Budget 2026: how to beat the new savings tax rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:00:36 UTC
16:00:36 KST

Savers were both winners and losers in Wednesday’s budget. In his first outing as chancellor, John Healey dropped a plan to cut the cash Isa limit for under-65s but surprised everyone with an extra tax charge on savings and property income. His predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had already announced a plan to increase the income tax rates for savers and landlords that was due to take effect in April 2027. But Healey went further, adding an additional two percentage points to each of the rates.
Jason Hollands, managing director at wealth manager Evelyn Partners, describes the higher rates as a “sting in the tail” for savers.
However, he says: “There are practical steps savers can consider to mitigate this interest tax crunch, although the right approach will depend on their circumstances.”
The new taxes
The levels of tax, which will apply to savers across the UK, will be 24% for basic-rate taxpayers, 44% for higher-rate taxpayers and 49% for those on the additional rate. They come into effect on 6 April.
This means it will get harder to find savings accounts that beat inflation – especially if, as expected, that stays high next year.
Anna Bowes, personal finance expert at advice firm The Private Office, says if inflation hits 3.5%, with the new tax to pay, a saver who pays basic-rate tax will need to earn 4.61% gross interest to retain the value of their money.
A higher-rate payer will need 6.25% gross, and an additional-rate taxpayer will need 6.86%. Currently, she says, these higher two rates “are impossible as far as I am aware” to find on a standard savings account.
There are, however, allowances you can use that will protect some savings, meaning you can beat inflation with a lower-paying account.
Your tax-free allowances
Most people can earn a chunk of interest from their savings without facing any tax bill. You don’t have to pay tax on anything earned on money held in cash Isas, and the maximum amount you can put into one in each tax year is going to stay at £20,000.
This was set to be slashed to £12,000 for anyone aged under 65 from April 2027. But Healey has ditched that plan.
Aside from Isas, other things come into play that reduce the tax you pay on savings, or mean you don’t pay any tax at all.
Your tax-free personal allowance covers all of your income, and for the 2026-27 tax year, this is £12,570.
If your personal allowance isn’t fully used up by your wages, pension or other income, HM Revenue and Customs will apply it to your savings interest.
And there are two more savings allowances that people can benefit from.
There’s the personal savings allowance (PSA), which means basic-rate taxpayers can receive £1,000 of interest each financial year without paying any tax, and higher-rate taxpayers can receive up to £500. Additional-rate taxpayers don’t get any PSA.
Until a few years ago, you would usually have needed to have a huge amount saved before exceeding the £500 or £1,000 threshold, but with accounts currently paying 5%-plus, it is much easier to get caught out.
There’s also the “starting rate for savings,” which some people on a low income can get on top of the PSA, where you can earn up to £5,000 of interest without paying tax on it. To benefit, the rest of your income (for example, wages or pension) has to be less than £17,570 a year.
What the higher taxes mean
The Isa allowance governs how much you put in each year while the PSA is based on how much you get back.
How quickly you use up the PSA depends on your tax position. A basic-rate taxpayer who puts £20,000 cash into a non-Isa savings account paying 5% interest will earn annual interest of exactly £1,000 – so will use up their entire PSA. If they found a higher paying account, they would face 24% tax on all the interest over £1,000, so they’d hand over 24p of every £1.
For a higher-rate taxpayer it would only take £10,000 in the same account to wipe out their £500 PSA. They would pay a rate of 44% on everything they earned over £500 – 44p in the £1.
When it comes to Isas you can put in up to £20,000 every tax year, as long as you are over 18. Once money is in a cash Isa it is protected from tax forever, so over time you can build up a huge amount of savings that don’t attract tax, as long as you don’t withdraw them.
You do not have to leave it with the same provider. You can move around to get better rates – subject to individual account rules – so it is wise to make the most of this shelter.
How to beat the rise
If you have a substantial savings nest egg you might want to review where they are held. Experts always recommend that you have emergency funds that are easy to access, so do not let a small tax bill deter you from doing that.
But Hollands says it is worth checking that you are not holding too much in savings. “Holding more cash than you need for several years can mean missing out on the potential for longer-term investment growth,” he says.
Look at your family situation. Hollands says couples who are married, or in a civil partnership, should look at their savings and allowances together.
If you have both used your Isa and personal savings allowances, but one partner pays tax at a lower rate, he says transferring cash to them could reduce an overall family tax bill.
“But this needs to be a genuine transfer: the money becomes theirs, legally and in practice, and they must be free to decide what to do with it, so trust is key,” he says.
If you’re saving for a child’s future, consider putting it in their name instead of holding it yourself. Pay into their child trust fund, or junior Isa if they already have one, or set up a junior Isa. You can pay up to £9,000 a year into a junior Isa, and all the returns are tax-free.
Outside the Isa wrapper there will still be a potential tax bill if you are the child’s parent. If the child earns more than £100 in interest from money you have put in their account, you will be taxed on the returns. This isn’t the case if you are a grandparent.
Check whether you could make your money work harder by overpaying on your mortgage (see right), or putting more into your pension. Money paid into your pension won’t just avoid the savings tax, it will also attract a nice tax break and, possibly, cut the rate you would need to pay on savings.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, says: “When you pay into your pension, you can get tax relief at your highest marginal rate and lower your ‘adjusted net income’.
“Not only does it mean you pay less tax on your income, but it could also help bring you back below other tax thresholds, while helping boost your prospects for retirement at the same time.”
If you do that, the cash will be locked in. For money that you need access to, there are options. Premium bonds are one. There’s no interest and prizes are all tax-free. Each person in the UK can hold up to £50,000, and they are government-backed so are a safe place for your cash. The prize fund recently increased so each bond has a 21,000-1 chance of winning.
Holland and Coates both suggest low coupon short-dated gilts as an alternative place to put cash. These are UK government bonds, paying a small annual interest rate, and set to mature within the next couple of years. When they mature the return you get will not be liable for capital gains tax (CGT).
This type of investment can be bought via an investment platform, and can be held in your stocks and shares Isa, or outside it. You will face some kind of fees for running the account. Most of the return comes from the CGT saving at the end, and this can make them very attractive in terms of the after-tax returns, when compared to the post-tax interest on a cash savings account, says Holland.
“This is especially the case for people subject to the higher and additional rates of tax,” he says.

Avanti West Coast paid out £20m in ‘delay repay’ passenger refunds this summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:00:35 UTC
16:00:35 KST

Avanti West Coast paid out more than £20m to passengers in just three months this summer in refunds for disrupted journeys on Britain’s main intercity rail network.
The intercity operator paid out almost as much in a four-week period to 25 July – £9.3m – as its annual profits for each of the past two years. It repaid a further £12.2m in the subsequent eight weeks.
The “delay repay” compensation bill for slow-running or cancelled services has been spiralling upwards across the railway network in recent years, according to official figures, with Avanti the biggest payer – although never before at this scale.
Most train operators are yet to publish this year’s payouts. According to the most recent published financial figures from the Department for Transport (DfT), covering all operators, the total passenger compensation for delays rose to £150m across the railway in 2024-25, up 8% compared with the previous year, of which about 27% was Avanti’s payouts (£40.5m).
Fare inflation and efforts to make passengers aware of their rights have contributed to the industry’s soaring bill, as well as the delays themselves. Compensation has become increasingly automated and some operators now proactively repay passengers who have been delayed.
Under the contracts that replaced the franchising system since the pandemic, train operators’ income comes from fees paid by the DfT instead of depending on fare revenue, with the taxpayer instead taking any profit or loss from ticketing income or refunds.
Avanti, which is due to be taken into public ownership next year as part of Great British Railways, paid out more than £50m in 2025-26, and is expected to pay out more than £70m this financial year.
As heatwaves hit the railway, fewer than half of Avanti trains ran on time in July with passengers delayed by an average 19 minutes, according to figures from the Office of Rail and Road. Its peak payout period also covered the incursion of a large herd of cows on the tracks for several hours one Tuesday.
Long-distance operators typically pay out the largest sums, with customers more likely to claim owing to the expense and the chance of delays reaching the 60-minute threshold where fares are refunded in full.
Avanti and GWR are unusually generous among long-distance operators in paying compensation for delays after 15 minutes, when passengers are eligible for refunds of 25% of the fare paid.
GWR, which runs trains from Wales and the south-west to London, and LNER, which runs London-Scotland trains on the east coast mainline, were the next highest refunders in 2025, paying back £29.7m and £28m respectively.
The number of compensation claims filed by passengers across Great Britain’s railway reached 9.1m in 2026, up almost 10% year on year, with 80% of the claims approved, according to data from the Office of Rail and Road.
An Avanti West Coast spokesperson said: “We apologise to customers affected by train delays. A range of factors can impact service performance, and we are working closely with our industry partners to improve punctuality and reliability across the network.
“To make it as easy as possible for customers to claim compensation when things don’t go to plan, we are committed to ensuring that customers are able to promptly receive any compensation for delays and offer automatic delay repay for journeys delayed by 15 minutes or more.”
According to Avanti, between May to August this year it was directly responsible for only 23% of those delays, with Network Rail or other operators responsible for the majority, as well as external factors such as trespassers on the line.
GWR said the increase in its delay repay payments this year was “driven largely by repeated heatwaves, with prolonged periods of unprecedented temperatures affecting both trains and railway infrastructure”, including track defects, points failures, speed restrictions and train cooling issues.
The operator said the payments recognised “the impact of disruption and helping maintain confidence in rail travel”, adding: “We’ve recently made efforts to increase publicity of the scheme, with clearer, more frequent announcements onboard delayed trains and on social media disruption updates.”
LNER, which compensates customers only after 30-minute delays, did not provide updated financial data.
According to DfT research, about half of disrupted passengers claim compensation, but an increasing number are satisfied with the process and results.
Most train operators now resolve more than 99% of claims within 20 days, according to data from the rail regulator.
A DfT spokesperson said it was “acting to tackle the root causes of disruption” and making it easier for passengers to get refunds, adding: “Under Great British Railways, we will make it quicker and easier to claim compensation through an easy-to-use service, which will also be available wherever passengers purchase their tickets.”

Syrian curriculum changes spark debate over removal of images and historical figures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:00:17 UTC
16:00:17 KST

Changes were not limited to the texts; images and illustrations were also edited in Photoshop, adding hijabs or long robes to female figures, deleting women's photos, and covering or replacing statues, sculptures and artworks.
A set of changes made to a number of school textbooks in Syria has sparked a wave of criticism and reactions on social media, after they included alterations to pictures and artworks, among them adding the hijab to drawn female figures, removing images of women and children, covering statues and replacing paintings and works of art. The revisions have also affected teaching content dealing with political life, citizenship, democratic participation, local administration and the media.
These changes have reopened the debate over the standards used by the Ministry of Education when it reviews curricula, and how far they take into account Syria's social and cultural diversity, amid questions about the nature and aims of the amendments, and whether they fall simply within a review of content linked to the former regime or go further towards reshaping how society is represented in school books.
Changes to images, illustrations and educational content
Comparisons posted on social media between different editions of school textbooks show amendments to material for several grades, including the early years and seventh grade, as well as the sixth-grade primary textbook "Social Studies".
It emerges that this last book, reissued for the current academic year, originally dates back to the 2012–2013 school year, with changes added that include the removal of material linked to the former regime, alongside lessons on local administration, political life, citizenship, the media and democratic participation.
The changes were not limited to texts; they also extended to images and illustrations using Photoshop. Hijabs were added – and in some cases long robes – to drawn female characters, entire pictures of women were deleted, statues were covered, and sculptures and artworks were removed or replaced with others.
The visual alterations to paintings and expressive illustrations became a main focus of controversy, after committees removed the world-famous painting "Mona Lisa" and deleted a drawing showing a girl skipping rope beside two children in textbooks for early age groups.
The revisions also extended to historical figures and symbols. The Phoenician princess Elissar, founder of Carthage, was affected when a painting depicting her on a hunting trip was dropped and replaced with another portrait that had been digitally modified to cover the chin and neck – a step critics saw as imposing contemporary ideological standards on an ancient historical era.
One of the examples that provoked ridicule and debate was dressing a pharaonic statue in a striped shirt, which many users likened to prison uniforms.
Accusations of "falsifying history" and erasing national symbols
A new batch of visual comparisons circulated on social media documented far-reaching changes introduced to the new Syrian school curricula in particular history books, with the new editions showing the removal of prominent national and pan-Arab figures and the alteration of the content of historical passages, amid sharp questions and concerns about systematic ideological and sectarian exclusion.
Activists highlighted information that caused widespread anger and was described as "a blatant falsification of history". The updated curriculum contains passages portraying the "martyrs" executed on 6 May by the Ottoman governor Jamal Pasha, known as the Butcher, as "agents of Britain and France", instead of their historical description as symbols of the national movement resisting Ottoman colonial rule.
The changes also include deleting the picture of Sultan Pasha al-Atrash and replacing it with that of Sheikh Saleh al-Ali, a move that raised fears of exclusion on sectarian grounds. The alterations further removed a photograph of the late Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser.
The revisions reached school maps too, with the district of Iskenderun and the occupied Syrian Golan omitted from one of the maps, as well as the deletion of a paragraph on the role of Syrian women in resisting the French Mandate. This has raised questions about the motives behind these changes and their impact on the historical narrative presented to pupils.
Artistic inconsistencies and satire on social media
The nature of these changes and how they were carried out unleashed a wave of sarcastic comments on social platforms, where many users felt some of the alterations were random and lacked unified artistic standards to ensure visual coherence within a single textbook.
The most widely shared example in this context is a female doctor character in first-grade books who appears wearing a hijab on one page and without a hijab on another.
The comments did not stop at the artistic side, but also questioned the rationale for removing artworks and illustrated characters from school textbooks, and the criteria used to decide which images should be kept, modified or removed.
Parents criticise the changes and warn of their consequences
Among parents, objections went beyond the quality of the illustrations or the inconsistencies in modifying them, to the implications of these changes and their possible impact on how children view society and diversity.
Speaking to Euronews, Alia, the mother of a lower-secondary pupil, said she had not at first noticed the amendments because of the poor print quality and lack of detail in the drawings, pointing out that the heavy academic content and padding make it difficult for both parents and pupils to focus on visual details.
She argued that editing images of historical figures by adding a hijab raises questions about the purpose of such a step, and felt that replacing the pictures with new drawings would have been a more logical option than tampering with the original works. She warned that imposing a single pattern in the way women are depicted could shape how social diversity is presented to children, instead of promoting values of harmony and coexistence.
She added that priority should be given to developing the curricula and keeping pace with global shifts in education, rather than becoming preoccupied with cosmetic changes that add no clear educational value. In her view, such practices risk deepening divisions and fuelling intolerance instead of reducing it.
Alia went on: "The highest priority in this critical phase should be to fundamentally develop the educational curricula and keep up with the latest global changes in the education sector", considering that focusing on superficial visual adjustments does not serve the learning process or offer pupils any clear educational benefit.
Concluding her remarks to Euronews, she warned that the persistence of such practices within educational institutions could produce the opposite effect, as they help to deepen ideological divisions in society and feed exclusionary and fanatical thinking rather than mitigating it and strengthening shared citizenship values.
In the same vein, Jaber, the father of a primary-school girl, expressed even stronger concerns in his interview with Euronews, arguing that these visual changes cannot be separated from ideological orientations that risk being entrenched in society's consciousness through the education system. Jaber called on international organisations concerned with children's rights to take urgent action to safeguard children's right to receive balanced and neutral education.
He summed up his objection with a stark contrast between global technological progress and the regression of local curricula, saying: "While the world has reached leaps forward in developing artificial intelligence, we in Syria are still drowning in sterile arguments over covering women's images and deleting artworks from school textbooks".
From satire to accusations of trying to impose an ideology
On the other hand, reactions went beyond mockery of how the changes were implemented and raised deeper questions about their cultural and social dimensions. Critics and observers accused the ministry of seeking to impose a specific ideology through the education system, arguing that changing the visual appearance of female characters and removing elements of global artistic heritage reflects a deliberate effort to reshape children's perceptions and build a new social identity.
Some believe these concerns are particularly sensitive in a country such as Syria, marked by religious, cultural and social diversity. Their fear is that, if adopted as a lasting approach, such changes could entrench a one-sided view of Syrian society and sideline its historical pluralism and the natural differences in ways of life that distinguish it.
Part of the controversy centres on the distinction between two separate steps: the first involves removing content linked to the former regime, and the second relates to altering artistic illustrations or deleting educational topics on citizenship, political life and democratic participation.
While some see purging the curricula of the previous era's legacy as part of a normal modernisation process, the other changes raise questions about the educational and cultural foundations that govern how content is selected and directed.
Others argue that the published amendments alone are not enough to conclusively prove the existence of a coherent policy to impose a specific ideology. To reach an objective assessment of this accusation, they say, it is essential to see the official standards adopted, define the real scope of the changes and their causes, and compare them with the broader orientations the new curricula will adopt in the coming phases.
Ministry of Education: curricula respect diversity and do not adopt a single line
For its part, Syria's Ministry of Education on Monday rejected, in an official statement, the reports circulating on social media about new changes to images and content in the school curricula, describing this information as "inaccurate" and asserting that no new changes have been approved to the curricula in force for the current academic year.
The ministry clarified in its statement that the changes carried out since the fall of the former regime were limited to a single amendment that was announced and fully detailed in January 2025. According to the statement, that change focused mainly on removing the symbols and ideological content of the ousted regime and correcting the images and material linked to it, especially in the social studies and Islamic education curricula after they were merged and unified, in order to safeguard the diversity of Syrian society and strengthen the presence of all its components and cultures.
The ministry stressed that its plans to develop the curricula aim first and foremost to meet Syrians' aspirations and to entrench the values of citizenship and belonging, a culture of law and respect for others. In this context, it announced the completion of the "national framework for curricula" and the adoption of modern scientific standards that place the learner at the centre of the educational process, with the aim of fostering critical thinking, analysis and creative problem-solving, as well as enhancing life and digital skills, with the new curricula to be introduced gradually in line with the approved procedures.
The ministry attached to its release original samples and images from school textbooks to demonstrate the visual and social diversity they contain and to counter the circulating claims, calling on the media and the public to verify information carefully, rely on official sources and avoid being drawn into rumours.
The ministry's official statement, however, failed to defuse the crisis. It was met with a broad and fierce wave of criticism from activists and education watchers, some of whom went as far as accusing the ministry of "lying and concealing the truth".
Critics argued that the ministry's denial of any new amendments is completely at odds with the evidence and live visual comparisons taken from the textbooks distributed in schools.
On 17 August 2026, the Syrian Ministry of Education announced the adoption of unified curricula in all provinces for the 2026–2027 academic year, based on the previous year's curricula known as the "Damascus curriculum". It stated that it had completed the preparation of national standards for the new curricula in preparation for moving to the drafting phase.
On 14 September 2026, Syrian Education Minister Mohammad Abdulrahman Turko told a parliamentary hearing that the ministry had removed images and symbols linked to the former regime from the last two editions of schoolbooks.
He indicated that a single curriculum had been adopted across the different provinces, with a two-year transition period granted to pupils who had studied under the previous curricula.
Turko added that the ministry had referred the national standards for building the new curricula to the Higher Council for Education in preparation for starting to write the textbooks once those standards are approved.

China joins global race to reawaken brain-injury patients through ultrasound therapy

After spending three months in a coma following a brain haemorrhage, a patient in China has regained the ability to speak, eat and walk with support – part of an early clinical trial using targeted sound waves to help “wake up” severely damaged brains, according to state media.
The technology, developed by a coalition including the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, used focused ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep within the brain without requiring invasive surgery or implanted electrodes, state broadcaster CCTV reported earlier this week.
It was presented at a brain-computer interface (BCI) industry conference that opened in Shenzhen earlier this month. While public attention around BCIs often centres on controlling computers or robotic limbs, the research showcased efforts to apply such technologies to neurological rehabilitation.

US midterms: 3 days to go – What latest polls say as early voting surges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

06:59:55 UTC

US midterms: 3 days to go – What latest polls say as early voting surges
More than 43 million Americans have voted early as Democrats lead national opinion polls and Trump prepares for final rallies.
With three days to go before the US midterm elections, Democrats are leading national polls as millions of Americans cast their ballots early.
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has announced he will carry on with his campaigns in Kansas and Iowa as both parties make their final push ahead of Election Day on Tuesday.
Here is what you need to know:
What do the US midterm polls say?
According to RealClearPolling’s latest national congressional ballot average, Democrats still lead Republicans by 8.2 percentage points. Democrats lead by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent.
A separate Economist/YouGov survey released on Thursday found that 44 percent of registered voters expect Democrats to control the House of Representatives after the election, compared with 31 percent who expect Republicans to retain control.
Expectations were much closer for the Senate, with 39 percent expecting a Democratic majority and 36 percent a Republican one.
Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, told Al Jazeera that the Democratic lead in national polling suggests a different picture for the two chambers.
“A big Democratic lead in House generic ballot polling suggests that the House is almost certain to flip to Democrats,” Kondik said.
“However, that does not mean the Senate is going to flip – it certainly could, but it is much more up in the air.”
How many Americans have already voted?
According to an Associated Press analysis released on Friday, more than 43 million Americans had voted early in person or returned mail ballots five days before Election Day.
That’s nearly 10 million more than at the same point before the 2022 midterms, with some of the biggest increases recorded in states having competitive Senate races.
In Texas, more than 6.3 million people had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point in 2022, an increase of 50 percent.
Al Jazeera’s Phil Lavelle reported from Houston on Friday that voters were continuing to arrive at polling stations as the state’s early voting period was drawing to a close.
In Georgia, more than 2.5 million ballots had been cast by Friday morning, surpassing the 2.3 million recorded during the early voting period in 2022, according to Al Jazeera’s Matthew Torres.
Torres reported long queues at an Atlanta polling station and more participation among young voters.
“We all just really want a better future for everyone, especially like the next generation,” one young voter told Al Jazeera.
Another young voter pointed to social media as a reason for the increased interest in the election. “Definitely social media. Social media and the media has put voting in the limelight,” the voter said.
Democratic political strategist Celinda Lake said many voters were looking for change.
“You got a lot of voters who say, ‘I’m going to do a Hail Mary for change, but I hope you do something,'” she said.
Early voting also increased by more than 30 percent compared with the same period in 2022 in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, according to the AP analysis.
However, early turnout figures don’t show which candidates voters have chosen or what the final results will be.
What’s happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?
Trump reversed his decision to cancel two weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa, with the White House confirming that both events would go ahead on Sunday.
The rallies had been cancelled on Thursday, with the White House saying Trump would instead take part in nearly 20 telephone campaign events.
But less than a day later, the president put the rallies back in his schedule.
Al Jazeera’s Tanya Nouri reported that Trump’s campaign team sees his personal appearances as a way to mobilise Republican voters.
“He is energised to go back and rally in person on Sunday,” Nouri said, quoting her campaign sources.
She also said that Trump’s team believes his appearances have a stimulating effect on Republican supporters, especially in states where the Republicans are running for Senate seats against strong opposition.
Trump also campaigned in Florida on Friday, where Republicans are defending Senate and gubernatorial seats.
“You got to vote. Bad things happen when you get too confident, right? So let’s pretend they’re one point down,” Trump told the rally crowd.
Meanwhile, in Texas, Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico were focusing their final campaign efforts on Houston, according to Al Jazeera’s Lavelle.
Paxton cancelled an event in El Paso to concentrate on Harris County, Texas’s most populous county, as early voting drew to a close.
On Friday, former President Bill Clinton campaigned for the Democratic Party in Mississippi.
He also urged people to vote.
“I can’t tell you how many people I care for that have lost in Mississippi because of those who did not vote at all,” Clinton said.
Where will Trump and the Democrats campaign this weekend?
Trump is scheduled to hold back-to-back rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday. In Iowa, he is expected to support Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, and later travel to Kansas, where he will campaign with Senator Roger Marshall.
Recent polls have shown competitive Senate races in traditionally Republican states. In Kansas, Marshall faces a tough race against his Democratic challenger, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton.
An Emerson College poll suggests that Hamilton is leading with 49 percent support, while Marshall has 45 percent. Democrats are also making their final appeals to voters. Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear will join Ohio governor candidate Amy Acton at a campaign event.
Democrat Senate nominee for Alaska Mary Peltola is also expected to attend a rally in Bethel, Alaska.
Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-ups that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in Congress’s upper chamber.
The race has been complicated by a dispute involving two candidates named Dan Sullivan. Trump has accused Democrats of recruiting an independent candidate with the same name as the Republican senator to confuse voters and draw support away from him.
The Department of Justice has taken legal action over the dispute, while Peltola has denied involvement in the alleged recruitment effort.
Separately, Republican candidate Mike Rogers is also expected to campaign with House Speaker Mike Johnson over the weekend.

Drug deaths in Finland reach record high in 2025
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:59:17 EET
15:59:17 KST

Drug-related deaths in Finland reached a record 333 in 2025, an increase of 35 per cent from the previous year, according to figures released by Statistics Finland on Thursday. Deaths increased across every age group, with the largest rise among young adults, while the number of women dying from drugs almost doubled.
The annual death toll rose by 86 from 247 in 2024, marking the largest year-on-year increase since records began. The figures show that drug-related deaths affected people across Finland, with substantial differences between regions.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Among people aged 15 to 24, deaths increased by 60 per cent to 64. Four of those who died were under 18. Drug-related causes accounted for one in five deaths in this age group during 2025.
"Drug deaths increased from the previous year in all age groups. The largest increase was among the youngest, those aged 15 to 24," said Kati Taskinen, an actuary at Statistics Finland.
People aged 25 to 34 accounted for the highest number of fatalities, with 85 deaths, followed by 83 among those aged 35 to 44.
The number of women who died from drugs rose from 50 to 94, the highest figure recorded. Women accounted for 28 per cent of drug deaths, compared with 20 per cent in 2024. The remaining 239 deaths involved men.
Men who died from drugs had a median age of 36, compared with 39 among women. Deaths among men were most frequent at ages 20 to 24, while women aged 40 to 44 formed the largest female group.
Regional figures showed Helsinki recording the highest number of deaths, at 58, followed by Pirkanmaa with 30, Southwest Finland with 28 and North Ostrobothnia with 25.
Päijät-Häme had the highest population-adjusted mortality rate, at 9.8 deaths per 100,000 residents. Satakunta followed with 9.0 and Kymenlaakso with 8.9, compared with the national rate of 5.9.
Accidental drug poisoning caused 195 deaths, an increase of 55 from 2024. Another 94 people died from drug dependence or the effects of long-term use, up from 63.
Statistics Finland reported that most deaths involved combinations of substances, often including alcohol or psychiatric medication.
Synthetic opioids were the most frequently identified primary substances in fatal accidental poisonings and poisonings of undetermined intent. Buprenorphine remained the most common individual substance, while deaths involving other synthetic opioids and stimulants increased.
The statistics also recorded 30 suicides involving drugs or medicines classified as narcotics. Women accounted for 22 of these deaths, despite men representing the majority of drug-related fatalities overall.

President nominates new chancellor of justice
President Ülle Madise has proposed to the Riigikogu that Justice of the Supreme Court Oliver Kask be appointed as the next chancellor of justice.
Madise served as chancellor of justice until she took office as president earlier this month.
On Saturday, in a statement posted on the president's website, Madise announced that she had nominated Kask as her replacement.
"Oliver Kask is a highly regarded expert on constitutional law and the protection of fundamental rights, both in Estonia and internationally. His work in the Administrative Chamber of Tallinn Circuit Court and his election as a justice of the Supreme Court confirm his professional competence, leadership and communication skills," the president explained.
She added that Kask's life and career to date give reason to believe that he understands how the system of separation and balance of powers functions.
"Estonia ranks among the very best in the world according to the rule of law index for a reason. In the international constitutional law community, the chancellor of justice's freedom from political affiliation is considered very important," the head of state said.
"Oliver Kask is fully capable of and has the legitimacy to stand up for the values of the rule of law as Estonia's chancellor of justice in the high-level international constitutional law community."
"Considering Oliver Kask's professional experience, knowledge and personal qualities, I believe he is a suitable candidate for the position of chancellor of justice," the president said.
Kask graduated from the University of Tartu's Faculty of Law. He has worked at the Ministry of Justice and, from 2004 to 2024, as a judge at Tallinn Circuit Court, including as chairman of its Administrative Chamber. Since September 2024, he has been a justice of the Supreme Court.
Before nominating Kask, the president held consultations with representatives of the parliamentary parties.

Four potential locations
The proposed base would cost around 3 billion zloty (€700 million), with several billion more needed for supporting infrastructure, General Dariusz Łukowski, former head of Poland’s National Security Bureau, told Polish daily Rzeczpospolita.
Łukowski identified four potential locations: Wrocław in southwestern Poland, suitable for an armored brigade; Szczecin in the northwest, offering port facilities; Bydgoszcz in the north-central part of the country, a hub for NATO command structures; and the western city of Poznań, home to the US Army’s V Corps forward command post.
The former security chief also warned that accommodating American troops and their families would require substantial investment in housing, schools, kindergartens and healthcare facilities.
“If there were 5,000 soldiers, that figure would rise to at least 15,000,” Łukowski said, referring to the total number of people requiring accommodation and services.

Diplomacy or war? Qatar signals Iran breakthrough as US warns Gulf states to prepare for war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:58:06 UTC
15:58:06 KST

Conflicting reports have emerged in the Arab world and the United States over the past 24 hours about what may unfold between Washington and Tehran in the coming week. President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly warned that he intends to bring the war with Iran to an end, one way or another, after the midterm elections, said Friday that he had time. But reports Friday night indicated that the United States had instructed Gulf states to prepare for the possibility of fighting resuming as early as next week. Meanwhile, the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported Saturday morning that a breakthrough had been reached in talks mediated by Qatar.
The Qatari report, citing unidentified sources, said that "a U.S. delegation will join the talks in Doha to negotiate directly with Iran."
Saudi channels Al Arabiya and Al Hadath reported overnight that they had obtained a draft proposal being discussed by mediators. The purported draft has not been confirmed by any of the parties, including Qatar. According to the reports, it includes a preliminary Iranian commitment regarding the future of its nuclear stockpile; discussions on arrangements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days; daily talks on confidence-building measures between Iran and the United States; an agreed timetable for implementing commitments by both countries; and a possible role for China as a guarantor of any agreement.
"Any Iranian action regarding its nuclear program will be met by a corresponding U.S. action on sanctions. Clear procedures will be established to address any delays or noncompliance by Iran," the Saudi channels claimed. "Neither Iran nor the United States will be required to make concessions without receiving a corresponding commitment." The reports also referred to "a clear definition of Iran's and the United States' obligations at every stage of the agreement."
The Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar, which is affiliated with Hezbollah, reported Saturday, citing "informed sources," that Iran does not oppose mutual commitments regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the lifting of the naval blockade. According to the report, Iran's reservations concern the clause on nuclear concessions, under which Tehran would allow inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) access to its nuclear facilities. In return, Washington would lift some sanctions and release some frozen Iranian assets. Tehran has repeatedly insisted that any negotiations over its nuclear program would take place only after a formal declaration ending the war and concrete steps to that effect.
The reports of negotiations and a possible breakthrough stand in contrast, to varying degrees, with a growing number of reports in the United States suggesting that Washington is preparing to resume the war, potentially as early as next week. U.S. network MS NOW reported Friday that the Trump administration had informed its Gulf allies that they should prepare for a "short and swift" round of fighting that could begin as early as Nov. 4, the day after the midterm elections. Three senior Gulf officials provided the information to the network.
However, Trump said Friday night that talks between the two sides were continuing. "There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking. We have time, frankly," he told reporters at the White House. He added that the conflict with Iran was "not a typical war" and claimed it was not imposing significant costs on American taxpayers. He also repeated his assertion that the United States had eliminated the nuclear threat posed by Iran. "I spent a lot of money in order to get rid of a nuclear weapon, which we've done," he said.
Earlier Friday, in an interview with Kansas City radio station KCMO, Trump expressed optimism about ending the conflict. "It will end soon," he declared, without explaining how. He emphasized that Washington's central condition for ending the war remained a guarantee that Iran would never possess a nuclear weapon. His remarks came just days before the U.S. midterm elections, scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 3. Trump has previously made clear that he would not order new strikes against Iran before the elections but has stopped short of promising not to resume military operations afterward.
According to an Associated Press report this week, U.S. officials warned several Middle Eastern countries and Washington's allies of possible renewed strikes against Iran after the elections. The countries were also asked to prepare for potential Iranian retaliation, including attacks on energy facilities and other critical infrastructure across the region. However, two diplomats familiar with the matter stressed that Trump had not yet made a final decision on whether to resume the strikes.

Different faces of goodness compete for the 2026 Awakener of the Year award
Saturday 31 October 2026 08:25
Saturday, 31 October 2026, 08:25
PHOTO BNR
Font size
National Awakeners Day is celebrated in Bulgaria on November 1, paying tribute to Bulgarian educators, men of letters, revolutionaries and cultural figures. It is a festive day for all Bulgarian educational institutions. The name “National Awakeners” is also borne by many Bulgarian Sunday schools abroad.
On November 1, the recipient of the honorary title “Awakener of the Year”, selected as part of the National Public Campaign of the same name, is also announced. The nominees are individuals dedicated to socially significant causes and supporting various social groups. A jury chaired by renowned journalist Iva Doichinova, who launched the campaign in 2014, selects ten candidates for the title. As in previous years, the public is invited to vote online to choose the person most deserving of the title “Awakener of the Year”.
Among dozens of nominations, the jury selected 10 candidates, including foundations united by a clear cause. Such a cause often begins with one person’s example and inspires many others to join. One such example is the “Podai Raka” (Lend a Hand) Foundation, which supports children and families through scholarships and provides healthcare and social support, as well as opportunities for social integration for elderly people and people with disabilities.
The team of the “Podai Raka” (Lend a Hand) Foundation
PHOTO personal archive
Dimitar Ivanov and his “Zaedno za dobroto” Foundation have also been nominated for the “Awakener of the Year” title. He started his initiative after discovering abandoned wheelchairs in an old house and deciding to repair them with his friends and donate them to people in need. Over time, this act of kindness developed into a cause that today brings together donors, volunteers and partners from across the country.
Dimitar Ivanov
PHOTO BNR
Slav Petkov, founder and chairman of the Federation of Adapted Physical Activity, has also been shortlisted for the award. For more than a decade, he has been working to provide people with intellectual disabilities and Down syndrome with opportunities for sports development and participation.
Slav Petkov
PHOTO BTA
A sign language interpreter has also made this year’s “Awakener of the Year” shortlist. Boris Bandev builds a bridge between the world of speech and the world of silence. Having grown up in a deaf family, Boris learned to communicate through sign language before he could speak. His personal experience laid the foundation for a cause that he now shares with his entire team of specialist interpreters: ensuring that deaf people have equal access to information, education and culture.
Boris Bandev
PHOTO personal archive
The jury’s shortlist also includes figures from the fields of science, music, theatre and the arts.

Explainer: A journey without pause: how a century-old political party governs itself
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:49:22 CST
15:49:22 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- How does a large ruling party that has long enjoyed the people's support keep moving forward without being lulled by its own success?
For the Communist Party of China (CPC), one key to doing so is to stay vigilant and never lose sight of potential risks that come with long-term governance. Faced with the dangers of complacency, inadequate competence, estrangement from the people and corruption, the Party has chosen to confront them head-on.
At the just-concluded fifth plenary session of its 20th Central Committee, the CPC reaffirmed its commitment to persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance.
The session took stock of what has been achieved and set out the fundamental task, guiding principles and plans needed to sustain that effort.
NOT A PASSING GUST
In 2014, when the term "full and rigorous Party self-governance" was first introduced, skeptics asked whether it would be a passing gust. Time has answered. The campaign has neither stopped nor softened.
The numbers show the scale of that sustained effort. From January to September 2026, disciplinary inspection and supervision organs across the country opened 800,000 cases and disciplined 680,000 people -- both figures well above the totals for the whole of 2014.
These increases require context. Broader oversight and stronger enforcement, aided by big data and other information technologies, have helped uncover more violations. The figures also point to an ongoing task: addressing corruption that has already taken root while preventing new abuses. This is no time to let up.
Looking at history, the pattern is evident. Attention to the Party's self-governance has never been an improvised matter. As early as 1926, just five years after the Party's founding, its Central Committee issued its first document aimed at combating corruption.
In recent decades, nearly every Central Committee of the Party has convened a dedicated plenary session on Party building. The emphasis has shifted with changing circumstances, but the issue remains a priority on the core political agenda of the Party, which now has more than 101 million members.
WHY PARTY SELF-GOVERNANCE MATTERS
This year marks the start of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) period, a critical stretch for advancing Chinese modernization. Next year, the Party will hold its pivotal 21st National Congress, a highly important meeting and an event of great political significance for both the Party and the country.
At this juncture, emphasizing the importance of persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance is particularly significant for the CPC, whose capacity to lead bears directly on whether Chinese modernization can ultimately succeed.
Much remains to be done: cultivating high-caliber officials, building a well-knit organizational system characterized by cross-level alignment and effective implementation, taking firm and coordinated action against corruption, and refining Party and state oversight systems.
The implications extend beyond China. As a major contributor to and stabilizer of global economic growth, China offers broad market prospects, stable policy expectations and a sound security environment as it advances Chinese modernization.
Through targeted oversight, disciplinary inspection and supervision organs are helping ensure certainty in development and provide strong guarantees for economic and social progress.
By persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, and combining Party self-supervision with supervision by the people, the CPC has offered the world new experience in supervising and constraining the exercise of power within a political party. ■

New renovation body may offer bigger subsidies for ageing Hong Kong districts
‘In places with a high elderly population, and in older districts and ageing buildings, there’s no harm in offering a larger subsidy when appropriate,’ finance chief says
Hong Kong’s planned renovation monitoring body will consider larger subsidies for homeowners of ageing buildings in older districts or with high elderly populations who use its supervision services for major repairs, the finance chief has said.
Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said on Saturday that the Building Maintenance Support and Services Council, set up to curb malpractice in the industry after the Tai Po fire report, would be non-profit but would have to recover its costs, since owners mainly bear responsibility for maintaining private residential property.
He said service charges would depend on factors such as the scope of the work, with fees estimated at several thousand Hong Kong dollars per household, but authorities would subsidise those in need.

After Louvre heist and string of thefts, Europe’s smaller museums are on guard
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:48:36 CET
15:48:36 KST

By Giselda Vagnoni, Gabriel Stargardter, Javi West Larrañaga and Jemima Denham
PARMA, Italy, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Two men wearing head torches climbed through a forced-open window at the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum near Parma on the night of March 22 and calmly lifted artworks by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse from the walls.
Within three minutes, they had passed the works, valued at about €9 million ($10 million), to an accomplice and fled. At the museum’s main gate, a fourth man discharged a fire extinguisher when the alarm sounded, distracting the custodian.
“Whatever could go wrong, did,” said Stefano Roffi, director of the private foundation that runs the museum.
The raid was one of a string of museum thefts in France, Italy and Spain since last year’s heist at the Louvre in Paris, raising concerns that criminals are increasingly targeting smaller institutions with fewer resources to protect valuable collections.
“This is where we see the ‘Louvre effect’,” said Marc Balcells, a Barcelona-based researcher specialising in crimes against cultural heritage. “If the Louvre was so easy to rob, just imagine a tiny museum in a rural area or a smaller town.”
Works by Antonello da Messina vanished from a museum in his Sicilian hometown in August, while two Renoirs were stolen from Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera the following month.
In Spain, thieves stole hundreds of historic gold coins from museums in Badajoz and Albacete and made off with a Bronze Age treasure in Villena, near Alicante.
A 2024 survey by France’s Culture Ministry found only one in four cultural institutions had an emergency and risk-prevention plan, while nearly half lacked video surveillance.
WHO CHECKS WHEN THE ALARM GOES OFF?
A French parliamentary report in May said museums lacked the resources and preparation to adequately protect artworks and artefacts.
In Italy, the challenge is amplified by the way the country’s cultural heritage is spread across hundreds of towns and institutions, a legacy of centuries of fragmented rule.
“That is also what makes our system distinctive: works remain in the places where they were created,” said Antonella Pinna, president of the Italian committee of the International Council of Museums. “But we need to make life harder for criminals.”
The council worked with Italy’s Culture Ministry and the Carabinieri on museum security guidelines published in 2015, but Pinna said technology alone was not enough.
“If an alarm goes off, someone has to make sure it is checked,” she said.
In a narrow street in the Tuscan town of Sansepolcro, the civic museum displays four works by Renaissance master Piero della Francesca, born just steps away in the 15th century.
The Louvre theft “affected us deeply because cultural heritage is central to Sansepolcro’s identity. It is our soul,” culture councillor Francesca Mercati told Reuters.
After the Louvre raid, officers from the Carabinieri’s cultural heritage protection unit recommended more cameras, longer retention of CCTV footage and tighter controls on bags and bulky clothing.
“We immediately implemented those recommendations,” Mercati said.
A VAST NETWORK TO PROTECT
The scale of the challenge is daunting.
Italy has more than 4,400 museums and similar institutions, according to national statistics agency ISTAT. Spain has about 1,500 museums, while France has more than 1,200 institutions carrying the official “Musees de France” designation, alongside hundreds of smaller collections.
Protecting such a broad network is particularly difficult for smaller institutions that depend on local funding.
Florence Imbert, a Paris-based security consultant for cultural institutions, said 85% of small French museums were run by local authorities with limited financial resources.
“The budget is key to winning the war,” she said.
France’s Culture Ministry announced a 33-point security plan in July, backed by €30 million over three years for local museums.
Recent figures suggest concern is warranted. The Carabinieri art squad recorded 17 thefts from Italian museums and galleries in 2025, up from 14 a year earlier.
Europol said in an August report that museum thefts were becoming more forceful and increasingly focused on precious metals, gemstones and other high-value artefacts.
A FAST BUCK?
Unlike gold or jewellery, which can be broken up or melted down, a well-known painting is difficult to turn into quick cash.
Celebrated works such as those by Renoir can rarely be sold openly, Pinna said. Instead, stolen art is more likely to be hidden, used as leverage in ransom attempts or offered privately.
Even when works are recovered, museums can face significant costs linked to investigations, recovery efforts and upgraded security.
The recent thefts have also reignited debate about insurance.
Most major state-backed museums in Western Europe rely on government indemnity schemes rather than commercial cover, but some institutions have begun reassessing the risks, said Filippo Guerrini-Maraldi, a private wealth and fine art insurance specialist at broker Howden Specialty.
“And for the first time, really, in my 40-year career, I’ve seen art theft now becoming more of a major, major risk. It was always the minor risk,” he said.
Insurers are also turning to technology. Beazley is exploring how AI can be used to analyse CCTV footage to identify suspicious behaviour in museums and galleries, helping security staff spot threats sooner, said fine art underwriter Dishni Mahendran.
SECURITY VS ACCESS
For museum directors and cultural officials, the challenge is how to tighten security without cutting collections off from local communities or diminishing the visitor experience.
“Ultimately, museums must remain easy to access,” Imbert said. “People should be able to enter without having to pass through 50 security checks.”
Julien Volper, a conservator at Belgium’s Africa Museum, said particularly vulnerable treasures should only be displayed when adequate security measures are in place.
“I’m not saying that’s the ultimate solution, but it seems better than displaying replicas,” he said. “We’re not at Disneyland.”
In August, the Carabinieri recovered the three artworks stolen from the Parma museum from a cardboard box hidden in an apartment. Five Moldovan nationals were arrested in connection with the theft.
Investigators said wiretaps indicated the suspects had unsuccessfully tried to find buyers in Eastern Europe and Russia.
The works have since returned to the museum in what Roffi called a “homecoming party”.
“The theft triggered an outpouring of solidarity in Italy and abroad,” he said. The museum now has round-the-clock guards funded by a local cheese consortium.
“It was seen not simply as a theft from a museum, but as an attack on art as a shared cultural heritage.”
(Reporting by Giselda Vagnoni in Rome, Gabriel Startgardter in Paris, Javi West Larrañaga in Gdansk, Jemima Denham in London; Additional reporting by Alex Fraser in Parma; Bart Biesemans in Brussels; Writing by Giselda Vagnoni; Editing by Ros Russell)

Travelling beyond the borders of Baku through fiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:45:07 UTC
15:45:07 KST

What connects an Iranian novelist exploring women's lives, a British children's author creating imaginary worlds and an Azerbaijani writer preserving her country's cultural identity? The answer is stories that cross borders, connect continents, and blend cultures through books.
From the poetry of medieval Azerbaijan to contemporary novels reaching readers from across different continents, Baku's relationship with the written word is rooted in centuries of cultural exchange.
Today, that literary heritage is finding new expression as authors, publishers and readers from Europe, Asia and beyond came together in the Azerbaijani capital for the twelfth year running.
The 12th Baku International Book Fair saw 32 countries taking part in an event which was not simply about discovering the latest books.
It was an opportunity to explore how literature connects hearts and minds across languages, generations, and geographical barriers by blending and sharing ideas and stories.
At a time when technology is transforming how tales are told, published, and consumed, the fair also questioned how books will remain an intrinsic and vital part of our futures.
Where history meets the modern word
Azerbaijan's literary traditions stretch back centuries and have been shaped by its position at the crossroads of Europe and Asia.
The 12th-century poet Nizami Ganjavi features heavily.
He was born in what is now Azerbaijan and became one of the most influential literary figures of the Persian-speaking world, with his works travelling the globe. He continues to be celebrated today.
Centuries later, writers and poets include Muhammad Fuzuli, who contributed to a rich literary tradition that developed across different languages and cultural influences.
This heritage provides a historical and rich backdrop to the country's modern relationship with international literature, where translation, publishing partnerships and literary festivals help stories reach audiences far beyond local borders and countries of origin.
For Iranian novelist Parinoush Saniee, literature offers a way of exploring the relationships between individuals and the societies in which they live.
Her internationally recognised novel The Book of Fate follows the life of an Iranian woman through decades of personal and political change, examining themes of identity, family, education and the expectations placed upon women.
Saniee explained that she initially assumed her work would only resonate regionally, but she was quickly surprised by the global reaction.
"The first translation of my book was into Italian," Saniee recalled.
"When I saw all that reception and various journalists came from different places, I asked them what was interesting about the book for you. They said it was close to us. We also had such experiences. It was very relatable."
Although rooted in Iranian society, the questions raised in her writing resonate far beyond its borders. The works have been translated into numerous languages and demonstrate how literature can offer readers an understanding of lives and experiences different from their own.
She observed this same phenomenon when the novel became a bestseller in Norway, proving that universal themes of suffering and endurance translate seamlessly.
"Human suffering, lifestyles, issues, and problems are overall very impactful for humanity, and we all understand it," Saniee stated. "Therefore, it doesn't matter where it is from."
Reaching younger minds
British author Darren Simpson, meanwhile, approaches storytelling through the imagination of younger readers.
He is known for novels such as Scavengers and The Memory Thieves, where he creates unusual worlds and characters exploring friendships, belonging, identity and the challenges of growing up.
Simpson echoed the sentiment that human emotion makes storytelling cross borders effortlessly, noting that children across the globe seek the exact same things from a narrative.
"When I see children from all around different countries connect to my stories in the same way, it speaks to me about the universal nature of a lot of feelings about people's needs and their desire to connect," Simpson explained.
His works reflect the importance of children's literature at a time when arguably young people have an unprecedented choice of digital entertainment and books are not necessarily the most popular choice. Yet, he highlighted that the local reception at the fair had been incredibly inspiring.
"I have been struck in Azerbaijan by how much passion there is here in the young readers," he added.
Championing local voices
Alongside its international offerings, the fair is also celebrating the locals who have helped to shape Azerbaijan's contemporary literary identity.
One of those is Reyhan Yusifgizi, a prominent voice in Azerbaijani children's science fiction who brings a unique academic background in computer science to her writing.
When discussing how to cultivate reading habits in a digital age, Yusifgizi explained that increasing a child's interest requires a two-step approach.
"First, this depends on the author," Yusifgizi noted. "They must write well, write in a modern way. With simple language, they must interest the child."
However, she stressed that the second factor is often the most fundamental.
"The parent directly influences the child. The parent stands between the author, the book, and the child," she said.
"First of all, the parent must demonstrate it through their own experience, their own example. They need to read."
Azerbaijani writer and publicist Elmira Akhundova reflected on the profound emotional weight that physical books carry compared to fleeting digital news. For her, literature's ultimate purpose is to promote peace and multiculturalism.
"What is at the end of the most difficult, the saddest book? It is light," Akhundova said.
"It is a call towards tolerance. We must hear these humanistic calls and instill them in our young generation," she told Euronews.
She challenged the next generation to seek out complex, philosophical narratives rather than settling for easy entertainment, noting that every story should ultimately lead the reader towards hope.
"A book must absolutely be geared toward humanism," she added, asserting that no matter what, a book "must be on the sunny side of the street."
The future of the written word
It is recognised that the relationship between books and their readers is changing.
Digital publishing, audiobooks and new forms of storytelling are reshaping the literary landscape, but rather than replacing traditional physical books entirely, there is an advantage to the technological advancements.
Books can now travel at lightning speed. A touch of a button can transport us to another universe, and perhaps that is what makes an international literary gathering even more relevant today.
Beyond the book stands, authors are choosing to move from the desktop to have those important physical discussions, drawn together by that love of narrative.
And what better place to have those conversations than the gateway between East and West?

Air defenses down 105 out of 134 Russian drones launched at Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force Command reported this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Friday, October 30, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 134 strike UAVs, including Shahed drones (72 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and Parodiya-type decoy drones. They were launched from the directions of Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo and Millerovo in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea.

Several enemy strike drones remain in the air space above Ukraine, and combat operations are ongoing.
Hits by enemy drones were recorded at 20 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.
As Ukrinform reported, several critical infrastructure facilities in Kyiv were left without power following a Russian attack.

Is AI killing art? No, but the human creative process still matters, Israeli study argues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:40:09 UTC
15:40:09 KST

For centuries, mastering an art form was inseparable from personal growth. A painter spent years learning to see the world before touching canvas, and a musician devoted decades to refining physical and emotional discipline.
Today, generative AI can produce sophisticated compositions at the click of a button, shattering that age-old connection.
But according to a new paper from Prof. Amit Zoran of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem (HUJI), this digital revolution isn’t rendering human artists obsolete; it is stripping away technical barriers so we can rediscover what made creativity meaningful in the first place.
The key question is not whether AI can generate attractive paintings or music; it is whether the process of creating something has value that cannot be captured by the finished product.
As AI becomes capable of producing sophisticated art in seconds, a new paper challenges us to rethink what makes human creativity valuable.
Zoran, who teaches and conducts research at HUJI’s The Rachel and Selim Benin School of Computer Science and Engineering, where he leads the Hybrid Design Lab, focuses on bridging the gap between emerging computational technologies (including AI, robotics, and 3D printing) and traditional human crafts, gastronomy, design, and consciousness.
He earned a bachelor’s degree in Communication Systems Engineering at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) in Beersheba and completed postdoctoral research at the prestigious Massachusetts Institute of Technology Media Lab, and also worked at Israel Aircraft Industries, followed by a master’s degree in industrial and product design at Jerusalem’s Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design.
He published his paper in the journal AI & Society, titled “More than we can make: Generative AI, artistic forms, and artistic becoming.”
Instead of focusing on whether AI-generated works qualify as art, Zoran argues that the significance of creativity lies not only in the finished product but also in the experiences that shape artists, audiences, and cultures.
For centuries, producing sophisticated art required years of learning, experimentation, and personal development. A painter developed not only technical skills but also a way of seeing the world, while a musician refined both physical abilities and emotional expression. Generative AI is fundamentally changing this relationship, he insisted.
Zoran introduces what he calls the “decoupling thesis,” arguing that AI “makes it possible to produce sophisticated artistic works without undergoing the personal development traditionally required to create them. Someone can now generate detailed illustrations without learning to draw or compose music without mastering an instrument.”
“For centuries, creating art meant going through a process of learning, experimenting, and changing as a person,” he explained. “Today, AI allows us to produce sophisticated works without necessarily undergoing that journey. But this doesn’t mean that human creativity has lost its value. It means we need to rethink where that value lies.”
“The real potential of AI is not just to help us produce more music, images, or designs, but to open new possibilities for how we experience, understand, and engage with the world around us,” he told The Jerusalem Post in an interview.
Rather than eliminating creativity, Zoran argues that AI is shifting it toward new activities, including experimentation, interpretation, and collaboration with technology. Importantly, the value of art also extends beyond its creator, influencing how audiences perceive the world and how cultures develop.
Human creativity has not lost its value
The paper highlights creative projects that show how technology can enrich human experiences rather than simply generate more content. In one example, a tree becomes the center of an interactive artistic experience that combines smell, taste, visual projections, recorded sounds, and AI-generated music. Instead of merely producing digital content, technology helps participants engage with nature in new ways.
The research also raises questions about how AI tools should be designed and evaluated. While current systems are often judged by speed, realism, and output quality, Zoran suggests considering whether they encourage curiosity, exploration, and new perspectives.
“As AI makes artistic production increasingly accessible, the future of creativity may depend less on what people can make and more on what they can discover, experience, and become through the creative process. Instead of making human creativity irrelevant, AI may make it possible to rediscover what makes it meaningful,” he said.
For artists, this could mean using the time saved by AI to experiment and develop richer experiences. For educational and cultural institutions, it could mean placing greater value on the creative process rather than focusing exclusively on finished products.
Ultimately, Zoran argues that as AI makes artistic production increasingly accessible, the future of creativity may depend less on what people can make and more on what they can discover, experience, and become through the creative process.
“Instead of making human creativity irrelevant, AI may offer an opportunity to rediscover what makes it meaningful,” he concluded.
Asked if creativity is valuable because of the finished product, the process of making it, the intentions of the creator, the skills acquired, the emotions involved, or the effect on an audience, Zoran said it’s not the technical complexity but actually creating changes in the artist or the culture, not how we did it. “It doesn’t matter if I drew something myself or a computer did it – but the impact.”
Asked whether someone could use AI to experience discovery, struggle, learning, and personal growth even if the system performs much of the technical work, he responded that “the experience behind it is important. We lose the experience and the authenticity. We have to think again. When musicians started using electric guitars, some said it didn’t sound good enough. But it became interesting when a computer was able to make it.”
Does the effort itself confer value, or does the value come from what the person learns and experiences? “The effort creates maturity.” AI-generated art might provoke the same emotional response as art made entirely by a human, he continued.
“Every era changed things. The Industrial Revolution changed the world. AI is the first technological revolution,” Zoran said. “I have faith in humanity, which finds a way to proceed. If there is painting on the wall of an ancient cave, with no name, there is a high level of art without credit.
“Debates surrounding generative AI and creativity have largely focused on artifacts: Who or what produced a given image or text, whether machine outputs qualify as art, and how authorship and value should be understood. Today, art is capitalist, but it’s not the end of humanity. Maybe it’s not so important exactly who writes a good book.”
While AI can bypass years of artistic training, it cannot replace the transformative experiences that give creativity its deeper meaning.
“The research suggests that the future of art may lie less in producing impressive works and more in using technology to inspire exploration, meaningful experiences, and new ways of seeing the world. For centuries, creating art meant going through a process of learning, experimenting, and changing as a person.
“Today, AI allows us to produce sophisticated works without necessarily undergoing that journey. But this doesn’t mean human creativity has lost its value. It means we need to rethink where that value lies. The real potential of AI is not simply to help us produce more images, music, or designs, but to open new possibilities for how we experience, understand, and engage with the world around us,” he concluded.

The ruling comes days before next week's US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Although several key races appear closely contested, polls favor Democrats to take control of the House and give them a plausible chance of a Senate majority.
In the months leading up to the midterms, President Donald Trump's administration has taken an aggressive approach to election oversight, such as pressing states for voter-registration data, saying stricter measures are needed to ensure election security and public confidence in the vote.
But the Justice Department went too far this month when it threatened to prosecute state and county officials who do not cooperate with the Trump administration's election-related initiatives, US District Judge Trina Thompson ruled in connection with a lawsuit brought by election workers' unions and some other groups.
"Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the Elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs' favor," Thompson wrote in her temporary restraining order.
The Justice Department had no immediate comment on the ruling.
Officials fear federal interference in the elections
Critics, including political experts as well as Democratic and some Republican election officials, have viewed the Trump administration's moves as federal overreach. Some election officials have told Reuters they were preparing for potential federal interference in the midterm elections.
Thompson, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, ordered the Trump administration to refrain from demanding that local election officials remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse ballots to specific voters, or segregate ballots cast in the midterm elections, based on a Trump administration list of alleged non-citizen voters.
Trump has made false claims related to elections in the past, including not acknowledging his defeat in the 2020 election.
