Cyclo-cross World Championships return to Ostend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:02:00 UTC
15:02:00 KST

100 days before the Cyclo-cross World Championships in Ostend (West Flanders) the official countdown to the final has begun. From 29 to 31 January, the city will host the World Championships. The World Championships are returning to Ostend after six years. It is also 11 years since Cyclo-cross World Championships with spectators took place in Belgium. The organisers are eager to turn them into a huge public celebration.
In 2021, the seaside resort of Ostend hosted the UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships. At that time, due to the coronavirus pandemic, no junior races were held and no spectators were allowed. Early next year, the atmosphere will be completely different, with a full sporting programme and tens of thousands of spectators lining the route.
“The countdown has now begun,” says Flemish Sports Minister Annick De Ridder (Flemish nationalist N-VA). “The Cyclo-cross World Championships are a highlight for this sport and a celebration of our sporting heritage and cycling DNA. We look forward to welcoming cycling fans from at home and abroad to Ostend.”
“Cyclo-cross is a sport with deep roots in Belgium and enjoys enormous popularity in Belgium,” says Ostend Mayor John Crombez. “Soon we will see the world’s very best competing for the world title in our city, on a unique course that links the sea, the beach, the city and our heritage.”
2 sand hills on the circuit
The countdown clock is located near King Leopold II’s statue and local landmark Drie Gapers, close to the Royal Galleries. Together with the beach and the Wellington Hippodrome racecourse, this site forms the circuit. The circuit is approximately 3.4 kilometres long. Unlike in 2021, there are now 2 bridges over the tram lines. Six years ago, there was just one bridge.
Two hills of sand will be erected on the beach. In front of one of these two, a paved section will be laid out using cycle path slabs. This will allow the riders to build up speed as they approach the hill. There will also be a paved section in the finish area. The riders will cross from the beach to the finish area via a long flight of steps just before the finish line.
‘We’re currently working on two fan zones, but a World Championship calls for something extra,’ says Tomas Van Den Spiegel, CEO of organisers Flanders Classics. "That’s why these zones will be a little more than just the classic, traditional marquees. We’re creating a festival atmosphere where everyone feels at home, from cyclo-cross fans to families. We’re looking into adding extra entertainment around the course and want to showcase Ostend’s culinary delights.”
Programme
On Friday 29 January, the Team Relay is scheduled as a rainbow race. After that, there will be an opportunity for adaptive or disability sports with the Belgian G-cyclo-cross Championships for riders with an intellectual disability or autism.
In Belgium and the Netherlands G-sport (where "G" stands for gehandicapt, meaning disabled) is the term used for adaptive or disability sports.
“The fact that a Belgian G-cyclo-cross Championship is being organised in Ostend on the Friday is a real bonus,” says Tom Van Damme, chair of Belgian Cycling. “It will undoubtedly be a unique experience for the participants to be able to compete for their Belgian title within the context of a World Championship. The combination of these two events is an example of how sport can be inclusive – something we at Belgian Cycling wholeheartedly welcome and are keen to support.”
Schools in Ostend will also play a part. Pupils will take part in various challenges attached to the World Championships. On Friday 29 January, a Schools’ World Championship will take place in a section of the course.

Jackson Boxer’s recipe for roast apples with toffee sauce and soured cream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:39 UTC
15:00:39 KST

I love a tarte tatin: it’s one of those perfect recipes that contains only a few key ingredients at its core – in this case, butter, sugar, apples and pastry – yet it brings out the absolute best qualities from each: the sugar dark, bittersweet, caramelised, and tempered by the acidity of the apples, the texture softened but held by the combination of butter and fruit pectin. The only problem is that the whole thing happens behind a screen of puff pastry, meaning that tarte tatin takes a great deal of practice and repetition to reach the right level of caramelisation blind. So, here, I’ve dispensed with the pastry altogether, making it a much easier preparation. For the intrepid, this is delicious cooked over a bonfire, where the smoke adds an incredible extra dimension; it also functions as a warming treat after a chilly evening out watching the fireworks.
Roast apples with walnuts and soured cream
This basically follows my method for making tarte tatin, but without the need for pastry – nor to turn out a pan of seething caramel at significant danger to the skin on your wrists. The butter and sugar in the presence of the apples produce a beautiful and slightly acidic toffee sauce, while the fruit retains enough bite to stand up for itself and avoid disintegrating into mush. By drying out the quartered fruit in the fridge first, you ensure a nice, even caramelisation of the sugar and helps the apples maintain their shape and integrity. That said, you can also dry them in an oven set to 80C (60C fan)/gas very low for 30 minutes.
Prep 5 min
  
Dry 2 hr
  
Cook 45 min
  
Serves 4
6 apples – braeburn or discovery, for preference
 
100g unsalted butter, softened
  
100g caster sugar
  
500g 
 soured cream, to serve
 
A few pinches ground cinnamon, to serve
  
100g toasted walnuts
 , to serve
 
Peel the apples, cut them in half and then into quarters, then cut out and discard the cores. Put the apple pieces on a tray and leave uncovered in the fridge for two hours to dry out.
Heat the oven to 210C (190C fan)/410F/gas 6½. Press the butter all over the base of an ovenproof nonstick pan, so it covers the entire flat surface, then scatter the sugar evenly over the top. Arrange the apples cut-side up on top (I like to shape them into a fan), then put the pan on a medium heat to melt the butter and caramelise the sugar for five to 10 minutes, gently shaking the pan every few minutes, until the sugar has melted to a dark caramel. Transfer to the oven and bake for 30 minutes, until everything is deliciously brown and bubbling.
Remove, leave to cool for 10 minutes, then divide between warmed bowls and serve with a generous spoon of soured cream, a dusting of cinnamon and some toasted walnuts.
- Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House, Vesper and Dove, all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London

====================================================================================================

As Trump fans the flames of a world on fire, can diplomacy take back control?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:38 UTC
15:00:38 KST

Never has there been a time when the world has been more interconnected than now. What happens in the secretive inner councils in Tehran, the mountains of south-west Yemen, the steppe of the Donbas, the still bloody wasteland that is Gaza and even the elegant boulevards of Paris and Milan have a common thread.
One cannot understand one set of conflicts without weaving them into another, and it is this very interdependence that is making each problem so contagious, layered and difficult to resolve, leaving the world to live as if trapped inside a pressure cooker on the brink of an explosion.
Each night it seems the world has reached a collective rock bottom, only to wake in the morning to the sound of knocking from below.
In this great age of noncooperation and lawlessness, the need for one crisis to be resolved before another can be addressed leads to a collective paralysis, especially in the total absence of clear leadership by the world’s leading power.
Speaking this week, the Indian external affairs minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, said: “The indivisibility of our existence permeates every aspect of human activity and it has deepened as globalisation has advanced. The fact now is that war anywhere threatens peace everywhere.”
Tom Barrack, Donald Trump’s envoy to Turkey and wider counsellor to the president on the Middle East, in remarks in Doha last week highlighted these threads, admitting the war on Iran launched by his president and Israel in late February had brought unexpected consequences, turning “camp fires into forest fires”.
He likened the Middle East to a Rubik’s Cube, whereby a single move can inadvertently affect the whole picture. “When you adjust one thing in the region what we have seen is everything then changes. Those unintended consequences, and the sequential pace of what is happening, is unexpected,” said Barrack.
He then admitted: “We started trying to do something with our allies in Iran that spread through Hamas, Hezbollah, to six Iranian militias, the Houthis and is now going to north Africa. So where does it stop? How much does this US intervention help or hurt?”
Without breaking from Trump, he answered his own question pretty unambiguously. “We have had 23 regime changes take place across the greater Middle East and Levant instituted one way or another by some American hand or influence, and none of them have worked.
“Every time we try to intervene and change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake,” Barrack said, pointing to Iraq, Libya and Afghanistan, but discreetly omitting Iran.
Deep tectonic transformations
So it is easy to blame what has gone wrong on excessive interventionism and failed multilateralism.
In his new book, the American international relations expert Charles Kupchan explains: “The world is experiencing deep tectonic transformations. Power is rapidly diffusing across the international system, decentering global politics and reawakening great power competition.
“At the same time the advance of the digital era is eroding the social contract of the industrial era producing massive socioeconomic disruption that is affecting political life inside nations as well as relations among them.”
Trump, he argues, is a symptom of a trend that is systemic and widespread.
But it is also hard not to believe that in this interconnected world the disruptive damage that a capricious, vain and amoral US president can inflict has grown tenfold, and that is what we are experiencing. World disorder meets personality disorder.
The Iran war, for instance, as Barrack implied, remains Trump’s most consequential and most mysterious mistake, and its repercussions reverberate across the world. Any US president would have had to address the Iran issue, itself a product of system failure, the inability of the multilateral system to incorporate and change Iran. But the way in which the Iran issue was addressed is down to Trump, and his psyche.
The Democratic candidate for senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, put it simply: “Everybody could have told you this is a dumb idea. There was really only one person in the whole world who had a 40-year project to get us to fight this war. He’s a prime minister of another government [Netanyahu]. And he finally found the dumbass who was willing to do it.”
The foreign minister of Oman, and mediator in the February Iran-US talks, speaking in Cambridge this week reminded his audience an agreement on the core issue – Iran’s nuclear programme – had been within reach before the bombing started.
On every test the war has been a catastrophic failure, whose consequence keeps spreading beyond its initial boundaries, pushing worldwide inflation to 4%. The strait of Hormuz, a waterway open to commercial traffic for centuries, has become an Iranian bargaining chip. Less than a fortnight before the midterms, the price of Brent oil per barrel reached $117 – 50% higher than prewar levels.
The GDP of Saudi Arabia, the Middle East’s economic powerhouse, is forecast by the IMF to contract 3.3%, a five percentage-point downgrade from the 1.7% growth forecast issued only in July.
As the House of Saud analysis explains: “The country’s Vision 2030 plan was constructed as a hedge against oil-price volatility. It assumed open sea lanes, functioning airports, and a US security umbrella that would deter kinetic threats to the kingdom’s export infrastructure. Every one of those assumptions has failed since February.”
On 30 September, Saudi Arabia’s government felt forced to raise its 2026 budget deficit projection to $65.3bn, 48% above the original forecast.
Nor did the conflict lead to a more stable Iran. The Iranian with most strategic nous, Ali Larijani, was blown up on the first day of the war. Hardliners around the new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, are more entrenched than ever. If anything the public debate inside Iran leans towards ending the fatwa on possessing nuclear weapons.
Regardless of the nuclear issue, after being attacked twice mid-negotiation, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps has already adjusted its defence doctrine to allow for preemptive strikes not just against US bases, but across the globe. “People can hurt us from a distance, and it doesn’t cost a fortune to be able to do so,” Tony Radakin, the UK chief of the defence staff, admitted.
Then there is the incoherence and lawlessness of the US-Israeli actions in Iran. Benjamin Netanyahu, spoiling to attack Iran for a third time in two years, wanted to order “the IDF, Mossad, and the security services” to “overthrow the regime in Iran”. The Americans focus was on nuclear weapons.
The chaos has left Trump’s domestic popularity in ruins. Yet as Dean Acheson, Harry S Truman’s secretary of state, asserted: “80% of the job of foreign policy is the management of your domestic ability to have a policy.”
Henry Kissinger said: “The acid test of policy is its ability to obtain domestic support.” A foreign policy has to be constructed to win popular backing and this one was not. As a result Trump feels entrapped, circling around solutions that failed before, making him ever more irascible and random.
The Republican pollster Karl Rove claimed Trump, as a result, “came across more as a heckler at a UFC match than as a reassuring wartime commander-in-chief. The more undisciplined the White House messages on war and the economy, the more at risk GOP candidates will be.”
Faced by the plunging poll numbers, incensed by Iran’s refusal to submit, incapable of self-criticism, Trump took the plunge and tried to deflect responsibility for high energy prices to a second theatre of war – Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Trump flung open the floodgates of his hatred for Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy that he first released in 2025 only for European leaders, and domestic pressure, to force them shut again.
The pent-up bile has poured out as he demanded Zelenskyy stand down, describing him as the real impediment to peace, and a new era of Russian US business cooperation.
But even in treachery the incompetence of the White House shone through.
Trump first announced an entirely fictional 60-day “energy truce” that neither Zelensky or Putin had agreed. Then the deal to release Russian diesel emerged to be so small that no serious commentator said it would have a serious impact on the US prices.
As to why Ukrainian forces were suddenly deprived of their previous levels of access to the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink, the US administration gave conflicting accounts over the rules that govern such systems, and what actually happened.
Even after the decision was supposedly reversed, some blamed a freelancing Musk, the billionaire owner of the system, implying a private company could determine the conduct of a putative US ally. Others, including the vice-president, JD Vance, said contractually Musk would have required the permission of the White House or the military to act. Musk said the Ukrainians had breached the terms of the Starlink contract by using it to attack Iran.
The Ukrainian author Illia Ponomarenko wrote: “There have, of course, been times in human history that were even darker and more terrible. But never, it seems, have there been times so despicable and, above all, so stupid.”
Trump’s intervention and his intertwining of these two wars has given the Russians the chance to pounce by proposing a three-way China, Russia and US great power summit at an already scheduled meeting in Shenzhen, China, on 18 November.
To make this more appealing to Trump, Putin sent his veteran foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, on 19 October to Tehran for the first time since the Iran war broke out to see if he could bring the conflict to an end on terms Trump could tolerate.
“The more Putin can persuade Tehran to move closer to Trump’s demands, the more concessions he can extract from Trump on Ukraine,” the Russia affairs analyst Amir Chahaki said. The Russian ambition is to use Trump’s difficulties to end the two wars – Ukraine and Iran – together, largely on Russian terms.
Trump is taking steps to help Putin, including by shedding his status as an international pariah, overruling the objections of some in his own party by inviting Putin to this winter’s G20 summit, which the US is hosting at a Trump golf club just outside Miami.
Quite why Trump feels so certain of Putin’s good intentions is a mystery, one that no one can unravel. David Frum, a former speech writer for George W Bush, posits it is a function of Trump’s decline. Trump was “much more of a self-aware conman when he entered politics a decade ago than he is now. He now may be kind of lost: truly in a world of illusions, where he no longer himself knows what is true and what is a lie.”
Waking up to Trump
But there is a consequence to all this. More and more countries are finally waking up to dangers of being excluded and abused by the US. The former Canadian foreign minister Chrystia Freeland admits it has taken a long time.
“There are leaders, thinking Trump is stupid, that decided: ‘I can win this guy over. I can give him the shiniest prize. I can give him a gold watch that’s encrusted with diamonds. I can flatter him in the most outrageous way.’”
For instance, Saudi Arabia offered gifts to Trump, and in return they have been left alone to fend off the attacks by Houthis that senior UN diplomats insist is entirely driven by a timetable that meets Iran’s needs.
In particular, Trump’s effort to deflect his Iranian disaster on to a largely innocent Ukraine has had a lethal effect inside Europe. The continent’s leaders are aghast at the gap between themselves and Trump on Russia.
Where Europe sees an existential threat, Trump sees a business opportunity. What is worse is that his pro-Russia rhetoric threatens the centre’s own political survival by feeding the populist narrative about the draining cost of Ukraine making lives unaffordable.
The torrent of propaganda about “peace with Russia” led the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, to exclaim: “My biggest concern at the moment is not our economy, not the USA or China, but Russia’s influence on our society.”
As a matter of self-protection, European leaders have no choice but to articulate their differences with Trump. As a result, they have had to become explicit in blaming the Iran war for the squeeze on living standards and to ask the rioters to criticise not them but Washington.
For instance, Emmanuel Macron, the French president, told the rioters that their anger about the cost of living was legitimate: “Demonstrators expressed concern about the cost of living and the price of fuel. Both are driven by the conflict launched in the Persian Gulf, a conflict in which France has taken no part but whose consequences we are suffering.”
The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, in his parliament admitted fuel prices for ordinary people were “devilishly expensive”, but added that the Donald responsible for this was not him but Trump, the hero of the Polish opposition.
The second knock-on impact is that Musk’s meddling with SpaceX has made it even more apparent to Europe that it has to end its debate on digital sovereignty and instead regulate to reduce its future dependence on US technology.
Freeland predicts: “Countries are going to think really hard before they buy another F-35 controlled by the Pentagon. Why would you want a jet that Americans control?”
The European Commission in May proposed reserving 70% of the 2GHz frequency spectrum, which allows smartphones to connect directly to satellites, for European enterprises, thus restricting access for players such as Starlink. Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone and Telefónica are already lining up to make the bid, prompting US diplomatic protests.
The Polish foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, accused Musk of digging his own grave in Europe, asking why “a Ketamine-addicted trillionaire in bed with foreign powers should think he deserves regulatory privileges and frequency permissions”.
Similarly, some Middle Eastern powers are waking up to the threat to their sovereignty posed by a US system that consistently privileges Israel’s priorities.
It is early days, but for a Gulf state leader to call for a Gulf security pact that includes Iran, as Badr Albusaidi, Oman’s foreign minister, did this week, is a potential Berlin Wall moment. The implication is that the US should no longer be the security provider for the Gulf.
Iran is viewed with deep suspicion across the Gulf, and Albusaidi admits his proposal is counterintuitive. But, as his team says, “war sometimes just happens; peace is always caused”.
Either way, at a time when people have lost faith in the problem-solving capacity of postwar institutions, it’s critical that those who believe in the efficacy of collective action and diplomacy show they mean it.
After three years of havoc and war, they finally need to take back control from the demolition men.

====================================================================================================

When you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters  | Hugh Muir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:38 UTC
15:00:38 KST

Pity Black History Month UK, assailed on all sides. Those on the right seek to end the celebration on the basis that it amounts to special treatment for a group that doesn’t deserve it. History should be colour-blind: society should not differentiate, they say. We are not racist, we just want fairness. But often, they are – and they really don’t.
On the other side of the argument are the progressives, notably minority progressives, who say the idea of a month to consider Black history is demeaning because it should already have a year-round place in our teaching and consciousness. There is a further view that any beneficial effect the month once had has been diluted by unimaginative repetition and commercially motivated virtue signalling. Players taking the knee in the Premier League? Been there, done that: yawn!
I have long taken the glass-half-full approach. The ideal would be for Black history to be incorporated into the social and educational culture – and perhaps one day it will be. But in the meantime, I’ll take a mandated, month-long focus on the Black contribution to the way our society has evolved. And it seems very necessary this year, when the very notion of belonging in Britain and other major western countries has been so under attack.
A year in which we have clearly seen that a political party, with pretensions to lead the country, attracts activists with ugly racist and nativist views – at national and local level – with the same efficiency that magnets attract iron filings. Our expectations are different now. When transcripts of the things Reform folk say in private reach the public domain, the old-fashioned Tory dog-whistle seems comparatively quaint.
This is a year in which we have again seen the confidence and daring of those who cuddle close to pseudo-scientific theories asserting white superiority and black inferiority. The racial eugenicists are back from the fringes, championed down their venal path by Donald Trump, whose leadership of the free world gladhands nativists, targets Black officials and routinely belittles Black enemies as “low IQ”.
It’s been a year in which toxic politics and the mainstreaming of intolerance – against minorities of many categories – has led to racist unpleasantness on our streets and in the workplace. There is a snapshot from the Royal College of Nursing: racist abuse of NHS nurses – including use of the N-word – up 86% in the recent past. All part of what one NHS official called “a rising tide of racism”.
Another snapshot of the increasingly hostile environment is from parliament. What happened, via social media, when Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy posted a video in support of Black History Month? Vile abuse, of course: “Some of a kind that I had not necessarily seen in that volume before. I had people calling me the N-word, people telling me to eff-off and go back to where I came from, and people sending monkey photographs.”
Another snapshot from Chichester, Sussex, where a diverse group of actors recently went to perform A Midsummer Night’s Dream and were shamefully menaced. “I don’t know if I have witnessed and/or experienced as much racism, xenophobia and homophobia as I saw in those six weeks,” said the actor and comedian Munya Chawawa. Britain is a good place. The vast majority of our fellow citizens are decent and kind. But it’s now easy, far too easy, to unwittingly enter hostile territory.
So in years like this, when there are obvious, concerted, targeted, and well-funded attempts to undermine Black people and the Black experience – not least the targeting of books by Black authors by “anti woke” crusaders – it becomes more difficult to be sanguine about concepts such as Black History Month. It then becomes a good thing, perhaps an essential one, to remember and to highlight – if only over a calendar month – who we are, who has shaped us and how we have indisputably helped to shape Britain as a vibrant, diverse, first world power.
Today, at the end of this Black History Month, Guardian Opinion has asked Black Britons representing four generations to tell us how their own Black British identities have evolved, for we have been here long enough now to compare notes on the different stages of our lives on this island. A twentysomething sees the joy and pain of being here very differently to their elderly siblings, to their parents, to their grandparents.
Call it reflection with a purpose. In a time like this, it seems more vital than ever to know who we were, who we are – and the foundations on which we all stand.
- Hugh Muir is executive editor, Opinion

Eight in 10 homes in London’s poshest postcodes now sell below asking price, Coutts finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:37 UTC
15:00:37 KST

Eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price, according to research by Coutts, which provides private banking services to wealthy clients.
Property prices in “prime central London”, which covers the city’s most expensive postcodes, have dropped 5% in the third quarter of 2026, as the slowdown in the UK’s property market hits its wealthiest residents.
It means some affluent people are facing hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of pounds in losses to the value of their homes, with properties selling at an average 10% discount to their asking price, Coutts found.
Prices in the highest end of London’s property market are now 14% below their peak in 2014, having been hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs. Buying and selling agents in the capital have also reported a slowdown in interest from foreign-born buyers after the abolition of the non-dom tax regime.
Exclusive areas such as Knightsbridge and Belgravia, and South Kensington have been hit the hardest, Coutts said, with prices 30.8% and 26.9% below their peaks respectively.
Alex Webster, head of lending at the bank, said buyers and sellers at the top end of the market were taking a more cautious approach, even before the chancellor, John Healey’s, first budget this week.
Sellers will now be watching to see if the budget “encourages some of that delayed activity to return”, she said. “But financing conditions and the wider economic environment will continue to influence the market.”
There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.
While the Bank of England has kept its key interest rate on hold at 3.75%, expectations are growing that next week its monetary policy committee will vote to increase the rate for the first time in three years to 4%.
In the meantime, sellers in prime central London are increasingly shying away, Coutts found, with new listings down 14% compared with the previous quarter and available stock down by 6% year-on-year.
Transactions were 9.1% lower in the third quarter of this year, it said, with the biggest slowdown in the £2m-£5m band, where transactions were down 22.3%.
However, separate research from the estate agent Savills found that buyers at the very top end of the market are driving activity, with 26 transactions above £10m in the third quarter of this year, taking the total to 127 over the past year. Together, these sales were worth £2.88bn, it found.

Massive Attack, Bob Marley, bell hooks and grime: the forces that shaped four generations of Black Britons | The panel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:35 UTC
15:00:35 KST

(L to R:) Lauryn Hill, Margaret Ekpo, Bob Marley, Skepta and Nelson Mandela. Composite: Redferns/Fourth Estate/Luath Press/Mariner/Corbis/VCG/Getty/Rex/Shutterstock/Alamy/Guardian Design View image in fullscreen (L to R:) Lauryn Hill, Margaret Ekpo, Bob Marley, Skepta and Nelson Mandela. Composite: Redferns/Fourth Estate/Luath Press/Mariner/Corbis/VCG/Getty/Rex/Shutterstock/Alamy/Guardian Design Massive Attack, Bob Marley, bell hooks and grime: what forces shaped four generations of Black Britons? Arlo Parks, Eunice Olumide, Ade Adepitan and Vanley Burke For Black History Month, figures from the arts, culture and sport reveal the people and ideas that made them who they are today When you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters | Hugh Muir ‘British music has shaped me completely’ Arlo Parks Singer and songwriter, 26 What book has most inspired you? All about love by bell hooks taught me so much about the nuances of connection and desire; it helped me make sense of the world and embrace my sensitivity. She had such a compassionate and inspired approach to truth-telling that I try to carry with me wherever I go. What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self? British music has shaped me completely. In Rainbows by Radiohead taught me to yearn, bend genres and embrace minimalism. Blue Lines and Mezzanine by Massive Attack moulded my taste in drums and song structure. Dummy by Portishead encouraged me to be as vocally naked and unafraid as possible. [The song] Archangel by Burial taught me to embrace the grime and the magic and the grey of London. What cultural moments have felt most significant to you? Radiohead headlining the Pyramid stage at Glastonbury. Tate Modern opening its programming into the late night. The founding of Notting Hill carnival, and Meltdown festival at the Southbank Centre. If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority? Protecting and advocating for young people’s health and education. Which Black historical figure has most influenced you? It would have to be a cluster of figures for their fearlessness, vulnerability and dedication to their crafts: Zadie Smith, Steve McQueen and the painter Donald Rodney. View image in fullscreen The writer Zadie Smith at her home in London, September 2020. Photograph: IBL/Shutterstock What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you? I’ve been most disappointed by the rise in anti-trans rhetoric and discrimination. I’ve been most uplifted by the Arts Everywhere fund and the general commitment to increasing public access to art. What is most misunderstood between generations? That it’s impossible for generations to truly connect. I think that with some care and attention we could find common ground, grow and truly understand each other. What is a “good life”? A life full of love, generosity and adventure. What would you change about your life? Nothing. I feel really lucky and am looking forward to seeing where life takes me. ‘I’m interested in people who refuse to be reduced to a single identity’ Eunice Olumide Model, actor, author and activist, 39 What book has most inspired you? I really did enjoy the Loud Black Girls anthology. It’s a wonderful constellation of extraordinary voices, contradictions, ambitions and histories. As someone who has spent much of her life moving between different worlds, I’m interested in the people who refuse to be reduced to a single identity. What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self? Growing up in Edinburgh, my relationship with identity has always been layered. Music was one of the places where those layers could coexist without requiring an explanation. I have toured the world with artists from Lauryn Hill, the Roots and Skepta to Wu-Tang Clan and Roots Manuva. They have all in different ways challenged the idea that we must make ourselves smaller to fit into the world. View image in fullscreen RZA and Ghostface Killah of Wu-Tang Clan performing at the O2 Arena in London, March 2026. Photograph: Simone Joyner/Getty Images What cultural moments have felt most significant to you? The emergence of grime as a defining British sound. It brought the ingenuity, language and lived realities of young people from communities too often treated as peripheral into the centre of British culture. It was a reminder that culture does not need permission to become influential. If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority? I would bring education, culture and economic opportunity much closer together. I’d usher in properly funded creative education, meaningful careers guidance, paid routes into industries that have historically relied on unpaid internships, and a serious commitment to ensuring that young people from every background can participate in Britain’s cultural and economic life. Which Black historical figure has most influenced you? Margaret Ekpo was an inspiring Nigerian women’s rights activist and politician who fought for equality and the empowerment of women. At a time when women were often denied a voice in politics, she bravely stood up for their rights and encouraged them to participate in decision making. What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you? The repeated pressure on public services, education and the arts concerns me deeply. These are not peripheral concerns; they shape our ability to participate in society, develop our talents and understand one another. What has uplifted me is the progress made in recognising the breadth of Britain’s history and the people who have shaped it. What is most misunderstood between generations? I think each generation underestimates the difficulty of the world the other has inherited. Older generations can sometimes mistake the language of younger people for a lack of resilience, when it may actually be a more sophisticated vocabulary for identifying problems that were previously endured in silence. Younger generations, meanwhile, can underestimate the ingenuity and sacrifices of those who navigated a world with fewer of the freedoms and resources we now take for granted. What is a “good life”? To have been a source of utter joy and kindness to the world. To use my inspiration to help and heal. Loving my family, doing good and letting the rest be. In the end it’s not what you own or worry about, it’s who you loved and the good you left behind. What would you change about your life? Absolutely nothing. ‘My first act as PM? Bring in conscription for teaching’ Ade Adepitan Presenter, disability advocate, former wheelchair basketball player and gold medal-winning Paralympian, 53 What book has most inspired you? King Leopold’s Ghost by Adam Hochschild opened my eyes to history. I have always had this craving for more knowledge about Africa, the world and why it is the way it is. It talks about the origins of racism and race theory, and where we are socially and politically in the world – you can see the roots of it from this book. What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self? I got Shut Up and Dance’s album Dance Before the Police Come when it came out in the 1990s. It is a seminal album from a time when British music was still trying to find itself. It is like a cross between hip-hop, breakbeat and dance – they were like the Prodigy before the Prodigy. I felt like the album had the right amount of anger and cultural references. Soul II Soul were pretty influential when I grew up, and Massive Attack were big for me as well. What cultural moments have felt most significant to you? The London 2012 Olympics and Paralympics. The opening ceremony was a real celebration of Britishness, of who we are and who we had become. It talked about everything from Black culture to white British culture, and we all celebrated it. View image in fullscreen The London 2012 Olympic opening ceremony in Stratford, London, 27 July 2012. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority? There are so many things like accessible housing and transport, but I just couldn’t get away from education. I get asked to go to a lot of schools to do talks and assemblies and I can’t understand how we can’t see that the difference between private and state education is so stark in terms of resources, facilities, everything. It is insane that we have a two-tier system with such a wide discrepancy. I would ringfence a certain percentage of GDP to go into state school education. Or introduce something like a kind of conscription for people who have been highly educated or have a degree to teach. I think everyone at some point should have to do a stint in teaching and put back into society. What Black historical figure has most influenced you? James Baldwin, because he was so articulate and an incredible communicator. He grew up in probably the most divisive and dysfunctional country in the world: the US. In a country where you could literally get shot for stating those types of views, he was brave enough to make it look at itself. What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you? What has most disappointed me is that a lot of our policies and political leaders have allowed their politics to be shaped by anger. Angry rhetoric about immigrants, about benefits; anger about taxes, or the country being overregulated. Arguably, if we hadn’t listened to some of these very vocal groups and allowed ourselves to be shaped by them, we may not have had Brexit. More appropriate regulation, rather than a focus on less regulation, might have avoided a tragedy such as Grenfell. What has most uplifted me is people starting to take more notice of politics. I think when I was growing up there was a lot of apathy when it came to political ideas. We were not as aware of what was going on. But people now have been forced to [take notice], because we have been in a period of high political flux and [experiences] like Covid have made us examine who we are. What is most misunderstood between generations? My generation thinks the millennials’ lives are really easy: “They are not as resilient as we were.” But then millennials will say: “You guys didn’t have to deal with the kind of world we had to.” We had 9/11 and that turned the world upside down. Then the next generation says: “Look at us; we are dealing with social media and cannot afford to buy a house.” We allow ourselves to be put into these groups and these groups are then put against each other. What is a “good life”? It’s about feeling happy and fulfilled. If you manage to find your thing, no matter whatever else happens to you in life you will always be able to go back to that. For me, it’s sports and family – they anchor me. What would you change about your life? What I regret is that a lot of my success came after my parents passed away or their health deteriorated, so we couldn’t enjoy as much. I would have loved my dad to have been a grandfather to [Ade’s children] Bolla and Zayla, and for my mum to have had more time while she was well with Bolla, and to have met Zayla. I would have liked things to have aligned when I was at my best and they were at their best. That would have been nice. ‘No political development has uplifted me – we always return to the status quo’ Vanley Burke Photographer and artist, 75 What book has most inspired you? The books by the Black photographers Gordon Parks and James Van Der Zee. They most influenced my visual style. What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self? Catch a Fireby Bob Marley and the Wailers undoubtedly had and continues to have an impact on me. His lyrics are so visual. Notable mentions: Burning Spear’s Marcus Garvey, Culture’s Two Sevens Clash, Stevie Wonder’s Songs in the Key of Life. The work of Nina Simone. So many great albums, it’s difficult to choose one. What cultural moments have felt most significant to you? The release of Nelson Mandela, perhaps because I was in Africa for the first time when it happened. This significant moment offered hope not just for South Africa but also beyond the shores of the continent. If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority? Acknowledging the evils of the enslavement of African people over centuries, the teachings of colonial history and its impact on British society, and having serious plans about how we can pay reparations for the labour of enslaved Africans. Which Black historical figure has most influenced you? The visionary Marcus Garvey offered hope for the Black people; he was not just a thinker but he also got things done. He was one of the most accomplished orators of all time. His thoughts and philosophy continue to reverberate throughout Africa and the diaspora. View image in fullscreen Marcus Garvey in 1924. Photograph: Photo 12/Universal Images Group/Getty Images What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you? No political development has uplifted me because we always return to the status quo, which is disappointing. Thatcher’s legacy and its continued legacy on the working classes, the selling of council houses, the dismantling of the manufacturing industry, privatisation and closing the coal mines. Her policies benefited a few but resulted in many of the issues that blight our communities today. What is most misunderstood between generations? Most people – especially the younger generation – are plugged in and switched on to their own universe, leaving very little time to communicate with each other. Meanwhile, the bridging generation is having to deal with an ever-changing work-life balance, making it difficult for them to provide the necessary support bringing both sides together. What is a “good life”? Not having to be conscious of race on a daily basis or even at all. But that isn’t going to be possible in my lifetime. And being able to pay your bills. What would you change about your life? I’ve been quite happy with my life. I’m not sure I would change anything, perhaps tweak a few things. Changing one thing can have detrimental consequences on the rest of your life. Is time up for backyard fireworks? UK ministers weigh partial ban over noise concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:34 UTC
15:00:34 KST

As the nights draw in, the season of sparklers begins, with Diwali, Bonfire Night and New Year’s Eve among the occasions typically celebrated with fireworks. But if campaigners get their way, this could be the last blast for bangers in the back yard.
In January concerns about the noise and availability of fireworks were aired in a parliamentary debate, with two petitions clocking up more than 180,000 signatures each, while earlier this month the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade closed a consultation on proposals including making louder fireworks only available to professional users.
Harriet Main, a public affairs manager at the RSPCA, said the charity was thrilled by the consultation: “For too long, pets, wildlife, and livestock have suffered from stress, fright and severe injury caused by loud unregulated back-yard DIY displays.
“Public appetite for change is overwhelming: the RSPCA hosted its own online action to help supporters submit their views to the consultation, and this generated over 51,000 responses eager to speak up for animals. This extraordinary turnout demonstrates just how deeply people across Britain care about protecting animals from the devastating impacts of unnecessarily loud fireworks.”
In recent years there have been reports of a host of animal fatalities linked to fireworks, from the death of a baby red panda at Edinburgh zoo to a dachshund in North Yorkshire.
Ministers have ruled out a complete ban on the public buying fireworks. Instead, their proposals include expanding the list of fireworks banned for general sale and reducing the permitted decibel level of consumer fireworks from 120dB to 110dB, meaning their loudness would be approximately halved.
Dr Gwen Rees, the president of the British Veterinary Association, said vets were acutely aware of the fear, distress, injury and lasting anxiety fireworks caused to animals in the UK each year. “Lower noise limits would reduce one of the main causes of firework-related distress while allowing celebrations to continue,” she said. “But quieter fireworks are not a complete solution. Flashes and unpredictable timing can still affect animals, so clearer labelling, responsible use, tighter controls on sales and private use, and better public awareness are also essential to protect animal welfare.”
A tightening of regulations has been backed by organisations including the National Farmers’ Union, which has cited animal welfare concerns and fire risks in relation to private firework displays. “One member reported losing around four acres of wheat after a firework landed in a standing crop during harvest,” the NFU noted.
Changes to pyrotechnics and fireworks regulations will be made as soon as parliamentary time allows after analysis of the feedback from the consultation, the government said, adding that there would be a six-month “transitional period” after the law was changed.
However, the British Fireworks Assocation has pushed back, noting that many of the behaviours that frustrate communities – such as setting off fireworks in a public place or after 1am – are already illegal, and that removing large numbers of legal and regulated products from the consumer market might push people towards finding hidden-market fireworks and pyrotechnics.
Recent efforts to tackle the use of fireworks and pyrotechnics in Scotland – including the introduction of “firework control zones” where the devices are banned – have had a mixed reception.
Helen Whitelegg, the campaigns manager at the charity Redwings Horse Sanctuary, said: “We believe the zones create a two-tier system of protection where they are put in place and risk pushing more use of fireworks to the surrounding areas.”
She added: “We are aware that the widely anticipated step of introducing a licencing requirement for anyone using fireworks has been shelved due to lack of resources and there is no indication when this part of the legislation is likely to be brought in.”
But it is not only the UK where firework fervour has cooled. In the Netherlands a countrywide ban on most consumer fireworks came into effect in August, while Czechia has also tightened its regulations. On 29 November, Swiss citzens will have their say on proposals to ban noisy fireworks.
In Germany, there is already a limited window in which fireworks can be bought or used, while there are also bans on fireworks in some zones and near certain facilities. Even then, there are calls for stronger regulations, with one survey suggesting almost half of those polled were in favour of a total ban, with exceptions only for very small fireworks such as sparklers.
Whitelegg said that among other measures, Redwings backed a reduction in the maximum loudness of fireworks to 90dB, as is the case in New Zealand, noting that while a Dutch-style ban would be preferable, the use of low-noise fireworks presented a practical compromise.
“I think the direction of travel does suggest that change is inevitable,” she said. “And because of what we’re seeing in other countries, it’s not unique to the UK by any stretch of the imagination.”

Lithuanian schools face a dilemma: embrace Halloween or stick to local traditions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Schools are deciding whether to celebrate Halloween. Some are changing its name and finding ways to adapt the festivities to their communities, while others are taking pupils to clean up graves. The Education Ministry does not ban Halloween celebrations in schools, but has sent them reminders that Lithuanian traditions should take priority.
The Taškius School of Science and Arts has come up with its own version of Halloween, renaming it “Autumn Revelry”. Each year, the school community chooses a new theme. This year, for example, pupils from Year 1 to Year 10 stepped into the world of Harry Potter.
“It was not just a day of learning. It also involved making costumes, because the pupils take part in a costume competition, and teachers transform themselves into professors. For example, in PE lessons, they played Quidditch, the game familiar from th Harry Potter films,” said Lina Jankauskaitė, head of Taškius school.
However, the school community has agreed on certain rules.
“Our masks and behaviour must not frighten anyone or be associated with cruelty. We want to create a celebration without spreading fear,” she says.
“They are children growing up in a secular society, and we are not raising them in isolation. I think they should know which celebrations are observed not only in Lithuania but around the world,” mother Dagnė told LRT TV..
“There are never too many celebrations in life. Halloween may not have originated here, but it is becoming a fun occasion, as the children themselves show,” said father Darius.
“It saddens me to see that, for example, people in our district no longer come together for Užgavėnės, our traditional pre-Lenten festival, while Halloween has become a huge district-wide celebration.
“All the houses are decorated, and the girls look forward to it tremendously. Since becoming a mother, I have come to appreciate this celebration more and have become more accepting of the fact that it came from abroad,” said mother Eglė.
Meanwhile, Abraham Kulvietis Classical Gymnasium in Vilnius chose not to celebrate Halloween.
“You cannot celebrate every holiday; we have traditional celebrations. This particular one simply has not become a tradition at our school,” said Kristina Gudelienė, head of the gymnasium.
Instead, pupils continue other traditions by visiting cemeteries and tending to graves.
“Neglected, forgotten graves – at Rasos Cemetery and Jerusalem Cemetery. It has become a tradition: teachers know they can go with their classes, and they do so practically every year,” Gudelienė said.
Every year, ahead of All Souls’ Day, the Education Ministry sends schools reminders to prioritise Lithuanian roots and traditions.
However, the ministry says it does not prohibit Halloween celebrations.
“We just need to make sure that cruelty, blood and violent games are not promoted, because these are forms of violence,” said Jolanta Navickaitė from the ministry.
According to Virginijus Jocys, chairman of the Council for the Protection of Ethnic Culture, the foundations of all holidays should be grounded in Lithuanian traditions.
“Perhaps teachers could explain the meaning in greater depth and make comparisons. Rather than imposing categorical bans, they should simply explain what it means. When a child dresses up as something, what are they trying to express?” he said.
According to the ministry, some schools are looking for alternatives.
For example, they invite people to donate whole pumpkins to organisations, which then make soup and distribute it to older people.

11 ‘extraordinary’ European hotels included on Fodor's Finest list for 2027

A new list of the 50 most incredible hotels in the world features 11 properties in Europe.
For some people, a hotel may simply be a place to lay their head when travelling. For others, it’s one of the biggest reasons to book a trip in the first place.
If you fall into the latter camp, the Fodor’s Finest list of the most incredible hotels in the world in 2027 is for you.
This latest edition features 50 "extraordinary" properties that offer more than just a stunning room. Impeccable service, luxurious amenities, extravagance and a deep connection to the surroundings are what set these stays apart.
In Europe, 11 hotels made the cut, including the Grand Hotel Tremezzo in Lake Como, the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo in Monaco, and the Orient Express La Minerva in Rome.
Housed in a 16th century building close to the gates of Edinburgh Castle, The Witchery was also included and offers guests an “immersive experience” with lavish rooms replete with Gothic interiors.
Opened in 2021, Acro Suites Crete combines luxury resort offerings with being a state-of-the-art wellness retreat. A night’s stay can be in a cave suite and by day, guests can take a dip in their private plunge pool.
Meanwhile, the five-star Charlotte Street Hotel in Fitzrovia, London, features rooms that each have a distinct design. It also has its own library, drawing room and screening room for film buffs.
Other European hotels on the list include Airelles La Bastide in Provence, Argos in Cappadocia, Hotel Pigalle in Gothenburg, Maison Souquet in Paris, and Pulitzer Amsterdam.
"An extraordinary hotel stay can mean something different to every traveller,” said Jeremy Tarr, Editorial Director at Fodor’s Travel. “It might be a remarkable sense of place, an unexpected level of personal service, or a setting that makes you see a destination in an entirely new way.
"By focusing on just 50 properties this year, we're spotlighting the hotels that truly stand apart and give travellers a compelling reason to make the journey."
How were the properties chosen?
Curated by Fodor’s editors in collaboration with hundreds of hospitality experts, the compilation features a range of stays from varying price points.
This includes properties that have a character-rich history, are design driven urban retreats to stays that are intimate hideaways. With only 50 places on this year’s list, “every selection has earned its place”, Fodor’s said.
Specifically in Europe, Fodor’s said the continent has been "perfecting the art of hospitality for centuries", with its portfolio of finest hotels having the history, character and occasional eccentricity to prove it.
Beyond price tags and copious marbling, the publication said its European curation is united by “a sense of personality”. It added: “Whether extravagantly opulent or quietly understated, these are places with stories to tell – and plenty of reasons to become part of them.”
Fodor’s ‘finest’ hotels in Europe
Out of the 50 properties on Fodor’s Finest list, 11 are in Europe:
- Acro Suites Crete, Crete, Greece
- Airelles La Bastide, Gordes, Provence, France
- Argos in Cappadocia, Uçhisar, Türkiye
- Charlotte Street Hotel, London, England
- Grand Hotel Tremezzo, Lake Como, Italy

A container-handling vehicle operates at the Global Container Terminals facility at Roberts Bank in Delta, British Columbia, Canada, on Oct. 30, 2026. The Canadian federal government on Friday announced that it has officially listed the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 project at the Port of Vancouver, Canada's largest port, as a project of national interest to strengthen trade infrastructure and reduce reliance on the U.S. market. (Photo by Liang Sen/Xinhua)
OTTAWA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The Canadian federal government on Friday announced that it has officially listed the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 project at the Port of Vancouver, Canada's largest port, as a project of national interest to strengthen trade infrastructure and reduce reliance on the U.S. market.
The move is part of Canada's broader strategy to double its exports to non-U.S. markets by 2035, according to Transport Canada.
With a planned investment of 5.9 billion Canadian dollars (about 4.2 billion U.S. dollars), the project is expected to increase the container capacity at the Port of Vancouver by approximately 50 percent. It will add 2.4 million containers of annual processing capacity and support up to 100 billion Canadian dollars (71.55 billion dollars) in annual trade.
Transport Canada said that the listing decision provides regulatory certainty, accelerating the project's commercial operations to 2035, up to four years ahead of schedule. The project is currently on a viable path to reach a Final Investment Decision by mid-2027. ■

Border with U.S. can not be changed by state-level government: Mexico
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:55:52 CST
14:55:52 KST

MEXICO CITY, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Mexican Foreign Ministry said Friday that border between Mexico and the United States can not be changed by the decision of a state-level government, and the demarcation of boundary between the two countries must follow standards established by international treaties.
The Texas General Land Office, a U.S. state agency led by Commissioner Dawn Buckingham, has declared nine islands in the Rio Grande (known as the Rio Bravo in Mexico) property of the state of Texas.
In response, the ministry said that under the 1970 Mexico-U.S. Boundary Treaty, the international boundary in the river follows the center line of the normal channel and that line determines sovereignty over the land on either side, regardless of who previously held sovereignty over it.
The International Boundary and Water Commission is the body authorized by the two governments to carry out the treaty and has the power to determine on which side of the boundary each island lies, the ministry said, noting that no state-level government body has the authority to make such determinations.
It stressed that under the treaty, neither side may build works that the International Boundary and Water Commission finds could alter or obstruct the normal flow of the river.
The ministry said Mexico will closely monitor any actions in the area and reiterated that it will abide by the treaty governing the two countries' shared border and continue to pursue dialogue through established mechanisms. ■

Protein may help identify breast cancers resistant to targeted drugs: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:55:33 CST
14:55:33 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Tracking a protein that drives cell division could help doctors tell which breast cancers are likely to respond to CDK4/6 inhibitors, a widely used class of targeted drugs, an Australian study has found.
Researchers at Australia's Garvan Institute of Medical Research found that the activity of a protein called CDK1 in breast cancers is linked to how they respond to a common therapy, an insight that could inform more personalized treatment approaches for patients, according to a statement of the institute released on Friday.
The study focused on estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer, the most common type, fueled by the hormone estrogen. Many people with this cancer now receive drugs called CDK4/6 inhibitors alongside hormone therapy. These drugs stop cancer cells from multiplying, but they don't work for everyone, and in advanced cancer, they eventually stop working for most patients.
In more than 400 patients' breast cancer biopsy samples, the researchers found CDK1 activity rose as the cancer became more aggressive, and higher activity was linked to worse outcomes.
The findings need to be tested in larger groups of patients treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors, and could eventually open the door to new drugs targeting CDK1, according to the study published in Advanced Science. ■

Australia launches new biodiversity restoration method to expand nature repair market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:55:28 CST
14:55:28 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government has launched a second method under its national Nature Repair Market, expanding opportunities for landholders to participate in biodiversity conservation and restoration projects.
Minister for the Environment and Water Murray Watt announced on Friday that the new method, known as enhancing native vegetation, would allow landholders to register projects aimed at improving and maintaining existing native vegetation or restoring vegetation in areas where it has been cleared.
The method also enables projects to improve habitats for threatened species and control invasive plants and animals, according to a government statement.
The Nature Repair Market was established to encourage landholders, farmers, Indigenous groups and conservation organisations to invest in activities that restore and protect biodiversity.
Under the market's first method, replanting native forest and woodland ecosystems, four projects have so far been registered, covering a total of 2,656 hectares of land being protected and restored.
The government said the new method would broaden eligibility for participation and allow certain projects to be used for environmental offsets, potentially stimulating demand for biodiversity restoration activities.
"The Nature Repair Market is still in its early stages, but by introducing more methods for use, we're incentivizing and rewarding landholders for protecting and restoring biodiversity on their land, including by controlling invasive species," Watt said.
He added that protecting habitats on private land was essential to improving conservation outcomes for Australia's threatened native species. ■

Dakar hosts Africa's first Olympic event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:53:45 UTC
14:53:45 KST

The 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympics ever to be held on African soil, open Saturday in the Senegalese capital marking an historic moment for the continent.
Signs proclaiming "Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates" are abundant across Dakar, which is hosting some 2,665 young competitors aged 14 to 17 from around the world.
The event marks the return of Russian athletes to the Olympics and also includes a refugee team. Overall, the athletes will compete across 25 sports and 153 medal events.
"We've got people from around the world that maybe had a very different idea about Africa and they're going to leave, hopefully, with something really positive in mind", International Olympic Committee (IOC) President Kirsty Coventry, a former Zimbabwean swimmer, said Thursday during a press conference in Dakar.
"I think that is really important for our continent", she said.
Events ranging from athletics to beach wrestling, rugby sevens to breaking, will be held across eight venues in three locations.
Dakar, the nearby suburb of Diamniadio and the beach town of Saly located some 80 kilometres (50 miles) from the capital, will all host events.
Sports culture
An opening ceremony Saturday evening in Diamniadio will kick off the Games.
A total of 136 Senegalese athletes will participate in the Youth Olympics, with some 6,000 volunteers from Senegal helping put on the event.
The west African nation is renowned for its sports culture, including its football team, traditional wrestling and surf scene.
Football enthusiasts and young people often organise impromptu matches in the evenings or weekends on the beach or in village squares.
And as the day cools, hundreds of people flock to Dakar's iconic coastal road, the Corniche, to run, do strength training or take part in group exercise.
While a sense of excitement is beginning to stir in the capital, the fourth summer edition of the Youth Olympics have struggled to stoke wild enthusiasm across Senegal.
Many are more concerned with the high cost of living, unemployment and economic hardship.
"Once the youth Olympic Games in Senegal begin, Dakar will become the capital of African youth," Senegal Prime Minister Ahmadou Al Aminou Lo said in an interview with AFP this week.
"Africa hosting the (Youth) Olympic Games, it's a symbol", he said.
Russian athletes
With the IOC effectively lifting the Russian Olympic Committee's (ROC) suspension in July, the Youth Games will mark the first Olympic competition since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 in which Russian athletes are allowed to compete under their own flag and colours.
According to the ROC, 13 Russian athletes will participate and 10 coaches will accompany them to Senegal.
"The kids are excited, it's good news that our legitimate right to participate with the national anthem and Russian flag has been restored", Anzor Gaunov, who coaches Anastasia Dobrovolskaya in judo, told AFP earlier this month in Moscow.
However, it is up to each sport's international federation whether to authorise the Russian athletes' participation.
The Dakar Youth Games will also welcome a refugee Olympic team, composed primarily of athletes based in Africa.
The IOC has called the Dakar Games an important milestone for the continent and an opportunity to showcase Senegal's cultural richness and Africa's growing role within the Olympics.
South Africa could potentially become the first African nation to host the Olympic Games, having already paved the way by hosting the men's FIFA World Cup in 2010. The country is officially in the running for the 2036 Summer Olympics.
