After the ‘martyr’s’ funeral: The families left behind by Yemen’s war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:48:25 UTC
14:48:25 KST

After the ‘martyr’s’ funeral: The families left behind by Yemen’s war
Rising fatalities in Yemen’s conflict deepen the burden on families of fighters, both emotionally and financially.
Sanaa, Yemen – Pickups carrying the bodies of Houthi fighters occasionally travel through the streets of Sanaa. Alongside them in the back, gunmen accompany the fallen fighters on their final journey to the cemetery.
A song known as “Our martyrs are our greats” echoes loudly from the moving vehicles, drawing the attention of passersby. At the cemetery, mourners solemnly pay their respects to the fallen fighters and show solidarity with their families.
Funerals of fighters have been a recurring sight in Yemen over the past few weeks.
Earlier this month, the Yemeni government said its forces killed or wounded 1,540 Houthis in 24 hours. Last week, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.
Houthis have also killed hundreds of pro-government troops over the past few weeks, with an October 19 missile attack on a security camp in Shabwa killing more than 70 government soldiers.
While the families of the deceased fighters receive fleeting public tributes at cemeteries, their grief and loss endure long after the funerals. For them, life has become more difficult, economic hardships have deepened and sorrow is a constant companion.
“The martyrdom of my brother, Abdulaziz, on October 10 broke us and robbed us of peace of mind. We could smile to hide our pain, but our hearts are filled with bottomless grief,” Akram, a 23-year-old resident of Sanaa, told Al Jazeera.
Abdulaziz, 21, was killed in Dhubab, in southwestern Yemen, while fighting alongside the Houthi group, two months after being recruited, Akram said.
‘Losing my pillar of strength’
Before Abdulaziz went to the front line, the two brothers worked in Sanaa as daily-wage workers in construction or agriculture. When they managed to get work, they pooled their earnings to cover the living expenses of their six-member family. That made the family’s financial difficulties “manageable”, said Akram.
Today, he struggles without his brother and covering the family’s basic needs has become a harder task.
“I lost my pillar of strength, Abdulaziz. His income, along with mine, used to cover water, electricity and food expenses. Without him, I am like a bird with one wing, burdened by so many responsibilities,” said Akram.
Over the past few days, petrol and diesel prices have risen by 10 percent in Houthi-controlled northwestern Yemen, adding to the cost of basic goods and increasing pressure on struggling families, such as Akram’s.
“When it comes to paying the fees for water, electricity, or buying groceries, it does not matter if your relative is a martyr or not. You have to pay or starve to death,” said Akram.
In recent months, Yemen has faced a major escalation in fighting between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi group that controls parts of the country.
The latest escalation “threatens to be absolutely devastating” for food security, said the World Food Programme’s Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations, Matthew Hollingworth, earlier this month.
“We are looking at a hunger crisis that is going to grow as it persists,” Hollingworth added.
The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in September 2014 and subsequently took control of much of northern and western Yemen. Since then, the conflict has remained unresolved.
‘A misery for the whole family’
Like many other deceased fighters’ families in Houthi-controlled areas, Houthi authorities gave Akram’s family a food basket, which included flour, cooking oil, rice and sugar.
However, the supply of food or financial assistance is irregular, Sanaa-based Ali Yahia, a 55-year-old father of a deceased fighter, told Al Jazeera.
“My son was killed four years ago on the Saudi-Yemen border when he was fighting for the Sanaa-based government. Since then, I have received food baskets at different times. Sometimes, I receive them twice a year or thrice a year, or four times a year,” he said.
For Yahia, this support is insufficient, and he argues that “fair compensation” would be a monthly salary of $200 at least. “This amount of money would help a family cover the basics each month,” he said.
Yahia has two other sons who support him. One is a delivery rider in Sanaa and the other works at a restaurant.
“With their support, my living conditions have improved. But if a family depends on a fighter’s income, the death of the fighter sparks a living and psychological ordeal for the whole family,” he said.
According to the World Food Programme, 18.3 million people across Yemen face severe food insecurity, while 2.2 million children under five suffer from acute malnutrition.
‘Too many martyrs’
As the number of fighters killed on the front lines rises, the authorities’ ability to support bereaved families is increasingly stretched, Ali Mohammed, a Houthi representative in Sanaa, told Al Jazeera.
“Martyrs today are too many and their families deserve due support. However, the rising number of martyrs affects the level of support they receive. Assistance is distributed so that every family gets some,” said Mohammed.
He argued that the “complete Houthi victory will lead to stability in the country and this will give authorities a better opportunity to look after the families of the martyrs.” He added: “This will take time”.
On October 25, the Sanaa-based Houthi Ministry of Youth and Sports commemorated Martyrs’ Day in the presence of many Houthi officials.
During the event, the group’s Undersecretary for the Sports Sector, Ali Hadban, emphasised the importance of observing the occasion to “draw inspiration from the lessons of sacrifice and selflessness, and to reflect on the enduring legacies of the martyrs who defended the nation”.
He noted that the victories achieved across various fronts are the direct result of the sacrifices made by “these noble martyrs”, emphasising the need to provide support and care for their families.
At the end of 2021, the UN estimated that 377,000 people had been killed directly or indirectly by the war in Yemen. The recent return of fighting has claimed more lives.
The continued burden
Adel Dashela, researcher at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, described the public celebration of fallen fighters as “an alien practice” that emerged during the war.
“This practice reflects the normalisation of violence and encourages children to risk their lives and die under various sectarian and political slogans. Yemenis did not witness this phenomenon until the Houthi group took control of the capital, Sanaa,” Dashela told Al Jazeera.
Families may be encouraged to participate in these rituals and may find themselves compelled to do so under social and political pressure, he said. “The reality, however, is that public displays of honour do not alleviate families’ suffering. Instead, the social, psychological and financial consequences of their loss remain their burden to bear.”
In many cases, women and children assume responsibility for supporting their families after the death of the breadwinner.
“Thus, women and children bear the real cost of these losses, while public celebrations remain detached from their everyday realities and the ongoing suffering of bereaved families,” Dashela added.

====================================================================================================

Where in Europe do people spend over 40% of their income on housing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:46:39 UTC
14:46:39 KST

Housing costs take up more than 40% of disposable income for millions of Europeans. Euronews Business takes a closer look at which countries are hit hardest, with experts explaining the drivers.
House prices in the EU have risen by 69% on average between 2015 and the second quarter of 2026, according to Eurostat. In some member states, prices have more than doubled. Rents and energy costs have also continued to climb.
“Europe faces a crisis driven by rising house prices and increasing housing costs,” the European Council said.
The housing crisis puts particular pressure on people who spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing. Eurostat calls this the housing cost overburden rate. In the EU, it stood at 7.7% on average in 2025.
“The main drivers of housing cost overburden are rising costs for housing (be it rents or house prices, which are spiking in many cities) in relation to the modest growth in incomes, especially for the lower quantiles of the income distribution,” Dr Hannah Widmer from ETH Zürich told Euronews Business.
So, which countries are hit hardest? Where in Europe is the housing cost overburden rate highest?
What are housing costs?
According to Eurostat, housing costs are the monthly expenses households pay for their homes. They include rent or mortgage interest, utilities such as water, electricity, gas and heating, and regular charges such as insurance, maintenance, repairs and taxes.
Disposable income refers to a household's total income after taxes and social contributions. It also includes social benefits such as pensions.
Greece has the highest housing cost overburden rate in Europe among countries with available data. This includes the 27 EU member states, two EFTA countries and five EU candidate countries.
In 2025, 26.4% of people in Greece lived in households that spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing. This is more than three times the EU average of 7.7%.
Denmark follows among EU countries, with 14.7%. Germany (11.2%) and Sweden (10.8%) are also well above the EU average.
The housing cost overburden rate is also above the EU average in Estonia (8.8%), Czechia (8.2%) and Luxembourg (8.1%).
Outside the EU, the rate is high in Switzerland (15.3%) and Norway (13.5%). Three candidate countries are also above the EU average: Turkey (10%), Montenegro (8.7%) and Serbia (7.9%).
“Given the very different contexts, not least in terms of economy and welfare system, the explanations for the level of the housing cost overburden in Greece, Switzerland and Denmark are not the same. And the consequences are not either,” Rikke Skovgaard Nielsen, senior researcher at Aalborg University, told Euronews Business.
She added that the money people have left after paying rent differs considerably between these three countries, as do living costs. As a result, the impact on households varies too.
Cyprus has the lowest rate. Only 2.4% of people spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing. Croatia (3.2%), Slovenia (3.5%) and Slovakia (3.5%) also have low rates.
Dr Marietta Haffner from TU Delft noted that when housing costs such as house prices, rents, energy prices, interest rates and inflation rise faster than income, the share of housing costs in income increases. Eventually, the share of those paying more than 40% of their income also increases.
“It is likely that the increasing energy costs will be a main driver in the next year of increasing housing costs,” she said.
Among the EU’s largest economies, Spain (7.2%), France (6.4%) and Italy (5.0%) are all below the EU average, while Germany (11.2%) ranks fifth overall.
Why does the burden differ across countries?
“It's probably the interplay between housing tenure structures (with tenants renting from the private rental market usually having the highest housing cost burden), welfare systems and the broader economic situation that explains higher or lower shares of housing cost overburden,” Widmer said.
However, she cautioned that comparing countries is complex. Experiencing housing cost overburden can mean something very different in Switzerland than in Greece, depending on welfare provisions and the quality of housing.
Over 34 million people in the EU are affected
The actual numbers tell a clearer story. More than 34 million people in the EU live in households that spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing.
Germany has the highest number of people affected by housing cost overburden, at 9.4 million. Turkey follows with 8.6 million, followed by France (4.4 million), Spain (3.5 million) and Italy (2.9 million).
Despite its relatively small population compared with these countries, Greece ranks sixth, with 2.7 million people living in households affected by housing cost overburden.
Of course, people on low incomes are hit harder. In the EU, the rate rises to 29.1% among people who are at risk of poverty. This group comprisespeople with an equivalised disposable income below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold, which is set at 60% of the national median equivalised disposable income.
In 2025, the EU’s median equivalised disposable income was €22,939 a year, or €1,912 a month. At EU level, 60% of this amounted to €1,147 a month.
Greece again tops the list. In 2025, 82.6% of people at risk of poverty in Greece lived in households that spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing. This means that more than four in five were affected. Denmark (59.8%) and Switzerland (56.1%) follow, while the rate is also above 40% in Sweden (46.8%), Norway (43.8%) and Czechia (43.4%).
Germany (35.0%) is above the EU average of 29.1%, while Spain (28.3%), France (25.4%) and Italy (21.7%) are below it.
Cyprus has the lowest rate, at 7.6%, followed by Albania (8.2%), Croatia (14.9%) and Slovakia (15.4%).

Spain train disaster clouds Sánchez chances of re-election
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:44:21 GMT
14:44:21 KST

Spain train disaster clouds Sánchez chances of re-election
- Published
The breaking news from Spain this week was shocking but also shockingly familiar: another collision on the high-speed rail line south from Madrid, with reports of dozens killed.
It is just nine months since two trains crashed near Cordoba, killing 46 people. Now 69 bodies have been recovered here in central Spain, from wreckage strewn over the tracks and down an embankment.
For the victims' families it is devastating; a personal tragedy.
But it is also a national disaster that has shattered confidence in the country's rail network and the Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez. It is playing out just weeks before the snap general election he called.
The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative.
From the first hours after the collision, Transport Minister Oscar Puente began suggesting "human error" was to blame, batting responsibility as far as possible from the cabinet.
On Friday, he appeared before the press for a second time to set out what he called the "objective facts" of the crash and counter a surge of criticism against the government.
The opposition People's Party (PP) is among those calling for his resignation as a "moral" and "ethical" move.
Instead after expressing "huge pain and sadness" for the victims, Puente went on the offensive.
He rejected talk of chronic underinvestment in infrastructure and insisted that Spain's high-speed signalling safety system, the LZB, was neither old nor inadequate: Germany and Austria use the same.
In Spain, it has already failed 170 times so far this year, he revealed, but called that "normal" and around the EU average.
The problem surrounds what happens next - when the system fails and control of the line shifts to manual.
In this case, the minister highlighted a series of human errors that proved catastrophic.
Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.
The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid.
"They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop.
"I'm no judge... But these are the facts."
So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister.
"I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."
But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading.
"This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.
An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz, near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails - very different to the latest collision.
But there is a similar impact.
"It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."
For Team Sánchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.
Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.
Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.
Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.
That's when Sánchez called an early election.
His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.
Most recent polls showed the centre-right PP coming first and forming a coalition with the far-right Vox.
"They have this majority in almost 95% of the simulations we have done," Prof Pablo Simon of Madrid's Carlos III University explains.
But Sánchez had been running a positive campaign, trying to lure apathetic voters to the polls to vote socialist.
Suddenly, the tone has changed.
"They've totally lost control of the agenda and the emotion of this campaign," Simon says. "It's going to be extremely difficult now. There is this general mood of decay, of a country that's not working properly. A depression."
There is also anger.
There have already been small protests over the train crash led by far-right groups in Madrid and large numbers of police are on stand-by this weekend ahead of further potential clashes, organised online.
Here in Toledo, the mood is nervous.
"We all travelled in silence and really sad," Paloma told me at the city station, where she had just pulled in on a half empty train.
She admitted she's scared of the high-speed network now and angry at the government.
"This crash will change all of our votes, completely," Paloma said. "We'll shift from the left wing to the right. Because of everything that's happened."
Lucia takes the high-speed AVE into Madrid each day, and is scared too.
"This was human error. But there's been two accidents now with more than 100 dead," she says. "Things here are really bad. They have to change."
Producer Davide Ghiglione contributed to this report

Taiwan gas demand set to outstrip winter supply capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:39:08 UTC
14:39:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — State-owned oil company CPC Corp. said Saturday that winter cooking gas demand could exceed its monthly supply capacity of 90,000 tonnes, adding to pressure from government price controls.
CNA reported that CPC Spokesperson Lin Ko-ju (林珂如) said demand for liquefied petroleum gas, widely used for cooking in homes and restaurants, is expected to peak between December and January. She said the company would give priority to domestic supplies and do its best to meet demand.
CPC expanded its facilities in Shenao, New Taipei, last year, raising its maximum monthly supply to 90,000 tonnes. The company sold about 678,000 tonnes of cooking gas from January to September, accounting for more than 90% of the domestic market.
The expected rise in demand comes as the government keeps household cooking gas prices at the same rate until the end of the year. The policy aims to protect consumers from rising fuel costs but has placed financial pressure on suppliers, per Economic Daily News.
CPC has raised cooking gas prices by just NT$3.15 (10 cents) per kilogram since December 2020. Taiwan Petroleum Workers' Union Chair Chen Chia-lin (陳嘉麟) said the company was absorbing NT$23.75 per kilogram in costs to keep its selling price at NT$20.01.
National Federation of Liquefied Gas Fuel Commercial Associations Chair Lai Fang-chuan (賴芳泉) said CPC sold gas for NT$1.80 less per kilogram than private supplier Formosa Petrochemical. The price gap has driven more dealers to CPC, where supplies have struggled to keep pace with demand, per CTS News.
Lai said dealers who buy from Formosa Petrochemical must either absorb the higher cost or risk losing customers by raising prices. The problem is especially serious in central Taiwan, where competition is strong and profit margins are tight.
Taiwan has more than 2,300 gas retailers and 110 plants that fill gas cylinders, Lai said. More than 10 retailers have closed this year, while some filling plants have merged in recent years to cut costs.
Lai warned that the supply gap could widen as winter and year-end holidays drive up demand. He urged CPC to increase supplies and called on the government to bring prices charged by the two producers closer together.
Energy Administration Deputy Director-General Chen Chung-hsien (陳崇憲) said the government would work with suppliers to keep gas supplies stable throughout winter. He said officials would seek to prevent shortages despite pressure on the market, per Rti.

Why are US, Russia and China racing to put nuclear reactors on the moon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:37:51 UTC
14:37:51 KST

Why are US, Russia and China racing to put nuclear reactors on the moon?
Lunar reactors could revolutionise moon exploration, providing energy for bases and mining, but risks of contamination remain.
The United States, Russia and China are racing to build nuclear reactors on the moon, as scientists warn about the possible risk of a radioactive mishap.
In January, NASA, the US space agency, announced plans to develop a nuclear reactor on the moon by the end of 2030. Russia, working with China, aims to do the same by 2036 as they strive to advance space exploration.
The reactors will be needed to power mining of frozen water trapped deep in the moon’s craters, which scientists believe could supply drinking water, air, and rocket fuel for future bases. The reactors would also provide power for lunar bases.
Here is what we know.
Which countries want to put nuclear reactors on the moon?
The US said NASA’s Lunar Reactor 1 would produce 20 kilowatts of electricity, creating enough power to run on its own for five years without maintenance.
NASA’s reactor is designed to be compact, weighing under 6,000kg (13,200 lbs) and will fit inside a rocket compartment measuring 3.7 metres (12 feet) long by 5.5 metres (18 ft) wide.
Russia is also building a nuclear reactor, which is expected to produce 10 kilowatts. The reactor, called Selena, will be able to run for a decade without maintenance. It will be ready to power a Chinese-led moon base by about 2036.
The Selena reactor is expected to be even lighter than NASA’s, weighing about 1,100 to 1,300kg (2,400 to 2,800 lbs) for an easier and softer landing on the lunar surface.
This would not be the first time nuclear reactors have been placed in outer space.
The Soviet Union launched more than 30 nuclear fission reactors into Earth’s orbit between the late 1960s and the 1980s to power spy satellites during the Cold War.
The small, 1,000kg (2,200 lbs) reactors powered radar-tracking spy satellites using heat from splitting uranium atoms into 3 to 5 kilowatts of electricity. They are no longer operational, and no other country has sent nuclear reactors into space.
The US has spent $20bn on advanced space nuclear programmes over the past 70 years, but has never successfully launched a nuclear reactor into space since an experiment in 1965.
That experiment was carried out to see if nuclear energy could power a satellite. It worked at first but accidentally shut down after just 43 days because a non-nuclear electrical part of the satellite broke down. It is still floating up in space today.
Previous attempts by the US to develop nuclear projects have stalled due to shifting budget priorities.
How do you put nuclear reactors on the moon?
First, scientists will have to build a reactor on Earth, which will then be transported to the moon using a robotic spacecraft that fires rocket engines for a slow and gentle touchdown.
Both the US and Russia say they would keep their reactors switched off until they reach the moon, to keep radioactive risk at a minimum until the last step.
Once set up on the moon, the reactors would be designed to run without maintenance for years, supplying power to bases engaged in mining on the lunar surface.
Why does the moon need a nuclear reactor?
The US, China and Russia want to build bases near the moon’s south pole, close to the known sources of water ice. The ice sits in the permanently shadowed craters, where sunlight has not reached for millions of years.
As well as powering the moon bases, the reactors would also supply enough power for mining. So far, the US, Russia and China want to mine for frozen water which, once released, could be used to support life on the moon at bases where people could live and conduct research.
Tech billionaire Elon Musk has also said he wants to extract minerals such as aluminium, titanium, and silicon, required for manufacturing satellites.
Solar power for such endeavours would be limited as the sun shines on any one spot on the moon only half the time, so solar panels would go dark for about two weeks every month.
Simon Middleburgh, director of Bangor University’s Nuclear Futures Institute (NFI), told Al Jazeera that solar power is too limited to provide the steady flow of energy a moon base would need, while batteries and diesel are too costly, because everything has to be launched from Earth.
Nuclear energy is the “obvious choice”, Middleburgh said, adding that it must be used “responsibly”.
It is likely that three or four reactors working together would be required to provide sufficient energy for mining lunar ice as well as supporting a moon base, he added.
Why the rush?
It comes down to geopolitics.
In a December 2025 executive order, US President Donald Trump ordered NASA to build a lunar reactor ready to launch by 2030. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin have revealed similar plans.
In August this year, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said the US is in a “race to the moon, in a race with China”.
Middleburgh said the 2030 deadline is likely for building the reactor itself, but the harder part will be landing on the moon and safely setting up the system.
“The biggest challenge isn’t really the nuclear technology at all; it is the regulation for launch, the availability of a launch platform itself, and the landing and setting up the system on the lunar surface ready for it to be operated sustainably and safely,” he said.
The race to the moon also comes amid growing military competition beyond Earth. In September, the US announced it had deployed weapons into orbit, which officials said would be used to defend US forces.
While the US did not provide details about these “weapons”, experts say they are likely to be space-based communications jammers, rather than kinetic ones that launch strikes.
The announcement raised concerns about the concept of “space weapons” or the use of space for military purposes, including the potential targeting of satellites that provide GPS, communications and intelligence.
What could go wrong?
Middleburgh told Al Jazeera that an accident during the launch of the reactors would be less frightening than it sounds because uranium alone, before it is used in a reactor, is not very radioactive. However, that changes once the reactor is switched on.
The risk is bigger if a running reactor falls back onto Earth, analysts say.
In 1978, a Soviet satellite carrying a reactor, Kosmos 954, scattered radioactive material across nearly 124,300 square km (48,000sq miles) of northern Canada.
The accident forced an expensive military cleanup of the highly radioactive fragments and microscopic particles.
On the moon, Middleburgh says, any contaminated area would be “extremely localised” if there were to be a similar accident.
Who has sovereignty over the moon?
Legally, no one. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans countries from “claiming” the moon or any part of it, though they have ownership of the equipment they send there. The treaty does not ban nuclear power in space.
Antonino Salmeri, director of the Lunar Policy Platform, a nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that a reactor can be lawful if it follows the treaty’s principles, including peaceful use and avoiding harmful contamination.
Norbert Schorghofer, a senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute in Arizona, US, told Al Jazeera all signatories “have the right to mine the lunar surface as long as it is for peaceful purposes”.
Whichever country’s reactor gets to the “best” water ice first could claim a “safety zone”, which would not be a land claim but could operate like one. Salmeri said declaring one creates no territorial rights, but a reactor shuts others out anyway, because nobody wants to enter a radioactive area.
A Lunar Policy Platform report released last month points to another problem: Who is responsible if something goes wrong? The report says existing liability rules have not been designed to regulate the use of long-term hazardous equipment on another celestial body.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski called for an immediate ceasefire in the Black Sea to secure grain shipments from Ukraine and Russia, while warning that Moscow must end its war against Ukraine on fair terms before being allowed to resume energy sales to Europe.
Speaking to reporters Friday, Oct. 30, during the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, Sikorski said restoring safe maritime trade was urgent for countries dependent on food imports, particularly in the Global South.

“I spoke in favor of doing something quickly because the people of the Global South need this grain,” Sikorski said, according to Reuters.
His proposal would allow grain shipments from both Ukraine and Russia to move safely through the Black Sea, a crucial route for agricultural exports to international markets.
But Sikorski made clear that a maritime ceasefire should not come at the expense of Ukraine’s broader security interests.
He insisted that Ukraine must participate in any negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s invasion and that Europe also has a legitimate role in shaping a settlement.

No return to Russian energy without a fair peace
Sikorski also linked any restoration of Russian energy sales to Europe to the outcome of the war.

Pentagon Says Ukraine’s Patriot Missile Production Request Requires ‘Further Review’
The position reflects Poland’s longstanding opposition to Europe’s reliance on Russian energy, which Warsaw has warned gives Moscow economic resources and political leverage over European governments.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov objected, arguing that Poland’s participation had been advanced without the consensus normally required for decisions involving G20 members.
Lavrov described the invitation as a violation of established diplomatic practice.
Sikorski welcomed Washington’s support and said he had discussed Poland’s candidacy with other G20 representatives.
Sikorski also confirmed that Britain, which will assume the G20 presidency in 2027, had invited Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to attend next year’s leaders’ summit in Manchester.

Country diary: An impromptu birding trip with a total stranger – and it was magical | Eben Muse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:30:33 UTC
14:30:33 KST

“What did you just see?” a bearded man asked, through the open window of his old Mini Cooper.
“Just some crows in that tree.”
“Slimbridge Wetland Centre is closed. I just missed it!”
We too had been greeted at Slimbridge by a shut door at the visitor centre, dashing our hopes of some late-afternoon birdwatching. “I’m going to find another way to the estuary. Want to hop in?”
Before I had a chance to contemplate this stranger’s offer, my partner, Beth, had jumped into the back seat of the Mini, and we motored away into the unknown.
We set off on foot down a promising track, following our new friend, Phil. With each step towards the shore he became more alive, extolling the weather, the ancient churches on the hills, and our fortuitous meeting.
I’m not an expert birdwatcher, but Phil has a lifetime of honed skill – he cupped his ear to the curlew’s cry, pointed to long-tailed tits, shelducks, dunlins and a medley of geese. We learned that he’s a composer, and helps to run a museum in the mid-Wales town where my sister lives.
As we approached the Severn seawall, roe deer with glowing antlers stared at us. I couldn’t help but think of Listers, a rip-roaring YouTube documentary about two young men who enter the cut-throat world of competitive birdwatching, spending a year chasing glory and rare birds across the US. They found that an ostensibly nature-based activity can become a Pokémon-style “Gotta catch ’em all” exercise, in which underhand strategy and toxic behaviour can be hard to avoid. Not so here, as we followed our excited leader’s stream of identifications and free-flowing observations.
The moment we mounted the seawall, we saw a horizon ablaze with a sunburst of burnished copper. The mudflats were dotted with countless waders and gulls, and the Severn’s mighty tide was already starting to rush in. “See the marsh harrier? Incredible, incredible,” Phil murmured. We watched as the harrier glided over, sublime, sending ripples through the assembly. And there wasn’t a whiff of competition.

Math Puzzle: Mysterious pyramid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:27:38 UTC
14:27:38 KST

The nine cells of the triangle contain nine zeros. Try to change the numbers, with any number of moves, so that they become nine consecutive positive integers, the smallest of which is a. The arrangement of these nine numbers in the triangle is irrelevant. A move is the increase or decrease by 1 of the two numbers occupying two adjacent cells, where adjacent cells share a side. For which values of a is the problem solvable?
A pair of adjacent cells always consists of one orange and one black triangle. Initially, the sum r of the numbers on the orange cells is equal to the sum b of the numbers on the black cells, namely, 0. A move does not change this equilibrium r = b. At the end, the nine numbers of the triangle should be a , a + 1, ..., and a + 8. Thus, because b is the sum of six of the numbers, b ≥ a + (a + 1) + (a + 2) + (a + 3) + (a + 4) + (a + 5) = 6a + 15, and because r is the sum of three of the numbers, r ≤ (a + 6) + (a + 7) + (a + 8) = 3a + 21. Because b = r, 6a + 15 ≤ 3a + 21, or a ≤ 2. Furthermore, r = b means that r + b = 2r, so r + b must be an even number. For a = 1, the sum of the nine numbers 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45, which is odd. Therefore, if there is a solution to the problem at all, it is only for a = 2.
Instead of increasing the numbers on the same pair of cells by 1 n times, one can directly increase both numbers by n. This does not change the problem in any way. The order of the individual moves also plays no role. The image shows in three steps that there is indeed a solution for a = 2.

"Thanked President Putin for confirming that Kenyans will no longer be enlisted into the Russian military because Kenya has been categorized as a non-source country for recruitment into the Russian military," Ruto said in a statement.

Kenya and Russia signed five cooperation instruments covering economic relations, employment promotion, labor inspection, transport, diplomatic training and visa-free travel for diplomatic and service passport holders.
The agreements include establishing an intergovernmental commission to coordinate economic cooperation between the two countries.
Ruto also invited Putin to Kenya as both governments seek to deepen diplomatic engagements.

India news: Oil tanker carrying 27 Indians attacked with limpet mines in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:06:00 UTC
14:06:00 KST

India news: Tanker carrying 27 Indians attacked in Strait of Hormuz
Published October 31, 2026last updated October 31, 2026
What you need to know
- The attack on the Panama-flagged Louise 1 occurred around 25 nautical miles (46 kilometers) northeast of Oman
- India's Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said all Indian seafarers aboard the vessel were safe and had sustained no injuries
- India successfully launches satellite to boost indigenous GPS alternative
- Delhi experiences coldest October day in 75 years
Here are the top headlines from India on Saturday, October 31:
India successfully launches satellite to boost indigenous GPS alternative
India's space agency successfully launched a navigation satellite on Friday night to strengthen the country's indigenous alternative to GPS.
The NVS-03 satellite, the third in Indian Space Research Organisation's (ISRO) next-generation navigation series, was carried into orbit by the "GSLV-F18" rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, located on an island in the Bay of Bengal.
According to ISRO the "the GSLV-F18 vehicle placed NVS-03 satellite into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit."
An earlier statement by the agency said the satellite is "intended to augment the NavIC constellation and support continuity of navigation services."
It is designed to provide navigation coverage across India and up to 1,500 kilometers (932 miles) beyond its borders.
NavIC is seen as an alternative to the Global Positioning System (GPS) system owned by the United States government and developed to reduce India's dependence on foreign navigation systems.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi celebrated the successful launch as a "great accomplishment."
Strait of Hormuz attacks: Two tankers carrying Indians hit by mines in two days
An oil tanker carrying 27 Indian seafarers was targeted with limpet mines in the Strait of Hormuz.A small boat attached two mines to the vessel's hull, causing a fire in the engine room, maritime security sources said on Friday.
Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said all Indian seafarers aboard the vessel were safe and had sustained no injuries. Sonowal also added that two Indians aboard another tanker that faced a separate attack on October 29 were also safe.
The attack on the Panama-flagged Louise 1 occurred on Thursday, around 25 nautical miles (46 km) northeast of Oman's Khasab.
The fire was extinguished, the crew was safe and there was no environmental impact, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said.
The incident marks the first known successful use of limpet mines against a vessel in the waterway since the US-Iran war began in February.
The identity of those behind the attacks was not immediately known.
The Strait of Hormuz,a vital chokepoint for oil and gas transport, is seeing attacks on ships at the highest level since the Iran war began, according to US-based think tank Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Incidentally, the Louise 1 was hit earlier with naval drones in the Black Sea by Ukrainian forces over its alleged role in transporting Russian oil and being part of the so-called shadow fleet of tankers deployed by Moscow.
Welcome to our coverage!
This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi studio bringing you the top updates from across India on the last day of the coldest October in 75 years. Brrr…must be true!
On a more serious note, two vessels with Indian crew members were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in the past two days. Thankfully, the Indian government has said all sailors were safe.
Meanwhile, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched the NVS-03 satellite to strengthen its indigenous navigation system and reduce reliance on the US-owned GPS.

Major water infrastructure project nears completion in N. Australia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:02:06 CST
14:02:06 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- A major water infrastructure project in Australia's Northern Territory has entered its commissioning stage and is expected to boost water supply to the Darwin region by the end of 2026, the territory government said.
The Manton Dam Return to Service project, one of the Northern Territory's most significant water infrastructure developments in the past 50 years, has reached the commissioning stage at 174 million Australian dollars (about 114 million U.S. dollars), coming in 15 million Australian dollars under budget, according to a government statement released Friday.
The project includes the modernization of an existing reservoir intake tower, construction of the new Strauss Water Treatment Plant, a new pump station and 22 kilometers of pipeline.
Once operational, Manton Dam will provide an additional 7,300 megaliters of water annually, strengthening water security for Darwin and surrounding areas.
The government said commissioning of the new water treatment plant was underway, with water from Manton Dam expected to enter the Darwin region's supply network by the end of 2026.
Construction of the project has engaged more than 111 employees and 500 contractors over the past two years, delivering economic benefits to local businesses.
The project forms part of the first stage of the Darwin Region Water Supply Infrastructure Program, jointly funded by the Australian federal and Northern Territory governments. ■

China calls for stronger global cooperation to advance right to development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:01:42 CST
14:01:42 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- China on Friday called for stronger international cooperation to advance the right to development, and urged countries to put development at the center of the global agenda amid widening inequalities and mounting challenges facing developing nations.
Speaking at a side event marking the 40th anniversary of the UN Declaration on the Right to Development, Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, said that "only through continuous development can people's aspirations for a better life and social stability be realized."
Development has been politicized and pushed to the margins when it is needed most, while divisions and confrontation are being fueled when solidarity is more critical than ever, he said.
Sun put forward four proposals to advance the right to development: defending the right to development, reinvigorating development partnerships, improving the development environment, and fostering new drivers of growth.
"The rights to subsistence and development are basic human rights of paramount importance," he said, adding that equal importance should be placed on different types of human rights.
"Without development, there would be no human rights to speak of, nor could any enjoyment of rights be sustainable," he said. "Development should be put front and center on the international agenda."
Sun also called for a more just and equitable international economic and financial architecture.
"Unilateral sanctions and long-arm jurisdiction are inimical to development and must be rejected," he said, urging the international community to promote "an inclusive economic globalization that benefits all."
On innovation, Sun called for speeding up technology transfer and knowledge sharing, so as to close the digital divide and artificial intelligence divide, and accelerate the low-carbon transition.
Sun said China's Global Development Initiative (GDI) has mobilized more than 23 billion U.S. dollars in funding and supported over 1,800 "small and beautiful" projects, benefiting local communities in more than 120 countries.
"China stands ready to work with all parties to strengthen international cooperation and create an enabling environment for the realization of the right to development," Sun said.
The event was co-organized by the Permanent Mission of China to the United Nations, the Coordinating Bureau of the Non-Aligned Movement and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
Godfrey Kwoba, charge d'affaires of Uganda's UN mission and chair of the Coordinating Bureau of the Non-Aligned Movement, said that the principles contained in the declaration must be translated into practical policies and actions at national, regional and international levels.
Claudia Fuentes Julio, UN assistant secretary-general for human rights, said development is not simply about economic growth; it is also about ensuring that the benefits of development are shared fairly and equitably.
Bjorg Sandkjaer, UN assistant secretary-general for policy coordination, welcomed the GDI as a contribution to global development efforts.
The emphasis on prioritizing development, adopting a people-centered approach and promoting practical cooperation is closely aligned with the right to development and the 2030 Agenda, she said.
Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1986, the Declaration on the Right to Development recognizes development as an inalienable human right, affirming that every person and all peoples are entitled to participate in, contribute to, and enjoy development. ■

Last year, Umm Khaled Fatoum returned from volunteering in a Jewish-Arab support centre for victims of war to find bulldozers tearing into her son’s house in the Bedouin village of Azzarnug.
The demolition crew, who arrived under police escort, did not even allow them to remove furniture or solar panels before reducing the home and its contents to a pile of rubble.
This week, she took action of her own at the ballot box, targeting the extremist national security minister who ordered – and boasts about – the mass destruction of Palestinian and Arab homes.
“I had one goal, to send [Itamar] Ben-Gvir home,” Fatoum said. “There isn’t a single family in the Bedouin community that hasn’t been hurt by his campaign against us.”
In the weeks before election day, she joined a grassroots campaign to educate other Bedouin women about their rights and potential power.
It had spectacular results, with voting rates tripling in some Bedouin villages in the southern Negev region in Tuesday’s election, amid a broader surge in turnout among Bedouin voters.
Years of violent, racist government opened the door for change in conservative communities, said Hanan Alsanah, a lawyer and activist whose Alnashmiat network led the grassroots programme.
“We said that even if all the men go to vote, it is only half the community. You need the power of all your votes, because Ben-Gvir has a lot of power.”
The rise in Bedouin votes came amid historically high turnout among Arab citizens of Israel. Their votes secured an unprecedented 19 seats in the Knesset for Palestinian-led parties and were critical to stripping the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his allies of their governing majority.
This year, the lowest turnout in any Bedouin community was 62%. The highest was more than 93%. With an estimated 180,000 eligible voters, their turnout was key to the Islamist Ra’am party beating polling expectations.
Netanyahu has repeatedly used racist fearmongering to try to boost voter turnout among his own base. This year, his attacks included an AI-generated image purporting to show a crowded polling station in a Palestinian area and Bedouin female voters.
In an apparent attempt to undermine the surge in votes for Palestinian-led parties, Netanyahu accused them of fraud and foreign support.
“The increase in voter turnout in the Bedouin community in particular, and the Arab community in general, is unprecedented in the history of the state,” said Amit Segal, a pundit and close confidant of the prime minister.
The allegations have been rejected by opposition leaders, election organisers, and the activists in the Negev.
“I am very proud of our turnout. They are talking about ‘corruption’ [as the reason for high voter turnout]. The correct word is ‘awareness’,” said Amira Habdoubi, an organiser from the village of Abu Talul.
For a community whose civil rights are policed by racist authorities, the election was a rare opportunity for political expression, she added. “We can’t protest, because they will arrest us. Voting is the only opportunity we have to make a political protest.”
The Muslim Bedouin are part of a marginalised minority inside Israel. Before the state was created, they roamed widely across the Negev desert.
Now, although their villages take up only 2.5% of the land in the region, many are deemed “unrecognised”, targeted by the state for demolition and left without basic services including electricity and water supplies. The majority of the Negev has been designated as military training grounds and firing ranges.
More than 100,000 people live in about 30 unrecognised communities in the Negev. Another 200,000 live in official towns, or places with some level of recognition.
Netanyahu’s pursuit of open-ended regional conflicts also drove Bedouin turnout. War is particularly terrifying in unrecognised villages because the state does not provide them with bomb shelters or warning sirens ahead of rocket, drone and missile attacks.
Rockets that hit Bedouin villages without shelters killed six of the 36 child victims of the 7 October attacks. Several adults were also killed that day in the villages and at least four people have been seriously injured by Iranian missiles.
Organised crime is another concern, rising almost unchecked under the current government.
“We had clear goals. Stop the home demolitions, stop the hatred, stop the war. Ben-Gvir talks all the time about security, but we feel no security and no one cares about us,” said Mayada Abu Khweida.
The activists worked to help women understand their rights and tackle logistical and practical obstacles to voting, as well as cultural ones.
“Because [residents of unrecognised villages] can’t vote in the municipal elections, a lot of women don’t know they have a right to vote in national elections,” said Abu Khweida. “We told them: ‘There is a legal way to express your anger and raise your voice.’”
For similar bureaucratic reasons, there are no polling stations in unrecognised villages, so voters have to travel to nearby towns. Men went any way they could, including on camel, horse, donkey and bike, on journeys that took up to an hour in each direction.
Jewish women offered lifts to Bedouin women, but because in 2019 Israel’s election committee ruled that organising transport volunteers was illegal, voters and drivers connected individually.
“Hundreds of women volunteers went to help Bedouin women to access the polls, and at the same time about 150 men went to do protective presence at the polling stations,” said Raluca Ganea, the founding executive director of the Jewish-Arab community action group Zazim.
“We wanted to have Jewish men standing there to de-escalate, in case there was a rightwing provocation of some kind. So it would not be the Bedouin men in front of the provocateurs, because if the police come or there is violence, they are much more likely to be arrested or worse.”
Netanyahu’s racist get-out-the-vote campaign on social media included photos of Bedouin women with their faces covered.
Some of these women covered their faces to avoid being seen by strangers from outside their own community. In recognised towns, where women could vote in their communities, most did not cover their faces, Alsanah said.
Others hid themselves to avoid becoming fodder for Ben-Gvir’s extremist social media feed, which regularly features humiliation of Arab citizens.
“The women were worried the extremists would take photos at the polling stations and covered their faces to protect themselves from being exploited on social media,” Abu Khweida said, adding that his campaign of humiliation has affected all of Bedouin society.
The grassroots mobilisation of Bedouin voters aimed in part to give children back their dreams, one reason why women responded so strongly.
“In the last election in 2022, turnout among women was around 20%. Now in the unrecognised villages, informal data shows more than 60% turnout among women,” Alsanah said, adding that Israel does not break down voting statistics by gender.
The project built on more than a decade of work with Alnashmiat, based in Arab and Jewish solidarity, that could set an example for a new government, Alsanah said.
“We learned an important lesson from this election campaign. We should work together, men and women, Arab and Jewish citizens, and we should bring this approach to the Israeli parliament to rebuild the state.”

UK historian says Taiwan can learn from Ukraine to defend itself against China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:52:09 UTC
13:52:09 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Royal Historical Society fellow Iain MacGregor said Taiwan could better defend itself against China by learning from Ukraine's use of drones, military training, and civilian preparedness.
In an article titled "Ukraine has shown Taiwan how to fight Goliath and survive," published by The Telegraph on Friday, MacGregor said Ukraine had shown how a smaller country can resist a stronger enemy. He said Taiwan faces a similar threat from China, which has far greater military resources.
Russia's failure to defeat Ukraine quickly showed that military strength alone does not ensure victory, MacGregor said. He credited Ukraine's military reforms, trained troops, and determination to fight for helping it resist Russia's invasion in February 2022.
MacGregor pointed to Ukraine's use of low-cost drones to destroy expensive Russian tanks. He also mentioned unmanned boats that have damaged Russian warships in the Black Sea.
Taipei has sought to apply those lessons by expanding domestic drone production and reducing its reliance on foreign suppliers. Its monthly production capacity reached about 15,000 drones by May 2026, according to government figures.
MacGregor also cited the country's decision to extend mandatory military service from four months to one year. The change took effect in January 2024 and applies to eligible men born in or after 2005.
He said Ukraine's experience showed that weapons alone were not enough to defend a country. Trained reserve troops, civilian volunteers, and reliable supplies were also vital during a long war.
MacGregor warned that Taiwan must prepare for power cuts, cyberattacks, and damage to transport and communications. The country has expanded emergency drills to keep essential services running and ensure people can obtain supplies during a crisis.
He also warned that Taiwan would face greater difficulties receiving foreign aid during a war. Unlike Ukraine, which can receive supplies across its land borders with European neighbors, it could face a Chinese blockade that cuts off sea and air routes.
However, the Taiwan Strait would also make an invasion difficult for China, as troops and equipment would have to cross the water under threat of attack. Taiwan, MacGregor argued, should convince Beijing that any attempt to seize the island would be costly, prolonged, and unlikely to succeed.

US greenlights $2.1bn Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:51:25 UTC
13:51:25 KST

US greenlights $2.1bn Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
Deal would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since Trump took office in 2025.
The United States says it has approved the possible sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn.
The package of missiles, parts and support, announced on Friday by the US State Department, would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second administration of President Donald Trump in January 2025.
The Patriot system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
Delayed missile deliveries, however, have stoked US-Ukraine tensions after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for his unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for Washington to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian energy and civilian infrastructure.
A Russian drone strike on Thursday killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro.
Five people were killed in daytime strikes on two other cities, and a late-evening missile strike killed one person in the capital, Kyiv, officials said.
Delivery years away
Despite Ukraine’s need for quick deliveries of the missiles, Kyiv is unlikely to receive the Patriot interceptors soon. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil.
Two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles, which have yet to be made, are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway through a programme called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in its statement.
US weapons manufacturer Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6bn to produce Patriot interceptor missiles in July.
Lockheed has said the deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 production capacity by the end of 2030. It has previously announced that Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would reach 2,000 units annually.
Pentagon negotiators are pressing weapons contractors to speed up production.
The US military’s supply of large quantities of weapons to allies and its own heavy munitions use for its operations in Iran have raised concerns about its inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.

PM Modi commemorates Sardar Patel's 151st birth anniversary at Statue of Unity
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday paid floral tributes to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel at the Statue of Unity in Ekta Nagar, Gujarat, on the occasion of the former deputy prime minister's 151st birth anniversary. The day is observed across the country as Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (National Unity Day), commemorating Patel's contribution to India's national integration after Independence.Patel had played a pivotal role in bringing hundreds of princely states into the Indian Union.
PM Modi calls Patel architect of Akhand Bharat
In a post on X, the Prime Minister described Patel as the "architect of Akhand Bharat and the Iron Man of the nation", highlighting his contribution to building a strong and united India."On the occasion of his birth anniversary, heartfelt salutations to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, the architect of Akhand Bharat and the Iron Man of the nation. He dedicated his life to the creation of a strong, prosperous, and capable India," PM Modi said.He further said Patel's "sacrifice and dedication in the service of Mother India" continued to serve as an inspiration for building a developed and self-reliant India.The Prime Minister also emphasised Patel's enduring contribution to nation-building, saying his commitment to the country remained a source of inspiration for future generations.
Union home minister Amit Shah also paid tribute to Patel and extended greetings to citizens on National Unity Day.In a post on X, Shah described Patel as the "architect of modern India" and "the symbol of national unity and integrity"."On the birth anniversary of the architect of modern India, the symbol of national unity and integrity, the Iron Man Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel ji, we offer him millions of salutations and extend our heartfelt greetings to all fellow citizens on ‘National Unity Day’," Shah said.Crediting Patel's courage and foresight with India's political integration, Shah said the leader had brought together a nation fragmented into princely states."With his indomitable courage and foresight, Sardar Sahab wove together a nation fragmented into princely states into a single thread, laying the foundation of a strong India," he said.

Patel's legacy and National Unity Day
Born on October 31, 1875, in Nadiad, Gujarat, Patel served as India's first home minister after Independence. He is widely credited with overseeing the integration of more than 560 princely states into the Indian Union. He died on December 15, 1950.HM Shah also recalled Patel's role in farmers' movements, particularly the Kheda and Bardoli Satyagrahas, describing his struggle for farmers' rights as an "unparalleled example of public service and leadership".The Centre has observed October 31 as Rashtriya Ekta Diwas since 2014 to commemorate Patel's contribution and reinforce the country's commitment to unity, integrity and security.

Power outages hit Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast, explosions reported in Ufa amid drone alerts
Widespread power outages hit Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast overnight on Oct. 31, while explosions were reportedly heard in the industrial area of Ufa, Bashkortostan, amid warnings of possible Ukrainian drone attacks.
Residents of Kaliningrad and several surrounding towns reported losing electricity around midnight, according to local media.
The outages affected several districts of Kaliningrad, as well as Guryevsk, Svetlogorsk, Pionersky, Yantarny, Gvardeysk, Bagrationovsk, and other settlements across the region. Disruptions to mobile internet services were also reported.
Regional authorities later attributed the blackout to the activation of an emergency protection system at the Kaliningrad CHP-2 power plant, which caused part of its equipment to shut down.
The Kyiv Independent can't immediately verify these claims.
Separately, the monitoring Exilenova+ Telegram channel reported explosions in an industrial area of Ufa, the capital of Russia's Bashkortostan Republic, and claimed Russian air defenses were operating amid a possible drone attack.
Earlier on Oct. 31, Bashkortostan authorities declared a drone threat across the republic and imposed temporary flight restrictions at Ufa Airport, according to Russian media.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify whether any facilities had been damaged.
Meanwhile, authorities in Russia's Perm Krai introduced airspace restrictions on the morning of Oct. 31, disrupting operations at Perm's Bolshoye Savino Airport.
Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, suspended flights after authorities introduced an emergency safety "carpet" protocol, covering an area within a 150-kilometer radius of the village of Beryozovka.
Several departing and arriving flights were delayed, according to local media.
Drone threat warnings had earlier been issued in neighboring Bashkortostan and Udmurtia, as well as Sverdlovsk Oblast. However, no drone threat alert was reported in Perm Krai itself, and the reason for the airspace restrictions remained unclear.
There was no confirmed connection between the incidents in Kaliningrad, Ufa, and Perm.

EKTA NAGAR, KEVADIA: Anand Math, the literary source of ‘Vande Mataram’, was adapted into a grand, multimedia-based play and showcased at Ekta Nagar, Kevadia, here on Friday in the presence of Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the eve of the Ekta Diwas, Sardar Patel’s birth anniversary.Sardar Patel’s birth anniversary on Oct 31 this year is focused on celebrating the end of armed Naxalism and 150 years of ‘Vande Mataram’. The prime minister is the chief guest at the Ekta Diwas events this year, organised here with the 'Statue of Unity’ as a backdrop. The one-and-a-half hour long play ‘Anand Math’ is directed by NSD, It is based on the abiding philosophy of Anand Math: that every person of India has a responsibility of building a bright future for the country and being aware of its cultural heritage.
Members of Anand Math author Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’ family sat beside the Prime minister, watching the dramatic recreation of the Bengali novel. The innovative use of digital screens to lend a cinematic edge to the sets, set the performance apart."The Chattopadhyay family is glad that Vande Mataram is being sung in full. Justice was not being done to the sentiment behind Anand Math when just two stanzas were sung," Shantanu Chatterjee, a member of the family who watched the play Anand Math, told TOI.
The play, in fact, ended with the rendition of Vande Mataram in full.Ekta Nagar, which houses the towering statue of Sardar Patel and other tourist attractions, is the venue of Rashtriya Ekta Diwas Parade, which is almost on the lines of Republic Day parade in Delhi, possibly grander with several events organised alongside the parade. The town is currently glowing with festive lights, with lit up pieces of art showcasing the culture and traditions of each state. Tourists from all over the country have descended here to watch the 'Unity Day' spectacle.On Saturday, 7,000 people from 126 districts that at some point of time were affected by Left-wing extremism, will participate both as performers and spectators in the event.Around 2,000 artists drawn from the 126 districts will join the celebrations by putting up a drama performance, also directed by the National School of Drama (NSD), through which they will recount how their life and property were threatened when Naxalism was rampant in their area.In addition, around 5,000 local people from these 126 districts have been invited. They will not only be spectators for all the performances but will also, through their interactions, share the hardships they had to undergo at the hands of Maoists and how their lives have changed now.“Their participation will underline the resilience of communities that have endured conflict and highlight the role of cultural expression in strengthening national integration,” said Govind Mohan.The 2026 edition of the parade will also feature march-past by contingents of all the central armed police forces (CAPFs) and state police personnel who were in the forefront of the decisive fight against left-wing extremist violence. A short film will play on LED screens at the venue as the contingents pass in front of the Prime Minister, the chief guest, summarising the salient feature of their achievements in eliminating armed Naxalism.The Ekta Diwas parade, to be held in the evening hours this year, will also feature tableaux designed around the theme of “Vande Mataram” and constructed by the people and private entities with corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds, with no involvement of the govt. The 15 designs for the tableaux, selected through competition, are based on the implications of ‘Vande Mataram’ on nationhood and development.
There will also be a cultural programme curated entirely by people from different states and communities who have made Gujarat their home. Around 5,000 artists will showcase dances and culture of their respective states through this mega-performance.

Trump's oil holdings surge 43% amid Iran war, raising conflict of interest concerns - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:41:39 UTC
13:41:39 KST

US President Donald Trump's oil and gas investments have risen sharply in value during the eight-month war with Iran, raising concerns among congressional Democrats about potential conflicts of interest as Americans face higher fuel prices, CBS News reported Monday.
According to a report by Democrats on the Congressional Joint Economic Committee, obtained by CBS, Trump's energy holdings increased in value by an average of 43% since the end of 2025, based on LSEG Data Analytics figures.
The estimated value of his holdings rose from a range of $12.6 million to $46 million at the end of 2025 to between $22.5 million and $81.6 million. Democrats on the committee also estimated that American families have spent an average of $856 more on gasoline since the war began.
The findings were based on Trump's financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics, which requires investments and transactions to be reported in value ranges rather than exact amounts.
Between March and the end of August, the latest period covered by available disclosures, Trump's investment accounts purchased between $4.7 million and $17.5 million in oil and gas stocks and sold between $2 million and $5.4 million, according to the committee's members.
Trump's energy holdings rise as fuel prices climb
Chevron and ExxonMobil account for Trump's largest oil and gas holdings, valued at up to $23.1 million and $18.4 million, respectively, CBS reported. Their shares have risen nearly 25% and 22% since February 20.
CBS also reported that Trump's investment accounts sold between $500,000 and $1 million in ExxonMobil shares on April 7, the same day he announced a ceasefire with Iran. ExxonMobil shares fell more than 6% at the open the following day.
The energy investments represent a relatively small portion of Trump's overall wealth, which Forbes estimated at approximately $7 billion in September.
Energy stocks have surged during the conflict, with the S&P 500 energy sector gaining more than 50% this year, compared with an approximately 11% rise in the broader index.
Since February, US gasoline prices have climbed from $2.87 to $4.29 per gallon, while diesel prices have risen from $3.68 to $6.28. Brent crude has also increased from below $75 to more than $115 a barrel.
White House denies conflicts of interest
The White House rejected allegations of conflicts of interest, saying Trump's investments are managed independently and that neither the president nor his family directs trading decisions.
White House spokesman Davis Ingle told CBS that Trump's financial portfolio is "independently managed by third-party financial institutions" through automated investment models that track established stock indexes.
"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold," Ingle added. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest."
Ingle also maintained that "President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public, which is why they overwhelmingly reelected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses."
Trump touts oil industry profits, blames Iran for rising prices
Trump has alternated between highlighting the financial benefits of the conflict for US energy companies and blaming Tehran for rising oil prices.
Speaking in Georgia on Saturday, Trump claimed American oil and gas companies were "making hundreds of billions of dollars" from the conflict and predicted that fuel prices would fall sharply once the war ended.
The previous week, Trump accused Iran of deliberately driving up oil prices ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections. In a Truth Social post, he claimed Tehran was fabricating reports of attacks and mines to influence energy markets.
Democrats raise concerns over Trump's investments
The rise in Trump's energy holdings has drawn criticism from congressional Democrats, who questioned whether his financial interests could conflict with his administration's decisions on Iran.
"Trump's Iran War has forced Americans to pay much more at the pump while Big Oil rakes in profits and the president's own stock wealth in the oil and gas industry continues to balloon," said Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee.
"As Trump, the country's highest-ranking public employee, continues to own and trade stocks in companies that stand to benefit from his decisions, his actions raise major concerns about conflicts of interest."
Trump has predicted that gas prices will "drop through the floor" once the war ends, although the timeline remains uncertain. He has not ruled out renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms, while US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told the Financial Times that the conflict could continue for another year, though he hoped Iranian leaders would "come to the table" before then.

US jails two Chinese nationals for spying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:41:32 UTC
13:41:32 KST

US jails two Chinese nationals for spying
Liren Lai and Yuance Chen admitted to facilitating ‘dead drop’ cash payments worth at least $30,000 to people in the US.
Two Chinese nationals have been jailed in the United States after admitting to trying to recruit US military service members to spy for Beijing.
Liren “Ryan” Lai, 40, and Yuance Chen, 39, were each sentenced to 30 months in prison and three years of supervised release, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) said in a statement on Friday.
The men sought to arrange “dead drop” cash payments in exchange for information related to US national security, the statement also said.
The pair operated a “long-running”, “extensive” and “brazen” scheme to undermine US national security and support Chinese intelligence operations and recruitment in the US, Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A Eisenberg said.
According to court documents, Lai and Chen began acting as agents of China’s foreign intelligence arm, the Ministry of State Security, no later than May 2021.
Lai, who arrived in the US on a tourist visa, recruited Chen, a permanent resident, into the scheme and initially served as an intermediary between Chen and intelligence officers – until Chen was able to receive his orders directly from his handler.
In May 2022, they facilitated a secret cash payment of $10,000 from China, ordering US-based individuals to drop the cash at a specified location for collection by someone else, an arrangement known as a “dead drop”.
The two later carried out another similar operation, facilitating a payment of $20,000.
Chen and Lai also engaged in other forms of espionage, including obtaining photographs of a naval facility, military recruits, and active-duty sailors. Chen collected personal information about a US Navy employee and maintained detailed biographical information about military personnel who were potential intelligence targets.
The DOJ did not say how many times the pair had facilitated payments, nor how many people they had successfully recruited in the US.
The men were found guilty of two charges: conspiracy to act as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the Attorney General; and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification.
Both pleaded guilty in court.
The pair were arrested and charged in June 2025.
In late August, US President Donald Trump said he knew China spied on the US, but “we spy on them too”.
In June, China announced that it had arrested a US citizen accused of espionage a day after US media reports said a scholar holding dual US and Myanmar citizenship was detained in early June.
The scholar, Min Zin, previously wrote opinion pieces on Myanmar politics that were critical of the military government, as well as the opposition groups it is fighting.
