New book 'Fairy Lights in God’s Backyard' is messy,  beautiful, and full of light - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:41:18 UTC
13:41:18 KST

Sarah Tuttle-Singer, author of Fairy Lights in God’s Backyard: A Jerusalem Love Story, finds the stories beyond the headlines. “I’m interested in the ways people connect across differences, and in the moments when someone surprises us by being more complicated, more generous, or more human than we expected,” she says. Jerusalem has taught her that “multiple truths can exist at once, and listening to someone else doesn’t require surrendering your own.”
“Jerusalem is always the main character in my work,” she explains. “And I’m still discovering her.”
The Magazine caught up with Tuttle-Singer, also author of 2018’s Jerusalem, Drawn and Quartered, to discuss her new book.
What is ‘Fairy Lights in God’s Backyard’ about?
It’s about love, loss, friendship, motherhood, faith, trauma, survival, and the peculiar magic of ordinary life in Jerusalem. Whereas my first book was about discovering the Old City and its communities, Fairy Lights is about what happens when a place becomes part of your identity – when the streets aren’t just history or scenery but the backdrop to your most intimate experiences.
What does the title mean?
For me, Jerusalem is God’s backyard. Not because everyone here agrees on God – quite the opposite – but because this is a place where the divine and the ridiculous, the sacred and the profane, the ancient and the ordinary are constantly bumping into each other. And the fairy lights are those little moments of beauty and human connection that illuminate the darkness. They’re the things we notice when we stop looking only at the headlines. They’re the conversations, friendships, acts of kindness, moments of tenderness, and flashes of unexpected joy that remind us why life is worth living.
Motherhood is part of your writing. Can you tell us about your children?
I’m the mother of three children: an 18-year-old daughter, a 16-year-old son, and a four-year-old son with special needs. Raising him has changed the way I experience the world, including Jerusalem. He notices things that other people overlook. He has his own relationship with the city’s sounds, textures, rhythms, and routines. Through him, I’ve learned to experience familiar places differently.
He features especially prominently in Fairy Lights. The book touches on the beauty, exhaustion, absurdity, tenderness, and occasional loneliness of raising a neurodivergent child, particularly as a single mother. And it’s about how the smallest moments – a familiar street corner, a favorite gate, a repeated phrase, a little hand reaching for mine – can become their own kind of sacred geography.
What inspired you to write this book?
The inspiration for the book came in the aftermath of the devastating explosion in June 2026 that destroyed our home in Jerusalem’s Old City and killed our neighbor. The experience left me trying to make sense of the trauma, the grief, and the disorienting experience of losing our home in a place I loved so deeply. It was after the explosion that Rabbi Menachem Creditor suggested I write a book as a way of processing the trauma, but it became something much larger: a love letter to Jerusalem, to the people who inhabit it, and to the fragile, beautiful, sometimes heartbreaking experience of being alive.
The book isn’t simply about the explosion. It’s about friendships formed in unlikely places, conversations that last until dawn, the strange intimacy of living in a city where everyone seems to know everyone, and the ways that ancient history and ordinary domestic life constantly collide. It’s about the little moments that might seem insignificant from the outside but become enormous when you’re living them.
I wanted to write about the darkness without allowing it to swallow the light.
How has the experience of losing your home affected you?
The experience of losing my home has changed the way I think about belonging.
A home isn’t only a building. It’s the people who know your name, the shopkeeper who remembers how you take your coffee, the neighbors who notice when you’re missing, and the streets that hold your memories.
And while I no longer live inside the Old City walls, in some ways I carry the Old City with me wherever I go.
How did you find your way to Jerusalem?
I grew up in Venice Beach, California, in a home filled with books, stories, Yiddish lullabies, civil rights anthems, and conversations about the world. It may seem a far cry from the Pacific Ocean to Jerusalem, but Jerusalem’s limestone hills were actually once an ancient seabed. I love that image, a California girl raised beside the ocean finding home in a city whose stones still remember the sea.
I first came as a teenager, on a Young Judaea summer program in 1997. I fell in love with Jerusalem, and that love affair continues to shape the rest of my life. I made aliyah in 2010 with my then-husband and our two young children. After our marriage ended, I stayed in Israel and eventually made my home in Jerusalem. I fell head over heels in love with this place through conversations with people from all backgrounds and walks of life.
Why the Old City?
I’ve always been fascinated by Jerusalem, particularly the Old City, where thousands of years of history exist in extraordinary proximity, and where people from radically different backgrounds live their daily lives against a backdrop that the rest of the world considers sacred. I wanted to understand it beyond the headlines, political arguments, and familiar narratives and to see what it would feel like to live in the hottest piece of spiritual real estate in the world.
So in 2016, I spent a year living in the four quarters of the Old City – Jewish, Muslim, Christian, and Armenian – spending approximately three months in each.
I wanted to understand Jerusalem from the inside, through the people who call it home. I met shopkeepers, religious leaders, neighbors, musicians, merchants, families, and people who challenged everything I thought I knew about the city.
That experience became my first book. And while the experiment officially ended, my relationship with the Old City never will. ■
Sarah Tuttle-Singer is a storyteller, journalist, author, and media personality. She also loves taking people for walks around the Old City.

Sneak preview: Excerpt from ‘Fairy Lights in God’s Backyard: A Jerusalem Love Story'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:41:18 UTC
13:41:18 KST

Every morning, my son’s shuttle to his special needs preschool is accompanied by the oddest couple – a man and a woman who, under almost any other circumstances, might never choose to spend time together. His melava is haredi – profoundly religious and right wing, and a big fan of Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The driver is as secular as they come, a regular at the protests who insisted his kids go to a mixed Jewish and Arab school, and who spends time on the front lines of Israel’s fight over its own democracy.
I have strong opinions about all of it
They’re on opposite sides of the argument about Israel’s future, its identity, its very soul.
Sometimes they debate in the car.
It’s mostly banter, really, though every now and then they try to pull me into the conversation.
I have strong opinions about all of it.
I love being Jewish. I also believe that being Jewish makes me neither better nor worse than anyone else. I have plenty to say about religion and politics and the future of this complicated little country.
But in that car, I usually stay out of it.
Because at the end of the day, these are two people who have dedicated part of every morning to helping keep my son safe.
I wouldn’t call them friends exactly.
But there is genuine warmth between them now.
And I love that special education can do that.
The morning was hard
It can take two people who might otherwise meet only across a protest line – or an argument – and gently compel them toward a common purpose.
Loving my son.
This morning was hard.
Lately, my little one has stopped asking to go back to his “castle” every day. That ache has softened.
But every time we walk through Jaffa Gate to wait for the shuttle, I still brace myself.
Maybe it was the heavy clouds. Maybe it was the wind. Maybe it was my own anxiety leaking through the brittle spaces in ways children always seem to sense.
Whatever it was, he had a full-blown meltdown in the back of the car.
His melava quietly handed him a book.
The driver reached over and put on The Beatles.
I climbed into the front seat, girding my mental loins, feeling profoundly tired – less like the pirate queen I usually aspire to be and more like a bedraggled castaway trying to get home to her own life.
Slowly, my son settled.
He began turning the pages, pointing to each letter, tracing every shape carefully with one small finger.
No one talked about politics.
No one argued about religion
We just listened to The Beatles.
“It has to be so hard for you,” the driver said.
“I’m praying for you every day,” the melava added.
And as we drove through Jaffa Gate into the morning, “With a Little Help from My Friends” came on.
It’s a cliché.
I’m willing to lean into it.
Jerusalem is heavy – layer upon layer. And sometimes those layers don’t impose, they support.
Yesterday I found another apartment – another house to add to the list of places this wandering Jew will shlep her suitcase.
It isn’t my Ottoman dollhouse.
But when I walked inside, I felt the faint possibility of home.
I’ll buy another pink tea kettle. I’ll hang more fairy lights.
I’ve lived in so many houses.
And I’ve learned that home is something you build with people far more than with stone.
Maybe one day I’ll live in my old house again.
Not anytime soon.
The Byzantine well courtyard is still buried beneath rubble.
There is still a bloodstain, in the shape of my neighbor, on the stone floor by the stone steps leading up to my teal door and shattered garden.
There are still moments when I feel haunted by every loss I’ve ever carried.
And yet…
I know I’m going to be okay.
Not because everything has been repaired.
But because people keep showing up.
A haredi woman.
A secular driver.
A little boy learning his letters.
Friends from all corners of Jerusalem who carry impossible things together every morning before breakfast and still make sure to check in on me.
So many people all around the world who’ve helped in both spiritual and practical ways.
Just then, the sun broke through the clouds.
The Beatles kept singing.
My son kept reading.
And I realized that, for all the heartbreak of this past year, I really am getting by with a little help from my friends.
It’s Tuesday. “Twice good,” our tradition teaches.
So, good morning, Jaffa Gate.
Good morning, magnificent city.
Good morning great grandmother and all the ancestors whose winding, broken paths somehow led to ours.
Good morning, Jerusalem.
Whatever happens next, I’ll bring fairy lights. ■
FAIRY LIGHTS
IN GOD’S BACKYARD: 
A JERUSALEM LOVE STORY
By Sarah Tuttle Singer

Riot police deployed to Poland’s constitutional court after judge suspended
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:27:25 UTC
13:27:25 KST

Riot police were locked in a tense standoff with protesters outside Poland’s constitutional court on Friday night after its top judge was suspended in the latest escalation in a decade-long dispute over the court’s legal status.
The clashes followed a controversial decision by a group of government-appointed judges to suspend the court’s contested president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, amid disagreements over the bench’s legitimacy.
The move prompted a furious reaction from the rightwing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, with its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, condemning what he claimed was an “assault” on the court.
The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over EU law and the European Union accused Poland’s highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time.
The PiS-backed conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, a close ally of Donald Trump, turned his plane around en route to a state visit in Senegal to return to Warsaw and intervene at the court on Friday night.
Hundreds of protesters – including opposition MPs – gathered outside the building to show their support for the suspended judges. Police said they detained three people after some protesters breached the tribunal’s fence and others threw objects at officers.
Shortly before 1am on Saturday, Nawrocki appeared outside the court and made his way through the police cordon, with one video showing the president tussling with security and other judges to force his entry into the building. As of 4am local time, the president remained inside the building.
In a clip posted online, Nawrocki was heard saying the government appointees “were not judges of the constitutional court”.
In a statement read out on his behalf outside the court at 5am, Nawrocki criticised “a violation of Poland’s constitutional order”, saying “a constitutional body was seized by force”. He called for security forces to leave the premises.
The latest clash is likely to further polarise the country, setting the scene for a dramatic showdown in next year’s parliamentary election, with polls showing the populist-right with a chance to return to power.
The court has been at the centre of a dispute dating back to 2015, when the outgoing centrist and the incoming rightwing governments moved in quick succession with legally questionable moves to stack the bench with their appointees.
The dispute over the appointments paralysed the court, followed by further attempts to cripple it during the PiS’s eight years of illiberal rule marred by clashes with the EU over the rule of law.
Since returning to power in 2023, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has repeatedly pledged to reverse controversial reforms as he sought to mend relations with Brussels, while refusing to recognise the court’s legitimacy in the current form.
However, his efforts have been thwarted by opposition-aligned presidents who used their veto powers and expansive interpretations of their powers to block reforms.
In the latest twist this year, Nawrocki, who unexpectedly won last year’s presidential election against Tusk’s candidate, refused to swear in five judges elected by the current parliament, further complicating the legal situation.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe’s advisory body on the rule of law, the Venice Commission, said the president’s refusal should not prevent judges from taking up their posts.
On Friday night, a group of judges elected by the current majority moved to suspend Święczkowski, a former minister under PiS, and seize procedural control of the court. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – who is one of the five judges not accepted by Nawrocki – said she had assumed the top position, citing the longest experience in the judiciary.
Experts are deeply divided in their opinion on the legality of the judge’s suspension. Marcin Matczak, a prominent law expert and outspoken critic of PiS, said he “did not think he would ever end up defending” Święczkowski, but believed the legal basis for his suspension was “non-existent”.
Separately, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said he had asked for Święczkowski and deputy chief Sochański to be stripped of their legal immunity to face prosecution for obstructing the court’s work.
Despite criticism, Tusk insisted that “restoring the rule of law is our duty.”
“After years of PiS’s lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he argued.
Earlier this month, he pledged “the court will begin its work in accordance with the constitution, whether people like it or not.”
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski told reporters on the margins of a G20 meeting in Atlanta that “the constitutional tribunal was politicised under the previous government.”
“What is happening has the purpose of allowing the majority of duly elected judges to make the tribunal function again,” he said.
Opposition leaders and the court’s social media account accused the government of carrying out a judicial “a coup d’état”. Several European far-right figures, including Britain’s Nigel Farage, Liz Truss and the Netherlands’ Geert Wilders, also condemned the move.
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said in a post on X: “The events unfolding tonight … are very serious.”
“Both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why,” he said. “Whatever the facts ultimately establish, thousands gathering outside the tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse.”

MUSCAT, Oman – Oman said on Oct 30 it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship set ablaze in an attack, as Iran reported three oil tankers were halted while crossing the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has restricted maritime traffic through the strait since the Middle East war erupted on Feb 28 with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic republic.
The narrow waterway, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil, has become a focal point of the conflict, with ships regularly coming under Iranian fire.
Muscat’s navy “carried out an evacuation operation for 25 crew members of the merchant ship RITI, flying the Panamanian flag, after it was targeted, which led to a fire breaking out on board”, Oman’s Maritime Security Centre said in a statement.
The crew members were provided with medical care, the Omani statement said, without giving details.
The Marine Traffic ship-tracking website described the RITI as a crude oil tanker.
US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said in a video released on Oct 30 that US forces had “successfully cleared the strait’s internationally recognised primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines”.
US forces remain “present to ensure that all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear”, he added.
Cooper said he visited some of the more than 50,000 US service members in the region, repeating earlier statements that Washington has helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude via the strait since summer.
British maritime security agency UKMTO said that a ship 40 nautical miles south of Lavan island in Iran was struck on Oct 30 by an unknown projectile, which caused a fire onboard.
“The crew of the vessel have been reported as safe and there is no reported environmental impact at this time,” the UKMTO said on X.
Blockade

“Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorised route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait,” the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has demanded that vessels use a designated route through the strait and coordinate their passage with the country’s armed forces, labelling a southern corridor closer to Oman’s shores as unauthorised.
The tankers had “switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist US military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorised route”, the Guards’ statement said.
The Guards did not specify the nature of the “incidents” the tankers encountered, which came a day after Iran’s armed forces said at least four tankers had stopped in the area after hitting mines.
They said the incidents on Oct 30 occurred after the vessels received several radio warnings but disregarded them.
The IRGC said in a later statement that a supertanker carrying two million barrels of oil had stopped following an explosion “after striking a naval mine while navigating an unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz”.
“This is the third oil tanker to have exploded and caught fire today as a result of attempting to pass through an unauthorised route,” it added.
The United States has responded to Iran’s blockade of the strait with a counterblockade of Iranian ports, further restricting Tehran’s ability to export oil and conduct trade. AFP

UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara to expire amid US, Russia vetoes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:24:00 UTC
13:24:00 KST

US, Russia block rival Western Sahara resolutions
October 31, 2026
The fate of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has been left in a limbo after Russia and the United States vetoed each other's draft resolutions on extending the mission that is over three decades long — just one day before the mandate expires.
The peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to oversee a settlement plan and ceasefire between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front in a territorial dispute spanning half a century.
Morocco considers Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, as its territory,
The Polisario Front, which is supported by Algeria and represents the indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.
US and Russia wield vetoes
On Friday, the US tabled a draft resolution at the UN Security Council (UNSC) that would have extended the mandate for one year, while making a Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara the only basis for negotiations to settle the conflict, and cutting the mission's military component.
Last year, the UNSC backed Morocco's autonomy proposal as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.
Friday's failed US draft resolution would have gone further and rebranded the peacekeeping force from MINURSO to MINUSO, dropping the 'R' which refers to referendum on the territory's self-determination.
The US proposal was vetoed by Russia, which slammed it as a "unilateral approach." A total of 11 of the 15 UNSC members voted in its favor and three abstained.
"We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty," Russia's permanent representative to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, said.
"The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach. Therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of the draft," he added.
The US, with its own veto, then blocked a Russian draft that proposed renewing the mission's mandate for another year while preserving the same terms as before.
"Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades," the US representative to the United Nations, Michael Waltz, said after the vote.
How did Morocco and the Polisario Front react?
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the peacekeeping mission and said that this "should mark the end of the Security Council's involvement and the removal of this issue from its agenda."
The Polisario Front's UN representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing the US resolution that he said "would have undermined the free exercise by the Sahrawi people of their inalienable right to self-determination and independence."

Five hundred missiles would be enough to protect our skies over the coming months – precisely when it is so important for Ukraine to be in a strong position in negotiations and for Russia NOT to succeed in breaking life in Ukrainian cities and communities,” the head of state said.
He recalled that the United States, European countries and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors: “Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach. And it is entirely feasible.”
Zelensky expressed gratitude to President Trump, the State Department and the U.S. administration as a whole for the authorization.
“But we are asking for decisions that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but at the very moment the threat is there – when Russia is killing and destroying. I thank everyone who stands with Ukraine!” the President concluded.
As Ukrinform reported, the U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale to Ukraine of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles for Patriot air defense systems, worth a total of $2.1 billion.

Europe has blown its chance to mediate Ukraine conflict – Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:15:00 UTC
13:15:00 KST

Europe has blown its chance to mediate Ukraine conflict – Lavrov
European countries have repeatedly failed to uphold agreements intended to resolve the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, undermining their credibility as potential peace guarantors, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Moscow has previously stated that European officials would not participate in the upcoming US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi.
Speaking at a press conference on the sidelines of a G20 meeting in Atlanta, Georgia on Friday, Lavrov said “the Europeans want to insert themselves into the negotiation process.”
“What matters is not what the Europeans want, but what added value they can actually bring to the table,” he said.
Lavrov accused European governments of failing to uphold agreements intended to resolve the crisis, beginning with the February 2014 deal between then-Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovich and opposition leaders. France, Germany and Poland helped broker the agreement, which was intended to end months of protests and deadly clashes in Kiev.
Yanukovich was ousted shortly afterward, an event Moscow maintains prompted Crimea to secede from Ukraine and join Russia, while also triggering a revolt in the largely Russian-speaking Donbass.
According to Lavrov, France and Germany also failed to ensure that Ukraine implemented political reforms and granted special status to Donbass under the 2014–2015 Minsk agreements which they had helped broker.
Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel and former French President Francois Hollande acknowledged in separate interviews in December 2022 that the agreements had given Ukraine time to strengthen its military. Moscow has cited their remarks as evidence that Western governments never intended to implement the accords in good faith.
Lavrov also cited the December 2019 summit in Paris, where the leaders of Russia, Ukraine, France and Germany reaffirmed their commitment to implementing the Minsk agreements. The diplomatic process ultimately failed to produce a lasting settlement.
“Over the past 12 years, they have had more than enough opportunities. Through their actions, they have demonstrated that their track record cannot be ignored the next time they seek to act as ‘guarantors,’” Lavrov stated.
His remarks followed a rare telephone conversation on Tuesday between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. The 90-minute call, which focused on the Ukraine conflict and upcoming peace negotiations, drew criticism from several European leaders. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the initiative had not been coordinated with other European countries, while Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said he had not been informed in advance.
Putin, however, welcomed the contact, describing the decision to call as a step towards establishing “some kind of constructive dialogue.”
Lavrov attended the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta at the invitation of the US, despite objections from some European governments to Russia’s participation. US President Donald Trump has also invited Putin to the G20 leaders’ summit scheduled for December in Miami.
European opposition to Russia’s participation was evident on Friday when the traditional G20 group photograph was canceled after several European diplomats objected to posing alongside Lavrov.

More than $3m spent on government merch, including condoms and lollies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:10:13 UTC
13:10:13 KST

Millions spent on government merchandise, including condoms, lollies, tote bags
In short:
The Commonwealth has banned federal agencies from using taxpayer funds to buy promotional merchandise "without exemption".
Figures provided to the Senate reveal government entities spent more than $3.4 million on merchandise last financial year.
What's next?
The new rules took effect from July, with departments required to report their expenditure on merchandise in their annual reports.
The Albanese government has launched a clampdown on taxpayer-funded merchandise in a bid to rein in the millions of dollars spent on promotional knick-knacks.
Stress balls, condoms, lollies, tote bags, pens and beanies were among thousands of branded or promotional products bought by federal entities in the past financial year.
The total cost across a range of government departments, agencies, independent statutory authorities, regulators and other entities came in at more than $3.4 million.
But under a new edict that came into effect from July, the government has banned agencies from using taxpayer funds to purchase promotional merchandise unless they seek approval.
There are some exemptions, such as if items are sold for profit or if they are considered critical to the government's policy objectives.
The policy, which was part of this year's budget, mandates that agencies must also publicly report details of their merchandise spend in their annual reports.
"The Department of Finance has issued guidance to agencies to support implementation of the government's policy," a government spokesperson told the ABC.
What the departments spent
The Department of Defence was among the biggest spenders in 2025–26, putting more than $1.4 million towards merchandise, according to figures provided to the Senate.
This included gifts for foreign militaries and dignitaries, as well as items for recruitment activities, employment expos and base open days.
A Defence spokesperson said officials must ensure spending on merchandise represented an efficient, effective, economic and ethical use of public resources.
Another $383,000 was also spent at the health department, which included 40,000 condoms in an initiative aimed at preventing sexually transmitted infections.
It also purchased 7,000 campaign-branded "condom wallets".
Among the other items the department bought were 5,000 stress balls, 5,000 mints packs, and 220 yo-yos — all with anti-vaping messages.
A department spokesperson defended its spend on merchandise, saying it was procured in limited circumstances for public health campaigns or strategies.
"Evaluation of these campaigns consistently show they are highly engaging, are well recognised by their target audiences and meet the campaign objectives," they said.
"Merchandise plays an important role in this.
"When used, merchandise carries important health messages and information, such as vaccine schedules, reminders of the importance of STI testing and scheduling, and strategies to assist in how to quit vaping and smoking."
Fewer 'branded generic keepsakes'
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) also incurred $176,000 in merchandise costs last financial year, with most of it aimed at spruiking this year's census.
This included census-themed beanies, mini AFL footballs, socks, reusable shopping bags, pencils, pens and "I heart census" button badge pins.
An ABS spokesperson said its agency had not purchased any further promotional material since the government's new merchandise policy came into effect.
"Census merchandise was used at community events, information hubs, during remote community engagement activities and to support the enumeration of people experiencing homelessness," they said.
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) spent more than $251,000, with a spokesperson saying it uses "standardised promotional material" for career expos and fairs.
The spokesperson also said it was "reasonable to expect" some of its reported expenditure on merchandise was used to purchase items from the AFP Legacy Shop.
"The AFP has formal governance on the acquisition of merchandise and has recently tightened this governance further to ensure a greater proportion of our merchandise has an educational element, rather than branded generic keepsakes," they said.

Hong Kong telecom company agrees to halt US operations under pressure
- HKT, a Hong Kong telecom and PCCW subsidiary, agreed to stop US services after the FCC moved to revoke its licence over national security concerns and China Unicom links.
- Under the consent decree, HKT must file to end services within 30 days and stop US operations by Sept 1, 2027. The FCC will not pursue the revocation case.
- The move is part of a wider US crackdown on Chinese telecom firms. China opposed the action and warned of countermeasures, while denying any wrongdoing.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – HKT, a leading Hong Kong telecom carrier and subsidiary of PCCW, agreed on Oct 30 to halt its operations in the United States under pressure from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC).
The FCC in October 2025 said it was moving to revoke the authority of HKT to operate in the US, citing national security concerns and its affiliation with China Unicom, which is a shareholder in PCCW.
Under a consent decree reviewed by Reuters, HKT has agreed to stop international and domestic telecom services to and within the US.
HKT must file an application with the FCC within 30 days to discontinue services and must discontinue US services by Sept 1, 2027. PCCW declined immediate comment.
The agreement means the FCC will not move forward with the revocation proceeding that could have offered more details on Washington’s national security concerns.
The FCC has previously barred China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom from providing international telecommunications services to the US, citing broad national security concerns.
The Trump administration has continued an extensive crackdown on Chinese telecoms over the past year.
The FCC on Oct 29 voted to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics starting from December 2028.
The telecom crackdown has sparked a strong reaction from Beijing.
China said on Oct 30 it firmly opposes the FCC action on labs, warning it would take necessary countermeasures “if the US side persists in acting unilaterally”.
The FCC also announced on Oct 29 it plans to soon ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers on national security grounds.
The plan would bar Chinese IP network service providers from direct access and those that use equipment from companies on the FCC’s list that pose national security risks, including Huawei and ZTE.
Other measures under consideration by the FCC include barring Chinese telecom firms from connecting to US networks and from operating their data centres in the US.
Concerns about the potential for spying and other harms to arise from Chinese access to US telecom data and infrastructure have grown in recent years.
In late 2024, Washington said a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group known as Salt Typhoon stole consumers’ call records and US call data and infiltrated US telecommunications and telecom infrastructure firms.
China has consistently denied any wrongdoing. REUTERS

Luigi Mangione’s lawyers file to dismiss state charges, citing double jeopardy law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:09:50 UTC
13:09:50 KST

Luigi Mangione’s lawyers filed paperwork on Friday once again pushing for dismissal of his state-level case in the killing of UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson following his federal guilty plea.
Mangione pleaded guilty on 14 August to federal charges in Thompson’s grisly death outside a Manhattan hotel on 4 December 2024. The shocking plea came less than a month before his state murder and weapons trial, which had been scheduled for 8 September.
Thompson’s death spurred a sprawling search for his killer. The incident simultaneously elicited an onslaught of anger against the for-profit US healthcare industry, which has long been decried for putting their bottom line ahead of patients, to the latter’s detriment.
About an hour after Mangione admitted to two federal stalking charges, his lawyers filed paperwork to dismiss his state case. They have contended that New York state’s double jeopardy laws bar him from being prosecuted by the Manhattan district attorney.
Double-jeopardy protection under the US constitution does not bar state prosecution for the same crimes as a federal case, and vice-versa. However, New York state statute maintains that “a person may not be twice prosecuted for the same offense” and “a person may not be separately prosecuted for two offenses based upon the same act or criminal transaction”.
In their new filing, Mangione’s lawyers reiterated their double-jeopardy arguments.
“The core misconduct of the federal and state prosecutions is the same: the intent to kill and the killing of Brian Thompson. Yes, stalking can also, in some circumstances, apply to conduct different and less extreme than intending to kill someone. But this has nothing to do with whether it also applies to intentional killing,” they wrote.
“One of the harms clearly addressed by the expansive federal stalking statute is stalking with the intent to kill and resulting in the killing of the person stalked,” they also said. “It is a statute that, like a state murder statute, is intended to keep people safe from being murdered—the oldest crime there is. That the stalking statute also criminalizes stalking conduct that does not result in death does not change that analysis.”
Manhattan prosecutors oppose Mangione’s push for dismissal. In paperwork filed on 9 October, they insisted his state proceedings can proceed “under an exception” of this state’s double-jeopardy provisions.
They have argued that federal stalking crimes, and state murder offenses, do not overlap in such a manner that state double-jeopardy protections would come into play.
“Statutory double jeopardy applies only when a defendant has been ‘separately prosecuted’ for the same misconduct, and dismissed federal charges do not constitute a separate prosecution,” they said.
The judge presiding over Mangione’s state case, Gregory Carro, pushed back these proceedings after the unexpected plea. Carro calendared the next court date for 10 December.

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- China's non-manufacturing activity moderated in October, while the services sector remained broadly stable, with holiday-related consumption and certain service industries showing relatively strong growth, official data showed Saturday.
The purchasing managers' index (PMI) for the non-manufacturing sector came in at 49.7 in October, down 0.5 points from September, partly due to weaker activity in some service industries, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 signifies contraction.
The business activity index for the services sector stood at 50.0, down 0.2 points from the previous month, indicating broadly stable activity.
By industry, business activity picked up in most major service categories. Railway transportation, accommodation, and culture, sports and entertainment services saw notable improvements, with their respective indexes rising into expansionary territory, supported by travel and consumer spending during the National Day holiday.
Meanwhile, business activity indexes for water transportation, postal services, and internet, software and information technology services all remained above 55.0, indicating relatively rapid growth in business activity.
The financial sector was the only major service category to register a decline in its business activity index, with a relatively sharp drop contributing to the overall moderation in services activity.
Business expectations remained positive, with the services sector's business activity expectations index standing at 55.2, suggesting that most surveyed enterprises remained confident about market prospects.
In the construction sector, the business activity index fell 2.3 points from September to 48.0, indicating a slowdown in construction activity.
The sector's business activity expectations index stood at 52.3, down 3.1 points from the previous month.
Saturday's data came as China's service sector has maintained strong growth momentum this year, underpinned by supportive policy expectations, growing market confidence, resilient consumption and opening up.
In the first half of the year, the service sector contributed 66.1 percent to the country's economic growth, up 5.9 percentage points from the same period a year earlier. ■

Interview: CIIE offers "gateway" for shared growth, says Indonesian expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:08:32 CST
13:08:32 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhang Yisheng, Feng Yulin
JAKARTA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The upcoming ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) offers a "gateway" for international businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), to tap into China's vast market and build resilient global trade networks, an Indonesian expert has said.
"The good thing is that China gives opportunities to countries all across the globe to come," Humprey Arnaldo Russel, head of the ASEAN-China Research Center at the University of Indonesia, told Xinhua in an interview ahead of the expo, scheduled to be held in Shanghai on Nov. 5-10.
Launched in 2018 as the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports, the CIIE aims to expand China's opening up and provide businesses worldwide with access to its large market. This year's edition will feature over 200 representative global debuts and first-time exhibits.
For smaller enterprises, entering a foreign market often involves navigating complex regulatory and compliance requirements. The CIIE helps address these challenges by providing a face-to-face platform for Indonesian SMEs to engage directly with Chinese businesses, Humprey said.
Indonesian businesses "can learn how to enter the Chinese market by meeting directly with their Chinese counterparts to discuss regulations," he said. "Sometimes an opportunity exists, but you must first meet the market requirements."
Amid ongoing shifts in global trade dynamics and unilateral tariff pressures, the Shanghai expo provides Indonesian exporters with "timely momentum" to diversify their export markets, build sustainable supply chains and integrate into broader economic ecosystems, Humprey said.
"Beyond accessing the Chinese market, our businesses can connect with international buyers and global distributors who convene in Shanghai. It is an invaluable platform for our export expansion," he said.
Highlighting the participation of companies from around the world, including U.S. firms that have maintained a strong presence at the CIIE over the years, Humprey said, "I think countries across the globe want to see China and the United States cooperate with each other for a better world."
"We need an open system where people with small and medium-sized enterprises, whether in Africa, Indonesia, Vanuatu, or Fiji, have the opportunity to trade across the globe based on WTO rules," he said.
Emphasizing that trade serves as a bridge for cooperation, Humprey noted that stronger economic ties and their positive spillover effects can help narrow differences among nations.
"A shared future is a must, because the future does not belong only to us. It belongs to the next generation," he said. "We have to prepare good things for them." ■

Feature: Mauritius' rare homegrown coffee embarks on aromatic journey to China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:08:26 CST
13:08:26 KST

PORT LOUIS, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Known for its striking multicolored volcanic dunes, southwestern Mauritius is also home to a less familiar attraction: the African island country's only coffee plantation.
Located in the Chamarel 7 Colored Earth Geopark in the Black River District, the plantation produces distinctive beans that remain little known outside Mauritius.
This signature coffee, grown amid the volcanic landscapes of Mauritius, is set to make its debut at this year's China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai.
"We would love the Chinese market to discover a rare coffee specialty from Mauritius," said Thomas Lehoux, development manager of coffee operations at Chamarel Coffee, the sole brand in Mauritius that grows coffee locally and makes products from its own beans.
At the plantation, humid conditions, gentle sunlight and mineral-rich soil provide a favorable environment for coffee trees, helping produce beans with a rich and balanced flavor.
Like wine, coffee derives much of its character from its origin, flavor and quality, Lehoux told Xinhua, adding that Chamarel Coffee uses beans grown on its own plantation and processed entirely by hand, producing flavors that distinguish from comparable products of other origins.
The plantation mainly grows two varieties of coffee, Arabica and Liberica. Lehoux will bring both to this year's CIIE, marking the brand's debut at the event.
Lehoux said coffee consumption in China has grown in recent years, along with increasing interest in bean varieties, flavor profiles and places of origin, creating opportunities for Mauritian coffee.
"I believe there can be a strong link between us as a small producer on a small island and a big market like China," he said.
At this year's CIIE, the brand hopes to connect with Chinese coffee importers, upscale restaurants, specialty coffee shops and roasters. For Lehoux, who has about 20 years of experience in coffee production, the expo will also offer a best chance to better understand Chinese consumers' preferences and explore ways to tailor products to the market.
To prepare for potential business opportunities following the CIIE, the company is expanding its plantation, which currently covers about 16 hectares and produces around one tonne of finished coffee beans for export annually. An additional 4 hectares were planted this year, with output expected to increase in two to three years.
The company has also been developing coffee-scented fragrances, perfumes and coffee cups as part of its efforts to diversify its business beyond coffee.
Walking through the plantation, Lehoux said he hoped the CIIE would help Chamarel Coffee build long-term relationships in China and find partners to support its growth.
Though separated by vast stretches of ocean, Mauritius and China have achieved fruitful results in practical economic and trade cooperation. Mauritius is the first African country to sign a free trade agreement with China. China, for consecutive years, has been Mauritius' largest trading partner and largest source of imports.
Mauritian sugar products, which have appeared at the CIIE for several editions, are a prominent example of the Indian Ocean island's efforts to reach Chinese buyers. With coffee and other new products to be presented at the expo this year, the two countries are poised to deepen trade cooperation and expand Mauritian exports to China. ■

Global wildlife trade involves over 107,000 species: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:08:20 CST
13:08:20 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- More than 107,000 species are used and traded worldwide, more than double previous estimates, according to a new study that warns the true scale could be far greater due to major gaps in global monitoring data.
Published in Science Advances and led by Australia's University of Melbourne, the study identified 107,356 species traded across plants, animals and fungi, compared with previous estimates of about 50,000 species in trade worldwide, according to a university statement released on Saturday.
Wildlife trade was a well-established driver of biodiversity loss, but information on its extent and sustainability remained incomplete and fragmented, said lead researcher Professor Alice Hughes from the university's School of BioSciences.
Wildlife trade extended far beyond the illegal trade of elephants, tigers and pangolins, encompassing timber, seafood, medicinal plants, pets, cut flowers, ornamental fish and fungi, most of which were legal, Hughes said.
"For most of these species we have little to no data. There is no data on quantity and origins, let alone the population level data to assess if trade poses a risk to species survival," she said, adding the global biodiversity framework's existing trade target covered only about 2 to 3 percent of species in trade, missing the remaining 97 percent.
The researchers called for standardized data collection and more comprehensive, transparent and globally coordinated reporting, saying existing customs and animal health inspection processes could be adapted to improve wildlife trade monitoring. ■

Large manufacturers continued to report expansion, with their PMI standing at 50.2, despite a slight decline of 0.4 points from the previous month. Meanwhile, the PMI readings for medium-sized and small enterprises came in at 48.4 and 47.5, respectively.
On the price front, both major raw material purchasing prices and factory-gate prices remained in expansionary territory, although their growth moderated.

Tens of thousands of Italians protested against prices and military spending
Kyiv • UNN
Mass protests against the rising cost of living and military spending took place in cities across Italy. Clashes with police occurred in Turin and Venice.
On Friday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets across Italy to protest the rising cost of living and increased military spending. ANSA reports, according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that students, truck drivers, farmers and other workers took to the streets of major cities — Rome, Turin, Palermo, Milan and Naples — protesting the rising cost of living.
Demonstrations proceeded peacefully in most cities; however, in Turin, police used a water cannon to push back protesters who approached the security cordons protecting the prefecture building.
Law enforcement officers launched an attack in central Turin after some protesters began throwing bottles at officers. Tear gas was also used
Clashes with law enforcement also took place in Venice. Seven police officers suffered minor injuries, bruises and cuts after clashing with march participants who attempted to break through the roadblocks.
In Rome, a large march took place near the Colosseum, where protesters said they planned to set up tents and remain there for the weekend. Demonstrators placed garbage bins across the streets and set them on fire.
In Milan, students blocked the ring road for an hour and a half, but later returned to the city center.
We remind you
On October 24 in Rome, the capital of Italy, several hundred protesters broke through onto the grounds of the Colosseum, where tourists were present at the time. The demonstrators broke through the entrance gates of the historic landmark.

Courtney Barnett's songs aren't just about Courtney Barnett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:58:53 UTC
12:58:53 KST

Courtney Barnett is in her late-30s, over a decade into an incredibly successful music career, and past the point of being Australia's next big thing: she arrived a while ago.
Where some artists fear maturity might dull their edge, Barnett recognises how experience works in her favour.
While making her latest album, Creature Of Habit, disjointed recording sessions and writer's block had the singer-songwriter feeling a little unstable. But this wasn't her first time at the big dance.
"There were moments where I thought it would never get finished," she says.
"It kind of comes in waves. I think that's just the creative process for me: it's ups and downs. I said to myself, 'I've been here before. I've made a few albums, and I've felt this feeling. I'm just going to trust that hopefully I'll pass whatever the difficult moment is and just get on with it.'"
Old habits die
Spoiler: it did pass, resulting in yet another remarkable collection of songs in which Barnett captures our insecurities and reflects them with startling clarity.
That's long been one of her great strengths as a songwriter. The details in a Courtney Barnett song often belong to her, but the feelings somehow belong to everybody.
"I know I got a sensitive heart, I'm always picking it apart when I throw it to the vultures. They don't want it either, probably too sincere," she sings on Sugar Plum, a highlight from Creature Of Habit.
Barnett won audiences over from the outset with sharply observed stories about the messy process of trying to figure out life. Her songs often felt intensely personal, but left enough room for listeners to find themselves inside them.
When the young, shy artist was thrust into the spotlight following the success of her early EPs, those innermost thoughts suddenly became open to scrutiny. Seeing her work picked apart by strangers was unsettling.
These days, she's more accustomed to it.
"It kind of adds up, time and experience and all those things … I just feel a little more comfortable doing what I do," Barnett says about her current standing.
While she feels the impact of years in the game, she still finds it a challenge to pinpoint what exactly has changed.
"I feel like I've learned a lot a lot of small but important lessons, but sometimes I don't quite know how to articulate them. One of them is just learning how to trust myself a bit more.
"In the past, I would often spiral into this self-doubt, which just doesn't feel very productive or enjoyable.
"Even just facing a difficult moment and just working through it, something that sounds kind of simple; it was hard to trust in that process.
"Sometimes you got to fake it till you make it. You've got to convince yourself that you 100 per cent know what you're doing."
Start somewhere
While experience helped, Barnett also benefited from coming back to her discipline with fresh eyes.
Making the 2023 instrumental album End of the Day — the soundtrack to the Anonymous Club documentary about her life on the road — gave her a chance to work in a different realm.
"When I started working on it, I was just kind of learning how to write again because I hadn't written a song for a little while," she says. "So, it felt in a way that I was kind of beginning again.
"I was doing a lot of free writing, trying not to go into writing with any kind of intention or idea. I was kind of just trying to understand what was rattling around in my head as unfiltered as humanly possible.
"I guess a lot of my writing is kind of like that. Then it shows me something and then I kind of piece a narrative or an idea together. I guess it was just a thing circling in my head."
Condensing swirling thoughts into compact and compelling cuts of relatable indie rock is not easy on a technical level. Making sense of that flood of thoughts can be just as challenging.
What's worse, there's not really anywhere to hide when you're bleeding onto the page.
"It can be confronting, because you're face to face with yourself and holding a mirror up to yourself and sometimes you see things that you don't like," Barnett says.
"I was exploring parts of my personality or just parts of my world or life. I guess that kind of plays into the album title.
"I was looking at parts of myself that I didn't really like or that I wanted to change or wanted to work on, and kind of gently and kindly doing that work or making those subtle changes."
The You and the I
In many of her best songs, Barnett tells stories about her own life. A medical incident in Avant Gardener, a trip to an open home she can't afford in Depreston, the general suburban malaise of Rae Street. But the inward focus is not always intentional.
"I think that sometimes when I do look out, or write something for someone else, or to someone else, it often makes its way back around to me somehow," she says.
"Whether that's putting myself in someone's shoes or finding some kind of level of connection or empathy or something. I don't know. But I often end up talking to myself in a weird roundabout way."
And if you see yourself in Barnett's songs, you're right. If you reckon she's singing about you, she's not going to argue.
"The 'you' and the 'me' and the 'I'… it's kind of interchangeable," she says.
"In some songs, I might be addressing multiple people or things in my head, but it might sound like it's to just one person."
Of course, the song and its intent don't necessarily belong to its creator. Perhaps music's most magical power is allowing us to interpret it how we feel, and project our own emotions and life onto it.
"It's why I don't like over explaining meanings of songs, I don't always find it necessary," Barnett says.
"I love learning what old songs are about and the story that is behind some old classic song, but also, it's nice that we get to project our own stuff onto music. I think that's really beautiful."
Making connections with those who see themselves in her songs brings the purpose of her endeavours into sharpest focus.
"I was just thinking of moments in my life where someone has come up to me and said exactly that. They've been the moments where I have really truly felt that connection. I'm really grateful for that," she says.
"I think it's sometimes it's so hard to know… you're just sitting in your room making music and then it goes on the internet and there's comments and all that stuff…
"But sometimes it doesn't really connect until a human says that or I play a show and I see people singing along or having an emotional moment. That's extremely powerful. I'm really grateful for those moments."
Courtney Barnett plays Brisbane on Wednesday before shows in Sydney and Melbourne on Friday and Saturday.
Creature Of Habit is out now.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 13 Chinese military aircraft, seven naval vessels, and two official ships between 6 a.m. on Friday and the same time Saturday.
In response, aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems were deployed. Six of the People’s Liberation Army aircraft sorties crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern, central and southwestern air defense identification zones, according to the ministry.
This month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 200 times and ships 354 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

Kazakhstan joins 5th UNESCO Global Forum against Racism and Discrimination
Ambassador of the Republic of Kazakhstan to the Kingdom of the Netherlands Akan Rakhmetullin participated in the 5th UNESCO Global Forum against Racism and Discrimination, held in The Hague on 29–30 October 2026, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of the Kazakh Foreign Ministry.
The Forum was organised jointly by the Government of the Netherlands and UNESCO under the theme “From Commitment to Accountability: Change the System, Change the Future.”
The opening ceremony was attended by His Majesty King Willem-Alexander of the Netherlands, Prime Minister of the Netherlands Rob Jetten, high-level representatives of UNESCO, the European Commission and the United Nations, as well as prominent international advocates engaged in combating racism and discrimination.
Bringing together representatives from more than 85 countries, the Forum served as an important international platform for discussing efforts to combat racism, discrimination and intolerance, promote equality, protect human rights and strengthen social cohesion. The Forum placed particular emphasis on translating political commitments into concrete measures to prevent discrimination and foster inclusive societies.
Kazakhstan's participation in the Forum reflects the country's national policy aimed at strengthening interethnic and interfaith harmony, ensuring equal rights for all citizens and promoting a culture of mutual respect. An important role in advancing these principles is played by the Kazakhstan People's Council, which contributes to strengthening social harmony and civic unity.
The Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions, initiated by Kazakhstan, makes a significant contribution to advancing international dialogue on tolerance and mutual respect. In particular, the 8th Congress, held in Astana in September 2025, reaffirmed the continued relevance of this platform in promoting interreligious understanding, countering intolerance and fostering a culture of peace.
These efforts were further advanced through the 2nd Joint Colloquium between Kazakhstan and the Holy See, dedicated to protecting the rights and dignity of vulnerable children, as well as the 24th Meeting of the Secretariat of the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions, both held in Astana in October 2026. The discussions focused particularly on safeguarding human dignity, strengthening interreligious solidarity, addressing the ethical implications of artificial intelligence and highlighting the role of religious communities in responding to global challenges.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Erdoğan, known for using public speeches to convey political messages, chose a traditional blessing from a figure deeply respected in both Turkey and Azerbaijan.
He wished that mountains would never collapse, trees would never be cut down, rivers would never run dry and swords would never break in battle.
But it was the prayer’s final line, invoking protection from the treacherous, that carried particular resonance amid the growing rift between Ankara and Baku.
Was Erdoğan indirectly warning Aliyev about the partners on whom Azerbaijan has chosen to rely?
One possible reading points to Israel, whose close military, security and energy relationship with Azerbaijan contrasts sharply with Erdoğan’s position toward the Israeli government.
Erdoğan had personally invited Aliyev to the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS). Instead, the Azerbaijani president remained in Baku to attend a FIFA youth football awards ceremony, sending Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov in his place.
US Approves 500 Patriot Missiles for Ukraine, but Zelensky Warns Deliveries May Not Begin for Years
In his remarks, Erdoğan appealed for unity, declaring that there was no room for division or discord within the Turkic family.
A dialogue without naming names
The apparent exchange of messages began weeks earlier.
Speaking at the ruling New Azerbaijan Party’s congress on Oct. 2, Aliyev declared that his country would not tolerate outside interference.
“We need no one’s help or patronage,” he said, insisting that no country had helped Azerbaijan when it needed assistance.
He also claimed that Azerbaijan had purchased every weapon it used, sometimes paying several times the market price.
Aliyev did not name Turkey. But the remarks came amid growing criticism from Turkish political and religious circles over Azerbaijan’s restrictions on headscarves in schools.
The dispute escalated when Azerbaijan declared 31 Turkish nationals persona non grata over criticism posted on social media.
Erdoğan reportedly attempted to contain the controversy, including by dismissing an adviser who had publicly criticized Baku.
Nevertheless, Aliyev skipped the summit despite Erdoğan’s invitation.
His absence became particularly significant because Turkey was taking over the organization’s rotating chairmanship from Azerbaijan.
A victory Aliyev does not want to share
The headscarf controversy may have dominated headlines, but another source of resentment lies in competing narratives surrounding Azerbaijan’s victory in Karabakh.
For Aliyev, the military victory has become the defining achievement of his presidency.
Yet Turkey’s support was crucial. Ankara provided military training, defense equipment, political backing and diplomatic support during Azerbaijan’s confrontation with Armenia.
In July 2024, Erdoğan sparked anger in Baku by invoking Turkey’s involvement in Karabakh and Libya while discussing possible action against Israel.
“Just as we entered Karabakh, just as we entered Libya,” Erdoğan said.
Azerbaijan’s Defense Ministry responded by insisting that no foreign military personnel had participated in its combat operations.
The exchange exposed an uncomfortable disagreement over who could claim credit for the victory.
Azerbaijani troops fought the war, but Turkey’s contribution went well beyond commercial arms sales.
In his Oct. 2 speech, Aliyev reinforced his preferred narrative.
“We stood alone,” he declared, adding that Azerbaijan had purchased its weapons “down to the last bullet.”
He also claimed that suppliers had sometimes charged prices several times higher than international rates.
There is, however, a difference between paying for military equipment and having an ally willing to provide it, alongside training, political backing and diplomatic support.
For many Azerbaijanis, recognizing Turkey’s role does not diminish their country’s victory.
But Aliyev’s insistence that Azerbaijan accomplished everything alone raises a political question: Is he reluctant to share the defining achievement of his presidency with Erdoğan?
A victory acknowledged as a joint strategic achievement would inevitably give Turkey a place in the historical narrative – something Aliyev’s increasingly personalized portrayal of Karabakh leaves little room for.
Why distancing Azerbaijan from Turkey is difficult
Aliyev faces a particular challenge in diminishing Turkey’s contribution: the relationship between the two peoples is older and deeper than either president.
Turkey was the first country to recognize Azerbaijan’s independence in 1991. It closed its border with Armenia in 1993 in solidarity with Baku during the first Karabakh war and maintained that position for more than three decades.
For many Azerbaijanis, Turkey’s importance is rooted in shared language, culture, history and a longstanding sense of brotherhood.
That attachment cannot easily be redefined by government messaging.
Pro-government arguments that Azerbaijan paid for Turkish weapons do not erase Ankara’s political and military support.
Nor does criticism of Aliyev from Turkey necessarily amount to hostility toward Azerbaijan.
Attempts to minimize Ankara’s contribution risk deepening the divide between the government’s narrative and Azerbaijanis who remain grateful for Turkey’s historical support.
The Karabakh victory can be both an Azerbaijani military achievement and a success made possible, in part, by Turkey’s strategic partnership. The two are not mutually exclusive.
Armenia moves closer to Turkey as Baku looks elsewhere
The growing friction comes as Armenia, Azerbaijan’s longtime adversary, is pursuing closer relations with Ankara.
Turkey and Armenia have been negotiating the reopening of their shared border, closed in 1993.
Turkey has linked normalization to progress in Armenian-Azerbaijani peace efforts. Yet the diplomatic contrast is striking: Armenia is seeking closer engagement with Turkey while Aliyev publicly distances himself from Erdoğan.
Another unexpected development came on Oct. 23, when Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Baku – the first such visit in eight years.
Aliyev personally received Jaishankar, whose country has supplied weapons to Armenia and has historically had strained relations with Azerbaijan because of Baku’s close ties with Pakistan.
The talks on expanded cooperation raise questions about Aliyev’s priorities as relations with Turkey, Azerbaijan’s closest strategic ally, grow strained.
Israel adds another layer of tension
Azerbaijan’s close partnership with Israel remains another sensitive issue.
Erdoğan has emerged as one of Israel’s fiercest critics over the war in Gaza, while Aliyev maintains extensive defense, intelligence and energy ties with Israel.
Baku insists it has the right to choose its strategic partners, regardless of Ankara’s objections. In a Jan. 5 interview, Aliyev defended his government’s position, arguing that Palestine had failed to support Azerbaijan during its conflict with Armenia.
“With all due respect and sympathy for Palestine, Palestine did not particularly protect us either,” he said.
His remarks echoed accusations in Azerbaijani political circles that Palestinian leaders had sided with Armenia.
The partnership has also given Aliyev influential allies in Washington, where pro-Israel advocacy groups have backed his government despite concerns about its human rights record.
Israeli military technology has played an important role in Azerbaijan’s military development.
Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR has also faced repeated protests in Turkey over Azerbaijani oil reaching Israel through the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline, despite Ankara’s ban on direct trade with Israel.
Russia enters the picture
Friday’s summit produced another unexpected development.
Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed inviting Russia to participate in the Organization of Turkic States through its OTS+ format or as an observer.
Tokayev cited Russia’s historical ties with Turkic peoples and argued that cooperation with Moscow could strengthen the organization.
No agreement was announced, and Russian President Vladimir Putin received no formal invitation.
The proposal was particularly notable given Russia’s continuing invasion of Ukraine and Moscow’s longstanding efforts to preserve its influence across the former Soviet space.
As Turkey ties cool, Aliyev moves closer to Moscow
The growing distance between Baku and Ankara comes as Aliyev’s government appears to be rebuilding its relationship with the Kremlin, following a period of tensions over the downing of an Azerbaijani passenger aircraft by Russian air defenses on Dec. 25, 2024.
On April 15, 2026, Azerbaijan and Russia issued a joint statement declaring that they had reached a settlement over the consequences of the crash, including compensation. The two governments pledged to deepen cooperation within what they described as their allied relationship.
A more revealing development followed on Oct. 16.
Speaking at Russian Energy Week in Moscow (an event attended by Putin), Elshad Nasirov, vice president of Azerbaijan’s state energy company SOCAR, announced that Baku intended to resume purchasing natural gas from Russia’s Gazprom.
“We can proudly say that our cooperation with such a giant company as Gazprom is a very good example,” Nasirov said, according to Russia’s state-run TASS news agency.
The announcement coincided with a significant shift in Washington’s Russia sanctions policy. On the same day, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order waiving sanctions and tariffs under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
For years, Azerbaijan has sought to establish itself as an alternative energy supplier to Europe, helping reduce the continent’s dependence on Russian gas.
The political implications extend beyond energy.
For years, Azerbaijan’s participation in the Turkic world provided Aliyev with a diplomatic alternative to Russian-led integration projects, including the Eurasian Economic Union and its customs arrangements. Baku could cultivate strong relations with Moscow without formally joining Russia-dominated economic structures.
The Organization of Turkic States offered another political center of gravity, with Turkey as Azerbaijan’s principal strategic partner.
Now, as Aliyev’s relationship with Erdoğan cools and cooperation with Moscow gains renewed momentum, that balance appears to be shifting.

US execution survivor Christa Pike says she is now in ‘constant pain’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:42:14 UTC
12:42:14 KST

US execution survivor Christa Pike says she is now in ‘constant pain’
Pike, 50, is being held in solitary confinement and faces an uncertain future after surviving a failed lethal injection.
An American woman who survived an execution in a Tennessee prison has spoken out for the first time.
In a statement released via her legal team on Friday, Christa Pike, 50, said she is now in constant pain and struggling to speak.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Pike said, adding that the pain is both “physical and emotional”.
“I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” Pike said.
Pike and her boyfriend tortured, stabbed and beat a 19-year-old classmate to death in 1995. As Pike was 18 at the time, she was handed the death sentence.
The victim’s mother travelled from Florida to witness Pike’s execution.
Pike said she “continues to think” about the victim’s family and the “terrible pain and loss they have endured”.
Pike’s lawyers say the two separate doses of the lethal drug phenobarbital administered to her on September 30 may have failed to kill her because the drug did not enter her bloodstream. Instead, it pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.
Pike was hospitalised and unconscious for days following the botched execution.
Despite her ordeal, Pike remains scheduled to die, and is being held in solitary confinement in the interim.
Her legal team has asked a federal judge to allow her to interact with other prisoners, saying her isolation in the wake of the failed execution has caused “significant psychological harm and trauma”.
Her legal team has also asked Tennessee’s Republican Governor Bill Lee to change her sentence to life in prison.
Last week, however, Lee told reporters that he “suspects” her sentence will be the same as before, “unless otherwise determined by the courts”.
The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences.
The Tennessee governor has organised an independent review of the failed execution and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled for this year.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction, announced his resignation in the wake of Pike’s failed execution.

Day of reflection in Bulgaria ahead of presidential runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:39:34 UTC
12:39:34 KST

Saturday 31 October 2026 05:00
Saturday, 31 October 2026, 05:00
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
October 31 is the official day of reflection ahead of the runoff in Bulgaria's presidential and vice-presidential elections. Election campaigning and the publication of opinion polls related to the vote are prohibited on this day.
Voters have just a few hours remaining to decide which of the two presidential tickets that made it to the runoff they will support. Both were nominated by initiative committees.
With voter turnout standing at 22.98% in the first round, Iliana Iotova and Kiril Valchev received 528,951 votes (34.76%), while Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev secured the support of 486,232 voters (31.95%). The October 25 first round saw an unprecedentedly low turnout, with only 1,525,034 of the 6,584,025 eligible voters casting their ballots in Bulgaria and abroad. There are hopes that the two presidential tickets will succeed in boosting turnout in the runoff and attracting new supporters.
The main issues concerning Bulgarian society during the election campaign were the role of the presidential institution in the country's governance, security amid the ongoing war in Ukraine, relations with Russia, and Bulgaria's policies within the EU and NATO. The incidents involving the sinking of merchant ships near the Bulgarian coast have heightened concerns over security in the Black Sea. The rising cost of living, low incomes and the 2027 state budget have also been sources of concern for voters.
Designed to serve as a mediator and balancing force between the three main branches of government - the legislative, executive and judicial - the presidency holds consultations with parliamentary groups and hands out mandates to form a government. If the parties represented in parliament fail to agree on a government, the Constitution gives the head of state a key role in forming a caretaker cabinet.
In the first round of the presidential election, a candidate ticket must receive more than half of the votes cast, provided that voter turnout exceeds 50%, to be declared the winner. In the runoff, however, the winner is the candidate who receives the highest number of votes, regardless of voter turnout.
