The National Medical Commission is seeking applications for standing counsels aimed at bolstering its legal expertise.
New Delhi: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has invited applications from advocates to empanel 17 standing counsels to represent it before the Supreme Court, High Courts and their benches across the country, with preference for lawyers experienced in medical institution and medical negligence cases.According to an Expression of Interest (EOI) issued on October 30, the commission is seeking one standing counsel for the Supreme Court and 16 positions across various High Courts. These include two positions each at the Delhi High Court and Himachal Pradesh High Court, and one each at the Karnataka High Court's Bengaluru, Dharwad and Kalaburagi benches, Uttarakhand High Court at Nainital, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh High Court's Srinagar and Jammu benches, Rajasthan High Court's Jodhpur bench, Bombay High Court's Nagpur and Goa benches, Gauhati High Court's Kohima and Aizawl benches, and Jharkhand High Court at Ranchi.The eligibility criteria require applicants to be between 35 and 70 years of age as on November 1, 2026, registered with the concerned State Bar Council and to have completed at least 100 appearances before the Supreme Court or a High Court in the preceding three years. Applicants must also have a minimum of 10 years' experience handling constitutional, civil, criminal or educational institution matters before High Courts.
For the Supreme Court position, applicants must be Advocates-on-Record with at least 10 years of experience.The NMC has said preference will be given to advocates with experience in medical institution and medical negligence cases, as well as those who have handled cases involving government organisations, institutions, departments and public sector undertakings.The empanelled advocates will represent the commission in court, draft petitions, counter-affidavits and other legal documents, conduct legal research, provide legal opinions and coordinate with government departments. They will also be required to keep the commission updated on important developments and hearing dates and submit monthly and annual statements of cases handled and their outcomes.The empanelment will be for three years or until further orders, whichever is earlier, and may be extended based on performance. There will be no fixed retainer fee, with payments governed by the revised fee structure prescribed by the Department of Legal Affairs, Union law ministry.
Applications must be submitted in the prescribed format by November 30, 2026. The commission will scrutinise applications through a screening committee, followed by interviews of shortlisted candidates, either physically or virtually.

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:25:02 CST
11:25:02 KST

NEW DELHI, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched its next-generation navigation satellite NVS-03 aboard the GSLV-F18 rocket to boost the country's independent navigation system, Navigation with Indian Constellation, it confirmed on Saturday.
The launch took place at 11:51 p.m. local time on Friday from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in the Sriharikota area of the southern state of Andhra Pradesh.
"GSLV-F18 has successfully placed NVS-03 in the intended orbit. Congratulations," stated ISRO in a post on X.
Congratulating ISRO scientists on the feat, the country's Science and Technology Minister Jitendra Singh said in a post on X that this achievement reflects India's growing prowess in space technology and its unwavering commitment to strengthening sovereign indigenous navigation capabilities.
According to ISRO, the GSLV-F18 was the 20th flight of India's Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle. The third satellite in the next-generation navigation satellite system, the NVS-03, is envisaged to provide continuity of navigation services for the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System series. ■

Mainz struggled to create clear chances and conceded again in the 26th minute. David Mokwa carried the ball forward and released Onyeka, who held off Paul Nebel before finishing for his first Bundesliga goal.

Lukas Petkov fired wide in the 40th minute, and Krattenmacher made it 3-0 in first-half stoppage time after Zentner failed to clear Keidel's corner, leaving Krattenmacher to evade Nadiem Amiri and Nebel and drive a low finish into the corner.
Mainz coach Urs Fischer made four changes in the 63rd minute, bringing on Hollerbach, Silvan Widmer, Ransford-Yeboah Konigsdorffer and Lennard Maloney. Campbell added a fourth for Elversberg in stoppage time, controlling Nicholas Mickelson's cross on his chest before acrobatically finishing. Hollerbach immediately reduced the deficit from Konigsdorffer's low delivery, but Mainz substitute Stefan Posch was then sent off for a second booking and will miss the next league match.

World Bank calls for translating African urbanization into growth, jobs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:24:34 CST
11:24:34 KST

ABIDJAN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The World Bank (WB) has called on countries in sub-Saharan Africa to turn the region's rapid urbanization into a powerful engine of economic growth and job creation.
The region's urban population grew from 170 million in 1975 to 913 million in 2025 and is projected to reach 1.7 billion by 2050, the international financial institution said in a report, adding that around 15 million young people enter the region's labor market each year.
Sustained population growth in particular underscores the need for creating more jobs correspondingly for youth while expanding access to productive, better-paying employment, according to the report titled "Africa's Urban Awakening: Catalyzing Economic Growth and Job Creation," which was published Wednesday.
The Bank recommends better planning for urban expansion, targeted investment in infrastructure and transport, and stronger regulatory frameworks and land governance. It also calls for greater mobilization of private capital to finance urban facilities and services.
Marie-Chantal Uwanyiligira, WB division director for Cote d'Ivoire, Benin, Guinea and Togo, noted that currently in the region, "productivity gains remain limited, incomes have grown slowly, and too many jobs remain informal and poorly paid."
In Cote d'Ivoire, official data showed it had 17.84 million urban residents out of an estimated total population of 32.8 million last year. The number of localities with more than 100,000 inhabitants increased from eight in 1998 to 17 in 2021.
The West African country has prioritized urban development, mobility and improvements in people's living conditions in its 2026-2030 national development plan. ■

By Kanishka Singh
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s administration plans to deport some Afghan immigrants to Afghanistan, a US official and a coalition of veterans and advocacy groups said on Friday.
• Many facing removal fled Afghanistan after the 2021 Taliban takeover and US withdrawal, said Shawn VanDiver, head of #AfghanEvac.
• Some facing deportation are “brothers and sons of men who served alongside US forces, families the Taliban already has every reason to target,” VanDiver added.
• Over 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be deported, the New York Times reported, in one of the largest single expulsions of Afghans.
• The administration detained dozens of Afghan immigrants in Louisiana and plans to deport them, the newspaper said, adding the first flight is expected as soon as Monday.
• A US official said deportations would be via Pakistan. Washington cannot directly arrange deportations to Afghanistan as it lacks diplomatic ties with the Taliban.
• Trump says his immigration crackdown and deportation drive aim to improve domestic security.
• Rights advocates say the crackdown violates due process and free speech and has created an unsafe environment for minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
• The Homeland Security Department said it would not confirm future removal operations, citing operational security.
• VanDiver urged Congress to pass legislation granting Afghans in the US temporary protected status to protect them from deportation.
• Pakistan has expelled over 2 million Afghan nationals to Afghanistan since 2023.

Trump, Milei under pressure to explain Bolsonaro flight from Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:20:00 UTC
11:20:00 KST

Trump, Milei under pressure to explain Bolsonaro flight from Brazil
BRASILIA – US President Donald Trump and Argentina’s Javier Milei faced mounting pressure on Oct 30 to explain the role their countries played in helping Flavio Bolsonaro flee Brazil after he had his passports cancelled.
The 45-year-old Brazilian senator bolted his country two days after being defeated by incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a presidential election on Oct 25.
He had been ordered to surrender all his passports due to an ongoing investigation into him on suspicion of money-laundering.
However, he left the country in a cloak-and-dagger operation via Argentina and Ecuador, and landed in Florida on Oct 28, where he declared himself the rightful “leader” of Brazil.
Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat after his loss, which came as a shock after he won a first-round election and had been seen as the narrow favourite.
According to the Argentine migration authority, Bolsonaro boarded a private plane on the evening of Oct 27 in north-eastern Puerto Iguazu, 40 minutes after entering Argentina by land.
While Bolsonaro’s Brazilian passport and diplomatic passport had been cancelled, he also holds an Italian passport, which he used to board a private jet in Argentina, according to a flight document seen by AFP.
A Brazilian diplomatic source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Argentina’s diplomatic representative had been summoned for a “routine meeting” to “provide explanations” on Oct 29.
Brasilia recalled its ambassador and downgraded diplomatic ties with Buenos Aires in August after repeated insults from Milei, who called Lula “a thief” and “corrupt”.
Argentina’s Foreign Minister on Oct 30 denied that Brazil had asked Buenos Aires to explain its role in Bolsonaro’s flight.
“False. There was no request for information,” Pablo Quirno wrote on social media platform X.
Outliers in not accepting result
Bolsonaro thanked Milei and Trump in his first statement after fleeing the country.
Milei has not recognised Lula’s election victory and Trump said the poll was a “disgrace” and “very strange”.
However, Lula’s victory has been recognised by global leaders from across the political spectrum, Brazil’s electoral court, Bolsonaro’s own party – which holds a majority in Congress – and other right-wing allies.
In the United States, Democrat lawmakers wrote a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio to request “an immediate accounting” of his department’s role in helping Bolsonaro leave Brazil.
Luis Grande, head of the Baires Fly airline that carried Bolsonaro, told AFP on Oct 29 that he had been hired by a broker “who lives in the United States”.
Some US media, including The New York Times and the Wall Street Journal, have reported that the plane was chartered by Jason Miller, an adviser to Trump.
The White House has not commented on the matter.
‘Difficult times’
Bolsonaro, who is the son of former far-right leader Jair Bolsonaro, has found himself isolated and the object of ridicule at home, after his departure and proclamation that he would lead the opposition from abroad.
Speculation has switched almost immediately to who would lead the right with Flavio out of the country, and the future of the Bolsonaro movement.
Jair Bolsonaro, 71, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup against Lula after his 2022 election loss.
His wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was just elected senator, released a statement on Instagram on Oct 30 referring to Jair Bolsonaro as “our leader”.
“We are living through difficult times. We need to reflect and only then act,” she wrote.
“My husband stresses that this is a time for unity, not for looking for people to blame,” she said. AFP

The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn, but Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned deliveries could take years and stockpiles were needed now to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the US state department said in a statement on Friday.
The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision by the US state department” but said in a post on X early on Saturday: “However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors.
“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.”
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Zelenskyy said US and European allies had sufficient stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to provide to Ukraine now, which could be replenished in the coming years through contracts already paid for by Ukraine and its partners.
He said this would “be the right approach” and was “entirely feasible”.
Delayed missile deliveries have added to Kyiv’s tensions with Washington after US president Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will probably not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense was encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US Jumpstart, along with national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, the state department said in a statement.
The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defense and precision-guided weapons.

Inside fraternities and why they are so important to US colleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:15:56 UTC
11:15:56 KST

What are frats and why is one at the centre of rape allegations at Cornell University?
New York state police have announced they will take charge of future sexual assault investigations at Cornell University in the latest fallout over the university's handling of an alleged gang rape on campus.
It comes as the university's faculty undertook a vote of no confidence in the school's administration over how it handled the allegation, with the results expected on November 6.
The alleged Cornell University incident in 2024 is not isolated, with the Associated Press reporting police were investigating allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity party at the University of Chicago on October 11.
A female student at the University of Arizona alleged she was sexually assaulted by two men at a fraternity house on August 26, according to AP.
A few weeks later, on October 8, the University of Arizona suspended fraternity activity after reports of hazing and sexual misconduct.
According to the AP, previous hazing at the university's fraternities included forcing new members to consume large quantities of alcohol, as well as live goldfish.
Australian attitudes to fraternities, also known as frats, have been mostly shaped by popular culture, but what are fraternities really? And why are they so ingrained in higher education in the US?
What are fraternities?
Social fraternities or sororities are exclusive clubs for undergraduate students who can live together, socialise together and participate in traditions, usually in a same-sex environment.
Kimberly Davis, data analyst at Pennsylvania State University's Piazza Centre for Fraternity and Sorority Research, said fraternities were "often built around a shared identity" and members could maintain fraternity relationships "long after graduation".
"For some students, that level of connection is especially appealing during a period of life that can feel uncertain and transitional,"
Dr Davis said.
The first fraternity-like organisation was founded in 1776 at the College of William and Mary in Virginia, but they became much more popular across the US by the mid 1800s, according to Dr Davis.
Why are fraternities so important to US universities?
Dr Davis said on a practical level, fraternities provided additional residential options for university campuses.
She said fraternities were also "valuable partners" for universities to foster leadership development, student involvement in community activities, service and philanthropy.
"The friendships and communities that fraternities create also offer benefits for universities," she said.
"Alumni who have favourable fraternity experiences often associate their experiences with the university, which in turn encourages alumni to stay connected to the institution through alumni mentor ship and financial donations."
What are the problems with frats?
Loading...
According to a 2019 survey by the Association of American Universities, 10 per cent of undergraduate women who reported being raped said the incident occurred at a fraternity house, and 20 per cent of women reporting unwanted sexual touching said it occurred in a fraternity house.
6.4 per cent of men and 6.7 per cent of transgender, gender queer or questioning students who reported being raped said the incident occurred in a fraternity house, and just under 10 per cent of men and 12.6 per cent queer students reported unwanted sexual touching.
Dr Davis said fraternities did not contribute to a culture of sexual violence by design, but "that does not mean that fraternity environments cannot contribute to risk".
"Some organisational environments can normalise attitudes and behaviours that increase the risk of sexual violence," she said.
"A chapter that prioritises accountability, healthy relationships, and intervention can create a very different environment from one that normalises excessive alcohol use or tolerates harmful behaviour."
As well as sexual assault allegations, fraternities are also often associated with hazing.
The University of Colorado defines hazing as any activity that humiliates, degrades, abuses, or endangers someone, regardless of consent, as condition for entering an organisation.
The Pennsylvania State University Piazza Centre is named after student Timothy Piazza, who died as the result of a hazing incident at the university's Beta Theta Pi fraternity.
Mr Piazza was given at least 18 drinks in 82 minutes, according to prosecutors, and fell down the fraternity house stairs, becoming unconscious.
He later died from a head injury after a delayed response by bystanders.
"Timothy Piazza was one of four IFC fraternity men who died in hazing incidents in 2017 alone; that was an especially deadly year and the catalyst for many revised state hazing laws,"
Dr Davis said
Hazing prevention organisation HazingInfo's database indicates about five deaths per year have been reported in the US since 2000.
Do we have anything like them in Australia?
In Australia, the frat niche is filled by residential colleges, which provide accommodation, meals, academic support and social activities for residents.
Southern Cross University professor Elizabeth Mackinlay said instances of sexual harassment, assault and violence persisted at Australian residential colleges.
She said under-reporting continued at a concerning level, because students feared potential consequences for them and those responsible.
Professor Mackinlay said what Australian residential colleges and US fraternities had in common was hazing.
Hazing, abuse and misogyny have been reported at some residential colleges, including at Sydney University when, in 2018, allegations emerged of sexual assault, excessive alcohol consumption and other incidents.
In 2024, the City of Sydney council recommended the abolition of the University of Sydney's Residential Colleges after an incident at St Paul's College "where 6 students were expelled and a further 21 suspended after engaging in acts of 'serious humiliation' and sexual violence against a student".
Professor Mackinlay said the issues reported at Cornell University, the University of Arizona and St Paul's College she experienced herself during her time at university in the late 80s and 90s.
"The alcohol abuse, the degradation, rape, everything happened," she said.
"Nobody reported it. Leadership in the student group took part."
Professor Mackinlay said the culture of hazing and alcohol abuse had to change and "cultural norms around respectful relationships have to be in place and reinforced".
"If there's gender-based violence, there's a good chance that you're going to have to sit at the breakfast table in halls the next morning with the perpetrator there," she said.

French economy ‘headed straight for a wall’ – finance minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:15:05 UTC
11:15:05 KST

French economy ‘headed straight for a wall’ – finance minister
France is “headed straight for a wall” unless it reins in its budget deficit, Finance Minister Roland Lescure has warned, as the country’s economy contracts and inflation accelerates.
Gross domestic product fell by 0.1% in the third quarter, following stagnation in the previous three months and a 0.2% decline at the start of the year, the national statistics agency reported on Friday. Annual inflation climbed to 3.4% in October from 3.1% in September, its highest level since January 2024.
Lescure also described the economy as being “at a standstill,” underscoring the mounting financial challenges facing President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
The downturn extended across key sectors. Exports dropped 1.7%, largely due to weaker overseas aerospace sales, while investment fell 0.6%. Manufacturing output declined 1.4%, with automobile production shrinking for the fourth consecutive quarter.
France is also struggling with public debt equivalent to roughly 119% of GDP and a substantial budget deficit. Government borrowing costs climbed following Friday’s figures, with yields on ten-year bonds approaching 5%, raising concerns about the cost of servicing the country’s debt.
The deteriorating outlook has increased pressure on Macron, whose government is pursuing spending cuts while boosting military expenditure and weapons deliveries to Kiev. France increased its 2026 military budget by €6.7 billion ($7.5 billion) despite its mounting debt.
The government’s austerity policies have also fueled nationwide unrest that began in September with protests over staff shortages and deteriorating conditions at a high school near Paris. The demonstrations quickly spread, with thousands of students demanding more education funding and accusing the authorities of prioritizing weapons over schools.
The unrest escalated into violence, with rioters looting shops, setting vehicles ablaze and damaging the historic city hall in Limoges. Thousands were arrested and hundreds injured.
The protests have drawn comparisons with the 2018 Yellow Vest movement, which challenged Macron’s economic policies. Activists, students and trade unions have called for fresh demonstrations on Saturday, prompting authorities to mobilize 70,000 security personnel nationwide. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder.
Macron has blamed the purchasing-power crisis on the US-Israeli war against Iran, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and surging fuel prices. He has also accused social media platforms of “damaging democracy” by circulating footage of protests and riots.
With the 2027 presidential election approaching, the economic downturn and continuing unrest have further weakened Macron’s position, complicating efforts to secure parliamentary approval for a deficit-cutting budget.

Flesh-eating Buruli ulcer cases are rising. Here's how to protect yourself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:13:29 UTC
11:13:29 KST

Flesh-eating Buruli ulcer cases are rising in Victoria and NSW. Here's how to protect yourself
It starts as a small, painless lump on the skin that is easy to ignore.
But under the seemingly innocuous lump, flesh-eating bacteria are burrowing through fat and muscle.
Warning: Readers are advised that this article includes an image of an open wound.
The skin over the lump then dies, turns black and eventually becomes an open sore that, if untreated, grows.
This is a typical case of Buruli ulcer, a condition that until recently was primarily found in West Africa.
Victoria is now considered the Buruli ulcer centre of the world, with a record 426 confirmed cases last year.
Buruli ulcer is typically acquired in summer and autumn.
It is endemic in the Mornington Peninsula, Bellarine Peninsula, Geelong and some Melbourne suburbs.
It is also found in other parts of Australia: pockets of coastal Queensland, where it is sometimes called Daintree ulcer, and around Darwin.
Most recently, cases have popped up on the New South Wales south coast around Batemans Bay.
Visitors to these popular tourism areas might unknowingly get infected, go home and, months later, develop a Buruli ulcer where local doctors may not be aware of the condition.
So, coming into summer holidays, how can you protect yourself from the disease?
What causes Buruli ulcer?
Buruli ulcer is caused by the microbe Mycobacterium ulcerans.
It can be transmitted to humans via mosquitoes, so ulcers usually appear in areas near bites, such as on arms and legs.
Loading...
Once in the skin, the bacteria secrete a cocktail of molecules that numb the area, slowly kill surrounding tissues and suppress the immune system.
"These things make it quite an impressive pathogen, and often, it's been there for a while before people actually know they've got it," Daniel O'Brien, an infectious diseases physician at Barwon Health in Geelong and Royal Melbourne Hospital, says.
The progression of lump to ulcer happens in about 90 per cent of Buruli ulcer cases he sees.
In less than 1 per cent of cases, the bacteria reach bone.
How is Buruli ulcer diagnosed and treated?
Buruli ulcer advances so slowly that the first symptoms usually are not noticed until five or six months after the infection.
It is diagnosed by sending a swab off for PCR testing to see whether the ulcer contains M. ulcerans bacteria.
Treatment starts with a six-to-eight-week course of antibiotics, but the drugs themselves can be problematic. They interact with many other medications and produce side effects so awful that about 20 per cent of patients cannot finish the whole course.
Dr O'Brien is leading a team trialling a new antibiotic that can be taken over just 10 days, which he says is less harsh on the body, yet still effective against M. ulcerans.
For most people, antibiotics will be enough, but if there is too much tissue damage or the wound is not healing properly, surgery is needed.
Even with treatment and good wound care, it can take months — even a year — for an ulcer to fully heal.
Dr O'Brien says outcomes for patients are generally better if the ulcer is diagnosed early.
For that reason, he recommends getting a health practitioner to look at any suspicious lumps sooner rather than later, especially if you live or holidayed in an area known to have the bacterium, and to specifically ask about Buruli ulcer.
How can I protect myself from Buruli ulcer?
While Buruli ulcer prevalence is rising, Dr O'Brien says it is important to remember that the disease is still uncommon in humans.
"If you protect yourself from the environment … you really minimise your risk of acquisition."
While mosquitoes are a main source of Buruli ulcers, they are not the only one.
Brushtail and ringtail possums are also known to get infected, and can develop nasty ulcers on their paws, face and tail.
A 2025 study found that analysing the poo of possums could help predict regions where Buruli ulcer might crop up next, with human cases usually appearing up to three years after the first positive possum poo test.
That is because possums shed the bacteria in droppings, introducing it to the soil, which can then get into cuts in our skin.
Dr O'Brien's advice is to:
- cover up as much as possible
- wear mosquito repellent on exposed skin
- cover any wounds while handling soil, and if you injure yourself, wash it immediately with soap and water, then apply antiseptic
- avoid handling sick or injured possums
A recent study found reducing mosquito numbers in Buruli ulcer areas also lowered human case numbers, so it is a good idea to tip out standing water where mosquitoes breed and put out mosquito traps.
It is also important to note that research shows not all possums in Buruli-endemic areas carry the bacteria, and it is illegal to trap, relocate or cull possums without a licence.
And, in good news for ringtails and bushies, an edible possum vaccine in the works could help reduce infections and ulcers in the future.
Hear more about Buruli ulcer on Outbreaks, a special series on Science Friction.

Ukraine’s efforts to manufacture American-made Patriot interceptor missiles domestically have encountered another obstacle, with the Pentagon opting for “further review” rather than granting the licensing authorization Kyiv has been seeking.
The response leaves Ukraine without a confirmed agreement or timetable for producing the critical air defense interceptors on its own territory, even as Russia continues its missile attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The development follows Washington’s approval Friday, Oct. 30, of a proposed $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) interceptors to Ukraine.
But President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that the newly approved missiles might not begin arriving for several years, highlighting the widening gap between Ukraine’s immediate defensive requirements and Western weapons production schedules.
“It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelensky wrote on X.
He urged Washington and European allies to release interceptors from their existing inventories, with newly manufactured missiles replacing them later.
The Pentagon’s decision to keep the licensing request under review raises a separate question: whether Ukraine will eventually be allowed to manufacture the weapons itself rather than remain dependent on overseas production and deliveries.
Russia Strikes Kharkiv With Jet-Powered Shahed Drone, Injuring 3, Damaging 10 Homes
No authorization or timeline for production in Ukraine
Ukraine has repeatedly sought to expand domestic weapons production as part of its broader effort to reduce dependence on foreign military assistance.
Manufacturing Patriot interceptors domestically would be a significant step toward that objective, potentially allowing Kyiv to build a more sustainable supply of missiles needed to counter Russian ballistic attacks.
However, the Pentagon’s response of “further review” does not constitute approval, nor does it establish when a decision might be made.
Production would require more than political authorization. It would involve licensing agreements, technology-transfer arrangements, industrial investment and the participation of the American companies responsible for manufacturing the interceptors and their components.
The PAC-3 MSE is produced by Lockheed Martin, while Boeing manufactures its advanced seeker components.
Even if Washington approved Ukrainian production, building the necessary manufacturing capabilities would take time and would not immediately resolve the country’s current shortage.
Lockheed Martin confirms ‘deep’ talks on overseas production
Lockheed Martin has acknowledged that it is exploring international manufacturing partnerships as demand for Patriot interceptors rises sharply.
In an exclusive interview with Kyiv Post, Dan Tenney, Lockheed Martin’s senior vice president for global business development and strategy, revealed that the company was engaged in advanced discussions with several countries about expanding production overseas.
“We are in pretty deep discussions on this,” Tenney said when asked about the prospect of international production partnerships.
He declined to identify the countries involved or confirm whether Ukraine was among them.
The company has outlined plans to expand annual PAC-3 MSE production capacity to approximately 2,000 interceptors by the end of 2030, compared with roughly 600 annually at the beginning of the expansion effort.

'Dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists': PM Modi hails ISRO after successful GSLV-F18 launch carrying NVS-03
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:04:02 UTC
11:04:02 KST

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday congratulated Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) scientists and engineers following the successful launch of the GSLV-F18 mission carrying the NVS-03 navigation satellite, saying the mission would strengthen India's indigenous satellite navigation system, NavIC.In a post on X, PM Modi said, "Congratulations to our scientists and engineers at ISRO on the successful launch of GSLV-F18 carrying NVS-03.
Also read: Success launch of navigation sat NVS-03 with desi atomic clock will make NaVIC up & running, and give military strategic independenceThis mission marks an important step in strengthening NavIC, our indigenous satellite navigation system. Equipped with enhanced capabilities, NVS-03 will further our pursuit of self-reliance in critical technologies and support navigation services that benefit our people.The dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists continue to make our nation proud."
The successful launch is expected to strengthen India's strategic autonomy by helping restore the operational capabilities of NavIC, India's indigenous alternative to global navigation systems such as the US-operated GPS and Russia's GLONASS.The NVS-03 satellite carries an indigenously developed atomic clock, alongside imported atomic clocks, marking an important step towards reducing India's dependence on foreign technologies for satellite-based navigation.
Atomic clocks provide highly precise time signals that are essential for determining location, navigation and timing.NavIC, which was originally designed around a seven-satellite constellation, had been operating with only three active satellites, below the minimum requirement of four satellites for standalone positioning services. This had limited its use for critical applications, including military navigation, precision positioning and coordination of naval assets.An operational NavIC constellation is particularly important for India's armed forces, which require reliable Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) signals for missile guidance, precision-guided weapons, troop movement, combat aircraft and naval operations.Dependence on foreign navigation networks can pose strategic vulnerabilities during conflicts, as access to such services could potentially be restricted or disrupted. India experienced the limitations of relying on foreign satellite navigation systems during the 1999 Kargil war.With NVS-03, India aims to strengthen the availability of indigenous navigation services for both civilian and strategic applications. NavIC is designed to provide coverage across India and up to 1,500 km beyond its geographical boundaries.
The original NavIC constellation comprised seven satellites supported by a network of ground stations operating round the clock. Three satellites were placed in geostationary orbit, while four were placed in inclined geosynchronous orbits.However, the constellation's operational strength declined over time as ageing satellites could not be replaced as planned. The launch of NVS-02 on January 29, 2025, also failed to deliver the intended results after a pyro valve signal loss in the engine prevented the satellite from reaching its designated orbit.The successful deployment of NVS-03 is expected to address some of these operational limitations and strengthen India's efforts to establish an independent satellite navigation capability.

The CCD advises against clicking links in emails about "debts" and downloading unknown archives.
"Check bills only on the official resources of service providers," the CCD added.

European diplomats shun Russia at G20 gathering in the US

European diplomats shun Russia at G20 gathering in the US
October 31, 2026
A Group of 20 foreign ministers' meeting in the US city of Atlanta got off to a rocky start on Friday after top diplomats from European nations refused to take a "family photo" along with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is hosting the gathering, decided to scrap the photo before the meeting got underway because Washington didn't want it to become a spectacle or distraction.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters before the first session on Friday that there wouldn't "be a family photo with European partners and Mr. Lavrov together because ... there is no normalcy with Russia."
The two-day gathering of the G20 grouping, which includes the EU, Russia, Germany, India, China, Brazil and other major countries, is meant to be a precursor to a G20 leaders summit later this December.
That G20 leaders meeting in December is set to be hosted by US President Donald Trump at his golf club in Miami.
Rubio stresses unity despite fractures
Rubio still opened the talks by stressing unity on major issues, telling his counterparts that they were in a "critical moment."
"We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises," he said.
He pointed to disruptions to global energy and trade and said many were posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order."
But several countries, including the United States and Russia, are involved in separate wars. Wars in Iran and Ukraine have resulted in a spike in food prices for people around the world.
While the message is about unity and finding solutions to problems like freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz during the G20 meeting, the reality is that finding common ground will likely be much tougher.
Given a renewed momentum to revive talks to end the war in Ukraine, there was also interest in getting Lavrov to talk about Russia's stance on future talks with Kyiv.
Russia willing to meet Zelenskyy in Moscow, Lavrov tells DW
The US has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 meeting in Miami, but it's unclear whether Russia has accepted the invitation.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has previously said that he would be open to traveling to Miami to hold talks with Putin if he were also there.
The Kremlin has so far declined direct meetings with Zelenskyy, with Russia's Sergey Lavrov telling DW on the sidelines of the meeting that Putin is willing to meet with the Ukrainian leader if he travels to Moscow.
"President Putin said if he [Zelenskyy] is willing to meet, let him come to Moscow," Lavrov said. "We will guarantee his safety."
Lavrov declined to say whether Putin will attend the G20 summit this December.
Putin has not attended a G20 leaders meeting since 2019 and only attended a session virtually in 2023.
Russia has also continued with its attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, stepping up drone strikes on water and energy infrastructure.
EU top diplomat calls out Lavrov's 'lies'
The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said ministers at the G20 meeting were able to call out Lavrov for his "lies" at the table.
"We were talking about the big geopolitical crises, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergey Lavrov head-on with this," Kallas said on the sidelines of the meeting.
"Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives that we were also able to then rebuke," she said.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also called out Lavrov, saying, "If we are serious about our values and our interests, we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine."
Lavrov says no easing of ties with US, 'no illusions' about diesel deal
Lavrov, who is under international sanctions for Russia's war in Ukraine, was invited to the US at a time when the two countries have appeared to have fostered warmer ties.
Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia earlier this month and also waived new sanctions on Russia's energy. The US announced the move just weeks away from the midterm elections on November 3.
Lavrov said on Friday that despite those efforts, "in practice, no real progress in relations with the US has so far been seen."
South Africa, a founding member of G20, excluded from US meeting
The Trump administration has been embroiled in disputes with South Africa, having imposed visa restrictions on South Africanswho it said were complicit in discriminating against white people.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year because US officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group.
But US officials didn't extend that invite to South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group.
"We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary," said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.
With this many issues on the table, it appeared less likely that there would be a joint consensus at the end of the talks.
Instead of a final declaration, the AFP news agency reported, the meeting is expected to end on Saturday with a chair summary drafted by the US.
Additional reporting from Benjamin Alvarez Gruber.

Is it legal to recruit spoiler candidates in US elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:46:00 UTC
10:46:00 KST

Is it legal to recruit spoiler candidates in US elections?
- The Justice Department is investigating claims that Democrats recruited spoiler candidates in Alaska’s Senate race. The case could affect certification if Republican Senator Daniel S. Sullivan loses narrowly.
- Legal experts say the DOJ faces a weak case because election rules are mainly set by states. A judge may rule soon on whether the lawsuit should be dismissed.
- Possible charges include conspiracy against rights, fraud, dishonesty, civil rights breaches and perjury. Experts say many “dirty tricks” are legal, but tricking voters may be different.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Justice Department is investigating allegations that Democrats recruited potential spoiler candidates to run in Alaska’s US Senate race, and has asked a US judge to prevent certification of the vote if incumbent Republican Senator Daniel S. Sullivan loses narrowly.
The race, in which Democratic former US representative Mary Peltola is challenging Sullivan, could prove critical for determining the balance of power in the Senate in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans are battling to maintain majorities in both chambers.
Here is an explanation of the legal issues at play and why the Justice Department will face challenges in its civil lawsuit or any criminal case.
What is the state of the Alaska race?
Alaska’s ranked-choice ballot will feature Sullivan, Peltola, a retired teacher whose name is also Daniel Sullivan, and another long-shot candidate.
Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Peltola’s aides worked with the campaign’s lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats’ campaign arm to recruit the retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan.
Reuters has not verified the report.
Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted, and Alaska’s Republican governor Mike Dunleavy has ordered a state law enforcement investigation.
Neither Trump nor Dunleavy specified which laws they believed may have been violated.
A Justice Department official said no charging decision had been made.
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement and said Republicans had also propped up other candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns.
Daniel J. Sullivan has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
Peltola’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Its lawyers have asked US District Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit, arguing the federal government lacks the legal authority to bring the case.
Alaska’s ballot will indicate that Daniel S. Sullivan is the incumbent.
Could the Times report affect the outcome of the DOJ lawsuit?
The Justice Department case seeking to prevent certification of election results if the incumbent Daniel S. Sullivan loses by a slim margin is pending.
The department plans to seek a preliminary injunction, Michael Heyman, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska, told reporters on Oct 30.
Alaska’s elections regulator earlier in 2026 blocked Daniel J. Sullivan from appearing on the ballot, finding that his candidacy was not filed in good faith and was instead an attempt to “confuse or mislead.”
State courts later restored him to the ballot, ruling that there was not enough evidence that he was trying to confuse voters and that there was no requirement under Alaska law that a candidacy be in good faith.
Legal experts have said the Justice Department’s case is weak because the US Constitution clearly assigns the responsibility for administering elections to the states, not the federal government.
Joshua Douglas, a law professor at the University of Kentucky, said the reporting asserting that Democrats helped recruit spoiler candidates was unlikely to help the Justice Department’s case.
“Regardless of who encouraged him to run, the second Dan Sullivan validly qualified for the ballot. And this is a matter of state law,” Douglas said.
Gleason’s decision on Peltola’s motion to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit could come as soon as Oct 31, though it is not certain when she will rule.
What criminal laws could be at play?
Legal experts said the Justice Department could seek to bring a criminal case under a federal statute that makes it illegal for any two people to conspire to deprive anyone of their constitutional rights, including the right to vote.
The law, originally passed in 1871 to combat the Ku Klux Klan, makes it illegal to conspire to “injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate any person” to prevent them from exercising a right.
In addition, if anyone lied under oath in earlier state-level litigation over whether Dan J. Sullivan could appear on the ballot, they could be prosecuted for perjury, UCLA law professor Rick Hasen wrote in an Oct 8 blog post.
A Justice Department official said the conduct under investigation could implicate statutes prohibiting fraud, dishonesty, and deprivations of civil rights.
Would any prosecution be viable?
Hasen said any federal criminal prosecution under the conspiracy-against-rights statute would likely fail because the free speech guarantees in the First Amendment to the US Constitution would likely protect the right to run for office with “impure motives.”
Michael Fragoso, a former lawyer for Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, said “dirty tricks” – such as one major party trying to help a fringe candidate win over voters from the other major party – were generally legal.
But he said convincing voters they were voting for their preferred candidate when they were not was different.
“It’s suppressing disfavoured votes by tricking voters into thinking that they’re voting one way when in fact, they aren’t,” Fragoso, now a fellow at the Washington-based think tank Ethics and Public Policy Centre, wrote in an Oct 28 blog post in the National Review.
Is there any legal precedent?
In a case brought by the Justice Department under Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration, a social media influencer was convicted in 2023 in Brooklyn federal court of conspiring against civil rights by using social media posts to spread false information about the 2016 election to help Trump win.
The Manhattan-based 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals in 2025 overturned that conviction, finding a lack of evidence he conspired with anyone.
The appeals court’s decision did not address the influencer’s argument that the First Amendment would protect speech deceiving voters. REUTERS

Jewish leaders for social change: Nine of history's most influential Jewish activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:40:57 UTC
10:40:57 KST

Jews are part of history and have made history, enriching the social, cultural, and scientific composition of mankind well out of proportion to their minuscule numbers.
The revolutionary Jewish innovation of monotheism, with its accompanying ethical principles, has contributed the highest values cherished by mankind: respect for life, justice, equality, peace, love, education, and social responsibility. From the beginning, the Jewish people have been improving the world and enriching lives at the forefront of virtually every major advance, cause, or social movement in world history.
Here are nine of them:
Lewis Gompertz and animal rights
Lewis Gompertz was an English writer and early animal rights advocate. He opposed animal suffering and argued it was morally wrong to kill animals or use them in ways (such as experimentation) that did not benefit the animals themselves. He avoided all animal products and even refused to travel by coach because of the exploitation of horses.
Gompertz set out his views in Moral Inquiries on the Situation of Man and of Brutes, published in 1824, later characterized as the most important work on the subject until the late 20th century. He was a founding member of the English Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (later the RSPCA), the world’s oldest animal welfare charity, and was appointed the society’s secretary.
He was forced to resign in 1832 as a resolution was adopted that “the proceedings of the Society were entirely based on the Christian faith and Christian principles.” He then co-founded the Animals’ Friend Society, which temporarily surpassed the RSPCA in membership. Many of Gompertz’s arguments remain relevant today to contemporary ethical debate.
Adolphe Cremieux, French defender of Jews
Adolphe Crémieux was a French lawyer, politician, and tireless defender of social justice and minority rights – above all, those of French Jews.
His first major struggle was to abolish the more Jewish oath that Jews were obliged to take since the Middle Ages in legal proceedings with non-Jews. Although equality of rights had been granted in 1791 to all French Jews, this humiliating discrimination had still been in force.
In 1840, Crémieux collaborated with Sir Moses Montefiore to successfully defend and liberate Jews falsely accused in the Damascus blood libel. Afterwards, fearful that accusations of ritual murder would be repeated, they convinced the Turkish Sultan to publish an edict protecting Jews of the Ottoman Empire against all manner of slander.
Crémieux served as justice minister in 1848 and again from 1870-1871. He secured decrees that instituted freedom of the press, association, and worship; abolished imprisonment for debt, ended punishment by public humiliation, reestablished the legality of divorce, abolished the death penalty for political crimes, granted French citizenship to the indigenous Jewish population of Algeria, and ended slavery in all French colonies, for which some have called him the “French Abraham Lincoln.”
Crémieux also founded the Alliance Israelite Universelle, which sought to protect the rights of Jews worldwide and established Jewish schools in countries of the Ottoman Empire. By 1900, it operated more than 100 schools in seven countries.
Baron de Rothschild and the right of Jews to a homeland
Baron Edmond de Rothschild, head of the French branch of the famed banking family, became known as the “Father of the Yishuv” due to his establishing and almost single-handedly financing the pre-state agricultural villages of Rishon Lezion, Zichron Ya’acov, Gedera, Rosh Pina, and 30 others.
He also played a pivotal role in establishing the Yishuv’s wine industry, when he helped Russian Jews fleeing pogroms in the 1880s immigrate to Israel, plant vineyards, and open major wineries in Rishon Lezion and Zichron Ya’acov (among the world’s largest at the time).
The Baron’s interest was by no means confined to agricultural settlement. Convinced that the growing Jewish community in the Land of Israel would ultimately become independent, he devoted financial resources and tireless energy to the Yishuv’s economic development.
With his assistance, the Yishuv’s first industries and basic infrastructure were established: a glass factory that would supply bottles for his wineries (the first Jewish-owned factory in pre-state Israel), factories for agricultural products, even the first electric generating station. In 1924, he established the Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, which purchased more than 125,000 acres of land and set up additional business ventures.
In his eulogy for Rothschild, prime minister David Ben-Gurion said, “I doubt that, in the entire history of the Jewish people in the Diaspora, a period of 2,000 years, one could ever find a man comparable in stature to the incredible character that was the Baron Edmond de Rothschild – the builder of the Jewish Yishuv in our renewed homeland.”
Louis Brandeis and the rights of the individual
Louis Brandeis was a lawyer and the first Jewish Supreme Court justice, who fundamentally shaped American jurisprudence around individual rights, civil liberties, and privacy. He is best known for:
• Articulating the foundational legal concept of a right to privacy, defining it as the “right to be let alone.”
• His argument that the Fourth and Fifth Amendments protected citizens’ private thoughts, emotions, and communications against technological and governmental surveillance.
• Formulating the principle that the appropriate response to dangerous or offensive speech is “more speech, not enforced silence,” helping shift the Supreme Court toward stronger protections for political dissent and free expression.
• Pioneering the “Brandeis Brief,” which incorporated economic data, medical research, and social science – rather than purely abstract legal precedent – to defend labor protections like maximum-hour laws for women.
• His decisions, which curbed the excessive powers of insurance companies, railroads, and utilities, clashed with the rights of individuals.
• His close ties with president Woodrow Wilson, which helped win US support for the Balfour Declaration.
Lillian Wald and public health care
Lillian Wald was a “practical idealist who worked to create a more just society.” She fought for public health care and the rights of women, children, and minorities, all while accomplishing unprecedented tangible achievements. She founded the Henry Street Settlement House on the Lower East Side of New York City in 1893, originally to help dislocated European immigrants adjust to the US.
After witnessing their crushing poverty and lack of any medical care, and guided by her belief that every New Yorker was entitled to equal and fair health care regardless of their socioeconomic status, race, gender, or age, she co-founded the world’s first visiting nurse service and was influential in developing the world’s first public school nursing system in 1902.
She emphasized the importance of community-based nursing, hygiene education, and disease prevention, which became fundamental principles in modern nursing and critical to steering New York through the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic. She also suggested a national health insurance plan and helped to found the Columbia University School of Nursing.
Wald provided employment and a unique career opportunity for women through the Settlement. Out of her concern for other women’s working conditions, she helped found the Women’s Trade Union League in 1903. She also lobbied for federal child labor laws and promoted childhood education, eventually inspiring the establishment of the federal Children’s Bureau. In 1909, she became a founding member of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP).
Samuel Gompers and the Labor Movement
Samuel Gompers founded and shaped the non-partisan American Federation of Labor (AFL) and later served as the organization’s president from 1886 to 1894, and from 1895 until he died in 1924. He organized the American labor movement and “business unionism,” and promoted collective bargaining, strikes, and boycotts to secure higher wages, shorter hours, and better work conditions for the member craft unions. Under his leadership, the AFL grew from a membership of 140,000 to three million by 1924.
Janusz Korczak and children’s rights
Janusz Korczak (Henryk Goldszmit) was a Polish pediatrician, educator, radio host, author, and early children’s rights advocate who developed an educational system based on love and respect for the child. He spoke against corporal punishment of children at a time when such treatment was considered a parental entitlement or even a duty.
In 1911, he founded a Jewish orphanage in Warsaw where he put his ideas into practice by creating a self-governing “children’s republic” with democratic and civic values, including their own parliament, a code of law, an independent court and a newspaper.
Korczak advocated a Declaration of Children’s Rights that demanded active societal obligations rather than passive goodwill or charity, long before any such document was drawn up by the Geneva Convention or the UN. Uncompleted at the time of his death, Betty Jean Lifton culled through his written works and compiled the rights that Korczak considered most essential:
• The right to love and respect as an individual.
• The right to optimal conditions for growth, free from hunger, neglect, and overcrowding.
• The right to live in the present (children are people today, not just “adults of tomorrow”).
• The right to make mistakes, have secrets, own property, and express grief.
During World War II, despite offers to secure his personal escape, Korczak moved in with his 192 orphans when forced to relocate to Warsaw’s Jewish ghetto. Together with his staff and pupils, they staged plays and concerts for the ghetto inhabitants. He was tragically murdered together with the entire population of the institution in the Treblinka extermination camp in 1942.
Betty Friedan and the women’s movement
Betty Friedan was a pioneering feminist activist before the modern women’s movement had fully formed. Her book The Feminine Mystique, published in 1963, launched the Women’s Liberation Movement in America.
As co-founder of the National Organization for Women (NOW) in 1966, which became one of the major organizations of the women’s movement, she led the battle for paid maternity leave, workplace equality, and other equal rights for women. Her central achievement was giving a public name and intellectual framework to questions many women experienced privately but didn’t yet understand as a political or social problem.
Natan Sharansky and the struggle for Soviet Jewry
Natan Sharansky was a founding member of the Helsinki Group, which monitored Soviet human rights, and also worked closely with Andrei Sakharov trying to secure the rights of Soviet Jews to emigrate. Arrested on false charges in 1977 and sentenced to 13 years of hard labor in the Soviet Gulag, he endured harsh conditions, long stretches in solitary confinement, and hunger strikes, refusing to compromise his conscience.
After an international campaign led by his wife Avital, he was released in February 1986 as part of a prisoner exchange, made aliyah on the day of his release, and continued leading the struggle for the release of Soviet Jews.
On December 7, 1987, he organized a rally in Washington, DC, attended by 250,000 people, which coincided with the first visit of Soviet president Gorbachev to the US, and was highly effective in pressuring him to ease the restriction on immigration.
In honor of his life’s work, he has received the Congressional Medal of Honor, the Presidential Medal of Freedom (the only living non-American citizen who is the recipient of these two highest American awards), the Israel Prize, and the Genesis Prize.
Sharansky has authored four books and remains a champion of the right of all people to live in freedom and the belief that the advancement of human rights is critical to peace and security around the world.■
The above has been compiled from the archives of Dust & Stars – Today in Jewish History, a day-by-day glance into 4,000 years of history, peopled by the remarkable Jews who have changed the world. Drawing from a total of over 1,800 entries, subscribers (free or paid) receive posts that combat ignorance, inspire pride, and integrate shared Jewish memory into the day-to-day: dustandstars.substack.com/subscribe

IDF demolishes monument previously damaged by MK Zvi Sukkot during West Bank ops - report

The IDF launched a counterterrorism operation in the Nablus area of the West Bank Monday night, targeting wanted suspects, weapons, and monuments commemorating terrorists, including a monument that Religious Zionist Party MK Zvi Sukkot damaged in August, KAN News reported Tuesday.
The operation also included the arrest of wanted suspects and searches for weapons, according to the IDF.
In August, Sukkot and several others were filmed damaging the monument in the village of Madama while accompanied by Israeli soldiers.
The monument appeared to be in honor of members of the al-Aqsa brigade and Palestinians killed in the intifada.
Sukkot defended his actions, saying at the time that he had repeatedly appealed to the IDF to remove monuments glorifying terrorists in the West Bank.
"Every child who sees every day a giant monument that glorifies murderers of Jews will dream of being a terrorist," Sukkot said in a post on X/Twitter in August.

“There is no place for support of terror in the State of Israel!" he wrote.
The IDF subsequently condemned the incident, saying Sukkot and those accompanying him had acted without authorization and violated the terms of their coordinated visit.
The military said at the time that it regularly removes monuments and symbols of incitement, subject to the necessary approvals and coordination with the Civil Administration.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Bennett condemned Sukkot's actions in August
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned Sukkot's unauthorized destruction of the monument in August, emphasizing that the IDF was responsible for maintaining security and carrying out government decisions in the West Bank.
"The IDF is the sovereign authority in Judea and Samaria and is responsible for implementing the decisions of the political echelon," Netanyahu said at the time.
"Taking the law into one's own hands, particularly by public figures, is unacceptable and hinders the IDF from focusing on its missions against terrorism and incitement."
Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot also criticized Sukkot, calling him a "violent provocateur" and accusing him of misleading the military and damaging Israel's security and international standing.
Sukkot's actions also drew criticism from B'Yachad leader Naftali Bennett, who accused Netanyahu's government of "undermining Israel's security and Israel's standing in the world just to rack up views on TikTok."
Palestinian village leader warns Sukkot's actions could fuel violence
Kafr Madama village council head Rami Nassar warned at the time that Sukkot's actions could encourage further violence against Palestinian residents.
“When an official Israeli politician acts like this, what can we expect from other radical settlers? It could push them to follow in his footsteps, leading to more raids and causing harm and harassment to residents and their property," Nassar said.
Nassar also criticized Netanyahu's condemnation of the incident, arguing that "words are not enough" and calling for measures to protect Palestinian residents from further incidents.

Hind Rajab Foundation accuses Israeli visiting London of 'using starvation as a method of warfare'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:40:40 UTC
10:40:40 KST

Pro-Palestinian organization the Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) announced on Monday that it had filed another criminal complaint with British authorities against an Israeli man in London.
HRF operates out of Belgium and regularly launches legal campaigns against IDF soldiers abroad.
This time, the complaint targets an Israeli man whom the organization claims served as a reserve soldier and D9 bulldozer operator in the 603rd Combat Engineering Battalion of the 7th Brigade, and who is currently staying in London.
In its complaint, the organization attributes alleged involvement in war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide to the man during his service in the Gaza Strip.
HRF accuses Israeli of 'using starvation as a method of warfare,' destroying buildings
At the center of the allegations is the demolition of an industrial flour production facility called Great Ocean Mills, located in the Morag Corridor between Khan Yunis and Rafah, on May 25, 2025.
According to HRF, the man documented a bulldozer demolishing the grain silos at the complex on social media. The foundation claims that the demolition of the facility, at a time when the Gaza Strip was experiencing a severe food shortage, constitutes part of what it describes as "using starvation as a method of warfare."
It further alleges that the 603rd Battalion was involved in more than 60 controlled demolition operations targeting buildings and the leveling of extensive areas across the Strip.
HRF also points to a photograph from November 2023 at a school in Gaza City, in which the soldier is allegedly seen holding a humorous sign, as well as additional footage of demolition operations in Khan Yunis and Rafah.
Later, according to the organization, the man also participated in military operations in Lebanon.
In its appeal to British authorities, the foundation is demanding that the young man be arrested and investigated immediately.
HRF demands UK question all Israelis about IDF service
Natasha Brack, the organization's head of legal affairs, argued that he should not be allowed to leave Britain, as he may return to reserve duty.
The foundation also broadened its demand, calling for every adult Israeli entering Britain to be questioned about their service in the IDF, particularly regarding activities in Gaza and Lebanon.
At this stage, it is unknown whether or not British authorities have initiated an investigation into the complaint.
The filing of the complaint itself does not indicate that criminal proceedings have been opened against the man or that HRF’s allegations have been accepted.
Not all of HRF’s complaints have led to action by local authorities. Last September, a complaint filed by the foundation against an Israeli reservist was rejected in Greece after it was determined that there was no legal basis for the country to hear allegations concerning acts that took place outside its territory. The foundation announced at the time that it had appealed the decision.
HRF founder allegedly trained with Hezbollah
The Hind Rajab Foundation, named after the six-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed in the Gaza Strip, is headed by Diab Abu Jahjah, a native of southern Lebanon who lives in Belgium. Abu Jahjah is known for his anti-Israel political activities and his past ties to Hezbollah.
Abu Jahjah himself is barred from entering Britain following a decision made by the country's authorities in the 2000s. His name has also been linked to the American no-fly list. In a past interview with the New York Times, he said that he had undergone military training in Hezbollah's ranks and expressed pride in doing so.
In recent years, he has led the foundation's activities from Brussels, seeking to locate Israeli soldiers while they are abroad and file complaints against them over actions attributed to them during their military service.
The current case in London joins the organization's efforts to initiate criminal proceedings against Israelis outside the country's borders, even when no enforcement measures have yet been taken following the complaints.

US conducting nightly missions to enforce Hormuz blockade, straining aircraft, crew - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:40:14 UTC
10:40:14 KST

The US military is conducting nightly missions over the Strait of Hormuz as American forces work to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports along the waterway and protect commercial vessels at risk of being struck by Iranian projectiles, according to a Wall Street Journal report on Thursday.
Pilots and aircrew aboard the USS George Washington aircraft carrier, deployed in the region since August, spoke to the WSJ about the warship’s daily operations and around-the-clock defense of the strait.
The airspace over the waterway is only about 20 miles wide but is full of aerial objects, US service members told WSJ, giving fighter jet pilots a small window to react to any projectiles launched from Iran’s coast.
US naval blockade support 'reliably' defending commercial shipping
Rear Adm. Jeffrey Heames, who commands the USS George Washington Carrier Strike Group, told WSJ that US forces have been reliably striking down threats to commercial shipping in the region.
“If there’s a threat that’s launched against those vessels, whether it’s an anti-ship cruise missile or a drone, those aircraft will go in and intercept it and shoot it down in a very short amount of time,” Heames stated.
According to US Central Command (CENTCOM), the protection provided by the US Navy has allowed Gulf partners to export over 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer. Over the past six months, more than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz without incident.
In a video statement released on X/Twitter on Friday, CENTCOM head Adm. Brad Cooper detailed that since the blockade was imposed, Iran has not been able to export any oil.
Nightly operations strain crew members, cost US billions of dollars
Despite the success of the nightly operations, US officials familiar with the missions told WSJ that the frequency of flight operations has put a strain on aircraft, crew members, and the mechanics responsible for maintaining fighter jets.
According to the WSJ, Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of the US’s naval operations, said that the Navy is taking the strain into account. Caudle stated that a ship maintenance hub has been set up on Diego Garcia, a base on an island in the Indian Ocean.
He added that they are learning from the conflict and are planning more port calls after naval personnel aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln completed a record-breaking deployment of 286 days at sea.
An officer in the aircraft carrier’s maintenance department, Ensign Addie Schaefer, told WSJ that the more the aircraft fly, the more they are prone to damage and wear, leading to frequent maintenance.
US military leaders say that their forces can maintain the blockade and protect the strait for as long as is needed, but some officials worry that the resource-intensive operations may impact the US’s ability to respond to other potential future crises in other regions.
According to the WSJ, the US currently has 50,000 troops and 20 ships deployed in the Middle East, costing the US between $2 billion and $3 billion a month on munitions, fuel, supplies, and other expenses necessary for maintaining its presence and operations in the region.

The main obstacle remains the sequence of steps toward a possible agreement. Washington insists that Iran's nuclear program be addressed from the beginning of negotiations, while Tehran is demanding that the United States first lift its blockade of Iranian ports and remove sanctions restricting Iranian oil exports.

He stressed that Iran was still giving diplomacy a chance, despite the substantial differences separating the two sides.

Trump, however, offered a different explanation Thursday, saying the purpose of the outreach was to discuss the delivery of medical supplies and humanitarian assistance to Iran.
With Qatar pressing ahead on the diplomatic front and Washington weighing its options after the midterm elections, the gap between the two sides remains substantial. The tanker fires and explosions reported in the Strait of Hormuz have added another dangerous complication to negotiations already overshadowed by the possibility of renewed U.S. military action.
