AI giants promise publishers new way to block some scraping
- OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic will offer one standard way for publishers to block content scraping for AI training.
- The change comes after complaints and court cases, including The New York Times' 2023 lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft over unauthorised use of articles.
- The tool will roll out slowly, and it only stops future AI training, not crawling by default; opt-outs may also reduce content visibility in AI apps.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO, California – OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic pledged on Oct 30 to give media outlets and other websites a single way to prevent their content from being scraped to train artificial intelligence models, amid growing criticisms and legal battles from news publishers.
Publishers currently have to implement multiple blocking commands for every bot that crawls the web to collect data, but the new proposed solution will allow them to enter a single, standardised instruction that is recognised and honoured by any AI company that adopts the protocol.
The solution will not fully take effect for months, though.
Microsoft will implement it beginning Feb 1, 2027, and Google sometime in 2027.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it will roll it out “in the coming months”, while Claude-maker Anthropic said it has “already started” rolling it out.
The announcement comes as publishers are facing a surge in bots that scrape their articles to feed AI models. Some, like the New York Times, have taken the matter to court.
In December 2023, the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft for allegedly using millions of its articles without authorisation or payment to train ChatGPT.
The two tech companies are invoking an exception to copyright law known as fair use.
Meanwhile, internet infrastructure provider Cloudflare has blocked AI bots by default on new customer sites since July 2025, and a standard called Really Simple Licensing already allows publishers to charge bots that visit their pages.
The new setting will apply only to future training of models but does not prevent bots from crawling otherwise, and content scraping will be allowed by default until the setting is changed by a publisher, Microsoft said in a blog post.
Opting out of AI training could reduce the chances that a publisher’s content will surface in AI apps and experiences, Microsoft and Google said in separate blog posts.
“We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step. And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry,” Meta spokesman Andy Stone wrote on X, conveying his support for the effort. AFP

====================================================================================================

War Is Hell—And The Mosquito Bowl Won’t Let Us Forget It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:33:07 UTC
10:33:07 KST

When you’re a kid, young men going off to war look like men. When you’re a grown-up, you see that they’re really just boys. If The Mosquito Bowl gets close to any essential truth, it’s that one. This is director Peter Berg’s retelling of a true story involving young football stars who went off to fight in the Pacific during World War II, focusing on four real-life figures: Dave Schreiner and Bob Bauman (played by Tom Francis and Bill Skarsgård) were teammates and close friends playing for the University of Wisconsin; Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson, son of Jack) was a fullback for Purdue; and John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine) had graduated from Brown University and been drafted into the NFL by the time the war had started. As Berg presents it, all four of these men went off believing they could win the war the same way you win a football game, with strategy and athleticism, only to learn how far off the mark they were. The film’s title refers to a legendary football game between two Marine regiments at Guadalcanal, on Christmas Eve, 1944. A few months later, three of the four would be dead in Okinawa: Of the 65 men who played in the Mosquito Bowl, 15 were killed on the island.
There’s a lot of drama inherent in that premise, and Berg—director of films like Hancock, The Kingdom, and Friday Night Lights, progenitor of the hit TV series—takes perhaps too much time drawing it out. He introduces the main characters with moderate efficiency: Schreiner is a solid, rather quiet guy who’s given to overthinking everything; as the film opens, his team has just lost to Purdue, and he’s still simmering with resentment toward Butkovich, who appears to be something of a hothead. Bauman is the solid Wisconsin country lad, giving his younger brother instructions on holding the family homestead together. And McLaughry is intelligent and grounded, if somewhat undersketched, though he does anchor the movie’s opening scene, which gives us some sense of what these young men left behind when they went to war, things they could never get back.
After some characteristically dehumanizing basic training, the men are hauled off to Tarawa. (In real life, the four weren’t in the same regiment, though it’s a forgivable dramatic tweak.) This occasions the movie’s first protracted battle sequence, in which these newly minted Marines get a swift education in what war is about. Legs are blown off. Pinwheeling men, having been set ablaze with flamethrowers, scream in agony. Blood burbles through gaping wounds. After we, and they, have made it through this ordeal, there’s a great deal of talking among the men about the grim circumstances they’ve found themselves in. Then there’s some football—the actual Mosquito Bowl—where they get to have some fun. This is the most exhilarating section of the film. It also feels like the shortest.
Because the deadly battle at Okinawa is yet to come, and Berg will spare us no bloody detail. (The script was adapted from the 2022 book of the same name by Buzz Bissinger, who also wrote the book that the 2004 film Friday Night Lights was based on.) More limbs are blasted off, more bullets end lives instantly or with agonizing slowness, more bayonets pierce tender flesh. War is hell, and Berg doesn’t want us to forget it.
In my early film-reviewing days, even before the existence of comments sections, I would sometimes get emails from veterans telling me what I had gotten wrong in writing about this or that war film. Most of those letters had a “Listen here, little lady” tone, but I didn’t mind them. The experience of watching a war movie is hardly the same as being in combat; it’s not supposed to be. Still, these guys had been to places I hadn’t. Even if they clearly didn’t understand my job, I’d have to admit to knowing next to nothing about theirs.
But from watching lots of war films—from the time I was a kid, when my World War II veteran dad would bring me along to see movies like the 1976 Midway, because no one else would go with him—I do know that when it comes to depicting the brutality of war, less is more. You can dramatize, or allude to, some truly horrific stuff—but choose your details wisely. One well-placed depiction of a combat atrocity can be enough to haunt a viewer forever. With The Mosquito Bowl, Berg throws so much violence at us that it comes to feel like padding, while the depiction of the Mosquito Bowl itself, the core of the movie, is pure joy. War doesn’t make a boy a man so much as it knocks the boyhood out of him, fast—which may be why it’s both freeing and poignant to watch these young men escaping, if only briefly, into versions of themselves that no longer exist.

Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to vote in US general election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:31:44 UTC
10:31:44 KST

Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to vote in US general election
Vatican confirms the pope submitted a mail-in ballot in his native Chicago ahead of November 3 midterm elections
Pope Leo XIV has become the first pontiff to vote in a United States general election after casting a mail-in ballot in Chicago, where he was born.
The Vatican confirmed on Friday that the pope submitted a mail-in ballot in the city ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, citing his longstanding belief in civic participation.
Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen”, as he has done “whenever he was eligible to do so”, the Vatican’s press office said.
“The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added.
The Vatican did not say which candidates Leo voted for.
In a note commenting on Leo’s vote, the US Conference of Catholic Bishops urged Catholics to put “our faith before our politics” and “uphold human dignity and the common good”.
“In voting, our Holy Father sets the example that encourages each citizen to exercise their civic responsibility,” said the conference’s director of public affairs, Chieko Noguchi.
Leo is a citizen not only of the US but also of Peru, where he lived as a priest and bishop for more than 20 years, as well as of the Vatican, where he is head of state.
US federal law allows citizens living abroad, even those working for foreign governments, to vote via absentee ballot.
Americans working for foreign governments are not automatically at risk of losing their US citizenship, but the US State Department says on its website that it may “actively review” the citizenship status of Americans who “serve as a foreign head of state, foreign head of government, or foreign minister”.
A regular voter
In this year’s midterm elections, voters in the solidly Democratic state of Illinois, where Chicago is located, will select a successor to retiring Senator Dick Durbin and choose whether to re-elect Governor JB Pritzker.
Leo requested a mail-in ballot on October 3, just 10 days before he underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung. He has slowly been resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital on October 17.
Since 2000, Leo has voted in five primary elections as Prevost, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections, which do not show which candidates he supported.
Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot.
While registered in heavily-Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
Clashes with Trump
Since Leo’s ascent to the papacy in May 2025, US President Donald Trump has clashed with the pontiff several times.
Trump criticised the pope for repeatedly condemning the US-Israel war on Iran and for challenging his administration’s crackdown on immigrants.
Earlier this year, Trump called Leo “weak” and captive to the “radical left”, kicking off a remarkable back-and-forth argument.
Leo responded by telling reporters: “I’m not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for.”

AI generated
WASHINGTON - A US federal judge on Oct 30 pushed back on government assertions that President Donald Trump’s planned massive arch in Washington is needed for national security.
Trump did not mention national security concerns when first announcing plans to build the 76m triumphal white arch, which is modelled after the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.
He said later, however, in a Truth Social post, that it would include a “top grade military complex” that could house drones and snipers.
District Judge Tanya Chutkan noted that the Republican president had also invoked national security in presenting the case for building a White House ballroom to the Supreme Court.
“It doesn’t make the use of national security talismanic in this case,” Chutkan said. “This is the first time the government has proffered a national security aspect to this case.”
Robert Stander, a Justice Department lawyer, said the arch is a “high priority project” for the administration.
The lawsuit being heard by Chutkan was brought by a group of Vietnam War veterans seeking to stop construction of the arch, which could begin as early as next week.
Wendy Liu, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said that given its massive size, the arch would obscure the sight lines between the Lincoln Memorial, one of Washington’s iconic landmarks, and Arlington National Cemetery, the final resting place for hundreds of thousands of American service members.
The arch is one of a number of projects launched by Trump in a bid to put his personal stamp on the capital.
They include the ballroom that is being built at the White House, for which Trump had an entire wing of the presidential mansion demolished.
Another is the laborious renovation of the Reflecting Pool, a massive rectangular water basin on the National Mall.
Trump has also proposed revamping the East Potomac Golf Links, a historic waterfront Washington golf course.
That project is the focus of a bitter legal battle: the judge presiding over the case launched an investigation on Oct 30 into whether lawyers for the Trump administration had lied to the court.
For a time, Trump also had his name placed on the walls of the Kennedy Centre, the culture and arts institute named after assassinated president John F. Kennedy, before a judge reversed the move.
Chutkan did not make an immediate ruling in the arch case but said she would do so “expeditiously.” AFP

A village that sent hundreds of men to one of imperial Japan’s most notorious wartime units is being demolished to make way for a runway at Tokyo’s Narita International Airport.
Unit 731 carried out lethal experiments on captives, many of them Chinese, to develop biological weapons during the second world war. A federal judge has barred the justice department from threatening or coercing election workers to stop processing ballots.

It marks another blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to assert control over local elections.
It comes after a federal appeals court on Friday rejected the justice department’s request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election, the latest setback for the Trump administration’s efforts to assert control over state-run elections.

A justice department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling. It is the Department’s job.”
Millions of people have already voted in California in the midterm election that concludes on Tuesday. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. Elections officials have said that processed votes can’t be matched back to the voters who submitted them.

Feature: Blind football team from Xinjiang makes mark on China's national stage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:27:52 CST
10:27:52 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- At 19, Bilali Yasen has emerged as one of the most promising players in Xinjiang's first blind football team, having gone from years of isolation after losing his sight as a child to becoming a potential candidate for China's national team.
Bilali, who lost his sight aged seven, recently returned to his hometown of Shache County in Kashgar, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, to recover from a recurring foot injury following a training camp in Guangdong Province.
Before losing his sight, Bilali had enjoyed playing football with friends in his village. But afterward, he withdrew from the outside world, afraid to leave his home.
"I always felt that I would spend the rest of my life in darkness," he recalled.
His fortunes changed when he discovered blind football, a sport that has since taken him and his teammates from the edge of the Taklamakan Desert to national competitions across China.
In March, Bilali was identified as a potential candidate for the national team, becoming the first player from Xinjiang's blind football squad to receive such recognition.
Hundreds of kilometers away, at Xinjiang Special Education Vocational Secondary School in Changji Hui Autonomous Prefecture, his teammates continue their training, calling out "wei, wei, wei" to communicate as they move across the pitch.
The team's origins date to 2021, when Su Yiyan, then a senior executive at a Shanghai film and television company, visited Shache County Special Education School to recruit young actors for a film about blind football.
"For the first time, I learned that even blind people can play football," said Abdumijiti Maimaiti, 19, one of Bilali's teammates.
Under the guidance of a coach from Shanghai, the students began learning the fundamentals of the sport, which uses a ball fitted with bells to help players track its movement.
For Bilali, football provided an opportunity to regain the confidence he had lost after becoming blind.
The original film project was suspended shortly after production began, threatening to bring the team's activities to an end.
Su, however, decided to continue supporting the players.
"You don't give people something, then take it back," she said.
She subsequently resigned from her position and, working with filmmakers Li Zhiwei and Liu Xiaoran, who had been involved in short films for the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics, began financing a documentary about the team.
With support from a physical education teacher at Shache County Special Education School, the players continued training while Su worked to keep the project alive.
The team faced another setback as its members approached graduation because their school did not offer upper secondary education.
The Xinjiang Disabled Persons' Federation intervened, helping establish the region's first blind football team in August 2024.
The following month, the players transferred to Xinjiang Special Education Vocational Secondary School, where they began studying traditional Chinese medicine rehabilitation while continuing their football training.
Their progress in national competition has been rapid.
The team made its national debut at the 2024 National Blind Football Championship in Fuzhou, finishing ninth.
At the 2025 National Games for Persons with Disabilities and National Special Olympics in Guangzhou, the players recorded their first victory in national competition by defeating Henan, eventually finishing seventh.
They improved further at the 2026 National Blind Football Championship in Korla, beating Shanghai 3-2 in a penalty shootout to reach the semifinals.
With an average age of 18, the squad is the youngest blind football team in China.
Its development has been supported by donations, educational opportunities and assistance from organizations and individuals across the country.
Su has raised more than 1 million yuan (140,000 U.S. dollars) to finance the documentary, titled "Wei Wei Wei, Football Team," while remaining closely involved with the players.
Years of training, travel and competition have made her an important figure in their lives.
"Without her, this blind football team as we know it today would never have existed," one player said.
The Xinjiang Disabled Persons' Federation has also played a central role in ensuring that the players can continue their education alongside their sporting development.
"Xinjiang Special Education Vocational Secondary School had never enrolled fully blind students before; we made an exception for this team," said Chen Jin, vice chairman of the federation.
Wang Jingrong, secretary-general of the Xinjiang Disabled Persons' Welfare Foundation, said businesses and organizations had provided equipment, clothing, financial assistance and training facilities.
A Chinese mobile phone manufacturer donated more than 100 accessible phones, while a local biotechnology company supplied clothing, footwear and nutritional supplements.
The Xinjiang branch of a centrally administered state-owned enterprise contributed tens of thousands of yuan, and a sports venue in Guangzhou provided accommodation and training facilities at a reduced cost during a monthlong training camp.
The team's story has also begun reaching audiences beyond the football pitch.
In July 2026, "Wei Wei Wei, Football Team" began limited preview screenings across China, documenting the players' journey from a special education school near the Taklamakan Desert to national-level competition.
For Bilali and his teammates, the ambition now extends beyond their own achievements.
"We cannot see the world with our eyes, but we are determined to make the world see us," the players said. ■

US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:27:31 CET
10:27:31 KST

By Mike Stone, Andrea Shalal and Tom Balmforth
Oct 30 (Reuters) - The US State Department said on Friday it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, in what would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration.
Delayed missile deliveries have added to Ukraine’s tensions with the US after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while 5 died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Zelenskiy said on Monday that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.
But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will likely not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfill, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles — which are yet to be manufactured — are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense is encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.
The program uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defense following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
The JUMPSTART program was used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $825 million made by Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defense and precision-guided weapons.
In July, the US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.
Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity by the end of 2030 and increase jobs at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50%, to about 1,850 from 1,200. Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units annually.
Pentagon negotiators are pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck earlier this year at the center of efforts to increase missile output.
(Reporting by Mike Stone, Andrea Shalal and Tom Balmforth; Additional reporting by Ryan Patrick Jones and Christian Martinez; Editing by Michelle Nichols, Don Durfee, Daniel Wallis and William Mallard)

Fake polls expose vulnerabilities in US elections ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:26:34 UTC
10:26:34 KST

Fake polls expose vulnerabilities in US elections ahead of midterms
Fabricated surveys are adding to tensions in the country’s increasingly polarised political environment.
Fabricated political polling has forced its way into the spotlight during the midterm election period in the United States.
Revelations that a small number of fraudulent firms have released fictitious results – some of which were picked up by news outlets and polling trackers – have raised concerns about how easily false information can acquire credibility.
Those datasets can be used to cast doubt on the electoral process. And when bad actors are unmasked, their existence can be leveraged to undermine voter confidence in election information overall.
The latest example occurred earlier this month, when Wedgewood Polls released a statement on social media admitting its statistics about a bevy of battleground states – like Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Kansas and Maine – were fake.
Wedgewood described its work as “an experimental project” designed to highlight the “vulnerabilities, lack of oversight and overall low barrier to entry” in the US polling industry.
“Having previously worked in the polling and research sector, we watched as the public’s trust in polling eroded alongside a rise in unverified, low-quality methodology,” the firm said in a statement posted to its social media account, which has now been deleted.
It justified its false data as a test to see how easy it would be for fabricated polling to gain traction among voters and the media.
“The short answer: Far too easy,” Wedgewood said.
But Wedgewood’s admission came after its surveys had already circulated through the political information ecosystem, reaching prominent media outlets like The New York Times.
The incident was the second such scandal in the 2026 election cycle, following the exposure of another operation, Median Strategies, which acknowledged in August it had also faked results as a “short-term social experiment”.
In an increasingly polarised US political environment, the incidents have roiled a polling industry – and a public – struggling to adapt to an ever-changing information landscape.
How fake polls gained credibility
Wedgewood, which launched in June, published surveys covering competitive races across several states. Its results attracted attention from political campaigns, commentators and organisations that compile polling data.
The New York Times said its polling tracker had listed 15 Wedgewood surveys between June and October. The newspaper subsequently removed them.
In the wake of the scandal, it explained that the firm had answered questions about its personnel, methodology and funding before its results were included.
While the Times said Wedgewood’s surveys were not incorporated into the newspaper’s own presidential approval or national congressional polling averages, the case revealed a vulnerability in the process by which polling information becomes established as credible.
Polling aggregators help journalists and voters make sense of a crowded field of surveys by collecting results from multiple research organisations. Their value depends partly on their ability to distinguish reliable research from poorly conducted or fraudulent work.
Wedgewood’s success in passing some of those checks suggests that transparency on paper is not necessarily proof that research has been conducted as claimed.
According to FiftyPlusOne, a polling and forecasting website that investigated the firm, inconsistencies in the raw data and the technical identifiers associated with survey responses helped raise suspicions about its authenticity.
The investigation prompted Wedgewood to acknowledge that most of its results were fabricated.
Though Wedgewood has denied trying to mislead the public, some pollsters are not convinced, suggesting the group could was up to something more nefarious.
“We were investigating Wedgewood for faking their data,” said data journalist G Elliott Morris, who was involved in FiftyPlusOne’s probe. “They are trying to cover up for their fraud with the ‘we were doing a social experiment’ excuse.”
How fake polling has impacted elections
The consequences of fake polling extend far beyond the polling industry.
Mallory McMorrow, who ran unsuccessfully in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, has argued that a Wedgewood survey showing her support in the single digits damaged her campaign.
McMorrow said the poll left her volunteers demoralised, and journalists repeatedly contacted her to ask whether she should abandon the race.
Donations, she added, also evaporated, with Democratic supporters looking to other campaigns to invest.
In a social media post, McMorrow described the poll from Wedgewood – and another from the firm Mitchell Research and Communications – as a “one-two punch” that “killed her campaign”. She suspended her Senate bid in July.
“By that point, we took a risk and we spend our money. We put our ads up. They were working. But the damage was done. And I was drowned out by outside spending and the narrative that we had completely collapsed,” she wrote.
Experts say McMorrow’s account illustrates a broader problem: Even when a poll does not accurately measure public opinion, its findings can still influence the decisions of people who believe it does.
Why it matters
The Wedgewood controversy demonstrates how fraudulent data can become ammunition in an already polarised political environment.
Researchers at the University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public tracked how discussion of Wedgewood’s admission spread across social media.
Initially, much of the conversation was concentrated among polling experts and people who followed election data. But the story subsequently gained traction among influential political commentators and partisan accounts.
Some posts focused on the fact that prominent outlets and polling aggregators had listed Wedgewood’s results. Others used the revelation to question polling more broadly, particularly surveys suggesting that Democrats were competitive in closely contested races.
The researchers found the controversy became intertwined with claims that polling was systematically misleading voters or understating support for particular political parties.
“Within 24 hours, the right-wing media ecosystem had succeeded in drawing attention to the story and setting some of the most salient frames: that poll numbers around the midterms, especially poll numbers favoring Democrats, cannot be trusted,” the Center for an Informed Public wrote in its analysis.
President Donald Trump, who has regularly made false claims about US election integrity, seized on the revelations to criticise the Times for including Wedgewood’s surveys in its polling tracker.
“The New York Times got caught,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. “Everything about The Failing New York Times is ‘ARTIFICIAL’.”
He also suggested the Wedgewood case would help his $15bn defamation suit against the Times.
“Our powerful Lawsuit against them is getting stronger and stronger everyday,” he added.
What can be done?
No laws exist in the US that criminalise fake polls outright.
Some advocacy groups and law scholars have argued that the publication of fake polls constitute commodities and wire fraud, warranting federal prosecution.
“Deterring this sort of fraud before it can happen – and raising awareness of it – is vital,” Tyler Yeargain wrote for the Missouri Law Review in 2020.
He argued that enforcement of election-related laws against fake pollsters has “not been fully utilized”.
“Prosecution would serve a strong federal interest,” he wrote. “The interest at stake is weightier than concerns over how fake polls can shade the accuracy of an academic endeavor in prediction markets. It is instead to deter other wrongdoers, the sort who would weaponize fake polls to manipulate elections.”
Brendan Carr, the head of the Federal Communication Commission (FCC), which regulates broadcasts in the US, said there has been “a significant surge” in fake polls during the 2026 midterms, urging networks not to amplify them. Otherwise, Carr said, they could lose their licence to operate.
“Broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in News Distortion or promoting Broadcast Hoaxes,” Carr wrote on social media. “It is important that broadcasters comply with their public interest obligations.”
But the FCC’s sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez, disagreed with Carr’s assessment.
“Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong,” she wrote on X. “FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.”
Without a clear legal remedy against fake polls, experts argue the onus is placed on media outlets and voters themselves to evaluate the quality of the election data they see.
Mark Baldassare, the survey director of the Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC), said there are ways to quickly spot which surveys are real – and which are not.
“Look for transparency,” Baldassare told PPIC’s Stephanie Barton in an interview. “A credible survey will list its mission, the purpose of its polling, and its sponsors or funders.”
“A poll guided by partisan groups or campaigns that is publicly released may have a message to relay to the public.”

Australia's basket is about to be reweighted. Here's why it matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:08:18 UTC
10:08:18 KST

in brief
- The latest CPI data shows inflation accelerating, with transport, housing and food among key drivers.
- The ABS is about to reweight the CPI basket of goods to produce a better measure of inflation.
Last week, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reported an unexpected spike in inflation in September, prompting fears of more interest rate hikes.
According to the ABS Consumer Price Index (CPI), Australia's annual inflation rate sits at 4.3 per cent — up from 4 per cent in August.
Amongst the largest contributors to rising inflation were housing, which rose 5.2 per cent; alcohol and tobacco, which rose 4.3 per cent and health, which rose 3.7 per cent.
The ABS will be reweighting the CPI basket of goods in January to better reflect current spending trends and produce a more accurate CPI, a crucial exercise as Australians adjust their spending amid continued rising costs.
According to retail expert at the University of Sydney Business School, Lisa Asher, a reweighting exercise is undertaken to "adequately reflect" what people are "actually spending" their money on.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
While a change usually occurs at the end of each year, the ABS had postponed the 2026 change to January. The last reweight was in late 2025.
"Some of the key changes or movements that we saw last year and this year focus much more on the increase in food and non-alcoholic beverages, as a larger percentage, as well as health costs and transport," Asher said.
While the ABS does not flag early what the new weightings may look like, previous changes offer some clues.
In 2025, the biggest weighting increases were in education, health and food and non-alcoholic beverages and the larger weight decreases were in furnishings, household equipment and services, alcohol and tobacco and housing.
What is the CPI and how is calculated?
The CPI is "really a measure of inflation" or "price changes in the economy" and it is based on a representative basket of goods and services for Australian households, head of price statistics at the ABS, Rachael McCririck, said.
The CPI provides a "sense of the underlying price pressures in the economy" but isn't a good measure for how the cost of living crisis is impacting individual households.
"The CPI is really an aggregate measure that informs policymakers and decision-makers about aggregate trends, it informs things like monetary and fiscal policy settings," she said.
"When we talk about the cost of living, we're really talking about an individual household and what pressures they're facing in their day-to-day lives — so to get a sense of that you have to look at the individual consumption basket."
To calculate the CPI, the ABS collects prices for items grouped into 87 categories and 11 groups. Every month, the ABS calculates the price changes of each item from the previous month and aggregates them to work out the inflation rate for the basket.
Prices are collected from a variety of retailers across the eight capital cities and the ABS uses methods like web-scraping and online and telephone interviews with retailers.
A knitter and an EV owner, McCririck said her basket would differ from the "average household's basket".
"But the weights that we give to the basket for the CPI are based on the average household experience," she said.
How are CPI items and weights chosen?
In deciding which goods and services to include in the CPI basket and what their weights should be, the ABS uses data about how much – and on what – households in Australia spend their income.
If households spend more of their income on one item, that item will have a larger weight in the CPI.
McCririck said reweights are based on the ABS' household expenditure survey.
"We've grown forward the CPI weights by looking ... at how trends in the household expenditure change — we've grown the weight forward each year manually," she said.
Looking at the reweight in 2025, the weight for alcohol and tobacco fell because sales of legal tobacco had fallen as smoking rates decline, although it did not include vapes and illicit tobacco.
The weight for housing also fell because home buying declined amid a shortage in new construction and supply. Dwelling commencements in 2024 were the lowest in over ten years.
In 2024, school fees rose in 2024 and there were more non-government school enrolments forcing the weight for education to go up for 2025.
Due to the rise in airfares, Australian household spending on overseas holidays rose so the weight for international holiday travel and accommodation increased.
Inflationary pressures are 'going to persist'
Regardless of the weights, Asher told SBS News that rising inflation is a trend that is likely to continue.
"The wars will continue, which means that fuel prices will continue to be high and that has a flow-on effect on goods, logistics and transport systems — which flows onto anything that's imported," she said.
"Many materials, even if they are locally produced here, will increase."
She said inflationary pressures have seen Australians reduce their spending — a habit she hopes can continue into the Christmas period.
"As we move into the Christmas period, people are worse off now than they were at the beginning of the year with inflation — wage growth hasn't kept up," Asher said.
"Some people will be inclined to still spend at Christmas because they feel obliged to do so. I really think that people should be okay to pull back and not overdo it or put things on credit.
"As we move into next year, it's still going to be incredibly tough. Many of the challenges we're seeing are going to persist."

“Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they’re going to get one,” he said. “Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election, they’ll answer for it.”
The Alaska contest is widely seen as one of the US Senate races that could sway control of the chamber, now narrowly held by Trump’s Republicans.
The Justice Department’s legal actions in Alaska and California, where the Trump administration is trying to prevent some ballots from being counted, represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution.
When the DOJ filed the civil suit against Alaska a week ago, Trump told reporters, “I’m the one that said do it.”
Heyman declined to offer specifics when asked what possible crimes were being examined, saying he would let the Alaska investigation proceed, although Trump has called for a prosecution of Senate candidate Mary Peltola, a Democrat.
“This is voter fraud at the highest level,” Trump told a Florida rally on Oct 30.

The court filing requested the judge’s help obtaining documents from the Democratic campaign and others to determine “whether Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy is frivolous or fraudulent.”
The DOJ also has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, loses due to the presence of a third candidate, named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken; both parties have engaged in “ballot stacking” by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents.
The New York Times this week reported that staffers from the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Party’s Senate campaign arm helped recruit a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village who is named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr to appear on the ballot.

McDonald’s must face lawsuit over McRib, US judge rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:46:00 UTC
09:46:00 KST

McDonald’s must face lawsuit over McRib, US judge rules
CHICAGO - A federal judge on Oct 30 rejected McDonald’s request to dismiss a proposed class action accusing it of defrauding consumers about the content of its McRib sandwich.
The plaintiffs accused McDonald’s of intentionally shaping McRib patties with ridges to resemble pork ribs and make diners believe the sandwich contains rib meat, an expensive cut known for its higher fat content and rich flavour.
Consumers said McDonald’s actual use of lower-grade pork products including shoulder, heart, tripe or stomach caused them to overpay for the McRib, one of its most expensive menu items.
While dismissing some claims, US District Judge April Perry in McDonald’s hometown of Chicago called it premature to accept the company’s argument that no reasonable consumer could expect the McRib to contain rib meat.
She said McDonald’s website describes the sandwich only as containing pork, and reasonable consumers need not do research before buying a US$7 (S$8.95) fast-food sandwich.
The judge also said ads highlighting the meat’s rib-like shape could support a claim of intent to defraud, though further proof was needed.
“Plaintiffs’ proffered understanding of ‘McRib’ is not unreasonable or fanciful,” Perry wrote.
McDonald’s has sold the McRib periodically since 1981.
It contended that distinctive product names do not fool reasonable consumers, and the plaintiffs’ preference for a certain cut of pork “doesn’t turn McDonald’s truthful marketing into consumer fraud.”
In a statement, McDonald’s maintained that it does not use hearts, tripe or stomach in the McRib, and has always been transparent about its ingredients. “This lawsuit distorts the facts and the claims are meritless,” it added.
Thiago Coelho, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said his clients will continue seeking accountability for deceptive marketing.
Fast-food chains have faced other lawsuits over product depictions in ads and on menu boards.
These include cases accusing McDonald’s, Burger King and Wendy’s of making burgers appear larger than they actually are. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Binance seeks to shore up confidence after record US$6.3 billion heist; Trump weighs in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:45:00 UTC
09:45:00 KST

Binance seeks to shore up confidence after record US$6.3 billion heist; Trump weighs in
BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS - Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, worked on Oct 31 to shore up public confidence after a record US$6.3 billion hack of its platform, promising it would cover all losses from company funds and allow clients to trade again within days.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on news of the hack, which analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. The publicly traded stocks of crypto-related firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood slid.
Binance said customer funds were safe and it is working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about US$3 billion located so far. It did not mention the status of the remaining US$3.3 billion, but Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that US$3 billion represented only about 2% of the company’s total user assets and public reserves.
The exchange also said on Oct 31 that its technical team was targeting a resumption of withdrawal services within approximately 34 hours. Binance said it is conducting a full security review and plans an initial proof-of-reserves snapshot in 12 hours, with the results expected to be available by Nov 2.
Binance said it has set aside around US$6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a US$1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. 
Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than US$1 billion.
Binance’s other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach was a “complex attack” that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, “making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate”.
The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called “hot” wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
“Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust,” Teng wrote.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained.
Bitcoin hit a six-week low of US$76,368, and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of US$2,178 before markets stabilised. Bitcoin last stood at US$76,447 and ether at US$2,226. Binance’s BNB token was down about 6.4% over the past 24 hours at US$696.
‘Largest known theft’
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. 
Last year, attackers stole US$2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
“This incident is almost certainly the single-largest-known theft of any kind,” British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.
The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Oct 29 and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
North Korea denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.
Trump weighs in
US President Donald Trump, asked on Oct 30 whether North Korean hackers were behind the theft, said he did not know but his administration is looking into it.
“It was a hack. That’s the problem. You know the old-fashioned way when you used to sign a cheque, take it out. These are different. People never see the money anymore. So I’ve always felt it was a little bit dangerous,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he thought any of the stolen funds could be retrieved. “But no, they (Binance) say they have it pretty much under control.”
Binance is working with the FBI and the US Secret Service, according to a person familiar with the situation.
The FBI said it is “aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps”.
The Secret Service said that its investigators “are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday”.
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it froze nearly US$1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than US$800 million.
Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating licence, said it is “engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident”. Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year.
Security implications
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which already was under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.
Investor Michael Saylor, among bitcoin’s most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expects Binance to “deliver” on ensuring no customers suffered losses.
“Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security and emerge stronger and more resilient,” Saylor wrote on Oct 30.
335 million registered users
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about US$162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
The heist at Binance drew a relatively measured response from crypto enthusiasts online.
On social media platform Reddit, discussions about the breach featured a mix of humour, confidence in the exchange’s financial resources and questions about how such an enormous theft could have occurred.
The reaction stood in contrast to the panic surrounding the collapse of FTX in November 2022, when mounting doubts about the exchange’s ability to repay customer funds triggered outrage online.
“Looking at all past data, we find that hot wallet hacks – even large ones – have historically not had a meaningful impact on future crypto returns,” said Matt Hougan, chief investment officer at Bitwise Asset Management. “Investors tend to treat them as ‘one-off events’.” REUTERS

France braces for fresh unrest, government vows tough response

09:36:48 KST

By Dominique Vidalon and Noemie Olive
PARIS, Oct 31 (Reuters) - France will deploy a 70,000-strong police presence to contain a widely expected bout of fresh unrest on Saturday in the latest nationwide protests driven by anger over living costs, public services and President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
The nationwide demonstrations, which fall on Halloween, come two weeks after riots and looting caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops, public buildings and businesses in cities across France. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has vowed not to let a repeat happen.
“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out details of security arrangements for a day he described as carrying “a very high risk” of unrest.
Authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez noted that laws already allow police to ban face coverings when public order is at risk.
The US Embassy advised travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.
The protests gathered pace in late September as Macron’s minority government launched 2027 budget talks. Facing public debt approaching 120% of economic output and rising borrowing costs, the government is under pressure to rein in spending, narrowing its room for manoeuvre.
Students angry at the dilapidated state of many schools, crowded classes and a university admissions system widely seen as unfair have been joined by trade unions and a re-emergent “Yellow Vest” movement demanding action on the cost of living.
PROTESTS SPREAD ACROSS EUROPE
The protests have inspired youth-led protests across Europe, with demonstrations planned in more than 30 German cities on Saturday.
The French government’s promises to reform education and ease fuel costs have failed to calm discontent.
“When I was little, I was told young people were the future,” said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student in the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne who plans to join his third consecutive weekend of protests.
“Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing.”
The unrest has handed a political boost to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of April’s presidential election, while potential centrist successors to Macron remain divided.
The troubles are the latest blow to an economy which, data on Friday showed, was already shrinking in the third quarter.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates losses to retailers exceed €1 billion ($1.1 billion). Other estimates put the total at double when including uninsured damage and lost revenue.
Along Paris’ main shopping boulevards, early Christmas lights glow around boarded-up windows and security grilles. Among the shops targeted in previous unrest were outlets belonging to luxury brands including Hermes, Louis Vuitton and Burberry.
The government is pushing ahead with a controversial law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 ($11,000) for damage caused either by themselves or by groups they are deemed to be part of. Rights groups and some lawyers say the measure risks undermining the right to peaceful protest.
(Reporting by Noemie Olive, Dominique Vidalon, Alessandro Parodi; Writing by Mark John; Editing by Ros Russell)

GEN Z TAKES CHARGE
For organisers, however, the focus is on what they see as the growing pressure on younger generations in Europe’s largest economy.

By Andrea Shalal
ATLANTA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged fellow G20 foreign ministers on Friday to work together for greater geopolitical stability and economic prosperity, warning that a series of crises posed serious threats to the global economic order.
But Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov’s participation in the two-day gathering in Atlanta - at Rubio’s invitation - has roiled many G20 ministers, aggravating deep rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East during a meeting that is expected to end without a joint declaration. Such statements require consensus that has been elusive if not impossible since Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband addressed Lavrov directly during the meeting, telling him: “Only yesterday your drones attacked and killed 15 people. And there are countless examples like this of you killing innocent civilians throughout this war. We all know you are the aggressor.”
Lavrov later told reporters that Moscow’s position on the Ukraine conflict was unchanged, and Russia could not accept Ukraine as a “military threat to the lawful security interests of the Russian Federation,” according to Russian news agencies.
US officials said they skipped a traditional G20 family photo after European officials refused to be photographed with Lavrov. One US official said Washington wanted to avoid a “spectacle” that could overshadow the meeting. A third of members objected, including Australia and Canada, a Western diplomat said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters a photograph with Lavrov was unacceptable because “there is no normalcy with Russia.” Lavrov himself acknowledged that there had been “concerns” about the family photo, drawing head nods from many in the room, one participant said.
Rubio, saying the world faced interconnected crises that threatened global energy and food supply, trade and the freedom of navigation, urged his counterparts to find areas of agreement during the final ministerial meeting before a leaders summit in Miami, Florida, from December 14 to 16.
“We are tasked, on behalf of the nations that we serve, to work together … to coordinate responses to emerging crises and to protect our shared interests,” he said. “We can help set the context for expanded geopolitical stability and the broader economic prosperity agenda that our leaders will tackle.”
Two Western officials said G20 members were in broad agreement about the severity of the economic challenges facing nearly every country as a result of the war in the Middle East. Many participants worried that renewed US strikes on Iran would send oil prices sharply higher, deepening the pain, they said.
“The possibility for a new military operation in Iran is on everybody’s mind,” said one of the officials, who spoken on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. “Everybody is under deep pressure.”
The foreign ministers’ meeting was expected to end with a chair’s statement, with the bigger effort focused on hammering out a joint declaration that could be signed by G20 leaders at their summit in December, Western officials said. It remains unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the December gathering.
With G20 members Russia, China and middle powers such as Brazil and India trying to navigate US-China strategic competition, you have “much more of a split than we’ve ever had,” said Heidi Crebo-Rediker, who was chief economist at the State Department during the Obama administration.
Over the past decade or so, G7 countries would at least “have agreed a coordinated platform before they came to the G20, but now we don’t even really have that,” she added.
Ministers are expected to discuss supply chain issues and challenges in procuring the critical minerals needed to produce advanced technologies during their discussion on Saturday.
Rubio has championed the Pax Silica initiative, aimed at uniting G20 countries concerned about China’s dominance in rare earths and other critical minerals.
But any movement on that front will probably come afterwards, experts said, pointing to a US-led statement on excess industrial capacity that some G20 trade ministers signed after the group failed to reach consensus.
Elaine Dezenski of the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies said such statements by ad hoc groups could offer a way forward in the current difficult environment.
“The right test is whether the US can build cooperation with partners when all-member consensus appears to be out of reach,” she said. She noted the Quad — a security grouping of the US, India, Japan and Australia — would also meet in Atlanta on Saturday, on the sidelines of the G20 gathering.
US President Donald Trump’s recent decisions on Russia, including a deal to buy diesel and waiving some sanctions, formed a challenging backdrop for the talks, along with Ukraine’s problems with its Starshield satellite services, participants said. Ukraine was not invited to attend.
Washington announced a multibillion-dollar sale of Patriot interceptors late on Friday, offering some good news to Kyiv.
Before the meeting, European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she would call for increased support for Ukraine, while pushing for progress on accountability measures through the Special Tribunal and Claims Commission.
“Russia must be accountable,” she wrote on X.
(Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Additional reporting by Simon Lewis; Editing by Don Durfee, Kate Mayberry, Sanjeev Miglani and Tom Hogue)

By Andrea Shalal
ATLANTA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski on Friday called for a rapid ceasefire in the Black Sea that would allow safe passage for grain shipments from both Ukraine and Russia and said Moscow must end its war against Ukraine before being allowed to resume energy sales to Europe.
“I spoke in favor of doing something quickly because the people of the Global South need this grain,” Sikorski told reporters during a two-day meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 20 major economies in Atlanta.
Sikorski, invited to attend the meeting by the US host nation, said that Ukraine must be included in any effort to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Europe also had “cards” in the issue and should be involved, he said.
He also called for a “fair end” to the war in Ukraine before Russia was able to sell its energy products once again to Europe, formerly its most lucrative market.
The United States, which holds the rotating presidency of the G20 this year, has proposed that Poland become a full member, much like Germany or France, which are also represented through the European Union.
Sikorski said he welcomed the push and had discussed it with a number of G20 member countries in bilateral meetings in Atlanta.
Western officials say it could take years for Poland to be accepted as a full member given Russia’s opposition and the G20’s requirement for consensual decisions.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told reporters that inviting Poland to attend G20 meetings was counterproductive and broke with diplomatic practice of seeking consensus at such gatherings, according to Russian news agencies.
“Of course, this violates the principles of diplomacy, and especially multilateral diplomacy, when members of associations such as the G20 work on the basis of consensus,” Lavrov was quoted as saying.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking at a reception for the ministers at Atlanta’s Georgia Aquarium, said Poland deserved to be made a full member.
“President (Donald) Trump believes their economic success and growing global influence is exactly what the G20 needs to tackle the major economic challenges we all face,” Rubio said.
Sikorski told reporters that Britain, which will head the G20 next year, had already invited Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to attend the 2027 leaders summit in Manchester, England.

US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:29:28 UTC
09:29:28 KST

The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

Saudi Arabian surgeons successfully separate Tanzanian conjoined twins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:26:57 UTC
09:26:57 KST

Saudi Arabian surgeons successfully separate Tanzanian conjoined twins
The medical and surgical team of the Saudi Conjoined Twins Programme has successfully separated Tanzanian conjoined twins Laityness and Loveness in a 14.5-hour operation in Riyadh, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Saudi Press Agency.
The operation was performed at King Abdullah Specialist Children’s Hospital in King Abdulaziz Medical City, affiliated with the Ministry of National Guard.
Dr. Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al Rabeeah, head of the programme’s medical and surgical team, said the operation was completed in nine stages.
A total of 44 consultants, specialists, nurses and technical staff from various medical disciplines took part in the procedure to ensure precision and safety at every stage.
The twins, aged two years and two months, were joined at the pelvis and hips and shared the lower part of the intestines, the spinal column, lumbar vertebrae and spinal cord. They had four lower limbs.
According to Dr. Al Rabeeah, this was the fourth successful separation of conjoined twins from Tanzania and the 75th operation conducted under the Saudi Conjoined Twins Programme.
Over more than 35 years, the programme has assessed 160 cases from 29 countries, highlighting Saudi Arabia’s role in humanitarian and medical care.
The programme receives direct support from the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, and Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud.
Earlier, a team of Saudi surgeons successfully separated Moroccan conjoined twins Saja and Doha during a six-hour operation.

SAN FRANCISCO - Meta reached a settlement in a landmark case over the alleged harms of social media, the plaintiffs’ lawyers said on Oct 30, leaving Snap as the only defendant in a trial set to open in Los Angeles next week.
“We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client,” Emily Jeffcott, a lawyer representing one of the young women suing both companies, said in a statement.
Jury selection began on Oct 28, and opening statements are scheduled for Nov 4.
The terms of the agreement are confidential, but sources close to Meta told AFP the company decided to settle for business reasons.
“Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception,” a Meta spokesperson said, referring to the series of test cases against the company being tried in Los Angeles.
If Snap does not settle, the trial will go ahead next week.
Snap did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
TikTok and YouTube were also named as defendants in the case, but both had already reached settlements with the plaintiffs, known by their initials SJ and KDB, their lawyers said.
Meta had also previously settled with SJ.
A California state judge consolidated the two cases into a single trial.
Snap, which makes Snapchat, will defend itself against the claims of both SJ and KDB.
Lawyers for SJ and KDB will argue that their clients were exposed to “addictive and problematic” social media apps when they started using them at ages 13 and 15, respectively, according to court documents.
“We believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed,” a Snap spokesperson said in a statement earlier this week.
Avoiding trial
Thousands of lawsuits have been filed in recent years in local, state and federal courtrooms across the country with various claims about alleged harms to children and teenagers caused by social media companies.
The cases – the first of which went to trial earlier in 2026 in Los Angeles – have taken twists and turns.
Meta and YouTube lost the first so-called bellwether case earlier in 2026, when a jury found them collectively liable for harming a young user known by the initials KGM, and ordered the tech companies to pay a combined US$6 million (S$7.67 million) penalty.
Snap and TikTok settled with KGM ahead of that trial.
Months later, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled another case that was set to go to trial in August; that plaintiff, known as RKC, then withdrew their remaining claims against Meta, allowing the Instagram and Facebook maker to avoid trial without a settlement.
By settling before a trial kicks off, the social media companies contain costs from lawyer fees and potential penalties; another benefit is that it shields their executives from testifying in court.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri were expected to be called as key witnesses in the upcoming Los Angeles trial.
Snap CEO Evan Spiegel is expected to testify if the trial proceeds without another settlement.
In August, Meta agreed to pay more than US$18 billion in penalties, in addition to making changes to Instagram and Facebook for teens, when it settled with 52 attorneys general several days into a trial held in California.
That settlement came just a day after Mosseri testified, and before Zuckerberg had been called to the stand.
Meta has faced other trials, though.
Earlier in October, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a case where the company was found liable for deceiving users in the state about how their data was used in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
A New Mexico jury also found the social media giant liable for harms to children, leading to a combined penalty of US$942 million earlier in 2026. AFP

In New Zealand’s bellwether seat, what are locals thinking as a knife-edge poll looms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:15:27 UTC
09:15:27 KST

It’s a hot spring day in the Auckland suburb of Onehunga, and the main strip is starting to hum with life. Builders slip into a bakery for a snack, retirees chat over coffee outside cafes and a shoeless man zips by on a scooter.
There are few signs New Zealand’s general election is looming along this shopping strip but Onehunga and neighbouring suburbs that make up the electorate Maungakiekie, will be closely watched when New Zealand heads to the polls on 7 November.
Over the past two elections, the Maungakiekie electorate has proven to be an “extraordinary” bellwether seat, accurately reflecting the mood of the nation.
In 2020, when Labour won 50% of the national vote, a near-identical 50.3% of Maungakiekie’s voters backed the party. Three years later, when Labour’s vote plunged to 26.9%, so too did Maungakiekie’s support for the party, falling to just 27.1%.
“[Maungakiekie] tracked the national number with extraordinary precision both times,” says Dr Michael Swanson, an honorary research fellow in politics at the University of Otago.
This year’s election is on a knife-edge. With voters frustrated by a sluggish economy and stubbornly high inflation, polls indicate neither the left nor right blocs will win an outright majority. Support for mainstream parties, National and Labour, is slipping in favour of minor parties – one of which, Opportunity, could decide who will next govern New Zealand.
Maungakiekie defies easy categorisation. Some parts are affluent – home to leafy streets and multimillion dollar homes. Others, such as Onehunga, were working class, but have been gentrified. The seat is ethnically diverse and home to a younger demographic than the Auckland average.
Maungakiekie is “a really interesting and relatively accurate” representation of modern New Zealand, Swanson says, and has been a consistently reliable barometer for which way support is leaning for parties.
When the Guardian visits the electorate in October, two key themes emerge: a grudging fealty to the National party – which has led the centre-right coalition government since 2023 – and growing support for minor parties.
Jemimah Fifita, a 25-year-old student who works at a local cafe, is about to ditch a family tradition of voting Labour.
“I’m very mindful of who I think I should vote for,” she says, “especially as a young person, because we are struggling” – nodding to high rates of youth unemployment and the rising costs of living.
Fifita is yet to decide who will get her vote, but the centrist Opportunity party has caught her attention. Opportunity has been consistently polling above the 5% threshold of seats needed to enter parliament, but it remains to be seen if that support translates into votes next Saturday.
Across the road, sitting outside a bakery are longtime Onehunga residents, Nigel Higgins and Lance Polmear. Higgins has not voted since the 1980s because he believes “all governments are oppressive”. But Polmear, who works in construction, says he will again vote for National, despite being unhappy with some of its policies, such as immigration.
At a cafe further up the street, retiree Margôt Phillipps reckons the government has been “shocking” this term, so she will be voting for the Green party, for its environmental stance and its policy of redistributing wealth.
In Ellerslie, a more affluent and less diverse suburb than Onehunga, locals are largely sticking with the status quo: the National-led coalition with the right-wing Act party and populist New Zealand First.
Kerry McCullough, a florist on the main street, is “very much against Labour” and will vote National even though she thinks party leader Christopher Luxon is “not very appealing”.
Across the road, butcher David Parsons is weighing cuts of meat for customers. He is switching his party vote from National to New Zealand First, led by Winston Peters, a politician who entered parliament in 1978 with National.
“It’s not something I ever thought I would do – my family has a long history of voting National – but its come to the point where I see a bit more eye-to-eye with Winston Peters,” Parsons says, adding he has become more concerned about immigration and believes the country should boost mining to grow the economy, issues that New Zealand First has campaigned on.
A mood of disillusionment could spell bad news for Luxon and National, who face the possibility of being the first one-term National-led government since the party was founded in 1936.
Polling in recent months has shown just a few points separating the winning and losing blocs. A RNZ-Reid Research poll released on Thursday shows National slumping under 25%, and Labour in a position to form a government alongside the Greens and Opportunity. A 1News-Verian poll released two days earlier had National slightly ahead and returning to power.
Support appears strong for the right-leaning coalition in Maungakiekie, but recent changes to the electorate’s boundary lines could alter the political landscape.
The new boundary lines add nearly 10,000 voters from a left-leaning suburb, but cut about 2,200 voters from a right-leaning suburb. The seat could inflate support for Labour compared with the national result and upset its bellwether status, Swanson says.
Regardless, Maungakiekie will remain one of the most closely watched seats when results roll in on election night, he says.
“They have earned, across several elections, the right to be taken seriously as a signal.”
