Russia-Ukraine humanitarian truce: What is happening in Alyoshki?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:47:05 UTC
03:47:05 KST

Russia-Ukraine humanitarian truce: What is happening in Alyoshki?
Russian and Ukrainian humanitarian teams have begun delivering aid and evacuating civilians from the frontline town of Alyoshki under a temporary ceasefire brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump.
Residents of the town in Russia’s Kherson Region have faced months of severe shortages, with Ukrainian drone attacks and mines disrupting supply routes, according to Russian officials and evacuees interviewed by RT.
An RT correspondent is on the ground covering the mission, which has brought representatives from both sides together to assist civilians. Here is how the agreement came about, what is happening on the ground and what residents have said about conditions in the town.
Where is Alyoshki?
Alyoshki lies on the left bank of the Dnieper River, opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson. It has been under Russian control since 2022 and is part of Russia’s Kherson Region, which Ukraine continues to claim.
The nearby Antonovsky Bridge, once a key crossing between the two cities, was put out of action in 2022. The river has since formed part of the front line separating Russian and Ukrainian forces.
The humanitarian mission is using land routes into Alyoshki, which Russian military engineers have been clearing of mines and unexploded ordnance.
Why was a humanitarian ceasefire needed?
Russian authorities estimated that between 1,500 and 2,000 civilians remained in Alyoshki before the operation, including elderly residents and children. Food, medicine, drinking water and fuel have been scarce, while damaged utilities have deprived residents of basic services.
Kherson Governor Vladimir Saldo has accused Ukrainian forces of attacking supply vehicles and remotely mining access roads. Russian Foreign Ministry envoy Rodion Miroshnik described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods.”
Ukraine, meanwhile, has accused Russia of preventing civilians from leaving. However, evacuees interviewed by RT blamed Ukrainian attacks for making both aid deliveries and evacuation attempts dangerous.
What have residents told RT?
“There’s nothing to eat. No medicine. Drones are constantly hovering above you,” one evacuee said. He described residents being unable to step outside without encountering drones and recalled three supply vehicles being destroyed in succession in the spring, leaving people to survive on vegetables grown in their gardens.
Others recounted receiving food, water and fuel from Russian soldiers and volunteers.
One woman said her husband was killed by a mine while collecting potatoes. She described how Russian troops guided her to safety using drones and a radio during a five-hour journey to a hospital.
Another resident, whose husband was killed in a Ukrainian attack, described houses being “blown away” during bombardments. Another evacuee noted that the people of Alyoshki were treated by Ukraine as “scum” and “traitors.”
Who negotiated the agreement?
The humanitarian crisis was raised during an October 9 telephone conversation between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump. The two leaders agreed to establish direct contact between Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova and Melania Trump’s office.
Subsequent negotiations secured a temporary pause in fighting around Alyoshki, with the US first lady and Pope Leo XIV helping advance the initiative.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has credited Melania Trump with coordinating the effort, linking her involvement to earlier work reuniting children separated from their families during the conflict.
Is the EU involved?
The EU has played no role in negotiating or carrying out the mission. The operation has instead relied on direct Russian-Ukrainian coordination, US mediation and logistical support from Belarus.
Who is leading the humanitarian teams?
Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, have coordinated the practical arrangements and are taking part in the mission.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has also participated in contacts and public announcements related to the operation.
Belarus has provided logistical assistance, with delegations from both countries traveling through the Belarusian city of Gomel before proceeding toward Alyoshki.
How long does the ceasefire last?
The truce took effect at 4am Moscow time on October 27 and is due to expire at 10:59pm on November 1. It covers the humanitarian mission and the routes used to bring in supplies and evacuate residents.
On Friday, Melania Trump said the ceasefire had held for 80 hours, allowing Russian and Ukrainian teams to deliver aid and prepare civilian evacuations.
Lantratova confirmed that both sides were honoring their commitments, reporting no violations.
What is happening on the ground?
Aid distribution and the boarding of evacuation buses were underway on Friday, according to Lantratova.
The humanitarian convoy includes 25 buses and vehicles carrying food, medicine, drinking water, hygiene supplies and fuel for generators.
Residents are free to stay or leave, with evacuation options available for those wishing to travel deeper into Russia or to Ukrainian-held territory.
Those remaining in Alyoshki are receiving essential supplies, Lantratova said. Some have chosen not to leave because they want to remain in their homes or care for relatives.
More than 50 journalists from several countries have arrived to cover the mission, according to Lantratova. They include an RT correspondent and four Newsmax reporters whom Melania Trump identified as observers documenting the operation.
What did securing the routes involve?
Military engineers had to clear mines and unexploded ordnance before humanitarian vehicles could enter Alyoshki.
The Russian Defense Ministry released footage of remotely operated mine-clearing equipment and said many of the explosives discovered along the routes had been dropped by Ukrainian drones.
The operation has already claimed a life. The ministry confirmed that Sergeant Andrey Vedernikov of the 98th Guards Airborne Division was killed on October 28 while clearing a road leading into the town.
According to the ministry, he was fatally wounded by a drone-laid explosive device equipped with a proximity sensor.
Could the operation be repeated?
Although the agreement applies only to Alyoshki, Peskov has suggested it could serve as a model for future humanitarian missions.
He said a successful truce “could set a precedent,” opening the way for similar ceasefires in other areas of the conflict zone.

Korean-owned Philly Shipyard lands $269 million U.S. Navy landing ship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:42:38 UTC
03:42:38 KST

- Hanwha Defense USA won a $269 million subcontract to build one Medium Landing Ship for the U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps in Philadelphia.
- TOTE Services, which manages the program, said construction can begin in late 2027, and the first ship is expected in 2030.
Hanwha Defense USA will build a Medium Landing Ship for the U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps at its Philadelphia shipyard under a $269 million subcontract from TOTE Services, the company announced, giving the South Korean-owned group its first contract to build a ship for the U.S. Navy.
The award covers one vessel at Hanwha Philly Shipyard, with options for three more. TOTE Services, which manages construction of the new class on the U.S. Navy’s behalf, said it has secured building slots that allow work to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027, and the program’s first ship is now expected to be delivered in 2030, later than the fall 2029 target cited when the management contract was awarded in July.
The deal follows an unusual buying arrangement. Instead of contracting directly with shipyards, the U.S. Navy hired TOTE Services as a vessel construction manager, a company that holds the prime contract, picks the builders and oversees their cost and schedule. The U.S. Navy awarded TOTE that $2.2 billion contract in July for up to eight ships, directing Bollinger Shipyards to build one and Fincantieri Marinette Marine to build four, while leaving TOTE to decide how to place up to three more. TOTE said Hanwha was the first shipbuilder selected through that process, based on its pricing and its acceptance of TOTE’s subcontract terms, and that talks with Bollinger and Fincantieri are continuing.
“This award shows the speed at which the VCM model can move from RFP to contract,” said Jeff Dixon, President of TOTE Services. “Through a competitive process, we secured strong terms that benefit the government, along with build positions that allow construction to start in the fourth quarter of 2027.”
The landing ship is based on the LST-100, a design by Dutch shipbuilder Damen that the U.S. Navy selected in December 2025 to speed up a program that had struggled to settle on a design. The ship is about 100 meters (328 feet) long, displaces roughly 4,000 tons and has a range of more than 6,300 km (3,400 nautical miles). It can run onto a beach and unload troops, vehicles and supplies through its bow doors without needing a port, which the U.S. Marine Corps wants for moving small units between islands and coastlines in the Pacific. The U.S. Navy describes the class as filling the gap between small, short-range landing craft and its large amphibious warships, and the services plan a fleet of 35. The same design is already in service with the Nigerian Navy and has been chosen by Australia.
“Since acquiring Philly Shipyard in 2024, Hanwha has made significant investments in its workforce and technology to pave the way to build ships for the U.S. Navy and other federal customers,” said HDUSA President and CEO Michael Coulter.
Hanwha bought the Philadelphia yard in December 2024 for $100 million, with Hanwha Systems taking a 60% stake and Hanwha Ocean the remaining 40%. Earlier this week, Hanwha Defense USA said it is acquiring the controlling stake through an HDUSA-led joint venture, placing the yard under its U.S. defense arm.
The company says the shipyard’s workforce has more than doubled since the purchase to nearly 2,500, and a Hanwha spokesperson told Janes the group has invested $350 million in the site.
Until now, the yard’s government work has come largely through TOTE. It has built National Security Multi-Mission Vessels, training ships for state maritime academies, for the U.S. Maritime Administration, with four delivered so far, and in July it was selected to build the Missile Defense Agency’s new missile-tracking ship, Golden Defender, which is due in 2030. Its only previous U.S. Navy work was a subcontract, announced in March, to help Vard Marine develop concept designs for a future logistics ship.

As Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent newspapers, is forced to close after 33 years, three former staffers look back on its legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:41:49 UTC
03:41:49 KST

As Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent newspapers, is forced to close after 33 years, three former staffers look back on its legacy
Novaya Gazeta has announced that it is closing. For more than 30 years, it covered Russia’s biggest events and told stories about Russians that readers couldn’t find anywhere else. Many outstanding journalists worked at Novaya. Some were killed for telling the truth. Meduza asked former Novaya Gazeta journalists Ekaterina Glikman, Elena Kostyuchenko, and Nadya Yurova to reflect on three decades of work by one of the country’s most important independent publications, which they were all part of.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
Ekaterina Glikman
Special correspondent and deputy editorial director at Novaya Gazeta from 2002 to 2022. Now deputy editor in chief of Novaya Gazeta Europe
My last years of high school coincided with Novaya Gazeta’s best years. I couldn’t get enough of it. Maybe that’s just my impression, but 1997 and 1998 were brilliant years. Above all, because of its star lineup of journalists. Novaya Gazeta was always a paper built around individual writers: Everyone had a very distinctive style, and the articles were fairly opinionated.
That’s not how people write now — everything has to be uniform, polished, and objective. There’s probably something to that; times have changed. But I miss that journalism, where the writer’s voice came through. You could start reading an article halfway through, without looking at the byline, and know who wrote it. Every writer was recognizable. I loved them all.
For my very first university internship, in 1998, I ran straight to Novaya — without arranging anything beforehand. I wanted to be like all those journalists, starting with [investigations editor Yuri] Shchekochikhin. I’m not sure Novaya deliberately recruited young people, but there were lots of kids like me.
Ekaterina Glikman on Yuri Shchekochikhin
I remember Novaya’s old website — it was terribly dated. There were two buttons in the menu linking to memorial pages: “Politkovskaya” and “Shchekochikhin.” For years afterward, I’d click on them to read their articles, until the old website was replaced. Shchekochikhin’s memorial site had an archive of his articles, people’s memories of him, and his prose.
For the first anniversary of his death, we put together a book of memories — a white cover with his signature on it. It was later reissued and expanded. We asked everyone who knew and loved him to write a short chapter. Those chapters were then posted on the memorial site.
Unfortunately, I don’t have any of it with me: I couldn’t take anything with me when the war began, and I can’t travel to Russia anymore. I’d like to reread it now — but I have neither the book nor the website. My whole library is still in Russia.
I joined Novaya in 2002, working in Yuri Shchekochikhin’s investigations department. Before that, I’d worked at the newspaper Segodnya, which was shut down [in 2001]. Salaries at Novaya were terribly low. You couldn’t survive on them. I really wanted to work there, but once you were no longer a student and had to pay rent, it was impossible. I’d stand at the newsstand at the journalism school, looking at the national newspapers — and I didn’t want to work for any of them. There was nowhere to go except Novaya. I had to resign myself to living in poverty but doing what I loved.
I think Shchekochikhin initially screened out most of my story ideas [for my safety]. Of course, that made me absolutely furious. But given how young I was then [Glikman was under 30 at the time], it’s understandable. My favorite kind of work was investigative reporting in the field: from Kuzbass, for example, about miners who’d died, or from Kamchatka, about a man wrongly sentenced to life in prison.
From 2004 to 2006, the last two years of Politkovskaya’s life, I was deputy to editorial director Sergei Sokolov. He handed some of his work over to me. That meant Politkovskaya’s articles, Chechnya — all the hardest stuff.
Novaya had like-minded colleagues at other outlets who reported on realities that made ordinary people uncomfortable. But some outlets were shut down, like Segodnya, and many others willingly turned to sensationalism to rake in cash. Novaya had to pick up the slack for everyone. There were so many stories that nobody but us would write that we could barely cram them into our poor little newspaper.
Everyone disliked us for that — except our loyal readers, who refused to give up access to information. Mainstream readers saw us as a fringe newspaper obsessed with misery. They preferred the sensationalist press, where they could find entertainment and gossip and hide from unpleasant information.
Of course, there are people now who read using a VPN. There aren’t that many of them, but it’s still worth it: This group will play an important role when change comes. But we’ve lost the mass audience. And that audience has lost more than objective information — it’s lost an understanding of the world.
To me, the scariest thing about propaganda isn’t the lies; it’s what gets left out. They don’t actually lie that much. Mostly, they leave things out. And we may even underestimate the effect. When refugees from the Belgorod region fled the shelling for neighboring regions, people there mistook them for Ukrainian refugees — they simply didn’t know the Belgorod region was being shelled.
Novaya was a very influential newspaper. Ministers were removed after our stories came out — remember what happened to [Yevgeny] Adamov. All the top officials read our investigations.
If you look through the print editions, you can barely find an issue without a piece by Politkovskaya. Because if someone had been abducted in Chechnya, the story had to be published as quickly as possible: If the person hadn’t been killed yet, there was a pretty good chance that publishing it in Novaya Gazeta could save them.
Here’s another example. It was 2003, the year Shchekochikhin was murdered. One of the investigations he did let me pursue was about the fishing mafia in the Far East (in fact, it wasn’t a mafia at all — it was the state). We planned a major series of investigations and published only a brief preview, not even the first installment. And after that tiny introduction, I was immediately invited to see the fisheries minister at the State Fisheries Committee, as it was called then. If we had no influence, why would the minister bother inviting a journalist in for a conversation?
On the other hand, many journalists felt disappointed, frustrated, and depressed. You write story after story about outrageous injustices, and nothing changes. Years go by, and suddenly you catch yourself describing the same situation you wrote about two years ago: a different region, a different official’s name, the same schemes. Sometimes even the region is the same — there was one governor, and now there’s another. A lot of people hit a wall with their work; some quit.
Journalism is an alarm that starts flashing and screeching when there’s smoke. Without it, one disaster follows another, until there’s no way out.
It’s very natural not to want to worry about other people’s problems. Why spoil a lovely moment by reading that a missile hit an apartment building in Ukraine today? Looking away isn’t a Russian trait — it’s a perfectly healthy reaction people have all over the world.
Real journalism gets in the way of that comfortable life. A thorn in your side. An irritant. But without it, we won’t have the very comfort we love so much.
Now I find myself wondering: Could we really do all that? When everything has been wiped out, censorship is total, and journalism and free speech have been destroyed, you keep thinking: Wow, back then we could actually write things, go places, talk to people.
Federal troops are killing people in one of the country’s regions [Chechnya]. Abducting civilians, carrying out “mop-up operations.” And Novaya Gazeta journalist Anna Politkovskaya goes to those villages to talk to the residents, and we publish it: who was abducted, who was killed, who was tortured, how they were tortured, where the body was found, and what condition it was in. In 2026, it’s hard to imagine that was ever possible.
Yes, journalists in Russia are threatened, beaten — even killed. But until 2022, we were publishing stories from inside the country about war crimes committed by our own country’s army.
Around the world, journalism is increasingly done at a desk rather than out in the field. But I hope reporting in the field survives. It’s the heart of real journalism — nothing can replace it. But the skills are disappearing, and there’s no one to learn from.
Because of the war and emigration, I suddenly found myself one of the few people in the [Novaya Gazeta Europe] newsroom who’d known Politkovskaya personally. All your life in Moscow, you were one of the younger ones, surrounded by so many people whose memories went back further — and suddenly people like me were the oldest.
I remember Shchekochikhin; I remember Politkovskaya. When she was killed, I was on the team putting that issue together. I was in the thick of so many events — I just never thought that was valuable. And then you suddenly realize you’re carrying all these memories, and you need to tell people how it happened.
Elena Kostyuchenko
Correspondent at Novaya Gazeta from 2005 to 2022
I remember exactly how I first found out about Novaya Gazeta.
I was 14, waiting to see the dentist, and I was really scared. It was going to be a long wait. There were some fashion magazines lying around, but I couldn’t look at them — I actually felt sick. I went outside. There was a newsstand nearby, and I decided to buy something. I noticed a newspaper I’d never seen before, because, as I later learned, Novaya Gazeta sold out very quickly.
I bought it, sat down on a bench in a little park, and opened it to an article. It was Anna Politkovskaya’s piece about a “mop-up operation” in the village of Mesker-Yurt, where Russian soldiers had killed 36 people, if I’m remembering correctly. And one of the local residents had been crucified. I was deeply shaken — I don’t even really remember the dentist’s appointment, because in my head I was still back there.
Afterward, I went to the library and asked for back issues of Novaya Gazeta. I sat there and read them all, one after another. And the more I read, the worse I felt, because I realized I knew absolutely nothing about my country, even though I’d thought I was a pretty well-informed girl, that I’d read a lot and seen a lot. And here were people writing things that didn’t fit my picture of the world at all — a picture that included, for example, “our boys,” “our valiant troops” in Chechnya protecting local people from terrorists.
After Politkovskaya’s articles, I didn’t believe that anymore. At first I was angry at Novaya Gazeta and at Politkovskaya personally. The way she writes, you can’t ignore it anymore, can’t push it out of your head — it stays with you.
Then I realized that this was what journalism was actually about. It has to bring people back to reality, even when they really don’t want to come back. That was when I decided I wanted to work at Novaya Gazeta and started thinking about how to get there.
I lived in Yaroslavl, and my family was dirt-poor. I needed to move to Moscow. The best idea I could come up with was to get into a university with a dorm. The only university I knew in Moscow was Moscow State University, so I applied there, and they accepted me. I’m still very grateful to Moscow State — it’s a wonderful place to grow up.
And here’s how I got into Novaya Gazeta. Russian media outlets usually hired people who’d made a name for themselves, who had experience and qualifications. Novaya Gazeta took us in when we were practically babies and helped us grow into journalists. My plan was to stand outside the newsroom door — like, “Take me on for anything, I’ll mop floors, make coffee, whatever you want.”
But I got lucky. I was writing poetry then, and I was shortlisted for a poetry competition whose judges included Oleg Khlebnikov, who worked on the paper’s culture desk. Oleg noticed me, this girl staring at him, found out from his colleagues that I was studying journalism, and came over: “Your writing’s quite good! You probably have an internship coming up. Would you like to do it at Novaya Gazeta?”
The first person I saw when I came to the newsroom was Politkovskaya. I didn’t recognize her, because Novaya Gazeta was in black and white then. So Oleg and I are walking along, and this incredibly beautiful woman comes flying down the hallway toward us. I ask Oleg, “Who’s that?” And he says, “Oh, that’s Politkovskaya.”
Oleg worked out pretty quickly that I wasn’t especially interested in writing about culture and sent me to the reporting team. That decision shaped my whole life. Nugzar Mikeladze — one of Novaya’s founders — taught an incredible number of reporters everything we know. Not just about journalism, but about being human.
When I joined Novaya Gazeta, I didn’t even know how to turn on a computer! And Nugzar sent me straight out into the field — to Khodorkovsky’s trial. Naturally, I had no idea who Khodorkovsky was or where the trial would be.
To me, one of the most important stories Novaya Gazeta covered was the shelling of parliament in 1993. That was a turning point: I think that was when Russia chose an undemocratic path. Putin won the election in part because people didn’t believe in democracy. Unlike many other supposedly “democratic” publications, Novaya Gazeta — which had only just been founded — didn’t support the shelling.
I also think everything Politkovskaya did was extremely important. Take her reporting on the Nord-Ost hostage crisis. That piece is special to me because it never lost sight of the human beings involved. Despite what was happening, Politkovskaya saw the terrorists as people.
That’s probably the most important thing she taught me and a whole generation of journalists — there’s no virtue in dehumanizing people. Even with an assault rifle pointed at them, journalists have a duty to see the person behind the gun. Such a simple rule. And such a difficult one.
Another hugely important story Novaya Gazeta covered, and a turning point for Russia, was Beslan. Lena Milashina flew there in place of Politkovskaya, who had been poisoned on the plane. Milashina was the first journalist to report that there weren’t 354 hostages, as the authorities were saying, but more than a thousand.
Novaya Gazeta investigated Beslan like no other newsroom. It found grenade launchers on the roof of a building near the school. It carried out a huge investigation whose findings were confirmed by the European Court of Human Rights. I’m talking about the fact that the assault wasn’t intended to save the hostages. I think that was when Putin stopped playing at democracy. Because why bother? You can literally blast a school full of hostages, children, with flamethrowers, tanks, and small arms on live television, and nothing will happen to you.
Novaya Gazeta published many other important stories — about the extermination of gay men in Chechnya, about events in the Donbas.
Why is it important to preserve this whole archive? On the wall of the journalism school in New York where I studied [after Moscow State], it said that journalism is the “rough draft of history.” Journalism is a way to understand what happened, what people thought, what the journalists themselves thought, what perspective they brought to it all.
The shorter the pieces and the smaller the events that prompted them, the more important it is to preserve them. Major events and investigations that make a lot of waves will be archived. But the small details of everyday life probably won’t be.
Novaya Gazeta’s archive is a chronicle of our fuckups as well as Putin’s. At Novaya Gazeta, we also wrote about how lots of small, individual choices lead to catastrophic consequences. I wouldn’t want my pieces “Internat” (“The Institution”), “Trassa” (“The Highway”), or any part of “Nam zdes zhit” (“We Have to Live Here”), about Kushchevka, to disappear.
Novaya Gazeta was founded by a group of journalists — and that same group owned it. We had no owner other than the staff. That meant we could elect the editor in chief, the editorial committee, and the editorial board. You listened to your bosses because you’d voted for them. And if you’d made the wrong choice, you could change it two years later. That made for much healthier relationships among the staff and a healthier approach to work in general. There was no authority you obeyed just because it was authority.
It was my home, my family, and the most important thing in my life.
Nadya Yurova
Podcast producer at Novaya Gazeta from 2020 to 2022. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, she moved to Latvia and continued working at Novaya Gazeta Europe as a YouTube and podcast host
I never particularly dreamed of becoming a journalist. After high school, I applied to drama school, but I hadn’t really dreamed of an acting career either. I spent two years at the Shchepkin drama school in Moscow and left — it was awful, and I decided I’d had enough.
The only option left that wouldn’t mean retaking entrance exams was journalism. I enrolled at the Higher School of Economics.
In my second or third year, I hosted a student talk show [“V tochku!” (“Right on Target!”)]. It was cool, a pretty big production. But in 2018, [Putin’s press secretary Dmitry] Peskov came on the show, and there was a scandal. They started censoring us and telling us who to invite and who not to invite. I really, really didn’t like that, and I started getting disillusioned.
I needed to earn money, so I started working at a coffee shop while I studied. Around the same time, I met Kirill Martynov — he taught us a course called “Media in the Post-Truth Era.”
Martynov noticed me because I worked really hard and always spoke up in his classes. At that point, I had pretty much no idea what my career was going to look like.
When COVID started, before the strictest restrictions came in, I was working at a small cafe that was part of a chain. Everyone wanted to support small businesses then, and Martynov came to my coffee shop. I remember taking off my apron, stepping outside for a smoke, and he goes, “Nadezhda, would you like to work at Novaya Gazeta?”
I had that feeling again that none of this was real, but I didn’t let it show and said with a straight face, “Well, maybe. Doing what?” He said, “What are you interested in?” I said I loved podcasts. He said, “We’re looking for someone for podcasts, actually. Come meet everyone.”
I’d been ready to give up and stay a barista for the rest of my life. Novaya Gazeta came out of nowhere. I’d grown up reading Politkovskaya; this was everything I could have dreamed of, but I had this feeling that it wasn’t real — like, “Is this possible?”
I suggested starting with the most straightforward thing — a news podcast. A Novaya Gazeta writer would write a piece, we’d invite them into the studio, and we’d talk about the article. I did the interviews.
During COVID, we recorded from home. I didn’t have a microphone, so I spoke into my iPhone’s voice recorder under a blanket. Interviewing someone for 30 minutes under a blanket is a bit tricky, but it was worth it.
It felt like fate handed me those first podcast episodes. The very first was with Elena Milashina, the second with Lena Kostyuchenko. It was freaking amazing: Here I was, a young employee who didn’t understand a thing, suddenly getting to know people across the whole newspaper.
A lot of young people joined the paper around the same time I did. We started doing YouTube, podcasts, TikTok — it was madness, and the best time of my career. This was the great Novaya Gazeta, with all these towering figures looking so serious. And we were just a bunch of goofballs and screwups. We sat on the floor during editorial meetings and rode skateboards down the newsroom hallways. They let us do all of it.
[Dmitry] Muratov told me that, in a way, we’d breathed new life into the newspaper.
Then February 24 came. During the first weeks of the war, we were in the newsroom around the clock, putting on daily livestreams with a team of four. We were shouting as loud as we could.
At the end of March 2022, Novaya Gazeta suspended publication. That was a huge blow. It felt like that was it — I no longer had the work that had kept me afloat.
Before I joined the paper, of course, I knew nobody could have written about Chechnya the way Novaya did. Nobody else had that enormous legacy handed down by Politkovskaya and Milashina. The newspaper had always been built around its writers’ individual voices. But only gradually did I come to understand just how great a newspaper I worked for.
Lena Kostyuchenko looks like a beautiful, delicate little flower, but then she goes and spends two weeks living in a residential institution for people with psychiatric and neurological disabilities. Right after Lena returned from the institution, she came onto my podcast [to talk about her piece “The Institution”]. It was as if you could still smell the horror on her — it chilled you to the bone. She was one of the first to say publicly that these institutions are a Gulag — and, in a way, to articulate that idea for the public. I remember not being able to believe I was part of all this.
There’s one project I’m very proud of. I’d dreamed of making a narrative podcast, and Kostyuchenko went to Taimyr to investigate the fuel spill in Norilsk. Around the same time, she also went on assignment to visit the Nganasans, an indigenous people of northern Russia.
When the oil spill happened, it polluted the river where they fished, and the fish disappeared. Lena went to talk to them, partly just to understand how they lived. I gave her a recorder to take along and asked her to record everything that happened to her. Lena brought me dozens of hours of material. That [the podcast “Poka ne vypal sneg” (“Before the Snow Falls”)] was the most interesting work I’ve ever done in my life.
That was also when I realized just how expendable people are to the authorities. This [what’s happening to the Nganasans] mirrors what’s happening across the country, including in the war.
I think that as long as I keep telling people what’s happening in Russia, as long as I keep the idea [of Novaya Gazeta] alive, it won’t be so easy to erase us and shut us up. In the newsroom, people are always talking about [Novaya Gazeta’s] legacy, remembering the journalists who were murdered.
From beginning to end, Novaya Gazeta was a thorn in the authorities’ side. In a country where nothing is allowed, there was one newspaper that caused them trouble — so much trouble that people were killed over it.
Novaya Gazeta is a memory, a record, and a chronicle of the Russian authorities’ fuckups.
On November 5, RIMA and Kronika will open the Novaya Gazeta archive. All 3,373 issues of the Moscow edition from 1993 to 2022, special editions, and much more will be freely available. Some of this material was previously inaccessible. It includes, for example, articles the newspaper was forced to remove on orders from the Prosecutor General’s Office and the media regulator Roskomnadzor. Among them are Elena Kostyuchenko’s reporting from occupied Kherson and the full versions of four issues from February to March 2022 whose contents are hidden on the newspaper’s website. For the first time, Novaya’s entire print archive will be available in one place. Researchers will also be able to request datasets containing the archive’s metadata from RIMA.

Isro’s GSLV-F18/NVS-03 mission successful: Next-generation navigation satellite placed in orbit; NavIC constellation gets a boost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:40:00 UTC
03:40:00 KST

It was the 20th flight of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle. (Photo by C Suresh Kumar)
SRIHARIKOTA: India's regional satellite navigation system, NavIC, which was facing a shortage of operational satellites, got a boost with the successful launch of NVS-03 on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday by Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro).GSLV-F18 carrying 2,250kg next-generation navigation satellite -- NVS-03 -- lifted off from the second launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) in Sriharikota at 11.51pm on Friday, as scheduled. It was the 20th flight of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV). Around 18 minutes later, NVS-03 satellite was placed in a geosynchronous transfer orbit (GTO) of 37,023km apogee and 170km perigee.
"The rocket has successfully and precisely placed the satellite into its intended elliptical orbit. It achieved a 170km perigee and 38,080km apogee. This is the 5th mission from Sriharikota this year. GSLV has carried 34 tonnes of spacecraft to space so far. We achieved this mission with a turnaround time of just 56 days after the GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission in September. With this launch, we have restored NavIC constellation operation as we need a minimum of four satellites to perform positioning, navigation and timing services," said Isro chairman V Narayanan.
He said, “The satellite is healthy, and the solar panel has been deployed. Already three pyro walls are operated, and we have lifted. Every system is totally healthy, and we are going to continue the operation and place the satellite in the intended circular orbit.”NVS-03 is the third satellite in Isro's next-generation navigation satellite system, designed to ensure continuity of services under the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS), operationally known as NavIC. The satellite carries an indigenously developed atomic clock along with procured atomic clocks. It also carries the L1 frequency signal in addition to the existing L5 and S-band signals.NavIC is India's independent regional satellite navigation system, designed to provide positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) services across the country and an area extending approximately 1,500km beyond the Indian landmass. The additional L1 signal, alongside the existing signals, is expected to improve compatibility with other satellite navigation systems and widen the potential use of NavIC in civilian applications.The NVS-03 mission is part of Isro's plan to deploy five second-generation navigation satellites -- NVS-01 to NVS-05 -- to augment the existing NavIC constellation and improve continuity and reliability of navigation services.The launch assumes significance as NavIC was unable to provide standalone positioning services because of a shortage of operational satellites. In a written reply to the Lok Sabha on July 29, Union minister of state for space Jitendra Singh said the constellation had only three satellites providing positioning, navigation and timing services, against the minimum four required for basic positioning services. While its timing service remains functional, the addition of NVS-03, once commissioned, could help restore standalone positioning capability."Since NavIC is being used in a multi-constellation environment for most of the use cases, there is no vulnerability for the users. The next NavIC satellite, NVS-03, is ready for launch and two more satellites, NVS-04 and NVS-05, are in an advanced stage of realisation," the minister had said then.The setback to the constellation followed the failure of NVS-02, launched on Jan 29, 2025, to complete its orbit-raising manoeuvres. An Isro review committee found that an electrical signal had failed to reach a pyro valve in the satellite's oxidiser line, preventing the propulsion system from firing and the satellite from reaching its intended orbit. The failure prompted Isro to undertake corrective measures for subsequent missions.
The first satellite in the second-generation series, NVS-01, was launched aboard the GSLV-F12 on May 29, 2023. It was also the first satellite in the series to carry an indigenous atomic clock.The Isro chief said five more launches are planned this financial year. “We are moving closer to Gaganyaan G1 uncrewed flight,” he added.

EU, Canada forge strategic alliance as Trump’s policies strain transatlantic ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:38:13 UTC
03:38:13 KST

The European Union and Canada have agreed to deepen their strategic partnership, announcing a series of initiatives on trade, technology and security as US President Donald Trump’s policies strain Washington’s relations with traditional allies.
The agreement was announced on Friday following a two-day summit in Montreal attended by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.
Canada will join the EU’s $103 billion (€90 billion) support loan for Ukraine, initially contributing $558 million (€500 million), while the two sides will expand cooperation across several strategic sectors.
“The world’s becoming more dangerous and divided. Our societies are being shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, pointing to eroding democratic norms and the “weaponization of trade”.
“Together, Canada and the European Union are anchoring the ground. Anchoring our ground to uphold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can all thrive,” he said.
Canada joins EU’s Ukraine support effort
Canada’s participation in the $103 billion loan comes as Brussels seeks additional support to address Ukraine’s financial needs amid its ongoing war with Russia.
Von der Leyen welcomed Ottawa’s contribution, saying the move sent a strong message of solidarity to Kiev.
“Together, we are stepping up our support for Ukraine,” she said.
The announcement also reflects broader efforts by Canada and the EU to strengthen ties following Trump’s return to the White House. Both have faced US tariffs and territorial rhetoric, prompting renewed discussions about reducing economic vulnerabilities and reinforcing cooperation among traditional partners.
Although Von der Leyen said Canada could not become a full EU member because of its geographical location, she stressed that the bloc wanted to bring the country “as close as possible”.
Critical minerals and AI at heart of economic partnership
Beyond Ukraine, the two sides outlined what a joint statement described as an “alliance for the future” aimed at building a shared space for prosperity and economic security.
They signed a digital trade agreement and a separate arrangement allowing the European Investment Bank to support Canadian critical mineral projects.
Canada has substantial reserves of rare earths and other critical minerals that Europe needs to diversify its supply chains, which currently depend heavily on China. However, developing Canada's mining sector will require significant investment in infrastructure.
The EU also opened access to its supercomputing infrastructure for Canadian researchers, businesses and start-ups, while the partners agreed to deepen cooperation on artificial intelligence, satellite connectivity and navigation.
The technology partnership comes as Europe and Canada seek to strengthen their positions in industries dominated by the United States and China.
On Thursday, Ottawa announced a $1.1 billion (CAN1.6 billion) investment in Canadian AI company Cohere. The firm recently partnered with Germany’s Aleph Alpha, a collaboration Carney cited as an example of the potential for closer transatlantic technology cooperation.
Cooperation extends to education and satellite navigation
The EU and Canada also launched work towards Canadian participation in European initiatives, including the Erasmus student exchange programme and the Galileo satellite navigation system.
Erasmus enables university students to study abroad, while Galileo provides a European alternative to the US-operated Global Positioning System (GPS).
The initiatives underline the expanding scope of the partnership, which now extends beyond traditional trade and diplomacy into technology, education, infrastructure and strategic security.

Urgent: Humanitarian mission in Oleshky completed: Russian official

MOSCOW, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- A humanitarian mission in Oleshky in the Kherson region in Ukraine has been completed, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said Friday. ■

'Five churches set on fire by Muslims?' Fake news by Islamophobic social media accounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:37:58 UTC
03:37:58 KST

'Five churches set on fire by Muslims?' Fake news by Islamophobic social media accounts
Several social media accounts associated with sharing anti-immigrant views claim French Muslims were responsible for burning five churches on October 17 – the day the nation was rocked by en masse protests. But both this number and story are fictitious. The French government agency that monitors religious heritage sites confirmed only one fire in a church occured in recent days; its cause unknown.
The fake claim that groups of Muslims are responsible for setting fire to five churches in France over the course of a single day has been circulating online. The acts supposedly took place on October 17 when violence erupted across several French cities, marring a series of planned peaceful demonstrations.
The claim has mainly been propagated by accounts known for anti-immigrant and islamophobic rhetoric, some of which have exploited footage of previous protests, taking them out of context.
'Muslims want to destroy Christianity'
American conspiracy theorist and podcaster Alex Jones made the claim originally via a post on X on October 25. It included a video purporting to be of one of the churches on fire, but the FRANCE 24 Observers team was able to geolocate the video to confirm in reality it actually showed a rubbish bin on fire in front of an apartment building in Lyon. In early October, Jones also made the unsubstanciated allegation that Catholic priests had been set alight during the protest led by French high schoolers.
"European heritage and history will soon be nothing but ashes without Remigration", read a post by a pro-Trump account, MAGA Nation 47, on X. The post featured a video of the Saint-Michel Church in Bordeaux, appearing to be on fire. But this post also used out-of-context images to deceive viewers. The video was actually filmed back in July and it shows a fire that started at a homeless encampment – which did not reach the church. Several media outlets misreported the false claims.
And such stories haven’t just come from the American far-right. The FRANCE 24 Observers team found one of the most widely shared posts to derive from an Italy-based account. In a Facebook post from October 23, a social media user claiming to be Catholic and with a history of Islamophobic posts – Mauro D. – declared five churches had been set on fire the day prior “by Muslims who want to destroy Christianity”. While he didn't specify details around the location of the churches, his post was shared nearly 10,000 times.
His post featured an image of a fire at the Parisian church of Saint-Sulpice. But the photo dates from 2019 when its door caught fire. Media coverage and early findings by the police laboratory indicated possible arson.
Our team contacted the author of the post but he did not respond.
One church fire, cause unknown
In reality, there have been no fires from October 17 attributed to anyone of Muslim faith, Vice President of the Observatory for Religious Heritage, Maxime Cumunel told FRANCE 24 Observers.
The association – which records any damage to religious structures – only recorded a single fire around this period: at Saint-Médard in Fenouillet, a village near Toulouse.
In a statement published on October 21 by the city council and picked up by a number of media outlets, it has not been possible to determine the exact cause of the fire.
Fires affect 20 to 30 churches a year
It isn’t the first time that false information about church fires has circulated in France. Back in July, the FRANCE 24 Observers team looked into misinformation about a fire at a disused church. At the time, the fake news story was shared by far-right Spanish accounts claiming the fire was linked to “mass immigration.”
Maxime Cumunel told our team that there are many causes for church fires – most often to do with disrepair.
"We are talking about numbers that remain relatively low, with only about 20 to 30 structures affected by fire each year,” he shared.
The Observatory for Religious Heritage published a letter on October 21 denouncing several acts of church vandalism that took place amid the general violence on the periphery of the October 17 protests, including “hateful graffiti” left on the Church of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine des Chartreux in Marseille.
In 2025, a total of 843 anti-Christian acts were recorded in France, representing 34% of all recorded anti-religious acts, according to data published by the Ministry of the Interior that cited the Observatory. This represents a 9% increase on 2024. In 87% of such cases, acts involve damage to property (including graffiti, damage, desecration and theft of sacred objects).
"We are seeing an increase in damage to cultural buildings because we are in a period of crisis. Notably, we are seeing the theft of objects made of precious metal, like chalices, because they have market value,” Hadrien Lacoste, vice president of the Observatory told our team.

Israel demolishes homes of Palestinians blamed for attack on soldiers

Israel demolishes homes of Palestinians blamed for attack on soldiers
Troops hold at least 12 Palestinians near demolished homes as nearly 5,000 remain displaced from Hebron neighbourhoods
Israeli forces have blown up the homes of two Palestinians who killed two Israeli soldiers in Hebron last week. The demolitions came on the eighth day of a military offensive and siege on the southern city in the occupied West Bank.
Troops demolished the homes of brothers Ahmad and Hammouda al-Jaabeh on Friday, after surrounding the buildings since the morning and sealing off the area. The brothers were killed after carrying out an attack on October 23 near the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint, at the western entrance to Hebron, killing two Israeli soldiers and wounding three others.
Reporting from Hebron, Al Jazeera’s Mohammed al-Atrash said army engineers spent at least nine hours inside the homes rigging explosives before detonating them.
When residents tried to approach the site afterwards, large numbers of troops backed by drones moved in and detained at least 12 Palestinians, he said. “Some of these Palestinians are still being detained up to this moment and we monitored live on air their abuse at the hands of the Israeli occupation army,” al-Atrash said.
Israeli forces have fully emptied the Ein Deir Bahha neighbourhood of its residents, he said. Some homes “have been turned into military barracks” and command centres. Hundreds of families in the neighbouring al-Jalda area remain trapped in their homes.
The Hebron municipality said on Tuesday that 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families had been displaced by the offensive. Al-Atrash said Israeli forces had arrested at least 120 Palestinians since the operation began and interrogated hundreds more. At least 13 businesses near the checkpoint have been demolished.
He said Israeli officials had threatened to speed up demolitions in Area C, the part of the West Bank under full Israeli control, in line with measures approved by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich after the attack.
On Friday, dozens of displaced residents, including women, children and older people, protested near the closed al-Jalda roundabout. They demanded an end to the siege and the right to return home.
Raed Nairat, an academic and expert on Israeli affairs speaking from Nablus, told Al Jazeera that the operation’s message had been clear “from day one”.
“It is effectively collective punishment, with the aim of breaking the Palestinians’ will and making him pay a price he cannot bear, as a result of an act he may not have been consulted about and may not be content with,” he said.
Nairat said the operation was driven by political rather than security aims. “It is as if you have turned Palestinian society back to 20 or 40 years ago in terms of fragmentation and turned the entire West Bank into a military zone ruled and controlled by the Israeli army,” he said.
Hamas described the forced displacement and demolitions in Hebron as part of a systematic campaign targeting the Palestinian presence and called for urgent international action.
Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces detained four Palestinians in raids south of Tulkarem. Soldiers and settlers also attacked or drove off olive harvesters in villages near Bethlehem and Nablus.
Israeli military and settler attacks across the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, have intensified since Israel’s war on Gaza began in October 2023.

Rain, snow, icy conditions, and dust storms forecast in Kazakhstan over next three days
Unsettled weather, bringing rain and snow, is expected across much of Kazakhstan from October 31 till November 2, with icy conditions forecast in the northern and eastern parts of the country, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Kazhydromet.

Oman rescues 25 from burning oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz

Oman rescues 25 from burning oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz
Incident comes as Iran says four oil tankers attempting to use ‘unauthorised routes’ to cross the waterway were halted.
Oman has rescued 25 crew members from a burning crude oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz as ships continue to be targeted in the besieged waterway.
The Omani Maritime Security Centre said in a statement on Friday that it had evacuated the people on board the RITI merchant ship. Oman said the vessel was flying the Panamanian flag, and the tracking website MarineTraffic identified it as a crude oil tanker.
The incident came as Iran said four tankers attempting to use “unauthorised routes” to cross the Strait of Hormuz were halted.
It is unclear whether one of the vessels was the tanker whose crew Omani maritime authorities evacuated.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said all four vessels were carrying oil and that the ships had been halted following “incidents” or after hitting mines.
“Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorised route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait,” the IRGC said in a statement on Friday.
Hours later, the IRGC said two more tankers – each carrying more than two million barrels of oil – “exploded and caught fire” as a result of hitting mines while attempting to pass through an “unauthorised route”.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Navy said on Friday that it struck and destroyed an unmanned enemy craft to the east of the strait.
Iran has repeatedly warned vessels against passing through the strait without Tehran’s permission.
It has claimed responsibility for attacks on ships and said last month that vessels attempting to transit Hormuz without authorisation would face “destruction”.
Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28.
The US military denies the naval mine claims. On Friday, United States Central Command chief Brad Cooper said the Strait of Hormuz’s “internationally recognised primary transit routes” had been successfully cleared of Iranian sea mines.
Shipping in the Strait of Hormuz is operating at about 70 percent below pre-war levels, the UK’s Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Friday.

Surging cost of living tops voter concerns ahead of US midterms
- Cost of living is the top US voter concern before midterm elections, with 84% of early voters naming the economy as their biggest issue, according to Pew Research Centre.
- Americans are facing higher gas, food, medicine and travel costs, and many say Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war have added to price pressure.
- Many households are struggling to cover basics, with United Way saying nearly 41% of US households fall below its ALICE threshold for food, housing and health care.
AI generated
FORT LAUDERDALE, United States - Soaring prices for gas, medicine and other cost of living essentials are preoccupying Americans as they start to cast their ballots ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
A whopping 84% of voters who have cast their ballots early listed the economy as their biggest concern this election cycle, according to a recent Pew Research Centre survey.
Kyler Daugherty, a 43-year-old health care worker, summed up the sentiment as he filled up his gas tank in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.
“It’s ridiculous. I mean, everything’s gone up, from food to transportation to gas prices,” he told AFP.
Fuel costs have skyrocketed around the world since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February.
US gas prices rose 9.1% in September alone, according to official figures, a headache for residents in a state like Florida, where most people rely on cars to get around.
“It affects transportation, it affects goods, it affects everything,” Matthew Moore, a 63-year-old attorney, said after he cast his ballot early.
“We transport a lot by truck. Air prices have gone up. My tickets home for Christmas have doubled since last year,” he said.
Broken promises
US President Donald Trump won reelection in 2024 in part because of his campaign promise to lower prices, which had also increased during the term of his predecessor Joe Biden.
“I didn’t believe that promise then, and I probably won’t continue to believe (it),” said Melissa Reer, a 49-year-old social worker worried by her car and home insurance costs.
“But I think there’s a lot more changes have to happen before prices can go down,” she said.
William Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution think-tank, said two of Trump’s decisions this term have directly contributed to cost pressures: launching the war on Iran and slapping tariffs on trade partners.
“It’s within the president’s power to remove most of the tariffs that he’s imposed. It’s within the president’s power to end the war that he began,” Galston told AFP.
For some voters, however, it’s too late.
“My vote was cast based upon my feelings about how they’ve handled the stewardship that the voters have given them,” said Michael Childs, 62.
The White House for its part insists that Trump’s policies are revitalising the US economy and making life more affordable for Americans.
Basic expenses
But millions of households across the United States find it harder than ever to make ends meet.
“The financial hardship is creeping up in America, particularly the middle class,” said Symeria Hudson, chief executive officer of United Way Miami, a non-profit non-partisan organisation focused on improving the health, education and financial well-being of local communities.
United Way’s ALICE metric – which stands for an Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed person – measures working people whose income does not cover basic expenses, such as food, housing and health care.
Nearly 41% of the 132 million households in the United States fall below the threshold.
“We continue to encourage those policymakers to really understand the data,” Hudson told AFP.
Many US voters are running out of ways to cut spending.
“I’m literally cutting back on certain meds because I’m like, ‘I can’t afford them.’ I don’t know what to do next,” Daugherty said. AFP

Misunderstood spooky women are at the heart of this new book
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

The Interview: Spooky Ladies takes bewitching look at lives of lady magicians, mediums and frauds
Were the great magicians and mediums of the 20th century actually women? That's the big question in author Kaz Cooke's surprising and seriously charming new book, Spooky Ladies, out just in time for Halloween.
The stalwart of Australian publishing became a household name for books like Up the Duff: The Real Guide to Pregnancy, Girl Stuff, Babies and Toddlers and It's the Menopause. But Cooke has recently published works such as You're Doing It Wrong, which looks at historically terrible advice for women about health and behaviour.
Her new one takes on the long history of magic and mediumship, especially the spiritualism movement of the late 19th century, through the lens of under-reported lives of the women — all with trademark wit.
From Lady Conan Doyle, wife of the famous Arthur, to the thriving mediumship scene of 1800s Melbourne, Cooke gives texture and context to the stories of women who used magic and vibes to make themselves rich and famous.
You're best known for helping women with books about pregnancy, birth and child-rearing. What inspired you to write about spooky ladies?
Well, over the last few years, I have found that an archive is my happy place. And I have loved looking at women who are no longer with us, who might have been forgotten or erased by history in some way, or misunderstood.
I became fascinated by the idea that there was a gender divide often between magicians and mediums. And then I realised, oh no, there were heaps of women magicians. They just didn't get written about.
And a lot of the famous wives, like Mrs Houdini, Bess, were just always kind of presumed to be timid or to be decorative by the male biographers of the magicians.
It's fascinating to me too that a lot of these women, they were opportunistic and they were frauds and they were incredibly talented at the acts they did.
The story of Lady Conan Doyle is one of the most interesting in the book and it seems you did not love her. She and Arthur Conan Doyle (author of Sherlock Holmes) and their social milieu intersected so much with 20th-century history. What did you learn there?
I really loved Sherlock Holmes as a big kid. So, I had not realised, like a lot of people, what an extraordinarily dim man he was and how he was a con man who didn't know he was a con man.
The way that his second wife Lady Conan Doyle has been written about before is that she was this marvellous English rose, you know, with fine upstanding morals.
But she was just a dreadful woman manipulating her husband by pretending to be a medium and doing the easiest version of mediuming that she could, which was automatic writing.
Why was spiritualism so appealing to the elites of the time?
Spiritualism was appealing to lots of people. I think all these women I've written about are emblematic of their times. Spiritualism started out as a girlish prank and then became a religion, and I think that's got a lot to do with people wanting to believe that we can communicate with people who have died.
Also, it was the age of scientific discovery. So, they were discovering things that you couldn't see, like magnetism and electricity. People kind of wanted to believe that maybe there was this whole spirit world that we couldn't see. A lot of people were just trying to make money and were just frauds.
But a lot of it had to do with the idea of women being ethereal and not very clever, so the spirits would kind of use them just as a conduit. Women were simply tubes!
Tubes! That's a theme in your work I suppose. That's what pregnancy is. You just get treated like a very large test tube.
Yes, absolutely.
One other thing about younger women dashing about in the drawing room after dark is that it's fun. I think it was entertainment. People didn't have streaming services. They used it to survive.
And what I realised was just how much, along with all the glamour, there was just so much grit and determination. They had no pensions, no health care, very often carrying the act if they were a magician, but just being dismissed as, you know, a bit of fluff on the side.
Tell me about the research you did for this book.
I got to go to Texas in between the two Trump presidencies, to the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas in Austin for a couple of weeks. They have a collection there of his magic files on other magicians.
So aside from obeying the sign that said I wasn't allowed to leave my handgun in the locker, I was in absolute heaven.
For example, I found the original love notes that Harry Houdini would leave on the pillow for Bess. Biographers and novelists have always said that Houdini's relationship with Bess was really childlike and he was sickly sweet and sentimental. But when you see and read the real thing, you can absolutely see that they were both in on the joke.
I got quite cross about the way that Bess Houdini had been written about as if she was this timid person who was always worried and didn't understand how the act worked. It's almost libellous. You can't libel the dead, as you well know, but I was sort of indignant on her behalf.
I think these women have been viewed in lots of ways, but all of the ways are one-dimensional.
Some of the research was also in Australia. Tell me about that.
There was a lot. I was so excited when I realised that Moi-Yo Miller, who was a girl from Geelong who escaped the Nazis, had living relatives. She was incredibly glamorous and clever and a recognised magician's assistant.
Her daughter, Charisse, and granddaughter, Celeste, live in Melbourne and they came over and chatted for hours. Then they so kindly left Moi-Yo's own scrapbooks with me for a couple of weeks so I could go through them.
After that I said to them: "Look, there's this guy in this other book that says this really sexist thing. I don't think that's right." They corrected a lot of stuff that was on the record, and that was incredibly useful.
Whereas for a lot of the others in the book, sometimes you'd have to read six books about a male magician to get a few paragraphs about his wife, who was an equal partner.
My final question for you is if you had to run a spooky grift, what would it be?
That's a great question! I've actually thought about finding some performers who'd be interested in doing the mind-reading act that Agnes Zancig did, but the problem with that is that we just haven't got the time. You have to memorise so many codes.
I think if I was to do a grift, I think it would have to involve dress-ups. I'd like to dress like Adelaide Herrmann. I could do with a tiara and a bit of diaphanous carry-on, I reckon.
Spooky Ladies is published by Scribner.

Mor Shamli, whose husband Alon was murdered before her eyes in a shooting attack in Egypt on October 8, 2023, has died after more than three years of suffering. Her parents, Ilan and Shoshi Cohen, said: "We cannot comprehend it, and we ask that our privacy be respected. Since the tragedy in Egypt and the trauma she endured, she was living but dead. Her husband was murdered beside her, and she never recovered. Her soul was murdered there in Egypt, and today she has simply died before her time."
"Mor was murdered along with Alon in Egypt. She continued living, but she could not bear the pain and the loss of her husband, Alon," her parents said. "She had no desire to live. She was simply living but dead, until today, when she is no longer with us."
In January, Mor announced to her Instagram followers that she intended to end her life through assisted suicide in Switzerland. The announcement sparked a wave of false rumors that the procedure had already taken place and that she had died. In Instagram Stories posted that month, she explained the painful decision she had made and the feelings that had accompanied her since the attack, which took place just one day after the October 7 massacre in communities near the Gaza Strip.
"The pain is unbearable. You wouldn't believe how many tears the heart and eyes can produce," she wrote in January. "I am not alive, but not entirely dead either. I exist as though I am floating above life. Here, but not here. My life ended there in Egypt on October 8, 2023, when they murdered us. The bullet that struck Alon's heart struck mine too."
"My pain did not end with the gunshot. It began there and continued for another two years," she wrote. "I used that time to try to obtain at least a minimum of justice, but I failed. Our country failed in that. What I hope we managed to achieve, at least to some extent, was to make people know who you were and give you the honor you deserve. You touched so many people during your life, and now in death as well. You will not be forgotten because you were, and still are, a true angel, and everyone has something to learn from you. I am sorry if we did things that seemed grandiose when modesty defined your entire being. But every act of remembrance and every cause reflected something connected to you: contributing to the community, to people, to sports and to matters of the heart."
She also apologized to those around her, thanked her loved ones and explained the reasons behind her decision. "I am sorry to everyone that for these past two years I have not been myself. Thank you to my wonderful family and Alon's family, who were always by my side, supporting and loving me even when I pushed you away. I was blessed with the most amazing parents. Every achievement of mine is thanks to you. Thank you to my beloved sisters, Shaked and Agam. Thank you to Alon's family, who always made me feel like a daughter and a sister. Thank you for bringing Alon into the world and making him the person he was. Thanks to you, I was blessed with the best husband and friend anyone could dream of."
"I am sorry that I am hurting everyone, that the suffering is being passed on to you. There are no words that can express how sorry I am. I hope you can understand and forgive me. I wish that every day of your lives could be like the life Alon and I shared together, full of love and happiness. I am sorry to the rest of the family and to my friends. I am sorry that we cannot say goodbye properly. Thank you for everything you were to me. Please try to remember me as I was before that terrible day. And do not hold anger in your hearts. Now I am no longer suffering. Now I am happy and at peace."
"Thank you for 32 wonderful years (34 minus 2), during which I managed to fulfill all my dreams. I managed to do everything," she wrote. She concluded with a line from Frank Sinatra's song: "I did it my way."
In the posts she shared online, expressing the pain and sorrow that never left her, Mor wrote her age as "34-2," subtracting the two years and three months that had passed since her beloved Alon was murdered. The couple had traveled together to many countries around the world. Since his murder, Mor had suffered profound emotional anguish, pain and psychological distress.
Alon, who coached a Hapoel Tel Aviv youth soccer team and worked as a physical education teacher, was murdered alongside Amnon Bezalel and Hagai Efrat by an Egyptian police officer who opened fire with his personal weapon during an organized tour in Alexandria. The attack took place just one day after the October 7 massacre, while the group was near Pompey's Pillar, a Roman triumphal column considered one of the best-known tourist attractions in Alexandria, Egypt's second-largest city.
Mor's uncle, Nahum Israeli, wrote Friday: "For three years, you have been gone. You have not been at peace, not been present, not been yourself. Now there is peace for you. You died back then, three years ago! When that bullet pierced the heart of your beloved Alon, it pierced yours too. But now there is peace for you. A huge crack opened in all our hearts three years ago, and now it has grown, widened and deepened. But at least now there is peace for you. We remain here to lick our wounds, mend what has been broken and preserve life. If only there is peace for you now. Give us a sign so that we know. Are you at peace now? Mor Shamli, my beloved niece."

Pentagon’s Top Military Planner Reportedly Fired After Admitting Ukraine and Iran Leaks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:28:10 UTC
03:28:10 KST

- Category
- World
Pentagon’s Top Military Planner Reportedly Fired After Admitting Ukraine and Iran Leaks
The Pentagon’s top military planner admitted to leaking classified information about Ukraine and Iran to two reporters from separate outlets over roughly a year, Axios reported on October 30.
Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was fired this week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the alleged disclosures, which a US official told Axios Sylvia acknowledged on video after failing four polygraph tests.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
An internal Pentagon report accused Sylvia of making “unauthorized disclosures to the media” and noted that he cooperated with investigators, including by providing his personal phone for forensic examination. The investigation was conducted by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
The report stated that Sylvia’s contacts with reporters began as early as June 2025 and continued through Signal and in-person meetings. In one case, he met a reporter at a Silver Diner in Arlington, Virginia, after the journalist’s Pentagon access had been revoked.
During that meeting, Sylvia allegedly relied on notes taken while reviewing a classified secret report and verbally disclosed information on US assistance to Ukraine, according to Axios. The reporter was writing a book and met Sylvia twice.
The report noted that Sylvia did not coordinate the meetings with the Pentagon’s Public Affairs Office or seek review of the information before providing it to the reporter.
Investigators also examined Sylvia’s Signal communications with another reporter. The report stated that Sylvia received messages believed to concern Iran and later deleted the entire message thread, removing records of Signal messages and calls from his personal phone.
US officials told Axios they suspected the deletion was intentional, while Sylvia maintained that he believed he had erased the thread accidentally.
The report further stated that Sylvia admitted being one of 20 officials cited in another story criticizing Pentagon leadership.
Another US official told Axios that Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle’s office had pushed the Joint Staff to release a statement supporting Sylvia before the reason for his dismissal became known internally. An Army official disputed that account, calling it “a coordinated campaign of lies” and stating that Telle’s office had not advocated for such a statement.
Sylvia’s dismissal comes amid a wider Pentagon crackdown on unauthorized disclosures. In July, the Defense Department announced a joint task force with the Justice Department aimed at identifying leakers and prioritizing prosecutions for unauthorized disclosures to the media, Axios reported.
Sylvia’s firing comes as Hegseth is separately withholding approval for a major transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. The missiles have already been paid for by Ukraine’s allies, but their delivery remains pending authorization from the US Defense Department.

Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:27:51 UTC
03:27:51 KST

A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
The S&P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less.
More than $2tn in market value is set to be wiped from the Nasdaq 100 this month, as big tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough.
The wipeout would amount to slightly more than SpaceX’s entire market value. The index has fallen more than 5.8% so far in October as the AI trade ran into turbulence, with hyperscalers Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon raising spending forecasts further as they race to expand AI infrastructure.
Intel tumbled nearly 30% and is flirting with its worst day since 1974, even though the chipmaker reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell far short of analysts’ expectations.
Amazon fell 1.8% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. The company also disclosed that it had spent more this year than anticipated.
A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12%, wiping $500bn from its market capitalization, to its worst day on record after telling investors that it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring because of similar, mammoth investments in AI.
Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make AI investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI datacenters have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward.
Such losses overshadowed an otherwise mixed day for the rest of Wall Street, with the S&P 500 roughly evenly split between gainers and losers.
Expectations are high broadly for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

Polish president turns back from Senegal trip as top court chief suspended

WARSAW, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Polish President Karol Nawrocki turned back to Poland on Friday while en route to Senegal after a far-right ally was suspended as head of the country’s top court, escalating a battle with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government over control of the judiciary.
Earlier on Friday, the Constitutional Tribunal said its longest-serving judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska had suspended Bogdan Swieczkowski, the tribunal’s president and an appointee of Tusk’s far-right predecessor, and was now in charge of the court.
Hundreds of protesters gathered outside the tribunal late on Friday amid a heavy police presence, while right-wing politicians addressed the crowd accusing Tusk’s government of carrying out a coup against the court.
“At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning,” Nawrocki said on X.
NEW DRAMA IN LONG-RUNNING CONFLICT OVER COURT
A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognise appointees put forward by the other side.
Tusk, writing on X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors — the Law and Justice Party — of subverting.
“This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he said.
The dispute dates back to 2015, when the nationalist Law and Justice sought to appoint judges to seats already filled by the previous government.
Its nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, while critics at home and abroad said the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.
After Tusk’s coalition took office in 2023 it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court, but Law and Justice ally Nawrocki has acted to thwart those efforts since his election as president in 2025.
Earlier this year, Nawrocki refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, declined to seat judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
Last month, the parliament appointed Tusk ally Maciej Berek to the tribunal, which critics said undermined the government’s stated goal of restoring checks and balances.
