Exclusive-Pakistan military ‘cautiously optimistic’ on Iran-US mediation
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:27:12 CET
03:27:12 KST

By Rick Noack
RAWALPINDI, Pakistan, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pakistan’s military is “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between Iran and the United States, its spokesman said on Friday in his first interview since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir — Pakistan’s chief mediator in its efforts to de-escalate the now eight-month-old Iran war — has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive sign.
PACT DOES NOT BAR NEW MEMBERS
“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
There were still “powerful spoilers and detractors,” who believed conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan’s armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed or whether the United States had backed the trip.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Munir in Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.
After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional countries without foreign intervention.
The wording of the pact does not bar new members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.
“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries’ political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. “We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict,” he added.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group has been reignited by the Iran conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.
HOME FRONT
On the home front, the federal government suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, led by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), on October 11 and detained Chief Minister Sohail Afridi.
The government had accused the provincial administration of failing to tackle militancy. The PTI rejected the allegations and says its government took part in counter-terrorism efforts. PTI leaders called the move a pretext to crush protests.
Asked if there would now be larger military-led campaigns in the province, Chaudhry said that was not how the army conducted counter-terrorism.
“Our counter-terrorism operations are based on what we call IBOs, intelligence-based operations… The tempo of the freedom of action of (those) IBOs will further increase,” he said.
Independents backed by Khan’s PTI won the most directly elected seats in the February 2024 election but fell short of a majority. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was the only province controlled by Khan’s party.
Khan has been in jail since 2023, and his supporters see the military behind his imprisonment and the dismantlement of the PTI. The army denies involvement in politics.
(Reporting by Rick Noack; Writing by Ariba Shahid; Editing by Andrew Heavens)

Ukraine initiated an urgent meeting of the UN Security Council over the massive Russian strikes on Dnipro, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk on October 29. As a result of the attacks by the Russian Armed Forces that day, 20 people were killed and dozens were injured. On October 30, Ukraine’s Permanent Representative to the UN Andrii Melnyk reported this on the social network "X", UNN reports.
Details
According to the diplomat, the Ukrainian side requested that an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council be convened over the latest Russian attacks on civilians. Melnyk said that he had signed the relevant letter addressed to the President of the UN Security Council, emphasizing the need for an international response to the deaths of civilians.
In light of Russia’s latest barbaric atrocities against Ukrainian civilians in Dnipro, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk, where Russian missiles deliberately killed 20 Ukrainians and wounded dozens of others, we are convening an urgent meeting of the UN Security Council
The Ukrainian diplomat also called for Russia to be expelled from the United Nations. He also noted that previous discussions at the UN had not yet produced sufficient practical results. Despite this, Ukraine will continue to use international platforms to draw attention to Russian attacks and their consequences.
Context
On October 29, Russian forces carried out a series of strikes on Dnipro, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk, killing at least 20 people.
In Dnipro, a Russian drone attacked the railway station platform, where passenger trains were located. Fifteen people were killed in the strike, and another 14 were injured.
In Chernihiv, a Russian drone struck the central part of the city. Two 15-year-old girls were killed, and dozens of people were injured. Children are among those injured.
In Kremenchuk, Poltava region, residential buildings came under Russian attack. Three people were killed and another 32 were injured, including six children.

US midterms: Could Texas break decades of Republican dominance and reshape Senate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:21:16 UTC
03:21:16 KST

Texas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since Lloyd Bentsen won re-election in 1988. The last Democrat to serve, Bob Krueger, briefly held Bentsen’s seat by appointment before leaving office in June 1993.
Now, more than three decades later, Democrat James Talarico is threatening to break that Republican hold. Recent public polls have generally shown him narrowly ahead of, or tied with, Republican Ken Paxton, although many of those leads fall within the margin of error.
A Democratic victory would mark a historic departure for Texas. But for some voters, the election turns on something more immediate than political history: how much it costs to get through the day.
"Everything is so expensive. To eat, it costs like $30 or $20, just to eat and feed yourself. Every day," Houston resident John McCary tells TRT World in a TV interview.
Another Houston resident, Heather Bromfield, describes the same pressure.
"Everything has gotten a lot more expensive… It's extremely expensive compared to a few years ago," she says.
Their concerns offer a glimpse of the household pressures surrounding a race now drawing national attention. With Republicans defending a narrow Senate majority, the outcome in Texas could help determine who controls the chamber.
Why is Texas important?
Donald Trump carried Texas by roughly 13.7 percentage points in 2024. Just two years later, the close Senate contest is testing how much of that Republican advantage Paxton can retain against Talarico.
Paxton defeated incumbent John Cornyn in the Republican primary contest, leaving the party to reunite after an internal battle while defending a seat long considered secure. For Democrats, that creates an opening, though competitive polls are no guarantee of victory.
The Washington Post identified Texas as one of seven states central to the Senate battle. Its emergence as a battleground complicates Republican calculations, putting pressure on the party to protect its own territory as it competes elsewhere.
Winning Texas also requires reaching voters across sharply different communities. Its major metropolitan centres, including Houston, Dallas, Austin and San Antonio, sit alongside fast-growing suburbs and vast rural areas. A large Latino electorate is central to both parties’ efforts, with neither candidate able to take its support for granted.
The longer-term significance lies in what a Democratic breakthrough might reveal. Would it reflect the particular strengths and weaknesses of these two candidates, or suggest a broader opening for the party?
One election would not settle that question. But it could change where both parties spend their money, recruit candidates and believe they can win.
The pivotal state
Texas also occupies a decisive place in an election model that uses prediction markets to assess the battle for the Senate.
In the analysis shared with TRT World, Yale economics professor Ray Fair ranks 14 contested states using market prices. Under his assumptions, Democrats need to win eight of those contests to secure a majority, with Texas sitting at the threshold.
"According to the ranking assumption, if the Democrats win Texas, they will win all the states above it," Fair says.
That makes Texas the pivotal state in his model: the estimated chance of a Democratic Senate majority matches the estimated chance of a Talarico victory.
The relationship rests on an assumption, however, rather than an electoral rule. Results need not follow the markets’ ranking, and Democrats could win some states while losing others placed above them.
Market prices have also shifted since Fair’s quoted snapshot. By late October, Kalshi and Polymarket were generally pricing a Talarico victory at around 70 percent, above the earlier readings in the low-to-mid 60s.
Those figures reflect market expectations, fluctuate continuously and should not be confused with polling leads.
For Republicans, the contest tests their ability to keep a familiar stronghold within reach. For Democrats, it tests whether a promising coalition can deliver an actual statewide victory.
Beyond November, both parties will be studying whether the forces making Texas competitive can travel elsewhere in the South.

Moscow accused of blocking the UN

As one of the council’s five permanent members, Russia holds veto power over its final resolutions, allowing Moscow to block action on its own war against Ukraine.

His remarks came as the Trump administration continues to ease economic pressure on Moscow.

The move came just three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which was intended to target Russia’s energy and defense sectors.
The Russian Direct Investment Fund, which helped arrange the diesel shipments, is now also seeking the removal of US sanctions against it, The New York Times reported.

Russian forces struck the city’s railway station again on Friday, injuring a woman, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
In Chernihiv, a Russian Banderol strike on the city center killed two 15-year-old girls and injured 27 people, among them a 10-month-old girl.
In Kremenchuk, attacks on two locations, including an area where a boarding school was damaged, killed three people and injured 32, six of them children.
Russian guided aerial bombs (KABs) also hit an apartment building in Izium, Kharkiv region, while late in the evening, ballistic missiles struck Kyiv, setting warehouses on fire and damaging residential buildings.
In the evening of that same day, Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
During the 81st UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York late September, 51 UN member states signed a joint statement backing Ukraine and urging Russia to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations.
On that same day, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council that Russia will not halt its aggression against Ukraine even during negotiations, rejecting growing international calls for a ceasefire.

Germany is accelerating military preparations amid the threat of a possible Russian attack on the Baltic states - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:10:34 EET
03:10:34 KST

Germany is accelerating military preparations amid the threat of a possible Russian attack on the Baltic states - media
Kyiv • UNN
More than 70 generals assessed the defense of the Baltic states and urged NATO to prepare more quickly for a confrontation with Russia. Germany plans to reinforce its troops and stockpiles.
More than 70 generals and senior officers from Germany and the Netherlands visited Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to assess potential combat areas on the border with Russia. The military leadership believes that NATO needs to accelerate preparations for a possible military confrontation. Die Welt reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication, since Tuesday, military leaders from both countries have been visiting border areas with Russia. The trip, which was largely organized in secret, is being called unprecedented. It is intended to demonstrate the seriousness of the European NATO members' intentions to fulfill their mutual assistance obligations.
Germany's Inspector of the Army, Christian Freuding, together with his Dutch counterpart, Jan Swillens, is studying possible areas for operations in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
We have all reached the shared conclusion that we need to prepare even faster for an immediate response, improve our capabilities every day, and only in this way will we be able to fulfill our great responsibility
Germany has already deployed the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania, whose formation is still under way. In addition, since July, the German-Dutch Corps has been responsible for the possible conduct of NATO ground operations in Estonia and Latvia.
Thus, the Baltic countries have become the main area of responsibility for the German Army. If necessary, German troops are to be rapidly redeployed there in large numbers.
Freuding said that he currently sees no indications that Russia is preparing for a possible limited attack on NATO territory. At the same time, he does not consider such a scenario entirely implausible.
According to him, Vladimir Putin could potentially use captured Alliance territory as an instrument of political pressure on the allies, demanding that they end support for Ukraine in exchange for ending the offensive.
The Russian armed forces will probably have a numerical advantage over us in this region
Among the preparation priorities, he named protection against threats in low-altitude airspace, countering electronic interference, and the development of unmanned systems and digital communications supported by artificial intelligence.
Germany also plans to pre-position weapons and material stocks in the Baltic countries to ensure that its troops are ready for prolonged defense.
Particular attention is being paid to long-range strike capabilities. The German Army is considering purchasing cheaper cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,500 km. They are planned for use in strikes against troop concentration areas and the enemy's supply routes. According to the publication, the purchases could be made both in Ukraine and in Germany.
Meanwhile, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are building the "Baltic Defense Line" along NATO's eastern flank. It involves constructing military obstacles and communications infrastructure, as well as deploying unmanned systems for attacks, defense and reconnaissance.
Directly near the Russian border, the Baltic countries are also digging trenches and building bunkers. One potential flashpoint is said to be the Estonian border city of Narva, where about 87% of the 52,000 residents are of Russian origin.
During the visit, the German and Dutch generals were presented with a detailed report on the defense preparations. At the same time, details of the military planning remain classified.
According to Die Welt, Estonian troops play loud music by the German band Rammstein from loudspeakers. The noise is intended to prevent Russian border guards from eavesdropping on conversations. Their post is reportedly located just over 100 meters from the site of the work.

Polish Army Received New Division-Sized Set of Krab Self-Propelled Artillery Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:09:54 UTC
03:09:54 KST

The Polish Armed Forces received another batch of Krab self-propelled artillery systems as part of the REGINA contract.
This was reported by the Armament Agency of the Polish Ministry of Defense.
The equipment was delivered to units of the 11th Lubusz Armored Cavalry Division named after King Jan III Sobieski.
The new delivery included a number of vehicles that make up a division: a command and staff vehicle, command and control vehicles, transport and loading vehicles, and Krab self-propelled howitzers.
The delivery was carried out by Huta Stalowa Wola (HSW), a subsidiary of the state-owned defense and industrial conglomerate Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa (PGZ).
REGINA is a Polish program to develop divisional artillery sets based on 155-mm self-propelled howitzers for the Polish Army. A standard division consists of 24 Krab self-propelled howitzers, as well as 11 support vehicles on tracked and wheeled chassis.
The Polish Ministry of Defense and HSW signed a contract for the delivery of the first four divisions in December 2016. In 2020, the parties concluded a supplementary agreement for the delivery of a fifth divisional set, and subsequently ordered additional vehicles to replace equipment transferred to Ukraine.
The Krab self-propelled howitzer is a Polish 155-mm self-propelled howitzer on a tracked chassis, developed by Huta Stalowa Wola. The artillery system’s design incorporates a licensed turret from the British AS-90 self-propelled howitzer with a 52-caliber barrel and a modified chassis from the South Korean K9 Thunder self-propelled howitzer.
The artillery system is capable of firing up to 40 km using active-reactive ammunition. The system’s maximum rate of fire is up to 6 rounds per minute, and the vehicle’s crew consists of 5 people.
The howitzer is equipped with the modern TOPAZ automated fire control system, digital communications, and night vision devices. The vehicle’s combat weight is approximately 48 metric tons, and its 1,000-horsepower diesel engine allows it to reach a highway speed of up to 60 km/h.
Another batch of American M1110 Joint Assault Bridge (JAB) tank bridge-layers has arrived in Poland.
The units are designed to facilitate the crossing of heavy armored vehicles over various obstacles.

Canada aims to become EU's first 'associate member' by June 2027, Carney says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:09:25 UTC
03:09:25 KST

Mark Carney has set June 2027 as the deadline to make Canada the European Union's first-ever "associate member". The category, which has no precedent, has been fiercely opposed by Germany.
Canada and the European Union aim to conclude negotiations on the country's potential "associate membership" of the bloc by June 2027, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday, following a bilateral summit in Montréal.
The proposed status, which has no basis in the EU treaties, is intended to bring the two allies closer across three areas: policy, programmes and governance. Its practical implications, however, remain to be negotiated.
Ahead of the summit, Germany opposed the term "associate member" during negotiations on a joint declaration. The final text instead refers to an "ever closer association". Carney, however, appeared determined to pursue the vision.
"We are working towards the deepest possible partnership short of accession, because of our geography, with Canada becoming the European Union's first associate member," Carney said at the closing press conference.
"In the coming months, we will determine the full substance, scale and scope of this new form of membership," he added.
Standing alongside him was European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who surprised EU capitals in September by proposing that Canada become the bloc's first-ever associate member. The idea had not been broadly discussed with member states beforehand.
Carney, who was in the audience for her announcement, initially appeared reluctant to embrace the proposal amid concerns over its implications for Canadian sovereignty.
On Friday, however, he defended the term.
"Today, we move towards associate membership for Canada, and we launch a new alliance for the future that will deliver now and in the future with like-minded nations," he said. "We're just getting started."
Von der Leyen pointed to several immediate benefits, including Canada's full integration into the Horizon and Erasmus programmes, and the €90 billion support loan for Ukraine.
The summit also expanded cooperation on digital trade, energy, critical raw materials, supercomputing, artificial intelligence and satellite technology.
"The concept of an associate member is uncharted territory, but we have the ambition, trust and creativity to shape it together," von der Leyen said.
"And to be crystal clear: this is a partnership, not against anyone else, but for our common strength. Bilaterally, this is the highest form of partnership."
The European Commission and Canadian government will hold a college-to-cabinet meeting in the spring to flesh out the proposal. Carney is then expected to attend an EU leaders' summit in June, when he hopes to conclude the negotiations.
How the arrangement would be ratified across Europe remains unclear. Carney has previously pledged to put the proposal to a vote in the Canadian parliament.
Asked about Germany's opposition, von der Leyen sidestepped the question, saying there was "broad support" among member states for bringing Canada closer to the bloc.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was the first to float an "associate member" definition in the context of Ukraine's own EU aspirations. Kyiv rejected the idea, saying it wants to be a full-time member.
Commission officials suspect Berlin's resistance to von der Leyen's initiative stems from the fact that Merz considers it his own.
"We would have loved to discuss full-fledged membership, but it is impossible. We know that," von der Leyen said, referring to EU treaties, which reserve membership for European states.
"This is the start of an intense work that we see here. We have the vision. We have an idea. We have to develop the framework. We have to fill it with life."
European Council President António Costa, who represents the collective position of EU countries, notably avoided the term "associate member", sticking instead to the joint declaration's wording of an "ever closer association".
"Our relationship is so special that we want to create something new, to go beyond a simple association," Costa said.
"Our association will be the closest, deepest and most unique of its kind."

US midterm early voting hits record 48 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:09:22 UTC
03:09:22 KST

US midterm early voting hits record 48 million
- A record 47.9 million Americans have already voted in the US midterm elections, beating the 2022 early vote total of 45.9 million.
- Turnout is strongest in battleground states like Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas and Georgia, with Democrats making up a larger share of early ballots.
- Experts say the figures do not predict the result, as many voters still have to cast ballots and Republicans often vote more on Election Day.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - A record 47.9 million Americans have already voted in next week’s US midterm elections, with participation surging in key battleground states and registered Democrats outpacing Republicans, figures showed Oct 30.
The University of Florida’s Election Lab had recorded 47,922,669 early votes nationwide by midday, surpassing the previous midterm record of 45.9 million cast ahead of Election Day in 2022.
The surge is especially pronounced in states with fiercely contested Senate races that could determine control of the chamber during the final two years of President Donald Trump’s presidency.
In Texas, more than six million people had voted early by Oct 28, according to official figures, with in-person turnout running around 50% ahead of the same stage in 2022.
North Carolina’s election board reported early voting up nearly 37% on the same point four years ago, while South Carolina surpassed its entire 2022 early vote total on Oct 26, with five days of early voting still to go.
In Kansas, where Republican Senator Roger Marshall faces a tough re-election fight, advance ballots were running around two-thirds ahead of 2022 last week, according to the secretary of state’s office.
In states that record voters’ party affiliation, registered Democrats have accounted for a substantially larger share of early ballots than Republicans.
Election Lab figures showed Democrats making up around 44% of early voters in those states, compared with 31% for Republicans and 25% for unaffiliated or minor-party voters.
University of Florida political scientist Michael McDonald, who oversees the Election Lab, has pointed to rising participation among Black and Hispanic voters in states that report racial and ethnic data, with particularly strong turnout in heavily Hispanic communities along the Texas-Mexico border.
In Georgia - where early in-person voting broke the state’s midterm record on Oct 29 - women accounted for 56% of ballots cast by that day, compared with 44% for men.
“Georgians continue to head to the polls in record numbers because they trust the system,” top elections official Brad Raffensperger said Oct 29.
But experts warn against interpreting the figures as a prediction of the election outcome.
A voter’s party registration does not reveal which candidates they supported, and tens of millions more Americans are expected to cast ballots on Oct 27.
In recent elections, Republicans have tended to turn out in greater numbers on Election Day, potentially narrowing or reversing the Democrats’ early advantage.
And higher early participation does not necessarily translate into higher overall turnout, since some voters may simply be casting ballots sooner than in previous elections. AFP

Binance loses $6.3 billion in record crypto hack linked to North Korea
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:06:20 EET
03:06:20 KST

Hackers have stolen approximately $6.3 billion (€5.4 billion) from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what investigators describe as the biggest known financial theft in history. Blockchain researchers have linked the attack to North Korean hackers, while US authorities have joined efforts to trace the stolen assets.
The breach occurred late on Thursday, with most of the cryptocurrency transferred from Binance-controlled wallets in approximately 20 minutes. The exchange suspended deposits and withdrawals and pledged to compensate users for any losses.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Binance said it had allocated $6.34 billion from company funds to cover the theft. Around $3 billion of the affected assets have been identified or frozen, although the company has not provided a full account of the remaining funds.
The attack targeted a cryptocurrency hot wallet, which remains connected to the internet to process transactions. Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng said hackers manipulated transaction authorisation systems to bypass the exchange's security controls.
The company's investigation initially identified a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer as a possible entry point. Subsequent findings indicated that attackers had gained access through additional systems.
"This was not carried out by one person," Teng said in a video statement. He added that the attackers deployed software designed to destroy evidence of their activities.
Blockchain intelligence companies TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic attributed the operation to North Korean state-linked hackers. TRM identified the TraderTraitor group, associated with the Lazarus hacking network, with high confidence.
Binance has not confirmed who carried out the theft. North Korea has consistently denied allegations of state-sponsored cryptocurrency hacking.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service have become involved in the case. The Secret Service said its investigators were working with financial companies to identify, freeze and recover stolen assets.
Stablecoin issuer Tether reported freezing approximately $1.57 billion linked to the attack, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
According to Reuters, Binance is cooperating with both US agencies as investigators follow transactions across blockchain networks.
The $6.3 billion theft exceeds the previous cryptocurrency hacking record of approximately $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in February 2025, an operation the FBI attributed to North Korea.
Blockchain analysis company Elliptic described the Binance incident as potentially the largest theft of any kind ever recorded.
Cryptocurrency markets declined following news of the breach. Bitcoin fell to $76,368, its lowest level in six weeks, while Ether dropped to $2,178. Binance's BNB token lost nearly 7% over 24 hours, according to Reuters.
Binance reported 335 million registered users worldwide and approximately $162.8 billion in assets under custody in its 2025 annual report.
Teng said customer funds remained protected and the exchange would publish a proof-of-reserves report by Monday. Withdrawal services will resume after security testing, with Binance targeting restoration within approximately 40 to 48 hours of the incident.

Smuggling, power, profit: Irregular migration out of eastern Libya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:06:00 UTC
03:06:00 KST

Smuggling, power, profit: Irregular migration out of eastern Libya
October 30, 2026
This year, almost 20,000 people have already tried to make the perilous crossing from Libya in north Africa to the Greek island of Crete.
The route, which runs from the east coast of Libya to Greece, has become an increasingly significant corridor for irregular migration into Europe, Greek daily Kathimerini recently reported.
On Oct. 20 alone, Greek authorities registered 710 people in 14 boats. Hundreds more arrived the next day.
Many of the boats depart from areas around Tobruk, a port city on Libya's eastern Mediterranean coast. According to Kathimerini, migrants pay as much as $4,000 (€3,600) for the crossing, which takes around a day and a half.
This particular route is becoming more popular in part because of crackdowns on alternative passages.
After eastern Libyan armed forces acted against people smugglers heading for Italy in 2023, the smuggling networks changed their methods, using smaller boats and sailing them towards Crete instead.
Fuelling the conflict economy
According to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a think tank based in Switzerland, other groups have since entered the people smuggling business too, including those who previously mostly moved goods, vehicles or drugs.
Human trafficking in Libya is closely connected with what is known as the "conflict economy."
This sees armed actors gaining economic resources and political influence by controlling informal markets and transport routes. It also sees local power brokers using measures against smuggling to obtain financial or political support for themselves.
"Conflict and subsequent instability in Libya have created a fertile environment for migrant smuggling and TIP [trafficking in persons] activities to develop, in turn leading to the growth of smuggling in other locations along an established route," researchers at British think tank Chatham House wrote, after looking in depth at three different transit hubs across Libya. "This has led to an increase in the number of migrants entering Libya and the expansion of Libya's conflict economy."
"It remains the case that an entire business has developed around smuggling routes, regardless of whether that [smuggling] involves weapons, goods, people or drugs," Hager Ali, a researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, or GIGA, told DW.
If there are already contacts, transportation and security arrangements in place, then these can also be used for illegal activities like people trafficking, Ali said. Since 2014, Libya has been split into two. In the west, a United Nations-backed administration is based in Tripol; and in the east, in Tobruk, the second Libyan leadership is backed by former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar.
Haftar has managed to consolidate control over various armed militias, ruling with an iron fist. His sons also hold important positions. However, there are no proven links between the Haftars' networks and people smugglers on that coast.
But, as Ali explained, even the appearance of having some influence over these sectors can confer political influence.
"The more apparent control one has over this market, the greater one's influence," Ali told DW.
Those Libyans who can influence, or even prevent, departures are demonstrating their importance to other actors. For example, high profile operations against the smuggling networks can serve as a sign of political legitimacy. "They present themselves as somebody who can restore order and curb migration," Ali noted.
There's also increasing geopolitical competition in the eastern Mediterranean. In late October, the Tobruk government signed a maritime agreement with Turkey, a deal that Turkey had actually originally concluded with Libya's other government in Tripoli.
Turkey previously fought Haftar-sponsored militias during the Libyan civil war, and this deal represents rapprochement between the two. It is also a way for Turkey to get what it wants in a rivalrous situation in this maritime area — Greece rejects the agreement, saying that it infringes on Greek economic rights around islands like Crete and Rhodes.
A direct link between the new agreement and rising numbers of irregular migrants in Crete is not clear. However, Ali suggested that it wouldn't be inconceivable that irregular migrants could be used as leverage in these kinds of geopolitical conflicts.
European cooperation
The European Union has been cooperating with Libyans to prevent irregular migrants from getting to Europe — despite the Libyan actors' links to armed groups and their disputed political legitimacy.
There's an obvious contradiction in that, argued Andreas Dittmann, a retired professor from Giessen University and expert on human geography and development. Such cooperation between the EU and Libyans can serve as a control on irregular migration but it also adds to the Libyans' local power.
"If those in charge in eastern Libya are actually able to influence the scale and timing of such [migrant] movements, they're demonstrating their own strategic importance to European governments," Dittmann told DW.
A report by the United Nations' International Organization for Migration, or IOM, illustrated how precarious the situation is for many migrants.
According to the report, which is based on data from May and June this year, around 950,000 migrants and refugees were registered as living in Libya. Many have only limited access to healthcare and tend not to have residence or work permits, all of which increases their dependence on informal markets as well as the risk of exploitation.
This story was originally published in German.

Hong Kong’s Deadly 2025 Fire: Accountability on Lee’s Terms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:05:00 UTC
03:05:00 KST

When Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee announced the resignation of Housing Secretary Winnie Ho over the Wang Fuk Court fire, a bereaved family member questioned why only one minister had been made to bear political responsibility. Yip Ka-kui, who lost his wife in the disaster, described the government’s approach as accountability calculated with nanometer precision. “All the secretaries for the departments named should step down,” he said.
When there is credit to claim, Yip observed, ministers take their share. When things go wrong, the responsibility falls on those working beneath them.
His criticism exposed a fundamental problem with Hong Kong’s response to the fire that killed 168 people in November 2025. Eleven months after the tragedy, the government has offered apologies, a ministerial resignation, investigations into dozens of civil servants, and extensive proposals for bureaucratic reform. Yet the authority to determine who should be held politically responsible, and what consequences they should face, remains firmly in the hands of the government itself.
The independent committee’s findings were unequivocal. Residents had raised “numerous complaints and enquiries about fire safety concerns at Wang Fuk Court,” while government departments neglected warnings, failed to exercise “real supervision,” and allowed dangerous construction practices – like “the extensive use of foam boards to cover all windows” – to continue. The report identified serious regulatory failures involving the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit (ICU), the Buildings Department, the Fire Services Department, and the Labor Department.
In explaining Ho’s resignation, Lee pointed to the Housing Bureau’s oversight of the ICU, while stressing that she had committed no personal wrongdoing. He described Ho’s departure as his political decision, made after considering departmental responsibilities and other factors. Yet he provided no clear standard explaining why failures within the Housing Bureau warranted its minister’s resignation, while those involving other departments did not produce equivalent consequences.
Development Secretary Bernadette Linn, whose bureau oversees the Buildings Department, acknowledged having considered resigning. She nevertheless compared the chief executive to the captain of a ship, explaining that, as a member of his “crew,” she was obliged to follow his instructions. Labor and Welfare Secretary Chris Sun similarly stressed that politically appointed officials must answer to the chief executive, maintain team spirit, and demonstrate an awareness of the broader interests of the administration. He would remain in office as instructed.
In other words, Ho left because Lee determined that she should assume political responsibility. Other ministers remained because Lee instructed them to continue their work. In both cases, the chief executive determined the outcome, while the public was left to accept or criticize his judgment. Without consistent and public standards, a ministerial resignation becomes a political concession granted at the discretion of the chief executive.
The independent committee itself was appointed by Lee and reported its findings to him. Despite extensive public hearings and detailed findings, it remained a non-statutory body without compulsory evidence-gathering powers. Its recommendations have been returned to the same executive authority responsible for determining their implementation and the political consequences for officials.
This concentration of discretion is particularly consequential in Hong Kong, where the chief executive is selected by a 1,500-member Election Committee rather than through universal suffrage. Only 20 of the Legislative Council’s 90 seats are directly elected, with candidates subject to political eligibility screening. Citizens consequently have limited electoral means to impose political consequences if they disapprove of the way an administration has handled a disaster.
Public pressure is limited in other ways as well. Shortly after the fire, student Miles Kwan was detained by police after distributing material demanding an independent investigation and government accountability. His detention illustrated the risks surrounding collective mobilization over the disaster. Without meaningful electoral leverage and with constraints on public organizing, citizens have few effective means to challenge the political settlement announced by the administration.
Against this background, the response from Beijing’s Liaison Office is revealing. Following the publication of the committee’s report, the office praised Lee’s leadership and described the government’s apologies, investigations, and reforms as evidence of a “a responsible government that is willing to take ownership and commit to reform.” It commended the administration’s “firm resolve to rectify long-standing, deep-rooted problems” before urging Hong Kong society to “unite and look to the future” under Lee’s leadership. The statement even explicitly connected the response to Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the broader goal of advancing the city’s “high-quality development.”
In the Liaison Office’s framing, a report exposing pervasive failures in government supervision became an occasion to celebrate the administration’s capacity for self-correction. The announced measures were presented as evidence of responsible leadership, while the public was encouraged to recognize the government’s efforts and turn its attention toward future development.
The emphasis on moving forward was already apparent in the government’s handling of displaced homeowners. Months before the independent committee completed its investigation, the administration introduced a scheme to acquire property titles at Wang Fuk Court. Owners were given until August 31 to accept the offer, with most required to execute sale agreements by October 15. Both deadlines preceded the publication of the committee’s findings on October 29.
The scheme offered urgently needed financial and housing arrangements to families who had lost their homes. Yet residents faced consequential decisions about surrendering their property rights while the full circumstances of the disaster remained under investigation. Some expressed concerns about the deadlines and their limited room to negotiate, particularly given the uncertainty surrounding alternatives to the government offer.
By early September, more than 99 percent of homeowners had indicated their willingness to sell. The government could point to this overwhelming response as progress in resolving the housing crisis created by the fire. But acceptance of a property acquisition offer says little about whether residents are satisfied with the government’s handling of the disaster. Families facing displacement and financial uncertainty have immediate needs that cannot be postponed until every question of responsibility has been answered.
The property acquisition process and the political accountability exercise share an important feature: the government largely determines the available options, the timetable, and the conditions under which decisions are made. Residents must navigate those arrangements while possessing limited influence over the broader political decisions that shape their futures.
The government’s 11-month investigation, criminal proceedings, and proposed reforms demonstrate its administrative capacity to respond to a major disaster. Whether these measures will prevent another tragedy remains to be seen. What the official response already reveals, however, is a political system in which accountability is largely defined and administered by the executive rather than enforced through public participation and democratic control.
For the bereaved families, the central questions remain unanswered. Why were residents’ repeated warnings ignored? Why was political responsibility assigned to one minister while others remained in office? What can citizens do when they consider the government’s answers inadequate?
Political accountability requires more than the willingness of those in power to acknowledge mistakes and impose consequences of their choosing. It depends on the ability of the public to demand explanations, challenge official decisions, and exercise influence over those who govern them.
In Hong Kong, the chief executive can decide which officials should resign, which should remain, and when the administration should move forward. The people who suffered the consequences of its failures have few options to demand a different outcome. That imbalance lies at the heart of Hong Kong’s accountability problem, and no amount of official contrition or administrative reform can resolve it on its own.

Russell Brand trial: accusers have ‘nothing to gain’ and were not led by media, court told
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:04:24 UTC
03:04:24 KST

Six women who have been “haunted” by their encounters with Russell Brand came forward to give evidence against him with nothing to gain and no appetite for fame, a court has heard.
The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said the women, who do not know one another, had not been compelled to make police complaints by the “magic force” of media reporting on Brand’s alleged misconduct.
In her closing speech, she told jurors at Southwark crown court that the women had “vivid recollections” and had “bravely” come forward to the tell “the truth” after realising they were not alone.
Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.
Karmy-Jones denied that a 2023 Dispatches documentary about Brand had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.
She said the complainants had described a similar pattern of behaviour, saying: “Six women who have nothing to gain, who have not sought the limelight, who have not looked out for some form of publicity, who have not taken part in a documentary, not made claims for compensation.
“There is no benefit to them, apart from perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago.”
She said the women described how Brand’s “demeanour changed” before he assaulted them. “Listen to their accounts,” the prosecutor told the jury. “Many said he was nice and then it was like there was a personality change. A pivot. His eyes changed, he snapped from charming to frightening and nasty.
“He didn’t listen when they said no, he didn’t stop, he didn’t care, he kept pulling, pushing, tugging, thrusting. In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim.”
She said the women had given the court “specific details” about Brand’s conduct. “What’s happened, we suggest, is these women have realised they’re not alone and they’ve bravely come before you to tell you the truth. The truth of what happened to them so many years ago.
“The truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years,” she said.
The prosecutor also accused Brand of using “gaslighting” to “good effect” by asking some of his accusers for their telephone numbers or emails after the alleged assaults.
She said women were a “disposable commodity” to Brand and later added: “He was a defendant who was rampant in his desire to have sexual contact whenever her wished, whenever he pleased.”
Karmy-Jones described the account of the youngest witness, a fan then in her early 20s who accused the TV personality of anally raping her at his London townhouse after meeting her at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.
He cared only about his “birthright orgasm” and ignored her pleas for him to stop, the prosecutor said, adding that she was “just another number to add to his 5,000 notches which he was marking up”.
The court heard Brand had a “flavour of disdain” towards the allegations, which the prosecution suggested was “a reflection” of his “whole approach to the female species at that time”.
“Women as a whole were disposable, they didn’t matter to him. He didn’t even need to know their names. They were just a means to an end.
“As he said in a 2017 interview, they were the amusements in what he described as his playground of orgasms,” Karmy-Jones continued.
Earlier on Friday the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, gave legal directions to the jury in which he pointed out that they would have “rival arguments” to consider.
Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
His barrister, Ian Winter KC, is due to deliver his closing speech on Monday.
The trial continues.

Vote for UAE candidate for UN chief will endorse genocide
TEHRAN - A vote for Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE's candidate for the post of UN secretary general, will mark an endorsement of genocide, mass atrocities and war, a former UN Security Council says.
Dino Mahtani, writing an article in Middle East Eye published on Oct. 29, says “evidence of the UAE's support for genocidal forces” by RSF militia in Sudan has piled up for years, yet Abu Dhabi denies it all while “cultivating a polished international reputation.”
Rights groups also say Nusseibeh has spent the last three years denying her country's role in the genocide in Sudan, deeming her “too dangerous” to the international order.
"We cannot afford to have the UN led by somebody who is a genocide denier, and indeed somebody who heads a government that has been aiding and abetting genocide, that is basically criminally complicit in that genocide, and she's a lead person in covering that up," Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, said on a joint virtual panel on Oct. 27 that called for Nusseibeh's disqualification.
Mahtani, also a former acting director of the Africa program at the International Crisis Group, writes that Anthropic established in September with "high confidence" that the UAE was behind an influence operation “targeting UN experts and critics of its role in Sudan.”
The following is the text of his article titled “The UAE Deals in the Darkest of Politics - its representative should be nowhere near the UN”:
A bid by the United Arab Emirates to install one of its top diplomats as secretary general of the United Nations, even as the country stands accused of supporting a genocidal paramilitary force in Sudan, has polarized opinion and left many wondering about the future of the world body’s moral authority.
The bid of Lana Nusseibeh, who is a switched-on, worldly diplomat, was pushed by UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, autocrat and sponsor of warlords, paramilitaries and mercenaries across the Middle East and Africa, and reflects the rapacious politics of our times.
Evidence of the UAE's support for genocidal forces in Sudan has piled up for years including in the form of UN investigations, yet the Persian Gulf Arab state denies it all while cultivating a polished international reputation.
In September, Anthropic established with "high confidence" that the UAE was behind an influence operation targeting UN experts and critics of its role in Sudan. Given the killings and disinformation and her role in denying them, placing Nusseibeh at the head of a world body already struggling to stay relevant and stem a deluge of wars would all but seal the coffin on its moral authority.
Until October, the race to succeed Antonio Guterres was dominated by centrist or left-leaning Latin American candidates. But US President Donald Trump, who has called the UN prone to "a far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats", rejected them all.
That opened the door for Bin Zayed, whom Trump calls a "warrior", to advance Nusseibeh’s bid. The monarch has committed $1.4 trillion of investment to the US, including in artificial intelligence. Bin Zayed is in contact with Trump on containing Iran, and is the Middle East's staunchest ally of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose separate genocide has decimated Gaza, where the UAE is helping Israel's redevelopment plans.
Of Palestinian descent herself and with an academic history in Israeli studies, she has secured the backing of her nomination by the Palestinian Authority, which is partially dependent on Israel for its revenues.
Denials and disinformation
Nusseibeh says that as the UN's first female leader she will act "with the interests of the United Nations only in view".
Many are skeptical.
The women-led Centre for International Policy, a US think tank, says her career will continue to owe itself to an "authoritarian regime that serves as a haven for global kleptocracy and corruption".
As UAE ambassador to the UN, then minister and foreign-policy envoy, Nusseibeh has led her government's categorical denials of UN and media reports that it supported Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, whom even the Trump administration has confirmed as committing genocide. The denials persist as UN investigators keep reporting the UAE's role to the Security Council.
Questioned at the UN this week about whether she would continue to reject the findings of UN investigations on the UAE’s support to the Rapid Support Forces, she sidestepped the question saying the allegations were something for the UAE to answer directly, as she has now taken a leave of absence from her ministry to focus on her candidacy.
Instead, she insisted, vaguely, that resolving Sudan’s conflict would be a "litmus test" for the success and credibility of any UN secretary general.
As a Security Council investigator, I saw first-hand how the UAE mission to the UN under Nusseibeh’s ambassadorship behaved when faced with overwhelming evidence of UAE complicity in sanctions-busting.
During 2013 and 2014, just after she took up her post, I documented over 160 shipments of charcoal shipped from Somalia to the UAE, in violation of a UN resolution linking the trade to the financing networks of the Al-Qaeda affiliated group al-Shabab.
During meetings with her team, I was always struck by how her office routinely dismissed the evidence at hand. My investigations culminated in the identification of a site in the UAE desert where I was able to find and photograph multiple warehouses stuffed with Somali charcoal, in flagrant violation of international law.
In 2022, long after I had left the UN but when Nusseibeh was still ambassador, I passed through the UAE in transit only to be detained on arrival, questioned for several hours and then expelled.
My own investigations, including enquiries made via a UAE-based lawyer, established that my detention was connected to the work I had previously done in the UAE and was provoked by renewed UN investigations on Somali charcoal. However, Nusseibeh’s office flatly denied her government’s involvement.
Regional supremacy
Back to today, the UAE is still not shy of intimidation tactics.
A UN report drafted this year and detailing the UAE's deployment of Colombian mercenaries in support of the RSF as they committed atrocities during last year's siege of the Darfuri city of El Fasher has been blocked for months, after the UAE's ally Bahrain, a non-permanent council member, requested a stay in proceedings.
In August, the UAE's UN ambassador demanded UN investigators to "immediately remedy the serious defects" in the report.
Controlling the Sudan narrative is vital to how the UAE shapes perceptions of its role in wars across the Red Sea region. It has backed a warlord controlling eastern Libya, supported pro-Israel secessionists in Yemen, and armed an Ethiopian regime now fighting several factions, including one in northern Tigray, where hundreds of thousands have been killed or starved since 2020.
These conflicts run parallel to the UAE's multi-billion-dollar port developments on the Red Sea's vital waterways, such as Berbera in the breakaway region of Somaliland, now recognized as independent by Israel.
The projects are partly designed to encircle and outflank Saudi Arabia, with which the UAE is locked in a contest for regional supremacy. They also cement its role as an indispensable hub of global capitalism; by some estimates its trading systems touch a third of humanity.
The cost of influence
The UAE has used its vast wealth to buy influence with the permanent Security Council members who could have vetoed Nusseibeh. It has committed billions of pounds to the UK, whose government now tiptoes around the UAE's role in Sudan and in the Manchester City football club scandal.
It has pledged billions of euros to France, while hosting a French military base and a branch of the Louvre in Abu Dhabi.
China's reticence about a candidate so heavily backed by Trump and so close to Israel may be tempered by Beijing's view of the UAE as its most important Middle Eastern strategic partner.
Some 60 percent of Chinese trade is re-exported through UAE ports to more than 400 cities. Beijing is still committed to a Latin American candidate, but may yet be swayed.
The UAE has also tightened ties with Russia, taking large volumes of Russian oil and refined products via intermediaries since Western sanctions were applied on Moscow.
Bin Zayed also recently mediated Trump's diesel supply deal with Putin, a trade Trump needs to lower fuel prices and soothe voters before US mid-term elections.
With all five Security Council permanent members so tied to and dependent on the UAE, it will be no surprise if they eventually wave Nusseibeh through. Her ascension may thus smooth the superpowers' collusive politics. But don't expect her to act in the interest of the victims of wars, mass atrocities and genocides.

====================================================================================================

Twice as many plants and animals sold in wildlife trade as previously thought, says report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:19 UTC
03:00:19 KST

The number of plant and animal species in use or sold in the wildlife trade is more than twice as high as previously thought, researchers have discovered.
A study, published in Science Advances, warns that there are huge gaps in global assessments of how wildlife is traded, and that past estimates have failed to keep up with changes such as the boom in the online exotic pet trade, where sellers offering to post spider eggs across the world or sneak reptiles on to planes are just a click away.
“The dimensions of trade have changed. Without monitoring it in a representative way, we cannot manage it,” said Alice Hughes, a professor at the University of Melbourne and lead author of the study. “At the moment, we are completely underestimating what modern trade looks like – for the pet trade and for the ornamental trade, we are not capturing it. And it poses a major risk to species.”
The study comes as the US-based nonprofit, the Center for Biological Diversity, filed a petition asking the US Fish and Wildlife Service to list the Javan slit-faced bat under the Endangered Species Act, warning that consumers are buying the bat for decor, placing it at risk of extinction. Taxidermy bats are sought after, particularly by US consumers, who are looking for gothic or spooky decorations for Halloween or Christmas gifts, the centre said.
The wildlife trade study identified 107,356 species that are either in use or traded globally – far higher than a previous estimate of about 50,000, which was made by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES).
The study draws on more comprehensive datasets, as well as newer research papers that have tracked species sold online for decoration. It shows flaws in our understanding of what species are at risk; for example, the number of butterfly species found to be traded is greater than the IPBES’ entire estimate for all traded terrestrial invertebrates.
Molly Brown, programme officer for wildlife use and trade at the International Union for Conservation of Nature and a co-author of the paper, said the findings were a reality check. “The number of species that we are talking about is still an underestimate, and that’s really clear in the paper, because we cannot access and we do not have the type of monitoring data that we really need,” she said.
Discussions about the wildlife trade often focus on criminal activities, such as illegal smuggling of ivory or pangolin scales. However, the wildlife trade encompasses sectors such as fisheries and the timber trade as well as fashion and the sale of species as ornaments. This includes activities that may be sustainable, as well as trade that is driving species to extinction.
Even assessing the value of the legal trade compared with the illegal trade is challenging. The under-regulation of wildlife trade has created loopholes that allow species, including sought-after exotic pets, to be “laundered into legality”, researchers said.
Four years ago, nearly 200 countries agreed to ensure that trade of wild species was “sustainable, safe and legal”, as part of a landmark set of targets aimed at ending the destruction of nature. Efforts to meet these targets are hampered by a lack of data about what is being sold and where it originated.
The main data point for measuring progress on a globally agreed wildlife trade target refers only to fish stocks, which would account for at most 3% of all traded species, said Hughes.
Experts say there needs to be more systematic data collection and sharing. Globally, fisheries are monitored by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, while the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites) monitors and regulates international trade in about 40,000 species to protect them from over exploitation.
However, researchers said that this excludes large numbers of potentially vulnerable species, warning the Cites system is too slow moving to keep up with new trends in threats to wildlife. Most countries lack any systematic data outside Cites, the study says. “Sometimes, it is years before things get listed and that means that they can be virtually extinct in the wild by that point,” said Hughes.
Species that are newly described are often rare and have a small range, meaning they are especially valuable to trade, and can be quickly wiped out.
Chris Shepherd, a conservation advocate at the Centre for Biological Diversity, who was not involved in the study, added that he had observed the wildlife trade for decades and that new species were continually appearing.
“The demand for wildlife, especially live wildlife traded for pets, is growing fast, as is the number of species involved,” he said. “This trade is pushing an ever-growing list of species towards extinction, and as such, putting in place mechanisms to better monitor this trade are essential.”

Low-fat diets do not prevent dementia deaths in older women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:17 UTC
03:00:17 KST

Adopting a diet low in fat and high in fruits, vegetables, and grains does not lower the risk of dying from dementia for most postmenopausal women. While earlier research hinted at potential cognitive benefits, a secondary look at a large clinical trial revealed that these dietary modifications did not prevent dementia related deaths over a twenty year period. The findings were published in the journal Menopause.
Dementia and cognitive impairment represent major health risks associated with aging. Women make up more than two thirds of people over the age of sixty five living with Alzheimer’s disease in the United States. Researchers want to understand whether modifying everyday habits like eating patterns can protect brain health and delay the onset of severe cognitive decline.
In the past, observational studies have linked diets lower in fat to better cognitive health. An observational study is one where researchers simply track people’s behaviors over time without asking them to change their habits. However, these studies can only show associations, rather than proving that a specific diet directly prevents cognitive decline. To find stronger evidence, scientists rely on randomized clinical trials, where participants are randomly assigned to follow a specific intervention or act as a control group.
A major project called the Women’s Health Initiative previously conducted one such trial. This large study tracked the health of tens of thousands of postmenopausal women, meaning women who had permanently stopped having menstrual periods. In previous reports from a subset of this trial, researchers noticed that women assigned to a low fat diet had lower rates of possible cognitive impairment, based on scores from a test of global cognitive functioning, compared to those eating their usual diet.
Based on those initial results, researchers wanted to test if this dietary pattern also translated to a lower risk of eventually dying from dementia. Rowan T. Chlebowski, a researcher at The Lundquist Institute in Torrance, California, led a team of investigators to examine this question. They looked at the long term survival data of the original trial participants. The goal was to see if the dietary intervention provided lasting protection against fatal neurodegenerative conditions.
The researchers analyzed data from a large randomized clinical trial that originally enrolled 48,835 postmenopausal women in the United States. The participants ranged in age from fifty to seventy nine years old. When they joined the study between 1993 and 1998, all of the women consumed diets where at least thirty two percent of their daily calories came from fat. Cognitive function was not a strict requirement for joining the study, but all participants had to be functionally independent.
The research team randomly assigned the women into two groups. Forty percent of the participants joined a dietary intervention group. Nutritionists guided this group to reduce their fat intake to twenty percent of their daily calories while increasing their consumption of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. The remaining sixty percent of the women served as a comparison group.
The women in the comparison group received standard health materials but did not receive ongoing counseling from study nutritionists. The intensive dietary intervention lasted for a median of eight and a half years. During this time, women in the intervention group successfully reduced their fat intake and increased their consumption of plant based foods. The differences in fat intake between the two groups remained measurable for up to thirteen years.
To determine how this dietary shift affected dementia mortality, the researchers tracked the participants for a median of twenty years. They verified causes of death using medical records, death certificates, and the National Death Index, which is a centralized database of death record information in the United States. They looked specifically at deaths caused by Alzheimer’s disease and non-Alzheimer’s forms of dementia.
The results showed that the dietary intervention did not prevent deaths from dementia. Out of the original study population, 1,386 women eventually died from dementia related causes. The rates of dementia mortality were almost identical between the group that ate a low fat diet and the group that consumed their usual diet. The difference between the two groups was not statistically significant.
The researchers also looked at specific types of dementia to see if the diet had a targeted effect. They found that the low fat eating pattern did not change the rate of death from Alzheimer’s disease. It also did not change the rate of death from other types of dementia, such as vascular dementia or Lewy body dementia. The overall impact on severe cognitive decline resulting in death was effectively zero.
The research team did perform analyses on specific subgroups of women based on their age at the start of the study. In one of these subgroup analyses, they noticed a trend toward lower dementia mortality for younger women, particularly those in their fifties and sixties when the trial began. The researchers noted a gradual decrease in dementia deaths for these younger age brackets compared to older participants. However, this trend did not extend to women who were seventy or older when they altered their diets.
The researchers noted that the low fat diet did produce other measurable health benefits during the trial. The intervention positively influenced body weight, physical activity levels, and the risk of developing diabetes and high blood pressure. Medical professionals widely consider these factors to be potential contributors to dementia risk. Because the diet improved these health markers but failed to reduce dementia mortality, the study suggests that improving cardiovascular health in later life may not be enough to reverse existing neurodegenerative processes.
While the study tracked thousands of participants over two decades, readers should consider a few important caveats. The researchers evaluated dementia mortality, which means they only counted cases where dementia was recorded as a cause of death. They did not measure dementia incidence, which is the number of people who developed the condition but perhaps died of something else. This distinction means the diet might still influence the onset of mild cognitive issues without necessarily changing the ultimate cause of death.
Determining the exact cause of death in older adults can also be imprecise. As people age, they often develop multiple overlapping health conditions, making it difficult for doctors to pinpoint a single fatal disease on a death certificate. This inherent ambiguity in medical records could obscure subtle benefits of the dietary intervention. The reliance on death certificates is a standard practice in long term studies, but it is an imperfect measure of cognitive health.
The positive trend observed in women under the age of seventy also requires cautious interpretation. Because the researchers analyzed many different subgroups, this single positive finding could simply be a result of statistical chance. Alternatively, it might suggest that lifestyle changes need to start much earlier in life to effectively protect the brain. Future clinical trials will need to test dietary interventions specifically in younger age groups to confirm if early changes offer true protection against dementia.
The study, “Low-fat dietary pattern and dementia mortality: a secondary analysis of the Women’s Health Initiative dietary modification randomized clinical trial with long-term follow-up,” was authored by Rowan T. Chlebowski, Stephen Rapp, Aaron K. Aragaki, JoAnn E. Manson, Kathy Pan, Marian L. Neuhouser, Karen C. Johnson, Linda G. Snetselaar, Victor W. Henderson, Lihong Qi, Kathleen M. Hayden, Laura D. Baker, Orena Garcia, Margaret D. Pichardo, Jean Wactawski-Wende, and Ross L. Prentice.

Politics is an image game, and the government needs to find better visuals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Politics is an image game, and the government needs to find better visuals
Politics at its most visceral is visual, which is why governments and oppositions spend so much time crafting the perfect image. Burnishing and beavering away to dispel the dismal, disguise the dishonest and nudge the narrative.
When it gets really fun is when the unexpected happens. Like a purposeful set-up that backfires, embarrassing the participants. Awks, as the kids might say.
There have been many examples over the years, but there was something in the air this week that rekindled memories of a 2015 photograph of then-prime minister Tony Abbott and his treasurer, Joe Hockey.
Taken in the prime minister's office on the eve of that year's budget, the photograph captured the two men side-by-side. Abbott leans to his left and puts a pastoral hand on Hockey's bare forearm.
Hockey looks miserable. Forlorn. Like a man beaten. Which it turned out he was. As was Abbott.
The photo was taken 12 months after what was regarded at the time as one of the least popular budgets in history: the notorious 2014 edition with all its broken-promise spending cuts.
A year later, still in its first term but with an eye on the coming election in 2016, the Coalition released its second budget at a time of deep poll trouble.
Hemmed in by the Senate and a popular backlash against the cuts, a politically battered and bruised Hockey was forced to shelve his ambitions for big reform that began when he declared an end to the "age of entitlement".
Instead, his second budget was a plodding affair full of cash handouts that spent almost every dollar saved. It was panned by the economic commentariat as a do-little effort that left the country drifting sideways.
Having Abbott sit with Hockey was intended to demonstrate unity and resolve. Instead, it produced snickering.
Four months later, almost to the day, both men were out of their jobs, rolled by Malcolm Turnbull who cited the fact Abbott had lost 30 straight NewsPolls to Labor.
What's the relevance of this?
Towards the end of Question Time on Wednesday — a day of bleak news on the economy, with rising inflation and interest rate worries — the prime minister got a question from the opposition about when he plans to replace Jim Chalmers with cabinet secretary Andrew Charlton.
The question was a political shit stir, designed to highlight the bad blood between the prime minister and treasurer.
Albanese used his answer to pump up the treasurer, who has made no secret in recent weeks of his frustration at being seen as the locus of blame for everything wrong with the government.
"This treasurer produced back-to-back surpluses," the prime minister began, before laying it on thick.
"This treasurer returned 75 per cent of revenue upgrades to the bottom line. He's one of only nine treasurers of finance ministers around the world to have a AAA credit rating from all of the agencies."
As he sat listening, Chalmers had the air of a man who wasn't entirely over the moon about the praise. How helpful it was, given tensions in the air, is debatable.
It certainly reminded those who saw it of the pressure Chalmers is under, which is looking more and more like an uncontrolled pile-on.
Going through some things
The risk when prime ministers have to defend their treasurers in a performative manner is that it sets tongues wagging.
Why now? What's the goal? Who is he trying to convince?
"If Jim could have flipped Albanese the bird in the middle of it, he would have," said one Labor observer.
A cynical interpretation is that the prime minister was also reminding the public that it's the treasurer who owns the government's economic story.
Which — as Donald Trump once said of an ill-fated US ambassador to Ukraine — is "going to go through some things".
Next week will almost certainly be brutal for the government, given the likelihood of another Reserve Bank rate hike on Tuesday, the fifth this year.
The prime minister will be in the Caribbean for a Commonwealth Heads Of Government Meeting (CHOGM), leaving Chalmers to face the music.
Like a rogue wave bouncing off a seawall, a story then appeared on Friday in the Sydney Morning Herald citing "government sources", suggesting Chalmers is a victim rather than villain of the government's deteriorating economic story.
The Herald quoted people saying that Chalmers' push for spending discipline was obstructed by the prime minister's razor gang in the lead-up to the May budget. And that his heroic fiscal rectitude was undermined by the prime minister's inner cabal of spendy left-faction ministers, led by Katy Gallagher, Mark Butler, Penny Wong and Tim Ayres.
This columnist has heard similar tales.
Alarmingly for the government more broadly, it hints at a shift in the underlying ecosystem of the government. It is far from irretrievable or terminal — and old hands speak of the current tensions as nothing compared to the Gillard-Rudd years. But the change is noticeable.
People are getting jittery, looking sideways. The easy confidence of key figures in the government is dwindling.
Loading
The souring reality
This week — like workers returning to the office on a Monday to discover the fridge stopped working over the weekend — drove home the sense that things that used to be certain have gone off.
Next to the soured milk sits the slightly whiffy items of the government's thus-far successful operating model — like the notion that cabinet stability is an unquestionable virtue. The government is in its fifth year, and many ministers have been in their portfolios since 2019.
As this columnist noted in February, some of Labor's frontbench is starting to look tired.
Nearly eight months on and that hasn't changed. Too many are carrying baggage. Punters have tired of them. Their lines resonate a little less each day.
One view is that it's also strange that Labor is not making opportunities for its next generation of leaders. The backbench is full of talent, some of whom are reduced to nodding for the Question Time camera.
Another souring reality is that Labor can no longer blame the previous government for all of today's problems, even if that were true.
Finally, on the war against Iran, it's not clear voters are as forgiving of the consequences as they were in March, April and May, when the government scrambled to secure fuel supplies. Back then, voters blamed Donald Trump.
Today's mood — as reflected in the polls, social media comments and political observers — suggests voters are blaming the government for rising transport costs.
It might be time for some better visuals.
Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.
