On a Remote Island, Japan Puts Its Deep-Sea Mining Ambitions on Display
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:37:00 UTC
02:37:00 KST

In February 2026, Japan became the first country in the world to successfully and continuously retrieve rare-earth mud, sediment rich in critical minerals, from a depth of 6,000 meters off Minamitorishima, its easternmost island, and bring it aboard a ship. For Japan – which relies on China for about 90 percent of its supply of rare earths, and which experienced a halt in exports from China in 2010 – this success sparked nationwide excitement as a major step toward breaking free from dependence on China.
As the first country to have continuously retrieved rare-earth mud from such depths, and as a member of the International Seabed Authority (ISA), Japan is in a position to influence the future of the maritime order. But there is an element of “political performance” surrounding the accomplishment.
The Asia-Pacific region has become the hottest battleground for commercial development in deep-sea mining. The competition over the deep sea is no longer just a battle for minerals. It shares a structure similar to the space race, in which nations seek to gain the upper hand in both resources and security, and plant their flag before the rules are set. Japan is no exception.
Experts argue that its rush at the island of Minamitorishima is driven less by the ore itself than by the political value of being seen to use the island – a way of reinforcing its claim of effective control over the vast waters around it.
The Special Significance of “Effective Control” Over Minamitorishima
The Japanese government continues to resist pressure from the international community to keep the brakes on commercialization of deep-sea mining at least until 2030. Shigeru Tanaka, director of the Asia-Pacific Resource Center (PARC), claims this relates to the hidden motive behind insisting on developing the sea around Minamitorishima Island, about 1,200 miles southeast of Tokyo, where rare earths were found in seabed sediment.
“A moratorium until 2030 shouldn’t really be a big deal for Japan. Researchers believe that commercialization by 2030 is impossible. Yet the reason they cannot support it is that there is political significance in continuing to show that Minamitorishima is being ‘used,’” said Tanaka.
In the past, China argued that Okinotorishima – a tiny, remote reef-islet at the southern edge of Japan’s territory – is just a rock, not an island, since no economic activity is taking place there. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the waters surrounding an island constitute a vast Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) for the country that owns the island. A “rock,” by contrast, generates no EEZ. Establishing a track record of economic activity – in this case, mining – on or around Minamitorishima could serve as evidence to demonstrate Japan’s effective control to the international community, and to elevate Minamitorishima’s legal status.
“They’re trying to show that economic viability exists on Minamitorishima. I suspect that’s actually the current government’s motivation,” said Tanaka. “It’s so far-fetched that it looks that way. Deep-sea mining, as things stand, is economically unfeasible.”
Three Different National Projects, All on Minamitorishima
Deep-sea mining isn’t the only project planned for the area around Minamitorishima. The Ministry of Defense has informed Ogasawara Village (which has jurisdiction over Minamitorishima) of its intention to begin missile launch drills starting next year. These drills, which are moving from the United States to Japan, involve launching missiles with a range of 200 to 300 kilometers from truck-mounted launchers.
Minamitorishima is also a candidate for something else entirely. In March 2026, a month after Japan’s first successful rare-earth extraction, the Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry (METI) asked Ogasawara Village to accept the first steps in selecting the island as a final disposal site for Japan’s high-level radioactive waste. The mayor consented in April.
That means not one but three national projects – rare earth mining, a potential final disposal facility for radioactive waste, and missile launch drills – are set to converge simultaneously on a single uninhabited island.
Masaaki Shibuya, mayor of Ogasawara Village, which administers the island, is cautious about drawing connections between them. The mayor said he has received explanations through separate channels: the rare earth mining project from the Cabinet Office and the literature survey for the nuclear waste disposal site from METI.
“The rare earth and nuclear waste issues have been presented to us as completely separate matters. Based on the explanations we’ve heard for each, I believe they are entirely distinct,” said Shibuya.
However, the fact remains that Minamitorishima is being considered for three very different initiatives of national importance to Japan. Furthermore, if a final disposal site for nuclear waste and a missile training range were to overlap on the same island, it could become an ideal target for an enemy nation.
Masashi Miyagi, a village council member in Ogasawara Village, shared a concern: “I might have just asked the wrong people, but when I asked the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, which is in charge of geological disposal, and to NUMO [responsible for managing national security risks], they only replied, ‘National defense is not within our jurisdiction, so we don’t know.’”
In other words, there is no one taking overall responsibility for the entire project surrounding Minamitorishima. Senator William Parkinson of the Guam Legislature described this situation as the “logic of the frontier” and is closely monitoring it as a fellow Pacific island sharing the same oceanic environment.
“Because Minamitorishima is uninhabited and far from mainland Japan, it can be treated as a convenient location from an administrative standpoint. However, being uninhabited does not mean it is ecologically empty or that it is cut off from the surrounding Pacific community,” said Parkinson.
Washington and Tokyo Aim to Curb China. Will It work?
In March 2026, an agreement on the joint development of rare earths on Minamitorishima was reached during a Japan-U.S. summit. Amid a rise in mining plans by Chinese state-owned enterprises in international waters off the coast of Minamitorishima – outside Japan’s EEZ – domestic media reported that this joint development initiative was intended to counter China.
Hiroyuki Yamamoto of the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC), who said he first learned of the Japan-U.S. joint development through media reports, remarked during the interview that he was “really surprised,” as he had not heard anything about it before.
“I have an acquaintance at the U.S. Department of the Interior, and I received an email from that person saying something like, ‘This kind of story is going to come out.’ I replied, ‘I don’t know anything about that,’” said Yamamoto during an interview conducted in April.
Yamamoto said that an announcement under these circumstances “would likely be more of a political stunt.”
If the issue were simply about resource development, there should be two options, according to Tanaka: Obtain an ISA exploration license for the same area around Japan’s EEZ, or object to China’s continued exploration as an ISA Council member.
“It is true that China’s vessel explores close to Japan’s territorial waters. However, this is in the high seas. It’s not that China is having a monopoly or anything,” said Tanaka.
Tom Hale, a researcher of critical mineral supply chains and the geopolitics of extraction at the University of Delaware, places Japan’s current push in a longer arc. “The original rare earth debate in Washington started with the incident around Senkaku Islands (a group of uninhabited islands in the East China Sea controlled by Japan but also claimed by China and Taiwan) in 2010,” he noted.
The 2024 Marine Energy and Mineral Resources Development Plan from Japan’s METI said that securing a stable supply of mineral resources is “a major challenge for our country,” and that tapping the resources in Japan’s own surrounding waters would “contribute to raising the nation’s self-sufficiency, insulated from international circumstances and geopolitical risk.”
The Cabinet Office’s Strategic Innovation Promotion program now running the Minamitorishima project, in its third phase since 2023, carries a telling name: “Building a Maritime Security Platform.” Resource development, in other words, has been placed squarely in the frame of national security.
Hale argued that there is a paradox here. Treating a resource as a national security problem creates a sense of urgency that actually leaves less room to solve it. “Urgency is reinforced through the securitization of supply chains,” he said.
Minamitorishima is where that tension becomes concrete. Japan is pouring resources into a project that its own scientists doubt is feasible, on a timeline they call unrealistic, all driven by a sense of strategic urgency. The more the island is framed as a matter of security and sovereignty, the harder it becomes to slow down, to wait for the science, or to weigh the alternatives.
“The more you securitize your resources, the less time you have to solve the challenges,” as Hale put it. “However, if you try to find diplomatic, international, and conflict de-escalation pathways, then your time broadens, and it becomes much easier to solve these issues.”

Report reveals campaign promoting racist, Islamophobic, anti-Qatar views
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:34:27 UTC
02:34:27 KST

Report reveals campaign promoting racist, Islamophobic, anti-Qatar views
Investigation finds that years-long operation sought to portray Qatar as driving force behind mass migration to Europe.
A years-long, paid-for influence operation promoting racist, Islamophobic and anti-Qatar views has been uncovered by two academics, with the evidence suggesting the campaign was intended to serve Israeli interests.
The investigation, which took three years, was published on Thursday. It detailed an operation that likely cost more than $11m and was carried out across 30 countries, including in Europe, the United States and Lebanon.
As part of the campaign, several million internet users were exposed to advertisements on sites like YouTube, TikTok and Facebook that pushed an agenda, according to the report titled Manufacturing the “Great Replacement”.
Marc Owen Jones, a professor at Northwestern University’s Doha campus, and independent researcher Sohan Dsouza, the academics who published the report, called it “perhaps one of the biggest digital influence and disinformation operations ever documented”.
Their report uncovered at least 533 million exposures of social media advertisements promoting anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, racist and anti-Qatar views between October 2023 and October 2026. It added that the advertisements were launched ahead of elections in some of the target countries.
One example, also reported by French newspaper Le Monde, looked at how the campaign had targeted France and found that “a historical analysis of the ads pushed by the campaign’s backers suggests that they repeatedly sought to align with national electoral calendars”, the newspaper said.
“Buying in France ran through the months before the June 2024 European Parliament elections, and UK buying stopped on 17 May 2024, days before the general election was called,” the researchers said.
“Its sustained promotion of anti-Muslim and anti-migrant narratives raises concerns about attempts to shape the political environment ahead of these votes, beyond the formal election campaign period,” they added.
Additionally, the report warned that “the campaign remains active in countries approaching major elections, including France and Italy in 2027”.
Qatar targeted
France accounted for about a third of the total number of advertisement placements, the highest share among the countries targeted, the report said. Meanwhile, the advertisements recorded the largest number of exposures in the United Kingdom, at 154 million. The US came second, with 100 million.
“In Europe, the ads use the structure of the Great Replacement conspiracy theory, that white people are being replaced by immigrants,” Jones said.
“Qatar takes the role that anti-Semitic versions give to George Soros: a hidden power directing Muslim immigration to ‘Islamise’ Europe,” he noted, referring to the Jewish billionaire philanthropist and frequent target of anti-Semitic conspiracy theories.
Separately, one of the campaigns that appeared on TikTok promoted regime change in Iran to audiences in Europe. The ads first began running on February 24, four days before the US and Israel launched their war on the country, the investigation found.
According to the report, the evidence suggests with “moderate to high confidence” that the influence operation was launched from within Israel and sought to portray Qatar as the driving force behind mass migration meant to allegedly “Islamise” Europe.
The researchers said metadata shows that video editors working on the campaign did so in the Israeli time zone. It also reveals that they used machines with Hebrew drive and folder names.
Qatar has been the focus of Israeli-linked campaigns before. Last month, the Israeli newspaper Haaretz found that a group of Israeli influence experts and political advisers had worked on a secret campaign targeting Doha in the weeks after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks.
Israeli politicians have also lashed out at Qatar several times in recent years, with former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett calling for the country to be declared an enemy state.
Most recently, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party accused Doha, without evidence, of interfering in Israeli elections held on Tuesday. The Qatari Foreign Ministry has denounced the allegations as a “disinformation campaign”.

The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that an oil leak from the Gem No. 2 tanker had been stopped, with no new leakage detected, as cleanup operations continued along coastlines affected by the spill.
The oil slick is concentrated off the northern emirate of Umm Al Quwain and extends partly towards coastal areas in the neighboring northern emirates of Ras Al Khaimah, Ajman and Sharjah, state news agency WAM reported, citing the environment ministry. The density of marine pollution has declined markedly, it added.
Authorities have temporarily closed some beaches and coastal areas as a precaution, though the ministry said this did not necessarily mean pollution had been detected at every site affected by the closures.
Environment ministry teams are carrying out field surveys, monitoring and cleanup operations in coastal areas reached by the pollution, in coordination with federal and local authorities, WAM said.
Authorities have not said what caused the spill, but shipping sources have told Reuters the vessel was struck by a projectile on October 9, causing a fire that was later extinguished.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
Technical teams work to repair tanker
Technical teams have repaired damaged parts of the tanker, restored some operating systems, and are assessing the integrity of its structure to determine the safest way to handle it, WAM added, citing the energy ministry.
The UAE also said fish and food products available in markets were safe for human consumption and that precautionary measures to protect drinking water supplies would not affect distribution.
The country relies heavily on desalination plants for drinking water, while much of its economy, including ports and industrial facilities, is concentrated along its coastline, making marine contamination particularly sensitive.

Israel lost the elections: An open letter to President Isaac Herzog - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:31:16 UTC
02:31:16 KST

Dear President Isaac Herzog,
Israel has voted. The ballots have been cast, the people have spoken, yet the country appears to have emerged from one of its most consequential elections without a clear winner.
Likud may be the largest party. The opposition may claim a mandate for change. Arab parties may wield considerable influence over the next government’s formation. But beyond the arithmetic of Knesset seats lies a more disturbing conclusion.
Israel lost the elections.
Not because democracy failed. Israelis exercised their democratic rights and demonstrated that the democratic spirit remains alive.
Israel lost because the election resolved little of the conflict dividing the nation. Millions awakened convinced that their country’s future remained at stake, regardless of who eventually forms a coalition.
Mr. President, this presents perhaps the most consequential opportunity of your presidency.
When democracy becomes existential
Democracy was never intended to guarantee that everyone wins. It was designed to ensure that losing an election does not mean losing one’s country. I trust that you have heard the conversations of those who claimed that if the outcome was not to their liking, they would plan on leaving Israel.
A healthy democracy requires more than majority rule. It requires confidence that institutions will endure, political opponents remain legitimate, and another election offers another opportunity to change direction.
Yet Israel has increasingly transformed electoral competition into an existential struggle. For too many, victory by the opposing bloc is portrayed not as an undesirable outcome but as a national catastrophe.
That is dangerous for any democracy, particularly one confronting Israel’s security challenges.
We remain engaged across military, diplomatic, economic, and cognitive fronts. Iran and its proxies remain threats.
Efforts to delegitimize the Jewish state continue internationally. The approaching American midterm elections introduce further uncertainty about Washington’s political direction and Israel’s strategic environment.
At home, increased electoral participation among Arab citizens and the potential parliamentary influence of anti-Zionist parties intensify debates over the state’s future character.
Only in the last few hours, before this column was submitted for printing, has it come to light that there is sufficient evidence for the chairman of the Central Elections Committee, Judge Noam Sohlberg, to call for the immediate investigation of the surprisingly massive voter turnout of the Arab Israelis, which was allegedly financed by foreign entities and funneled via Arab organized crime members to Arab Israeli voters.
While this disturbing news might actually invalidate the election results, there is now a need to also investigate, even through the use of polygraph testing, whether any Arab Israeli party leaders were aware of this horrific crime.
Mr. President, my unusual request for polygraph testing of Arab Israeli party leadership is further strengthened by MK Ahmad Tibi’s reported visit to Qatar two days before the elections.
The truth is that the terrible division in the Israeli electorate was an issue before and after this discovery.
Therefore, the opportunity for the Israeli president to find new pathways toward resolving the counterproductive electoral stalemate is, in my humble opinion, unchanged by this disturbing attack on our democracy.
Israel cannot afford political paralysis while its adversaries exploit national weakness. But neither can it afford to mistake another appeal for unity for a solution.
Unity is not the answer
Mr. President, I suggest a different objective.
Not unity. Interoperability.
Unity implies ideological reconciliation that may be impossible in the foreseeable future. Israeli society is divided across political, religious, cultural, and philosophical lines. Democracy should not demand uniformity.
Interoperability means that independent, even competing, groups can function within a common system while preserving their convictions and identities.
We do not all have to row in the same direction. But we must understand that we are all in the same boat.
History demonstrates that cooperation is possible. During the Yom Kippur War, Israelis confronted a common threat despite their differences. After October 7, 2023, citizens across the political and religious spectrum mobilized to defend the country, assist soldiers, and support displaced families.
These experiences did not erase disagreement. They demonstrated that cooperation does not require agreement.
The challenge is to institutionalize that understanding before another emergency forces it upon us.
A remarkable historical parallel
Mr. President, history has placed you in a position reminiscent of one confronted during your father’s presidency.
In 1984, president Chaim Herzog witnessed an election that left neither major political bloc able to govern independently. Israel faced the consequences of war in Lebanon, severe economic distress, and bitter political division.
What followed was an extraordinary accommodation: Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Shamir, representing opposing political traditions, agreed to share power through a rotating premiership.
They did not embrace each other’s ideologies. They found a mechanism through which their movements could function together.
That was interoperability before we had a name for it.
Forty-two years later, another President Herzog faces a divided electorate amid extraordinary challenges. History does not demand that you reproduce the 1984 solution. It reminds us that deadlock need not become paralysis.
Your father’s presidency witnessed a political accommodation transcending electoral arithmetic. Yours could establish a precedent for confidence in the constitutional process itself.
The presidency’s defining test
Your immediate responsibility is constitutionally straightforward but politically extraordinary: deciding which Knesset member receives the mandate to form a government.
The law does not require you to choose the leader of the largest party. Following consultations with parliamentary factions, you must assign the mandate to a consenting member of the Knesset.
That discretion places you in an almost impossible position. Whichever candidate you choose, millions may question not merely your judgment but your impartiality. The problem is not necessarily a lack of good intentions. It is a shortage of public trust.
You have already experienced the consequences of irreconcilable expectations.
The controversy over possible clemency for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu placed your office under intense domestic and international pressure. US President Donald Trump publicly urged you to act; others demanded the opposite.
Whatever one’s position on clemency, the episode exposed the difficulty of navigating a deeply divisive national question through presidential authority alone.
The decision now before you could be even more consequential. Do not repeat that experience.
An eminent council for national confidence
There is another way.
Before assigning the mandate, establish a small, temporary council of eminent advisers: two individuals of exceptional national standing acceptable to Netanyahu’s bloc, and two similarly respected figures acceptable to Gadi Eisenkot and the principal opposition parties.
They should not be party operatives or political negotiators, but individuals whose integrity, judgment, and service command respect beyond their affiliations.
They would not select the next prime minister. That constitutional responsibility remains yours. Instead, they would examine competing possibilities, advise on a fair process, and help demonstrate that your decision follows balanced deliberation.
The council must supplement, never replace, the legally required consultations with parliamentary factions. Its role and the principles guiding its work should be explained publicly.
There is a relevant precedent. In the 1990s, an independent committee of eminent persons chaired by former Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker examined dormant Swiss bank accounts linked to Holocaust victims.
Its composition brought together interests divided by profound distrust, establishing a credible investigative process.
The circumstances differed, but the lesson applies: when trust is scarce, respected individuals and credible procedures can help bridge competing interests.
That is interoperability in practice.
The opportunity of a presidency
Israel’s presidency possesses limited executive power but extraordinary symbolic potential. Your greatest contribution may not be the identity of the next prime minister or the survival of the next coalition.
It may be establishing a precedent for public confidence when elections produce uncertainty rather than resolution.
This advisory council would advise the President only during the formal seven-day consultation window, ensuring no appearance of circumventing the statutory faction consultations mandated by the Basic Law.
The council would be a first step toward identifying the minimum common commitments that allow our democracy to survive political disagreement.
Not ideological unity. Not artificial reconciliation. Not abandoning convictions. Rather, accepting that no election should become a referendum on whether the state itself can survive its result.
A government will eventually be formed, or Israel may vote again. Either way, the nation will remain divided.
Mr. President, history rarely offers leaders the opportunity to define their legacy through a single institutional decision. This may be such a moment.
Israel does not need you to make everyone agree. It needs you to help ensure that Israelis can continue to live, compete, and govern together even when they do not.
We are all in the same boat. And its survival must remain more important than who holds the oars.
The writer is a global strategist and a strategic adviser at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs. Follow him on X: @jeffkahn

Sudan civilians face drone strikes and arbitrary arrests: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:30:36 UTC
02:30:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan: El Obeid's civilians face RSF drone strikes and arbitrary arrests by army, UN warns
Civilians in the Sudanese city of El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, are facing the threat of drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and an increase in arbitrary arrests by Sudanese army-affiliated forces amid escalating violence in the war-torn country, UN-appointed investigators have warned this week.
In its latest report, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan said that, more than three years after the conflict broke out in April 2023, the war was becoming increasingly widespread and dangerous for civilians.
The latest warnings also highlight deteriorating humanitarian conditions in El Obeid, which had already been identified as being at risk of famine, alongside other parts of Sudan.
"Thousands have been arrested by SAF security cells, detained and tortured in unofficial locations and in El Obeid Central Prison, kept under appalling conditions,” said Mona Rishmawi, an expert member of the UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan.
“These practices must stop immediately.”
Roughly 30% of hospitals in El Obeid are currently functioning following RSF drone attacks, according to the UN report.
It added that the strikes had continued to kill and injure civilians in the city, while also targeting homes, schools, displacement sites, and electricity and water systems.
The report cited a drone attack on a market in Abyei earlier this month, reportedly carried out by forces aligned with the military government, which killed at least 80 people.
The UN also said it would investigate reports of Egyptian airstrikes on goldmining sites near the Sudan-Egypt border, which reportedly killed at least 72 miners.
The UN further highlighted an increase in detentions, with approximately 2,000 people reportedly being held at El Obeid Central Prison.
The report cited a former detainee who said people were being confined in a cell measuring roughly 2.5 metres by 2 metres.
UN investigators have warned that security actors affiliated with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have increased surveillance and are "targeted people engaged in humanitarian, human rights and peace work".
The latest findings come a year after the brutal RSF takeover of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, where more than 10,000 people were reportedly massacred by the paramilitary group over two days after it seized the city in October 2025, following an 18-month siege.
A reported surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas since June has prompted the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of the atrocities in El Fasher.
Joy Ngozi Ezeilo, another expert member of the UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan, has renewed calls to extend the UN arms embargo to cover the whole of Sudan, as it is currently limited to Darfur.
"Sovereignty should not shield mass atrocity crimes, period," Ezeilo said.
"One year after the devastation of El Fasher, civilians in other parts of Sudan continue to pay the price of a conflict that is becoming increasingly destructive and difficult to escape."
She added: "In El Obeid, attacks on electricity networks, water facilities, hospitals, schools and displacement sites demonstrate how damage to critical civilian infrastructure can reverberate through entire communities long after an attack has occurred."
“The passage of time should not diminish attention to what has happened in El Fasher. On the contrary, it should remind us of the cost of impunity.”
Now in its fourth year, Sudan's war began in April 2023, when fighting broke out in Khartoum between the RSF and the Sudanese military before spreading across the country.
The conflict has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, although other aid groups argue that the true death toll is likely to be higher.

Will Islamic Finance Expand Financial Inclusion in Uzbekistan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:29:00 UTC
02:29:00 KST

On October 23, the Central Bank of Uzbekistan (CBU) issued its first license granting official permission to provide Islamic banking services to Open Bank Joint-Stock Company, marking a new page in the country’s attempt to expand financial inclusion.
Uzbekistan has been trying to expand access to financial services and bring more money into the formal banking system for years. In 2019, Uzbekistan became a member of the International Islamic Trade and Finance Corporation and the Investment and Export Credit Insurance Islamic Corporation.
President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, in his 2020 address to the parliament, highlighted the need to introduce Islamic financing. “The time has come to create a legal framework for the introduction of Islamic financial services in our country,” Mirziyoyev said. “Experts from the Islamic Development Bank and other international financial organizations will be involved in this regard.”
In a 2023 pre-election meeting with potential voters in Namangan, one of the most populated areas of Uzbekistan historically following a stricter form of Islam, Mirziyoyev even promised to have Islamic financing system operating in Namangan.
Although Uzbekistan allowed microfinance organizations to provide Islamic financing from 2022, the CBU only approved regulations governing such services in 2024. That year, the CBU joined the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB). In 2025, Tashkent hosted the 20th International Shariah Scholars Forum in Islamic Finance (ISSF) – the first time the event was held outside Malaysia.
Also in 2024, the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis adopted a draft law on introducing Islamic banking activities.
In 2026, progress accelerated. In March, Mirziyoyev signed a law that established the legal framework for organizing Islamic banking, including establishing licensing, regulating, and taxing requirements. By mid-July, the CBU established a Islamic Finance Council of five people, including members from the Muslim Board of Uzbekistan.
While Tashkent’s ambitions are clear, the economic case rests on two expectations: that people use Islamic financing and savers will place their savings in Islamic investment accounts.
Uzbekistan is a Muslim-majority country with a total population exceeding 39 million. The exact number of Muslims is hard to gauge – while both the U.S. Department of State and Human Rights Watch estimate that over 80 percent of the population follow Islam, the Committee on Religious Affairs of Uzbekistan reported that figure to be 94 percent as of 2015. Neither, however, estimates how many Uzbek citizens would prefer Islamic financing, regardless of their faith.
In 2023, Bakhrom Nomonov, then chairman of the board of Apex Bank, noted that 20 percent of Uzbek citizens do not take out traditional loans from banks due to their religious beliefs. Therefore, he argued, Islamic financing could attract up to $10 billion a year to the country. A 2020 survey conducted within the framework of the United Nations Development Program on “Analysis of Islamic financial products in Uzbekistan” also indicated religious beliefs as one of the main reasons many Uzbek people not to take out traditional bank loans.
The Muslim Board of Uzbekistan, as well as popular imams, all interpret riba – taking an interest-based loan from a bank (locally known as taking a credit) – as a sinful act, while other forms of Islamic financing – such as leasing, and murabaha –are deemed permissible.
This, however, does not mean a nationwide strict observation of Islam, including in finance. Many Uzbeks consider Islam a part of their culture. It is something that they are born into and many people simply do not follow every single fatwa or recommendation from an imam. (Uzbekistan is a secular state and the fatwas issued by imams are not binding by law.) The existence of some strict observers is matched by those with more lax approaches. The latest report from the Central Bank shows that as of 2025, 20 percent of adults in the country have an active bank credit account with almost one-third of them having taken 1.7 loans on average.
Whether Uzbek citizens take out bank loans or put their savings into investment accounts is not entirely – or even predominantly – a religious question. The availability of halal loans might create more chances, but if Islamic financing costs more than conventional bank loans – when a new product is launched, it usually competes with other similar products in the market – there is no guarantee that the Muslims of Uzbekistan will choose a more expensive halal one.
Another obstacle lies with reputation. Inclusion of members from the Muslim Board of Uzbekistan into the CBU’s Islamic Finance Council will increase its credibility among the public as the majority of Muslims in Uzbekistan trust official religious endorsements. However, this also raises the question of who checks these systems for compliance and conducts audits. IMAN invest, a company that offers Islamic investment products, is currently embroiled in a huge scandal. The Islamic Finance Consulting Board (IFCB) terminated its cooperation with the company, with board member Mahmud Usmon alleging misuse of investor funds in violation of Islamic finance principles and a deficit of $20 million in its investment portfolio. The company has disputed the allegation and is trying to restore public trust.
This one dispute does not mean that licensed Islamic banks will face the same difficulties or allegations, but the risks remain. It just takes one respected scholar questioning a product’s Islamic compliance to undermine public trust, and without public trust even the devout might shy away from Islamic financing options.
Reportedly, more than 10 commercial banks in Uzbekistan are preparing to introduce Islamic finance products. Their success with previously underserved populations is to be seen in the coming years and is subject to competing services and credibility. The number of licenses is an initial indicator of interest, not a guarantee of success.
This research was supported by a Marie Curie Staff Exchange within the Horizon Europe Programme (CARSI, no: 101086415)

Hezbollah chief declares US-brokered framework agreement 'effectively nonexistent'

Hezbollah chief declares US-brokered framework agreement 'effectively nonexistent'
TEHRAN — Hezbollah Secretary General Sheikh Naim Qassem said in a speech on October 28 that the resistance will keep its weapons for as long as Israel occupies Lebanese land.
There is "no room for discussion" on disarmament while the occupation and aggression continue, he said, declaring the U.S.-brokered framework agreement signed in June "effectively nonexistent."
Addressing the "sacrificing and honorable" people of Lebanon, Sheikh Qassem placed the resistance on legal ground. It acts, he said, under a legitimate right that the Taif Agreement and the constitution protect.
His demand was concrete: an Israeli pullout under the November 27, 2024 ceasefire and UN Security Council Resolution 1701, with the Lebanese army deployed south of the Litani River.
Israel has delivered neither. After the November ceasefire, it kept troops at five positions it deems strategic and went on striking Lebanon almost daily.
Sheikh Qassem sees a pattern older than any of this. He said the resistance exists because of an occupation backed by the world's tyrants, America first among them.
Israel's wars, launched on flimsy pretexts, serve the "Greater Israel" agenda, he said, adding accords such as Madrid and Oslo were stops on the way to the next war.
Without American and Western backing, Israel could neither hold its gains nor expand, and the same backing sustains the genocide in Gaza and the West Bank. Israel quit south Lebanon in 2000 under fire, with no agreement to sign.
A framework with no withdrawal date
Sheikh Qassem said the June 26 text of the framework agreement has no legitimacy because it contradicts the constitution, Taif, the president's inaugural speech and the government's own policy statement.
It gives the enemy what is not his, surrenders sources of Lebanon's strength and feeds on strife, he lamented.
The terms help his case. A "phased" Israeli withdrawal is tied to Hezbollah's verified disarmament, and no date is set. The resistance is supposed to disarm first, and Israel is supposed to leave when it decides it is satisfied.
Four months on, President Joseph Aoun told a visiting German minister Thursday that a ceasefire, Israeli withdrawal, border demarcation and the release of prisoners had still not materialized, a week after trilateral talks at CENTCOM headquarters in Tampa.
War Minister Israel Katz said on October 14 that Israeli forces remain in "security zones" in Lebanon and Syria.
Sheikh Qassem wants an end to American tutelage over parts of the Lebanese state. "Tutelage is like occupation," he said, adding, “Both violate sovereignty."
Lebanon's Health Ministry counts 4,389 people killed and 12,424 wounded between March 2 and October 12.
A so-called ceasefire took effect on April 17 and has not stopped the drones. On October 12, Israeli aircraft hit Kfar Tibnit and Tallousah while artillery shelled Beit Lif, Majdal Zoun and Yater.
Even Aoun has said Israel has demolished homes, bulldozed lands and kept farmers out of their fields.
Iran, America and Israel's election
Sheikh Qassem said Hezbollah follows the diplomatic moves between Iran and the U.S. closely.
The Iran-U.S. memorandum in June earned its keep as soon as it was announced, he said, by lowering Israeli aggression on Lebanon.
Iran has placed an end to that aggression and an Israeli withdrawal at the top of its priorities, "a great sacrifice we appreciate" from "the icon of the free people of the world," the Hezbollah chief said.
On Washington, Sheikh Qassem said "tyrannical America" is in no better shape. Iran buried the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Sayyed Ali Khamenei, his family and many commanders, yet frustrated the American and Israeli aim of toppling the government and disintegrating the country, the resistance leader pointed out.
He credited the Iranian people and the leadership of Ayatollah Sayyed Mojtaba Khamenei.
The U.S., by contrast, is mired in erratic decisions and a severe economic crisis, has lost its global standing and is preparing to leave the region, Naim Qassem noted.
Israel's election earned no kinder review. Results from the October 27 vote left Netanyahu's bloc with 53 seats, eight short of a majority, which Sheikh Qassem called "one of the expressions of defeat."
"We do not concern ourselves with who governs the usurping Israeli entity," he said. "But it must know it cannot continue its occupation, and it must leave our land."
Unity, with conditions
At home, Sheikh Qassem renewed Hezbollah's "promise and commitment" pledge to provide shelter, repairs and reconstruction, and to press the state to do its part with help from friendly countries.
He affirmed the bond with the Amal Movement and allied forces, support for the army, rejection of sedition and readiness for dialogue within the constitution. He attached a condition: "actions from others" that prove they mean it.
"The cost of resistance is heavy," he said, "but surrender and concession leave nothing." He closed with the Quranic verse: "Allah will surely support those who support Him."

The return of an icon and a revolution in its segment — Renault Twingo E-Tech Electric
Launched in 1992, the Renault Twingo radically changed the A-segment with its bold new concept for a city car. Fun, bright and modular, the Twingo invited customers to “invent a life that suits it.” At the time, the market offered a wide choice of city cars, and their number grew every year. Today, this segment accounts for less than 5% of the European market.
Contrary to popular belief, the current size of the A-segment does not reflect low demand: drivers across Europe are still looking for compact, affordable cars designed for urban life or as a second car for the family. The problem lies in the limited supply. Faced with the difficulties of combining competitiveness, regulatory compliance and modern customer expectations, most manufacturers have simply abandoned this segment.
Since 1992, the Twingo has established itself as an iconic city car. It was a huge success: more than 4.1 million units sold in 25 countries, winning over several generations thanks to its innovative one-box design, spacious and modular interior, and cheerful character.
The Twingo E-Tech electric was created to achieve three main goals:
-  to make electric mobility more affordable and sustainable: with an
entry price of less than €20,000 (excluding subsidies), the Twingo E-Tech
electric is an affordable and more environmentally friendly solution for European families; 
-  to reduce the vehicle development period to two years:
for the first time in Renault’s history, this achievement became part of a pilot project that
provides valuable experience for the company’s future initiatives; 
-  to maintain a competitive production base in Europe:
assembling the model in Novo Mesto (Slovenia) became possible thanks to optimized
industrial organization and a local supply chain. 
The car is equipped with a 60 kW (82 hp) motor producing 175 N·m of torque, allowing it to accelerate to 130 km/h and deliver a range of up to 263 km.

Ukraine hits Russian Mi-8 during raid on supply lines in Luhansk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:25:50 UTC
02:25:50 KST

- Ukraine’s Third Assault Brigade said it destroyed a Russian Mi-8 helicopter in the Luhansk region with two Hornet attack drones after it landed.
- The helicopter outran the first drone in flight, so the crew struck it near its fuel tanks once it touched down, the brigade said.
Ukraine’s Third Assault Brigade destroyed a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter in the Luhansk region with two Hornet one-way attack drones after waiting for it to land, the brigade said on social media on Oct. 30.
A drone crew from the SKYFOM strike-wing platoon of the brigade’s unmanned systems battalion spotted the helicopter during a raid on Russian supply lines and launched a Hornet to intercept it in the air. The Russian crew changed course after noticing the drone, but the helicopter was faster than the Hornet and pulled away, the brigade said. The brigade did not say where in the Luhansk region the strike took place or when.
“The helicopter’s cruising speed exceeded the speed of the strike drones, but as soon as the Russian aircraft landed, the fighters struck it in the area of the fuel tanks. The second Hornet successfully finished off the target,” the Third Assault Brigade said.
The brigade said the helicopter burned out completely. Russia uses the twin-engine Mi-8 as the workhorse of its military helicopter fleet, flying troops and cargo, evacuating wounded and providing fire support. Russia has not commented on the loss.
The Hornet is a fixed-wing one-way attack drone built by Perennial Autonomy, a U.S.-based company that multiple published reports have linked to a network of firms connected to former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Ukrainian units use it to hit Russian supply routes deep behind the front, and Ukraine’s 1st Azov Corps has flown it more than 50 km (31 miles) from the front line over occupied Donetsk. In May, Ukraine tested launching a Hornet from an aerostat at about 8 km altitude.
Ukrainian drone units have increasingly gone after Russian helicopters, usually catching them on the ground or while hovering, since most strike drones cannot match a helicopter’s speed in level flight. In February, Ukrainian strike drones destroyed a Ka-52 attack helicopter and a Mi-8 at a forward airfield in Russia’s Oryol region. In September, a single drone destroyed a Mi-8AMTSh at a helipad near Anapa, Russian sources reported. In July, the Unmanned Systems Forces’ Rarog unit said it brought down a Mi-28 attack helicopter, and in April a joint team struck a Mi-28 and a Mi-8 together at a Russian airstrip in the Voronezh region more than 150 km (93 miles) from the front line.

Satellite photos confirm Ukraine destroyed two Russian Su-34s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:22:04 UTC
02:22:04 KST

- Satellite imagery shows two Su-34 fighter-bombers destroyed at Russia’s Marinovka air base after a Ukrainian Neptune missile strike on Oct. 29.
- Ukraine’s Navy says the jets belonged to the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment; Russia has not confirmed any losses at the Volgograd region base.
Satellite imagery shows the wreckage of two Su-34 fighter-bombers destroyed at Russia’s Marinovka air base in the Volgograd region, confirming Ukraine’s claim that its Neptune cruise missiles knocked out the jets on Oct. 29, open-source analysts said.
The open-source monitoring group CyberBoroshno said the post-strike image shows the effects of hits in two parking spaces where Su-34s were stationed, with the remains of the aircraft visible. It compared the image with a Sentinel satellite picture taken on Oct. 28, which shows a Su-34 standing at the same spot, a sign the location was the aircraft’s regular parking position.
“This confirms that the strike hit the places where the aircraft were based, not random points on the airfield,” CyberBoroshno said.
The Russian aviation-focused account Avivector also published satellite frames showing the destroyed aircraft, writing that the Ukrainian Navy’s Oct. 29 strike on Marinovka “destroyed two Su-34 fighter-bombers.” Russia has not publicly confirmed any losses at the base.
The Ukrainian Navy said on Oct. 29 that its units hit the base near the settlement of Oktyabrsky with a coastal Neptune missile system, in what it called a “Long Neptune” strike, the extended-range land-attack version of the Ukrainian-made cruise missile. The Navy said the two Su-34s belonged to the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment of Russia’s 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army, Ukrainska Pravda reported. President Volodymyr Zelensky later confirmed the result. NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-detection system picked up a fire at the airfield on the night of the attack, and the base lies more than 400 km (250 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
The Su-34 is the main aircraft Russia uses to drop glide bombs, known in Ukraine as KABs, on Ukrainian cities, frontline positions and the troops holding them. Each jet can carry up to 8 metric tons of weapons. Russia had about 140 Su-34s in service as of Oct. 22, Ukrinform reported, and Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR has estimated that Russian industry can build only 14 to 18 of the aircraft a year.
Marinovka has been hit before. In June 2025, Ukrainian drones struck the base, and Ukraine’s General Staff said four Su-34s and a maintenance area were hit, with a Russian air force-linked Telegram channel later acknowledging losses. Earlier this month, on Oct. 15, Ukraine said Neptune missiles struck Su-34s at Borisoglebsk airfield in the Voronezh region, and satellite imagery of that base also showed destruction.
Ukraine has not said how many Neptune missiles it fired at Marinovka or whether other aircraft at the base were damaged in the strike.

Taiz governor says city 'didn’t choose war' as supplies dwindle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:21:41 UTC
02:21:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Taiz governor says city 'didn’t choose this war' as supplies dwindle, rubbish fills streets
The governor of Yemen's Taiz province has urged the international community to help reopen supply routes to its besieged capital, Taiz, as litter piles up on streets and essential supplies dwindle.
Speaking to the Sanaa Centre, a Yemeni think tank, on Thursday, Nabil Shamsan described a dire situation, with remaining food and water supplies being distributed at minimum levels, and pregnant women unable to access healthcare facilities.
"Civilians must not be made to pay the price for the [Houthis] militia's recklessness in their failed attempt to storm the city," he said from his office in Taiz, adding, "Their basic needs must not be used as a means of applying pressure or achieving military gains."
Since the war in Yemen reignited in early September with fighting on the Red Sea Coast, Taiz has been one of the focal fronts of the renewed escalation, with the Houthis closing an encirclement of the city in early October.
According to Shamsan, the encirclement placed six of the province's districts, housing two million of Taiz's 4.47 million people, under Houthi control.
The gains, which cut the main supply corridor to the southern city of Aden, have affected access to water, food and fuel, much of which was imported from outside the city's boundaries.
Only 500 cubic metres of the 5,000 cubic metres of water Taiz received per day before the latest escalation is available to those residing in the city. The city is estimated to need 35,000 cubic meters under normal circumstances.
Shamsan said that there is also a deficit of 2,314 tonnes of wheat per day in relation to the city's needs, leading to famine and around 275,000 children suffering from malnutrition.
According to the UN's World Food Programme, the city is experiencing high levels of food insecurity, with 10 out of 16 districts classified at emergency level, or the equivalent of IPC Level 4 of food insecurity.
In addition to food insecurity, the governor added that services were also breaking down, with the city's 12 hospitals and 18 health centres seeing a deterioration of service provision. Cancer patients and pregnant women are unable to obtain treatment, while surrounding districts have seen 120 health centres close and 66 partially close.
The situation has become so dire that some 15 ambulances and 22 intensive care beds have been looted, Shamsan said, with rubbish being dumped on Taiz’s streets as the city lost access to dumps, leading to a spread of disease.
"We call on the United Nations, the Security Council, influential countries and international organisations to take practical action to ensure that roads are open, and that water tankers and supplies can pass without conditions or obstacles," Shamsan said.
"Taiz did not choose this war, nor is it seeking special privileges. It is asking only for its people's right to live in safety, to have access to water, food and medicine, to move freely, and to manage their own affairs within a state that protects everyone."
Accusations of child soldiers as war continues
The governor also accused the Houthis of violations against civilians in the areas newly under their control, including the forcible conscription of child soldiers who have been sent to fight in the northern province of Saada.
He also said that the Houthis were entrenching themselves in civil institutions in newly-controlled areas.
"They have become the people in control and the decision-makers. They decide what can and cannot be done."
"They have taken up residence inside mosques and schools. They have taken control of water projects and everything else. They have left nothing in the districts untouched."
He added that, as part of increasing their mechanisms of control, Houthis have forced tribal leaders to fill out forms that declare they are now supportive of the Houthis.
Taiz is known for having been a bastion of opposition to the Houthis since the war began, as well as being central to the 2011 revolution that toppled longtime president Ali Abdullah Saleh.
"This is not simply a military war; it is a war aimed at changing identity. Taiz will never accept that," Shamsan said.
The New Arab was unable to verify the claims made by the governor.
Taiz has been a frontline city since the war erupted in 2014 when Houthis took over the capital of Yemen, Sanaa, having been placed under a complete siege in 2015, and later a partial siege.
According to the governor, the Houthis have mobilised 60,000 fighters in their campaign to take over the city, which has seen residential buildings shelled and ongoing fighting in the areas of Saber, al-Mawadem, Mashra'a and Hadnan.
The Houthi offensive on Taiz, though managing to encircle the city, has slowed following an uptick in Saudi airstrikes aimed at supporting government forces in the pocket.
Those airstrikes have also killed Yemeni civilians, with the Houthi health ministry reporting that Saudi airstrikes killed at least 13 people in Taiz on Thursday.
Shamsan said that some 271 people have been killed and 1,129 injured in fighting around Taiz since the start of the Houthi offensive.
Alongside the death toll, which the World Health Organisation records as 1,677 killed and 7,395 wounded, hundreds of thousands have been displaced, mostly from Taiz province.

Tensions in the Black Sea region do not affect tourist bookings in Bulgaria
Friday 30 October 2026 17:46
Friday, 30 October 2026, 17:46
Minister of Tourism Ilin Dimitrov
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Despite the tensions in the Black Sea and recent drone-related incidents, there has been no impact so far on early bookings for vacations in Bulgaria. This was stated by Minister of Tourism Ilin Dimitrov, who emphasized that the country continues to be perceived as a safe and peaceful tourist destination. He drew a comparison with the situation in several popular tourist destinations - such as France, Italy, and Spain - where, unlike in Bulgaria, there is social unrest and protests.
According to him, data also indicates strong interest in the upcoming winter season.
Legislative amendments are being prepared that would require municipalities to allocate at least 50% of the revenue generated from tourist taxes toward promotion and the improvement of transport connectivity.

Polymarket to investigate 'suspicious' Israel election bets

02:19:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Polymarket to investigate 'suspicious' Israel election bets
Polymarket is launching an investigation into users who placed suspicious bets on Tuesday's Israeli election, a spokesperson for the prediction market announced.
Hundreds of new accounts placed bets that Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party would win the election just before polls closed in Israel.
As of Thursday, nobody has been able to form the majority required to form a government in Israel. Netanyahu's coalition bloc did, however, receive the most votes, surpassing most expectations for the prime minister, who is wanted by the ICC for war crimes.
Polysights, a Polymarket analytics firm, noticed the unusual activity on Wednesday, posting on X, "What on earth is going on in Israel?" The firm says the bets were placed on "fresh wallets" -- newly created accounts.
What on earth is going on in Israel??? 🇮🇱 Odds of Benjamin Netanyahu winning the election have sky rocketed over 35c in the last 2 days In the last 24 hours our tools picked up massive inflows of YES buys on fresh wallets This is definitely worth investigating...
— Polysights (@Polysights) October 28, 2026
By Wednesday, one user made a $28,000 profit on a $14,000 bet placed twelve minutes before the polls closed, according to analysis by The New York Times.
This is the latest in a series of suspicious political bets on prediction markets.
Prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi allow users to place bets on the probability of events happening. Bettors can make wagers on a wide range of events and issues, including elections and the release dates of popular video games.
Kalshi requires users to complete an identity check before placing bets. In August, disgraced former Congressman George Santos was banned from Kalshi after he allegedly placed bets on his own attendance at US President Donald Trump's state of the union address in February.
However, Polymarket users can create anonymous accounts, raising questions about insider trading.
In February, two Israelis were charged with using classified military information to place bets on Polymarket. The individuals placed bets ahead of Israel's June 2025 invasion of Iran, resulting in winnings of roughly $150,000.
On Tuesday, Polymarket's head of Global Intelligence & Investigations Shana Bautista said the company had rolled out a new election surveillance system ahead of the upcoming US midterms in an interview with NPR.
"We will find you," she said.

Russia will extend the ban on diesel fuel exports until 2027, but will make exceptions

Russia will extend the ban on diesel fuel exports until 2027, but will make exceptions
Kyiv • UNN
Moscow plans to extend restrictions on diesel exports until January 2027, while retaining certain exceptions. Supplies will depend on Ukrainian attacks.
Russia plans to extend the ban on most diesel fuel exports for another three months, until January 2027. At the same time, Moscow intends to allow certain volumes of fuel to be supplied to global markets. Bloomberg reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to him, the government is preparing the relevant order. The restrictions are expected to be extended until January 2027, while maintaining exceptions for certain export shipments.
In November, Russia expects to export about 2.15 million tonnes of diesel fuel. By comparison, in October the figure stands at 510,000 tonnes.
Novak suggested that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries could somewhat alter export plans, but no significant reduction is expected.
At the same time, after an approximately two-week pause, Ukraine again attacked a major oil refinery owned by Rosneft.
As the publication notes, Russia previously eased restrictions on diesel exports following a statement by U.S. President Donald Trump that he had reached agreements with Vladimir Putin on returning Russian fuel to global markets.
According to analysts' estimates, the export volumes planned for October are too small to affect high diesel prices in the United States.
At the same time, Novak said that by the end of the year Russia could increase monthly exports to 3.5 million tonnes, provided the domestic market is adequately supplied. This would allow the country to restore its share of global seaborne diesel shipments to approximately 10%.
The publication emphasizes that implementation of these plans depends on Ukraine's further actions, since Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries were the reason the export ban was introduced in July.
As of the end of October, four tankers carrying diesel fuel had departed from Russian ports on the Baltic Sea.
Despite this, finding American buyers for Russian diesel proved difficult. Democratic U.S. lawmakers promised to investigate the Trump–Putin agreements if, after next week's midterm elections, they gain control of one or both chambers of Congress.
According to Bloomberg, one of the tankers that previously listed its destination as "Atlantic Coast — by order" changed course for the Bahamas. Three other vessels continue to list an unspecified destination — the Atlantic Coast or "by order." None of them currently indicates a specific U.S. port.

BELGRADE, October 30. /TASS/. The US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has extended the operating license for the sanctioned Serbian oil company NIS (Naftna Industrija Srbije) until December 11, according to the national broadcaster Radio Television of Serbia (RTS).
NIS submitted an extension request to OFAC for its current operating license on October 24, which was set to expire on October 30.
The owners of NIS have been compelled to sell their assets due to US sanctions. In January 2025, the US Treasury added the Serbian company, along with its majority shareholder Gazprom Neft, to its sanctions list. Following several deferrals, the restrictions took effect on October 9 of that year. On November 11, 2025, the Serbian Ministry of Energy reported that the Russian owners of NIS had notified the US of their readiness to transfer control of the company to a third party.
On January 19, Gazprom and the Hungarian group MOL announced the signing of a memorandum of intent regarding the sale of a stake in NIS. Serbian authorities have announced plans to increase their own stake in the company by 5%, which will allow Belgrade to influence certain shareholder meeting decisions.

‘Paleo lighting’ can fix your brain’s clock after daylight savings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:16:00 UTC
02:16:00 KST

At 2 A.M. on November 1, the clocks will fall back, and for one weekend out of the year, the whole country will think about light and time. Most people will spend the extra hour asleep and the following week complaining that it’s nearly dark at 5 P.M. Regardless of how you feel about the time change, for the next four months the sun will rise in the sky closer to the time you do. That alignment is the best thing that could happen to your body clock—and your sleep—all year.
Of course, you can try to buy your way into a better night’s sleep right now: mouth tape, tablets of magnesium glycinate, blackout curtains, a wearable sensor that grades your sleep, a mattress that maintains a chill 62-degree-Fahrenheit temperature. The stack of such approaches can run into the thousands of dollars and has a name on social media—“sleep maxxing.” It’s the wellness market’s latest way of turning a basic human function into a product line.
But the two things that will do the most for your sleep cost nothing. That is because nobody has figured out how to package them.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
I’m talking about light: bright days, dark nights. Think of it as a return to nature. Call it Paleo lighting.
I shamelessly borrowed the term from the “Paleo diet,” which sold the premise that human physiology took shape under conditions that no longer exist and that the mismatch costs us something. We built an industry around what goes into our mouths. We left the eyes alone. Our ancestors could not dim the day, postpone the night, or order light at midnight. That is not an argument for candlelight or for unplugging the grid. It is the same dietary logic aimed at the organ that sets our internal clock.
This clock sits at the base of the brain, about 40,000 nerve cells in a structure called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus, and it generally runs slightly long. Shut a person in a laboratory with no windows and no clocks, and typically the body settles into a day of roughly 24 hours and 12 minutes.
Light early in the morning is what pulls the clock back in line with the sun. Bright light at night does the opposite, telling it the day isn’t finished. And the clock in your head is not the only clock you own. Your liver, pancreas and immune cells all run on their own daily schedules, taking their cues from that cluster of cells in the hypothalamus linked to the sun. When the SCN loses alignment with the sun, these rhythms drift apart and optimal functioning may be lost.
The disruption to our circadian rhythms comes at a physiological price. Light at the wrong hour can suppress melatonin, the hormone that tells your body it is night. And from there, the effects may spread to digestion, heart rate and the timing of metabolic and immune programs evolved to run on a 24-hour schedule. How far that reach extends is still being mapped. The clearest view comes from animals, for which you can hold everything else steady and change only the light.
In my laboratory, we have kept mice at night with lights set to five lux, roughly the brightness of a night-light in a kid’s bedroom. They gained more weight than mice sleeping in genuine darkness. They were not sleep-deprived; the night-light just disrupted their clock-gene rhythms, subsequently shifting their food intake to the wrong part of the day. In the case of nocturnal mice, they shifted their food intake from night to daytime. Because they generally sleep during the day, light at night can scramble their circadian timing without touching their sleep or rest time. Related work found the same dim night worsened weight gain, glucose control and inflammation in animals on a high-fat diet. Sleep, metabolism and immunity seem to act as gears in a clock: if there’s one misalignment, the whole system is disrupted.
The obvious objection is fair: these are mice, they are nocturnal, they live in cages, and nobody has ever asked one how it slept. What happens when you run the experiment on people?
Researchers at Northwestern University put healthy young adults to bed for a single night in a room lit to 100 lux—dimmer than a well-lit kitchen, brighter than a night-light—and measured them in the morning. Their heart rates ran higher through the night. And by breakfast, they were measurably worse at handling sugar, assessed by increasing insulin resistance, than another group that slept in the dark.
That was one night in a laboratory, with 20 participants. “What happens over years in ordinary bedrooms?” is the harder question, and the best answer we have comes from 43,722 women, none of them shift workers, who were tracked for about five years. Those who slept with a television or a light on in the room were 17 percent more likely to gain 11 pounds or more and 33 percent more likely to develop obesity over that time, after researchers accounted for diet, exercise and sleep duration. Night-shift workers, who experience the extreme case of circadian rhythm disruption, carry higher rates of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, mood disorders and several cancers—though people who live that far out of phase with the sun differ from non-shift workers in many ways besides light.
The prescription costs almost nothing. Within an hour of waking, get outside for 10 to 30 minutes in whatever the sky is offering—an overcast morning outdoors still runs to thousands of lux; a well-lit kitchen only manages a few hundred. Sit near a window if you have one. In one small study, office workers with windows got far more daytime light than colleagues without them and slept the better part of an hour longer at night. When indoors in the evening, dim the lights and use warm light bulbs rather than overhead and blue lighting.
Then deal with the bedroom, which is the part everyone skips. Stand in yours tonight with the lights off and count what still glows: the router, the smoke detector, the charger, the standby light on the television, the sliver where the curtains refuse to meet.
Nobody is ever going to sell you a dark night. You will have to make it on your own.

Trump’s falling popularity hangs over a midterm vote shaped by Iran war, inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:15:51 UTC
02:15:51 KST

Trump’s falling popularity hangs over a midterm vote shaped by Iran war, inflation
TEHRAN — Donald Trump is not on the ballot, yet the election is about little else. On November 3, roughly 210 million registered voters will decide all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships.
Their verdict on the war on Iran, inflation and the campaign his party has run will determine how much power Trump keeps for the last two years of his term.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on October 26 put Trump’s approval at 32 percent, one point above the record low set a week earlier. Registered voters preferred Democrats on the congressional ballot, 47 percent to 36 percent. Counting undecided voters who lean toward a party, the gap is 50 to 41.
History offers Republicans little comfort. Since 1946, the president’s party has lost an average of 26.5 House seats in midterms. No president has entered midterm election so unpopular since Harry Truman, and Trump sits nearly 10 points below where he stood in 2018, when Republicans still held onto several Senate seats in friendly territory.
Democrats need a net gain of three seats for the House. The Senate is a steeper climb. Republicans hold 53 seats, Democrats and their two independent allies hold 47, and a 50-50 split would still favor Republicans because Vice President JD Vance breaks ties. Democrats need four seats, and many of the contests lie in states Trump won comfortably two years ago.
The price problem
Prices are the one issue Trump promised to fix. In 2024 he vowed to “rapidly bring down costs.” Since then, they have outrun wages, and households feel it in gasoline, groceries, insurance premiums, rent, mortgages and credit-card balances.
The White House answers with “growth” figures. Output rose at a 3.4 percent annual rate over the summer, and consumer spending climbed 3.8 percent in the third quarter. Voters are unmoved.
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett has called worries about affordability a “myth,” and Trump has called the issue a “hoax.” At a rally in Lubbock, he insisted prices had fallen while signs in the crowd demanded “LOWER PRICES.”
Gasoline costs more than $1 a gallon above its level on the day Trump returned to office, according to AAA. Tariffs, tax cuts that pushed the federal debt past $40 trillion, and cuts to food and health benefits have added to the strain.
The war on Iran added more. The blockade and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz lifted oil prices and, with them, the cost of farming, trucking, heating and shipping. About 73 percent of Americans say they are extremely or very concerned about fuel prices driven by the war.
The Iran war quagmire
Nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose U.S. involvement in the war on Iran, and the aggressive campaign has split both parties. The fighting has hardened into an open-ended confrontation with no political settlement in sight.
At least 21 U.S. service members have died and more than 800 have been wounded. Iranian missiles and drones have damaged American bases, including Al Udeid in Qatar. Even so, the Pentagon blocked Senator Chris Murphy from visiting the base on a fact-finding trip.
“War” Secretary Pete Hegseth, who helped lead the campaign, has run the department with secrecy, purges of senior officers and open hostility toward Congress.
Democrats are preparing to answer in kind. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has promised to “run Pete Hegseth out of town” if his party wins the House.
A Politico poll found 63 percent of Democratic midterm voters support impeaching him, and Republican Representative Thomas Massie has already filed eight articles accusing Hegseth of plotting an illegal war and obstructing oversight.
Conviction in the Senate is unlikely. Hearings would still put the legal and human cost of a war Trump never asked Congress to authorize on the public record.
Campaigning on fear
Candidates who cannot run on prices or the war have found another subject. In Michigan, Trump and his allies have turned the Senate race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed into a sustained attack on Muslims.
Trump has mocked El-Sayed’s name, called him a “jihadist” and suggested he should pass through a metal detector before entering the Capitol. Republican nominee Mike Rogers has baselessly tied him to Hamas, Hezbollah, Iran and the Muslim Brotherhood.
The rhetoric has gone mainstream within the GOP. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. claimed “Arabs do not produce literature or science and do not win Nobel Prizes.” Senator Ted Cruz called El-Sayed a “jihadist leprechaun.”
Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud says his city receives daily threats, and Muslim advocates describe a climate worse than the weeks after September 11.
Ohio supplied a different kind of ugliness. Vivek Ramaswamy promoted an advertisement featuring the estranged birth mother of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, using her childhood abuse and homelessness to suggest instability.
Republican Governor Mike DeWine asked for it to come down. Trump and Vance defended it. Campaigning in the Midwest, Barack Obama called the approach “cruelty” and “indecency.”
Billionaires bankrolling
Money is meant to do the work persuasion cannot. Elon Musk has given more than $445 million to federal political committees this cycle, the largest disclosed donation total in modern midterm history.
He put $77 million into America PAC in the first half of October and $158 million into the Senate Leadership Fund in September, aimed at the Senate seats Republicans must hold.
He has company. Public Citizen reports that 515 donors giving at least $1 million have supplied $4.2 billion to super PACs in 2026, with Musk alone responsible for about 10 percent. Trump-aligned committees and Republican congressional super PACs raised $2.1 billion through the third quarter, against $1.3 billion for Democratic groups.
Spending on that scale reads as an attempt to buy protection, taken out on an unpopular president, an unpopular war and a message built on scapegoats.
After November comes the fight over inheritance. Who will carry a failing GOP?

Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:13:48 UTC
02:13:48 KST

People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.
The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children.
The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine.
The localised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region allowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible.
While Ukrainian territory lies just 3 miles (5km) from Oleshky, evacuees will need to travel to the southern Russian city of Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.
Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to Anapa.
“From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he said.
Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post: “At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky.” Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky.
While earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled in the convoy.
Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay.
Asked if she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a woman who identified herself as “Anna” was shown on video saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.”
Oleshky’s population has declined to about 2,000 since the star of the war, according to authorities and volunteers, and many of those who stayed have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.
Some say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.
“We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in a report broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.”
Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city.
“They are currently checking empty houses and, in some cases, moving into them,” she told the Associated Press. “They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine,” she added.
The convoy arrived under a ceasefire in the area, which the US first lady, Melania Trump, claimed to have helped broker – a rare example of cooperation between the warring sides.
On Friday, the Kremlin, however, described it as a special case that was “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for a peace settlement.
Oleshky was seized by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
It has suffered extensive damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the huge upriver Kakhovka dam in June 2023.
“The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.
“I’ve been told that it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.”
He added: “This is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established across such an extensive stretch of the frontline and has been maintained for such a significant duration.”
