Bukele secures Trump’s green light for Salvadoran troop deployment to Haiti: reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:13:26 UTC
02:13:26 KST

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele secured US President Donald Trump’s approval before proceeding with a major military deployment to Haiti, where up to 2,000 Salvadoran troops are expected to help combat powerful armed gangs, Axios reported on Friday.
Bukele called Trump on Tuesday to ensure Washington would not oppose the operation, which has received approval from the Haitian government, according to the report.
“Do what you have to do,” Trump reportedly told Bukele, while also expressing sympathy over four Salvadoran military personnel who went missing following an ambush in Haiti.
The Salvadoran leader had previously proposed that his country take charge of efforts to pacify Haiti, effectively acting as a US-backed force.
However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly opposed the proposal, preferring to keep Washington at a distance.
US declines requests for military equipment
According to Axios, Bukele also asked Washington to provide military equipment, including drones and transport aircraft, but the requests were rejected.
Colombia could potentially act as an unofficial channel for supplying equipment, allowing the operation to move forward without direct US involvement, the report said.
El Salvador announced on Wednesday that it would send up to 2,000 troops to Haiti, with the possibility of increasing the deployment.
Bukele defended the mission in a post on X on Thursday, saying his country was not seeking financial gain from the operation.
“We didn't come to Haiti to make money, because no one is paying us to do it. We came to Haiti to fight against the wicked,” he wrote.
Haiti grapples with escalating gang violence
Haiti has struggled for years to contain heavily armed gangs, which control large areas of the country and have undermined security, displaced communities and disrupted access to essential services.
More than 5,700 people have been killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, according to the figures cited in the report.
The proposed Salvadoran deployment comes as Haitian authorities seek international support to restore security and strengthen efforts against armed groups.
The operation would mark a significant expansion of El Salvador's role in international security efforts beyond its borders.

Oleshky: No access to basic needs, ceasefire offers limited opportunity for humanitarian assistance
Issued on:

Catherine Viette is pleased to welcome Jens Schumacher, Field Coordinator in Mykolaiv and Kherson with Solidarity International. Just a few kilometers separate the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson from Russian-occupied Oleshky. For civilians caught between military occupation, disrupted essential services and uncertain evacuation arrangements, geographical proximity offers little guarantee of access to life-saving assistance. Schumacher examines the humanitarian implications of a temporary ceasefire around Oleshky, where approximately 2,000 civilians were reported to remain. Although the cessation of attacks has created a limited opportunity for humanitarian operations, the geographical scope of the agreement, the prospects for evacuation and the possibility of sustained humanitarian access remain uncertain.

This budget fails to live up to Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:11:06 UTC
02:11:06 KST

Aditya Chakrabortty was spot-on in his analysis of John Healey’s budget (Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget, 28 October). It was a drop in the ocean of what is needed to bring about the scale of change this country needs and, importantly, was promised by Andy Burnham.
As the affordability crisis rages on, people may feel some relief at the small cost of living measures announced for households and businesses. But when we’ve been told we’ll get a wholesale reset and an end to neoliberalism, 4p off the price of gherkins and a temporary tiny bank tax isn’t going to cut it.
So, what’s the solution? The government must fairly tax the vast fortunes of the richest people and corporations, left mostly untouched. Recouping the massive wealth and profits siphoned off to shady tax havens each year, equalising how the tax system treats income from wealth and work, and building HMRC’s capacity to properly measure and collect tax from the very richest would raise tens of billions to help pay for targeted, meaningful cost of living support and Burnham’s ambitious plans to fix the housing crisis, fund social care and devolve power and wealth to every region.
Reforming capital gains tax – a proposal supported by members of his own party – would make things fairer and raise around £19.7bn a year, enough to build 90,000 new council homes (the number needed each year to end the housing crisis) and train 128,000 new NHS nurses.
This government cannot survive much longer on vibes alone, and Labour is already on its last chance. Burnham must use his 10-year plan and spending review to lay out a proper roadmap to genuinely improve lives and transform the country, otherwise he risks being remembered for gherkins, which isn’t much better than Liz Truss’s lettuce.
 
Caitlin Boswell
 
Deputy director, external affairs, Tax Justice UK
 Aditya Chakrabortty is right to say that Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric and romantic notions need to be translated into a bold programme of change. Unless this government tackles income and wealth inequality seriously, people’s anger will unceremoniously sweep it from office at the next election.

Saudi Arabia on Friday announced additional precautionary measures against the Ebola virus, including suspending travel to and entry from Kenya, according to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
The measures, introduced following an assessment of the epidemiological situation by health authorities, include suspending travel by Saudi citizens to Kenya and halting the issuance of all types of visas to travelers from the East African country.
The kingdom will also prohibit entry to travelers arriving from Kenya, including those traveling through third countries who have stayed in Kenya or other Ebola-affected countries during the 21 days preceding their arrival.
The restrictions are part of preventive measures introduced in 2019 and strengthened this May for travelers arriving from countries facing Ebola outbreak risks, SPA reported.
This June, Saudi Arabia suspended travel to and entry from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan.
The kingdom also strengthened preventive measures for arrivals from countries neighboring Ebola-affected areas, including screening at entry points, epidemiological investigations, and early health response mechanisms.
The Saudi Public Health Authority, known as Weqaya, said the country’s public health situation remains reassuring and under continuous monitoring.
It added that authorities are closely following epidemiological developments regionally and internationally and coordinating with relevant agencies to implement preventive measures as necessary.
Ebola is a severe viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of infected people. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.

Pedestrianisation won’t save Oxford Street | Letters

The real causes of the problems seen in Oxford Street (The long read, 22 October) are high rents, the chaotic system of business rates and the replacement of many smaller footprints with larger ones; these are the main factors that have made the street less viable. The large flagship shops depend on being surrounded by good-quality small businesses to attract customers.
Much of what the mayor of London is doing here is a de facto part-privatisation – stopping up a very important public highway for a large number of users of “unwelcome” modes of transport, to benefit private landowners.
Rather than buses being a main culprit here, it is much more likely that the gradual downgrading of bus services along Oxford Street has contributed significantly to its decline.
The strategic mistake of routing Crossrail along Oxford Street – long after this plan lost its part-justification (dating from when it was conceived decades ago) of stimulating the West End – has caused the dangerously high footfall levels that have become a main motivation for pedestrianisation.
The Crossrail route should have been changed to connect Heathrow and Stratford through centres in south London, but we have to live with it now. There is a natural limit to how much footfall is beneficial for urban centres, and disadvantaging everyone who doesn’t want to get there by underground railway isn’t going to change this.
The factors at play that have weakened Oxford Street are not unique to it, and none of them will be affected by these actions from the mayor of London, who is largely powerless to address them without central government taking corrective action.

London

Pope Leo XIV, who has repeatedly clashed with US President Donald Trump over immigration and the war in Iran, has cast his ballot in the US midterm elections by mail – officially becoming the first pontiff to do so.
Describing the vote as an expression of his belief in “the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” the pontiff submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago, according to Vatican News on Friday, Oct. 30.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I have no fear of the Trump administration or speaking out loudly of the message of the Gospel,” the pontiff said during his papal flight to Algeria earlier in April.
Before becoming pope, Robert Francis Prevost had voted in every election for which he was eligible, including those during his years living in Peru. Friday’s vote continues that long-standing practice, the Vatican said.
The vote comes two weeks after the first American pope personally intervened over Russian-occupied Oleshky. In two separate telephone discussions, he urged Russian President Vladimir Putin and President Volodymyr Zelensky to agree to a humanitarian ceasefire for the town.
The evacuation of Oleshky’s residents began earlier on Friday, marking the first humanitarian operation of such scale since Russian forces occupied it in February, 2022.
Long-standing disputes with Trump
Since being elected pope in May 2025, the pontiff has repeatedly found himself at odds with the Trump administration, particularly over immigration enforcement, the US-Israeli war with Iran and Venezuela.
Dnipro Station Hit Again as Russian Strikes Spark Fire
He has been a long-standing, outspoken critic of mass deportations and family separations, and has even warned against the risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI).
Tensions with Trump, however, peaked in April, when the pontiff called for peace following strikes on Iran. “I don’t think he’s doing a very good job,” Trump said about Pope Leo XIV at the time, BBC reported, adding that he is “not a big fan” of him.
Trump also drew criticism for sharing an AI-generated image of himself as Jesus, which he later deleted, the CST reported.
A registered Illinois voter
The pope remains registered to vote at an address in New Lenox, Kim Fladhammer, Will County’s clerk office chief of staff, told the Chicago Sun-Times.
According to county records, Prevost voted in Democratic primaries in 2008 and 2010 and in Republican primaries in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
He also voted in general elections of 2012, 2014, 2018 and 2024, but did not vote in this year’s March primary.
The elections will be held on Tuesday, Nov. 3, to elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives, 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats and governors in 36 states.
The 71-year-old pope, who grew up in the Chicago suburb of Dolton, returned to the Vatican on Oct. 18 following surgery to remove part of his right lung due to cancer.
He has since gradually resumed his public duties, and the Vatican confirmed he is planning to travel to Peru, Argentina and Uruguay in early November.
Diesel deal ahead of the vote
The elections come as Trump faces severe pressure over record-high diesel prices, for which he has previously blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries instead of US-Israeli war on Iran.
On Oct. 9, Trump struck an abrupt diesel deal with Putin, after which the US Treasury authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
During the same time, a Ukrainian delegation was in Miami holding negotiations with Trump’s administration, hoping to reach a breakthrough in Russia’s war.
The following day, Trump blamed Zelensky for high fuel prices again, criticizing Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries and saying it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The deal has drawn criticism from both Washington and Kyiv, as well as from European leaders.
Meanwhile, the Russian Direct Investment Fund, which helped arrange the diesel shipments, is now seeking the removal of US sanctions against it, The New York Times reported.

The Greatest Is a Biographical Drama That Understands Why Muhammad Ali Became a Legend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:05:37 UTC
02:05:37 KST

“What do you think it is about Cassius that makes him able to do things that other men find impossible?” Malcolm X (Michael Ealy) asks Muhammad Ali’s stalwart trainer, Angelo Dundee (Giovanni Ribisi), in Prime Video’s stylistically conventional yet unusually insightful The Greatest. “What spark inside him makes him so different from other people?”
These questions fuel the series, streaming in full on Nov. 4, which finds in the relative newcomer Jaalen Best an ideal young Cassius Clay, a bold boxing phenom on a quest to become the heavyweight champion of the world—and a spiritual journey that will change both his faith and his name. There are reasons to be skeptical of this show. It counts his widow, Lonnie Ali, among its executive producers. (Michael B. Jordan, who played the Ali-esque title character in the Creed movies, is another.) Such projects can default to hagiography. And Ali has already been portrayed many times on screen. But creator Ben Watkins (Cross) doesn’t dodge the tougher aspects of his subject’s life. What justifies this retelling is not only the care he and Best take in recounting what Ali achieved, but also conveying what made him capable of greatness.
The Greatest is bookended by career highlights: the 1960 Rome Olympics, where Ali won gold at 18, and his first heavyweight championship in 1964. That fight, against Sonny Liston, must be his most extensively documented moment. Michael Mann opened his 2001 biopic Ali, starring Will Smith, with an immersive restaging of the match. Regina King’s 2020 film One Night in Miami imagines its afterparty, a meeting of the minds between Eli Goree’s Ali, Malcolm X, Jim Brown, and Sam Cooke. In ending where these predecessors begin, the series traces how the upstart Cassius Clay crafted Muhammad Ali, the legend.
Best’s Ali reads as a significantly younger man than the versions in Mann’s and King’s movies. Instead of detracting from his astonishing self-possession, Cassius’ fresh face makes those qualities seem more remarkable. Upon his return from Italy, where he enjoyed a relative reprieve from anti-Black racism, to his segregated hometown of Louisville, Ky., he is again a teenager in his parents’ humble household. He has a mutually adoring bond with his mother, Odessa (Dana Gourrier, excellent), a domestic servant who wants nothing fancier than to give her children a better life. His father, Cash (Omari Hardwick), had dreams of becoming a great artist but settled for painting signs and drowning his disappointment in alcohol and women. Cassius’ younger brother Rudy (Kai Parham) is also a boxer. But any rivalry is outweighed by Rudy’s sincere wish to help a sibling he recognizes as a generational talent.
An 18-year-old rocketing to the top of a lucrative sport is sure to meet many people eager to buy stock in his future. Especially if he is Black and working-class, he’ll be treated as though he owes them something. As he prepares to go pro, Cassius is swarmed by this type. “I knew you had the skill,” one tells the gold medalist. “Wasn’t sure you had the work ethic.” The prejudice underlying this comment would be obvious even if we didn’t see Cassius exhaust himself in training sessions. But he knows he deserves respect, and he refuses to work with anyone, Black or white, who tries to humble him. This can look like arrogance, but it’s also an accurate self-assessment. As Angelo puts it: “You don’t teach Michelangelo how to paint.”
How does a person as systemically disadvantaged as Cassius come to believe so fervently in himself? Watkins offers three compelling explanations, all implied through his behavior rather than overstated via exposition. One is the strength of his will—his innate ability to tune out skeptics and distractions. Another is his mother and brother’s unwavering love, which counteracts the hatred he experiences. Finally, in rare instances when his poise wavers, he can fall back on the rhyming, boasting showmanship he gleans from the flamboyant pro wrestling heel Gorgeous George (WWE alum Chris Jericho, in an apt cameo).
Cassius’ singular personality is thrown into relief by Sonny (Amin Joseph), who is depicted as his antithesis in life as in the ring. An ex-con and abuse survivor, he has internalized every monstrous caricature of Black manhood Cassius actively resists. Even as the champ, with the love and guidance of a canny wife (Erica Tazel), he’s poisoned by self-hatred. Ultimately, he behaves like the beast a racist press makes him out to be. Watkins lets us sit in discomfort, watching Cassius use the same stereotypes (“big, ugly bear”) to taunt Sonny.
The Greatest rarely deviates from the bio-drama template, with its archetypal hero’s journey. But the approach suits this story of a man figuring out who he is and what he values through a noble quest. It’s when the show tries to loosen up, as in boxing montages scored to energetic hip-hop that feel like Gatorade ads, that it rings false. It occasionally struggles to balance complex truths. On the Nation of Islam, it makes clear-eyed distinctions between Malcolm X, framed as a true mentor to Cassius, and the tactics of polarizing Nation leader Elijah Muhammad (Hill Harper). Yet in illustrating why Cassius chooses the Nation’s militance over turn-the-other-cheek Christianity, hurting his mother in the process, it minimizes the Black church’s centrality to the civil rights struggle.
Even so, as it distinguishes Malcolm from Elijah, Odessa from Cash, Angelo from a legion of white guys with dollar-sign eyes, and most of all Cassius from Sonny, The Greatest builds a strong case for integrity as the key ingredient of greatness. A hero of Ali’s magnitude doesn’t just embody that virtue. He demands it from the people who surround him.

Pope Leo makes history with US midterm vote

Breadcrumb
Pope Leo makes history with US midterm vote
Pope Leo XIV, the Catholic Church's first US-born pontiff, has voted in the United States midterm elections, the first known time a pope has voted in a political election.
The head of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, who has clashed with US President Donald Trump, submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago, the Vatican said Friday.
The Chicago-born pontiff "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so" and believes in "the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," it said.
A rift earlier this year between US President Donald Trump and the pope sparked global headlines.
Leo and Trump repeatedly clashed over papal criticism of the harsh crackdown on immigration in the United States and of the war on Iran, with Trump calling the pontiff "weak" on crime and "terrible" on foreign policy.
The pope said he was "not afraid" of Trump.
In April, after Trump's threat to destroy Iran, Leo called on everyone to do their part for peace, urging them to "contact the authorities - political leaders, congressmen - to ask them, to tell them, to work for peace and to reject war and violence."
The crucial US midterm elections are scheduled to be held on 3 November.
In September, Leo urged the faithful to shake off "all passivity and indifference" toward current events.
"We cannot remain as unengaged spectators; rather, we must listen with our hearts, allow ourselves to be challenged, and become involved," he said during the weekly general audience in St Peter's Square.
Robert Francis Prevost, as he was known before his papal election, voted in Democratic primaries in 2008 and 2010 and in three Republican primaries in the years that followed, according to the New York Times, citing state and local records.
In primary elections in Illinois, voters may choose any party's ballot at the polls, and Prevost varied in his selection, it said.
Prevost spent nearly two decades as a missionary in Peru and has both US and Peruvian citizenship.
"The Holy Father has also confirmed that, during his years of residence in Peru he exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so," the Vatican said.

Am I too old to have best friends?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:02:37 UTC
02:02:37 KST

Hello everybody,
This week we’re looking at best friends.
I flew to America last week.
I packed a travel bag full of books, articles, and intellectual fodder to gorge myself on. Which was either aspirational or hopelessly naive, depending on how you look at it. I spent the entire flight messaging people, staring absently at clouds, and watching Deadpool & Wolverine.
I was flying to America to meet some friends. Now, I might still be jet-lagged and deliriously sleep-deprived, but I hope you will forgive me a moment of sentimentality. Because I would say that these friends have very quickly become some of my best friends. If I had my way, I’d see them every week. But in the meantime, I’ll have to settle for the occasional transatlantic jaunt.
I’m limping my way into middle age. I’ve more salt than pepper in my beard, and my forehead is a crinkly mesh. I’m too old to have “best friends.” You have best friends when you’re ten years old. You swap notes, play video games, and giggle over sexual innuendos. As it happens, I still do all those things. So, what does a best friend look like to me?
Well, of course there’s no one simple thing. I trust these friends totally. I think each of them embodies certain characteristics I want to develop in myself. I love them and have told them so. But one thing I want to examine today is something overlooked but oh so important. It’s overlooked because we often take it for granted: You have to enjoy being around your best friends.
So, this week we look at the philosophy of best friends.
Go well,
Jonny
We were sitting around a table, playing the guitar.
I’m not especially good at the guitar. I can shuffle my way around something that sounds a bit like the twelve-bar blues, but my friend is one of those people who can hold a coherent conversation while absently plucking something straight out of a recording studio. I was shuffling, he was riffing, his wife was singing. It sounded okay, but, more importantly, it felt good.
There’s an ancient need in all humans to both make music and participate with one another. Chanting, drumming, dancing, and playing the blues are primal. Music is nice in itself, of course, but playing music with someone is a different kind of nice.
Because there are sounds and songs you can never play on your own. There are things in life you need others for. In philosophy, an “emergent property” is something that emerges only when you put various parts together. A traffic jam made up of cars. Birds swooping in hundred-winged union. And the music you get from “jamming” or “just playing” is a kind of emergent property. Join a choir, join a band, sing around the campfire after a few too many beers. You’ll feel it.
The best kinds of friendships are emergent properties. Yes, there’s a form of therapy that involves “making friends with yourself,” but friendship is usually seen as an interaction between different people. You are who you are, I am who I am, and we’ll whip up a jazzy infusion. This is what some psychologists call an “ecosystemic” relationship — where all members not only take a place within the whole but are conscious of being part of the whole.
The opposite of an ecosystemic friendship is an “egosystemic” one. This is where everyone fixates on themselves. They stay in their own heads, obsessed with their own thoughts, and see “listening” only as a necessary pause before they can talk about what they want. An egosystemic friend is like a guitarist who changes tune in the middle of a song. It’s the chorister who refuses to read the sheet. It’s the drum soloist who won’t stop drumming. An egosystemic table is really just a collection of discrete individuals who happen to be near each other. I wouldn’t be so categorical as to say these aren’t friendships. I follow Aristotle on this and think there are a few kinds of friendships — some better, some worse. And ecosystemic friendships are the best kind.
One good way to identify an ecosystemic friendship is by listening to what it sounds like. Because when you’re sitting around the table with your best friends, the conversation often flows. It adapts to what one person says and picks up the same rhythm. You listen, and you reply. You offer a bit of yourself, and you nudge the conversation somewhere else. Another friend picks up that nudge and joins in. It could be funny, sentimental, or philosophical, but the point is that the conversation plays with the swinging joy of a jazz band lost in the jam. Hi-hats tapping, trumpets blaring, and the bass thumping. On and on in a sweaty, joyous euphoria.
Best friendships are ecosystemic, and they are rare because they require two things:
First, a basic degree of empathy and other-regardingness. Ecosystemic friendships need you to attend to another person. They take your partner’s step and dance with it. Second, they require that far more elusive je ne sais quoi we often call “being on the same wavelength.” When one person finishes a thought, someone else knows where to take it. It’s not quite finishing each other’s sentences, but it’s the feeling of union that explains why best friendships often feel so relaxed. So familiar. Because for the briefest of moments around a table, your thoughts are dancing together.
Of course, this goes beyond just nattering around a table for a few hours with a guitar, and an ecosystemic relationship will look different to each of us. It might be a breathless, cackling back-and-forth in the pub. It might be a slower, contemplative unearthing of the soul. It might be years or decades of mutual support. “They’ve always been there for me.” But in each case, best friends reach beyond the self-concerned parameters of their own minds to engage with someone else.
In an ecosystemic relationship, all members care for each other, and each feels cared for. This is why the members of an ecosystemic group work hard to nurture the friendship itself. The ecosystemic friendship is treated as a thing — an identifiable emergent property.
“I like jamming; let’s keep doing it. I love not only you, but this relationship. I will protect it.”
As I touch on in this week’s Mini Philosophy column, this je ne sais quoi factor of clicking with someone isn’t necessarily common. We need to meet a lot of people, try a lot of things, and accept that not all friends are meant to last forever. Not all friends have to be best friends. But if you are lucky enough to find them as you’re limping into middle age, it’s important to pause and appreciate them. Invest, nurture, protect. And book another flight to America as soon as you can.
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

Taxes on online sales from 2027: who will pay and how the State Tax Service will calculate the amounts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:02:18 EET
02:02:18 KST

Taxes on online sales from 2027: who will pay and how the State Tax Service will calculate the amounts
Kyiv • UNN
From January 1, 2027, income from digital platforms will be taxed at rates of 10% and 23%. The limit for sales of goods will be €2,000.
Starting January 1, 2027, new rules for taxing income received by Ukrainians through digital platforms will take effect in Ukraine. They provide for accounting for income from various platforms, special rates, and reporting by platforms. In certain cases, the State Tax Service will calculate the tax amount itself. UNN explains who will pay into the state budget and how the amounts of the new tax will be calculated.
Details
The changes were established by Law No. 4903-IX dated June 9, 2026. It applies both to online sales and to income from providing services, transportation, and rentals through the respective services. Ordinary transfers between individuals are not covered.
Which sales income will not be taxed
For individuals, the authors of the law provided for an annual tax-free threshold of EUR 2,000 for selling goods through digital platforms. This will allow people to sell personal belongings without paying tax if their total income does not exceed the threshold.
Importantly, the threshold applies not to each individual website but to total income for the calendar year. For example, if a person sells items on two platforms, proceeds from both platforms will be taken into account together. The equivalent amount in hryvnias will be determined using the official exchange rate of the National Bank of Ukraine as of January 1 of the relevant reporting year. If income from the sale of goods exceeds EUR 2,000, tax under the special regime will be charged on the excess amount.
When the State Tax Service will calculate the tax itself
The tax authority at the seller’s tax address will determine the liability if total annual income from the sale of goods through several digital platforms exceeds the EUR 2,000 tax-free threshold. Another basis provided by law is income exceeding the threshold of 834 minimum wages established as of January 1 of the reporting year. This amount determines the threshold for applying the special tax rate. If the established conditions are met, income within this threshold will be taxed at a rate of 10%, while a rate of 23% will apply to the excess amount. Tax previously withheld by the platform will be taken into account during the final calculation.
To determine liabilities, the State Tax Service will use reports from digital platform operators, simplified tax calculations, information from foreign tax authorities exchanged במסגרת international exchange, and other data provided for by law. Amounts in foreign currency will be converted into hryvnias at the NBU exchange rate as of January 1 of the reporting year.
Who will withhold tax from income
As a general rule, the digital platform operator will perform the function of a tax agent. Under the conditions established by law, it will withhold tax from the user’s income and transfer it to the budget. To apply the 10% rate, the seller must meet specified requirements, including having no employees, not selling excisable goods, and operating through a registered platform operator.
In other words, for most citizens who meet the criteria of the special regime, separate declaration of such income is not required. However, if a seller loses the right to the special rate, they may become obligated to file a declaration and pay the tax independently under the general rules.
When a notice from the tax authorities will arrive and how much time there will be to pay
If the State Tax Service determines the amount of the tax liability, the citizen will be sent or served with a tax notice-decision containing a detailed calculation. The notice will be sent by July 1 of the following year. From the date of service of this document, the seller will have 60 days to pay the specified amount. Thus, for income received during 2027, notices in the relevant cases will be sent by July 1, 2028. The payment period will be calculated from the date the document is received, not from the beginning of the calendar year.
When the new rules and international exchange will take effect
The law has already been adopted and officially published; however, the new procedure for taxing income from platforms will apply from January 1, 2027. Operators of such services must register with the State Tax Service by the end of 2026 and subsequently report users’ income.
On October 29, 2026, Ukraine joined the multilateral DPI MCAA agreement on the automatic exchange of information about income from digital platforms. This creates a legal basis for receiving the relevant data from partner states. The provisions on international exchange are to enter into force on November 1, 2026. At the same time, income unrelated to work through digital platforms will continue to be taxed under the general rules of the Tax Code. Citizens who use several online marketplaces should track their total receipts throughout the year, since it is the aggregate amount that matters for determining tax liabilities.
Let us remind you
At the beginning of June 2026, the Verkhovna Rada approved the taxation of income earned through online platforms at a rate of 10%. The services are expected to automatically report users’ earnings.

Japan-Taiwan Relations Enter ‘Deep Waters.’ Will They Sink or Swim?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:02:00 UTC
02:02:00 KST

On August 10, Taiwan’s representative to Japan, Lee Yi-yang, declined to attend the atomic bombing memorial ceremony in Nagasaki after Taiwan’s delegation was seated outside the area reserved for diplomatic representatives. Lee denounced the arrangement as a symbolic slight to Taiwan’s status and a concession to Beijing’s efforts to restrict Taiwan’s international space. Nagasaki officials, however, maintained that the seating arrangement reflected Japan’s longstanding “One China” policy rather than an effort to single out Taiwan. Yet while Taipei protested the decision, it was equally careful to ensure that the controversy did not overshadow the broader trajectory of Japan-Taiwan relations.
The episode exposed a central paradox in contemporary Japan-Taiwan relations. Economic, technological, and societal ties between the two sides have never been stronger, yet political sensitivities surrounding Taiwan’s international status continue to constrain how far the relationship can advance. The Nagasaki dispute was therefore more than a disagreement over diplomatic protocol. It illustrated how a relationship characterized by growing interdependence remains embedded within a diplomatic framework shaped by Japan’s “One China” policy and the broader dynamics of Sino-Japanese relations. As Taiwan and Japan become increasingly interconnected, both their expanding cooperation and the political constraints surrounding it have become more visible.
Taiwan and Japan have entered what many Taiwanese policymakers describe as the “deep waters” of bilateral relations. Economic integration, technological collaboration, and societal exchange have reached unprecedented levels, even as enduring political and security constraints continue to limit closer cooperation. The challenge ahead is not merely to expand areas of engagement, but to translate growing convergence of interests into sustainable forms of cooperation. Doing so will require both stronger institutional frameworks and the political will to advance the relationship despite persistent geopolitical constraints.
From Economic Partnership to Strategic Convergence
The most visible driver of Japan-Taiwan cooperation has been Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s investment in Kumamoto. What began as a commercial decision has evolved into one of the most important strategic projects in East Asia. For Japan, TSMC’s presence supports the revitalization of a domestic semiconductor industry that had steadily declined over the past three decades. For Taiwan, the project deepens integration with one of its most important political and economic partners.
The Kumamoto project links Taiwan’s manufacturing leadership with Japan’s strengths in semiconductor equipment, specialty chemicals, advanced materials, and precision machinery. The result is a more resilient and geographically diversified supply chain.
But cooperation linked to the project extends beyond the economic realm. In Kyushu, local governments, universities, research institutes, and businesses have forged new partnerships with Taiwanese counterparts. Educational exchanges, workforce training programs, and joint research initiatives have expanded rapidly, creating new channels of cooperation. TSMC’s single investment has therefore become a platform for broader regional integration.
Beyond semiconductors, both sides are increasingly collaborating in sectors such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, drone technology, digital governance, and economic security. The signing of a Japan-Taiwan Digital Trade Agreement in 2025 reflected the growing importance of these emerging domains. Clearly, Japan-Taiwan cooperation is entering a new phase.
In the past, economic cooperation with Taiwan was relatively uncontroversial. But today, the distinction between economics and security is blurring. Semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and supply chains are no longer merely commercial issues. They have become central components of national competitiveness and strategic resilience. As a result, Japan-Taiwan relations have evolved beyond a traditional economic partnership, with growing convergence in economic security, advanced technology, and regional strategic interests. Yet important political constraints remain.
The Institutional Constraints
The institutional foundations of the relationship have not kept pace with its strategic transformation. Although Taiwan and Japan have signed numerous practical agreements over the past decade, most of the recent arrangements have been narrowly focused and technical in nature. Major agreements in the areas of fisheries, taxation, customs cooperation, investment, and aviation were largely concluded during the 2010s. More recent agreements have concentrated on specialized areas such as railway cooperation, customs information sharing, plant variety certification, and digital trade.
That’s because Japan’s approach to Taiwan cannot be separated from its management of relations with China. Since the normalization of diplomatic relations between Japan and the People’s Republic of China (PRC) in 1972, Beijing has consistently sought to limit Japan’s engagement with Taiwan whenever Tokyo has appeared to move beyond the bounds of an unofficial relationship. Beijing cites the 1972 Japan-China Joint Communiqué, in which the Japanese government stated that it “fully understands and respects” the PRC’s position that Taiwan is an inalienable part of Chinese territory.
Although Japan did not formally recognize Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan, the communiqué became the foundation of Japan’s One China policy and remains the principal reference point for Beijing’s criticism of expanded Japan-Taiwan ties. Whenever Japan has sought to expand exchanges, support Taiwan’s international participation, or deepen political engagement, Beijing has invoked the 1972 communiqué to argue that such actions violate the spirit of bilateral understandings.
Consequently, while Tokyo has supported practical cooperation with Taiwan in many areas, it has been reluctant to pursue measures that could be interpreted as a significant upgrade in official relations. The result is a relationship that continues to deepen in practice while advancing more cautiously at the institutional level.
To see this in practice, look at the debate over a bilateral Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA). As economic ties have deepened, Taipei has repeatedly called for an EPA to provide a more comprehensive framework for trade and investment. Tokyo, however, remains reluctant, and prefers to discuss smaller, sector-specific agreements like the 2025 digital trade agreement.
Taiwan’s bid to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) faces the same reluctance. Japan has consistently expressed support for Taiwan’s participation, and Taiwan has undertaken significant domestic reforms to align itself with CPTPP standards. Yet progress toward accession has remained slow, reflecting the reality that economic considerations alone do not determine the pace of institutional integration. The challenge is not a lack of cooperation or goodwill, but the broader political environment for Taiwan’s international participation. Consequently, formal integration continues to lag behind the growing depth of Japan-Taiwan economic relations.
The Nagasaki controversy was yet another illustration of this enduring tension. Political constraints rooted in the “One China” policy continue to influence Japan-Taiwan relations despite their growing economic and strategic significance.
The growing complexity of Japan-Taiwan relations has exposed a mismatch between shared interests and the frameworks available to advance them. Progress has been most visible in semiconductors, digital governance, supply chain resilience, and other emerging technologies – all of which require sustained coordination on regulations, talent, and investment. Yet the areas where strategic interests overlap most directly remain the most politically sensitive. Although concerns about economic security and cross-strait stability have drawn Taipei and Tokyo closer together, cooperation on defense and security issues remains limited. Consequently, the challenge facing both sides is how to build institutions capable of supporting deeper collaboration despite the substantial political constraints.
Taiwan’s Coordination Problem
The institutional challenge isn’t only on Japan’s side; it also exists within Taiwan itself. As bilateral cooperation expands into increasingly interconnected areas such as semiconductors and economic security, responsibility for Japan policy is spread across multiple agencies, including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the National Security Council, the Ministry of Economic Affairs, and Taiwan’s representative institutions in Japan.
The coordination challenge is not unique to Japan policy, but the issue is particularly acute because Japan-Taiwan relations now span multiple policy domains that cut across traditional bureaucratic boundaries. In addition to trade and people-to-people exchanges, the bilateral agenda now encompasses economic security and supply chain resilience – issues that require coordination across Taiwan’s diplomatic, economic, scientific, educational, and security institutions. As the relationship becomes more multidimensional, the costs of fragmented policymaking become increasingly apparent.
Compounding this challenge is a shortage of Japan specialists within Taiwan’s policy community. Compared with the resources devoted to China and U.S. affairs, Taiwan maintains a relatively small pool of experts on Japanese politics, foreign policy, economic security, business networks, and the Japan-U.S. alliance. As Japan-Taiwan cooperation expands into strategically important areas, this lack of expertise becomes increasingly consequential. Without a deeper bench of Japan specialists, Taiwan may struggle to develop the long-term policy coordination and strategic planning needed to sustain a more complex bilateral relationship.
Building a Sustainable Partnership
The future of Japan-Taiwan relations will depend not only on identifying new areas of cooperation, but also on developing the political will and institutional capacity needed to sustain an increasingly complex partnership. Three priorities stand out.
First, Taipei and Tokyo should continue expanding practical cooperation through sector-specific agreements in areas such as economic security, talent mobility, digital governance, and emerging technologies. While broader initiatives such as a bilateral Economic Partnership Agreement may remain politically difficult, targeted arrangements can help advance cooperation in areas of shared interest.
Second, Taiwan should strengthen the coordination of its Japan policy. As the bilateral agenda increasingly spans diplomacy, technology, economic security, supply chains, and regional affairs, more effective coordination among the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the National Security Council, economic ministries, and Taiwan’s representative institutions in Japan will be essential. Whether through an existing mechanism or a strengthened interagency framework, Taiwan needs a more integrated approach to one of its most consequential external relationships.
Third, both sides should invest in cultivating a new generation of specialists with expertise in Japanese politics, foreign and security policy, economic governance, business networks, and the Japan-U.S. alliance. Universities, think tanks, and government agencies should expand language training, research collaboration, policy exchanges, and professional development programs. As Japan-Taiwan relations become more technologically sophisticated and strategically significant, human capital will be as important as semiconductors in shaping the future of the partnership.
The Nagasaki controversy demonstrated that the political constraints surrounding Taiwan have not disappeared. Yet a comparison with Hiroshima shows the other side of the coin. Despite operating within the same national framework, Hiroshima has generally taken a more accommodating approach toward Taiwan’s participation at its atomic bombing commemorations, underscoring the importance of political will and leadership.
Whether the Japan-Taiwan relationship continues to deepen will thus depend not only on stronger institutions, but also on the willingness of leaders in Taipei and Tokyo to translate shared interests into sustained cooperation despite geopolitical pressures. If they can do so, the “deep waters” of Japan-Taiwan relations may become the foundation of a more resilient and sustainable partnership in the Asia-Pacific.

BRUSSELS, October 30. /TASS/. The European Commission (EC) has received about €8 billion in revenue generated from the reinvestment of frozen Russian sovereign assets held at Belgium-based Euroclear since 2024, according to the depository’s report.
The latest tranche of €1.4 billion was transferred to the EC in August.

In December 2025, the Russian Central Bank filed an 18.2-trillion-ruble ($225.5 bln) lawsuit against Euroclear with the Moscow Arbitration Court amid EU plans to use frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine. This sum includes frozen funds, the value of blocked securities, and lost profits. The EU and G7 countries have frozen about €300 billion in Russian assets, with around €180 billion held at Euroclear.
On May 15, 2026, the court ruled in favor of the Russian Central Bank, ordering the recovery of 18.2 trillion rubles ($225.5 bln) from Euroclear Bank. On May 20, the Bank of Russia petitioned the court for immediate enforcement of the judgment.

‘Exhumed’ recounts the true story of America’s first vampire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Exhumed recounts the true story of America’s first vampire
A historian digs deep to show how fear shapes culture
Exhumed
Aaron Mahnke
Running Press, $30.00
October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.
Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.
Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”
Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.
Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.
Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.
Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy. Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.
He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.
Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.
At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!
More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.
Macabre Trivia
If you are the type of person who has 50 tabs open at any given moment, then you will appreciate Exhumed’s myriad quirky facts. Here are three of my favorites:
- Leonardo da Vinci was a fan of corpse medicine, the practice of reusing body parts from dead people for medicinal purposes. Like many of his peers, da Vinci believed the human body contained “vital spirits.” When someone died, there’d be leftover spirits for the living to make use of.
- In 17th century Europe, the tomato was known as the “poison apple.” Many people became sick after eating tomatoes and some even died. For two centuries, society wrongly blamed the fruit. The real killer turned out to be lead leached out of pewter dishes by tomatoes’ acidic juice.
- The spinning red, white and blue poles on barbershops were born out of the business’ former specialty, bloodletting. Red stripes stand for blood, blue for veins and white for the rags used for clean-up. The ball on top is said to represent the bowl that captured the blood. And the pole itself represents the wand patients squeezed during the procedure. Feeling sick in 1705? Head to the local barber with the spinning pole outside.

The CEO Summit will draw on ABAC's policy recommendations for the year and discussions held during the summit to jointly issue a Shenzhen initiative with the Asia-Pacific business community, Wang noted.

Feature: South Sudan's young climate advocates urge leaders to turn pledges into action
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:59:42 CST
01:59:42 KST

JUBA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- For 17-year-old Siama Santino, attending school in flood-stricken South Sudan often means taking off her shoes and wading through deep water just to reach her classroom.
"Every morning when you wake up, you have to think of how much you are going to move in water or first remove your shoes to reach school," Siama told Xinhua in a recent interview in Juba, the capital of South Sudan.
Santino is not alone. Across this country, worsening climate conditions, including severe flooding, drought and extreme heat, increasingly threaten education, food security and public health.
As global leaders prepare for the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, from Nov. 9 to 20, young climate advocates in South Sudan are urging national authorities and international partners to turn high-level pledges into practical protection for vulnerable communities.
At an event about climate conditions in Juba organized by Save the Children in South Sudan and the country's Ministry of Environment and Forestry, young delegates demanded climate-resilient school infrastructure, upgraded early warning systems and direct relief for disaster-affected families.
Amoko Ronny, an 18-year-old student and children's council representative, highlighted how climate shocks exacerbate poverty.
He noted that extreme heat forced local children out of classrooms for two weeks in 2024, while recurring floods destroyed crops, compounding severe food shortages and leaving many families unable to afford basic meals.
"Children must be the top priority," Ronny said, calling for greater investment in climate education, resilient school infrastructure and early warning systems to help children and communities get prepared for disasters.
He also urged the government and civil society organizations to invest in sustainable agriculture and promote clean energy, emphasizing the need for practical alternatives to reduce reliance on charcoal and curb environmental degradation.
For Siama, effective adaptation requires empowering families with a clearer understanding of climate risks.
She called for expanded climate education, emergency preparedness training and targeted humanitarian aid for households displaced by flooding and other climate disasters, and urged the world leaders to prioritize immediate action over unfulfilled promises.
Eva Hegedus, director of strategic partnerships and influence at Save the Children in South Sudan, noted that the climate crisis impacts education far beyond physical structural damage.
"Climate-related disasters interrupt learning while simultaneously undermining children's nutrition, healthcare, protection and psycho-social well-being," Hegedus said.
To address these compounding threats, Hegedus called for embedding climate resilience into national adaptation plans, education frameworks and school preparedness protocols.
She stressed that educators, students and administrators must be equipped to ensure safe, continuous learning during disasters alongside targeted investments to construct and rebuild climate-resilient school facilities.
At the state level, climate adaptation and access to international climate finance remain central priorities for South Sudan ahead of COP31.
Payai Manyok John, director for climate change and the national focal person for the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change at the Ministry of Environment and Forestry, emphasized that South Sudan is pressing developed nations to expand funding for vulnerable states.
"We want to make sure that developed countries increase climate finance for the least developed countries, particularly for South Sudan and other highly vulnerable nations," Manyok said.
He noted that the government has established national climate frameworks covering both adaptation and mitigation, with a heavy focus on building resilience for smallholder farmers.
The ministry is collaborating with international partners to secure funding for climate adaptation projects, targeting small-scale agriculture and nature-based solutions in Jonglei and Unity states, alongside direct aid for flood-affected communities.
Additionally, the government is upgrading its early warning capabilities by modernizing the national meteorological department and expanding climate information sharing through media and civic networks.
Timely forecasts and practical support are vital for flood-prone regions, Manyok added, stressing that climate policies must account for the distinct needs of farmers, pastoralists and water-dependent communities.
"Whatever negotiation that has come here has to be put into policies and also translated from policies to projects," Manyok said.
For South Sudan's young advocates, the central goal is ensuring that climate policies and international commitments translate into tangible outcomes: safer classrooms, fewer learning disruptions and stronger protections for families on the frontlines of extreme weather.
As COP31 approaches, their calls underscore an urgent priority, placing children's education and well-being at the heart of climate adaptation strategies, especially in communities where severe flooding and extreme heat already threaten daily life. ■

China, Switzerland sign protocol to upgrade free trade agreement
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:59:27 CST
01:59:27 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- China and Switzerland on Friday signed a protocol to upgrade their free trade agreement (FTA). The move is expected to expand market access, promote two-way investment, and deepen bilateral economic and trade cooperation, according to China's Ministry of Commerce.
Under the protocol, the two sides will make high-standard commitments to further opening up trade in goods, services and investment, while upgrading rules covering rules of origin, trade facilitation, technical barriers to trade, digital trade, competition, and trade and sustainable development.
The upgrade is expected to provide stronger institutional support for bilateral trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, said the ministry, adding that it underscores both countries' commitment to free trade, open cooperation and a rules-based multilateral trading system amid global uncertainties.
Switzerland is China's seventh-largest trading partner in Europe, while China is Switzerland's largest trading partner in Asia, an official with the ministry noted. Bilateral trade reached 49.04 billion U.S. dollars in 2025.
The official explained that the upgraded agreement would help unlock greater potential for bilateral trade and investment, and bring new opportunities to businesses and people in both countries.
China and Switzerland signed their original FTA in 2013, and the agreement entered into force in July 2014. The two countries launched negotiations to upgrade the agreement in September 2024 and announced their completion in August 2026, after five rounds of talks.
Following the signing, both sides will complete their respective domestic legal approval procedures and work to bring the upgraded agreement into force as soon as possible, the ministry said. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- China on Friday called on the United States to immediately rescind new restrictions adopted by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on testing, certification and accreditation bodies based in China, and other so-called "non-reciprocal economies," a Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said.
The remarks came after the FCC voted Thursday to end its recognition of testing laboratories, telecommunications certification bodies and laboratory accreditation bodies located in China, and other so-called "non-reciprocal economies" starting Dec. 1, 2028. These new rules will prohibit FCC-related testing, certification and accreditation activities from being conducted in these economies.
China expressed strong dissatisfaction with and firm opposition to the move, the spokesperson said, noting that the FCC has repeatedly introduced restrictions targeting China, disregarding repeated representations from the Chinese side and violating the important consensus reached by the two heads of state.
Such measures have seriously harmed the interests of China and other trading partners, undermined the stability of China-U.S. economic and trade relations, and disrupted global industrial and supply chains, the spokesperson said.
Chinese testing laboratories are an important part of the global testing and certification system, providing cost-effective support for the production and trade of communications electronics and smart manufacturing products worldwide, according to the spokesperson.
The United States is disregarding the objective realities of global economic development and the international division of labor in industrial cooperation, interfering with market choices through administrative measures, and pushing ahead with the so-called "onshoring" of testing, the spokesperson said. Such moves will drive up testing costs for businesses, lengthen product delivery and iteration cycles, and ultimately harm U.S. businesses and consumers.
The spokesperson noted that China had repeatedly proposed talks on a bilateral mutual recognition agreement, but the U.S. side had responded negatively.
China remains open to resolving differences via consultation and hopes the United States will heed industry concerns, respect market rules, and work with China in the same direction, the spokesperson said.
"If the U.S. side insists on going its own way, China will take further necessary measures to firmly safeguard its legitimate rights and interests," the spokesperson said. ■

Xinhua Headlines: CPC advances Party self-governance with resolute anti-graft efforts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31

01:59:13 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Communist Party of China (CPC) remains resolute in its fight against corruption as part of broader efforts to advance full and rigorous Party self-governance, according to Party officials.
At a plenum that concluded Thursday, the CPC Central Committee adopted a resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, stressing the need to maintain a tough stance against corruption and strengthen checks on and oversight over the exercise of power.
The Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th CPC Central Committee also called for fortifying the cultural-ethical foundations for championing integrity and disdaining graft, and enhancing coordinated efforts to ensure that officials do not have the audacity, opportunity, or desire to commit corruption.
"The anti-graft fight remains a grave and complex challenge, and much remains to be done to eliminate the conditions and fertile ground that give rise to corruption," senior anti-graft official Zhang Fuhai said on Friday at a press conference held by the CPC Central Committee on the guiding principles from the plenum.
Since 2012, discipline inspection and supervisory organs across the country have filed 8.105 million cases and punished 7.922 million people, including 963 officials registered with and supervised by the CPC Central Committee, said Zhang, deputy secretary of the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and deputy head of the National Commission of Supervision.
China has over the years launched an unprecedented anti-graft campaign that has reached every level of the Party and government, netting both high-ranking "tigers" and lower-level "flies."
Some of the most senior officials -- including former members of the Political Bureau and its Standing Committee, senior military officials, and retirees who left their leading positions years ago -- have been brought to justice.
The campaign has continued unabated. In 2025 alone, 115 officials at ministerial level or above were placed under investigation, while 627,000 people were disciplined in cases involving misconduct and graft that affect the people's immediate interests. The same year, China also opened investigations into more than 500 cases of cross-border corruption.
It was noted at the plenum this week that the Party must steadfastly follow a distinctive Chinese path of anti-graft and strengthen the Party Central Committee's centralized, unified leadership over anti-corruption work.
"We must take systematic steps to address both symptoms and root causes of corruption and adopt a holistic approach that combines severe punishment, targeted remedy, and effective prevention, carrying this fight through to the end," said a communique issued after the plenary session.
Zhang said anti-graft authorities will, in line with the arrangements made at the plenum, resolutely win the battle against corruption. "This is a battle that we cannot afford to lose and must never lose."
The plenum pledged to take targeted, well-designed measures to select and appoint officials, inspire them to foster and act on the correct view of performance, and enhance their competence in fulfilling duties and breaking new ground.
Huang Jianfa, deputy head of the Organization Department of the CPC Central Committee, said at the press conference that strict discipline is not intended to stifle initiative or constrain officials' actions.
"Rather, it seeks to set clear direction, enforce rules, promote sound conduct and guard against corruption, fostering a clean political environment and enabling officials to take initiative in their work," he said.
The resolution stresses that everyone is equal before the rules, no one enjoys privileges and no exceptions are allowed in their enforcement, said Xie Chuntao, vice president of the Party School of the CPC Central Committee.
It also calls for enforcement and oversight to be integrated into every stage of the work of Party organizations, members and officials, ensuring that institutional rules remain authoritative at all times and effective at every level, Xie said at the press conference.
FULL, RIGOROUS PARTY SELF-GOVERNANCE
The plenum made systematic plans for persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance.
Key priorities include strengthening the Party spirit, improving conduct and tightening discipline, taking firm and coordinated action against corruption, running the Party with systems and regulations, and refining Party and state oversight systems.
With over 100 million members, the Party has attached great importance to its own building since it was founded in 1921, said Liu Haixing, a member of the CPC Central Committee and head of the International Department of the CPC Central Committee.
For 105 years, he added, Party members have treated Party building as a great project, pressing ahead one generation after another -- forging and tempering the Party into the great, glorious and correct CPC that stands today.
"The Party demonstrates the strong vitality of Marxism," he said.
As profound changes unseen in a century gather pace across the world, political parties around the globe are confronting a stream of new issues and challenges.
"Many political parties are turning their eyes to us in the hope of finding paths and solutions for reference," said Liu.
That attention, he noted, attests to the valuable experience the CPC has accumulated during the periods of revolution, development and reform -- experience that progressive forces around the world can draw on.
Wu Hansheng, head of the Society Work Department of the CPC Central Committee, underscored the importance of Party building in emerging sectors.
Wu's department will work to expand the coverage of Party organizations in these sectors, strengthen Party building and improve services and management for people in new forms of employment.
Built on internet platforms, new forms of employment now engage some 84 million workers nationwide, including couriers, ride-hailing drivers and e-commerce workers.
Zhong Baijun, party chief of Xijidang Village in Lianyungang City in east China's Jiangsu Province, who attended the plenum as a non-voting participant, said that for communities like the one he leads, the latest arrangements from the meeting mean power at the micro level must be kept in check, affairs handled fairly, and petty graft close to the people rooted out.
The aim, he said, is to win public trust with integrity and clean governance.
"Weeds don't stop growing just because you've pulled them once," said Zhong, adding that the same goes for the Party's full and rigorous self-governance.■

DAKAR, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- With the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games (YOG) fast approaching, Marieme Diallo is putting the finishing touches on her preparations after recently returning from a training camp in China.

Diallo trained in Changsha City, central China's Hunan Province, where she was struck by the dedication and consistency of her Chinese counterparts. "They have good training methods, which helped us," she recalled.
Accompanying Diallo as a coach with the Senegalese Table Tennis Federation, Marie Fara Mendy also made the trip to China.
"What impressed me most was the rigor, discipline and sports facilities. I was also impressed by the attention paid to technical details, the volume of ball practice and the role played by sparring partners," Mendy noted.
"There was also the physical conditioning, as well as the patience and kindness of the Chinese coaches despite the language barrier."
The 2026 China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges finds Senegalese youth table tennis players back in China for their second consecutive year of intensive training.
"In technical terms, the players improved their serves, returns, consistency on the backhand and footwork. Mentally, they gained more confidence and developed the ability to sustain training sessions lasting four to five hours," Mendy observed.

Wu partnered with Zhao Qingjian, an associate professor at the Capital University of Physical Education and Sports, to design a curriculum covering physical endurance, flexibility, and sport-specific techniques.
After each session, the Chinese coaches checked in with each athlete through an interpreter to monitor muscle condition and physical responses, adjusting training intensity in real time.
Ndiaye Woreye had practiced wushu for several years, though her technique had yet to be shaped by a formal discipline. "The Chinese coaches have been teaching me the finer details of the movements. I hope to achieve good results at the Youth Olympics," she said.
Ousmane Sako, head coach of Senegal's national wushu team, watched closely as the Chinese instructors demonstrated each movement.
Sako said that Chinese martial arts had changed him, making him more focused and patient.
He also hoped to guide his athletes through thorough preparation so they could deliver their best performances, while expecting the Dakar 2026 YOG to inspire more young Senegalese to discover and embrace wushu.
With wushu set to make its debut as an official medal sport at the upcoming Youth Olympics, 17-year-old Tunisian athlete Zaineb Manai spent two weeks at the Tianjin Huoyuanjia School as well.
It was her fourth visit to China, but unlike previous trips for competitions, this one was dedicated entirely to training and preparation. She began practicing wushu at the age of four but took up taijiquan only two years ago.
"My main goal is to help elevate her technical specifications from the perspective of both a coach and a judge, as technical specifications carry significant weight in competition," said Chinese coach Cui Ru.
The two sides developed a packed schedule with five hours of daily training. "I train her just as I train my Chinese students, holding nothing back," said Cui.
Manai shared that the Chinese coaches were wonderful and her Chinese training partners were exceptionally warm and hospitable. Beyond training, they chatted about fun topics like food and culture.
Taijiquan is not just a competitive sport, but also a philosophy of how to live in harmony with oneself and others, she said, adding that the training camp brought her both technical refinement and a boost in confidence.
Manai has already fixed her gaze on Dakar, aiming not merely for a podium finish but for gold.
"In Tunisia, not many people practice wushu yet," she said. "I hope to inspire more Tunisians to practice wushu and taijiquan so that more people will grow to love it." ■

Drones have not killed tank: Ukrainian analyst says Operation Vivaldi shows NATO how to make armor work again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:58:59 UTC
01:58:59 KST

The lesson for NATO is not to abandon armored warfare, but to rethink how it is conducted. That is the argument Ukrainian military observer Oleksandr Kovalenko draws from Operation Vivaldi, the Third Army Corps’ counteroffensive near Lyman, which he says proves tanks still have a place on a battlefield many had already written them off.
Vivaldi is Ukraine's counteroffensive aimed at disrupting Russian forces' plans to encircle the fortress-belt cities in Donetsk Oblast from the north and south that protect the region from the entire occupation. Among them are Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka. These cities have helped hold back Russian forces since 2014.
Kovalenko's claim runs against a view that hardened as drones came to dominate the front: that massed armor is finished, kept alive only by habit.
It matters because NATO’s own recent exercises have fed that view, with small Ukrainian drone teams beating Alliance armor again and again. Kovalenko says the Alliance now risks taking the wrong lesson from its own defeats.
What NATO’s war games got wrong about the tank
Kovalenko points to two drills. At Estonia’s Hedgehog exercises in May 2025, Ukrainian FPV-drone units ran rings around NATO troops, who he says lost vehicles by the dozen and failed one task after another.
In one episode, Ukrainian pilots notionally knocked out a large combat group built around a British brigade.
A year later, during the Aurora 26 exercises on the Swedish island of Gotland, the pattern repeated, and the NATO units, in his telling, in a sense lost control of the island.
The skeptics’ case leaned on exactly these results, Kovalenko says, with many concluding that the Alliance faltered in part because it still fielded large amounts of armor, a tool they believe has lost its relevance in modern warfare.
How the Third Army Corps made armor move again
Vivaldi is the counterexample, Kovalenko argues. During it, the Third Army Corps carried out two mechanized assaults that pushed into the Russian rear, not armor used the old way.
A similar idea appeared in the 2024 Kursk operation, he notes, paired there with intense electronic warfare; Vivaldi widened the package, with deeper reconnaissance and dedicated work against the enemy’s own strike systems.
The vehicles carried extra passive and active protection, and crews trained for the task, and Ukrainian forces moved to suppress Russian surveillance and communications.
None of these ingredients is new on its own, he says. What mattered was adapting the working formulas to attack a heavily outnumbered enemy.
“Ukrainian forces are showing that even what seems at first glance to be a battlefield anachronism can be adapted and given a new function,” Kovalenko says.
The corps’ commander made the same point about armor specifically.
“These operations prove that maneuver by armor remains possible on a battlefield increasingly dominated by reconnaissance drones, loitering munitions and precision weapons,” Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, who leads the Third Army Corps, said in a comment Kovalenko cites.
His own conclusion is a warning: NATO armies are stuck near Cold War templates for attack and defense, and unless they study and absorb what Vivaldi did, the Alliance could one day find itself routed not in an exercise but on a real battlefield.
