Investigation: The coordinated campaign to drive hate against Ukrainians in Central Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:57:24 UTC
01:57:24 KST

Investigation: Rising hate against Ukrainians in Central Europe part of a coordinated campaign
"Dealers of Hate", a documentary published by The Kyiv Independent’s War Crimes Investigations Unit. (The Kyiv Independent)
Ukrainians in the three EU countries that have taken in the largest numbers of Ukrainian refugees are increasingly facing aggression — from insults on public transport to knife attacks. Journalists at the Kyiv Independent analyzed tens of thousands of posts on X and found that the same narratives circulating online are picked up and amplified by popular local politicians.
Editor's Note: The story is based on the documentary "Dealers of Hate," published by the Kyiv Independent's War Crimes Investigations Unit.
Left unprotected
Eva Yakubovska and Vladyslava Vorobiova have lived in Germany for nine years, where they founded the organization Vitsche. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the two began holding regular rallies in support of their home country. At these rallies, they have found not only support but, increasingly, faced aggression.
"We've seen all kinds of things at those rallies. People spat at those who came, shouted at them, and got right up in their faces, screaming at them aggressively," Vorobiova said.
In the first months of Russia's full-scale invasion, Ukrainian refugees in EU countries were met with a wave of support that began right at the border. Today, aggression against Ukrainians is increasingly common in those EU countries that have taken in the largest numbers of Ukrainian refugees — Poland, Germany, and Czechia.
On Ukraine's Independence Day, Aug. 24, 2024, as Vorobiova and Yakubovska held a rally near the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, Vorobiova noticed a man approaching them with a knife in his hand. Yakubovska only remembers that he was shouting something about Russia.
"I thought I would protect Vlada because I'm older — I could die," she said.
When the attacker realized the activists had noticed the knife, he began cutting his arms and chest and dropped to his knees. The women called for the police over and over but received no help initially. "They didn't respond," Yakubovska said.
Although the police did eventually subdue and detain the man, it later turned out that the officers had not logged the incident. The women had to go to the police again, where they were told the attacker had a mental illness and would undergo a brief rehabilitation program.
Yakubovska and Vorobiova do not feel protected by German police, and they are not alone.
"There have been many pro-Ukrainian German activists who have ultimately decided, 'Okay, I'm not going to do this because I can't protect my family.' For example, at the beginning of the full-scale invasion, we had a head of logistics whose home was simply broken into. And the police never logged it," Yakubovska said.
read also
'I'm afraid to speak Ukrainian'
Kateryna Lebed fled the war from Zaporizhzhia to Czechia with her young son in 2022. In Prague, she opened a laser hair-removal studio. In June 2025, she was attacked while walking through the city with a friend. Near a tram stop, a local man started shouting at the women.
"He shouted, 'Ukrainian whores!' That's the first thing I heard," Lebed said. The man blew smoke in her face, shoved her, kicked her, then grabbed her and threw her hard onto the road.
Unlike their German counterparts, Czech law enforcement reacted quickly. The attacker, Patrik Slastan, was identified, arrested, and sentenced to 20 months in prison for assaulting Lebed. He had already assaulted two Ukrainian women in Prague in 2023.
In Warsaw, Oleksandra Iwaniuk, who has lived in Poland since 2010 and teaches at the University of Warsaw, was verbally abused on a tram. She was speaking Ukrainian with a friend when a man began loudly repeating, "Russian whores."
"What struck me most was the reaction — or lack of reaction — from the other people on the tram," Iwaniuk said. In the past, she said, someone would always step in when something like this happened. "I felt like it had become normal for someone to publicly insult another person simply because of the language they speak."
"My friend stopped speaking Ukrainian to her child on public transport. I haven't, because it's really important to me that my child never sees that I'm afraid to speak Ukrainian. But the truth is I am afraid," she said.
Both Lebed and Iwaniuk wrote about these incidents on social media. In the comments under their posts, many others shared stories of anti-Ukrainian aggression on public transport, in stores, and on the streets.
Beyond the statistics
How many Ukrainians exactly fall victim to such attacks is unknown. Statistics that the Kyiv Independent requested from Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office showed that thousands of crimes against Ukrainians had been logged in the country since Feb. 24, 2022. Police classified only 139 of them as politically motivated attacks against Ukrainians, 137 of those involving physical assault.
Human rights activist Oleksandra Bienert, director of CineMova Ukrainian Empowerment Network, which collects statistics on attacks against Ukrainians, stressed that the data is far from complete. "We don't know about these cases because people don't report them or register incidents of discrimination," she said.
Seemingly minor violations of rights, such as bullying of Ukrainian children at school or refusals to book doctor's appointments for people who don't speak German, also remain outside the statistics.
In Czechia, the human rights organization In Iustitia had documented 129 anti-Ukrainian attacks since 2022 as of early 2026 — roughly half of all hate-motivated violent incidents recorded in the country. Klara Kalibova, head of In Iustitia, said the Czech Republic has never seen a wave of aggression against a particular group as intense as the one now targeting Ukrainians.
But Ukrainians often do not report incidents to the police, even in cases of outright violence. According to a study by PAQ Research cited by Kalibova, 57% of Ukrainians who arrived in Czechia have experienced verbal abuse, and 5% have experienced physical attacks. In actual figures, that is about 216,000 and 19,000 people, respectively.
Ukrainians are not the only victims of anti-Ukrainian sentiment in EU countries. In Iustitia human rights activists documented a case in which an adult man kicked and punched a 13-year-old Czech girl near her home — he had mistaken her for a Ukrainian.
Polish media reported similar cases in the summer of 2026. In Gdansk, a Polish man attacked two fellow Poles after mistaking them for Ukrainians, breaking one person's arm.
read also
'We're not in Ukraine'
In each of the three countries, influential politicians have made grievances against Ukraine and Ukrainians part of their political agenda.
In Germany, the most prominent example is the increasingly popular Alternative for Germany (AfD). "No aid to Ukraine, no money for Ukraine, no weapons for Ukraine — and no German troops!" AfD co-chair Alice Weidel said at a rally in July 2026.
The party's other co-chair, Tino Chrupalla, regularly claims that 700,000 Ukrainians in Germany do not work and receive Buergergeld, Germany's basic welfare benefit. This claim has been repeatedly debunked by German fact-checkers and contradicted by official statistics.
About a quarter of the 700,000 people cited are children or people unable to work, and only about 200,000 able-bodied Ukrainian recipients of Buergergeld are unemployed.
Last year in Czechia, Andrej Babis repeatedly claimed that Ukrainian refugees placed an excessive burden on the state budget, including during the televised debates with then-Prime Minister Petr Fiala ahead of the 2025 parliamentary election. "We don't have enough money here for our own people," Babis said. "We're not in Ukraine… We're in the Czech Republic!" Babis won the election and became prime minister.
The Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD), led by Japanese-born Czech nationalist Tomio Okamura, has promoted anti-Ukrainian rhetoric since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion. As early as May 2022, Okamura told parliament about Ukrainian refugees, quoting a regional politician, "We're talking about people who can't write, can't read, can't even use a simple toilet or turn on an electric kettle… Obviously, they've never worked and never will."
The SPD also campaigned on explicitly anti-Ukrainian slogans in the 2025 parliamentary election, which saw Okamura emerge as speaker of the lower house of parliament. In November 2025, he made a point of removing the Ukrainian flag from the parliamentary building.
In Poland, the first sources of hate speech toward Ukrainians were far-right organizations and politicians, said Rafal Pankowski, professor at the Institute of Sociology of Civitas University in Warsaw and president of the Never Again Association (Nigdy Wiecej), a human rights organization.
Grzegorz Braun, leader of the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown, launched the slogan "Stop the Ukrainianization of Poland!" In 2023, he was reelected to the Polish parliament, and in 2024, he was elected to the European Parliament.
"What Ukrainianization of Poland could there possibly be? Yes, it's a large group of refugees, but it's roughly 1 million people in a country of roughly 40 million, so talking about the 'Ukrainianization of Poland' is absurd," Pankowski said.
During the 2025 presidential campaign, the eventual winner of the election, Karol Nawrocki, also used anti-Ukrainian narratives. He posted a campaign video captioned with "Ukrainians — to the back of the line."
"In queues for doctors and clinics, Polish citizens should have priority. In schools and kindergartens, Polish children should come first," he said.
American researcher Susan Benesch, founder of the Dangerous Speech Project, stressed that hate speech is "a very useful political tool."
"If you want to get more supporters or you want your supporters to be more loyal to you, it's very effective, unfortunately, to tell them that their problems are caused by this other group of awful people," she said.
Vorobiova in Berlin also pointed to a clear overlap between politics and spikes in anti-Ukrainian hate, saying, "The closer we get to elections, the more these narratives spread, fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiments, opinions, and conclusions."
In Czechia, Kalibova also pointed to a direct link between the spread of anti-Ukrainian rhetoric and elections.
Iwaniuk in Poland has made the same observation. "When the presidential campaign began, it only took a few months for us to see a rise in hatred on the streets," she said.
After Nawrocki clashed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky this summer and revoked his Order of the White Eagle, Poland's highest state honor, a wave of attacks on Ukrainians swept across the country.
A virtual mirror of hate
The anti-Ukrainian narratives heard on the political stage are almost the same as those spreading en masse on social media, especially on X, formerly Twitter.
Journalists from the Kyiv Independent collected about 140,000 posts on X in German, Czech, and Polish, published between the summer of 2024 and the summer of 2025, a period that coincided with a number of election campaigns, to investigate anti-Ukrainian sentiment in these countries.
From those, they filtered 98,000 posts "that we considered substantive — meaning they actually contained meaningful content," data analyst Denys Hubashov said. The narratives in these posts were identified by an AI model, which journalists trained on hundreds of posts they had labeled themselves. The model's results were then manually reviewed and verified.
For Germany, the journalists analyzed 12,000 German-language posts about Ukrainians. A quarter of them focused on the alleged harm Ukrainian refugees cause to German society, including the strain on the welfare system cited by politicians. "Why don't we finally send all those Ukros who are living entirely off our dime back home?" one post read.
More than 1,000 other posts accused Ukrainians of Nazism. This is a common Kremlin narrative, but it taps into particularly sensitive issues in German society. "This narrative works in Germany… Because Germany has a memory, Germany has a history, and Germany has a responsibility," Vorobiova said.
For Czechia, the journalists analyzed 23,000 Czech-language posts and replies. Some 2,500 of them focused on the claim that Ukrainians were bringing crime and danger to Czechia. "How much longer are Ukrainians going to terrorize us in our own country?" one user wrote.
For the past 15 years, roughly two-thirds of Czechs have consistently viewed foreigners as a security threat to their country. Czech journalists and the fact-checking organization Demagog have repeatedly shown that the crime rate among Ukrainians in Czechia is about the same as in Czech society as a whole. Police statistics confirm this reporting. Nevertheless, Okamura has spread claims that Ukrainians are behind rising crime in Czechia.
"If you really want to make people condone or commit violence, you want to make them afraid."
Most of the analyzed posts about Ukraine and Ukrainians were in Polish. The dominant theme was also the alleged danger posed by Ukrainians, particularly claims about rising crime. But another popular topic was the shared history between the two nations. Ukrainians are called Banderites and Nazis, in reference to the ethnic conflict between Ukrainians and Poles that escalated into mass killings in Volyn in the 1940s. "The only enemy nation is the Banderites," one user wrote.
Many of these narratives bear the hallmarks of Russian propaganda. But Pankowski warned against blaming everything on Russia.
"It is equally important to recognize the problem posed by the far-right groups operating in Poland. They act in Russia's interests and against Ukraine and Ukrainians in Poland. Groups whose base is in Poland itself, not outside the country, not in Moscow, not in Minsk, and not elsewhere," he said.
read also
Drops of hatred
"When we see big surges of hate speech and dangerous speech, it is typically because somebody starts it and then spreads it… It always starts because it's useful to someone," Benesch said.
She stressed that the operative emotion here is not hatred but fear, which is usually unfounded. "If you really want to make people condone or commit violence, you want to make them afraid," she added.
Benesch cited the example of Rwanda, where the 1994 genocide was accompanied by an intense campaign of hate speech, spread mainly through radio. One witness at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda said that the propagandists "dripped petrol little by little all over the country until one day you could strike a match and it would burst into flames."
Pankowski said the link between hate speech — online or offline — and real violence against Ukrainians is obvious to him.
"We had a case at a school in Slupsk where a teacher was spreading anti-Ukrainian narratives among the class. Some of the students also held anti-Ukrainian views, and eventually, Ukrainian students were beaten by Polish students. So we're dealing with an ideological, xenophobic message that ultimately, in a sense, leads to physical aggression," he said.
Because of this link, Benesch prefers the term dangerous speech to hate speech — defining it not by the intent of the speaker but by the consequences of their words, "by the harm that it causes to other people."
Benesch said that even if a politician does not explicitly call for violence but their supporters take their words that way, this "should not exonerate that person of at least a very strong moral responsibility, though they may not have a legal one."

G20 foreign ministers meet in US amid economic, security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:57:16 UTC
01:57:16 KST

A G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has kicked off in the US, bringing together top diplomats from the world’s leading economies for two days of discussions of pressing global economic challenges, geopolitical tensions, and international security issues.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting the gathering, which opened on Friday, in the Southern city of Atlanta, Georgia, where the main focus will be on economic growth, energy and food security, freedom of navigation, and the resilience of global supply chains.
Opening the meeting, Rubio urged members to work together to address interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, warning of growing threats to energy and food supplies, international trade and freedom of navigation.
He described the current period as a “moment of choosing”, saying challenges facing the US also had implications for the wider world.
The gathering opened with Rubio’s remarks, without the traditional group photo, after several European officials indicated they would not appear alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
Asked on the sidelines whether he would join a photo with Lavrov, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said: “I assume there will be no family photograph at all.”
He added that European partners would not pose alongside the Russian minister. “There is no normality with Russia,” he said.
'Series of interconnected economic, geopolitical crises'
“We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, many of which pose severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order,” said Rubio.
He identified disruptions to global energy and food supplies, supply chains, trade, and freedom of navigation as major challenges requiring a coordinated response.
Rubio called on G20 partners to strengthen economic resilience, safeguard markets, and protect the economies that depend on them.
He also stressed the role of foreign ministers and political leaders in coordinating responses to emerging crises and protecting shared interests.
“By translating our shared interests into practical cooperation and real action, we can reinforce global stability and, more importantly, deliver meaningful results for our citizens,” he said.
Rubio said the assembled officials faced a busy two-day agenda, with the opening plenary session focusing on freedom of navigation and food security.
Fidan to address Gaza, regional tensions
Fidan is set to address the situation in Gaza, tensions between the US and Iran, and the importance of safeguarding strategic maritime routes. He is also expected to underline Türkiye’s diplomatic efforts to promote regional security and stability.
Lavrov, who is leading the Russian delegation, is expected to call for greater economic cooperation and equal dialogue among G20 members. Moscow has also criticised Washington’s decision to exclude South Africa from the G20 process, calling for its membership rights to be restored.
US President Donald Trump earlier announced that South Africa would not receive an invitation to the 2026 summit. The decision followed Washington’s boycott of the Johannesburg summit and stemmed from Trump’s claims of persecution of white farmers in South Africa.
The Group of Twenty (G20) is an international forum bringing together the world's major advanced and emerging economies to discuss and coordinate global economic policies and address key international challenges.
Established in 1999 in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis, its membership now consists of 19 countries and the European Union and the African Union, which joined in 2023.

Israeli arms firms face fresh restrictions at Paris exhibition
Israeli arms firms are facing fresh restrictions at France’s upcoming naval arms exhibition, with offensive weapons barred from display and Israeli government representatives excluded, amid two years of restrictions on Israeli exhibitors.
Euronaval, the world’s largest naval defence exhibition, is due to take place in Villepinte, near Paris, on 3 November. French officials have informed organisers that Israeli exhibitors will once again be subject to a "clearly defined and highly restrictive framework", according to Israeli media reports.
French authorities have reportedly also made clear that Israeli companies will only be permitted to showcase defensive technology, specifically air defence and missile interception systems.
The measures have sparked anger among Israeli defence officials, according to reports.
Israeli companies have also reportedly been told they will not be allocated significant exhibition space at the next Paris Air Show in 2027, with organisers citing limited availability.
This follows the 2025 edition at Le Bourget, when organisers erected black walls overnight around the stands of Israel Aerospace Industries, Rafael and Elbit Systems shortly before the exhibition opened.
In June, Israeli exhibitors faced further restrictions at Eurosatory, another defence exhibition held in France. Local inspectors classified the exhibits as displaying offensive weapons, which were then concealed behind black walls. Official Israeli government representation was also prohibited, and the establishment of an Israeli national pavilion was blocked.
Israeli arms firms frequently market their products as being "battle tested" — often meaning that the weapons and technology have been used against Palestinians living under occupation.
France’s continued restrictions over the past two years have fuelled tensions between Paris and Tel Aviv amid Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, particularly following France’s recognition of Palestinian statehood last year.
Last month, France, alongside the United Kingdom, Canada and nine other countries, announced plans to introduce an import ban on goods originating from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

How do you bounce back from Liz Truss-level public failure? Don’t be shameless; do show remorse | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:55:53 UTC
01:55:53 KST

Gabriel Weston made a mistake at work this summer. It doesn’t define her – she was and is a well-regarded NHS surgeon and author – but it was serious enough, as she explained in an extraordinarily candid series of Instagram and Substack posts this month, to prompt an investigation that left her feeling “ashamed and alone and really quite nervous”. Whatever went wrong in the operating theatre was bad enough to be classed a “never event” (something that should never be able to happen if the process is working properly) and triggered a nagging anxiety that she might somehow do it again, unless she figured out where she had unexpectedly gone wrong.
It’s a fascinating insight into a process that most people never have the courage to talk about openly. But it also highlights why it’s so hard in practice for doctors and other professionals to acknowledge and learn from mistakes – as every public inquiry into every public scandal ends up recommending, only to repeat it all over again after the next one – rather than close ranks and cover up. Weston says she only spoke up out of frustration with what she saw as her employers’ failure to support her (she had asked to reduce what she considered an overloaded operating list to take some pressure off, which she says has now happened, leaving her full of praise for the hospital’s ultimate response). Judging by the responses to her posts, she’s not alone.
I thought of Weston this week when Liz Truss published Bank Job, the second book she has written in two years circling the drain of her career. This one seems if anything even less self-aware, blaming the Bank of England, not herself, for the spectacular failure of her mini-budget (even her old cheerleaders at the Telegraph called it deranged). But it’s also oddly sad. There’s something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure, as if the truth would shatter her. She can’t seem to leave the whole episode alone – can’t withdraw, as Keir Starmer has, into stony silence about his own prematurely curtailed time in Downing Street – yet can’t really face it head-on either.
How does anyone learn from cataclysmic failure? I don’t mean the frothy, early-career kind that seemed the end of the world at the time, but which you can laugh about now from the security of knowing that eventually everything turned out fine. Those aren’t the kind of failures the state really cares about avoiding. Nor do I mean the kind whose authors somehow manage to fail upwards anyway – or at least onwards, like Truss, into some strange reincarnation on YouTube. The failures that most haunt their authors, but which often hold the most useful lessons for preventing such a thing ever happening again, are often of the “there but for the grace of God go you and I” kind, involving formerly blameless and conscientious people who make one inexplicably dumb mistake, often under pressure or when exhausted.
Richard Jackson was a high-flying civil servant working on counter-terrorism, who one night accidentally scooped up two classified documents that should never have left the building along with some routine papers he was taking home. Realising his error that night, he fatally compounded it by deciding to sneak the files back before their absence was noticed, only to accidentally leave them on the train – where they were found and handed into a BBC reporter, resulting in a security scandal that cost Jackson his job and left him close to suicide. The advice on coping he shared in a recent episode of BBC Radio 4’s Life Changing series – get dark thoughts out of your head by writing them down or telling someone; keep a note of all the nice things people have ever said to you; don’t let your life be defined by one mistake – seems useful for individuals in the eye of the storm. But so perhaps is what Weston calls a degree of professional “care and acceptance” for good people who have failed, and want help working out why.
Shamelessness has a deservedly terrible reputation in public life, and for some mistakes forgiveness can be too much to ask.
But it’s shame that prevents thoughtful people learning from failure; shame that drives the cover-up; shame that ruins, and sometimes even ends, lives. People willing to honestly examine their own mistakes for others’ benefit deserve some grace in return. The true shame lies with those refusing to offer it.
- Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist
- In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

Report: Israel pleaded with Britain to delay Palestinian recognition until hostages freed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:54:30 UTC
01:54:30 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- Report: Israel pleaded with Britain to delay Palestinian recognition until hostages freed
Report: Israel pleaded with Britain to delay Palestinian recognition until hostages freed
Israeli officials warned unconditional recognition could endanger hostages and undermine talks; Britain said there was no evidence it put either at risk
Israel pleaded with Britain to make the release of hostages held in Gaza a condition for recognizing a Palestinian state, warning that unconditional recognition could endanger them and undermine negotiations, The Jewish Chronicle reported on Friday.
“During hostage negotiations Israel pleaded with the UK not to recognise a Palestinian state unconditionally as it could harm the remaining hostages and put their lives at risk,” an Israeli government official told the newspaper.
Then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced recognition on September 21, 2025, while 48 hostages remained in Gaza. He insisted the decision was “not a reward for Hamas.” The remaining living hostages were released 22 days later under a US-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Adam Rose, a lawyer representing British and British-linked hostage families, told the newspaper that the families’ representatives repeatedly argued that recognition would reward Hamas, but British officials rejected that argument in four meetings.
“We were led to believe that recognition ultimately was a transactional decision given to the Arab states who in return made a statement calling for the release of the hostages,” Rose said.
Rose also said Starmer promised the families on September 11, 2025, that Britain would expand sanctions against those supporting Hamas and other terrorist organizations. That promise had yet to be fulfilled, he said.
The Foreign Office defended recognition and rejected the suggestion that it endangered the hostages. “There is no evidence to suggest recognition risked the lives of hostages, nor the negotiations mediated by President Trump, which subsequently resulted in an agreement to release the remaining hostages,” a spokesperson told the newspaper.

Ukraine is working to expedite the delivery and maintenance of F-16 fighter jets, which have proven highly effective in combating Russian jet drones, Spokesperson for the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) Heorhiy Tykhy said.
"Yes, work is underway to secure additional platforms – that is, additional aircraft – to expedite the delivery of those already promised, to secure additional parts, and expediting aircraft maintenance," he said at a briefing in Kyiv on Friday, responding to a question from an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.

Zelenskyy said the U.S.-made F-16 fighter jets have proven effective against new Russian jet-powered drones, but too many of the aircraft – about half – have been in Europe for an extended period for repairs and maintenance.
Zelenskyy said he aims to move the maintenance of the F-16s to Ukraine to save time.

Mass protests sweep Italy during nationwide strike

Thousands of students, workers hold peaceful protests in Italy
- Thousands of students and workers protested across Italy on Oct 30 for more school funding and help with the rising cost of living. The demonstrations were mostly peaceful.
- USB union said 1 million to 1.5 million people joined nationwide. Students said unsafe schools, high fees and rent left them “at a breaking point”.
- Some clashes still broke out in Turin and Rome. Meloni’s government has tightened protest laws and plans more youth support in the 2027 budget.
AI generated
ROME - Thousands of students and workers took to the streets across Italy on Oct 30, calling for more school funding and relief from the soaring cost of living, in massive protests that remained mostly peaceful.
The protests were the biggest in a recent wave of demonstrations inspired by those in France and Spain, led by students who have set up tent camps and occupied schools to make their demands heard.
A general strike called by Italy’s USB trade union drew thousands of workers to Oct 30’s protests, including truck drivers, taxi drivers and farmers who have rallied in recent weeks over the spike in fuel prices and to oppose rising defence spending.
The USB union estimated to AFP that between 1 million to 1.5 million people across Italy participated on Oct 30. The authorities did not publish official numbers.
Roman student Sofia Cataldi said conditions in her high school were not safe.
“We don’t want windows falling on our heads, and we don’t want mice in our schools. We want clean buildings, and I want to live in a better world than this one,” the 16-year-old told AFP.
University student Beatrice Chilelli said students were “at a breaking point”.
“They can’t afford to pay exorbitant tuition fees, and rent... which weighs heavily on their parents’ shoulders,” said the 21-year-old, citing student housing in Rome that could reach €1,200 (S$1,720) per month for a single room.
Two tractors and a taxi were at the start of the Rome procession that began at the main train station and made its way past the Colosseum and the economy ministry building, with protesters waving flags and shouting into megaphones.
“We need more houses, not bombs!” sang one group in the crowd.
‘Reclaim our future’
The Milan protest also began at the central train station, but then headed outside the city – far from the centre where young vandals had looted stores, destroyed property and clashed with police two weeks ago after another sanctioned cost-of-living demonstration.
“Let’s reclaim our future” read one banner unfurled by students in Milan.
In the Milan crowd was Stefano De Finis, 25, who said he hoped the various protests would lead to something “lasting”.
“Because next year we’ll have elections and honestly, when it comes to voting for real change, we honestly don’t know how it could happen,” he said.
“The problem is that in Italy there are many elderly people and few young people, so we need to make sure the elderly start getting mobilised... otherwise we’re alone in this struggle,” he said, citing the political power of Italy’s ageing union workers.
Across the country, police in riot gear were seen on the sidelines of the various protests.
In one of the few reported clashes, protesters in Turin were beaten back with batons by the police, who used a water cannon to keep them away from the prefecture.
In Rome, AFP reporters saw young protesters throwing bottles and knocking over rubbish bins and setting one on fire towards the end of the demonstration.
Following the Oct 17 to Oct 18 weekend of clashes between youth and police in Milan, Meloni’s hard-right government toughened laws on public gatherings while easing rules on detaining minors.
The government also last week agreed a €175.2 million aid package for truck drivers, farmers and fishermen hit by soaring fuel prices linked to the war in the Middle East.
Measures in favour of young people and families are also planned in the draft 2027 budget being discussed among the various governing parties, such as an annual bonus of €2,500 for workers under 30.
“I hope this can provide answers for young people in general... who feel that the state doesn’t care about them,” Meloni told journalists on Oct 28, stressing that these measures were “not for those who smash windows”. AFP

Tennessee woman Christa Pike describes pain after failed execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:51:00 UTC
01:51:00 KST

Tennessee woman Christa Pike describes pain after failed execution
October 30, 2026
Death row inmate Christa Pike said Friday that she remained in constant pain and struggled to speak a month after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee.
Her lawyers have urged Governor Bill Lee to reduce her death sentence to life imprisonment, but he has indicated that it will remain unchanged unless the courts intervene.
In her first public statement since the failed execution, Pike said she had expected to die but instead woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said. "My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak."
What happened during the execution attempt?
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital during the September 30 execution attempt. Her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered. She spent the first few days in hospital unconscious and on a ventilator.
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the intravenous line caused the drug to collect in surrounding tissue rather than enter her bloodstream.
Lee ordered an investigation and postponed Tennessee's other lethal injection scheduled this year. The state's prison chief resigned.
What did Pike say?
Pike blamed the failed execution on "incompetence" and said her suffering extended beyond her physical injuries.
"There is pain in my mind and in my soul," she said.
She also expressed gratitude to the medical workers who saved her life and acknowledged the suffering of her victim's family.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and killing of her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time of the crime, which she committed with her boyfriend.
"I continue to think about my victim's family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured," she said.
What happens next?
Lee told reporters this week: "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts."
Pike dictated her statement to her legal team from the infirmary at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she returned after hospitalization.
"I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next," she said. "For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time."

Ukraine Imposed Sanctions Against 10 Companies Involved in Production of Rassvet System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:50:30 UTC
01:50:30 KST

Ukraine imposed sanctions against 10 companies and 19 individuals involved in the development and expansion of the Russian Rassvet low-Earth orbit satellite communications system.
This was announced by the Commissioner of the President of Ukraine for Sanctions Policy, Vladyslav Vlasiuk.
“Rassvet is not just an attempt to create a Russian internet from space. It is future military communications infrastructure: drone control, data transmission, troop coordination, and the operation of command posts and strike systems,” emphasized Vladyslav Vlasiuk.
Among those targeted by the sanctions was, in particular, the network’s chief developer and operator—Bureau 1440—headed by Alexey Shelobkov. Restrictions were also imposed on its affiliated companies, Labs 1440, which manufactures solar panels for spacecraft, and FAB Rassvet, which, under the leadership of Boris Kanunnikov, develops and manufactures communications satellites, subscriber terminals, and telecommunications equipment. Both executives were also added to the sanctions list.
Sanctions were also imposed on the Belarusian company Aerokosmichnye Prybory, which is wholly owned by Bureau 1440 and develops prototypes of aerospace system components.
The restrictions apply not only to legal entities and individuals within the Bureau 1440 structure but also to companies and their management involved in industrial cooperation. In particular, the Russian manufacturing association Akvamash, which produces high-precision metal parts and assemblies for the aviation, rocket and space, and defense industries, and the company Small Spacecraft, which specializes in space technology and ground-based satellite communications equipment.
The sanctions list also includes 5S Group, which supplies industrial computers, networking equipment, and automation systems, and the Novosibirsk-based company Eltex, which manufactures switches, routers, and other telecommunications equipment.
Restrictions were also imposed on the Moscow-based El-Optics, which supplies and integrates optical, laser, and telecommunications equipment, photonics components, and quantum communication systems, and on the St. Petersburg-based Elesar Group, which supplies Russian companies with foreign electronic components and equipment.
Personal sanctions were also imposed against Pavel Dronov, director of the Fakel Design Bureau, and Vladimir Koshlakov, head of the Keldysh Center. The Fakel Design Bureau manufactures electric propulsion systems for Rassvet satellites, while the Keldysh Center produces compensator cathodes for these systems.
Sergey Kasaev, CEO of the radio-electronics manufacturer Mikran, and his predecessor, Vera Paramonova, were also added to the list. The company supplies ultra-high-frequency, radio-frequency, and antenna equipment for Rassvet.
In total, the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine identified 49 Russian and Belarusian companies involved in the project, including IT companies, microelectronics manufacturers, research institutions, enterprises of the Roscosmos corporation, and entities of the Russian Defense Ministry.
“In other words, this is not the final sanctions decision,” emphasized Vladyslav Vlasiuk.
The next step will be to coordinate sanctions with partner countries and cut off supply channels for critical components.

Billions stolen in minutes: Inside world's biggest crypto heists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:49:17 UTC
01:49:17 KST

A cyberattack on Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, on Thursday has drawn fresh attention to cryptocurrency theft, with blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs estimating that about $6.36 billion was transferred out of its wallets across 10 blockchains.
Most transfers took place within about 20 minutes. TRM Labs attributed the operation, with high confidence, to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group.
Binance said its preliminary investigation pointed to a potentially compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer.
In a statement on Friday, it estimated the impact at around $6.3 billion and said about $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen.
The exchange said user funds were safe, pledged to cover losses through its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company funds, and reported no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. The investigation remains ongoing.
The incident ranks among the largest reported cryptocurrency thefts.
Here are some of the biggest cases, based on the estimated value of assets at the time.
Bybit, February 2025
Cryptocurrency exchange Bybit suffered one of the largest digital asset thefts on February 21, 2025, when hackers stole approximately $1.5 billion in cryptocurrency from an Ethereum cold wallet.
The attackers compromised the transaction approval process, tricking authorised signers into approving a malicious transaction.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) attributed the attack to North Korea, identifying the operation as part of a hacking campaign known as TraderTraitor.
The FBI said the attackers rapidly converted some of the stolen assets into bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, distributing them across thousands of addresses on multiple blockchains.
Ronin Network, March 2022
The Ronin Network, a blockchain platform associated with the online game Axie Infinity, lost cryptocurrency worth almost $620 million after attackers compromised its transaction-validation system.
Hackers gained control of private keys belonging to validators, enabling them to approve unauthorised withdrawals.
The US Treasury Department attributed the March 2022 attack to Lazarus Group, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking organisation.
The department said the group had stolen almost $620 million from the blockchain project.
Poly Network, August 2021
A hacker exploited a vulnerability in Poly Network, a decentralised finance platform that enables transfers between different blockchains, stealing digital assets worth more than $610 million.
The platform said the attacker began returning the assets within days of the incident.
By August 2023, media reported that almost all the funds had been returned, except for some stablecoins frozen by their issuer.
The hacker claimed the attack was intended to expose a security weakness in the platform.
Poly Network offered a $500,000 reward for information about the vulnerability and for returning the funds.
BNB Chain, October 2022
An attacker exploited a vulnerability in the BSC Token Hub, a cross-chain bridge connecting two BNB blockchain networks, and withdrew around 2 million BNB tokens worth approximately $586 million.
BNB Chain said the attacker exploited a flaw in cross-chain message verification.
The network coordinated with validators to suspend operations and limit the movement of the affected assets.
Coinbase's threat intelligence team later published a technical analysis explaining how the attacker forged security proofs to exploit the bridge.
The initial amount involved did not translate into an equivalent financial loss, as much of the cryptocurrency remained on the network or was frozen.
Coincheck, January 2018
Japanese cryptocurrency exchange Coincheck suffered a major attack in January 2018, when hackers stole approximately 526.3 million NEM tokens from an internet-connected wallet.
Media reports said the stolen assets were valued at around $530 million at the time.
The incident prompted Japan's Financial Services Agency to order improvements to Coincheck's operations and examine security arrangements at other cryptocurrency exchanges.
Coincheck later said it had compensated affected customers for the stolen funds, according to company filings.
Mt. Gox, 2011–2014
Tokyo-based bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox collapsed in 2014 after disclosing that hundreds of thousands of bitcoins had gone missing through thefts spanning several years.
The missing cryptocurrency was valued at close to $500 million at the time, according to reports.
Mt. Gox, which once handled a large share of global bitcoin trading, filed for bankruptcy in 2014, leaving thousands of customers unable to access their funds.
Wormhole, February 2022
Wormhole, a platform connecting different blockchain networks, was exploited in February 2022, resulting in the theft of approximately $320 million in cryptocurrency.
Hackers exploited a vulnerability in the platform's verification process to create tokens without providing the required backing.
Media reported that Jump Crypto, whose parent company had acquired Wormhole's developer, replaced the stolen funds.
Liquid Network, September 2026
Attackers drained about $319 million in bitcoin from Liquid Network, a Bitcoin sidechain operated by Blockstream, on September 6, 2026.
TRM Labs said the attackers exploited a software vulnerability to create unbacked synthetic bitcoin tokens and exchange them for real bitcoin.
About 85 percent of the funds, worth roughly $272 million, were later returned after Blockstream patched the vulnerability.
The firm said around $47 million remained with the attackers.

“Our Dear Ones”: First Footage Shows Oleshky Residents Greeting Ukrainian Ombudsman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:48:05 UTC
01:48:05 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
“Our Dear Ones”: First Footage Shows Oleshky Residents Greeting Ukrainian Ombudsman
The first footage from a Ukrainian humanitarian mission inside Russian-occupied Oleshky shows residents packed and waiting for buses that are expected to evacuate them to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets arrived in Oleshky as part of the humanitarian mission and met residents preparing to leave the occupied city, his office reported on October 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
At the beginning of the footage, one woman greets Lubinets emotionally: “Our dear ones.”
Residents said they had already prepared for evacuation, labeling their bags with their names and phone numbers while waiting for transportation.
“We are bringing the buses in now. Everyone who is going to Ukraine—we will tell you which buses will take you,” Lubinets told residents.
Another woman, who introduced herself as Anna Leonidivna, recognized the Ukrainian ombudsman during the meeting.
The mission is intended both to deliver humanitarian assistance and to evacuate civilians who want to leave Oleshky. A temporary ceasefire was arranged for the operation, with Ukraine’s Ombudsman Office crediting US First Lady Melania Trump with helping facilitate and coordinate the process.
Ahead of the mission, Ukrainian and Russian human rights commissioners said designated routes had been cleared of mines and that the sides had agreed on the conditions needed for the humanitarian operation.
The Ukrainian delegation traveled first to Gomel in Belarus, then to Anapa in Russia, before continuing through occupied Crimea to Oleshky. The same route is expected to be used to evacuate residents who choose to leave.
Lubinets has said civilians will be able to decide for themselves whether they want to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory or to Russia.
Organizers prepared 25 buses with capacity for around 750 people, along with ambulances for residents with limited mobility.
Particular attention is being given to elderly people, people with disabilities, and those unable to care for themselves.
The humanitarian cargo reportedly includes food, medicine, drinking water, hygiene products, and fuel for generators.
Melania Trump has continued drawing attention to the mission and sharing updates from Lubinets as it progresses. Ukraine’s Ombudsman Office has publicly thanked her for helping create the conditions for the operation.
“May this humanitarian mission bring an end to suffering and open a new chapter of lasting peace between Russia and Ukraine,” Melania Trump wrote.
Previously, Lubinets reported that a ceasefire in the temporarily occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region has remained in effect for more than 75 hours without any reported incidents.

Russia Spent Decades Modernizing One Giant Cruiser—Now Its Flagship Is Headed for Scrap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:56 UTC
01:47:56 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Spent Decades Modernizing One Giant Cruiser—Now Its Flagship Is Headed for Scrap
Russia’s flagship nuclear-powered battlecruiser Pyotr Velikiy is no longer considered worth repairing or modernizing after years of accumulated wear, according to a preliminary assessment by a special commission.
Vladimir Maltsev, head of the All-Russian Fleet Support Movement, told Russian state media agency TASS that specialists had concluded the massive warship could not realistically be restored to service.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The cruiser cannot be restored. The ship has a certain degree of wear,” Maltsev said on the sidelines of the “330 Years of the Russian Fleet” forum.
He stressed that the finding remains preliminary and that a final decision will be announced later.
According to a TASS source in Russia’s defense industry, Moscow had originally planned to begin modernizing Pyotr Velikiy immediately after completing work on its sister ship, Admiral Nakhimov. The idea was to ensure that the Russian Navy always retained at least one nuclear-powered cruiser of the class.
That plan fell apart as work on Admiral Nakhimov dragged on eight years beyond the original schedule. By the time the overhaul was finally nearing completion, Pyotr Velikiy had reportedly exhausted its remaining service life.
The cruiser serves as the flagship of Russia’s Northern Fleet and is the last active ship of the Soviet-designed Orlan nuclear-powered cruiser family.
Russian sources have long described it as the Navy’s most heavily armed surface strike vessel and one of the world’s largest surface combatants outside the aircraft-carrier category.
Four ships of the class were built at the Baltic Shipyard between 1977 and 1996. Two—Admiral Ushakov and Admiral Lazarev—have already been retired.
The modernization of Admiral Nakhimov, meanwhile, stretched across decades and was completed this summer. The cruiser is currently undergoing trials and is expected to return to the Northern Fleet before the end of 2026.
Sevmash, the Severodvinsk shipyard responsible for the overhaul program, has capacity to accommodate only one cruiser of the class at a time.
Work on Admiral Nakhimov had originally been expected to finish in 2018, but repeated delays pushed the program far beyond schedule. Its reported cost more than doubled during the process, eventually exceeding 200 billion rubles.
If Pyotr Velikiy is retired, Admiral Nakhimov will become Russia’s principal heavy surface combatant of the type.
The modernized ship is expected to carry Fort-M and Pantsir-M air-defense systems, Paket-NK and Otvet anti-submarine weapons, and universal vertical launch cells capable of holding as many as 80 Kalibr, Oniks, and Zircon missiles.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia was preparing to retire its only aircraft carrier, Admiral Kuznetsov, effectively shutting down its fixed-wing carrier aviation.

Ukraine’s FPV Drone Hits Loaded Russian Grad and Sets Off Massive Explosion, Video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:50 UTC
01:47:50 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s FPV Drone Hits Loaded Russian Grad and Sets Off Massive Explosion, Video
Russian BM-21 Grad multiple-launch rocket system was hit by a powerful blast after being struck by an FPV drone while still positioned for firing, according to footage released by the Signum Battalion of Ukraine’s 59th Unmanned Systems Brigade.
The Russian crew reportedly managed to fire only two ranging rockets before the Ukrainian drone reached the launcher.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The forecast says the hail is canceled. SIGNUM fighters hunted down a Russian BM-21 Grad multiple-launch rocket system right on its firing position,” the unit said.
Footage of the strike shows the launcher erupting after impact, with the remaining rockets apparently contributing to the violent secondary detonation.
The Signum operators also struck several other Russian vehicles used to move personnel and supplies toward the front.
According to the unit, the additional targets included a pickup truck from which Russian troops were seen jumping out, an ATV, a camouflaged vehicle, and other logistics equipment.
The BM-21 Grad remains one of Russia’s most widely used multiple-launch rocket systems in its war of aggression against Ukraine.
Developed in the early 1960s and introduced into Soviet service in 1963, the system is mounted on a Ural truck chassis and carries 40 launch tubes for 122mm rockets.
A Grad can fire its full load in roughly 20 seconds, saturating an area of up to about 14.5 hectares, or 36 acres.
Depending on the ammunition used, the system can strike targets at distances of up to roughly 40 kilometers, or 25 miles, making it particularly dangerous against troop concentrations, defensive positions, and infrastructure.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces tracked down and destroyed a Russian BM-30 Smerch multiple launch rocket system (MLRS) and its accompanying reloading vehicle hidden approximately 60 kilometers behind the frontline.

Binance hack losses exceed total market theft over past two years — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:37 UTC
01:47:37 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. The scale of the hacker attack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance, which resulted in the withdrawal of approximately $6.3 billion, has exceeded the combined losses suffered by the crypto market from hacks over the previous two years, Olga Goncharova, head of the Digital Financial Assets and Digital Currencies Expert Center of the Association of Banks of Russia, told TASS.
"The bulk of the funds was siphoned off in just 20 minutes – more was taken from the exchange than hackers stole from the entire crypto market over the last two years. This is a classic 'black swan' – an event no one anticipated that has instantly rewritten the industry's entire statistics. Hundreds of minor incidents occur over the years, and then one single event happens that overshadows years of data. You cannot prepare for this based on average figures. Security must be built with the worst-case scenario in mind," she noted.
According to the expert, despite the scale of the attack, it is premature to speak of critical flaws in Binance’s security system. "I know Binance from the inside. Their security team has always been one of the strongest in the industry, so I wouldn't call it a critical error just yet. It is more likely a case of social engineering," Goncharova explained.
Earlier, the Binance press office stated that the attackers may have gained access to the exchange’s internal infrastructure via a compromised work laptop belonging to one of its engineers. The exchange estimated the scale of the incident at approximately $6.3 billion and announced plans to compensate all losses using its SAFU insurance fund and corporate resources.

01:47:23 KST

Israel’s final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead.
The results released early yesterday showed Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge.
Photo: AP
“Now comes the truly hard part,” centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding: “If you want to know if something’s happening behind the silence you’re hearing now, the answer is yes.”
Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government?
Much of Israel yesterday started winding down for Shabbat, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Israel to take a deep breath and embrace them.
“There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties,” said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv.
The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president on Wednesday, then Israeli President Isaac Herzog would task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited.
If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he would do everything in his power to avoid that scenario.
In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance.
The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population, which makes up 20 percent of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over Netanyahu’s far-right allies such as Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir. His party lost seats.
In Netanyahu’s first public comment yesterday, he posted on X asserting it is forbidden to form a coalition with Arab parties.
The head of Israel’s election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims, but asked the agency to investigate.
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar of involvement — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas. Qatar issued a denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.”
As it announced results, the election committee said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Central Elections Committee Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the investigation had been “entirely unfounded.”
“It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said.

China expels record number of officials from CCP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:22 UTC
01:47:22 KST

China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25 percent of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
Photo: EPA
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia (張又俠), the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui (馬興瑞), the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society think tank, said in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. However, in recent years the campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey.”
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi and the military’s anti-graft czar, Zhang Shengmin (張升民).
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of next year. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of communist China since Mao Zedong (毛澤東).
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo would be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

Ministry approves first carbon sequestration exploration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:21 UTC
01:47:21 KST

The Ministry of Environment yesterday said it has approved the nation’s first carbon sequestration geological exploration plan, marking a shift from policy to practice in Taiwan’s carbon sequestration efforts.
The plan was proposed by Formosa Petrochemical Corp (FPC, 台塑石化), based in Yunlin County’s Mailiao Township (麥寮).
Last month, media reports said that Formosa Plastics Group (FPG, 台塑集團), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) and US oil giant Exxon Mobil Corp were jointly planning and evaluating a carbon capture and storage project in deep waters off the township. The project is expected to help TSMC acquire low-carbon electricity in line with its net zero target.
Photo: Taipei Times
The ministry yesterday said that FPC proposed the geological exploration plan last month in accordance with the Regulations for the Management of Carbon Dioxide Capture and Storage (二氧化碳補捉後封存管理辦法), which were promulgated in August.
The project is to conduct a geological exploration of a 2,500km2 area that covers the FPG-run Mailiao Industrial Park and offshore waters, the ministry said.
The exploration work includes onshore and offshore seismic surveys, exploratory well drilling, well testing, petrophysical and core mechanics analysis, monitoring facility and model evaluation, it said.
The goal is to assess whether the area has reservoir stratum and caprock at 1,000m to 1,800m below ground level to ensure the safety of the sequestration site, it said.
Geological exploration is critical to selecting a carbon storage site, which must have a storage reservoir that is thick, continuous and topped by a compact, intact caprock layer to serve as a reliable sealing barrier, it said.
Such geological conditions and potential leakage pathways must be examined based on field measured data obtained through seismic surveys and hydrocarbon exploration, the ministry said.
FPC may start geological exploration after the ministry approved the plan on Thursday, but it may not apply for carbon storage at the site until its carbon sequestration project has completed an environmental impact assessment, it added.
The ministry held two meetings with authorities and experts to review the plan, it said.
They approved the exploration methods proposed by FPC as well as the plan’s scope of implementation and duration from Thursday to Dec. 31, 2031, it said.
No carbon dioxide injection test is allowed in future evaluation of the site’s injection reservoir, the ministry said.
Approving the exploration does not mean the site’s sequestration potential has become exclusionary, nor does it guarantee that the company’s future application for carbon storage would be prioritized, it said.
The plan’s reviewers have asked the company to do an environmental base line survey and take environmental protection measures before it starts drilling exploratory wells, the ministry said, urging the company to conduct environmental impact assessments based on exploration results.

Indigenous ancestry travel book launched
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:21 UTC
01:47:21 KST

A book written by a Bunun man about his journey through an abandoned hunting path in search of “tears of the moon” has been launched in Taipei, the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Nantou branch said on Wednesday.
Titled Mudadadan — meaning “go on foot” in the Bunun language — the book documents ancestry trips taken by a group of young Bunun people of Tumpu Village (東埔部落) in Nantou County’s Sinyi Township (信義).
The trips began with a Bunun tale that author Ibi Takiludun Takisbisazuan’s father used to tell him, in which a sun was shot down by an arrow and turned into the moon with its tears left on a rock.
Photo courtesy of the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Nantou Branch
Takisbisazuan on Wednesday told a news conference that he used to be scared of the dark when he was little.
“However, I realized when I grew older that what scares me more is the gradual loss of people who can lead me out of the dark,” he said.
Bunun mythology is rooted in the village’s surrounding topographic landscapes, Takisbisazuan said, adding that he learned about such stories while staying with village elders.
“Bunun hunters of younger generations lack the environment for them to become a cultured hunter,” he said, adding that a hunter is educated through experiences in the mountains rather than classroom learning or secondhand stories.
Takisbisazuan also encouraged younger Bunun people returning to their hometowns to learn more about elders’ traditional wisdom with a humble attitude.
Village members performed two songs at the news conference, Pasibutbut and Pislahi.
Pastor Supina said Pasibutbut is a prayer for a good millet harvest where each singer imitates sounds of everything in nature, such as sounds of winds, streams, waterfalls, bees and cicadas.
The resonant voices integrate into one melody echoing through the sky, she said, adding that the beautiful resonance is considered worthy of God’s blessing.
Pislahi is a song that Bunun hunting groups would chant before they enter the mountains to hunt for food, Supina said.
It prepares hunters with a godly mindset about their hunting trip when they sing to invite different animals to their hunting guns, she said.
“Muntjac, please come to my gun. Sambar deer, please come to my gun,” Supina said, reciting the lyrics.
“The song reflects Bunun people’s outlook on hunting,” she said. “Hunting while walking in the woods is not slaughter, plunder or brutal conquest, but to accept God’s blessings and arrangements.”
Hunters invite the animals to their guns and accept them with a reverent and grateful mind, she added.
Forestry agency Director-General Lin Hwa-ching (林華慶) said the book originated from forestry authorities’ collaborations with local indigenous people in indigenous hunting self-management.
Traditional indigenous hunting is not just about food; it has deep significance, he said.
That includes how indigenous people safeguard their land and resources, as well as their understanding of the land and nature after generations of migration, Lin said.
The book is expected to help the public understand the significance of traditional indigenous hunting and how indigenous people’s traditional wisdom can benefit today’s sustainable governance of natural and wildlife resources, he said.
Indigenous hunting self-management is not only about setting guidelines or a convention, but to help the government work with indigenous communities to apply their wisdom to forestry conservation, Lin said, adding that such a vision has been achieved with Tumpu Village.
Taiwan Biodiversity Research Institute Director Yang Jia-dong (楊嘉棟) said cultural diversity is often overlooked in biodiversity conservation.
Tumpu Village has long been assisting the institute in biodiversity investigations and ecological conservation, he said, adding that the book helps readers understand Bunun people’s culture and emotional bond with the land.
Council of Indigenous Peoples Deputy Minister Qucung Qalavangan, who is also a Bunun member from the township, thanked the forestry agency and the branch for closely collaborating with the village.
The collaboration marks the start of reconciliation between the government and indigenous people since they were forced out of their traditional territories, he said.

‘Star Trek,’ Shakespeare actor Patrick Stewart dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:20 UTC
01:47:20 KST

Patrick Stewart, the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the Star Trek and X-Men franchises, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died on Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed.
“We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today,” Hugh Jackman, a frequent Stewart costar in the X-Men universe, said on social media. “And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”
Photo: Reuters
While best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation series and professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.
Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of A Christmas Carol and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land and Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot in repertory with buddy Ian McKellen.
He won three Olivier Awards, including one for playing Claudius in Hamlet opposite David Tennant. He also had a Grammy — in 1996 for best spoken word album for his recording of Peter and the Wolf.
He achieved some of the best reviews of his career when he finally tackled Macbeth for the first time. The production, under the direction of Rupert Goold, debuted in May 2007 at England’s Chichester Festival Theatre, switched to London’s West End and then moved to the Brooklyn Academy of Music before transferring to Broadway in 2008.
Stewart’s performance earned him his sole Tony Award nomination. The Times of London said his Macbeth was “an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humor.”
The Daily Telegraph said he had turned in “a truly great performance” and the New York Times said it was “a must-see.”
Raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working-class corner of northern England, the future 24th-century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.
Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor.
He had been bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family.
His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of “repeated violence against my mother,” as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. “Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it.”
In his memoir, Making It So, Stewart wrote about how he and his older brother, Trevor, braced for the nights when their dad came home drunk and angry, and attacked their mother.
“Sometimes it was with an open hand, other times a closed fist. Always he aimed for her head.”
The son would later become a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims.
Stewart was accepted into the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing everything from Mark Antony to Henry IV to Shylock to Oberon.
“People who were not in the company would say to me, ‘Give it a break. Why don’t you go somewhere else?’ And I would say, ‘To do what?’” he said. “Telly?”
Stewart eventually left to look for more varied work, including the 1981 film Excalibur. He had just done a production of Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? in 1987 when an interesting offer came along.
“I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail,” he wrote.
It did not, of course. Thanks to Stewart’s rich baritone and noble bearing, the Star Trek franchise ran for seven years, 178 episodes and produced four feature films. He was known for his slogan “Make it so.”
His adoration for Shakespeare would serve him well when he began to play Jean-Luc Picard, a 24th century starship commander.
“There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that remind me of numerous Shakespearean situations I’d been in onstage. I should play Jean Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in Henry IV, which is about brave men,” Stewart wrote in his memoir.
Stewart died just a few days after Walter Koenig, another Star Trek icon, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original NBC TV show from 1966 to 1969.
“What a heartbreaking week it has been,” William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk in the franchise, wrote on Instagram. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did.”

Advocates criticize handling of river silt buildup issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:18 UTC
01:47:18 KST

Environmental advocates yesterday questioned the government’s handling of a river siltation problem in northern Tainan in which NT$1.3 billion (US$40 million) was allocated for bridge rebuilding without taking any action against allegedly illegal upstream land clearing.
The advocates convened a news conference in Taipei where they presented aerial photos showing that patches of woodland in Baihe District (白河) had been cleared, mostly within Baihe Reservoir’s water source quality protection area.
They said illegal land clearing has caused the build up of silt not only in downstream rivers such as the Jishuei River (急水溪), but also across local farmland.
Photo: CNA
Farmer Chang Ling-teng (張令騰) said he has eight hectares of farmland near the river and the Chianan Irrigation Canal (嘉南大圳), which faces serious siltation issues, especially following typhoons.
The silt erodes cultivation areas and can build up to 2m on the farmland, he said.
“Our fields are flooded with silt whenever Baihe Reservoir releases water during typhoons,” Chang said, adding that Typhoon Gaemi in 2024 caused the most severe agricultural losses.
Siltation issues forced Chang to abandon six hectares of green bamboo cultivation, he said.
Taiwan Water Resources Conservation Union chair Chen Jiau-hua (陳椒華) said the government has built Baihe Reservoir sediment bypass tunnels, which brings sediment into the Jishuei River.
Downstream siltation worsened around the Jishueisi Bridge (急水溪橋) — which spans the river’s main stream — as well as Cingye Bridge (青葉橋) and Baihe Bridge, which cross the river’s tributaries, she said.
Union executive director Wu Li-hui (吳麗慧) said that the government allocated NT$1.3 billion to reconstructing the three bridges, including NT$100 million for Baihe Bridge, NT$350 million for Cingye Bridge and NT$850 million for Jishueisi Bridge.
Combined with the Forward-Looking Infrastructure Development Program’s NT$1.75 billion budget invested in the reservoir sediment bypass project, the government has spent a great amount to solve the issue, she said.
However, it failed to stop upstream illegal land clearing and more than 10,000 tonnes of sediment continues to be discharged into the Jishuei River whenever heavy rainfall occurs, Wu said.
The Tainan Water Resources Bureau said that operators have been penalized for illegal land development in accordance with the Soil and Water Conservation Act (水土保持法).
Removing vegetation without changing the terrain is not punishable by the act, it said.
Regarding which agency is responsible for inspecting such land clearing, it was agreed that the Ministry of Agriculture’s Irrigation Agency is responsible.
However, the broader water source quality protection area requires coordination between the Irrigation Agency’s Chianan Management Office and the city government, the Water Resources Agency said.
