“The enemy has again struck the railway station in Dnipro. A fire broke out there,” he said.
Ukrzaliznytsia separately confirmed that Russian forces had carried out several targeted strikes on the station during the evening.
The railway operator said evacuation had been announced in advance and passengers and employees were in shelters. Its initial statement reported no casualties among those groups, while Hanzha’s update identified one wounded woman.
Neither statement specified the weapon used in the evening attack. The claim circulating on local channels that a jet-powered Shahed was involved has not been confirmed in those official accounts.
Passengers shelter underground
Ukrzaliznytsia said it had set up areas for extended stays in the station’s underground spaces as passengers waited through the danger.
The company asked everyone at the station to remain in shelter until the air raid alert ended.
Passengers whose journeys were not essential were encouraged to postpone their trips. The operator said tickets could be returned for a 100% refund, allowing passengers to choose another travel date.

The initial evening statement did not provide a detailed assessment of damage to the station or a revised timetable for affected services. It focused on evacuation, shelter arrangements and options for passengers who could defer travel.
Earlier attacks already disrupt journeys
The evening strikes followed renewed attacks on the station overnight into Oct. 30.
Ukrzaliznytsia chief Oleksandr Pertsovskyi had reported repeated strikes and regional power outages, saying railway staff were helping passengers and arranging solutions for disrupted journeys.
He said train managers were gathering information about passengers’ connections so that alternatives could be offered. He also stressed that departures depended on safety conditions.
Substantial delays were already being reported before the evening attack.
On Friday morning, Dnepr.info reported, citing railway information, that the Dnipro-Lviv service No. 127/128 was running 16 hours and 15 minutes late. Services from Dnipro to Chernivtsi and Ivano-Frankivsk were each listed as delayed by 14 hours and 20 minutes.
Those figures describe the morning disruption, rather than the consequences of the evening strikes.
Elsewhere in Dnipro earlier on Oct. 30, an attack damaged at least five apartment buildings and a school, Mayor Borys Filatov said. Municipal services and charities were deployed to assess damage and assist residents.
Oct. 29 platform strike kills 15
The latest attack came a day after a Russian jet-powered drone struck a railway platform where train No. 866, bound for Zaporizhzhia, was standing.
The death toll from that attack rose to 15 after another wounded man died in hospital, Hanzha said on Oct. 30.
Five railway employees were among those killed, according to Ukrzaliznytsia memorial accounts reported by Suspilne. They included staff helping passengers reach shelter and an engine driver returning home while on leave.
Following the deadly attack, Ukrzaliznytsia announced a review of its safety protocols. The company said it had issued warnings and ordered an evacuation before the drone hit, but people remained near the train at the time of impact.
The Oct. 29 station strike was part of a series of deadly daytime attacks across Ukraine. Two 15-year-old girls were killed in Chernihiv, while strikes in Kremenchuk killed three people.

At the Third Russia-Africa Summit, Moscow Talked Big. But Who Was Listening?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:10:00 UTC
01:10:00 KST

Every three years, the leaders of some of Africa’s largest nations descend on a major Russian city for a few days of shmoozing, media-ready photo opportunities and closed-door meetings with Kremlin officials.
Now in its third iteration, the Russia-Africa Summit has few surprises to offer. Each time, Moscow makes its pitch as an anti-imperialist bulwark, drawing on historic ties to African independence movements, while African leaders vie for trade deals and prestige.
The result is a mutually beneficial diplomatic concoction. Russia shows that it doesn’t need the West to have reliable allies, and African nations can boast of winning a global power’s favor.
This year’s event, which took place over the course of two jam-packed days this week, presented an altogether more pressing question: Nearly five years into the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, is cooperation with Russia still worth it?
The answer depends on who you ask, analysts told The Moscow Times this week.
The Russia-Africa Summit has become a staple diplomatic initiative for Moscow, one whose key attraction is the opportunity to meet with Russian officials including President Vladimir Putin. This year, delegations from 48 countries were in attendance, including 22 heads of state.
As with other regions where it has longstanding ties, Moscow’s relationship with Africa has been made trickier by the war in Ukraine.
Nowhere is this more visible than in the issue of military recruitment. African countries have been some of the biggest targets of Moscow’s shady efforts to fill a gap in manpower for the war in Ukraine by enlisting foreign citizens to serve, a practice that rights advocates say meets the criteria of human trafficking.
Meanwhile, fighting on land and sea continues to sporadically disrupt supply lines to longstanding buyers of Ukrainian agricultural products, like Kenya, Libya and Tunisia, driving up food costs as importers pivot to other providers.
These issues were present in a nascent form at the last Russia-Africa Summit in 2023. But three years on, the picture of how the war is reverberating across the continent is much clearer, and it doesn’t look reassuring for Moscow.
In countries like Kenya and South Africa, the recruitment of foreign citizens for the war has become a matter of national outrage, drawing attention from government investigators.
This week, human rights watchdog Amnesty International called on African officials to raise the issue with their Russian counterparts, saying it would be “a profound disservice to the people of their countries” to “remain silent.”
At the same time, Moscow continues to take a hands-off approach with managing its vast mercenary network. Rebranded as the Africa Corps and placed under the control of the Defense Ministry after the Wagner Group’s dissolution in 2023, the organization is still trailed by stories of human rights abuses in countries like Mali.
All of this complicates the image that the Russia-Africa Summit puts forward of two places “united by truly strong bonds of friendship and close partnership,” as Putin said during the second day of the summit.
In reality, those words might only apply to a limited number of countries in the region.
Many of the attending nations depend on Russian military or diplomatic support in one way or another, noted Joseph Siegle, a senior research associate at the University of Maryland’s Center for International and Security Studies and expert on African security issues.
“These are the majority of the 22 heads of state that are there,” Siegle told The Moscow Times. “Their rationale for being there is political rather than anything else. There’s a mutual interest in supporting that perception of Russia’s broader ambitions with Africa.”
The spectacle around the Russia-Africa Summit shouldn’t be taken as widespread approval of Moscow’s conduct, he added. Indeed, many countries in Africa are at worst skeptical and at best modestly enthusiastic of Russia’s ability to be a transformative partner.
There’s also fear of the potential reputational hit of engaging with Moscow.
For evidence of that, look no further than the number of participants. The Russia-Africa Summit’s strongest showing was in its first year, in 2019, when 43 heads of state attended. Both iterations since then have taken place during the war in Ukraine, and participation each time shrunk by nearly half.
What’s more, while the summit sells itself on being a venue for dealmaking, there are some basic discrepancies in the macro Russia-Africa economic relationship, Siegle said.
Russia is not in Africa’s top 10 trading partners, what trade that does occur is lopsided, seeing Moscow export about seven times more than it imports, and Russia provides only about 1% of the total foreign direct investment going into the continent.
“From the African perspective, the primary interest for most external partners is what they can do to help with Africa’s economic prospects, and there’s a realization that Russia offers relatively little there,” he said.
Some countries, however, are coming away from this year’s summit with tangible agreements. In what was perhaps the summit’s highest-profile deal, Ethiopia, a country teetering on the brink of civil war, received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets. Officials did not say how much the deal would be worth.
Elsewhere, promises were abundant but light on details. Putin said that Russian firms are interested in opening production plants in African countries to circumvent Western sanctions, while officials from Rosatom, the state nuclear agency, announced that they are in talks with multiple countries to build power plants, including some that could float in coastal waters.
African attendees were clear that this is the kind of thing they want more of.
“We invite Russian companies to invest in Mozambique and establish reliable partnerships,” the state-run TASS news agency quoted Mozambique President Daniel Chapo as saying.
If this year is any indication, that’s not lost on the Russian side. While the summit is unavoidably a politicized affair, Russian officials appear to have “refined their pitch to their African counterparts” by this point, at least in their rhetoric, said Ivan Klyszcz, a research fellow at Estonia’s International Center for Defense and Security.
“The themes gesture more consistently at topics that are important for African development, which has always been a big kind of flaw in Russia’s offer to Africa,” Klyszcz said. “What it can offer cannot match what African governments seek.”
The biggest question going forward, then, will be whether Russia can actually deliver on the economic opportunities it promises, especially as it remains preoccupied by the war in Ukraine.
Even after two summits that promised a substantial expansion of the economic relationship, Russia’s trade with Africa is still falling short of targets, and its ties to many African nations remain primarily based on security assistance.
Those kinds of assistance “are important in the way African governments define their foreign policies — but not always,” Klyszcz said. “They’re less focused on these big political issues and more on concrete development.”

“We need asymmetric effect,” Defense Minister Khmara says, as Ukraine funds its own missiles and radars to stop burning costly interceptors on cheap Russia’s drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:09:56 UTC
01:09:56 KST

Ukraine is opening grant money for home-built air-to-air missiles and radars, aiming to shoot down Russia’s fastest drones without paying a huge price. The Defense Ministry, the Ministry of Digital Transformation, and the Brave1 defense-tech cluster are launching the competitions, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara announced in an address to manufacturers, adding that a grant contest for turbojet engines will follow.
Ukraine is being forced to use expensive air defense missiles against relatively inexpensive Russian drones and cruise missiles. Developing cheaper interceptors, domestically produced radars and engines could change the economics of warfare.
The move comes as Russia leans harder on faster, jet-powered drones that strain the cheapest layer of Ukraine’s defenses. It also follows an earlier round of Brave1 grants that had already flagged anti-bomb systems and Ukrainian radars as priorities.
What Kyiv wants built, from navigation to radars that see the faint targets
Khmara laid out the threats the money is meant to answer: ballistic missiles, cheap cruise missiles, high-speed drones and guided bombs.
From Ukrainian producers, the ministry wants domestic navigation systems, stronger electronic warfare, radars able to pick out low-signature targets, and affordable designs that can be developed in quantity.
“Our requirements are clear: effectiveness, affordable cost, interoperability between systems, and sufficient volume of supply,” Khmara says.
The grants are one tool among others, meant to carry developments that can later scale for the Security and Defense Forces. Earlier, the ministry and Brave1 ran a large-scale test of drones with AI-assisted targeting.
The next contest targets the guided bombs Ukraine still cannot reliably stop
The minister singled out a separate job for manufacturers: new ways to counter Russia’s guided aerial bombs, known in Ukraine as KABs, and to blunt their use.
These are the glide bombs Russian aircraft release from a distance, and Ukraine has struggled to answer them without reaching the launch aircraft themselves.
“It is important to create innovative solutions that let us act ahead and prevail. We need asymmetric effect. We need technologies that change the rules of the game in our favor,” he argues.
Grants for turbojet engines, the ministry says, are the next step after the missiles and radars.

Sofia Sapega, ex-girlfriend of former Belarusian opposition journalist Roman Protasevich, recounts her time in prison and his testimony against her after the 2021 Ryanair diversion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:09:54 UTC
01:09:54 KST

Sofia Sapega, ex-girlfriend of former Belarusian opposition journalist Roman Protasevich, recounts her time in prison and his testimony against her after the 2021 Ryanair diversion
The Belarusian news outlet Zerkalo has published the second part of an extensive interview with Sofia Sapega, the former girlfriend of Roman Protasevich, a former editor-in-chief of the opposition Telegram channel Nexta. In May 2021, Belarusian authorities used false pretenses to force a plane flying from Athens to Vilnius to land in Minsk so they could arrest Protasevich. Sapega was detained along with him. Since then, she has lived under house arrest with Protasevich and broken up with him, been sentenced to six years in prison, spent a year in a penal colony, received a pardon, and returned to her old life in Lithuania.
Unlike Protasevich, Sapega kept a low profile after her detention and release. This is her first in-depth interview since her arrest. Yesterday, we compiled the most interesting quotes from the first part. Today, we’re sharing excerpts from the second.
House arrest with Protasevich
[After a month in a cottage outside Minsk, they moved us to Roman’s apartment to continue our house arrest] at Roman’s apartment — his parents were in Poland. A few days before we moved in, they [the security officers] took his keys and set everything up so they could watch us 24/7. The apartment had a living room and a bedroom. Officers from the KGB’s Alpha special forces unit took the living room, and Roma and I had the bedroom.
***
Life under house arrest was pretty monotonous. […] We were still allowed to drink alcohol then, and every so often we used it to escape reality, even if just for a little while. I couldn’t take antidepressants or sedatives, see a psychologist, or talk openly about what was happening to me. And alcohol seemed like the only way we had to quiet our thoughts, at least for a while.
Suicide attempt and breakup
Gradually, things between Roman and me got much worse. Then something terrible happened. It was late October. It was morning, Roman was still asleep, and I woke up and decided to scroll through Instagram. I picked up his phone (we shared one) — his account was open, and I saw his messages with his ex-wife. I’m reading her replies to his messages, seeing the pictures she’s sending him of underwear, herself, her body… In normal life, I would’ve just packed my things and left. But here, I’m a hostage.
***
I lost control and drank quite a lot [that day], silently, alone, with a blank expression. […] Then I did something unthinkable, something I’d never done before. The window was open (and this was the sixth floor). I sat on the windowsill, swung my legs outside, and was ready to jump. I guess I have the people walking past to thank. They were cutting across to another courtyard — a mom, a dad, and a child. And I realize I don’t want them to see this, to have the child watch me fall. So I waited for them to pass. But they were walking so slowly. And that’s when someone pulls me back in through the window.
***
After that suicide attempt, they [the security officers] realized it was too dangerous to keep Protasevich around me. […] From late October on, I lived [in my parents’ apartment] in Lida. They still only let me out for an hour-long walk each day. It must have looked pretty absurd: me in a bulletproof vest, a woman and a man with pistols beside me, two more police officers a little farther away, and a police SUV behind us. Can you imagine that kind of security? Like I was the president’s wife or some especially dangerous criminal.
At first, I thought, “How humiliating!” Especially since this was my own courtyard, the street where I grew up. But over time, I got used to it and started seeing the funny side, almost treating it like a joke.
The trial
There wasn’t a single victim at the trial. Protasevich did show up, though — as a [prosecution] witness. What a disgrace. By then, I’d lost all respect for him. They called him into the courtroom, and I could tell he was nervous, but he kept saying everything I’d already learned from the volume of the case file devoted to me. He didn’t even dare look at me. Only after he’d finished testifying did he glance in my direction.
***
The security officers [whose personal information had been published in Black Book of Belarus] filed civil claims seeking compensation for emotional distress. I’m so grateful to my family: My loved ones took on that financial burden and paid about $70,000 to cover the claims.
The penal colony
To them [the security officers at the penal colony], I was a personal enemy, because my job had been to expose them and publish information about what they did. Of course they didn’t like that.
I remember one of the women at the colony talking to the warden — Colonel Denis Tolstenkov at the time — and putting in a word for me: “Please leave her alone. She’s behaving herself.” […] Tolstenkov’s reaction to that request was completely unexpected. He made a gun with his fingers, pretended to fire it, and said, “If Sapega ever comes to my home, I won’t hesitate to pull the trigger.” I still don’t understand why I’d ever go to his home in the first place — to have tea or something?
***
I was already in the colony when the officers told me the news [about Protasevich’s wedding] with obvious delight. They were gloating: “Ha-ha-ha, look at this!” It really hurt. Not that I still cared about Roman. It was more about my own pain. I felt sorry for myself and couldn’t understand how someone could treat another person so horribly.
***
Warning: The next paragraph contains profanity.
[In the colony, I was in a unit where] the girls tormented each other, practically tortured each other. One day, a girl with a yellow tag was put in our unit. She openly defied the system: She refused to work and simply didn’t want to obey or accept the rules. […] It all came to a head when, one day, she called our officer a fucking moron and a useless idiot in front of everyone. One of the women told him what she’d said. That same evening, the girl was beaten. I still remember her screams.
Release
On the day [I was released], Tolstenkov called me by my first name for the first time. Instead of “Sapega,” “bitch,” “animal,” and his other favorite names. I knew I was going free, but I felt no joy, no euphoria. I felt empty inside. I was just waiting for them to let me out at last. […] That same day, I flew to Moscow, [and from there] through the UAE to Thailand, because my father has lived there full-time for more than 10 years.
I spent about nine months in Thailand. It was amazing there. It was as if I’d just walked out of one door and through another — stepped over the threshold, and that was it. No particular emotions, no distress.
***
For the first six or seven months [after returning to Vilnius], I felt fine. Then it hit me. Everything that had happened seemed to catch up with me all at once. I had severe depression. I felt like I was all alone with my pain, with everything I’d been through. I didn’t understand what was happening to me or how to cope with any of it.
Life afterward
I used to think constantly about who might see me, what people would say about me, and what might happen as a result. […] I was afraid people would start accusing me of things I hadn’t done. Of supposedly being the one who’d informed on people. I was afraid people would spread stories about me, that all of it could affect my parents and they’d end up having problems because of me, too. So I tried to keep as low a profile as possible, to avoid appearing in public any more than I had to or drawing attention to myself. But at some point, I realized I couldn’t spend my whole life afraid of what other people might think or say about me.
***
I can’t say I’m living some perfect dream life now. Life as an immigrant comes with plenty of difficulties: the language, paperwork, finding work, having to build a life all over again practically from scratch. But all of that is much better than living in a country where you can’t even get together peacefully with other people and clap your hands without being afraid of the consequences. I don’t want to go back to that kind of life.
How she sees Protasevich
In my view, he’s a victim of his own weakness. I feel sorry for him because he made a decision that I believe turned out to be fundamentally wrong. And I’m sorry he couldn’t find the strength to accept his fate. If he’d come to terms from the start with what he thought was in store for him, if he hadn’t tried at any cost to avoid the fate he’d imagined, maybe he could have come through it with some dignity.
***
I don’t think he can put anything right anymore. I once tried to imagine myself in his place. And the way I saw it, you’re an outsider here, and there, in Belarus, you’re an enemy and an outsider, too. So where do you belong? Nowhere. You’re not accepted in Europe or in Belarus. And I don’t think that can change now. No matter how hard you try, how much you maneuver, how carefully you choose your words, or how much you tell people what they want to hear — none of it will change anything. You’ll still be an outsider.

The Mossad is reportedly joining the investigation into suspected foreign interference in the elections and will assist the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) in areas falling under its remit, namely, the possibility that Qatar was behind payments to the Joint List’s apparatus, according to reports from Israeli media on Friday.
The referral follows the Shin Bet's initial investigation into suspicions that foreign entities, potentially including Qatar and Turkey, funneled money into Israel to influence voting in Arab communities, following a directive from Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg to investigate suspected foreign funding and election bribery.
Investigators are examining, among other possibilities, whether Qatar was behind payments to the Joint List’s party apparatus. However, according to the information provided, the suspicions have no bearing on the election results and are not expected to affect them later.
Elections Committee: “The reports that were published are unfounded”
Acting Central Elections Committee director-general Dean Livne said overnight that reports of suspected attempts to sway the election for the 26th Knesset were unfounded.
“Further details cannot be disclosed, but reports published during the day are entirely unfounded,” he said in a recorded statement issued with the approval of committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg.
Livne said the Shin Bet opened the investigation after classified intelligence was presented to Sohlberg.
“Yesterday, the head of the Shin Bet presented classified intelligence to the committee chairman, which led to the opening of the investigation,” he said.
He added that, with Sohlberg’s approval, the main points of the intelligence were also presented to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, opposition leader Yair Lapid and Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot.
Livne stressed that very few people had access to the information because of its high security classification. He said the investigation did not focus on any particular community and would not change the election results submitted to Israel’s president.
Once the investigation is complete, its findings will be submitted to the Central Elections Committee chairman to assess its scope and implications. The committee pledged to update the public as soon as possible, subject to security restrictions.
Jonah Davidov and Corinne Baum contributed to this report.

Herzog can secure his presidential legacy by bringing Netanyahu and Eisenkot together - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:08:26 UTC
01:08:26 KST

The politics of delegitimization and defamation, particularly the demonization of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by the Left, make the establishment of a broad Israeli government of repair an unlikely scenario.
Yet this is exactly what Israel needs now – the partnership in government of Netanyahu and one of his major rivals, say, the political parties led by Yashar head Gadi Eisenkot and/or Naftali Bennett – to together tackle Israel’s major challenges.
The question is: Who is going to disabuse both the Left and the Right of their belligerent, separatist, extremist dreams of establishing a one-sided government that relies on haredi (ultra-Orthodox) or Arab parties? Who is going to cajole Likud and Yashar and/or B’Yachad into a pseudo “unity” coalition government?
The answer, of course, should be the Israeli president. But I wonder whether President Isaac Herzog is up to the task.
Herzog comes from the Left (a former leader of the Labor Party), and he is already under pressure from his political home base to mandate and approve a narrow Eisenkot government based on an alliance with anti-Israel Islamists or anti-Zionist ultra-Orthodox Jews; a government that defiantly excludes Netanyahu.
The camp’s overriding priority is to dethrone Netanyahu under any circumstances and at any cost. This camp expects Herzog to play along; nay, they demand that he brandish his bully pulpit to legitimize a government that embraces Mansour Abbas and Prof. Yousef Jabareen, or alternatively Yakov Asher and Yitzhak Goldknopf.
Such a government would handcuff the IDF in fighting Palestinian enemies and kill the hope of recapturing the Negev from Bedouin mafia gangs, and it would quash any plan for drafting haredim into the IDF. But so what? In the view of the hard Left, terminating Netanyahu is the higher goal that makes anything and everything kosher.
Herzog needs to repel the pressures and demands of the hard Left and wedge the mainstream parties, the two or three largest in Knesset, into a governing coalition, uneasy and fractious as it may be.
It is not enough for Herzog to say that he “will do everything in his power to avoid a repeat election scenario.” He must actively agitate for a broad Zionist government. He should aggressively intervene in the political process beyond the usual presidential consultative role following elections.
Herzog should declare that he will give the mandate to form a government first and foremost only to a political party leader that is up-front committed to seeking unity as his priority plan of action. And then he should reject any proto-government coalition brought to him that is not broad-based; that is, contingent on fractional Arab or haredi parties.
Herzog can and should go further in making a broad-based government possible by getting into the nitty-gritty of the issues that stand in the way, from Netanyahu’s future (rotation in the prime minister’s post, a timetable for retirement from politics, and a pardon) to good governance (formation of a national commission of investigation into the October 7 disaster, judicial reform, settlement policy, and haredi draft).
Don’t tell me that this isn’t the role of the Israeli president and that he has no powers for such interposition. Indeed, it is not the president’s classic role, and legally he has no such powers.
Herzog can play hardball with Netanyahu, Eisenkot
But unique times call for emergency measures and for gutsy leadership. Herzog can and should buck convention and play hardball; use his elbows and knuckles, and the prestige of the presidency, to strong-arm Netanyahu and Eisenkot into teamwork.
Clobber them into cooperation. Stymie and shame them, if necessary.
Herzog should hold up the process until he gets his way; our way, the way that most Israelis want and Israel needs.
The problem is that Herzog is too nice. He’s a scholar and a gentleman. He likes to be loved by everybody and to express uncontroversial sentiments. He is prone to opinions that are motherhood and apple pie, like concern for the hostages, victims of terror, and battered women, like empathy for new immigrants and Diaspora Jews.
And to be fair, that has been the traditional, limited purview and approach of previous Israeli presidents too, and there is a noble “peoplehood” logic behind it.
But occasionally Israeli presidents are presented with a moment where more is demanded of them, when they have a unique opportunity to make a substantial difference in the country’s political life.
Herzog had one such previous opportunity, and he blew it. That was during the vigorous public debate over judicial reform in spring 2023. The thinkers and activists behind the controversial judicial reform plan and those violently opposed to it brought a compromise plan to Herzog, which he should have embraced and promoted.
The plan was a daring piece of work. It brought compromises to the table that were incredibly hard for both sides. That is exactly why it was such a brave and hopeful effort. It could have saved Israel from six months of continued internal warfare and perhaps saved Israel from the debilitating military unreadiness that led to the October 7 slaughter.
So, Herzog should have grabbed the judicial reform compromise and promoted it as his initiative. He should have assertively advanced it against the out-of-control passions and political vendettas raging at the time.
But he didn’t. Herzog would not buck the uncompromising dictates of former Supreme Court president Aharon Barak, who declared all-out war on the Likud government’s judicial reform agenda. Herzog did not have the gumption to defy the overheated Left that was banging on drums, blocking roads in Tel Aviv, and burning effigies of Netanyahu in Jerusalem.
Herzog rejected the judicial compromise proposal. He buried the best prospect for healing a badly divided nation. He missed a critical chance to make a difference, and in my eyes, this stands to his eternal discredit.
Now, following this week’s election that ended in a stalemate, Herzog has the option to do teshuva, to repent and repair his ways. He holds the gargantuan opportunity to embrace and insist on a broad government of repair.
Does Herzog have the courage to confront the forces of anti-Netanyahu paroxysm, to buck the pressures for Netanyahu’s political annihilation? Will he break from and defy his natural home base on the Left and drive relentlessly toward a unity government that includes Netanyahu?
Herzog has 20 months left in his seven-year term as president, and he is unlikely to face a greater challenge than this. He can make this moment his signature presidential legacy. However, if he fails to rise to the occasion, you can mark this moment as the end of an inconsequential presidency.
The writer is managing senior fellow at the Jerusalem-based Misgav Institute for National Security & Zionist Strategy. The views expressed here are his own. His diplomatic, defense, political, and Jewish world columns over the past 30 years are at davidmweinberg.com.

Vance offers to meet with former IRGC commander Rezaei as Pentagon preps new attack - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:08:14 UTC
01:08:14 KST

The White House believes Mohsen Rezaei, one of the Iranian regime’s staunchest hardliners, could be the key to an agreement that would prevent renewed war between the US and Iran, Washington Post columnist David Ignatius reported Thursday evening.
Ignatius, a veteran Washington journalist who covers foreign affairs and national security, cited conversations with a US official familiar with the negotiations, providing new details about the Trump administration’s latest effort to reach an agreement with Tehran.
Previous reports revealed that Vice President JD Vance sent a personal letter last week to Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In the letter, Vance expressed willingness to meet with him personally to discuss ending the war through negotiations.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the letter’s existence. Ignatius disclosed additional details about its contents and why the White House chose to approach a senior member of Tehran’s hardline camp.
According to the US official who spoke with Ignatius, the letter emphasized putting both countries’ national interests at the center of negotiations. Vance made clear that Washington’s primary interest was ensuring Iran did not acquire nuclear weapons.
He also pointed to Iran’s interest in rebuilding its economy, which has been severely damaged by the war and sanctions, and preserving its national sovereignty. Vance stressed that Iran must send representatives with the authority to negotiate the nuclear issue and reach binding agreements.
Rezaei the only person capable of building support for deal, US official says
A central finding in Ignatius’s report concerns US intelligence assessments of Rezaei’s influence within the Iranian regime. According to the US official, the Trump administration has concluded that Rezaei is its most important negotiating contact in Tehran and effectively the only person capable of building broad support for an agreement limiting Iran’s nuclear program.
US intelligence officials assess that Rezaei maintains regular contact with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The two are believed to have spoken in recent days, after the American letter arrived.
Rezaei, who commanded the Revolutionary Guards for years, is believed by US officials to retain the trust of commanders who previously served under him. Over the past year, he has also strengthened his position by reorganizing the Supreme National Security Council and appointing allies to influential posts.
He maintains close ties with senior officials responsible for Iran’s economy, which has been severely damaged by the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and economic sanctions.
The Trump administration believes Rezaei understands the severity of Iran’s situation. His standing among hardliners could enable him to persuade opponents of compromise to accept an agreement.
If the two sides agree to meet, Istanbul or the Qatari capital, Doha, would be the most likely locations.
Ignatius noted that Vance has already played a central role in US efforts to reach an agreement with Iran. In April, he traveled to Islamabad, Pakistan’s capital, and met with Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.
During those talks, the administration offered to lift economic sanctions on Iran and pursue broad economic cooperation, an approach Trump officials called the “golden bridge,” in exchange for a binding nuclear agreement.
Ghalibaf, however, failed to secure support from the regime’s leadership in Tehran. The two countries signed a limited, vaguely worded memorandum of understanding, but it collapsed after exchanges of fire resumed in the Strait of Hormuz.
Since then, according to Ignatius, US intelligence has concluded that the Iranian regime’s real power rests with Rezaei, rather than necessarily with those who have led the formal negotiations.
Qatar continues to play a central role as a mediator, with its representatives maintaining regular contact with Rezaei and other senior Iranian officials.
Iran sees Vance's letter as respectful gesture
According to the report, Iran’s leadership viewed Vance’s personal outreach as a respectful gesture. However, there is still no indication that Iranian officials have softened their positions on the nuclear issue, which remains the main obstacle to an agreement.
The report comes as military tensions surrounding Iran rise and the Pentagon prepares for the possibility of renewed, large-scale combat operations.
Earlier Thursday, US Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper reportedly visited the White House and presented Trump with options for further military action against Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine also attended the meeting.
Ignatius wrote that White House officials fear time is running out to reach an agreement without resuming the war.
He also highlighted a significant difference between Washington’s and Jerusalem’s approaches. According to Ignatius, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for regime change in Iran, believing it is the only way to eliminate the threat once and for all.
Trump, meanwhile, continues to say he wants to “finish the job” in Iran as additional US forces deploy to the region. In Ignatius’s assessment, however, Trump and Vance clearly prefer a diplomatic agreement to another round of fighting.
Even as the US military prepares for a possible attack, a significant diplomatic effort is underway to reach an agreement with one of the figures most closely associated with the Iranian regime’s anti-American stance.
Ignatius, who has covered US foreign policy and the intelligence community for decades, expressed skepticism about the initiative’s prospects. He noted that Rezaei has effectively built his entire career on staunch opposition to the US and Israel.
Although Rezaei has the political influence needed to secure an agreement with Washington, doing so would represent a dramatic change of direction for him.
The initiative also illustrates Vance’s growing role in leading diplomatic efforts with Iran and his reservations about continuing a war that lacks broad support among the American public.
According to Ignatius, the political timing also matters. The initiative comes just days before the November 3 congressional midterm elections, as the Trump administration faces public criticism over the war and its economic consequences.
Beyond those political considerations, however, Ignatius concluded that pursuing a diplomatic solution is a worthwhile alternative to another round of fighting.
It remains to be seen whether Rezaei, whom Washington identifies as Tehran’s true center of power, will take the step US officials hope for: moving from decades of opposition to any agreement with the US to becoming the person capable of bringing the war to an end.

Joint Statement from the International Contact Group for the Great Lakes region…

Joint Statement from the International Contact Group for the Great Lakes region (ICG) Democratic Republic of the Congo Conflicts Joint statement On : October 30th 2026 Belgium, Canada, Denmark, the European Union, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the United States of America as members of the International Contact Group (ICG) for the Great Lakes region, chaired by France, issue the following statement on the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The International Contact Group for the Great Lakes region (ICG) encourages all parties to the Washington Accords and Doha Framework to remain committed and engage in good faith to find a lasting and peaceful resolution of the conflict and to fulfil their obligations without delay. The ICG supports the efforts of the mediators, including those of the African Union, led by the President of the Council of the Togolese Republic, welcomes the co-facilitators’ recent visit to the region and reaffirms the importance of regional leadership. In light of recent political and security-related developments in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the ICG welcomes the statement issued on 19 October by the President of the African Union Commission calling on all parties to exercise restraint. The ICG categorically rejects the pursuit of political objectives through the use of violence, as advocated by the recently created FRN (Front pour la Refondation de la Nation). It underscores the need for all parties to respect the rule of law and the Constitution of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and reiterates its commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of the DRC. It recalls the importance of a peaceful and inclusive inter-Congolese dialogue involving all key Congolese stakeholders as an essential prerequisite for lasting peace in the DRC. Political differences and grievances cannot be resolved by military means. Guaranteeing rule of law and protection of fundamental rights is crucial to ensure that all political parties and civil society organisations can freely exercise their role. The ICG reiterates its deep concern over the continued fighting in eastern DRC and deplores the suffering inflicted on civilian populations. It urges all parties to honour their commitments made in Doha on 19 July 2025 to observe a ceasefire. The escalating use of drones has grave consequences for civilians and humanitarian workers. The ICG reminds the parties to implement UN Security Council Resolution 2773, which calls for the Rwanda Defence Forces to cease support to the M23 and immediately withdraw from DRC territory without preconditions, the dismantling of illegitimate parallel administrations in the DRC territory, and the neutralization of the FDLR. On the last point, recalling the ICG statement of August taking good note of the plan put forward by the DRC government, the ICG encourages them to present a clear action plan and timeline aimed at swiftly implementing the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration protocol for FDLR groups. Against the backdrop of increasing humanitarian needs and the Ebola epidemic, the ICG urges all parties and armed groups to respect international humanitarian law and to ensure that humanitarian actors have full, safe and unimpeded access to populations in need.

Not Enough Money: Russia Plans to Postpone Pay for Troops Not Involved in Combat Operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:05:35 UTC
01:05:35 KST

The Russian Defense Ministry plans to postpone December pay for troops not participating in the war against Ukraine until January.
If the draft order is approved, this will mark the first time in at least 18 years that payments have been postponed, as noted by the publication Verstka.
Currently, Russian servicemembers are supposed to receive their pay between the 10th and 20th of each month for the previous month, and by December 25 for December.
The draft order proposes postponing December payments to the period from January 11 to 21.
An exception is to be made for those participating in the aggression against Ukraine. This applies, in particular, to bonuses.
Verstka notes that military personnel have been receiving their December pay by the end of the year since at least 2008.
The postponement of December payments is likely due to financial difficulties faced by the Russian Defense Ministry or budgetary constraints.
This is especially true given that this is not a change to the usual payment schedule, but rather an exception that applies specifically to military personnel not participating in the war against Ukraine.
The postponement of payments until January may indicate the Russian Defense Ministry’s desire to defer part of its budgetary expenditures and shift the financial burden to the next fiscal period.
The current payment procedure in the Russian Federation is established by an order from 2019 and has not changed since then.
Prior to that, a similar order dated December 30, 2011, was in effect, which required that December’s pay be disbursed by the last working day of that month.
At the same time, according to this order, the Minister of Defense could decide to make payments earlier.
Additionally, in one of the decisions of the Bryansk Garrison Military Court, a document for official use is cited—Order No. 250 of the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation dated May 7, 2008, “On Financial Support and Specifics of Budget Accounting in the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation.” According to this order, military pay was disbursed between the 20th and 25th of each month for the current month.
Thus, for at least the past 18 years, Russian military personnel have received their December pay before New Year’s. Presumably, this practice has existed for much longer.
For example, paragraph 37 of the 1986 Instructions of the State Bank of the USSR states that military personnel receive their pay between the 13th and 29th ‘for the current month.’

A woman processes a discarded glass bottle at a workshop in Zanzibar, Tanzania, Oct. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman)
DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- For Mwanamkuu Mussa, 52, a discarded glass bottle is more than waste. It represents school fees paid, medical expenses covered, and a step closer to building a home for herself and her four children.
Before joining Chako Zanzibar in 2021, the mother of four worked as a nursery school teacher. She has since built a new livelihood around transforming discarded glass into useful products. She now helps train new artisans, assists with bottle collection, and keeps the workshop organized.
The income has enabled her to open her own DVD library and contribute to her children's education and healthcare. Her next ambition is to build a house for her family.
"Working at Chako has helped me become an independent woman," Mussa said.
Her journey reflects the mission of Chako Zanzibar, a social enterprise tackling two challenges facing the Indian Ocean island: mounting waste from tourism and limited economic opportunities for parts of the local community, particularly women.
For women like Mussa, the enterprise offers more than employment. It provides practical skills, a source of income, and the opportunity to make decisions about their families' futures.
The idea began with a question that Dutch entrepreneur Anneloes Roelandschap and her partner confronted after entering Zanzibar's tourism industry.
After opening a hotel in Stone Town in 2008, they saw how tourism created jobs and business opportunities but also generated waste that the island struggled to manage. They also recognized that the benefits of the expanding industry did not reach everyone equally.
In 2012, they founded Chako to address these challenges by collecting waste from hotels and resorts, turning it into new products, creating local jobs, and selling the finished goods back to the tourism industry.
The enterprise now collects glass bottles and plastic from hospitality businesses, cleans and processes the materials, and transforms them into drinking glasses, vases, lamps, and decorative items. Tourists can also buy the products as souvenirs, taking home a reminder of Zanzibar while supporting local livelihoods.
Since its establishment, Chako has prevented more than five million bottles from ending up in Zanzibar's landfills and has trained more than 400 local people, Roelandschap said.
Yet the environmental gains tell only part of the story. At the heart of the business is an effort to help women develop skills and earning power, Roelandschap said.
"By giving women more power, an income, and skills, they can bring money home and gain more respect from their families and husbands. They can also send their children to school," she said.
The workshop offers women opportunities to take on tasks traditionally associated with men, including woodcarving and other forms of skilled production. Through training and hands-on experience, workers discover abilities they may never previously have considered developing.
Ada Juma, 36, is one such artisan. Before joining Chako in 2023, she ran a small business selling cashew nuts. Seeking a new direction, she joined the enterprise and gradually acquired skills in woodcarving, glass processing, and plastic weaving.
She now leads the plastic department, where she also teaches other artisans. Her work has expanded beyond learning a new trade to helping others gain the skills to earn an income themselves.
For Juma, the greatest satisfaction is supporting her children and paying their school fees. Like Mussa, she dreams of building a house for her family.
Her advice to other women is to stay active, work hard, and pursue independence rather than wait for opportunities.
These individual ambitions are central to Chako's approach. Its artisans are paid for each piece they produce, at rates agreed upon in advance. The arrangement gives them flexibility in how much time they devote to the enterprise while leaving room for family responsibilities or personal businesses.
The company currently works with about 25 artisans, though the number varies with production needs and orders. Some trained workers eventually move into other jobs or start their own businesses.
Helena Benedict, Chako's 26-year-old operations manager, said this combination of income generation and skills development was particularly valuable to women supporting their families and young people seeking ways to enter the workforce.
"By empowering women and young people, we give them opportunities to recycle and upcycle waste, which provides them with jobs and allows them to earn an income," Benedict said.
Chako's work also extends beyond its workshop. The enterprise welcomes students, community groups, nongovernmental organizations and government representatives to learn about waste management and environmental conservation. It also works with hotels and their staff to encourage waste separation and demonstrate how discarded materials can be reused.
The approach reflects the founders' belief that waste management on an island requires participation from businesses, residents and visitors alike.
But turning that vision into a sustainable business remains challenging. Collecting bottles, washing materials, training artisans and marketing finished products all require time and money.
Roelandschap said some consumers and businesses still needed convincing that locally made upcycled products were worth choosing over imported goods.
For now, the connection between environmental protection and economic opportunity is visible in the lives of women like Mussa and Juma. Their work gives discarded materials a new purpose while helping them provide for their children and pursue goals that once seemed more difficult to achieve.
In Zanzibar, where tourism continues to generate both opportunities and waste, Chako is showing how one can help address the other.
For the women turning bottles and plastic into marketable products, the process is also creating something less tangible but equally valuable: the means to shape their own futures. ■
A woman displays a hanging lamp made of a recycled glass bottle at the showroom of a workshop in Zanzibar, Tanzania, Oct. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman)

Feature: "One day, I want to visit her in China" -- Dutch visitors see off giant panda Lang Yue
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:03:43 CST
01:03:43 KST

Zhang Yi, charge d'affaires ad interim at the Chinese Embassy in the Netherlands, delivers a speech during a farewell ceremony for giant panda Lang Yue in Rhenen, the Netherlands, Oct. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Lyu You)
RHENEN, the Netherlands, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Four-year-old Freya's eyes filled with tears as she watched a vehicle carrying giant panda Lang Yue slowly pull away from Ouwehands Zoo in Rhenen, the Netherlands.
Her family had bought annual zoo passes so they could visit the panda regularly. For Freya, watching Lang Yue's progress had been an important part of her own growth. "One day, I want to visit her in China," she said.
Nearly 100 people came to the zoo on Friday morning to bid farewell to the panda, who was born there in July 2024. Children wearing baseball caps and waving small flags bearing images of Lang Yue gathered outside the Chinese-style panda house for the farewell ceremony.
Dragon and lion dances accompanied the farewell. On the departing vehicle, a message wished Lang Yue good luck.
Zhang Yi, charge d'affaires ad interim at the Chinese Embassy in the Netherlands, said at the ceremony that giant pandas were envoys of friendship between the two countries. He added that cooperation on panda conservation reflects their shared commitment to protecting wildlife and preserving biodiversity.
Zhang also invited Dutch visitors to explore China, especially Sichuan, home of the giant panda.
Lang Yue is the second cub born to Wu Wen and Xing Ya, who arrived in the Netherlands in 2017. Their first cub, Fan Xing, was born in May 2020 and left for China in September 2023.
For giant panda keeper Brenda van Ekeren, who has cared for Lang Yue since birth, the departure brought back memories of their first encounter.
"She was very soft," van Ekeren recalled. The cub was curious and willing to approach, but still kept checking for her mother.
Lang Yue has a more timid personality than her older sister Fan Xing, the keeper explained. Faced with an unfamiliar situation, Lang Yue would watch her mother before trying it herself. However, once she feels reassured, she becomes playful and eager to explore, van Ekeren said.
Zoo Director Robin de Lange said it was an emotional day for the staff. However, alongside his sadness, he said he was happy that Lang Yue would help with the conservation of giant pandas in China.
The zoo is proud to have raised two cubs, he added. Behind those births were years of cooperation with Chinese colleagues.
Van Ekeren has visited China several times, learning from keepers, veterinarians and managers about daily care, breeding and raising cubs. The Dutch team records the pandas' growth, sharing information and exchanging questions with their Chinese counterparts. Comparing the two cubs has also taught keepers how differently individual pandas can behave.
Rhenen Mayor Geran Kaai told Xinhua that the pandas mean a great deal to the town and are a source of pride for its residents. He said they have helped bring Chinese and Dutch people and cultures together, pointing to the zoo's Chinese-style buildings, music and dragon and lion dances.
The area was dotted with colorful lanterns shaped like giant pandas and other figures, bringing a touch of Sichuan, the pandas' home province, to the Dutch farewell.
De Lange said the displays were part of the zoo's years-long cooperation with partners from Zigong, a city in Sichuan known for its lantern-making tradition.
Visitors Jesse and Judith, who came from nearby Ede for the farewell, said they had watched Lang Yue grow through almost monthly visits.
For van Ekeren, meanwhile, the goodbye came with a wish to meet again. "I would love to visit her when she's in China," she said. ■

Last independent newspaper in Russia forced to shut down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:03:43 UTC
01:03:43 KST

Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last independent newspaper, "no longer exists," as Putin erases the free press
Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last independent newspaper, announced Friday that it will cease operations from Nov. 9, marking a major milestone for President Vladimir Putin's years-long effort to silence the country's free press.
Novaya Gazeta said it was being forced to close under pressure from Russian authorities and security services.
"The newspaper no longer exists," editor in chief Sergei Sokolov said in a video statement shared Friday on YouTube. "The Russian government, Russian special services, forced the editorial team to stop its work."
The announcement came a day after the newspaper's staff learned they were being evicted from their Moscow newsroom on Potapovsky Lane, where journalists had worked for nearly 30 years. At the same time, the system that enabled readers to donate to the paper was switched off, cutting its only remaining source of funding.
The Anna Politkovskaya Museum, a memorial to the paper's renowned investigative journalist who was shot dead two decades ago, will close with the newspaper, as it has been housed in her former office.
Sokolov said authorities had left the team no choice but closure. In his statement he said the newspaper's staff would now "end on the street, with no means of subsistence and under the constant threat of repression."
Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993 with money donated by former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, from his Nobel Peace Prize award. It became the standard-bearer for investigative reporting in post-Soviet Russia, exposing corruption and human rights abuses, including Politkovskaya's reporting on the war in Chechnya.
She was gunned down in Moscow in 2006, becoming one of multiple journalists killed over the years in allegedly politically motivated assassinations, including at least two others who were with Novaya Gazeta. Politkovskaya's convicted murderer was pardoned by Russian authorities in 2023 after he joined the military to fight in Ukraine.
In 2021, the newspaper's then-editor Dmitry Muratov was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, along with Philippine journalist Maria Ressa, for defending freedom of expression.
Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Novaya Gazeta suspended its print and online operations following repeated warnings from Russia's state media regulator about violating laws on alleged "false information," and a court stripped the outlet of its media license that September.
With the closure of Novaya Gazeta on Friday, there are now no major independent newspapers still operating inside Russia.
Independent radio station Ekho Moskvy and the TV Rain network had already shut down operations inside Russia under similar pressure from authorities. Some Novaya Gazeta staff left Russia and launched a sister outlet in Europe, which Russian authorities have also blocked access to inside the country.
Katya Kotrikadze, news director for TV Rain, which now operates in exile from Europe and is not accessible in Russia, told CBS News on Friday that Novaya Gazeta's closure did not come as a surprise.
"There was no freedom of speech and media in Russia for years now, it has been destroyed for years now," she said, adding that Novaya Gazeta had not been able to objectively cover the war in Ukraine due to censorship that was tightened at the start of the full-scale invasion.
Putin "has burned all the bridges and has stopped all the imitation of democracy and freedom of everything in Russia," she said.
Novaya Gazeta said it would provide more information about its future in the coming days.

Noting Switzerland is an important partner of China in Europe, Xi said Swiss cooperation with China has always been at the forefront among European countries. He added that free trade cooperation has become the brightest highlight of China-Switzerland relations, which fully demonstrates the political courage and responsibility of the two countries in adhering to open cooperation, and highlights the unique leading role of both sides in promoting the building of an open world economy.
China is willing to work with Switzerland to uphold openness, strengthen cooperation, promote a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, and jointly inject confidence and more certainty into the economic and trade cooperation between China and European countries, as well as into the global economic development, Xi said.

Switzerland firmly adheres to the one-China policy and looks forward to strengthening dialogue and exchanges with China, upholding mutually beneficial cooperation, and promoting greater development in cooperation in various fields, he said.
The Swiss side attaches great importance to the positive role played by China in international affairs and is willing to closely coordinate with China, adhere to multilateralism, safeguard free trade, and contribute to world development, prosperity, peace and stability, Parmelin added.
After their meeting, the two leaders witnessed the signing of the protocol on upgrading free trade agreement and multiple cooperation documents in areas like scientific research, employment and the media. ■

DPRK weightlifter Pak shatters two world records for 70kg gold as Ningbo local He takes bronze
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31

01:03:23 KST

Pak Pyol of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) competes during the men's 70kg snatch event at the 2026 IWF World Championships in Ningbo, east China's Zhejiang Province, Oct. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Jiang Han)
NINGBO, China, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- DPR Korea's Pak Pyol broke two world records to win the men's 70kg title at the IWF World Championships here on Friday, while China's He Baozhen took bronze in the city where he grew up.
Pak lifted 157kg in the snatch and 198kg in the clean and jerk for a 355kg total, setting new records in the snatch and total. He, 22, won three medals, including silver in the snatch and bronze medals in the clean and jerk and total.
He made all three snatch attempts to finish on 151kg. "I was nervous on the first lift, but relaxed on the second. By the third, I stopped overthinking and it felt easy," he said.
Pak opened at 150kg before twice rewriting the snatch record at 155kg and 157kg. The previous 154kg mark was set by Japan's Masanori Miyamoto in Nagoya a month ago. DPRK's Ri Won-ju also made 151kg, but He took silver thanks to a lighter bodyweight, 69.60kg against 69.95kg.
He opened his clean and jerk at 182kg and then made 188kg, while both DPRK lifters started higher, Pak at 190kg and Nagoya champion Ri at 192kg. He failed his third attempt and took bronze at 188kg.
"I rushed it; otherwise I could have made it look easy," He said.
Pak then made 195kg for a 352kg total, breaking Ri's previous record of 349kg, and pushed it to 355kg with 198kg. Ri, chasing his own 198kg clean and jerk record, went for 205kg but failed and appeared to injure his arm before withdrawing. Ri took silver at 343kg, with the Philippines' Albert Ian Delos Santos fourth at 331kg.
"This gives me so much motivation, because I grew up as a lifter right here in Ningbo," He said. Since 70kg not an Olympic category, He plans to move up to 75kg to chase a 2028 Los Angeles Olympics spot.
The men's 75kg competition takes place on Saturday, with Indonesia's Rahmat Erwin Abdullah facing DPRK lifters. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) announced Friday that Terquavion Lamont Smith of the Shenzhen Aviators has been provisionally suspended from competition for an anti-doping violation.

Li Xi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and secretary of the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), presides over a meeting of the CCDI Standing Committee to study the guiding principles from the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Yue Yuewei)
BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Standing Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), China's top anti-corruption body, on Friday convened to study the guiding principles from the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee.
Li Xi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and secretary of the CCDI, presided over the meeting, urging disciplinary inspection and supervision authorities to thoroughly study and implement the guiding principles from this plenum.
They should adopt higher standards and more concrete measures to promote high-quality development of the disciplinary inspection and supervision work, and persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance to provide strong guarantees for building a great country and advancing national rejuvenation on all fronts through Chinese modernization, Li stressed.
Speaking about the resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance adopted at the plenary session, Li said it serves as a programmatic document for continuously advancing the great new project of Party building in the new era, and called for a full, accurate and comprehensive grasp of its principles.
Li urged disciplinary inspection and supervision bodies to make sustained efforts to strengthen political oversight, implement the central Party leadership's eight-point decision on improving work conduct, strictly enforce Party discipline and rules, take integrated steps against corruption, and promote the regularized, law-based and standardized development of discipline inspection and supervision work.
The fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee was held from Monday to Thursday this week. ■

Feature: Rwandan honey producer eyes sweet opportunities in Chinese market ahead of CIIE
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:03:05 CST
01:03:05 KST

Grace Mbabazi, founder and chief executive officer of M&M Sozo Ltd., a honey-producing company based in Kigali's Kicukiro District, receives an interview with Xinhua in Kigali, Rwanda, Oct. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Ju Yinhe)
KIGALI, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Rwandan entrepreneur Grace Mbabazi has spent years producing and selling honey in the domestic market. Now, she is setting her sights on a market that once seemed beyond reach: China.
Her ambitions are gaining momentum thanks to the China International Import Expo (CIIE) and China's zero-tariff policy for 53 African countries, which offer new opportunities for Rwandan honey to reach Chinese consumers.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Mbabazi, founder and chief executive officer of M&M Sozo Ltd., a honey-producing company based in Kigali's Kicukiro District, said the CIIE had helped her company explore the Chinese market by providing direct access to Chinese buyers, importers, distributors and business partners.
Rwanda has participated in all eight previous editions of the CIIE since the expo's launch in 2018, with honey among its featured products. The country has also designated honey as its priority product under the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations' One Country One Priority Product initiative.
According to data released in 2022 by the Rwanda Agriculture and Animal Resources Development Board, the country has approximately 120,000 beekeepers operating across five major beekeeping zones, including Akagera National Park and Kigali City.
As M&M Sozo Ltd. prepares to showcase its honey products at the ninth CIIE, scheduled for Nov. 5 to 10 in Shanghai, Mbabazi looks back on her first participation in 2024 as a valuable stepping stone toward the Chinese market.
Mbabazi said the expo gave her a rare opportunity to introduce her products to an international audience, raise brand awareness, engage with potential customers, importers, and distributors, and gain a better understanding of the Chinese market.
"Our experience at the CIIE showed that the expo can help local businesses build commercial partnerships and introduce products such as honey to Chinese consumers," she said.
Mbabazi highlighted the free exhibition booths, "green channel" arrangements for products exported to China, and other preferential measures available to exhibitors from Rwanda and several other African countries, saying these policies could help businesses reduce marketing and participation costs.
Such support enables her company to showcase its honey to Chinese buyers and international visitors while allocating more resources to product development, packaging, and business promotion.
She also described China's zero-tariff policy as "a big motivation," saying it offered Rwanda "a good opportunity to increase honey exports."
Mbabazi hopes to capitalize on the policy to "use the potential savings from eligible tariff-free imports to improve price competitiveness, negotiate attractive commercial terms, and reinvest in business expansion."
Her immediate goal is to build long-term relationships with importers and distributors in China, creating a reliable market for her honey, increasing export volumes, and raising the company's international profile.
Producing seven tons of honey monthly, the company now works with 36 permanent beekeepers as well as several outgrowers across various districts of the country.
Since its inception in 2018, the company has expanded its operations to almost all districts in the Eastern Province, working mainly with women and young people. Mbabazi aims to increase the number of beehives associated with the business from 5,000 to approximately 25,000 by 2028.
At this year's CIIE, the company plans to showcase two signature products, Sozo Pure Gold Honey and Sozo Pure Natural Honey, both produced in Rwanda. Mbabazi said the products stand out for their natural production process: the honey is collected straight from beehives and sold without heating, processing, or pasteurization.
"Our beehives are located in forests where no pesticides are used," she emphasized.
As the business grows, Mbabazi hopes to create greater economic opportunities for the beekeepers who supply her company. She said the prospect of higher earnings for beekeepers has reinforced the importance of accessing larger markets, including China.
Looking ahead, she hopes to establish a reliable and sustainable honey supply chain from Rwanda to China, increase export revenue, and build lasting business relationships with Chinese partners. ■

Ukraine Reports First Drone Interception of Russian KUB-2E Loitering Munition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:02:57 UTC
01:02:57 KST

Ukraine’s Posipaky drone unit shot down a Russian KUB-2E loitering munition in the Zaporizhzhia sector in what the National Association of Ukrainian Defense Industries (NAUDI) described as the first confirmed interception of the weapon by a frontline interceptor drone.
The pilots used a General Chereshnia AIR interceptor, NAUDI said in a Facebook post.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The General Chereshnia FPV team also reported the interception, congratulating the Posipaky unit.
“There is now one more page in our ‘Red Book’,” the team said, referring to its registry of rare or destroyed equipment.
Both statements included a short video of the engagement recorded by the interceptor’s onboard camera. Kyiv Post could not independently verify the footage’s time or location.
What is Russia’s KUB-2E?
The KUB-2E is a Russian-made loitering munition developed by the Kalashnikov concern. Russian forces use it against Ukraine, while the manufacturer also markets the system for export.
The weapon is designed to strike personnel, military equipment and drone operator positions. It typically works alongside a reconnaissance drone that identifies targets, with an operator using the munition’s onboard video feed to guide the attack.
The KUB family includes several variants with different payloads and ranges. According to the Vash Visnyk news outlet, the basic model carries a warhead weighing about 3 kilograms (6.6 pounds) and has a reported range of 25–40 kilometers (16–25 miles).
Su-57 Fighter Reportedly Burned Down at Russia’s Akhtubinsk Airfield
Other KUB-2E versions reportedly carry thermobaric warheads and have a range of up to 40 kilometers (25 miles).
Heavier models, including the KUB-10E and KUB-10ME, reportedly have ranges exceeding 100 kilometers (62 miles) and optical guidance systems. Their intended targets include lightly armored vehicles, artillery positions, command posts and personnel.
The family’s electric propulsion reduces its acoustic signature. Newer variants are also reported to have improved resistance to electronic warfare.
Interceptors also target Russian reconnaissance drones
Ukrainian interceptor crews have also downed Russian reconnaissance aircraft, including the ZALA Z-20, a drone reportedly worth about $200,000.
In early January 2026, a crew from the 55th Separate Artillery Brigade, Zaporizhzhia Sich, shot down a Z-20 using a General Chereshnia AIR interceptor.
The electrically powered Z-20 monitors the battlefield, identifies targets and adjusts artillery fire. It is also believed to help locate targets for Russia’s Lancet loitering munitions.
Its manufacturer, ZALA Aero, part of the Kalashnikov concern, claims the drone can remain airborne for more than six hours and transmit video over distances exceeding 100 kilometers (62 miles).
The General Chereshnia AIR interceptor has been used by dozens of Ukrainian units. According to the Brave1 defense innovation cluster, it had been credited with more than 300 confirmed interceptions of Russian reconnaissance drones by December 2025, including Orlan-10, ZALA, Supercam and Merlin models.

Pope Leo votes in US midterms in first known political ballot for any pontiff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:01:21 UTC
01:01:21 KST

Pope Leo has voted in the US midterm elections – the first time a sitting pontiff is known to have cast a ballot in any political election at any time in history.
Leo, who has clashed with the US president, Donald Trump, over several issues, submitted his vote by post in Chicago, where he was born, the Vatican said on Friday. Leo became the first American leader of the Catholic church last year after the death of Pope Francis.
The Vatican said Leo “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so”, including in Peru, where he lived for years as a missionary. “The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” the statement added.
Leo, who before being elected pope was known as Robert Prevost, reportedly made his request for the mail-in ballot on 3 October, registering at an address in New Lenox, Illinois.
That was 10 days before he had surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung. The pontiff has gradually been resuming activities since being discharged from hospital on 17 October.
The crucial midterm elections are due to be held on 3 November.
Leo and Trump have clashed over the US president’s harsh immigration polices, with the pontiff describing them as “inhuman”.
Earlier this year, Trump lashed out in response to Leo’s criticisms of the US-Israeli war on Iran, calling the pontiff “weak on crime” and “terrible on foreign policy”. The US president also said Leo had only been elected pope because Trump himself was in the White House.
In response to the tirade, Leo said he was “not afraid” of Trump.
In his first key address to the US on the eve of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, Leo praised the country’s history of welcoming migrants, while urging Americans to live up to the ideals put forward in the declaration, in what was seen a further rebuke to Trump.
In an interview with the US broadcaster in late July, Leo expressed “great love” for his home country and its core principles of freedom, opportunity and welcoming immigrants but qualified that he just “happens to be American”.
Leo will travel to Latin America in November for an 11-day trip covering 10 cities. Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s foreign minister, told reporters at Rome’s foreign press association this week that a papal visit to the US was expected in the “not too distant future”, adding that the outcome of the midterms might influence whether the trip went ahead in 2027 or later.
