‘Need a Plan B’: Yemenis in Aden prepare for another war as missiles fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:26:00 UTC
00:26:00 KST

‘Need a Plan B’: Yemenis in Aden prepare for another war as missiles fall
As Houthi missiles strike Aden, residents stockpile food and prepare escape plans, fearing a return to all-out war.
For Mohammed Abdul Malik, the powerful explosions that have hit Yemen’s southern city of Aden repeatedly over the past month are an ominous warning of darker days ahead.
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed attacks against several locations in Aden, including the international airport, military camps, the city’s port, and the presidential palace – which serves as a base for Yemen’s government.
Fearing that the city could once again descend into widespread violence, Abdul Malik has begun taking precautions. He has stockpiled food and prepared his car for a long journey if he needs to leave.
“I’ll tell you about myself and my close friends: We’ve started buying and stockpiling basic provisions, like sugar and other staples,” Abdul Malik told Al Jazeera.
If the security situation deteriorates further and state institutions collapse, his Plan B is to flee Aden with his family and seek refuge in Shabwa, to the northeast, or Hadramout, to the east.
“We’ve mapped out an exit route from the city. I’ve prepared my car, checked it over, and set aside an emergency supply of fuel. I’m ready to pack up my family and head out at a moment’s notice,” he said.
Daily life disrupted
After four years of relative calm, Yemen’s war has reignited in recent months, particularly since early September, when the Houthis launched a major offensive to seize government-held areas in the west of the country from the Saudi-backed, pro-government National Resistance Forces (NRF).
Within a week, the Iran-backed armed group – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – had seized districts in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces, including the port city of Mocha, a stronghold of the NRF, and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.
A government counteroffensive launched in early October has made limited gains along the Red Sea coast, but at the same time the Houthis have tightened their siege of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, after capturing a vital road linking it to Aden.
Aden had remained relatively peaceful despite the fierce fighting elsewhere, and had become a refuge for thousands of people displaced by the conflict.
The wave of Houthi missile and drone attacks this month has shattered that calm, and has raised fears that the Houthis may be seeking to capture Aden.
Accounts from friends who fled Taiz, where fighting and the siege have driven up prices and disrupted supplies, have deepened his concerns about what could happen to his city.
“Prices in Taiz have already doubled, and the same could easily happen in Aden. If the [Aden] port were to be struck, prices would skyrocket,” he said.
“At work, my colleagues and I talk about what we should buy, what food we ought to store, what our contingency plan is, and where we would go if we had to leave,” he added.
Abdul Malik described how the Houthi attacks have disrupted daily life in Aden, with some families limiting their movements – especially at night.
“When the [first missile] explosion occurred, one of my colleagues went to the school to pick up her son and found the students frightened and gathered together in one place. We go to work and take our children to school, but there is a sense of anxiety and tension,” he told Al Jazeera.
Airport attacks
Aden international airport, currently Yemen’s busiest airport, has borne the brunt of the Houthi missile and drone attacks, which have repeatedly disrupted air travel, forcing airlines to cancel or delay flights and divert others to airports elsewhere in Yemen or abroad.
For residents living near the airport, the repeated strikes and explosions have taken a psychological toll on families, prompting some to consider moving to safer areas inside and outside Aden. Ahmed Awadh, a resident of Aden’s Khor Maksar district, near the airport, said the attacks have left children struggling with fear and anxiety.
“An explosion jolts the children awake in terror, leaving them unable to sleep for the rest of the night. Even the sound of an ordinary airplane now strikes fear into my family,” Awadh told Al Jazeera.
He said the attacks have disrupted schools and businesses, prompting families to rush home and some parents to keep their children away from school. Some families have sent vulnerable relatives, including children and elderly people, to neighbouring Lahj and Abyan provinces or other districts of Aden. Others have rented homes further away from the airport.
Awadh, who lives with 10 other family members, said they have taken precautions by keeping children away from windows during attacks. He and his neighbours have also created a WhatsApp group to check on one another after each explosion.
“The [Aden] airport, which serves the civilian population, as well as other civilian infrastructure and residential areas, must not be targeted,” Awadh said.
Aden remains vulnerable
Aden, Yemen’s second-most important city after the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, suffered extensive destruction in early 2015 during fierce fighting between the Houthis and their opponents, as well as air strikes by the Saudi-led coalition.
Even after the Houthis were driven out, the city continued to experience sporadic clashes between rival anti-Houthi factions, which sometimes turned their weapons on each other.
Adeeb al-Shatri, a professor of journalism at Aden and Hadramout universities, said the latest wave of Houthi missile attacks had compounded the suffering of a city already plagued by lawlessness and insecurity.
He questioned why Yemen’s internationally recognised government had left Aden, its temporary capital and seat of government, vulnerable to Houthi attacks without adequate air defences to intercept missiles and drones.
“Aden is currently the capital, housing both major and minor state institutions. Therefore, the legitimate government must protect it,” al-Shatri told Al Jazeera.
The Yemeni military has claimed to have air defence forces in Aden, with reports of drone interceptions before they reached civilian areas.
Yemen’s Information Minister, Moammar al-Eryani, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on criticism that air defence systems have been inadequate in protecting Aden.
Al-Shatri argued that only a small proportion of Aden’s wealthier residents could afford to stockpile food and other essential supplies in preparation for an emergency. Most residents, he said, were already struggling to feed their families.
“In Europe and other stable Arab countries, people stockpile food during crises, but in Aden, people need three times their current salaries just to live a simple life,” he said.
Al-Shatri also challenged the notion that Houthi attacks had brought businesses and education in Aden to a complete standstill.
“People’s movement in the city returned to normal just an hour after the explosion because they have to keep moving to earn money and secure their daily bread,” he said. “If work were to stop, it would lead to a financial crisis, and they would be unable to provide food for themselves.”

Russia Designates Opposition Delegation at PACE as ‘Undesirable’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:25:00 UTC
00:25:00 KST

Russia’s Justice Ministry has added the Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces at the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) to its list of “undesirable” organizations, a move that renders affiliation with the anti-war group illegal.
The delegation of Russian exiles was set up in January after years of lobbying efforts by leading opposition figures like former businessman Mikhail Khodorkovsky.
Several members of the anti-war group, including dissident Vladimir Kara-Murza and Pussy Riot co-founder Nadya Tolokonnikova, already face criminal prosecution in Russia.
Under Russian law, individuals affiliated with an “undesirable” entity can face up to four years in prison. Organizing the work of an “undesirable” group carries a maximum sentence of six years in prison.
Neither the Prosecutor General’s Office, which ruled to designate the Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces as “undesirable” on Oct. 21, nor the Justice Ministry, which approved the designation on Thursday, have officially commented on the decision.
Besides the PACE delegation, the Justice Ministry blacklisted another 11 foreign entities on Thursday, including Vidim Books, a publishing house founded in Slovakia in 2023 to print books that are censored or banned inside Russia.
Russia was expelled from the Council of Europe and PACE in March 2022, shortly after launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It had been a member for 26 years.
Introduced in 2015, Russia’s “undesirable” designation has been used to hinder the work of independent media outlets, civil society groups and the political opposition. Hundreds of entities have since been added to the registry, including The Moscow Times.

Queen Ursula comes to Canada with velvet handcuffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:24:26 UTC
00:24:26 KST

Queen Ursula comes to Canada with velvet handcuffs
I’m trying to spend a few weeks back in Canada for some peace and quiet from the usual European drama. Just my luck that Queen Ursula would follow me here, circus and all.
She hadn’t even landed in Montreal for the EU-Canada Summit, and already everyone around me was saying that Canada’s “associate membership” had been canceled. They’d heard that countries like France and Germany objected to the idea, even as Von der Leyen was saddling up her broom for a trip across the Atlantic.
Someone even asked me if that meant that we’re now kicked out of Eurovision. I had to explain that the title never existed in the first place. EU treaties refer only to association agreements. It’s just the usual sort of branding that von der Leyen, the unelected EU chief executive, likes to roll out, much like her endless riffs about unity, as though dissent weren’t an actual virtue in a functioning democracy.
Or like the way she talks a good game about sticking it to Russia while simultaneously celebrating the €977 million spent this winter alone on gas purchases for Ukraine – much of which comes from Russia via Hungary and Slovakia. The EU writes cheques to Kiev. Kiev pays Hungary and Slovakia, who then pay Moscow.
Those middlemen exist mainly so that Queen Ursula can maintain a certain public image while engaging in more practical considerations behind the scenes, albeit at considerably greater expense to the European taxpayer.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney got a taste of the spectacle when Ursula’s marketing campaign became the focus of the event. He was forced to acknowledge that he honestly didn’t give a damn what they called this new cooperation, so long as it was good for Canadians. Meanwhile, other EU leaders, like German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, had started referring to it instead as an “alliance for the future.”
But von der Leyen had already landed in Canada and continued promoting the “associate membership” label, smiling as Carney, sitting beside her, subsequently echoed the term.
Of course, all that the mental midgets are going to take away from this whole event is the intrigue over whether or not Canada is joining the EU. Spoiler alert: it isn’t. And never will. It’s not even legally possible. But this idiotic intrigue is distracting from the details of what lurks underneath, which could amount to a whole lot of iron-fisting through velvet gloves.
Turns out someone had already leaked a draft statement on these future relations to Politico, dated September 22, 2026. Cut out the diplomatic fluff and here’s what you’re left with.
Both sides are clearly looking for new markets as they diversify trade away from the US. Great. But it seems rather stupid for the EU to be begging Canada for its natural resources – gas, metals and minerals – while simultaneously slapping on carbon tariffs that get downloaded onto European citizens and companies. What’s the point of trying to bring prices down by increasing supply if you’re just going to top up the cost anyway.
You jokers also killed off your own nuclear industries, only to realize (a bit late) that perhaps it was preferable to having to resort to coal, before subsequently reviving it as the future of clean energy. So maybe you’re not exactly the best people to be doing commie-style central planning.
Technology is already advancing in favor of the environment, with those improvements increasingly built into the conditions for funding and financing. Just let it breathe already. Not every industry needs a Brussels bureaucrat hovering over it.
It also sounds like they’ve roped Canada into their scheme to skim Russian cash from its Western-held assets to pimp themselves out under the pretext of Ukraine’s defence and their own, then just hope that Russia’s ultimately cool with that so they don’t have to stick their own taxpayers either the final bill.
Perhaps the most troubling part is the Orwellian digital cooperation section of the agreement, which aims to “advance cooperation on artificial intelligence security and sovereignty, trusted data flows and digital governance and to align emerging AI and digital regulatory frameworks through associated country status for Canada.”
Does this mean Canadians get to have Queen Ursula block their bank accounts now, too, since we’ll all be connected and harmonized inside one giant digital panopticon? Or worse, some AI bot? It’s hardly reassuring that Carney’s government has just appealed the federal court decision condemning his predecessor Justin Trudeau’s government for unconstitutionally invoking the Emergencies Act, which allowed it to block the bank accounts of Covid-era anti-mandate Freedom Convoy participants without a court order – all for the crime of honking too loudly. Nor is it reassuring that Canada and the EU have already signed an agreement on digital “trust services” involving things like government-controlled digital identity wallets.
One honk too many, one wrong opinion on some social media platform linked to the online ID system that they’re all ushering in – ostensibly under the pretext of adults needing to prove that they aren’t children requiring protection from online pedos – and there goes your whole life with the flip of a switch. It’s not like Queen Ursula’s European Commission isn’t already doing that with sanctions and asset freezes, in the absence of due process, for those whose views it qualifies as “propaganda.”
And if this is what they mean by an alliance for the future, then Canadians – the average citizens of this country – need full and open debate over the fine print before anyone signs us up.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Up to 10,000 Turbojet Engines Per Year: PBS Group Invests $100 Million in U.S. Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

The Czech company PBS Group plans to invest an additional $100 million in expanding the production of small turbojet engines in the United States.
The funds will be directed toward expanding the production capacity of the PBS Aerospace plant in Roswell, Georgia, according to Armádní noviny.
By 2028, the company expects to reach an annual production volume of up to 10,000 engines, which will nearly double its current output.
This volume will correspond to the production of approximately 40 power units per working day.
In parallel with its U.S. operations, the PBS Group is expanding its capacity in the Czech Republic. In Velká Bíteš, the company is investing approximately €40 million in the creation of a new aviation technology division.
The expansion of the plant in Georgia extends beyond the assembly lines. The facility’s floor space has already been increased by 930 m², two new test chambers have been built to double engine testing capacity, and preparations are underway to launch a second production shift.
It is worth noting that the company’s initial plans called for reaching an annual production capacity of 20,000 engines as early as 2026–2027. PBS Group has not yet specified whether these figures remain relevant for later stages.
The U.S. facility is mass-producing the TJ40 and TJ80 turbojet engines, which are being actively integrated into various drones and missile systems.
Among the company’s key customers is the American firm Zone 5 Technologies, which develops and manufactures the Rusty Dagger and White Spike missiles. PBS has signed a long-term contract with the company to supply turbojet engines.
Additional opportunities for cooperation arose after Zone 5 Technologies became part of the Norwegian defense group Kongsberg Gruppen earlier this year.
In addition, the Ukrainian company Airlogix and the Czech company PBS Velká Bíteš signed a memorandum on organizing licensed production of small turbine engines in Ukraine.
The process will begin with engine assembly and the establishment of a certified service center, followed by the expansion of manufacturing operations.

Lula’s Victory Preserves Kremlin Ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:23:00 UTC
00:23:00 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election preserved an important relationship for Moscow just as Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted African leaders at the Kremlin.
“We welcome Mr. Lula’s victory,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday, Oct. 26, praising the Brazilian president’s contribution to bilateral relations and the BRICS grouping.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Three days later, Russia concluded a summit attended by delegations from 48 African countries, including 22 heads of state, according to the Kremlin. Its declaration called for closer economic and security cooperation, opposing unilateral sanctions and the unlawful seizure of sovereign assets.
The developments showcase a continuing challenge for Ukraine and its allies: Despite Russia’s invasion, Moscow retains governments willing to maintain trade, participate in its diplomatic forums, and resist Western efforts to isolate it.
Lula’s approach to Moscow is personal and practical
Lula has spoken openly about the value he places on his relationship with Putin.
During a May 2025 meeting at the Kremlin, he praised the Russian president’s attentive approach to their discussions and the dialogue between their foreign ministers. He was visiting Moscow for the 80th anniversary of the Soviet victory over Nazi Germany, joining other foreign leaders at the commemorations while Russia’s war against Ukraine continued.
His reluctance to confront Moscow has also surfaced outside discussions about Ukraine. After Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic penal colony in February 2024, Lula urged an investigation before assigning responsibility.
Ukraine Reports First Drone Interception of Russian KUB-2E Loitering Munition
“Why the rush to accuse?” he asked, arguing that conclusions should await the results of an autopsy. His remarks contrasted with Western leaders who held the Kremlin responsible.
Commercial interests only serve to reinforce that diplomatic caution.
During an Aug. 4 telephone conversation, Lula and Putin discussed Russian diesel and fertilizer supplies, alongside cooperation in energy, science, technology, and shipbuilding. Brazil’s presidency said both leaders intended to continue working together in BRICS.
Those supplies matter to Brazil’s economy. Its agriculture ministry says imports account for 93% of fertilizer consumption, with Russia and China leading the country’s supply. Restricting those relationships would therefore present practical challenges for Brazilian agriculture.
A setback for Trump’s regional ambitions
Lula won the Oct. 25 runoff with 51.79% of valid votes against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, according to Brazil’s electoral court. The result secured a fourth presidential term, and a second consecutive term since his return to office in 2023.
It also interrupted a regional trend toward governments aligned with US President Donald Trump.
Christopher Sabatini, director of Chatham House’s Latin America Program, described Bolsonaro’s defeat as a setback for a White House that had hoped to consolidate a network of conservative governments across the hemisphere. Lula nevertheless faces conservative majorities in both houses of Brazil’s Congress, which could constrain his domestic agenda.
Trump responded by questioning the election. On Thursday, Oct. 29, according to Al Jazeera, he called the contest a “disgrace,” while maintaining that he had not taken sides. His remarks followed Bolsonaro’s departure for the US and unsupported allegations that the vote had been stolen.
Such tensions create an opening for Moscow and Beijing. Lula can present those relationships as evidence that Brazil has alternatives to Washington, particularly when US pressure is perceived as interference in Brazilian sovereignty.
The economic relationships differ substantially. Brazilian exports to China reached $100 billion in 2025, compared with $38 billion to the US, according to Chatham House. Russia’s importance rests more heavily on particular commodities and cooperation in diplomatic forums.
BRICS keeps Russia at the table
Lula’s re-election provides continuity for BRICS, which he helped establish during his earlier presidency.
While Bolsonaro had questioned Brazil’s role in the grouping, Lula supports expanding financial cooperation, including greater use of national currencies in trade. His victory reduces the prospect of a Brazilian retreat, although the members’ differing economic and geopolitical interests remain.
For Moscow, Brazil’s participation helps keep BRICS broader than a gathering of Russia’s closest security partners. It places Putin’s government alongside major economies that also maintain extensive relationships with Europe and the US.
Still, there are limits to that accommodation. Putin did not attend the 2025 BRICS summit in Rio in person as Brazil could not provide assurances concerning the International Criminal Court warrant for his arrest.
Nevertheless, continued engagement provides Russia with opportunities to negotiate, trade, and influence international debates without first ending its war against Ukraine.
In Africa, Putin seeks partners and investment opportunities
This week’s Moscow summit followed a similar approach.
Putin presented Russia as a partner in a multipolar international order, invoking Soviet support for African anti-colonial movements. He said Russia had supplied 13 million metric tons, approximately 14.3 million US tons, of grain to Africa in the first nine months of 2026, according to ABC News.
He also highlighted educational and diplomatic ties, saying approximately 40,000 African students were studying in Russia and that Moscow had opened eight embassies on the continent since the previous summit in 2023.
The economic pitch extended beyond trade. Putin said Russian companies were interested in moving some production operations to African countries, explicitly linking that interest to sanctions against Russia’s economy and businesses.
He called for guarantees protecting Russian investments but did not identify particular factories, destinations, or a relocation timetable. Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who chairs the African Union, meanwhile urged investment that would help African economies move beyond exporting raw materials and importing finished goods.
The summit’s declaration emphasized cooperation in nuclear energy, critical minerals, agriculture, and security. Its opposition to unilateral sanctions also aligned with Moscow’s position on Western restrictions.
Russia’s outreach addresses African demands for investment, security, and greater representation in international institutions. It also allows the Kremlin to present itself as a defender of sovereignty abroad while violating Ukraine’s.
Kyiv has doubts
In spite of cooperating with the Kremlin, Lula has encouraged Putin to negotiate with President Volodymyr Zelensky and has publicly said that he asked the Russian leader to end the war.
Several African countries have expressed diplomatic support for Kyiv, including Ghana, Kenya, Côte d’Ivoire, and Zambia. They were among 14 African states that endorsed the communiqué from the 2024 Ukraine peace summit in Switzerland, reaffirming support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Ghana and Kenya have also backed Ukraine-related resolutions at the UN. Yet, Kyiv remains unconvinced.
In September, Zelensky criticized the absence of a consistently strong position from countries including Brazil and South Africa, arguing that they possess influence over Russia and could use it to help secure peace.
Lula’s re-election and the African summit illustrate the difficulty of that appeal. Governments may favor negotiations while prioritzing their commercial and diplomatic relationships with Moscow.
For Putin, those relationships provide room to maneuver. Even if these countries don’t endorse the invasion, continued trade, diplomatic access, and resistance to sanctions help sustain Russia’s international position while the deadly fighting continues.

“No movement” in cabinet talks amid left-right stalemate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

“No movement” in cabinet talks amid left-right stalemate
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet’s attempt to win over left- and right-wing opposition parties in its ongoing tax plan talks failed again on Friday.
Prime minister Rob Jetten and other senior ministers met opposition leaders a day after three right-wing parties, the far-right JA21, orthodox Protestant SGP and farmer-citizen movement BBB, banded together to push their demands as a single bloc. The demands range from harsher asylum measures and changes to abortion rules to scrapping a tax rise to pay for defence.
The move was the latest attempt by the opposition to force the cabinet to pick a side. Opposition parties have said for weeks that the cabinet will never get a broad agreement, because the two sides of the aisle have incompatible demands.
The offer presented on Friday covered how to pay for changes to box 3, the tax on savings and investments, without raising taxes on wealth, sources told the Telegraaf.
The cabinet would use money left over from a fund to refund people who were overtaxed under box 3 in past years, and cut taxes for business owners who pay themselves profits from their own companies. It would also keep a tax deduction for healthcare costs that was due to be scrapped in 2028.
Regardless of the offer, the stalemate appears to continue. Centre-left PRO leader Jesse Klaver said he saw “no movement at all” on his party’s demand for higher taxes on the wealthy and lower taxes on workers.
JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans called it “a tough, complicated conversation”, but said the new right-wing alliance remained intact.
The coalition of D66, VVD and CDA does not have a majority, so it needs support from opposition parties to get its tax plan through parliament.

EU says it is prepared for peace talks with Russia, awaits Moscow's 'readiness'

Melike Pala

 The European Union is ready to engage in peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine and has been preparing for such a possibility for a long time, a bloc spokesperson said Friday.

Explainer-Why is the evacuation of Oleshky by Russia and Ukraine happening now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:21:34 UTC
00:21:34 KST

Key questions around the Russian and Ukrainian evacuation of Oleshky
MOSCOW, Oct 30 - Residents of the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine began evacuating on Friday as part of a joint relief operation by the two sides, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.
Many questions have been asked about the humanitarian operation and its wider significance under a deal that US first lady Melania Trump was involved in brokering, with the additional involvement of Pope Leo.
WHAT DO RUSSIA AND UKRAINE WANT FROM THE OPERATION?
Besides the safe evacuation of many of Oleshky's residents, Moscow and Kyiv are trying to use the operation to show US President Donald Trump they are serious about his efforts to secure an overall peace settlement.
Neither side wants to be blamed by Trump for something going wrong in Oleshky, an event that could burnish his self-professed credentials as a peacemaker before US midterm legislative elections.
But the two sides remain far apart on potential terms for ending the conflict in Ukraine, and there appears to be no immediate prospect of it ending.
Both sides want to keep Trump engaged in the peace process, even if it is moving slowly, as even if Trump's Republican Party performs badly in the midterms, he will be president for two more years and able to influence what is happening in Ukraine.
Moscow hopes Trump can pressure Kyiv into agreeing a deal that meets many of its conditions, such as full Russian control of Ukraine's Donbas region and a bar on Ukraine joining NATO.
Kyiv wants to ensure US intelligence sharing continues, along with full access to Elon Musk's battlefield communications system Starshield, and that European-bought US military hardware, including Patriot interceptor missiles, continues to flow.
HOW ARE THE SIDES TRYING TO INFLUENCE TRUMP'S VIEW OF THE OPERATION?
Moscow and Kyiv, keen to court the US president, have lavishly praised Melania Trump's role in making the operation happen.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has publicly recognised her importance in bringing about the ceasefire and aid operation, and Dmitry Peskov, his spokesman, cited her proven experience in reuniting children affected by the Ukraine conflict with their families as one of the reasons why Moscow agreed to the Oleshky operation. Special Envoy Kirill Dmitriev has repeatedly taken to X to highlight her role in what is happening.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets has paid tribute to Melania Trump too, saying Kyiv wanted to extend its "special thanks" to someone who was "personally devoting her time and attention to the humanitarian mission and assistance to civilians in Oleshky".
Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky with what state media said was about 50 journalists, including four US journalists from Newsmax, an outlet whose founder has said it is supportive of Trump and his policies.
Russian state TV has shown humanitarian aid boxes destined for Oleshky decorated with Russia's flag being loaded by people wearing T-shirts saying "Putin's Team - The People's Front."
DOES THE HUMANITARIAN MISSION MEET INTERNATIONAL STANDARDS?
The International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva said on Friday its teams had not been asked to provide support, but stood ready to help within its mandate if requested.
Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, said the UN had not received any request to help but officials were closely monitoring the situation.
He said the question of why the UN had not been invited to observe was one for Ukraine as Oleshky is in territory internationally recognised as Ukrainian.
"What we do know is that we have advocated for and will continue to advocate that all international rules, laws, and practices are upheld during this evacuation," Laerke said.
The fact that human rights commissioners from Ukraine and Russia were involved inspired some confidence, he added.
COULD OLESHKY BE A MODEL FOR SIMILAR LOCAL CEASEFIRES?
Kremlin statements suggest the operation could be a one-off — at least for now. Asked if the operation meant Russia and Ukraine could find other areas where they could cooperate, Peskov said it was a specific and isolated case that, for now, did not have wider implications for the peace process.
The ceasefire, which was extended to the wider Kherson region, expires on Sunday. There has been no easing of fighting in the other three Ukrainian regions Russia says it has incorporated as its own.
After holding talks with US negotiators, Putin this month agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine next month.
But Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, unhappy about attempted Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow, has hinted at a possible rethink if the attacks continue, while Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian oil refineries after a pause.
There has also been no let-up in Russian airstrikes on infrastructure targets across Ukraine. REUTERS

European politicians urge EU to use frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:19:34 UTC
00:19:34 KST

Melike Pala
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Four leading politicians from Europe and Canada on Friday called on the European Union to take custody of €210 billion ($234 billion) in frozen Russian sovereign assets and use the funds to support Ukraine's needs.
In a joint op-ed published by Poland’s TVP World, Germany’s Handelsblatt, Le Monde, The Times of London, and the UK’s Globe and Mail, the politicians argued that the EU should transfer the assets to a special EU custodian before the end of this year, calling the move an urgent step to secure funding for Kyiv.
The signatories are former German Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer, former French European Affairs Minister Nathalie Loiseau, former UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves, and former Canadian Deputy Prime Minister Chrystia Freeland.
"The time to act is now," they wrote, warning that Ukraine faces a €70 billion funding shortfall next year as Russian aerial attacks continue and the country struggles to sustain its defense.
They said the frozen assets, immobilized following the start of the war in Ukraine, could provide a financial bridge for Kyiv through 2029 and reduce the risk of political changes in European countries disrupting support.
The proposal, which they call the "Russian Transfer," would move custody of the immobilized Russian Central Bank accounts from financial institutions, primarily Belgium-based Euroclear, to the EU itself. 
EU leaders had failed to reach agreement
The politicians stressed that the arrangement would not amount to confiscation, as Russia would retain ownership of the assets, while the associated liabilities would also be transferred.
They argued that the arrangement could address Belgium's legal concerns over the concentration of Russian assets at Euroclear, which holds approximately €185 billion of the total.
The signatories also proposed that the EU compensate member states and private companies for potential losses resulting from the transfer, arguing that such safeguards would not require additional guarantees from individual member states.
The call comes amid continuing disagreements within the EU over how to finance Ukraine's military and budgetary needs.
EU leaders previously failed to reach agreement on using approximately €210 billion in frozen Russian assets to underpin a large loan to Kyiv, largely due to Belgium's objections and its demand for guarantees against potential legal and financial retaliation from Moscow.
Instead, the bloc agreed to raise €90 billion in common debt to finance a loan to Ukraine over 18 months. However, the funding is expected to fall short of Kyiv's requirements.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has requested an additional €70 billion for next year.

European countries fear being sidelined in Russia–Ukraine peace talks but can’t agree on how to secure a seat at the table, FT reports
European countries fear they could be shut out of talks to end Russia’s war with Ukraine, but they cannot agree among themselves on how to secure a seat at the negotiating table, or who should represent their interests and how, the Financial Times reported.
That anxiety has grown since Washington eased sanctions on Moscow and accused Kyiv of being unwilling to end the conflict. European countries worry that, ahead of talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, Washington and Moscow could reach a deal without them on issues that affect European interests, including security guarantees for Russia and restrictions on NATO.
Driven by these concerns, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Vladimir Putin on October 27. The call drew criticism from other European countries because the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had not secured their allies’ support beforehand.
According to the newspaper’s sources — European diplomats and officials — these uncoordinated attempts at contact, and the backlash they triggered, highlight the dilemma facing Europe: how best to convey its interests to Putin and Trump.
“Before we can talk about choosing a representative [for Europe at the talks] we need a chair at the table. Putin doesn’t want to include us, he wants to talk to Trump and so to put [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelensky in a corner,” one senior European diplomat said.
The United States is still involving Europeans in the negotiating process to some extent, the Financial Times reported. Washington and Kyiv have been considering the so-called European troika — the United Kingdom, France, and Germany — as the most likely representatives of Europe at the upcoming talks, but diplomats say that option risks provoking objections from other European countries.
Pentagon officials recently asked several NATO countries to tone down their statements about the Russian threat. The countries that received these requests include the Baltic states — Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia — among others, Reuters reported.
Moscow says there is no need for European involvement. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov, for example, commented on the possible participation of European representatives in the new round of talks:
If they buy plane tickets, fly to Abu Dhabi, and hang around there somewhere, then from time to time the same Ukrainians, or even the same Americans, might report something to them, consult with them, maybe take some points of view into account — in other words, the process there could become more complicated.

Bulgaria Faces Cold, Wet Days Ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:18:00 UTC
00:18:00 KST

Bulgaria Faces Cold, Wet Days Ahead
Meteorologist Petar Yankov has forecast prolonged rainfall, falling temperatures and the first significant snowfall in Bulgaria's mountains, while predicting a return of an "Indian summer" in November, with temperatures reaching 20 degrees, in an interview with Bulgaria ON AIR.
Yankov said the unsettled weather would continue into next week, making the upcoming weekend unsuitable for trips to the mountains or the Black Sea coast.
Rain is expected across different parts of the country over the coming days. Saturday will also bring rain, with showers concentrated mainly in western and central Bulgaria on Sunday.
"Sofia will be the coolest Balkan capital, with maximum temperatures hovering around 9 degrees. In the far southern regions of the country, temperatures will reach 13–14 degrees. Over the weekend, the weather will be unsuitable for outings in the mountains or along the Black Sea coast. In Greece, Sunday will see heavy, torrential rainfall," Yankov said.
Rainfall in Western Bulgaria is expected to reach 10 to 20 liters per square meter on Sunday.
The cold conditions will persist into next week, accompanied by frequent precipitation. At higher elevations, rain will turn to snow, with the first significant accumulation expected in the mountains.
"From Wednesday afternoon, the cloud cover will gradually begin to break. Snow will fall in our mountains, with a snow cover of 10 to 20 cm forming above 2,000 meters, and up to 4-5 cm at an altitude of 1,500 meters. On Musala, temperatures will drop to minus 6 degrees. In populated areas, temperatures will range between 6 and 9–10 degrees. On Tuesday, in the high-altitude western plains, rain may temporarily turn into snow," Yankov said.
The meteorologist also warned that prolonged rainfall would leave roads throughout Bulgaria wet and slippery.
"Drivers should be mindful of slippery road surfaces throughout the country. Those who have switched to winter tires will feel more at ease. For those still using summer tires, I advise reducing speed by 10–15 km/h below the posted limits," he recommended.
Yankov also addressed the conditions for switching on Sofia's heating system, saying the average temperature must stay at 12 degrees Celsius for three consecutive days. He expects this threshold to be met in the coming days.
The first 10 days of November are forecast to bring changeable weather, precipitation and low temperatures. Yankov expects the cold spell to last until November 7, followed by more sunshine and a moderate rise in temperatures.
"During the first ten days of November, the weather will be more unsettled, with periods of precipitation. This cold spell will persist until November 7. By November 10, we expect more sunshine and a rise in temperatures to between 10°C and 12°C," he said.
The improvement is expected to be brief, with another period of heavy rainfall forecast for November 11-13.
A warmer spell is then expected between November 14 and 20, when temperatures could climb to 20 degrees.
"Between November 14 and 20, an 'Indian summer' is expected to make an appearance, with temperatures rising to as high as 20 degrees," Yankov forecast.
The warmer weather is also expected to cause the snow accumulated in the mountains to melt quickly.
"The snow cover will melt quickly in the middle of the month," the meteorologist said.
From November 21 to 25, cloud cover is expected to increase, with frequent rainfall and a slight drop in temperatures. More sunshine is forecast toward the end of the month's final 10-day period.

African football body reverses decision, keeps Africa Cup of Nations on 2-year cycle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:17:07 UTC
00:17:07 KST

Halis Sünnetci
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The Confederation of African Football (CAF) announced Thursday that the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) would continue to be held every two years, reversing a decision last year to switch to a four-year cycle.
CAF's Executive Committee unanimously approved the reversal after reviewing plans to introduce a new Africa Nations League competition.
The governing body said the proposed tournament would take several years to generate enough revenue to support African football development and make its competitions financially self-sustaining.
CAF President Patrice Motsepe said the decision was intended to protect the interests of the continent's football community, its 54 member associations and African players competing for clubs abroad. 
"We were also concerned by the several years required before the proposed new Africa Nations League Pan-African competition, (which was supposed to be identical to the current AFCON and take place Every Two Years), could make the substantial financial and football development contributions for African Football and CAF competitions to be globally competitive and self-supporting," Motsepe said.
The next AFCON will be jointly hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda in 2027, with subsequent editions scheduled for 2028, 2031 and 2033.
Motsepe said the competition would not be held in 2030 to avoid a clash with the FIFA World Cup.
CAF announced plans in December 2025 to move AFCON to a four-year cycle, drawing criticism across African football.
Earlier this month, Motsepe said at a strategy conference in Cabo Verde that the governing body would reconsider the change.

‘The Right to Be Named’: Russians in Amsterdam Remember Victims of Political Repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:16:50 UTC
00:16:50 KST

AMSTERDAM — On a dark October evening in Amsterdam’s Frederiksplein square, around 50 people quietly wait their turn to read out the names of strangers into a microphone.
“Nikolai Khristoforovich Bashlykov. 26 years old. Timber receiver, serviceman. Executed on Dec. 2, 1937.”
“Sabina Savelyevna Bogusevich. 42 years old. Polish. Cook at a sugar factory in the Krasnodar region. Executed on Dec. 14, 1937.”
One by one, participants take a card from a volunteer, read the names into a microphone and step aside. Acquaintances greet each other in hushed voices. Others move quietly around the gathering, photographing the crowd and the flickering candles.
Organizers repeatedly remind them to only photograph people who had given their consent. Many people are afraid of being seen at a public commemoration, even abroad, due to the ongoing threat of repression in Russia, they say.
The gathering was part of Returning the Names, an annual initiative commemorating victims of political repression held every year on Oct. 29.
Established nearly two decades ago to remember people killed during Stalin’s Great Terror, it has since become an occasion to reflect on the relationship between Soviet violence and political repression in present-day Russia.
For years, its main gathering took place at the Solovetsky Stone on Moscow’s Lubyanka Square, just steps from the headquarters used by the Soviet security services and now occupied by the Federal Security Service (FSB).
The event was organized by Memorial, the human rights organization founded to document Soviet political repression. With Memorial now designated an “extremist” organization in Russia, Returning the Names is no longer formally affiliated with it.
Despite this, activists continue to gather to read the victims’ names every Oct. 29. Events took place in more than 100 cities worldwide this year, from Russia’s Irkutsk and Kirov to Melbourne, San Jose and Miami.
In Amsterdam, the commemoration has been organized by writer and historical memory researcher Nikolai Epple since 2022.
“After the Russian experience, it’s surprising,” he told The Moscow Times. “This year, the Dutch police called me just to ask how they could help. It’s very strange and sweet.”
But he lamented the challenges of persuading people to turn out to the event.
“We’re holding it for the fifth time in the Netherlands. Around 50 people always turn up, which feels strange when the diaspora here is so large, around 11,000 people,” Epple said. “I think Russians are still afraid of taking part in any public event. The willingness to do so was systematically stamped out of people over the years.”
Some local Russian-language Telegram channels declined to share announcements for the event, including those aimed at Russians who left after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he said.
“They told us: ‘We’re about culture, not politics’,” he said.
He said he believes this reluctance reflects Russians’ tendency to avoid politics as much as a fear of personal consequences.
For the non-Russian participants who regularly attend Returning the Names, organizers make announcements in English and prepare the name cards in several languages so that people who do not speak Russian can participate.
“Maria Georgiyevna Babek. 41 years old. Slovak. Head of the council of Kazan’s Catholic community. Executed on July 7, 1938,” says a man with a Dutch accent, stumbling slightly over the place names and dates. Those who had already taken their turn stood nearby and listened.
“People here have a strong culture of participating in events like this. Showing solidarity matters to them,” Epple said. “And not just over things happening in their own country. When Navalny was killed, a lot of Dutch people came to the rally that day.”
The gathering took place beside the memorial to Walraven van Hall, a leading figure in the Dutch resistance during World War II. Nearby, candles and photographs formed a memorial to the late Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny beneath a large tree.
“Our history and Dutch history are linked,” he said.
Toward the end of the gathering, Navalny’s name was read aloud.
“Alexei Anatolyevich Navalny. Killed on Feb. 16, 2024, in a penal colony in the settlement of Kharp.”
Returning the Names was traditionally understood in Russia as a memorial event rather than a political protest, Epple said.
“But the fact that it was held right on Lubyanka, of course, gave it immense political significance — an event in memory of victims right in front of the building of the organization responsible for that terror,” he said.
Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, that meaning has become more pronounced.
Last year, the event took place in 150 cities worldwide. The initiative’s decentralized structure means that organizers in each city can choose what they would like to emphasize. Some read only the names of Soviet victims, while others include current political prisoners.
“For us, the crucial thing is to make that direct connection [between past and present] explicit,” Epple said. “Because Soviet terror was never properly examined, reckoned with and condemned, it continues to block any movement toward democracy. Today’s war and today’s terror are a direct consequence of those historical lessons going unlearned.”
Among those waiting to read out the names was Polina, a 37-year-old psychologist who left Russia in 2022 and has lived in Amsterdam for several years.
“Justice is my most important value,” she said, asking to withhold her last name for safety reasons. “Hundreds of thousands of people were executed in Soviet times, and more than 1.5 million died in the camps.”
She said that behind every name was a life, a family, a job and plans that were cut short.
“When I read a name, I give that person back something that was taken from them: the right to be named, rather than remain a number in a case file,” Polina said. “It’s my way of showing that I do not accept this injustice and that we will not forget.”
She agreed with Epple’s belief that remembering the past is inseparable from Russia’s present.
“Unfortunately, those lessons haven’t been learned. Today, Russia once again has thousands of political prisoners, and the sentences keep getting longer,” she said. “We will do everything we can to ensure that the lives swallowed up by the regime are not forgotten.”

The café attraction combines refreshments with close encounters, allowing visitors to observe the animals' behaviour and interact with them through the enclosure fence. With alpacas and llamas sharing the space, the unusual setting has become a place where a family outing can include both a cup of coffee and a meeting with some curious four-legged neighbours.

Washington has been easing pressure on Moscow piece by piece. On 9 October, the Treasury issued a general license allowing sales of Russian diesel, including into the US. A week later, President Trump waived new sanctions under the Graham Act, a Russia sanctions law he had signed on 18 September. Meanwhile, Kyiv is still waiting for the next round of three-way peace talks. Freeing a Kremlin fund now would lift another cost from Moscow before any settlement on Ukraine.
A review in Washington
The fund is run by Kirill Dmitriev, Vladimir Putin’s envoy in talks with Washington. The official said the administration was weighing the application through established procedures, as part of an effort to “improve US-Russia relations and help end the war.”
The official also praised Dmitriev as “a helpful envoy.” Russian officials pushed for delisting during talks on the fund’s role in shipping Russian diesel to the US, people familiar with the negotiations told the NYT. The Treasury, however, held that its 9 October license already let the fund handle diesel transactions, the paper reported.
Talks, according to Moscow
Ushakov described a two-way conversation rather than a review. He said on 28 October that it had been going on for some time and that he did not know the outcome. He pointed in particular to Dmitriev’s active contacts, saying that was why the issue had come up.
Blocked four days into the invasion
The Treasury fully blocked the fund and Dmitriev on 28 February 2022, four days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. At the time, it said the fund was widely considered a slush fund for Putin. The Treasury is handling the new request under its normal process, and the fund will have to prove the grounds for its sanctions no longer apply, people familiar with the process told the NYT.
Russia resumes diesel exports to Türkiye, Brazil, after Trump lifts sanctions on fuel supplies, boosting Moscow’s war revenue – Reuters
Eric Green oversaw Russia policy at the White House National Security Council under President Joe Biden. He told the paper that lifting the sanctions would send a strong message. In his view, Washington would be relaxing its position of not easing sanctions and other costs until a settlement in Ukraine.
This is not Dmitriev’s first push this year. On 7 February, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence had shown him a so-called “Dmitriev package” of US-Russia cooperation, worth about $12 trillion, that Dmitriev presented in the US. In April, he arrived in Washington as a US oil waiver for Russia neared expiry. US delisting would not touch UK and EU restrictions on the fund. But it would reopen American finance to a fund the Treasury said Putin’s inner circle relied on to raise money abroad.

Roundups to force men into the war are surging again in Russia. Families in Omsk and other cities say men are being seized off the streets.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:15:48 UTC
00:15:48 KST

Roundups to force men into the war are surging again in Russia. Families in Omsk and other cities say men are being seized off the streets.
What happened?
Roundups of men forced to sign contracts with the Defense Ministry and then sent to fight in Ukraine have become more frequent again in Russia.
The situation in Omsk has drawn widespread attention. On October 27, opposition activists from the Omsk Civic Association flagged reviews of the Sirius-55 military recruitment center on the mapping service 2GIS. Many relatives of local men have posted complaints there, saying the men are being picked up off the streets, subjected to violence, and prevented from contacting anyone. Journalists from the investigative outlet iStories examined the complaints and found that the first accounts appeared in the spring, but there are now far more. Similar accounts have also appeared in comments on local news websites — for example, under an August article on the subject published by NGS55.
The current wave of roundups extends beyond Omsk. Timofey Vaskin, head of the legal department at the School of Conscripts, told Novaya Gazeta Europe that rights advocates are receiving similar complaints from dozens of regions. The news outlet Verstka, for example, reported similar complaints from 34 regions, including the Arkhangelsk, Kemerovo, and Novosibirsk regions. Other organizations helping men in Russia have received similar accounts.
The surge in complaints shows that the practice of forcing men en masse to sign contracts, which began in Penza in June, is continuing.
Are the current roundups any different from those the authorities carried out in Penza and other cities over the summer?
Yes and no.
It’s hard to compare the current roundups with those in Moscow, for example. In the capital, officials detain specific conscripts to send them into compulsory military service.
In Penza, by contrast, they grabbed “everyone in sight,” according to Artyom Klyga, head of the legal department at the Movement of Conscientious Objectors. That resembles recent accounts from Omsk and other regions.
The roundups also share a purpose. Both in Penza over the summer and in Omsk this fall, detained men have been pressured to sign military contracts. Contract soldiers are now the Russian military’s main source of new personnel: They make up the bulk of those sent into the combat zone and killed at the front. Roundups are among the methods the authorities use to keep recruits coming.
There is a difference, too. In Penza, detained men were mostly taken to police stations and could then be taken straight to a military unit. In Omsk, they are first sent to the Sirius recruitment center for contract soldiers. Experts say this intermediate stop may give detainees time to seek help. While being processed at Sirius or a similar facility, they may still be able to contact loved ones or lawyers.
But having a large recruitment center for contract soldiers in a city may itself encourage larger roundups. The Movement of Conscientious Objectors puts it this way:
Sirius-55 is one of Russia’s first specialized centers of this size. It’s unlikely they built it to stand empty. So we expect detentions in Omsk to continue.
It’s too early to say much about other details. Lawyers working on these cases don’t have enough information to say exactly who is being picked up, how it happens, which cities will see more cases, or what the chances are of getting loved ones out.
But it doesn’t hurt to know some basic safety rules in case you’re detained.
How can men in Russia protect themselves?
Here are the main recommendations. We originally compiled them during the roundups in Penza and have now expanded them:
Put together a support group. If you think you’re at risk, make arrangements with several people you trust who are ready to act quickly if necessary.
Have a power of attorney notarized. You need to do this in advance. The document will allow your loved ones to represent you, hire lawyers, and submit requests and complaints to government agencies.
Get a spare basic cellphone with a keypad and save important contacts on it. This will let you stay in touch even if your main smartphone is confiscated, so you can seek help from loved ones, lawyers, rights advocates, and relevant government agencies.
Remember that signing a contract is voluntary, and don’t sign anything. Be clear on this: No one has the right to force you into military service. To feel more confident, read the federal law “On Military Duty and Military Service,” which sets out all the basic rules.
Turn on your camera and audio recorder. If you’re detained, record everything the officers do. Say the time, address, and the officers’ full names and ranks aloud as you record. If possible, post the recordings online — they will be crucial evidence that you were forced to sign a contract.
Flood the authorities with complaints. You or your support group should write to the Investigative Committee, the military prosecutor’s office, the Defense Ministry, and human rights commissioners. You can also file lawsuits to challenge the officers’ unlawful actions.
If intense pressure does lead you to sign a contract, try to leave the place where you signed it immediately.

This is the hard lesson from Israel’s election: to stop national populists, you can’t play by gentlemen’s rules | Jonathan Freedland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:12:57 UTC
00:12:57 KST

It’s less an election result than a philosophical puzzle: what happens when a win contains a loss, a loss contains a win and the two collide? That’s the question posed by the confused and confusing outcome of this week’s Israeli election, one that, despite its murky uncertainty, offers clear, sharp lessons – both for that country and for those locked in combat with nationalist populists across the globe.
Start with the result that has simultaneously handed Benjamin Netanyahu a devastating defeat and a strong chance of staying on as prime minister, extending a run that has seen him lead Israel, on and off, for more than 19 of the past 30 years. The defeat is clear enough. At a stroke, his parliamentary majority was wiped out. Before Tuesday, the parties that together comprised his ruling coalition controlled 68 of the Knesset’s 120 seats: that tally has now shrunk to just 53, far short of the 61 seats needed for power. That’s a loss in anybody’s language.
And yet, Netanyahu does not look or sound like a man defeated. That’s because he knows that while the parties arrayed against him won many more seats than he did – 67 to his 53 – their chances of forming a government are slim. If they fail, one or two of them might peel away and enter a so-called national-unity government – under Netanyahu as PM – or there will have to be fresh elections, ones from which, most analysts agree, Netanyahu would emerge stronger.
The opposition’s problem is not arithmetical. It goes much deeper. Put simply, a big chunk of the anti-Netanyahu seats were won by parties that chiefly represent the one in five Israeli citizens who are Palestinian. This was the big twist of Tuesday’s election, a huge surge in turnout for what Israelis refer to as the Arab parties. Usually, far more Jewish than Arab Israelis participate in the country’s elections, but this year that pattern was flipped: turnout in Palestinian communities inside Israel hit 80%. The result is a record total of 19 seats for Arab-led parties. The anti-Netanyahu bloc cannot form a government without them. In today’s Israel, Palestinian politicians are the kingmakers.
On paper, the next step might look straightforward enough. All Netanyahu’s Jewish opponents need do is team up with their Arab colleagues and they can send the PM packing. But such an alliance would mark a watershed in Israeli history. It would mean breaking a taboo that has endured, with only fleeting exceptions, since the founding of the state, a taboo rooted in mutual suspicion.
On the one hand, Israel’s Jewish-led parties have long shunned the mainly Arab parties because the latter identify as anti- or non-Zionist, meaning they reject Israel’s self-definition as a Jewish state. For that same reason, Arab-led parties have maintained a boycott, refusing to legitimate the Israeli state by participating in its government.
In 2021, a short-lived “government of change” broke the taboo by including in its ranks Ra’am, an Islamist party regarded, improbably enough, as the most moderate of the Arab groupings. But after the Hamas massacres of 7 October 2023, the taboo was restored – and hardened. Netanyahu cast Palestinian-Israeli politicians as an enemy within, as tacit allies of the Hamas killers, a framing buttressed by a crude anti-Arab racism voiced most explicitly by his coalition allies – the likes of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich – and which sought to delegitimise Israel’s entire Arab minority.
This was Netanyahu’s core message throughout the campaign: you can’t trust my opponents because, when the moment comes, they will sit with “the Arabs”. In recent days, he and his allies have doubled down on that message, claiming high Palestinian turnout means that “the Arabs are stealing the election” – rather than merely exercising their democratic rights – and, on Thursday, alleging that Qatar paid Palestinian-Israeli citizens to vote, thereby rendering the entire result void.
Instead of challenging Netanyahu’s framing, and insisting that the vote of every citizen, Arab or Jewish, is of equal worth, most of the main opposition parties – Yair Golan’s Democrats were the exception – bowed to it, pledging that they would not forge a coalition with the largely Arab parties, and certainly not with any group more radical than Ra’am. Now they find themselves in a bind. On their own, the Jewish-led opposition cannot form a government. Unless they somehow manage to lure defectors from Netanyahu’s bloc – perhaps one or both of the ultra-Orthodox parties – even Ra’am’s support won’t be enough to reach the magic number of 61. They need Arab partners – and probably several of them.
This, then, is the big lesson for Israel. That group that has long opposed Netanyahu – Jewish-Israelis who despise a PM on trial for corruption, who has mounted serial assaults on Israel’s institutions, including the supreme court, and brought isolation, if not pariah status, upon the country – are now confronted with a fact that has long been true but which they have preferred not to see: that they are a minority in the land they once dominated. As Aluf Benn, editor of the liberal daily Haaretz, told me: “The Jewish vote is predominantly rightwing in Israel and has been for decades.”
That means the Jewish Israeli opposition cannot win alone. This week stands as proof, because this was their perfect opportunity. Netanyahu was at his lowest ebb, the leader on whose watch the most calamitous day in Israeli history took place, the leader who promised to destroy Hamas in Gaza, but who succeeded only in turning that place into a ruin, killing tens of thousands and, in the process, destroying Israel’s standing in the world. He faced in Gadi Eisenkot, his lead challenger, a decorated former general rooted in the Mizrahi working class, a man universally regarded as honest and decent, a bereaved father whose own son fell in the Gaza war – a man, in other words, who might have been designed to appeal to the very voters who for so long have been beyond the opposition’s reach. And yet none of that was enough to win.
The only way the opposition can succeed is by making common cause with their Palestinian fellow citizens, just as Democrats in the US – who have not won a majority of the white vote since 1964 – could never win the presidency without the support of Black Americans. No one should underestimate the scale of the task, which requires a deep cultural shift as much as a political one. It should have been the work of decades, rather than a panicked scramble in a few rushed weeks of coalition horse-trading. It demands a reshaping of Israeli society, breaking a pattern of systemic discrimination and inequality within the country that has existed since the founding of the state (to say nothing of the post-1967 occupied territories where, of course, millions of Palestinians have no vote at all in Israeli elections). That task was always essential, but this week has confirmed that, if the right’s lock on power is ever to be broken, it can be delayed no longer.
Much of this is peculiar to the unique political terrain of Israel. But there are broader lessons for all those fighting nationalist populism, whether that be Donald Trump in next week’s US midterms, Marine Le Pen in France or Nigel Farage in Britain. First, don’t accept the terms laid down by the other side: that was the cardinal error made by Netanyahu’s challengers. Second, mere opposition and criticism is not enough. The nationalist populists will always tell a compelling story; you have to tell an equally compelling one of your own. And, last, you need to be every bit as determined as they are. Too often you play by gentlemen’s rules, when those you are fighting are anything but gentlemen. Netanyahu is without shame and will do anything – cross every line, cut any deal – to keep power. The opponents of such a man will prevail only if they show an equal resolve in seizing it.
- Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

FACTBOX - With all votes counted, how Israel’s legislative election results compare with previous vote

- Voter turnout reaches 77.9%, highest since 1999
- Final vote count gives Netanyahu-led bloc 53 seats, Eisenkot’s bloc 48, while Arab parties secure 19 seats, nearly doubling their tally from the 2022 election
- Final official results to be presented to President Herzog on Nov. 4, once Central Elections Committee completes review of reported errors, complaints
Israel's Central Elections Committee (CEC) released the final results of the 2026 legislative elections early Friday, with neither bloc securing the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset and the formation of a government.
The final official results are expected to be presented to President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday, Nov. 4, once the committee has completed its review of any reported errors and complaints.
Herzog will then meet with the leaders of each party, who will recommend a candidate to form the next government.
Voter turnout reached 77.9%, the highest since 1999, with 5,716,665 eligible voters casting ballots. 
Pro-Netanyahu bloc
The final results show Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party winning 27 seats, down from the 32 it secured in the 2022 parliamentary elections.
The ultra-Orthodox alliance United Torah Judaism, headed by Ya’akov Asher, and far-right Otzma Yehudit, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, also secured seven seats each.
They were followed by the ultra-Orthodox Shas party, led by Aryeh Deri, and the far-right Religious Zionism party, headed by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, with each securing six seats.
Shas’s tally marked a decline from the 11 seats it won in the previous election.
In 2022, the Religious Zionist alliance, comprising the Religious Zionism Party, Otzma Yehudit and Noam, led by Avi Maoz, won 14 seats. In the 2026 election, the Religious Zionism Party and Otzma Yehudit secured a combined 13 seats, while Noam failed to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold. 
Jewish opposition bloc
The Yashar party, led by Netanyahu's main challenger and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, won 21 seats.
The results give the Together alliance, formed by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid and their respective parties, Bennett 2026 and Yesh Atid, a total of 12 seats -- down from the 24 seats won by Yesh Atid alone in the 2022 elections.
The Democrats, a left-wing party chaired by Yair Golan, secured eight seats, doubling its four-seat tally in 2022.
The Democrats were followed by Yisrael Beiteinu, a right-wing opposition party led by former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman, which secured seven seats, up one from the previous vote. 
Arab parties
Arab parties — including the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am) — which are neither aligned with the governing coalition nor the Jewish opposition bloc, secured a combined 19 seats, with 11 of them going to the Joint List and eight to Ra’am.
This marks a significant increase from the 10 seats won by the Joint List and Ra’am combined in the 2022 elections, when each secured five seats. 
Coalition formation
The results give the pro-Netanyahu bloc 53 seats, compared with 48 for the Jewish opposition bloc and 19 for the Arab parties.
The pro-Netanyahu parties, which make up the current governing coalition, held 68 seats in the outgoing Knesset, a considerable decline from their previous total.
The Arab parties — the Joint List and Ra’am — secured a record 19 seats, nearly doubling their combined 10 seats in the outgoing Knesset.
The Arab factions' support would have been enough to give the opposition bloc a comfortable majority. However, most Jewish opposition parties, including Eisenkot’s bloc, had previously ruled out cooperation with the Arab parties.
The exception was Yair Golan, leader of The Democrats, who urged Eisenkot’s bloc to work with the Arab-majority parties to oust Netanyahu.
The new Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on Nov. 10, regardless of the progress of coalition talks, which are expected to be difficult and could last more than two months.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot asserted that each would be the one to form the next government, despite neither bloc being close to the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
Tuesday’s vote also marked Israel’s first election since the Israeli army launched its war on Gaza in October 2023, in which more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 others wounded.

News Analysis: Warming oceans pose mounting risks to coral species, reef ecosystems
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:10:10 CST
00:10:10 KST

LONDON, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Warming oceans pose mounting risks to coral species and reef ecosystems, recent global assessments have warned, raising concerns for marine biodiversity and coastal livelihoods.
An assessment of 892 reef-building coral species found that 340 were threatened with extinction, according to a study published in Nature in October.
Marine ecologist and co-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) SSC Coral Specialist Group Francoise Cabada-Blanco is one of the lead authors of the study. She told Xinhua that species extinction and ecosystem collapse are distinct but interconnected risks.
The former concerns the risk of losing individual coral species, while the latter concerns whole reef systems collapsing, with living coral largely replaced by algae, rubble and other organisms, she said.
A separate IUCN assessment released on Oct. 22 classified 122 of 127 shallow-water coral reef ecosystems, or 96 percent, as Critically Endangered when projected climate change was included.
Under a scenario projected by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, marine heatwaves will become so frequent over the next 50 years that reefs may lack sufficient recovery time, IUCN explained.
However, the classification does not mean these ecosystems have already collapsed. Most still retain living coral and continue to function as reef ecosystems. "There is still time to act, but the window is closing," IUCN said.
For Cabada-Blanco, the growing frequency of bleaching is particularly worrying. The phenomenon, whereby corals eject algae and can eventually die, is caused by warming waters. "We are now moving towards near-annual bleaching, which leaves no recovery window at all."
The study published in Nature combined coral-cover trends, projections of severe bleaching, and biological traits affecting vulnerability. Nevertheless, its underlying data ended in 2020, before the global bleaching event of 2023-2025.
Cabada-Blanco said conditions had most likely worsened since 2020, as bleaching events have become more widespread and longer-lasting.
LOSSES BEYOND THE REEF
Coral reefs occupy less than 1 percent of the ocean floor but support around a quarter of all marine fish species, according to IUCN. Their contribution to food supplies, tourism and coastal protection makes reef degradation a concern whose implications reach far beyond conservation.
Coral reef decline is depriving countless species of the food, shelter and breeding grounds they depend on, said Grethel Aguilar, IUCN Director General, noting that it is also threatening the safety and livelihoods of coastal communities, and undermining key economic sectors such as fisheries, aquaculture and coastal tourism.
"Reef-building corals are ecosystem engineers," Cabada-Blanco said. "When they die, reefs flatten, and the fish and invertebrates that depend on them lose their homes." Small-scale reef fisheries often feed local families, she said.
Regional findings show that even reefs that appear healthier reefs face substantial risks. In East Asia, 22 out of 25 ecoregions are under threat, despite comparatively high coral cover. All 25 are Critically Endangered when future climate projections are included, IUCN said.
Cabada-Blanco said overall coral cover could remain stable while sensitive species were replaced by tougher ones. "Coral cover alone can therefore mask a real loss of diversity, and it may hide how close a reef is to a sudden decline."
The Nature study provided a warning over that vulnerability: 191 of 279 Indo-Pacific species in the Acroporidae family, which includes branching and plating corals that shape reef structure, are classified as Endangered.
For communities relying on reefs, recovery could also come too late. Cabada-Blanco said reef structures could rebuild over centuries, but not on timescales relevant to people depending on them today. "Some losses would be irreversible. Extinction is permanent."
ACTION STILL MATTERS
IUCN said that, based only on observed changes over the past 50 years, 24 percent of the assessed reef ecosystems would be Critically Endangered, compared with 96 percent when future climate projections were included. The contrast highlights how strongly future warming influences the outlook.
"Emissions reductions come first. No local action can protect reefs from unlimited warming," Cabada-Blanco said. Every tenth of a degree of warming avoided would help retain more coral species and reef function, she underlined.
Local pressures also affect reefs' ability to withstand heat. IUCN found disrupted ecological relationships among corals, algae and fish in 63 percent of assessed ecosystems. Overfishing, pollution and sediment can weaken the balance needed for recovery.
Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the global IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment, urged governments to cut emissions while keeping coastal waters clean and making fishing sustainable.
Scaling up restoration and improving coral heat tolerance are important areas of research, Cabado-Blanco said, but warned that a single heatwave could erase years of restoration work if warming continues. "Restoration is a complement, not a substitute," she stressed.
According to IUCN, reefs in areas such as the Northern Red Sea, Papua New Guinea, and Bermuda have maintained living coral and a healthy ecological balance despite repeated heatwaves, making them priorities for protection.
Scientific cooperation is another essential part of the response. Cabada-Blanco said that although her team's assessment involved more than 60 experts, only 15 of the 892 coral species had population data across their ranges. Open data and taxonomic research would improve future assessments, she emphasized.
David Obura, Cabada-Blanco's fellow co-chair of the IUCN SSC Coral Specialist Group, said that major knowledge gaps must be addressed alongside urgent efforts to reduce the pressures that are driving the decline of species and ecosystems.
"Reefs have repeatedly shown they can recover when given the chance," Cabada-Blanco said. "Our task is to give them that chance." ■
