Ukrainian photographer Sasha Kurmaz shortlisted for prestigious Deutsche Börse Prize – photos
Ukrainian photographer Sasha Kurmaz has been shortlisted for the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize 2027, one of the most prestigious international awards in contemporary photography.
Source: the prize's website
Details: Kurmaz was nominated for his photo book Red Horse, published by Éditions Images Vevey in November 2025. It is a visual diary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The photographer began the project in 2022. It combines documentary photos with personal notes, as well as materials and images found on the streets. The book was designed by graphic designer Nicolas Polli and runs to around 800 pages.
"Red Horse is a powerful reflection on how war transforms our lives and collective memory, and on what it means to create art in times of armed conflict," the foundation said.
The other artists shortlisted alongside Kurmaz are:
- Iranian documentary photographer Hoda Afshar, for her exhibition Performing the Invisible at the Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac in Paris
- Canadian photographer Lotus L. Kang, for her installation The face of desire is loss at the Bulgari Pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale in Italy
- Italian artist and photographer Salvatore Vitale, for his exhibition SABOTAGE at Photo Elysée in Lausanne, Switzerland.
"The compelling shortlist examines how images shape our understanding of bodies, war, labour and power. Together, the shortlisted artists investigate desire and memory; the human costs of the digital economy; surviving in times of conflict; and the politics of looking," the foundation said.
The winner will be announced on 29 April 2027 and will receive £30,000. The other shortlisted artists will each receive £5,000.
An exhibition of the shortlisted projects will be held at The Photographers' Gallery in London from 10 March to 6 June 2027. It will then move to the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation in Eschborn, near Frankfurt, where it will run from 19 June to 26 September 2027.
The Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize was established by The Photographers' Gallery in London in 1996. It recognises and supports innovative approaches to contemporary photography that reflect current social, political and philosophical issues.
Sasha Kurmaz began his artistic career with graffiti writing in the early 2000s. By 2010, he was a member of the informal Kyiv-based group Psia Krev.
Since 2010, he has worked on independent art projects and photography. Since 2011, he has also collaborated with the Viktor Marushchenko School of Photography.
Kurmaz's artistic practice combines various media and genres, particularly photography, video, performance and interventions in public spaces.
His projects explore the relationship between individuals, society and power, questioning mechanisms of control, representation and visibility.
Earlier, the photographer won the 2026 Kraszna-Krausz Photography Book Award.

====================================================================================================

The Heartbreaking True Story of War and Football in The Mosquito Bowl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:09:16 UTC
00:09:16 KST

In the wet heat of a Guadalcanal afternoon on Christmas Eve 1944, two regiments of the 6th Marine Division met on a football field of packed earth and broken coral. They had come to settle a question argued over beer: Which of them had the better team? The island where the Pacific War’s first major American offensive was fought had been quiet for nearly two years, a staging ground of tents and supply depots where men trained and waited and swatted at the insects that gave the island’s Armed Forces Radio network its name. The game was a serious to-do: There were printed programs, numbered T-shirts, goalposts the Marines built themselves, and an announcer whose call went out over the Mosquito Network to men on ships and islands across the Pacific. At least 1,500 Marines lined the field, some with money on the outcome. Neither team scored. Three months later, the division sailed for Okinawa, an island on Japan’s doorstep, where 15 of the 65 men who played that day were killed.
That game is the short reprieve at the heart of Peter Berg’s The Mosquito Bowl, in select theaters Oct. 30 and arriving Nov. 25 on Netflix. Directed by Berg, who wrote the screenplay with Mark L. Smith, the film adapts Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Buzz Bissinger’s book and follows four of those players from the Saturday afternoons when the best of their lives still seemed to lie ahead, through weeks of training that could not prepare them for what came next, to one of the bloodiest battles of World War II. Nicholas Galitzine plays John McLaughry, alongside Tom Francis as Dave Schreiner, Bill Skarsgård as Bob Bauman, and Ray Nicholson as Tony Butkovich. Three of those men would die on Okinawa. The fourth would live to 90.
The stadiums give way to boot camp, boot camp to the reef at Tarawa, Tarawa to the long crossing toward Okinawa, where the familiar idea of victory becomes a contest with no whistle, no clock, and survival as the only trophy. What the film is after, once the pageantry is stripped away, is that moment of recognition: young men who thought they had been sent to win learning what they have really been sent to do.
Berg has made films (and a massively popular TV show) about football and films about war. Here the same young men must do both. “They got out there and very quickly found that it wasn’t a game,” Berg tells TIME. “They weren’t really qualified for it, but they were going to do their very best. The tragedy is the death of that innocence.”
The lives before the uniforms
What the four men shared, after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941, was an assumption. Their country had been attacked, and young men like them were expected to go to war.
Schreiner, from Lancaster, Wisconsin, had twice been named an All-American in his career with the University of Wisconsin; in 1942 he was named the Big Ten’s most valuable player, and the Detroit Lions drafted him. The letters he left behind, now at the Wisconsin Historical Society, show a more private side of the star athlete. He was engaged to Odette Hendrickson, wrote to her and to his parents constantly and judged himself without mercy. “Tightly, tightly woven,” Bissinger says of the man. Francis found in him a care and a vulnerability that colored everything, and a mind that would not rest. “He overthinks everything, but then as soon as one of his brothers comes to him and isn’t quite there, he just can find a way to be like, ‘I’ve got you,’” the actor says.
Schreiner had options. “Dave could have gotten out of it because of who he was,” Bissinger says. “He could have easily been a phys ed instructor somewhere at one of the bases in the United States, and he said, ‘No, I got to go. My friends are going. I’m just sitting around doing nothing, and I can’t live with that.’”
The man who kept Schreiner loose was his teammate Bob Bauman, a tackle from Harvey, Ill. Bauman’s father died when he was a boy, and he grew up holding his family together. “Bob was more happy-go-lucky,” Bissinger says. When Schreiner tightened up, Bauman’s advice, as the author renders it, came down to a single line: “Dave, don’t overthink, Dave.” The two enlisted within months of each other and would serve in the same company.
Butkovich was the son of Croatian immigrants who settled in a coal town in central Illinois. He played two seasons at Illinois before the Marines sent him to Purdue, where he rushed for 833 yards in seven games in 1943. The team went undefeated, but the Marines called him away before the season ended, and he cried in the locker room over having to go. The Cleveland Rams made him a first-round pick in 1944, and he kept up a pen-pal correspondence with a 9-year-old fan. “He was really on this high level,” says Nicholson of Butkovich’s stature as a football star. “But at the same time, he was a mama’s boy.”
The oldest of the four, McLaughry was the only one already out of college. His father, Tuss McLaughry, coached at Brown, and John captained his father’s team in 1939 before playing a season for the New York Giants. He also painted. “Steady, solid, almost a Renaissance man,” Bissinger says. Galitzine was drawn to both McLaughry’s intellect and his artistic sensibility. He and Berg discussed McLaughry’s “ability to intellectualize things and how that kind of dissipates, given the trauma and the grotesque violence that he sees,” the actor recalls. What remains is a sense of duty more immediate than politics. “The loyalty you have really is not even to your nation necessarily, or to the men who send you to war, but it’s to your brothers who are in the foxhole next to you,” Galitzine says.
By the autumn of 1944, the war had brought all four to Guadalcanal. Though the film has them all in the same regiment, in reality, Schreiner, Bauman, and McLaughry were officers in the 4th Marines, and Butkovich served in the 29th, the other regiment on the field that Christmas Eve.
The game they made for themselves
Bissinger first learned of the Mosquito Bowl by chance, through a passing mention he found while working on another book. “It sounded ludicrous to me and totally unimaginable,” he says. A program survived, with both teams’ rosters, and then he learned that all but one of the men on them had since died. The lives behind those names emerged from what their families had kept: letters, report cards, pictures drawn in childhood.
The game stemmed from an argument. The former college players in the 29th were sure they could beat the former college players in the 4th. The rosters held three All-Americans, seven former captains, and close to 20 men who had been drafted by NFL teams or would go on to play in the league. By December, the regiments had drilled for months, and the drilling had gone stale; men were getting antsy, Bissinger says, and antsy men “get this thousand-yard stare.” The division’s commander, Major General Lemuel Shepherd, was looking for a way to lift their spirits. “When morale flags, Marines get worried,” Bissinger explains, reconstructing the general’s reasoning. “They preoccupy themselves with death, and we need some diversion.” Shepherd approved the game, and the Marines worked hard to make it resemble the real thing. “This was about joy,” Bissinger says. “It was about doing something that they loved, that for many of them would be the last thing they would ever do that they loved.”
Little of the game itself survives: the date, the printed program, a few photographs, and a final score of 0-0. The men wore T-shirts and cut-off dungarees. Nobody stuck to the intended mode of touch football for long, and the coral in the dirt drew blood. What matters about the Mosquito Bowl is not anything that happened on the field but that it happened at all, an afternoon in which the war paused and these men got to be what they had been raised to be. “The football of it all never really mattered. I think it wasn’t about who scored what, what tackle here, who had this many rushing yards,” Berg says. “It must have given them an opportunity in the middle of this descent into hell to stop, to get out of hell, to be free again, to be young again, and just play a game. That’s what kind of hooked me on Buzz’s book, and that’s what we tried to recreate.”
In the film, the game plays as a respite, beautiful and painful at once: everything they get back is exactly what the war will take. Most of the plays are lost, and Berg is untroubled by it. “I don’t even know what the score of the game is in our movie. I truly don’t know,” he says. “You ask me who won. I don’t know. Was it a tie? I think so. Did they have fun? Yes.”
There would be no rematch. On March 15, 1945, the division sailed from Guadalcanal, by way of the Navy anchorage at Ulithi, for Okinawa.
What Okinawa took
On the morning of April 1, 1945, Easter Sunday, the Americans came ashore on the western beaches of Okinawa, 350 miles south of mainland Japan, in the largest landing of the Pacific War. The defenders did not meet them at the beaches; they had dug into the ridges and limestone caves of the island’s southern third and waited. The 6th Marine Division swept north, cleared the island’s northern reaches in three weeks, then turned around and marched south.
The rains came in late May, and for days they did not stop. The roads dissolved, supplies went forward on men’s backs, and the wounded came back the same way. The terraced hills were cut with caves and family tombs the Japanese had turned into firing positions, so that an advance of a few hundred yards could last an entire day of sealing holes with dynamite and flame. Civilians hid in the same caves the soldiers fought from, and many died in them too. By late June, more than 12,000 Americans were dead or missing and nearly three times as many wounded. The Japanese defenders, told not to surrender, mostly did not. The Okinawans are the ones no one can count; estimates of the civilian dead run from about 94,000 to more than 140,000. The Cornerstone of Peace at the island’s southern tip carries more than 240,000 names, soldiers and civilians from every side, and names are still being added.
The worst of it came at a hill the Marines called Sugar Loaf. It stood only some 50 feet high, but it sat between the division and Naha, the island’s capital, and Japanese guns covered it from three directions. It changed hands again and again, and in the 10 days before the Marines finally held it, on May 18, more than 2,600 men from the division were killed or wounded. Three days before the hill fell, George Murphy, the former captain of Notre Dame, who had played in the Mosquito Bowl the previous Christmas Eve, was leading a platoon of the 29th Marines on its slopes.
As Bissinger tells it, Murphy was ordered to make another assault and protested. “We don’t have enough hand grenades,” he said. He would fight for his country, but this was a death assignment. “The captain said, ‘I don’t give a sh-t. You got to go up there,’” Bissinger says. The Army’s official history of the campaign tells it slightly differently. In that version, it was Murphy who asked to fall back and his captain who refused: the hill was to be held, whatever the cost. Murphy brought his men down anyway, through the mortar smoke. He stopped for one of the wounded on the way, and a fragment killed him there. Only 11 of his platoon’s 60 men were left. Bissinger, who refused to soften the book’s combat, puts it plainly: “War is not about glory. War is not about heroism. War is about death.”
Butkovich had been dead for a month by then. He was killed on April 18, during the division’s push through the north of the island. He had been on Okinawa less than three weeks. He was 24, the first of the four to die.
Bauman and Schreiner were still paired up. On the morning of June 4, the 4th Marines landed from the sea on the Oroku Peninsula, southwest of Naha. Bauman had been wounded in April and returned to the front. On June 6, his captain went forward with a scouting party, and Company A of the 4th Marines was Bauman’s to lead. He did not lead it long: a Japanese machine gun on the high ground nearby opened fire, and Bauman was killed. Schreiner, a platoon leader in the same company, had two more weeks to live.
There is no agreed-upon account of Schreiner’s final patrol. By June 20, the Japanese defense had collapsed into the island’s southern tip, and the Marines were clearing the last pockets of resistance there. Schreiner was mortally wounded on patrol. Accounts collected by Terry Frei, a chronicler of Schreiner’s Wisconsin team, differ on how: some cite grenade fragments, others a sniper or Japanese soldiers who appeared to surrender before opening fire. He died the following day, June 21, as the battle was drawing to a close. Japan announced its surrender less than two months later. McLaughry, whose platoon of self-propelled guns was supporting Schreiner’s battalion that day, was told at the time that a sniper had shot his friend, and later heard that the bullet had lodged in his spine.
McLaughry fought through all of it and lived. He came home to his wife, raised three children, led the football programs at three colleges, the last of them Brown, and kept painting, but the war stayed with him.
Bringing the men back
Bissinger never met any of the four, though his father, a rifleman in the 4th Marines, fought on Okinawa and never talked about it. “Can you make guys come alive you’ve never met, and never will meet?” he says. He is candid about how he chose them to tell this story: “I picked those people because they had the most readily accessible material.” The McLaughrys kept everything, down to letters John wrote at 4. Schreiner had a niece. Butkovich had a cousin, still living when Bissinger was writing. “Tony had really nothing, so I compiled as much as I could,” he says. “But I felt he had to be in there, particularly since he was the best of the football players.” Their stories reach only as far as their families, and the war, allowed.
The book found its way to the screen through family. Berg and Bissinger are cousins, and The Mosquito Bowl is the second of Bissinger’s books Berg has adapted, after Friday Night Lights. The book follows a wide cast of Marines through several battles; a two-hour film could not, and Berg took his cuts to its author. “I presented my kind of outline to Buzz. I’m like, how would you feel if I did this?” he recalls. “He thought about it, and he said, ‘Do it.’” The film takes dramatic license in places, including a grudge between Schreiner and Butkovich and a battle at Tarawa, the bloody November 1943 assault on a Pacific atoll, where none of the four fought; Marines stranded on a reef under fire was the first image Berg knew the film had to contain. “There were some areas in which Pete had to create his own narrative, and that was going to veer from the book. But that doesn’t bother me, because the essence was there,” Bissinger says.
Berg found his own way in on the ground. He walked Okinawa’s battlefields with Marines stationed there, and came away ready to write.
On set, Berg gave up some of the control a director usually keeps. “I like not being in complete control and allowing something to grow out of that,” he says. Filming in Australia, that meant a director who kept noticing terrain no one had checked. Wildlife handlers cleared the ground before the actors lay in it, Galitzine says, because the local snakes could kill. Berg would look past the cleared area to some unvetted cliff and announce that the actors should climb it. “We just did it,” Galitzine says. Crawling through the Australian bush made the four actors feel as though they were on an adventure together. “It really was an exercise in trust, in a lot of ways.”
Berg had never shot anything like the reef landing. The production put stuntmen, then actors, then camera operators into heavy Australian surf. “You can drown in that surf,” Berg says. “They call that ‘washing machine.’ You’re in the ‘washing machine.’ Think about doing that while you’re being shot at.” Elsewhere, a sand quarry near the coast stood in for the battlefield below Shuri Castle, the Japanese command post at the heart of the island’s defenses. Production designer Philip Ivey scattered scorched books, broken dishes, and clothing across it, the wreckage of ordinary life. The resulting film is intimate and enormous at once, the camera close enough to see fear, with cutaways from the ground to the planet itself that set the men’s suffering inside a scale too large to take in.
In the editing room, the question became how much football the film needed. Early versions spent considerably more time on the game. The finished film instead begins with McLaughry after his experience in combat, before going back to the men’s football years. “The football is there to serve a purpose, and that’s to illustrate that these men were living it up. They were at a good spot in their lives,” Berg says. “So I felt like we needed just enough football to tell that story, and then move on.” The actors trained for much more than made the final cut. Before cameras rolled, they spent weeks in training that was part football practice, part Marine boot camp, each actor drilled at a position, enabling the production to make limited use of stunt doubles.
Four actors, four men
Each of the four actors went looking for the man he was playing, and each found him somewhere different. Francis found his in a joke. The Mosquito Bowl was his first film, and early in the shoot he went to Skarsgård with a stage actor’s questions: Where do I look, what do I do, how do I make it all happen? Skarsgård’s answer was, “You’re overthinking, Schreiner.” Francis heard the character in it. “I was like, this is the man,” he recalls. Skarsgård leaned on the one fact that set Bauman and Schreiner apart from the others. They played beside each other at Wisconsin, joined the Marines a few months apart, and went to war together. “Tom can always come to me and lean on me, and I could always come to lean on him, both as actors, but also as our characters,” Skarsgård says. “The way that they worked was that Bob could pull Dave out.”
Nicholson found his in letters. He read Butkovich as a performer whose confidence was real and whose tenderness ran underneath it. “Once they go through this experience, that version of Tony Butkovich is forever gone,” he says. A five-page handwritten letter Nicholson sent Berg, one the director calls among the “most beautiful” he has ever received, showed him the passion he was casting for. Butkovich’s letters to a young fan, meanwhile, gave the actor a way into the man. Nicholson wrote letters of his own to his father, actor Jack Nicholson, who would have been about that boy’s age during the war. “How do you be someone’s hero?” he asks. “What is that like?” Purdue also sent him restored film of Butkovich with the ball. By chance it came on the anniversary of Butkovich’s death, and Nicholson watched it by himself with the lights off, feeling as if the two of them had somehow met.
Skarsgård went to the place itself. While researching the role, he spent three days on Okinawa with Marine guides, and at the end he asked them to take him to where Bauman was shot. It is in Naha now, a residential neighborhood with a playground and a convenience store. “I’m standing where he took his last breath,” Skarsgård recalls, describing the “immense amount of responsibility” he felt. He was struck by the unlikely connection between his own life and Bauman’s. “Here I am, a Swedish actor, 80 years after this happened, and I’m thinking about this man, and I’m connected with this man, and I feel just so much gratitude towards him.”
Galitzine carried a different weight, the survivor’s, and it came into sharper focus toward the end of filming. The production shot the last scene for Nicholson, Francis, and Skarsgård on a boat, and when it was done, they wrapped and he did not, because McLaughry’s story continued. “There was just this underlying sense of dread, for a lot of the movie, and guilt,” he says. He had spent months alongside the three actors, “knowing that they were going to have to say goodbye in a way that I didn’t.”
The lives that remained
Late in The Mosquito Bowl, in a scene Berg wrote, Schreiner talks with McLaughry on a secluded beach about having children and what a man might leave behind. “The contrast of being in one of the most beautiful places I’ve ever been, and then thinking about Dave going through that thought process, it was almost like an out-of-body experience,” Francis says. Galitzine, playing a version of McLaughry beginning to unravel, says that in the scene Schreiner helps “crystallize the reason why they’re doing what they’re doing,” and that Francis’s portrayal gave him “something larger than the chaos and the brutality.”
Schreiner never had those children. Bissinger keeps a photograph of him on his wall, and when he looks at it, he reaches for a word he acknowledges is probably not the right one: waste. “Here was a life that really should have been lived,” he says. “He should have had kids. He should have been married. He should have had a career. He should have had laughter. He should have had glory. He should have had disappointment. All the things that we have in life, and he’s never going to get that.”
The film frames the four men’s lives with a warning and a number: the Herbert Hoover line it opens on, about old men declaring wars the young must fight, and the loss it closes on, 75 million dead worldwide. Berg wants the audience to leave carrying both. “That wasn’t that long ago,” he says. “We live in a very violent planet today, and I really hope that never happens again. I don’t think a movie can change that. But taking a personal responsibility for each and every human being to think about how we can prevent people from having to go kill each other. If we can, let’s do it.”
Against that death toll, four men may seem like nothing. Yet the enormity of the war begins to register through the three lives it cut short and the one it forever changed. Of the dead, traces remain: Schreiner’s letters, Bauman’s snapshots, and restored footage of Butkovich running with the ball. The war left a fuller record of these men than ordinary lives would have, had they simply been allowed to go on living them uninterrupted. Had Schreiner come home, his handwriting might never have left Lancaster.
In the few photographs of the game, young men in T-shirts stand on the makeshift field, the jungle a dark line behind them. For one afternoon on Christmas Eve 1944, nothing was decided. Nobody lost.
McLaughry grew old with the years his friend never had. Then, in 1993, nearly half a century after Okinawa, he wrote out what he could remember of the day Schreiner was hit, a man in his seventies setting down what a young officer had seen, heard, and been told. Much of what he knew had reached him secondhand, and he doubted the version that had settled into the record. He returned to it all the same, because he was the last of the four men who could, and because somewhere on a field of coral in the flat afternoon light, with the ball sailing through the air, the other three were still 23, and in that borrowed moment, always would be.

Dozens of Palestinians forcibly displaced by the Israeli army rallied Friday in the southern occupied West Bank city of Hebron, demanding to return to their homes as Israeli raids and closures continued for an eighth consecutive day.
The protesters, including women, children and elderly people from displaced families, gathered near Al-Jalda Square, which remains closed off by Israeli forces, an Anadolu correspondent reported.

The raids have included incursions into residential neighborhoods, closures of city entrances and orders forcing Palestinian families from their homes.
During the first days of the campaign, homes, commercial properties and infrastructure were also demolished or damaged, while Israeli flags were raised over some homes seized for military use.
Hebron Municipality said Tuesday that 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families had been displaced by the continuing Israeli campaign.
The Palestinian Prisoner Society said Israeli forces arrested 110 Palestinians across Hebron governorate between Friday and Wednesday.
Military closures have also disrupted in-person education at 66 schools, affecting 2,872 students.
Of those, 2,198 students are living under direct closure, while another 674 are from forcibly displaced families and have been unable to reach their schools.
The displaced families are demanding that Israeli forces lift the closures and allow them to return to their homes and resume their daily lives.

Manosphere's impact on boys and men calls for public health action, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:08:01 UTC
00:08:01 KST

The ‘manosphere’ is fuelling harmful attitudes and worsening health inequalities among boys and men, prompting calls for a public health response that addresses the root causes of its growing appeal.
Increasingly, boys and young men who feel misunderstood or overlooked by society are seeking a sense of community online. Some find it in groups within the manosphere, where men share a preoccupation with the so-called crisis of masculinity and a common conviction: that feminism has systematically disadvantaged men.
“The manosphere offers boys and young men belonging, identity and an explanation for why life feels hard,” said Sarah Hawkes, co-founder of the think tank Global 50/50 and co-author of the report.
However, the sense of belonging these communities offer can come at a cost.
The manosphere — a loose network of online communities that claim to address men’s struggles while often blaming women and feminism — causes underrecognised harm to health and should be addressed through social and economic policies, requiring a coordinated response, according to a new Lancet report.
The harm caused to boys and men, women and girls and wider society includes social isolation, reluctance to seek mental health care and gender-based violence. Reducing these risks requires tackling the societal and economic conditions, commercial structures and social norms that sustain the manosphere's appeal.
This could include tackling economic insecurity through employment and social protection policies, encouraging boys to re-engage with education, and improving access to mental health support and other essential services for boys and young men.
Therefore, the report argues that content moderation alone is insufficient: restricting manosphere content does nothing to address the unmet needs that make its explanations attractive in the first place.
“We need to offer boys something better, not just tell them what to avoid,” Hawkes said.
The report also highlights broader challenges facing boys and men. Boys are increasingly disengaging from education systems, while men are over-represented in suicide statistics and incarceration rates. In health and social care, men and boys — particularly those marginalised by social and structural factors — experience substantial unmet needs that are not adequately addressed by existing policies, systems and services.
The manosphere operates with clear hierarchies of masculinity that are “mainly based on physical attractiveness and socioeconomic status”, the authors wrote.
Idealised representations of the male body, including low body fat, muscularity and hypermasculine features, are widely circulated online and have been linked to mental health harms, such as body dissatisfaction and psychological distress.
Incentives behind the manosphere
The authors also point to the commercial incentives behind the manosphere, arguing that maintaining these online communities can be a lucrative model.
“Boys and men are not the problem,” said Kent Buse, co-author of the report. “The problem is the conditions that leave them isolated and without a secure future, and the companies that profit from their anger and insecurity.”
He added that the manosphere operates as a business model that exploits outrage and grievance, rewarding the most extreme content.
Beyond the manosphere, public health strategies have been used to address complex issues such as gender-based violence and drug use by tackling their root causes, challenging stigma, improving access to support services and shifting public attitudes, rather than relying mainly on punishment and law enforcement.
A similar approach should be applied to the manosphere, authors argued. “Public health has a tested toolkit for commercial harms and we should use it,” Buse added.

Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta says it will shut down following pressure from Kremlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:08:00 UTC
00:08:00 KST

The paper is one of the few Russian outlets that has been openly critical of Russia's war in Ukraine, but it has come under increasing pressure from Moscow.
"We have been killed," reads a statement from the editorial team behind the Russian independent news outlet Novaya Gazeta, as it announced on Friday that it would be ceasing operations.
"On November 9th, we will turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down our servers, and leave," the paper said. "The newspaper no longer exists. The Russian authorities and the Russian security services have forced our editorial team to cease its operations."
The paper is one of the few Russian outlets that has been openly critical of Russia's war in Ukraine, but it has come under increasing pressure from Moscow, which revoked its media licence in 2022 and has detained its journalists.
The outlet said its team were now also being evicted from its headquarters on Potapovsky Lane in Moscow and that the donations platform it used to receive financial support from readers had also been closed down.
"We have been stripped of all our resources. Entirely," it said, calling it a "coordinated campaign."
"Banks which have cut us off tell us they are merely following internal corporate rules. They don’t tell us that the rules they follow are set by the FSB, the state security service, embedded in every organsiation. They see the country as their personal fiefdom," the statement continued.
It added that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, it had been unable to report on the "most critical and tragic events of our time" and that censorship applied to "virtually every sphere of civic life."
One final issue of the paper is still set to be published, however.
Independent Russian journalists have issued a statement in support of Novaya Gazeta.
"The story of the most important independent publication in modern Russia has come to an end. Novaya was a unique newspaper from the moment it was founded right up to the very end. There is not a single other newsroom on the market with such a curriculum vitae: this refers both to the list of phenomenal investigations and outstanding texts, and to the list of awards, including Dmitry Muratov's Nobel Prize, and to the list of murdered journalists," a text published by the Meduza outlet reads.
"By all measures this was the best media outlet in the history of Russia," it added.
Along with the newsroom, the museum of journalist Anna Politkovskaya is also closing; it was opened in her office on 7 October 2021, on the 15th anniversary of her murder.
Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993 by Sergei Kushnerev, Pavel Voshchanov, Akram Murtazaev, Dmitry Sabov and Dmitry Muratov.
The editorial office's first computers were purchased with the help of former USSR president Mikhail Gorbachev.
At the end of March 2022, after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, Novaya suspended its work due to warnings from media monitoring agency Roskomnadzor but later resumed operations.
After the start of the war, some of its journalists left Russia and set up Novaya Gazeta Europe, which has its main office in Latvia.

Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:06:39 UTC
00:06:39 KST

Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii.
The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii.
The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern.
But the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury.
The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified.
“A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park.
“It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.”
The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson.
The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said.
Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home.
The home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its facade was first excavated in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project.
There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century.
“It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters.
“So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.”
Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, a large and sophisticated thermal bath complex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city.
A home containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.

Putin rounds off diplomatic week in talks with African leaders (PHOTOS)
Russian President Vladimir Putin is holding a series of bilateral meetings with African leaders at the Kremlin on Friday, following the third Russia-Africa Summit.
The talks involve African heads of state, including from Sudan, Madagascar, Ghana, Mali, South Sudan, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Eritrea, as well as the prime minister of Togo.
The meetings follow the two-day summit, held in Moscow on October 28-29, which focused on expanding trade, investment, energy, security, and humanitarian cooperation between Russia and African nations.
During Friday’s talks with Sudan’s Sovereign Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the Sudanese leader proposed establishing a free economic zone on the Red Sea for Russian fuel and wheat storage facilities, as well as cooperation on a railway linking Port Sudan to Chad.
Burhan also offered Russian investors access to Sudan’s gold and copper deposits.
Putin presented a roadmap for bilateral cooperation and said Russia-Sudan trade had more than doubled in 2025, rising by a further 25% in January-August 2026.
Addressing the ongoing conflict in Sudan, Putin reiterated Moscow’s support for a political settlement and proposed discussing additional steps Russia could take to help resolve the crisis.
In a separate meeting with Madagascar President Michael Randrianirina, Putin highlighted expanding educational ties, noting that around 5,000 Malagasy students have studied in Russia and that MGIMO University signed a cooperation memorandum with Madagascar’s Foreign Ministry in June.
Putin also welcomed the Russian Orthodox Church’s recognition as a legal entity in Madagascar in April, noting that it has more than 1,500 parishioners on the island.
Randrianirina called for stronger practical cooperation and urged Moscow to accelerate work on debt conversion.
During talks with Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama, Putin said bilateral trade had grown by 6% between January and August. He added that Ghana ranks 12th among Russia’s African trading partners. The Russian leader also praised Ghana’s independent foreign policy and its opposition to neocolonialism, thanking Accra for its support for Russian resolutions at the UN.
Mahama expressed interest in expanding economic and investment cooperation with Moscow. The leader praised Russia for having “always stood by Africa” during the struggle against apartheid and for supporting the continent during the Covid-19 pandemic through supplies of Sputnik V vaccines.
At a meeting with Mali’s transitional president, Assimi Goita, Putin said Russia had increased its scholarship quota for Malian students to 300 places for the 2026-27 academic year, citing growing interest in Russian education and language studies. He added that six Russian language and cultural centers are operating in the West African country.
During the summit, Putin also held at least nine more bilateral meetings with other African leaders, including the presidents of Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Mozambique, Namibia, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Kenya, as well as Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Libya’s Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed al-Menfi.

Poland holds a suspect for stabbing two Ukrainians for their nationality, the latest case in a year of rising hate crimes against them

00:05:12 KST

Warsaw police have arrested a man suspected of stabbing two Ukrainians on a bus over their nationality, police said. A court ordered him held in custody, and the charges he faces carry long prison terms.
Russia's full-scale war drove nearly a million Ukrainians to seek protection in Poland, and attacks on them for their nationality grew this year. Polish police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, over 30% more than a year earlier.
Police tracked the suspect to a forest
The attack took place on a Warsaw city bus in mid-October. The attacker stabbed and slashed two passengers, both Ukrainian citizens, and fled before police arrived. Both victims went to hospital with multiple stab and cut wounds. Police found that he attacked them because of their nationality.
Officers quickly identified the suspect but spent days locating him. The 30-year-old was hiding and living in a forest in Warsaw's northern Bielany district, where police detained him last weekend.
He faces three charges. Two concern the bus attack: attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and causing injuries lasting more than seven days. The third covers threats against another man at a Warsaw venue in August 2024.
Police said he acted as a repeat offender, within five years of serving a prison term for a similar crime. The charges carry three to 20 years in prison. At prosecutors' request, a court ordered him held for three months.
This year's attacks on Ukrainians in Poland
In early August, Ukraine's ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, said anti-Ukrainian remarks and attacks had risen by about 30%. Days later, people rallied in 22 Polish cities against violence toward Ukrainians and other minorities.
Poland paused a military aid package over Lviv’s vote honoring WWII nationalists, Ukrainian source says. Polish ministry denies it
Other recent cases this year include:
- In late July, police in Wrocław detained two of three men suspected of beating a young Ukrainian couple.
- On 14 August, a woman allegedly attacked a Ukrainian girl and her younger brother in a Bydgoszcz park after hearing them speak Ukrainian. Prosecutors charged her four days later.
- In September, a man punched a 20-year-old Ukrainian tourist in the head at a crossing in central Warsaw, knocking him unconscious. Police detained the attacker, who gave no motive.
Tensions rose again in late September, when a Ukrainian man allegedly killed a priest in a knife attack at a monastery in Jarosław. Bodnar said some Polish politicians and journalists used it to argue for deporting Ukrainians.
Meanwhile, police in southwestern Poland detained a Russian citizen suspected of spying, after catching him photographing trains and railway infrastructure. Russia's suspected sabotage campaign keeps reaching Poland and the rest of Europe, and Ukraine's intelligence warned last week that Russia may stage sabotage in Eastern Europe and try to pin it on Kyiv.

Details: The European Commission proposes approving €8.04 billion for Ukraine under the Ukraine Facility mechanism, but points out unfulfilled reforms.
Quote: "Ukraine has satisfactorily fulfilled the relevant conditions for the partial payment... of the fourth, seventh, eighth and ninth instalments of financial assistance under the Ukraine Plan. Such assistance shall amount to EUR 8 040 665 425 before clearing the pre-financing, of which EUR 298 747 120 corresponds to the fourth instalment, EUR 368 010 368 corresponds to the seventh instalment, EUR 95 530 669 corresponds to the eighth instalment and EUR 7 278 377 268 corresponds to the ninth instalment."
Details: EU sources familiar with the matter told European Pravda that after deductions for the repayment of previously disbursed pre-financing, the actual amount payable to Ukraine will be around €7.8 billion.
A Council of the EU decision is required to approve the proposed payment, which is expected by the end of November.
For the ninth instalment, the European Commission assessed 16 of the 18 required steps as satisfactorily fulfilled. Among them were the modernisation of the IT system for enforcing court decisions; approval of the Human Rights Protection Strategy; adoption of an anti-human trafficking programme, a strategy to reduce state ownership in banks and an Employment Strategy; investment in education, healthcare and housing for veterans with disabilities, families of fallen veterans and internally displaced persons; preparations for an independent assessment of the National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission (NEURC); and measures relating to electronic identification and water monitoring.
The two outstanding steps concern the appointment of supervisory boards with a majority of independent members at state-owned businesses (completed at 10 of the required 15) and the adoption of a roadmap for gradually liberalising the gas and electricity markets.
In determining the payment amount, the Commission proposed taking into account partial fulfilment of the requirement regarding supervisory boards and the early fulfilment of one step scheduled for the 10th instalment: submitting a request for an IAEA Integrated Regulatory Review Service mission.
Factoring in these elements, the Commission proposed paying Ukraine an additional €529.4 million. Consequently, the difference between Ukraine's request and the proposed payment amount is only €264.6 million (rather than nearly €800 million, as it could have been).
Background:
- On 2 October, Ukraine received €2.9 billion from the EU under the Ukraine Facility. European Pravda previously covered in detail the reforms Ukraine completed to receive that tranche.
- EU Commissioner Marta Kos called on Ukrainian authorities to unite in exchange for funding.

The latter provides for the development of land and air, passenger and cargo transportation, including through international transport corridors.

What Tokayev’s Economic Agenda Means for Kazakhstan’s International Partnerships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

For Kazakhstan, a country linking China and Europe while sharing a long border with Russia, infrastructure is never entirely a domestic matter. Railways determine how goods move across Eurasia, electricity supplies shape industrial investment, and the ability to process minerals affects the country’s place in international supply chains. These connections offer a useful way to read President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s October 28 State of the Nation address, which was mostly about economic development but had also important implications for foreign relations.
Tokayev began by warning of deepening mistrust among major powers and a more unpredictable international environment. Rather than proposing a new diplomatic alignment, he emphasized a stronger economy, modern infrastructure, technology, and effective institutions. For Kazakhstan’s longstanding balanced and multivector foreign policy, the underlying logic is that domestic capacity can widen the scope for cooperation with different partners at the same time.
The most visible proposal was the nationwide “People’s Construction” program, backed by 6.5 trillion tenge (approximately $14 billion) from the National Fund through 2029, including 1.5 trillion tenge earmarked for early social projects. Roads, utilities, housing, and public facilities are central to the plan. Tokayev also proposed a higher minimum wage and new healthcare facilities. These measures principally address domestic needs, but more reliable services and regional infrastructure can also reduce costs for investors and make industrial projects more viable outside the largest cities. The president’s insistence that public spending mobilize private capital, rather than substitute for it, gives the initiative an international dimension.
The clearest connection between domestic investment and foreign relations is transport. Tokayev said the Bakhty-Ayagoz railway should enter service in 2027, adding 20 million tons of capacity on routes toward China. Construction has also begun on an Aral-Caspian corridor intended to shorten the Trans-Caspian route by roughly 1,000 kilometers. Both projects respond to an established demand for more dependable links between Asian production centers and European markets. In February, the World Bank approved an $846 million guarantee designed to mobilize $1.41 billion in commercial financing for Kazakhstan’s rail network along the Middle Corridor.
The geopolitical value of these routes lies in their usefulness to multiple economies. China gains additional westward capacity, European businesses gain another option for moving goods, and Kazakhstan can expand its role in services surrounding that trade. Tokayev’s call for freight consolidation centers, logistics operators, and factories near transport junctions suggests an ambition to capture value beyond transit fees. Yet the route’s performance will depend not only on Kazakh construction but also on ports, customs procedures and coordination with Azerbaijan, Georgia, and other corridor partners. Greater connectivity is a regional undertaking, not simply a national project.
The same logic applies to data. On October 15, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan inaugurated a 380-kilometer fiber-optic link beneath the Caspian Sea, designed to carry information between Central Asia and Europe. Mentioned again in the address, the cable shows how physical and digital connectivity can reinforce one another. Reliable cross-border data links matter to cloud services, financial transactions, and the data centers Kazakhstan wants to attract.
China’s role is notable in other spheres too. At a September China-Kazakhstan investment forum, Tokayev described a portfolio of 260 joint industrial projects valued at more than $62 billion, spanning manufacturing, metallurgy, agriculture, and energy storage. Its composition indicates how the relationship is developing from commodity trade and transport toward local production and technology. The address’s emphasis on manufacturing capacity and domestic suppliers is consistent with this direction.
Energy provides a second intersection between internal requirements and external partnerships. Kazakhstan generates about 123 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually but still faces shortages. Tokayev set a goal of achieving a sustained surplus by 2029 through new generation, modernized grids and a broader mix of energy sources. Russia is an established partner in this sector. During President Vladimir Putin’s May visit, the two countries signed a nuclear power agreement and arrangements for Russian export-credit financing. Chinese companies have also proposed nuclear cooperation, including technology transfer and specialist training, as Tokayev noted in the address.
These projects are significant because a nuclear partnership can encompass engineering, fuel services, training and maintenance over decades. They should not, however, be mistaken for an immediate solution to the 2029 electricity target: the first planned reactor is not expected to begin operating before the following decade. In the nearer term, grid upgrades and other generation projects will remain decisive. For Kazakhstan’s partners, a more dependable power system would also improve the prospects for energy-intensive manufacturing, mineral processing and computing infrastructure.
Critical minerals offer another area in which domestic reforms can produce international effects. Tokayev called for modern geological exploration, better access to geological data, long-term financing and offtake arrangements, alongside consideration of a dedicated mechanism for nonferrous and rare-earth metals. The objective is to develop processing and other parts of industrial value chains. This meets interests expressed by both Western and Asian partners, although turning resource potential into competitive production will require technology, investment and skills.
During Tokayev’s June visit to Brussels, EU leaders identified critical raw materials, energy, transport and digitalization as priorities for expanded cooperation. As Kazakhstan’s largest trading and investment partner, the EU has a particularly strong interest in the development of these sectors. The United States and Kazakhstan have also agreed to cooperate on mineral supply chains, including a proposed American-backed tungsten mining and processing project. These relationships have distinct commercial purposes, but each could support Kazakhstan’s stated goal of producing more value domestically. They complement its established energy and industrial ties with Russia and China rather than necessarily displacing them.
Technology is becoming a further point of international engagement. The address highlighted two operating supercomputers, another planned before year’s end, and efforts to apply artificial intelligence to agriculture, industry and public services. In June, Kazakhstan joined the U.S.-backed Pax Silica initiative and signed an AI Opportunity Partnership statement, connecting cooperation on computing, semiconductors, energy, critical minerals and research. On October 23, Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana and met Tokayev. Nvidia’s own account of the visit described planned computing investments and potential applications in mining, agriculture and industrial automation. These developments give the digital agenda a tangible international dimension, although the economic benefits will depend on adoption by ordinary businesses as much as high-profile infrastructure.
The final link is institutional. Tokayev acknowledged weaknesses in investment coordination and proposed a larger role for the Baiterek development holding, a new civil code, adjustments to tax rules and an English common law-based investment court in Alatau. Such changes will matter to foreign partners only insofar as they create predictable conditions in practice. The same is true of financing: public construction spending can initiate projects, but sustained industrial cooperation requires viable businesses, long-term credit and confidence in dispute resolution.
The address did not signify a departure from Kazakhstan’s established diplomatic approach. It suggests rather how that approach might acquire greater economic substance. China’s industrial and transport links, Russia’s energy cooperation, the EU’s connectivity and raw-materials partnerships, and emerging U.S. ties in minerals and artificial intelligence each intersect with priorities set out by Tokayev. Delivery remains the essential test. If infrastructure is completed, power becomes more reliable and investment rules improve, Kazakhstan could become a stronger participant in the production, services and technology networks that connect Eurasia.

Poland's coalition politicians slam opposition leader's EU exit remarks
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:02:51 CET

Poland's coalition politicians slam opposition leader's EU exit remarks
Poland's ruling coalition politicians on Thursday condemned the suggestion by the leader of the main opposition, Law and Justice (PiS) party, Jaroslaw Kaczynski, that Poland could initiate formal EU withdrawal negotiations as a high-stakes pressure tactic to force institutional changes within the bloc.
Reacting sharply on X, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that the very future of the country's Western integration is now up for debate.
"Jaroslaw Kaczynski has just announced that Poland should begin negotiations on the conditions of leaving the European Union," Tusk wrote on Thursday morning. "This is precisely what is at stake in today's fierce struggle in Poland. A tough battle—and I do not intend to lose it, even if not everyone plays on my side."
Kaczynski countered on X later that day, writing that "Tusk, as usual, is lying." He added that "the European Union is needed, but it requires thorough reform," attributing the bloc's current crisis to the past governance of former German Chancellor Angela Merkel and Tusk himself during his tenure as European Council President. Kaczynski declared that PiS wants an EU focused on lowering energy prices, strengthening security, and eliminating unnecessary bureaucracy for ordinary citizens. "We will restore the European Union to its citizens," Kaczynski wrote, adding that allowing the current systemic crisis to continue is what truly threatens Europe's future.
Earlier on Thursday, PiS Vice-Chairman Przemyslaw Czarnek also said that the party has no plans for Polexit, clarifying that Kaczynski's remarks were aimed entirely at the necessity of reshaping and reforming the face of the EU.
The political firestorm follows Kaczynski's speech at the Krynica Forum 2026, a major political, economic, and geopolitical conference held in southern Poland on Wednesday. There, Kaczynski expressed his "deep conviction" that the European Union requires fundamental changes. In addition to shifting public opinion and drafting a new treaty with delayed implementation, the opposition leader proposed a "hard and risky" approach using the exit clauses of the Treaty on European Union
"It all begins with negotiations, and simply starting these negotiations," Kaczynski told the forum, referring to the EU's treaty provisions for member state withdrawal. "It is a hard method, a risky one, but things are really so bad... that it is worth employing such a method if others fail." He admitted that the strategy would require immense determination and aligning positions among like-minded member states whose views, particularly on Eastern policy, remain far apart.
Senior coalition figures swiftly linked Kaczynski's remarks to a broader pro-Russian and anti-Western agenda, tying the opposition's actions to far-right, Euroskeptic Confederation of the Polish Crown leader Grzegorz Braun. The row comes amid public friction over whether President Karol Nawrocki should invite Braun's faction to the upcoming National Security Bureau (RBN) meeting on November 3.
Special Services Coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak criticised Kaczynski for entertaining EU exit talks "at such a sensitive moment for our security", adding that "even Kremlin dreamers would not have predicted a significant Polish politician speaking directly against Poland's interests." Government spokesman Adam Szlapka said that "Kaczynski is implementing Braun's agenda, and we all know whose agenda Braun implements."
Speaker of the Sejm, lower house, Wlodzimierz Czarzasty said that while Nawrocki normalises the "pro-Russian Braun", Kaczynski is "familiarising the public with the topic of Poland leaving the EU," concluding: "They are moving East. We are staying."
Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the rhetoric follows the opposition's recent votes against the EU's SAFE programme, a loan fund providing up to EUR 150 billion for defence industry investments, which President Nawrocki vetoed in March. Kosiniak-Kamysz added that the EU must be reformed "where improvement is needed, not threatened with an exit," demanding that PiS and Confederation explicitly state ahead of the parliamentary elections whether they want Polexit.
Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned that leaving the EU would trigger severe everyday consequences, including "a customs border with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Lithuania, passport controls at airports, and an end to EU subsidies for farmers and investments." New Left MEP Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus and Infrastructure Minister Dariusz Klimczak echoed these concerns, with Klimczak warning that the UK's severe post-Brexit national losses should serve as a stark warning to Poland. (PAP)

CineCrossroads: Five films to make your Halloween weekend unforgettable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:01:15 UTC
00:01:15 KST

CineCrossroads: Five films to make your Halloween weekend unforgettable
With Halloween arriving this weekend, CineCrossroads presents a special selection of five films that explore the holiday from different angles. From supernatural terror and a genre-defining classic to gothic suspense, playful comedy and family animation, this edition offers something for every kind of Halloween viewer. Qazinform News Agency wishes you an enjoyable and suitably spooky viewing experience.
Movie of the week: Other Mommy (2026)
This week’s main release is Other Mommy, a supernatural horror film directed by Rob Savage and based on Josh Malerman’s novel Incidents Around the House.
The story follows Bela, a young girl whose family home is invaded by a sinister entity she calls Other Mommy. Appearing in the shape of Bela’s mother, the creature tries to gain the child’s trust while gradually tightening its hold over the household.
Jessica Chastain takes on a disturbing dual role as Bela’s mother and the entity imitating her. She is joined by Jay Duplass and Arabella Olivia Clark, while filmmaker James Wan serves as one of the producers.
Rather than relying only on sudden scares, Other Mommy draws its tension from a fear familiar to many children: the possibility that something frightening may be hiding inside an apparently safe home. Its domestic setting and unsettling central figure make it an appropriate choice for viewers seeking a chilling start to the Halloween weekend.
Classic pick: Halloween (1978)
No Halloween selection would be complete without John Carpenter’s Halloween, one of the most influential horror films ever made.
The film follows escaped killer Michael Myers as he returns to the fictional town of Haddonfield on Halloween night. There, teenager Laurie Strode, played by Jamie Lee Curtis, gradually realizes that a silent masked stranger is following her.
Carpenter creates suspense through patient camerawork, carefully framed shadows and an unforgettable minimalist score. Much of the film’s power comes from what remains unseen. Quiet streets, darkened houses and empty doorways become sources of danger long before violence occurs.
More than four decades after its release, Halloween remains a model of economical filmmaking. Its imagery and music have become inseparable from the holiday itself, making it an essential classic for anyone interested in the history of horror cinema.
Gothic pick: The Others (2001)
For viewers who prefer atmosphere to bloodshed, Alejandro Amenábar’s The Others offers an elegant and haunting alternative.
Nicole Kidman stars as Grace, a deeply religious mother living with her two children in an isolated mansion shortly after the Second World War. Because the children suffer from an extreme sensitivity to sunlight, the curtains must remain closed and every door must be locked before another is opened.
When unexplained footsteps, voices and strange figures begin appearing in the house, Grace becomes convinced that the family is no longer alone. Yet the truth behind the disturbances proves far more complicated than she expects.
With its candlelit rooms, heavy fog and growing sense of isolation, The Others captures the spirit of a traditional ghost story. Its restrained approach and carefully constructed mystery make it an excellent Halloween choice for audiences who enjoy psychological suspense.
Horror comedy pick: What We Do in the Shadows (2014)
Halloween does not have to be entirely frightening. Taika Waititi and Jemaine Clement’s What We Do in the Shadows turns a household of ancient vampires into the subjects of a mock documentary.
The vampires share a home in Wellington, New Zealand, where their supernatural abilities do little to solve ordinary domestic problems. They argue about cleaning, struggle to enter nightclubs without an invitation and attempt to understand contemporary fashion and technology.
The film affectionately parodies familiar vampire traditions while giving each of its immortal characters a distinct and surprisingly relatable personality. Its humor comes from placing legendary creatures in mundane situations, without losing sight of the darker mythology surrounding them.
Inventive, quotable and consistently charming, What We Do in the Shadows is ideal for viewers who want costumes, creatures and Halloween atmosphere without an evening of intense scares.
Family pick: ParaNorman (2012)
The final recommendation is ParaNorman, a stop-motion animated adventure that combines ghosts, zombies and witchcraft with a compassionate story about fear and prejudice.
Norman is an eleven-year-old boy who can see and speak with the dead. His unusual ability makes him an outsider in his small town, but it also leaves him as the only person capable of stopping an old curse when the dead begin rising from their graves.
Although the film embraces spooky imagery, its monsters are never quite what they initially appear to be. Beneath the supernatural adventure is a thoughtful message about misunderstanding others and the harm caused when fear turns into cruelty.
With its detailed animation, lively humor and emotional depth, ParaNorman is a strong choice for families with older children. It provides plenty of Halloween excitement while ending this special edition on a warm and meaningful note.
Whether the weekend calls for supernatural terror, classic suspense, gothic mystery, vampire comedy or animated adventure, these five films offer different ways to enter the Halloween spirit.

Nations agree on push to get nature goals on track at UN summit
- Nearly 200 nations approved key UN biodiversity texts in overtime at COP17 in Yerevan, after two weeks of tense talks aimed at reversing nature loss by 2030.
- Countries still face major gaps on targets, including protecting 30% of land and oceans, cutting pollution, and raising conservation finance. The UN says the world needs US$700 billion more a year.
- Talks were dogged by disputes over harmful subsidies, new funding sources, the weak Cali Fund, and attacks on science. Leaders and indigenous groups urged urgent action, and the next summit host may be Panama or Ecuador.
AI generated
YEREVAN – Nearly 200 nations on Oct 30 adopted hard-fought agreements at a UN biodiversity summit aimed at putting the world back on track in efforts to halt nature’s destruction by 2030.
The outcome, however, was accompanied by disappointment over missed opportunities to address humanity’s destructive toll on nature.
Delegates cheered as the crucial texts were approved in overtime but the celebrations were tempered by acrimonious debates and regret over limited progress on some of the most contentious issues.
The COP17 summit in Armenia sought to revive a landmark commitment to halt and reverse the destruction of nature by 2030 after global efforts to meet that goal fell short.
Over two bruising weeks in Armenia’s capital, Yerevan, nations were urged to correct course to keep the pact alive and protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on earth.
“And that’s it. Perfect,” said COP17 president Hambardzum Matevosyan to applause, as he brought down the gavel on the documents, the final versions of which were not immediately available.
The world adopted a historic pact in 2022 setting ambitious targets to halt biodiversity loss by 2030.
But ahead of the summit, the UN warned that countries would fail to meet the goal unless they urgently correct course.
Most of the objectives are falling short, including targets to protect 30% of Earth’s land and oceans, tackle pollution, and provide poorer countries with greater conservation finance.
A draft COP17 text had called on countries to “accelerate” efforts to keep the pact alive.
The much-anticipated text stressed that “increased action” was needed to tackle the root drivers of nature loss.
Highlighting the disagreements that dogged the talks, the document proposed various options to achieve the 2030 goal.
It was not immediately clear which of those options made the cut.
The text “needed to respond to the irrefutable evidence that we are off track for our 2030 deadline, and while not particularly exciting or detailed, it’s good news that countries could reach agreement,” Catherine Weller from Fauna and Flora told AFP.
Kirsty Leong, of WWF International, told AFP the “outcome has its strengths and weaknesses, but, on balance, it’s a good outcome”.
‘Weak terms’
During negotiations, countries wrangled over reforming subsidies and other incentives that encourage activities harmful to nature, such as fossil fuels, intensive agriculture and overfishing.
Governments had pledged to reduce this spending but made little progress, with an estimated US$2.4 trillion still flowing every year to harmful subsidies.
An Lambrechts from Greenpeace International said it was crucial that spending was switched to nature protection and restoration.
“Even though the agreed decision text expresses it in weak terms, COP17 saw important political momentum to address harmful financial incentives - including subsidies - and that’s urgently needed,” she told AFP.
A separate row revolved around finding new cash sources to fund conservation efforts around the globe - a hot-button issue with public budgets under strain amid an energy crisis and conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
To restore degraded ecosystems, save endangered species and conserve forests, wetlands and other vital natural habitats, the world needs an estimated US$700 billion (S$890 billion) more every year than it currently spends.
The European Union led a charge for wealthy emerging economies such as China to join in paying for global conservation efforts, a contentious issue at COP17.
In a sign of possible compromise, another draft text that circulated on Oct 30 invited countries outside the developed country donors to voluntarily join the group.
It did not compel any country to contribute to biodiversity finance but asked for volunteers to “signal interest”.
Science under attack
Efforts to refine the lacklustre Cali Fund – a UN mechanism for sharing profits from corporations that use genetic data from plants and other organisms - also proved difficult.
The fund set out to raise US$1 billion a year for conservation in developing countries when it launched in early 2025. So far, it has attracted around US$10,000.
Nations have also feuded over key scientific reports, with a handful of countries accused of stonewalling efforts to accept the benchmark findings of a UN-backed biodiversity body.
“The attacks on science have bothered me a lot,” French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said.
Around 70 ministers joined the negotiations this week, in an effort to nudge things along, while indigenous leaders and civil society activists appealed to nations to act with greater urgency.
At the last biodiversity summit in Colombia in 2024, talks ran overtime as nations haggled over conservation finance and ended without a deal. Negotiations resumed in Rome in 2025 where an agreement was reached.
The COP17 summit was also expected to decide on Oct 30 whether Panama or Ecuador will host the next biodiversity summit in 2028. AFP

Mussolini's great-grandson scores first Lazio goal in 6-2 win over Sassuolo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:00:18 UTC
00:00:18 KST

Halis Sünnetci
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Romano Floriani Mussolini, the great-grandson of Italian fascist dictator Benito Mussolini, scored his first goal for Lazio in a 6-2 victory over Sassuolo on Tuesday, helping the Rome-based club move provisionally to the top of Serie A.
The 23-year-old right-back converted a low cross from Kenneth Taylor in the 16th minute to put Lazio 3-1 ahead, with the goal initially ruled out for offside before being awarded following a video assistant referee (VAR) review.
It was his first goal for Lazio and his first in Italy's top flight, having previously scored in Serie B while on loan at Juve Stabia.
"I'm really happy to have scored that first goal, but even more so about this win, which is crucial for us," Floriani Mussolini said after the match.
Lazio's 6-2 victory over Sassuolo, which saw the hosts reduced to 10 men in the first half, extended their unbeaten Serie A run to nine matches, leaving them level with Inter Milan on 25 points at the top of the standings. 
Mussolini's family legacy and Lazio's far-right history
Floriani Mussolini's family background has attracted attention throughout his career, particularly because of Lazio's historical association with far-right supporter groups.
The 23-year-old is the son of former Italian politician Alessandra Mussolini and a great-grandson of Benito Mussolini, who ruled fascist Italy from 1922 to 1943.
Sections of Lazio's organized supporters have been associated with far-right politics since the 1970s, with the club's Curva Nord later becoming particularly linked to the Irriducibili, a group founded in 1987 and known for its far-right ideology and controversies involving fascist symbols and racist behavior.
Floriani Mussolini, who developed through Lazio's academy before loan spells at several Italian clubs, has sought to keep his football career separate from discussions about his family history.
"My surname has never caused me any problems and, from my point of view, the less said about it, the better," he said in July 2025, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
"I'm here to express myself on the pitch, nothing else."
His first senior goal, scored while playing for Juve Stabia in December 2024, also sparked controversy after some supporters appeared to perform fascist salutes during the celebrations.
The Italian Football Federation opened an investigation into the incident, while Juve Stabia denied the allegations, saying supporters were raising their arms as part of a customary goal celebration.
