Israel's opposition must break its promise, rely on Arab parties to oust Netanyahu - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:40:13 UTC
23:40:13 KST

As in previous elections, the opposition can only point to a majority in the Knesset when the seats won by Arab parties are included in the electoral count. This was the case with the parliamentary camps that backed Yitzhak Rabin in 1992, Ehud Barak in 1999, and Yair Lapid in 2021.
The precise circumstances of those earlier governments differed, but the underlying principle was the same: Arab citizens vote in Israeli elections, their representatives sit in the Knesset, their seats count toward the parliamentary balance, and they do not approve of the Likud and its racist, ultra-nationalist fellow travelers.
However, there is one spectacular complication. Leading opposition politicians promised during the campaign that they would not form a government dependent on Arab parties. Having (pathetically) accepted Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s contention that such dependence would somehow taint a government, they may now find themselves unable to take office without violating their solemn commitments.
It’s understandable, up to a point. Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, and other opposition leaders reassured right-wing voters that replacing Netanyahu would not mean relying on parties with positions on the Palestinian conflict and Israel’s national identity that many of those voters find objectionable. It is hard to dismiss this as meaningless campaign rhetoric.
Which campaign promises will the opposition break?
But the opposition also made a far more consequential promise, one that constituted the very essence of its campaign: to replace Netanyahu and reverse the direction in which his government has taken Israel.
If the only parliamentary route to do so requires Arab support, the two commitments cannot both be honored. The question is whether fidelity to a tactical electoral pledge should outweigh the broader responsibility that opposition leaders themselves placed at the center of the election.
The practical circumstances make the dilemma especially unusual. Arab political leaders have indicated that they are prepared to support an alternative minority government from outside the coalition, without demanding cabinet positions.
Their support would not be unconditional, but their concerns are very reasonable: representatives of the Joint List have raised demands regarding crime in Arab communities and the Palestinian question.
Whether breaking the promise can be justified raises a question philosophers and statesmen have debated for centuries. Promises underpin political legitimacy, yet circumstances can make honoring them more damaging than breaking them. The question is whether fidelity to one’s word outweighs responsibility for its consequences.
Niccolò Machiavelli argued in The Prince that rulers cannot always honor commitments when circumstances change and doing so threatens their interests. The German sociologist Max Weber offered a more ethically serious framework in Politics as a Vocation, contrasting an ethic of conviction with an ethic of responsibility. The former emphasizes fidelity to principle; the latter demands accountability for foreseeable consequences.
Edmund Burke approached the question differently. In his famous 1774 address to the electors of Bristol, he argued that representatives owe voters judgment, not blind obedience. A politician who clings to an earlier position despite recognizing its harm may be sacrificing the very judgment voters elected him to exercise.
History provides examples in which the tension involved matters considerably more serious than an abandoned tax pledge or an inconvenient coalition agreement.
Abraham Lincoln entered office in 1861 explicitly assuring the Southern states that he had no intention of interfering with slavery where it already existed. Yet in 1863, he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring enslaved people in areas then in rebellion to be free.
Possibility of Netanyahu remaining prime minister
This brings us to the disastrous possibility that honoring their promise leaves the opposition clearing the way for Netanyahu to stay in power. The man who was in charge on October 7, who risks lives every day by blocking an inquiry meant to prevent a similar disaster, who is undermining Israeli democracy and enabling the outrages of the haredim to continue, who is on trial for corruption, and who is dedicated to sowing divisions, will get away with it and continue causing the nation his destructive harm.
There is also a rather delicious irony in any notion of honesty and the main quality in any context featuring the prime minister. Netanyahu’s political career has featured repeated lies, distortions, betrayals, and prevarications.
This is a person who promised that Itamar Ben-Gvir would never be a cabinet minister; who promised (in a court affidavit!) to recuse himself from interfering with the courts; who enthusiastically backed term limits; who called on prime minister Ehud Olmert to resign over a mere police investigation (while he himself is actually on trial); and who broke his promise to rotate the premiership with Benny Gantz.
Hilariously, he is also the man who, having lost the election in 2021, negotiated with Mansour Abbas to bring the Arab party Ra’am in a government based on a completely new political alignment. It was only the veto by Bezalel Smotrich that blew up that machination – and yet today he dares argue that Ra’am (led by an Arab who has emphatically accepted Israel as the Jewish state) is beyond the pale.
Arab citizens constitute roughly one-fifth of Israel’s population, vote under the same electoral laws as Jewish citizens, and elect representatives to the same parliament.
Their parties hold positions on the Palestinian conflict and national identity that many Jewish Israelis oppose, and those disagreements would create genuine difficulties for a government dependent on their support. But they must be embraced if this country is to have any sort of future. They will never sing “Hatikva” with great gusto, but they have not caused damage and have been remarkably loyal citizens.
Boycotting them is not just stupid politics for the opposition; it is devastating to the future of Israel as a functional country.
Besides, Netanyahu has long relied on ultra-Orthodox parties whose demands concerning military service, education, and public spending have profound consequences for Israel’s security, economy, and social cohesion. Some of those parties are non-Zionist, yet their seats are treated as an entirely normal component of the parliamentary arithmetic.
The opposition should stop overthinking, get out of its own way, thank the Arabs for their support, and get on with saving the country.
The writer is the former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press, the former chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem, and publisher of danperry.substack.com.

Houthis continue to engage in ‘fierce battles’ in mountains near Aden, Taiz - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:40:04 UTC
23:40:04 KST

The Houthis continue to attack Saudi Arabia and are also continuing to engage in “fierce battles” in Yemen. This is an important issue because any talks with Iran, which appear to be happening, will take the Houthis into account. Arab News in Saudi Arabia said on October 30 that the “Saudi-led coalition said on Friday it intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region a drone fired by Yemen’s Houthis.”
According to the Saudis, “a drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Makkah region.” The report noted that “the Iran-backed militia has for weeks targeted airports, energy infrastructure and cities across the Kingdom with drones and missiles.”
Now, Al-Ain media in the UAE also says that “dozens of government forces and Houthis were killed and wounded on Friday in fierce battles in Al-Maqatra district of Lahj, following a large-scale attack by the militias.”
Sources in Yemen told Al-Ain News that the Houthi militias launched a large-scale ground attack on government forces’ positions in Al-Maqatirah district, the northern gateway to Lahj, in an attempt to make progress on the ground and control key mountain ranges in the area.
This is an area in southern Yemen where the Houthis are fighting a tough and complex war against the Yemeni government and also other factions aligned with the government. Some of these factions were linked to the Southern Transitional Council, which had been backed by the UAE.
The UAE has excellent sources in this area.
“The sources confirmed that the Houthi militias aim, through the attack, to control the ‘Al-Muqatara Tunnel’ area and the strategically important Al-Muqatara mountain fortress, as well as to reach the Al-Rubu’ market located in the Heijah Al-Abd valley, where the main road linking Taiz and Aden is located.” The sources explained that the battles extended to the Haifan front, where the militias are trying to reach Mount An’an, which overlooks large areas between Haifan and Al-Maqatirah.
Events in Yemen could affect Iran, UAE, Qatar, US
This area appears to be only around 40 to 50 miles from Aden. This means the battles in these mountains, amid palm trees and scrub brush and steep terrain, could determine the next moves in Yemen. What happens here, could also matter in Tehran, Doha, Riyadh and Washington.
Let’s recall why the Houthis matters. The Iran-backed Houthis have emerged as one of the most important armed terrorist armies in the Middle East, using Yemen as a base to threaten Saudi Arabia, Israel and international shipping. The movement, also known as Ansar Allah, emerged from northern Yemen's Zaydi Shi'ite community and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
In early 2015, Houthi forces advanced south toward Aden, forcing Yemen's internationally recognized government to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in March 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition seeking to restore the government and prevent the Houthis from consolidating control over Yemen.
The war devastated the country but failed to defeat the Houthis. Iran's support helped the movement develop an increasingly sophisticated arsenal of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. These weapons enabled the Houthis to strike Saudi Arabia and eventually target Israel.
Following the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, the Houthis began launching missiles and drones toward Israel and attacking commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Israel, the United States and Britain subsequently carried out strikes against Houthi targets. The Houthis resumed attacks on Israel during the 2026 conflict involving Iran.
Yemen's war escalated again in July 2026, when the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi targets and shipping. In September, Houthi forces advanced along the Red Sea coast, capturing Mocha and reaching the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait. The strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a vital route for international trade and energy shipments.
Fighting has also intensified around Taiz, where the Houthis have sought to threaten the road linking the city to Aden, the internationally recognized government's main base.
The renewed conflict illustrates how Yemen's civil war has become intertwined with the wider regional confrontation involving Iran, Saudi Arabia and Israel. Control of territory around Bab al-Mandab gives the Houthis additional leverage over regional security and international commerce.
Al-Ain says that as the battles in the mountains have continued, “warplanes launched a series of raids on Houthi positions and gatherings to repel the militia's attack on Al-Maqatirah district in Lahj governorate.” Al-Ain concludes that “by attacking Al-Maqatirah, the Houthi militias are trying to reach Tur Al-Bahah district in Lahj, a coastal province that is the main gateway to the capital, Aden.”
Yemen has been witnessing fierce battles since the beginning of last September, following a large-scale, multi-pronged attack launched by the Houthis on areas of the western coast, Bab al-Mandab and Taiz, which resulted in thousands of deaths and injuries.
Houthis lay seige to Taiz
The Houthis are also laying siege to the city of Taiz in the mountains. Arab News says that the Houthis are also facing growing international criticism over their detention of United Nations personnel and the worsening humanitarian crisis in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
According to Arab News, the Houthis are holding 71 UN staff members, severely restricting the organization's ability to operate in areas under their control. “These actions render the delivery of humanitarian aid in areas under the control of the Houthis untenable at this time,” Shirin Yaseen, associate spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, told Arab News.
The reports indicate that the humanitarian situation has deteriorated further around Taiz, where more than 800,000 people have been cut off from essential supplies. The Houthis intensified their siege in early October after seizing the road connecting Taiz with Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government. According to the World Food Programme, approximately three-quarters of the affected population depend on humanitarian assistance. Taiz has faced varying degrees of Houthi siege since 2015.

Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen. Now what?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:39:20 UTC
23:39:20 KST

What next as Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen?
Tel Aviv — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party alleged Thursday that Israel's election earlier in the week was stolen by Arab-majority parties, helped by foreign funding that amounted to vote-buying, as final results showed Netanyahu's bloc has lost its majority in Israel's parliament, the Knesset.
Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Their success is one of the main reasons Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority and can't now form a new government.
The final election results show the far-right wing bloc's share of Knesset seats fell from 68 to 53.
Israel's Arab minority, also called Palestinian citizens of Israel, makes up about 20% of the country's population.
"Israel's elections have been stolen," Netanyahu's Likud party declared in a statement Thursday, claiming "an attack on democracy aimed at leading to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of the right-wing government to cause a withdrawal and defeat of the IDF (Israeli military) on all fronts — first and foremost, Iran."
The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats, so they would need some support from the Arab parties to try to form a coalition government, assuming none of the lawmakers currently aligned with Netanyahu's bloc defect.
The heads of Israel's two biggest Arab parties, which collectively won 19 seats, have said they would be willing to help the main opposition bloc oust Netanyahu from power.
Most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from Arab parties to form a government, however, leaving a question mark over whether they might now be willing to cooperate to build a coalition to unseat the incumbent prime minister.
"No basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise"
The Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency, said it had opened an investigation into possible foreign influence in the election, but the scope of that investigation has not been made clear.
"An investigation of this type is also focused and bounded, and does not cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally," the agency said in a Thursday statement.
The Acting Director-General of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."
Israel media reports said one of the allegations the Shin Bet investigation would consider was whether Qatar had sent money to Arab parties in order to increase turnout among Arab Israeli voters.
Qatar's foreign ministry has denied the accusation.
"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," ministry spokesperson Majid Al-Ansari said. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians."
"An improper influence operation?"
While vote counting is now officially complete, the election results must still be certified and sent to President Issac Herzog before a new parliament can be sworn in and the process of forming a new government begins.
Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar party and the top candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said he was worried that Netanyahu could be using the allegation of a stolen election to justify delaying or disqualifying the results.
"Netanyahu, who has accustomed himself to dealing with reality through lies, consciousness engineering, and the spreading of chaos, is leading alongside his partners an improper influence operation on the Israeli public aimed at delaying the publication of the election results on time and creating fictitious delegitimization of the activity of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot said Thursday in a social media post.
Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on — Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament.
Netanyahu, who President Trump endorsed enthusiastically, will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim.

Ukraine’s SOF ambush enemy in Russia and seize documents

Ukraine’s SOF ambush enemy in Russia and seize documents
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this in a Telegram post.
“Operators of the 73rd Maritime Center of the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine carried out an ambush on Russian territory, struck the enemy, destroyed a vehicle and seized important documents and communications equipment,” the statement said.
Having overcome enemy minefields, the soldiers of the 73rd Maritime Center entered the enemy’s rear, where they conducted reconnaissance for several days and identified targets for fire strikes.
During the mission, the special forces operators spotted enemy personnel traveling in a vehicle. The operators reacted swiftly and launched a strike.
The Ukrainian defenders found drone equipment, radios, weapons, mobile phones, combat orders, movement routes and enemy personnel lists inside the vehicle.
Following the successful ambush, the operators of the 73rd Maritime Center continued their mission behind enemy lines.

The program was presented at the Casa de Italia headquarters in the Colonial City of Santo Domingo, in the presence of Ambassador Sergio Maffettone, Politur Central Director General Minoru Matsunaga, and the president of the cultural institution, Angelo Viro. “With this initiative, we want to make the Italian language a practical tool for protecting our compatriots. Poland Received New Batch of M1110 JAB Tank-Mounted Bridge-Laying Vehicles Based on Abrams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:33:28 UTC
23:33:28 KST

Another batch of American M1110 Joint Assault Bridge (JAB) tank bridge-layers has arrived in Poland.
This was reported by the Armaments Agency of the Polish Ministry of National Defence.
According to Defence24, the equipment will be received by the 18th Mechanized Division. The first batch arrived in the country in July.
The delivered units are designed to facilitate the crossing of heavy armored vehicles over various obstacles.
In particular, the assault bridges will operate in conjunction with units equipped with M1 Abrams main battle tanks.
The procurement of this specialized equipment is being carried out as part of large-scale contracts with the United States for the supply of this armored equipment.
In total, Poland has ordered 25 M1110 JAB bridge-layers: 8 units under the agreement from January 2023 for 116 M1A1 FEP units and 17 under the contract from April 2022 for 250 M1A2 SEPv3 versions.
The M1110 was developed by Leonardo DRS based on a modified M1A1 chassis with suspension components from the M1A2 variant.
This provides the engineering vehicle with a level of armor protection, cross-country capability, and speed comparable to that of tanks.
The vehicle is equipped with a hydraulic deployment system and a new release mechanism. It uses a standard 18.3-meter-long Heavy Assault Scissor Bridge (HASB).
The bridge-laying vehicle’s crew consists of two people—a driver-mechanic and a commander. The vehicle is capable of deploying a bridge across obstacles up to 11 meters wide in just 3–5 minutes.
The structure’s load-bearing capacity meets the MLC 115 class standard. This allows even the heaviest tracked platforms—including the M1A2 SEPv3, weighing over 65 metric tons, and the M88A2 Hercules armored recovery vehicles—to safely cross water and land obstacles.

Ukraine to co-found defense bank aimed at financing weapons production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:33:15 UTC
23:33:15 KST

Ukraine and eight partner countries plan to sign an agreement establishing a new international defense bank on Nov. 30, potentially opening another source of long-term financing for weapons production, the governments said in a joint statement published Oct. 29.
The Canada-led Defense, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) aims to begin operations in 2027. It would help governments finance their defense needs, and manufacturers expand production, with benefits tied to participation in the institution.
As Russia’s war drags on, Ukraine needs sustained funding to keep its military supplied. The proposed bank could give allies another way to help finance Ukraine’s defense over the long term, supporting weapons production and military purchases.
Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said on Oct. 26 that the bank would be headquartered in Canada, with a European hub in Luxembourg. Its mandate would cover industrial expansion, critical supply chains and eligible procurement, including financing gaps affecting smaller defense companies.
read also
Reuters reported in August that the project was targeting about 100 billion euros ($111.3 billion) in capital: 20 billion euros ($22.3 billion) paid in and 80 billion euros ($89 billion) callable from members if required. The latest official statements do not specify a capital target or announce funding earmarked for Ukraine.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Canada's invitation for Ukraine to become a founding member back in July in a Telegram post following talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
“It will work to attract capital and develop defense-industrial capacity and technologies tested in real combat conditions,” Zelensky said.
Alongside Ukraine and Canada, the founding group includes Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania and Turkey.
The announcements do not specify Ukraine's contribution, borrowing terms or potential allocation. The November signing would mark another step toward establishment, rather than the start of lending.

How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:32:31 UTC
23:32:31 KST

How US and Israeli money turned Latvia into a drone workshop for Ukraine
NATO’s aggressive eastward expansion was one of the key reasons for the initiation of the military operation in Ukraine in February 2022. This is supported by RT’s findings about a drone production cluster established by NATO-affiliated enterprises near Riga.
The Baltic states had become a hub for developing combat drones as early as 2020. According to RT’s findings, companies in Latvia generated €283 million in revenue from producing UAVs, robotics, and military aerospace systems in 2022-2025 alone. More than half of that revenue came from companies with foreign investment. The two largest factories are under US and Israeli ownership, while another is partly Ukrainian-owned. Several factories form a single industrial cluster near Riga. Experts say this suggests Latvia was preparing for a conflict with Russia well in advance.
Presently, we will focus on eight UAV production factories in Latvia that are backed by foreign investments. RT uncovered the details about these companies in financial reports, aided by the G8 OSINT team that advises the Russian Defense Ministry.
According to the data, the companies collectively earned €282.98 million from 2022 to 2025.
The bulk of the revenue came from three companies: Redwire Defense Tech Riga (€131.4 million), Belss (€77.7 million), and Brasa Defense Systems (€46.7 million). The following companies contributed lesser amounts: Origin Robotics (€10.6 million), Eraser ( €6.04 million), LV-Teh (€5.98 million), Atlas Aerospace (€3.52 million), and Natrix (€0.98 million).
The Drone Coalition, which also includes the UK, was established in 2024 at Latvia’s initiative. The aim is to collaboratively supply Ukraine with drones. Collective commitments reached €600 million, and the coalition’s fund raised €1.8 billion from investors in 2024. Since then, over 100,000 drones have already been delivered to Ukraine.
Drones abound in quiet Marupe
The heart of Latvia’s drone assembly industry is located in Marupe, a suburb of Riga. Just a couple of kilometers from the international airport, five companies form a bustling UAV production cluster: Belss, its subsidiary Eraser, Brasa Defense Systems, Origin Robotics, and Redwire Defense Tech Riga.
At the center of this cluster lies SIRIN Park Marupe, a logistics hub situated near the runway. This is where Redwire Defense Tech, the industry leader in terms of revenue, is located. The company produces Penguin drones. Since 2022, they have delivered around 250 to 300 drones to Ukraine. Smaller models start at around $20,000, while some modifications can reach up to $70,000 each. The facility employs 279 people.
Nearby, at 26 Dzirnieku Street, there is Origin Robotics, which has around 60 employees. They specialize in building BEAK portable strike drones and BLAZE autonomous drone interceptors. Both models are used in Ukraine and are also part of Latvia’s military arsenal. By the end of November 2026, Origin Robotics aims to complete the development of a cargo drone system designed for precise automated delivery of cargo (i.e. explosives). In simple terms, the Latvians plan to equip quadcopters with guided mini-munitions.
Further on, in the direction of Riga, there is Brasa Defense, which occupies around 6,000 square meters of warehouse and office space at 16 Plienciema Street. They manufacture UNHUMAN ground robotic platforms designed to support infantry on the battlefield.
Located furthest from the airport, Belss operates in Ezisi Industrial Park. It is the largest defense communications integrator in Latvia (operating since 1994). The company formerly focused on secure military communications but pivoted in 2023 to develop its own line of UAVs. By 2024, they were supplying thousands of modular military drones to Ukraine. In June 2024, Belss spun off its drone division into a separate subsidiary named Eraser.
There are no doubts as to who is the primary consumer of Belss products: Latvian and Ukrainian flags are proudly displayed at the entrance. A satellite view reveals a private runway just 100 meters from the fence, used for testing equipment.
The other production facilities are located in Riga, but the difference isn’t critical since Marupe is very close to Riga. The area is home to the NATRIX, LV-Teh, and AeroVictory Baltic factories. The latter is a Baltic subsidiary of a Ukrainian company that has relocated UAV production to Latvia and has yet to submit financial reports.
Also registered in Riga is Atlas Aerospace – a company with Ukrainian roots and Israeli ownership – producing reconnaissance drones like the AtlasPRO, Atlas UAVs, and AtlasTETHER tethered systems. These devices are supplied to Ukraine and NATO countries. The company has 43 official employees.
The choice of location is strategic, according to specialists from the G8 group. In addition to proximity to the airport, a railway runs through Marupe that will soon connect with tracks leading to Ukraine via Moldova.
The father of ‘Penguins’ in the service of NATO
Latvia has its own key figure uniting several companies backed by American and European capital: Konstantins Popiks, a serial entrepreneur in the military industry. He was introduced to aeromodeling as a child and even represented Latvia in aeromodeling competitions. After enrolling at the University of Liverpool in 2005, he graduated in 2009 with a Master’s degree in aerospace engineering.
The Penguin reconnaissance drone and its combat versions, which are in service with the Latvian military and are being sold in large quantities to Ukraine, originated as Popiks’ student project. Upon returning to his homeland, he founded UAV Factory, which produces Penguin drones. Within ten years, the company reached the international level, and in 2021, it attracted an investor from the US: AE Industrial Partners. By 2022, Popiks departed, and the factory changed ownership and rebranded as Edge Autonomy.
In June 2025, the facility announced plans to double its production footprint, enabling it to produce up to ten heavy fixed-wing UAVs per month. According to documents, there were 270 employees at the time, and the company had contracts with the Latvian Defense Ministry.
In 2025, Edge Autonomy Holdings signed a merger agreement, becoming a subsidiary of American company Redwire Corp. By March 2026, it was rebranded as Redwire Defense Tech Riga, emerging as the leading company in the sector by revenue. Its reported income of €131.4 million accounts for nearly half of the total UAV sector earnings.
This defense contract not only brought Popiks fame but also significant wealth. As RT discovered, he resides in an upscale neighborhood of Jurmala (Kapu Street), where he owns a small castle. The property is surrounded by tall Baltic pines, with the Riga seashore and a beach just beyond the backyard. The property borders the Gulf of Riga.
After selling the factory, Popiks established another company – Origin Robotics. Funds from European investors began flowing in. In 2025, Belgium’s defense minister signed a €50 million contract with the company for the procurement of BLAZE drone interceptors. Currently, Origin is experiencing remarkable growth. Revenues soared from 2023 to 2025, reaching €10.6 million.
Under the wing of the IDF
Among the entrepreneurs in this cluster is Ivan Tolchinsky, an Israeli citizen of Ukrainian descent. Born in Gorlovka, Donetsk Region, he moved to Israel at the age of 10. As an adult, he served in the special forces and took part in combat operations in Lebanon. For around five years, he worked as an engineer in Israel’s aerospace industry and spent a year in China studying mass electronics production.
In 2015, Tolchinsky relocated to Latvia, where he co-founded Atlas Dynamics with Igor Zhidanov, a fellow native of Gorlovka. Zhidanov is a seasoned engineer with 35 years of experience and holds three world records in aeromodeling. He had his own club back in Gorlovka, which Tolchinsky was also a part of.
In interviews with Latvian and Ukrainian media, Tolchinsky revealed that his production facility produces over 300 Atlas drones per month – which, he says, is five times more than in previous years. He doesn’t conceal his collaboration with the Ukrainian Armed Forces. “We have a direct contract with the Ministry of Defense, which we’ve already fulfilled. Now we are working towards another contract,” he told Ukrainian journalists.
A few years before the conflict, in 2020, Tolchinsky established a subsidiary in Ireland called Atlas Dynamics UK. Originally registered at a residential address in Moreton-on-Lugg, Herefordshire, it soon changed its legal address.
The company had Israeli roots, as indicated by its founding documents drafted in Hebrew and English by a notary from Israel.
In the 2020s, Atlas Dynamics was rebranded as Atlas Aerospace SIA. In November 2025, Tolchinsky sold the company to Israel’s Xtend Reality Expansion Ltd – a company focused on creating FPV drones for entertainment and gaming prior to its collaboration with the IDF.
Russia is identified as the main adversary
Latvian UAV factories do not publicly mention contracts with Ukraine in their annual reports. Some only mention that Ukraine is among their clients, without disclosing what portion of their profits comes from supplying Kiev.
One thing is clear: Nearly all the above-mentioned companies receive investments from the Latvian Defense Ministry and EU agencies. This is part of measures to enhance defense capabilities, with Russia identified as the chief adversary.
According to EU Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, “Russia is outproducing Europe in key armaments.” This has been cited as a reason for increased defense spending, which is reflected in official documents.
According to reports reviewed by RT, one of the main sources of funding for SIA Belss is the European Defense Fund (EDF). In 2024-2025, the fund allocated €470,800 to the company under the European Extended Mine Countermeasures program, aimed at developing demining technologies. Earlier, RT reported on how the EU channels military expenditures through the guise of ‘humanitarian’ demining initiatives.
Even before 2022, Latvia’s drone sector was already experiencing rapid growth and consolidation. LV-Teh has been operating since 2020, while Brasa Defense Systems officially became a separate entity on September 13, 2021. Origin Robotics was registered on January 31, 2022 – just weeks before the start of the Ukraine conflict.
Belss has been in business since 1994, but significantly expanded its capabilities in 2022 and 2023. UAV Factory, known for its Penguin drones, was founded in 2009, and Atlas Aerospace emerged in 2015.
Only three new companies appeared after the start of hostilities: Natrix in February 2024, Eraser in June 2024, and AeroVictory Baltic (a company with direct Ukrainian roots) in February 2026.
In one of the reports, RT uncovered evidence of Latvia’s preparations for the conflict. In December 2021, just two months before the start of hostilities, the Latvian Defense Ministry allocated €88,000 to Belss for upgrading British infantry fighting vehicles in service with the Latvian army. This included installing automatic fire control systems on turrets, allowing operators to engage targets without exposing themselves, thereby enhancing crew survival on the modern battlefield, which is increasingly dominated by drones. This suggests that Latvians were gearing up for drone warfare well before the start of the conflict.
Long before the events of 2014 and 2022, a coalition of three countries with a firm anti-Russia stance formed in the Baltics, Vadim Avva, a Russian writer and political scientist born in Daugavpils, Latvia, says.
“The statehood of the Baltic nations led to the establishment of three sparsely-populated forts along [Russia’s] northwestern borders; their primary function is to support expanding NATO military bases and other infrastructure clearly being prepared for an operation to invade and occupy the territories of Russia and Belarus,” Avva says.
A launchpad for hatred
Avva recalled a viral video in which Estonian teenagers were asked which country should be erased from the world map, and many named Russia. He notes that during World War II, the national bourgeoisie of Latvia and Estonia “became a foundation for Latvian and Estonian SS legions,” and today, local schools are named after Lithuanian collaborators with Nazi Germany. He explains that the oppression of the Russian-speaking population in these regions began in the late 19th century and only intensified with the collapse of the Soviet Union.
“What has returned to the Baltics is not just bourgeois nationalism; it’s a blend of bourgeois Nazism and ‘brown’ [ultra-right] emigration,” Avva says. “What fate could befall this territory after the establishment of property monopoly and political monopoly and the welcoming back of the descendants of fascist collaborators? Obviously, it could only become a military launchpad.”
Latvian UAVs are occasionally identified and shot down by Russian drone interceptors. However, their share among the various models used by Ukraine remains small, according to a drone operator with the call sign ‘Baks’, who neutralizes enemy drones approaching Russian borders.
“Ukrainians definitely try out everything produced by the Balts and purchase a lot of their equipment, but it’s a question of scale and quantity. We don’t have much information on the BLAZE and BEAK models, but there is some info on ‘Penguins’ – our colleagues at Rubicon [Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies] managed to take down a few. The number of downed UAVs directly relates to their quantity. Compared to the Shark, Leleka, and other [Ukrainian drones], Latvian models represent a mere fraction [of the deployed drones].”
It’s not just Penguin drones that are being targeted, however, but their manufacturers as well. Redwire Defense Tech Riga, the company producing these drones, relocated to Sirin Park after their previous facility in Marupe unexpectedly burned down.
Similar incidents often occur at European companies that supply drones to Ukraine. In August 2026 alone, there were several incidents: A production facility belonging to Polish arms maker WB Electronics caught fire at the end of August; an explosion rocked the KNDS Ammo plant near Rome on August 13; and on August 15, unknown arsonists set fire to the building of Estonian military robotics manufacturer Milrem Robotics, which RT wrote about in the first part of its investigation.

Scaramucci described two ways of handling Trump: the Carney approach and the Rutte approach.
Advertisement
“There’s two models of behavior: one is [NATO Secretary-General] Mark Rutte and one is [Canadian Prime Minister] Mark Carney. I think Mark Carney is handling him better. The Canadian people are with him, even if it causes some level of economic hardship,” Scaramucci said.
“Rutte, on the other hand, is making a big mistake. Because when you equivocate or flatter him, when you act in the manner that Mark Rutte has acted, all you’re doing is losing his respect. You’re not gaining anything,” he added.
Rutte has often lauded the U.S. president: “I just like the man. I think what he is doing for NATO is great news,” the military alliance chief said in an interview with POLITICO this summer.
Europe has seemingly yielded to Trump’s wishes on numerous occasions. The EU-U.S. trade deal was criticized as playing in Washington’s favor, while European allies agreed to a 5% of GDP spending target by 2035 at last year’s NATO summit in The Hague, matching Trump’s headline demand.
Carney, by contrast, has been more unwilling to bow to Trump’s pressure. He walked away from U.S. trade talks, saying Ottawa could not accept the offer or the demands — and promised to match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.
In the interview, Scaramucci also lambasted members of Trump’s own Republican Party. “That is the other side of this story: the cowardice of the political servants that are supposed to check Donald Trump, the members of the Republican Senate caucus and the House caucus,” he said.

23:31:21 KST

Continental champions will compete in Qatar this December as PSG seek a second successive Intercontinental Cup title. The final stages return for a third year, following earlier matches in Saudi Arabia and South Africa.
Paris Saint-Germain will return to Qatar in December to defend their FIFA Intercontinental Cup title, after the country was confirmed as host of the tournament’s final three matches for a third consecutive year.
The French club will play in the final on 16 December at Ahmad bin Ali Stadium in Al Rayyan, returning to the venue where they lifted the trophy last year. The other two matches will take place on 9 and 12 December, organisers announced on Thursday.
PSG secured their place by retaining the UEFA Champions League title in the 2025-26 season. Under the competition’s format, Europe’s champions enter directly into the final, while clubs representing the other five continental confederations compete for the remaining place.
Last December, PSG beat Brazil’s Flamengo 2-1 on penalties after a 1-1 draw following extra time, winning their first Intercontinental Cup in front of 42,150 spectators.
Three clubs, one place in the final
Mexico’s Toluca, winners of the Concacaf Champions Cup, will face this year’s Copa Libertadores winners in the Derby of the Americas on 9 December at Jassim bin Hamad Stadium in Doha.
The winners will then meet South Africa’s Mamelodi Sundowns in the Challenger Cup at the same venue on 12 December, with a place against PSG in the final at stake.
Sundowns reached that stage by beating Saudi Arabia’s Al Ahli 2-1 in Pretoria on 19 September to win the African-Asian-Pacific Cup. Al Ahli had opened the tournament with a 1-0 victory over New Zealand’s Auckland FC in Jeddah on 26 August.
The South American representative will be decided in the Copa Libertadores final on 28 November.
The Intercontinental Cup is FIFA’s annual competition for the champions of its six continental confederations. It is separate from the expanded Club World Cup, which is held every four years.
Qatar hosted the final stages of the first two editions of the Intercontinental Cup in 2024 and 2025, having previously staged the 2019 and 2020 editions of the former annual Club World Cup.
This year’s December fixtures will overlap with the closing stages of the Under-17 World Cup, which Qatar is hosting from 19 November to 13 December.

In Germany, 70 rescuers removed a drunk man from a tree after he was unable to climb down following a party
Kyiv • UNN
A 25-year-old man became stuck in a treehouse six meters above the ground after a party. Rescuers brought him down with a blood alcohol level of 2.5 per mille.
In the German federal state of Saxony, around 70 emergency service workers took part in rescuing a 25-year-old man who was unable to descend from a treehouse on his own after a party. Bild reports, writes UNN.
Details
The incident occurred on the evening of October 29 near the settlement of Sehmatal in the Ore Mountains. A group of young people held a party in a treehouse about six meters above the ground. When one of the participants was unable to climb down because of severe alcohol intoxication, his friends called the firefighters.
Because of the treehouse’s hard-to-reach location near railway tracks, rescuers had to reach the site on a rail trolley. Height-rescue specialists climbed up to the man, secured him in a rescue stretcher, and carefully lowered him to the ground using ropes. The injured man was then transported by rail trolley to an ambulance and taken to hospital.
Before hospitalization, police checked the man’s blood alcohol level. The breathalyzer showed 2.5 parts per thousand, which corresponds to severe alcohol intoxication and may be accompanied by serious disruptions in the functioning of the body.
Firefighters, police officers, medical personnel, and height-rescue specialists took part in the rescue operation.

New Bulgarian Drone to Monitor Maritime Threats and Protect Shipping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

New Bulgarian Drone to Monitor Maritime Threats and Protect Shipping
A Bulgarian company has developed an autonomous drone designed to protect shipping and support maritime security in the Black Sea, with controlled tests scheduled in the Bay of Burgas over the next two weeks.
The drone was presented at an International Forum on Security and Innovation in Burgas. It was developed by a 20-member team led by Dragomir Enchev, a software engineer, and can perform autonomous maritime missions while also allowing manual control by an operator. The device runs on batteries and solar panels.
Enchev said the project aims to offer a more affordable alternative to similar autonomous drones, which can cost millions. The plan is to deploy dozens of units along Bulgaria's coastline, where they would work in coordination with radar systems and provide continuous, real-time information to enable rapid responses.
The drone is still being tested, and its developers are open to discussions with interested parties. It is electrically powered and communicates with the shore through several channels. Its capabilities include jamming hostile devices and establishing "green corridors" for safe passage.
The device can also be deployed for environmental monitoring, collecting samples at regular intervals from areas affected by spills.
Burgas Mayor Dimitar Nikolov said he had checked whether rising tensions in the Black Sea could affect commercial shipping and the city's preparations to host the upcoming Eurovision contest. "I made inquiries yesterday regarding any restrictions on commercial traffic to or from the ports in Burgas. There have been no disruptions or interruptions," he said.
Nikolov also said he felt secure as mayor of a Black Sea city because Bulgaria is a member of the EU and NATO. While acknowledging the unease caused by instability in the region in recent days and months, he said the forum was focused on a different agenda.
"I hope this concerning situation ends soon, allowing us to shift our focus back toward development and the future - toward new transport corridors and the new technologies that will take root along our coastline," Nikolov said.
Atanaska Nikolova, chair of the association Prospecti M, which is organizing the forum together with the Municipality of Burgas, said this year's event focused on sustainability, security and innovation.
The forum brought together representatives of European and national institutions, businesses and the scientific community to discuss security challenges facing Black Sea countries and opportunities for joint solutions. Discussions covered the protection of marine resources, coastal development and the introduction of new technologies.
An exhibition area also presented technological developments intended to strengthen security in the Black Sea. The event took place against a backdrop of increasingly frequent drone attacks on commercial vessels and heightened regional tensions.
Enchev said the drone was produced using 3D printing, with manufacturing taking just 48 hours. He described it as one of the first devices of its kind worldwide and said it could be produced at a relatively low cost.
"When deployed in groups, especially given the current situation, these drones can rapidly generate comprehensive, interactive maps of high-risk areas, such as our Black Sea coast, and provide instant alerts whenever a danger arises," Enchev said.

7 candidates nominated to lead World Health Organization
Unknown

2026-10-30

23:29:36 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Seven candidates have been nominated by member states to become the next director-general of the World Health Organization (WHO), the UN health agency announced Thursday.
The nominees include Qatar's Hanan Mohammed Al-Kuwari, a former health minister and current adviser to the prime minister on public health; Saudi Arabia's Hanan Balkhy, WHO regional director for the Eastern Mediterranean; and Belgium's Hans Henri P. Kluge, WHO regional director for Europe.
Also nominated are Spain's Maria P. Neira, a former director of WHO's environment and health department; Indonesian Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin; and China's Li Song, secretary of the All-China Women's Federation and former senior health official.
The seventh candidate is Armenian pediatric oncologist Gevorg Tamamyan, a professor and department chair at Yerevan State Medical University, who was nominated by Botswana.
They will participate in a public forum at the organization's headquarters in Geneva on Nov. 18-19, allowing member states to engage directly with them.
The WHO Executive Board will narrow the field to five candidates in early 2027 before conducting interviews and nominating up to three for consideration by the World Health Assembly.
A second public forum will be held March 15, 2027, for those shortlisted.
The assembly is scheduled to appoint the next director-general in May, with the successful candidate taking office Aug. 16, 2027.

Nvidia CEO sees Kazakhstan as potential AI hub for Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:29:33 UTC
23:29:33 KST

During his first visit to Kazakhstan, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the country's growing computing capacity could make it a major AI hub for Europe, as Kazakhstan expands its energy and digital infrastructure.
Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang has visited Kazakhstan for the first time, saying the Central Asian country could emerge as a major AI computing hub for Europe.
Huang made the remarks during a fireside chat with Zhaslan Madiyev, Kazakhstan's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, at the Alem.ai International Artificial Intelligence Centre in Astana.
During the discussion, Madiyev said Kazakhstan plans to nearly double its installed power capacity to more than 40 gigawatts by 2035 as the country expands the infrastructure needed to support its growing AI sector.
One of its flagship projects is the Data Center Valley, a large-scale AI computing campus under development in Ekibastuz, one of Kazakhstan's main power-generating centres. Its first 50-megawatt phase is expected to begin operations in 2027, while the project's energy infrastructure could eventually scale up to one gigawatt.
Huang said Kazakhstan's energy resources and growing computing capacity could give the country a significant role in Europe's AI ecosystem.
“Kazakhstan has a lot of real estate. It also has a lot of energy,” Huang said. “You're going to have a lot of compute right here in Kazakhstan. It's going to be a hub, a computing hub, an AI factory hub for all of Europe.”
Huang described the country's abundant energy resources as a potential competitive advantage in the AI economy, arguing that electricity could increasingly be used to generate computing power and AI rather than simply being exported as energy.
“Kazakhstan has a fundamental advantage because you have so much natural resource already. You have so much energy, and instead of just exporting energy in the future, you could transform the energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” Huang said.
Sovereign AI
But energy alone, Huang argued, will not be enough. Kazakhstan will also need to retain control over another resource — its data.
Madiyev said the country is already developing Kazakh-language large language models based on open-source foundation models and asked whether Kazakhstan should eventually build its own foundation model from scratch.
Huang said building a domestic foundation model “makes complete sense”, describing it as a national security concern.
He argued that countries should retain control over both their data and the AI infrastructure used to serve their citizens, comparing it to other essential national infrastructure.
“In the future, you will have your own electric grid, your own internet, your own telecommunications and your own intelligence grid,” Huang said.
The potential of Physical AI
Beyond computing infrastructure and sovereign AI, Kazakhstan is also looking to position itself in the emerging field of Physical AI — systems that can interact with and operate in the physical world.
Pointing to Kazakhstan's industrial base in mining, agriculture, transport and logistics, Madiyev asked whether the country could become a hub for developing and training Physical AI models and robots. Huang called the idea “fantastic”, saying these industries could be among the first to benefit.
“Physical AI is not just robotics,” Huang said. “It includes everything from seismic understanding to mapping mines and wells, to understanding geography and geology — where to mine, how best to mine — understanding material science, the processing of chemicals.”
With the technology still at an early stage, Huang said Kazakhstan has an opportunity to help shape the emerging industry.
Investing in AI startups
The discussion also turned to Higgsfield AI, a Kazakh-founded generative video startup in which Nvidia has invested.
Asked what attracted Nvidia to the company, Huang said the decision ultimately came down to its founders.
“The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” Huang said, describing Higgsfield's founders as “visionary” and capable of competing with leading AI companies globally.
Huang also pointed to the company's presence in both Kazakhstan and the United States, saying it could help bridge the two ecosystems.
Later that day, Huang met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who described the development of artificial intelligence and digitalisation as a national priority.
“This visit is very important for us in terms of giving a serious boost to cooperation with Nvidia,” Tokayev said.
Huang welcomed Kazakhstan's ambition to become an “AI nation” and said the country had the potential to become a global hub for Physical AI.
Huang's first visit to Kazakhstan came at the close of AI Month, a nationwide initiative launched in September as part of the country's Year of Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence.

Russia-Africa Summit: Four days of dealmaking the West wanted Africa to skip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:28:55 UTC
23:28:55 KST

Russia-Africa Summit by the numbers: What was achieved despite Western pressure
Delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 leaders, gathered in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit under the motto “For Peace, Security and Development.” The gathering concluded on Thursday with a final declaration and a new cooperation plan. Organizers reported 146 documents signed across the Summit and its accompanying economic, humanitarian and media forums, comprising 92 agreements and 54 memorandums.
More than 3,500 participants from 74 countries attended, including over 1,200 business representatives from around 630 companies.The forum hosted more than 40 sessions.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has already held at least nine bilateral meetings with African leaders, including the presidents of Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Mozambique, Namibia, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Kenya, as well as Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Libya’s Presidential Council Chairman Mohamed Al-Menfi.
Bilateral talks continued on Friday, with the day’s lineup including the leaders of Sudan, Madagascar, Ghana, Mali, South Sudan, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, and Eritrea, as well as Togo’s prime minister.
The October 28-29 summit capped four days of events, beginning with Monday’s media forum and including Tuesday’s separate gas exporters’ summit. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told RT that Western governments had tried to discourage African leaders from attending.
An overnight Ukrainian drone attack also prompted temporary restrictions at three Moscow airports before Thursday’s proceedings. Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported 231 drones destroyed on the approaches to the capital. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov questioned the timing during an international gathering and praised air defenses.
Here are the main outcomes and key moments.
A framework through 2029
Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the African Union chair, co-chaired Wednesday's and Thursday’s proceedings. Leaders addressed a plenary session in Kremlin before continuing over a working breakfast.
They adopted the Moscow Declaration, a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum action plan for 2027-2029 and a declaration on civilian applications of artificial intelligence.
The political declaration backed greater African representation in international institutions, opposed unlawful unilateral sanctions, and supported efforts to address colonial-era damage. It also called for South Africa’s full G20 participation to be restored, following its exclusion from meetings under the US presidency. Pretoria remains a member.
At their closing press conference, Putin emphasized the potential for further cooperation, while Ndayishimiye pressed for measurable benefits. Another summit will follow, with its date and location to be agreed.
Partnership: ‘Africa has not come to ask for aid’
Russia and Africa are “natural allies in building a multipolar, genuinely democratic world order,” Putin told the plenary. He backed stronger African representation in global decision-making and described Russian businesses as partners investing in host countries rather than pursuing colonial exploitation.
African leaders also stressed that cooperation should strengthen their ability to make independent decisions and develop their economies.
“Contrary to what malevolent forces might think, Africa has not come to ask for aid,” Ndayishimiye told the Kremlin plenary. He called for commitments to become concrete investment programs and for international cooperation to follow African priorities.
Democratic Republic of Congo President Felix Tshisekedi made a similar distinction. “Diversifying our partnerships is not about choosing sides: it is about strengthening our freedom of decision-making in the service of our populations,” he said.
Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa highlighted the need to turn agreements into action while processing more minerals domestically. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi presented his country’s cooperation with Russia, including the El Dabaa nuclear plant and planned Suez Canal industrial zone, as a model for wider partnerships.
Russia also signed several documents to deepen cooperation with African regional organizations. These included memorandums with the East African Community, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, and the African Continental Free Trade Area Secretariat, alongside an action plan with the African Union Commission.
Sergey Lavrov met counterparts from 41 African states.
Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said Lavrov pledged support for Accra’s application for BRICS partner status and would seek consensus among founding members.
Peskov said Putin presented country-specific cooperation roadmaps during bilateral meetings. Putin also highlighted expanding diplomatic representation: eight Russian embassies have opened in Africa since 2023, bringing the total to 48. Six trade missions cover 16 countries, while Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo plan embassies in Moscow.
Financing and nuclear cooperation
Signings included a Wednesday memorandum between Russia’s development institution VEB.RF and BCID-AES, the joint investment bank serving Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, to identify and assess development and integration projects.
Rosatom also signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation memorandum with Togo, establishing working groups to examine potential projects and training. Floating nuclear power units are among the possibilities.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed sought priority for nuclear cooperation, including financing, engineering training and medical isotopes. A roadmap for Ethiopia’s first nuclear plant was signed in March, Rosatom chief Aleksey Likhachev said in an interview published Friday. Site-selection preparations are underway. Burundi expressed interest in small modular reactors. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi highlighted El Dabaa and the planned Russian industrial zone near the Suez Canal as examples of bilateral cooperation.
Trade and technology at Gostiny Dvor
Wednesday’s Economic and Humanitarian Forum at Gostiny Dvor in the Russian capital set much of the practical agenda. Putin proposed at least doubling Russia-Africa trade to more than $50 billion. On Thursday, he reported that the ruble accounted for up to 85% of commercial transactions between the two sides.
Putin and African leaders toured the “Platform for Sovereign Development” exhibition, showcasing energy, healthcare, agricultural, and digital technologies.
Elsewhere, Kenyan President William Ruto visited Sberbank’s smart city development and highlighted potential AI cooperation in healthcare and education.
Gas diplomacy alongside the summit
Tuesday’s eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit adopted its own Moscow Declaration, separate from the Russia-Africa documents. It reaffirmed sovereign rights over gas resources and supported supply security, investment, and a balanced transition toward lower-carbon energy.
At Monday’s ministerial meeting, Russian Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilev promoted a proposed gas bank for long-term infrastructure financing, including in Africa. The initiative remained under discussion.
Media cooperation and liberation legacies
The Russia-Africa Media Forum ran from Monday to Thursday, organized by RT alongside Sputnik and TASS. Organizers welcomed more than 200 participants from 46 African countries for discussions on reporting, professional cooperation, and media sovereignty.
The forum also produced several media partnerships. These included Ethiopia’s Fana renewing its agreement with RT and Libya’s national news agency signing with RT Arabic. Rossiya Segodnya concluded partnerships with outlets in Algeria, Chad, Morocco, Ghana, and Zimbabwe, as well as Ethiopia’s Debre Markos University and Niger’s Higher School of Journalism and Communication.
RT’s Thursday session, “Forging Independence: Lessons from the Founders of African Nations,” featured descendants of African liberation leaders. Samia Nkrumah, daughter of Ghana’s first president Kwame Nkrumah, credited Russian support during Africa’s independence struggles, saying, “We are all here in Russia for a reason.” Ndileka Mandela, granddaughter of South Africa’s Nelson Mandela, recalled first meeting him through a prison window on Robben Island in 1981, aged 16: “I touched the window on one side and he touched on the other.”
Education and healthcare commitments
Putin extended Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for Africa through 2029.
Eight countries have received 15 mobile laboratories, and around 450 African specialists have been trained under the program, he said.
Among the healthcare agreements was a five-year memorandum with DR Congo covering training, research, maternal and child health, nuclear medicine, and digital healthcare.
Nearly 40,000 Africans study at Russian universities, up 50% since 2020, according to Putin. Government-funded scholarship places have nearly tripled over that period, reaching 5,500 for 2026-2027. Announced initiatives include ten centers helping African applicants enter Russian universities and vocational training programs.
Andrey Maslov, director of HSE University’s Center for African Studies, told RT that extended visits by African leaders and their separate business programs showed political ties with Moscow are gaining practical substance.

India’s China+1 Dilemma: It May Need China to Depend Less on China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:28:00 UTC
23:28:00 KST

On July 8, New Delhi cleared a smartphone joint venture between Dixon Technologies, an Indian firm, and the Indian arm of Vivo, a Chinese one. Dixon will hold 51 percent, Vivo 49. The partnership was first announced in December 2024 – its approval took nearly 19 months. That is a fair measure of the scrutiny Chinese money attracts in India.
The deal captures the dilemma of India’s China+1 ambitions. India wants to reduce its dependence on China, but building the manufacturing capabilities to do so may need more Chinese involvement, not less. Whether Dixon-Vivo merely adds assembly capacity or helps build Indian technology and Indian suppliers remains to be seen.
The tension came up repeatedly in 50 interviews with executives, policymakers and industry experts, conducted in 2025 for research at the East Asian Institute, National University of Singapore, and published in Global Policy.
Few executives talked of China+1 as leaving China. Most described a portfolio: keep China’s scale, add India as a second site. One automotive executive spoke of “two supply chains for the same product — one will come from India, one will come from China.” Another explained why that is hard: “China’s strength is its mature local supply chain, which doesn’t exist yet in Southeast Asia or India.”
India’s electronics boom shows the problem. Smartphone assembly and exports have grown fast, but many of the components, machines and materials still arrive from China. Making more in India does not mean buying less from Chinese suppliers. In the short term, it can mean buying more.
Dependence also brings fragility. In July 2025, Bloomberg reported that Foxconn, the Taiwan-based electronics maker that assembles iPhones for Apple, had asked hundreds of Chinese engineers and technicians to return home, and that more than 300 had already left its Indian iPhone operations. The reasons remain unclear, but the episode showed how much Indian manufacturing leans on skills that sit in China. Some executives we spoke to also worried about sudden interruptions to supply, and about the safety of proprietary designs handed to Chinese vendors. Those are perceptions of risk rather than documented cases of government interference.
India’s caution is understandable. Press Note 3, introduced in April 2020, made investment from countries sharing a land border with India subject to government approval. Two months later, in June 2020, Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in the Himalayas, reportedly killing 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers. India also barred Huawei from its 5G networks and banned hundreds of Chinese apps.
Yet restrictions have a price. Chinese equity investment into India fell from about $229 million in 2018-19 to $2.67 million in 2024-25. Several interviewees argued that investment screening, together with visa restrictions and political uncertainty, had put off Chinese component and equipment suppliers from setting up in India. One described restricting Chinese investment while carrying on importing Chinese products as “shooting yourself twice over in your foot.”
While that’s probably an overstatement, it does point to a real trade-off: Keeping Chinese capital out does not remove dependence on Chinese production. It may leave Indian manufacturers importing inputs that, in principle, they could make at home.
New Delhi has started to loosen up. In March 2026 the government relaxed parts of its investment-screening rules. Investors from land-border countries with non-controlling beneficial ownership of up to 10 percent can now use the automatic route, subject to conditions. Proposals in specified manufacturing activities, including electronic components and capital goods, are due a decision within 60 days. Direct Chinese investments that need approval are still screened.
The question is what India does with this opening.
First, security-sensitive activities should stay under tight scrutiny, while ordinary manufacturing investment deserves clearer, more predictable rules. Second, Chinese participation should be judged by what it adds to Indian capabilities: engineering skills, supplier development, competitive component production, access to technology and markets. Indian majority ownership, as in Dixon-Vivo, may help, but a 51 percent stake does not guarantee any meaningful transfer of technology. Third, India needs other sources of critical inputs – in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Europe and elsewhere. Not everything has to be made at home. The aim is to be less exposed to disruption while building capability where India can actually compete.
The result is managed dependence, and it should not be permanent. Chinese participation can help build India’s manufacturing base, but the test is whether Indian firms end up with more capabilities and more choices than they have now.
Chinese firms have their own reasons to come. India offers a big domestic market and a growing manufacturing base for global customers. As multinationals spread production beyond China, Chinese suppliers must choose: follow their customers to India, or lose business to rivals who do. What suits the firms, though, may not always suit Beijing.
New Delhi can set the terms on which Chinese firms take part in India’s industrial development. Or it can go on depending on the terms on which Beijing lets Chinese goods, technology and expertise flow.

Russia: Closure of Novaya Gazeta is a devastating loss for embattled media freedom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:27:13 UTC
23:27:13 KST

Responding to the announcement that Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s last independent newspapers, will cease operations on 9 November, Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Deputy Director, said:
“The closure of Novaya Gazeta is a devastating loss for everyone in Russia who turns to independent, investigative journalism to uncover the truth. This long-respected newspaper has withstood years of mounting state pressure, including criminal prosecutions, raids and attacks on staff members. Its journalists have been killed for doing their jobs. Its website has been blocked, its official registration cancelled and just last month, it was designated a “foreign agent.”
“The final blow has come with an eviction notice demanding that the newsroom vacate its premises, in addition to being cut off from online donations. While these measures were carried out by private actors, the authorities’ role is not in question. Their decades-long predatory campaign has resulted in the near complete annihilation of free media in Russia, and now, of its most celebrated and distinguished champion.
“Russian authorities must immediately end their persecution of independent media, including Novaya Gazeta, and abolish laws stifling freedom of expression and imposing censorship. Journalists must be able to work without fear of harassment, prosecution or violence.”
[The authorities’] decades-long predatory campaign has resulted in the near complete annihilation of free media in Russia, and now, of its most celebrated and distinguished champion
Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Deputy Direct
Background
On 30 October, Novaya Gazeta announced it would cease operations on 9 November, closing its Moscow office where staff had worked for 29 years, after the landlords told the newsroom to vacate the premises. The editorial statement said the newspaper had been deprived of the means to operate, including access to its donation system, due to financial organizations’ unwillingness to provide services to it following the 4 September 2026 designation of the newspaper’s entire editorial team as “foreign agents.”
In the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the authorities blocked Novaya Gazeta’s online resources and stripped it of its media registration. On 9 April 2026, Investigative Committee officers searched its newsroom for 13 hours in connection with a criminal case involving alleged “unlawful access to computer information” and “illegal use of personal data.” Investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested in connection with the case and later placed under house arrest. On 15 October, officers searched the home of editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov.

Turkish first lady highlights women's influential role in social heritage of Turkic world

Orhan Onur Gemici and Zehra Nur Celik
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Women holding strong, influential positions in social life is not a new development in the heritage of Turkic civilizations, said Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan on Friday.
“What we need to do is transform this experience into a perspective unique to the Turkic world that is in harmony with the cultural sensitivities, priorities, and social realities of our societies,” Erdogan said at the first meeting of the High Honorary Council of the Council on Family and Women in the Turkish capital Ankara.
Hosted by Erdogan, the meeting was attended by the spouses of leaders visiting Ankara for the 13th Heads of State Summit of the Organization of Turkic States as well as Turkish Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas, and senior representatives from member countries.
The meeting aimed to transform the shared commitment to family and women's issues across the Turkic world into lasting cooperation.
Addressing the gathering, Emine Erdogan said: “We aim to make our council a lasting platform for cooperation. Today, together with you, we have taken the first steps toward establishing our council here in Ankara.”
“I hope that we will hold our council's first official meeting next year during the 14th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States in Uzbekistan, hosted by my dear sister Ziroat Mirziyoyeva,” the wife of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, she added.
Later on Friday, Erdogan shared a post about the meeting on Turkish social media platform NSosyal.
“With our council having taken its first step towards establishment, we aim to bring together our efforts to empower families and women on a common platform,” she said.
“We believe that keeping families, the unseen stronghold of our societies, strong is possible by supporting women in every sphere of life,” she also said.
“With this understanding, we attach importance to drawing on the experience of our countries and developing solutions to the challenges we face through collective wisdom.”
Erdogan voiced hope that the council will reinforce cooperation in the fields of family and women across the Turkic world and further strengthen their bonds of fellowship.

On again: Trump restores weekend campaign rallies in Iowa, Kansas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trump backtracks on rallies in turbulent end to midterms campaign
- Trump reversed his cancelled rallies in Kansas and Iowa, after questions about his health and energy. He said Republicans still “have a shot” in the midterms.
- Republicans are defending their Senate majority, while Democrats want to win a chamber and slow Trump’s agenda. Trump’s low approval ratings and public anger over costs and war may hurt Republicans.
- Early voting has reached a record 47.9 million. Pope Leo XIV, the first known pope to vote in a political election, mailed his ballot in Chicago, the Vatican said.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump on Oct 30 insisted Republicans “have a shot” at success in the US midterms despite a feverish end to the campaign for elections that will decide control of Congress.
Trump reversed course and reinstated two rallies in Kansas and Iowa a day after cancelling them, a move which had raised questions about his health and about the state of the race.
“Typically, a president, whether he’s good or bad, Republican or Democrat, loses the midterms,” Trump told reporters as he hosted Stephen Hubbard, a US detainee recently freed by Russia, in the Oval Office.
“I think we have a shot at doing well. Maybe very well, but you know, pretty well.”
Trump said that he had cancelled the two events to hold virtual rallies but that Republicans in Iowa and Kansas called “and they said if you could go, it would be better than a tele-rally.”
But the 80-year-old’s comments were far from a robust assessment of Republican chances in the Nov 3 vote.
Republicans are defending their 53-47 majority in the Senate in Nov 3’s elections, while Democrats are seeking to capture at least one chamber of Congress and curb Trump’s legislative agenda during his final two years in office.
Trump has put himself at the centre of the Republicans’ midterm strategy, hoping it will fire up his MAGA (Make America Great Again) base.
But his Trump’s dismal approval ratings and public anger over the Iran war and the cost of living may be a drag on Republican chances.
Trump, who complained of losing his voice earlier this week, had lashed out on Oct 29 when he was asked if he was scrapping the Kansas trip because he was “sick of travelling.”
“I feel perfect,” Trump snapped, saying he no longer needed to visit Kansas because Republican Senator Roger Marshall was “doing very well.”
But Trump’s about-face was likely the result of the questions over the energy levels of America’s oldest-ever elected president, political strategist Mike Fahey told AFP.
“My suspicion is that Trump didn’t particularly like that narrative, and putting the events back on the calendar was the fastest way to kill it,” said Fahey, a veteran of multiple election campaigns.
Both Kansas and Iowa voted comfortably for Trump in 2024, but have emerged as unexpected battlegrounds for Republicans.
Marshall faces a competitive challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in Kansas, which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932. In Iowa, Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson is fighting a close race against Democrat Josh Turek.
Pope Leo votes
A record 47.9 million Americans have already voted in the US midterms, with participation surging in key battleground states and registered Democrats outpacing Republicans, figures showed on Oct 30.
The surge is especially pronounced in states with fiercely contested Senate races.
Among the early midterm voters is Pope Leo XIV, the Catholic Church’s first US-born pontiff – the first known time a pope has voted in a political election.
The head of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, who has clashed with US President Donald Trump, submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago, the Vatican said on Oct 30.
A rift earlier in 2026 between the pope and Trump sparked global headlines.
Trump has urged Republicans to “pretend I’m on the ballot” in the midterms, pointing to his presidential election wins in 2016 and 2024 which largely defied the polls.
He has promised a US$5,000 “dividend” for every American citizen if Republicans keep control of Congress, and stepped up harsh rhetoric against migrants, Muslims and transgender people.
Trump has also repeatedly warned that he will face a third impeachment if Republicans lose, although Democrats may be more likely to focus on the 2028 presidential election.
Democrats, meanwhile, fear Trump won’t accept a Republican loss in the midterms – as he did in the 2020 presidential election – after he recently ramped up claims of voter fraud.
“We had a rigged election in 2020. We cannot ever let that happen again,” Trump said in an interview with the KCMO radio station in Kansas City. AFP
