UN finds Israel persecuted Palestinian children based on age. Can justice follow?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:10:53 UTC
23:10:53 KST

The deliberate killing and injuring of Palestinian children in Gaza and the occupied West Bank by Israeli forces amounts to age-based persecution, a United Nations commission of inquiry has found.
In a report presented on Monday to the UN General Assembly, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel concluded that Israeli forces had persecuted Palestinian children on the basis of age in the occupied West Bank, extending its earlier finding on Gaza.
The commission said the repeated attacks and severe physical and psychological harm inflicted on children were part of a broader pattern of intentional violence.
Persecution as a crime against humanity entails a severe deprivation of fundamental rights on discriminatory grounds, according to Nasir Qadri, an international law practitioner and critical legal scholar at Koc University.
“Age-based persecution applies that discriminatory ground specifically to children as a group. In this context, their age was the basis for the use of lethal and injurious force against them, rather than children simply being part of the population caught up in a military campaign,” Qadri tells TRT World.
“War crimes require proof of specific prohibited acts, while genocide requires proof of the intent to destroy a group as such,” he adds.
“Persecution falls into a different legal category. It requires a widespread or systematic attack, a severe deprivation of rights, and discriminatory intent directed at the group being targeted.”
“The Commission found all three, with age as the discriminatory ground, across the occupied Palestinian territory as a whole. The West Bank finding extends a conclusion previously confined to Gaza. Age-based persecution is now the Commission’s determination for both,” he says.
The commission investigated seven cases involving killings and serious harm to Palestinians in the occupied West Bank between November 2023 and June 2026, and documented six.
In most cases, the victims were children, including an infant. The commission found that they were unarmed, posed no imminent threat, and were targeted without warning, often in the head or upper body.
It concluded that Israeli soldiers intentionally killed the victims, despite being in a position to recognise that they posed no immediate danger.
In one case, an Israeli soldier fired on a car carrying a Palestinian family in Hebron on June 5, 2026, killing a seven-month-old baby with a shot to the head and injuring both parents.
Video footage showed the father slowing down, stopping the car and raising his hands as he approached the soldiers.
The Israeli army said the soldier had fired because the vehicle was accelerating towards them, but the commission found that the soldier had a clear, unobstructed view of the occupants from a distance of about 10 metres. The family received no medical assistance.
In another incident, a 14-year-old Palestinian boy was shot in the chest and killed near the entrance to Jenin refugee camp on September 8, 2025.
Israeli forces had closed the camp in January, displacing its residents.
When rumours spread that troops might be withdrawing, around 50 to 60 residents went back to check on their homes. Israeli forces arrived by vehicle and opened fire without warning, killing the boy.
What is age-based persecution?
Persecution is a crime against humanity under international criminal law. It involves the intentional, severe deprivation of fundamental rights because of a person’s identity or membership in a particular group, with discriminatory intent.
Age-based persecution applies this legal framework to harm inflicted on people because of their age.
Not every killing or injury of a child automatically amounts to persecution. The legal determination depends on the severity of the harm, evidence of discriminatory intent, and the broader context in which the acts took place.
In the case of Palestinian children, the commission concluded that the attacks’ recurrence and widespread nature revealed a pattern of intentional violence, rather than children merely being caught up in military operations.
The legal finding depends on the nature and severity of the harm, evidence of discriminatory intent and the wider context in which the acts took place.
The report also found that Palestinians in the occupied West Bank were being targeted on the basis of their nationality, race, ethnicity, gender and age.
Qadri points to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia's (ICTY) Kupreskic case, which examined the persecution and killing of Bosnian Muslim civilians during the 1993 attack on Ahmici, Bosnia and Herzegovina.
“In the Kupreskic case, the ICTY established that discriminatory intent can be demonstrated through the cumulative effect of acts that may appear ambiguous when viewed individually, but which reveal a pattern when considered alongside an established policy,” Qadri says.
In other words, discriminatory intent need not be established by any single incident if the evidence as a whole demonstrates a pattern.
“The Commission found that Israeli forces applied permissive rules of engagement exclusively against Palestinians, concentrating lethal force on children approaching designated lines, as part of a coordinated attack across the occupied Palestinian territory,” Qadri adds.
A wider pattern of violence
The report describes a sharp deterioration in the human rights situation in the occupied West Bank since October 7, 2023, as Israeli forces' attacks and sustained settler violence have increasingly endangered Palestinian civilians.
The scale of lethal force has changed dramatically. According to the commission, six Palestinians were killed by air strikes in the occupied West Bank between 2008 and October 6, 2023.
Between October 7, 2023, and September 30, 2026, air strikes killed 254 Palestinians.
The commission concluded that Israeli military operations and settler violence were part of a widespread, systematic attack on Palestinian civilians in the occupied West Bank.
It also linked the violence to territorial expansion and displacement.
Israeli military operations since January 2025 have led to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 people still displaced as of August 2026, according to the report.
The findings add to a growing body of evidence concerning alleged and established violations of international law against Palestinians. But documenting crimes and securing accountability remain separate challenges.
“The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant mean that the situation in Gaza is already part of active proceedings. The Commission’s finding of age-based persecution could also provide evidentiary material for the Office of the Prosecutor as it builds its case,” Qadri says.
“The ICJ is continuing to hear South Africa’s case under the Genocide Convention, and the Commission’s findings on the West Bank add to the factual record the Court can consider when assessing Israel’s compliance with its January 2024 provisional measures order.”
“So the legal avenues are already open and active. The main obstacle is not jurisdiction, but enforcement,” Qadri adds.
Accountability efforts
The commission's conclusions go beyond documenting individual abuses.
By classifying the deliberate killing of Palestinian children and the serious physical and psychological harm inflicted on them as age-based persecution, the commission has identified this conduct in both Gaza and the occupied West Bank as a crime against humanity.
The report also found that Israeli authorities and forces continued to commit genocidal acts in Gaza after the October 2025 ceasefire, with the intent to destroy Palestinians, in whole or in part.
In the occupied West Bank, it documented other crimes against humanity, including extermination, torture, rape, and other forms of sexual violence.
The commission called on Israel to end its unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory, remove settlements and settlers, reverse the confiscation of Palestinian land, and return seized property to its owners.
“Under Article 41 of the Articles on State Responsibility, all states must refrain from recognising as lawful situations resulting from serious breaches of peremptory norms of international law, and must cooperate to bring those breaches to an end,” Qadri says.
“States that continue to provide military, financial or political support to Israel in the face of this evidence may also face legal consequences. The Commission made clear that states must use all means available to prevent and punish genocide and cooperate with the ICC.”
“When states choose not to act despite the evidence available, that is a political choice. The Commission has already set out its legal assessment,” he adds.
As of September 30, 2026, the commission was unaware of any effective investigations, disciplinary proceedings, or judicial measures in the cases it had examined.
Even in four cases where Israeli authorities acknowledged mistakes, the victims' families had received no remedy.
The commission warned that this lack of accountability had helped entrench a discriminatory system in which violations against Palestinian children were repeatedly committed with impunity.

Five Questions About Trump’s ‘America First’ Approach to Fighting Corruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:10:00 UTC
23:10:00 KST

Shortly after taking office in early 2025, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump paused the enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), the nearly 50-year-old law that prohibits American citizens or companies from bribing foreign officials for business.
When the FCPA was resumed six months later, the U.S. Department of Justice was ordered to narrow its focus to limit “undue burdens” on American companies operating outside the country. That action was in line with the Trump administration’s “America First” unilateral approach to foreign policy, which has seen the U.S. withdraw from dozens of international organizations on the grounds that they are inefficient and not in line with the country’s priorities.
Lorenzo Crippa, a lecturer at the University of Strathclyde who quantitatively studies how recorded instances of corruption affect financial flows, discusses the repercussions of these changes and worrying trends that have emerged under the new U.S. approach to global anti-corruption enforcement.
The U.S. has changed the way it applies the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and last month it was announced it will officially withdraw from GRECO, the Council of Europe’s anti-corruption body. U.S. officials reportedly said the government would instead use unilateral tools like sanctions and visa restrictions to fight corruption, which they described as more effective. Based on your research, do you think the rejection of collaborative global standards in favor of mechanisms a country controls itself can be more effective?
I would say hardly so. In the anti-corruption space, likely the opposite is true. It's just enough to look at history: the U.S. adopted the FCPA (Foreign Corrupt Practices Act) in 1977, and for 20 years, the law was basically silent until a global regime on anti-corruption was passed at the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) with the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention.
The law was on the books, but it was effectively not enforced, because the fear was that enforcing the law would disadvantage American companies at a time when German competitors and French competitors could even deduct bribes from tax statements.
That all changed with the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention. At the end of the ‘90s, that's the moment we see enforcement of the FCPA, effectively for the first time.
The same could be said when we think of other areas of governance, more generally. There's research in political science and international relations that clearly shows that coordination among countries is the most effective way to address global issues, rather than unilateral actions. So, I'm at the very least skeptical that that could be the case.
In unrelated research of mine with some co-authors, we looked at the effect of American sanctions on financial markets, and we find that they can actually backfire for American firms that are connected to the sanctioned entities. So there's even evidence that a multilateral solution could probably be more desirable.
You co-authored an article in Foreign Affairs this year on how Washington may now be weaponizing anti-corruption law. Many critics of the U.S. say that its laws were hardly neutral before, and often applied for geopolitical or economic leverage, or even amounted to a form of imperialism. How would you respond to that line of argument?
Certainly it's true that the FCPA had been enforced in the past also for geopolitical reasons. I'm sympathetic to these claims. What has changed is that the approach of the Trump administration seems to be one where American firms get a free pass, and non-American firms would be subject to harsher enforcement. Or at least the expectation seems to be this one. And if that's the case, this is a significant change from the past.
If we compare it from the past situation, [despite] the fact that non-U.S. firms might have been significantly charged under the FCPA, American firms were still subject to this policy to a full extent. Whereas here, what we're observing is the possibility of a double standard. That could genuinely be concerning, because that would be outright weaponization.
Like I said, I'm sympathetic with these critics of the FCPA but it did manage to get some massive cases of corruption brought to justice — even of American firms. I think the largest fine in FCPA history is Goldman Sachs. It was certainly far from ideal, but probably closest to the best that was realistically adoptable as an anti-corruption policy. So its reshaping under the Trump administration is, to me, concerning.
What are your specific concerns? What could be the broader effects on corruption around the globe if they don't target U.S. firms and selectively target non-U.S. firms?
When Trump initially halted enforcement of the FCPA in 2025, I was initially puzzled. The FCPA has been used as a tool of foreign policy as well, so getting rid of this or pausing it altogether, was puzzling to me.
But when the period of pause was over and enforcement resumed, under new revised guidelines, what seems to be the case is that it's going to be enforced primarily with the purpose of defending American foreign interests. At the moment we just have a handful of new cases after this change in enforcement, which makes it a little bit difficult as of now to understand if that's really the direction that this is going.
What my co-authors and I found was that at the very least markets seem to have priced in that expectation. We found that the moment the FCPA was suspended, firms that had been targets of FCPA actions in the past significantly experienced a boost in their stock price, which reflects the idea that probably investors expected a lax enforcement environment coming, for the rest of the Trump administration at least. That essentially means putting a bonus on the possibility of corrupt activity. It's a very robust change that we observe from the moment enforcement was made laxer.
In the past decades, we got used to the idea that corruption was bad for business, that investors would prefer a cleaner firm. These results, at least in this historical moment, seem to indicate the opposite: That these market actors would be willing to bet on more corruption. This is somewhat of a step change when it comes to corporate governance and good governance of business. Then again, this gain in stock price was concentrated on American firms. Non-American firms saw no improvement to their valuation, which seems to reflect this idea that there's going to be weaponization going forward.
With those same co-authors, you published another paper this year studying the effects of the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention, finding that the drop in bribery by companies who comply with the convention was basically offset by an increase in bribery from non-signatory competitors. What can we conclude from this? Is it casting doubt on whether the OECD convention or any “supply side” treaty targeting bribers can work?
That's a tricky question, because that paper clearly shows two faces of the same coin. On the one hand, it shows that these treaties are working because they generate strong incentives for those outside the treaty to make the most out of the advantage that they can get. That shows firms covered by the treaty that cannot bribe with impunity. The other face of the coin, that this is offset by corruption from firms outside the treaty, is really concerning. It means that something should be done.
We had a meeting with the OECD working group on bribery about this when we were disseminating the results of our findings. I think they're very aware of this problem. My main takeaway from this is that the solution is [an] expansion of these treaties. As long as there are double standards, as long as there are firms outside of the treaty who can bribe with impunity, the risk of this leakage (that’s what we call it where corruption sort of leaks to the group of firms outside of the treaty) becomes larger.
Historically, the way this has been solved was by trying to expand participation to the treaty. In the ‘90s, that meant having France, Germany, and Japan in the treaty. Right now, probably that means trying to expand to China, Singapore, Taiwan — jurisdictions with firms that are very heavily involved in business, but who can bribe with impunity. I understand that calling for more multilateralism these days seems idealistic, but really that's the only way that we can ensure that these supply side treaties can work in a sense.
My research doesn't do much on this, but existing research of others does show that in the past a strategy has been to use domestic anti-corruption needs of countries. When the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention was signed, the U.S., who was heavily pushing for this treaty, managed to sort of exploit the fact that European countries were facing their own domestic corruption scandals. In Italy, for example, the Mani pulite [“clean hands”] scandal was a big thing in the ‘90s, and that was a significant reason why the U.S. managed to put pressure on this treaty to exist. So if treaty members were able to exploit the fact that, domestically in other parts of the world, there might be a need for more anti-corruption reforms, this could be one lever to try and extend participation.
I wouldn't be certain that these [multilateral treaties] are the ideal solutions, but of the ones that have been tried, they seem to have been quite effective. At least in the shape that they used to have, with a multilateral agreement, and within that agreement, the United States playing a significant role in enforcement, for the good and bad that that was. This role as a global sheriff, in a sense, has managed to reduce corruption and bring large cases of bribery to justice. Now, whether that is the ideal solution, I'm not sure. There certainly is evidence that this was working, and jeopardizing that with the recent moves of the Trump administration makes me somewhat worried.
Could the U.S. look to resume its role as “global sheriff” if U.S. President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffers the kind of losses currently being predicted in polling for next week’s U.S. midterm elections?
There's a group of senators led by Elizabeth Warren who are trying to propose a bill called the FCPA Reinforcement Act. The idea is to extend the statute of limitations of the FCPA so that it could effectively be protected by future political decisions to halt enforcement again. This specific bill is very unlikely to pass — it’s mostly like a signalling device.
But under a flip [of congressional power in next week’s elections] … that’s a hypothetical. [but] Mmy expectation would be that it would counteract the negative effect that we saw on stock market movements at least. By protecting the FCPA from political swings it should reinforce the idea that enforcement is going to happen, and that good anti-corruption governance is the expectation, and that companies and investors shouldn't deviate from that. So at the very least, I would expect it should reassure markets of that and prevent investors from betting on corruption. I'm not sure this would do much to change this idea of enforcing the FCPA more strongly on non-American companies. I'm not sure that would be something that the bill itself could address. But at the very least, it should remove part of the problem.

Finland to establish military space operations center at Tikkakoski
Finland will establish a military space operations center at Tikkakoski, according to Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen, Qazinform News Agency reports.
In a post on X, the Finnish minister said that the Defence Forces' Space Operations Centre will be located at the Air Force Headquarters in Tikkakoski. It will start operating on January 1, 2027.
“It will serve as the command and control of defence space activities and the space operations of the Finnish Defence Forces, while also developing the Defence Forces’ space capabilities,” an official statement reads.
The center will initially employ 20 personnel, and the number will increase in the coming years.
“The founding of a space operations centre is part of a broader process to improve Finland’s defence by reinforcing the Finnish Defence Forces’ space capabilities. It is also our response to the growing importance of space as an operational domain for defence,” Minister Häkkänen said.
The Ministry of Defence is also preparing a space strategy for defence to create a long-term vision for developing space defence in the defence administration. The strategy is nearly complete, and the establishment of the space operations centre is one of the first tangible steps towards reaching the objectives set out in the strategy.
The priorities and objectives for space defence are outlined in the Government Defence Report. As part of its Programme, the Government has also adopted a Space Strategy, which sets out Finland’s vision and objectives for space activities through 2030, highlighting the importance of the space economy, security and defence policy, and security of supply.
Earlier, it was reported that Finland's Licensing and Supervision Agency had ordered Google's subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, to suspend environment-altering preparatory work at two planned data center sites in Muhos and Kajaani until environmental impact assessments are completed.

Six killed in helicopter crash en route from Indian holy site

Six killed in helicopter crash en route from Indian holy site
A helicopter crash in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand has killed all six people on board, including the pilot, officials said on Friday.
The helicopter owned by Trans Bharat Aviation Private Limited, with the call sign VT-HCX, was heading from Badrinath in Chamoli district to Dehradun when contact with it was lost at around 1:15 PM IST. It crashed into a hillside, local officials said.
“We have received the unfortunate news of a helicopter crash near Chayee village, close to Joshimath,” Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami posted on X. Joshimath is a sacred hill town in the Garhwal Himalayas.
Indian Army and local rescue teams were rushed to the scene of the crash. The Chamoli district administration later confirmed the deaths of all on board the chopper.
The five passengers on board the chopper were from the southern Indian state of Karnataka. The pilot, Capt. Himanshu Sabharwal, was from Delhi, reports said.
The Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority has grounded Trans Bharat’s helicopter fleet as a precautionary step.
Heavy rains and poor visibility have been reported in the area, which is under an “orange” alert issued by the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD). The IMD has forecast thunderstorms, hail, and gusty winds accompanied by heavy rainfall in many areas of the Himalayan state bordering China and Nepal.
The pilgrim site of Badrinath, from where the chopper took off, is part of the Char Dham pilgrimage route along with Kedarnath, Gangotri, and Yamunotri. Pilgrims take chopper rides to avoid difficult mountain treks on the route.
Aviation authorities have boosted inspections and imposed flight curbs following a spate of mishaps in the hill state’s pilgrim routes.
Seven people were killed in a helicopter crash involving pilgrims near Kedarnath in June last year, and a similar number of casualties were reported in another crash on the same pilgrimage route in October, 2022.

‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:08:41 UTC
23:08:41 KST

Flávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.
Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the US after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – to declare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.
“If it served any purpose at all, Flávio’s foolishness liberated the democratic right from a family of coup-mongers, which for far too long held it hostage to their reckless folly and irremediable disdain for Brazil,” the conservative Estado de São Paulo newspaper thundered on Friday.
Bolsonaro fled to Miami on Tuesday night, 48 hours after being beaten by his leftwing adversary, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, by 4.4m votes. Lula’s victory has been recognised by rightwing leaders from around the world, including El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, not to mention Bolsonaro’s own party and many key allies.
But on Wednesday after landing in the US, Bolsonaro published an outlandish letter – reportedly produced with the help of ChatGPT – in which he declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil” and made phoney claims about election fraud.
Perhaps most bizarrely, he claimed he would continue to lead Brazil’s opposition from abroad, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who in the 1940s led a French government-in-exile against the Nazis from London, and the 19th-century Cuban independence hero José Martí, who challenged the Spanish empire from New York.
“They were all treated as criminals by the regimes they confronted. History called them something else,” Bolsonaro said, also likening himself to Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado and Rui Barbosa, a Brazilian politician who went into exile in London in the late 19th century after challenging an authoritarian president known as “the Iron Marshal”.
Just under an hour after Bolsonaro’s proclamation was first published on social media, a corrected version was issued, altering his claimed status to “leader of Brazil” – reportedly after he was upbraided by Trump administration officials keen to avoid a full-blown diplomatic split with Brazil’s actual leaders.
The amended letter also updated the out-of-date Brazilian coat of arms that had been used erroneously in the letterhead of the first version referring to the “United States of Brazil” – a name the South American country has not used since 1967.
Bolsonaro’s flight – and his brief but bogus claim to be “president-elect” of one of the world’s largest democracies – prompted an outpouring of opprobrium and ridicule.
“[This letter] seems to have been written by a foolhardy, loony halfwit,” Flávia Oliveira, a prominent political commentator, told the network GloboNews.
The Estado de São Paulo’s leader writers said: “Flávio’s letter isn’t worth the ink of this newspaper, but there’s no way the embarrassment can be ignored,” before savaging a man they called “a con artist of the highest order”.
The Rio broadsheet O Globo said Bolsonaro’s “shameful and sneaky” decision to abscond laid bare the “pathetic” nature of his political movement, Bolsonarismo, while the Folha de São Paulo said it exposed the true nature of the “authoritarian, ignorant, incompetent” Bolsonaro family.
José Casado, a columnist for the conservative magazine Veja, wrote: “The comedy storyline has already guaranteed him a spot in the pages of political satire.”
Merval Pereira, a conservative columnist for O Globo, called Bolsonaro “a madhouse Napoleon”.
Even Silas Malafaia, a pugnacious televangelist who is close to Bolsonaro’s jailed father, Jair Bolsonaro, had harsh words. “Bolsonaro’s kids are jackasses … A bunch of amateur morons,” Malafaia was quoted as saying by O Globo.
Some observers see Bolsonaro’s post-defeat getaway as proof that his dispirited movement is dead. “I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, said this week, calling the result “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.
The Estado de São Paulo’s editorial board agreed. “Flávio belongs to the past and will soon vanish into the basement of political irrelevance from which he should never have emerged,” they predicted, urging conservatives to ditch Bolsonaro and throw their weight behind his ally Tarcísio de Freitas, the São Paulo governor.
Others warned Bolsonarismo would remain a powerful political force, even if the Bolsonaro family’s leadership of the far-right movement was now in doubt.
Social media users were also merciless in their reaction to Bolsonaro’s short-lived claim to be “president-elect”. One meme invited supporters to attend his January inauguration – at Cinderella Castle in Walt Disney World, Orlando. Another parodied his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan “God, homeland and family”, which became “Goodbye, homeland and family”.
Donald Trump has declined to publicly recognise the result of an election he has called “a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil”. But a US diplomatic cable obtained by the Folha de São Paulo called Lula’s victory “surprising but definitive”.
Asked if he saw Bolsonaro as Brazil’s “rightful” leader, the US president replied: “I won’t get involved.”

Seoul fears being left out as US reaches out to North Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

Seoul fears being sidelined as US reaches out to North Korea
October 30, 2026
South Korea's relationship with the North, always strained, seems to be going through a particularly hostile patch in recent weeks.
Last month, Seoul accused North Korea of planting a mine on the southern side of the heavily fortified border. The device exploded, injuring three South Korean soldiers. Pyongyang refused to apologize and insisted this was a false-flag incident designed to tarnish the isolated nation. The North Korean regime has since conducted multiple weapons tests, held its first-ever exhibition of military drones attended by Kim Jong Un, brought up self-propelled artillery units to the border and started preparing loudspeaker systems that will blast propaganda into the South.
On Thursday, North Korea also fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the Sea of Japan just before a scheduled visit to South Korea by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
On top of South Korea's issues with its arch rival, many in Seoul are growing increasingly wary of their most important ally, the United States. South Korean politicians are worried that the US could push for a diplomatic breakthrough with North Korea at the cost of ignoring South Korea's security, or even leave it exposed to Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal.
Who gets a voice on South Korea's future?
US President Donald Trump famously claimed he and Kim Jong Un "fell in love" during Trump's first term. More recently, Trump has indicated he would like to resume talks . There have been suggestions that a meeting could take place on November 18 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
The North Korean side has made no official response to Washington's hints, although South Korea's National Intelligence Service informed a closed-door meeting of Seoul's intelligence committee on Thursday that Kim Jong Un discussed the possibility of meeting Trump when he met with senior members of China's politburo in Dandong on Saturday.
Seoul's fears were also fueled by the US proposing three-way talks with Russia and China on the fate of Ukraine without inviting a representative of Kyiv to attend. The worry in Seoul is that President Donald Trump may conduct a similar bypass manoeuvre on the Korean Peninsula.
Washington-Seoul relationship shaken by tariffs, funding disputes
"Right now, there is a problem of trust between the two governments," said Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation.
A security and trade relationship that was previously considered secure has been rocked by tariffs, trade restrictions and demands from Washington that the South pay more for the US troops stationed in the country, Kim told DW.
President Lee's diplomats have lost access to key decision-making personnel in this White House, he added.
"I do not think this US administration is thinking long-term in the relationship with South Korea," Kim said. "They do not see South Korea as a part of their wider national security network and I do not think they are listening to experts on the importance of allies in the region."
"I also think that Trump is eager to meet with Kim because of his personal quest to obtain a Nobel Peace Prize."
Trump's widely publicized efforts to secure a Nobel have been thwarted so far. However, this might change if Trump somehow manages to formally end the Korean War that was put on hold by the 1953 armistice.
South Korea eyeing its own nuclear deterrent
"The most serious concern is that the US recognizes Pyongyang as a nuclear power, which would legitimize the North's program and undermine efforts to convince it to abolish its nuclear weapons as well as the broader non-proliferation system," said Lim Eun-jung, a professor of international studies at Kongju National University.
In parallel, she said, there are fears that Trump could reach an agreement with North Korea that requires it to scrap its long-range nuclear missiles — those that are capable of hitting targets in the United States — but permits it to retain short-range weapons that can still easily reach South Korea and Japan.
That would raise questions about the US commitment to defend South Korea in case of a nuclear attack. That uncertainty, in turn, is likely to give credence to voices arguing that South Korea needs to develop its own nuclear deterrent.
"For years, we have depended on US extended deterrence guarantees under the nuclear umbrella, but this US administration is unpredictable and there are more and more people asking why we don't just go it alone," Lim told DW.
"Virtually, all our neighbors have nuclear weapons, and while no-one wants the dominoes to start falling, it could happen."
Merz says Korean security affects Europe
The latest escalation between Seoul and Pyongyang comes amid repeated attempts by South Korean President Lee to improve communication with Pyongyang. The perceived outreach has irritated South Korea's European allies, who are angry over North Korea deploying soldiers and supplying munition and missiles to help Russia in the Ukraine war.
Moscow is believed to be repaying Pyongyang's support with money, military technology and security guarantees.
During his visit to South Korea, Germany's Merz pointed out that "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects the security of Korea."
"The world is small — even in war," Merz added.
South Korea needs allies
Berlin, just like Seoul, has been disoriented by the Trump administration turning hostile on many of its allies while seeking reproachment with geopolitical rivals such as Russia and China. During his Asia tour, Merz pushed for an alliance of middle powers to protect free trade and oppose "unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law."
"The fact remains that the United States is shifting its foreign policy, its foreign economic policy, and redefining its interests. As they do so, we must do the same," he said in South Korea.
It was not clear if Seoul will respond to Merz's appeal by moving closer to the European Union. At the moment, however, it seems apparent that the South Korean government is struggling to communicate with either North Korea or the US.
"It is a very difficult situation," said Kim Sang-woo. "There is no trust and no connections and that, to me, is very worrisome."

50 students and 9 startup teams take part in Zubr Capital Young AI Hackathon in Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:07:10 UTC
23:07:10 KST

On October 24, Zubr Capital hosted the Zubr Capital Young AI Hackathon in Cyprus, bringing together university students and early-stage startup founders. The event attracted applications from more than 50 students and nine startup teams. During the hackathon, participants built AI-powered products from scratch or developed existing projects.
Over the course of a single day, participants researched their target audiences, tested key assumptions, set priorities and worked on minimum viable products (MVPs), experiencing the kinds of challenges startup teams face in practice.
Throughout the hackathon, teams received guidance from investors, entrepreneurs and senior executives from Zubr Capital’s portfolio companies. Mentors helped participants critically assess their ideas, refine product hypotheses and focus on the most important tasks.
The event concluded with final presentations before a panel of investors and industry experts. Teams pitched the products they had developed or improved during the day, explaining their key assumptions and the results of their work.
“In a startup, there is rarely enough time or information to make decisions with complete confidence. A hackathon makes this particularly clear: teams have to test assumptions quickly, distinguish what matters from what does not, take feedback on board and, when necessary, change their original approach. Ultimately, it is not just the idea that counts, but how quickly a team can learn and make decisions under uncertainty,” said Alena Padalnitskaya, Head of Student Programs at Zubr Capital.
The event marked the return of Zubr Capital Young Hackathon to Cyprus, where the first edition took place in October 2025, bringing together 50 participants and eight startup teams. The initiative has also been held in Warsaw and Almaty. This year’s Cyprus edition introduced a dedicated focus on AI, giving students and early-stage founders an opportunity to explore how the technology can be used to build and develop new products.
“Cyprus has a growing technology ecosystem, an international business environment and talented young people. We believe that building globally competitive technology companies starts long before their first investment round — at universities and through early entrepreneurial projects. That is why supporting the next generation of founders and helping them turn ideas into viable products is important to us,” said Oleg Khusaenov, founder and CEO of Zubr Capital.
The event marked the second edition of Zubr Capital Young Hackathon in Cyprus, following its debut on the island in October 2025. The initiative has also brought together aspiring founders in Warsaw, Poland and, most recently, in Almaty, Kazakhstan, where an AI-focused hackathon took place in September 2026. Together, these events form a growing international series connecting young tech talent with investors and experienced entrepreneurs.

Kyiv will begin connecting residential buildings to heating from Monday, November 2, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko has reported.
"We were the first in Ukraine to start the heating season, on October 16. At first it was for social-sector facilities. At the request of their managers, almost 50% of social facilities have already been connected to heating. In particular, 157 medical facilities, 402 kindergartens and 85 schools. And from Monday, November 2, we will begin supplying heat to residential buildings as well," Klitschko wrote on Telegram on Friday.
According to him, launching Kyiv's centralized heating system takes up to a week, so the capital decided to start the heating season in the residential sector a few days before a sharp drop in temperature.
Klitschko also added that the length of heating networks in Kyiv is about 3,000 km. The capital's entire heating system is one of the largest in Europe.
As reported, Klitschko announced the start of the heating season in Kyiv on October 16. According to him, the heating season began, as usual, with social-sector facilities, "in particular in hospitals, schools and kindergartens," at the individual requests of their managers.
Heating is usually switched on when the average daily temperature stays below 8 degrees Celsius above zero for three days, and switched off when it is higher than that. The decision is made by local authorities.

Andreas Malm condemns UK travel ban as ‘drift into authoritarianism’

23:06:23 KST

The Swedish climate academic Andreas Malm has condemned a travel ban imposed on him by the UK government as a “drift into authoritarianism” amid criticism of the move.
Malm, the author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, said he had been “kept in the dark” by the UK’s immigration authorities over the reasons for his electronic travel authorisation (ETA) being revoked.
He said he had only been told that his presence in the UK was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”, as the Guardian revealed.
Speaking to Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, he speculated that the only plausible rationale for the ban was his advertised appearance at a conference next Wednesday alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed group Palestine Action.
He said: “I cannot see any other explanation than the scheduled appearance of me on stage for a panel on Wednesday evening in London, together with Huda Ammori. That … makes me somehow a terrorist or associated with terrorism, and therefore barred from travelling to the UK. That’s pretty scandalous.”
He added: “What I am going through here is just a very small part of a major trend: this drift into authoritarianism that is targeting the Palestine movement, the climate movement, and others who oppose the destructive forces that are in control of this world. And that’s a very sad thing.”
Malm confirmed to the Guardian that he would speak via video link at the event organised by Tribune magazine.
In his BBC interview, he denied supporting or helping to finance Palestine Action. But Malm, who has long campaigned for Palestinian rights, added: “You might be able to guess my opinions and sympathies.”
The Home Office said it could not discuss individual cases. However, a source said: “Decisions to refuse or cancel an ETA on the grounds that presence in the UK may not be conducive to public good are based solely on an assessment of the potential risk an individual may pose to UK society.”
Malm said: “I don’t have any concrete evidence for what this is all about. I’m left in the dark. I have asked for clarification, explanation. I haven’t received any.”
Malm was challenged on Today over whether his description of the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 as an “act of liberation” could be the reason for the ban.
He replied: “It could be. But my views about what happened on 7 October and in Palestine have been in the public realm for a long time. I was most recently in the UK in May.”
Malm added: “I’ve done nothing in public that is associated with Palestine Action. I have not publicly supported them or promoted them in any way.”
Malm said he was invited to speak alongside Ammori to discuss the war in Iran.
“So, what they’re preventing here is for us to have a discussion about the drivers of the imperial aggression in the Middle East,” he said.
“The only link to Palestine Action is her [Ammori] as a person. If you continue with these guilt-by-association links, then presumably if I am a threat to the public good in the UK by dint of talking to her, then someone who talks to me presumably is also a threat to the public good. Where does that end?”
The travel ban has been widely criticised. The author Sally Rooney said it was a “sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm”.
In a post on X, the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said: “This all feels very much Starmer’s Labour government 2.0. An extraordinary attack on free speech from Andy Burnham.”
The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who last year offered to stand down from his Norwich South seat to allow Andy Burnham the chance to return to parliament, said: “When any government starts barring academics for their political views, alarm bells should be ringing.
“If ministers have evidence Andreas Malm is dangerous, produce it. Otherwise, this looks like political censorship dressed up as public safety. That’s a dangerous road for any democracy.”
Ammori said in a post on X: “Banning academic and author Andreas Malm from entering Britain to stop him from speaking alongside myself, a Palestine Action co-founder, is another disgusting attack on free speech as a result of the draconian ban. The ban must be overturned.”
Neal Lawson, the director of the thinktank Compass, tweeted: “This makes me ashamed to be British and ashamed of an @UKLabour government that enacts illiberal attempts to stifle legitimate voices.”
The former shadow chancellor John McDonnell wrote: “You would have thought there was someone in government to appreciate the irony of effectively censoring someone who wanted to come here to discuss censorship. Home Office policy-making has degenerated into dangerous farce.”
How to Blow Up a Pipeline, which inspired a film of the same name, argues that sabotage and destroying property are morally and strategically justified forms of activism.

Strikes on camp in Ethiopia kill at least 15, sources say
NAIROBI, Oct 30 - At least 15 people, many of them children, died in a series of drone strikes that hit a camp for displaced civilians in Ethiopia's Amhara region, two sources involved in a rescue operation said on Friday.
It was not clear why the camp was targeted or who was behind the attack, but the strikes highlight continuing clashes in the area despite a lull in the heavy fighting that erupted last month between an alliance of rebels from northern Tigray region and the government in Addis Ababa.
"There were around five explosions. Then ... we started collecting bodies," a community representative involved in the burials told Reuters, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue.
The representative said they helped bury 13 people at the camp, which is known as Jari 2 and is home to more than 1,700 people who fled previous violence.
Two of the injured later died at a hospital in Hayk, a town 17 km away.
A spokesperson for Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment but a local official said they were aware of the incident and were helping get medical treatment to 36 people who had been injured.
A resident of Hayk who was helping provide shelter to survivors also said 15 people had been killed. "Those from the camp are now sheltering in a school," they said.
The dead included five children, the two sources said.
Both sources said there had been no fighting in the area when the strike took place, but members of the Amhara Fano National Movement, which is part of the rebel alliance spearheaded by fighters from Tigray, had been nearby.
Government troops have driven back the rebel alliance since their offensive was launched on September 23.
They retook the capital of Tigray region earlier this month and advanced towards the border with Eritrea, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebellion by sending troops over the border.
Asmara denies the accusation and says Addis Ababa's allegations of an invasion by Eritrean forces amounted to a "declaration of war".
Given the web of interconnected conflicts in the Horn of Africa, with neighbouring countries and powers further afield backing their respective proxies, experts have warned that war in Ethiopia could trigger a broader conflict in the region. REUTERS

Christa Pike describes 'pain in my mind and in my soul' in first statement after failed execution

Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital during her attempted execution on 30 September. She was sentenced to death for torturing and killing her classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when she was 18.
Christa Pike said she has been in constant pain since surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month, but remains grateful for the love and support she has received.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said in her first public statement, released through her attorneys on Friday.
Pike dictated the statement to her legal team from the infirmary at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she is being held.
Pike said she entered the execution chamber prepared to die peacefully, only to wake up alone and confused in a hospital bed. The 50-year-old added that she had never imagined living beyond her scheduled execution date.
“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she said.
Pike also criticised the handling of her execution attempt, while expressing sympathy for her victim’s family.
"I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position. I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured,” Pike said.
Pike’s lawyers have called on Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life imprisonment.
However, Lee told reporters this week that he expected her sentence to remain unchanged unless the courts ruled otherwise.
“I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
The governor has ordered an investigation into the failed execution and postponed the state's other lethal injection scheduled for this year.
She was initially hospitalised following the failed execution before being transferred back to prison.

Pope Leo casts US midterm ballot after row with Trump
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo XIV, the Catholic Church’s first US-born pontiff, has voted in the United States midterm elections, submitting his mail-in ballot in Chicago, the Vatican said on Oct 30.
It is the first known time a pope has voted in a political election.
The head of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, who has clashed with US President Donald Trump, believes in “the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes”, the Vatican said in a statement.
The Chicago-born pontiff “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so”, the Vatican said.
“The Holy See Press Office confirms that, in keeping with this longstanding practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago,” it added.
A rift earlier in 2026 between US President Donald Trump and the Pope sparked global headlines.
Leo and Trump repeatedly clashed over papal criticism of the harsh crackdown on immigration in the United States and of the war on Iran, with Trump calling the pontiff “weak” on crime and “terrible” on foreign policy.
The Pope said he was “not afraid” of Trump.
The crucial US midterm elections are scheduled to be held on Nov 3.
Robert Francis Prevost, as he was known before his election to the papacy, spent nearly two decades as a missionary, then bishop, in Peru, and has both US and Peruvian citizenship.
“The Holy Father has also confirmed that, during his years of residence in Peru, he exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Vatican said. AFP

From the most powerful fleet to “disarmament for gas” - how Ukraine lost its strategic aviation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:03:15 EET
23:03:15 KST

From the most powerful fleet to “disarmament for gas” - how Ukraine lost its strategic aviation
Kyiv • UNN
In 1999, Ukraine transferred 11 strategic bombers and 575 Kh-55 missiles to Russia in exchange for writing off its gas debt. The remaining aircraft were dismantled.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Ukraine inherited the world's third-largest aviation arsenal, including the newest Tu-160 and Tu-95MS strategic bombers. However, by the late 1990s, under pressure from the West, some of the aircraft were cut up for scrap, while another portion was transferred to russia in November 1999 in exchange for the write-off of gas debts, UNN writes.
State of aviation as of August 1991
At the end of 1991, following the collapse of the USSR, a strategic military (forces) grouping remained on the territory of Ukraine, consisting of three military districts (the Carpathian, Kyiv, and Odesa districts), as well as the Black Sea Fleet.
According to available information, the following were stationed on the territory of Ukraine:
-  3 combined-arms armies and 2 tank armies; 
-  an army corps; 
-  four air armies; 
-  a separate air defense army (9 air defense brigades); 
-  the 43rd Rocket Army of the USSR's strategic nuclear forces; 
-  the Black Sea Fleet, with a fleet of more than 850 vessels (warships, boats, and support vessels, including the unique vessels "Akademik Sergey Korolyov" and the flagship of the space fleet, "Kosmonavt Yuriy Gagarin"); 
-  two nodes of the missile-attack early-warning system,
other military formations. 
The total personnel strength exceeded 800,000; there were more than 9,000 tanks, more than 11,000 armored infantry and airborne vehicles, and approximately 3,000 aircraft, of which 1,090 were combat aircraft: Su-27 and MiG-29 fighters; Su-24M bombers and Su-25 attack aircraft; 25 Tu-95 and 19 Tu-160 strategic bombers, as well as approximately 200 other bombers, including Tu-22 bombers of various modifications; Su-24MR reconnaissance aircraft, military transport aircraft, and more; 900 helicopters (Mi-24 attack helicopters, Mi-8 multipurpose helicopters, and others, of which 330 were combat helicopters); and more than 850 ships and support vessels.
Photo: Tu-160 "White Swan"
Transfer of strategic aviation in exchange for gas
However, on October 8, 1999, Ukraine and russia signed an agreement in Yalta under which Ukraine was to transfer 8 Tu-160s, 3 Tu-95s, and 575 Kh-55 air-launched cruise missiles to russia as part of the "gas deal".
On November 2, 1999, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine, headed by Prime Minister Valeriy Pustovoitenko, without the approval of the Verkhovna Rada, approved an agreement between the government of the russian federation and Ukraine, under which Kyiv transferred to moscow 8 Tu-160s, 3 Tu-95s, and 575 Kh-55 air-launched cruise missiles as payment toward the debt owed by NJSC "Naftogaz of Ukraine" to OJSC "Gazprom," amounting to $275 million.
In 2019, the Verkhovna Rada's Temporary Investigative Commission, established to investigate information concerning the embezzlement of assets in the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the undermining of the state's defense capability between 2004 and 2017, established that the stated amount was not approximately commensurate with the value of the transferred property.
As already noted, Ukraine had 19 Tu-160s and 25 Tu-95MSs, of which 8 and 3 aircraft, respectively, were transferred to russia. The remaining aircraft were cut up for scrap under the Nunn–Lugar program. In particular, 10 aircraft were scrapped in 1998–2001 at the airfield in Pryluky, Chernihiv region. The destruction of the first Ukrainian Tu-160 began on November 16, 1998, in the presence of American senators.
Photo: Tu-160 with tail number 32 being dismantled at the airbase in Pryluky. 2001.
Nineteen Tu-95MS aircraft were scrapped at the airbases in Uzyn and Bila Tserkva. One Tu-160 (tail number 26) also flew from Pryluky to Poltava in 2000. It is now an exhibit at the Museum of Heavy Bomber Aviation. One Tu-95MS is also located there, while another was left at the base in Uzyn as a training or museum-display airframe and was subsequently scrapped.
Photo: Tu-95MS "Bear"
On November 5, 1999, the first flight took place—the first Tu-160 flew from the airfield in Pryluky to the Russian "Engels" airbase. The transfer of the remaining aircraft and equipment was completed in February 2000.
This is a weapon that determines both a state's political and military potential, and also makes it possible to speak as an equal with any partner. If the potential of this strategic aviation complex allows territories on almost every continent to be kept under control, then this suggests that, apparently, some officials responsible in both the government and our ministries approached this issue without sufficient awareness. At one time, the aircraft could have been converted to carry conventional weapons. Such projects were even developed here at the Pryluky air base
Aviation expert Bohdan Dolintse told UNN that the Tu-160 is a supersonic bomber capable of changing the shape of its wings to increase flight speed. It can fly at what is known as supersonic speed, that is, more than 1,000 km per hour, and launch so-called supersonic missiles; in fact, these are missiles with a speed of 1,000 to 1,500 or more kilometers per hour.
Secondly, if we are talking about Tu-95MS aircraft, this is in fact a fairly old platform. It is a turboprop aircraft, but its key feature and advantage is significantly lower fuel consumption and the ability to fly over very long distances.
Kh-55 missiles are, in fact, long-range cruise missiles with a range of up to 2,500 kilometers. They can carry either a nuclear or a non-nuclear warhead. These are essentially offensive missiles. Their task is to penetrate an air defense system and destroy it.
If we are talking about their importance specifically for Russia, virtually the main part of the most modern and newest Tu-160 aircraft was based in Ukraine, in Pryluky. Therefore, Russia was interested in obtaining these aircraft, because this was not simply a matter of acquiring some additional Tu-160s, but the most modern and newest aircraft, with essentially the greatest remaining flight-service life. As for the Tu-95... although Russia was the main operator of these aircraft, at the time of the collapse of the Soviet Union a significant number of them were located in Ukraine. Therefore, they effectively remained in Ukraine. At that time, before the transfer, overall, since 1991, Ukraine had more than 1,600 Kh-55 missiles and over 40 strategic aviation aircraft, including 19 Tu-160s and 25 Tu-95s. Russia, meanwhile, had only a few Tu-160 aircraft
Could Ukraine have refused to transfer the aircraft?
According to him, from the moment Western partners began pressuring Ukraine to effectively disarm it, and Kyiv gave up its nuclear weapons, this involved not only the nuclear warheads themselves, but also the aircraft capable of carrying nuclear weapons and the delivery vehicles for tactical and nuclear weapons.
Of course, Tu-95 and Tu-160 aircraft, as well as Kh-55 missiles, were the items that the Western world understood to be elements of nuclear weapons, and Ukraine, if it did not want to face sanctions and wanted to receive at least some support or assistance from the West, had to give up these weapons
As already noted, Ukraine had more than 40 aircraft of this type, but Russia received only some of them.
Why? Because by the time the aircraft were transferred to Russia in 1999, some of them had already been destroyed, dismantled, and effectively torn apart. There is a considerable amount of footage showing specialized equipment financed by Western countries arriving and effectively cutting these aircraft into scrap metal. Of course, no one in Ukraine compensated the value of these aircraft. In fact, some minimal funds may have been provided based on the price of scrap metal. And even then, only to compensate for the costs of destroying these aircraft
He emphasizes that, speaking of alternatives, Ukraine, first of all, could hardly have maintained these aircraft, since virtually all technical maintenance and repairs were based in Russia.
Secondly, according to the expert, it was necessary to have a complete set of the relevant technical documentation for these aircraft, and it also remains an open question whether at least part of this documentation was available.
We need to understand that their operation required appropriate flight-testing facilities and training centers capable of preparing pilots to operate these aircraft. After all, over 10–15 or 20 years, virtually no one remained who could operate these aviation platforms. Another important component… we need to understand that this is not some ordinary passenger or transport aircraft. It is impossible to use it for any non-military purposes. In other words, this meant that hundreds of millions of dollars would have had to be spent constantly on maintaining such an aircraft fleet—something Ukraine could hardly have afforded at that time, given the already difficult situation with budgetary funds
How many Tu-160 and Tu-95MS aircraft could Russia have
In August, Defense Express, citing data from the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense, reported that after the destruction of a Tu-95MS strategic bomber at the "Engels" airbase, Russia could have been left with about 37 combat-ready aircraft of this type.
Defense Express also reported, citing data from the AviVector analyst, that Russia officially has 18 Tu-160 strategic bombers in service, but in fact uses only seven aircraft of this type for missile strikes against Ukraine.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russia may have lost between 10 and 15 Tu-95 aircraft of various modifications. Since December 2022, Engels-2 airport has become a regular target for Ukrainian drones. The first strikes, on December 5 and 26, 2022, damaged Tu-95MS aircraft and resulted in the deaths of technicians.
In 2025, as a result of the SBU’s "Spider Web" special operation, Russia lost up to 8 aircraft at the Belaya airfield in Irkutsk Oblast.
On July 17 this year, the SBU Forces destroyed a Tu-95 military aircraft in Engels that was used for Russian missile strikes against Ukraine.
On August 28, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the strike on the Yaroslavl Oil Refinery, the Russian Tu-95MS missile-carrying aircraft in Engels, as well as the responses in the Black Sea.

Egyptian court orders closure of news site Mada Masr and fines editor Lina Attalah, sparking international outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:02:55 UTC
23:02:55 KST

PRESS FREEDOM
Egyptian court orders closure of news site Mada Masr and fines editor Lina Attalah, sparking international outcry
Attalah was briefly detained and ordered to pay more than $50,000 amid a government crackdown on independent media.
A Cairo court on Tuesday ordered the closure of news outlet Mada Masr and convicted its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah of managing an unlicensed website. The ruling sparked outrage among press freedom advocates, who warned it marked a significant escalation in ongoing attacks against independent media in Egypt.
Attalah was briefly detained and ordered to pay the maximum penalty of 3 million Egyptian pounds, equivalent to more than $50,000, according to Mada Masr. Upon her release, Attalah learned a one-year prison sentence was issued against her in absentia in 2024 on separate charges of publishing false news and operating an unlicensed website. Her lawyers challenged the ruling, and a retrial is scheduled for Nov. 11, Mada Masr reported.
“If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe,” Sara Qudah, regional director of the Committee to Protect Journalists, said in a public statement.
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013 and authorities blocked its website in Egypt four years later during a crackdown on more than a dozen sites, including Al Jazeera. Even so, the newsroom has spent more than a decade reporting on government corruption and human rights violations in the country, and took part in ICIJ’s 2021 Pandora Papers investigation. Most recently, the outlet covered protests spreading through Egypt’s prisons.
The court hearing on Tuesday was marred with legal controversies. Human rights and press freedom advocates reported that the court rejected requests from Attalah’s lawyers to review the case file and appointed Attalah a new attorney despite the presence of her legal team. The court ruled that Mada Masr’s site had been operating without a license, despite the outlet’s repeated, unanswered requests to authorities for a license since 2018, according to Amnesty International.
Timothy E. Kaldas, deputy director of the Washington-based think tank Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, called the court’s decision “unprecedented on multiple fronts.” Mada Masr has not been referred to trial previously — or convicted of any crime — and an Egyptian court has not ordered the closure of a news site since 2013. “It’s an alarming escalation,” he told ICIJ.
If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe.
— Sara Qudah, regional director of the Committee to Protect Journalists
The Mada Masr closure comes just one month after authorities detained the entire newsroom of the Egyptian fact-checking website Matsadaash, accusing the journalists of associating with the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood. Mada Masr had rallied behind the Matsadaash newsroom and reported that the staff was forced to read false confessions and subjected to torture. On the same day as Attalah’s hearing, Egypt’s Supreme State Security Prosecution extended the journalists’ pretrial detention for another 15 days without providing new evidence. In September, ICIJ joined more than 40 organizations worldwide to call for their release.
The recent flurry of cases signifies a growing hostility toward independent media in a country that is already one of the world’s top jailers of journalists. The Committee to Protect Journalists reported that 25 journalists are currently behind bars in Egypt, the highest number since 2021. Egypt ranks 169 out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders World Press Freedom Index.
“We’re in uncharted territory in terms of these escalations,” Kaldas said.
He warned that the attack on Mada Masr, one of Egypt’s most prominent independent news outlets, without pushback could encourage the government “to take out virtually all the independent media that remains in the country and, in so doing, denying the Egyptian public access to any kind of credible information.”

"The Russian Threat" - Borissov Leads High-Profile Group of Former Bulgarian Leaders Calling for Gyurov's Election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:02:00 UTC
23:02:00 KST

A group of Bulgarian politicians, former prime ministers, ministers, senior military officers, diplomats and public figures has urged voters to support presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov and vice-presidential candidate Georgi Kandev in the November 1 runoff, warning that Bulgaria risks international isolation and another national catastrophe.
The appeal was signed by former prime ministers Boyko Borissov, Ivan Kostov and Nikolai Denkov, as well as President Rosen Plevneliev and Sofia Mayor Vasil Terziev. Its signatories called for national unity in response to what they described as an escalating Russian threat in the Black Sea and the wider region.
The statement argues that national security should take priority over political differences and that Bulgaria must defend its interests while fully participating in the collective security efforts of the European Union and NATO.
The signatories warn that the country should not wait for another sunken vessel, an attack on infrastructure, a terrorist act or loss of life before recognizing the seriousness of the threat. They accuse the President and the government of playing down the danger instead of preparing an adequate response, arguing that this approach fails to deter the aggressor and creates conditions for further attacks.
They also criticize what they describe as Bulgaria's reluctance to acknowledge the Russian threat, including in its contiguous zone, and to hold the Kremlin responsible for the escalation in the Black Sea. The failure to make full use of Bulgaria's own capabilities and those of its allies, they say, increases the country's vulnerability and geopolitical risks.
The appeal argues that allies can make up for military capability shortages, but cannot compensate for a lack of political will.
The signatories warn against the belief that Russian President Vladimir Putin can be appeased through concessions and submissiveness. They say the consequences of such an approach extend beyond military and geopolitical issues to affect Bulgarian citizens, businesses, trade and the safety of shipping to and from the country's ports.
The statement also criticizes the fact that Bulgaria has reached a point where it questions Romania's decision to defend itself and shoot down Russian drones, despite relying on the neighboring country as an ally. The signatories refer to claims that Romania's actions could be considered provocative toward Russia.
Another central concern is Putin's demand that NATO return to its pre-1997 borders. According to the appeal, accepting such a demand would put Bulgaria and the rest of Eastern Europe back within Russia's sphere of influence and effectively mean their withdrawal from NATO.
The signatories accuse Bulgarian political leaders of failing to address this strategic threat, specifically naming Iliana Yotova and Rumen Radev. They also argue that Bulgarian society is being denied an accurate assessment of the danger through the repeated use of statements that mirror the Kremlin's positions and contradict the assessments of the EU and NATO.
“Therefore, we call upon all those who identify as patriots and defenders of Bulgaria’s civilizational choice, its place within the family of European democracies and NATO, to make their choice and vote for Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev,” the appeal states.
The signatories describe Gyurov and Kandev as the only genuine opportunity to stop Bulgaria from drifting toward international isolation and another national catastrophe. They also call for a political counterweight to Radev's policies, arguing that the country needs an institutional and political check at the highest level.
The appeal says previous political disagreements should not prevent the signatories from recognizing the common danger and accepting responsibility for Bulgaria's future. It calls on voters to make a decisive choice in defense of the country's European future and the security of its citizens.
Diplomat Iliyan Vassilev also publicized the appeal on Facebook, emphasizing the need for a clear assessment of the threat and Bulgaria's full participation in the collective defense of the EU and NATO.
Here is the complete list of signatories, in alphabetical order:
President: Rosen Plevneliev.
Prime ministers: Boyko Borissov, Ivan Kostov and Nikolai Denkov.
Mayor of Sofia: Vasil Terziev.
Ministers: Anyu Angelov, Atanas Zapryanov, Boyko Noev, Valentin Radev, Velizar Shalamanov, Daniel Mitov, Korman Ismailov, Meglena Kuneva, Nadezhda Neynski, Nikolay Vasilev, Nikolay Nenchev, Nikolay Svinarov, Rumyana Bachvarova, Todor Tagarev and Traycho Traykov.
Senior officers, reserve and retired: Lieutenant General Dimitar Iliev, Vice Admiral Georgi Fidanov, Major General Lyuben Stoykov Pandev, Major General Stefan Dimitrov and Brigadier General Dinko Ivanov.
Diplomats and public figures: Valeri Rachev, Vesela Cherneva, Evgeniya Koldanova, Iliyan Vassilev, Radan Kanev and Stefan Tafrov.

Explosion at Spanish ammunitions factory supplying Ukraine injures 3

An explosion at the Fabrica de Municiones de Granada (FMG), an ammunition factory on the outskirts of Granada, Spain, injured three people on the morning of Oct. 30, Spanish newspaper ABC reported.
The explosion occurred shortly before 9 a.m. in the plant's gunpowder-burning area, a restricted site where no one is normally supposed to be present, Granada's local police said, according to ABC.
Emergency services received multiple calls reporting the blast, which was felt in nearby towns, including Fuente Vaqueros and La Zubia, Spanish outlet El Espanol reported.
All three people sustained minor injuries, including hearing damage, ABC reported.
Sources from UGT, one of Spain's two major trade unions, said the explosion occurred during a routine test in a fenced-off area of the factory.
The incident was the second at the facility in two weeks. On Oct. 13, a company truck carrying mortar rounds overturned on the road to El Fargue, ABC reported.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, the Spanish factory has produced ammunition of various calibers and missile components for Ukraine.
The factory is owned by Slovakia's MSM Group, which is part of the defense division of Czechoslovak Group (CSG), one of Central Europe's largest defense holdings. The Czech holding is a key supplier of ammunition to Ukraine under the Czech ammunition initiative, according to CSG Executive Director Michal Strnad.
Launched in early 2024 amid severe ammunition shortages in Ukraine, the Czech-led program has been hailed by its proponents as one of Prague's most significant international efforts and has since delivered millions of shells to Ukrainian forces.

Bhutan hot springs hit by flood from glacial lake burst
No injuries reported after glacial lake burst, causing a flash flood and disrupting Bhutan’s Gasa Tshachu hot springs.
A flood caused by the Shintaphu glacial lake bursting its banks has washed away infrastructure at the Gasa Tshachu natural hot springs in the Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan.
According to state broadcaster BBS on Friday, no injuries or loss of life had been reported from Thursday night’s flash flood.
It added that the extent of the damage was unknown because of “darkness and the strong flow” of floodwaters.
Two Bailey bridges, which are bridges built in portable, prefabricated sections, may also have been washed away, BBS said.
According to Kuensel, Bhutan’s national newspaper, part of the road leading to the village of Laya, where the springs are located, had also been washed away, rendering it impassable. It added that the road has been closed to traffic indefinitely.
Kuensel said that as authorities assess the damage, concerns have emerged about a large artificial lake formed after the flood-affected river channels conjoined following the outburst.
Residents along the Mochhu and Punatsangchhu river valleys were also advised to remain vigilant and avoid riverbanks and flood-prone areas, the report added.
Moreover, in neighbouring India, flood warnings were issued in parts of West Bengal and Assam following the glacial lake outburst, India’s NDTV broadcaster reported.
The hot springs at Gasa Tshachu are a major tourist attraction in the northern part of Bhutan, nestled between India and China.
They were also hit by a flash flood in 2021 when the Mochhu River changed course and swept through the area.
In neighbouring Nepal, a mountainous area about 600km (380 miles) to the west, a flash flood on its border with China in August killed more than 1,500 people and left more than 5,000 missing.
