New study finds narcissism is linked to violent intentions on both sides of the abortion debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:00:55 UTC
23:00:55 KST

People who score high in hostile, manipulative forms of narcissism are more likely to endorse illegal and violent political actions on both sides of the American abortion debate, according to new research published in Current Psychology. The researchers argue that this pattern fits their view that some aggressive, self-centered people may treat political movements on either the left or the right as a vehicle for conflict and excitement, rather than being driven purely by moral convictions about reproductive rights or the unborn.
Political scientists generally distinguish between everyday activism and political radicalism. Activism involves legal, peaceful efforts to bring about social or political change, such as signing petitions, donating money, or marching in permitted rallies. Radicalism, by contrast, involves a willingness to break the law and use violence to achieve political goals, such as vandalizing property or attacking police officers and political opponents. While many psychological models focus on how social pressures or feelings of exclusion push ordinary citizens toward extremism, psychologists have increasingly examined how underlying personality traits attract certain people to political conflict in the first place.
To explain this attraction, psychologist Ann Krispenz and psychology professor Alex Bertrams of the Division of Educational Psychology at the University of Bern in Switzerland developed a framework called the dark-ego-vehicle principle (DEVP). According to this principle, people with socially aversive personality traits sometimes join noble-sounding causes not because they genuinely care about the issue, but because the movement serves as a convenient vehicle to satisfy their own selfish desires.
A central trait in this framework is antagonistic narcissism, the hostile core of narcissism characterized by arrogance, manipulation, a sense of entitlement, a lack of empathy, reactive anger, and thrill-seeking. Unlike extraverted narcissism, which involves outgoing leadership and charm, or neurotic narcissism, which centers on insecurity and sensitivity to shame, antagonistic narcissism is associated with tendencies to pick fights, demean others, and seek out dangerous excitement.
Early tests of this principle grew out of a 2023 study, in which Krispenz and Bertrams found that antagonistic narcissism and psychopathic tendencies predicted support for violent left-wing revolution, whereas concern for social justice and helping others did not. The pair later linked narcissistic traits to greater involvement in environmental activism and, in a 2024 study of sexual minority and gender identity movements, found a similar pattern among people with grandiose narcissistic traits and a desire to show off their own virtue. Research in 2024, conducted by a different researcher, also linked dark personality traits to environmental activism.
Because those initial studies focused on causes typically associated with the political left, observers could question whether the phenomenon applied only to progressive movements. Krispenz and Bertrams argued that their principle is ideologically impartial, meaning that hostile narcissists may be drawn to any political cause on the left or the right as long as it gives them an outlet for aggression.
Following their own 2024 longitudinal study that linked dark personality traits to both left-leaning and right-leaning forms of antisemitism, the authors sought to test whether this nonpartisan pattern holds true in the context of political activism. The U.S. abortion debate provided a fitting test case, as the 2022 Supreme Court decision overturning Roe v. Wade sparked renewed protests and some militant activity on both sides.
“Our hypothesis was based on the Dark-Ego-Vehicle Principle,” study authors Krispenz and Bertrams told PsyPost. “The DEVP assumes that individuals high in dark personality traits participate in prosocial activism if and as long as they can instrumentalize their participation to satisfy their ego-focused needs (e.g., for aggression). However, the scope of application for the DEVP should not be restricted to a specific political/ideological side; rather, individuals high in dark personality traits should be drawn to either form of activism as long as it allows for the satisfaction of their own dark-ego needs. Thus, we investigated the validity of this assumption regarding both pro-choice and pro-life activism in a U.S. sample.”
To test whether antagonistic narcissism predicts radicalism on both sides of the abortion divide, the researchers recruited a diverse sample of U.S. adults through the online research platform Prolific. After removing incomplete entries, duplicate submissions, participants who failed an attention check, and 81 respondents who did not take a side on abortion, the final sample included 872 adults with an average age of 43. Within this group, 501 participants (57.5 percent) identified as pro-choice and 371 participants (42.5 percent) identified as pro-life. The study’s main hypotheses and analyses were preregistered.
Participants completed a 60-item personality questionnaire that measured antagonistic narcissism alongside extraverted narcissism and neurotic narcissism on a 1-to-5 scale. They also rated their willingness to engage in legal, nonviolent activism (such as traveling an hour to attend a peaceful rally for their abortion stance) and illegal, violent radicalism (such as attacking security forces or engaging in unlawful actions for their group) on a 1-to-7 scale. In addition, the survey measured everyday altruism, such as giving money or help to strangers, along with three ideological attitudes: left-wing authoritarianism, right-wing authoritarianism, and social dominance orientation.
Across the entire sample, participants generally favored peaceful action over violence, reporting an average score of 4.12 out of 7 for legal activism intention compared to a relatively low average of 2.26 out of 7 for radicalism intention. Average scores for antagonistic narcissism were also modest at 2.07 out of 5, and pro-choice and pro-life participants did not differ in a statistically significant way in their levels of antagonistic narcissism. In line with the researchers’ primary expectations, higher antagonistic narcissism was strongly associated with a greater willingness to engage in illegal and violent abortion-related actions across the total sample (a correlation of .41). This relationship held true within both the pro-choice group (a correlation of .37) and the pro-life group (a correlation of .46).
“We found a meaningful and positive relationship of antagonistic narcissism and abortion-related radicalism intention,” the researchers noted. “Thus, on both political/ideological sides (i.e., for pro-choice as well as pro-life activism), narcissistic individuals seem to participate in abortion-related activism for the satisfaction of their antagonistic needs (e.g., for aggression).”
The link between antagonistic narcissism and radicalism intention remained robust even after the researchers statistically controlled for age, gender, altruism, extraverted narcissism, and neurotic narcissism. The association also held up when the authors accounted for participants’ willingness to engage in legal, peaceful activism. Peaceful activism intention correlated moderately with altruism across the sample (a correlation of .33), suggesting that lawful advocacy tends to go hand in hand with a habit of helping others.
Before peaceful activism was controlled for, altruism showed a small positive link to radicalism intention, but once peaceful activism was factored in, altruism showed no statistically significant link to violent radicalism, whereas antagonistic narcissism remained a strong predictor.
Before analyzing the data, the authors predicted that the link between antagonistic narcissism and radicalism would be stronger among pro-choice supporters than pro-life supporters, reasoning that pro-life conservatives typically value law and order and might feel reluctant to endorse illegal tactics. While the overall strength of the correlation did not differ in a statistically significant way between the two camps (and was, if anything, numerically larger among pro-life participants), an exploratory analysis of the data curves uncovered a notable difference in how radicalism emerged across the two groups.
Among pro-choice participants, the willingness to use illegal or violent tactics rose steadily in a straight line as antagonistic narcissism increased. Among pro-life participants, the relationship followed a curved, U-shaped trajectory.
For the majority of participants who scored in the low-to-moderate range of antagonistic narcissism (representing 71.1 percent of the sample), pro-choice individuals expressed higher radicalism intentions than pro-life individuals. At the highest levels of antagonistic narcissism, however, pro-life radicalism intentions accelerated sharply and caught up with the pro-choice group.
Because this curved pattern came from an exploratory analysis, it warrants caution: the difference in curvature between the groups weakened to a statistical trend when the researchers reran the analysis using a method less sensitive to extreme scores. Relatively few participants scored at the very top of the narcissism scale, with about 13 percent scoring well above the sample average.
“We originally assumed a linear relationship between antagonistic narcissism and individuals’ abortion-related radicalism intention,” Krispenz and Bertrams said. “However, we found such a relationship only for the individuals of the pro-choice group. For the pro-life group, results unexpectedly revealed a u-shaped effect.”
The authors suggest that because conservative circles generally emphasize respect for authority and law enforcement, moderate levels of hostility may not be enough to push a pro-life supporter toward endorsing law-breaking. “Hence, radicalized pro-life activism including violent and aggressive acts seems – just like pro-choice activism – to be a fitting dark-ego vehicle for some antagonistic individuals, but only at more extreme levels of antagonistic narcissism when self-restriction is particularly low,” the researchers added.
The researchers also examined how broader political attitudes related to violent intentions within each camp. Among pro-choice participants, radicalism intention was strongly associated with left-wing authoritarianism (a correlation of .44), a mindset that endorses using force and censorship to overthrow established hierarchies in the name of progressive values. Among pro-life participants, radicalism intention was not statistically significantly related to right-wing authoritarianism (a correlation of -.07), which emphasizes strict obedience to traditional authorities and social norms. Instead, pro-life radicalism showed a small positive association with social dominance orientation (a correlation of .11), a trait characterized by a desire to aggressively dominate rival groups and maintain group-based hierarchies.
“The most important takeaway is that the association between antagonistic narcissism and radicalism intentions was found among people on both sides of the abortion debate,” Dominika Adamczyk, a researcher at the Political Cognition Laboratory at the Institute of Psychology of the Polish Academy of Sciences, who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “I think this is interesting because it suggests that, when trying to understand extreme political engagement, we should look not only at people’s political views, but also at individual psychological characteristics.”
These results align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2020, which found that socially aversive personality traits were linked to both authoritarian political correctness on the left and white identitarian beliefs on the right. While that earlier research examined a broader set of traits (psychopathy, general narcissism, Machiavellianism, and entitlement) in relation to extreme ideological beliefs rather than violent activism intentions around abortion, both studies link hostile, self-serving personality traits to authoritarian attitudes on both the left and the right.
“This finding fits with previous studies suggesting that narcissism can be associated with extreme political views on both sides of the political spectrum,” Adamczyk noted. “However, narcissism has often been discussed in relation to right-wing political attitudes, and relatively few studies have examined different forms of political beliefs and action among narcissistic individuals across the ideological spectrum. The present study extends this work by looking at intentions to engage in radical political action among people with opposing political positions.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Pro-choice and pro-life participants had similar levels of antagonistic narcissism, average scores for both antagonistic narcissism and radicalism intention were relatively low, and willingness to engage in peaceful activism was more closely tied to altruism than to antagonistic narcissism.
“The results of the present research do not demonstrate that any abortion-related stance or activism is per se radical or narcissistic,” Krispenz and Bertrams emphasized. “This interpretation of the results is supported by the results of the present study which show that altruism was significantly associated with abortion-related activism intention as well. These results demonstrate that individuals also participate in abortion-related activism in the pursuit of pro-social goals (e.g., to protect the women’s rights or the life of the unborn respectively).”
“We should also remember that political engagement or political activism, both violent and non-violent, is shaped by more than individual personality traits, and group dynamics and social context are crucial as well,” Adamczyk added.
The authors argue that a subset of antagonistic individuals could harm peaceful advocacy groups on either side, though the study surveyed members of the public who identified with a stance rather than members of activist organizations.
“Our results show that abortion-related activism on both ideological sides can be attractive for antagonistic narcissists,” the authors explained. “The potential for illegal and violent behavior of such narcissistic individuals may seriously harm the activism, for example by causing irreparable reputational damage to the activist movement. Such reputational damage may lead to dwindling support for the activist movement by the public and could even be wielded against the movement. Thus, the respective activist groups striving for social change in a peaceful way as well as the public should be made aware of the narcissistic ‘enemies’ from within activist movements.”
Methodological constraints also limit what the data can show. Because the study relied on survey responses collected at a single point in time, it cannot establish that narcissistic traits cause people to radicalize, nor can it track whether narcissistic individuals abandon a movement once it stops providing thrills. In addition, the researchers measured self-reported willingness to commit illegal or violent acts rather than actual real-world behavior, and they did not directly measure whether specific motives like thrill-seeking or anger expression drove those intentions.
“I have high confidence in the observed associations,” Adamczyk said. “The study has a relatively large sample, preregistered hypotheses, and the findings remained robust after controlling for several relevant variables. However, I would be more cautious about interpreting what causes this association. I see the results as convincing evidence of an association, but not as a definitive explanation of why it occurs.”
Future studies could track real-world activist groups over time and test other polarizing debates, such as gun control, to see how antagonistic personalities operate across different cultural and political landscapes.
“Currently, we are investigating the DEVP with regard to the need for chaos (i.e., the desire for the destruction of the established order and societal structures),” Krispenz and Bertrams told PsyPost. “Thus, we are adapting the need for chaos scale for German, French, and Italian samples. This will allow us to investigate the DEVP regarding phenomena like the current violent protests in France and Italy.”
“I would like to see research examining how individual characteristics interact with group processes and social context to shape political engagement,” Adamczyk said. “I think we need to understand not just who is drawn to radical political action, but also under what conditions and through what processes this willingness develops.”
The study, “Ideological impartiality of the dark-ego-vehicle principle: antagonistic narcissism is associated with pro-choice as well as pro-life radicalism intention,” was authored by Ann Krispenz and Alex Bertrams.

Ukraine Strikes Iskander-M Launcher Inside Russia—Cutting Into Moscow’s Ballistic Missile Threat
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile system in the Kursk region, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 30. The attack directly reduces Moscow’s ability to launch ballistic strikes against Ukrainian cities.
The Iskander-M is a mobile short-range ballistic missile system designed to hit high-value targets well behind the front line.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Its transporter-launchers and support vehicles allow Russian missile units to relocate quickly, fire from dispersed positions, and move again before they can be targeted.
Ukraine’s General Staff stressed that every Iskander-M launcher destroyed reduces the Russian military’s capacity to conduct ballistic missile attacks.
The strike in Kursk was part of a broader series of Ukrainian attacks against Russian military infrastructure.
Ukrainian forces also hit ammunition depots near Maloyanisol in the temporarily occupied parts of the Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Luhansk regions.
Other strikes targeted logistics storage facilities near Bilovodsk in temporarily occupied Luhansk region, a Russian repair unit near Rubizhne, and a repair-and-recovery base near Pysarivka.
The Iskander threat has also continued to evolve. Russia used its newest 9M723-2 ballistic missile—commonly referred to as the Iskander-1000—against Kyiv for the first time during a combined strike on the Ukrainian capital this summer.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the upgraded missile offers significantly greater range than the earlier 9M723-1 used by the standard Iskander-M system.
The most important changes include a larger rocket motor and a correspondingly enlarged launcher. Ukrainian military intelligence says those modifications increase the missile’s maximum range to roughly 550 kilometers, compared with around 390 kilometers for the earlier 9M723-1.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine’s intensified hunt for Russian missile systems has reportedly forced Moscow to move some launchers roughly twice as far from the Ukrainian border.
Russian forces had previously launched ballistic missiles from positions around 100 kilometers, or 62 miles, from Ukraine. That pressure has reportedly pushed some Russian systems back to positions roughly 200 kilometers, or 124 miles, from the border.

French patrol plane spots sea drones before strike on ship off Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:00:12 UTC
23:00:12 KST

- A French Navy Atlantique 2 detected three sea drones targeting the container ship Contship Jet off Bulgaria on Oct. 28, helping save all 18 crew.
- The ship sank the next day; Bulgaria’s navy said it could not intercept the drones, which struck in its exclusive economic zone.
A French Navy Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft spotted three Russian uncrewed surface vessels heading for a civilian container ship in the Black Sea on Oct. 28 and raised the alarm, helping Bulgarian naval forces rescue all 18 crew members after the drones struck, the French military said in a post.
The Liberian-flagged container ship Contship Jet was hit about 16 nautical miles east of Cape Kaliakra, inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone but outside its territorial waters, the Bulgarian Navy said. The Greek-managed ship was sailing from Haifa, Israel, to Constanța, Romania, with 421 containers, some carrying fuel and other hazardous cargo. It sank the following day, Bulgaria’s maritime administration said.
The French military said the Atlantique 2, flying a routine maritime surveillance mission, detected the threat and warned the ship’s crew, passed the vessel’s position to Bulgarian authorities, helped coordinate the rescue with Bulgarian naval forces and alerted other ships in the area.
Photos released by the French military also show the Bulgarian Navy corvette Reshitelni, hull number 13, one of the ships sent to the scene.
Bulgarian Navy commander Rear Adm. Kiril Mihaylov said the French crew first saw two uncrewed boats and then a third, all heading west toward several merchant ships crossing the area, Bulgarian news site Dnes.bg reported. The first strike hit the Contship Jet at exactly noon, followed by two more, and he said the third drone was destroyed with small-arms fire. The open-source account GeoInsider said the aircraft spotted the drones about 40 minutes before they reached the ship, a figure Bulgarian and French officials have not confirmed.
The drones were traveling at about 26 knots (48 km/h), and the Bulgarian Navy said it had no forces able to react that quickly or any technical means to destroy them before impact, 24 Chasa reported. Mihaylov said the early warning likely helped save the crew. The corvette Reshitelni, the rescue ship Proteo and fast boat 223 joined the search, and all 18 sailors, 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians, were taken aboard the Proteo and brought to Varna without injuries.
The Atlantique 2 is a twin-turboprop patrol aircraft that the French Navy uses to hunt submarines and watch surface shipping over long distances. France deployed the aircraft to Constanța earlier this month to support search and rescue after the attacks began, while a U.S. Navy P-8A Poseidon started patrolling the Black Sea at Bulgaria’s request. Their job is to detect and track threats; the decision to intercept rests with the coastal state, and the attack took place in waters patrolled by Bulgaria.
The strike was the fifth drone attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone this month, the Associated Press reported. On Oct. 6, sea and aerial drones hit two Turkish-owned ships about 70 nautical miles east of Byala, sinking one. On Oct. 13, drones struck two more cargo ships off Bulgaria, damaging the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3 and sinking a second vessel with 11 crew missing. On Oct. 23, a cargo ship capsized and sank off Romania after a drone strike, killing one sailor, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen blamed Russia.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told parliament earlier this month that “the logic points” toward Russia but that Bulgaria cannot prove it. The Bulgarian Navy commander declined to say whether the drones’ course indicated where they came from or whether debris had been recovered.
The attack came as the defense ministers of Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey met in Sofia. The three NATO countries condemned the attacks on merchant shipping and agreed to strengthen intelligence sharing, early warning and coordination in the Black Sea, but did not announce new patrols or air defense measures.

From Lenin to Star Trek captain – screen legend dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:00:10 UTC
23:00:10 KST

British screen legend Patrick Stewart, who portrayed Soviet leader Vladimir Lenin and a powerful KGB chief before finding global fame as Captain Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men, has died aged 86.
Stewart passed away at his Los Angeles home on Wednesday after battling Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, his representatives confirmed on Thursday. His family said he spent his final days surrounded by loved ones following “a brief and poignant journey” with the illnesses.
Born in Yorkshire in 1940, Stewart built his reputation on the British stage, spending decades performing Shakespeare and joining the prestigious Royal Shakespeare Company in the 1960s.
Long before commanding the USS Enterprise, Stewart had already brought some of the most prominent figures in Russian and Soviet history and literature to the screen. In the 1974 BBC historical drama Fall of Eagles, he portrayed Soviet leader Vladimir Lenin in a series chronicling the collapse of Europe’s great empires, including Russia’s Romanov dynasty.
Five years later, Stewart took on one of his most intriguing Cold War roles. He played Karla, the formidable Soviet intelligence chief and principal rival of British spy George Smiley, portrayed by Alec Guinness, in the BBC adaptation of John le Carré’s Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy (1979).
Stewart returned as Karla in Smiley’s People (1982), another adaptation of le Carré’s espionage novels. Despite his character’s central role in the intelligence struggle between Moscow and London, Stewart delivered the entire performance without uttering a single word.
His ties to Russian literature went beyond Cold War espionage. In 1973, Stewart appeared as Gurvich in the BBC adaptation of The Love-Girl and the Innocent, a play by Alexander Solzhenitsyn set in a Soviet labor camp. The production aired months before the Nobel Prize-winning Russian writer was expelled from the USSR in 1974.
The actor’s career took a dramatic turn in 1987 when he landed the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation. The series propelled Stewart to international stardom, spawning several films and a later spin-off centered on his character.
He went on to portray the wheelchair-bound telepath Professor Charles Xavier in the blockbuster X-Men franchise, sharing the screen with longtime friend Ian McKellen.
Stewart was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his services to drama.
His death prompted tributes from across the entertainment industry, with fellow Star Trek actor William Shatner remembering him as “a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor.”

From derelict food market to futuristic Centre of Excellence: inside a Cyprus success story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:00:03 UTC
23:00:03 KST

It is housed in what once was a derelict food market building. It is now a thriving regional hub for immersive technologies. Its urban regeneration project has been shortlisted as one of the EU´s top social cohesion projects. An ongoing metamorphosis… made in Europe.
At the very heart of Nicosia, the capital of the Republic of Cyprus, lies a Centre of Excellence (CYENS) specialising in interactive media, smart systems and emerging technologies.
Partially funded by the EU, CYENS employs around 110 people — mostly researchers, developers and technicians — across multidisciplinary research groups, affiliated start-ups and spin-offs. They work across more than 50 projects, mostly European, but also through local, national and industry grants.
For example, computer scientist Panayiotis Charalambous´team is using AI-driven tools and augmented and virtual reality technologies to create a variety of visual content. These include interactive urban maps displaying real-time data on traffic, noise, environment and pollution, along with reproductions of historical monuments where access is limited or restricted.
“Virtual reality is one of those technologies that can enable different modes of interaction with visual elements”, Charalambous, also a Team Leader at the Centre, explains. “One of the things that can enable you [to do] is to be immersed in an environment that maybe it's difficult for you to go to. Either because it's in a remote location, something in a different country, or maybe you also have mobility issues. Being immersed in that environment allows you to feel like, yes, I'm there, right?”.
His team is also developing innovative technologies to allow interactive experiences. One of their recent projects will let children create their own scenarios with actor avatars in a theatre museum.
“You can basically give the actors in the scene different emotional temperaments, different actions that they can do and effectively create your own play”, game engineer programmer Ismail Hadjri explains. “There's also the stage designer table where functionally you place the different objects in the space, you tell the actors where they need to go, you put spotlights where they need to be”
Another intriguing technology from the Centre is called Senssos, which involves utilising sensors to monitor interactions between body motion and muscles. This could help musicians reduce imbalances in performance, or physiotherapists propose better treatments for their patients.
“We have developed our own hardware to replace the commercially available systems with something which is cheaper, easy to install and fast. So, it can be easy for consumers to use this either at home or at jobs during rehabilitation, during training, to enhance performance and for rehabilitation reasons as well”, explains Christos Ioannou, research assistant professor and co-founder of Senssos.
The small sensors being tested here are also already helping professional athletes to enhance their performances by measuring real-time cadence, ground contact, heart rate, and many other parameters that could improve their training techniques.
“Main applications of the technology is for the athlete to have real-time feedback on when they are running, indoors or outdoors, without having a coach with them, or to analyse the data afterwards alone, with a coach or with a clinician,” explains computer engineer Panayiotis Kyriakou, who is also the CTO & Co-Founder of biomechanics company Darefore.
The Centre of Excellence was established with the goal of becoming a regional hub for technology and knowledge transfer. It has now turned into a useful tool to fight against brain drain in Cyprus — a small EU member with highly skilled engineers, researchers and students, claims CYENS´ CEO, Yiorgos Chrysanthou.
“Cyprus is a small place, and we cannot really compete with heavy industry or anything else”, he says. “I believe the only way to help the economy and take it forward and move a little bit beyond tourism, which was the main economic driving force for all these years, is to keep this critical mass of talent. And build it and expand it to create an economic activity which relates on technology”.
Software engineer Haris Psallidopoulous, for instance, is working to help farmers improve their farming techniques with AI-driven virtual reality apps.
“Farmers were really open to the idea of using AI, extended reality and robots, but they didn't know such technology was available to them, which was actually mind-blowing to me because I am in the tech field: I know they exist”, he says. “Farmers should be using technology more because it's a really helpful tool”.
Other researchers are developing solutions to help cities better map, identify, quantify, protect and manage their trees and urban green spaces.
“We wanted to provide more time to the municipal staff for creative work rather than having to do micro tasks”, explains Penélope Vásquez, project coordinator of the Cyprus Trees Initiative. “It's easier for them to know where they need to go and trim the trees geographically, where they should plant trees because there's something lacking. And also, we combine this platform with other projects that relate to the urban heat island effect, so the rising of temperatures. Now, the municipality will be able to plan with more information and strategically plan to reduce temperatures in the city.”
The City of Nicosia is already actively using some of these solutions.
The Municipality was a founding partner of the Centre; the mayor himself chairs its Board of Directors. The institution, he claims, is a key socio-economic actor in the city.
“We are between Europe, Asia, and Africa. And this is very attractive for people from the wider region to come”, Prountzos says. “The presence of CYENS in Nicosia brings together top-class academics and top-class research together with the municipality, the city, and of course the business community in order to create research that will be used in the sphere of innovation, but also to create applicable solutions.”
These solutions are already in use by municipal services, including this platform DumpMapper, a platform that helps track and report illegal landfills, even tiny ones, across the city.
“This area is 50 square kilometres, and we have identified through our technology 98 incidents”, Andreas Kamilaris, Managing Director at DumpMapper says while pointing at different points across a map of the city of Nicosia on the computer screen. “Each colour indicates a different type of waste. You can also see a hotspot where most of the waste is located.”
As Managing Director for the DeepCamera research group, associate research professor Alessandro Artusi works with his team to develop new image processing, and computer graphics for a variety of applications.
DeepCamera focuses on the development of AI-powered vision pipelines that drive real-time detection, tracking, and decision making across complex environments; “from entertainment to maritime safety”, Artusi explains, while sharing a preview alongside his senior research associate, medical physicist Xenios Milidonis.
Research associate Charithea Stylianides, a PhD student in Mathematics, also works for CYENS on the application of data science and machine/deep learning on patient data for enhanced diagnosis, prognosis and therapeutic outcomes.
Other initiatives promote cultural heritage. Magic Lantern, for example, aims to develop an interactive, augmented-reality-based book designed for museums, galleries, libraries, or archives. The project taps into consumers’ desire to not only witness art and literature, but to connect with it in a more tangible way.
“The tangible feeling of an actual physical book provides a different sense and a different engagement for the actual user compared to just touching on a screen”, explains Magic Lantern CEO Fotos Frangoudes. “There are a lot of studies and research behind this that [suggest] more tangible technologies can improve overall learning capacity”, he explains.
The Centre has also become a magnet for artists —including Ting-Hun Liu and Leon-Etienne Kühr, who recently experimented with AI’s creative capabilities by asking it to generate its own images without any human prompt.
“We all have the feeling that AI images have this own aesthetic quality to them. And we kind of want to distil this, get only this out of it”, the artistic duo explains. “And what happens if these machines only interact with themselves and there's no more human input? And we can see here, it's very mundane pictures of nature, advertising, and politicians.”
A recent art festival “FLOWS” co-hosted by the Centre of Excellence gathered the proposals of 60 artists from 15 countries.

Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
October 31, 2026
"In the entire film industry, whoever works without aligning with us, or works with Salman Khan, will be killed."
This warning was delivered in an audio message by presumed attackers on Indian actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai earlier this month, as they claimed responsibility for the shooting.
The apparent perpetrators said they were connected to Lawrence Bishnoi, a student-politician-turned-gangster who has been in prison since 2014. Notably, police have not confirmed the gang's involvement.
The shots fired at Shroff, which injured his driver, were only the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent figures from the Mumbai-based film industry, popularly known as "Bollywood".
Since 2022, gunmen fired shots at actor Salman Khan's apartment and at the home of filmmaker Rohit Shetty in Mumbai, as well as actor Disha Patani's family home in northern India. Actor Ranveer Singh also reportedly received an extortion demand of nearly $1.1 million (around €980,000).
The attacks have spread to the other side of the globe, with a cafe owned by comedian Kapil Sharma in Surrey, Canada, also hit three times.
For an industry that once lived in the shadow of organized crime, the attacks have revived old fears, harking back to the crime bosses of the 1990s. But experts say the threat facing Bollywood today looks very different from the one it faced three decades ago.
When the underworld ruled Bollywood
In the 1990s, Mumbai's underworld was deeply entangled with the Hindi film industry.
"The mafia was always fascinated with the movie industry," said S. Hussain Zaidi, crime journalist and author of "Dongri to Dubai: Six Decades of the Mumbai Mafia," who has covered organized crime in the city for over three decades.
Gangsters like Dawood Ibrahim, Abu Salem and Chhota Shakeel "were totally obsessed" with Bollywood, he told DW, much like mafiosi who sought a foothold in Hollywood.
To the gangsters, films offered glitz and glamor, but also a way to launder their profits. They invested in films "so that they could control the industry and have a legitimate way of making money," Zaidi added.
When producers didn't cooperate, the consequences could be fatal. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar, founder of the label T-Series, was shot dead. In 2000, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan, father of Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, was shot and wounded.
Mumbai's streets were "made red with blood" in 1998, Zaidi said, describing the year as the pinnacle of gang killings.
D. Sivanandhan, the former Police Commissioner of Mumbai, who led the crackdown, says 101 businessmen were shot dead in 1998 alone, or one "every third day," mostly over unpaid extortion demands.
Police efforts were reinforced by a tough new organized crime law passed in 1999, which Sivanandhan calls the "ultimate weapon." Security forces used electronic surveillance and preventive detention, and seized some 2,500 illegal weapons.
"A few encounters also happened, but that is not a policy nor a strategy,” he told DW, referring to police shootouts.
By the early 2000s, the gangs' hold had been broken, and a new Mumbai seemed to be emerging.
A gang run from a prison cell
The man believed to be behind the latest wave of attacks is not from Mumbai.
Bishnoi, 33, comes from a landowning family in the northern state of Punjab and was studying in Chandigarh when he was drawn into violent student politics. Then, he was arrested, incarcerated and eventually turned to crime, says journalist Jupinderjit Singh, author of "Gangs of Punjab."
"He was introduced to the University of Crime through the jail," Singh told DW.
Bishnoi went on to build what Singh describes as one of the first criminal syndicates spanning several northern Indian states. Investigators say he still directs operations from prison using concealed phones and messaging apps.
Currently, Bishnoi is held in a jail in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat.
His network stretches beyond India's borders. In September 2025, Canada designated the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity. Last month, the FBI added Satinderjeet Singh, popularly known as Goldy Brar, to its Ten Most Wanted list, offering up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest. US prosecutors described him as the alleged leader of Bishnoi's group in North America.
While Bishnoi comes from an affluent landowning family, his shooters are mostly poor. The gang usually recruits them online.
"There are so many youngsters who want to do something… they are just pulled by the lore attached to Lawrence Bishnoi," Singh explained. "Recruiting is no big issue… They offer money, protection, weapons."
Why target film stars?
For Bishnoi, it seems personal.
In 1998, Salman Khan was accused of killing a blackbuck, an antelope revered by Bishnoi's community. Bishnoi vowed revenge, and many of the attacks targeted people close to the actor, including the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique, which police have linked to the gang.
Singh sees the feud as a bid for respectability. Criminals "always try to find something that makes them a moral guardian," he says, and this case was Bishnoi's "chance to redeem himself."
But money and intimidation matter too.
"Bollywood has a lot of money," Singh added, pointing that the previous generation of gangsters was no longer in position to take advantage.
"With Dawood Ibrahim and his counterparts away, there was a vacuum, and Lawrence Bishnoi is trying to exploit that."
Sivanandhan explained the old Mumbai gangs ran a whole "basket" of illegal businesses, from smuggling to protection rackets and cricket match-fixing. Their members were "local boys," while the Bishnoi gang has “nothing to do with Mumbai,” he added. It targets Bollywood because the industry is "loaded with money" and a "soft underbelly."
"They are using Bollywood as an ATM," he told DW. "Insert a card and collect your money."
Meanwhile, Zaidi sees the attacks mainly as publicity. "It's a way to grab headlines," he told DW. Within hours of the recent attack on Shroff, someone claimed on social media that he was targeted for being close to Khan, a logic Zaidi called "absolutely illogical and absurd."
But publicity is useful to gangs that live off extortion. "The base material of extortion is: create fear," a security professional responsible for the protection of several Bollywood stars, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue, told DW.
Is Bollywood under siege?
Still, experts say its hard to argue that the ongoing violence is comparable to the 1990s crime wave.
"I won't say resurgence, because that would be a bit of an exaggeration," Zaidi said. In the 1990s, several rival gangs fought for control of Mumbai. Today, other than Bishnoi's faction, other gangs are not considered active in Mumbai.
The film industry is also not paying up the way it once did, because the shift to digital payments has made large cash transactions hard to hide, he added.
Sivanandhan disagrees. The shootings at walls and gates, followed by quick claims on social media, are "all aimed at collecting… extortion money," he said. In his view, "cash-rich Bollywood would be coughing up so much, which is enough to run an army of people."
At any case, the fear remains real.
And even if violence is not as prevalent, hundreds of thousands of people rely on the Mumbai film industry for their livelihoods.
"If the fear of the underworld continues, leading names may be forced to leave Mumbai," the All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) President Suresh Shyamlal Gupta wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah.
"Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, and Bollywood will not be allowed to work in the shadow of fear," Gupta wrote.
With security forces seemingly on the back foot, gangsters are likely to continue their campaign.
Several Bollywood stars have already stepped up their security.
Edited by: Darko Janjevic

Two men dead, baby critically ill after migrant boat reaches Spain’s El Hierro island
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:59:39 CET
22:59:39 KST

MADRID, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Two men were found dead aboard a migrant boat that reached Spain’s Canary Islands early on Friday after departing from Gambia, and a baby was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition, Spanish rescue services said.
The vessel, carrying 113 people, was located about 37 nautical miles south of the tiny island of El Hierro after emergency services received distress calls late on Thursday. Rescuers brought 110 survivors ashore, including eight women and eight minors.
The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats, seeking to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances.
Arrivals typically pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favourable for crossings.
Migrant arrivals have declined so far this year compared with 2025, but crossings increased sharply this month, putting additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some of the Canary Islands, particularly the smaller and less populated ones.
Migrant arrivals in the archipelago fell 18% year-on-year to 11,527 people to date, according to the office of the Spanish government’s representative in the Canary Islands.
(Reporting by Emma Pinedo; Editing by David Latona and Timothy Heritage)

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine called on UNESCO to respond to Russian propaganda events at the Khan's Palace in Crimea
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is protesting against Russian events at the Khan's Palace on October 31–November 1. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is asking UNESCO to strengthen the protection of the heritage site.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine has expressed its protest over propaganda events planned by Russia on the grounds of the Khan's Palace in occupied Bakhchysarai, scheduled to take place from October 31 to November 1. The MFA called on UNESCO to respond to the actions of the Russian Federation and strengthen the protection of Crimean Tatar cultural heritage. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine reports this, writes UNN.
The Khan's Palace is a historical and cultural landmark of global significance, included by Ukraine on the Tentative List of UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Russian Federation continues to systematically wage war against the Crimean Tatar people, their culture, historical memory, and the world's cultural heritage. The occupiers' criminal actions are documented during monitoring conducted by UNESCO in temporarily occupied Crimea since 2014
The ministry noted that Ukraine had already officially informed UNESCO's leadership and the organization's member states of the Russians' intention to hold the event in temporarily occupied Bakhchysarai.
We call on the Director-General of UNESCO, its relevant bodies, and the Organization's member states to immediately employ all available international instruments aimed at ending Russia's practice, as the power temporarily occupying Crimea, of turning the cultural monuments of the indigenous Crimean Tatar people into an instrument of imperial propaganda and the justification and glorification of the occupation
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine calls on UNESCO to take the following measures:
-  Provide a principled assessment of Russia's propaganda activities in the temporarily occupied Crimea. 
-  Strengthen international mechanisms for protecting Ukraine's and the Crimean Tatars' cultural heritage. 
-  Consider strengthening the Russian Federation's accountability for the systematic destruction of Ukraine's cultural heritage, which bears signs of war crimes.

Pope Leo XIV has voted in US midterm elections, Vatican says

The US midterm elections, scheduled for 3 November, will determine the make-up of Congress for President Donald Trump's final two years in office.
Pope Leo XIV has submitted a mail-in ballot for the US' midterm elections, the Vatican announced on Friday, marking the first known time a pontiff has voted in a political election.
The Vatican Press Office said in a statement that Chicago-born Leo had "exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen."
"The Holy Father has also confirmed that, during his years of residence in Peru he exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so," the statement continued. Leo spent years working as a missionary and later bishop in Peru and has Peruvian citizenship.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," it added.
The US midterm elections, scheduled for 3 November, will determine the make-up of Congress for President Donald Trump's final two years in office.
Since his return to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly clashed with Leo, accusing him of being "weak on crime" and "terrible for foreign policy."
"He wasn’t on any list to be pope, and was only put there by the church because he was an American, and they thought that would be the best way to deal with President Donald J. Trump," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account in April.
For his part, Leo has been critical of the US' harsh stance on immigration and Trump's threats to Iran.
The 71-year-old pontiff would have been able to vote in both the race for the Illinois Senate and in the contest for governor of the state, where incumbent Democrat JB Pritzker is up against Republican Darren Bailey and independent Collin Corbett.

Ice hockey federation fumes after being ordered to readmit Russians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ice hockey federation fumes after being ordered to readmit Russians
The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) has reluctantly accepted this week’s ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) overturning its exclusion of Russian teams from international competitions.
The ban was challenged at the Lausanne-based court by the Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) in August, after the IIHF resisted a broader trend toward readmitting Russian and Belarusian competitors in July.
The IIHF said on Friday that it respected CAS' authority and would comply with its ruling, but maintained that the restrictions on Russian teams were “necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions” – an argument the court found was not supported by sufficient evidence. The federation also complained that the decision carried “significant practical implications” for upcoming championships.
The RIHF said that it would work with the IIHF to implement the CAS-mandated reinstatement. The World Junior Championship, scheduled to take place in Canada from December through January, is set to become the first major tournament featuring Russia following the ruling.
Russian and Belarusian athletes were barred from competitions organized by numerous international federations following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Over the following years, arguments that the exclusions were politically motivated and inherently discriminatory increasingly gained traction.
The International Olympic Committee (IOC), which wields considerable influence over international sports, withdrew its recommendations restricting Russian participation in July, clearing the way for athletes and teams to return.
The IIHF was among several federations that maintained restrictions, alongside track and field governing body World Athletics, the International Biathlon Union (IBU), and football authorities FIFA and UEFA. Other organizations retained partial exclusions, including requirements that Russian and Belarusian athletes compete without displaying their national symbols.
Moscow has argued that Western nations pressured international sports organizations into excluding Russian athletes as part of their broader strategy to contain Russia. It has also maintained that the restrictions have undermined the quality of international competitions by denying some of the strongest contenders an opportunity to demonstrate their skills.
Efforts to prevent Russian athletes from participating in international competitions have continued, with supporters of Ukraine resorting to visa restrictions, public ostracism, and other measures, sometimes at a cost to themselves.
Earlier this year, Estonia and Poland lost the right to host European fencing and weightlifting championships, respectively, after refusing to guarantee entry to Russian competitors. Both decisions preceded the IOC’s July policy change.
This month, the Netherlands denied entry visas to three prominent Russian gymnasts, prompting Moscow to demand that the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam be stripped of their status as an Olympic qualifying event.

Singapore braces as Indonesia slaps back at neighbours amid haze, political woes
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:59:12 CET
22:59:12 KST

By Xinghui Kok and Stanley Widianto
SINGAPORE, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Indonesia’s swipes at its neighbours are set to last as its embattled government tries to blunt criticism of its handling of welfare programmes, market regulation and persistent wildfires that have choked the region in haze.
Singapore, in particular has been the target of sharpened rhetoric from Jakarta, with Indonesian officials warning pilgrims to avoid transiting through the city-state.
Jakarta has also trimmed gas supply to Singapore with its energy minister saying “so-called brothers and sisters” should not lecture Indonesia on honouring contracts.
Singapore has tried to play down the spat and its foreign minister made a visit to Indonesia this week to meet President Prabowo Subianto.
But the city-state has also summoned representatives of companies suspected of having fires on their plantations in Indonesia.
Analysts say Jakarta’s nationalistic rhetoric, which intensified when Singapore and Malaysia complained about the haze, will likely stay as long as Indonesia’s woes remain.
Prabowo has often blamed foreign actors for problems and Singapore, with its majority Chinese population, is an easy target, said Yohanes Sulaiman, of Indonesia’s Universitas Jenderal Achmad Yani.
“The intensity is pushed to 11 under this administration,” he said.
Syahganda Nainggolan, chief of the Indonesian government’s communications office, told Reuters on Friday that Jakarta continues to seek close relations with Singapore, and the visit by the foreign minister proves the two countries’ relations are not strained.
He said the gas cuts were due to domestic supply considerations and only “coincided with a seemingly tense situation.”
PROTESTS AND PRESSURE
Prabowo has pushed back against international criticism, including a downgrade threat from global index provider MSCI, which has sent Indonesia’s markets into turmoil.
One former Indonesian official blamed Singapore sovereign wealth funds for having a role in the MSCI pressure, but offered no evidence, with the accusation amplified by social media accounts that were “liked” by prominent government figures. The funds denied any involvement.
Yohanes said the MSCI downgrade threat compounded problems for Prabowo’s administration after the fires, as well as food poisoning and corruption issues at a signature free lunch programme.
Prabowo’s popularity has fallen sharply, with his approval rating reaching 44.5% this month according to one survey, from 81.2% late last year.
Protests occurred in several Indonesian cities this week over his government’s response to the fires.
The latest tensions mirror previous episodes where Indonesia has criticised external forces such as Singapore, Malaysia and the West during periods of domestic strife.
Singapore, roughly the size of New York City and with a 6.2 million population, was in 1998 disparaged by Indonesia’s president at the time as a “little red dot” that was not a friend when talking about the Asian Financial Crisis.
In the 1960s, there was outright violence when Indonesian President Sukarno launched a campaign that resulted in 42 bombing attempts in Singapore during a period called the “konfrontasi”, while Indonesia faced hyperinflation and instability at home.
‘STORM IN A TEACUP’
Current and former officials from both countries sought to calm the waters this week.
“Differences are to be expected,” Singapore’s foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan told media on Wednesday. “Even polemic statements sometimes, from time to time,” he said.
Suryo Pratomo, a former Indonesian ambassador to Singapore, said the comments made by some Indonesian ministers were immediate reactions and not administration policy.
“Indonesia and Singapore’s relationship is complementary, not competitive,” he said.
Singapore is Indonesia’s largest source of foreign direct investment at $17.4 billion last year. Indonesia is also reliant on fuel imports and global internet cables through Singapore.
“It’s a storm in a teacup,” said Dewi Fortuna Anwar, a foreign policy analyst.
But there is “prickly nationalism” that leads Indonesia to be more sensitive to perceived slights and interference from other countries, she added.
(Reporting by Xinghui Kok in Singapore and Stanley Widianto in Jakarta; Editing by Josh Smith and Toby Chopra)

Pakistan’s Trump Bet Meets the US Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

Pakistan’s improved relations with Washington rest almost solely on the relationship between Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and President Donald Trump. Allies of the United States, from Europe to East Asia, have faced Trump’s tariffs and been publicly criticized by the U.S. president. Trump, however, praised Sharif during his address to the U.N. General Assembly. Trump’s praise of a world leader, however, means little without a U.S. institutional partnership, and Pakistan has done little to secure that. With the U.S. midterm elections scheduled for November 3, if the Republican Party loses its majority in either house of Congress, as polls suggest it might, the limits of this “reset” will be harder to ignore.
The “reset” has been more of a closer relationship between two people than between two countries. Field Marshal Asim Munir earned Trump’s endorsement as his “favorite field marshal” after Munir visited Trump at the White House. At the same time, the democratically elected government of Pakistan has worked in close coordination with the army leadership. The tactics of Pakistani foreign policy were made clear when Pakistan credited Trump for ending the May 2025 war with India, a claim India has denied. Similarly, Pakistan’s nomination of Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize has pleased the U.S. president but hasn’t won favor with anyone else in Washington. With an approval rating at 30 percent and widespread expectations that Republicans will lose control of Congress, Pakistan’s foreign policy has pursued a sinking political ship.
Few tangible benefits have materialized from the public fanfare surrounding Pakistan’s relations with the United States. In July 2025, the U.S. reduced tariffs on Pakistani goods from 29 to 19 percent. While some analysts see this as a win for Pakistan, others say these reductions benefited Pakistan very little. The memorandums of understanding (MOUs) signed since 2025 remain largely on paper, including those for critical minerals and cryptocurrency. A trade pact has also not been signed. Even worse, some of these deals include companies related to Trump’s circle, while a drone partner Pakistan took on also sells drones to India. Islamabad has received no assurances, and, in the meantime, has given away a lot through commercial favors.
Pakistan’s brokering of the April 2026 Iran-U.S. ceasefire and Tehran talks shows the limitations of negotiating a single major crisis. The window for follow-up talks closed without renewal. On October 20, Munir made his fifth visit to Tehran, but it yielded no results. A go-between is valuable only if both sides want to talk, and Pakistan has no control over this. Islamabad staked much of its relevance on something it has little control over.
A change in the U.S. Congress could expose how narrow Pakistan’s base in Washington truly is. Even though foreign policy largely resides with the executive, Congress controls the purse strings, reviews arms sales, and sets the terms of debate through its oversight and hearings. Analysts in Islamabad expect that a Democratic Congress would mean a shift in policy toward New Delhi and American treaty allies. Critics in Washington argue that Trump’s successor would feel no obligation to uphold the promises Trump has made to Munir. After nearly two years of cultivating a relationship with one person, Pakistan has few friends in the institutions that will outlast him.
Meanwhile, Pakistan’s domestic politics make it an easy target for those who would roll back the reset. The current government in Islamabad, already under fire at home from critics who accuse it of sidelining political opposition, is likely to face increased scrutiny from the next U.S. Congress. Under a Democrat-controlled Congress, oversight committees would routinely examine these concerns. For Democrats looking to distinguish themselves from Trump, Pakistan is a case study of diplomacy based on personal relationships and deal-making
There are legitimate criticisms of U.S. policy toward South Asia as well. Fostering long-term stability on the subcontinent and in the region, particularly with Pakistan’s huge and growing population and its nuclear weapons, is clearly in the U.S. interest. However, successive U.S. administrations have focused solely on near-term interests when dealing with Pakistan and addressing South Asia. Each has developed and strengthened relationships with Pakistan’s security establishment. Washington has also prioritized security cooperation with Pakistan, providing economic and military assistance in return for short-term alignment, which critics argue has come at the expense of Pakistan’s civilian institutions. As a result, what the United States has developed with Pakistan has ultimately served to weaken U.S. interests in the region. It has also fostered the sentiment in Washington that building relationships with Pakistan is a zero-sum game.
If Pakistan wants the recent improvements in its relationships with Washington to grow, then, like the U.S., it needs to shift from a “closing” to a “developing” relationship with Washington and the rest of the world. Nothing would better demonstrate Pakistan’s seriousness than finishing the trade deal now under negotiation and turning its mineral memorandums into real contracts. Such steps would create supporters in U.S. farm states and boardrooms whose interest in Pakistan does not depend on who sits in the Oval Office.
The weeks after November 3 will test whether Pakistan’s moment in Washington was a strategy or a stroke of luck. Some analysts warn that a weaker Trump could mark the beginning of the end of Islamabad’s current importance. In contrast, others argue that alienating Pakistan would shut the door on much of U.S. influence in the region. Islamabad should stop counting on Trump’s Republicans to hold on and start building ties that can survive their defeat.

Russian Northern Fleet warships complete long-distance Arctic voyage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:58:19 UTC
22:58:19 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. A detachment of the Russian Navy’s Northern Fleet ships has completed its long-distance Arctic deployment and returned to base, the fleet’s press service reported.
"Today, on the Day of surface fleet personnel, a reception was held at the Northern Fleet’s main base in Severomorsk for the detachment of warships and support vessels, which has completed its latest, fifteenth, Arctic voyage across the waters of the Arctic Ocean. Northern Fleet Commander Admiral Konstantin Kabantsov received a report on the successful completion of the assigned tasks by the crews of the combat ships and support vessels," the press service reported.
The fleet commander congratulated the Northern Fleet sailors who took part in the long-distance voyage on the 330th anniversary of the Russian Navy and surface fleet personnel day, as well as on the successful completion of all assigned tasks and their return home. He noted that the detachment carried out strategic deterrence missions in the Arctic waters stretching from the Novosibirsk Islands to Franz Josef Land. For the first time, the detachment sailed through the Shokalsky Strait, thereby confirming the suitability of this new navigation area for Russian Navy ships. Also for the first time, amphibious landing was carried out on the coast of the Sedov Archipelago.
"Once again, you have confirmed the fleet’s readiness to defend Russia’s national interests in the Arctic," emphasized Konstantin Kabantsov at the welcoming ceremony, according to the press service. The commander noted that the crews of the warships and support vessels demonstrated a high level of naval training, coordination, and professional skills while carrying out their assigned tasks. In keeping with tradition, the commanders of the ice-class patrol ship Ivan Papanin, the large landing ship Kondopoga, and the captains of the support vessels--the rescue tug Pamir and the ocean-going tanker Sergey Osipov-- were presented with roast piglets by the fleet commander, while distinguished sailors received awards and certificates of commendation.
The Arctic deployment of the Northern Fleet’s ships was conducted to safeguard Russia’s maritime navigation and economic activities in the Arctic.

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. African countries have shown interest in Rosatom’s floating nuclear power plants (NPPs), Chief Executive Officer of Russia’s state corporation Alexey Likhachev said following the Russia-Africa forum in Moscow.
"Nine countries have shown significant interest in this technology (floating nuclear power plants - TASS). We are currently in substantive discussions regarding the implementation of projects in the interests of Egypt, Tanzania, Togo, and Namibia. Four more countries are in talks with us about the construction of high-capacity power plants. We are also working on specific proposals with Uganda and Ghana. In Ethiopia, we plan to start site survey works in the near future. In Egypt, we plan an expansion of the largest construction project of its kind globally, the El Dabaa NPP, from four to six high-capacity reactor units," he said.

Dozens of Russian drones fell to gun turrets over Kyiv in a month, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:57:16 UTC
22:57:16 KST

Automated gun turrets now serve in Ukraine’s Air Force and are destroying Russia’s jet-powered weapons, the Defense Ministry reported on 29 October. It gave no count for those jet kills, and it did not say what type of drones the turrets downed over Kyiv.
Jet drones are where Ukraine struggles most. From 1 to 26 September, Ukraine downed 55% of jet-powered drones against 90% of slower ones, partly because its interceptor drones fly at about 300 km/h, too slow to catch them. Yurii Cherevashenko, Deputy Commander of the Air Force, told a parliamentary inquiry commission on 6 October that jet-drone interceptors would arrive in the needed numbers no earlier than late November. Guns have limits too. On 5 October, Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said turrets had already downed Geran-5s, but that their range is short because their main weapon is a machine gun.
Air Force turrets against jet weapons
According to the ministry, Brave1, a defense innovation cluster, began developing automated turrets in 2024. The systems have since “moved beyond the experimental stage and become an integral part of air defense,” it said. In Air Force service, the turrets are destroying jet-powered Banderol munitions and Geran-5 drones.
To scale up air defense without straining the front, Ukraine enlists business. In under year nearly 100 companies have joined, their crews downing 60-plus targets
Russia first used the Geran-5, a 6-meter jet-powered strike drone, in early 2026. The Banderol, a jet-powered cruise missile, flies at 520–560 km/h and can reach 650 km/h.
Private teams, a familiar number
Separately, the ministry said turrets have destroyed more than 60 targets within the private air defense project. The project lets companies form anti-drone teams that work under Air Force command.
Postal service Nova Post says it has already shot down Russian Shahed drones, as Ukrainian businesses take air defense into their own hands
Yet on 14 October, the ministry gave the same 60-plus total for all private teams. At the time, it named interceptor drones and heavy machine-gun turrets as their main weapons. Groups from six companies were on combat duty, about 50 groups had been formed in total, and some were still training. Nearly 100 companies had joined by then, up from 81 in mid-September.
The ministry says the project expands air defense “without placing an additional burden” on the military’s own air defense. It and Brave1 say they will keep integrating automated turrets into the air defense system.

- From making interceptors to guarding sky: Ukrainian drone maker gets its own private air defense unit and will pay for it from weapon sales
- Ukraine’s private air defense has quadrupled since spring: businesses are now shooting down Shaheds over their own sites
- Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January

Islamic states prosecutors call for global enforcement coalition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:56:06 UTC
22:56:06 KST

Law enforcement heads from 46 Islamic states gather in Baku to tackle cross-border financial crime, artificial intelligence and international asset recovery.
As transnational criminal networks deploy increasingly sophisticated technology to conceal illicit wealth, authorities across the globe are accelerating efforts to dismantle international financial crime.
These priorities framed the agenda in Azerbaijan as delegates convened for the Third High-Level Meeting of the Heads of Anti-Corruption Law Enforcement Agencies of Member States of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
At the core of the summit was the implementation of the Makkah al-Mukarramah Convention.
According to the OIC, the landmark treaty represents the first multilateral anti-corruption law enforcement agreement tailored specifically for Islamic Cooperation member states, establishing a unified legal foundation to track illicit financial flows across borders.
Overcoming bureaucratic borders
Cross-border financial investigations often face significant legal barriers, a challenge highlighted alongside Malaysia’s recent asset recovery experience.
Abd Halim Bin Aman, Chief Commissioner of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission, detailed his agency’s multi-year effort to trace and repatriate stolen funds following the 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) case.
"We managed to achieve our goal of tackling the 1MDB matter and as of today we managed to bring back home about 75% to 80% to outside countries, and we managed to bring back about 33 billion Malaysian ringgit worth of loss," he revealed.
Originally established in 2009 as a state-owned strategic development fund, 1MDB became well-known for being embroiled in one of the world's largest financial kleptocracy scandals, after billions of dollars were systematically siphoned off through offshore shell companies and international bank accounts.
According to the US Justice Department’s website, between 2009 and 2015, money was "laundered through major financial institutions worldwide, including in the United States, Switzerland, Singapore, and Luxembourg" and "misappropriated more than $4.5 billion (approximately €4 billion) in funds belonging to 1MDB through a criminal scheme."
The Justice Department stated it "repatriated an additional $156 million (approximately €139 million) in misappropriated 1MDB funds" to people from Malaysia and brought the total of returned funds to approximately $1.4 billion (approximately €1.2 billion).
Bin Aman also shared his views on what typically slows down such international matters.
"Bureaucracy is always being an obstacle to any investigation," he said.
He said that the summit provides a necessary platform to share legislation and best practices to speed up investigations irrespective of legal backgrounds.
Ivica Bošnjak, Deputy Minister of Security for Bosnia and Herzegovina, outlined the unique structural and geographical pressures facing his country.
"Bosnia and Herzegovina is complicated and complex in the political part, and therefore the organization of the entire security system is complex," Bošnjak stated.
He noted that national authorities must coordinate "16 police agencies and a whole series of other law enforcement agencies" operating across the security sector.
While the state has adopted extensive legal regulations and action plans, Bošnjak told Euronews that "much still needs to be done to refine a couple of more crucial laws" and operational strategies to tackle cross-border financial crime effectively.
Building a global enforcement coalition
Tugay Rahimli, Special Assistant to the Prosecutor General of Azerbaijan, outlined the scale and primary objective of the summit.
"Today's event brings together more than 250 participants from 46 member and service states as well as eight international organisations," Rahimli said.
"The main objective of today's event is to facilitate and foster international cooperation among member states, facilitate exchange of information and best practices, as well as to enhance the joint efforts to recover the assets obtained through crime," he added.
Rahimli also pointed to a key leadership development for the host nation.
"Particularly important outcomes of today's event that I would like to highlight is the election of Azerbaijan to chair the bureau for the next two years," he told Euronews.
A unified legal framework
Kamran Aliyev, Prosecutor General of the Republic of Azerbaijan, confirmed the host nation's immediate legislative steps regarding the agreement, the Makkah al-Mukarramah Convention, which is an agreement designed to facilitate mutual legal assistance, the exchange of information, and the recovery of assets derived through corruption.
"This convention first was adopted in 2022 in the city of Makkah, of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and this is a new platform in fighting corruption at a regional level," Aliyev said.
The agreement operates under a framework, which incorporates 57 nations, with the intention to bypass lengthy diplomatic channels and to allow law enforcement agencies to share intelligence quickly, conduct joint investigations, and trace, freeze, and return stolen state funds to their countries of origin.
Aliyev said that Azerbaijan has joined international initiatives and international and regional conventions against corruption and has also "implemented all provisions of the conventions into our legislation."
Fighting tech with tech
Imed Hazgui, President of the High Authority for Administrative and Financial Control in Tunisia, talked about the global nature of the conference and how the meeting "brings together about fifty Islamic states who are interested in the development of cooperation between them in the fight against corruption."
He warned about the methods modern criminals may use to evade international sanctions.
"Today we all know that terrorist groups and organised crime groups are increasingly using developed technologies to commit their crimes, to hide the necessary means of having them, and also to escape all sanctions," he said.
He is urging member states to integrate advanced digital tools into their law enforcement strategies to keep pace with these threats, which he says "requires a great cooperation at the level of the exchange of developed technologies, of the exchanges of the good practices in this sense, through also the increasingly use of artificial intelligence today in the fight against corruption, in the prediction of dangers and in the treatment of dangers."

Ukrainian Forces Struck Iskander-M SRBM Launcher in Kursk Region

Unknown Publisher

Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a launcher of the Iskander-M operational-tactical ballistic missile system in the Kursk region.
This was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The strike was carried out over the past 24 hours near the town of Fatezh, where the enemy was reloading ballistic missiles.
Destroying such launchers reduces Russia’s ability to launch ballistic strikes against Ukrainian cities.
The Ukrainian military also struck Russian military targets in other regions. Specifically, they hit enemy ammunition depots, logistics facilities, and repair units.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported on the destruction of an Iskander-M repair base in the Kursk region. On October 12–13, strikes were carried out against a facility near Kondrinka, where self-propelled launchers and transport-loading vehicles for the missile system were being repaired.
