UN refugee agency warns of worsening crisis affecting over 65,000 refugees in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:33:17 UTC
22:33:17 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The UN refugee agency warned Friday of a rapidly deteriorating humanitarian situation affecting more than 65,000 refugees and asylum seekers in Yemen, as intensifying fighting, economic hardship and restrictions on humanitarian access leave thousands struggling to survive.
"UNHCR is alarmed at the rapidly worsening humanitarian crisis," spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh told reporters in Geneva, citing insecurity, dwindling resources and rising prices.
He said conditions were particularly concerning at Kharaz refugee camp in southwestern Lahj governorate, which shelters approximately 9,500 refugees from Somalia and Ethiopia.
Although no refugee casualties have been verified, shelling near the camp has disrupted essential services and restricted movement. Schools have closed, while legal assistance and documentation services have been suspended.
Saltmarsh said some families were fleeing toward southern areas, including Aden, using roads frequented by parties to the conflict and exposing themselves to further danger.
Since fighting escalated in August, UNHCR has helped approximately 600 Somali refugees return voluntarily from Aden to Mogadishu on three flights. More than 1,100 others have expressed interest in returning, but continued attacks and insecurity have complicated further operations.
Meanwhile, over 134,000 asylum seekers and migrants arrived in Yemen by sea during the first nine months of 2026, an increase of approximately 22% compared with the same period last year.
Saltmarsh recalled that at least 139 people reportedly died off Djibouti in October while attempting to reach Yemen.
He added that more than 280,000 Yemenis had been displaced in the past month, while UNHCR's humanitarian appeal for the country was only 19% funded.
Regional shipping disruptions have further complicated aid deliveries, although the agency has secured free transportation for 11 containers of emergency supplies from Dubai to Yemen.

Sassanid-era ossuary inscription discovered near Naqsh-e Rostam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:32:02 UTC
22:32:02 KST

Sassanid-era ossuary inscription discovered near Naqsh-e Rostam
TEHRAN - A newly identified Sassanid-era inscription has been discovered during recent archaeological surveys around Naqsh-e Rostam in Fars province, southern Iran, marking the “fifth ossuary-related inscription” documented in the latest investigations of the area.
Archaeologist and historian Abolhassan Atabaki announced the discovery, saying the three-line inscription dates to the late Sassanid period (224–651 CE) and was found in an area known as Darreh-ye Barre’i, also referred to as the Shahzadeh Esmail Rock, approximately 500 meters north of Naqsh-e Rostam, Jamaran news agency reported on Thursday.
Atabaki said the inscription is among five ossuary inscriptions identified during recent surveys around the ancient archaeological complex. Two of the five inscriptions were found in the Darreh-ye Barre’I area.
In that regard, historian and researcher Najmeh Ebrahimi said six Pahlavi inscriptions associated with ossuaries at the site had previously been identified and documented.
Photographic records of several of these inscriptions are preserved in the archives of the Smithsonian Institution, including images taken by German archaeologist Ernst Herzfeld, who documented archaeological remains in the area, the report said.
Although some of the previously recorded inscriptions have been examined in earlier studies, damage to the stones and the erosion of their inscriptions have made parts of the texts difficult to decipher, Ebrahimi said.
She added that recent investigations had led to the identification of two additional inscriptions in the area, both of which have suffered considerable damage. The inscription reported in the latest discovery is one of the newly documented examples.
Naqsh-e Rostam, situated near Persepolis in Fars province, is one of Iran's most significant archaeological sites, preserving monuments from different periods of ancient Iranian history.

Chinese firms broaden role in Australia's energy storage market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:30:51 CST
22:30:51 KST

by Xinhua writer Xiong Wenyuan
MELBOURNE, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese companies are taking on a broader role in Australia's growing energy storage market, moving beyond battery cell supply to help integrate systems into the grid and support their long-term operation.
The opportunities are expanding alongside investment. Nine utility-scale battery storage projects representing a combined investment of 4.3 billion Australian dollars began operating in Australia in the first half of this year, according to the latest report from Australia's Clean Energy Council.
At All Energy Australia 2026, an exhibition held in Melbourne on Oct. 28-29, Australian project developers and engineering firms said Chinese suppliers' technology, manufacturing capacity and delivery capabilities were helping bring local storage projects into operation.
One example is the Waratah Super Battery in New South Wales, which reached full commercial operation in September. Using cells supplied by China's EVE Energy and REPT BATTERO, the facility acts as a grid "shock absorber," responding rapidly to disturbances and allowing more renewable electricity to reach consumers through the transmission network.
Paul Curnow, managing director and chief commercial officer of Australian storage developer and operator Akaysha Energy, told Xinhua that technical performance, competitive pricing and local technical support were key reasons for choosing the two Chinese suppliers.
For engineering contractors, Chinese manufacturers' scale and speed of delivery also make a difference.
Chris Kennedy, commissioning director of Australian power engineering company EPEC Group, said those strengths, combined with cost competitiveness, helped improve project economics and move projects forward.
EPEC is working alongside Chinese battery maker CATL at the Maryvale solar and storage project, also in New South Wales. CATL is supplying the storage system, while EPEC is responsible for the high-voltage substation's design and construction and related control systems.
Integrating the batteries with the plant's control systems is a key area of cooperation, said EPEC Group Executive Director Mark Parker.
"We're very appreciative of what Chinese companies have done for the energy transition," he said.
As Australia's energy needs evolve, customers are also asking suppliers for different kinds of storage.
Andrew Tang, chief executive officer of REPT BATTERO's overseas business, said demand for four-hour systems was growing, with customers also asking about six- and eight-hour options that would allow surplus electricity to be stored for use at other times.
EVE Energy's cooperation with Akaysha is likewise expanding beyond cell supply to a broader range of products and solutions, including batteries, battery packs and battery systems, said Chen Mengmeng, head of the company's international power products department.
Envision Energy, meanwhile, is pursuing opportunities to combine wind power, storage and artificial intelligence in Australia.
Li Tao, its general manager for Australia, the Middle East and Africa, said a rising share of renewable power, efforts to decarbonize mining operations and growing electricity demand from data centers were driving demand for storage.
Serving that market requires more than equipment. Companies are also strengthening their local presence to support project delivery and maintenance.
EVE Energy has established a subsidiary in Melbourne and plans to expand its local service team. Chen said Australia's demanding requirements for grid connection modeling, product reliability and compliance made it essential to understand how equipment would be used and provide timely technical support.
Envision is developing local spare-parts warehouses and a round-the-clock operations and maintenance service center, while training local delivery and service teams, Li said. With projects scattered across Australia's vast territory, the aim is to maintain equipment promptly and reduce losses from downtime.
Jackie Trad, chief executive officer of the Clean Energy Council, told Xinhua that China was at the forefront of energy technology innovation, making continued close engagement with Chinese companies and technical experts important.
The benefits also extend to households, she said, pointing to Chinese-made batteries that help Australians manage electricity consumption and storage while cutting energy bills.
Describing China as an important partner in Australia's energy transition, Trad called for cooperation to continue.
"It needs to continue if our transition is going to be a success," she said. ■

News Analysis: What China's new consumption trends say about its economy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:30:34 CST
22:30:34 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- For years, China's consumption story was told through shopping bags. Now, it is increasingly measured via concert tickets, travel itineraries, health services and smart devices. More than a change in taste, this shift amounts to a structural turning point that is reshaping how household spending is understood.
In the first three quarters of 2026, China's total retail sales of goods and services rose 2.6 percent year on year. Notably, retail sales of services grew 5 percent, 4 percentage points faster than sales of goods.
Experts said, while the growth pace may look moderate, its scale and quality are significant. Domestic consumption contributed nearly half of economic growth, driving GDP growth up by 2.1 percentage points.
In particular, the engine is switching. Traditional high-consumption drivers, namely demographic dividends, housing-related spending and durable goods, are giving way to new ones: service consumption, upgraded consumer goods, and green and smart products.
That is why, in June this year, the National Bureau of Statistics unveiled a new indicator -- total retail sales of goods and services, a telling marker of consumption trends.
The deeper impetus stems from a historic leap in the development stage. International experience shows that once per-capita gross domestic product (GDP) approaches the 15,000-U.S.-dollar benchmark, consumption structures typically shift from goods-led to service-oriented patterns, said Wang Yiming, former vice president of the Development Research Center of the State Council, who noted that China is at a key phase of this transition.
Holiday spending has highlighted the trend. During the seven-day National Day holiday this year, domestic tourist trips and total spending rose 6.3 percent and 4.3 percent year on year, respectively.
Even birdwatching is contributing to this momentum. At the Yellow River estuary in east China's Shandong Province, visitors flock there each year during the migratory season for the spectacular "bird waves."
Local birdwatching sites have received about 400,000 visitors each year during the season, according to local authorities, generating more than 300 million yuan (about 44.7 million U.S. dollars) in revenue from accommodation, catering, and cultural and creative products, while hotel occupancy has risen by more than 10 percent year on year.
Service consumption is not simply replacing goods spending but rebalancing the consumption basket at a higher level. Travel, culture, sports, health and information services are growing faster, while demand for outdoor gear, smart wearables and health-related products is being stimulated as a result.
International sports brands are also benefiting. Amer Sports' revenue in China climbed 35.5 percent year on year in the second quarter of 2026, while direct-to-consumer sales surged 52 percent. Executives said the Chinese market remains one of the company's most productive and profitable markets, supported by demand across performance running, trail running and lifestyle footwear.
With a population of more than 1.4 billion and increasingly segmented demand, China's market provides ample room for service supply to expand, iterate and improve, reflecting the upgrading of people's needs.
China has consciously rejected the playbook of "helicopter money," which temporarily inflates consumer data but triggers severe long-term inflationary hangovers and fiscal degradation, a commentator, Bi Jianlu, wrote in an article carried by the Foreign Policy in Focus website.
Instead, the country has laid out its first five-year plan dedicated solely to expanding consumption. The blueprint made "enhancing consumption capacity" a standalone chapter, with systematic arrangements for employment, income growth, social security and public services.
The aim is not only to encourage people to spend today but also to build an institutional architecture in which they feel secure enough to spend tomorrow, analysts said.
When incomes are supported, safety nets are in place and the business environment improves, consumption growth follows in a natural way.
Meanwhile, China's efforts such as consumer goods trade-in programs are gaining traction. Since the beginning of 2026, the trade-in program has supported 250 million purchases, creating product sales worth a total of 2 trillion yuan.
However, challenges still remain. The pace of household consumption recovery remains to be seen, while it takes time for improvements in income expectations to translate into stronger willingness to spend. Another key issue is whether the quality of service can keep pace with upgrading demand.
The friction between robust supply and lackluster demand is, in essence, not one of absolute oversupply or insufficient demand, but a mismatch caused by the transition in the development stage and model, reads a commentary in Qiushi Journal, a flagship magazine of the Communist Party of China Central Committee.
"By persistently deepening reform and fostering more domestic demand-led, consumption-driven and endogenous growth, this mismatch can be fundamentally resolved," it said. ■

Interview: Dakar 2026 YOG makes once far-away dream "reachable," says Role Model Chajira
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:30:17 CST
22:30:17 KST

Kenyan rugby player Sheila Chajira (C) organizes a training session for club players in Nairobi, Kenya, on Aug. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Qi)
DAKAR, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- As Africa counts down to its first Olympic event, Kenyan rugby veteran and Athlete Role Model Sheila Chajira believes that a "reachable" dream can inspire hundreds of millions of young hearts across the continent.
Africa is home to the world's largest concentration of childhood, and its young population is growing faster than anywhere else, according to the United Nations Children's Fund. Nearly 691 million under-18s live in African Union member states, roughly 46 percent of the continent's population.
Speaking of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games (YOG), Chajira recently told Xinhua that this historic event could be a game-changer for young Africans who dream of reaching the world's top sporting stage one day.
"The YOG, for the first time being held in Africa, is a platform for African girls and boys who have a dream to one day play in the Olympics. It brings them closer to their ultimate goal," she said. "Many playing in local tournaments now have something tangible to look forward to."
At just 22, Chajira was part of Kenya's inaugural women's rugby sevens team at the Olympics, as the sport made its Games debut at Rio 2016. "Being part of the team selected for the Olympics was a dream, but at the same time, I didn't know what to expect when I went out there," she recalled.
Excited yet humbled, Chajira found herself facing her idol Portia Woodman. She recalled Woodman telling her that even a powerhouse like New Zealand had not started at the top, but had built its success through patience and consistency.
The Lionesses may have left Rio in 11th place, but they did so with their heads held high.
"Knowing where we come from, the facilities we have, and the small things we get has motivated us or helped us reach where we are and we can perform and play against the best of the best," said Chajira.
The early exit still gave them a taste of "what Olympics are all about," and they went home with a clear sense of "what to expect and how to train" to compete at the next level.
"When we got a chance to participate and compete in the 2020 Olympics, we knew what it entailed. To the younger girls who were coming in, we were able to tell them about how incredible it is to play in the Olympics," she noted.
"We had to fight as a team and make sure that every game that we play, we play it like it's a final. Even if we lose, we know we win; we tick the small boxes that we are able to tick. Going to Tokyo, our minds are different."
Now 32, Chajira looked back on her journey, drawing lessons that go well beyond medals and results. "Being an Olympian is a dream for every athlete," she said. "I love being an Olympian because of the commitment it demands."
"Through the Olympics, I have been able to get unexpected opportunities and a relentless drive. Training and competing among the best athletes in the world instills values that help you not only in sport, but in life in general. It is a massive, life-changing thing," she noted.
While still playing as Kenya's national team captain and a mainstay at the Harlequins Women, Chajira also served as the club's head coach, completed strength and conditioning courses, as well as introduced the sport to more girls, including those in the Kibera informal settlement.
As an Athlete Role Model recognized by the International Olympic Committee, Chajira did not take the title lightly.
"It's a big responsibility, because you are helping athletes stay on the right path to attain their goals through your example and mentorship ... I am proud to be who I am and to help others navigate their athletic path to the Olympics," she said.
For Chajira, the Olympics were long perceived as "a distant dream" for Africans when hosted abroad, whereas staging the sporting spectacle on African soil "means it is reachable."
"It motivates training athletes to realize that if the Games can come to Africa, we as Africans can also reach the highest levels in world sports. I am truly looking forward to watching the girls and boys play," she added.
Since Chajira first picked up a rugby ball in her high school years, the game in Kenya has come a long way.
Community clubs have multiplied, domestic tournaments are flourishing, national teams are playing more on the continental and world stage, and Kenya has even hosted a leg of the global circuit earlier this year.
"We couldn't have said that rugby was a career then. We were just doing it for fun or just getting out of a dark space," she said. "But right now, I'm happy to say that rugby pays. Players can get something back home and sustain themselves through it. The table has turned. Things are far better than how I started."
Chajira has set sights on a lasting legacy from the Dakar YOG, stressing that Africa can only unlock its full athletic potential by moving beyond stop-start preparation and committing to long-term, structured youth programs.
"Africa has talent," she said. "I would love to see more youth competitions, because in many African countries, we often only start training when a tournament is approaching."
"If we get a consistent program running -- moving a player seamlessly from under-15 to under-18, under-20, and then to the senior level -- we will leave a better sports legacy. Consistency creates the best of the best players," she added. ■

KINSHASA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is approaching 5,000, according to the latest official report released Friday, as the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) paid tribute to a doctor who died from the disease in the country's conflict-hit east.

The outbreak has affected 67 health zones across eight of the country's 26 provinces.
Meanwhile, Africa CDC paid tribute on social media platform X to Dr. Marie-France Shogogo, who died of Ebola in Beni, North Kivu Province, calling for greater protection of frontline health workers.
"Protect those who protect us," the continental health agency said.
According to local health sources, three doctors died of Ebola within less than 72 hours at an Ebola treatment center in Beni, underscoring the risks facing medical personnel battling the outbreak.
The Beni health zone reported in total 661 cases, including 443 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 67.0 percent, according to the INSP report.
Across North Kivu, a total of 2,391 confirmed cases and 1,341 deaths have been recorded. The report also highlighted mounting pressure on the province's healthcare system, with Ebola treatment facilities operating at 86.3 percent capacity and only 82.2 percent of identified contacts being monitored, below the target of 95 percent.
The outbreak, declared on May 15 and caused by the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, has become the world's second-largest recorded Ebola outbreak. ■

Finland's diesel prices hit record high amid Mideast conflict

22:30:01 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Diesel prices in Finland reached a record high in October, surging 54.7 percent from a year earlier as the Middle East conflict continued to disrupt global energy supplies.
Statistics Finland said on Friday that the average retail price of diesel had climbed to 2.49 euros (2.79 U.S. dollars) per liter, surpassing the previous record set in June 2022.
Other fuel prices also rose sharply. The average price of 95-octane petrol reached 2.28 euros (2.55 dollars) per liter, up 33.3 percent year-on-year, while 98-octane petrol rose 31.5 percent to 2.38 euros (2.66 dollars). Light fuel oil surged 70 percent to 2.04 euros (2.28 dollars) per liter.
The conflict in the Middle East, which began with airstrikes by the United States and Israel on Iran in late February, has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy trade.
Kristiina Nieminen, a senior statistician at Statistics Finland, said that oil continues to reach global markets despite the conflict, but transport-related uncertainty is affecting supplies and driving up consumer prices.
Citing the International Energy Agency (IEA), Nieminen said the global oil market is expected to remain in deficit through the end of 2026. Meanwhile, shortages of middle distillates, including diesel, could persist well into 2027.
Further price pressures could also emerge as winter approaches. Hanna Kalenoja, a transport expert at the Finland Chamber of Commerce, told Finnish public broadcaster Yle that demand for diesel and heating oil would increase with the start of the heating season.
The surge in diesel prices is also raising concerns about broader economic consequences. Ville Kaitila, a senior researcher at the Finnish economic research institute Etla, told Yle that commercial transport prices have already begun to rise.
He warned that higher transport costs could eventually feed inflation, increase wage pressures, weaken Finland's cost competitiveness and affect exports. ■

SHENZHEN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Andrea Triboldi stepped into Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei, the well-known electronics hub, with a handwritten shopping list of more than 20 products, noting model numbers, prices and stall locations. At the top was a DJI drone for the Italian tourist's 11-year-old son.
Next month, leaders of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) economies are expected to gather in Shenzhen for an annual summit. The theme of this year's summit is "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," while China has identified openness, innovation and cooperation as the three priority areas for this year's APEC cooperation.
The city's Huaqiangbei, one of the world's largest wholesale markets for electronic products, offered a tangible window to see how these priorities translate into commercial reality.
Long known for bulk electronic components and low-cost gadgets, the bustling market's merchandise mix has shifted toward a growing range of smart consumer goods, a reflection of the city's push for digital innovation. This ability to roll out new items quickly grows out of its tightly integrated industrial cluster.
Spanning just 1.45 square kilometers, Huaqiangbei hosts 35 specialized markets and over 115,000 registered businesses, stocking more than a million kinds of parts and finished goods. Designers, suppliers, prototyping workshops and exporters operate in close proximity, creating an environment where new product ideas can move swiftly from concept to market.
"Foreign buyers used to come mainly for electronic accessories," said Meng Hangfang, co-founder of local supply-chain platform Zhipinku. "Now smart robots, wearable AI devices and small home appliances are popular. Many visitors come as soon as new items launch."
On the market floors, travelers from across the region test these new offerings. A Vietnamese visitor tried a sensor-controlled aircraft model, drawing onlookers to film. Nearby, a group of Vietnamese tourists picked up portable neck massagers. Nguyen Thi Hong Ngoc said the 150-yuan (about 22 U.S. dollars) massager outperformed pricier alternatives back home, and nearly everyone in her group bought one.
Figures from Huaqiangbei subdistrict authorities show that AI-related products accounted for 61 percent of electronic products in the area as of July, up from 41 percent in 2025.
Sales of AI products rose more than 55 percent year on year in the first seven months of 2026. Sales of AI glasses doubled, while those of drones and robots increased by 60 to 70 percent.
Choi Minjee, a journalist with the Republic of Korea (ROK)'s Kyunghyang Shinmun newspaper who previously covered the technology industry, said she was surprised by the low prices of AI-enabled accessories in Huaqiangbei.
"Such accessories are not yet widely available in the ROK, but they are ubiquitous in Shenzhen," she said. "You can directly feel the advantages brought by the city's complete and mature electronic information industrial chain."
Overseas customers favor smartwatches, headphones, game consoles, affordable phones and hair dryers, as well as foldable electric bikes and smart suitcases, said trader Xiao Wenlong. Some 70 percent to 80 percent of his orders are from abroad, mainly Europe, the United States, the Middle East and Southeast Asia.
"There used to be more large bulk buyers," Xiao said. "Now foreign visitors often combine family travel with shopping." He added that China's visa waiver and tax refund policies have made it easier for individual shoppers to cross borders, supporting broader open trade exchanges.
In the first half of 2026, Shenzhen's trade with other APEC members rose 33 percent year-on-year to 1.98 trillion yuan, nearly 70 percent of the city's total foreign trade.
Huaqiangbei sees roughly 750,000 visits daily, including more than 8,000 overseas business visitors, said local official Chen Jiongwen.
Janwick Hattingh, a Hong Kong-based South African, squeezed in a day trip. He bought a power bank, got his MacBook and daughter's watch repaired, and headed home by late afternoon.
"You can find everything," he said. "If you can't find it here, it doesn't exist." ■

Economic Watch: AI takes on bigger role in China's express delivery during Singles' Day peak
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:29:57 CST
22:29:57 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- A drone hovers overhead, calibrating its position as a smart locker below opens its double doors. A package is lowered precisely into the compartment before the doors close. Later, a customer collects it with a code, with no courier on site.
Scenes like this are becoming common during this year's Singles' Day shopping rush, as China's express delivery industry pushes artificial intelligence (AI) deeper into frontline operations. From sorting centers to last-mile delivery, delivery companies are deploying intelligent agents, robots and predictive models to streamline the entire delivery chain.
The Singles' Day shopping festival, also known as Double 11 because it falls on Nov. 11, is China's annual online shopping carnival and one of the world's biggest retail events.
The most visible change this year is that AI is no longer confined to back-office analytics. STO Express, one of China's major couriers, has deployed AI "digital employees" through its SClaw intelligent-agent platform. The system can assist with customer inquiries, intercept abnormal shipments, plan trunk-line routes and help couriers make outbound calls and optimize delivery sequences. A digital quality-control system is also flagging risks for fresh produce and other sensitive parcels.
"The core change at STO Express this year is using AI computing power to take on part of the frontline physical workload, while proactive services help absorb peak pressure. We are raising efficiency without compromising safety, ensuring the entire network can steadily handle this prolonged peak season," said Luo Jian, who oversees Double 11 operations at STO Express.
Beyond frontline support, delivery companies are using intelligent decision systems to improve resource allocation. JD Logistics, the logistics arm of Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com, has rolled out its upgraded Super Brain 3.0 large model as a decision-making hub, forecasting order volumes by region and adjusting nationwide logistics capacity in real time. The company said AI-recommended delivery routes have an adoption rate of more than 90.2 percent.
In specific operational scenarios, logistics robots are expanding their reach. JD Logistics is deploying embodied intelligent robotic arms at scale in sorting centers, and the arms have achieved a parcel tracking accuracy rate of 99.9 percent. Drones are also delivering to remote villages in southwest China, where mountainous terrain and river crossings have long made last-mile delivery difficult.
AI applications are also extending into broader supply-chain management. SF Express is using sales forecasts and digital supply-chain tools to move inventory closer to consumers in advance, shortening the last-mile delivery distance. YTO Express has embedded more than 100 intelligent agents into route optimization, dispatch analysis and customer-service workflows, and put 28 digital employees to work in operations and customer service. Digital-twin systems now cover its entire network of consolidation hubs.
The changes are not limited to the logistics chain itself. Zhang Yi, vice-president of the Guangdong Internet Society, said AI applications are now used across the entire e-commerce operation cycle, from product selection and content creation to traffic acquisition, customer service and competitor analysis.
This shift is reflected in the latest data. A recent report by the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing showed that AI adoption in China's logistics and supply chains had exceeded 37 percent, with transport at 78 percent, safety and compliance at 52.73 percent, and smart warehousing at 47.27 percent.
China's express delivery sector handled 151.3 billion parcels in the first nine months of 2026, up 4.3 percent from a year earlier, according to the State Post Bureau. The scale of the market continues to provide diverse real-world scenarios for AI deployment across the logistics chain.
Hu Dajian, vice-president of the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing, said AI is shifting from isolated applications to whole-chain coordination, extending from single enterprises to broader industrial-chain collaboration.
This whole-chain push is backed by national policy. The deployment comes as China promotes deeper integration of AI into the real economy. In 2025, China released a policy document to advance the "AI Plus" initiative, setting out goals and priorities for integrating AI across the economy and society.
As these efforts take hold, industry observers said the broad commercial rollout of AI, from drones and unmanned vehicles to robotics and digital employees, has become a major highlight of this year's Singles' Day shopping peak, signaling that the next competitive edge will come less from scale than from AI embedded across the entire operational chain. ■

Ukraine invests in firepower as it inflicts a new Russian casualty record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

22:29:57 KST

Ukraine invests in firepower as it inflicts a new Russian casualty record
Recent Starlink suspension did not much affect Ukrainian lethality, but Kyiv shows it is losing trust in the US.
Ukraine’s military says Russian casualties reached 49,040 in October – a new monthly record.
The General Staff’s estimate of dead and incapacitated Russian troops, as of October 28, comes close to fulfilling Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s goal set in January of at least 50,000 enemy casualties a month by the end of 2026.
Zelenskyy had said that was “a level of destruction of the occupier at which Russian losses exceed the number of reinforcements they can send.”
The previous monthly high of 46,230 was set in September, with both records marking a sharp increase in reported Russian dead and wounded since the summer.
Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert Brovdi called it a “massive industrial slaughter”.
Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty estimates by either side. Ukraine’s military says it has video documentation of each strike.
Aerial drones are responsible for most of the casualties Ukraine inflicts, and Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara this week asked his European allies for funding to double drone production next year to about 16 million units.
The goal, he said, was “to scale up joint production of Ukrainian drones in other countries”.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine could even triple drone production given enough money. Ukraine has decided that mass is the key to winning the war against Russia in terms of firepower.
“We see signs that mass production is preferred over technological sophistication,” said Ukrainian Defence Ministry adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov. “Mass production and simplicity will overcome technology.”
On October 28, the Netherlands and UK took steps to help Ukraine achieve its goal.
The Netherlands said it would provide 500 million euros ($560m) in immediate additional military aid and 1.2 billion euros ($1.34bn) in additional financing.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham upped Britain’s commitments by 10 billion pounds ($13.4bn) over three years, of which 3 billion pounds ($4bn) will be for weapons.
Ukraine announced its Starlink satellite navigation services were back to normal on October 24. “Communication remains stable at speeds exceeding 400km/h,” said the Defence Ministry.
On October 14, Ukraine had reported it was losing control of its drones above about 150km/h (100mph), making it difficult to mount defence against Russian jet-powered drones travelling above 500km/h.
After initially denying involvement, Starlink owner Elon Musk said on October 24 that he had “closed a loophole” that had allowed Ukraine to use Starlink offensively.
But Ukraine appeared to be thinking beyond Starlink and its Pentagon-owned military-grade service, Starshield.
On October 22, Ukraine and Finland announced they were jointly developing an independent sovereign military satellite system. Poland-based ICEYE and Finnish Nokia said they were partnering to realise the system, which would begin to launch satellites in 2028.
Other Europeans may be interested. On October 28, Zelenskyy also discussed satellite technology collaboration with Dutch premier Rob Jetten.
Ukraine said while they lasted, Starlink’s speed restrictions damaged its interception of Russian jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said the 10-day outage caused Ukraine’s interception rate to fall from 77 percent to 74 percent.
Yet the rate seemed to be improving regardless.
According to Ukrainian Air Force data, Ukraine managed to shoot down at least 75 percent of jet-powered drones during the week ending October 29.
That was far above the three-month average shoot-down rate of 60 percent for jet-powered drones, suggesting that Ukraine is adapting fast.
Still, many Russian drones are getting through. One struck a train platform in the central city of Dnipro on October 29, killing at least 14 people.
Ukraine is also concerned that the US administration is hesitating about sending ballistic missile interceptors European allies have paid for.
“The artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems, which unfortunately have been occurring recently, are directly helping Russia achieve the goals of its terrorist campaign,” Zelenskyy said, after Russian ballistics hit a university campus in downtown Kyiv on October 27.
The previous day, Khmara had asked European allies to transfer 10 percent of their existing stocks of interceptors as an advance on future orders.
Ukraine struck Russia during the past week, too.
On October 23, Ukrainian missiles destroyed the main microchip production building of Proton-Electrotex in the city of Orel, which makes missile components.
During the week, Ukraine damaged five chemical plants, NAK Azot, Toliattykauchuk, Omskiy Kauchuk, Energiya and Voronezhsintezkauchuk, which make solid rocket propellants used in missiles.
It also damaged the Voronezh Aircraft Company and VSMPO-AVISMA, two factories building airframes or the metals for them.
Notes from underground
Ukraine has also been developing underground warfare, far from the battlefields monitored by drones, planes and satellites.
On October 22, its Khartiia Corps, originally a volunteer unit but now part of the National Guard, announced it had successfully completed an operation to flush Russian infiltrators out of a disused gas pipeline.
The Russians were using the pipeline to move troops from occupied parts of Kharkiv to the front line city of Kupiansk.
“The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to move past our positions. Our warriors turned this tactic against the Russians and used this system of underground pipelines against the occupiers with extraordinary success,” said Zelenskyy.
Ukraine’s Operation Veles advanced 15km (10 miles) underground through the pipeline and tunnels to emerge behind Russian positions, said Brigadier General Ihor Oboloenskyi.
Khartiia Corps said it coordinated underground attacks from pipes and tunnels with overland attacks and drones to surprise the enemy from several different directions at once, killing or wounding 100 Russian soldiers and capturing 30.
Russian forces had used the pipelines to evacuate their wounded, too, and were filmed marching Ukrainian civilians among them as human shields, said Viktor Tregubov, United Forces Group spokesman.
Ukraine’s forces besieged the Russians inside the pipeline, said Vladimir Dektyarev, an officer of Khartiia Corps. “Even after they were surrounded, they sat for over a month, until their food ran out, waiting for a command from their command for permission to surrender.”
Veles marked the third operation this year where Ukrainian forces have pushed Russian forces back and reclaimed land.
In the south of the country, too, Ukrainian forces were reported to have liberated three settlements – Peredubova, Komar and Fedorivka – on the Donetsk-Zaporizhia border, expanding an area of reclaimed territory there.
Although the US is still on track to bring Ukrainian and Russian technical teams to the negotiating table on November 10, and Zelenskyy supported a ceasefire on energy infrastructure and grain exports, Russia downplayed expectations.
Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke of Ukraine as “the territory of historical Russia” on October 22, denying the existence of a Ukrainian people and refusing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
His foreign policy adviser, Valery Ushakov, said the talks “will not resolve much”.
When Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb held a call with Putin on October 27 – their first contact with him since assuming office – Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov dismissed the conversation as “Europeans’ desire to squeeze into the negotiation process.”

Ukraine sanctions companies, individuals linked to Russia's Rassvet satellite system, shadow fleet
President Volodymyr Zelensky signed decrees on Oct. 30 imposing sanctions on 10 companies and 19 Russian citizens involved in developing the Rassvet satellite system, as well as 39 vessels in Russia's shadow fleet, according to a statement on the Presidential Office's website.
Since February, Russian Starlink terminals have been blocked, with only verified devices allowed to connect. The Rassvet low-Earth orbit satellite network could provide Russian forces with their own satellite communications link, enabling them to control drones and missiles over long distances.
The Rassvet system could pose a threat to the entire world, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, said.
"The (Rassvet) project depends on foreign technologies, equipment, and components, so we are targeting these supply chains at the development stage and calling on our partners to coordinate sanctions," Vlasiuk added.
Among the sanctioned entities are Bureau 1440, the developer, coordinator, and system integrator of the Rassvet system, and two affiliated companies: Labs 1440, which manufactures solar panels for spacecraft, and FAB Rassvet, which develops low-Earth orbit communications satellites, the Presidential Office said.
The sanctions also targeted Belarusian company Aerospace Instruments, which develops components for aerospace systems, the office added.
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) said on Oct. 28 that 49 Russian and Belarusian companies were involved in developing Russia's Rassvet low-Earth orbit satellite communications system.
Besides the satellite system-related entities, the sanctions target 39 vessels belonging to Russia's shadow fleet. The vessels sail under the flags of Russia, Barbados, Liberia, the Marshall Islands, Panama, Hong Kong, Djibouti, the Bahamas, Equatorial Guinea, Zimbabwe, Cameroon, Palau, and Sierra Leone, the Presidential Office said.
The vessels transport Russian oil, petroleum products, and gas condensate to China, India, Egypt, Turkey, and other countries, the office said.
One tanker, the Vasily Dinkov, made 15 voyages carrying approximately 726,000 tons of Russian crude oil in the first half of 2026 alone. Some of the vessels are already under sanctions imposed by the EU, U.K., U.S., Canada, Switzerland, and Australia, the statement read.
Russia's shadow fleet consists of aging, poorly insured tankers used to transport Russian oil in violation of international sanctions. Western governments have also accused Moscow of using the fleet to support its hybrid war against Europe.

Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot are adamantly opposed to two-state politics. France and the international community have no chance of diplomatic gains with either option. What France, like the rest of the world, refuses to concede is that the two-state paradigm enables colonialism. Only by departing from the colonial-serving international consensus can a challenge to Israel be truly presented.
So, when France says its position remains unchanged, while Israel will prioritise ongoing forced displacement and colonial expansion, the only dissonance is in the way France describes the two-state paradigm.
Decades of calling for two states living side by side in peace and security have achieved the total opposite, because while the hypothesis allows space for Israeli colonialism, it does not allow space for legitimate Palestinian anti-colonial resistance. If the two-state paradigm is discarded in favour of decolonisation, France can find cohesion between the words uttered and their meaning. There will be no two-state framework to use as a colonial shield for Israel’s impunity.
In the absence of decolonisation, France’s position, like that of the rest of the world in persistently advocating for the defunct two-state paradigm, supports all measures undertaken by the Israeli government to forcibly displace Palestinians from their land. It is the insistence on pretending that Israel is not a colonial entity that provides the space for world leaders to state that a paradigm based upon territorial appropriation can bring peace and equality.
If the two-state paradigm has achieved nothing but colonial expansion, forced displacement and genocide, then the status quo to which France and the international community adhere is replete with war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Qalamkari: The centuries-old art of printing stories on fabric in Isfahan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:28:33 UTC
22:28:33 KST

Qalamkari: The centuries-old art of printing stories on fabric in Isfahan
TEHRAN - In the historic Iranian city of Isfahan, where centuries of artistic ingenuity have shaped one of the country's richest cultural landscapes, an age-old craft continues to bring colour, patterns and stories to life on fabric. Known as Qalamkari, this traditional textile art combines hand-carved wooden stamps, carefully prepared dyes and intricate Persian designs to produce decorative fabrics that are both functional and artistic.
Rooted in Iran's long tradition of craftsmanship, Qalamkari became particularly prominent in Isfahan, especially during the Qajar era, when its printed textiles developed into some of the city's best-known artistic products. Beyond their decorative appeal, some of these fabrics served as visual narratives, portraying episodes from Persian epics, historical events and religious traditions.
Isfahan, nicknamed Nesf-e Jahan, meaning "Half the World", was the capital of Persia during the Safavid era and a major crossroads of international trade, diplomacy and artistic exchange. Under the Safavid monarch Shah Abbas I, the city experienced a remarkable cultural and architectural flourishing, helping establish its reputation as one of the most important centers of Persian art and craftsmanship. Today, it remains one of Iran's leading tourist destinations and a prominent hub of traditional handicrafts.
An art shaped by wood, color and fabric
Qalamkari, also known as Kalamkari in some transliterations, is a traditional method of decorating textiles through printing with hand-carved wooden blocks. Artisans use these stamps to transfer elaborate patterns onto fabric, often combining several colors and motifs to create richly detailed compositions.
The designs draw inspiration from a broad range of Iranian artistic traditions, including Persian carpets, architectural ornamentation and the elaborate tilework of historic mosques. Floral and botanical patterns, animals, arabesques, geometric arrangements, hunting scenes and Persian calligraphy are among the recurring motifs.
Flowers, cypress trees and other elements of nature feature prominently, often evoking the visual richness of traditional Persian gardens. The resulting compositions reflect a distinctive aesthetic in which symmetry, repetition and a harmonious combination of colors play central roles.
Cotton is among the most widely used materials for Qalamkari because of its ability to absorb dyes. Silk, canvas and fustian have also been used, depending on the intended purpose and desired finish.
The traditional production process requires considerable precision. First, an artisan prepares the design and selects the appropriate wooden stamps, each carved with a particular section of the intended pattern. The raised surfaces of the blocks are coated with dye and pressed onto the fabric to transfer the design.
Producing multicolored patterns requires several stamps, each corresponding to a different color or part of the composition. Their placement must be carefully coordinated so that the separate elements align correctly. Even a slight misalignment can disrupt the overall design.
The craft therefore involves much more than simply pressing a wooden block onto cloth. Knowledge of dyes, fabric preparation, pressure, spacing and the precise registration of patterns is essential. In some examples, hand painting is also combined with block printing to achieve more elaborate effects.
A craft with a long history
The precise origins of Qalamkari in Iran remain uncertain, and no definitive historical reference establishes when the craft first emerged. However, according to the renowned art historian Arthur Upham Pope, the art was already practiced in Iran during the Ghaznavid period.
It subsequently developed through different historical periods, reaching particular prominence under the Safavids. The reign of Shah Abbas I was especially significant for Isfahan's artistic and commercial development, as the city became an important center for the production and exchange of Persian handicrafts.
Although Qalamkari flourished under the Safavids, it was during the Qajar period that Isfahan's printed textiles became especially well known. Their popularity extended beyond decorative applications, with different fabrics serving as garments, tablecloths, curtains and large wall hangings.
Some pieces featured repeating floral and geometric patterns, while others incorporated elaborate figurative compositions. In the latter, the fabric became a surface for storytelling, bringing together characters, landscapes and historical or religious episodes.
When fabric became a storytelling medium
One particularly interesting aspect of Iranian Qalamkari is its ability to communicate narratives through images.
A number of historical examples preserved in international museum collections demonstrate that these textiles were not always intended merely as household decorations. Some depicted scenes from Persian heroic literature, while others illustrated religious beliefs and historical events.
The Weltmuseum Wien (Vienna's World Museum), for instance, houses several examples of Iranian printed and painted textiles attributed to Isfahan and dating from the 19th century.
One of them is a cotton wall hanging from the mid-19th century, during the Qajar period, measuring 176 centimeters in height and 116 centimeters in width. Originally part of the collection of Austria's Museum of Trade, the piece features a variety of traditional Iranian motifs, including scenes inspired by Persian epic stories, floral compositions, cypress trees emerging from vases and animal figures.
Another notable example, titled The Day of Judgment, is a late-19th-century cotton wall hanging attributed to Isfahan. Combining printing and hand painting, it depicts scenes associated with the Day of Resurrection from a Shiite religious perspective, including references to the Battle of Karbala and the fate of its martyrs and opponents.
The museum also preserves another late-Qajar textile, catalogued as a pictorial Qalamkari, which incorporates verses attributed to the Persian poet Omar Khayyam. Its message reflects on the passage of time and the importance of appreciating life's fleeting moments.
Together, these works illustrate the remarkable range of subjects that Iranian textile artisans could accommodate within a single piece of fabric. They also demonstrate how Qalamkari could preserve aspects of Persian literary, historical and religious culture through visual storytelling.
Challenges, decline and revival
Like many traditional Iranian crafts, Qalamkari experienced significant challenges as economic conditions and international markets changed.
During the 19th century, the arrival of cheaper and, in some cases, higher-quality textiles from Britain and Russia made competition increasingly difficult for Isfahan's producers. According to Encyclopaedia Iranica, the quality and price of locally produced Qalamkari fabrics were not always competitive with imported alternatives.
To maintain production, some manufacturers began importing unfinished white textiles and printing their designs in Iran before selling the finished products. Although this helped sustain the industry for a time, it could not fully address its underlying difficulties.
Keeping a living heritage alive
Today, Qalamkari continues to be produced in Isfahan, where generations of artisans have worked to preserve the techniques and knowledge associated with the craft.
Its products include tablecloths, curtains, decorative wall hangings and other household textiles. While traditional floral, geometric and figurative designs remain popular, contemporary producers have also adapted their products to changing tastes and practical uses.
In 2023, Isfahan's Qalamkari received international recognition from the World Crafts Council, reflecting the craft's cultural significance and the city's continuing contribution to traditional textile production.
Isfahan is widely regarded as one of the crown jewels of Iran's handicraft industry, with artisans working to safeguard skills passed down from one generation to the next. Qalamkari represents an important part of this heritage, bringing together textile production, wood carving, color-making and visual design in a single artistic tradition.
For visitors to Isfahan, discovering Qalamkari offers an opportunity to look beyond the city's celebrated mosques, palaces, bridges and historic squares and explore another dimension of its cultural identity.

Pentagon tells Baltic hawks to stop ‘poking’ Russia – Reuters

The warning came after Baltic officials issued a frenzy of aggressive statements against Moscow. In September, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal likened Russian President Vladimir Putin to a “rat in a corner.” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda made similar remarks as he warned that Ukrainian strikes deep into Russia – many of which target civilian facilities – could trigger Moscow’s retaliation. The Russian leader has also repeatedly dismissed speculation that Moscow could attack NATO and the EU, describing it as “political schizophrenia.”
The reported Pentagon intervention comes amid US President Donald Trump’s renewed diplomatic overtures to Moscow. Following an October 9 call with Putin, Washington temporarily eased sanctions to allow Russian diesel shipments to the US and global markets, with Trump suggesting the move would alleviate pressure on American truckers and farmers.

Trump’s deal with Putin triggered backlash from Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky, who denounced it as a “weak decision,” prompting the US president to suggest that Zelensky should be ousted to open the path to peace. Is Israel behind the ‘inexplicable’ safety errors causing train wrecks in Spain?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:27:49 UTC
22:27:49 KST

Spain has faced three deadly train accidents this year, drawing heavy scrutiny to falling safety and security standards in the second-largest country in the European Union.
What has, however, given a new twist after the latest accident earlier this week is the growing online clamour over a potential Israeli hand in the deadly accidents, which have killed at least 115 people since January.
A surge of commentary on social media points fingers at Israel for allegedly carrying out repeated acts of sabotage in Spain.
The two countries recently locked horns over Madrid’s recognition of a Palestinian state and heavy criticism of the Israeli genocide in Gaza.
The tussle follows Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatening the European nation that it would pay an “immediate price” for its pro-Palestinian diplomatic stance.
The subsequent recruitment of Spain’s former railways safety chief and transport secretary by an Israeli railways cyber firm also gave rise to suspicions about Tel Aviv’s alleged role in the fatal train accidents.
A series of human and system errors
A high-speed train ran into the back of a stationary train near the town of Urda in Spain’s Toledo province on October 28, killing at least 68 people and injuring more than 100.
Initial investigations point to a combination of a computer system failure and an “inexplicable” human error as the cause of the deadly accident.
Reports say a technical glitch knocked out the automated signalling safety system across a 65-kilometre stretch of the railway track, bringing all trains in the area to a halt. This led railway traffic controllers to take manual control of the trains.
One controller in Madrid then gave an “inexplicable” order allowing the trailing train to resume normal operations with no speed limits.
The resulting high-speed rear-end collision gave rise to suspicions that it was a planned act of sabotage instead of an accident.
Earlier, another high-speed train derailed on January 18 and crossed into the opposite track on the exact same Madrid-Seville line near Adamuz in the Cordoba province.
An oncoming train then crashed into the derailed train, killing 46 people and injuring more than 150.
Investigations held a broken section of the rail track responsible for the deadly accident. Reports said Spain's train drivers’ union had raised safety alarms before the accident.
Two days later, on January 20, another commuter train derailed close to Barcelona, killing the train driver and injuring dozens of passengers.
Investigations attributed the accident to a structural collapse – a support wall crumbled alongside the tracks, and the debris caused the fatal derailment.
Why is Israel being blamed?
There are two main reasons why an increasing number of online commentators are pointing fingers at Israel for allegedly orchestrating the deadly train accidents.
First, Netanyahu had threatened in an official statement earlier this year that Spain would pay an “immediate price” following a long string of diplomatic clashes.
Spain has taken a strong position against Israel by recognising the Palestinian state, criticising Israel’s genocidal bombing of Gaza, enacting a weapons embargo against Tel Aviv, and closing its airspace to US military flights bound for strikes against Iran.
Netanyahu said that he would not tolerate Spain's “hypocrisy and hostility” or allow it to wage a diplomatic war.
Two, the reason many people have accused Israel of playing an alleged role in the deadly train accidents is the recruitment of Spain’s former transport secretary and railway chief by an Israeli rail cybersecurity firm.
In February 2024, the Tel Aviv-based rail cybersecurity firm Cylus appointed Isabel Pardo de Vera to its advisory board.
Previously, she served as the president of Spain's state-owned railways infrastructure company, and later worked as the country’s secretary of state for transport from July 2021 until early 2023.
Always under the spotlight
Historically, Israel has been frequently accused of conducting covert sabotage, cyberattacks, and targeted operations in countries that it considers hostile.
Its foreign intelligence agency, the Mossad, along with military cyber units like Unit 8200, has a well-documented history of alleged meddling in foreign countries.
In the 2000s, Tel Aviv deployed what is widely considered the world's first publicly known state-sponsored cyber weapon against Iran. It used the Stuxnet computer virus to specifically target and physically destroy nearly 1,000 centrifuges at Iran’s Natanz nuclear enrichment facility.
In 2020, Israel was found to be behind a massive cyberattack that paralysed the computers regulating traffic, shipping, and tugboats at the strategic Shahid Rajaee port terminal in Iran’s Bandar Abbas, causing miles-long traffic jams on land and sea.
In another highly sophisticated supply-chain operation, Israeli intelligence detonated thousands of modified pagers and handheld radios used by Hezbollah members simultaneously in 2024 across Lebanon, killing dozens and injuring many more.
Israel and the online chatter
Israel is being widely accused of playing a secretive role behind the high-speed train collision in Spain on October 28.
Users are connecting the widespread computer communications failure that preceded the crash to Netanyahu’s earlier warning that Spain would pay an “immediate price” for its diplomatic stance.
They are also pointing to the integration of Israeli cybersecurity firms within Spain’s rail systems.
“Israel is crashing Spanish trains,” Joe Black, a social media user, posted on X.
Another social media user highlighted that the crash was caused by a technical malfunction.
“Israeli companies are embedded into the Spanish train system and Spanish trains keep crashing after Israel threatened them,” the post said.
“Really unfortunate coincidence how these accidents keep happening when countries upset Israel and their computer/security contracts are with Israel. It's inexplicable,” said another social media user.

9M people need winter assistance across 4 crisis-hit countries: UN refugee agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:23:07 UTC
22:23:07 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
An estimated 9 million people across Afghanistan, Ukraine, Syria and Lebanon will require additional assistance this winter, the UN refugee agency warned Friday, launching a $50 million fundraising appeal to help vulnerable families withstand freezing temperatures.
"Winter is fast approaching, and we expect 9 million people across Afghanistan, Ukraine, Syria, and Lebanon to need additional support," Dominique Hyde, UNHCR's director of external relations, told reporters in Geneva.
Hyde said the campaign seeks contributions from individuals and the private sector to provide heating equipment, blankets, warm clothing, fuel assistance and materials to repair damaged homes.
She warned that rising oil, transportation and food prices were placing additional pressure on displaced populations.
"All of us are feeling it. The cost of living is increasing," she said, stressing that the impact was particularly severe for refugees.
In Ukraine, escalating drone and missile attacks have damaged civilian infrastructure and contributed to daily power outages, while approximately 10.8 million people will require humanitarian assistance this year.
Hyde said a $135 donation could provide a winterization kit containing a heater and materials to insulate and repair damaged windows.
In Afghanistan, which has recorded an estimated 6.5 million returns since September 2023, a $35 contribution could provide a traditional heating device for a family.
Separately, approximately 1.7 million refugees and nearly 1.9 million internally displaced people have returned to Syria since December 2024.
Hyde said about 2.4 million people in priority areas of Syria are expected to need winter assistance this year, but the agency anticipates reaching far fewer people.
"Our ability right now to help is being squeezed at precisely the moment when that help is most needed," she warned.

The Knesset election and the prospect of meaningful Palestinian political participation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:22:00 UTC
22:22:00 KST

Could this election usher in a new era of meaningful Palestinian political participation?
Tuesday’s election took place amid deep polarisation in Israeli society between those seeking to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in power and those determined to remove him. This divide may make little difference to Palestinians on fundamental issues concerning the future of their cause, but it could bring immediate changes to their living conditions, both within the Green Line – the 1949 armistice line separating Israel from the territories it occupied in 1967 – and beyond it. These changes chiefly concern a reduction in the current escalation, which Netanyahu’s government has fuelled since taking office in 2022, particularly following the events of 7 October the following year.
What could mark the beginning of a more profound change, however, is the scale of Palestinian participation in this election. Preliminary estimates put Palestinian turnout at around 80 per cent; between 1999 and 2022, it ranged from a high of approximately 75 per cent in 1999 to a low of 44.6 per cent in 2021. What prompted Palestinian citizens of Israel to turn out in such large numbers? Did elites play a role in the success of this mobilisation? More importantly, what role might the Palestinian vote play in future decision-making within a state where Palestinians constitute roughly one-fifth of the population, yet which makes no attempt to conceal its drive to entrench religious purity?
A study examining Palestinian towns within the Green Line suggests that Palestinian voter turnout in Knesset elections is closely linked to political considerations. It found a substantial decline in turnout in the elections following the Al-Aqsa Intifada at the beginning of this century, attributing the decline to political exclusion and the repercussions of the events of October 2000, when Israeli police killed 13 Palestinian protesters, for relations between Palestinians and the state.
By contrast, Arab turnout rose markedly in the first election after the Oslo Accords, held on 29 May, 1996, reaching approximately 77 per cent, compared with 69.7 per cent in 1992, an increase of 7.3 percentage points. Palestinian participation in the current Knesset election is being described as historic, with preliminary turnout figures reaching 80 per cent.
Palestinian citizens of Israel have faced worsening challenges under Netanyahu’s current government compared with previous periods, including personal security, civil liberties, development budgets and housing. These problems did not begin with this government. Long-standing social and economic disparities between Arab and Jewish communities were already evident in educational and employment opportunities, infrastructure and public services, alongside an intractable and escalating crisis of violence and crime within Palestinian society.
Personal security has become the most pressing of these challenges. Figures documented by The Abraham Initiatives, an Arab-Jewish civil society organisation, show that the number of Palestinian victims of violence and crime rose from 116 in 2022 to 244 in 2023, followed by 230 in 2024 and 252 in 2025, more than double the figure recorded before the current government took office. This escalation has not been accompanied by effective accountability. The Times of Israel reported that Israeli police solved only around 10 per cent of murders within the Palestinian community in 2025. A 2024 opinion poll identified violence and crime as the greatest challenge facing Palestinian society within the Green Line.
Alongside the deterioration in personal security, Palestinian citizens of Israel have faced increasing restrictions on freedom of opinion, expression and protest under Netanyahu’s current government, particularly since 7 October, 2023. Adalah – The Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel has documented investigations, arrests and legal proceedings arising from social media posts and online protest activities, including statements falling within the scope of freedom of expression, such as opposition to the targeting of civilians and solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. These restrictions have extended beyond the online sphere to include sweeping limitations on organising anti-war demonstrations and the use of measures to silence Palestinian criticism.
These challenges extend to education, employment, infrastructure and the capacity of local authorities to provide services in Palestinian communities. A report published by the Knesset Research and Information Center in March 2026 documented a decline in both funding allocations and the implementation of development programmes for Palestinian towns between 2022 and 2024. Press reports revealed that in December 2025 the government approved the transfer of approximately 220 million shekels ($68 million) from a civilian development plan to the police and the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, diverting resources partly earmarked for building classrooms and supporting cultural institutions and youth centres in Palestinian towns. Human rights organisations and the National Committee of Heads of Arab Local Authorities also filed a petition with the High Court challenging the government’s decision in July to reallocate 496.9 million shekels ($162 million) from the five-year development plan (Government Resolution 550) to the police and the Shin Bet.
These pressures also extend to escalating demolitions and displacement in the Negev, where the Negev Coexistence Forum for Civil Equality, an Arab-Jewish rights group, documented 5,187 demolitions of buildings and structures in 2024, an increase of 58 per cent over the previous year. Among the most prominent cases was the demolition of dozens of homes in the village of Wadi Al-Khalil, leaving hundreds of Palestinians homeless. These policies pursued by Netanyahu’s government against Palestinians within the Green Line intersect with even harsher and more complex policies targeting Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank, which explains the anxiety and mounting fears surrounding the government’s intentions.
These factors, together with Palestinian party elites’ awareness of them, may have played a significant role in guiding, mobilising and encouraging the public to vote in this election. The two Palestinian electoral lists, the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am), conducted campaigns relatively free of mutual attacks compared with previous campaigns. They emphasised that strengthening the lists’ electoral position would make it harder to form a new government including extremist ministers.
Activists and community leaders also played a role in encouraging different segments of society to vote and avoid provocations that could obstruct access to polling stations. The electoral messaging of some of these elites reflected a political evolution that had unfolded over the years and matured in response to the Netanyahu government’s policies targeting Palestinians.
The significance of Palestinian participation in Knesset elections lies in its ability to tip the political balance, as Palestinian seats in the Knesset can help determine whether a government is formed or remains in power. Following the withdrawal of the ultra-Orthodox Shas party from Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin’s government in 1993, the government remained in office despite its parliamentary support falling to 56 seats, relying on outside backing from five Knesset members belonging to factions representing Palestinian society.
In 2021, the participation of Ra’am in the coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid helped form the government that replaced Netanyahu’s. The influence of Palestinian parliamentary factions also extends to the passage of legislation and budgets benefiting Palestinian communities within the Green Line. Palestinian parties, working alongside local authority leaders and civil society organisations, have helped advance government plans to narrow disparities between Jewish and Palestinian communities. Palestinian representation in the Knesset has also enabled issues affecting Palestinians to be placed on the parliamentary agenda and referred to its committees, including the demolition of homes in Qalansawe, which was brought before the Interior Committee, and the issue of Palestinian workers’ wages, which was raised before the Labour Committee.
Broader Palestinian representation could place Palestinian parties among the larger forces in the Knesset and enable them to influence decision-making to a limited extent. As past experience suggests, however, an increase in seats does not automatically translate into substantive influence over decisions or a change in political direction. Such influence remains confined to the avenues outlined above, particularly when it comes to decisions affecting the fate of Palestinians. It is therefore necessary not only to sustain and organise greater Palestinian electoral participation, but also to draw on left-wing and centrist voices within the Green Line, particularly those sympathetic to Palestinian rights and the justice of their cause, both in the Knesset and on the streets. These voices should be supported, both to strengthen their standing and to invest in partnership with them.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Australia Raises Student Visa Costs and Cuts Working Holiday Maker Slots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:22:00 UTC
22:22:00 KST

The biggest strategic mistake in politics is letting another political party set the terms of debate. This is especially true when the party setting the debate is deeply ignorant of Australia’s structural realities and is driven primarily by a series of reactionary emotions.
The rise of One Nation as a major political force in Australia has not only created deep problems for the Liberal and National parties as One Nation cannibalizes their electoral bases, but it has led the current federal Labor government to make a number of decisions around Australia’s migration program that undermine the country’s capabilities.
To placate those drifting off toward One Nation, the government saw a couple of easy targets in international student and working holiday makers to signal that it was “doing something” about immigration.
Labor has raised the cost of student visas to the highest in the world, with a 252 percent increase in just over two years. It has also tightened international student visas by restricting family members accompanying students and requiring new visas when students change courses or institutions. It has also increased financial-capacity requirements and scrutiny of applicants’ intentions.
Some of this is in response to genuine problems within the system, namely exploitative education providers. Yet the crackdown has created a refusal rate of around a quarter of all applicants, with a particular focus on refusing Indian and Nepalese students. It has also sent an unwelcoming message to international students that is discouraging applications – something the government has now acknowledged.
The university sector has highlighted that these measures will cost an estimated $1.4 billion over three years. Universities argue that these restrictions threaten an already fragile funding model. Successive federal governments have underfunded higher education, with real government funding per domestic student falling around 6 percent since 2017. Universities have consequently become reliant on international student fees to subsidize domestic teaching and fund research not covered by government grants. International students now account for just over a quarter of university revenue, and falling enrollments threaten cuts to research programs, academic positions, and infrastructure. Universities warn this will weaken Australia’s research capacity and international competitiveness.
The same ill-thought out response to international students has also guided Labor’s desire to restrict Working Holiday Maker visas. Under changes announced by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke in September, second-year working holiday visas will be capped at 45,000 places, down from approximately 57,000 people who qualified in the previous year. Third-year places will fall from around 31,000 to just 5,000.
The Working Holiday Maker scheme has been used by Australia to fill labor shortages in agriculture and horticulture, where seasonal harvesting requires a large number of workers for short periods. The scheme allows young people, typically from Europe, North America, and East Asia, to gain a second and third year work visa if they complete 88 days of work in a rural or regional setting. This has now become an essential component of Australia’s ability to feed itself and its agriculture export market.
Working holiday makers provide a particularly useful form of labor as without major life ties in Australia they can move quickly between regions and work for short periods as different crops become ready for harvest. This flexibility matters. Fruit especially cannot wait for a workforce to become available. Neither can grain harvests. When the crop is ready to pick, farms need lots of available hands at short notice.
The Working Holiday Maker scheme is also essential to the revitalization of smaller towns and rural areas that struggle to retain younger people, who tend to chase opportunities in cities. Beyond this, participants in the scheme are exactly the kind of migrants Australia should be targeting – young, well-educated, adventurous, and initiative-showing. Many have the ability, given their countries of origin, to integrate into Australian society very easily. Retaining as many as possible after three years should be the Australian government’s objective.
One Nation’s persistent advocacy for substantially lower – or “net negative” – migration has created a political environment where migration numbers have become a test of government resolve. Rather than explaining to the public that Australia’s below replacement level birthrate combined with many industries’ reliance on international students or migrant labor make this irresponsible, the Labor government has decided to submit to One Nation’s premise.
The problem is that One Nation lacks the knowledge of how the country actually functions to make credible policy recommendations. The party itself doesn’t actually want to take on the responsibility of governing, but it wishes to be a permanent agitating force, amplifying grievances and using this to bend other parties to their will. Yet when the government allows such a party to set the rules of the game they themselves become detached from the practical responsibilities of governing.

Haze-fueled protests engulf Jakarta – RT reports (VIDEO)
A wave of protests fueled by toxic haze from massive wildfires continues in Indonesia, with thousands of demonstrators rallying in central Jakarta last week.
Anti-government demonstrations began earlier this month, around the second anniversary of President Prabowo Subianto’s inauguration.
Anger over the government’s handling of the wildfire crisis, described as the worst in more than a decade and linked to widespread respiratory illnesses, has compounded discontent over the rising cost of living, perceived corruption and other grievances.
Protesters are demanding that the government declare a national emergency, a step officials have argued is unnecessary because sufficient resources have already been allocated to tackle the situation. The administration says it has deployed an additional 70,000 firefighting personnel. Combined with improving weather conditions, the effort has helped reduce air pollution in affected parts of Indonesia and neighboring Malaysia and Singapore, according to officials.
Scientists say extreme heat and an intensifying El Nino phenomenon in the Pacific have made Indonesia’s forests and peatlands particularly vulnerable to fires this year. The government has also alleged that some of the fires may have been deliberately started and has launched investigations.

Poland may reconsider transferring additional MiG-29s to Ukraine if Bulgaria deal falls through – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
