Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:03:34 GMT
22:03:34 KST

Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
- Published
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.
Óscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.
The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.
Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.
A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.
In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.
Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.
Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".
Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".
But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".
"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.
The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.
But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.
"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.
A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of Wednesday's disaster, but many families are still waiting for information from authorities about their loved ones.
Esther San Emeterio, whose 54-year-old brother Pepe is still missing, told reporters in Toledo, near Urda, that officials were forcing families to wait in "uncertainty".
"We went to bed crying, outraged and full of shame," she said. "We are desperate and I want all of Spain to know. How can they keep us like this?"
Additional reporting by Sergi Forcada Freixas

Bear Yavor finds new home at Belitsa sanctuary after 14 years in captivity
Friday 30 October 2026 13:30
Friday, 30 October 2026, 13:30
PHOTO facebook.com/FOURPAWS.Bulgaria
Font size
After 14 years in cramped concrete enclosures, Yavor the brown bear has found a new home at the Bear Sanctuary in Belitsa, Bulgaria. The 22-year-old bear now has room to roam, a pool to bathe in and a den where he can retreat, the international animal welfare organisation Four Paws announced.
Yavor had lived at Lovech Zoo since 2012, in enclosures without vegetation or the opportunity to behave naturally.
He was transported to Belitsa in a specially equipped bear ambulance and is reportedly doing well. He is currently in a 3,000-square-metre quarantine enclosure with an artificial den and a large pool, where he will gradually adjust to his new surroundings under the supervision of a veterinarian and the sanctuary's keepers.
Yavor's new home is the result of Four Paws' long-running Change for Zoos campaign, which aims to improve living conditions for animals in Bulgarian zoos.
The relocation was proposed by Blagoevgrad Mayor Metodi Baykushev after Four Paws offered to take in the bear and provide suitable living conditions.
In captivity, brown bears can live for 40 to 50 years.

Swiss economists expects strong winter tourism season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:02:07 UTC
22:02:07 KST

Swiss economists expects strong winter tourism season
Following a strong summer season, the winter is also likely to be a success for the tourism sector, according to the KOF Swiss Economic Institute.
Specifically, the KOF Institute forecasts around 18.7 million overnight stays for the 2026/27 winter season, which begins on Sunday in November. That would be 0.1%, or around 15,000, fewer than in the previous record winter of 2025/26.
The figure would therefore remain very high and exceed that of 2024/25, according to a statement issued on Friday. The forecast has remained largely unchanged since the spring. Slightly rising demand from Europe is largely offsetting the weaker long-haul markets, whilst domestic demand remains stable.
Swiss visitors are by far the most important visitor group during the winter season. With around 9.5 million overnight stays, they are expected to maintain the record level of the previous year, according to the forecast.
The robust economy in Switzerland is underpinning demand. Furthermore, the weaker Swiss franc is making holidays abroad more expensive, which keeps winter holidays at home attractive, according to KOF.
KOF forecasters expect slightly more visitors from Europe than last winter. They anticipate around 5.6 million overnight stays, which would represent an increase of 0.8%. However, subdued consumer sentiment is limiting growth.
The situation is different for long-haul markets, which are likely to remain subdued due to the political situation, with wars and high oil prices. The forecast anticipates around 3.6 million overnight stays, which would be 1.7% lower.
Demand from Asia and the Gulf states is likely to remain below pre-war levels due to high airfares, according to the KOF Institute.
American guests are also expected to be somewhat more cautious about travelling, given the gloomy consumer sentiment. According to KOF, fewer guests are also likely to arrive from other long-haul markets.

‘No food, no medicine’: Alyoshki evacuees recount Ukrainian siege (VIDEO)
People who were evacuated from Alyoshki in Kherson Region, Russia told RT of hunger, relentless Ukrainian drone attacks, and homes being destroyed, describing how Russian soldiers brought supplies and helped them escape.
The frontline town, across the Dnieper River from Ukrainian-held Kherson, has been largely cut off from essential supplies for months. Evacuees described the targeting and destruction of vehicles carrying food and the threat of drones making even a few minutes outdoors dangerous.
“There’s nothing to eat. No medicine. Drones are constantly hovering above you,” one resident said, adding that people could barely step outside for a cigarette before another drone appeared.
He said three vehicles attempted to bring supplies in the spring. “They blew up the first one, then the second, then the third. So they wouldn’t let us get anything in.” People had to rely on vegetables from their gardens, he said, with no vehicles able to reach them.
Another evacuee, Sergey, described living without running water, electricity, and gas after flooding devastated the area. Russian soldiers and volunteers brought supplies. “That’s how we survived,” he said.
For some, escape followed the loss of family members. One woman said her husband died after encountering mines while cycling to collect potatoes. Russian troops guided her to safety using drones and a radio during a five-hour journey from her village to a hospital.
Another woman, whose husband was killed in a Ukrainian attack, described repeated bombardments that forced her to move out of her damaged home and shelter in an adjoining kitchen.
“Houses were just being blown away,” she said. Russian soldiers supplied food, drinks, and gas as residents struggled to survive.
One evacuee said Ukrainian forces were responsible for the attacks, while Russian soldiers evacuated them.
“Ukraine believes that we are traitors, that we are scum. We just want to live a normal life, a regular life,” he said, noting that soldiers shared cigarettes, canned meat, grains, and offered further help.
The humanitarian operation is underway under a temporary Russia-Ukraine ceasefire around Alyoshki. The ceasefire began on October 27 and is scheduled to continue through November 1, following mediation involving US First Lady Melania Trump.
A convoy carrying food, medicine, drinking water, hygiene supplies, and fuel for generators arrived in the town on Friday. The operation also provides the opportunity for those who wish to leave to evacuate.
Russian officials accused Ukrainian forces of obstructing deliveries and evacuations by targeting access roads and scattering mines from drones. Russian military engineers have been clearing the routes to allow the humanitarian convoy through.

Irish government to assess potential for united Ireland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:01:15 UTC

Irish government to assess potential for united Ireland
London has to call a referendum on Irish unity if it appears likely that most Northern Irish voters would back it.
The Irish government plans to set up a government body that would assess the possibility of a united Ireland.
Prime Minister Micheal Martin told The Irish Times in an interview published on Friday that Dublin will, for the first time , research and prepare for a union with British-run Northern Ireland.
Martin said that the body would be tasked to research models and challenges for various potential outcomes, including Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom or maintaining some autonomy as part of a united Ireland.
Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday peace agreement, which put an end to decades of conflict, the British government is obliged to call a referendum on Irish unity – or “border poll” – if it appears likely that a majority of Northern Irish voters would back it.
“What has concerned me about this push for a border poll since Brexit is that it’s partisan, it’s a one-sided advocacy approach,” Martin told The Irish Times.
“It’s sort of putting forward the idea that this would be easy and that it’s inevitable and our time has come. And it’s almost that this would be a victory for nationalism, as opposed to an approach which genuinely seeks to hear all voices.”
While opinion polls consistently suggest a majority in favour of remaining in the United Kingdom, the gap has narrowed since the UK voted to leave the European Union a decade ago, with Irish nationalist parties like Sinn Fein stepping up calls for a referendum.
Martin’s proposal, the first steps of which he said he would bring to cabinet before the end of the year, is the latest move by government parties south of the border to consider what a united Ireland might look like.
His government partner Fine Gael is expected to publish what it has described as a blueprint for a unified island at its annual conference next week.

Cocktail of the week: Ayllu’s sakura no hana – recipe | The good mixer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:00:54 UTC
22:00:54 KST

Inspired by our restaurant’s Japanese-Peruvian roots, and to mark the 1-2 November Day of the Dead celebrations, this drink combines white rum and sake with a dash of bitters and a red-wine float: the result is a light, layered cocktail with delicate, floral notes, juicy berry fruit and just enough theatre to impress without being hard to make.
Sakura no hana
Serves 1
50ml white rum – we use Bacardi
 
25ml sake
 
10ml standard 1:1 sugar syrup
  
2 dashes bitters
  – we use Angostura
 
15ml red wine, ideally malbec, to float on top
 
1 edible flower (we use a cherry blossom when it’s in season), to garnish (optional)
 
Fill an old fashioned glass with ice, then add all the liquids except the wine and stir to combine. Slowly pour in the malbec, so it sits as a separate layer on top of everything else, garnish with the edible flower, if using, and serve.
- Shak Nematulloev, bar manager, Ayllu, London W2

Intelligence alone may not win you status. A new evolutionary psychology study hints at what does.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

A new study suggests that intelligence may raise a person’s standing in a group mainly through what it allows them to do for others. In research published in Evolution and Human Behavior, university students with higher cognitive test scores tended to devise better solutions to a group planning puzzle, and those who devised better solutions received more respect from a partner after a brief exchange. The authors see the results as initial support for the idea that human intelligence evolved partly as a way to earn status by providing useful mental services to one’s group.
In human groups, social status often takes the form of prestige, which is standing freely granted to individuals through respect, admiration, and voluntary deference rather than fear or physical intimidation. Evolutionary psychologists link prestige closely to what they call coalitional value, a term that describes how useful a person is to their social group or alliance in achieving shared goals. Because group living requires constant cooperation, humans tend to track who contributes the most to collective success and reward those high-value partners with influence and social standing.
Understanding how these group dynamics work may help answer a major question in biology: why the human brain nearly tripled in size over the past two to three million years. Much of this expansion occurred in the prefrontal cortex, the front region of the brain responsible for complex planning, decision-making, and flexible behavior. Although an analysis of ancient DNA from West Eurasia indicates that natural selection actively favored genetic variants linked to higher cognitive ability over the past 10,000 years, scientists still debate what specific survival or reproductive advantages drove that trend.
One set of evolutionary explanations suggests that bigger brains evolved to solve ecological challenges like crafting tools, hunting, or surviving harsh climates, yet many other animal species face identical environmental pressures without developing human-level intellect. Another view proposes that intelligence evolved through sexual selection as a courtship display to attract mates, much like a peacock’s tail. However, that idea struggles to explain why men and women show virtually identical general intelligence and why objective cognitive test scores often fail to predict romantic attractiveness in live dating studies.
A third perspective holds that human brainpower was shaped primarily by social competition and the need to navigate group living. Proponents of this view argue that once early humans mastered their physical environments, other humans became their main evolutionary rivals, forcing individuals to form cooperative alliances in order to compete against rival groups. Within these alliances, people who could think ahead and coordinate others became highly sought-after partners.
Psychological research offers some support for a link between mental ability and group hierarchy. A 2004 analysis that pooled results from earlier studies found that more intelligent people tend to emerge as leaders and be seen as effective, although the connection was more modest than earlier researchers had assumed. To explain why groups elevate capable leaders, the authors of a 2014 theoretical paper proposed a “service-for-prestige” model, arguing that followers voluntarily grant respect and deference to leaders as payback for solving coordination problems that benefit everyone.
Three of the new study’s authors built on these ideas in a 2026 theoretical paper that laid out the Coalitional Intelligence Hypothesis, which argues that human intelligence evolved because its outward behaviors signal a person’s capacity to provide demanding mental services to their group in exchange for status.
“The broader motivation is a long-standing puzzle: why did humans evolve such high levels of intelligence?” said study lead author Jonathan Egeland, a researcher at the University of Agder and the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. “We build on an idea from the evolutionary biologist Richard Alexander, who argued that ancestral humans ‘had to cooperate to compete.’ Our Coalitional Intelligence Hypothesis develops this idea by proposing that human intelligence evolved due to reciprocity: Intelligent individuals provide useful services or benefits to their group, such as helping members coordinate, and they are rewarded with status in return.”
“To test this, we had to address a gap between two research traditions,” Egeland told PsyPost. “Research in personality and differential psychology has shown that cognitive ability predicts status, but status there is usually measured as socioeconomic status (income, education, or occupation). Anthropologists, by contrast, focus on prestige: the respect, admiration, and voluntary deference people give to valued group members, which is the kind of status most relevant to human evolution. However, those studies usually rely on subjective rather than objective measures of intelligence.”
To bring these two traditions together and put the hypothesis to its first direct test, Egeland and his colleagues designed a laboratory study that paired a formal intelligence test with ratings of how much respect and admiration people earned from a partner. The study was preregistered, meaning the researchers publicly recorded their hypotheses and analysis plan before collecting data. They wanted to see whether higher test scores go along with more prestige after working on a group problem, whether any such link runs through how well a person actually solves that problem, and whether people can accurately judge a partner’s intelligence during a brief interaction.
The researchers recruited 175 university students in Norway with an average age of about 23 years and an average of 1.6 years of college education. The sample was 58.3 percent female and 38.3 percent male, with the remaining participants identifying as another gender or choosing not to report their sex. Participants formed 85 complete pairs, known in psychology as dyads, and were compensated with either a cafeteria gift card worth 100 Norwegian kroner or a one-in-five raffle chance to win movie tickets.
The experiment took place in three stages, starting with individual assessments. Participants first viewed a diagram of a standard bell curve showing how intelligence scores are distributed in the general population, with an average score of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, and estimated their own score on that scale, a measure collected for a broader project and not analyzed in this paper. Next, they completed a 16-item cognitive ability test that the bilingual research team had translated into Norwegian and verified using blind back-translation into English. This test measured four distinct mental skills: completing letter and number sequences, solving visual pattern matrices, answering verbal logic questions, and mentally rotating three-dimensional shapes.
In the second stage, participants were placed into pairs and given five minutes to work silently and independently on a social coordination puzzle titled “Gathering Food for the Winter.” The scenario asked each participant to figure out the optimal number of hours members of a hypothetical tribe should spend foraging before winter arrived. Because more hours spent foraging brought in more food but also caused greater physical exhaustion for the tribe, participants had to calculate the mathematical sweet spot that maximized food supplies while minimizing group fatigue. The researchers treated each participant’s score on this puzzle as a measure of coalitional value, since a good answer amounts to a useful planning service for the group.
Once the five minutes ended, the partners showed each other their written answers so neither person could copy the other’s work. Each person then had exactly one minute to verbally present their proposed foraging strategy and explain the reasoning behind it to their partner. Because the researchers never told participants what counted as a good or bad answer, partners had to form their own judgments about the quality of each other’s reasoning. In the final stage, the partners were separated to privately rate how intelligent they thought their partner was on the 100-average bell curve, and to evaluate their partner’s social status across three items measuring respect and admiration, leadership qualities, and usefulness as a group member on a 1-to-7 scale.
Before testing their main evolutionary predictions, the authors verified that their Norwegian translation of the cognitive test worked as intended. Using a statistical technique that groups test questions by the underlying skills they measure, they confirmed that the test showed the expected structure, capturing four specific reasoning skills as well as general intelligence, the overarching mental capacity that influences performance across diverse cognitive tasks, which accounted for nearly half of the score variation.
Across the sample, participants answered an average of 7.22 out of 16 cognitive items correctly and earned an average score of 31.37 on the winter foraging task, where scores ranged from 0 to 60 and were calculated by subtracting total tribe fatigue from the amount of food gathered. After removing two extreme outlier ratings below 70, partners estimated each other’s intelligence at an average of 104.65 and gave relatively favorable status ratings averaging 5.38 out of 7.
To analyze how intelligence, task performance, and status fit together, the scientists used a specialized statistical model designed for paired data that accounts for the mutual influence two interacting partners have on one another. Within this framework, they ran a mediation analysis, which tests whether an intermediate factor explains the link between a starting trait and a final outcome. The results showed that participants with higher cognitive test scores performed better on the winter foraging coordination task, with a standardized effect size of 0.44, a moderate association. In turn, coming up with a better foraging strategy positively predicted the social status rating received from the partner, showing a standardized effect of 0.28.
Before accounting for task performance, the overall link between cognitive test scores and the status a person received was small (0.16) and fell just short of statistical significance. Once the researchers factored in how well participants solved the foraging task, the direct link dropped to near zero (0.03), while the indirect pathway running from cognitive ability through task performance to status (0.13) was statistically significant. In statistical terms, task performance fully mediated the relationship, a pattern consistent with the idea that participants with higher test scores earned more prestige because they came up with better group strategies.
A separate analysis, which also accounted for the paired structure of the data, found that a person’s actual test score predicted their partner’s estimate of their intelligence (0.37). This suggests that people can gauge a peer’s mental ability with some accuracy after hearing them explain their reasoning for just a minute.
“Intelligence does not seem to raise a person’s rank in a group simply because others are impressed by it,” Egeland explained. “In our study, more intelligent people were granted more prestige mainly because they were better at providing something useful to the group, namely good solutions to a coordination problem. Once we accounted for this ability to benefit others, intelligence itself no longer had a meaningful direct effect on status. In other words, people seem to reward intelligence because of what it can do for the group.”
The authors argue that because deferring to someone carried costs in ancestral environments, early humans likely evolved to grant status selectively to peers who could provide benefits in return. In their view, quickly spotting who offers sound reasoning would let group members rally behind capable coordinators and share in the rewards of better collective decisions.
The study does have some limitations to keep in mind. Because a person’s cognitive ability cannot be experimentally altered in a laboratory, the study relied on an observational design, which means it cannot establish that intelligence directly caused the higher status ratings. For instance, unmeasured traits like speaking confidence, charisma, or verbal fluency during the one-minute presentation could have influenced how impressed partners felt. In addition, the participants were all Norwegian university students whose judgments were based on a two-minute exchange about a hypothetical paper-and-pencil foraging puzzle, whereas real-world reputations and hierarchies typically develop over months or years of repeated interaction.
The study also captures a present-day pattern among modern university students, so it cannot directly show why human intelligence evolved, only that the results are consistent with one evolutionary explanation. Helping a group succeed in everyday life involves many skills beyond mathematical resource optimization, such as mediating interpersonal conflicts, building alliances, and sharing cultural knowledge.
Future research will need to test whether these findings hold up in larger, more diverse populations outside of university classrooms and over longer periods of social contact. Exploring additional ways that people contribute mental effort to their teams will help clarify how different aspects of human intelligence shape social standing in the real world.
The study, “Coalitional value mediates status allocation based on cognitive ability,” was authored by Jonathan Egeland, Leif Edward Ottesen Kennair, Thomas Haarklau Kleppestø, and Mons Bendixen.

A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine
Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers
A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.
Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.
Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”
Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.
The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.
Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

Bulgaria’s Revenue Agency Finds 19 Violations at Sofia Restaurants and Hotel

Unknown Publisher

13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Bulgaria’s National Revenue Agency (NRA) found 16 violations during inspections of five restaurants in Sofia and identified three more at a hotel belonging to a global chain, the agency said.
During checks conducted by its Main Directorate for Fiscal Control, inspectors visited five well-known restaurants in the capital and uncovered violations including failure to issue receipts, differences between the amounts recorded by fiscal devices and actual cash balances, and the issuing of non-fiscal receipts.
The NRA also detected three violations during control operations at a hotel representing a global chain over the weekend. These involved failure to issue cash receipts, the provision of a non-fiscal receipt, and discrepancies between cash balances and the amounts recorded in the cash register.
The inspections at the restaurants and the hotel began with test purchases conducted by undercover customers. In three cases, customers were not given a fiscal receipt after paying, or received a counterfeit-style payment slip printed by a non-fiscal device when they specifically requested a cash receipt.
The established violations could lead to the administrative measure of sealing the hotel or restaurants.
The NRA reminded consumers that they can help monitor how businesses report their income by using the agency’s NRA Mobile app to scan the QR code on a receipt. The application is available through the App Store for iOS devices and Google Play.
Reports of missing receipts, false payment documents, missing details, and other tax or social insurance violations can be submitted to the NRA Information Center at +359 700 18 700 or by email at infocenter@nra.bg.

Repeaters for Russian drones continue to operate in Belarus - Demchenko
Kyiv • UNN
Repeaters periodically transmit signals from Belarus for Russian drones. During massive attacks, the UAVs move along the border.
In Belarus, repeaters for Russian drones continue to operate. This was stated by State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko during a national telethon on October 30, UNN reports.
Unfortunately, they are operating. Signals originating from the territory of Belarus are periodically detected, which allow Russian drones to move more freely toward our western regions. And it cannot be said that the repeaters operate 24 hours a day, but those components of the Defense Forces that have the technical capabilities continue to note that, in various locations, the repeaters resume operation for a certain period of time—especially when a more massive attack is underway as Russia launches drones toward Ukraine. The routes are specifically plotted so that these drones follow the border line with Belarus

Shmyhal: Russia has carried out more than 350 attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector since September
This was stated by First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Denys Shmyhal during Question Time with the government in the Verkhovna Rada, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Since September, the enemy has carried out more than 350 strikes, damaging more than 800 units of various types at substations and power generation facilities,” Shmyhal said.

As reported by Ukrinform, a number of Ukrainian energy companies have called on international partners to expedite the provision of assistance—particularly in the area of air defense—and to intensify sanctions pressure on Russia.

Nature recovery is falling behind. Can COP17 get global action back on track?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:57:54 UTC
21:57:54 KST

Biodiversity goals are off track as the UN nature summit faces funding and political tensions on its final day.
The United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP17 CBD) is due to close later today (30 October) in Armenia after two weeks of heated debate.
The 2026 summit has largely served as an evaluation of progress towards promises made in previous years, with a focus on implementation and long-term results.
Delegates are trying to finalise the Yerevan Pathway, a package of decisions meant to speed up delivery of the world’s nature goals.
“We need to see concrete priorities coming out of the negotiations. But unfortunately, this is not the case yet,” Irene Wabiwa from Greenpeace International told reporters on Thursday (29 October).
A number of topics remain unresolved in the final hours of the summit, ranging from the role of science in the negotiations to how to fund conservation and tackle harmful subsidies.
Indigenous peoples are also calling on governments to uphold their rights, respect traditional knowledge and guarantee meaningful participation in decisions about the lands and waters they protect.
How far have countries come in the global effort to protect and restore nature?
The first global assessment of progress on the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) – known as the ‘Paris Agreement for nature’ – was launched by UN Secretary-General António Guterres on 15 October. The report, ‘State of Biodiversity Action’, found that fewer than half of the assessed national targets are on track.
The report covers all 23 global targets adopted by 196 parties in the landmark agreement during COP15 in 2022. Now at the halfway point towards the 2030 deadline, the report revealed progress is being made, but much too slowly.
On the headline ‘30x30’ goal of protecting at least 30 per cent of the planet’s land and sea by the end of the decade, data from the Protected Planet database shows about 19 per cent of land and inland waters and 10 per cent of oceans are currently protected.
World leaders adopted the ‘Yerevan Declaration: Taking Action for Nature’ at a leaders’ summit on 16 October – just ahead of COP17 – reaffirming the 2030 goal.
A separate UNEP report published on 29 October, ‘Nature’s comeback’, looked at the related target of putting at least 30 per cent of degraded ecosystems under effective restoration by 2030.
It found land restoration has reached nearly half of that goal, but progress in marine and coastal ecosystems has reached only 23 per cent of the global target and freshwater ecosystems – which are degrading the fastest – are at five per cent. However, the report cautions that gaps in monitoring and reporting likely mean this figure is underestimated.
One of COP17’s major outcomes is meant to be the ‘global review’: a set of concrete recommendations for turning lagging pledges into action and speeding up progress to the 2030 deadline as part of the Yerevan Pathway. But this remains in limbo after days of deliberations.
In a process where ambitious commitments are made but few mechanisms exist to ensure they are translated into action, the global review is meant to strengthen accountability by identifying gaps and tracking collective progress.
There are also growing calls to reform the consensus-based COP process itself, with critics arguing that the requirement for unanimity allows a small number of countries to block progress.
Financing for nature restoration falls short
A lack of money is a major barrier to meeting the 2030 biodiversity goals and has been a key focus of the Yerevan summit, where governments are seeking ways to raise funding from public and private sources.
Last year, delegates agreed a strategy to mobilise at least $200 billion (€180bn) annually by 2030 to close the global biodiversity finance gap. Currently, the annual shortfall in funding needed for nature is estimated at around $700 billion (€628bn).
Yearly investment in ecosystem restoration alone must increase more than four-fold, according to the UNEP report, from $64 billion (€57.5bn) to $296 billion (€266bn) by 2030. It cites the challenge of paybacks – such as flood protection, cleaner water, carbon storage and healthier ecosystems – taking years to materialise as a barrier to mobilising immediate funds.
Urging a shift from financing individual projects to building “restoration economies”, UNEP has called on governments and financial institutions to recognise the economic value of healthy ecosystems, attract private investment, and reduce incentives that encourage environmental degradation.
More than $1.8 billion (€1.6bn) in new funding has been announced during the summit, according to the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).
But COP17 has seen flare-ups over who should fund global conservation. The EU has argued that wealthy emerging economies – such as the Gulf states and China – should join the group of around two dozen mostly Western nations formally expected to provide biodiversity finance for developing countries.
Saudi Arabia and Qatar have reportedly opposed this and talks have drifted into stalemate.
Efforts to boost the lacklustre Cali Fund – a UN mechanism for sharing profits from corporations that use genetic data from plants and other organisms – have also proved difficult.
The fund set out to raise $1 billion (€893m) a year for conservation in developing countries when it launched in early 2025. So far, it has attracted around $10,000 (€8,900). Contributions are voluntary, which is at the heart of the dispute.
Harmful subsidies are another sticking point. The framework’s Target 18 calls for cutting subsidies that damage nature by at least $500 billion (€447bn) a year by 2030. Countries remain divided over language on reducing or phasing out such incentives, including agricultural subsidies.
On 27 October, the EU launched the Friends of Credits for Nature and Biodiversity, aiming to attract investment in nature restoration and protection by turning these efforts into something tangible and tradable.
However, critics warn that nature credits are hard to verify and can encourage greenwashing by allowing companies to offset environmental damage rather than reducing their impact.
Synergising climate and nature action
The biennial biodiversity COP is often overshadowed by the larger annual climate COP, although the topics they address are inextricably linked – with biodiversity loss and climate change accelerating one another.
In recognition of this, the COP17 agenda covers cooperation between the three Rio Conventions, on biodiversity, climate and desertification, including a call to enhance collaboration between national departments responsible for compliance.
“Finding synergies between the Rio Conventions, and between climate and nature action plans more widely, has never been more essential – or a more obvious win,” says Catherine Weller, global policy director for conservation charity Fauna & Flora.
“This really just makes a lot of sense. When the right hand doesn’t know what the left hand is doing, you risk making a mess.”
But, speaking on condition of anonymity, a French government delegate at COP17 told news agency AFP that a small number of countries were frustrating progress.
Saudi Arabia, Russia, Argentina and Brazil have reportedly pushed back against taking on board guidance from two landmark scientific assessments on the overlap between the nature and climate crises and the economic forces driving them.
The dispute echoes a growing pattern in consensus-based global negotiations, where oil-producing countries are accused of frustrating efforts to tackle fossil fuels, plastic waste and other environmental harms.
A push by countries including Saudi Arabia, India, Russia and China to delay publication of the IPCC’s next set of benchmark reports on global warming remains unresolved. The IPCC’s October meeting was suspended without agreement on a timetable, and talks are due to resume in December.
This matters because the reports are meant to feed into the second Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement, a process that begins at COP31 in November and will see countries assess collective progress towards climate goals before concluding at COP33 in 2028.
Tackling invasive species
As the climate and oceans warm, the shift in which species survive and thrive is gathering pace. Invasive species are migrating into new environments, causing ecological and economic damage as they disrupt the delicate balance among native species.
“In order to tackle this top-five driver of biodiversity loss, we need a collaborative, cross-sector approach,” says Weller. “Many of the pathways through which invasive alien species are spread are linked to trade, transport and supply chains, and so businesses have a significant role to play in both prevention and removal of invasives.”
Acknowledging this, invasive species have been on the negotiating agenda at COP17. A decision on invasive alien species was one of four adopted in the opening week, alongside gender equality, environmental education and information sharing.
It calls for stronger early detection of invasive species and rapid response systems, better sharing of scientific data, and improved access to funding and technology to help countries tackle the problem.
Beyond the talks, Weller urges stronger prevention, biosecurity and better sharing of data on invasive species in the private sector, alongside closer collaboration with governments and conservation organisations.
The COP17 summit is also expected to decide whether Panama or Ecuador will host the next biodiversity summit in 2028.

‘Trust in high-speed rail shattered,’ says Spanish premier after deadly accident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:57:50 UTC
21:57:50 KST

Alyssa Mcmurtry
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday acknowledged that "trust in high-speed rail has been shattered" after a deadly accident earlier this week killed at least 69 people and injured 110.
Wednesday's collision near Urda in central Spain was the country's second major high-speed rail disaster this year. 
A derailment and collision near the town of Adamuz in January killed 46 people, with preliminary findings pointing to a fractured rail.
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain, with such a strong high-speed rail system, to suffer two accidents of these characteristics and magnitude in one year," Sanchez said at a press conference.
He pledged to "provide solutions to further strengthen the high-speed rail system so a tragedy of this kind … doesn't happen again."
Spain has the world's second-largest high-speed rail network after China and the largest in Europe, according to the International Union of Railways.
Castile-La Mancha regional President Emiliano Garcia-Page said Friday the death toll could rise slightly as identification work continued. Authorities had received 70 missing-person reports.
Of the 110 people hospitalized in the region, 39 remained admitted, all progressing reasonably well, he said.
Failures under scrutiny
Scrutiny is growing over the failures that allowed a Renfe high-speed train to slam into the back of a stationary Iryo train on the Madrid-Seville line.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said a technical failure in the automatic signaling system halted several trains, prompting controllers in Madrid to take over. Similar glitches have occurred 160 times in Spain this year, Puente said Friday, adding that the figure was within the EU norm.
A worker at the control center then authorized the Renfe train to proceed at normal speed – up to 200 kilometers (124 miles) per hour – despite the stationary train ahead, violating safety protocols, according to Puente.
"If there are two trains in the same block section, the train behind should not move. Second, in these conditions, if the first train moves, the train should be authorized to move at a maximum of 40 kilometers (25 miles) per hour," Puente said.
Around five minutes before the accident, the stationary train had also contacted the control center to warn that it was unable to resume moving.
A preliminary investigation estimated that the Renfe train was traveling at around 160-200 kilometers (99-124 miles) per hour when it struck the stationary train.
The investigation has not established final responsibility, and railway workers and experts have questioned whether the controller's decision, which Puente called "inexplicable," reflects wider weaknesses.
Vicente Almenar, a Renfe train driver with the UGT union, urged caution, warning of intense pressure to speed up operations to prevent delays, Spanish news agency EFE reported.
Antonio Tobal, UGT’s safety representative at Adif, cautioned against focusing solely on human error. He called for examining working conditions, organizational procedures and staff training for emergencies.
Other experts have pointed to Spain's rapid high-speed rail expansion and relatively low maintenance spending compared with other European countries. They have also questioned delays in replacing the Madrid-Seville line's aging automatic signaling system with the European Rail Traffic Management System.
Spain's rail safety record
Spain’s disasters contrast with high-speed rail’s strong safety record elsewhere.
Japan’s Shinkansen has recorded no passenger deaths from collisions or derailments since services began in 1964. 
China’s two documented fatal high-speed crashes killed 41 people. France, which has Europe’s second-largest high-speed network, has recorded 14 deaths aboard TGV trains in three accidents, including 11 during a test run.
Spain's two crashes this year have killed at least 115 people. Another 80 died in the 2013 Santiago de Compostela derailment.
On Friday, Spain’s transport minister rejected calls to resign.

Government seeks to ban smoking where children congregate

Government seeks to ban smoking where children congregate
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch cabinet wants to prohibit smoking at locations dominated by children, including petting zoos and after-school and other managed playgrounds.
Sources told broadcaster NOS the proposed ban will be discussed at Friday’s Council of Ministers.
While most such places are already smoke-free, the government wants to ensure that the remaining few ban smoking. The House of Representatives also supports the ban and wanted to extend it to other kid-friendly locations like zoos and amusement parks.
That may come in the future, along with bans at unattended playgrounds and outdoor swimming pools, but for now, the government will focus on managed playgrounds and day care centres where there is wide support for the plan.
The ban is part of the government’s efforts to have a smoke-free generation by 2040. Measures already in place include a display ban, unattractive packaging and fewer locations to purchase cigarettes.

Destinus says it now makes more cruise missiles a month than Europe did a year before 2022, but engines are what Ukraine’s strike programs are short of
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:57:04 UTC
21:57:04 KST

Destinus has completed 1,750 Ruta B1 cruise missiles and reached monthly output of nearly 300, the company said on 29 October, telling Reuters this exceeds Europe’s annual cruise-missile production before Russia’s full-scale invasion.
That gives a date for easing a shortage. A looming shortage of mini jet engines threatened to hold back Ukraine’s deep-strike drones, Reuters reported in April. Czech maker ZofiTech was then producing about 200 a month, nearly all for Ukraine, and expected demand to reach thousands within months. Both Ruta versions use the 1.5-kN engines Destinus is promising. Ukraine plans to build more jet drones and cruise missiles, so engine output next year will have to keep up, Defense Express notes.
Destinus builds its own engines, but hasn’t said how many
Destinus CEO Mikhail Kokorich said the company already produces turbojets in the roughly 1.5-kilonewton class in series, supplying them both for its own missiles and to other manufacturers. The Ruta B1 runs on the company’s own T150 engine. In June, Destinus announced its 1,000th T150 and said the line was designed to sustain production of thousands of missile systems a year. The company has not disclosed its current engine output.
Block 2 enters production, Block 3 is due to fly in 2027
Meanwhile, Destinus said it has begun production of the larger Ruta Block 2, designed to carry a 250-kg payload more than 700 km. Unlike the roughly 300-km Block 1, Block 2 is designed to be stored, transported, and launched from the same container. A third version, Block 3, is planned with a 2,000-km range, with flight tests scheduled for 2027.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged the Ruta’s combat use in October 2025. Days later, he said Ukraine expected mass production of Ruta and Flamingo missiles by the end of that year. In June 2026, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the Netherlands was ready to finance about 700 Rutas for Ukraine, without specifying the version.
Deterrence takes “tens of thousands of missiles”
At the same time, Kokorich said Europe’s problem is shifting from production to integration.
“To have sufficient deterrence, you need to have tens of thousands of missiles,” he said.
European customers, he added, still need to build the military units and logistics to operate missiles in such numbers. Those arsenals would also need storage, transport, maintenance, and targeting infrastructure, he said, and European militaries would need to rethink how they stockpile and deploy precision-strike weapons.
No Chinese parts, and a bet on cheaper, shorter-range missiles
Kokorich said Destinus uses no Chinese components, unlike wartime production in Ukraine, and said access to Chinese suppliers would make manufacturing cheaper, faster, and easier.
Kokorich also argued that cheaper missiles with ranges under 1,000 km would make up most future demand. Separately, Destinus is working with Rheinmetall on cruise missiles and ammunition for multiple-launch rocket systems, including a planned European equivalent of the GMLRS rockets fired by HIMARS.

Trump: US-Iran war will 'get wrapped up soon,' speaking ahead of midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:56:04 UTC
21:56:04 KST

US President Donald Trump said Friday evening that he sees no urgency to reach an agreement with Iran, citing the difficult situation facing the Iranian regime as negotiations between Washington and Tehran continue.
Trump made the remarks during an Oval Office meeting with Stephen Hubbard, an American citizen recently released from prison in Russia.
Asked by a reporter for further details about the talks with Iran, Trump replied: "There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking, but look, they're not paying their soldiers. They're not paying their police officers. You know, they're in big trouble, and we have time."
The president also dismissed criticism of the financial costs of the US military campaign against Iran.
"I heard somebody say we're wasting money," he said. "I spent a lot of money to get rid of nuclear weapons, and that's what we did. But every dollar we spent in Iran, we got back many times over through what we did in Venezuela."
Trump added: "Frankly, it's a war, but it's not a typical war. We've been there for seven months. We're spending very little money, relatively speaking."
Trump also claimed that US operations in Venezuela had generated hundreds of billions of dollars for the United States, although he offered no figures to substantiate the claim.
Trump says Iran war could end soon, insists on nuclear guarantees
Despite dismissing concerns over the cost of the military campaign, Trump suggested that the conflict with Iran could soon come to an end, while reiterating his demand that Tehran be prevented from acquiring nuclear weapons.
During an interview with Kansas City radio station KCMO, just days before the November 3 midterm elections, Trump said the war "It's going to get wrapped up soon," adding, "We need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon."
Trump had previously said the US would not launch further strikes against Iran before the elections.
Qatar submits proposal to Iran to end the war
Trump's remarks come amid renewed diplomatic efforts to prevent another round of US strikes on Iran.
Qatari mediators arrived in Tehran on Friday to meet with senior Iranian officials as part of an initiative coordinated with Washington.
Qatar presented Iran with a draft proposal to end the war on Sunday, but a senior Iranian official rejected it, saying the terms were unacceptable to Tehran.
The central disagreement concerns the sequence of negotiations. Washington insists that Iran's nuclear program be discussed from the outset, while Tehran is demanding that the US lift its blockade of Iranian ports and remove sanctions on Iranian oil exports before the talks can move forward.
The diplomatic efforts also follow a letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Mohsen Rezaei, a senior Iranian regime official, delivered through Qatari mediators.
The letter was intended to explore the possibility of resuming direct negotiations, although Trump said Thursday that it concerned the delivery of medical equipment to Iran.
Trump defends Russia sanctions decision amid Iran negotiations
Trump's comments Friday suggest that Washington believes time is on its side as Iran faces mounting economic pressure.
However, the president announced no breakthrough in the talks and made no commitment to refrain from further military action.
Later in the Oval Office meeting, Trump addressed the negotiations that led to Hubbard's release from Russia, defending his decision not to impose additional sanctions on Moscow while those talks were underway.
Trump argued that imposing sanctions at that stage could have jeopardized Hubbard's release.

MEP Marina Kaljurand not running in Riigikogu election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

MEP Marina Kaljurand not running in Riigikogu election
Long serving Social Democratic Party (SDE) MEP Marina Kaljurand is not running in next spring's Riigikogu elections, the party has announced.
SDE leader Lauri Läänemets confirmed that Kaljurand, who ran in the same electoral district (Harju and Rapla counties) in the previous Riigikogu elections in 2023, wlll not be running this time around, and outgoing Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov will take her place as a candidate.
"We have indeed taken Marina Kaljurand's wishes into account, as she has said that she will not be taking part in the Riigikogu elections this time," Läänemets said.
Kaljurand had said in an interview with ERR in April this year that she did not see herself continuing in politics after her current mandate at the European Parliament ends. Kaljurand, a former foreign minister and ambassador to both Russia and the United States, has been an MEP since 2019.
"As for the Harju and Rapla counties electoral district, that is where the prime ministerial candidate usually runs. If the party council confirms Jonatan Vseviov as its candidate for prime minister this Sunday, then naturally Jonatan Vseviov will also be at the top of the list in that electoral district," Läänemets said.
"And this also fits with the logic of having the prime ministerial candidate run in Harju and Rapla counties, so we will not have to make choices there, but can go into the elections with strong candidates competing against one another," Läänemets went on.
SDE is known for frequently placing its leading candidates at the bottom of its national list, even though this has backfired on the party on several occasions — for example, it led to former Riigikogu Speaker Eiki Nestor leaving politics.
Estonia's modified d'Hondt system means parties can position prominent names to maximize their share of compensation mandates – where candidates lower down on a list receive the excess votes from higher profile candidates who have already won a seat. With a higher profile candidate lower on a list, this cannot happen, however.
"The same procedure still applies in our party. The national list is discussed by the party's board, but this is the very last stage in the process of drawing up the electoral lists. This means we will get to that sometime around the beginning of January," Läänemets said.
Läänemets acknowledged that the Nestor case was not the party's greatest success, but said the system, established 15 years ago, has generally served the party by making candidates work harder and giving more people a chance of entering parliament.
Since Kaljurand is an MEP she did not take up the Riigikogu seat she won in any case; again, the next candidate on the list who has not won a seat in their own right gets that seat. In general this brings a situation where parties run high profile candidates with no intention of them taking up a Riigikogu seat if won, usually because they cannot – for instance if they hold a local government leadership position or, as in Kaljruand's case, a European Parliament seat.
SDE is to hold an electoral assembly in January, where its national list, district lists across all 12 districts, and platform will all be approved. Läänemets said experience shows minor and major changes alike are often needed at the last instant, hence the board's final decision on the national list coming relatively late – the election itself is March 7.
Vseviov was a long-serving Foreign Ministry secretary general and security expert who joined SDE earlier this month, meaning he will be stepping down from the secretary general post in November. He is also running as the party's prime ministerial candidate.

French court gives Irish man suspended sentence for antisemitic threat to Jewish couple
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:55:50 UTC
21:55:50 KST

A court in Avignon, in southern France, gave Patrick O’Brien, a 60-year-old Irish citizen, a six-month suspended prison sentence on Friday after convicting him of making antisemitically motivated death threats and of justifying crimes against humanity, a criminal offense in France. O’Brien had threatened to kill a Jewish couple from Australia during a confrontation at a supermarket.
The judges also ordered him to pay the woman and her husband €500 [$560] each, and rejected prosecutors’ request to ban him from France for three years. Jewish organizations that joined the case criticized the sentence, arguing that it was too lenient to serve as a deterrent.
The incident took place on August 11 at an Auchan superstore in Le Pontet, near Avignon. The Australian couple had struck up a friendly conversation with O’Brien, a Dublin native, about the French national soccer team jersey the husband was wearing. When the conversation turned to Ireland’s policy toward Israel, O’Brien became aggressive and made antisemitic remarks.
'It’s a shame Hitler didn’t finish the job'
“It’s a shame Hitler didn’t finish the job,” he told the couple, according to their testimony. When the woman took out her cellphone and began recording, O’Brien threatened to put a bullet in her head. The video went viral on social media, sparking outrage in France and beyond. The woman’s father is a Holocaust survivor, and members of her family were murdered at the Auschwitz death camp.
C.H.A.R., a French organization that fights hatred, antisemitism, and racism, joined the case as a civil party, a status under French law that allows victims and advocacy groups to take part in criminal proceedings and seek damages, and was represented by attorney Annie Cohen. The group welcomed the conviction but said it was deeply disappointed by the sentence.
“To publicly wish for the completion of the Holocaust, and then to threaten to murder a woman because she is Jewish, and to come away with a suspended sentence and a payment of just a few hundred euros: this is a message that minimizes the gravity of these acts, and we cannot accept it,” a spokesperson for the organization said after the sentencing.
The group also emphasized the victim’s family history. “The victim’s father survived the Holocaust; members of her family were murdered in Auschwitz. What was said to her was, in effect, an expression of regret that her family had not been wiped out entirely,” it said.
B’nai B’rith also joined the case as a civil party. The court ordered O’Brien to pay each of the two organizations €300 [$335].
After the video spread online, investigators from France’s gendarmerie, a national police force, identified O’Brien using the supermarket’s security cameras and tracked him down at his home in the Avignon area. He was arrested on August 26. Digital devices seized from his home contained additional racist content, according to prosecutors, including remarks targeting people from developing countries.
O’Brien admitted making the statements but claimed they came during a heated argument
Avignon prosecutor Stéphanie Huin said O’Brien admitted making the statements but claimed they came during a heated argument about Ireland’s policy toward Israel. She said he expressed remorse and explained that he had lost his temper. During the trial, he portrayed himself as someone opposed to violence, described himself as “a committed humanist,” and said he has health problems.
Despite convicting him on both counts, the court chose not to send him to prison.
The case drew condemnation as early as August, when French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez praised the investigators’ work, stressing that “antisemitism must be fought with determination and without respite.” Now, following the sentencing, Jewish organizations are warning that lenient sentences for explicit death threats and statements praising the Holocaust could send a dangerous message at a time of growing concern over antisemitism in France.

Tanker hit by explosives in Strait of Hormuz as Iran claims two vessels disabled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:55:46 UTC
21:55:46 KST

An oil tanker was struck by explosives attached to its hull in the Strait of Hormuz, setting its engine room ablaze and temporarily disabling the vessel, Reuters reported, as Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed Friday that two tankers attempting to cross the strategic waterway without Tehran's authorization had been forced to stop.
The latest incidents underscore the growing threat to commercial shipping in one of the world's most important oil transit routes, where Iran has intensified attacks on vessels in an apparent effort to frustrate a U.S.-led operation to reopen the strait without a negotiated agreement.
According to Reuters, citing shipping industry sources, a small boat approached the Panama-flagged tanker Louise 1 on Thursday and attached two limpet mines, explosive devices designed to adhere to the hull of a vessel. The mines detonated, igniting a fire in the ship's engine room and temporarily putting it out of operation.
No crew members were injured, the fire was extinguished and no environmental damage was reported. The tanker has since resumed its voyage.
The attack occurred approximately 46 kilometers (29 miles) northeast of Khasab, Oman, on the southern side of the Strait of Hormuz.
Reuters said it was not immediately clear who was responsible for the attack.
The incident marks the first reported successful use of such explosives in the strait since the outbreak of the war with Iran in late February, according to Reuters. A similar attempt to disable a vessel last month failed when the explosives did not detonate, two sources told the news agency.
The apparent ability of attackers aboard a small vessel to approach a moving tanker, attach explosives and escape has raised serious concerns about the vulnerability of commercial shipping in the narrow and heavily trafficked waterway.
Marisks, a Greece-based maritime risk management company, warned that the method could pose a particularly difficult challenge for shipping operators because of its simplicity and low cost.
"The apparent ability of a small craft to approach a transiting tanker, deploy explosive devices and withdraw presents a significant security concern, particularly in the Strait's congested shipping lanes," the company said.
Marisks noted that limpet mines are relatively inexpensive and readily available, describing their deployment against moving ships from small boats as a technologically simple but highly effective method of attack.
Iran claims two tankers stopped in Hormuz
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' navy said Friday that two oil tankers had been stopped off the strait's southern coast after attempting to cross without coordinating their movements with Iranian authorities.
In a statement, the Guard claimed the vessels had disabled their navigation and positioning systems and attempted to leave the strait through an unauthorized route with assistance from the U.S. military.
"After several unanswered radio warnings, the two tankers entered an unsafe area, became involved in incidents and were stopped off the southern coast of the Strait of Hormuz," the statement said.
The Guard did not identify the vessels or explain what it meant by the incidents that caused them to stop.
It was not immediately clear whether the Louise 1 was one of the two tankers mentioned in the Iranian statement. The Guard's account could not be independently verified.
The reported location of the vessels, near the southern shore of the strait, is notable because Iran's coastline lies along the northern side of the waterway, while Oman occupies much of its southern shore.
In recent weeks, Iranian authorities have repeatedly claimed that tankers crossing the strait were damaged after striking mines.
The incidents come amid reports that Tehran has stepped up deliberate attacks on commercial vessels in an effort to disrupt Washington's campaign to restore maritime traffic and the flow of oil to international markets.
The United States has sought to reopen the waterway without reaching an agreement with Iran while maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington has so far refrained from directly responding to the latest reported Iranian attacks, potentially to avoid an escalation that could drive fuel prices higher just days before Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections.
President Donald Trump has recently dismissed some Iranian claims of damage to vessels as "fake hits."
The continued disruption of shipping through the strait has become a central point of contention between Washington and Tehran, with both sides seeking to use maritime access as leverage in negotiations over ending the conflict.
Trump says Iran deal possible as Qatari mediators arrive
Despite the continued attacks, diplomatic efforts to prevent a renewed American military offensive against Iran appeared to be gaining momentum Friday.
Speaking to a local radio station in Kansas, Trump was asked about his ultimate objective in Iran and whether military action could resume after Tuesday's midterm elections.
"It will be over soon," Trump said, while suggesting that a negotiated settlement remained possible.
"They want to make a deal, they have to make a deal with a guarantee. We have to have a guarantee that they will never have a nuclear weapon," he said.
Earlier Friday, Reuters reported, citing a source familiar with the discussions, that Qatari mediators had arrived in Tehran in an effort to advance negotiations and prevent further escalation.
Qatar presented Iran with a draft agreement Sunday, according to an earlier Reuters report, but a senior Iranian official rejected the proposals Wednesday as "unacceptable" and said Tehran would maintain its position on the nuclear issue.
The central dispute concerns the sequence of concessions each side is prepared to make.
Washington wants Iran's nuclear program included in negotiations from the outset, while Tehran insists that the United States must first lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, remove sanctions on Iranian oil exports and meet additional conditions included in an Iranian proposal Trump rejected last month.
CBS News also reported Friday that a Qatari delegation had arrived in Tehran, citing a source familiar with the negotiations who said the mediators were carrying revisions to the proposed agreement to end the war.
The source said there were signs of progress and that an Iranian response was expected by the end of the week.
"The goal of the proposal is to prevent a return to U.S. military action against Iran, which Trump has repeatedly threatened to resume in recent weeks," CBS reported.
Meanwhile, The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance recently sent a letter to senior Iranian official Mohsen Rezaei offering to meet him personally to advance the negotiations.
Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, is a close associate of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and is widely regarded as a hard-liner.
Despite his hawkish positions, the Trump administration reportedly views Rezaei as its "best hope for peace."
The diplomatic contacts come as Washington weighs whether to resume military operations against Iran, with a decision widely expected to come only after the U.S. midterm elections.
Air defenses deployed around Trump's Florida estate
Amid the heightened tensions with Iran, U.S. media reported that security around Trump's private Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, has been significantly reinforced at the direction of the Secret Service.
Photographs circulated in American media show two Avenger air defense systems equipped with Stinger missiles positioned on a floating platform in a lake adjoining the presidential estate.
The systems were first spotted near Mar-a-Lago on Oct. 23, shortly before Trump arrived at the property that day, according to the reports.
The Palm Beach Daily News reported that an additional Avenger system had been deployed in the southern section of Palm Beach's international airport, which was renamed after Trump earlier this year.
That system was reportedly positioned near the area where Air Force One typically parks during presidential visits.
In a statement to the local newspaper, the Secret Service said it continued to operate in an elevated threat environment.
"The U.S. Secret Service continues to operate in a heightened threat environment, and the agency continually adapts its protective operations to incorporate the most advanced tools, technologies and methods to protect those in its care," the agency said.
The Avenger system, manufactured by Boeing, consists of a modified Humvee equipped with a rotating turret carrying two missile launchers, each holding four Stinger missiles.
The short-range surface-to-air missiles use infrared guidance to track the heat signatures of their targets. The system also carries a heavy machine gun.
According to the U.S. military, the Avenger is designed to counter aerial threats including cruise missiles, drones, helicopters and low-flying aircraft.
Neither the Secret Service nor the U.S. military has publicly explained why the additional defenses were deployed.
Local media noted that placing such conspicuous air defense systems in a civilian area, where they are clearly visible to people passing the estate, is highly unusual.
Retired Lt. Col. Octavio Perez, a security intelligence expert, told NBC's Miami affiliate that the deployment could reflect concerns about a drone attack on the property or even an attempt to strike it using a larger aircraft, such as a helicopter or small plane.
Perez also pointed to the upcoming Group of 20 summit, scheduled to take place at Trump's golf resort in Miami in December, as a possible factor behind the heightened security.
He suggested that the deployment could also be connected to threats from Iran, whose leadership has previously threatened to assassinate Trump or members of his family.
With Washington considering renewed military operations against Tehran, Perez warned that an escalation could create incentives for an attack on the president's Florida residence.
If the war resumes, "a sleeper cell or a lone actor in the United States could try to do something at Mar-a-Lago," Perez said. "That's essentially what's behind this preparation."
The deployment highlights the broader security concerns accompanying the standoff with Iran, even as negotiators attempt to reach an agreement that would end the war, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and avert another round of military confrontation.
