Israel cannot afford another election - its leaders must compromise for unity - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:55:39 UTC
21:55:39 KST

Here is the question Israel’s political leaders need to ask themselves in the aftermath of Tuesday’s election: Do we really want to go through this all over again?
It is a simple question, but one with enormous implications for the country’s future. And if the answer is no, as it should be, then the parties elected to the Knesset this week need to start thinking differently about what comes next.
There is no question that Israelis who voted for Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan did not want Tuesday’s result. They voted with the overriding objective of removing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from office. That was the purpose of their vote and the promise they made to their supporters.
For months, it seemed like it might actually happen. The opposition had momentum, and unlike previous elections, no votes were going to be wasted on parties failing to cross the threshold.
Tens of thousands of Israelis flew in from abroad to cast their ballots, and while the polls did not show a clear 61-seat majority, they suggested that the opposition would emerge with the larger bloc, potentially allowing Eisenkot to establish a minority government and begin advancing at least part of his agenda.
But that is not what happened.
Instead, Netanyahu emerged as the political winner. Likud is the largest party with approximately 27 seats, while his bloc has about 53, more than the 48 won by the Eisenkot bloc. That is a remarkable achievement considering that almost all polls predicted the exact opposite.
It is true that the opposition, together with the Arab parties, is projected to hold approximately 67 seats, meaning that a majority of the next Knesset will be represented by parties opposed to Netanyahu, but that is not how governments are formed in Israel.
What matters is who can assemble 61 seats and turn them into a functioning coalition. Neither side can do that right now, but Netanyahu appears to be in the stronger position, and his success can be explained by two factors.
The first is that Israeli politics remains deeply tribal. Despite the massacre on October 7, 2023, the failures of his government, and the momentum against him, Netanyahu’s traditional voters largely remained loyal. They might have reservations about his policies and even his leadership, but when they enter the voting booth, they come home.
The second is that Netanyahu ran an extremely effective closing campaign. He focused on two fears: Iran and massive Arab turnout. To his critics, it looked like desperation. But Netanyahu understood something about the Israeli electorate. These messages tapped into deep, visceral fears about the country’s security and future.
For many Israelis, he remains the known commodity, the leader they instinctively turn to when danger looms. Whatever they think of his record, the alternative was perceived as an even greater gamble.
That is the political reality. And whether we like it or not, it is the reality from which the next government needs to emerge.
Which brings us back to the question of what happens now. I would argue that if we accept two basic premises, there is only one responsible path forward.
The first is that Eisenkot does not have a realistic path to forming a government. Some on the Left have suggested that he take the roughly 48 seats of the Zionist opposition parties and establish a government with the support of the Arab parties.
That is almost impossible to imagine happening. It would have been one thing had Eisenkot emerged with a bloc in the mid-50s and needed just a handful of votes from Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am party. But relying on both Ra’am and the Joint List is something entirely different.
Bennett and Liberman would almost certainly reject such an arrangement, even if Eisenkot was willing to consider it, which itself is unlikely.
Looking back at multiple elections
That leaves us with the second premise: Israel cannot afford another election.
Consider what this country is confronting. Iran remains a threat, with another military confrontation possible as early as next week. In Gaza, Hamas has yet to disarm; in Lebanon, Hezbollah is rebuilding its military capabilities while terrorism in the West Bank is increasing. The unresolved issue of the haredi draft continues to tear Israel apart.
The cost of living remains high, the deficit is growing, and Israel faces an increasingly isolated situation on the international stage than ever before. And hovering over all of this is a society that remains deeply divided, still struggling to recover from the trauma of October 7 and the wars that followed.
Does anyone seriously believe another election would help solve any of these problems?
On the contrary: it would paralyze the political system for months, postpone critical decisions, and deepen divisions that Israel desperately needs to begin healing.
We know this because we saw this exact process happen before.
When Israelis look back at the years leading up to October 7, they tend to focus on 2023 and the government’s judicial reform, which tore the country apart. But we often forget what preceded it: five elections in less than three-and-a-half years. Judicial reform did not create all those divisions. It poured fuel on a fire that had already been burning for years.
And as October 7 demonstrated, the erosion of social cohesion is not just a political problem. It is directly tied to national security. Israel’s enemies watch what happens inside this country; they study our divisions and look for opportunities to exploit them.
Why would we willingly send ourselves back into that destructive cycle?
Now consider something else. What, exactly, are the ideological differences between Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Bennett, and Liberman that make it impossible for them to sit together in a government?
Their four parties would have about 68 seats. That is more than enough to form a stable coalition, one that would not be held hostage by the demands of small sectoral parties or the extremes of either side of the political spectrum.
Do they fundamentally disagree about Iran? Is it as if one believes the Islamic Republic should be allowed to obtain nuclear weapons while the others oppose it? Do they have radically different approaches to Gaza? Is any one of them advocating that Israel simply withdraw and allow Hamas to rebuild its military capabilities?
What about the Palestinians, the traditional divide between Israel’s Right and Left? Also, no real difference here. Netanyahu opposes Palestinian statehood; Bennett advocates annexing Area C, which comprises about 60% of the West Bank; and Liberman has proposed having Jordan take over while Eisenkot has called a two-state solution delusional.
On the economy, none are socialists. All broadly support the free market, private enterprise, and economic growth.
And what about the haredi draft?
Here, Netanyahu’s record is certainly different. For years, he has accommodated the demands of his ultra-Orthodox coalition partners, but that was when his political survival depended on the haredim.
Put him in a different coalition, one that does not depend on Shas and United Torah Judaism, and the political equation changes.
None of this means these four leaders agree on everything. They do not. There are real differences over governance, the judiciary, the handling of October 7, and, most importantly, accountability for what went wrong. But those differences are not necessarily insurmountable. Certainly not when compared with the challenges Israel faces.
So what is really preventing such a government from being formed?
The answer is not ideology but rather personalities and a profound lack of trust between them.
That distrust is not imaginary, and Netanyahu has earned much of it. His political history is filled with broken commitments and efforts to undermine partners when doing so served his interests. Bennett, Eisenkot and Liberman have legitimate reasons to doubt that an agreement signed today would be honored tomorrow. And their voters did not send them to the Knesset to rescue Netanyahu. They voted for change, accountability and a different direction.
These concerns cannot simply be brushed aside in the name of national unity. But neither can they become an excuse for condemning Israel to another election.
If the obstacle is trust, then the challenge is to create mechanisms to try to verify it, since if they can do that, such a government could tackle the real challenges Israel faces. It would be difficult. Perhaps extraordinarily difficult. But is it really more difficult than sending the country to another election, with all the damage that would entail?
Imagine what a government representing such a broad cross-section of Israeli society could accomplish. A government that could make decisions on Iran and Gaza without constantly calculating their impact on coalition survival. That could finally confront the ultra-Orthodox draft crisis, begin repairing Israel’s standing internationally, and tackle the economic challenges that have been neglected for far too long.
Most importantly, imagine what it would mean for Israeli society to see political leaders who have spent years attacking one another decide that the country matters more than their personal rivalries.
I am not naive about the obstacles. Netanyahu would need to demonstrate that he can be trusted. Eisenkot, Bennett, and Liberman would need to explain to their voters why joining him does not mean abandoning the principles for which they were elected. All four would have to give up something they desperately want.
But that is what leadership is supposed to be about: recognizing when the circumstances have changed and finding the courage to adapt.
Israel has been through too much over the last four years. Too many lives have been lost, too many families have suffered, and too many opportunities have been missed. Another election would be the easy way out since everyone could stand by their promises, blame the other side, and return to the campaign.
The harder path would be to compromise, try to create trust, and form a government capable of governing.
After everything this country has been through, perhaps it is time for our leaders to try it.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.

Middle Israel: Netanyahu and Eisenkot both lost, but Israel may have emerged the winner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:55:27 UTC
21:55:27 KST

The people have spoken.
The electoral fog is still thick at this writing, but several facts – personal, moral, and social – have already emerged, and they are as clear as they are harsh. The personal truth is that Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu both lost.
Eisenkot, as argued here last week, displayed no vision, articulated no idea, and presented no plan other than to replace a failed government. That’s not how you win an election.
That Eisenkot is not charismatic is perfectly fine, and after the Netanyahu era this flaw is even welcome. But it’s no excuse for failing to say anything about our overcrowded hospitals, substandard schools, rampant crime, municipal corruption, and traffic congestion, to mention but a few of the crises that frustrate millions of citizens every day.
That is how the opposition blew it, despite having had all the reason in the world to win by a landslide. Having said this, Eisenkot’s failure pales compared with Netanyahu’s.
The man who thought he would turn this country into a one-man show has been dealt an emphatic vote of no confidence.
Though the final count is yet to be known, there is no ambiguity about where Netanyahu has led his flock: Likud has lost some 15% of its voters, and the ruling coalition has shrunk by one-fifth. Moreover, among the Zionist electorate, namely, voters who do military or national service, Netanyahu was defeated 55:45.
The working assumption among Likud’s voters that Netanyahu is their biggest asset has proven unfounded. He was their liability, and will remain such as long as they don’t replace him. Otherwise, the swing vote that Netanyahu ignored, provoked, and lost will grow even larger.
And the reason the swing vote abandoned the ruling party and its leader is their moral record. It began with the judicial coup Netanyahu tried to launch back in January 2023.
Netanyahu’s plan, to have the government select the Supreme Court justices, limit the judiciary’s oversight of government decisions, restrict the grounds for Supreme Court rulings, and dilute the powers of the attorney-general and the rest of the government’s legal advisers – has now been buried for good.
Having ignored the need to pass such constitutional reforms through a broad consensus, Netanyahu tore Israeli society apart, only to see multitudes take to the streets and force him to stage a retreat.
Still, Netanyahu and his party hoped to return to this plan, had they won. But they did not win. The swing vote, it turned out, did not like the sight of a prime minister besmirching our judges and laying siege to their courts.
Yes, the 30% that constitute die-hard Likudniks and far-right zealots fully backed his urge to conquer the judiciary.
The swing vote, however, did not share this hope, and was particularly appalled by the Likud’s barbarian assault on the Supreme Court and its president.
Even worse, both morally and electorally, was Netanyahu’s flight from responsibility.
The trauma of October 7 predominated millions of citizens’ thoughts as they made their electoral choices. Recalling what they endured, voters were disgusted when they saw their prime minister shirk responsibility for the catastrophe, and personally block the establishment of a state commission of inquiry.
And hovering above these moral failures was Netanyahu’s alliance with ultra-Orthodoxy. Too many Israelis arrived at the polls fed up with the deal that exempted thousands from military service, while they and their children spent hundreds of days risking their lives for this embattled country’s defense.
Like the judicial reform, the ludicrous plan to make ultra-Orthodox draft exemption a constitutional right is now dead. This audacious scheme is probably what chased the swing vote away from the Likud more than anything else.
Lastly, swing voters were displeased with the Netanyahu government’s inept treatment of the war’s displaced population, collapsed businesses, and damaged homes, and with its failure to uproot Jewish terrorism and lawlessness in the West Bank.
These, in brief, are the issues that shaped this election’s results. At the same time, this election exposed a new, far-reaching social transition.
What's changed?
The incoming Knesset will be recalled for the unprecedented size of its Arab factions. At this writing, they appear to have won 16 seats, as opposed to the 10 they had in the outgoing Knesset. That’s an astonishing feat, and it, too, is a result of Netanyahu’s incompetence.
Arab voters flocked to the polls for two reasons: rampant crime in their streets, and unconcealed hostility from Netanyahu’s National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir. In this narrow electoral sense, Netanyahu has only himself to blame for this development.
Yet this massive vote bears deeper implications, one ominous, the other actually optimistic. The ominous meaning is that the crime crisis in Arab towns has become unbearable. If not treated by the next government systematically and forcefully, it might boil over.
The happy part of this is that Arab Israel finally went to the polls. In doing so, many of them have now, for the first time, joined Israel’s political process. Arab Israel has thus arrived in 2026, where ultra-Orthodox Israel arrived back in 1977, when it first joined an Israeli government as a key partner.
And then there is the flip side of Arab Israelis’ political zenith: ultra-Orthodoxy’s political decline.
Ultra-Orthodoxy emerges from this election disempowered. Its brazen effort to make its boys’ draft dodging a constitutional right has backfired. The law will never pass, and the attempt may soon cause the emergence of a broad coalition of Zionist parties in which ultra-Orthodoxy will lose its disproportionate leverage.
It follows that 2026 may be recalled as the year in which Arab Israeli politics matured, while ultra-Orthodox politics came of age, returning to its pre-1977 position, in the political margins. Seen this way, Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot may have both lost, but the State of Israel won.
The writer, a Hartman Institute fellow, is the author of the bestseller, The Jewish March of Folly (Yedioth Books 2026), now available in English on Amazon.

US oil giants report profit surge again on Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:54:43 UTC
21:54:43 KST

Breadcrumb
US oil giants report profit surge again on Iran war
US oil giants reported Friday another quarter of soaring profits reflecting higher oil prices and refining margins due to the US-Israeli war on Iran.
ExxonMobil's profits in the period came in at $15.4 billion, slightly more than double the $7.5 billion in the year-ago period, while Chevron's profits were $9.9 billion, compared with $3.5 billion in the year-ago quarter.
The surge in US petroleum earnings comes on the heels of similar increases at European companies as the US-Israeli war on Iran drags on. The impacts have been most dramatic in refining, where the profit margins for processing crude oil into gasoline, diesel and other petroleum products have exploded in recent months.
Steep price increases and supply shortfalls in some cases have sparked protests in parts of Asia, Latin America and Europe. In the United States, President Donald Trump's Republican party faces a stern test in next week's midterm elections, with high gasoline and diesel prices souring the mood of consumers.
At ExxonMobil, oil prices averaged around $85 per barrel during the period, about a third more than in the 2025 quarter.
Refining margins were $50.3 per barrel, almost three times the level in the year-ago period as the company cited efforts to boost output of diesel and other key products that have seen supplies tighten.
"Refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East remained curtailed, with roughly 10 percent of global capacity offline," the company said in prepared remarks ahead of a conference call.
"North American refineries sustained high operating rates during the quarter but were unable to fully offset reduced global refining capacity availability," according to the remarks.
The efforts to boost output translated into 100 percent crude unit utilization at US Gulf Coast refineries, ExxonMobil said in its press release.
Chevron scored higher profits in its upstream business, but also won its greatest increases in the downstream area, where profits of $4.9 billion were more than four times the level in the year-ago period.
The NGO 350.org, which advocates for clean energy and other measures to address climate change, called for "permanent levies" on "exceptional" oil industry profits, with the funds going to consumers and to finance the energy transition.
"As we head into the midterms, energy affordability is on everyone's minds," said Candice Forten, US campaigns manager for 350.0rg.
"Families and small businesses want reliable electricity they can afford, and communities want a say in how their land, water and energy resources are used," Forten said. "Yet as people struggle with energy bills and the impacts of extreme weather, the biggest oil companies are forecast to make billions."
Forten called for policies to ensure that data centers for artificial intelligence do not drive up electricity bills and that oil companies "pay their fair share towards the costs of the crisis, rather than leaving the public to pick up the bill."
Shares of ExxonMobil rose 2.0 percent in pre-market trading, while Chevron climbed 1.7 percent.

Royal Navy film remembers submarines that never returned
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:54:26 GMT
21:54:26 KST

The Royal Navy has released a remembrance film marking 125 years of the Submarine Service, made in memory of the nearly 6,000 submariners and more than 150 submarines that never came home.
The film, called The Echo, follows a Cold War era submarine beneath the waves alongside a submarine veteran volunteering at his local museum, and was shot aboard HMS Alliance at the Royal Navy Submarine Museum in Gosport.
The Royal Navy has released a remembrance film marking 125 years of the Submarine Service, made in memory of the nearly 6,000 submariners and more than 150 submarines that never came home pic.twitter.com/Px0fGbrhe0
— UK Defence Journal (@UKDefJournal) October 30, 2026
Rear Admiral Andrew Perks, Director Submarines and head of the Submarine Service, said: “This year being the 125th anniversary of the Royal Navy’s Submarine Service makes it an even more poignant Remembrance for us. As we stand at the Westminster Garden of Remembrance and name aloud every submarine that did not return, we remember those we have lost in the last 125 years.
“This film, for me, encapsulates the experience of being a submariner. Whilst it’s set in the Cold War and is significantly different from the cutting-edge technology, we use today it still captures the jeopardy of being under the waves perfectly.”
Petty Officer James Clark, head of the Royal Navy’s video production branch, said: “We wanted to capture people’s imaginations and leave them with questions unanswered. We wanted audiences to think about what they’d seen and wonder what really happened.
“The film’s ambiguous ending reflects the reality that, for many submarines lost at sea, the circumstances of their disappearance remain a mystery.”
The ambiguity points at a particular boat, because Alliance’s sister HMS Affray sailed from Portsmouth in April 1951 and was lost in the English Channel with seventy five men aboard, the last British submarine lost at sea, and although the wreck was found two months later the cause was never established beyond doubt. Among the theories was a fractured snort mast, the induction pipe that lets a diesel submarine run its engines while submerged.
Alliance herself is an A-class boat ordered for the war in the Pacific and completed after it ended, serving through the early Cold War before becoming a memorial to submariners lost in service. She has been on display at Gosport since 1981 and was restored at a cost of several million pounds in the last decade.
The Submarine Service dates its existence from the launch of Holland 1 in October 1901, a five-man boat bought against the opposition of admirals who regarded the submarine as underhand, and the service spent its first decades proving otherwise. Its losses include the 1950s accidents that followed the war, the men of HMS Thetis who died in Liverpool Bay before commissioning in 1939, and the seventy four boats lost in the Second World War.
Britain has maintained continuous at sea deterrence for fifty seven years, and the Dreadnought class now being built at Barrow will take that task on from the Vanguard boats in the early 2030s.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea on Friday, as he wrapped up his Asia tour amid heightened tensions between the two countries.
"We Germans know how painful the division of a country is," he said, adding that those who "stand firmly" by their values and have the "courage" to engage in dialogue can tear down walls.

Kiev ‘ignoring’ Trump – Kremlin
Ukraine, emboldened by continued European support, is ignoring US President Donald Trump’s calls to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
Three Russian oil refineries and a gas chemical complex were targeted in overnight attacks on Friday, according to Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak.
Commenting on the latest attacks, Ushakov told journalist Pavel Zarubin that Kiev had once again defied Trump. “I would even say they are simply ignoring him,” he added.
According to Novak, one of the targeted facilities sustained minor damage, but Russian air defenses largely repelled the attacks. Samara Region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Friday that two people involved in dealing with the aftermath of the drone strikes had been killed, while several others were injured.
Trump has repeatedly demanded that Kiev stop targeting Russian oil refineries, accusing it of worsening the global fuel crisis and driving up prices for American consumers and farmers – a sensitive issue ahead of the November 3 US midterms. Vladimir Zelensky rejected the criticism, calling Trump’s claims “totally false.”
Ushakov suggested that Kiev was emboldened by continued European support. “They would hardly have dared to do this on their own,” he said.
“Trump has been persistent on this issue and continues to be, but they are not listening,” Ushakov said. The aide noted that trilateral talks are being planned under US mediation, which he described as crucial to resolving the conflict.
Moscow agreed in principle to a fourth round of trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine following last week’s meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. The negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi in November, with European countries not invited, according to the Kremlin.
Ukraine’s European backers have been excluded from all three rounds of trilateral negotiations so far and have increasingly sought direct participation in the peace process. Moscow has accused the EU of acting as the principal side arming Ukraine and prolonging the conflict.
Novak said on Friday that the Russian government was preparing to extend its diesel export ban until the end of January 2027, while maintaining exemptions for certain shipments to international markets.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel have been dispatched to the US under an agreement reached between Putin and Trump following their October 9 phone call. Washington temporarily waived sanctions on Russian fuel imports to facilitate the deliveries.

Bayer wins Roundup weedkiller cancer trial while awaiting settlement ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:52:00 UTC
21:52:00 KST

Bayer wins Roundup weedkiller cancer trial while awaiting settlement ruling
- Bayer won a St Louis trial over three women’s claims that Roundup caused their cancer. The jury ruled for Monsanto after the US Supreme Court limited legal claims.
- The verdict matters because Bayer still faces about 65,000 Roundup cases and a proposed US$7.25 billion settlement is waiting for a Missouri judge’s decision.
- Bayer says glyphosate is safe and the EPA sees no need for a cancer warning. Plaintiffs argue Roundup was dangerous, while the EPA is again reviewing its safety.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Bayer won a trial on Oct 29 over claims by three women that its Roundup weedkiller caused their cancer, while awaiting a broader ruling from a separate court on the company’s US$7.25 billion (S$9 billion) effort to settle other Roundup cases.
The trial was a test for the continued viability of Roundup lawsuits after a US Supreme Court ruling in Bayer’s favour limited the legal claims that plaintiffs can bring.
Bayer is also separately seeking to resolve tens of thousands of other Roundup lawsuits through a proposed US$7.25 billion settlement, which is under review by a Missouri state court judge in St Louis.
A St Louis jury unanimously ruled for Bayer-owned Monsanto in the first case to go to trial after June’s Supreme Court ruling. The litigation has weighed on Bayer since its 2018 acquisition of Monsanto, costing the company billions of dollars and driving down its share price.
Bayer shares rose 4% to a one-month high at 1011 GMT.
Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Frankfurt-based Union Investment, said the verdict was one of the most important trial wins for the company.
“Plaintiffs have failed in their new litigation strategy to prove that Bayer had ignored the risks as early as the development stage of glyphosate,” he said.
Bill Dodero, Bayer’s US general counsel and global head of litigation, said the verdict showed how difficult it would be for other plaintiffs to win cases after the Supreme Court ruling.
“This verdict should send a strong signal that plaintiffs who wish to pursue claims in the court system following the Durnell ruling will face significant challenges both in demonstrating they have viable claims and putting forth the necessary evidence to prove them in court,” he said in a statement.
Plaintiffs sued in 2020
Plaintiffs Theresa Aretino, Cynthia Fernandez and Betty Larkin sued Bayer unit Monsanto in 2020 in St Louis, saying they used Roundup regularly and later developed non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Their attorneys argued that Roundup was defectively designed and unreasonably dangerous, and that Bayer was negligent in selling it.
The three women are not participating in Bayer’s proposed settlement. Fernandez died before the trial began.
Reuters viewed the trial and verdict on Courtroom View Network. Attorneys for Aretino, Fernandez and Larkin did not immediately respond to a request for comment late on Oct 29.
Bayer has denied the claims and said that decades of studies have shown glyphosate, Roundup’s active ingredient, is safe and does not cause cancer.
Bayer faces around 65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from plaintiffs who say they developed cancer after using Roundup at home or on the job.
Before the Supreme Court ruling in 2026, most lawsuits had alleged that Roundup’s label failed to warn consumers about cancer risks. But the court blocked those legal arguments in June, ruling that federal law requires herbicide makers to use the exact label approved by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
The EPA has concluded that Roundup’s label does not require a cancer warning.
Bayer has argued that other legal claims, including design-defect and negligence, are also foreclosed by the US Supreme Court’s ruling, but plaintiffs’ attorneys have argued that those claims are not affected by the ruling.
The EPA has previously concluded that glyphosate is probably not carcinogenic, but it is in the middle of a new review of its safety.
In 2015, the International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded that glyphosate was “probably carcinogenic” to humans, but Bayer has said that is an outlier opinion based on flawed methodology. REUTERS

Qais Abu Samra, Lina Altawell
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
A Palestinian was injured and two others were arrested Friday in attacks by the Israeli army and Israeli occupiers targeting olive pickers across the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian sources.
In the northern West Bank, a 36-year-old Palestinian suffered bruises and other injuries after Israeli occupiers beat him in the town of Burqa, northwest of Nablus.
The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said its teams treated the man after he fell from a height during the attack.
In Beit Dajan, east of Nablus, Israeli occupiers attacked farmers harvesting olives in the northern part of the town, prevented them from continuing their work and forced them to leave their fields, local sources told Anadolu.
In Al-Lubban Al-Sharqiya, south of Nablus, Israeli soldiers chased olive pickers in the southern and eastern parts of the village and fired sound grenades toward them.
More than 30 Palestinians were forced to leave agricultural land located just dozens of meters from village homes, according to local sources.
In the Al-Masoudiya area northwest of Nablus, Israeli occupiers broke into a house, damaged its door and belongings and cut power lines.
In Jenin governorate, Israeli occupiers entered the eastern part of Jaba early Friday and stole equipment from a vehicle repair workshop.
They also damaged three vehicles by smashing their windows and slashing their tires, and stole a car radio, other equipment and two sheep from outside Palestinian homes.
Jaba Mayor Mohammad Al-Baddad told the official Palestinian news agency Wafa that the occupiers entered the area in a vehicle and carried out the thefts and vandalism.
In the central West Bank, Israeli occupiers attacked olive pickers and a foreign solidarity activist in Kafr Malik, northeast of Ramallah, according to local sources.
The activist was assaulted while accompanying Palestinian farmers, while Israeli forces arrested two Palestinians harvesting olives east of the town.
In Al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, Israeli occupiers attacked olive pickers near the Jabr family's homes and opened fire toward Palestinian houses, according to local sources.
On Oct. 22, the Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said it had documented 409 attacks on olive farmers, trees, land and agricultural equipment across the occupied West Bank between Oct. 1 and 21.
Of those, 317 were carried out by Israeli occupiers and 92 by the Israeli army, according to the commission.
The attacks included preventing farmers from reaching their fields, forcing them to leave their land, stealing crops and damaging trees and agricultural equipment.
Israeli army raids and attacks by Israeli occupiers have intensified across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since October 2023, with reports of killings, arrests, home demolitions, arson attacks, the bulldozing of land and the displacement of Palestinian communities.

A former regional lawmaker and head of the Murmansk chapter of Russia’s Communist Party is facing treason charges following his arrest earlier this month, Russian media reported Thursday, citing the FSB security service.
Law enforcement officials arrested 76-year-old Gennady Stepakhno on Oct. 9, after which a judge ruled that he be placed in pre-trial detention for two months. The exact charges against him were not immediately made public.
Stepakhno had served as a lawmaker in the Murmansk region’s legislative assembly since 2007 before losing his seat in elections last month. He also headed the Communist Party’s regional chapter between 2004 and 2021.
In an FSB statement carried by the Interfax news agency, Stepakhno was accused of using his position in office to share sensitive government documents and details about “engineering facilities” with Ukrainian intelligence agencies.
Under Russian law, treason carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment for men. It was not immediately clear whether Stepakhno pleaded guilty.
Local media outlets in Murmansk, citing anonymous sources close to the former lawmaker, reported that law enforcement officials may be investigating Stepakhno based on a phone call he made about the construction of an Indian pharmaceutical plant in Murmansk. According to those reports, he discussed sensitive information about the project with a relative who lives abroad.
In a separate report, the exiled news outlet The Insider suggested that Stepakhno’s criminal prosecution may be connected to his alleged long-running feud with fellow Communist Party member Oleg Ryabtsev over questions of party finances.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify either report.
Stepakhno is the latest Communist Party member to face criminal prosecution following State Duma and regional elections late last month, during which the ruling United Russia party gained a supermajority in the lower house of Russian parliament.

Unrest in France is nightmare fuel for Macron’s heirs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:48:37 UTC
21:48:37 KST

PARIS — France’s center-right presidential candidates are bracing for more doom and gloom ahead of another tense day of protests Saturday, as polls suggest the combined effect of massive marches and the connected violence is fueling their rivals on both ends of the political spectrum.
Five polls, including one commissioned by POLITICO, conducted in the aftermath of the unrest in France on Oct. 17 — when hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets while violence and looting broke out across the country — have all shown the same thing: The potential successors from President Emmanuel Macron’s coalition would be eliminated in the first round.
Both Marine Le Pen on the far right and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the far left have been able to capitalize on the movement: the former “by presenting herself as a candidate who guarantees law and order,” and the latter acting as a “hero and herald of protest,” said Gaël Sliman, the head of French polling firm Odoxa.
Advertisement
They are facing a divided field of mainstream candidates on the center and center-right, including two former prime ministers under Macron in Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, and Bruno Retailleau, a former interior minister. These candidates have struggled to settle on a common message in response to the crisis — let alone agree on who the best candidate would be to avoid their nightmare scenario of a runoff between Mélenchon and Le Pen.
‘Out of ideas’
Three officials supporting centrist and conservative candidates told POLITICO that they were concerned the events of the past few weeks would cause lasting damage to their campaigns.
“It’s definitely going to kill us,” said one campaign official who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “We cannot be the solution anymore, only the problem.”
A Philippe supporter went as far as suggesting his champion was ill-equipped for the moment. “It’s exactly what he doesn’t need,” the supporter said last week, drawing parallels between the protests and the 2018–2019 Yellow Vest movement under Philippe’s premiership. “He doesn’t know how to do this. He’s not empathetic, and he’s not pretending to be.”
“Honestly, I don’t know how we’re going to get through this. Things are tough, and we’re out of ideas,” a centrist MP said.
The protests have taken place two Saturdays in a row and are expected to continue in the weeks to come. High school students are demanding better learning conditions while the wider public are protesting the cost-of-living crisis. The movement has been marred by scenes of vandalism and looting, especially on Oct. 17, when Macron’s government appeared to have underestimated both the scale of the protests and the potential for violent unrest.
Advertisement
In the following days, the government and center-right candidates focused on attacking Mélenchon and his party, France Unbowed, for fanning the flames that led to dramatic scenes of violence and looting. The strategy may have further dented his image among voters who already oppose him, polls suggest. But it did little to weaken his particularly young voter base.
“There is a kind of synergy between the social movement and France Unbowed,” a party strategist said. “This leads participants to see Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s impending victory as a logical conclusion.”
Le Pen, meanwhile, pushed her “protective vision” while her deputy Jordan Bardella said a far-right victory was “the only solution to allow the return of order and return of authority.”
As things stand, Le Pen is leading the race by a double-digit margin, while Mélenchon appears best placed to take second place and qualify for a runoff.
‘Muddled and hazardous’
Centrists and conservatives have been hindered by their persisting inability to agree on a single candidacy to take Macron’s mantle.
Attal, the candidate for Macron’s Renaissance party, made a surprise pitch for a “large primary of democrats” Wednesday, in a bid to narrow down the field of candidates against the far left and the far right.
Advertisement
Such a primary could see him face Philippe and Retailleau as well as David Lisnard, the mayor of Cannes running as an outsider on a conservative, small-state platform.
But Attal’s proposal was swiftly dismissed by rival campaigns. Laurent Marcangeli, who leads Philippe’s Horizons party in the National Assembly, called it “muddled and hazardous” Wednesday evening. “Without Philippe, there’s no primary,” a Retailleau backer said.
Despite these rebuffs, Attal on Thursday kept pushing for a contest to avoid the “cataclysm” of a Le Pen-Mélenchon runoff. “Our country wouldn’t recover from this,” he told public broadcaster France 5.

People of 27 nationalities may be among those killed or injured in Spain train crash, Sánchez says – Europe live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:47:48 UTC
21:47:48 KST

Spain’s trust in high-speed rail ‘broken’ after second deadly crash this year, says PM
Sam Jones
in Madrid
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’s deadly train collision that killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network.
Sánchez said the Spanish state was “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims – who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding that his government was committed to finding what had caused Spain’s second deadly train collision this year.
Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.
The crash came nine months after 46 people were killed and dozens injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
“It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain – which has such a powerful high-speed rail system – to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,” the prime minister said on Friday.
“Therefore, our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system.
Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.”
Shortly after Sánchez spoke, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente – who is under growing pressure to resign – gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down, promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust.
“My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can. If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.”
Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif. He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but stressed that such incidents were not at all uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers ultimately reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors.

Bulgaria’s next president will be elected in a runoff vote on Sunday, after a close race between the two main contenders ended inconclusively in the first round.
The incumbent Iliana Yotova, former vice-president to Bulgaria’s former president and current prime minister Rumen Radev, faces pro-European opposition candidate, Andrey Gyurov.
The two candidates will pit contrasting political visions against each other in a highly polarised contest on Sunday, AP noted.

Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta to close, citing pressure from ‘special services’
The Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it is closing, citing pressure from authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor and earlier this year detained one of its journalists.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” the editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, said in a video statement published on YouTube on Friday. “The Russian authorities – the Russian special services – have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
Russia has introduced near-Soviet levels of censorship since sending troops to Ukraine, pushing the vast majority of independent journalists into exile. Novaya Gazeta, a bastion of independent journalism in Russia, is classed by Moscow as a “foreign agent”, a label used to stifle dissent.
Sokolov said: “Novaya Gazeta has been killed … On 9 November we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”
This month Sokolov was taken in for questioning and Russian authorities searched his home over a criminal case involving one of his colleagues, Oleg Roldugin, who was arrested in April.
Russia has intensified its crackdown on independent news outlets since its offensive on Ukraine in February 2022. Novaya Gazeta cut down production inside Russia after the offensive began. Authorities revoked its media licence the same year.
The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel peace prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.

Spain’s trust in high-speed rail ‘broken’ after second deadly crash this year, says PM
Sam Jones
in Madrid
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’s deadly train collision that killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network.
Sánchez said the Spanish state was “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims – who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding that his government was committed to finding what had caused Spain’s second deadly train collision this year.
Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.
The crash came nine months after 46 people were killed and dozens injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
“It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain – which has such a powerful high-speed rail system – to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,” the prime minister said on Friday.
“Therefore, our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system.
Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.”
Shortly after Sánchez spoke, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente – who is under growing pressure to resign – gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down, promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust.
“My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can. If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.”
Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif. He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but stressed that such incidents were not at all uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers ultimately reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors.
Another effect of the crash may be to change the way that Spanish railway authorities handle upgrades and engineering works in the future.
In his press conference, transport minister Óscar Puente noted that he was considering closing the Madrid-Barcelona line while it is upgraded. In Spain the usual practice has been to remodel and upgrade lines while they still have traffic moving on them, unlike in other nations where the approach is typically to completely close lines for engineering.
He said:
It is currently one of the things we are evaluating, not only for safety reasons, but for multiple reasons. I don’t know if, under these circumstances, the most prudent course of action is to suspend service and significantly shorten the construction time. It’s something we have to consider.
Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor who now leads the leftwing Frente Amplio coalition that is running in the election, also said Puente needed to go.
“We’re not going to engage in the triviality of debating whether that resignation should take place today, tomorrow, or the day after,” she said. “It must happen as soon as possible.”
'If they don’t resign, we will force them to resign at the ballot box,' opposition leader says
Despite all these detailed answers, it does not look like the opposition is convinced by Puente’s explanations at all.
El Mundo reported that the opposition People’s Party’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, took aim at Puente this morning, demanding political responsibility for the crash.
Puente also points out that in all modes of transport, the ultimate responsibility – despite supporting systems – falls on humans running them.
“In the maritime sector, if a ship loses its onboard equipment or the plotter used to chart its course, who takes control? Do we just leave the vessel adrift? No: a person takes control.
If three aircraft are waiting to land and their control and approach systems fail, who takes charge? A person does. In fact, in aviation, there have been instance, even with redundant, ‘double-check’ systems, where human controllers have made errors; this is because the final recourse … is always a human being.
In its standard, day-to-day operation, the system does not rely on human intervention; it relies on automated systems. However, these are always subject to human supervision, and in exceptional cases – when the automated systems fail – humans step in to take control.”

Details
Lawmakers ranging from House Representative Hakeem Jeffries to Republican Thom Tillis have made it clear that they plan to focus attention on Hegseth, seeking to hold him accountable for U.S. President Donald Trump's war with Iran.
These threats include a new impeachment effort against the defense secretary, led by Republican Representative Thomas Massie. They underscore that all Democrats and a growing number of Republicans view Hegseth as a vulnerable representative of Trump.
Hegseth has been the subject of close scrutiny by members of both parties since the day Trump nominated him. His relationship with Congress has only worsened after aggressive congressional hearings and accusations that he refused to share information about the cost of the war. He also fired dozens of generals and admirals with virtually no explanation and announced that he would livestream an execution by firing squad before Trump rejected the plan.
Even Republicans are frustrated by what they say is the Pentagon's refusal to give them answers about an unpopular war that has driven up fuel prices and contributed to predictions that Democrats could gain control of both chambers of Congress.
"Pete Hegseth started this job with no room for error," said Republican strategist Lisa Camuso Miller. "Hegseth came from the Fox News studio and had never built a network of contacts on Capitol Hill. In Washington, relationships are your insurance policy. He never bought one."

‘People’s Republic of the Disappeared’: Stories of Horror But Also Resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:47:00 UTC
21:47:00 KST

A Czech citizen, taken this summer by Chinese police – or more likely by the Ministry of State Security (MSS) – as part of hostage diplomacy, to pressure the Czech government into releasing an alleged Chinese spy. One U.S. citizen taken by the MSS after being lured into the country. Another U.S. citizen only just moved into formal arrest. A British citizen whose release from prison was only recently made public. Two Japanese businessmen working in the sensitive field of rare earth materials. A Chinese journalist whose whereabouts and condition remain unknown to this day. An endless parade of Chinese lawyers, journalists, and NGO workers.
These people all have one thing in common: they are – or were – disappeared. Not detained. Not arrested. Disappeared into what China euphemistically calls “residential surveillance at a designated location,” better known these days as RSDL. The fact that these cases are so disjointed and vary so much from one another is simple to explain: RSDL is becoming a go-to tool for the CCP in an ever-growing number of scenarios. And these cases cited above are just the tip of the iceberg.
It has long been known that China has used the system on foreigners in the past – myself included. However, the sheer number of cases only now coming to light suggests that past foreign victims were either just a small fraction of the real number, or, more likely, that Chinese police and the MSS alike are becoming more carefree about placing foreign citizens into the system, especially when the victim is intended as a tool of foreign policy. Or, to put it plainly: hostage diplomacy.
It is with this in mind that Safeguard Defenders, the NGO I work with, has released the third edition of the book “The People’s Republic of the Disappeared,” a collection of first-person testimonies from these secret prisons. When we first started on the book, we knew we wanted to focus on foreign citizens as victims – first because it seemed to be happening more and more, but also because we have worked for years with RSDL victims, often Chinese lawyers, journalists, and activists, and knew their experiences well. But what about those foreign citizens? How did their experiences compare? And what about the cases where the system was so clearly being used merely as a tool of hostage diplomacy?
The book, an anthology of sorts, contains first-person short stories from a myriad of victims. Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig, a prime example of such hostage diplomacy, didn’t just write his own story – he wrote the book’s foreword. Australian news anchor Cheng Lei and Taiwanese activist Lee Ming-che are other contributors. As a former NGO worker in China who ended up in RSDL myself, I contributed too. And so did many others.
The stories are not exactly an easy read, but they should be mandatory reading for those in foreign governments working to protect their citizens abroad from arbitrary detention – both governments with recent or current victims, and those who will almost certainly have their own citizens taken into the system the next time the CCP feels it can use them as leverage in trade negotiations, “prisoner” exchanges, or other foreign policy goals. For those in foreign ministries tasked with keeping their citizens safe from such treatment, failure to learn how the system actually works should not be an option.
In fact, foreign ministries in countries whose citizens have been disappeared into the system have been consistently slow – at best – or have downright avoided learning about RSDL from past victims, when they have every reason, and indeed an obligation, to learn as much as they can: both to better help their own citizens, and as a means of pressuring the CCP to roll back its use of arbitrary detention and hostage diplomacy against other countries.
The book, of course, also includes numerous testimonies from Chinese victims – from lawyers to media workers to those who were merely collateral damage – and shows how the system is used as a tool of political terror within and against China’s fledgling human rights community, whose members seek something as audacious as basic rights, religious freedom, and the rule of law.
While we continue to publish new analysis and data showing how many tens of thousands are being put into the system, and to expose how the facilities are built and what they look like inside, none of that can ever compare with letting readers hear directly from those who have the real experience of going through the system, and how it changes everyone who has been through it.
The one positive thing one can take from these testimonies is the often incredible stories of resilience – how people, domestic activists and foreign victims alike, draw strength from these experiences. Few who have gone through it ever give up; most return even more determined. Others, having faced such horror, become public advocates against the system, or work to help both future and past victims. And there is much to be learned from this, as people have made clear in the past: by reading how others have experienced RSDL, those at risk of becoming future victims have been able to prepare themselves and work out strategies to protect themselves, their partners, and their loved ones, should they face it themselves.
Which is why the book – also available in a Chinese-language edition – is being made available for free, for all Chinese activists, dissidents, and others to freely access.

Gamble on democracy: Inside suspicious election-contracts trading on prediction markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:45:16 UTC
21:45:16 KST

Spencer Pratt appeared to be a shoo-in to win the June primary in the Los Angeles mayor's race, based on millions of dollars wagered on prediction markets aiming to call the race.
Pratt was an unlikely candidate for mayor. The former reality TV star had never held elective office, but after the Palisades fire destroyed his home, he turned his criticism of the city's response into a campaign rallying cry.
Using prediction markets including Kalshi, Polymarket U.S. and Polymarket International, speculators flocked to the race, which drew more than $47 million in trades, making it the most heavily traded mayoral contest of 2026. On the eve of the June primary, one market gave Pratt a 78% chance of advancing to the November runoff.
The prediction markets were wildly off base, and Pratt finished third.
Pratt supporters, though, used the failed speculation to cast doubt on the integrity of the election. That drew a response from the city: "Prediction markets can add to that confusion when people treat their projections as more authoritative than the actual votes being counted," Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder for the Los Angeles County Clerk's Office, said in a statement to CNBC.
Prediction markets' failure to call the election correctly also raised the possibility that markets can be manipulated to make candidates appear to have more support than they really do. Exclusive reporting from CNBC shows that this risk is real.
The dissonance between voter polling, speculation-fueled prediction markets and the actual outcome has grown in importance as election wagers become a prominent feature of elections. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.
Polymarket and Kalshi are the two largest prediction market platforms. They let people speculate on almost anything — from which team will be the 2027 NBA champions to whether the U.S. will confirm that aliens exist.
Already, on these platforms the amount wagered on contracts related to the 2026 congressional elections has more than tripled wagers on the 2024 races, according to the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, or ACDC, a nonprofit based in Washington, D.C. And people are increasingly using the platforms as a source of information. For midterm election markets specifically, Kalshi reports that viewers outnumber actual traders by a 5-to-1 ratio.
Spotting suspicious trades
Despite the Pratt race being a heavily traded, liquid contract, Kalshi detected and reported on price spikes that occurred during trading on that race in a case study it published in July. A price spike is a temporary but large price jump that can make an outcome look more likely to happen, according to experts. Price spikes can happen for a variety of reasons, such as new information changing trader expectations or a trader buying a large number of contracts, which can drive up contract prices as cheaper ones get bought up.
On May 20, the company said, a trader on Kalshi spent $1.25 million on "Yes" contracts on Pratt becoming LA's next mayor. One of the trades caused the price of contracts on Pratt's victory to jump from 29 cents to 45 cents, suggesting that traders saw his chances of winning rise from 29% to 45%. However, according to Kalshi's case study, within nine seconds, the price reverted to earlier levels and the markets self-corrected.
"You can absolutely guarantee there are rational traders in that market willing to take those trades and bring that price right back down to where it belongs," said Robert DeNault, the head of enforcement at Kalshi, who is tasked with tracking unusual activity on the platform. "And by the end of the day, his price was lower than when it began."
But during the LA mayoral race, there were numerous price spikes across Kalshi and Polymarket International that pushed the odds in Pratt's favor, according to an analysis for CNBC by ACDC. The group didn't consider trades from Polymarket U.S. in its analysis.
Data that ACDC collected confirms Kalshi's findings. In the case study, Kalshi provided insight through about 30 minutes after the large order was placed. However, the group found that if you expand the time frame to three hours after the spike, the price lands three cents higher and that level is sustained for about two hours. In the long term, the price does correct. But according to ACDC's research, the longer a price increase lasts, the greater the risk of that information being interpreted as market sentiment.
And as ACDC's research suggests, election contracts are vulnerable to unusual price spikes — similar to those in the Pratt race.
The group found that of 167 congressional markets across Polymarket International and Kalshi worth more than $100,000, 38 markets — or about 23% — experienced price spikes moving the contract price 30 cents or more.
One example of such a spike was the Kalshi contract on whether Juliana Stratton would be the Democratic nominee for the Senate in Illinois. On March 3, according to ACDC, two purchases stood out as large — the median order was $12 before election day. One buyer spent $5,000 on contracts that favored the longtime public official's candidacy, taking the price from 47 cents to 79 cents. The price normalized after three seconds, going back down to 47 cents, but about one minute later, it shot back up to 99 cents after $3,000 of additional contracts were purchased. The price eventually sank back to 52 cents — 5 cents more than where it started — meaning a person or persons spent $8,000, and, in the process, drove up the price that made a Stratton victory look more likely.
Two weeks later, Stratton won the Democratic primary. Stratton declined to comment on this story, but a spokesperson from her office pointed CNBC to a poll from Public Policy Polling released on the same day as the price spike. It showed Stratton leading.
In a statement to CNBC, a spokesperson for Kalshi wrote, "As is common on Kalshi, the market corrected quickly to a price near fair value."
ACDC said it's impossible to know the motive behind these wagers. While profit could be a factor, it is an imperfect one. On prediction markets, participants can buy and sell contracts valued between $0 and $1, with the price reflecting how likely traders think an event is to happen. The more expensive a contract, the smaller the potential payout. Winning contracts settle at $1, while losing contracts become worthless. So traders buying in at 99 cents expect to earn only 1 cent if their predicted outcome happens, and transaction fees charged by prediction markets can also eat into that profit.
"If the theory is that prediction markets are accurate because of a price motive, [a lack thereof] begs the question: What type of goal does someone making a trade like that really have for themselves?" said Michelle Kendler-Kretsch, a researcher at ACDC.
Influencing election outcomes may be an answer.
Voters were between 10 and 20 percentage points more likely to believe a candidate would win if prediction markets favored the candidate, no matter what the polls reported, according to a new study funded by the Brennan Center for Justice, a New York City-based left-leaning advocacy organization. That survey, which took place in September, included the perspective of 1,994 registered voters.
Data ACDC shared with CNBC also shows shifting the odds is even easier and cheaper in markets where not many wagers are placed. Across 18,000 active congressional markets on Polymarket International, Polymarket U.S., and Kalshi, 88% could have their prices moved by 10 cents with a single wager under $1,000.
Policing market manipulation
Still, Kalshi market outcomes are often correct. "Across U.S. elections since 2024, when Kalshi's markets favored a candidate to win, that candidate went on to win roughly 9 times out of 10," the company wrote in a website post. Further, The Washington Post examined 268 candidates in this year's primaries who received a 70% to 80% chance of winning on Kalshi or Polymarket on any day in the two months before the primary election. Three-quarters of them won.
Kalshi says it's working to assuage election distortion concerns. It added new transparency-centered features to its midterm election markets earlier this month to help users understand how much confidence to place in a contract's odds, including labels for markets with little trading activity and live feeds showing individual trades. Polymarket also rolled out its own election-specific surveillance system "to detect potential attempts to manipulate election markets, distort probabilities, or manufacture apparent market consensus."
Kalshi told CNBC it uses algorithms to generate alerts based on parameters for unusual trading activity, including fishy trading times and volumes as well as price jumps. It's unclear if Kalshi's internal protocols alerted over the Pratt trades; the company didn't respond to CNBC's request for clarity.
Both Kalshi and Polymarket U.S. are governed by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or CFTC, an independent federal agency whose rules are designed to prevent market manipulation and insider trading. Trading prices and activity are publicly visible, and at least in the case of Kalshi, its order book is public on derivatives exchanges and people can escalate and flag unusual trades to the exchanges. In addition, Kalshi and Polymarket U.S. collect "know your customer" information including full legal names and Social Security numbers.
The outside world, however, has no insight into who is behind each trade.
"I formerly worked at the FBI and in centralized finance off the blockchain," said Shana Bautista, the head of global intelligence and investigations at Polymarket. "If you want to get information on a case or a certain transaction, you have to serve either a subpoena or a search warrant to be able to get that information."
In April, Polymarket International announced a partnership with blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, which helps the blockchain-based platform track suspicious trading on its international platform.
Adam Hart, a senior product manager at Chainalysis, showed CNBC the data the firm collects on each Polymarket trader. Polymarket can, for example, see the number of trades being made, the total value of buys and sells, how much traders are wagering relative to their overall activity, and their total profits and losses.
Hart walked CNBC through an investigation his team conducted in collaboration with Polymarket: the case of Gannon Ken Van Dyke, a U.S. soldier charged with using classified information to bet on the removal of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and the entry of U.S. forces into Venezuela. Van Dyke pleaded not guilty.
Hart said the wallet was flagged because it made unusually profitable bets and never lost. Van Dyke was ultimately identified in part because he did little to conceal his identity: His wallets were funded through cryptocurrency exchanges that require users to verify their identities. Hart said Van Dyke also transferred his approximately $400,000 in winnings to a mainstream U.S. exchange.
Of course, trades that may look suspicious could be the wagers of a sharp speculator or an enthusiastic backer. That was the case of "Theo," the anonymous French whale who made about $85 million on contracts favoring Donald Trump in the 2024 elections. Bubblemaps, an on-chain analytics firm, was one of the platforms to trace Theo's approximately $60 million in wagers across at least 10 Polymarket accounts. Bubblemaps traced the activity to two crypto exchanges' deposit wallets owned by Theo, who said he based his wagers on his own neighbor polling and calls to battleground states.
Engineering election integrity
That internal sleuthing does little to reassure Jared DeMarinis. As the administrator of the Maryland State Board of Elections, DeMarinis is convinced that the only way to protect election integrity is an outright ban on wagering on election outcomes.
In July, he asked the office of the state prosecutor to investigate whether prediction markets violate state laws prohibiting wagering on election outcomes. A few months later, in September, he prohibited certain individuals and election staff, including election judges and members of the state board of elections, from trading in election markets.
"We employ 26,000 election judges that are poll workers," DeMarinis said. "They have access to information right before it's getting tallied officially and counted. They'll know certain things. This is all problematic because it goes to the legitimacy, integrity of the electoral process."
More than half of all states have laws making election betting illegal in all or some circumstances, according to the Pew Research Center. Prediction markets argue that the CFTC, not states, has jurisdiction over their contracts because they classify them as swaps, which fall under federal law. The CFTC has backed that argument.
But these laws may not apply to federally regulated prediction markets. New Jersey, backed by dozens of states, has asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on whether the CFTC rules go far enough to counter election concerns and whether the states themselves have additional standing.
In the meantime, the prediction markets are only ramping up their election offerings.
"We don't have a lot of information on whether prediction markets are accurate," Kendler-Kretsch said. "When [a trade] doesn't go the way of an election, instead of sowing doubt in prediction markets and their accuracy, it's sowing doubt in the election itself."
— Ananya Chetia contributed to this report.

Italy: Students and workers rally over living costs

Italy: Students and workers rally over living costs
October 30, 2026
Tens of thousands of students and workers marched across Italy on Friday, demanding more education funding and relief from rising living costs.
The rallies followed weeks of student tent camps and school occupations, with a general strike bringing workers into the streets alongside them.
Demonstrations took place in dozens of cities, including Rome, Milan, Turin, Bologna, Genoa and Naples. Police were deployed in large numbers after earlier protests descended into rioting.
Why were students and workers protesting?
Demonstrators criticized Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's right-wing government over low wages, rising fuel prices and military spending. Students demanded more money for schools and universities.
In Rome, university student Beatrice Chilelli said students were "at a breaking point."
"They can't afford to pay exorbitant tuition fees, and rent... which weighs heavily on their parents' shoulders," the 21-year-old told AFP.
The USB trade union called a general strike, with truck drivers, taxi drivers and farmers among those joining the protests. Disruption to public transport remained limited on Friday morning.
Thousands marched from Rome's Termini station past the Colosseum, accompanied by two tractors and a taxi. "We need more houses, not bombs!" one group chanted.
Did the protests turn violent?
Minor scuffles broke out between demonstrators and riot police in Turin at the start of the march. No major clashes had been reported by midday.
In Milan, the procession headed away from the city center, where rioters looted shops, damaged property and clashed with police after a cost-of-living demonstration two weeks earlier.
Authorities also increased protection around landmarks, including Rome's Colosseum and Milan's cathedral.
The student protests have drawn momentum from similar movements in France and Spain. Teachers, retirees and other workers also joined Friday's rallies.
