Three years of the Gaza genocide serving Western capitalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:26:35 UTC
21:26:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Three years of the Gaza genocide serving Western capitalism
To my knowledge, the first public, English-language warning that a genocide was unfolding in the Gaza Strip came from Israeli genocide scholar Raz Segal, five days after the events of 7 October 2023. Amnesty International confirmed Segal's conclusions fourteen months later, by which time at least 40,000 more Palestinians were killed.
The Amnesty Report still failed, however, to compel Western governments to act, despite being the first of its kind the organisation issued in the midst of a genocide.
Instead, the live-stream slaughter continued broadcasting for another ten months when a ceasefire finally came into effect in October 2025. By that time, at least 72,000 Palestinian were killed, and virtually all of Gaza’s urban infrastructure had been transformed into rubble.
The question of why and how Israel’s genocide persisted for so long despite repeated warnings and full knowledge of its unfolding is a question that must not slip from public conscience.
Indeed, it is the proverbial 800-pound gorilla in the room that world powers pretend isn’t there, and the continued failure to explain its presence tempts others to repeat similar crimes elsewhere.
However, the danger of the genocide resuming full-throttled in Gaza is also very real, particularly after Israeli and US mid-term elections. Almost daily, Israel’s politicians and military brass vow to complete their ethnic cleansing of Gaza, and bicker over whether the slaughter they already committed there was enough.
Furthermore, the US has also recently resupplied Israel with 40,000 two-tonne bombs - the chief weapon of the genocide.
The daily toll of those killed also reminds us that the ceasefire itself was never observed.
Collectively, these factors remind us that the forces that committed the genocide, protected it and pushed it forward, are all still very much alive today, and have used the passage of time to reposition.
Ending the genocide
So how does the solidarity movement get rid of the guerrilla, especially given that Western democratic institutions and representatives have proven themselves to be so spineless, paralysed and complicit?
To its credit, the movement did an impressive job shining a flashlight into the institutional undercarriage of Western capitalism, trying to discover what made the killing machine run.
Of course, its work was assisted by the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, whose longstanding work documents where the bloody shoes that stomped all over Gaza were initially purchased and tread.
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese also produced an important report that mapped key political-economic connections running between government, the private sector and universities.
The report admitted, however, that it could only document “the tip of the iceberg” and warned that complicity around the genocide would not end “without holding the private sector accountable, including its executives."
This is precisely what lies behind the US State Department’s recent declaration of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC). This extraordinary measure was not just another Trump administration swipe against multilateralism but was a specific attempt to protect US citizens and corporations from possible future prosecution.
Both the ICJ (which prosecutes states) and the ICC (which prosecutes individuals) are deeply engaged in investigating Israel’s genocide and the individuals responsible for it. While article 25(1) of the Rome Statute prevents the ICC from prosecuting corporations, the Court can target individual corporate officers, including directors and employees.
In sum, the US knows it needs to get ahead of the curve because there is no shortage of US corporations and executives that are targets of these courts.
The political economy of the genocide
As time passes, more research surfaces explaining the political economy of the genocide. One of the most effective of these is a visualisation recently produced by an anonymous collective tracing the genocide’s “blood money”.
This impressive set of figures and visualisations exposes a tangled web of inter-permeated interests and actors, chiefly focused around the military-industrial, big tech, and financial services sectors. While none of these sectors is entirely surprising given their profiteering role, the scale and depth of their complicity were both active and conscious, rather than circumstantial or passive.
Microsoft, Google and Amazon provided cloud services to the Israeli government and its main arms producers that enabled Israel to draw up the genocide’s kill lists. This included collecting 200 million hours of audio files that these companies helped Israel browse and analyse.
How many of these recordings document the last horrific screams of 20,000 children killed when daddy finally did come home? Thousands, certainly.
Google and Amazon even had a secret “winking” mechanism to tip Israel off when foreign courts asked them for information on their servers.
In a just world, the heads of these corporations would all be on trial for these crimes, right next to Netanyahu, Trump, Biden and Starmer.
The audio and video resources these execs helped Israel process should also be made public through enforced court disclosure procedures. They are the records that document the banality of evil in today’s world, and should be interred in a future version of the Palestinian genocide museum when the time comes.
For years, big tech’s relations with Israel have been like a kid in a candy store, as Silicon Valley shopped in Silicon Wadi to see the latest Unit 8200 spinoffs and gadgets. Israeli start-ups were showered with billions in venture capital, encouraging innovation in the dark arts of occupation, apartheid and genocide for the purpose of commercial hyper-scaling.
The blood money visualisations also show that even larger behemoths of Western capitalism sit behind big tech, also profiteering from genocide - the major index funds like BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street and others.
These funds oversee assets larger than virtually every country in the world, except the US. They own significant chunks of big tech, and virtually everything profitable on the S&P 500.
The index funds link genocide profits to public and private sector pension plans, making individual Western employees unwitting benefactors of Gaza’s blood money.
Profit and interest
All of this speaks to how the genocide was hardly the act of a Zionist cabal that penetrated Western government and corporations. Instead, it was a set of interests, relations, and inclinations that saturated the heart and nervous system of Western capitalism, particularly its big tech, financial services, and military-industrial wings.
These wings have come to dominate Western capitalism today and are deemed ‘too big to fail’ by the political class, as they also lie at the centre of Western geo-economic strategies to compete with China in this post-neoliberal age of imperial anxiety.
Their power transcends the domain of states, and they use their resources to manipulate the markets, states, and international systems they operate across.
These corporations also hide their wealth in tax havens and defy regulation because they operate at the frontiers of technological and economic ‘innovation’ the world has never seen. It will take years for lawmakers to catch up to their tax-beating chicanery, if ever.
By serving as parastate actors, they undermine traditional bourgeois liberal capitalism and its elementary associated values - not only of free trade and competition, but also of privacy, free expression, the free press, the right to organise, and academic freedom. It is not by chance that critics have come to describe this era as one marked by technofeudalism that is ushering in authoritarianism and fascism.
Indeed, this is the anatomy of the 800-pound gorilla that explains its self-righteous staid. The gorilla that hangs about the room smashing up Gaza has also plundered the public assets of social democracy, to say nothing of the resources of the Third World. He is king because we are in his jungle.
Like the ‘disposable’ people of Gaza, the Western working class now awaits an inevitable culling, be it from mass AI-induced redundancy, WWIII or both.
Seen in this light, Palestine and the Gaza genocide are but one frontier in a fragmented global dystopia where AI technologies now juice the gorilla with amphetamine.
This is also why the movement to end the genocide in Gaza has such a historic role: it is the key global political actor that understands the political-economic connections that animate the gorilla and which make it so dangerous - not only in Palestine and the Middle East, but also in Porto, Paris and Milan. It has also built and mobilised an inchoate global infrastructure of movement to contain the gorilla, even though the task of actually disempowering him is now down to the ropes and arrows of the global Lilliputian class in our millions.
God save us all if we fail.
Toufic Haddad is a Palestinian-American academic and author of “Palestine Ltd: Neoliberalism and Nationalism in the Occupied Territory.” He has worked in various capacities across the OPT as a journalist, researcher, consultant, editor, and publisher, including in Gaza for several UN bodies since 1997, and was most recently the Director of the Council for British Research in the Levant's Jerusalem Branch - the Kenyon Institute. He also writes for the Palestinian policy network Al Shabaka.

James Comey lawyers seek to have third criminal case dismissed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:26:17 UTC
21:26:17 KST

Lawyers for the former FBI director James Comey will ask a federal judge on Friday to block the US justice department from pursuing its third criminal case against him.
Comey is an outspoken critic of Donald Trump, in open feud since the US president fired him from that post early in his first term, and he is a frequent target of Republican outrage.
Court documents unsealed on Monday showed that the Trump administration this month bypassed a grand jury and filed a charging document known as a “criminal information” over allegations of a decade-old and previously investigated news media leak.
The justice department defended the maneuver as an effort to extend the legal time limit for seeking a grand jury indictment, but Comey’s lawyers have called the case legally invalid.
US district judge Trevor McFadden in Washington, DC was expected to hear arguments on that question on Friday. He was appointed by Trump.
The latest effort to prosecute Comey, who says he is innocent of the allegations, is part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week’s midterm elections.
Comey was FBI director when Trump first took office, having been appointed to that role in 2013 by Barack Obama. He oversaw an investigation into whether Trump’s presidential campaign conspired with Russia to tip the 2016 election in the Republican’s favor over the Democratic party nominee, Hillary Clinton. The two men have been bitterly at odds since, with Comey likening Trump to a corrupt mafia don “untethered to the truth” in a book he published, and the president accusing him of treason and calling for his imprisonment.
The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of lying to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed.
A separate, pending indictment charges Comey with threatening Trump via a snapshot posted on Instagram of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47” – 86 is slang meaning “to throw out”, “to get rid of” or “to refuse service to”, and Trump is the 47th president. The former FBI director has sought to dismiss the case.
The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the foreign intelligence surveillance court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.
Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI’s conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey’s attorneys said in a recent court filing.
In 2019, the US attorney’s office for the District of Columbia, the federal prosecutors in that district, opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name Tropical Vortex. But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in early 2020.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

Residents leave devastated Russian-occupied Oleshky as evacuation corridor opens
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:25:53 GMT
21:25:53 KST

Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire
- Published
Hundreds of residents of the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have been evacuated, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have said, following a humanitarian ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
"Everything unfolded without any incidents, and both sides noted the high level of organisation," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed the evacuees were on their way to southern Russia, from where they will travel on to Ukraine through Belarus.
Melania Trump said that "all elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders".
Speaking to journalists on Friday evening, Lantratova put out a joint request with her Ukrainian counterpart "to the US First Lady... that humanitarian missions such as this one, delivering aid to residents in need, be conducted on a regular basis under the coordination of Mrs Melania Trump".
A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.
Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning.
"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."
Ukrainian military positions lie 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.
They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.
Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.
Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.
Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. He will also become the first to visit Russia when he escorts the evacuees back into Ukraine on Saturday.
The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.
But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.
Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.
In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.
An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."
Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind.
"The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise."
Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter.
"She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said.
"That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."
The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Residents of Kherson told the BBC they were "overjoyed" by the ceasefire. However, they are concerned the truce has given Russia time to build up its military presence on the banks of the Dnipro river, which could result in a renewed assault once the ceasefire expires.
On Friday, the Kremlin made it clear that the success of the Oleshky ceasefire should not be interpreted as willingness to extend the truce to the rest of Ukraine.
A handful of foreign journalists have been invited to witness the evacuation of the town, which Moscow is expected to present as a humanitarian mission conducted with mercy to protect the people of Oleshky.
Many Ukrainians suspect Russia's real intention is to earn credit with the White House, and to provide US President Donald Trump with a boost ahead of next week's midterm elections.

China Owes Climate Accountability to South Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:25:00 UTC
21:25:00 KST

Over the last two decades, China has emerged as a Global South leader in green technology innovation and development, facilitating the green transition both domestically and abroad. This feat also positioned it as central to the climate discourse in South Asia pertaining to Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (the CBDR-RC principle). And this is rightly so. China accounts for 33 percent of the share of global greenhouse gas emissions, with around 13.1 billion tons, making it the top emitter in Asia. India, in second place, emits around four times less than China (around 3.15 billion tons).
But the discourse on Beijing’s responsibility and accountability stems not only from its massive contribution to global gas emissions, but also from its capability as a green technology provider, and to a large extent, from its position as an upstream actor that affects shared regional ecosystems and vulnerable neighbors.
We begin with geography. There are two facts to note here. One, China’s upstream disposition. Second, and related, the fact that the South Asian nations rank among the most vulnerable to climate-induced heatwaves, floods, and sea-level rise, despite a smaller share of historical global emissions. Various catastrophic incidents back this.
After the devastation of Nepal’s Rasuwa district in August 2026 in a transborder glacial flood, environmental specialists noted around 25 glacial lakes within China that can affect Nepal and the adjacent region. Just over a year before, in July 2025, there was another flood outburst that began in China’s Gyirong County before causing damage and deaths in Nepal. Without commenting on causation, one can note that these hazards are highly asymmetric: risks originate upstream and casualties are borne downstream. This risk asymmetry makes the tasks of real-time hydrological data sharing and joint monitoring a matter of accountability and responsibility. Similarly, China-India collaboration on climate security can be operationalized to enable accurate forecasting and create shared data for tracking glacier melt. However, China has resisted this transparent climate cooperation, increasing India’s vulnerability to floods and water shocks.
China holds itself up as the leader of the Global South in climate negotiations. However, the actual outcomes from this claim are rather feeble. Between 2013 and 2022, China provided and mobilized about $45 billion to support developing countries’ climate actions. Indeed, under the UNFCCC, China, being a developing country, is under no formal obligation to provide climate finance and hence all its efforts are voluntary rather than mandatory. This may be appreciable, but given its claim as the Global South’s representative, one must invoke the CBDR principle to hold Beijing accountable for cross-border hazard prevention and mitigation.
Given the clean technology economic boom in China, it stands out from other developing countries for its growing participation in climate finance via private investment channels. Consequently, there are growing conversations about Beijing’s funding obligation to the $1.3 trillion corpus to support climate action in other developing countries.
China is the world’s largest producer of renewable power. However, the rise in the clean energy system is supplementing, not replacing, fossil fuels. China added 78 GW of new coal power capacity in 2025, reaching a multi-year record. Although annual tallies of new coal power projects are down slightly from the 2022-23 peak, in the first half of 2025 China approved more coal-fired plants than it had in a decade.
The long-term contractual lock-ins guarantee minimum purchase of coal-generated power by utilities, compelling grid operators to prioritize coal even when clean, cheaper wind and solar power are abundant. These guaranteed offtakes by the state, which are no less than a subsidy to coal plants in effect, lead to a fall in emissions in percentage terms without impacting it much in absolute terms.
And China’s climatically vulnerable neighbors like Nepal, Bhutan, and Bangladesh bear the real cost. Becoming a leader in clean energy by showcasing good emissions figures relative to GDP is one thing; an actual reduction in emissions in absolute figures is another question entirely. Thus, one sees an externality problem. Beijing captures the economic benefits from coal plants by providing them purchase guarantees. Meanwhile, its emissions increase the risk of climate disaster for its neighbors – a risk that China is not proactively addressing through timely information-sharing.
Of course, discussions of China’s responsibility can’t take away from the West’s still-greater responsibility to address climate issues. However, given geographical proximity and leadership, discussions of climate responsibility and accountability must include China, given the recent environmental hazards in the fragile ecosystem of the Himalayas in South Asia. The task on the Chinese side is rather doable: embrace real-time transboundary data-sharing with Nepal and India, co-fund early-warning infrastructure, and make an action-oriented and measurable South-South climate finance commitment.

Northrop Grumman gets $56M to upgrade one MQ-4C Triton drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:24:29 UTC
21:24:29 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Northrop Grumman a $56 million modification on Oct. 28 to install the B7 retrofit material kit on one MQ-4C Triton.
- Work runs through May 2030, mostly in Palmdale and San Diego, funded entirely by fiscal 2027 U.S. Navy aircraft procurement money.
The U.S. Navy has ordered a $56 million retrofit for a single MQ-4C Triton, paying Northrop Grumman to install the B7 retrofit material kit on one of its high-altitude maritime surveillance drones. Naval Air Systems Command awarded the firm-fixed-price modification on Oct. 28, and the work is scheduled to run until May 2030.
The full $55,986,538 comes from fiscal 2027 U.S. Navy aircraft procurement funds and was obligated at award, with no competition. The award is modification P00003 to delivery order N00019-26-F-1093, placed under basic ordering agreement N00019-25-G-0003. Northrop Grumman will do 64% of the work in Palmdale, California, where the Triton is built, 34% in San Diego and the remaining 2% at other U.S. sites.
The announcement does not say which configuration the kit brings, what it changes on the aircraft or which airframe will receive it. B7 matches the construction numbers the Navy and Northrop Grumman use for individual Triton airframes, and earlier contracts used the same scheme. A 2023 order worth $83.1 million retrofitted air vehicles B9 and B10 and one main operating base to the multi-intelligence configuration known as Integrated Functional Capability 4, or IFC-4. Northrop Grumman delivered B8, the first production Triton upgraded to that standard, to Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, on Feb. 1, 2022. If B7 is an airframe, it was built just before that aircraft, but the Navy has not said the new kit is an IFC-4 upgrade.
The cost and work split closely track the retrofit of air vehicle B5. In late 2025, the U.S. Navy exercised a $45.75 million option for continued engineering, tooling and labor to complete IFC-4 change requests and engineering change proposals on B5, with completion set for June 2029 and the same 64% Palmdale, 34% San Diego and 2% elsewhere division. Retrofit kits for B5 and B11 were bought under a separate order in August 2024, and installation was awarded in May 2025, so a single airframe’s upgrade has been spread across several contract actions covering parts, engineering and labor.
IFC-4 is the configuration that gave the Triton a signals intelligence role. According to Northrop Grumman, the upgrade adds two sensors, one for electronic intelligence and one for communications intelligence, and their stricter data security requirements forced hardware and software changes across both the aircraft and its ground segment. The rest of the sensor suite centers on the AN/ZPY-3 Multi-Function Active Sensor, an X-band electronically scanned surveillance radar under the fuselage, and the Raytheon AN/DAS-3 electro-optical and infrared turret. The U.S. Navy flew the first Triton in IFC-4 configuration on July 29, 2021, and the configuration is intended to let the service retire its crewed EP-3E Aries II signals intelligence aircraft.
The Triton is a heavily reworked RQ-4 Global Hawk. Northrop Grumman strengthened the airframe and wing and added de-icing and lightning protection so the unarmed drone can descend from around 15,000 m (50,000 feet) to about 3,000 m (10,000 feet) to identify ships, then climb back to patrol altitude. The aircraft first flew on May 22, 2013, and the U.S. Navy originally planned to buy 68.
Operational use has grown since the first two baseline IFC-3 aircraft deployed to Guam in 2020 with Unmanned Patrol Squadron 19. The U.S. Navy sent a Triton to Naval Air Station Sigonella, Italy, for the first time on March 30, 2024. On April 9, 2026, one was lost: the Naval Safety Command listed it as a Class A mishap with no injuries and withheld the location for operational security. The aircraft had vanished from public flight tracking over the Persian Gulf. The Navy has not said what caused the crash, and the new contract announcement does not connect the B7 work to that loss.
Retrofits are now a steady stream of business for Northrop Grumman. Earlier in October, the U.S. Navy placed a $66 million order under the same basic ordering agreement to install 17 U.S. Navy and 16 Australian engineering changes on fielded Tritons. On Oct. 22, Naval Air Systems Command posted a notice on the federal government’s contracting website saying it intends to award Northrop Grumman a sole-source indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract for Triton engineering, software and cyber sustainment, logistics and engineering change proposals for the U.S. Navy and the Royal Australian Air Force, with award expected in the third quarter of fiscal 2027.
The customer base is widening. Australia buys its Tritons through a cooperative program with the U.S. Navy that covers development, production and sustainment. On July 7, 2026, Denmark, Finland, Germany and Norway signed a letter of intent at the NATO summit defense industry forum in Ankara to buy up to five Tritons for NATO’s own intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance force.

Trump cancels campaign appearances days before midterm votes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:22:42 UTC
21:22:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump reverses cancellation of Iowa, Kansas campaign appearances
US President Donald Trump will go ahead with scheduled rallies in Iowa and Kansas ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections, after the Republican National Committee (RNC) previously announced the appearances would be cancelled.
The RNC initially announced the cancellation on Thursday, saying the president would instead appear at a series of tele-rallies, which the White House says will still go ahead in addition to the in person rallies.
“Rallies are BACK ON! President Trump loves his supporters, and in addition to nearly 20 tele-rallies, he will hold back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday,” the White House said in a statement hours after the cancellation announcement.
The RNC said in the cancellation announcement that their party is "in a strong position in Kansas and Iowa", and the tele-rallies will "reach more voters in the limited time left before polls close".
In Kansas, Republican Senator Roger Marshall is up for reelection in a close race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. The state will also elect its governor in a race between Republican Ty Masterson and Democrat Cindy Holscher. The position is currently held by Democrat Laura Kelly, who cannot run for re-election due to term limits.
Iowans will vote in a key Senate race between Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek. The state will also elect two new member of congress, and its governor in a race between Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand. Current Republican Governor Kim Reynolds announced in last year that she would not run for re-election.
"I think what's interesting about these two states is they're traditionally quite red," Andrew Proctor, lecturer of US politics at University College London's Institute of the Americas, told The New Arab.
"I do think [Trump's decision to cancel the campaign appearances] is an indicator that they might think they could lose them," Proctor said, speaking before the announcement that the in-person rallies are back on the president's schedule.
Many Republican candidates are reluctant to show support for the president, with two-thirds who are running in close races having distanced themselves from Trump, according to analysis by Reuters.
An NPR/PBS/Marist poll published Tuesday found that 40% of likely voters approve of his presidency, while 59% disapprove.
"One thing we also don't know, did those candidates tell him not to come, which could've been another reason why these events were cancelled," Proctor said.
The choice to hold tele-rallies is a departure from Trump's usual style of campaigning, which is known for his in-person rally speeches that typically run for well over an hour.
"His supporters usually like to see him in person, so I think this is more digital format isn't really in line with what we know his approach to politics to be," Proctor said.
He added that if the Republicans lose both Congress and the Senate, "I think you could expect to see a lot of distancing from the president in the next couple of years. I definitely think that that's how that will play out".
"If there's a world where they actually hold onto the Senate and maybe the House, the House is looking very unlikely, but if there was a world where did that did happen, I think you would see people cozy back up with him after after the midterms."

Spain’s deadly train crash redraws electoral battle lines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:20:22 UTC
21:20:22 KST

Spain’s deadly train crash redraws electoral battle lines
The tragedy has upended the November 29 election campaign, shifting attention from housing to security.
A few minutes past 9am on Wednesday, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez posted a message on X declaring there were “lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country”.
His left-wing Socialist Party (PSOE) had sought to seize upon anger over Spain’s housing crisis as a campaign issue ahead of the November 29 election.
Less than an hour later, news of a deadly train crash began to emerge, transforming the campaign. The safety of Spain’s railways, its infrastructure and the government’s ability to deliver essential public services are now key issues after 69 people were killed nine months after a similar disaster.
The mood has changed and Sanchez’s Socialists could be in trouble, analysts say, as the conservative opposition has been handed new grounds to challenge the government on competence and security.
“There are no winners in this tragedy, but it marks a new tone for the campaign where the conservative party could be more comfortable,” said Yolanda Roman, global director for public affairs at ATREVIA, referring to the Popular Party (PP) that has been leading in the polls.
Sanchez’s Socialists were heading for a public debate they could manage, “but after this major tragedy the political framing for the election changed dramatically in all senses”, she added.
PP’s leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the prime minister’s main rival, has demanded accountability.
“This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families. That does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers,” he said.
In the wake of the crash, he said the PP would suspend campaign activities for two days.
The far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, who is likely hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives, did not show the same restraint.
“We, too, are in mourning – but do not expect us to stay quiet. We will not maintain a complicit silence. It is my duty to denounce Sanchez’s criminal handling of affairs and to work tirelessly so that this coming November 29th … Spain may rid itself of this mafia-like gang,” he said on X.
Hundreds of mostly far-right demonstrators gathered in front of Spain’s Transport Ministry to call for the prime minister’s resignation. “Spain can’t take it anymore,” read a banner.
The political fallout unfolded as questions mounted over what caused the crash. At 8.53am (7:53 GMT) on Wednesday, a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to Seville slammed into the back of another stationary train on the same track. The incident took place close to Toledo, south of the capital.
Spanish officials pointed to a failure involving the LZB train-control system, which has been used on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line since it opened in the 1990s.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente rejected claims that the accident showed Spain’s railway system was unsafe, describing it as “reliable and safe”, while acknowledging the limits imposed by equipment and human error. His remarks did little to quell the debate over the condition of the country’s rail infrastructure.
Isabel Pardo de Vera, the former president of Adif, the state-owned company responsible for managing Spain’s railway infrastructure, criticised the government over the transition from the older LZB system to the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS). Her comments raised further questions about the pace of modernisation and whether warnings about the network had been adequately addressed.
The crash has revived memories of other fatal accidents. In 2013, 80 people died in a derailment at Angrois, near Santiago de Compostela in the country’s northwest.
Spain’s high-speed rail network has long been regarded as one of the country’s flagship public services, alongside its healthcare system. It carried about 45 million passengers last year, including millions of tourists.
A survey conducted by Spanish media in January, after the previous fatal crash, found that 57 percent of respondents believed rail services had deteriorated since Sanchez took office, while nearly 60 percent said they had little or no confidence in the country’s railway system.
For Sanchez, the timing could not have been worse.
His party has faced corruption scandals involving his inner circle. Separate investigations have targeted Sanchez’s wife, Begona Gomez, over alleged influence-peddling and business corruption, and his brother, David Sanchez, over the circumstances of his public-sector appointment. Both deny wrongdoing.
The government had also been criticised after 80,000 migrants crossed into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta in late July. The Socialists had faced a backlash from right-wing parties and security personnel over alleged failures to adequately invest in border infrastructure, despite repeated warnings from staff.
And opinion polls have been predicting gains for the far-right Vox party, which lies at the opposite end of the political spectrum.
Sanchez’s election bid
But in late September, images of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal being evicted from her apartment in Madrid went viral. The episode triggered uproar, channelling discontent over the cost of living and the housing crisis.
Sanchez seized the momentum and called for snap elections: social policy was at the centre of the debate, and the party was hoping to build an electoral campaign. It had even prepared a series of measures dubbed “Social Tuesdays” to make it clear what its agenda was focused on. His campaign was upbeat.
Then the train crash happened, shifting the campaign away from the social issues the PSOE had hoped to highlight.
The government, Roman explained, would now have to spend more time defending its record and answering questions about accountability. And it could make it harder for Sanchez to mobilise the hundreds of thousands of undecided left-wing voters he had hoped to bring to the polls with his social agenda, she said.
His PSOE appeared to gain some traction in early October, but was still trailing in most surveys. The latest polls this week show the Socialists at 26.7 percent, still behind the PP at 31.5 percent. The far-right Vox party remains in third position at 19.1 percent.

Armenian Parliament erupts into mass brawl (VIDEO)

Armenian Parliament erupts into mass brawl (VIDEO)
The Armenian Parliament erupted into an all-out brawl, with ruling-party and opposition lawmakers trading punches and hurling chairs as deepening political divisions spill into violence.
The confrontation broke out on Thursday after MP Taron Chakhoyan, from Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s ruling Civil Contract party, launched personal attacks against the family of Narek Karapetyan, the head of the opposition Strong Armenia faction, during a debate over the party’s election campaign.
Opposition lawmakers approached the podium, triggering a scuffle that rapidly descended into a mass brawl. Footage from the chamber shows Deputy Speaker Vahagn Aleksanyan, a ruling-party member, throwing a chair at opposition MPs. Lawmakers also reportedly wielded bottles, and one deputy was knocked to the floor.
At least one opposition MP suffered a bloody nose, and another had his clothes torn, according to local media. The session was eventually suspended, but clashes reportedly continued in the corridors before security personnel intervened.
Pashinyan blamed the opposition, defending his party’s lawmakers and describing their response as “proportionate and appropriate.”
“If anyone thinks they can lay a hand on a member of parliament and hit them, we will simply break that hand. If necessary, we will break it with a chair,” the prime minister said.
Opposition lawmakers accused Deputy Speaker Ruben Rubinyan, who was presiding over the session, of allowing the violence to unfold by failing to intervene. Armenia Faction leader Anna Grigoryan accused the ruling party of deliberately provoking the confrontation and suggested that the incident may have been orchestrated.
The parliament is no stranger to fistfights – the clash on Thursday is reportedly the third this month. The incident comes amid an increasingly bitter struggle between Pashinyan’s government and its opponents following June’s disputed parliamentary elections.
Post-election power struggle
Pashinyan’s pro-EU Civil Contract party won a decisive victory in the elections in June, which was viewed as a referendum on Armenia’s geopolitical future. Two opposition blocs – billionaire Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia and former President Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance – entered parliament, while Prosperous Armenia narrowly missed out, helping Pashinyan retain a constitutional majority.
All three opposition parties favor closer ties with Russia, a key trade partner that supplies discounted gas. Pashinyan has pursued EU integration while continuing to reap the economic benefits of ties with Moscow.
The opposition has rejected the election results, alleging widespread vote-rigging and pressure on public-sector employees and military personnel. Pashinyan has escalated his attacks on his rivals, calling them “criminal oligarchs” who serve foreign interests. He claimed that the newly elected opposition emerged through “absolutely illegal actions” and threatened to bar them from political activity.
Opposition figures condemned the moves as a political crackdown, citing criminal cases against prominent rivals and plans to nationalize Strong Armenia founder Samvel Karapetyan’s electricity distribution network. They also accuse the West of giving Pashinyan free rein to suppress dissent in exchange for his anti-Russia pivot.
The political crisis is compounded by Pashinyan’s escalating confrontation with the Armenian Apostolic Church, one of the country’s most influential institutions and a critic of his government. Pashinyan accused senior clergy of political meddling and having ties to foreign intelligence services, including Russia, which the church denies.
The rift deepened in August with the unprecedented criminal prosecution of the church’s supreme leader, Catholicos Karekin II. Opposition and church figures denounced the case as part of a broader crackdown on dissent.

AstraZeneca profit jumps 23% on cancer drugs as it unveils major savings plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:17:41 UTC
21:17:41 KST

AstraZeneca's net profit jumped 23% in the third quarter on booming sales of its cancer drugs, as the British drugmaker unveiled a programme to save $1.5 billion (€1.34bn) a year to invest back into developing new medicines.
AstraZeneca, Britain's biggest pharmaceutical company, said on Friday that its profit after tax rose 23% to $3.12 billion (€2.79bn) for the July to September period, driven largely by its cancer treatments.
That marks a sharp pick-up from the rise of just over 2% in the previous quarter. The firm also launched a plan to generate $1.5 billion (€1.34bn) in annual savings, which it intends to reinvest mainly in the drugs it has in development.
Revenue grew 7% to $16.2 billion (€14.5bn).
Oncology, its biggest business, accounted for 48% of the total, with sales up 17% to $7.8 billion (€6.99bn), led by lung cancer drug Tagrisso and immunotherapy Imfinzi. Core earnings per share, which exclude items such as restructuring costs and the amortisation of acquired drugs, rose 17% to $2.79.
The savings drive, called Reshaping for Sustainable Growth, will cost up to $2 billion (€1.79bn) in one-off restructuring charges and is due to be largely complete by the end of 2029.
AstraZeneca said the savings would be reinvested in the company, principally in its pipeline of new drugs, as it plans to "redeploy resources" across its existing business to back more than 180 projects in development.
Such restructuring could mean job cuts, though none have been announced.
"With multiple potential blockbuster assets in late-stage development and transformative technologies scaling rapidly, we are on track to deliver our 2030 ambition," CEO Pascal Soriot said in a statement.
Generics and China weigh
The growth came despite pressure on older medicines.
Sales of Farxiga, its treatment for diabetes, heart and kidney disease, fell 25% to $1.6 billion (€1.43bn) after cheaper generic versions hit the US market, while blood thinner Brilinta also lost patent protection.
AstraZeneca is also facing volume-based procurement in China, a state bulk-buying scheme that forces drugmakers to cut prices in exchange for large orders.
The company confirmed its outlook for 2026, expecting revenue to grow by a mid-to-high single-digit percentage and core earnings per share by a low double-digit percentage, excluding currency swings.
It remains on track for its target of $80 billion (€71.7bn) in annual revenue by 2030, compared with almost $59 billion (€52.9bn) in 2025, and expects half of that to come from the US.
The company has been leaning further into the American market, adding a direct share listing in New York in February, while also pledging to invest $15 billion (€13.4bn) in China by 2030.
It has reported 12 positive results from late-stage trials so far this year, and is also developing a weight-loss treatment to compete with drugs such as Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro.
AstraZeneca shares were up over 4.5% in early trading on Friday.

Estonian Drama Theater limits ticket sales

Estonian Drama Theater limits ticket sales
The Estonian Drama Theater has limited ticket sales to four per customer for a single performance, down from the previous eight, but an increase on the two tickets announced earlier this week.
The theater changed its proposed policy of two tickets per performance after an outcry from customers earlier this week.
"Since many theatergoers contacted us, we decided to change the restriction so that instead of two tickets, four tickets can be purchased for a single performance at a time. Hopefully, this will allow us to ensure a good purchasing experience for more people while not excessively restricting theater visits by families and groups of friends," the Drama Theater said in a newsletter.
Newspaper Postimees reported on Thursday that the theater would also discontinue group bookings because waiting lists are extremely long.
Drama Theater marketing manager Katre Väli said the decision had to be made because of exceptionally high demand.
"The waiting lists for group bookings for the most popular productions listed on our website are four to six years long, with thousands of people interested. We generally suspend group bookings when calculations show that fulfilling the orders would extend beyond two seasons," she explained.
Väli could not say when group bookings for these productions would reopen.
Group bookings started at 20 tickets, with a maximum of 50 tickets available for reservation.

China successfully launches stealthy UAV from Sichuan amphibious assault ship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:14:58 UTC
21:14:58 KST

SHANGHAI, October 30. /TASS/. Sailors of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) successfully tested the launch and landing of the GJ-21 (Gongji-21) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) from the Sichuan multi-purpose amphibious assault ship, the Xinhua news agency reported.
The tests mark a breakthrough in the development of China’s amphibious assault ships and demonstrate the PLA Navy’s capability to launch and recover fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles from large naval combat platforms, the agency said.
The GJ-21 is a heavy, low-observable, shipborne reconnaissance and strike UAV. It is 12.2 meters long and 14.4 meters wide.
The Sichuan was launched in Shanghai in December 2024. Its maximum displacement exceeds 40,000 tons. It features a flight deck that spans the entire length of the ship. It is the first of China’s Type 076 ships. The Sichuan is equipped with an electromagnetic catapult and an arresting gear. It can carry fixed-wing UAVs, helicopters, and amphibious assault vehicles. The ship is designed for amphibious and long-distance maritime operations.

Novaya Gazeta has announced it is shutting down. We never thought we would have to write these words — and yet that’s the reality. The story of the most important independent news outlet in modern Russia has come to an end.
Novaya was a unique newspaper from its founding to its final day. No other newsroom has a record like this: an extraordinary body of investigative reporting and exceptional journalism, an impressive array of awards — including Dmitry Muratov’s Nobel Peace Prize — and a list of journalists who were murdered.
By every measure, it was the best media outlet in Russian history. In a testament to that distinction, Novaya Gazeta was the only major independent outlet that kept operating inside the country after 2022, in defiance of wartime censorship, dictatorship, and even the instinct for self-preservation.
We admire your loyalty to the profession. We thank you for everything. And we promise to continue your work for as long as we can. We also know that you are unbreakable and never give up. You’ll find a way, as you have so many times before.
That is why we refuse to say goodbye to you. Novaya Gazeta will not disappear.
Thank you.

Britain bars entry to Swedish academic ahead of appearance with Palestine Action founder
LONDON, Oct 30 - Swedish climate academic Andreas Malm said on Friday he had been denied entry to Britain, where he was due to speak alongside the co-founder of Palestine Action, a group banned as a terrorist organisation.
Malm, an academic at Sweden's Lund University, has been a vocal critic of Israel and expressed strong support for the Palestinian movement.
Britain's Home Office (interior ministry) said it did not comment on individual cases.
Malm told the BBC's Radio 4 he had received a message from the Home Office saying his "presence in the UK is not conducive to the public good" with no further clarification.
He said he suspected he was barred because he had been due to appear at an event next Wednesday organised by a socialist magazine alongside Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori, where he said he had been due to speak about the war in Iran. He added he had not publicly endorsed, promoted or financially supported Palestine Action.
"I've been going back and forth to the UK for years, for decades, to do my scientific work, my archival research, my participation in conferences. This is the main purpose of my visit to the UK this time too," Malm said.
"What this means is that I am banned from doing my work as an intellectual, as an academic."
Asked by the BBC whether the ban could be linked to previous comments he made calling Hamas's October 7 attack on Israel "an act of liberation", Malm said "it could be".
Malm is most known for his book "How to Blow Up a Pipeline", which argues radical action is necessary to stop fossil fuel extraction.
Britain's Supreme Court is due to hear an appeal next week on the proscription of Palestine Action under terrorism laws, which has made expressing support for the group a criminal offence.
Earlier in October, Irish novelist Sally Rooney said her books will no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.
In June, Britain blocked left-wing Turkish-American media personality Cenk Uygur and his nephew Hasan Piker from entering the country to speak at events.
Britain has also imposed travel bans on far-right Israeli ministers and banned Israelis from attending a prestigious London defence studies college. REUTERS

Iran’s IRGC navy says two tankers stopped south of Hormuz after incidents
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:10:29 CET
21:10:29 KST

DUBAI, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Friday that four oil tankers had caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, while attempting to use what it described as unauthorised routes, Iranian state media reported.
In its latest statement, the IRGC Navy said a fourth vessel, a tanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, had hit a mine, suffered a powerful explosion and was burning.
An IRGC Navy statement had said earlier that one of the tankers, which was also carrying 2 million barrels of crude oil, had hit a naval mine.
Reuters was unable to immediately verify the statement.
Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said it had received a report of an incident in the Strait of Hormuz. A verified source told the agency that a crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while completing an outbound transit of the waterway.
Earlier, UKMTO said it had received a report that a vessel was hit by an unknown projectile on its port side about 40 nautical miles (74 km) south of Iran’s Lavan Island, causing a fire on board. The crew were reported safe and there was no reported environmental impact, it said.
Lavan Island lies in the Gulf, off Iran’s southern coast. It was not immediately clear whether the vessels cited by UKMTO were among the four tankers referred to by the IRGC Navy.
Tensions have persisted in the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which around one-fifth of global oil supplies pass, since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran at the end of February.
State media said Iranian forces also downed and captured an MQM-170 US drone over Iran’s Qeshm island near the Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate reaction from the US military and Reuters could not independently verify the report.
Iran also said it had destroyed an unmanned US vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
But the US military’s Central Command denied this and said in a statement on X: “All U.S. military unmanned surface vessels in the Middle East are accounted for, including a squadron of advanced sea drones on patrol in the Strait of Hormuz.”

As US airlines deploy AI pricing tools, start-ups help travellers cash in on fare drops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:10:00 UTC
21:10:00 KST

As US airlines deploy AI pricing tools, start-ups help travellers cash in on fare drops
- US airlines are using AI to improve pricing, while start-ups like JetBack, Junova and Refare use AI to spot fare drops and claim refunds or credits for travellers.
- The services grew after Covid-19, when airlines removed many change fees, making it easier to recover price differences on non-refundable tickets. JetBack says it has recovered US$2.4 million.
- The model may face risks if airlines tighten rules. Alaska Airlines has already stopped honouring fare drops through customer service, worrying start-ups that other carriers may follow.
AI generated
NEW YORK – US airlines are turning to artificial intelligence to help maximise revenue from airfares. Now startups are putting AI to work on the other side of the transaction, helping passengers automatically claw back savings when ticket prices fall.
Companies including JetBack, Junova and Refare monitor fares after customers have booked and seek refunds or flight credits when prices drop. Their pitch is simple: airlines have spent decades building sophisticated pricing systems, while travellers have largely been left to check the prices themselves.
The services are emerging as airlines face scrutiny over how they use AI in pricing. While AI’s role in aviation continues to evolve, airlines are using the technology to monitor competitors’ fares while testing applications aimed at optimising pricing and improving flight operations.
The use of AI has garnered questions from lawmakers over whether the technology could harm consumers if it is used to set individualised pricing based on consumer data and behaviour.
For travellers, the startups are exploiting a change that followed the Covid-19 pandemic, when many US airlines eliminated change fees on most non-refundable tickets as travellers grew hesitant to book travel amid testing requirements, quarantine rules and border closures.
That means a passenger who buys a ticket for US$500 (S$638) may be able to claim the difference if the fare later falls to US$400, without additional charges, though airline policies vary.
“Airlines have spent decades investing in incredibly sophisticated pricing technology, while consumers are still expected to do the equivalent of refreshing a webpage and crossing their fingers,” said Bryan Dubno, founder of JetBack, which says it has recovered US$2.4 million in credits and refunds since launching in early 2025. “AI doesn’t have to be a one-sided advantage.”
Junova said that among 10,000 flights it monitored from September 2025 through July 2026, about 22% experienced at least one fare drop. About 40% of those saw prices decline more than once, illustrating how rapidly fares can change after a passenger has booked.
Airfares fluctuate like stock market prices, said AJ Brustein, Junova’s co-founder: “They go up and down, often up. But when it goes down, you have an opportunity to get that difference in price back.”
Junova and Refare charge customers only when they recover money, taking 20% and 25%, respectively, of the savings, while JetBack charges US$100 a year.
Airlines can change the rules
The business model, however, depends heavily on airlines continuing to accommodate fare drops without imposing large penalties. The Covid-19 crisis weakened a revenue stream for US air carriers, which collected US$2.84 billion in reservation cancellation or change fees in 2019.
Before the pandemic, change fees on many non-refundable tickets made recovering a modest fare decline impractical. The widespread elimination of those fees created an opening for companies that can continuously monitor prices and pursue credits on customers’ behalf.
That opening could close. In early October, Alaska Airlines stopped honouring fare drops through customer service, instead directing travellers seeking to capture a lower fare to cancel and rebook under the applicable fare rules.
Alaska said it does not charge cancellation fees for its main and first-class fares. But its basic economy tickets are eligible for a credit of 50% of the ticket value when cancelled at least 14 days prior to departure.
“We’re fearful that we could be shut out if other airlines go that route,” said Justin Dombrow, founder of Refare.
Airlines may nevertheless have reason to tolerate the services. Many fare adjustments on non-refundable tickets are issued as credits rather than cash, requiring passengers to spend the money with the same carrier.
“Depending on how you look at it, the refunds are still a win for the airline,” Brustein said. REUTERS

King Charles’ sorrow over slavery faces test as reparations movement gains ground
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:09:49 CET
21:09:49 KST

By Sam Tabahriti
LONDON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - King Charles has since 2022 expressed sorrow for the suffering caused by slavery without crossing a line that Britain has long resisted: an apology.
That balancing act is likely to be tested at next week’s Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, where Caribbean leaders who back a reparations campaign through the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) are expected to press their case.
Buckingham Palace has indicated Charles would not apologise on behalf of Britain, which has repeatedly ruled out financial reparations over its role in the transatlantic slave trade.
Speaking in the Bahamas on Tuesday ahead of a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting that begins on Sunday, Charles said it was “only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past,” and said leaders from affected countries would discuss the issue at the summit.
But Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas’ National Reparations Committee, said that did not go far enough. “We do not need more carefully crafted words about healing,” she said in a statement. “We need action equal with the scale of the harm inflicted.”
On Friday, about 15 people protested ahead of the king’s arrival in Georgetown, Guyana. They gathered outside the Umana Yana, a conical palm-thatched hut originally built for the 1972 Non-Aligned Foreign Ministers Conference, where Charles later delivered a speech.
“It’s an opportunity to try to impress upon him this historic responsibility for what took place here,” said Terence Campbell, a member of parliament for the opposition APNU, who stood among the protesters holding a banner that read: “No apology will return what was stolen. Reparations now!”
ROYAL LINKS TO SLAVERY UNDER SCRUTINY
From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations, according to the Transatlantic Slave Trade Database.
Alan Lester, a University of Sussex historian whose research spans the legacies of slavery and empire, said opponents of the reparations movement had “successfully weaponised” the idea that reparations simply meant writing a cheque, an idea that few Western governments will countenance.
Instead, Caribbean leaders often frame their demands in terms of debt relief, development finance, education, healthcare and climate resilience, measures they say would address inequalities rooted in slavery and colonialism.
“I think King Charles III is in a difficult position because you can express sorrow about something, but an apology goes much further,” royal commentator Afua Hagan said.
Buckingham Palace said in 2023 that Charles had given his support to research that was examining the monarchy’s links to slavery after the Guardian newspaper reported on a document showing a historical connection.
In a more recent finding, independent researcher Desiree Baptiste told Reuters her forthcoming book, “George IV, Empire, and Objects of Prestige,” would cite House of Lords papers and other British government records showing that profits derived from enslaved labour helped fund furniture and decorative work commissioned by George IV at royal residences.
In a response, the Royal Collection Trust, a charity that maintains and displays artworks and historic objects held in trust by the king, said constant research helped it to keep its records “continually under review in order to improve the information presented on an object or subject”.
(Reporting by Sam Tabahriti; Aditional reporting by Kemol King and Isabel Infantes in Georgetown; Editing by Sharon Singleton, Xevi Fontdegloria and Raul Cortes)

Slovakia has reopened the investigation into the transfer of MiG-29s to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Slovakia’s chief prosecutor ordered the investigation into the transfer of MiG-29 fighter jets and KUB systems to Ukraine in 2023 to be reopened. The case had previously been closed.
Slovakia’s chief prosecutor ordered a new investigation on October 30 into the transfer of MiG-29 fighter jets and air defense systems to Ukraine by the country’s previous government, reopening an investigation that had been completed earlier this year. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico’s current government, which is pursuing a more pro-Russian foreign policy and has halted military aid to Ukraine, has repeatedly criticized the transfer, made in 2023, the publication writes.
The decision reopens a criminal case at the heart of the dispute between Fico’s government and its predecessors over military support for Ukraine.
Fico said the donation had made the country dependent on allied air force patrols, while a senior official from his party called it sabotage.
The country’s chief prosecutor, Maroš Žilinka, said on Facebook on Friday that he had ordered a new investigation because the previous one had ended prematurely.
"In the course of the preliminary proceedings, the facts were not established to the extent necessary for a decision to be made," he said.
When concluding the previous investigation in February this year, Bratislava regional prosecutor Rastislav Remeta said that a dozen Soviet-era MiG-29 fighter jets and KUB surface-to-air missile systems were obsolete, not fully operational, and lacked pilots and missiles. He said their donation did not constitute a crime.
The then-defense minister, Jaroslav Naď, denies any wrongdoing.
The case illustrates Slovakia’s deeply polarized political scene, where Fico has repeatedly accused his predecessors of bringing cases against his party when he was in opposition, the publication notes.

Georgia midterm elections: Why this is a key US battleground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:09:03 UTC
21:09:03 KST

Georgia midterm elections: Why this is a key US battleground
Obama and Trump campaign in key battleground state ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
Georgia is among a number of key “swing” or “battleground” states being fought for hardest in the run-up to the United States midterm elections next week.
The southern state has been so competitive in recent federal election cycles that its three most recent Senate matchups went to runoffs.
Both the Republican and the Democratic parties have spent considerable time and resources trying to win the state during the closing stretch of their campaigns.
US President Donald Trump and former US President Barack Obama both held rallies in Georgia this week, as the parties present their closing messages ahead of next week’s vote.
Why is Georgia such a key state for the midterms?
Georgia is a major focus for Trump, and he has campaigned twice in Dalton, Georgia, in the past two weeks.
The state is a source of personal grievance for the president, primarily because it was where he disputed his preelection loss in 2020.
Trump refused to concede to Joe Biden following his defeat but failed to overturn the results in several states, including Georgia.
In January, Trump urged a Georgia official to recalculate the state’s presidential election results in his favour. Trump said “I just want to find 11,780 votes, which is one more than we have”.
In 2023, Trump and others were charged with attempting to overturn the 2020 US election loss in Georgia. That case was dismissed “in its entirety” after Trump was returned to office.
During his re-election campaign in 2024, Trump revived unfounded claims that his loss in 2020 was the result of “massive fraud”, despite audits which upheld Biden’s win.
In 2024, Georgia voted for Trump by a 2.2 percentage point margin. It was the 28th largest margin for Trump among the 50 states, leaving the state as one which could go either way this time, observers say.
What does polling in Georgia show?
Georgia will be voting for its Governor, one senator and its House representatives.
For the Senate, incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff has a solid lead of 52.6 percent to Republican Mike Collins’ 42.4 percent, according to MS NOW polling averages.
Polls indicate a tight Governor’s race, however. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is up against Republican Rick Jackson. They are running to succeed Republican Brian Kemp, who cannot seek a third term.
Voters will also be choosing representatives for Georgia’s 14 congressional districts as well as Lieutenant Governor, Attorney General and Secretary of State. Of the 14 representatives Georgia sends to Congress, nine are currently Republican, while five are Democratic.
Who are the key contenders for the Senate?
Incumbent Ossoff is seeking a second term as a Georgia senator. He won his seat in 2021, narrowly defeating Republican Senator David Perdue in a run-off. He was the youngest Democrat elected to the Senate in almost four decades and Georgia’s first Jewish senator.
He is campaigning on affordability, healthcare and government accountability.
Ossoff has accused Trump and his allies of corruption and conflicts of interest in many of his rallies.
Corruption was also a theme for Obama during his rally in Georgia on Wednesday, in which he said Trump was “very much focused on enriching himself and his family and his cronies”.
“The guy has made billions of dollars while in office. We have never seen a president so intent on selling favours like this,” he said, echoing a speech he made days earlier in Michigan, another swing state.
Ossoff’s Republican rival won his nomination in June in a run-off. Collins is campaigning on Trump’s agenda, immigration enforcement and smaller government.
During his last-minute rallies ahead of next week’s midterms, Trump has repeatedly said he will reward states that vote for him.
Trump told Collins he can call him whenever he wants help for his state. But he warned that if Georgia reelects Ossoff, it could be another story.
Trump acted out a hypothetical scenario at his rally where Ossoff called to ask for money for his state, with Trump responding, “I don’t give a damn what he wants.”
NBC, which carries out its own polling, has forecast Georgia as “Likely Democratic”.
Who are the key contenders for governor?
NBC polling points to a potential “toss-up” between the Democratic and Republican parties.
Former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic contender, is campaigning on affordability, healthcare access, education funding, and environmental regulation. Her campaign says she aims to “deliver for working families and bring steady leadership to Georgia in the midst of uncertainty and chaos coming from Washington”.
If she wins, she would become the first black woman elected governor in the US.
Bottoms is up against 72-year-old billionaire Rick Jackson, who has accused her of failing to deal with crime during her tenure as Atlanta mayor.
Jackson has spent more than $200m of his own money on advertisements featuring demonstrations and violence in Atlanta following the killing of Rayshard Brooks, an unarmed black man, by a white Atlanta police officer in 2020. The killing happened while Bottoms was Atlanta mayor.
Americans have been voting for weeks, with 40 million ballots already cast, according to the University of Florida’s election lab. A total of 45.9 million Americans voted early in the last midterm elections in 2022.

Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:06:56 UTC
21:06:56 KST

Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).
Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.
The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.
Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.
The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.
It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.
Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.
The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.
Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.
“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

China News Service: We notice that the Committee on Disarmament and International Security (First Committee) of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly approved resolutions on “Further practical measures for the prevention of an arms race in outer space” and “No first placement of weapons in outer space.” The vision of a community with a shared future for humanity was again included in the resolutions. Could you share more details?
Guo Jiakun: China advocates the peaceful use and safety of outer space, and promotes the building of a community with a shared future for humanity in the domain of outer space. Since 2017, China has, together with relevant countries, jointly submitted to the First Committee of the UN General Assembly each year the two resolutions on “Further practical measures for the prevention of an arms race in outer space” and “No first placement of weapons in outer space.” China firmly opposes the weaponization of and any arms race in outer space, and calls for negotiations on an international legal instrument to safeguard lasting peace and common security and build a community with a shared future for humanity in the domain of outer space.
The First Committee of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly once again adopted the above resolutions by a majority. This marks the tenth consecutive year that the vision of a community with a shared future for humanity has been incorporated into UNGA resolutions on outer space. It fully demonstrates that the vision conforms to the trend of the times and meets the common expectations of the international community, and has become an international public good of major significance in today’s world. The recently released China’s Position on Strengthening Outer Space Governance is consistent with this vision. China stands ready to work with the international community to jointly build a peaceful, secure, open and cooperative outer space, and to ensure that the outcomes of outer space exploration benefit all humanity.
