====================================================================================================

Robotize this: Despite apocalyptic forecasts, AI will make society richer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:52:15 UTC
20:52:15 KST

In his controversial new book, Russian economist Igor Lipsitz predicts that the adoption of AI will lead to a global catastrophe in the labor market. In the author’s (highly debatable) view, growth in labor productivity will not offset this reduction. Of course, the emergence of new technologies does make some professions redundant, but only because people and machines begin to perform more tasks in less time — the very definition of an increase in productivity. As a result, society gains the opportunity either to increase overall consumption or to shorten working hours: a repeating pattern clearly visible in the history of technological development. In the end, society as a whole reaps the fruits of progress, even if any technological transition does indeed produce both winners and losers. Still, it is not technology that is to blame for this unevenness, but inefficient institutions. After all, on average, high-tech economies tend to distribute income significantly more evenly than commodity-based ones.
Lessons learned
Humanity’s historical experience shows that new technologies and automation do not bring about total unemployment. Studies of long-term labor market trends confirm the benefits of automation.
In the U.S., for example, in the year 1900, 41% of all workers were employed in the agricultural sector, but by 2000, this figure had fallen to 2%. Without question, the appearance of combines and other specialized machinery drove people out of the fields, but they did not simply become unemployed. Instead, they moved to factories and the service sector, which were growing rapidly at the time. In addition, mechanization sharply lowered food prices, leaving more money to be devoted to satisfying other needs.
In another example, the invention of the standard shipping container in the 1950s cut the cost of loading one metric ton of cargo from $5.86 to $0.16, and the profession of dockworker disappeared almost entirely. However, shipping became so cheap that its positive impact on world trade exceeded that of all postwar international agreements combined.
After that, the advent of personal computers led to the closure of typing pools, and with the appearance of automatic telephone exchanges, telephone switchboard operators disappeared. At the same time, however, tens of millions of new jobs were created: for programmers, systems analysts, marketers, and designers.
Data gathered by Our World in Data show that from the start of the common era up to 1820, average world income per person remained within the range of 1,100–1,300 international dollars a year. The turning point came during the Industrial Revolution — thanks to the mechanization of labor, output outpaced population growth for the first time. As a result, in the two centuries that followed, global GDP per capita grew by a factor of 15, to exceed $18,000.
In the countries that spearheaded industrialization (Great Britain, and then the U.S. and Western European nations), the gap turned out to be even more impressive, with per capita GDP growing 25–30 times from 1820 to today (from $2,000–$3,000 to a present-day $60,000–$75,000).
Contrary to stereotypes, statistics show that the multiple growth of output over the past two centuries was accompanied not by increased “exploitation of workers,” but by a steady reduction in working hours and an increase in paid leisure.
In the 19th century, the prevailing opinion was that factory production had to rely on continuous and exhausting labor. In the 1870s, the working day in Europe and the U.S. usually lasted 10–12 hours, with a six-day workweek and no right to vacation. Workers agreed to such conditions simply because the alternative of peasant labor in the fields was even less attractive.
However, as mechanization and automation progressed, this trajectory changed. Today, in most developed economies, average working time has almost halved, with a standard five-day 40-hour workweek (and as low as 35 in some countries). Benefits appeared that did not exist in the preindustrial era: paid vacation and maternity leave, sick leave, public holidays, a ban on child labor, and old-age pensions.
So what is the origin of the fear that the development of algorithms will leave almost half of the planet’s population without work? This is a misunderstood estimate released in 2013 by University of Oxford researchers, who argued that 47% of jobs in the U.S. are at risk of disappearing because of AI. However, the researchers themselves stressed that 47% is merely the share of work tasks that computers are technically capable of performing, and not at all a forecast that half of people would actually be laid off. In other words, researchers examined the fundamental possibility of replacing a human with an algorithm in individual operations, not real job losses.
Later, OECD researchers approached the question by breaking down each occupation into specific repetitive operations. Having studied the structure of work of thousands of workers in 21 developed countries, the researchers found that people holding seemingly identical positions often perform fundamentally different tasks. Their calculation showed that the real risk of full replacement by machines applies not to 47%, but to only 9% of jobs, ranging from 6% in South Korea to 12% in Austria. For the vast majority of people, technology does not abolish an entire profession but takes over routine functions and complements human labor.
The real risk of full replacement by machines applies not to 47% but to only 9% of jobs, ranging from 6% in South Korea to 12% in Austria
In the history of the world, no country has achieved sustained growth in its population’s incomes without regularly adopting major technical inventions, such as the steam engine, electricity, the internal combustion engine, and computers. But technology is not the only growth factor, as it delivers results only when combined with quality education, intelligent investment, and functioning government institutions. After all, a transition period is always accompanied by difficulties that require effective management.
How AI is changing the labor market
Artificial intelligence largely repeats the path of earlier technological revolutions, but it features several fundamental differences. The main similarity is that technologies rarely destroy professions instantly. Any job consists of many small operations, and a machine that performs two or three of them cannot replace the human specialist completely.
Experts at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) stress that automating individual tasks changes the structure of the workday, as its calculations showed that 27% of jobs in developed countries are in occupations with a high share of potentially automatable operations. However, even in those, algorithms take over only 20% to 40% of specific routine duties, while tasks requiring critical judgment, communication, and personal responsibility remain with humans, who continue to be responsible for goal-setting and decision-making in disputed or nonstandard situations.
Humans continue to be responsible for goal-setting and decision-making in disputed or nonstandard situations
The link between falling costs and rising demand is clearly visible in the market for language translation and digital services. According to industry associations, the appearance of machine translation systems cut the cost of rough processing one page of text by more than 70%. However, rather than destroying the translator’s profession, it led to a significant increase in the volume of material processed: companies began translating dozens of times more internal documentation, instructions, and customer reviews. As a result, overall employment in localization and editing grew, shifting from mechanical translation to review, semantic adaptation, and fact-checking.
The falling price of services such as writing software code and performing legal and financial consulting tasks makes them accessible to those who could not afford them in the past. As a result, the market expands, and demand for labor remains.
Just like previous technologies, AI needs time to lead to an explosive rise in macroeconomic indicators. Economist Paul David described this pattern in a 1990 study by using the electrification of factories as an example. Three decades passed between the appearance of reliable electric motors in the 1880s and the surge in labor productivity in U.S. manufacturing. The share of electrified factories exceeded 50% only by 1920, and for many years annual growth in factory output did not exceed 1.5%.
At first, enterprises simply replaced the old steam boiler with a single electric motor, keeping the existing layout and belt drives in place. The real leap in productivity — to a record 5% a year — began only when factory owners rebuilt the environment from scratch, erecting spacious single-story shops, connecting an individual motor to each machine, and training managers in new work schemes.
The good news for us is, the adaptation process for today’s office and service workers is far milder than the upheaval of past eras. And this is an important difference between the adoption of AI and that of classical technologies. In the 19th century, the mass departure of illiterate peasants to factories was accompanied by severe disruption of everyday life and required the creation of school education.
Today, the threshold for changing career paths within the services and information sector is incomparably lower. Most specialists already possess basic literacy, as well as business communication and information-search skills, allowing them to master adjacent fields without the need to spend years retraining.
AI also differs from earlier technologies in that the algorithms themselves help people master new duties, taking on the role of a personal instructor. Studies of software assistants in corporate support showed that by using model prompts, even the least experienced employees tend to reach the level of qualified specialists in just two months rather than the previous transition time of six months, and the speed and success of their task resolution rose by 34%.
A micro effect and faith in the future
To assess the impact of AI on the modern economy objectively, researchers divide the available data into three different levels.
The first is direct measurements inside individual enterprises, where it is possible to empirically compare the performance of employees with and without a neural network.
The second is general statistics of national labor markets in the first years after the appearance of mass chatbots, showing changes in real wages, hours worked, and the hiring process.
The third is predictive macroeconomic calculations that model the technology’s impact on aggregate productivity and the country’s GDP years ahead.
The most accurate evidence of real productivity growth today has been obtained at the first level. A study published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics analyzed the work of a tech giant’s customer support department. The authors observed 5,172 employees and processed 3 million conversations during the phased rollout of a software assistant based on the GPT-3 model. In the baseline calculation, the number of successfully resolved inquiries per hour rose by 15%. The program essentially accumulated the best phrasing of experienced specialists and passed it on to newcomers.
PwC calculated that productivity growth is 40% higher in the companies that are most exposed to AI. Since 2022, the leaders in corporate AI use have tripled their lead in labor productivity growth over those that have barely adopted it. A link was also established with growth in wages and headcount, which both grow faster in companies where AI is widely used.
If we turn to labor market data for the first years of ChatGPT’s existence, the macroeconomic picture looks more restrained. Researchers studied survey data and the official state employment register in Denmark, presenting their findings in a paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research.
The analysis showed that although employees began actively using algorithms for tasks and rated their convenience positively, this had no statistically significant effect on their earnings or recorded working hours over the first two years.
At the same time, a study by the Stanford University Digital Economy Lab recorded a worrying trend in the U.S. labor market. While no mass layoffs have been observed, employment of people aged 22 to 25 in the occupations most exposed to automation has been lagging noticeably behind that of other fields.
By June 2026, the hiring gap with occupations less affected by the technology had reached 19%, though the Stanford authors stress that this link is descriptive and does not in itself prove the negative impact of algorithms. However, it still suggests that many young specialists are having a problematic start to their careers.
In long-term macroeconomic scenarios, researchers’ conclusions vary substantially. The OECD’s 2024 model suggests that the use of AI could bring the U.S. economy an additional annual labor productivity gain of 0.4–0.9 percentage points in ten years’ time. However, economist Daron Acemoglu offers a much more cautious estimate. By his baseline calculations, the increase in total factor productivity (TFP) over the decade will not exceed 0.66% — that is, less than 0.1% a year. Still, taking into account investment in fixed capital, the impact on overall GDP should be somewhat higher, Acemoglu notes.
To compare these models, it is important to use a single indicator: the OECD’s corresponding TFP calculation projects from 0.25 to 0.6 percentage points of additional growth each year — noticeably higher than Acemoglu’s estimate.
This discrepancy in figures illustrates the subject of present-day debates. Economists no longer argue about whether algorithms can speed up specific intellectual operations. After all, at the level of individual work tasks, the productivity gain has already been reliably recorded and measured. The main question now is how quickly and to what extent the benefit from innovative software at individual workplaces can translate to the national level.
In aggregate indicators — real wages, the number of jobs, and GDP growth — the effect has been barely noticeable. This inconsistency forces researchers to be more conservative in their forecasts, but this does not mean that the technology will not become the basis for powerful long-term development.
How robots close the demographic hole
The optimistic scenario for adopting artificial intelligence does not mean that the labor market will automatically adjust to the new conditions. A positive result is possible only through a combination of objective demographic processes and well-considered actions by the government and business, which can soften the loss of jobs and help people find new roles in the economy.
The demographic crisis in developed countries has become the most important backdrop for current automation. According to Employment Outlook 2025, the working-age population has begun to decline in many OECD countries. According to demographic forecasts, by 2030 the number of people aged 20 to 64 in European Union countries will fall by more than 10 million. In Japan and Germany, a shortage of workers is already holding back business development.
Under these conditions, adopting software algorithms helps maintain production volumes despite the growing shortage of personnel. However, the deficit of employees is distributed extremely unevenly across sectors and regions, affecting health care, home nursing care, construction, and technical trades most acutely. Meanwhile, generative models are most actively adopted in the corporate sector, marketing, basic programming, and workflow management.
Generative models are most actively adopted in the corporate sector, marketing, basic programming, and workflow management
An acute shortage of nurses or workers does not guarantee that a laid-off office analyst or lawyer can easily change profession and fill such a vacancy, meaning that the development of solutions to the imbalance in workforce availability across sectors requires a targeted government policy. Restrictions on the adoption of AI are not the answer, as attempts to ban technologies or force enterprises to keep unneeded jobs only slow productivity growth across the whole country.
An effective strategy consists of supporting specialists during their transition by providing guaranteed income insurance upon job loss, free retraining programs, and compensation of relocation costs to regions with high demand for personnel. For example, in Denmark about 20% of workers change profession or employer every year, but thanks to targeted payments and short-term retraining courses, this process does not lead to prolonged unemployment or a social crisis.
Young specialists require special attention. Since neural networks are taking over the drafting of simple reports, data collection, and the writing of initial code, the customary chain of internships is beginning to break. As studies show, when entry-level tasks disappear, companies need to rebuild their on-the-job training and mentoring programs. Instead of routine manual work, students and interns are taught to check generated results, set tasks for algorithms, and coordinate work chains.
Finally, a key role in distributing the benefits brought by new technologies belongs to market competition. If advanced models and infrastructure end up concentrated in the hands of a few monopolies, the savings from lower costs will remain inside these corporations in the form of excess profits. By contrast, active rivalry between companies forces businesses to lower selling prices for goods and services for end consumers.
Economic history shows that the decline in the cost of computing and communications in the late 20th century was the result of market competition — consumers got higher-quality and cheaper hardware and services, which in turn expanded the overall market and created new jobs in adjacent sectors.
In 2004, William Nordhaus calculated that thanks to market competition, the creators of new technologies capture only about 2% of the total economic value of their innovations, while the remaining 98% “flows” to consumers, who get much cheaper and better products — and therefore a higher purchasing power.
The authors of another study proved mathematically that the fall in prices of computer components (caused by progress in semiconductors and competition among manufacturers) triggered an avalanche-like accumulation of capital across the entire economy: in banking, logistics, trade, and media. This did not reduce aggregate demand for labor but led to an employment boom in adjacent sectors like distribution and applied software development.
How productivity turns into prosperity
A person’s well-being is determined by their real, not nominal, income. If algorithms lower the cost of a service without reducing its quality, the consumer benefits even if they do not receive a pay raise, because the same amount of money buys more. Here it is more appropriate to speak of relative cost: specific goods and services become cheaper compared with what they would have cost without the adoption of new tools.
Whether cost savings are reflected in the consumer price depends on external conditions — above all market competition, the absence of artificial scarcity, and the buyer’s real ability to switch to another supplier.
As already mentioned, from the end of the 19th century to the middle of the 20th, working time fell sharply in developed countries, but then the reduction slowed and almost stopped as society on the whole opted to direct further efficiency growth not toward a larger share of free time but toward the volume and quality of consumption (sophisticated medicine, higher education, electronics, improved housing, and the service sector).
High productivity opens room for wage growth. However, the median wage of an ordinary worker will not necessarily rise at the same pace. An OECD study showed that in 24 developed countries between 1995 and 2014, the gap between growth in labor productivity and growth in the real median wage averaged 13%. Productivity rose by about 28%, while median pay for workers rose by only 15%.
The study notes a fall in labor’s share of national income and a rise in market concentration — that is, high returns on capital go to a narrow circle of those who control the algorithms, computing power, databases, or the business that adopts the technologies. On the other hand, the development of technology creates new areas of activity that complement automated systems. If demand for people with scarce skills in such adjacent tasks grows, this helps sustain the overall level of employment and pay.
The fact that automation does not simply replace people but creates complementary tasks was shown by an MIT study. About 60% of all jobs in today’s developed economies did not exist at all in 1940. In fact, they arose directly as a result of technological growth.
A win for everyone or just for the chosen few?
Debates about who will benefit from the spread of artificial intelligence are dominated by two opposing views. Some consider growing inequality an inevitable consequence of the use of algorithms, while others attribute it solely to government policy. In reality though, the result depends on the joint action of technology players and public institutions.
The aforementioned Acemoglu and fellow economist Pascual Restrepo studied the impact of automation on the labor market in detail. In their 2022 paper, they showed that 50% to 70% of the growth in wage inequality in the U.S. over the period from 1980 to 2016 was linked to technological displacement — a situation in which machines and software replaced people in routine operations.
Computer systems do indeed devalue repetitive labor, but at the same time they raise the value of other skills, such as the ability to set a task correctly, to double-check a machine’s result, to take on legal or professional responsibility, and to communicate effectively with people. The adoption of algorithms stimulates demand for specialists who prepare quality data, train and adapt systems for narrow industries, or coordinate complex automated processes.
Another important change concerns the concentration of capital. Training large models and maintaining server infrastructure require billions in investment, which gives a gigantic head start to a small number of technology corporations. This monopoly, of course, is not guaranteed to last. The emergence of open and lightweight architectures, as well as a sharp drop in the cost of computing, creates accessible alternatives and prevents a narrow circle of players from closing off the market completely.
The viability of open-source architectures proves that total monopolization of the AI market is unlikely, and the gap in performance between commercial giants and open systems has rapidly narrowed on key benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval). This democratization is confirmed by statistics: by March 2026, total downloads of open AI models on Hugging Face reached 2 billion — an almost sixfold rise from the 340 million recorded a year earlier.
Today there is no need to pay for a ChatGPT subscription or other popular neural networks every month. Powerful artificial intelligence can be downloaded from the internet and run on a laptop retailing for $1,500. Such a program will work solely on your computer’s resources and deliver results on a par with paid services. The rule here is simple: the more powerful your “hardware,” the smarter and more complex a model you can install on it.
This opens huge opportunities for business. Any company can install free neural network models on its servers and build powerful, customized AI tools for its tasks without depending on giant corporations or purchasing expensive access. Everything works on-premises, securely and under full control. Thus open source forms a powerful market counterweight, turning basic AI tools into publicly available infrastructure.
Any company can install free neural network models on its servers and build powerful, customized AI tools for its tasks
Under such circumstances, antitrust regulation decides whether competition ultimately forces companies to lower prices for buyers or allows them to retain technological rent in the form of excess profits. Labor market rules are equally important — where there are strong trade unions, a transparent system of collective agreements, and a clear minimum wage level, the gain from productivity reaches ordinary workers faster. The experience of the Nordic countries shows that, with the same level of digital tool adoption as in the U.S., developed labor institutions keep income inequality at a significantly lower level.
The transition to new kinds of activity requires support from the tax system and social insurance. Accessible retraining programs allow people whose professional tasks are being automated to master adjacent fields without a catastrophic drop in income. An example is the Danish flexible employment system (flexicurity), in which ease of hiring and firing is combined with high government payments during the job search and mandatory training in new specialties.
Finally, rules of professional responsibility and quality control are critically important in industries such as health care, education, and law. Clear standards prevent service providers from lowering quality to save money, which protects consumers from the hidden costs of automation.
Studies show that high levels of technology adoption do not necessarily lead to income polarization, as inequality is consistently lower in high-tech states than in commodity-based countries. A high Economic Complexity Index, reflecting the diversity and technological knowledge intensity of the goods produced, usually means a lower level of income inequality. A high-tech economy requires distributed human capital, whereas a commodity-based one concentrates wealth around narrow rent-extraction chokepoints.
Countries with the highest density of technology and complex industrial production (Germany, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, the Nordic states) keep the Gini coefficient after taxes and transfers in the range of 0.26–0.33. However, large resource exporters (the oil monarchies of the Persian Gulf when migrants are counted, commodity economies of Latin America, and also Nigeria and Angola) show a Gini coefficient at the level of 0.42–0.55 and higher, with a colossal gap between the top decile and the rest of the population.
Overall, the history of technological development shows one stable pattern: the advent of more efficient tools has invariably made society richer as a whole. Even when entire professions became a thing of the past and individual workers had to change occupations or go without work, the resulting standard of living, the availability of goods, and the quality of everyday life for the majority invariably rose.
The foundation for well-founded optimism about artificial intelligence is built precisely on this proven mechanism. When new solutions make it possible to achieve the same or a better result at lower total cost, the economy gets a real surplus of resources. Even if it does not take advantage of the opportunity, society at least gains the chance to direct this surplus where it is needed most: raising the quality of medicine and education, increasing the affordability of goods, developing public services, and increasing free time. Attempts to hold on to every familiar job and preserve obsolete labor operations have historically always led to a dead end. Instead, adaptability is the key to prosperity.

‘dismantling should be designed, not improvised’: THISS studio on radical reuse in architecture

‘dismantling should be designed, not improvised’: THISS studio on radical reuse in architecture
from salvaged barn beams to an upturned boat, the london practice lets available materials shape the design while embracing uncertainty as part of the process.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
THISS STUDIO PUTS RADICAL REUSE BEFORE THE FINISHED DRAWING
An old barn, a pontoon boat, and a dismantled exhibition might seem like unlikely starting points for an architectural brief. For THISS Studio, they offer materials with which to begin designing. Founded by architects Tamsin Hanke and Sash Scott, the London practice works across cultural spaces, fashion, retail, and public installations, developing projects around the people and resources available to make them. Hanke’s research into low-impact design meets Scott’s interest in material experimentation and structural invention, an approach informed in part by his experience designing and flying high-performance kites. In an exclusive interview with designboom, Hanke explains how working with reclaimed components changes the architect’s role, the construction process, and the expectations attached to a finished space.
‘Primarily, reuse changes the order in which we design,’ Hanke tells designboom. A project can no longer be fully resolved on paper before its materials have been found. Instead, the studio establishes its intentions, gathers available stock, and revisits the design as that stock arrives, continuing to make adjustments during construction. Suppliers, craftspeople, and the dimensions and condition of individual components all influence the outcome. ‘With reuse, necessity means we can no longer be the sole authors of the outcome,’ he explains. This requires a strong concept and details capable of accommodating differences between materials. As Hanke puts it, ‘The work becomes a conversation rather than a monologue.’
SALVAGED TIMBER AND AN UPTURNED BOAT SHAPE NEW SPACES
That willingness to let existing objects redirect a project is visible in Barn Again, developed with architect Tom Svilans for the 2025 Copenhagen Architecture Biennial. Beams recovered from disused Norwegian barns are stacked into a tapering pavilion, retaining weathered surfaces and traces of previous connections. Designed for disassembly and further use, the structure gives those irregularities a place in its architectural expression. At Kiko Kostadinov’s London flagship, a pontoon boat installation by artist Ryan Trecartin provides a very different starting point: inverted railings become a ceiling-mounted support system for the shop’s shelving. ‘Often the material will suggest a move we would never have drawn from scratch,’ Hanke says. Both projects make that possibility tangible, finding a new spatial role for something with an established identity.
The same attention to available resources extends to Pergola, a public outdoor theater in Cairo developed with CLUSTER and Orient Productions. Its red structure incorporates materials from local reuse initiatives, including textiles made from recovered river plastic by VeryNile and recycled-plastic bricks from Rebloxx. Elsewhere, the studio’s work on PoliNations demonstrates how a temporary installation can continue beyond its original setting. First presented in Birmingham in 2022, its monumental tree structures returned at Glastonbury’s Shangri-La in 2025. These projects approach material life at different scales, from individual components to substantial structures that can be used again. ‘Reuse should never dilute the conceptual ambition of a project,’ Hanke argues. ‘We are happily now in a position in the industry where reuse is not even enough to drive the design, it is just part of the process.’
EXHIBITION DESIGN STARTS WITH WHAT HAPPENS AFTERWARDS
For THISS Studio, exhibition design brings these questions into particularly sharp focus. A display may occupy a gallery briefly, yet its construction can determine whether its materials remain useful long after visitors leave. ‘Exhibition design is never neutral,’ Hanke says. ‘It participates in the conversation the exhibition is having with the work, and that conversation is ideological, even political.’ Discussing work with the V&A, he describes an all-timber assembly without metal fixings, conceived to preserve the components for subsequent use. The design considers how pieces will come apart and what condition they will be in when they do. ‘As we see it, an exhibition should be an interruption in a material’s life not the end of it.’
Working with the Design Museum has prompted another shift in method: taking stock before drawing. The studio catalogued and assessed existing exhibition infrastructure, then tracked design decisions against that inventory, scrutinizing each proposed addition. ‘We worked more like archaeologists or archivists than conventional architects,’ Hanke explains. Here, the challenge becomes how to alter the experience of a space through careful adjustments to what is already available. ‘The creative challenge is restraint: making something feel new while touching as little as possible.’ The approach gives the less visible work of sorting, documenting, and evaluating materials a direct influence on the architecture visitors eventually encounter.
MAKING REUSE WORK MEANS CHANGING THE COMMISSION
Turning this approach into routine practice requires institutions to reconsider how they commission and fund design. Hanke identifies a tension between the certainty clients expect at the outset and the adjustments that reclaimed materials can demand later. Design programs need to accommodate those revisions, while funding must arrive early enough to secure stock before rapid exhibition construction schedules take over. He points to organizations such as Yes Make, which can source and hold materials while a design develops. ‘Money and materials need to move earlier,’ he says. A willingness to reuse therefore has practical consequences for budgets, procurement, and decision-making, well before the first component reaches the gallery.
Long-term galleries introduce further pressures, particularly around maintenance and durability. Hanke argues that these requirements need not exclude previously used materials, citing the studio’s research into the recovery of hardwoods and cross-laminated timber after extended service. What matters is designing both the assembly and its eventual separation with sufficient care. ‘Dismantling should be designed, not improvised. The materials should leave as a resource not as waste.’ For THISS Studio, the architect’s responsibility consequently extends beyond the appearance and performance of an installation during its public life. It includes organizing the collaboration that produces it and anticipating what its parts might become once the exhibition is over.
project info:
studio: THISS Studio | @thiss.studio
location: London, United Kingdom
This article is part of designboom’s POSTHUMAN UTOPIAS chapter, exploring what happens when humans are no longer the measure of all things. These stories rethink our relationship with the planet through interspecies architecture, living materials, regenerative landscapes and emerging technologies – learn more here! How the Binance hack happened and who was behind it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:50:49 UTC
20:50:49 KST

Investigators say several factors may have been involved, including a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, with signs pointing to North Korean actors being responsible.
Investigators are looking into how hackers stole $6.3 billion (€5.6 billion) from cryptocurrency exchange Binance in what is being described as the “biggest hack in history”, with signs suggesting a North Korean hacking group was behind the attack.
The figures involved dwarf those of previous crypto hacks, such as Bybit ($1.5 billion, €1.39 billion), Poly Network ($610 million, €545 million) and Ronin Network ($540 million, €482 million). The Binance incident is the latest in a series of cybersecurity incidents this October, with the expanding use of AI to find vulnerabilities largely being blamed by cybersecurity experts.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, controlling roughly 35% of the total crypto market share, according to the company. It functions as a key pillar of the crypto ecosystem, allowing people to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.
Like traditional currency exchanges, it keeps its customers’ coins in wallets it controls and processes withdrawals from a few of those wallets that stay online all the time.
The attack took place in just under four hours, as hackers gained access to several wallets via a compromised laptop and sent the funds from Binance's wallets to their own. Fortunately, Binance and its partners managed to freeze $2.7 billion (€2.4 billion) of the stolen funds, but the remaining funds sits untouched in the attacker’s wallets.
Here’s a timeline of how it happened:
Thursday
22:29 CET Binance says it is actively investigating reports of a potential security issue and reassures customers that their funds are “completely safe”, but warns of “scams”.
23:15 CET The company says it is conducting security checks, with withdrawals to resume as soon as the security issue is resolved.
Friday
00:06 CET The company suspends Binance Alpha trading, saying trading will resume once the security issue is resolved. It again reassures customers that their funds remain safe.
00:22 CET Binance makes its first announcement that assets are being affected. The company says it is aware of reports of frozen funds, clarifying that $2.54 billion (€2.26 billion) has currently been frozen. It adds that the figure may rise as it works closely with law enforcement and relevant authorities to trace and freeze assets.
01:13 CET Binance issues a statement saying it will “cover all losses” and that, as a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals have been temporarily suspended.
01:52 CET The company updates the frozen asset figure, which has risen to $3 billion (€2.68 billion).
03:25 CET Binance reveals the total impact is around $6.3 billion (€5.6 billion), with its investigation suggesting a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop may have been the entry point for an attack that allowed access to a service container and the submission of unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
The company adds that there is no evidence of any wallet private key leak. As a precaution, it has revoked the affected address authorisation and engaged law enforcement and blockchain partners to trace and recover funds, in addition to freezing accounts.
05:36 CET The company says in an update that the incident stems from multiple factors, and not just the compromised laptop.
09:47 CET Binance confirms its previous statement that a compromised laptop may have been the entry point, but says investigators have found other breaches in what was a “complex attack”. The company says it is on track to resume withdrawal services in 45 hours.
11:55 CET The company says it has begun recovering affected assets for users and will cover losses through company funds, with $6.34 billion (€5.66 billion) reserved to cover the incident.
“We will weather this storm,” says the company on social media platform X.
How did they do it?
Binance has said the incident was a “complex attack” that stemmed from multiple factors.
Its initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
Blockchain data infrastructure company Bitquery reports that Binance’s own withdrawal system signed away $6.3 billion (€5.6 billion) from 17 of its hot wallets in just under four hours, from Thursday night at 21:04 to 00:56 CET on Friday morning.
This prompted stablecoin issuers Tether, Circle and Arbitrum, along with four smaller issuers, to freeze $2.7 billion to prevent the funds from being stolen, says Bitquery, while Bitcoin confirmed that $3 billion had been frozen in total.
The attacker swapped another $729 million of stablecoins before the freezes began. In the end, the attacker still held roughly $3.1 billion, mostly in Ether and Bitcoin, according to Bitquery.
Bitquery also reports that the funds were sent to new addresses across nine blockchains, with Ethereum, Bitcoin and TRON hit hardest.
The company is still investigating the issue in liaison with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds.
Binance has temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed, revoked the affected address authorisation and engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds.
The company has said it will publish a detailed technical post-mortem after the investigation is complete and the facts have been verified.
It also plans to publish an updated Proof of Reserves after remediation is complete.
Who was behind it?
Blockchain intelligence and cybersecurity firm TRM Labs claims that TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group, was behind the attack.
“Based on robust on- and off-chain intelligence, we make this judgment with high confidence,” the company said in a statement.
It also points out that the FBI named the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion (€1.34 billion) Bybit hack in February 2025.

Feature: Australian community remembers Chinese student who died saving a life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:49:08 CST
20:49:08 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- For Justin Peng, Oct. 29 marks the anniversary of the day his life was saved.
Three years ago, Chinese student Jiang Antong lost his life while trying to rescue Peng from danger in the sea off Wollongong, Australia.
"I feel like I've been given a second chance at life," Peng told Xinhua on Thursday at the University of Wollongong, where a memorial ceremony was held to honor Jiang.
Jiang's parents, former classmates and people from various sectors in China and Australia gathered beneath a tree planted in his memory and laid flowers before a memorial stone.
On Sept. 1, Australia's Governor-General announced the 2026 bravery awards, with Jiang posthumously receiving the Commendation for Brave Conduct.
Born in 1995, Jiang arrived at the University of Wollongong in July 2023 to pursue a master's degree. On Oct. 29 that year, he saw Peng in danger while visiting Fairy Meadow Beach with several classmates. Jiang joined the rescue effort but was swept away by a rip current and lost his life.
Peng said that whenever he encounters difficulties, remembering Jiang's sacrifice gives him the courage to face them.
Jiang's father, Jiang Yu, said his son's actions reflected his habitual kindness and willingness to help others. During a cycling trip, Jiang once called an ambulance for an injured classmate and stayed with him in the hospital's emergency department throughout the night.
His parents also learned only after his death, while sorting through his belongings and talking with classmates, that he had donated blood and taken part in volunteer activities.
"There were so many things he never told us," Jiang Yu said, reflecting on the many admirable qualities they had discovered about their son after his death.
Over the past three years, the University of Wollongong has established a scholarship in Jiang's name and organized memorial football matches. Helen Partridge, the university's deputy vice-chancellor for education, said Jiang remained part of the university community and that even students who had never met him were sharing his story.
"We remember Antong not only for the courage he showed in a moment of danger, but also for his kindness, sincerity and love of life," said his former classmate Yan Lingzhi.
Wang Chunsheng, acting consul general of the Chinese Consulate General in Sydney, said the continued remembrance of Jiang by people in China and Australia reflected their shared appreciation of kindness, courage and life.
An Jingkun, Jiang's mother, said at the ceremony that the care shown by his teachers, classmates and friends had reassured his parents that their son had not been forgotten.
Jiang Yu said they had named their son Antong in the hope that he would grow up safely and, like a tall tree, provide shade for others.
Three years after it was planted in his memory, the tree on campus has grown taller, its branches spreading out.
"That tree is rooted in the soil of Wollongong. Like an invisible thread, it connects him to his mum and dad across the distance between us," An Jingkun said. ■

‘Removing Netanyahu is the most important thing’, Mustafa Barghouti tells Euronews

Changing the government in Israel is the top priority for Palestinians, according to one of the West Bank’s most prominent political figures. Arab parties hold the balance of power after Israel’s election and would be key to forming a new government.
An Israeli government led by Gadi Eisenkot would be better for Palestinians because removing current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from power is the most pressing issue, says Mustafa Barghouti, leader of the Palestinian National Initiative, a political party active in the occupied West Bank.
Speaking on Euronews' Europe Today, he argued that the opposition leader should rely on Arab members of the new Knesset to form a government, sidelining ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, whom he labelled “fascist.”
The Arab parties - Joint List and United Arab List (Ra’am) - made significant gains in the election, winning a record 19 seats between them, effectively turning them into kingmakers. Their support would be crucial for Eisenkot, as the opposition camp led by the centrist Yashar party fell short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
“Netanyahu has been responsible not only for slaughtering Palestinians in Gaza and for enhancing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, but [also] for creating wars with Lebanon, with Syria, threatening Jordan, and trying to impose Israel as an imperial force controlling the Middle East,” Barghouti said.
Working with Arab parties requires breaking campaign pledges
However, Eisenkot declared after the election that he will do his utmost to form “a Zionist government.”
Almost all parties in the opposition “Change Bloc” are reluctant to ally with Arab parties. Eisenkot’s Yashar, B’Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu and the Democrats all more or less explicitly ruled out cooperating with Joint List and Ra’am before the election, and any agreement would likely require them to abandon campaign pledges.
“All Zionist parties in Israel, whether in government with Netanyahu or in opposition, share the same views of rejecting Palestinian rights, including a Palestinian state, right of the Palestinians to self-determination, the idea of ending the Israeli illegal occupation,” Barghouti said, adding that all these political forces "are supportive of continuing the genocidal war on Gaza."
Arab parties represent the just over 2 million Palestinians who are citizens of Israel, roughly 21% of the country’s population, and do not include the 5.5 million non-citizen Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank and Gaza
That segment of Israel's electorate supports ending the war in Gaza, stopping illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and is largely in favour of a two-state solution, all sensitive topics for Israeli public opinion.
'We are not leaving'
Removing illegal Israeli settlements from the West Bank is the only way to save Palestinian statehood, according to Barghouti.
“For these extreme Israeli parties who reject a two-state solution, the only solution is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. But we are not leaving. We are here. We’re going to stay. We will resist,” he said.
Settlement activity has surged to an unprecedented level over the past two years, according to a UN report on the topic. The UN says there are more than 400 settlements and outposts in total, all illegal under international law.
The coming weeks will be crucial for forming a government in Israel.
President Isaac Herzog will now consult party leaders before tasking the candidate he believes has the best chance of securing enough support.
That leader has a maximum of 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension. If he fails, the president can give a second candidate a maximum of 28 days. If this second attempt also fails, the Knesset can request that a third candidate be given 14 days.
If all attempts fail and the deadlock proves impossible to resolve, another election is called, as happened four times between 2019 and 2022.

EAEU national currency payments reach 93.5 pct of intra-bloc trade, says bank chief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:49:03 CST
20:49:03 KST

MINSK, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Member states of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) are increasingly using national currencies in mutual trade and financial transactions, said Roman Golovchenko, chairman of the Board of the National Bank of the Republic of Belarus.
Speaking at a meeting of the advisory council on currency policy of the central banks of EAEU member states on Thursday, Golovchenko said that the share of payments in national currencies for exports and imports of goods and services within the bloc has reached 93.5 percent.
The shift is being driven by market mechanisms, with businesses favoring reliable and predictable payment instruments without administrative coercion, the banker said, adding that expanding settlements in national currencies helps reduce transaction costs and currency risks for the bloc.
The meeting also addressed the current economic situation and monetary policy, measures to combat unauthorized payments, and the potential use and regulation of central bank digital currencies and virtual assets within the union.
Established in 2015, the EAEU comprises Russia, Kazakhstan, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia. ■

UK to require foreign defense contractors to invest in domestic industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:46:42 UTC
20:46:42 KST

Aysu Bicer
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The UK announced a new defense procurement policy Friday requiring overseas companies awarded major military contracts to invest in British jobs, businesses and industrial capacity.
Under the policy, foreign suppliers securing selected contracts worth more than £50 million ($68 million) will be required to generate economic benefits in the UK, potentially equal to the full value of their contracts, the Ministry of Defense (MoD) said.
For example, a £100 million contract could require the supplier to deliver up to £100 million in domestic economic benefits through job creation, skills development or industrial investment.
The policy, which will apply to selected procurements from April 2027, was announced by Defense Secretary Wes Streeting and Chancellor John Healey during a visit to BAE Systems' Scotstoun shipyard in Glasgow.
"Every pound we invest in defense should be judged by what it does for Britain. That's why we are backing British by buying British wherever we can," Streeting said.
"Even when that is not possible, we are acting to ensure that any investment brings jobs, skills and investment back home, strengthening our national security by boosting our domestic industry," he added.
The MoD said the initiative would prioritize domestic procurement while ensuring that purchases from overseas suppliers also support the UK economy.
A new Offset Authority will oversee agreements and monitor their implementation, with requirements applied on a case-by-case basis.
The ministry noted that Poland, Norway and the Netherlands already operate similar arrangements.
Further details were outlined in an offset policy paper published Friday.

Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center employees are suspected of abducting and torturing conscripts and taking bribes. They could face up to 12 years in prison.
In Bukovyna, five servicemen of a district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center (TCC and SP) and a law enforcement officer were detained on suspicion of torturing conscripts, unlawfully depriving them of their liberty, and accepting illicit benefits. This was reported by the press service of the State Bureau of Investigation, UNN writes.
Details
According to the investigation, in the city of Kitsman, officials forcibly detained men in the streets and later subjected them to violence on the premises of the TCC. Thus, according to law enforcement, they sought to force the men to agree to mobilization.
Among the documented episodes is a case that came to public attention in early February 2026. At that time, a conscript was shot with a non-lethal weapon during his detention, sustaining a leg injury. The man was then taken to the TCC, where, according to the investigation, he was not provided with the necessary medical assistance and was forced to remove the bullet from the wound himself.
Another episode occurred on September 30, 2026. Investigators established the circumstances of the alleged abduction of a man following a personal conflict with certain TCC officials.
According to the criminal case materials, the man was followed, and when he approached a pedestrian crossing, he was forcibly dragged into a car. The victim is a combatant. Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, he had defended Ukraine and taken part in the battles for Kyiv, Irpin, and Bakhmut.
In addition, law enforcement documented the extortion and receipt of €5,500 from a conscript for his release after detention.
Overall, the investigation documented one episode of abduction, four episodes of alleged torture, as well as the extortion and receipt of an illicit benefit
On October 21, 2026, during a special operation, the State Bureau of Investigation detained all five suspects.
The head of the department and three of his subordinates were notified of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 146 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — unlawful deprivation of liberty or abduction committed by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy and accompanied by the infliction of physical suffering on the victim.
Four subordinates were also notified of suspicion under Part 3 of Article 368 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — accepting an illicit benefit by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy.
Two of them were additionally charged with torture committed by a state representative (Part 3 of Article 127 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
The most severe sanction under the articles charged carries a sentence of up to 12 years in prison.
The pretrial investigation is ongoing. Investigators are verifying possible other episodes of unlawful activity by the officials and identifying people who may have suffered from their actions.

Swiss court upholds 20 year jail term for ex-Liberian warlord
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:44:15 UTC
20:44:15 KST

Swiss court upholds 20 year jail term for ex-Liberian warlord
The Swiss Federal Supreme Court has upheld a 20 year prison sentence handed down to former Liberian rebel commander Alieu Kosiah.
The court acquitted him of crimes against humanity, but the conviction for war crimes stands.
In its judgement published on Friday, the Federal Supreme Court examined whether Kosiah’s actions during the civil war in the West African country between 1993 and 1995 could be classified as crimes against humanity. Switzerland did not incorporate this offence into its Criminal Code until 2011.
Judges ruled that applying the law retrospectively would contravene the principle of legality. It therefore acquitted Kosiah of this charge.
But the court upheld the remaining convictions. The war crimes included, amongst other things, the recruitment of child soldiers, murder, rape and the desecration of graves.
Kosiah, now aged 51, was arrested in Switzerland in 2014.

====================================================================================================

AI chatbots face scrutiny over failure to report criminal confessions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:43:53 UTC
20:43:53 KST

Emirhan Demir, Emir Yildirim
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots can be told about crimes, but uncertainties surrounding legal frameworks or measures that would mandate these tools to report confessions to law enforcement cast doubt on the pace of AI development.  
AI chatbots have entered daily life, with many users worldwide using and sometimes misusing these tools, often making headlines around the world.
In August, a 19-year-old University of Missouri student reportedly confessed to ChatGPT that he damaged 17 parked cars on campus late at night and asked, “Will I go to jail?”
ChatGPT responded with “tips about the potential outcome of getting caught” but urged the user to dial 911 after the messages grew increasingly aggressive, police documents showed.
The chat history was uncovered after the student allowed investigators to examine his phone, and the history was used as evidence against him in court, becoming instrumental in the felony property-damage charges against him.
In a similar instance, court records in Florida showed that days before two college students went missing in April and were later found dead, their roommate had asked ChatGPT, “What happens if a human has put in a black garbage bag and thrown in a dumpster.”
Canada’s British Columbia provincial government filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT.
The lawsuit, filed in February, concerned a mass school shooting that left nine people, mostly children, dead and 27 injured.
The case alleged that the firm failed to report the shooter’s chat with ChatGPT to law enforcement and argued that the attack could have been prevented if OpenAI had warned police.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologized in a letter, but whistleblowers told The Wall Street Journal newspaper that the conversation between the shooter and ChatGPT had allegedly already been flagged in June 2025. However, Altman and the firm’s leadership reportedly overrode the safety team’s recommendations to contact police.
The ethical implications of these interactions continue to deepen, as a study in Australia found that children are more likely to report sexual abuse online to chatbots than to responsible adults.
The same privacy principles that apply between lawyers and clients or doctors and patients do not apply to AI chatbot conversations, so tech firms can share logs with investigators.
While researchers debate whether chatbots should report crimes, the prospect is further complicated by algorithms misinterpreting intent.
For instance, Anthropic’s Claude 5 gave a false tip about an unsolved murder to a US police hotline in July. 
AI chatbots should not be used in crime prediction  
Matthew Trail, an American legal scholar and researcher at Goethe University in Germany, told Anadolu that each company developing AI chatbots adopts different rules and that these chatbots are not designed to respond to inquiries about planning murders and similar acts.
Trail stated that chatbots are trained to avoid certain topics, especially those regarding child sexual abuse, and refer these conversations to human moderators. However, users can compose their prompts in a certain way, such as by pretending to ask for help with writing fiction, to circumvent these filters and obtain AI-generated answers to otherwise inappropriate questions or requests.
Trail noted that while law enforcement could request a person’s chat history from AI firms when the person is suspected of having committed a crime, the primary goal of AI chatbots must not be to predict crimes before they are committed, as laws and policies surrounding this prospect are very unclear.
He added that allowing these AI models to collect more data than they already do to make more accurate assessments of crime potential is not a good idea, either. 
Can AI chatbot conversations ever be private?  
People across the globe discuss a myriad of topics with AI chatbots, especially personal matters ranging from health issues to psychological support and life advice.
As more and more people turn to AI for conversations, ethical debates over privacy have come to the fore.
Altman said in July 2025 that conversations with AI chatbots must be based on confidentiality.
Robert Diab, a law professor at Thompson Rivers University in Canada, stated that laws do not treat communications between accomplices as confidential, arguing that chats between humans and AI chatbots could be treated according to the same principle.
Diab said models like ChatGPT appear to be capable of detecting when users are prone to criminal behavior and argued that chatbot developers could prevent crime by notifying law enforcement.
He mentioned that alerting law enforcement based on all suspicious messages could also increase the workload of human teams due to false alarms.
He added that users will always find a way to circumvent security measures to use AI to commit a crime.

At around noon, David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's parliamentary faction, confirmed that humanitarian aid had reached Oleshky and that technical assistance was being provided to residents wishing to evacuate.
The operation marks a rare moment of direct humanitarian cooperation between Ukraine and Russia after years of occupation, with the ceasefire negotiated through their respective human rights representatives and supported by US First Lady Melania Trump.
But the most sensitive phase of the mission is ensuring that civilians who want to leave can do so safely and reach Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi initially said that 527 residents intended to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory, but later withdrew the figure, saying the number remained uncertain as the operation continued.
Twenty-five buses with a combined capacity of 750 passengers have been prepared for the evacuation, alongside ambulances for people with limited mobility, Lubinets said.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to leave safely. At the same time, those who have decided to stay can stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian support," he said.
The assurances come amid claims that Russian forces began evacuating residents before the agreed date, raising questions over whether the operation will proceed according to the arrangements reached by both sides.
The fate of those leaving remains a particular concern, given fears that civilians could be transported through Russian-controlled territory rather than being allowed to return to areas under Ukrainian government control.

The decline is sparking concern as there remains an ongoing need for new wigs made from natural hair for patients who have lost their hair following chemotherapy treatments, according to data published as part of the "Braid of Strength" campaign.
The campaign is run by the non-profit organization Zichron Menachem, sponsored by the Pantene Association.
During the event, barbers reportedly volunteered to cut hair free of charge for anyone who donates a braid. There is no requirement to schedule an appointment or register beforehand, and donors will receive a gift from Pantene in appreciation for their donation.
“Donating hair allows the public to take part in responding to this need,” said Beersheba and Negev News.
Donations halved since the war
In late 2023, Zichron Menachem reported that monthly donations dropped from about 3,000 to about 1,500 after the outbreak of the war. In November 2025, it announced that hair donations to women with cancer had dropped by about 50% over the two years before the report.
According to estimates by the Israel Cancer Association for 2026, approximately 34,000 new cancer cases are expected to be diagnosed in Israel, which equals about 93 new patients per day.
The preparation process reportedly allows the wigs to be tailored to the patients' personal characteristics, including length, color, and hair type. In order for hair to be used to make a wig, a donation of at least 30 centimeters in length is required, and dyed hair may also be suitable for donation, subject to the organization's guidelines.
The hair drive was open to the general public, and professional hairdressers, including Haim Pitousi, Rami Lagaziel, Hagit Emakias, and ‘LICABRUSH’ (an Israeli haircare brand), volunteered their time to perform the haircuts, according to Beersheba and Negev News.

Earlier drive in Kfar Saba

Zichron Menachem’s guidelines applied the same at both events, whereby hair donations were required to be at least 30 centimeters long, there was no requirement to schedule an appointment or register beforehand, and donors also received a small gift for their donation.
Arim Mall regularly hosts dedicated national hair drive events in collaboration with non-profits like Zichron Menachem. The donations derived from this project make wigs from natural hair, which are given free of charge to cancer patients, according to Tzomet Hasharon.
“For many women dealing with cancer, hair loss following treatment is one of the most difficult changes in coping with the disease,” added Tzomet Hasharon.

Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:42:36 UTC
20:42:36 KST

Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- University of Birmingham
- Summary:
- Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.
- Share:
What if time is not a fundamental part of the universe, but something that emerges from the changes taking place inside it? A physicist at the University of Birmingham has created a miniature universe in the laboratory that offers a surprising new way to investigate this possibility.
Using thousands of atoms cooled to temperatures barely above absolute zero, Professor Giovanni Barontini demonstrated that the passage of time can be measured without relying on an external clock. Instead, a form of time emerges naturally from the behavior of particles within the experimental system.
The findings, published in Physical Review Research, provide experimental evidence for an intriguing idea in theoretical physics: Time may not be an essential ingredient of reality. It could arise from the relationships and changes occurring within the universe itself.
Why Some Physicists Think Time May Not Be Fundamental
We usually think of time as something that continuously moves forward, regardless of what happens around us. Seconds pass, planets orbit stars, and the universe evolves. But some theories of physics suggest that time may work very differently at the most fundamental level.
One example is the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, which appears in attempts to combine quantum mechanics with gravity. In this framework, the universe can be described as a single, unchanging quantum state, with no external clock marking the passage of time. Quantum particles can exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties, but the universe as a whole does not necessarily have a built-in time variable.
This creates a major puzzle. If the universe has no external clock, how can anything happen in a particular order? What determines which events come first and which happen later?
One possibility is that time emerges from the changing relationships between different parts of the universe. Barontini designed an experiment to investigate whether such a process could be observed in the laboratory.
Creating a Miniature Universe With 24,000 Atoms
To build his miniature cosmos, Barontini used a cloud of approximately 24,000 atoms cooled to just a few billionths of a degree above absolute zero. At these extraordinarily low temperatures, quantum effects become especially important, allowing researchers to study behaviors that are normally difficult to observe.
The atoms were confined inside a carefully controlled quantum system designed to remain isolated from its surroundings. Two laser beams operating at different frequencies created a thin barrier that divided the system into two regions: an observed ('bright') region and an unobserved ('dark') region.
Although the overall system was isolated from the outside world, atoms could move between these two regions.
The bright region underwent repeated cycles of expansion and contraction, resembling simplified versions of two dramatic cosmological events. The expansion was analogous to the Big Bang, while the contraction resembled a Big Crunch, a hypothetical fate of the universe in which cosmic expansion eventually reverses and everything collapses inward.
The experiment did not recreate these actual cosmic events. Instead, it provided a simplified quantum model in which researchers could investigate how a sequence of events might be reconstructed without referring to a clock outside the system.
How Time Emerged Without a Clock
The key to the experiment was entropy, a concept in physics associated with the spread or disorder (entropy) of particles and energy.
Rather than using seconds or minutes, Barontini developed a way to track time through changes in how atoms were distributed within the miniature universe.
As atoms moved between the bright and dark regions, the distribution of particles in the bright region changed. These changes provided a way to define the system's progression through time, even when the bright region alternated between expansion and contraction.
When the particle distribution increased or decreased in its spread, the system continued moving forward according to this internal measure of time. When the distribution remained unchanged, the progression of this particular form of time effectively stopped.
Importantly, this did not mean that time literally stopped in the laboratory. It meant that the internal measure of time ceased advancing when the relevant changes in the system disappeared.
Barontini called this concept "entropic time." The experiment showed that this form of time has several important properties. It moves consistently in one direction, establishing what physicists call the "arrow of time," the distinction between past and future. It also places events in the correct sequence, even as the miniature universe expands and contracts.
Perhaps most surprisingly, entropic time does not always advance at the same rate. Its progression can speed up or slow down depending on how entropy changes within the system.
A New Clue to One of Physics' Biggest Mysteries
Professor Barontini said: "In some theories of the universe, especially quantum gravity, time doesn't appear as a built-in feature. Yet in everyday life, time flows from past to future -- why is this so, when most basic laws of physics work the same way forwards and backwards?
"This study provides the first controlled experimental evidence that 'time' can be defined by changes within a system rather than as the external 'ticking clock' we think of as time. It offers new insight into the nature of time in quantum gravity that could be used to describe dynamics just as effectively as conventional time."
The distinction between everyday time and the underlying laws of physics is especially important. Many fundamental physical equations work equally well whether time is mathematically reversed or allowed to move forward. Yet our experience of the world has a clear direction: We remember the past, not the future, and events unfold in a recognizable sequence.
Entropy has long played a central role in explaining this difference. Barontini's experiment takes that connection further by demonstrating how changes in entropy can provide an operational measure of time inside a controlled quantum system.
The findings also go beyond simply arranging events in the correct order.
Barontini demonstrated that a version of the Schrödinger equation, one of the foundational equations of quantum mechanics (Schrödinger), can be expressed using entropic time. This equation describes how the quantum state of a system evolves, including changes in the probability of finding particles in particular locations or states.
In other words, the internally generated measure of time could still be used to make predictions about the quantum system's behavior, much as conventional time is used in standard quantum mechanics.
Could a Tiny Universe Help Explain the Big Bang?
For decades, questions about the origin and fundamental nature of time have largely belonged to theoretical physics, particularly quantum cosmology and quantum gravity. These fields attempt to understand how the universe behaves when quantum effects and gravity must be considered together, including under the extreme conditions associated with the early cosmos.
Barontini's experiment offers a way to investigate some of these ideas using physical systems that scientists can create, manipulate, and observe.
The miniature universe continued to obey the established equations of quantum physics while providing a different way to describe its evolution. That makes it a potentially valuable testing ground for theories in which time is not assumed to exist independently of the system being studied.
Future experiments could extend this approach to more complicated quantum systems, allowing researchers to explore models of the Big Bang and the Big Crunch in greater detail. Similar techniques might eventually help simulate aspects of black holes or distinguish between competing explanations of how time emerges.
The experiment does not establish that time is an illusion or prove that our universe lacks fundamental time. Instead, it demonstrates something that was previously difficult to test: A quantum system can possess a meaningful internal measure of time without depending on an external clock.
By creating a miniature universe from just 24,000 atoms, researchers have gained a new experimental tool for investigating a question that has challenged physicists and philosophers for centuries: What makes time flow?

Ofcom introduced 'unprecedented' regulation, social media companies say

Meta, TikTok and X argued the notices create unprecedented regulatory burdens, but their case was rejected by London's High Court.
Neither the companies nor Ofcom immediately responded to requests for comment.
