Iranian, Greek universities seek to beef up scientific ties
TEHRAN – A delegation from Greek universities has visited Shahid Beheshti University to explore ways to expand academic ties between the two countries.
The delegation visited the university on Wednesday and attended a scientific roundtable at the Faculty of Economics and Political Sciences, where Shahid Beheshti University Chancellor Mahmoud-Reza Aqamiri and Greek academic officials emphasized the importance of strengthening scientific, research, and educational cooperation.
During the meeting, the two sides explored areas for collaboration, including exchanges of professors and researchers, sharing expertise, conducting joint research and educational projects, and attracting students.
Underscoring the need to address human and legal dimensions of the war against Iran, the Greek delegation called for the expansion of scientific, interdisciplinary, and international cooperation to strengthen social justice and confront shared challenges.
Iranian academic officials, for their part, emphasized the historical interactions between the two nations and stressed the need to address challenges, such as financial constraints, difficulties with travel, bank transactions, visa-related issues, and administrative obstacles, prior to developing joint scientific efforts.
Also, they suggested holding online meetings, publishing joint articles, promoting library cooperation, and implementing ongoing research projects as practical measures for the enhancement of academic ties between the two countries.
According to Aqamiri, Shahid Beheshti University would follow up on the implementation of the reached agreements and lay the basis for sustainable scientific interactions between the two sides.
Iran ranks first in key scientific output among Islamic countries
Iran ranks first among Islamic nations in key fields of scientific output such as quantum science, cognitive sciences, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced materials, the head of the Presidential Affairs Office at the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC) announced in August.
The country is in close competition with Turkey and Saudi Arabia in these fields, IRNA quoted Saeed Bakhtiari as saying.
He made the remarks in a press briefing on August 17, noting that the development of science in these fields has also been emphasized in national development plans.
Based on the reputable Web of Science database, Iran ranks first among Islamic countries in scientific output in some of these fields, while placing second or third in others. Overall, however, Iran holds the top position, he said.
Bakhtiari noted that in advanced materials—a multidisciplinary field spanning physics, chemistry, mechanics and materials science—Iran ranks second among Islamic countries and ninth worldwide.
He added that Iran ranks third in artificial intelligence, behind Saudi Arabia and Turkey, while in quantum science it ranks second, after Saudi Arabia.
The ISC official further said that Iran holds the top position among Islamic countries in scientific output in cognitive sciences and ranks first overall.
According to Web of Science (WoS) data, over a five-year period (from 2021 to 2025), Iran (with 32 documents) ranks first in cognitive sciences among Islamic countries.
Turkey, with 23 documents, and Saudi Arabia, with 22 documents, are placed second and third, respectively, IRNA reported.
From 2014 to 2023, Iran ranked either first or second in most fields of cognitive sciences among Islamic countries. Over the course of the decade, the country ranked first in cognitive neuroscience, cognitive rehabilitation, and cognitive linguistics with 387, 156, and 30 documents, respectively.
The country is placed second in quantum (with 216 documents) and advanced materials (with 5975 documents), after Saudi Arabia, with 283 and 6160 documents in quantum and advanced materials. Malaysia (with 154 documents) and Egypt (with 3151 documents) are placed third in quantum and advanced materials, respectively.
Despite illegal sanctions, Iran secures first place in cognitive sciences among Islamic nations and ranks ninth globally in advanced materials. Numerous prestigious Iranian universities and institutions are included in international rankings. These accomplishments underscore the country’s scientific capabilities, IRIB quoted Science Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf as saying, addressing the 7th Turkey Educational Technologies Summit (known as TETZ 2026), held in Istanbul from June 26 to 28.
Iran serves as a great opportunity to invest in higher education and modern technologies. The country has one of the largest higher education systems in the region, with more than three million students and over seventy thousand faculty members and researchers.
Highlighting that the rapid development of emerging technologies, including AI, is fundamentally transforming human relationships and higher education systems around the world at an unprecedented pace, Simaei-Sarraf said that effective use of smart technologies requires the establishment of a system based on algorithmic transparency, educational justice, accountability, protection of learners’ rights, and responsible data governance.

Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles late on 29 October, killing a man and injuring a 35-year-old woman, Kyiv city prosecutors said. The strikes damaged eight apartment blocks in Dniprovskyi district, a gas station, a restaurant, a dental clinic, warehouses, and cars. A warehouse building caught fire in Darnytskyi district, the city administration reported.
Overnight, Russia fired Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 ballistic missiles, four Kh-59/69 guided missiles, and 113 drones, 83 of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force said. The attack mainly targeted Kyiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. Air defenses downed three missiles and 96 drones, but strikes hit 17 locations.
Russia is waging its war on Ukraine's cities around the clock as winter approaches, striking homes, transport, and the power grid that keeps them running. On 29 October, including the late attack on Kyiv, Russian strikes killed at least 27 civilians and injured more than 140 across six regions, by EP's tally of regional authorities' reports. It was one of the deadliest days of the autumn. Most died in daylight, on a train platform in Dnipro, in an apartment block in Kremenchuk, in central Chernihiv, and under guided bombs in Izium.
Dnipro and Kyiv's right bank lose power
A Russian strike on Dnipro left more than 350,000 customers in the city and nearby towns without power, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast's administration said shortly after midnight. Water pumping stations switched to backup power. By morning, engineers had restored electricity to most customers in the oblast, but more than 200,000 were still without power.
It was the only transport serving a village where more than 1,600 people still live: Russian forces strike a social bus with a drone in Bilenke, killing a woman and injuring other passengers
In Kyiv, equipment damaged in earlier strikes failed on the right bank, forcing emergency outages, the city administration said. Russia attacked an industrial plant in Poltava Oblast's Kremenchuk district overnight and again in the morning, with no casualties reported, the regional administration said.
In the morning, a Russian drone hit a shopping center in Kharkiv's Kyivskyi district, injuring four women, Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian drones destroyed the house of culture in Mena late on 29 October, and in the morning a drone hit a house in Bobrovytsia and injured a woman, the regional administration said. In Chernihiv itself, 37 people sought medical help after the 29 October strike on the city center that killed two 15-year-old girls, Yana and Mariia.
Two oblasts in mourning as the Dnipro toll rises to 15
A 40-year-old man wounded in the 29 October jet drone strike on Dnipro's railway station died in hospital, raising the toll to 15, the regional administration said. Eleven people remain in hospital. Dnipropetrovsk Oblast declared 30 October a day of mourning.
Poltava Oblast also mourns three people killed when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in Kremenchuk on 29 October. Another 32 were injured, six of them children, the regional administration said.
Russian jet drone hits Dnipro railway platform, killing 14 people next to a Zaporizhzhia-bound train
In Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, Russian guided bombs hit a five-story building on 29 October, killing four people and injuring 14, police reported. In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people in Bilenke and injured 23 across the region, 13 of them when Russia sent seven FPV drones at vehicles and public transport in Zaporizhzhia city, police said. EP reported the city faced a record number of such attacks.

Former US ambassadors: America must stand with Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:28:44 UTC
20:28:44 KST

Flags for the United States and Ukraine billow in the wind off an activist's bicycle on April 23, 2024 in Washington, DC. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
The United States cannot credibly defend freedom around the world while treating the survival of a democracy under attack as a bargaining chip.
Russia’s war against Ukraine is not simply a territorial dispute. It is a test of whether democratic nations will defend the principles that sustain their freedom — or allow an authoritarian aggressor to destroy these principles through military force, terror and economic coercion.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine was unlawful. Its conduct has included attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and in March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova over alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. All grave allegations that demand accountability.
Advertisement
As Ukraine continues to fight for its survival, current U.S. policy raises a fundamental question: Does Washington understand what is at stake?
If Moscow succeeds in subjugating Ukraine, other authoritarian leaders will also ask whether military conquest can succeed. Can U.S. commitments be trusted? Will democratic nations stand together when the price becomes politically inconvenient?
Ukraine’s defense is not charity. It is a strategic investment in American and European security, Washington’s credibility and the deterrence of future conflicts.
The U.S. emerged from World War II understanding that an international order based on sovereignty, freedom and rule of law serves its interests. And successive Republican and Democratic administrations recognized that unchecked authoritarian expansion threatens both American security and the independence of its allies.
That understanding must guide U.S. policy toward Russia today.
Diplomacy is essential. Negotiations to end the war should be pursued seriously. But peace cannot mean rewarding aggression, compelling Ukraine to surrender its sovereignty or giving Moscow time to rearm for another invasion.
Advertisement
Appeasement does not necessarily prevent conflict. It can encourage aggression by convincing dictators the free world lacks the will to resist them. And a ceasefire without effective safeguards could become merely a pause before the next assault. A settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless would postpone the conflict, not resolve it.
Peace should be measured not by the speed with which an agreement is signed, but by whether it protects Ukraine’s independence and makes another war less likely. And economic pressure is among the most important nonmilitary instruments available to the U.S. in this process, as Russia’s ability to wage war depends substantially on energy revenues, access to international markets and networks that facilitate sanctions evasion.
On Sept.18, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law. Then, on Oct. 16, he issued an executive order waiving specified sanctions, restrictions and duties authorized under the legislation, citing the national interest. This order raises a legitimate question about how Washington intends to use the economic leverage Congress provided.
The measurable objectives these waivers are intended to achieve, why they serve American national security and what conditions would trigger their reconsideration need to be explained.
The U.S. needs to enforce restrictions consistently, close avenues for evasion and impose consequences when countries or companies knowingly provide material assistance to Russia’s war effort in violation of applicable law.
This does not require abandoning diplomacy. It requires a coherent policy in which economic relief advances clearly defined security objectives.
Advertisement
If Washington weakens its own pressure without obtaining meaningful concessions, it risks surrendering leverage while leaving Russia’s aggression unresolved. Every source of revenue helping Moscow sustain its military campaign has consequences for Ukrainian civilians, who bear them in destroyed homes, shattered families and lost lives.
U.S. policy should not make it easier for Russia to finance a war Washington says it wants to end.
American history has a bipartisan tradition of leadership that combines the defense of freedom with strategic judgment.
Harry Truman understood U.S. security depended on resisting authoritarian expansion. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, John F. Kennedy demonstrated that strength and diplomacy are not opposites. Ronald Reagan understood freedom must be defended against those who seek to suppress it. And George H. W. Bush knew sovereignty and alliances are essential to an international order where nations cannot redraw borders by force.
Though from different eras, the leadership of these presidents reflected a common principle: American security is strengthened when the U.S. combines military strength, alliances, diplomacy and a commitment to the independence of free nations.
A policy that pressures Ukraine more than Russia, offers Moscow economic relief without substantial concessions or asks Ukrainians to accept an insecure future is not a strategy for lasting peace. It risks rewarding aggression and inviting further conflict.
Advertisement
And above all, Ukraine’s future should not be decided over the heads of Ukrainians.
Democratic institutions can be attacked and dismantled far faster than they can be rebuilt. Ukraine’s struggle is therefore about more than one war. It is about whether the democratic world will remain a community of nations bound by common principles or become a collection of states left to negotiate individually with authoritarian regimes.
History will not judge U.S. policy solely by the immediate cost of weapons, energy or sanctions. It will judge whether America stood by a nation fighting for survival, upheld the principles it asks others to respect and helped prevent future wars by demonstrating that aggression does not pay.
Adrian Zuckerman is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2019-2021); Mark Gitenstein is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2009-2012) and to the EU (2022-2025); Ron Gidwitz is a former U.S. ambassador to Belgium (2018-2021) and acting U.S. ambassador to the EU (2020-2021); Jim Gilmore is a former U.S. ambassador to the OSCE (2019-2021); Kathleen Kavalec is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (2023-2025); Jim Rosapepe is a former U.S. ambassador to Romania (1998-2001).
POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

Senior officials from several countries have flown to Tehran in recent days as fears rise of a return to hostilities in the Middle East war, which started eight months ago.

Iran attends World Young Scientist Summit 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:27:28 UTC
20:27:28 KST

Iran attends World Young Scientist Summit 2026
TEHRAN – The head of the National Institute for Oceanography and Atmospheric Sciences has represented Iran at the World Young Scientist Summit (WYSS) 2026.
The event took place on October 24 and 25 in Wenzhou, China, ISNA reported.
Attending the WYSS Deep-Sea Resources and Environment Forum, Ali Mahdinia delivered a talk on ‘Deep-Sea Natural Resources Survey in the Oman Sea: Experiences and Evidence’, presenting Iran’s scientific findings and research experiences in studying natural resources in the deep waters of the Sea of Oman. The official also elaborated on the country’s research capacities in marine science.
The forum was held under the theme “Marching to the Deep and Distant Sea — Marine Resources Empowering the Blue Economy Future”, bringing together young scientific and technological talents in the deep-sea field from more than 20 countries and regions to exchange views on key topics such as green development of deep-sea resources and ecological synergy.
Nearly 800 representatives, including scientists, educators, and entrepreneurs from more than 60 countries and regions, attended the World Association of Young Scientists.
With the theme “Gathering Talents Worldwide to Create a Better Future,” the summit’s annual agenda was “Global Youth Action in the AI Era: Building a Sustainable Future.” It aimed to draw on the insights of young people around the world, deepen international sci-tech cooperation, and jointly address questions about young people, science, the world and the future.
This year’s summit placed greater emphasis on the growth needs of young scientists, with young talents under the age of 45 accounting for 88 percent of participants.
It aimed to build a cluster of international journals, bring together young scientific talent, facilitate a batch of international collaborative projects and advance the application and commercialization of scientific and technological achievements.
Iran deepens scientific ties with China through new ocean research pact
In November 2025, Iran’s National Institute of Oceanography and Atmospheric Science signed a cooperation agreement with the Second Institute of Oceanography of China’s Ministry of Natural Resources, aiming to expand joint research in deep-sea studies under the framework of Iran’s BRICS membership.
According to Mahdinia, the memorandum was designed to strengthen scientific and technological collaboration between the two sides as part of Iran’s active participation in the BRICS “Working Group on Ocean and Polar Science and Technology.”
He said the agreement included joint deep-sea research projects, scientific and technological events, exchange of professors, researchers and students, shared access to research facilities, and the exchange of scientific data, books and journals.
“The agreement builds on Iran’s integration into the expanded BRICS group, whose members include Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, the United Arab Emirates, Iran, Indonesia, Bolivia and Nigeria,” he added.
Iranian scholars dispatched to Chinese scientific centers via TYSP
The Iran-China Talented Young Scientist Program (TYSP) has so far facilitated the dispatch of 71 Iranian scholars to the top Chinese scientific center to conduct research, laying the groundwork for expanding scientific and research cooperation between the two countries.
The TYSP is an international mobility scheme funded by the Chinese government aimed at cultivating future leading scientists, together with other countries.
According to the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology, and Knowledge-Based Economy, the two countries started the young scientists exchange program in 2017, IRNA reported.
The program, which includes scholarships and financial support from Chinese universities, as well as educational and research institutes, came to a halt following the Covid-19 pandemic. The program restarted in October 2024.
The new edition of the Iran-China TYSP, announced in January 2025, opened up 53 opportunities for young scientists from the two countries.
The majority of Iranian applicants are associate professors or those with higher degrees, and the rest are selected among faculty members and researchers.
TYSP offers sponsorship for talented young scientists from other countries to work in China on a full-time basis for 6 or 12 months together with China’s team; the Ministry of Science and Technology of China has allocated 12,500 yuan per month to support the implementation of research activities of the young talented scientists in China.
Iranian scholars are primarily working with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Tongji University, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and China Agricultural University.
Agricultural sciences and plant protection, earth sciences and natural hazard management, physics and optics, mathematics and computer science, materials science and engineering, energy, and bioinformatics are among the most important scientific fields in the TYSP program.
TYSP promotes cross-border exchanges of excellent young scientists, scholars, and researchers. The program also enhances cooperation among research institutes, universities, and enterprises.
When the program is over, participant will receive a TYSP Certificate based on their performance evaluation.

Indian exports to cross $1 trillion in current financial year – top Modi aide
Indian exports are set to cross $1 trillion in the 2026-27 financial year, government Chief Economic Adviser V Anantha Nageswaran has said.
The South Asian nation’s cumulative exports, including goods and services, totaled $476.20 billion in the April-September period, government data showed.
“We are on track to exceed or even achieve $1 trillion exports this year,” he said, pointing to the 13.84% growth recorded in the first half of the fiscal, from the year-ago period.
India’s total exports in the financial year ended March was 863.1 billion, with merchandize exports reaching 441.8 billion, and services exports at $421.3 billion.
To compare, China’s goods exports alone stood at $3.77 trillion in 2025, while overall US exports, including services, came in at $3.43 trillion.
Achieving the ambitious export targets would, however, require New Delhi to strengthen its manufacturing amid geopolitical tensions and supply-chain disruptions.
Sectors that received robust federal government backing should help deliver strong export numbers and provide the country with the ability to compete on import prices, the government’s chief economist said.
India is on course to exceed $1 trillion in exports in 2026-27, according to Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran. He described 2025-26 as a critical economic inflection point for India — comparable to 1991 in significance, not in crisis terms — after years of global supply-side shocks from the pandemic, the Ukrainian conflict, and tensions in the Gulf. https://t.co/hpFV5iIYKE
— Sputnik India (@Sputnik_India) October 29, 2026
“We have to insist on quid pro quo from the industry in terms of export competitiveness, and/or import parity,” he said.
Nageswaran also advocated setting up reservoirs of essential commodities as a way to deal with supply chain issues.
India’s Niti Aayog pointed out in its executive summary for the Jan-March quarter that challenging global trade conditions, along with continued uncertainty surrounding trade policies, investment flows, and supply chains were weighing on economic activity.
The South Asian nation clocked real GDP growth of 7.8% in the first quarter of 2026-27, making it one of the fastest-growing major economies in the world.
The US remained India’s largest export destination in the first-half of the fiscal year, with exports of $50.81 billion, up from $45.82 billion a year ago despite the tariff uncertainties and continuing negotiations over a trade deal.

Serbian election winners plan gas talks with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:27:15 UTC
20:27:15 KST

Serbian election winners plan gas talks with Russia
Serbia’s incoming leadership plans to hold talks with Russia to negotiate a long-term natural gas supply agreement, prominent Student List candidate Radomir Saicic has said.
The student-backed movement, which defeated the coalition of longtime Serbian leader Aleksandar Vucic in a parliamentary election this month, previously indicated that Belgrade would not join Western sanctions against Moscow.
Vucic himself, however, has warned that the Student List would renege on its position, while some high-profile members of the movement have suggested that Serbia’s relations with Russia could be reconsidered.
The Student List secured around 52.5% of the vote in Sunday’s snap election. The movement emerged from mass protests triggered by the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people and sparked widespread accusations of government corruption.
While the authorities launched an investigation into the tragedy and made several major concessions, the protests continued. Vucic eventually called snap parliamentary elections and resigned the presidency in September to seek a return to power as prime minister. The Serbian leader denounced the protests as an attempted Western-backed ‘color revolution’, but pledged to respect the election results and avoid bloodshed, ultimately conceding defeat.
Moscow, which had shared Vucic’s concerns about possible foreign interference, acknowledged the election results. Earlier this week, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic’s contribution to bilateral ties, expressing hope that the incoming leadership would continue developing constructive relations with Russia. He stressed that cooperation with Moscow was in Serbia’s interests, adding that “it takes two to tango.”
Speaking to Serbian weekly NIN in an interview published on Wednesday, Saicic, a founding signatory of the Student List who is reportedly viewed as a possible prime minister, outlined ties with Russia as one of the incoming government’s priorities.
“In the first 30 days… energy supply, which includes oil, gas and the functioning of the Electric Power Company of Serbia, will be ensured. To this end, our delegations will hold talks in Washington (expiration of OFAC’s decision on the temporary suspension of NIS sanctions) and in Moscow (gas arrangement), in order to conclude longer-term arrangements,” he said.
Saicic also previously reaffirmed the movement’s opposition to sanctions against Russia over Ukraine despite pressure from the EU, stressing that “problems should be resolved through dialogue, negotiations, and agreements, not sanctions.”
Another Student List representative, university professor Jovo Bakic, gave similar assurances in an interview with RT Balkan on Monday, saying that “we respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector.”
At the same time, Ilija Srdanovic, another prominent member of the movement, delivered a different message, signaling in an interview with US-funded RFE/RL that all options remain on the table, saying that “there will certainly be a dialogue within our society.”
Russia is Serbia’s dominant natural gas supplier, accounting for up to 90% of its imports in 2025, with most deliveries arriving through the TurkStream pipeline via Türkiye and Bulgaria. However, the two countries have yet to negotiate a new long-term gas contract since their previous three-year agreement expired in May 2025, relying instead on successive short-term extensions. The current gas agreement is valid until December 31.
The overall talks have been complicated by the uncertainty over the fate of NIS, which operates Serbia’s only oil refinery and faces US sanctions over its majority Russian ownership. Hungarian energy company MOL has been negotiating to acquire the Russian stake, while Washington has issued temporary waivers to keep the company operating.
Moscow said that long-term contracts were complicated by EU energy policies, Serbia’s European integration ambitions, and uncertainty over gas transit through Bulgaria. Nevertheless, Russia has repeatedly stressed it is open to supplying gas to any interested European customers.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Vucic discussed energy cooperation and NIS in late September before the elections, with the Serbian leader saying at the time he was confident that Russian gas deliveries would continue at favorable prices – €318 ($356) per 1,000 cubic meters, compared with a European market benchmark of more than €800.

$6.3 billion Binance hack likely work of North Korea, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:26:55 UTC
20:26:55 KST

$6.3 billion Binance hack was likely work of North Korea, blockchain intel firms say
A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.
What is TraderTraitor?
In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said.
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.
Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain research firm Chainalysis, also said on social media that the Binance hack was "likely done" by TraderTraitor.
Analysts believe that TraderTraitor members are part of a wider North Korean hacking unit known as Lazarus Group, which targets multiple institutions across government, finance and other fields, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.
The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.
Working "around the clock"
Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. President Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.
Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:26:00 UTC
20:26:00 KST

Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results
October 30, 2026
Though it has been two days since Israel's parliamentary elections, German politicians are still being cautious to respond, as it is still unclear who will lead Israel's new government.
Although the right-wing bloc, including religious hardliners, led by incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, neither has a clear path to a governing majority in the Knesset.
Forming a coalition government is likely to be extremely difficult.
Martin Giese, spokesperson for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, declined to comment at Wednesday's regular government press conference in Berlin.
But he did stress that Germany has been in contact with numerous officials and politicians in Israel via Germany's ambassador. "The Jewish state and Germany are inextricably linked by our history, and we will do everything we can to work well with any future government," Wadephul said.
Alabali Radovan: 'Winter in Gaza will be difficult'
One concern for the German government is providing aid to the people in Gaza, and protracted coalition negotiations could delay necessary progress.
"Winter is coming, and it will be difficult," Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan, currently visiting Lebanon, warned in an interview with Politico. She underlined that there must be more opportunities for aid organizations to provide crucial assistance in Gaza and that it cannot wait for coalition negotiations.
In interviews with DW and broadcaster RTL, she spoke about the recent increase in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.
"The radical settler violence must be stopped. The Netanyahu government remains in office on an interim basis, and this means that this situation must still be brought to an end," she said.
All settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territories is considered illegal under international law.
More distanced from Netanyahu's government
Relations between Germany and Israel are traditionally close, in part because of Germany's historical responsibility for Nazi Germany's murder of millions of Jews during the Holocaust.
Recently, however, the German government has distanced itself from Netanyahu's policies, at least in its public rhetoric.
Most recently, Wadephul said after a major Israeli military operation near the city of Hebron: "Under international law, Israel is quite clearly obligated to uphold and protect the rights of Palestinians as well." Around 3,000 Palestinians were driven from their homes during the operation, which followed the reported killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinians.
In Berlin, there has long been speculation about whether Germany's policy toward Israel might change after Israel's 2026 election.
So far, one thing is clear: Unlike numerous other countries, including some in Europe, Germany does not intend to recognize a Palestinian state for the time being.
CDU hoping for a centrist government
At the same time, Germany hopes that the future government will no longer include religious extremists, and in some cases far-right, politicians such as the current Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
"I think it would be best for Israel to form a government that is closer to the center of the political spectrum," Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy expert for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in the Bundestag, told DW. "Of course, that's something the people, and above all the elected politicians, will have to figure out. But it's encouraging that so many people participated in the election."
The Arab-majority parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel made large gains in this election. They are usually classified as part of the current opposition camp. The historic results by these parties could lead them to play a kingmaker role in coalition formation.
However, Netanyahu’s bloc have ruled out working with the Arab-majority parties.
Eisenkot's opposition bloc has not yet said whether it would be willing to form such a coalition, but one of the Arab-majority parties, United Arab List/Ra'am, featured a Jewish candidate, and has stated its willingness to work with Eisenkot’s bloc to unseat Netanyahu.
Hardt believes a minority government led by Eisenkot and supported by parties representing Arab Israelis is conceivable.
"The major campaign carried out by Netanyahu's camp, aimed primarily against Arab Israelis, greatly mobilized the opposition, to the point where his camp no longer has a majority."
The vice president of the German Bundestag, Green Party politician Omid Nouripour, told DW: "Frankly, after all the turmoil that has occurred — for example, regarding judicial reform — this is good news for Israeli democracy."
This article was originally published in German.

WHO: Yemen escalation leaves over 9,000 dead or injured, displaces 276,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:25:58 UTC
20:25:58 KST

The World Health Organisation (WHO) says the death and injury toll from the latest military escalation in Yemen has reached 9,072, warning that health services are deteriorating and medical supplies, fuel and water are in short supply, particularly in Taiz governorate.
In a report released on Thursday, the WHO said 1,677 people had been killed and 7,395 injured as of 25 October, with 559 casualties recorded over six days.
The average number of casualties during the reporting period stands at 93 a day, almost half the daily average of 168 recorded in the previous report. However, deaths and injuries continue to be reported across several governorates.
Marib has recorded the highest number of deaths among the governorates covered by the data, with 45 deaths out of 143 casualties. Taiz follows with 34 deaths out of 237 casualties, while Lahj has recorded 21 deaths out of 158 casualties.
The WHO says 276,301 people are displaced across Yemen as of 24 October, including more than 46,000 families. Taiz hosts around 46 per cent of all registered displaced people.
The report says restrictions on access from Aden to Taiz and the western coast are delaying the delivery of supplies. Severe shortages of medicines, fuel and water, alongside disruptions to waste management services, are increasing the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.
It adds that only six of the 31 hospitals in Marib remain operational.
The developments come amid continued military escalation in Yemen, following the resumption of clashes between government forces and the Houthi movement in late June.

By Tuvan Gumrukcu
ANKARA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev skipped a summit of Turkic states on Friday despite a personal invitation from his Turkish counterpart, highlighting growing tensions between the historic allies over domestic and regional policies.
Ties between Turkey and Azerbaijan have become strained in recent weeks over some Turkish officials’ criticism of Baku’s decision to impose restrictions on the use of headscarves under new secular school uniform regulations.
Aliyev and other Azeri officials warned against interference in Baku’s affairs, without mentioning Turkey — a rare crack in an alliance of nations at the heart of a fractured region. Any worse break could hurt Turkey’s ambitions of increasing its influence in an area where Russia traditionally holds sway.
HEADSCARF DISPUTE IS ‘SYMPTOM OF A DEEPER RIFT’
The two countries are also at odds over Israel. Ankara is a fierce critic of Israel over the war in Gaza, while Azerbaijan has strong ties with it.
Turkish officials have sought to downplay tensions and Erdogan delivered a message of unity at the opening of Friday’s summit of countries united by language, culture and roots.
“There is no place for separation, division, or conflict in our family picture. We are all one, together and, God willing, we are brothers forever,” he said at the meeting in Ankara, without naming Azerbaijan.
Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov represented Azerbaijan at the summit. Speaking after Erdogan, he did not mention the tensions, thanking Turkey for its hospitality.
The tensions are unusual. The two countries describe their relationship as “two states, one nation”. Ties deepened after Turkey backed Azerbaijan during the 2023 Nagorno-Karabakh war and they have built strong ties in defence and energy. Ankara is a major buyer of Azeri natural gas.
Erdogan this week removed one of his advisers, Oktay Saral, after his public criticism of the headscarf decision. He also personally invited Aliyev to the Organisation of Turkic States summit during a phone call last week, according to his office.
The Azeri-Press Agency said, without citing sources, that Aliyev skipped the summit arranged months ago due to “previously planned events and the tightness of his work schedule”, including a ceremony and festival at the FIFA U-15 World Cup in Baku.
There has been no official comment from Azerbaijan, while Turkey’s presidency and foreign ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
Gonul Tol, director of the Washington-based Middle East Institute’s Turkish programme, said that Aliyev skipping the summit was the latest sign of growing tensions between the allies.
“Beneath the ‘two states, one nation’ rhetoric, tensions have long simmered over a number of issues including Azerbaijan’s sovereignty, Ankara’s influence in Baku, diverging policies toward Israel, and Turkey’s rapprochement with Armenia. The hijab dispute is a symptom of a deeper rift,” she said on X.
Turkey has been working to normalise relations with Armenia but has said that this would depend on peace efforts between Azerbaijan and Armenia. Turkish officials have said Ankara has been looking for progress there so it can take concrete steps like opening borders with Armenia.
Amid the tacit warnings against Turkey, Azerbaijan’s foreign ministry this month declared 31 Turkish nationals persona non grata over social media posts criticising Baku.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said this month after meeting Aliyev at a Baku summit that disinformation was being spread on social media about Turkey-Azerbaijan ties.
He said that while the countries may not agree on everything, they could “sit and discuss our own problems” in a civil way that befits their close ties.
“Can there be different perspectives, different views on certain issues? There can be. Brothers then sit amongst themselves and discuss it in line with their brotherly ties,” he said.

Hong Kong fire exposes entrenched triad networks in building renovation industry
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:24:28 CET
20:24:28 KST

By Clare Jim
HONG KONG, Oct 30 (Reuters) - A deadly fire at a Hong Kong housing estate has exposed how bid-rigging networks linked to criminal gangs exploited weaknesses in the city’s lucrative building renovation industry to influence contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Organised crime groups known as triads were mentioned more than 40 times in the report on the government-subsidised Wang Fuk Court inferno, which killed 168 people and displaced thousands of residents.
In response to the report’s findings, the government proposed to make bid-rigging in building renovation a criminal offence, punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a HK$10 million ($1.3 million) fine. Laws against triads will also be tightened.
“After all these years, the syndicates are so sophisticated that they make use of all the legal loopholes,” said Chiu Yan Loy, founder and spokesperson of the All-Hong Kong Owners’ Anti-Corruption and Anti-Bid-Rigging Alliance.
Some networks delay distributing profits for months and use channels including cryptocurrencies, making money flows difficult to trace, he added.
Lawyers and law enforcement officers say the new offence will only work if it helps investigators gather hard evidence.
“We’re talking about offences that exist in a kind of twilight world. There aren’t always transactions between offenders, bribery or a paper trail to prove collusive behaviour or a cartel,” said one law enforcement officer, who declined to be identified due to the sensitivity of the issue.
LOOSE REGULATORY FRAMEWORK
Triad gangs — fraternal brotherhoods whose members swear blood oaths of loyalty and secrecy — have for decades been linked to extortion, prostitution, drug trafficking and loan-sharking.
Less prominent than in the 1980s and 1990s, they remain active and operate more complex white-collar scams, police and academics say.
The report explained that loose regulation and lax enforcement around vetting and hiring contractors let them enter the construction ecosystem.
Industry experts say bid rigging worsened when the government introduced hundreds of millions in subsidies in 2012 alongside a scheme requiring owners to repair buildings more than 30 years old, creating a lucrative market for contractors.
Tommy Leung, an associate professor at Wake Forest University, said his research showed renovation prices rose about 40% after the scheme began.
BID-RIGGING AT PLAY
The Wang Fuk Court renovation, whose cost rose from an initial HK$152 million estimate to more than HK$330 million, provides a window into alleged methods used to manipulate projects.
According to the report, the alleged scheme began with gaining influence over the consultant who helps owners select contractors.
Will Power Architects secured that role with a HK$220,000 ($28,000) bid, well below an estimated HK$500,000 market rate, then issued misleading tender assessments, including giving main contractor Prestige Construction full marks for safety compliance despite previous convictions.
Authorities have brought at least 25 criminal charges related to Wang Fuk Court, which housed more than 5,000 people in eight 31-storey towers, against Prestige, Will Power and seven individuals. The report did not say whether the firms had triad links.
Prestige and Will Power could not be reached for comment.
Security Secretary Chris Tang, the former police chief, said on Friday the government would “dismantle the criminal networks behind such activities.”
Hong Kong now plans to give law enforcement greater investigative powers, create a joint task force involving police, the Independent Commission Against Corruption and Competition Commission, and a new bureau overseeing renovation work.
Some former Wang Fuk Court residents were unconvinced.
“It’s just a slogan. They’ll say, ‘we’ll crack down on bid-rigging,’ but ultimately, nothing gets done,” said Betty, who declined to give her full name.
(Reporting By Clare Jim in Hong Kong, additional reporting by Greg Torode and Carol Mang; Editing by Anne Marie Roantree and Saad Sayeed)

Exclusive-Japan pushes to remove Myanmar from global financial watchdog’s blacklist
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:24:13 CET
20:24:13 KST

By Tamiyuki Kihara and Poppy McPherson
TOKYO/BANGKOK, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Japan is pushing a global financial crimes watchdog to remove Myanmar from its blacklist to make it easier to do business there, the latest sign that some major countries are looking to bring the pariah state’s military-backed government in from the cold.
Japan wants the Financial Action Task Force to drop requirements that its members apply enhanced screening to financial transactions with Myanmar to avoid money laundering and terrorist financing, said a senior Japanese government official and another person familiar with the matter.
Removing Myanmar from the list would ease checks on business with a country whose military seized power in a 2021 coup and which remains under scrutiny over scam centres and illicit finance.
The only other countries currently on FATF’s blacklist are Iran and North Korea. The 40-member body will conclude its third and last plenary meeting of the year in Paris on Friday.
It was not immediately clear whether a change is imminent, though the second source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said at least one other major Asian country was pushing for Myanmar’s removal.
A spokesperson for the FATF Secretariat said meetings were ongoing, discussions were confidential, and any changes to the blacklist would be announced after their conclusion on Friday. A spokesperson for Myanmar’s military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment.
Myanmar was added to the blacklist in 2022 as the country plunged into turmoil and widespread civil war after the coup.
The chaos has fuelled illicit drug production, trafficking and the growth of industrial-scale scam centres in the Golden Triangle, some of them run by militia aligned to the military-backed government.
Myanmar’s government has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centres. It has also said it has been making efforts to seize narcotics and that drug production and trafficking is carried out by armed groups.
On Monday, Reuters reported Myanmar imported sanctioned jet fuel from Iran, used for deadly bombing campaigns, in shipments disguised with sham paperwork. Myanmar government officials did not return requests for comment.
DIPLOMATIC ENGAGEMENT
The push to remove Myanmar from the blacklist is the latest effort by some nations including Japan to re-engage with Myanmar after a period of international isolation that followed the ousting of leader Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021.
The coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including for his role in the coup and the crushing of a popular uprising that followed.
The United States last month held direct talks with Myanmar’s military-backed government in Naypyidaw, the highest-level contact since the coup. Those talks, which focused on shutting down scam centres but could pave the way for negotiations on access to Myanmar’s abundant rare earth deposits, were quickly followed by more secretive talks in Tokyo earlier this month.
Japan, whose companies have maintained a large corporate presence in Myanmar even as other firms fled following the coup, believes that getting Myanmar off FATF’s blacklist will make it easier for countries to do business there and help its economy recover, the Japanese government official said.
Myanmar was added to FATF’s blacklist, formally known as the High-Risk Jurisdictions Subject to a Call for Action list, in October 2022 after missing a deadline to address deficiencies.
The global watchdog said at the time that its members must apply enhanced due diligence to business relations and transactions with Myanmar, while ensuring that funds for humanitarian purposes, legitimate non-profit activity and remittances were not disrupted.
In a June assessment, FATF said Myanmar had demonstrated some progress but urgently needed to address deficiencies including ensuring money laundering was investigated and prosecuted, while illicit finance from cyberfraud remained a concern.
(Reporting by Tamiyuki Kihara in Tokyo and Poppy McPherson in Bangkok; Writing by John Geddie; Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan)

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Friday that two oil tankers that switched off their navigation systems were involved in an incident and stopped in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz, after ignoring radio warnings and attempting to use what it described as an unauthorized route through the strategic waterway.
Iran also said on Friday that it destroyed a US unmanned vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate confirmation from the US military.
In a separate incident, a small boat attached two limpet mines to the hull of a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz causing a fire in its engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel, in the first successful use of such explosives in the waterway since the US war with Iran began in February, maritime sources said on Friday.
The crew was safe, there was no environmental impact and the fire had been extinguished, British navy agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said in an advisory note, adding that the vessel, which it did not name, was continuing to its next port of call.
The incident occurred on Thursday, 25 nautical miles (46 km) northeast of Oman's Khasab, UKMTO said.
IRGC claims responsibility for both tanker attacks
"Early this morning, an enemy vessel operating within the operational zone east of the Strait of Hormuz was struck and destroyed by the brave personnel of the Army Navy," a spokesperson for the IRGC's Navy said in a statement.
"Furthermore, two enemy oil tankers - which had violated regulations by disabling their tracking systems and navigating through prohibited and unsafe waters east of the Strait of Hormuz, despite receiving warnings - sustained damage and caught fire after striking naval mines.
"The owners of the oil tankers shall bear full responsibility for all consequences resulting from this unauthorized transit and the disregard for safety and maritime warnings," the statement added.
"We warn the enemy that any movement, infiltration, or provocative action within areas under the surveillance of the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran will be met with a decisive and proportionate response."
Iran has repeatedly attacked commercial tankers transiting Hormuz
The incident comes amid repeated attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important oil export routes, since the outbreak of the conflict between the US and Iran in February.
Iran has hit vessels it says have violated its restrictions on passage through the strategic waterway, as it seeks to assert control over the strait and exert pressure on Washington.
The tanker - the Panama-flagged Louise 1 - was targeted with limpet mines, according to assessments from three maritime security sources.
This is the first known successful strike using limpet mines in the area since the beginning of the US war with Iran and followed a separate attempt in September using such devices which did not detonate, two of the sources said.
"The apparent ability of a small craft to approach a transiting tanker, deploy explosive devices and withdraw presents a significant security concern, particularly in the Strait's congested shipping lanes," Greece-based maritime risk management group Marisks said in a note on Friday.
Limpet mines have been deployed in Hormuz since 2017
Marisks said limpet mines were first deployed in the region in 2017 and used against tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in subsequent years, adding that "limpet mines are cheap and easily available."
"The methodology of a small craft attaching these mines on the hulls of vessels in transit is cheap, low-tech and very efficient," it said.
Ukrainian forces also hit the Louise 1 in July with naval drones in the Black Sea over what Ukraine’s SBU security service said was its role in transporting Russian oil and being part of the so-called shadow fleet of tankers deployed by Moscow to keep oil exports flowing.
The vessel's Panama-based operator, listed in shipping databases as Aquarius Maritime Ventures, could not be immediately reached for comment.

Preliminary results of the “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” subregional anti-drug operation have been summed up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:23:45 UTC
20:23:45 KST

On October 30, 2026, the results of the “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” subregional anti-drug operation were summed up as part of the implementation of the 2026 Plan of Key Activities of the Coordinating Council of Heads of Competent Drug Control Authorities of CSTO Member States (CCHCDCA).
From October 18 to 23 this year, in accordance with the 2026 Plan for the Joint Training of Command and Control Bodies and Formations of Forces and Assets of the Collective Security System of the Collective Security Treaty Organization, the “Cobalt-2026” special exercise was held at the Magob training range of the Special Purpose Units Training Center of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Tajikistan.
	 An international scientific and practical conference entitled “Greater Eurasia: Institutions, Development, Cooperation” was held at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO) of the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, jointly organized with the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences (ICCA RAS). CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov took part in the conference.
A working meeting between CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov and Kazem Jalali, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Islamic Republic of Iran to the Russian Federation, was held at the Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the Russian Federation.
	 An international scientific and practical conference entitled “Transformation of the Global Security System and the Shaping of a Eurasian Security Framework” was held at Moscow State Linguistic University (MSLU).
Preliminary results of the “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” subregional anti-drug operation have been summed up
30.10.2026
On October 30, 2026, as part of the implementation of the 2026 Plan of Key Activities of the Coordinating Council of Heads of Competent Drug Control Authorities of CSTO Member States (CCHCDCA), the preliminary results of the “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” subregional anti-drug operation were summed up by CSTO CCHCDCA Secretary, Deputy Head of the Main Directorate for Drug Control of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Russia, Police Major General Boris Yakovchenko, together with Chairman of the Committee for Combating Drug-Related Crime of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Police Colonel Abay Zhusupov, a representative of the CSTO Secretariat, heads of anti-drug agencies of Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan, and experts from relevant international organizations who participated in the operation.
The operation was conducted from October 26 to 30 this year across the territories of CSTO member states. Participants included law enforcement agencies, border and customs services, state security agencies, and financial intelligence units of CSTO member states. Observers included officers from the law enforcement agencies of Iran and China, representatives of the Eurasian Group on Combating Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism, the Committee of Heads of Law Enforcement Units of the Council of Heads of Customs Services of CIS Member States, the Central Asian Regional Information and Coordination Centre (CARICC), the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.
The operation aimed to block drug supply routes into the CSTO area of responsibility, enhance efforts to counter drug trafficking along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, neutralize international transnational drug-trafficking groups, dismantle clandestine drug laboratories, and undermine the economic foundations of the drug trade.
Nearly 9,000 personnel from Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan, as well as more than 2,000 personnel from China and Iran, were involved in the operation. Joint measures resulted in the detection of 790 drug-related crimes (445 by CSTO member states), including 81 cases of smuggling, and the exposure of 101 drug-trafficking groups (12 and 61, respectively, by CSTO member states).
In addition, through coordinated efforts by CSTO member states and observer countries, more than 11.4 tonnes of prohibited substances were seized from illicit circulation in the territories of CSTO member states, China and Iran (1.7 tonnes by CSTO member states). These included approximately 11 tonnes of narcotic drugs, 9.4 kg of psychotropic substances, 23 kg of potent substances and 8 tonnes of precursors. Approximately 200,000 drug-containing plants, more than 153,000 tablets containing prohibited substances, 213 firearms and 1,722 rounds of ammunition of various calibers were also seized.
A total of 376 people were detained for drug-related offences, including 135 citizens of countries outside the CSTO. Another 59 wanted individuals were apprehended.
A total of 674 websites disseminating prohibited drug-related information were identified.
According to preliminary data, more than 1 tonne and 260 kg of marijuana, over 232 kg of hashish, 47 kg of alpha-PVP, more than 68 kg of mephedrone, 31 kg of heroin and approximately 3 kg of precursors were seized from illicit circulation in CSTO member states.
To prevent the smuggling of narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances and their precursors, the Main Directorate for Drug Control of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, together with the Main Directorate for Combating Smuggling of the Federal Customs Service of Russia and the competent authorities of Kazakhstan, organized and is conducting a dedicated anti-drug operation in the Chelyabinsk Region targeting individuals and vehicles crossing the Russian-Kazakh border.
A joint delegation of financial intelligence units of the Eurasian Group reported that, during the active phase of the operation, more than 80,000 financial transactions had been identified. A significant proportion involved transfers to individuals’ accounts, including those of drug couriers used to receive and move illicit funds, the accumulation of assets in such accounts followed by cash withdrawals, and cryptocurrency conversions. The total value of these transactions exceeded 1 billion rubles.
Information provided by financial intelligence units to law enforcement agencies contributed to the initiation of six criminal cases involving money laundering.
During the operation, participants exchanged best practices for combating cross-border drug trafficking.
The “Channel-Caspian Lighthouse” operation helped address practical challenges related to stabilizing the drug situation in the CSTO area of responsibility. New joint measures to ensure anti-drug security have been outlined.
Joint efforts to combat illicit drug trafficking within the CSTO framework will continue.

Everywhere I look there are cardboard boxes and plastic bags. Everything must go.
For thirty years this has been Russia's most prominent independent newspaper, featuring investigative journalism fiercely critical of those in power.
Now Novaya Gazeta is being evicted from its home of three decades. The paper also says it's been blocked from receiving donations.
It's accusing the Russian authorities of killing it off.
"There are different ways to commit murder," journalist and co-founder of the paper Dmitry Muratov tells me. "They chose to strangle us."
"First, they blocked our websites and banned the paper edition. Then they revoked our media licence. One by one we were declared 'foreign agents', and our journalists were attacked.
"Now we can't earn any more money. The banks are refusing to accept donations from our readers. In our country there are political repressions going on. Those have reached us."
In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".
The award didn't stop the Russian authorities from designating him a 'foreign agent' in 2023. The label is often used to punish critics of the government.
Over the years Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.
The paper says that six colleagues were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty". Those journalists include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block twenty years ago this month. She had written extensively on the wars in Chechnya.
As I walk down a corridor, I spot the office Anna had used. Following her killing, the room and all the items in it were preserved and became a museum in her memory. Since the eviction order, most of the objects have already been removed. All that's left is the desk and, lying on top, a portrait of Anna.
In a statement on its website announcing the closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities.
"They've killed us," it starts. "The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."
The publication claims it is the victim of "a coordinated act" and blames "the repressive state apparatus".
"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime… The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.
Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the 'special military operation', new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
Earlier this year there was a police search of Novaya Gazeta's editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".
In connection with the case the newspaper's current editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.
Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form. Loyal readers used VPNs, virtual private networks, to circumvent official blocking of the website. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions were a major blow to the publication.
How does Dmitry Muratov view the future?
"We are in the middle of a terrible catastrophe," Mr Muratov tells me. "Different dictatorships in the world seek chaos. They use chaos to rule their countries and peoples and to strengthen their personal power.
"I don't know what will happen next. I do know that we will do everything to stay true to our values: the human right to life. Human rights override the rights of states."
Novaya Gazeta's demise is very much the end of an era.
In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.

Atlantic bonito abundance delights Turkish consumers but worries fishermen
An abundance of Atlantic bonito in Turkish waters of the Black Sea, unprecedented in 40 years, is delighting market customers with low prices but also raising concerns about the ecological balance, the Nefes newspaper's website (nefes.com.tr) reports.
Selling at affordable prices of between 30 and 50 lira per fish (EUR 0.54–EUR 0.90), Atlantic bonito are being snapped up by customers in large quantities. However, fishermen warn that Atlantic bonito, being one of the most voracious species, prey on numerous other marine creatures, including crustaceans. They say the fish must be caught quickly to protect marine biodiversity.
Towards the end of spring, Atlantic bonito migrate to the Black Sea to spawn, where they lay their eggs, grow in size and build up fat reserves. From October onwards, as the waters begin to cool, the shoals migrate back through the straits towards the Sea of Marmara and the Mediterranean.

"We've been killed by secret services": Independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta to close after 30 years
Novaya Gazeta, an independent Russian newspaper, has announced its permanent closure after more than 30 years, blaming pressure from the authorities, law enforcement agencies and secret services.
Source: Novaya Gazeta
Quote: "We have been killed. On 9 November, we will turn off the lights in our home, where we lived for 30 years, shut down the servers and leave. The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian intelligence services have forced the editorial board to stop working...
We managed to work for almost five years completely surrounded by intelligence services... This is being done by the FSB, the Ministry of Justice, the prosecutor's office, and others who have appropriated the state and usurped power. This is not merely nostalgia for the Soviet past and bitterness over its loss. Behind that façade, a military dictatorship has all but been established."
Details: Novaya Gazeta has received an eviction notice for its office in central Moscow, where its journalists had worked for 29 years. Its system for accepting reader donations has been disabled. Novaya Gazeta says it has now been stripped of everything it needs to keep operating.
The newspaper also recalled that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the authorities had blocked all its online resources and seized its printing house. Intelligence officers and censors had also intervened to stop other printers from producing the paper.
Many of Novaya Gazeta's employees were forced to leave the country. Its editor-in-chief was the target of an assassination attempt. The authorities later revoked the newspaper's media registration and began designating its journalists as "foreign agents", starting with the editor-in-chief. The designation carries strict reporting requirements and other restrictions and is widely used to target independent media and Kremlin critics.
In September, the authorities designated Novaya Gazeta's entire editorial board as a "foreign agent" and added more than 100 journalists and contributors to the register.
For reference: Founded in 1993, Novaya Gazeta became a platform for some of the most outspoken critics of Vladimir Putin and his inner circle in the early 2000s. Among them was human rights activist Anna Politkovskaya, who was murdered in 2006.
Background:
- In 2021, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, received the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts to protect freedom of speech. On 22 March 2022, Muratov announced that he would sell his Nobel Committee medal and donate the proceeds to support Ukrainian refugees affected by Russia's war.
- After the Kremlin adopted the so-called "law on fakes about the Russian army" in early 2022, Novaya Gazeta changed the phrase "Russia's war against Ukraine" to "special military operation" to be able to continue publishing materials in Russia.

A draft of Ukraine's new Cybersecurity Strategy is being prepared for submission to the National Security and Defense Council, and the document will provide for developing the state's capacity to detect and neutralize threats linked to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko said.
"One of the key challenges the Strategy takes into account is the rapid development of AI. So the document must provide for developing the state's capacity to detect and neutralize new threats in good time," he said after a meeting of the National Cybersecurity Coordination Center at the Council on Friday.
Klymenko said participants also discussed strengthening the state's cyber resilience, protecting energy infrastructure, military systems and defense industry enterprises, and countering cybercrime and fraud.
He said Russia is increasing the number of cyberattacks, makes growing use of artificial intelligence tools and synchronizes attacks in cyberspace with missile and drone strikes.
At the same time, despite the overall rise in the number of cyberattacks since 2022, the number of critical incidents has fallen by more than 98%, he said. Ukraine currently ranks 19th in the National Cyber Security Index (NCSI).
Representatives of the Security Service of Ukraine, the Defense Ministry, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the Digital Transformation Ministry, the State Special Communications Service, the National Police, the Foreign Ministry, the Energy Ministry, intelligence bodies and the National Bank took part in the center's work.
"Specific measures were determined for each area, including training of specialists, development of the necessary infrastructure and solutions for early detection and neutralization of threats in cyberspace," the statement posted on Telegram said.
Officials responsible for overseeing the tasks have also been named in government bodies.
The proposals will form the basis for further consideration at a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief. "We must build the cybersecurity system taking into account not only current risks but also challenges that may face Ukraine in the future," Klymenko said.

Ukrainian Defense Forces have destroyed or disabled 1,039 Russian military boats and small vessels using unmanned aerial vehicles since the beginning of 2026, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense.
The ministry reported that all recorded strikes were documented on video through the DELTA battlefield management system and subsequently verified by Ukraine’s Brave1 defense innovation cluster.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the ministry, Russian forces sustained their highest monthly losses in July, when Ukrainian drone operators struck 236 boats and small vessels.
The second-highest number of strikes was recorded in March, with 155 vessels targeted, followed by August with 118, September with 106, and June with 103.
In April, Ukrainian forces struck 92 Russian vessels, while May accounted for 76. During the first 25 days of October, another 67 boats and small vessels were destroyed or disabled.
The lowest monthly figures were recorded at the beginning of the year, with 51 vessels struck in January and 35 in February.
Beyond operations targeting Russian vessels, Ukrainian forces have also carried out major ground offensives aimed at reclaiming occupied territory and disrupting Russian military plans.

North Korean Hackers Suspected in Record $6.36 Billion Binance Crypto Heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:19:00 UTC
20:19:00 KST

- Category
- World
North Korean Hackers Suspected in Record $6.36 Billion Binance Crypto Heist
North Korean hackers are believed to be responsible for a cyberattack on the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange Binance that resulted in the theft of approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets, making it the largest cryptocurrency heist on record, according to Reuters on October 30.
US blockchain analytics company TRM Labs identified TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit, as the group behind the attack, citing evidence gathered from blockchain activity and other intelligence sources.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“An attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM Labs said in a statement.
According to CNN, the attack took place on October 29 with hackers gaining unauthorized access to digital wallets belonging to Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said its preliminary investigation indicated that hackers gained access through an employee engineer’s laptop, enabling them to infiltrate a service container and initiate unauthorized cryptocurrency withdrawals.
In response to the breach, Binance halted deposits and withdrawals pending security reviews, withdrew authorization for the compromised address, and began working with law enforcement and blockchain analysis companies to track down and recover the stolen cryptocurrency.
The exchange also assured customers that their assets remained safe, promising to cover any losses through company resources and its emergency reserve fund.
At the same time, cryptocurrency firms launched efforts to prevent the hackers from accessing the stolen funds. According to CNN, approximately $3 billion worth of digital assets had been frozen by October 29 night in the United States through a joint effort involving several companies.
“It’s the biggest hack in history,” Aravind Srinivasan, head of systematic over-the-counter trading at cryptocurrency market maker GSR, said, as reported by CNN.
Other blockchain intelligence companies also identified North Korean hackers as the likely perpetrators, supporting the findings published by TRM Labs.
Among them was Singapore-based Pangolin Intelligence, which told CNN that its conclusions were drawn from examining blockchain transactions associated with the theft and comparing them with patterns observed in earlier cyberattacks linked to North Korean groups.
One of the company's analysts, who requested anonymity, suggested that the hackers could rely on established money laundering networks to transfer and eventually convert the stolen cryptocurrency into accessible funds.
“I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet,” the analyst told CNN.
Meanwhile, blockchain tracking firm Chainalysis said it was monitoring the movement of stolen assets across several cryptocurrency networks, including Bitcoin and Ethereum. A company representative told CNN that the firm was highly confident North Korean hackers were responsible for the operation.
If North Korea’s involvement is conclusively established, the incident would mark a significant increase in the scale of cryptocurrency theft attributed to the country’s hacking operations.
The attack also comes amid previous scrutiny of Binance over its handling of cryptocurrency transactions involving Russia.
In August, Reuters reported that Binance had provided Russian authorities with information about cryptocurrency donations to Ukrainian fundraising campaigns. The data was subsequently used as evidence in a terrorism financing case against a Russian IT specialist.
According to the outlet, the disclosure occurred despite Binance announcing in 2023 that it had fully withdrawn from the Russian market. Although cryptocurrency exchanges generally comply with legitimate law enforcement requests for customer information in countries where they operate, Binance had already exited Russia when it shared the data.
