The report examined Sino-Russian collaboration surrounding advanced conventional weapons—including industrial supply chains, joint research and development, and academic links between defense-affiliated institutions—identifying 314 shipments involving 52 Russian suppliers and 21 Chinese recipients that transferred military dual-use inputs, manufacturing capabilities, intellectual property, and advanced weapon technologies.
Researchers found that Russian companies increasingly partnered with Chinese counterparts to meet wartime demand by relocating parts of their defense production into China, while joint R&D allowed both nations to test designs, lower costs, and accelerate serial production.
Although the relationship remained uneven—with Russia contributing Soviet-era engineering expertise and China offering industrial scale and heavily funded tech-to-military applications—academic ties and joint publications helped institutionalize long-term cooperation, building upon the "no limits" partnership declared shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Russia’s most powerful warship, the nuclear-powered battlecruiser Pyotr Veliky, deemed too worn out to repair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:18:18 UTC
20:18:18 KST

Russia’s most powerful warship, the nuclear-powered battlecruiser Pyotr Veliky, deemed too worn out to repair
A special commission has concluded that repairing and modernizing the heavy nuclear-powered missile cruiser Pyotr Veliky is not practical, said Vladimir Maltsev, head of the All-Russian Movement in Support of the Navy.
“The cruiser cannot be restored. The ship has a certain degree of wear,” he said. Maltsev stressed that this is a preliminary conclusion, and a final decision has not yet been announced.
A source in the naval sector told the Russian state news agency TASS as early as 2023 about plans to retire the Pyotr Veliky from service. According to the source, the idea of decommissioning it emerged because of the prolonged repair of the cruiser Admiral Nakhimov.
A source who spoke to the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti claimed the same year that there were no plans to decommission the Pyotr Veliky or remove it from the Navy’s active service.
The Pyotr Veliky is the flagship of Russia’s Northern Fleet and the only active nuclear-powered cruiser of the Project 1144 Orlan class. Aside from aircraft carriers, it ranks among the largest warships in the world and is one of the most powerful surface ships in the Russian navy.
Four such ships were built under the project between 1977 and 1996. The Admiral Ushakov and Admiral Lazarev have already been decommissioned, while the heavy nuclear-powered cruiser Admiral Nakhimov went to sea this year for the first time after 28 years of repairs. Plans called for returning it to the Navy by the end of the year.
The Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk, which handles the cruisers’ modernization, can take on only one ship of the series at a time. Repairs on the Pyotr Veliky were initially planned to begin after work on the Admiral Nakhimov was completed in 2018. However, the repairs dragged on, and the cost doubled over that time, exceeding 200 billion rubles.

Indonesia: nine orangutans rescued from wildfires return to the forest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:17:45 UTC
20:17:45 KST

Deep in the protected Batu Nyambu forest, conservationists opened the transport cages on Thursday, 29 October, allowing the animals to scramble up nearby trees and vanish into the canopy. The group included four mothers accompanied by their young, three of whom had also been found to be pregnant during their final veterinary examinations.
The orangutans had been rescued in August and September from an oil palm plantation in Ketapang, where fires had swept through their habitat. Some suffered burns to their hands and feet, while others were severely underweight and malnourished, according to Karmele Llano Sanchez, head of the YIARI wildlife rehabilitation foundation.
After spending four to eight weeks recovering at a rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, the orangutans faced a difficult journey to their new home. Conservationists transported them by vehicle, boat and on foot, carrying heavy cages through steep, slippery forest terrain to reach Batu Nyambu, a 23,000-hectare protected area chosen for its largely undisturbed habitat and abundant food.
The release comes amid growing concern over the survival of Borneo's critically endangered orangutans. Indonesia's forestry ministry says at least 51 have been rescued from burning forests in West Kalimantan since early August, while monitoring group Nusantara Atlas estimates that fires consumed more than 1.9 million hectares of land across Indonesia in the first nine months of 2026.

Investigators suspect him of involvement in a criminal group that caused losses to the Odesa hromada A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories .

Swedish climate scholar Andreas Malm has been barred from entering the UK ahead of a planned appearance at a London conference, with immigration officials saying his presence "may not be considered to be conducive to the public good," The Guardian reported on Friday.
Malm was scheduled to speak alongside Huda Ammori, co-founder of Palestine Action, a pro-Palestine group banned under UK law, at a conference organised by Tribune magazine next week.
The event was set to discuss the impact of Palestine Action's proscription and coincide with a Supreme Court challenge to the group's designation.
Malm, an associate professor of human ecology at Lund University in Sweden, was notified of the decision before travelling to the UK.
He described the decision to deny him entry as "scandalous" and urged the government to reverse it, saying he had travelled to the country for decades for academic research, lectures and conferences.
In comments reported by The Guardian, Malm said Britain had been a central part of his academic life. He conducted archival research in the country for his PhD dissertation, lectured at dozens of universities and participated in numerous conferences. His previous engagements included institutions such as Oxford, Cambridge and King's College London.
"I have always considered the UK a centre of the world of ideas, where differences in opinions and scientific approaches can be aired freely," Malm said, describing his longstanding relationship with the country.
He also expressed dismay at the decision, saying he had expected greater respect for freedom of expression and other democratic rights. He appealed to the government to reverse the ban.
Malm was also scheduled to appear on BBC Radio 4's ‘Radical with Gabriel Gatehouse’ during his visit. His planned appearance would have provided an opportunity for public discussion of the issues surrounding Palestine Action's proscription.
Tribune editor Oliver Eagleton said Malm had been due to speak about attacks on freedom of speech, including the implications of Palestine Action's proscription, but had now himself been prevented from entering the country.
“He is being censored for speaking out about censorship, in truly Orwellian fashion,” Eagleton said in comments to the Guardian.
Author Sally Rooney criticised the decision as "a sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm", describing Malm as one of Europe's influential intellectuals.
Malm has won international awards for his books, and his writings have inspired many to take action for Palestinian rights and environmental justice, according to the Guardian.
The Home Office declined to comment on individual cases, according to the report.

Swiss supermarket chain plays down job loss rumours
A planned merger of the regional co-operatives at Swiss supermarket chain Migros will not cost thousands of jobs, according to chair Mario Irminger.
“Incorrect figures are circulating in the media,” he told the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ). “It is certainly not a matter of thousands of jobs. These estimates are probably based on an analysis of the merger with Coop that took place 25 years ago, but the situation at Migros is different.”
More
Scandals and losses force revamp of Swiss supermarket chain Migros
The SonntagsZeitung has suggested potential annual savings of between CHF300 million and CHF400 million, resulting from 3,000 job cuts. Based on its own calculations, the NZZ estimates that 400 to 600 administrative jobs could be shed.
“At the moment, I don’t wish to comment on a figure like that,” Irminger said. “One thing is certain: at management and administrative level, we will be phasing out parallel structures over time. At Migros Supermarkets, we employ 55,000 staff, and if we take staff turnover within the group into account, we’re talking about 10,000 vacancies that we need to fill every year.”
“Our concern is that we may not have enough specialists to manage our business.”
Irminger will be leaving the company next summer. “The last few months have been very intense. The transformation will continue beyond my retirement,” he said.
For the merger proposal to be approved, the consent of all ten regional co-operatives is required with a two-thirds majority and a 25% turnout.

Modern Aesthetics and Democratic Life: The Struggle for Aesthetic Freedom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:14:00 UTC
20:14:00 KST

It’s hard to imagine a timelier appearance of a monograph than Jörg Schaub’s Modern Aesthetics and Democratic Life. Right now, the same democratically elected representatives who make a show of gilding the pillars of democracy in faux gold are at the same time steadily chipping away at its already shaky foundations. It’s no wonder a generation and a half of skeptics (younger folks in particular) are beginning to wonder if this unquestionably precious thing called “democracy” is all it’s cracked up to be. More worrisome still is that some aren’t sure it’s worth all the effort of preserving it from undemocratic forces. The beauty of Schaub’s book is how convincingly it shows us that it is. Drawing on the best insights of a philosophical legacy that perceived government by and for the people as something more than campaigning and casting ballots, he argues that democracy is a way of life—and indeed, at its best, a richly aesthetic way of life.
Schaub situates this argument at the often-overlooked intersection of political philosophy and aesthetics. The original and attractive thesis it offers is roughly this: that a crucial dimension of freedom concerns our liberation with respect to perception, emotion, and imagination. He argues that the aesthetic is not a peripheral or merely decorative concern for political philosophy, but essential to the achievement—and, just as importantly, the failure—of recognition. “Recognition” here has all the weight originally ascribed to it in the nineteenth century, as the crux of G. W. F. Hegel’s expansive, and often contested, account of mutual freedom. But Schaub lightens it, makes it more familiar, by showing us the fascinating aesthetic dimension of recognition, a dimension strangely absent from a very active tradition of recognition theory. Through well-chosen and highly relevant case studies (socialist critiques of capitalism, feminist consciousness-raising, campus “safe spaces”), the argument moves well beyond the abstract moral, legal, and political forms of Hegelian recognition and illustrates nicely how the achievement of recognition also depends on how we engage in the world aesthetically.
Schaub’s book is not the first (or the last) to diagnose contemporary social and political conflict through a lens considerably broader than the liberal vocabulary of rights and freedoms dominating much Anglophone political philosophy today. But it certainly is a welcome and meaningful contribution to recognition theory in that it turns us away from a fixation on finding new institutional arrangements or revised principles of justice, and points us—in true Hegelian fashion—to the myriad ways the aesthetic operates in everyday social and political life. Here, Schaub tells us, is where we discover (or re-discover) democracy in lived form.
The argument unfolds across three major movements. The first recovers a capacity-based view of modern aesthetics from figures such as Baumgarten, Du Bos, and Addison, and develops a notion of aesthetic subjectivity as the “self” constructed from sense perception, emotion, and imagination. This is more than antiquarian scene-setting: it establishes the conceptual resources Schaub needs to argue that aesthetic experience, properly understood, involves capacities that can be developed, exercised well or badly, and—here’s where recognition comes in—thwarted or denied. The second movement shows where Schaub’s thesis is grounded in Hegel’s writing. A novel reading of Hegel’s Aesthetics shows that the theory of ethical life (Sittlichkeit) discussed there seems to require something like aesthetic recognition if it is to do justice to the full range of ways individuals can be recognized (or misrecognized) by others. On this Hegelian foundation, the argument builds a critical theory of aesthetic recognition in its own right. The advantage is that it clarifies a broader set of conditions on which recognition succeeds or fails. But it also addresses the ways aesthetic recognition co-exists (or conflicts) with other forms of recognition, such as the moral and political. Schaub’s book closes a notable gap in our theoretical picture of recognition. But more importantly, it helps diagnose at least some of what has gone wrong in contemporary politics by getting political philosophy to take seriously the sensory, emotional, and imaginative experience of democratic life.
One of the most significant outcomes of Modern Aesthetics and Democratic Life is that it puts into conversation philosophical traditions that rarely speak to one another with this degree of fluency. First, Schaub shows that the tradition of political philosophy concerned with recognition, freedom, and democratic life has much to discuss with the rich tradition of aesthetic theory running from Hegel through critical theory and beyond. Further, Schaub draws on an impressively wide catalog of sources, the productive interchange between them doing much to overcome the analytic/continental divide that continues to constrain both traditions. Above all, Schaub makes an original and compelling case that how we experience the world aesthetically—in the broadest sense of that term—matters enormously to our sense of self and to whether we are able to live full, autonomous lives. If freedom really does rest on recognition, then Schaub makes a convincing case that it rests in part on the quality and availability of our sensuous and imaginative engagement with the world, and further, that any theory of freedom that ignores this is incomplete.
So I agree fully with the argument’s conclusion that a healthy democratic society is one in which individuals experience recognition in the aesthetic register. But I think there are places where the argument’s premises could be strengthened, particularly if it is to convince skeptics of the philosophical traditions it leans on. For example, “aesthetic” does a lot of work here. And I think Schaub is right to treat the term in its most expansive sense. But this inclusiveness runs the risk of flattening important distinctions. It’s not obvious that we ought to treat the aesthetic experience of art as identical or even similar to, say, the aesthetic experience of nature—especially from a Hegelian perspective. Plenty of Hegelians (Danto, Rockhill, myself, etc.) find plausible reasons to hold engagement with art in higher regard than most everyday experiences. That’s not to say we’re right in holding these different kinds of aesthetic experience. But I’d at least want to be convinced that aesthetic experience of art is qualitatively similar enough to other forms of aesthetic experience (sunsets, daydreaming, a good meal, etc.) to warrant any claims concerning a general aesthetic experience and its role in mutual recognition.
Further, it’s worth acknowledging that Schaub’s account of aesthetic recognition is primarily of negative utility. Really, it’s an account of misrecognition, intended to identify clear cases of recognition’s denial or failure, as in each of the case studies discussed. It’s not his aim, nor should it be, to specify the exact conditions under which recognition is successfully achieved. And, in any case, providing a conceptual framework to identify and understand instances of misrecognition strikes me as a more practical (and interesting) goal than analytic precision. But one does want perhaps a little more guidance in the basics of recognition successfully achieved, especially since, as Schaub notes, norms of aesthetic recognition are “typically contested”, always “subject to re-interpretation”, and are therefore even less settled and less well understood than other norms of recognition (e.g. norms of legal recognition)” (p. 166). So a fuller picture of what these norms look like and how they operate within the aesthetic seems like fertile soil for Schaub’s theory.
The final point, related to the last, concerns how this emphasis on misrecognition applies to one of the book’s central case studies: Hegel’s notoriously brash critique of romantic irony (Friedrich Schlegel’s, in particular). Schaub uses this material effectively to illustrate the kind of pathology that underwrites aesthetic misrecognition. As a diagnostic tool, this deployment of the concept works well. But I’d push back a bit against the claim, made around page 225, that Hegel offers no indication of what a non-pathological form of aesthetic freedom might look like. The seeds of such an account are already present in Hegel’s distinction between Socratic and romantic irony, and there is a further, though brief, discussion of K.W.F. Solger’s concept of irony toward the end of the section of the Lectures on Fine Art devoted to Schlegelian irony that gestures toward a fundamentally different and potentially non-pathological account of irony. It’s not exactly an alternative, positive account of irony Hegel offers here, but it does point in that direction, and further developed, it might strengthen Schaub’s case that Hegel’s resources extend beyond diagnosis to something more constructive.
These are relatively minor quibbles in the context of the book’s considerable achievement. This is an excellent and original manuscript that deserves a wide readership across modern political, aesthetic, and critical theory, as well as across the analytic-continental divide. Schaub has identified a genuine lacuna in the recognition-theoretic tradition and filled it with an account that is historically grounded, philosophically rigorous, and attentive to pressing contemporary controversies. Modern Aesthetics and Democratic Life represents a major contribution to modern political and aesthetic thought, and it deserves widespread attention from scholars across both analytic and continental traditions.

A Confucian Theory of Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:14:00 UTC
20:14:00 KST

The main body of this book is an extensive essay by Sungmoon Kim on the concept of power and its evolution in Confucian political thought. While arguably underlying any attempt to theorize politics, power “remains one of the least examined concepts” in the Confucian tradition (7). This lack of attention to power, as Kim claims, correlates with scholars’ overemphasis on Confucian moral virtue (3) but weakens the potential for Confucianism to thrive as a robust political theory in contemporary East Asia (8). To mitigate it, Kim begins by interpreting several moments in the ancient history of Confucian political thought in China and Korea to defend his idea that Confucian power is best understood in terms of responsibility (16-59). Next, he explores this idea’s implications for contemporary Confucian democracy by focusing on two kinds of responsibility. The first is the liability public officials bear for the suffering of their citizens, even if such suffering is not directly caused by the officials; and the second is the capacity of citizens to attend actively to one another’s concerns (59-71). In this way, Kim issues another challenge to contemporary Confucian meritocrats who attempt to base state legitimacy on performance rather than on responsibility, as these scholars often devalue citizens’ active political participation (69) but hardly develop a realistic way to prevent officials from abusing their power once they assume office (62). Following this essay are six critical responses and Kim’s replies to these responses.
In light of Kim’s meticulous attempt to highlight the role of power in Confucian political theory as well as the creative idea of power as responsibility that he proposes, this book is undoubtedly original and thought provoking for those who care about the future of East Asian societies. Moreover, as a leading expert on Confucian political theory, Kim maintains an extraordinarily high level of historical and philosophical rigor throughout his essay. This allows him to present exegeses with great accuracy and analyses with clear logic, thereby forestalling many potential criticisms on these fronts. Finally, if readers still manage to raise questions about Kim’s account, they will likely find that their questions have been well elaborated in one of the critical responses and that Kim’s thoughtful reply has more or less addressed them. Thus, the remainder of this review focuses on a topic that I believe neither Kim’s essay nor his six critics have adequately covered: the possibility of interpreting the same intellectual history of Confucianism differently.
Kim intends to offer a Confucian “political theory of power”, which is explicitly distinguished from “a conceptual study of power” (14), or an exploration of the ways to comprehend power per se. Instead, Kim aims to “investigate how power was made sense of, often tacitly, within the Confucian political tradition animated by specific political ideas…and to realize a specific goal” (15). As I understand this aim, Kim begins with a rough concept of power and uses it as a handy torch to shed light on several important topics in Confucian political discourses that remain relatively underexamined today. But once illuminated, these topics also enable him to reflect on that torch itself and hence to gain a better sense of the concept of power.
For example, in the second section of the essay, Kim revisits the Confucian distinction between “the Kingly Way” and “the Way of the Hegemon”, a distinction that bears far greater normative weight than contemporary Confucian performance meritocrats have acknowledged (17). Whereas hegemons rely on raw force to coerce, real kings rely on moral virtue to guide. Although both may increase the wellbeing of the ruled, the Way of the Hegemon is widely considered morally inferior to the Kingly Way in the Confucian tradition. Kim explores this distinction in light of its relevance to power. As he contends, for many pre-Qin Confucians, the wellbeing of the people under the rulership of a hegemon is always contingent upon the use of coercion, but coercive force can be easily abused (24). Thus, such uncertain wellbeing is never as appealing as the more solid one under the rulership of a king. It follows that, in neglecting the Confucian rejection of the Way of the Hegemon, contemporary Confucian performance meritocrats mistakenly assume that all ways to make the people happy are equal (25).
Moreover, when the distinction between the two Ways is understood in terms of power, it also becomes possible for Kim to abstract the pre-Qin Confucian understanding of power primarily as force-based coercion in light of its contrast to virtue-based guidance. On this basis, Kim proposes that the idea of power as responsibility can be largely understood as the result of post-Qin Confucian scholars’ attempt to tame coercion in the historical context of hereditary kingship, thereby leading to a reconceived understanding of power that aims to displace force (26).
This is a brilliant methodological move: without imposing an elaborate but likely exogenous definition of power on the Confucian tradition that does not even use any single term to capture that concept (15), Kim allows power to be a theme for the study of Confucian political thought and lets power reveal its own meaning within the Confucian tradition as its political and intellectual history unfolds. As such, in a somewhat Hegelian way, this approach also helps resolve the chicken-or-egg issue regarding the relationship between concept and phenomenon: in exerting influence on each other, they evolve with each other.
Meanwhile, readers may still wonder whether Kim nevertheless begins with a thin understanding of power to operationalize his approach, and if so, why he prefers this to another understanding of power. At first glance, this may not appear to matter much because the initial understanding of power, whatever it is, will eventually evolve into power as responsibility. However, I argue that the starting point exerts tremendous influence on the way in which the ensuing history is interpreted, as different starting points may give rise to vastly different interpretations even if historical facts themselves remain the same. Let me elaborate.
Kim summarizes three Western ways to understand the concept of power: “power-over”, “power-to”, and “power-with” (14). Whereas “power-over” roughly corresponds to the idea of power as coercive force, “power-to” captures the idea of power as enabling. As mentioned above, although Kim rightly insists that “power-over” and “power-to” coexist in the Confucian tradition, he seems to privilege “power-over” a little more in his discussion of pre-Qin Confucianism, as this “negative” understanding of power leads to Confucians’ worry about the abuse of coercive force (22). “Power-over”, in this sense, becomes the starting point of Kim’s inquiry, and the remainder of the history is largely interpreted as a series of attempts by Confucians to enrich and transform the meaning of power in order to tame and even sideline “power-over”. Put differently, post-Qin Confucians often appear in Kim’s essay as conscientious defenders of “power-to”, who attempt to impose moral restraints on hereditary rulers and allow ministers and even the ruled to share political responsibility with their rulers. The democratic implications at the end of the essay hence follow.
But what if Kim treated “power-to” as the starting point of his inquiry instead? Doing so may have produced a different interpretation of the Confucian tradition. In pre-Qin texts, sage-kings are frequently depicted as offering non-coercive guidance to their people by means of virtue and rituals. Such guidance allows the people themselves to become virtuous so as to harmonize with one another. Accordingly, virtue and rituals enable the people’s self-rule, which is exactly what “power-to” means. However, generations of ambitious rulers constantly attempt to achieve political hegemony and hence bring “power-over” to the table, and their political success gradually culminates in the displacement of virtue-based legitimacy (the Sagely-Line) by force-based legitimacy that passes down through the bloodline (the Princely-Line). Accordingly, one may cast a very different light upon post-Qin Confucians’ endeavor to theorize power as responsibility: rather than standing their ground to defend “power-to”, they retreat from their initial emphasis and give in to “power-over” whenever hegemonic rulers forcefully assert their dominance.
Admittedly, this is a much less appealing way to interpret what these Confucians do than Kim’s interpretation, in as much as it portrays their endeavor instead as (a) an abandonment of the “rectification of names”, arguably the most important thing that Confucius himself urges his followers to do, and (b) a compromise with the status quo in a world where hereditary kingship eventually becomes an unchallengeable fact. What follows, then, is not the democratic implications of Confucian power but an exhibition of Confucians’ failure to resist both the lure and the intimidation of Legalist absolutism.
This is definitely not to say that the alternative interpretation above is more faithful to historical facts than is Kim’s. Nor is Kim unaware of alternative interpretations of the examined thinkers. Quite the contrary, he takes one such alternative seriously. In his discussion of imperial Confucianism through the lens of Dong Zhongshu in the third section of the essay, Kim mentions a conventional way to read the Han-dynasty thinker as “a Legalist posing as a Confucian” (36) and rejects it. This is a welcome rejection, but not much is said about alternative readings of other examined thinkers. Such silence, in turn, may give rise to new questions regarding his portrayal of them.
For example, in the fourth section, Kim examines Northern Song Confucian scholar-officials’ attempt to advance Dong’s project by claiming their shared responsibility with the emperors. In this examination, Kim invokes these scholar-officials’ practice of citing classical Confucian texts to boost their moral power and support their claim. Such a practice may appear to show that the authority of Confucianism is independent of the authority of the emperors, but Kim rightly pushes back by reaffirming that the scholar-officials’ quasi-constitutional claim is still based on their acknowledgment of the ruler’s undivided political power (43). Rather, the real breakthrough is better observed in Chŏng Tojŏn’s account later (52-56).
Yet Kim could have further emphasized some nuances in Northern Song politics, as doing so may cast a different light on those scholar-officials. Despite their significance, Confucian classics are just one source of scholar-officials’ authority. Northern Song is distinguished from almost all other Chinese imperial dynasties in its insistence on the authority of so-called zu zong zhi fa 祖宗之法, or a changing, vague, but still recognizable series of rules and instructions initiated especially by Taizu and Taizong, the first two Song emperors. By the time of Emperor Renzong, zu zong zhi fa already takes on a life of its own, potentially creating a conceptual and practical distinction between the monarchy and its incumbent monarch (hence something comparable to the famous problem of the King’s Two Bodies in medieval political thought).
In claiming their share of responsibility in ruling, Song scholar-officials often resort to zu zong zhi fa, even when it has become obviously inconvenient due to its conservative nature. In fact, the blind adherence to zu zong zhi fa is precisely a major target of Wang Anshi’s unsuccessful reforms during the reign of Emperor Shenzong. Accordingly, Song scholar-officials’ endeavor is perhaps less morally laudable than Kim shows: their motivation to participate in the process of ruling may be less “a sense of responsibility” to the wellbeing of the people (45) than an unreasonable devotion to past rulers’ hegemonic legacies, hence less a desire to endorse “power-to” than a desire to preserve “power-over”. At the very least, the line drawn between the two sides is more obscure than it may appear at first glance.[1]
To be sure, it is in no way surprising that the same series of accurately portrayed historical facts may yield multiple competing interpretations, and asking an author to thoroughly reject all other possible interpretations before proposing one’s own is also an uncharitable demand. Nevertheless, I believe that some reasonable burden of proof still remains on the author’s shoulders to defend one’s interpretation not only on its own terms but also against its alternatives. Perhaps a more effective way for Kim to do so is precisely to reflect on the very beginning of his inquiry and argue that “power-over” is indeed more suitable than “power-to” and “power-with” as the starting point for his examination of the birth of power as responsibility. Doing so would spare him from the need to defend his interpretation of each examined thinker one by one. More importantly, it would allow him to assert that the implications of his Confucian theory of power are unmistakably, and even unavoidably, democratic. This is a stronger assertion than the one he has offered. It is also an assertion that contemporary East Asian societies urgently need.
REFERENCES
Deng Xiaonan, Invoking Imperial Ancestors’ Instructions in Early Northern Song Politics (Beijing: Joint Publishing, 2014).
[1] This brief discussion of zu zong zhi fa relies entirely on the seminal work by historian Deng Xiaonan, Invoking Imperial Ancestors’ Instructions in Early Northern Song Politics (Beijing: Joint Publishing, 2014). She is particularly skeptical of Northern Song scholar-officials’ pronounced moralism in light of their factional conflicts that often revolve around zu zong zhi fa: “At that time, the moral depravity of any single scholar-official was often despised, but these scholar-officials’ collective moral depravity in political struggles was often hidden behind the banner of the absolute moral standard” (454).

20:13:46 KST

A Russian FPV drone struck a social bus operated by the Proliska Humanitarian Mission in the frontline village of Bilenke, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, while it was carrying 23 passengers and a driver. The mission’s head, Yevhen Kaplin, reported the attack on Facebook on 29 October. In a comment to Ukrainska Pravda, he later gave slightly different details: 20 passengers and around 14:50.
Earlier that day, Russian attacks on Bilenke killed a 49-year-old man and wounded three other men, acting Zaporizhzhia Oblast head Mykhailo Semikin said. The village of Bilenke is likely to face the most difficult conditions in Zaporizhzhia Oblast this winter, then-head of the oblast Ivan Fedorov said in an interview with Ukrinform on 15 August. Russian forces use the village as a testing ground because the front line runs roughly across the river, he said.
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, this marks the 121st attack on the mission’s staff and volunteers while they were providing aid, as well as on its vehicles, offices, and warehouse infrastructure, Kaplin said.
The drone was reportedly lying in wait
The attack killed a female passenger born in 1952. The bus driver sustained serious injuries and was evacuated to a medical facility, Kaplin said. Another passenger, a man born in 1947, sustained multiple shrapnel wounds, while another woman suffered injuries from flying glass. The remaining passengers suffered acoustic barotrauma. Most of the people on board were elderly.
According to preliminary information, this was a drone that was lying in wait, Kaplin said. The attack took place at around 14:30 in the center of the village, on a section of road protected by an anti-drone net.
The bus was clearly marked with the humanitarian mission’s logo on the hood and roof, as well as the words “social bus,” Kaplin said.
National Police special units and military personnel evacuated the wounded, accompanied by aerial cover teams, due to the threat of further drone attacks.
It was the only transport serving the village, Kaplin said
Commercial transport operators no longer serve the village of Bilenke, but more than 1,600 people still live there.
As a result, residents had no way to reach the Oblast center to access essential services, or to buy food and medicine, Kaplin said. They also could not collect their pensions or winter aid payments from the state and humanitarian organizations.
The Proliska team launched the social bus at the request of regional and local authorities.
Russians attack public transport in Zaporizhzhia with drones
Russian drones also hit civilian transport in the Oblast capital several times on 29 October. The city came under a record number of FPV drone attacks that day, Semikin said, adding that Russia had changed its tactics and modified its drones.
- In the morning, a Russian FPV drone struck a municipal bus in the city, Semikin said on 29 October. He first said the strike injured a woman and a man, then said four people were injured.
- Russia launched two strikes on Zaporizhzhia, Semikin reported the same day. Two men, aged 66 and 41, were injured. The strikes damaged 15 vehicles, a warehouse building, a power line, and a nearby apartment block. A fire broke out at the site, he added.
- Later, a Russian drone struck a minibus in central Zaporizhzhia, Semikin reported. According to preliminary information, one person was injured.
- A Russian FPV drone struck a municipal trolleybus in Zaporizhzhia again, Semikin said. He initially reported one woman injured, then said the number rose to three. They included a 56-year-old woman in serious condition and two other women, aged 71 and 66, who sustained minor shrapnel wounds to their legs, he said.

The court began proceedings on 20 September against 47 French nationals accused of belonging to Islamic State, scheduling hearings in stages.
Iraqi lawyers have been appointed to defend the defendants after French lawyers requested by them were unable to attend.

Wall Street braces for Democratic gains as 2026 midterm election nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:12:17 UTC
20:12:17 KST

Investors expect a blue wave in next week's midterm election, as Democrats surge in polls and President Donald Trump's approval rating remains low.
Public polling suggests Democrats are likely to take control of the House of Representatives, and analysts who parse what politics means for investors are in overdrive to tell their clients how to prepare for what Congress will look like after the Tuesday election.
Concern about the spending plans and priorities of a Democratic-controlled Congress permeates analyst reports reviewed by CNBC. But because Trump has another two years of his presidency, a divided government would likely create gridlock that would prevent congressional leadership in opposition to the president from getting much done, analysts are advising their clients.
Most analysts believe Democrats are also within striking distance of a Senate majority, though that outcome is significantly less likely than a House flip according to the polls. Next Tuesday's elections will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress for the remainder of Trump's presidency, after two years of full Republican control.
Divided government typically makes must-pass legislation, like government funding and raising the debt ceiling, harder to enact. A debt ceiling standoff — or first-ever default on federal debt — could be particularly damaging.
Wall Street watchers are also expecting Democrats to try to advance an ambitious and expensive agenda should they gain control of Congress. An Oct. 29 report from Piper Sandler analyzing Congressional Budget Office data projected that policy proposals from Democrats "would add $5 trillion to the deficit over the coming decade." The analysis assumes repeals of Trump's tariffs and reversing cuts to Medicaid, nutrition programs and Affordable Care Act subsidies.
Major policy swings — and big spending packages — become less likely as a divided government is unlikely to agree on issues. That's a dynamic the market typically enjoys. Trump's veto power would effectively block major Democratic policies from becoming law.
"A blue House is the obvious consensus base case," Wolfe Research said in an Oct. 27 report. The firm surveyed 138 investors and found 96% of those polled believed Democrats would prevail in House control.
"The scale of polling error that would be required for Republicans to retain House control would be unprecedented in modern history, well above the polling error in the famously bad 2020 cycle," Wolfe wrote.
Wolfe is less bullish on a Democratic Senate, though investors clearly see a possibility that Democrats regain control of both chambers of Congress.
Fifty-eight percent of investors the firm surveyed believed Democrats would gain control of the Senate, while 42% believed Republicans would retain control of the chamber. The investors surveyed were more bullish than Wolfe itself, which puts the chances of a Democratic Senate at 49%.
Other analysts are largely coalescing around the potential for a good night for Democrats.
"A blue wave scenario has become our base case," an Oct. 20 report from TD Securities reads. An Oct. 23 Raymond James report says "Democrats are in a solid position to win a majority in the House of Representatives and are increasingly likely to win enough seats to capture a Senate majority."
Even if Democrats sweep both chambers, protracted battles could still play out as Republicans maintain the White House and the Senate must still surpass the 60-vote filibuster threshold.
Democrats winning control of the Senate could allay concerns about the Federal Reserve's independence from Trump, TD predicted.
That's because any new Fed members would need to be confirmed by the Senate, which would be unlikely to support a nominee who wouldn't support the central bank charting its own course.
Democrats are also expected to investigate companies that have done business with the Trump administration should they win control of a chamber. The majority party in Congress holds subpoena power on committees. Some Democrats have already telegraphed their investigative priorities ahead of the election.
The debt ceiling is likely the most critical sticking point for the economy that lawmakers will need to address during the next Congress, unless Republicans raise it during the lame-duck session between the election and the start of the next Congress in January. The Bipartisan Policy Center expects the U.S. will reach the debt limit between late-winter and mid-summer 2027.
"While negotiations around the debt ceiling may come down to the wire, a Democratic Congress would make it slightly more likely that a bill is passed than a divided Congress," TD said.
If Congress does not raise the debt ceiling, the U.S. could default on its debt, causing catastrophic economic consequences.
Democrats, should they control one slice of government, are expected to demand concessions from Republicans in exchange for their votes to raise the debt ceiling. That sets up a potential standoff, which analysts note Republicans could avoid if they lose next week and raise the debt ceiling during the lame duck.
"[R]aising the debt limit before January could substantially reduce leverage Democrats have over healthcare, Medicaid, SNAP, and broader domestic spending priorities in the next Congress," Raymond James told its clients.
Correction: This story has been corrected to reflect that the Bipartisan Policy Center projects the U.S. will reach its debt limit next year. An earlier version mischaracterized the center's projection.

A day earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that the Armed Forces of Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes on Russian territory, destroying two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers and hitting an Iskander missile launcher, though he did not specify the exact location. Previously, the press service of the Ukrainian Navy reported that the Su-34s were destroyed in a strike by a Neptune coastal missile system on the Marinovka airfield in Russia’s Volgograd region.

Police launch criminal investigation into Google data centre works
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
13:08:48 EET
20:08:48 KST

Finnish police have launched a criminal investigation into preparatory work at Google's planned data centre in Muhos, northern Finland, over suspected environmental damage. The investigation follows concerns about drainage and water management at the site, where the company cleared hundreds of hectares of forest before completing environmental assessments.
The Oulu Police Department announced on Thursday that it had begun investigating activities carried out by Tuike Finland, Google's Finnish subsidiary, following a request from the Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV).
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Police have received five requests for an investigation concerning the Muhos project. All five will form part of the same criminal inquiry.
According to the police statement, preliminary findings indicate irregularities and shortcomings in drainage arrangements and water management at the construction site. Investigators will examine these activities to establish whether environmental offences have occurred.
Police said the investigation also covers potential lesser offences.
The case follows weeks of scrutiny over Google's preparations for data centres in Muhos and Kajaani, where extensive forest clearance and earthworks began before the completion of environmental impact assessments.
Tuike Finland cleared approximately 330 hectares of forest in Muhos. Finnish legislation requires the assessments when permanent forest removal exceeds 200 hectares in a continuous area.
The Finnish Supervisory Agency intervened in early October, instructing Tuike Finland to suspend work affecting the environment at both locations. The restrictions covered logging, excavation, drainage, soil removal and the construction of roads and storage areas.
Google confirmed on 14 October that preparatory activities had stopped at both sites.
The agency had raised concerns that the scale of the work risked changing the environment before the assessment process established its potential consequences.
Google has maintained that it acted in accordance with Finnish legislation and understood from discussions with municipal authorities that preparatory work was permitted.
In an earlier statement, Google communications manager Sondre Ronander acknowledged concerns about the company's handling of the projects.
“We understand the concern caused by the situation. In this case, we did not meet the high standards we set ourselves,” Ronander said.
Google previously claimed it had conducted nature surveys and taken measures to protect environmentally sensitive areas. It also announced plans to plant trees across 130 hectares in Muhos.
The projects form part of Google's announced €13 billion investment programme in Finnish data centre infrastructure.
The Oulu Police Department aims to complete the preliminary inquiry during 2027 and plans to release further information in December 2026.

Russia ‘forces’ closure of investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

Russia ‘forces’ closure of investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta
A symbol of independent journalism, Novaya Gazeta has been classed as a ‘foreign agent’ by Moscow.
Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it will shut down, citing pressure from the authorities.
The independent outlet’s editorial board said in a statement released on Friday that the newspaper has been forced to end its operations.
The Russian media has come under increased scrutiny from the state amid Moscow’s war on Ukraine. The authorities recently searched the home of Novaya Gazeta’s senior editor and arrested the editor-in-chief.
“The newspaper is gone. The Russian authorities and … intelligence services forced the editorial staff to cease operations,” the editorial board said in the statement, which was entitled: “We were killed.”
Viewed as a relative bastion of independent journalism in Russia, Novaya Gazeta has been classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow, a label used to stifle dissent.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a video statement published on YouTube. “On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”
Earlier this month, Sokolov was taken in for questioning as Russian authorities searched his home due, they said, to a link to a criminal case involving his colleague Oleg Roldugin.
Roldugin was arrested in April and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”.
“How far will the Kremlin’s relentless campaign against Novaya Gazeta go?” asked media watchdog Reporters Without Borders in a statement after Sokolov was arrested on October 15.
“Six of its journalists and staff members have been murdered, its newsroom has been raided, its journalists have been prosecuted, and the publication has been designated a ‘foreign agent’,” the press freedom organisation noted.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, said he was “deeply concerned and saddened” by the closure, describing it as another “devastating blow” for remaining independent media in Russia.
Turk said pressure on independent journalism had intensified significantly since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, through increasingly restrictive legislation, tighter state controls and the persecution of journalists.
He noted that his office has repeatedly raised concerns about the wider media clampdown, including the “foreign agent” law and its effect on civil and political rights.
The forced closure of Novaya Gazeta marks another escalation in Russia’s crackdown on press freedom, with few independent media outlets or journalists left in the country, as censorship levels and arrests of regime critics have skyrocketed since it launched the Ukraine war in February 2022.
The newspaper had already trimmed production inside Russia after Moscow invaded Ukraine, as authorities revoked its media licence.
The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.

October marks record high for reported strikes in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. navy says
There were more strikes reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz than any other month during the Iran-U.S. war, according to the U.K. Marine Trade Operations Centre, which is supported by the Royal Navy.
There were just over 30 attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman or Persian Gulf reported in October, with only March, the first month of the war, reporting even 30 attacks, according to the UKMTO. There were twice as many attacks in October as there were in September. While there were likely more attacks in the month, the UKMTO only counts attacks reported by verified vessels in the region.
The war also crossed the eight-month mark this week as it started on Feb. 28. Since the war started, there have been 145 reported incidents, the UKMTO said. While the UKMTO does not track who fired the projectiles that hit vessels, the vast majority of strikes came via Iran. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps often claims responsibility for the attacks.
Iran has started to claim a large number of ships hitting mines in the region as well, though they largely do not appear on the list of incidents from the UKMTO.
Since July 6, 59 of the 81 projectile strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz region came along the southern route, the UKMTO said. The U.S. has championed the southern route, and used it to escort oil tankers out of the Persian Gulf, while Iran calls the route illegal and says ships need to travel north, along the Iranian coast.

But ongoing conflicts have deepened rifts even as the United States seeks to focus on economic growth, trade imbalances and supply chain challenges in areas like energy and critical minerals.
Rubio warned at an opening plenary session that the world faces "interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, many of which pose severe threats" to the global economy.
He urged the G20 to work together against threats including strains to global energy and food supply chains, and on freedom of navigation.
Still, few breakthroughs are expected this week from the Group of 20 economies — which include China, India, Russia, Japan, Germany and France — as officials face divisions over Moscow's war on Ukraine and fallout from the conflict with Iran.
Global energy prices have rocketed since U.S.-Israel strikes on Iran from late February triggered Tehran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
"This is the last test case the G20 has, at least under the US G20 presidency, until Miami," Alisha Chhangani of the Atlantic Council told AFP. Its outcomes will affect how the December summit shapes up.

BP profit quadruples as Iran war sends refining margins soaring and debt tumbles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:07:31 UTC
20:07:31 KST

BP's net profit quadrupled between July and September as the Iran war sent refining margins and oil prices soaring, with the British energy giant beating forecasts and cutting its net debt by $8.4 billion (€7.5bn) ahead of a strategy update in December.
BP's profit attributable to shareholders rose to $4.7 billion (€4.2bn) for the July to September period, four times the $1.16 billion (€1.04bn) of a year earlier, it said on Friday, as disruption from the Iran war boosted its refining and trading earnings.
The British oil and gas major also beat analysts' forecasts and cut its net debt by $8.4 billion (€7.5bn), weeks before its new CEO sets out her strategy in December.
Its underlying replacement cost profit, the figure investors judge BP on, nearly quadrupled to $8.5 billion (€7.6bn) from $2.2 billion (€1.96bn), well above the $6.2 billion (€5.55bn) expected.
It strips out swings in the value of BP's oil and fuel stocks and one-off items, such as $4 billion (€3.58bn) of writedowns this quarter, mostly on what it called "transition businesses".
Like its rivals, BP cashed in on refining margins, the difference between what refiners pay for crude and what they earn from fuels such as diesel. With the war choking off fuel exports from the Middle East, refineries elsewhere are profiting from tight global supplies.
CEO Meg O'Neill, who took over in April, described "a strong set of results, supported by the higher-price, higher-margin environment".
Net debt also fell to $13.9 billion (€12.4bn) from $22.3 billion (€19.9bn) three months earlier, helped by BP suspending share buybacks in February to put spare cash towards its balance sheet. The company said it had now met its targets for cutting debt and costs, and kept its quarterly dividend at 8.66 cents a share.
BP also said it intends to prioritise using spare cash to settle its remaining liabilities from Deepwater Horizon, the 2010 explosion and oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico that killed 11 workers, after agreeing last week to speed up payments of the $16 billion (€14.3bn) settlement to the US state of Louisiana.
O'Neill unveils her strategy on 15 December as BP, long seen as lagging its peers, had already cut back clean energy spending to refocus on more lucrative oil and gas. Rivals Shell and TotalEnergies also posted bumper profits on Thursday.
BP shares were up 0.3% in early trading on Friday.
Where oil stands
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, traded at around $113.6 a barrel on Friday morning, up roughly 2.5% on the week, after falling more than 6% on Monday as diplomacy over the Iran war seemingly gathered pace.
That is still far above the roughly $72 per barrel that Brent fetched before the Iran war began in late February.
US benchmark West Texas Intermediate stood at around $104.2 a barrel, up roughly 1.5% on the week.
BP has also raised the oil price it uses to value its assets, and now assumes Brent will average $87 a barrel this year, up from $70, both adjusted for inflation to 2024 prices.
It expects supply disruptions in the Middle East to last into 2027, and refining margins to "remain elevated" in the final quarter of this year.

Slovak prosecutor reopens probe into fighter jet donation to Ukraine
Oct 30 - Slovakia's top prosecutor ordered on Friday a new probe into the donation of MiG-29 fighter jets and air defence systems to Ukraine by the country's previous government, restarting an investigation ended earlier this year.
The current government of Prime Minister Robert Fico, which pursues a more pro-Russian foreign policy and ended military aid for Ukraine, has repeatedly attacked the donation made in 2023.
The decision reopens a criminal case at the centre of a dispute between Fico's government and its predecessors over military support for Ukraine.
Fico has said the donations left the country dependent on allied air patrolling, and a senior official in his party called it sabotage.
The country's chief prosecutor, Maros Zilinka, said on Facebook on Friday he had ordered a new investigation as the previous one ended prematurely.
"In the preparatory proceedings, facts were not established in an extent necessary for a decision," he said.
A Bratislava regional prosecutor, Rastislav Remeta, said in ending the previous probe in February this year that the dozen Soviet-era MiG-29 jets and the KUB air defence systems were outdated, not fully operational and lacked pilots and missiles. He said their donation was no crime.
The defence minister at the time, Jaroslav Nad, has denied any wrongdoing.
The case is an illustration of the highly polarised Slovak political scene, where Fico has repeatedly accused his predecessors of pursuing criminal prosecutions against his party when he was in opposition. REUTERS

Pranksters fake US$10 theft from struggling Minnesota dad – viewers raise over US$250,000 for him
- Two pranksters faked a US$10 theft on a struggling Michigan father, Walt Z, while he worked at a Minnesota grocery store.
- The video of the prank went viral on X, drawing more than 2.2 million views and strong backlash. The Instagram account was later taken down after the pranksters faced online anger.
- Viewers raised more than US$250,000 on GoFundMe for Walt. Red Baron said it had spoken to the employee involved and was supporting him after the August incident.
AI generated
It was a simple prank, but the two trolls behind it picked the wrong mark: a Michigan father of four with bills to pay, shelves to stock and a whole universe of frustrations to unload.
So, in a two-minute video that has been watched more than 2.2 million times on social media platform X, he let the pranksters have it.
He berated them and angrily told them why they should not be making fun of someone like him who was nearly at the end of his rope, just so they could entertain their Instagram followers.
Viewers responded to that raw emotion with more than just sympathy. They chipped in, raising more than US$250,000 (S$319,000) as at Oct 29 for the man, publicly identified only as Walt Z.
The encounter began when two men approached Walt, who was wearing a Red Baron pizza shirt, as he stocked a grocery store freezer, and asked for the time.
When Walt took out his phone to check the time, one of the men held another phone near it and set off a fake Apply Pay sound and a simulated money transfer.
“I just took US$10,” the prankster told Walt, laughing and trying to provoke a reaction. “I just took your money.”
Walt’s response was immediate.
“My life is hard enough as it is, okay? I don’t need this crap,” he told the two men.
“Bro, bro, it’s just a joke! It’s just a prank,” the man recording the video replied, trying to pacify Walt.
But Walt had more to say.
“I got kids at home that went to bed without me right now! I was supposed to be off an hour ago! I gotta wake up at five in the morning and do 10 more stores!” he told them.
One of the men then said: “I’m sorry, bro, chill. We’re just filming a video, it was just a joke.”
“No, you don’t!” Walt replied. “You’re probably making money off of this! I can’t even pay my goddamn mortgage, and I got four kids at home! So not funny!”
The pair uploaded the video onto their Instagram channel before taking it down and deactivating their account following huge online backlash.
“Real people have real emotions, and they shouldn’t have to become content just so someone can get views,” wrote one X user.
“In America, hard work is punished, while laziness and goofiness are rewarded,” added another.
After coming across the video, Luke Oakenshield, who identified himself as a homeless veteran, organised a fund-raiser on GoFundMe for Walt.
“This fundraiser is about standing up for a working person who is busting his butt and should not have to fear losing stability because someone wanted content and clicks,” Oakenshield wrote.
By Oct 29, the campaign had raised more than US$280,000.
In an update, Oakenshield said Walt had been found and made aware of the fund-raiser.
“Walt Z out of Michigan sends a heartfelt thank you, and is absolutely blown away by how much people have cared over this,” he wrote.
“They are requesting privacy, and GoFundMe is taking the lead in transferring all of this to him. You’re all Rockstars, and it shows,” he added.
A spokesman for Red Baron’s parent company told The New York Post that it was aware of the video and had spoken to the employee involved.
Red Baron is a Minnesota-based frozen-food manufacturer and distributor.
“We are aware of the video circulating on social media involving one of our direct store delivery employees during an incident that occurred in August,” said the spokesman.
“Following the incident, we connected directly with our team member to check on his well-being, and we continue to offer our support. We are pleased to share that he is doing well and remains a valued member of our team,” he added.

Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:04:12 UTC
20:04:12 KST

Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.
In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.
Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.
The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.
Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.
Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.
“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.
In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.
Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

Internal documents show failed scramble to save "forever cruise"

2026-10-30
11:03:26 UTC

Internal documents reveal scramble for funds before around-the-world "forever cruise" was stranded
When the journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship came to a sudden end earlier this week in Cambodia, giving residents on the ship just hours to disembark, it marked the culmination of several attempts over a period of about three months to save the unique voyage.
According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, those included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.
The voyage of the Odyssey, which is operated by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, was billed as a continuous around-the-world cruise when it launched in October 2024. It allowed passengers to become residents of the ship by purchasing cabins for several hundred thousand dollars.
However, more than 200 passengers and dozens of crew members became stranded in Cambodia on Tuesday when Villa Vie suddenly suspended operations because of major financial issues.
In early August, the Odyssey was docked in Singapore when Villa Vie warned that the ship was at risk of being detained and the operator said it urgently needed to raise money.
"There's no question that we ran out of money in Singapore," said Darrell Carp, a Villa Vie resident who told CBS News he is out $250,000.
Residents believed finances were being mismanaged by cruise operator
Multiple residents told CBS News they were concerned about giving money directly to the company because they believed the finances were being mismanaged by Villa Vie.
"We never fully understood the level of their debt," Carp said. "They were already behind on their payments on crew, and provisions, and fuel, and things like that."
A source close to the company said that when fuel prices spiked this year after the U.S. attacked Iran, it was a disaster for the company's business model.
After some passengers raised money while the ship was stuck in Singapore, $400,000 was paid to a fuel supplier directly out of one resident's personal checking account so the Odyssey could continue its journey, sources said.
At that time, Villa Vie was in the hole for several million dollars, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. Hundreds of thousands of dollars were owed to a port agent, fueling companies, food vendors and the crew.
Those internal documents showed that in a town hall on Aug. 4, residents were warned there was a real possibility of halting operations, laying off staff and repatriating the crew.
According to documents reviewed by CBS News, the ship was potentially days away from losing its insurance. It said that it would cut internet service to save money and was paying just enough to keep sailing.
Villa Vie introduced VIP program to raise emergency funds
In early August, Villa Vie introduced a so-called VIP "Villa Incentive Program" to help raise emergency funds, according to the documents. The VIP program was only open to current Villa Vie passengers so they could purchase more cabins at a discounted rate.
By Aug. 18, the company posted: "We have the commitment of over 20 cabins on the VIP sales!"
The program was initially an idea by the residents. Instead of just raising funds, it was designed to give passengers an even greater ownership stake in the ship, according to passengers and a source close to the company.
There was urgency to sell the cabins. The last slide of a PowerPoint presentation by Villa Vie on the VIP program read, "Funds are due today."
The VIP program was able to raise enough funds to keep the ship operating, but it continued to struggle, sources said.
A source with knowledge of the VIP program also said cabins aboard the Odyssey were still being sold to Villa Vie residents despite the company operating at a loss at that point.
According to one document, the ship's finances showed that even at full occupancy, it would operate at a $600,000 loss. Average monthly operating costs were $3.1 million, but revenue at 100% occupancy with everyone paying full fees would only have been $2.5 million, the document showed.
A source close to the company disputes the $3.1 million number and claims that the ship's monthly operating costs were under $1 million.
In August, 139 of 490 cabins were unsold, according to the documents.
Ship director had to bribe Vietnam officials to get food aboard, source says
When the ship reached Vietnam, crew members allegedly had to buy food from local grocery stores to feed passengers because the company owed money to a food vendor that would no longer deliver food, according to sources familiar with the situation.
According to one source, the ship's hotel director allegedly had to bribe local customs officials in Vietnam in order to get food onto the ship.
Later, in Hong Kong, court records obtained by CBS News showed the ship was detained until the company paid $167,844.48 to a fuel provider.
Villa Vie founder Mike Petterson has said skyrocketing fuel costs were what ultimately caused the ship's journey to come to an end.
When asked by CBS News Wednesday if creditors might seize the ship, Petterson told CBS News: "We will likely file for Chapter 11 here any day, right, which will put a stay on that while we go through the restructure process."
A source close to the company said Villa Vie stopped conducting cabin sales externally after Aug. 4, once the ship knew it was essentially out of money and needed to raise funds.
Yet on July 27, just a week before the ship ran out of money, Villa Vie had announced it was in the process of purchasing a second ship, the Legacy, and offered residents who were buying a cabin on the future ship an opportunity to take up immediate residency on the Odyssey.
A source close to the company said it was necessary to buy more ships to scale up for the business model to work.

Brazil's new anti-gang law: Can it curb organized crime?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:03:00 UTC
20:03:00 KST

One year after deadly favela raids, does Brazil's anti-gang law work?
October 30, 2026
One year after the deadliest police operation in the history of Brazil, human rights organization Human Rights Watch (HRW) has leveled serious accusations against the country's authorities.
Contrary to legal regulations, most of the 2,500 police officers who were deployed to the "Complexo do Alemao" and "Complexo da Penha" favelas on October 28, 2025, did not wear body cameras.
In the course of "Operacao Contencao" ("Operation Containment"), police officers were expected to execute dozens of arrest warrants against members of the Comando Vermelho drug cartel that day.
The result: During hours-long firefights in the favelas, 117 alleged gang members and five police officers were killed.
Body cameras don't show the full picture
After analyzing more than 4,000 hours of video material, HRW concluded in its investigation that only around one quarter of the deployed police officers were wearing body cameras and that some were manipulated. Not a single deadly shooting was captured on camera.
"It's clear to us that a decision by the Supreme Court according to which the police in Rio must wear body cameras was violated," said HRW Brazil director Cesar Munoz.
The organization published its report in Rio de Janeiro on October 28.
Having analyzed the autopsy findings, HRW also concludes that many bodies show signs of execution, i.e. the killing of persons already incapable of fighting.
For example, 40% of those killed were shot in the head, and 75% were shot in the back. There were reasons to believe, Munoz said, that the operation "was obviously designed to be lethal."
The police operation carried out under the supervision of the state government of Rio de Janeiro shocked the country. However, there were soon calls to intensify the fight against organized crime.
Fighting drug gangs and militias
In response, the "Anti-gang Law" ("Lei Antifaccao") came into force in March 2026. It is aimed at combating criminal gangs like the PCC, a drug gang based in Sao Paulo, or the Comando Vermelho (CV), which dominates Rio.
However, militias (gangs made up of corrupt police officers and soldiers) are also to be dismantled, both criminally and economically. "The law addresses a real problem," Rodrigo Ghiringhelli de Azevedo of the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety (FBSP) NGO told DW.
This was because the ability of criminal organizations to control territories, move funds and make inroads into economic activities and public institutions had expanded.
It was positive, he added, that the law extends tools for asset tracing, finance tracking, institutional cooperation and capital withdrawal to these organizations.
Another improvement, said HRW Brazil's Cesar Munoz, was closer cooperation between state security agencies. The federal police, which reports to the central government, was to play a greater role in combating gangs in the future.
In Brazil, military and civil police report to state governments. During the deadly operations in Rio de Janeiro's favelas, one year ago, command was under the authority of the state government of Rio de Janeiro — and, consequently, under the influence of local politics.
Overcrowded prisons and recruitment behind bars
On the other hand, however, the law was raising constitutional concerns, said the FBSP's Azevedo. For example, it provides for the automatic imposition of pretrial detention on suspects.
Other plans included expansion of grounds for arrest, restrictions on the easing of prison conditions — such as furloughs and the suspension of the remainder of a sentence — as well as an extension of the length of stay in prisons.
This could further exacerbate Brazil's chronic prison overcrowding. "Brazil already has one of the largest prison populations worldwide, and the law could accelerate its growth," said Azevedo.
In addition, prison overcrowding in Brazil had the perverse side effect of allowing crime syndicates such as the PCC and Comando Vermelho to recruit new members there.
"Overcrowded prisons without adequate government control facilitate recruitment and strengthening of the very criminal factions that legislation intend to combat," Azevedo concluded.
"It would be important to prevent gangs from recruiting young people and to show those who've committed crimes new prospects in life," HRW's Cesar Munoz told DW.
Rodrigo Ghiringhelli de Azevedo of FBSP also sees a constitutional problem in the cancellation of prison assistance — a benefit that the state paid to the prisoners' dependents.
"Its cancellation means economic punishment for those who haven't committed any crime at all, including children. This runs afoul of the constitutional principle according to which punishments must not extend beyond the convicted person," Azevedo said.
This article was originally published in German.
