Report: Israel gives Gaza terrorists choice between dying alone or with family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:57:56 UTC
19:57:56 KST

Israeli intelligence officers have reportedly been calling Palestinian terrorists in the Gaza Strip and warning them that they must leave their families before being targeted in airstrikes or risk having their relatives killed alongside them, according to an investigation published Thursday by the London-based pan-Arab newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat.
The newspaper reported that at least five such incidents have occurred over the past three months, citing Palestinian field sources familiar with the cases. The accounts, which could not be independently verified, suggest Israeli forces have used advance telephone warnings to isolate suspected terrorists before carrying out targeted killings.
The latest reported incident occurred Wednesday afternoon in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip, where a Palestinian man identified as Muhammad al-Bayouk was killed in an Israeli drone strike after allegedly receiving a telephone call from an officer of the Shin Bet, Israel's domestic security agency.
According to Asharq Al-Awsat, the officer presented al-Bayouk with a choice: remain with his family and risk their deaths in an airstrike or go alone to the roof of a building at a shelter for displaced Palestinians, where he would be targeted.
Al-Bayouk reportedly chose to leave his relatives and climbed onto the roof of a room inside the shelter, where he was struck by a small missile fired from an Israeli drone.
Several members of the al-Bayouk family declined to comment when approached by the newspaper. Others confirmed the account, including a cousin who was present at the scene.
The relative said another family member, al-Bayouk's aunt, was seriously injured while attempting to stop him from leaving after receiving the alleged warning call.
The report did not establish al-Bayouk's organizational affiliation or describe the intelligence underlying Israel's decision to target him.
At least five reported cases in three months
Palestinian field sources told Asharq Al-Awsat that similar incidents have occurred repeatedly in recent months, although they cautioned that some claims circulating locally had exaggerated their frequency.
One source said initial rumors suggested the practice was widespread, but subsequent security reviews identified at least five cases over the preceding three months.
According to the source, individuals receiving such calls from Israeli intelligence officers felt compelled to comply with the instructions because they feared their families would otherwise be killed.
The source accused Israel of using the threat of harm to relatives to pressure targeted individuals into exposing themselves to military strikes.
He also drew parallels with allegations that Israeli interrogators had threatened Palestinian detainees with harm to their relatives if they refused to provide intelligence.
In some cases, the source alleged, detainees were shown photographs of dead family members as a means of psychological pressure.
Those allegations were not independently substantiated in the report.
The source said all the documented telephone-warning cases involved individuals with connections to terrorist activity.
By contrast, he claimed, Israel has continued to target senior commanders and prominent field operatives through larger strikes involving multiple missiles and attack drones, including attacks that have caused civilian casualties.
Palestinian sources reject suggestion of a more restrained approach
Sources interviewed by Asharq Al-Awsat rejected the suggestion that advance warnings reflected a broader effort by Israel to protect Palestinian civilians.
They argued that the practice should not be interpreted as evidence that Israeli forces had adopted a more humanitarian approach or were attempting to improve Israel's international image.
The sources pointed to continued Israeli strikes that they said had killed civilians, including women and children.
Nevertheless, the newspaper suggested that the reported use of smaller precision weapons and attempts to separate terrorists from their families could reflect an Israeli effort to reduce civilian casualties amid sustained international criticism.
The report also cited a September article in the Israeli newspaper Haaretz describing an understanding between Washington and Jerusalem over the use of force in Gaza.
According to that account, the Trump administration has generally refrained from intervening in Israeli military operations except in exceptional circumstances, while President Donald Trump has not demanded that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu broadly restrain Israeli forces in the territory.
The Haaretz report said American attention had focused particularly on civilian casualties, which had declined relatively as Israeli forces increasingly used drones armed with smaller bombs and missiles to target Hamas operatives.
A Palestinian field source disputed that assessment, telling Asharq Al-Awsat that civilians continued to be killed in strikes targeting terrorists and in what he described as indiscriminate shelling.
The source cited a strike Wednesday in southern Khan Younis that reportedly killed civilians, government employees and representatives of merchants.
According to the account, the strike hit a facility operated by government ministries responsible for monitoring the movement of goods entering the Gaza Strip.
The report did not provide an independently verified casualty toll for that incident.
Additional strikes reported across Gaza
The Asharq Al-Awsat report also described several Israeli military operations across the Gaza Strip amid continuing accusations of ceasefire violations.
Two Palestinians were reportedly killed in an Israeli strike targeting a vehicle in the Maghazi refugee camp in central Gaza.
Another Palestinian sustained moderate injuries in a separate strike in the Safatawi area, west of the Jabaliya refugee camp in northern Gaza.
The Palestinian Shehab News Agency reported that two bodies and several wounded people were brought to Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital following the Maghazi strike.
The agency characterized the attack as part of what it described as continuing Israeli violations of the ceasefire agreement.
Elsewhere, several Palestinians were reportedly wounded by gunfire and artillery shelling in different parts of the territory.
In eastern Gaza City, a helicopter fired a missile early Wednesday at an unoccupied apartment on Yafa Street that had previously been struck, according to the report. No injuries were reported in that incident.
Shehab also reported additional Israeli military activity across the Gaza Strip, including gunfire directed toward tents housing displaced Palestinians, artillery strikes, a drone attack on a residential apartment, bulldozing operations and gunfire from naval vessels.
The casualty reports and circumstances of the individual incidents could not be independently verified.
The report did not include an IDF or Shin Bet response to the allegations.

Sports court orders Russia’s return to ice hockey world championships from 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:57:24 UTC
19:57:24 KST

The Court of Arbitration for Sport, known as CAS, has ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to ice hockey world championships from 2027, despite the international federation’s decision to maintain its exclusion.
The ruling covers several youth world championships and the men’s World Championship in Germany in May 2027, according to a statement on the court’s website.
The International Ice Hockey Federation, or IIHF, said it was disappointed by the decision but respected it. It warned, however, that Russia’s return would require changes to tournaments already organized.
The men’s championship has its 16 participating countries divided into two groups, and the match schedule has already been set.
“The change requires extensive coordination with the relevant national member associations, organizing committees, and host authorities.”
“This includes, among other things, a review of tournament formats, match schedules, travel and accommodation arrangements, as well as security measures,” the IIHF said.
The federation said the ruling did not account for practical changes that could not be implemented immediately.
Russia challenged exclusion
The IIHF decided earlier this year to maintain Russia’s exclusion on safety and security grounds. Russia appealed, but the federation’s appeals body upheld the decision.
Russia then took the case to CAS, which ruled in its favor following a hearing.
Russian national and club teams have been excluded from IIHF tournaments since February 28, 2022, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s ranking points have been frozen during its exclusion, leaving it with enough points to return at the top of the world rankings. Ukraine is the lowest-ranked participant in the upcoming men’s championship.
The women’s World Championship begins next week in Herning and Esbjerg, Denmark, without Russia. CAS said its ruling would apply to the women’s World Championship at the end of 2027.

Trump cancels Kansas and Iowa rallies, switches to telephone events before midterms

U.S. President Donald Trump has canceled weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa and will instead hold telephone campaign events ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election.
The Republican National Committee, the party’s national organization, announced the change overnight into Friday, according to The Associated Press.
Trump will spend the next 72 hours holding “telerallies,” speaking remotely to voters. The committee said the aim was to reach as many voters as possible across the country before the November 3 vote.
Events are planned in 20 states, with more potentially to be announced.
The change means Trump’s rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, scheduled for overnight into Saturday Danish time, will be his final in-person rally before the election.
Trump began a 32-day campaign push in early October to support Republican candidates. According to AP, he had set a goal of holding more than 30 rallies and has held 25 so far.
AP reported signs this week that the travel schedule and lengthy speeches were taking a toll on his voice.
“God did not create your vocal cords to hold rallies every day,” Trump said in a hoarse voice at a rally in Mississippi on Monday.
Asked overnight into Friday whether his health was behind the canceled Kansas trip, Trump responded sharply.
“You have followed me for two weeks. I am doing perfect,” he said, before telling the journalist to “get in shape.”
Several polls suggest Republicans could struggle to retain their narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress, the Senate and the House of Representatives.
Kansas is traditionally a Republican stronghold, while Iowa voted decisively for Trump in the 2024 presidential election. AP nevertheless expects tight races in both states, as well as in Alaska, Ohio, Texas and South Carolina.

Parcels arriving from outside the EU to Denmark and other EU countries will face a new fee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:57:13 UTC
19:57:13 KST

Cheap goods from Chinese online shops are arriving in EU in huge numbers, raising concerns about product safety.
In 2025 alone, Danish customs registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Therefore, the European Union will introduce a permanent handling fee of 2 euros per line item in parcels arriving from outside the bloc starting Sunday, November 1, the Danish Customs Agency said Friday.
The fee, equivalent to about 15 Danish kroner, will apply regardless of a parcel’s total value. It will be added to the temporary customs duty introduced this summer on parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Items with the same commodity code count as one line item. Three cotton T-shirts, for example, would incur a handling fee of 2 euros. A cotton T-shirt and a pair of denim jeans would count as two line items, bringing the fee to 4 euros.
The existing customs duty is 3 euros per line item in parcels with a total value below 150 euros.
Christian Lützen, director of the Danish Customs Agency, said the number of low-value parcels sent to consumers from outside the EU had fallen since the customs duty took effect.
“With the handling fee, we are stepping up efforts even further to, among other things, strengthen member states’ opportunities to inspect the contents of parcels,” he said in the press release.
“There are still problems with many of the goods in relation to consumer safety, and as an authority at the border, we must take that seriously.”
When the customs duty was introduced this summer, Lützen said the agency had previously seen a sharp increase in goods arriving from Chinese online shops. He called it “a major problem across EU countries” and said the duty should help make shopping with Danish businesses more attractive.
In 2025, the agency registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros. A count showed that more than 90% of parcels entering Denmark contained Chinese goods.
Shein and Temu were among the 10 online shops most used by Danish consumers in the latest survey by Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, a business organization.
The two platforms sell products ranging from clothing to kitchen equipment and have faced criticism over poor quality and illegal chemicals in their products.

Danish court rejects disabled woman’s discrimination claim over citizenship refusal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:57:08 UTC
19:57:08 KST

The Danish government hopes to allow wolf hunting as early as 2027. Researchers will now determine how large the country’s wolf population needs to be to remain viable.
Denmark is taking another step towards allowing wolves to be hunted, after EU rules protecting the species were relaxed last year.
The government has commissioned work to determine how many wolves Denmark needs to maintain a stable and viable population in the long term.
At the same time, authorities want to introduce more precise monitoring using DNA to identify individual wolves.
Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of the Social Democrats said the scientific work could pave the way for hunting as early as 2027.
“We need a population model in place. It is a step towards being able to regulate – that is, hunt wolves in Denmark,” he said.
The Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV) will put the development of the population model out to public tender. A separate tender will cover individual monitoring of wolves.
At least 49 adult wolves
Denmark does not currently have an exact count of its wolf population.
In spring 2026, researchers from the Natural History Museum Aarhus and Aarhus University estimated that there were at least 49 adult wolves in Denmark.
The government now wants a more precise assessment based on DNA, making it possible to identify individual animals.
“We need a scientific count of the wolves, and we need a model for a minimum population,” Rabjerg Madsen said.
Once that work has been completed, the government hopes it will provide the scientific basis for introducing regulated hunting.
EU rules on wolves were relaxed in 2025
Wolves remain protected under EU law, but their protection status was changed in 2025.
The species was moved from Annex IV to Annex V of the EU Habitats Directive, changing its status from “strictly protected” to “protected”.
The change gives EU countries greater flexibility to manage their wolf populations, including through hunting.
However, it does not mean Denmark can simply introduce unrestricted wolf hunting.
Any hunting or population management must be compatible with maintaining the wolf at what EU rules call a “favourable conservation status”.
Determining that status involves more than simply counting wolves. Authorities must also consider factors including the population’s geographical range, habitat and long-term prospects.
The population model being commissioned by the Danish authorities is expected to be ready during 2027.
Minister hopes for hunting in 2027
Rabjerg Madsen said his ambition is to allow wolf hunting that same year.
“It is my ambition that we can have wolf hunting in 2027, because that is when we will start getting the numbers,” he said.
“My expectation is that they will show that we have a viable wolf population and that we therefore can have hunting of the wolf.”
Asked whether he was anticipating the researchers’ conclusion before the calculations had been made, the minister said the outcome would have to remain within the scientific and international rules governing Denmark.
“I have been very careful to say that it is my assessment and hope that we have a viable wolf population, so that we can have wolf hunting within the scientific boundaries we are committed to by international rules,” he said.
Individual wolves can already be killed under certain circumstances in Denmark. This can include wolves that repeatedly attack livestock protected by approved wolf-proof fencing or animals that display an abnormal lack of fear of humans.
Sources: Ritzau, European Commission and Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV)

"Now comes the truly difficult part: attempting to form a government," he said.
"Forming a government is the exact opposite. It takes place in small rooms, slowly, away from the cameras," he added, referring to the difference between election campaigning and coalition negotiations.
"It will be difficult. I have no guarantees," Lapid said, urging supporters to remain patient.
Rival parties explore coalition options
Separately, far-right Jewish Power party leader Itamar Ben-Gvir met Netanyahu on Thursday to discuss efforts to preserve a right-wing government, according to Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth.

Meanwhile, Democrats party leader Yair Golan urged leaders of the Change bloc to reconsider their positions on cooperation with Arab parties.
Golan met United Arab List (Ra'am) leader Mansour Abbas on Thursday as part of efforts to accelerate the formation of an alternative government.
He has previously supported including Ra'am in a future coalition, while Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman opposes forming a government that includes Arab parties.

‘Swift justice’: Student List supporters focus on cleaning up Serbia’s rotten institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:54:17 UTC
19:54:17 KST

In Belgrade’s Pioneers Park, just across from the national assembly, a small crowd craned their necks to listen. One woman held aloft a placard reading “Love prevailed for the people and Serbia”. With a bouquet of media microphones in front of them, members of the Student List, the direct democracy movement that won an improbable but decisive victory in Sunday’s election, gathered under the trees.
Having spent days bathing in the euphoria of their unexpected triumph, the candidates’ focus was now clear: the cleaning up of the rotten institutions that had increasingly blighted the lives of Serbs over the 14 years of government by the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS). They called for the dismissal of many senior law enforcement officials, among them the chiefs of the criminal police, the paramilitary gendarmerie and an anti-terrorism unit.
Student List candidate Svetlana Stanarević was applauded when she accused the officials of violating the law. She also called for the director of Serbia’s internal intelligence agency to resign, accusing him of running the organisation as “a party security service, not a state security service”.
There was approval, too, for the “reopening or expediting of cases” related to the disaster that sparked the student protest movement. Sunday will mark the second anniversary of the canopy collapse that killed 16 people at a renovated railway station in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. There have yet to be any convictions.
The announcements on Thursday were the Student List’s way of stressing they intended to put anti-corruption efforts at the heart of government.
“For years, for decades, people have been really frustrated,” said Iva Marković, a Student List candidate and political ecologist who founded the Right to Water initiative. “We see this as a time where everyone who was honestly and credibly working within [public] institutions can do their jobs. They are no longer under political pressure, and we ask them to do their jobs, which also means for prosecutors to prosecute, and police to investigate.”
Reinforcing the student movement’s key principles is also a way, perhaps, to allay concerns that the Student List might not know how to handle its stunning victory over Vučić and the SNS. The movement is not a traditional party. It does not have a hierarchy or leader – and although the students selected the list of candidates, they will not have any direct control over the people who have been elected, once they have been sworn in as MPs.
Marković said the common commitment the students and their parliamentary candidates had made should not be underestimated.
“The process didn’t start with the elections,” she noted, adding that preventing “individualism” from undermining core goals had been key to the student movement’s success. “When you dream together with some people, it’s very hard to forget this dream, even if you are in parliament.”
Borko Stefanović’s choice of a pizzeria themed around ’Allo ’Allo! as a meeting place reflects Serbia’s enthusiasm for British sitcoms of a certain vintage. Only Fools and Horses is a particular favourite, with its tales of thwarted schemes and broken dreams chiming strongly in a country that has been through turbulent times since the early 1990s.
Stefanović knows this better than most. He was part of the political movement opposed to Slobodan Milošević – and saw the democratic coalition that emerged from the overthrow of Serbia’s notorious former president fritter away its early promise. It is not a film he cares to watch a second time.
“There is this almost legendary saying in Serbia that we won on the 5th of October [2000] over Milošević, but we never had the 6th of October,” he said, adding that the Student List was correct to prioritise the dismissal of corrupt officials.
“Get the right people in the right places, bring swift legal justice, liberate institutions and the media, and allow the prosecutor’s office to arrest criminals. Everyone who wants to contribute to the reforms needs to get on board and to do everything we can to make this excellent example in Europe a lasting one.”
Perched on a sofa in a coffee roastery in Belgrade’s old town, Tara Blagojević was convinced the movement she has been a part of already had the right people in place. With the elections over, she said it was down to the successful candidates to form a government. The student assemblies will take a less active role, acting as “advisers or kind of supervisors”.
“Everything’s going to be fine,” Blagojević insisted, adding that although the Student List was “kind of a political experiment”, the people who will soon be sworn in as MPs “recognise each other’s strengths and are able to project who can be suitable to do certain things within the new government”.
Slobodan Tomić is optimistic about the Student List’s prospects. The Belgrade-born political scientist at the University of York has been following the student movement since its inception. “It is an extraordinary change,” he said of the party’s unconventional structure. “I couldn’t find any example across the world of anything similar happening.
“The MPs had to sign a pledge that they would follow through the programme that the Student List had created. So on paper, there isn’t much space for drift.”
The organisers of the famous Exit music festival are also convinced. They moved the event out of the country this year in protest at the policies of Vučić and the SNS. They confirmed that Exit would return to its home in Novi Sad next year.
The news further energised the crowd at Belgrade’s first big gig since the election, where the euphoria showed no sign of subsiding. Chants of “Victory!” welcomed Fontaines DC on stage among the shipping containers at the port of Belgrade. “Congratulations,” responded the Irish singer Grian Chatten. “This is your moment, not ours.”
A former punk rock bassist himself, Stefanović is sure that assessment is correct. “These wonderful, wonderful people from the Student List and the student movement, they know exactly what needs to be done,” he said. He added just one caveat from experience: “Don’t blow it.”

Average headcount in January-September 2026 was 29,300, compared with 27,600 in 2025, and headcount at the end of September was 35,200, compared with 32,000 a year earlier.
In the first half of 2026 Nova Poshta raised consolidated net profit 24.3% year-on-year to UAH 2.195 billion and revenue 31.8% to UAH 39.127 billion. Gross profit rose 19.9% to UAH 8.474 billion and operating profit 29.5% to UAH 4.633 billion.

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- South Africa is approaching its local elections on Nov. 4 amid mounting social tensions, with demonstrations and anti-immigrant protests, raising concerns over public security.
Recent unrest in Johannesburg's Soweto township and Durban, triggered by protests against illegal immigration earlier this month, has highlighted longstanding challenges facing the country, including unemployment, poverty, and immigration management.

Dissatisfaction with municipal services is another source of tension.
Residents in several communities have voiced concerns over unreliable water and electricity supplies, deteriorating roads, inadequate sanitation, poor waste management and delays in housing provision.
Against this backdrop, immigration, crime and unemployment have become increasingly prominent campaign issues ahead of the local elections.
The challenge for political leaders is to address public concerns without fueling hostility toward particular communities or undermining the country's constitutional principles.
Despite the heightened tensions, the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has continued preparations for the local elections.

MBDA expands German plant to build more missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:52:33 UTC
19:52:33 KST

- MBDA is expanding its Schrobenhausen site to about 100 hectares to build air defense and deep strike missiles faster and in larger numbers.
- Defense Minister Boris Pistorius visited on Oct. 29; the site will produce Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors and the Taurus Neo cruise missile.
MBDA is expanding its main German site at Schrobenhausen in Bavaria to about 100 hectares (247 acres) as it turns the plant into what it calls Germany’s “missile hub” for air defense and long-range strike weapons, MBDA Deutschland said in a post after a visit by Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Oct. 29.
The company said the expansion adds new production areas for complex weapon systems and new manufacturing technology, so it can deliver deep precision strike and air defense weapons faster and in larger numbers. Schrobenhausen develops, builds, maintains and upgrades air defense systems, guided missiles and laser weapons for the Bundeswehr and NATO partners. MBDA did not say how much the expansion will cost, how many jobs it will add or when the new areas will be finished.
Pistorius stopped at Schrobenhausen as part of a day of visits to defense companies around Munich, which also included Airbus Defence and Space, drone maker Helsing and hypersonics startup Hypersonica, the German Defense Ministry said. Almost two years earlier, he had broken ground at the same site on a new production building for Patriot interceptors.
That building is at the center of the plant’s growth. COMLOG, a joint venture of MBDA Deutschland and Raytheon, is setting up Europe’s first production line for the Patriot PAC-2 GEM-T interceptor at Schrobenhausen, with a €250 million (about $280 million) investment covering a 31,000-square-meter (334,000-square-foot) production hall. The NATO Support and Procurement Agency has ordered up to 1,000 GEM-Ts from COMLOG for Germany, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain, and Raytheon has said the plant will help fill a $3.7 billion order for Ukraine. Pistorius said in September that production of the newer PAC-3 MSE, which destroys incoming missiles by hitting them directly, is also set to begin at Schrobenhausen later this year.
On the strike side, MBDA is preparing series production of the Taurus Neo, an upgraded version of the Taurus KEPD 350 air-launched cruise missile developed with Sweden’s Saab, after signing a contract with Germany’s procurement agency at the end of 2025. Germany aims to buy about 600 Taurus Neo missiles for around €2 billion (about $2.23 billion), Reuters has reported, with production planned from 2029.
Schrobenhausen will also build the DefendAir anti-drone missile for Rheinmetall’s Skyranger 30 air defense vehicle under a contract signed in November 2025, and it hosts a final assembly line for Brimstone 3 precision strike missiles for German Eurofighters, the first outside the U.K. The plant also produces the Enforcer shoulder-fired missile.
MBDA doubled its missile production capacity across its European sites between 2023 and 2025 and plans to invest another €2.4 billion (about $2.68 billion) between 2025 and 2029 to raise output further.

Apple Pay and Google Pay launch in Uzbekistan amid wider fintech reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:52:18 UTC
19:52:18 KST

The rollout follows changes to personal data laws and high-level talks with Google. The Central Bank tells Euronews that work is underway to include domestic payment networks Uzcard and HUMO.
Uzbekistan has introduced Apple Pay and Google Pay following regulatory reforms aimed at opening its financial services market to international technology providers.
In written responses to Euronews, the Central Bank of Uzbekistan confirmed that work is underway to extend the services to cards issued through the country's domestic payment networks, Uzcard and HUMO, although no timetable has been provided.
The availability of both services for locally issued cards was announced on 27 October by Saida Mirziyoyeva, Head of the Presidential Administration, who had met Google Vice President Karan Bhatia in New York a month earlier to discuss technological cooperation and the conditions for international payment services to operate in Uzbekistan.
From domestic payments to global platforms
Mobile and contactless payments were already available in Uzbekistan through domestic services such as HUMO Pay and UZCARD PAY, alongside QR code payment systems.
The introduction of Apple Pay and Google Pay allows customers with eligible locally issued cards to use the international platforms, rather than relying solely on existing domestic payment solutions.
Apple Pay initially supports Visa and Mastercard cards issued by eight local banks and financial institutions: Uzum Bank, Orient Finans Bank, the National Bank of Uzbekistan (NBU), Kapitalbank, Hamkorbank, Ipak Yuli Bank, TBC Bank and Octobank. Uzum Bank and Hamkorbank currently support Visa cards only.
Google Pay supports cards from nine banks: AVO Bank, Octobank, Uzum Bank, TBC Bank, Aloqabank, Kapitalbank, Ipak Yuli Bank, NBU and Orient Finans Bank.
Customers are advised to check with their bank which cards are eligible for Apple Pay and Google Pay.
The Central Bank told Euronews that both services protect customers' card information during transactions, while cashback and other benefits remain subject to individual banks' conditions.
Regulatory reforms open the market
The rollout follows amendments to Uzbekistan's personal data legislation in March 2026, which eased restrictions on processing and storing certain categories of personal information outside the country.
During her September meeting with Google's vice president, Mirziyoyeva explicitly linked the regulatory changes to the introduction of international payment systems.
“As a result, broader opportunities are opening up for the unrestricted use of international payment systems in Uzbekistan,” she said.
The September talks also addressed cooperation with Google, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity training and support for the country's technology sector.
The developments coincide with Uzbekistan's National Fintech Strategy for 2026–2030, approved by the Central Bank in September.
The strategy includes plans to attract investment, develop cross-border payments, introduce Open Banking and improve connectivity between financial systems.

Feature: Border county on Pamir Plateau sees growing China-Pakistan economic exchanges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:52:06 CST
19:52:06 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- As night falls over the Pamir Plateau in northwest China, a bustling border market comes alive with bright lights, lively chatter and the aroma of Pakistani cuisine.
At a market near the China-Pakistan border in Tashkurgan Tajik Autonomous County, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Chinese tourists browse and bargain over Pakistani crafts, including jade bracelets, wool scarfs and embroidered round-top caps.
After they find items they like and agree on the price, they scan QR codes to pay. Some pose for photos with Pakistani stallholders and exchange contact details on WeChat.
The region's snow-capped peaks and crystal-clear lakes have long drawn visitors. Now, easier cross-border travel and expanding trade are adding to its appeal.
In December 2024, the Khunjerab Pass, a key gateway between China and Pakistan, shifted from seasonal to year-round operation to facilitate commerce and people-to-people exchanges. In the first three quarters of 2026, over 55,000 cross-border visits were recorded, including tourists from 42 countries and regions such as Pakistan, the Republic of Korea, France and Malaysia.
Karim Anim, a Pakistani trader, moved to Tashkurgan 15 years ago from Islamabad. His father and uncle had come to China and opened a small 50-square-meter shop in 1993, then expanded it into a two-story, 200-square-meter store in 2000. Learning the small-commodity trade from them after moving to Tashkurgan in 2011, he teamed up with his cousin to establish a company and has expanded the product range from food and beverages to jade, bronzes and high-value handicrafts.
As tourism grows, more Chinese visitors from across the country are coming to Tashkurgan, giving his store a welcome boost in sales. "Customers have strong purchasing power," he said. Meanwhile, thanks to an improved cross-border road system, when he misses his hometown, he can leave Tashkurgan by bus in the morning and be home in Pakistan by the afternoon.
Many restaurants line the streets of Tashkurgan, and Aslam Muhammad is one of their owners. A decade ago he was a truck driver working along the border. But seeing how growing business exchanges were creating opportunities in restaurants and tourism, he decided to open a Pakistani restaurant -- now it attracts a steady stream of Chinese tourists and Pakistani traders.
"I used to drive trucks on the China-Pakistan logistics route, but now I connect people from both countries through the taste of Pakistani food," he said.
Curious and satisfied comments about Pakistani food have been popping up on Xiaohongshu, a Chinese lifestyle-sharing platform. One consumer shared that she and her friend ordered chickpeas with chicken, cheese and potatoes, and Pakistani tea, and packed a Pamir sandwich to go.
"Looking at my empty plates in the photos I posted, the meal was clearly a hit," she wrote.
Nearly 460 Pakistani nationals now live and work in Tashkurgan, engaging in trade, catering and border-market businesses. Their daily interactions with local residents have fostered closer ties, with people from both countries sharing work and helping one another.
Booming tourism has created jobs and investment. Tashkurgan has 107 hotels and 640 guesthouses, offering more than 32,000 beds. The tourism industry directly employs about 6,000 people, according to Yang Qingling, head of the county's culture and tourism bureau.
Meanwhile, year-round customs clearance is helping goods move more freely across the border. Chinese machinery, new-energy vehicles and consumer goods are heading to Pakistan, while Pakistani fresh produce and handicrafts are finding their way into Chinese households.
According to Khunjerab customs, cargo throughput in the first seven months of 2026 had already exceeded the total for all of 2025. The figure is expected to surpass 100,000 tonnes for the full year.
Zhang Yaqiang, head of Xinjiang Huayingtai International Trade Company, has witnessed an increase in goods transported from Pakistan through China for re-export to Central Asian markets, supporting Pakistan's trade links with countries in the region.
To accommodate growing demand, major projects with investment of 450 million yuan (about 67 million U.S. dollars) are underway to upgrade the port, modernize facilities and increase handling capacity, according to the county's commerce and industry bureau. Plans also include improving infrastructure for the border economic cooperation zone, bonded warehouses and customs-supervised areas.
From bustling market stalls to expanding trade routes, the town on the Pamir Plateau is showing how improved connectivity can turn a remote border crossing into a hub of commerce, tourism and friendship.
Looking ahead, local authorities aim to make better use of Tashkurgan's strategic location to deepen economic cooperation and people-to-people exchanges between China and Pakistan, said Li Feng, the county's Party chief. ■

Australia faces million-tonne solar panel waste challenge by 2035: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:52:03 CST
19:52:03 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Australia is facing a growing waste challenge from its rooftop solar boom, with more than one million tonnes of end-of-life solar panels expected to accumulate by 2035, a new report has warned.
The report, led by Australia's RMIT University in partnership with global think tank RAND, found that much of the waste could end up in stockpiling, landfill, or informal disposal rather than being reused or recycled.
Although Australia has more rooftop solar panels installed per person than any other country, recycling remains more expensive than landfill disposal, while systems to recover, refurbish or recycle them at scale are not yet in place, RMIT University said in a statement on Thursday.
The report recommended establishing a national marketplace for used solar panels, introducing a product stewardship scheme by mid-2027 and improving the commercial viability of recycling.
Between 45 and 65 percent of decommissioned panels remain suitable for reuse, but only about 10 percent are currently tested for that purpose, the report noted.
Australia already has more than 40.6 gigawatts of installed solar capacity across over four million systems, generating about 40,000 tonnes of end-of-life panels annually, which could exceed 100,000 tonnes a year by the early 2030s.
Recovered materials, led by silver, could be worth more than 1 billion Australian dollars (about 700 million U.S. dollars) cumulatively by 2035, the report said, adding that reinstalling usable panels could increase the country's solar generation capacity by up to 17 percent. ■

BANGKOK, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's industrial output grew in September, as global demand for electronics tied to artificial intelligence and data centers, along with government stimulus, supported production, official data showed on Friday.
The Southeast Asian country's manufacturing production index (MPI) rose 2.05 percent last month from a year earlier, slowing from a revised 4.20 percent increase in August, according to the Ministry of Industry.
The index stood at 101.37 in September, with capacity utilization at 60.58 percent, up from 59.83 percent in August.
The MPI is now compiled with a chain-link method, which the ministry's Office of Industrial Economics (OIE) adopted to follow United Nations recommendations.
This approach allows the index to more quickly reflect changes in the industrial production structure and to keep pace with shifts in technology and global demand, said OIE director-general Supakit Boonsiri.
The government's co-payment scheme kept supporting consumer spending, which helped food, beverage, and packaging producers. A cut in electricity tariffs for September to December also lowered costs for businesses and households, Supakit told a news conference.
The biggest gains in September came from electronic components and circuit boards, communications equipment, and computers and peripherals, he said, adding that declines were led by refined petroleum products, primary plastics and synthetic rubber, and vehicles.
Supakit also warned that the Middle East conflict still threatens energy and shipping costs. Manufacturers may struggle to pass higher costs on to customers, which could squeeze margins and erode competitiveness. ■

Leaders signed a joint declaration Friday at the 13th Heads of State Summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara.
Hosted by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan under the theme "Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed," the gathering brought together leaders and officials from participating countries.
The declaration was signed following addresses by Erdogan and visiting heads of state and officials.
The Ankara Declaration, released after the summit at the Bestepe National Congress and Culture Center's Exhibition Hall, reaffirmed member states' determination to strengthen the OTS as an increasingly influential platform representing the shared vision of the Turkic world and contributing constructively to regional and international peace, stability and prosperity.
It said the summit reaffirmed a shared commitment to transforming growing solidarity across the Turkic world into lasting strategic cooperation and making the coming century an era of greater unity and prosperity.
It emphasized that unity, solidarity and common resilience among Turkic states had become increasingly important at a time when confidence in international cooperation was declining. The leaders reiterated their determination to build a more resilient, interconnected and globally influential Turkic world.
The declaration also recognized the valuable contributions of Hungary, Turkmenistan and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) to the OTS as observers, describing them as integral parts of the Turkic world.
The declaration encouraged the completion of the OTS Strategy for 2027-2031 as the next phase of the Turkic World Vision 2040 and welcomed progress on the draft Treaty on Strategic Partnership, Eternal Friendship and Brotherhood among Turkic States.
It urged mutual support among member states for candidacies in international organizations and stronger coordination on joint decisions and initiatives.
The leaders also supported regular meetings of the Council of Elders and welcomed the establishment of the Group of Turkic States at UNESCO.
The declaration urged member states' foreign ministers to maintain frequent contact to ensure timely consultations, closer coordination and joint action on regional and global developments of common interest.
On Cyprus, the declaration stressed the need for a negotiated, mutually acceptable and sustainable settlement based on the realities on the island. It expressed support for efforts to secure the inherent equal rights of the Turkish Cypriot people, whom it described as "an integral part of the Turkic world."
Regarding the Gaza Strip, the declaration highlighted the need for full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 2803 (2025) and the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict to address the difficult humanitarian situation, establish security and stability and pave the way for recovery.
It also underlined the need for "a just and lasting solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the implementation of the two-state solution in accordance with relevant UN resolutions."
The leaders reaffirmed support for Syria's territorial integrity and unity, as well as its security, stability and reconstruction. They also pledged to continue efforts, including through the OTS Afghanistan Working Group, to contribute to peace, stability and sustainable development in Afghanistan.
The declaration welcomed the outcomes of meetings of the secretaries of the member states' security councils and heads of defense industry institutions. It urged authorities to continue holding regular political and security consultations on regional and international issues of mutual interest.
The leaders reaffirmed their commitment to expanding multilateral cooperation in the defense industry.
They encouraged exploring the establishment of an OTS Defense Industry College program hosted by Türkiye to promote the exchange of information and experience, train qualified personnel, develop theoretical and practical expertise in the defense industry, and keep pace with technological advances.
The declaration also emphasized continued cooperation and coordination in combating terrorism, extremism, separatism, organized crime, drug trafficking, arms smuggling and cybercrime.
It encouraged the signing of an agreement on the establishment of a council for combating crime among OTS member states and observers. It also urged accelerating the signing of a memorandum of understanding on cybersecurity and consultations on establishing an OTS Cybersecurity Council.
The leaders reiterated their commitment to cooperation against racism, discrimination, xenophobia, Islamophobia, hate speech and disinformation. They also noted that the possibility of establishing an International Biological Security Agency based on the Biological Weapons Convention was being considered to strengthen international biosecurity.
The declaration welcomed growth in intra-regional trade and encouraged continued negotiations on a draft Agreement on the Facilitation of Services and Investments for Sustainable Development, aimed at deepening economic integration. It highlighted the critical role of the OTS Trade Facilitation Committee in optimizing customs procedures, removing technical barriers and reducing trade costs.
It also welcomed the outcomes of meetings of relevant institutional heads responsible for economy, competition, taxation, industry, financial intelligence and customs, while emphasizing the establishment of digital platforms and stronger cooperation on standardization.
The leaders highlighted the importance of sustainable mountain development and expressed expectations regarding the second Global Mountain Summit, Bishkek+25. They also stressed the importance of fast-track customs mechanisms and electronic document sharing for shipments of agricultural and food products.
The declaration underlined the strategic importance of the Trans-Caspian International East-West Middle Corridor, the Zangezur Corridor, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway and the Trans-Afghan Railway for regional connectivity and trade. It encouraged the preparation of an OTS Transport Corridors Strategy.
In transport, digital infrastructure and energy, the declaration supported cooperation agreements on developing the Middle Corridor, the creation of dedicated passenger lanes at airports, the Digital Silk Road initiative involving a fiber-optic cable line between Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan, and implementation of the e-CMR Memorandum of Understanding.
The member states also pledged to deepen cooperation on pipelines, green energy corridors, critical minerals, energy efficiency and the peaceful use of nuclear energy to strengthen energy security.
The declaration welcomed meetings among space agencies and digitalization initiatives. It also welcomed the completion of production of the 12U OTS-SAT CubeSat and the signing of the first Framework Agreement on Developing Cooperation Capacity in the Space Industry within the OTS. Kyrgyzstan was congratulated on launching its first national satellite.
The leaders highlighted the Digital Turkic World concept, TEKNOFEST, artificial intelligence governance and efforts to protect intellectual property rights. They also welcomed the outcomes of Azerbaijan's COP29 presidency.
On the environment, climate change and urban development, the declaration supported Türkiye's hosting COP31 and its identified priorities. It welcomed the International Day of Greening the Planet, proclaimed at the UN, and the partnership between the OTS and the Islamic Organization for Food Security.
The leaders encouraged practical steps to implement the Memorandum of Understanding on Urban and Spatial Planning signed on the sidelines of the 13th World Urban Forum in Azerbaijan, focusing on sustainable urban development and affordable housing.
In cultural tourism, social protection and legal cooperation, the declaration supported the Common Museum Card project, the Tabarruk Ziyorat tourism routes, and the designation of Ankara and Tashkent as Tourism Capitals of the Turkic World.
It also welcomed memorandums of understanding and cooperation mechanisms established in areas including labor, employment, migration management, health tourism, forensic science networks, judicial ethics, supreme courts and prosecutor generals' offices.
The declaration further highlighted regional humanitarian cooperation activities carried out by the Turkic States Red Crescent and Red Cross Network, bringing together Red Crescent and Red Cross societies within the OTS framework.
The declaration emphasized support for women's empowerment, strengthening the family institution, promoting traditional family and cultural values among younger generations, and recognizing the role of older generations in preserving and passing on cultural heritage.
It acknowledged that a healthy and dynamic population was essential to the development and sustainability of societies and encouraged cooperation among member states on family and population policies.
The leaders also encouraged discussions on establishing a voluntary Supreme Council of Honor, composed of the spouses of heads of state and representatives appointed by the presidents of OTS member states, to increase cooperation on family and women's issues.
The declaration welcomed the inaugural meeting held within the framework of the Ankara summit under the auspices of Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan. It supported holding subsequent meetings on the sidelines of future OTS summits.
The leaders reaffirmed the importance of strengthening cultural, linguistic and social ties between Turkic states and global communities. They urged ministers and heads of relevant institutions responsible for diaspora affairs to enhance cooperation and coordination in line with the Joint Action Strategy of Turkic-Speaking Diasporas, annual Joint Action Plans for Turkic Diasporas and the Turkic World Vision 2040.
The declaration welcomed the implementation of joint OTS diaspora scholarship programs under the Türkiye Scholarships initiative, describing them as a contribution to strengthening ties between Turkic states and their diasporas. It also welcomed the outcomes of the ninth meeting of OTS education ministers, held on June 8 in Turkistan.
The leaders welcomed consultations on treating football players who are citizens of OTS member states as "non-foreign players" in each other's domestic competitions and organizing a Turkic Cup tournament among national teams at various levels. They encouraged further efforts to turn the proposals into concrete initiatives.
The declaration stressed the importance of strengthening cooperation in strategic communications, combating disinformation and using emerging technologies in the media sector. It also welcomed the outcomes of the eighth meeting of OTS ministers and senior officials responsible for media and information, held in Astana on Oct. 16.
The declaration welcomed the Turkic Culture and Heritage Foundation's designation of 2026 as the Year of Ziya Gokalp, a Turkish sociologist and writer, and appreciated commemorative activities organized throughout the year to honor his intellectual legacy and contributions to Turkic culture and thought.
Türkiye was commended for its efforts to preserve the Bilge Tonyukuk Monument, while the leaders expressed satisfaction with recent archaeological excavations conducted across the Turkic world.
The declaration recognized Aktau's designation as the 2025 Cultural Capital of the Turkic World and welcomed Andijan's designation as the 2026 Cultural Capital.
It also welcomed the outcomes of the seventh meeting of the Council of Heads of Muslim Religious Boards of the OTS, held in Baku, and noted the recommendations and joint fatwas adopted within the framework of the OTS Fatwa Committee.
The leaders praised the efforts of the Turkic Academy to promote the common Turkic alphabet, adopt proposed guidelines for its use, and publish literary and scientific works written in the alphabet.
The declaration also recognized the Union of Turkic Chambers of Commerce and Industry as an important mechanism bringing together the national chambers of commerce of all Turkic states to strengthen economic cooperation, trade, investment and business-to-business relations.
The declaration welcomed growing interest from third countries and international organizations in establishing institutional cooperation with the OTS. It urged authorities in member states to accelerate joint efforts to secure observer status for the organization at the UN General Assembly and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
The OTS secretariat was instructed to accelerate efforts to develop institutional relations with international and regional organizations, with particular emphasis on expanding cooperation with relevant external partners through the OTS+ format.
The leaders supported strengthening the secretariat's capacity to effectively carry out its expanding responsibilities and extended their best wishes to incoming Secretary-General Mirvahid Azimov.
The declaration said the 14th OTS Summit would be held in Uzbekistan in 2027. It also welcomed with great appreciation Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov's proposal to host the 2027 informal OTS summit in his country.
The heads of state expressed their deep gratitude to President Erdogan for successfully concluding the negotiations of the 13th OTS Summit and praised the Turkish government and people for their warm hospitality.
The declaration also welcomed Türkiye's assumption of the OTS chairmanship until the next summit.

Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:50:22 UTC
19:50:22 KST

Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- University of Michigan
- Summary:
- A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead.
- Share:
A surprising discovery made with NASA's Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from darkness. The findings suggest that powerful explosions from dying stars may have actually interfered with a process scientists once believed they helped drive.
An international research team, including astronomers from the University of Michigan, found that powerful winds produced by exploding stars can prevent ultraviolet radiation from escaping galaxies. This is the opposite of what a widely accepted theory had predicted, and it could change how scientists understand one of the most important transformations in cosmic history.
The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, offers new clues about how the universe became transparent to ultraviolet light roughly 13 billion years ago.
How the Early Universe Emerged From Its Cosmic Fog
During the first billion years after the Big Bang, vast amounts of neutral hydrogen filled the space between galaxies. This hydrogen formed a kind of cosmic fog that absorbed ultraviolet radiation, preventing that light from traveling freely across the universe.
That changed during a period known as reionization, which began approximately 13 billion years ago. Intense radiation from early galaxies gradually transformed the hydrogen by stripping electrons from its atoms, leaving behind positively charged protons and free electrons.
As more hydrogen became ionized, ultraviolet light could travel much farther through intergalactic space. This transformation helped establish the relatively transparent universe that astronomers observe today.
"Eventually, when it ionized the majority of hydrogen filling intergalactic space, that was the end of reionization and we see the universe today," said Cody Carr, a postdoctoral researcher in the University of Michigan's Department of Astronomy. "We call reionization the last major phase transition of the universe."
Despite its enormous importance, astronomers still do not fully understand which objects supplied the radiation responsible for reionization or how enough of that radiation managed to escape from early galaxies.
"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," said Carr, who conducted and led the research while working as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China, before joining the University of Michigan. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."
Hubble Challenges a Leading Theory About Exploding Stars
For years, one prominent explanation centered on supernovae, the powerful explosions that occur when certain stars reach the ends of their lives. These explosions can generate enormous winds that sweep through galaxies, pushing gas and other material outward.
Scientists proposed that these winds cleared pathways through the gas surrounding young stars, allowing ultraviolet radiation to escape into the space between galaxies. Once outside, that radiation could help break apart the neutral hydrogen responsible for the universe's ancient fog.
However, new observations from Hubble suggest that this explanation may have the process backward.
Rather than opening routes for radiation to escape, the researchers found that stronger galactic winds were associated with less escaping ionizing radiation. The observations indicate that the winds generated by supernovae can actually make it harder for the radiation to leave a galaxy.
"Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn't what we thought," Carr said.
The results lend support to a different possibility. Radiation from young, massive stars may escape their galaxies before those stars explode as supernovae and generate large winds that reshape the surrounding environment.
"Our observations show that these photons are escaping before galactic winds form," Carr said.
Photons are individual packets of light energy. In this case, the researchers are interested in ultraviolet photons energetic enough to ionize hydrogen, making them essential to understanding how the early universe became transparent.
What Hubble Discovered in Nearby Starburst Galaxies
To investigate how radiation escapes, the international team used the Hubble Space Telescope to examine nearby starburst galaxies. These are galaxies experiencing exceptionally intense periods of star formation, making them useful modern examples of the kinds of galaxies believed to have contributed to reionization.
Hubble, a NASA mission launched with contributions from the European Space Agency, allowed researchers to study the light coming from these galaxies in detail.
The team examined their spectra, which reveal how much light is present at different wavelengths. By studying the patterns in those spectra, astronomers can learn about the gas surrounding stars and determine how quickly it is moving.
Gas absorbs particular wavelengths of light, creating recognizable dips in a galaxy's spectrum. The locations and shapes of these dips provide clues about the speed and movement of galactic winds.
When the researchers compared wind speeds with the amount of ionizing radiation escaping from each galaxy, they uncovered a surprising relationship. Galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of ionizing radiation to escape.
That result directly challenges the expectation that stronger winds should clear away more gas and make it easier for radiation to reach intergalactic space.
"It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape," said Stephan McCandliss, a senior author of the study and director of the Center for Astrophysical Sciences at Johns Hopkins University.
In other words, instead of clearing a path for ultraviolet light, energy from exploding stars appears to redistribute gas and dust in ways that can block more of it.
Young Stars May Hold the Key to Cosmic Reionization
Although large galactic winds appear to suppress escaping radiation, smaller winds and other activity around young stars could still help create openings in the surrounding gas.
These processes may occur before the first supernova explosions, giving radiation a chance to escape while conditions are more favorable.
The findings suggest that astronomers may need to pay greater attention to what happens during the earliest stages of star formation, rather than focusing primarily on the effects of exploding stars.
Carr and his colleagues are seeking additional observing time with Hubble to examine more galaxies and investigate whether the same patterns appear elsewhere. More observations could help establish how important the activity of young stars is in allowing ionizing radiation to escape.
The results also have implications for computer simulations of the early universe. These simulations attempt to recreate how galaxies formed, how gas moved through them, and how radiation eventually transformed the hydrogen filling intergalactic space.
"Supernovae play a central role in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that explain how ionizing radiation escapes from galaxies," said Renyue Cen, a senior author of the study and professor and director of the Center for Cosmology and Computational Astrophysics at Zhejiang University. "Our findings highlight the need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode."
By accounting more accurately for these early interactions between stars, radiation, and gas, researchers may be able to build better models of how reionization unfolded.
The discovery does not yet settle the question of what caused the universe's last major phase transition. However, it provides an important new clue, suggesting that the radiation that helped lift the universe's ancient fog may have escaped galaxies before powerful stellar explosions began to alter their surroundings.
International Research Collaboration and Funding
The research brought together nearly 30 scientists from more than a dozen institutions around the world. Sally Oey, a professor of astronomy at the University of Michigan, also contributed to the study.
The project received additional financial support from Zhejiang University, the Zhejiang Provincial Top-Level Research Support Program, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities in Spain, the European Regional Development Fund, and the European Union's Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Program.
The research was also supported in part by federal funding from NASA and the U.S. National Science Foundation. Additional support for the Hubble Space Telescope observations came through a grant administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute.

How can Israel break its election deadlock?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:50:21 UTC
19:50:21 KST

How can Israel break its election deadlock?
No political party has achieved the 61-seat majority required in the Knesset to form a government in Israel.
No clear winner has emerged from Israel’s election, raising speculation over which party could form the next government.
Early on Friday, the Central Elections Committee (CEC) published the final results of the October 27 vote, which had a high voter turnout of 77.9 percent.
Neither Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition grouping led by Gadi Eisenkot has secured the majority necessary to form a government. Both leaders have also ruled out working with the two main electoral lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List.
So how can Israel break its political deadlock?
Here’s what we know:
Have all votes been counted?
Yes. On Thursday, at least 500,000 “double envelope” votes which came in from soldiers and diplomats were counted. These voters use two envelopes: the first contains their ballot without any identifying information, while the second bears their personal details. The anonymous envelope is placed inside the second envelope, allowing officials to check that voters have not cast ballots elsewhere, without compromising the secrecy of their choice.
What was the final result?
Netanyahu’s bloc secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48 seats.
The United Arab List, or Ra’am, and the Joint List secured a combined 19 seats.
To form a government, a political party must hold at least 61 seats. No single party has ever won that majority and alliances have led to governing coalitions, with a prime minister at the helm.
What happens next?
Political consultations to form a coalition are reported to be under way.
If the process fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog could choose which candidate has the best chance to form a government. That candidate is then given about 28 days to do so – a period that could be extended.
If the candidate fails, the president can then choose another. If that candidate is unable to form a government, then a 21-day window opens in which 61 members of the Knesset can submit a request to Herzog to assign the task to a Knesset member.
Is a second election possible?
Yes, because if all the processes listed above fail, Israelis will have to return to the polls.
Are Arab parties being considered for coalitions?
Many Israeli leaders have rejected the idea of partnering with Arab-led parties.
Netanyahu has ruled out working alongside them and demonised them following their strong showing.
“It is forbidden to form a government with them,” Netanyahu posted on X on Friday.
Netanyahu’s Likud party has accused the Arab-led parties of “stealing” the election, after his own coalition lost its majority.
According to a Times of Israel report this week, Eisenkot has said he would only consider partnering with any party that recognises Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, endorses the values of the Declaration of Independence and commits to all Israelis performing national service.
He has not said whether the Arab-led parties would meet those criteria.
On Thursday, another opposition figure, Avigdor Lieberman, the hard-right leader of Yisrael Beytenu, also ruled out certain coalitions. “Neither Bibi nor Tibi”, he said, using Netanyahu’s nickname and invoking Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Ta’al party – part of the Joint List.
Where do the Arab parties stand?
The Arab parties have shown interest in partnering with anti-Netanyahu factions.
Yousef Jabareen from the Joint List said that his party was ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”, which he called one of “bloodshed”.
“Against a politics of supremacy, racism, and exclusion, we offer a completely different alternative. The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote on X.
Political analyst Ahmed Najar said the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel have shown considerably more pragmatism than Eisenkot and most of his allies.
“Ra’am has indicated that it is open to participating in an Eisenkot-led government, while the Joint List has left open the possibility of supporting a minority government from outside the coalition, provided that such support delivers meaningful commitments on equality, violent crime in Palestinian communities, home demolitions and a political pathway for the wider Palestinian question,” he said.
Can Arab parties break the political deadlock?
It is still too soon to say, according to analysts.
“The numbers don’t add up for any side,” Roi Zur, a lecturer at Essex University and specialist in Israeli voting behaviour and election strategies, told Al Jazeera. “However, there are rumours that Eisenkot will ask for the support of the Arab parties in a government investiture vote in return for financial investment in their communities. Yet, this is unlikely on both sides, and even if both sides go forward with this idea, it might fall due to Lieberman objecting to the idea.”
Zur said that if the four parties in Eisenkot’s “change bloc” were closer to a majority, outside support would have been more likely because Ra’am is perceived as a more “moderate” Arab party.
“Then a European-style confidence-and-supply agreement would be more probable,” he added.
Nimrod Flaschenberg, a Berlin-based political analyst, told Al Jazeera that it is still unclear whether Eisenkot is willing to rely on Ra‘am and the Joint List.
“If Eisenkot will be willing to go for such cooperation, then there are three options: The first is the Israeli-Arab parties could be part of the government. This is what Ra‘am wants; the Joint List does not want this at this stage. The second option is they could be a coalition member but without any government seats. This is what Ra‘am was in the Bennet government from 2021-2022,” he said.
“The third option is they could support from the outside as a preventive bloc that does not vote down the government. Most predict that if there is such a government, it will include Ra‘am in the coalition and will rely on the Joint List from the outside,” he added.
Palestinian political analyst Najar said that the real obstacle at this stage is not a lack of pragmatism from Arab parties, but rather “the refusal of Eisenkot and several of his partners to recognise Palestinian citizens of Israel – and the 19 representatives they elected – as legitimate political partners”.
“The election produced 67 seats outside Netanyahu’s bloc, but Israel’s political system continues to behave as though 19 of those seats do not fully count. Eisenkot wants Palestinian votes to remove Netanyahu while insisting on a ‘Zionist government’ that excludes the representatives of those same voters,” he noted.
“That is not merely coalition arithmetic; it exposes a profound democratic contradiction. Palestinian citizens are permitted to vote, but when their votes become decisive, their political legitimacy is immediately questioned,” he added.
What options does Netanyahu have?
To keep power, the prime minister could yet form a coalition, according to Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House.
“He can try and persuade Eisenkot and others to form a coalition with him and in the meantime he can delegitimise the Arab parties to make it difficult to form an alternative government,” he told Al Jazeera.
Flaschenberg said Netanyahu will likely push for another round of elections.
“In his calculation – the Arabs will not turn out as before and the opposition would be discouraged and stagnant. He believes that in another round of elections his bloc could get to 61,” he said.
“The other option that [Netanyahu] is working on is getting one or two parties from the Change bloc to join his government. Most likely Bennet and Liberman. But at the moment it doesn’t look like they are going to join him,” he added.
How do Palestinians view the deadlock?
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, called the election “an existential moment for Palestinian Israelis”.
Palestinian analyst Najar said that for Palestinian citizens of Israel, the result represents both an achievement and a test.
“They turned out in large numbers, secured unprecedented representation and may now have the power to prevent another Netanyahu government. Yet they are again being told that their votes are acceptable only if they do not translate into real political power,” he said.
“For Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, however, there is little reason to see this as a contest between occupation and peace, or between oppression and equality. It is principally a struggle over who will govern Israel and how Israel will present itself — not whether Palestinians will continue to live under military occupation, settlement expansion, dispossession and systemic inequality,” he added.
“But Palestinians will judge any successor by policy, not personality – whether it ends the genocide in Gaza, stops settlement expansion and settler violence, and recognises Palestinian freedom and self-determination,” he said.

Apple takes "monumental step forward" with first touchscreen MacBook

Apple takes “monumental step forward” with first touchscreen MacBook
Apple has revealed its latest MacBook Pro model, which features the technology brand’s first laptop touchscreen and what it claims is “the world’s best laptop display”.
Sixteen years after Steve Jobs described touchscreen laptops as “ergonomically terrible”, Apple has ventured into the market with its new MacBook Pro, which is available from 6 November at prices ranging from £2,899 to £14,549.
As well as being touchscreen, the laptop features a PROLED XDR display, which Apple said is “the world’s best laptop display”, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, 128 gigabytes of memory, 16 terabytes of storage, up to 24 hours of battery life and a thinner, lighter design compared to previous models.
It comes in 14- and 16-inch models, weighing three and four pounds respectively. The laptop was designed to be both portable and a powerful tool for professional creatives on the go, whether they’re working on 3D models or playing musical instruments onscreen.
“The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is a monumental step forward for the Mac,” said Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji.
“PROLED XDR is the world’s best laptop display,” he continued. “And with the magic of Touch coming to MacBook Pro, combined with the game-changing performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, we’ve created a whole new way for pros to interact with their content, taking their workflows to a completely new level.”
“The new MacBook Pro is the result of the deep integration between Apple silicon, hardware, and software, and there’s simply nothing else like it.”
Aiming to provide an intuitive experience, the Touch technology allows users to scroll through a webpage by swiping, zoom in on a photo by pinching, drag and drop slides in presentations and double-tap a window to fill the screen.
The touch sensor is built into the display panel rather than layered over it, to give the feel of touching the displayed content itself.
To support the Touch feature, Apple redesigned the laptop hinge for better stability and created real-time video stabilisation to smooth the camera feed when using the touchscreen on a video call.
Apple said that the macOS operating system automatically translates touches into clicks, meaning multiple existing apps will work with Touch right away. These include Adobe Lightroom, Blender, Maxon Cinema 4D, Maxon ZBrush, Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint.
“Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing,” said Apple.
“Musicians can play software instruments right onscreen, and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display.”
Apple said the new PROLED XDR display offers “true-to-life colour and unparalleled brightness and contrast”, made possible by combining OLED technology with algorithms that control light across the display.
“The PROLED XDR display offers tandem OLED technology unlike any other, with deep innovations in its layers that keep brightness and grayscale uniform across the entire display, while minimising internal reflections common in traditional OLED designs,” said Apple.
“It’s all backed by advanced algorithms in the display engine that precisely control each pixel in real time, plus a meticulous manufacturing process and precise calibration of every panel for consistency from display to display.”
The MacBook Pro also has a six-speaker sound system, designed for deeper bass and improved sound clarity compared to previous models, and the Dynamic Island search and notification feature currently used in iPhones.
Other recent releases from Apple include its first folding smartphone, the HomeView dashboard for home controls and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.
The images are courtesy of Apple.
