The psychology behind our undying fascination with vampires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:44:55 UTC
19:44:55 KST

Rachel Feltman: Happy Halloween, listeners. For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
When I was about 13 years old, I stumbled upon a vampire story that I became obsessed with. I wrote reams of fan fiction and made my crush on all three members of the main love triangle into an entire personality. Many girls on the cusp of teenhood in 2005 could no doubt say the same, though most of them were probably fixated on the recently released book Twilight, and I, ever the contrarian, had gone to my local Blockbuster and discovered a movie from 1987.
[CLIP: Kiefer Sutherland as David in The Lost Boys. “Now you know what we are. Now you know what you are. You’ll never grow old, Michael, and you’ll never die. But you must feed.”]
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
It’s been more than 20 years, but I’m still firmly Team Kiefer. So you can imagine my delight when, just this past April, a musical based on The Lost Boys made its Broadway debut. And that’s far from the only vampire media people are paying to see in droves: With his award-winning movie Sinners, Ryan Coogler brought creatures of the night into prestige cinema like never before. And AMC’s adaptation of Anne Rice’s The Vampire Chronicles series has launched her beloved character Lestat into the stratosphere.
[CLIP: Sam Reid as Lestat in Interview with a Vampire: “Are there any readers in the audience tonight?”]
Then, of course there’s Robert Eggers’s Nosferatu, Cynthia Erivo’s solo Dracula show on the West End, the delightful comedy What We Do in the Shadows, which sadly has ended, Dimension 20’s “City Council of Darkness”—I could go on.
So today we’re going to talk about what makes vampires so fascinating that they keep showing up in our media—and how these seductive fictional figures can actually be traced back to public health horror stories.
Tales of humanoid creatures that feed on life are about as old as stories get, but the use of the term “vampire” for a bloodsucking monster seems to have emerged around 18th-century Europe. And throughout the [1700s] and 1800s, many people saw vampires as a real and present danger.
Aaron Mahnke: It’s just a bizarre story, you know. And there’s some grief involved in it, there’s some tragedy and some weirdness and some grossness, but at the core of it, it’s a fascinating story.
Feltman: That’s Aaron Mahnke, a historian who hosts the hit podcast Lore. His latest book is called Exhumed: Unearthing the History of the American Vampire.
Mahnke: What we think was going on was essentially a community would experience an outbreak, usually of what we think was tuberculosis because of the symptoms.
Feltman: Basically, people got it into their heads that certain illnesses could be transmitted posthumously, with the dead somehow staying tethered to the living and draining their health away. Because tuberculosis could spread between family members and then slowly kill several of them in a row, the disease might seem almost like a curse. Inventing vampires as an explanation helped people feel like there was something they could do to keep tragedies from multiplying.
Similar “epidemics” show up in earlier historical records around the world and were particularly common in Europe in the 1700s. But Mahnke’s book focuses on the story of Mercy Brown, who died of what was likely tuberculosis in Exeter, Rhode Island, in 1892.
Mahnke: You have to imagine these are people in the early to mid-1800s who had no concept of virology and how illness was passed around. So what people were doing was reacting to this belief that the reason why people in their family were sick was because someone who had already died from the sickness in their family was literally lying in their grave, drinking the life force from those who were still above ground. So not in a sense—like the vampire that we think of today as running around in leather pants with handguns and, you know, battling werewolves and drinking the blood out of someone’s neck. So in the century of the New England vampire panic, it was more Colin, the emotional vampire from What We Do in the Shadows. They were sucking the life from someone from a distance.
Feltman: You can see the threads that would eventually weave into the bloody vampire myths we know today in the methods New Englanders used to “prove” a vampire’s existence. Mahnke says folks had a pretty binary understanding of decomposition and the degradation of blood in particular. If a body was really and truly dead, they figured, blood would be dried into powder. The presence of liquid meant something was still kicking around in there. But there are a few reasons someone might see what seemed to be fresh blood in a definitely actually dead corpse: Liquids produced by decomposition might ooze out of orifices tinted red by dried blood, for one thing. And in New England and much of Europe, where death during winter meant loved ones were temporarily interred aboveground to wait for the ground to thaw, blood and tissue might freeze instead of rotting.
Mercy Brown, for instance, died in January and was “exhumed” that March.
Mahnke: Her exhumation was literally just opening a shed and removing her coffin. They miraculously discovered that she looked very well preserved, but that’s kind of what you’d expect from somebody who’d spent two months in a walk-in freezer.
Feltman: As Mahnke’s latest book makes clear, this visceral fear of the undead was really quite recent. Mercy Brown’s sister lived until 1954. But during her lifetime, our attitude toward vampires made a radical shift from a manifestation of grief and fear to, well, maybe still a manifestation of grief and fear but one that we might also be interested in dating. So how did they make the transition from rotting spectres of disease to hot anti-heroes?
In her 1995 book Our Vampires, Ourselves the late literary scholar Nina Auerbach argued that vampire stories take on the fears and desires of the people telling them. The folk vampires Mahnke described, where dead relatives drain the living and doom a whole family, are one version of that. Another is the predatory aristocrat figure introduced in John Polidori’s 1819 novella The Vampyre—which took cues from his notoriously rakish associate Lord Byron—and then popularized by Bram Stoker in 1897. So what does the influx of cool, sexy vampires say about our current cultural needs? Speaking personally—which I hope you’ll allow me to do since this is more of a question of cultural analysis than empirical research—I think it might have something to do with a shift in what it means to be “other.” The fears that once built monstrous figures like Nosferatu, like xenophobia, still exist especially systemically but are perhaps less popular with mainstream audiences than they were in the 1800s. When Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu published Carmilla in 1872, it was radical in its presentation of a lesbian vampire—but she was also literally a monster. Her otherness was compelling but horrifying. In the latest TV adaptation of Interview with the Vampire, queerness and colorism make the bloodsuckers all the more “other” in the context of their own worlds but actually serve to humanize them for the audience. So maybe our modern vampires reflect a more modern sense of how many of us are the “other” in one way or another.
I spoke about that a bit with Jenny Hamilton, a senior lecturer in counseling and psychological therapy at the University of Lincoln. Her professional work on monsters focuses on how people use them to help process trauma, but she has some thoughts on how monstrous characters have changed with the times. On the one hand, she says, our monsters have shifted from less physical to more psychological in nature as our fears have gotten less primal and more existential.
Jenny Hamilton: In modern and postmodern societies, our anxieties are often less tangible: things like climate change, pandemics, AI, uncertainty about the future.
Feltman: Now, obviously vampires are not the only monster game in town but it makes a lot of sense that being humanoid figures that still engage in very human activities and relationships, they offer a really good template for exploring anxieties that are more social and cultural than physical.
And as figures that sit more firmly on the fuzzy line between human and monster than, say, goblins or dragons, it makes sense that they’ve also been at the forefront of our increasingly complex sense of what makes a monster.
Hamilton: They kind of sit on a lot of boundaries that are a bit difficult for us or taboo. So, you know, the boundaries between life and death, being human and animal.
Feltman: Jenny says that vampires have always been these very contradictory figures who are on the fringes but that our own relationship with the idea of good and bad, villain and hero, is what’s become more nuanced. It’s become more complex as binary traditional ideas about who belongs and who doesn’t have been shed in modern society. In other words, we’ve thankfully come to value a lot of the qualities that used to keep people on the fringes of certain kinds of society.
Now, I’ll pause here to say that of course I know vampires aren’t the only monstrous characters that have gotten the romance treatment, especially in recent years. Just off the top of the dome, I got classic [choices] like Beauty and the Beast, avant-garde ones like The Shape of Water, even zombies thanks to Warm Bodies. We had Lisa Frankenstein, not to mention all of the werewolves in the Twilight franchise and Teen Wolf and similar fiction. We’ve even got that new Olivia Colman movie where she’s married to a big, giant, beautiful man made of wicker, which I cannot wait to see. But I do think vampires are a little unique because most of the other monsters I talked about, you know, they occasionally show up as the love interest in kind of a subversive way. Vampires have become so synonymous with sensuality that, at this point, it’s actually surprising and subversive when a movie makes them gross and not sexy. I’m looking at you, Robert Eggers.
But when it comes to how and why we’re able to find literal monsters so attractive, from a purely physical point of view, there’s no clear-cut scientific answer—but there are a lot of really interesting angles to explore.
To get into this I spoke to Mathias Clasen. He’s the co-director of Aarhus University’s Recreational Fear Lab, which is exactly what it sounds like: its mission is to investigate the kinds of things people do because they scare them.
Mathias Clasen: It’s not just watching horror movies.... It’s also some of the earliest playful activities that we expose kids to like, you know, peekaboo, which is a sort of baby jump scare…, running after kids pretending to be a monster. It’s also so-called risky play, you know, kids riding their bikes too fast, climbing trees until they feel butterflies flapping their wings in their stomachs. It’s young women listening to true crime podcasts. It’s middle-aged guys buying fast cars and driving too fast. So there’s a whole range of things people do to get pleasure out of being scared, and that’s what we’re trying to understand.
Feltman: Clasen doesn’t currently research our love of monsters, but it’s something he’s thought about a lot.
Clasen: Before, I spent most of my time doing empirical research, like going to haunted attractions to measure the heart rate of guests or try to draw blood samples to look at immune activation, I did a lot of more kind of conceptual theoretical work, including an attempt to explain why monsters are ubiquitous in the landscape of popular culture.
Feltman: One of his favorite examples is the movie Jaws, which led to an actual drop in beach tourism while drawing huge crowds at the theater.
Clasen: The odds of being eaten by a big white shark are, you know, as close to zero as you can get. But there’s something about that monster with the mouth brimming with sharp teeth and the, you know, the dead black eyes that just, I think it triggers something deep within us, and I think that’s what good monsters do, is they trigger, you know, an ancient defense system that evolved way before we were human.
Feltman: Basically, some evolutionary psychologists think that scary play—which includes telling stories about monsters—taps into the same mechanisms for learning and adapting that helped our ancient ancestors survive real threats.
Clasen: We’re kind of hardwired to not just keep our distance but to actually, you know pay attention because that’s the way to learn about different kinds of threats in the environment. So it makes sense that there would be that sort of push-pull ambivalence associated with, you know, monsters and frightening creatures.
And so the reason why there are many more monsters in popular culture than in the real world is that we’re still sort of at the core kind of these cowering, you know, Stone Age hominins, you know, sitting around the bonfire telling stories about all the horrors that exist outside that protective circle of light.
Feltman: But why have so many of those campfire stories turned so sexy? For some reason there don’t seem to be any psychology labs working on what to me is obviously an urgent question. But there’s some adjacent research that’s worth unpacking a little bit.
As Mathias pointed out, we have sort of a push-pull relationship with our favorite monsters, where they intrigue us while also, on some level, freaking us out. The push and the pull might not always feel at odds with each other because fear and attraction share a lot of the same physiology. In 1974 psychologists ran a now infamous experiment on the so-called misattribution of arousal where male study subjects met with female interviewers on either wobbly rope suspension bridges or low, sturdy bridges. The ones on shaky footing apparently were more likely to call the interviewer, who offered her number in case they had “follow-up questions.” As you might guess based on the absolutely bonkers nature of that methodology, this study isn’t considered a particularly strong piece of research. But while the idea that we can literally misinterpret fear as sexual arousal is shaky, other research suggests that a fearful rush of physiological arousal could amp up the perceived intensity of whatever else we’re feeling.
In other words, maybe seeing Spike skulk into a room on Buffy can simultaneously trigger both standard physical attraction—because, I mean, have you looked at a picture of James Marsters lately?—and something deep-seated that tells us to sit up and pay close attention to the apex predator in our midst. I’m picturing my nervous system flooding itself with chemicals à la that one scene in Flashdance.
Another idea I’ve seen bandied about is that vampires are, generally speaking, just so evolutionarily fit that we can’t look away. You might hear people mention the so-called dark triad personality traits of narcissism, psychopathy and Machiavellianism. Some research argues that these noxious traits make men more successful at reproducing, and I’ve seen a lot of pop psychology arguing that this is some kind of explanation for the bad boy stereotype and our love of hot villains. But the reproductive edge actually goes away for everything but short-term mating strategies, and women generally don’t rate those traits as attractive in long-term relationships or necessarily at all—so it’s probably more that those qualities lend themselves to seeking out lots of partners and saying whatever it takes to get them into bed them and not that psychopathy makes the average gal go, “Awoooooga.”
It is true that, broadly speaking, humans look for signs of health and reproductive fitness in their potential partners. And it’s technically true that there’s no greater sign of fitness than eternal life. But I personally think that our attraction to vampire characters is less about them short-circuiting our unconscious search for a reproductive mate and more about our own complicated relationship with the idea of sitting at the top of the evolutionary food chain.
Clasen: I think the reason why that figure won’t go away is that it embodies, at the same time, some of our, you know, the things we really fear and detest, the most nasty impulses in human nature, the, kind of, animalistic, predatory, power-seeking, selfish drives. But there’s also something appealing about, you know, eternal youth and not dying and, you know, never changing, and it’s just a sort of symbolic container for our deepest fears and our, you know, their most burning desires—for example, to not die.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. I hope you’ve enjoyed this very freaky Friday Fascination. We’ll be back on Monday with our usual science news roundup.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Sushmita Pathak, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great weekend!

New Humvee-type air defense vehicle spotted in China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:44:29 UTC
19:44:29 KST

- Images show an upgraded Yitian-L air defense vehicle carrying two six-round missile packs, up from the four TY-90 missiles on the standard version.
- NORINCO has not commented, and it remains unclear whether the vehicle is for the Chinese military or for export.
An upgraded version of China’s Yitian-L short-range air defense system has been spotted on the move with two six-round missile packs, apparently tripling its ready-to-fire load to 12 missiles from the four carried by the production model, images shared on social media show.
The vehicle was photographed while being transported, and the images show a reworked launcher on the platform of the Dongfeng Mengshi 4×4, the Chinese equivalent of the Humvee, with two boxes of six launch tubes each in place of the four separate canisters on earlier Yitian-Ls. It was not clear where or when the photos were taken, whether the vehicle belongs to the Chinese military or is an export version, and whether the missiles are the standard TY-90 or a smaller derivative. NORINCO, which builds the Yitian family, has not publicly commented on the new configuration.
The Yitian-L is a lightweight version of China’s Yitian air defense system, meant to protect troops and fixed sites from low-flying helicopters, drones and cruise missiles. In its known form, it carries four TY-90 infrared-guided missiles and a folding 3D X-band radar on the roof. NORINCO says the radar can detect targets at up to 18 km (11 miles) and the TY-90 can hit them from 500 m out to 6 km (3.7 miles) and at altitudes of up to 4 km, Janes reported. Two operators run the system from inside the vehicle using a joystick-based digital console.
The TY-90 was originally developed as a short-range air-to-air missile for Chinese helicopters before being adapted for ground launch. It homes in on the heat from its target, so it can be fired and left to guide itself without the launcher keeping a radar beam on the target. That passive guidance also means the vehicle does not give away its position by emitting radar signals during the engagement.
Packing more missiles onto a single light vehicle addresses a problem air defense units have faced in Ukraine and the Middle East, where small drones arrive in large numbers and a four-missile launcher can empty quickly. The original Yitian and the newer Yitian II, both mounted on armored personnel carriers, carry eight TY-90s each, so a 12-round Yitian-L would carry more missiles than either of the heavier versions.
The Yitian-L has so far been an export product. Mauritania was the first known operator, displaying eight systems in June 2024, and Mali received Yitian-L systems earlier this year under a 2024 contract with NORINCO. In 2025, NORINCO also showed another lightweight Yitian variant on a Yema 4×4 chassis. The Chinese army has meanwhile fielded its own Mengshi-based short-range system, believed to be designated HQ-13, armed with FB-10A missiles.
The images do not show whether the upgraded Yitian-L keeps the same radar and fire control, whether the extra missiles cost it range or performance.

US weighs new Iran strikes as Vance reaches out: Is war or a deal closer?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:40:52 UTC
19:40:52 KST

US weighs new Iran strikes as Vance reaches out: Is war or a deal closer?
As Washington and Tehran send mixed signals, analysts say trust remains a key obstacle to any deal.
Over the past week, Washington and Tehran have sent mixed signals about whether their eight-month war is heading back to full-scale strikes or towards a peace deal.
On Thursday, the head of United States Central Command (CENTCOM), Admiral Brad Cooper, briefed US President Donald Trump on options for renewed attacks on Iran, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.
The US and Israel have drawn up joint plans to attack Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections, The New York Times (NYT) reported last week.
Yet on the same day, The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance had offered to meet Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, in person to negotiate an end to the war.
On Friday, Qatari mediators returned to Tehran for talks coordinated with the US, an official told Reuters.
So is Washington heading back to war, or towards a deal? Here’s what we know:
Why are there conflicting reports?
Essentially, Washington is preparing for war while keeping a diplomatic channel open.
The WSJ reported that the US has boosted air defences and munitions in the region and moved some troops away from bases vulnerable to Iranian retaliation.
Ten US military cargo planes landed at the Ovda and Nevatim air bases in Israel’s Negev region on Thursday, with more sent to Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, the Israeli public broadcaster Kan reported.
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, who said he had been briefed on the plans, called them “insane” and warned of a devastating escalation.
Can diplomatic efforts hold off a return to strikes?
Diplomacy has not stopped.
Vance’s letter, delivered to Rezaei through Qatari mediators on Sunday, proposed direct talks led by Vance, with Iran’s nuclear programme on the table from the start, according to the NYT, in a bid to prevent a renewal of strikes.
Whether it might have any influence over what happens next is a matter for debate. Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst who is an affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies in Sweden, described Vance as the “voice of reason” on Iran within the Trump administration, saying his signals have been “the least volatile and unpredictable”.
But he also told Al Jazeera that Vance’s position has “never proven to be sturdy enough to actually sway Trump”.
“Thus, while the optics with Vance look better than anyone else in the Trump administration, I doubt that they [Iranian officials] give the outreach much credence until Vance proves able to actually deliver something on his own,” he said.
Furthermore, Nader Hashemi, a professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera that “Rezaei is just one voice among many” adding that the “reality is that decisions are made collectively inside the Islamic republic”.
Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, has a different view, however, telling Al Jazeera, “There is no doubt that the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] currently calls the shots in Iran.”
In February, Iran’s then supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in the initial attacks by Israel and the United States, and his son became the new supreme leader, but Pusztai says he “simply does not have the influence his father did”.
“Without the IRGC’s approval, there will be no agreement with Iran,” Pusztai said, adding it is safe to assume that when Rezaei makes a statement or endorses a proposal, “it reflects the position of the IRGC leadership” and that the US was “absolutely right to negotiate with him”.
Pusztai said it is unclear whether Rezaei is indeed ready to make a serious compromise, but under sustained US pressure, Rezaei, who holds a doctorate in economics, could come to see that “Iran’s interests and the regime’s survival can be better secured without nuclear weapons and through a less aggressive foreign policy”.
“He certainly knows that peak oil is approaching and that time is running out for Iran’s economic recovery through the use of its oil revenues,” he said.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said progress depends on Iran’s seven conditions being met – including the lifting of sanctions, ending the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, guarantees to an end to US-Israeli strikes, and the unfreezing of Iranian assets – adding that the “carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran”, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Vance, meanwhile, told Fox News on Thursday that Trump would “never” let the conflict become “a forever war”.
Which of all these signals matter most?
The diplomacy may say more than the threats.
Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Vance’s offer of direct talks “suggests that the Americans do have second thoughts” and that they are less ready to strike than they publicly suggest.
But he warned that Cooper, whom he called “quite hawkish”, could give Trump false confidence “that there is a military way out of it, when in reality there isn’t a military way out of it”.
“This idea that there is a short and crisp military operation to solve this issue is obviously an illusion,” he said.
Paul Musgrave, an associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera the White House could be sending signals to coerce Tehran, but that “the better interpretation is the simplest one”.
He believes “the United States is getting ready to carry out substantial attacks relatively soon”. He said he does not expect Washington to accept what he called the unfavourable deal Tehran is offering “without another round of attacks”.
Pusztai said Trump’s main focus is now the midterms, making it “very unlikely that he will order another large-scale attack on Iran before the elections”.
“Starting in mid to late November, there could be a major wave of attacks aimed at advancing the American agenda,” he said, adding that the aim would be to weaken the IRGC enough to push it towards a deal on US terms.
Whatever the vote’s result, “in the short term it will not change much”, Musgrave said.
A strong Republican showing could encourage more aggressive tactics, while a Democratic win could push Trump to show his unilateral powers, including by attacking, he said.
Hasn’t this all happened before?
It has. Iran was attacked by Israel or the US while talks were under way in both 2025 and 2026.
“We’ve seen this pattern of behaviour before from the United States,” Hashemi said, describing it as “talking diplomacy while preparing for war”.
On June 13, 2025, Israel launched major strikes on Iranian nuclear and military sites, two days before a sixth round of US-Iran talks was due in Oman. The US joined on June 22, bombing Iran’s Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan nuclear sites.
This year, the US and Israel attacked on February 28, two days after talks in Geneva that mediator Oman said had made “significant progress”.
A day before the strikes, Oman’s foreign minister said Iran had agreed to reduce its nuclear stockpiles to “the lowest level possible”.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera in September that Iran no longer trusts negotiations with Washington because attacks had come during previous rounds of talks.
Hashemi said he suspects “the same pattern is repeating itself”, with the US preparing “a massive bombing campaign in Iran, replete with war crimes like we haven’t seen before”, citing his reading of Murphy’s comments.
What is blocking a deal?
“The issue is mostly around sequencing and the lack of trust on the Iranian side that the Americans will actually follow through with their commitments,” Krieg said.
Tehran wants sanctions and the US naval blockade lifted quickly, fearing that a slow process gives Trump room to backtrack, he said.
Some IRGC hardliners do not necessarily see war as a bad thing if it tightens their grip on the Hormuz strait, he added, and “the Iranians have been prepping for this war for the last three weeks, so they are ready to fight”.
Krieg said he expects “nothing is going to happen until the 3rd of November [the date of the US midterm elections]”. After that, he said, the likelihood of war will “increase exponentially”.
Any new escalation would be worse than in February and March, he said, with Iran readier to strike critical infrastructure in Gulf countries.
He said the threat to the Gulf “will be unprecedented”.

Taipei Fine Arts Museum scores with Sakamoto exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:40:33 UTC
19:40:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Piano keys and the hum of a bassline introduce Taipei Fine Arts Museum’s latest exhibition, a retrospective on the life and work of Ryuichi Sakamoto — providing a counterpoint to the usual focus on visual arts.
The Japanese musician, who passed away three years ago at 71, was an Oscar-, Grammy-, and Golden Globe-award-winning pop star, film composer, and the voice of a generation.
A classically trained pianist, he co-founded the influential early electronic music band Yellow Magic Orchestra in the late 1970s. He then struck out on his own, or in collaborations with leading lights such as David Bowie, David Sylvian, David Byrne, Alva Noto (Carsten Nicolai), DJ Spooky, and many others.
His works ranged from the earwormy theme tune for the movie “Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence,” the score for “The Last Emperor,” and well-known solo piano pieces such as “Energy Flow.”
Starting around the beginning of the new millennium, Sakamoto focused more on large-scale installations at museums and festivals that incorporated visual elements. At the same time, he continued to experiment with sound, presenting field recordings, working with unconventional instruments, and using technology to expand the horizons of electronic music.
In doing so, he profoundly influenced contemporary music and interdisciplinary art, according to TFAM. Appropriately, it is this part of his oeuvre that the art museum focuses on in its latest exhibition, which opens Saturday and continues until March 14 next year.
TFAM Director Loh Li-chen (駱麗真) commented: “While presenting Ryuichi Sakamoto’s explorations of the forms that art can take, this exhibition also leads visitors to ponder the relationships among sound, time, space, technology, and bodily sensation.
“We hope that when visitors enter our museum, they will listen and see in new ways, and so experience how art changes our understanding of the world around us.”
“Ryuichi Sakamoto, Seeing Sound, Hearing Time, New Ways to Sense the World through Sound, Space, and Image” is curated by Sachiko Namba and comprises seven large-scale installations, in addition to providing archival materials about the works and his collaborations. They sum up Sakamoto’s vision of music being “an ‘art of time’ and existing only in time.”
The first exhibit of note is not technically a Sakamoto piece. However, as TFAM points out, it does echo his belief that all sounds are equal and is an extension of the artist’s “prepared piano” works.
Two “sound boxes” have been installed in the entryway to the exhibition, which allow visitors to generate their own soundscapes using field drums, percussive elements, levers, and dials. Ambient noise from outside the art museum is also incorporated, and afterward the result can be downloaded to a phone via a QR code. It’s a neat start.
Afterwards, visitors are encouraged to stroll around and examine the rest of the installations, or take a seat and immerse themselves in rooms that offer mindful visions and stimulating soundscapes.
“Async-immersion” by Sakamoto and Shiro Takatani presents a long LED video wall and a multichannel sound system. It is based on Sakamoto’s 2017 album “Async,” and was first shown at “Ambient Kyoto” in 2023.
The setup means visitors stand inside the music rather than simply listen to it. Scenes such as reeds on a riverbank, a grove of trees, or a coastal view are gradually erased by horizontal bands of light that move from one side to the other.
At the same time, ambient music rises and falls with the appearance and reappearance of either natural scenes or visual representations of electronic interference. The loop continues, bringing forth a feeling of endless repetition and rhythm that is both hypnotic and reflective.
“Async-volume” from 2017 is a collaboration with Zakkubalan, a Tokyo- and New York–based artist and filmmaking collective. The video and sound installation is eerie in that it feels like breaking into the artist’s house after it has just been vacated.
A film continues to play in the empty sitting room, while a gong in the studio moves slightly as if it was hit and is now coming to rest. Outside the house, there is a broken window, and branches on a tree move in the wind. It is as though we are peeking surreptitiously into Sakamoto’s private life.
Elsewhere, there is a container of water, which is disturbed by water dripping from above, creating plops and plinks, and bubbles. Alternatively, the container is shaken or stirred, creating ripples across the water’s surface.
Another exhibit sees a penguin drift by on the screen and bleached bones in a natural history museum, all elegantly accompanied by Sakamoto on the piano. Time slows while the sound and visuals create a contemplative atmosphere.
TFAM Media Associate Daisy Tian-Rong Shiou (修天容) said the art museum team saw the original Sakamoto exhibition that was presented in Tokyo in 2023 and wanted to reproduce that here. She described the original show as “marvelous” and added that the team felt that TFAM’s high ceilings and acoustics would suit it perfectly.
It does.
“Another reason for the exhibition is that our museum is expanding and will be completed in 2029,” Shiou said. “For that museum we are thinking of having experimental art or new media arts, so in the years before then we will also try not only visual arts, but cross-media arts.”
The NT$5.2 billion (US$160 million) extension is being framed as “art within a forest,” since it is being built within Taipei Art Park. It will have one above-ground level and two underground levels, making it Taiwan’s first earth-sheltered museum.
There is a dedicated third-floor observatory of sorts at the back of TFAM that presides over the ongoing construction of the museum extension. After sampling Sakamoto, it is a cool space to rest and decompress for a while.

Who are Germany’s Gen Z protesters and what do they want?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:38:52 UTC
19:38:52 KST

- ‘If politicians aren’t going to do anything, then we young people have to take action,’ says organizer Akram Selo
- Ruling CDU/CSU bloc calls protesters far-left extremists and criminals, likening them to recent protests in France
A growing culture of protest and resistance has been taking shape among young people in Germany.
Following a series of blockades at high schools, members of Generation Z – teens and young adults between the ages of 14 and 30 – will take to the streets on Saturday.
The newly founded initiative, Gen Z regelt (Gen Z takes charge), has called for a protest at the historic Brandenburg Gate in Berlin.
More than 154,000 people have registered for the protest, according to the group's website.
Similar demonstrations are planned in 30 other cities across Germany, with protesters opposing cuts to education and social services, as well as mandatory military service.
“We are young people who are no longer willing to stand by and watch as decisions about our future are made without our voices being heard,” the group said on its website.
“We call for policies that invest in education, social security, health care, climate protection, and an affordable standard of living, rather than cutting back on the younger generation,” it added.
It also calls for consistent climate action and opposes the expansion of government surveillance.
 
Young people worry about future, organizer says
One of the organizers of Saturday’s protests, Akram Selo, said it is the fear for their future which brings young people to the streets of Germany.
“There are many young people who are worried about their future … If politicians aren’t going to do anything, then we young people have to take action,” Selo, 18, told daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.
Asked whether he was concerned that the demonstrations in Germany could turn violent like in France, the activist replied: “This movement didn’t just start last week. We’ve been planning this for more than three weeks. When we started, the demonstrations in France were still peaceful.”
 
We have to stand up for our rights, students say
The view was echoed by Ruediger F, a political science student at Berlin’s Free University.
“The fact that tens of thousands of students are planning to take to the streets this weekend to press for their demands shows that our concerns have not been taken seriously,” Ruediger F. told Anadolu.
“We are investing hundreds of billions of euros in our military instead of our educational system, combating poverty and climate change. We have to set our priorities straight and that is why I strongly support the protests,” he added.
Marie S., a political science student at the same university, said: “For years, there have been budget cuts in the education and social sectors.
“While there is supposedly no money for schools and universities, massive investments are being made in militarization; and if conscription were to be introduced, it would once again be at the expense of the younger generation, which is already bearing the brunt of the climate crisis,” she told Anadolu.
“The upcoming protests are part of a series of protest movements around the world, most recently in France,” she noted.
It is a “positive sign that young people are joining forces internationally and standing up for these causes,” she said.
 
Left and Green youth organizations support protests
The initiative, however, has received support from the youth organizations of the opposition Greens and The Left Party.
The Federal Association of the Left Youth criticized the prejudgment of the protests, which are planned to be peaceful.
“As Left Youth, we welcome the fact that young people are taking to the streets to protest the Merz-Klingbeil government’s austerity policies.”
The Green Youth also backed the protests. Their spokesperson, Luis Bobga, called it “right and important that our generation is now also applying pressure on the streets.”
Both parties are calling for participation in the International Youth Strike Day, which is planned to take place simultaneously in various European countries on Nov. 20.
 
Police vows ‘no mercy’ if protests turn violent
Alexander Throm, the domestic policy spokesperson for the co-ruling Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) parliamentary group, alleged in an interview with business daily Handelsblatt that the youth protest movement have been taken over by far-left extremists and criminal elements from the migrant community.
Baden-Wuerttemberg’s Interior Minister Manuel Hagel, also a member of the CDU, vowed to strike back “with the full force of the rule of law.”
The CDU’s city council caucus in the southern city of Stuttgart is considering a ban on public gatherings.
The CDU youth organization in Berlin’s district of Mitte has floated the idea of calling in the German army. It said that Paris has shown what “those who hate the free, democratic order” are capable of.
On Instagram, they posted an AI-generated photo of children with school backpacks at the Brandenburg Gate, with soldiers in bulletproof vests and combat helmets standing in front of them.
The police have also joined in the campaign against the youth protests.

Berlin's Police Union leader Stephan Weh said: “We have to be extremely careful that radical forces don’t co-opt democratic protest—as they did in France.

Swiss and Chinese presidents sign free trade agreement
The presidents of Switzerland and China, Guy Parmelin and Xi Jinping, have signed a modernised free trade agreement in Beijing.
Many previous tariffs previously imposed on Swiss exports to China are to be abolished if the deal is ratified by the Swiss parliament.
More
‘Glass half full’ rating for Swiss-Chinese trade deal
The new text represents an improvement on the trade agreement between the two countries that came into force in 2014, according to the Federal Department of Economic Affairs. It promises to improve access to the Chinese market for Swiss goods and investments.
Rules on environmental protection and labour standards will be further strengthened within a legally binding chapter on trade and sustainable development. This is a first in any free trade agreement concluded by China, according to Switzerland.
In addition to this agreement, Switzerland and China have also signed a related agreement on cooperation in the field of labour and employment, and an agreement on regulated cooperation in research and development.

French customs seize thousands of THC sweets bound for NL

French customs seize thousands of THC sweets bound for NL
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
French customs officers have intercepted 3,560 packs of cannabis-laced sweets that were being shipped from the US to the Netherlands, the European anti-fraud office OLAF said on Thursday.
The sweets contained THC, the main psychoactive substance in cannabis. Of the packs, 3,213 copied the look of a “very well-known European gummy brand”, using altered lettering to resemble its name. OLAF did not name the brand. All the packs have been destroyed.
OLAF did not say who the sweets were meant to be delivered to in the Netherlands.
In a statement, the agency said the familiar packaging gives the false impression of an ordinary, safe product, but that a single product could contain a high amount of THC, and children could be at risk.
Cannabis sweets have caused several scares in the Netherlands. This summer, Utrecht police warned parents after two children became ill from sweets found in a school playground, broadcaster NOS reported.

The helicopter took off from Badrinath for Sahastradhara Heliport at 1.14 pm today.

Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:37:00 UTC
19:37:00 KST

Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A startling new study suggests that venomous snakebites are killing far more people worldwide than official statistics indicate, with an estimated 274,000 to 513,000 deaths every year. Researchers found that as many as 7 million people could suffer snake envenoming annually, while more than 800,000 survivors are left with long-term disabilities.
- Share:
Not every snakebite injects venom. When venom enters the body, however, it can cause snake envenoming. This is a potentially fatal condition and it mostly affects poor rural communities across tropical and subtropical regions who don’t have easy access to medical care.
As researchers with decades of combined experience in snakebite and tropical disease epidemiology, we came to realise that snake envenoming faces a data crisis. Over half of the countries where venomous snakes pose a threat don’t keep count of how many people are bitten or envenomed.
In rural sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia, many victims live hours away from the nearest clinic, lack transport, or seek care from traditional healers. As a result, their cases are never captured in national health statistics.
To bridge this massive gap, we conducted a study to map the global burden of snake envenoming and related deaths.
We looked at data from 79 countries by reviewing studies published up to March 31, 2025. This allowed us to update the findings from our milestone 2008 global burden study. To fill the remaining data gaps, we built a geostatistical model that combines real-world data with local environmental and socioeconomic factors. This allowed us to estimate envenoming and fatality rates.
We conclude from our findings that snake envenoming is a public health crisis on a far greater scale than official statistics have shown. Our results show that sub-Saharan Africa bears the heaviest toll.
The World Health Organization has set an ambitious target to halve snakebite mortality and disability by 2030. Mapping the problem at the country level is the first crucial step.
Uncovering the hidden burden
To overcome the lack of reliable data, we turned to a model-based geostatistics framework.
To understand how this modelling works, think of it as predicting invisible patterns by combining known data points with environmental signals. Instead of assuming data for every region, this modelling uses statistical probability to calculate a range of likely outcomes based on environmental signals.
We fed our model with data including climate, snake species richness and socioeconomic indicators. The model then calculated the probability of snakebites occurring in specific locations, even where official health records were completely blank.
By comparing different data sources (including hospital-reported data and regional statistics) against ground level community-survey data, our framework allowed us to account for unreported snake envenomings. It produced both a baseline floor and a potential upper ceiling for snake envenomings and fatalities.
Based on this, we estimate that at least 2.1 million people experience snake envenoming each year globally. The true number could be high as 7 million. Using our model, which adjusts for substantial under-reporting, annual deaths may range from 274,000 to 513,000.
The geographic distribution of this burden is uneven. Our research shows that sub-Saharan Africa alone accounts for 45% of all global envenomings and fatalities. That burden has likely been underestimated for decades. People in sub-Saharan Africa experience snake envenoming and death at nearly three times the rate seen in south Asia.
Countries like Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ethiopia face a high burden, driven by dense rural populations and high exposure in agricultural fields.
Why sub-Saharan Africa is hit hardest
The reasons sub-Saharan Africa suffers such disproportionate harm are structural rather than accidental.
Firstly, the continent hosts a rich diversity of medically important venomous species. These include saw-scaled vipers (Echis spp.), puff adders (Bitis arietans), African cobras (Naja spp.) and mambas (Dendroaspis spp.). They are responsible for substantial morbidity and mortality across the continent.
Secondly, millions of rural agricultural workers labor in open fields without protective boots and walk on unlit footpaths at night. When a bite occurs, fragile health systems, long travel distances to regional facilities and the high cost or total absence of effective antivenom mean a treatable medical emergency can quickly become fatal. Similar conditions exist in parts of Asia.
We estimate that over 800,000 survivors are left with long-term physical disabilities each year, including amputations and other permanent impairments. These disabilities can reduce household income, increase healthcare costs and push already vulnerable farming families deeper into poverty.
Going forward
Meeting the World Health Organization’s goal requires moving away from guesswork and using spatial risk data to guide real-world policy.
By identifying high-risk hotspots, governments and global health partners can strategically stockpile antivenom where it is needed most, train primary healthcare workers in high-burden rural zones and improve rapid transport infrastructure.
Snake envenoming has remained hidden for too long. Better data cannot solve the problem, but can help ensure that antivenom, healthcare services and prevention efforts reach the communities that need them most.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Dileepa Ediriweera, Health Data Scientist, Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov on Friday called for stronger economic and transport links among Turkic states, saying their geographical position and energy resources offered significant opportunities to expand their role in global trade and energy security.
Addressing the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in the Turkish capital Ankara, Bayramov highlighted the development of the Middle Corridor and expanded transport connections between member countries as ways to boost their collective economic potential.
"Our primary objective is to leverage these opportunities not merely for transit transport, but also to foster mutual trade, industrial cooperation, and investment," he said.
Bayramov said cooperation in energy, digital connectivity and emerging technologies had reached a new stage among OTS member states, with Azerbaijan playing a key role in establishing green energy and digital links between Central Asia and Europe.
He also highlighted the OTS+ format as a means of expanding ties with third countries and international organizations, while urging continued efforts to secure observer status for the OTS at the UN General Assembly.
Recalling that Azerbaijan assumed the organization's chairmanship at its 12th summit in Gabala last year, Bayramov said regional peace and security had been central priorities.
He noted that global developments over the past year had reinforced their importance amid growing tensions in international relations.
"In such an environment, Azerbaijan continues to serve as a zone of stability and security. Our country not only ensures its own security but also plays a stabilizing role in strengthening peace and stability across a broader region," he said.
Armenia urged to take steps toward peace treaty
Bayramov said Azerbaijan's restoration of its territorial integrity and sovereignty had resolved the long-standing conflict in the South Caucasus, with normalization efforts now underway with neighboring Armenia.
"A de facto state of peace exists in the region. Nevertheless, we expect Armenia to take the necessary political and legal steps toward the signing of a peace treaty," he said.
He stressed Baku's commitment to establishing a "long-term, reliable" peace and replacing the "era of conflict" in the South Caucasus with an "era of cooperation."
Bayramov also thanked Türkiye for hosting the summit and congratulated the Turkish people on the country's 103rd Republic Day, celebrated Oct. 29.
He wished Türkiye success as it assumed the OTS chairmanship from Azerbaijan and congratulated Mirvokhid Azimov on his appointment as the organization's new secretary general.

Will diversifying fuel imports be enough to fix Indonesia’s energy shortfall?

Resty Woro Yuniarin Jakarta
Indonesia is looking beyond Singapore for petrol supplies as it seeks to reduce its dependence on a single source, but analysts say diversifying imports will do little to address the country’s fuel production shortfall without faster refinery modernisation and investment in alternative fuels.
Indonesia has long sourced petroleum products from Singapore, including RON 90 petrol, which has a minimum octane rating of 90 and is marketed domestically as Pertalite. Finnish military creates space operations center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:32:19 UTC
19:32:19 KST

- Finland will open a military Space Operations Center at Air Force headquarters in Tikkakoski on Jan. 1, 2027, with about 20 initial staff.
- The center will take over operation of three ICEYE radar satellites from the company on April 1, 2027.
Finland will set up a military Space Operations Center on Jan. 1, 2027, to run the country’s space defense and take over the three radar imaging satellites the Finnish Defence Forces bought from ICEYE, the Finnish Air Force announced on Oct. 30.
Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen approved the new center, which will sit within Air Force headquarters at Tikkakoski, near Jyväskylä in central Finland. It will start with about 20 military and civilian specialists transferred from elsewhere in the Defence Forces, a number the Air Force expects to grow as Finland’s military space capabilities expand. The Air Force did not give a budget for the center.
The center will build a military picture of what is happening in space, coordinate space activity with NATO and partner countries, and plan and run the Defence Forces’ own space systems. It will work with the civilian space situational awareness center at the Finnish Meteorological Institute and with allies, combining national, allied, commercial and open-source data to issue warnings, threat assessments and analysis to military commanders.
“The importance of space has grown rapidly in recent years, both for civilian society and for warfare. Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine has shown in concrete terms that space technology supports the operations of forces fighting on land, at sea and in the air, and that as an operating environment it is an essential part of modern multi-domain operations,” said Col. Jari Kumpuniemi of the Air Force headquarters.
Finland’s first military satellites form the core of the new center’s work. The Defence Forces signed a contract with ICEYE in September 2025 for a satellite remote sensing system, valued at about €158 million (about $176 million), including options to extend the satellites’ service life and expand the system. The Air Force has now confirmed it includes three satellites carrying synthetic aperture radar, or SAR, which were launched in 2025 and 2026. ICEYE has operated them under the contract until now, and the Defence Forces will take over operations on April 1, 2027.
SAR satellites bounce radar signals off the ground to build images, so they can see through clouds and at night, an advantage in Finland’s often overcast northern climate. The Air Force said the satellites give the Defence Forces an initial independent space-based intelligence and surveillance capability, and that their data can also be shared with other Finnish authorities and NATO allies.
ICEYE, based in Espoo, Finland, has sold satellites or ordered systems to several NATO members, including the United States, the Netherlands, Poland, Germany, Sweden and Portugal. Poland took control of its own ICEYE constellation less than a year after signing its contract, a similar model of buying satellites and then running them in-house that Finland is now following. The Finnish Defence Forces said they are also building cooperation with allies that operate SAR satellites.
Commercial radar satellites have also drawn Russian attention. A Russian military satellite maneuvered to within about 5 km (3 miles) of an ICEYE satellite in October and has held position near it, according to tracking data.

Rifts over wars in Ukraine, Iran loom over G20 meeting in US

Breadcrumb
Rifts over wars in Ukraine, Iran wars loom over G20 meeting in US
Deep rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the US-Israeli war on Iran are likely to derail unified actions or statements at a two-day meeting of foreign ministers from the world's 20 largest economies in Atlanta, experts and diplomats said.
The US, which holds the rotating presidency of the G20 this year, has sought to focus its allies on trade imbalances while building a coalition to counter China's control of critical minerals, but the wars—and their economic impact—remain the top concern for many G20 members.
The US has not invited South Africa to the ministerial, which takes place from 30 to 31 October, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov is attending, adding to tensions. Even the traditional G20 family photo has caused some headaches, with some European officials now suggesting two separate pictures—one with Lavrov, one without.
With G20 members Russia, China and many middle powers such as Brazil and India trying to navigate US-China strategic competition, you have "much more of a split than we've ever had," said Heidi Crebo-Rediker, who was chief economist at the State Department during the Obama administration.
Over the past decade or so, G7 countries would at least "have agreed a coordinated platform before they came to the G20, but now we don’t even really have that," she added.
A State Department official told reporters on Thursday the Atlanta meeting would focus on energy and supply chain challenges, seen as crucial to the development of AI. The official said four G20 ministerial-level meetings held this year had achieved some consensus, but more work was needed before the 14 to 16 December leaders' summit in Miami.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is hosting the gathering, has championed the Pax Silica initiative, aimed at uniting G20 countries concerned about China's dominance in rare earths and other critical minerals.
But any movement on that front will probably come afterwards, experts said, pointing to a US-led statement on excess industrial capacity that some G20 trade ministers signed after the group failed to reach consensus.
"It's going to be very hard to have complete agreement on any of the larger strategic questions that you would ordinarily have on the agenda," Crebo-Rediker said.
Elaine Dezenski, a former US official who heads the Center on Economic and Financial Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington-based think tank, said such statements by ad hoc groups could prove the way forward.
"The Atlanta meeting takes place within an environment of widening disagreement over the global economic order, and the right test is whether the US can build cooperation with partners when all-member consensus appears to be out of reach," she told reporters this week. She noted the Quad—a security grouping of the US, India, Japan and Australia—would also meet in Atlanta in coming days.
Disagreement over Russia
US President Donald Trump's recent decisions on Russia, including a deal to buy diesel and waiving some sanctions, could also weigh on discussions, along with Ukraine's problems with its Starshield satellite services.
“If it's not brought up, it’s certainly the elephant in the room that the US—and Trump in particular—has taken a very solid stance together with (Russian President) Vladimir Putin and against Ukraine," Crebo-Rediker said.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she would call for increased support for Ukraine, while pushing for progress on accountability measures through the Special Tribunal and Claims Commission.
"Russia must be accountable," she wrote on X on 29 October.
Some countries may seek to avoid conflict, including Canada, Mexico, India and others still negotiating trade agreements with the US, said one G20 diplomat who declined to be named. "Everyone is trying to keep a low profile."
The meetings take place a day after Commerce Department data showed the US economy grew at its fastest pace in a year in the third quarter, buoyed by AI investment despite higher oil prices from the war on Iran, even as other countries face slower growth or even contractions.
They also fall just days before the 3 November midterm elections, which polls indicate could leave Trump without majorities in either house of Congress, and amid reports the US might launch fresh attacks on Iran.
Although Ukraine has not been invited to join the G20 ministers in Atlanta, Trump is also pushing hard for a ceasefire in Russia's war in Ukraine. Russia, Ukraine and the US are expected to hold technical-level trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next month.

Ukraine joins digital platform tax data swap - tax service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:31:50 EET
19:31:50 KST

The State Tax Service of Ukraine has signed a declaration of accession to the multilateral competent authority agreement on automatic exchange of information on income earned through digital platforms (DPI MCAA), the service said on its website.
Signing the agreement is the first stage in implementing law No. 4903-IX of June 9, 2026 on implementing international automatic exchange of information on income from digital platforms and taxation of such income (bill No. 15111-d), it said.
The DPI mechanism provides for regular automatic exchange of data between the tax authorities of participating countries on income of individuals and legal entities earned through marketplaces and digital services. This will make it possible to obtain information on foreign income of Ukrainian taxpayers, increase the transparency of the e-commerce market and implement the OECD Model Rules and the EU's DAC7 Directive, the service said.
On October 22, 2026 President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the law (bill No. 15111-d). Adopting it and joining the exchange mechanism is a structural benchmark of the International Monetary Fund's Extended Fund Facility program and a condition for macro-financial assistance from the European Union under the Ukraine Support Loan.
The law implements the European DAC7 standard and requires operators of digital platforms (marketplaces, taxi services, property rental and so on) to register with the State Tax Service, identify users and submit an annual report on their income. It also introduces a special preferential tax regime for individuals at a rate of 10% (instead of the standard 23%), provided they have no hired employees, do not trade in excise goods and stay within an annual income limit of 834 minimum wages. For sales of used personal items by individuals, there is a tax-free threshold of up to EUR 2,000 a year.

Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta says it is shutting down after ‘coordinated campaign’
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:31:36 CET
19:31:36 KST

By Andrew Osborn and Nika Khutsieva
MOSCOW, Oct 30 (Reuters) - The Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta said on Friday it was winding up its remaining operations after a campaign of state pressure in which a senior editor has been prosecuted and its financial support and premises have been taken away.
“We have been killed,” the publication, set up with money from the Nobel Peace Prize of the last Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, said in a statement.
The paper halted its print edition inside Russia in 2022, but had continued to produce online content and operate from its office in central Moscow.
“On November 9, we will turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down our servers, and leave,” it said. “The newspaper no longer exists. The Russian authorities and the Russian security services have forced our editorial team to cease its operations.”
At its office, employees quietly packed cardboard boxes, shuffling through rooms lined with awards and photos of colleagues killed because of their work.
“We represent the interests of that enormous part of society that opposed war and bloodshed. And that is why they are doing to us what they are doing now,” said co-founder and former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov.
“When people are dying in war and political prisoners are dying, we do not cry over ourselves, we simply pack our things,” he said, adding that one final issue was in the works.
A THORN IN RUSSIAN AUTHORITIES’ SIDE
There was no immediate comment from Russian authorities, which designated the publication a “foreign agent”.
But the Kremlin - which accuses foreign intelligence services of trying to stir discontent in Russian society - has said previously that some censorship is necessary when Russia is locked in what it calls an existential struggle with the West over Ukraine.
Prominent war blogger Rybar offered a taste of how the publication is seen in some official circles, reposting a diatribe accusing Novaya Gazeta of systematically promoting an anti-Russian narrative and of relishing the difficulties faced by the Russian state.
Founded in 1993 in line with Gorbachev’s vision of “glasnost,” or openness, Novaya Gazeta (“New Newspaper”) became one of Russia’s most influential newspapers and defenders of democracy with investigations into corruption and critical coverage of Russian politics.
Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize, dedicating it to six slain colleagues including investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya, who wrote about Moscow’s wars in the restive Chechnya region.
PRESSURE FROM UKRAINE FALLOUT
Like other media outlets not run by the state but critical of it, Novaya Gazeta came under increasing pressure after the conflict in Ukraine began in 2022. Sweeping censorship rules were introduced that mandated long jail terms for “discrediting” the Russian army or disseminating what the authorities deem to be fake news.
The newspaper said it “cannot report on the most critical and tragic events of our time,” adding: “Censorship applies to virtually every sphere of civic life.”
It said many of its journalists and those from other outlets had fled Russia in 2022. Some of its former employees began a separate Latvia-based print and online publication, Novaya Gazeta Europe, which the Moscow authorities designated an “undesirable organisation”, effectively banning it in Russia. It will continue to operate.
Novaya Gazeta said that in Russia its website had been blocked, its print licence revoked and its presses seized, and that one editor, Oleg Roldugin, was under house arrest awaiting trial on allegations that he misused personal data, an offence carrying a prison term of up to 10 years.
Its Moscow offices - from which it is being evicted - have been searched, and the home of Sergei Sokolov, its editor-in-chief, was searched this month.
“Now they have truly killed us, meaning this is not a suspension, this is a closure,” Sokolov told Reuters. “We buried our friends, we buried our hopes. We saw everything that was happening and tried as adequately as possible to tell our readers and everyone else about it.”
(Editing by Kevin Liffey, Alessandra Prentice and Timothy Heritage)

Trump escalates legal challenges against states as Election Day nears
Italy

2026-10-30
11:31:14 CET
19:31:14 KST

By Andrew Goudsward and Nathan Frandino
WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s administration stepped up criminal and civil investigations into allegations that Democrats conspired to recruit a spoiler candidate in a critical Senate race in Alaska, US officials said on Friday, injecting fresh uncertainty into Tuesday’s congressional midterm election.
The Justice Department’s top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a press conference that a Wednesday New York Times article about the effort had driven a “surge” of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the case and that investigative steps were taking place “intensely and swiftly.”
“Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they’re going to get one,” he said. “Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election, they’ll answer for it.”
Separately, the department on Friday asked a federal judge to block Alaska from certifying the election results if the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, loses due to the presence of a third candidate, also named Daniel Sullivan.
The contest between Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is widely seen as one of the few Senate races that could sway control of the chamber on November 3.
A record 48 million people have cast early ballots, more than any other midterm election in US history, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, with even the American-born Pope Leo casting a ballot by mail.
If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they intend to launch investigations into Trump’s administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war against Iran.
KEY PATH FOR DEMOCRATS
If Democrats cannot flip the seat, their path to a majority narrows considerably, with the party needing to win at least two other races in mostly Republican states such as Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Kansas. Trump’s fellow Republicans are likely to lose their slim majority in the US House of Representatives, according to nonpartisan analysts.
The New York Times this week reported that staffers from the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Party’s Senate campaign arm helped recruit a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village who is named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr to appear on the ballot. Reuters has not been able to independently confirm the Times’ reporting.
Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has also denied involvement. Sullivan, the retired teacher, has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken; both parties have engaged in “ballot stacking” by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents. Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted.
Heyman declined to offer specifics when asked what possible crimes were being examined, saying he would let the investigation proceed. He also said the probe had been ongoing for months and that the Times report had added urgency to the investigation, but did not explain how.
Peltola’s campaign has asked a judge to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit, arguing it has no legal basis.
CALIFORNIA PROBE
The Justice Department has also pushed forward a legal case in California, issuing subpoenas to election officials as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by noncitizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters.
A US appeals court on Friday rejected the department’s request to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens, the second time the court has done so this week.
A lower court judge had already denied the administration’s request, finding it would potentially disenfranchise thousands of legal voters. California officials have said the Justice Department’s assertions relied on suspect data.
The administration’s legal moves represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution. Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington.
Trump has long sought to sow distrust of election results, falsely claiming for years that his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden was the result of widespread fraud. Voter fraud in the US is extremely rare, studies and investigations have found.
The president will campaign on Friday in Florida, the latest in a series of rallies he has headlined in states he won handily in 2024 but where Democrats are now competitive, as he tries to stave off Republican losses on Tuesday.
Trump said on Friday he would attend weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas after all, a day after canceling them, telling reporters at the White House that Republicans in those states had called him and asked him to reconsider.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris, whom Trump defeated in the 2024 election, will rally for Democrats in Atlanta on Friday.
