Fran Luin Beijing
Chinese people use the phrase “yao chan wan guan,” or “carrying ten thousand strings of cash around the waist,” to describe wealth. But how much was a string of cash, and what could one buy in ancient China?
Guan was a traditional Chinese unit of account. Literally referring to the string used to thread coins together, it emerged alongside the round coin with a square hole, which first appeared during the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC).
A guan generally equalled a string of 1,000 individual copper or bronze coins, known as wen.

Hello from Tokyo. We are now just four days away from the U.S. midterm elections. With about one-third of the Senate and every House of Representatives seat up for grabs, the outcome could significantly shape President Donald Trump's behavior in the second half of his term. Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress, but pre-election forecasts suggest Democrats could retake the House, and the Senate is shaping up to be a tight race.
The results will have ramifications far beyond U.S. politics, affecting the global economy and geopolitics. While media around the world will be watching the midterms closely, Nikkei Asia will focus on what the results mean for Asia. On Tuesday, we published an explainer, "5 things to know about the midterms and what they mean for Asia." We have more related stories in the works; and on election day, please stay tuned to our live blog for the latest developments.
For American voters, the rising cost of living, from fuel and food to housing and consumer goods, remains the biggest concern. But another issue with potentially significant implications for Asian economies has rapidly gained attention in this election: the backlash against data centers. The race is expected to be particularly tight in Ohio, the home state of Vice President JD Vance, where the Democratic Senate candidate has made data centers' rising electricity costs a major issue in the campaign against the Republican incumbent.
Many advanced semiconductors and pieces of equipment that fill these data centers are produced in Asia, particularly in Taiwan and South Korea. If the midterm results strengthen the backlash against data center construction in the U.S., major technology companies in Taiwan and South Korea could feel the consequences, potentially weighing on earnings and share prices. Nikkei Asia is closely watching this emerging issue, and we have been reporting on it from Ohio.
Two weeks after Americans go to the polls, leaders from the U.S., China and other Asia-Pacific economies are scheduled to gather in Shenzhen for the APEC summit. Coming soon after the midterm results, the gathering will offer an important indication of how Trump will approach diplomacy after receiving the verdict of voters at home. The ASEAN summit in Manila will also be held around the same time.
With just over two months left in 2026 and major events still ahead, the Nikkei Asia newsroom is heading into one of the busiest stretches of the year. We hope you'll follow our reporting as these stories unfold.

U.S.-China tensions that led to trade restrictions and a "China+1" diversification strategy for the tech supply chain have been trumped by pressures created by the artificial intelligence buildout. Press review: EU, NATO try to hinder Ukraine peace and Russia seeks constructive G20 talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Moscow suspects EU and NATO leaders are obstructing efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict; Russia and African nations called for closer economic and political cooperation at a major summit in Moscow; and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov travels to G20 talks in Atlanta against a backdrop of tensions with Western countries. These stories topped Friday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Russia says EU, NATO leadership is hindering efforts to resolve Ukraine conflict
Despite some European politicians expressing readiness to engage in dialogue with Russia, Moscow has noted attempts by the leadership of NATO and the EU to hamper efforts to resolve the Ukrainian conflict, the Russian Foreign Ministry told Izvestia. Vladimir Putin has said that Russia supports any steps toward rebuilding relations with both the European Union as a whole and individual European countries. At the same time, he warned that "there would be no winners" in a potential military conflict between Russia and Europe and urged caution against a repeat of the Strait of Hormuz scenario in the Baltic Sea.
Russia is ready for contacts with the EU and NATO, but it was not Moscow that cut off those ties, and "accordingly, the initiative for dialogue must come from the Europeans," Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Department of European Affairs at the Russian Foreign Ministry, told Izvestia.
"Some European politicians are beginning to acknowledge the need to restore contacts. At the same time, the leadership of both the European Union and the North Atlantic Alliance, along with many of their member states, has been striving for months to block any settlement of the Ukrainian conflict, hampering US negotiating efforts. Yet they publicly claim that it is Russia that is taking maximalist positions and displaying no willingness to negotiate," the diplomat added.
According to Maslennikov, the Europeans’ desire to "squeeze into" the negotiations and avoid being left on the sidelines is also plainly apparent. "Without the Europeans factoring in the realities on the ground, it would, frankly, be strange to engage in talks," he emphasized.
According to Andrey Kortunov, research director of the Russian International Affairs Council, the prolonged nature of the Ukrainian crisis is driven by the interests of a coalition of Western forces that can be classified into three main groups. First are economic and political circles linked to the military-industrial complex and the militarization of Europe. Second, the ongoing confrontation benefits the political leadership of European countries. Third, proponents of neoliberalism play an important role in hindering a settlement. For them, confrontation with Moscow is a matter of ideological dogma, he added.
Vedomosti: Russia, African nations discuss boosting cooperation at Moscow summit attended by 48 countries
The third Russia-Africa summit was held at the Kremlin on October 29, bringing together delegations from 48 of Africa’s 54 countries. The gathering featured more than 20 countries represented at the highest level in Moscow. At the conclusion of the event, participants adopted a final declaration and a declaration on cooperation in the civilian use of artificial intelligence technologies. According to experts interviewed by Vedomosti, Africa’s increasing role in global politics and the business contacts made at the Russia-Africa summit could assist Russian companies in strengthening their presence in African markets.
The summit comprised two sessions lasting more than eight hours in total. The first included speeches by heads of state, while the second was held behind closed doors in the format of a working breakfast. Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov had previously stated that this part of the summit would feature an exchange of views on its agenda. The opening session began with remarks by Vladimir Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, whose country currently chairs the African Union.
Several heads of delegation brought up the issue of conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, stressing the need for peace. Many heads of state also spoke about food security. Trade between Russia and African countries surpassed $27 bln in 2025, representing a 1.5-fold increase since the previous summit in 2023. Russia delivered 18 mln metric tons of grain in 2025 and 13 mln metric tons in the first nine months of 2026, while fertilizer shipments totaled 1.5 mln metric tons last year and surpassed 2.2 mln metric tons this year.
The need for an equitable partnership between Russia and Africa was another key issue at the summit. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called the model of cooperation between Russia and the African continent successful, pointing to the construction of Egypt’s El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant as an example.
Africa’s role in global politics has been increasing since the 2010s, as demonstrated by objective economic indicators, Ivan Kopyttsev, an expert at the Africa Center of the Russian Institute for Strategic Studies, told Vedomosti.
The expert also pointed out that dozens of business representatives were present at the event. "Undoubtedly, the personal contacts forged at the forum are of enormous importance for the further expansion of Russian businesses into African markets, since establishing that initial connection can sometimes prove decisive," he added.
Kommersant: Russia seeks constructive G20 dialogue as Lavrov gets ready for talks in Atlanta
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will participate in a Group of Twenty (G20) ministerial meeting in Atlanta, United States, on October 30-31. The trip is expected to be a difficult one: it remained uncertain until the last moment as US authorities held up the issuance of visas, while the Russian minister is expected to come under fire from his Western counterparts at the meeting, Kommersant writes. Nevertheless, the Russian Foreign Ministry voiced optimism that the gathering would "proceed in a constructive and unbiased manner."
It was not until October 28, just one day before his scheduled departure, that Lavrov’s trip to Atlanta was officially confirmed. According to Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, the Russian side "had the impression, particularly in light of the situation surrounding the issuance of US visas to Russian delegates by the US Embassy in Moscow, that not everyone in Washington was in favor of the Russian delegation’s planned visit." Most of the outstanding issues, she added, were settled literally at the last moment.
Apart from the difficulties surrounding the trip’s organization, the Russian delegation is expected to face criticism from Western countries at the G20 meeting. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, for example, has vowed to hold Iran and Russia responsible for increasing global energy prices and problems with international food security, arguing that the two countries are hampering the normal functioning of trade routes.
Nevertheless, before Lavrov’s departure for Atlanta, the Russian Foreign Ministry voiced confidence that the meeting would take place "in a constructive and unbiased manner." At the same time, the ministry indicated that Russia’s top diplomat also has concerns to raise with his Western counterparts.
According to the ministry, Lavrov’s remarks at the G20 will present "Russia’s perspective on the main factors behind international tensions, focusing on the refusal of certain powers to acknowledge the rise of new centers of power; the use of economic ‘weapons’ against opponents, including sanctions, trade wars, and supply chain disruptions; and the persistent North-South imbalances stemming from this destructive approach."
US authorities have also extended an invitation to Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami on December 14-15, but Moscow has yet to make a decision on whether he will attend. It appears that the decision will depend on several factors, including the outcome of Lavrov’s visit to Atlanta and how the Russian president’s trip to the APEC summit in China on November 18-19 develops, Kommersant writes. The latter event could serve as the venue for the first-ever trilateral summit between Russia, China, and the United States.
Izvestia: EU plans to request €20-25 bln from UK, Canada for Ukraine amid rising funding needs
The European Union plans to seek €20-25 bln from the United Kingdom and Canada to fund Ukraine in 2027. Brussels intends to raise the matter at upcoming summits with the two countries, a European source told Izvestia. The EU hopes to meet some of Kiev’s additional funding requirements of €70 bln, which persist despite an already agreed two-year loan of €90 bln. However, experts believe London and Ottawa are unlikely to consent to providing such a substantial amount.
"The EU will certainly request around €20-25 bln from the United Kingdom and Canada for Ukraine next year at the upcoming summits. Zelensky has asked for approximately €70 bln for next year. Japan and Australia may also contribute more modest sums of assistance. The outstanding funds could be provided by the European Union," a European source told Izvestia.
Financial assistance to Kiev also has political implications. According to the source, it is important for the EU to demonstrate to Vladimir Putin that Brussels "can outlast Russia."
If Kiev’s allies beyond the EU are unable to supply the necessary amount, the financial responsibility will fall on Brussels. The bloc is already considering the possibility of issuing debt instruments to finance Ukraine. Media reports indicate that some member states support providing a €45 bln loan. The funds could be secured through borrowing backed by guarantees from the EU budget.
The issue has already triggered heated discussions in the European Parliament. Slovak Member of the European Parliament Milan Uhrik is against increasing the EU’s debt obligations. "Brussels is seeking yet another decision to allocate €70 bln to Ukraine, but this uninterrupted flow of funds into a ‘black hole’ must come to an end. Officials are discussing irresponsible mechanisms, ranging from joint EU debt backed by European taxpayers’ money to the use of extraordinary returns from frozen assets," he told Izvestia.
The European Commission argues that the bloc has enough financial capacity to meet these expenditures. However, no concrete funding source has yet been identified. The situation is further complicated by the stance of Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Bulgaria, which, according to Politico, have already declined to contribute to interest payments on future loans to Ukraine.
Vedomosti: Gold prices forecast to stay above $4,000 through 2030 amid worldwide uncertainty
The average global gold price is projected to stay above $4,000 per troy ounce until at least 2030, according to a forecast featured in a report by consulting firm Kept, seen by Vedomosti. The report presents two scenarios. The first presumes that the current global geopolitical situation and elevated energy prices will continue, alongside further tightening of US monetary policy. The second anticipates progress toward resolving major geopolitical conflicts and a halt in interest rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve.
Under the first scenario, Kept analysts project that the average gold price will climb to $4,523 per ounce this year, representing a 31.5% increase from the previous year. Under the second scenario, the price is expected to average $4,560 per ounce, up 33%, according to the report. In 2025, the metal gained 44% in price to $3,439 per ounce.
Gold prices climbed sharply in January and February of 2026, hitting record highs and exceeding $5,000 per ounce. However, prices subsequently started falling despite the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, even though gold has traditionally functioned as a safe-haven asset during periods of increased global risk. Experts link the decline to gold sales by several countries seeking to replenish their energy stocks.
Andrey Smirnov, a stock market expert at BCS World of Investments, believes that deglobalization and the dedollarization of the global economy will fuel stronger demand for gold and drive prices upward. Elena Kozhukhova, an analyst at Veles Capital investment company, regards the geopolitical situation as the main factor determining price movements.
Gold could climb to $4,500-4,700 per ounce in 2027, Boris Krasnozhenov, head of the Investment and Industry Analysis Directorate at Alfa-Bank, told Vedomosti. Meanwhile, Nikolay Dudchenko, an analyst at Finam Financial Group, believes prices could reach $5,000 per ounce.

Samsung S95H OLED TV Review (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Another major difference has to do with the breakout box, called the Samsung One Connect. With the S95H, it’s no longer required or included in the box, so you have to connect all of your devices like a video game console or a streaming device directly to the television. That means the S95H is thicker at 1.04 inches compared to just 0.4 inches for the S95F. However, I actually preferred not using the One Connect. It meant less hassle with another device to plug in and set up. You can always buy the One Connect box later if you decide you want less clutter by your TV stand or on the wall.
The S95H has four HDMI ports on the right side (including one for gaming at 165 Hz and one for eARC passthrough audio for surround sound), an Ethernet jack, optical audio out, two USB ports for playing files off a storage drive, and a headphone jack. It supports Wi-Fi 6E for faster speeds and compatibility than older standards (like the Wi-Fi 5 used on the S95F). Both TVs mount flush to the wall, although I used the included pedestal stand, which attached easily.
For the UI, Tizen OS is not terrible, but as we noted in our previous S95F review, it’s still a bit of a maze. The setup process including adding apps and tweaking picture settings is far easier on a Google TV model like the Sony Bravia 7 II. I’m used to Tizen OS, since I test TVs often, but I still don’t love it. (At least I didn’t need to use the Samsung SmartThings app for setup.)
I really like the Samsung remote—It doesn’t overwhelm you with buttons. Hisense remotes tend to have way too many buttons, in my experience. Most of us need channel, mute, and volume, plus maybe a few shortcuts to apps like Netflix.
Samsung doesn’t officially list the color gamut specs like DCI-P3 or BT.2020 for the S95H. Equally so, there is no official mention of brightness rating in nits or contrast ratio, but I’m okay with that as well. Those specs can be misleading and really depend on the picture quality settings, the brightness of the room, and (mostly) the content you watch. Instead, I subjected the S95H to rigorous real-world testing to see how it measures up to recent models.
Competitive Color Quality
The S95H measures up to the competition quite nicely when it comes to color quality. It excels in many areas but is not always the de facto winner for every movie, show or game. Once again, there is so much competition that buying a flagship OLED like this one is no longer the obvious choice.
I started with the movie Awake because several scenes in that movie (about people who can no longer sleep) are extremely dark. Time and again, even top-end televisions can’t seem to show key scenes with enough color or clarity. The S95H performed surprisingly well, but it took some tweaks. On Filmmaker, Dynamic, and even Standard and Eco modes, scenes with the main character biking at night looked too dark. Enabling AI Optimized picture mode helped a lot, beating out what was possible on the Samsung Micro RGB R95H in the same scenes.

Crematoria Are Being Used to Heat Homes and Swimming Pools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

In 2011, Redditch Borough Council in England tried something that hardly anyone in the UK had heard of before. Staff announced they were going to warm the local swimming pool with heat from a nearby crematorium.
A public firestorm ensued. The plans were met with international headlines, and a labor union official branded them “sick and an insult to residents.” (A spokesman for the union, Unison, says this was not—and is not currently—the organization’s official position.)
“All you’re doing is basically heating a radiator and sending the heat down a tube,” says Guy Revans, of Redditch and Bromsgrove Councils, just south of Birmingham. “But death is always an emotive subject, isn’t it?”
Eventually, the relentless press coverage faded away. The project won a green award, and the crematorium has warmed Redditch’s swimming pool since 2013.
Although extremely rare in North America, European countries have been harvesting warmth from crematoria for years. The total volume of heat available from crematoria is modest, but as people search for ways of reducing the environmental impact of funeral rites, utilizing crematoria waste heat provides a way to lower their carbon intensity.
Roughly 1,200 cremations are carried out every year in Redditch. A heat exchanger captures heat from flue gases emitted by the facility’s two gas-fired ovens as part of a process to remove vaporized mercury from dental fillings, before venting the remaining gas into the atmosphere.
That’s a common process at many crematoria. In other words, excess heat is often captured by default, meaning the next question is, does it make sense to waste the heat—or use it? In Redditch, the heat exchanger connects to a water loop that travels 200 meters underground, eventually reaching another heat exchanger supplying the swimming pool.
Helpfully, such a sizable body of water “acts as a heat sink”, adds Revans. “You put heat into it during the day, it retains that heat for a considerable length of time.” The recreation center also has gas-fired boilers that can provide more heat when necessary. Overall, the system has saved the council tens of thousands of pounds per year in fuel costs.
Similar projects have emerged elsewhere recently. A school currently under construction in Aberdeen, Scotland, will receive excess heat from the city’s crematorium. The crematorium already relies on waste heat to warm its own premises.
“They were only utilizing a tiny amount of the heat available; the rest was going to the atmosphere,” says Ian Davidson, chief executive of Aberdeen Heat & Power, who says that the system now has full planning permission. The crematorium will provide just under 1 gigawatt-hour of heat annually, roughly half the school’s total requirement. A heat pump will cover the rest of the facility’s needs, and the entire system should be fully operational by February 2027.
Some crematoria are going even further in their pursuit of green credentials. The crematorium that will open in Kangasala, Finland, in 2028 will be connected to the town’s district heat network, a system of pipes that supplies more than 6,500 homes with hot water for heating. The crematorium will be fully electric, powered partly by solar panels on its roof.
“It’s a special thing,” says Timo Heikkilä, an energy and building systems consultant at Thenco Oy, who is working on the project. “I’m really glad I get to be a part of this.”
Winter temperatures in Kangasala can remain below 0 degrees Celsius for weeks on end. In Finland, there is a push to use less natural gas for heating, says Heikkilä. Although once cheaply available from neighbouring Russia, that country’s invasion of Ukraine and concerns over climate change have prompted Finland to seek alternatives. In some locations, this means utilizing waste heat from unusual sources, including crematoria.
“Finns,” says Heikkilä, “are quite practical.”
Ian Rudkin, who has managed multiple crematoria in the UK and is currently a board member of the Cremation Society of Great Britain, says many crematoria are becoming more eco-conscious. Today, software can schedule the firing of gas ovens to align with funeral services, ensuring they don’t waste energy and are only turned on when needed, for example. And some crematoria hold coffins for up to 72 hours, so that several may be cremated in a sequence, which is more efficient.
“When we first brought that in, [families] seemed a little bit shocked,” says Rudkin. Soon, however, people became more accepting. “They’d make comments like, ‘Dad always used to turn the light off at home to save energy.’”
But implementing heat recovery tech at crematoria in the US is more difficult, says Paul Seyler, director of strategy at Matthews Environmental Solutions. There, district heat networks are rare, and crematoria tend to be privately owned. That means the investment needed for heat exchangers and pipework necessary to link buildings together is higher.
“We’re studying this and watching it closely because, when the economics align, we’d like to be in a position to offer a solution,” says Seyler. Wasted heat is, after all, just a waste of resources, he adds. Besides a few small-scale experiments, Seyler says he isn’t aware of any fully operational systems in the US that utilize heat from crematoria.
The closest example is in Canada at a funeral complex in Sainte-Thérèse, Quebec. This 3,255-square-meter building houses family rooms, a large chapel, a crematorium, and a kitchen, among other facilities. Heat exchangers installed just over a decade ago soak up heat from cremation flue gases and distribute it around the complex, including the sidewalks to melt snow in the winter.
“The owner was not immediately on board as he thought it may have posed an ethical dilemma,” recall design engineers Martin Roy and Lianne Cockerton in an article about the project, published in the ASHRAE Journal.
Now, visitors pass an LED screen in the reception area that displays the energy performance of the building, based partly on the heat exchanger’s operation. While gas is still used for some of the building’s heating needs, as well as for cremations, the new system saves an estimated 29 metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually.
Recovering heat from cremations is one way of attempting to counter the “devastating impact” that humans have had on the environment, says Hannah Rumble, an associate at the University of Bath’s Centre for Death and Society. “I can see that would be a reason why people might choose to be cremated at a particular crematorium.”
Most crematoria contacted by WIRED say they do not emphasize the presence of heat recovery technology to families or mourners, though a spokeswoman for Aberdeen City Council adds that the council there will “undertake some public awareness-raising on the new system before it is operational to ensure transparency.”
Gaynor Doherty, an independent humanist funeral and wedding celebrant in the UK, says using waste heat from crematoria is “sensible,” though she suggests a natural burial, where bodies are simply shrouded or placed in biodegradable coffins and allowed to decompose in the environment, might be preferable to many eco-minded people. The carbon intensity of cremation varies from facility to facility, but could be around 250 kilograms of carbon per gas-fired cremation. Recovering heat from the process offsets some of those emissions (one company claims savings of 100 kilograms) but not all.
A study published in 2024 estimated that, if all crematoria in the UK were tapped for waste heat, they might only meet 1 percent of the county’s total heating needs. This sounds small, but decarbonizing heat is notoriously difficult, so any interventions to achieve that can be valuable. Plus, some people may feel that sharing the heat from their cremation could carry a lot of meaning.
In Finland, the all-electric crematorium in Kangasala will not produce as much heat as a gas-fired equivalent, though it will run 24/7 because it’s more efficient to operate by using electricity to gently top up heat retained in ceramic materials within the ovens. The connection to the district heat network means that, when mourners return home from funeral services at the new crematorium, it is conceivable that at least a small portion of that warmth they feel after stepping through their front doors will come from the cremation of the person they loved.
Heikkilä says working on the project has prompted some big questions for him. “I have thought about it, and once my time is up, I would like to be cremated, and I would like my waste heat to be recycled,” he says. “It’s the sensible thing. The last favor you can do for the world.”

Election denialism is on the ballot in Arizona. These volunteers are pushing back
Unknown

Election denialism is on the ballot in Arizona. These volunteers are pushing back
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- President Trump has undertaken a sweeping effort to exert control over and cast doubt on U.S. elections.
- Election protection organizers emphasize that the goal is to ensure every voter casts their vote and the person who gets the most votes is declared the winner — regardless of political party.
CHANDLER, Ariz. — At balloon-adorned tables in red, white and blue, a handful of voters inside a church gymnasium listened as Medina Moore explained what to do if federal agents show up at the polls.
Call a hotline, she told volunteers, where attorneys will be ready to respond. Take videos, report what you see and remove yourself from any situation that becomes intense, she advised.
It was one of Moore’s final poll monitor trainings in the Phoenix area before election day, preparing a few new “peacekeepers” to join the ranks of about 200 she has recruited from local faith groups in the Phoenix area to greet voters, answer questions and keep an eye out for issues at voting sites on Tuesday.
“It feels very urgent this year,” said Moore, the voting rights organizer for the Arizona Faith Network, a coalition of religious groups. “We’re in an era of information overload. Being able to educate voters on what’s true and what’s not is very important.”
As lawyers nationwide prepare defenses against possible election interference by the Trump administration and election officials train for worst-case scenarios, ordinary citizens across the country are also readying to help. Through nonpartisan groups, parents are training to be poll monitors, law students are staffing legal hotlines, veterans are holding voting events and business owners are signing pledges to back local election officials.
The grassroots efforts, underpinned by various voting and democracy nonprofits, amount to a striking push by American voters to help uphold the nation’s election system in the face of possible threats from its own government. More than 21,000 people nationwide have been trained as nonpartisan poll monitors through the Election Protection coalition, the program that Moore used, along with thousands of others through other nonprofit and partisan efforts.
Thousands of observers are expected to descend on polling places to monitor the vote on election day
A sprawling election protection effort on the left that is expected to deploy tens of thousands of monitors will be met by the largest-ever monitoring program by the Justice Department and still more observers from Republican-aligned groups.
The effort is aimed at helping ensure voter turnout at a time when Trump’s rhetoric has eroded public trust in the system and many GOP-led states have enacted new ballot rules for voters to navigate. Worry among voters about whether their ballots will be counted has accelerated, according to organizers; in a recent AP-NORC poll, just under half of American voters expressed confidence that midterm votes will be counted accurately.
“People who vote occasionally or it’s their first time voting or they haven’t voted in a while, they all have questions on ‘If I vote, will my vote count?’” said Rebekah Caruthers, president of the Fair Elections Center, a nonpartisan voting rights group that is working with college students to monitor voting on campuses. The best way to combat those fears, she said, is for as many people as possible to “show up and exercise their right.”
Since returning to office, Trump has undertaken a sweeping effort to exert control over and cast doubt on U.S. elections, and the administration has intensified its efforts as the midterms draw closer.
In recent days, the Justice Department has sued California, arrested residents and threatened to prosecute election officials over an unsubstantiated government claim of 20,000 “likely noncitizen” voters; moved to block certification of Alaska’s election results if the Republican candidate for Senate there loses narrowly; and began notifying counties of its plan to send federal monitors to polling places in every state.
“Be careful of the voter fraud,” Trump said at a Texas rally Tuesday. “We’re going to watch that voter fraud.”
This week, Trump offered $1 million to anyone who reports voter fraud that leads to a conviction, the latest in a string of incentives he has floated related to the midterms and another suggestion of rampant election fraud.
U.S. Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche last week said the Justice Department did not intend to interfere with elections. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) committed to a peaceful transfer of power if Democrats win a majority, saying, “We’re going to follow the Constitution,” but predicted there would be no transfer because Republicans would win the majority. Trump told reporters Tuesday that he would respect the election results “if they’re honest elections.”
Preparations by lawyers, nonprofits and Democratic lawmakers to anticipate how the Trump administration could try to interfere with the midterms have been underway for months. Courts have already blocked many of the administration’s steps, including attempts to access state voter rolls, restrict voting by mail and demand states change some election rules.
The grassroots effort has grown out of existing programs — the Election Protection coalition has been operating since 2000 — but interest from volunteers is particularly high this year, organizers from several groups said.
“Voters are responding to the moment that we’re in right now,” said Saige Draeger, a senior policy associate at Verified Voting, a nonprofit that advises states on the use of voting technology and is part of the Election Protection coalition. “I think they feel like it’s incumbent upon everybody to make sure this election goes smoothly.”
In Arizona, an epicenter of Republican efforts to deny the 2020 election results, partisan tensions have long been high, and residents cite concerns about potential political violence surrounding the election.
Now, election denialism is on the ballot: The Republican nominees for governor, secretary of state and attorney general each played a role in Trump’s denial of the 2020 results. Alex Kolodin, the Republican candidate for secretary of state, filed lawsuits challenging the 2020 election results.
The outcome of the race could be consequential for the 2028 election, because secretaries of state play a key role in certifying their states’ results, and presidential elections can come down to a single swing state. Along with the Arizona race, those in Nevada, Michigan and Georgia are being closely watched by pro-democracy groups.
On street corners, the campaign signs for Kolodin and Secretary of State Adrian Fontes, the Democratic incumbent, duel: “Protect every vote,” say Kolodin’s. “Protect your vote,” Fontes’ read.
Organizers focused on election protection efforts stress that the goal is to ensure every voter casts their vote and the person who gets the most votes is declared the winner — all regardless of political party.
“With the level of polarization that we have nationally right now, people might mistake and think that calling for a free, fair, democratic election is somehow partisan,” said Hardy Merriman, an organizer with the Hold the Line project, which has recruited about 650 volunteers to ask their local leaders to sign on to a pledge affirming they back free and fair elections. “It’s really important for actors to get off the sidelines ... and say, no, actually it’s not.”
California election skeptics filed dozens of public records requests. Some are soliciting donations from people who believe election results can’t be trusted.
The mission of the poll monitors is to answer voters’ procedural questions, ensure no one is incorrectly turned away from voting and provide a friendly nonpartisan face — “be a peaceful presence,” Moore said. They can help voters navigate state laws — in Arizona, for instance, a requirement to show an approved form of identification when voting.
The monitors are also trained to call the attorney-staffed hotline to report anything out of the ordinary: long lines that may deter people from voting, people being turned away from the polls, aggressive electioneering from partisans outside the polling place or law enforcement showing up at voting locations.
Monitors trained through the Election Protection coalition will be stationed in 40 states and the District of Columbia, while about 3,000 legal professionals will be staffing the hotline, said Camille Wimbish, national director of campaigns and field programs for the Election Protection coalition, which is a project of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law.
“It gives voters reassurance that there is someone who has their back at voting locations,” Wimbish said. “It also just shows our determination as a community to stand up and say that we care about our elections, we want election day to be a joyful, peaceful, celebratory experience for all of us.”
PJ Boone-Edgerton Longoni, 70, who attended Moore’s mid-October training in Chandler at Holy Trinity Lutheran Church, said the idea of poll monitoring made her a little nervous, but she believes there is a “high-stakes need” for citizens to show up.
“I want to be a support,” she said. “All this misinformation gets people not to trust anything, and that lack of trust causes things to fall apart — because democracy is based on trust.”

Borissov Urges the Bulgarian Government to Take Clear Stance on Black Sea Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

GERB leader Boyko Borissov has called on the Bulgarian government to take a clear political stance on rising tensions in the Black Sea, warning that drone attacks on commercial vessels pose a direct threat to national and European security.
Borissov made the statement after meeting with a delegation of Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) who came to Sofia to discuss the growing tensions in the region and the attacks against commercial ships.
The visit by Angelika Winzig of Austria, Sven Simon of Germany, and Jacek Protas of Poland was organized at the invitation of Bulgarian MEPs Andrey Novakov and Emil Radev.
Borissov said the government could not respond to the latest incident in the Black Sea with silence, hesitation, or measures taken only after events unfold, arguing that such an approach does not safeguard Bulgaria's national interests.
He stressed that the drone attacks had moved beyond the scope of a regional problem and now threatened the security of both Bulgaria and Europe.
“GERB’s position is clear and consistent: Bulgaria is part of the EU and NATO, and security in the Black Sea must be upheld through collective action,” Borissov wrote in a social media post.
He also insisted that Bulgaria should have a more active role in determining Europe's security policy.
“I stated unequivocally that the Black Sea is no place for geopolitical maneuvering. Bulgaria must be an active participant in shaping European security policy, rather than a passive observer,” he added.
Borissov concluded by reaffirming GERB's position that Bulgaria belongs in a strong Europe, alongside a strong NATO, and must remain firmly committed to protecting its national interests.

China slams U.S. suppression of Chinese telecom firms

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- China expresses firm opposition and strong dissatisfaction over the U.S. side's unreasonable suppression of Chinese enterprises, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Friday.
Guo made the remarks at a regular news briefing when asked to comment on the U.S. Federal Communications Commission's plan to ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to U.S. telephone numbers over national security grounds.
The U.S. side has overstretched the concept of national security and abused state power to unreasonably suppress Chinese companies, Guo said.
Such moves have seriously impeded normal economic and trade exchanges between Chinese and U.S. businesses and do not serve the interests of any party, including U.S. companies and consumers, he said.
China will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests, he added. ■

Column: China International Import Expo widens gateway for African products to Chinese market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:59:11 CST
18:59:11 KST

by Sizo Nkala
Trade has long been an important pillar of Africa-China cooperation. As China continues to open its vast domestic market, African countries and businesses are gaining more opportunities to bring their products to Chinese consumers.
A series of measures is helping turn these opportunities into greater market access, including the zero-tariff treatment for products from 53 African countries that have diplomatic relations with China from May 1, the establishment of green channels for African agricultural products, and wider use of China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, or CIPS, by African financial institutions to lower trade transaction costs.
Such measures are designed to strengthen Africa's export capacity and competitiveness while demonstrating China's commitment to a more open, inclusive and development-oriented trade relationship with the continent.
Meanwhile, market access is meaningful only when businesses can find buyers. This makes the China International Import Expo (CIIE) an increasingly important platform for African exporters.
Launched in 2018 as the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports, the CIIE was designed to expand China's opening-up and turn its vast market into a shared opportunity for the world.
The ninth CIIE will be held in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10. Preparations are basically complete. A total of 162 countries, regions and international organizations will take part, with 4,142 overseas companies exhibiting.
For African exporters, however, the significance of the CIIE lies not simply in its size, but in its ability to connect relatively small businesses with a market that may otherwise be difficult to reach.
Zambian honey, Nigerian cashew nuts, Beninese pineapples and Kenyan flowers have all made breakthroughs and secured markets in China through the CIIE. South African exporters of rooibos tea, wine, avocados, and jewelry have also secured contracts at previous editions of the expo.
South Africa's Standard Bank hosted 21 export clients at the 2025 CIIE. According to the bank, clients from four African markets secured export contracts with Chinese importers worth approximately 140 million U.S. dollars that year through its Africa-China Trade Solutions initiative.
These contracts are not just numbers. They have tangible benefits for ordinary people in Africa by creating job opportunities and thereby contributing to poverty eradication.
Another welcome development is the further upgrade of the Asia-Africa Products Zone, first introduced at last year's CIIE, with more exhibition space for African businesses this year.
To encourage greater African participation, particularly by micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), organizers will also hold a dedicated business matchmaking event for Asian and African food and agricultural products, helping connect exporters with potential Chinese buyers.
Moreover, small businesses from least developed countries, most of which are in Africa, can participate in the expo at reduced cost through free exhibition booths and other logistical and operational support. Such measures make the CIIE more inclusive and accessible, particularly for Africa's MSMEs, which account for nearly 90 percent of businesses across the continent.
By lowering the barriers to participation, the CIIE ensures that small businesses, the engines of economic growth and development in most African countries, have access to China's large import market.
For African governments and businesses, therefore, the CIIE is more than a trade fair. It is a platform through which market-opening measures can be translated into commercial opportunities.
As the ninth CIIE approaches, African exporters have another opportunity to show their presence to Chinese buyers.
Editor's note: Sizo Nkala is a senior research fellow at the University of Johannesburg's Center for Africa-China Studies.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

Foreign arms firms to pay benefits back into Britain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:57:58 GMT
18:57:58 KST

Overseas companies winning British defence contracts worth more than £50 million will be required to put benefits back into the country that could match the full value of the contract, through jobs, apprenticeships, factories, investment in British suppliers and transfers of technology, under an offsets policy published today, according to the government.
A contract worth £100 million could carry an obligation to deliver up to £100 million of new jobs, facilities or skills training in Britain, and a new central Offset Authority will agree, value and monitor what each supplier owes through dedicated Offset Agreements.
The policy was announced by the Chancellor and the Defence Secretary on a visit to BAE Systems at Scotstoun in Glasgow, and forms part of the Back British approach set out in the Budget.
John Healey, Chancellor of the Exchequer, said: “We are putting British jobs and British businesses at the heart of how Government spends taxpayers’ money.
“When a big contract goes overseas, these changes will ensure 100% of the value creates new opportunities for workers and businesses here at home, strengthening our industrial base and supporting growth across Britain.”
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “Every pound we invest in defence should be judged by what it does for Britain. That’s why we are backing British by buying British wherever we can.
“Even when that is not possible, we are acting to ensure that any investment brings jobs, skills and investment back home, strengthening our national security by boosting our domestic industry.”
The money at stake is the eleven per cent of departmental spending with industry that goes abroad. More than £35.2 billion has been spent on defence contracts and services with overseas industry since 2016, measured against total direct expenditure with industry and commerce between 2016-17 and 2025-26, while 85 per cent of spending already goes to British firms. Last year defence investment supported 274,000 jobs in British industry, up ten per cent on the year before, with £34.1 billion going to businesses based in Britain.
Companies holding qualifying contracts will be able to meet the obligation by creating British jobs and apprenticeships, opening or expanding factories here, investing in British suppliers, transferring technology and know-how to British firms, or using more British-made components.
Offsets of this kind are standard practice among allies, and the government named Poland, Norway and the Netherlands as countries already running similar schemes. Britain abandoned its own industrial participation requirements more than a decade ago in favour of open competition, so the policy reverses a position held across several governments.
Scotland was chosen for the announcement because the defence economy there is worth £2.5 billion and directly supports 12,200 jobs, with the £10 billion Norwegian order for Type 26 frigates supporting 2,000 local jobs and a £453 million Typhoon radar contract supporting 300 roles in Edinburgh.
The policy delivers commitments from the Defence Investment Plan and the Defence Industrial Strategy, and follows the Chancellor’s confirmation on Wednesday that the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank will deploy up to £5 billion over four years into defence, dual use and other sectors supporting national security, alongside the start of treaty negotiations with the Netherlands, Poland and Finland on a Multilateral Defence Mechanism to procure and stockpile equipment at scale.

Iran’s most decorated para swimmer Izadyar calls time on career
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:56:33 UTC
18:56:33 KST

Iran’s most decorated para swimmer Izadyar calls time on career
TEHRAN – Shahin Izadyar, Iran’s most decorated Paralympic swimmer, has announced his retirement from competitive swimming after an illustrious career that saw him claim 28 medals across five editions of the Asian Para Games.
Despite bringing down the curtain on his remarkable career, Izadyar insists his journey in the pool is far from over, revealing plans to return to the sport as a coach in the near future.
In an exclusive interview with the Tehran Times, Izadyar reflected on his achievements, memorable performances and the milestones that shaped his career.
“My first Asian Para Games were in Guangzhou, China, in 2010. I was just 17 years old and managed to win two gold, one silver and three bronze medals, becoming the most decorated athlete in the Iranian delegation. I also broke the Asian record in both events in which I won gold,” he said.
“In 2012, I competed at the London Paralympics as Iran’s first and only representative in swimming. For the first time in history, an Iranian Para swimmer reached the final of the men’s 100m breaststroke. It was a huge achievement for our sport.”
Izadyar continued his medal-winning run at the 2014 Asian Para Games in Incheon, South Korea, where he collected five silver medals and one bronze.
“Although I delivered some strong performances in Incheon, I couldn't win gold. However, with five silvers and one bronze, I once again became the most decorated athlete in the Iranian delegation,” he recalled.
Two years later, Izadyar made his second Paralympic appearance at Rio 2016, again carrying Iran’s hopes as the country’s sole representative in Para swimming.
“I reached the 100m breaststroke final once again and clocked an impressive 1:09.63. I also recorded 25.32 seconds in the 50m freestyle, a record that still stands,” he said.
The highlight of Izadyar’s career came at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, where he delivered a sensational performance, capturing six gold medals and one silver.
“Jakarta was my third Asian Para Games, and it was an unforgettable experience. With six gold medals and one silver, I became the most decorated athlete among approximately 3,700 competitors at the Games,” he said.
Although Izadyar missed the Tokyo Paralympics, he returned to the continental stage at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games in 2023, competing at the age of 30.
“In Hangzhou, I won two silver and three bronze medals and once again finished as the most decorated athlete in the Iranian delegation,” he explained.
Izadyar also represented Iran at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games alongside fellow swimmer Sina Zeighaminejad, but an injury prevented him from reaching the final.
His final competitive appearance came at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya, where he added three silver medals and one bronze to his impressive collection.
“Competing in Nagoya marked my fifth appearance at the Asian Para Games. I won three silver medals and one bronze and once again shared the distinction of being the most decorated athlete in the Iranian delegation,” Izadyar said.
“That was my final competition, and I decided to say goodbye to competitive swimming. But I hope it won't be long before I return to the pool, this time as a coach, to continue serving the sport I love.”
With 28 Asian Para Games medals and a career spanning multiple Paralympic appearances, Izadyar leaves behind an extraordinary legacy as one of the most successful figures in Iranian Para swimming.

French presidential candidate Édouard Philippe designated 'assisted witness' in embezzlement case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:54:09 UTC
18:54:09 KST

Through his lawyer, Philippe welcomed the decision to have been given assisted witness status, which is less serious than being formally investigated. "This confirms that there is nothing to reproach him for in this case," his lawyer told the AFP news agency.
Former French Prime Minister Édouard Philippe has been placed under the status of assisted witness in an investigation into the alleged misuse of public funds at the Le Havre metropolitan authority.
Philippe, a 2027 presidential candidate for the Horizons party and mayor of Le Havre, appeared before two investigating financial judges on Thursday to answer questions relating to the case.
Following the hearings, Philippe released a statement through his lawyer, Emmanuel Marsigny, welcoming the decision to have been given assisted witness status, which is less serious than being formally investigated.
"This confirms that there is nothing to reproach him for in this case," his lawyer told the AFP news agency.
The case dates back to 2020 following allegations raised by Cornelia Findeisen, a former deputy director general of the Le Havre metropolitan authority.
She subsequently filed two complaints, one in 2023 that led to the opening of a preliminary investigation and searches carried out by the National Financial Prosecutor's Office.
A second complaint, filed two years later, included a request to join the proceedings as a civil party and resulted in the case being referred to financial investigating judges in Paris.
Philippe became president of the Le Havre Seine Métropole authority in July 2020. He later signed a multi-year agreement with Stéphanie de Bazelaire, voluntary president of the LH French Tech association, for running the Cité Numérique innovation hub in Le Havre.
LH French Tech was the only organisation to respond to calls from the authority for expressions of interest. The association was to receive €2.154 million in public funding to carry out various projects.
Investigators are now working to establish whether Philippe and de Bazelaire struck a deal involving "political, financial and networking support in return for the management of the Cité Numérique."
Findeisen said she was sidelined and subjected to harassment after exposing the alleged arrangement. In January last year, she was granted whistleblower status.
Philippe's questioning "shows that my alert deserved to be examined," she has said.
Assisted witness status
The Picovschi law firm says that an assisted witness is an individual "involved in a criminal case whose situation sits between that of a witness and that of a person under formal investigation."
This status can change as a case progresses and as new evidence emerges.
"A person is granted the status of 'assisted witness' when the investigating judge’s case file contains evidence suggesting alleged guilt in relation to an offence," the firm says on its website.
"The assisted witness is implicated in a judicial investigation; however, they are not directly charged with the offence in question."

Irish government to scope out possibility of unity with Northern Ireland for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

09:51:25 UTC
18:51:25 KST

Irish government to scope out possibility of unity with Northern Ireland for first time
DUBLIN, Oct 30 - Ireland will set up a government body that would for the first time undertake research and preparations for the possibility of future unity with British-run Northern Ireland, Prime Minister Micheal Martin was quoted as saying on Friday.
Martin told the Irish Times that the new body would be tasked with scoping out the models and challenges for different potential outcomes, including Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom or maintaining its devolved entity but as part of a united Ireland.
He was fleshing out an idea first referenced in a speech this week, when he said a new approach was required to carefully address the need for an "independent and dispassionate base of knowledge on which you can have a credible discussion about constitutional futures."
"What has concerned me about this push for a border poll since Brexit is that it's partisan, it's a one-sided advocacy approach," Martin told the Irish Times.
"It's sort of putting forward the idea that this would be easy and that it's inevitable and our time has come. And it's almost that this would be a victory for nationalism, as opposed to an approach which genuinely seeks to hear all voices."
Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday peace agreement, the British government is obliged to call a referendum on Irish unity if it appears likely that a majority of Northern Irish voters would back it.
While opinion polls consistently show a majority in favour of remaining in the UK, the gap has narrowed since the UK voted to leave the European Union a decade ago and Irish nationalist parties like Sinn Fein stepped up calls for a referendum.
Martin's proposal, the first steps of which he said he would bring to cabinet before the end of the year, is the latest gradual move by the dominant government parties south of the border to consider what a united Ireland might look like.
His government partner Fine Gael will publish what it has described as a blueprint for a unified island at its annual conference next week. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Why is India's dam project near China border facing local opposition?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:50:58 UTC
18:50:58 KST

India has deployed paramilitary troops in parts of its northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh amid protests against a proposed mega hydropower project near the Chinese border.
The deployment follows a protest last week in the Siang Valley, which borders Tibet, during which four women were injured during a clash with police, according to reports. At least 21 arrests were also made.
The protesters were opposing the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP), a proposed 11,200-megawatt project, saying the dam would submerge ancestral villages, destroy farmlands, displace large populations and disrupt livelihoods
Police claimed protesters vandalised police vehicles and pelted stones at security personnel.
What is the project?
First proposed as a national project by the Congress-led government in 2008, the Siang River project has since emerged as one of Arunachal Pradesh’s most contentious infrastructure proposals. The Congress party is now the main opposition party.
The project is considered strategically significant for India, particularly in light of China's plans for a major hydropower project upstream on the same river.
India views the proposed dam as a major water storage facility to regulate river flows and strengthen the country's water and energy security.
In December 2024, China announced plans to construct the world's largest hydropower dam upstream, officially known as the Medog Hydropower Station.
The proposed Chinese project has raised concerns in Arunachal Pradesh, where the state government has described it as an "existential threat."
China and India both claim Arunachal Pradesh, which China refers to as Zangnan and considers part of southern Tibet.
The Siang River flows into Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet, where it is known as the Yarlung Zangbo.
Why the protests?
The proposed project, to be developed by the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation, is located in the Siang Valley, where opposition has largely come from local communities, particularly members of the Adi tribe.
Residents fear the proposed dam could submerge ancestral villages, displace communities and disrupt their way of life.
The Adi Bane Kebang Youth (ABKU), a local grassroots movement, has warned that the dam could submerge several villages and cause extensive losses.
This week, it demanded the immediate release of its workers detained or arrested in connection with the protests.
Former Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Gegong Apang has called for the immediate cancellation of the proposed dam.
In New Delhi, the Congress has linked the protests to a wider movement among young people to protect the "environment and local communities'" rights.
"Gen Z across the country is taking to the streets. In Delhi, it is for education. In Arunachal Pradesh, it is to protect the forests, rivers and ecosystems that the Adi people have depended on for centuries," Congress leader Pawan Khera wrote on X.
Government response
Apart from strengthening security to counter the protests, the Arunachal Pradesh government has attributed growing apprehensions about the project to what it described as "misinformation and misconceptions."
Chief Minister Pema Khandu this week held a meeting with various groups to discuss the project and strengthen efforts to spread awareness across the state.
"Our people deserve accurate information to understand the project, its strategic importance and the concerns associated with it," he said.
At a separate meeting with legislators from different political parties, Khandu said discussions covered national security, environmental concerns and the apprehensions of local residents.
"Our priority is to protect national interests while respecting the rights and aspirations of the people of Siang Valley," he said.
Arunachal Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister Chowna Mein recently took to X to explain how India's proposed dam could help address concerns arising from China's planned 60,000-MW hydropower project upstream.
"The answer lies in understanding that MW measures power, not water. The proposed Medog Dam in China is primarily designed for hydropower generation, with an estimated height of around 2,000 metres (2 km) and storage capacity of 5.5 billion cubic metres," he said.
Mein said India's proposed dam, with a height of around 280-300 metres and live storage capacity of approximately 9.2 billion cubic metres, was primarily intended to store, regulate and manage water, alongside generating electricity.
"In the event of sudden releases or extreme flows upstream, this storage can help regulate downstream discharge and reduce the risk of flooding in the Siang basin and downstream areas of Arunachal Pradesh and Assam," he said.

The letters that gave five human rights activists hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:50:31 UTC
18:50:31 KST

For the past 25 years, Amnesty International’s Write for Rights campaign has been bringing people together to fight for justice and dignity. Millions of people have changed the lives of those whose human rights had been stripped from them, giving them hope in times of darkness.
Amnesty’s brilliant supporters have written letters both to those whose rights are being violated, and the people in authority who can make change happen.
For many, a simple letter made so much difference, letting them know that there were people out there rooting for them.
Here, five people who were part of Amnesty’s Write for Rights campaign share a letter that meant the most to them…
Wendy Galarza
Wendy Galarza was shot after attending a protest in Cancún, Mexico. She almost lost her life speaking out for women’s rights in her country. She lodged a complaint against the police, though it took months for the State Prosecutor to accept her additional evidence, which included clothing showing bullet holes from the day of the protest. While the case continues, Wendy has set up a collective with other persons who were assaulted that day.
People across the world came together to demand justice and support Wendy in Write for Rights 2021.
“These letters are among my favourites, though it was difficult to choose them from the vast number I received.
“One key reason is the hope I felt knowing my case had reached as far as Taiwan – a place that sent some of the most creative letters, most of which were written by teenagers.
“This particular letter inspired me with its clear message reminding us that ‘no one should face gender-based violence.’ It led me to reflect on the main reason I attended the march on 9 November 2020: to raise my voice and demand justice for the femicide of Bianca Alejandrina Lorenzana Alvarado in Cancún in the State of Quintana Roo.
“I would also like to thank everyone who wrote a letter to show their support; though it may sound like a cliché, those words provided me with emotional strength and became a beacon of hope on a dark path toward justice.”
Germain Rukuki
On 30 June 2021, Burundian human rights defender Germain Rukuki was released from prison four years into a 32-year sentence. He had been found guilty on a number of sham charges relating to his human rights work. He was jailed before getting a chance to hold his youngest child, born just weeks after he was arrested in July 2017.
Through Write for Rights 2020, hundreds of thousands of people around the world demanded Germain’s release.
“I chose this pink letter with the drawing of an elephant, balloons and a little purple heart. But more than the drawings, it was the words that touched me and spoke to me. The phrase ‘you are strong’ immediately takes me back to the moment I was arrested. It was a very difficult moment. I was trying to hold myself together. To leave the house without alarming my family and those around me. Deep down, it felt like a farewell, like I would never see them again. But I did not want to show that, and I did not.
“In that moment, I felt truly strong and perhaps a bit extraordinary. What stays with me are the words ‘strong and extraordinary’, which take me back to everything I went through that day and during my detention.
“It wasn’t easy to choose one letter. Each letter is important to me. I received them after my release. In prison, we were not allowed to receive letters or cards, but I was well aware of Amnesty International’s Write for Rights campaign, and the authorities saw the wave of international solidarity.
“One day, I would like to create a work of art from all these letters, cards and messages. Each letter has a place in my heart.”
Magai Matiop Ngong
Magai Matiop Ngong was a 15-year-old schoolboy in South Sudan when he was sentenced to death in 2017 for murder. Magai told the judge the death was an accident and that he was only a child; despite this, Magai faced trial for capital murder without any access to a lawyer. More than 700,000 actions were taken for Magai during Write for Rights 2019, and in March 2022 the High Court agreed that given his age at the time of the conviction, he should be released.
“Out of all the letters I received during the Write for Rights campaign, this one stayed with me the most. Joy was only 19, yet she chose to believe in my future when I was struggling to believe in it myself. She didn’t pretend to understand everything I had been through; she simply reminded me that I was not alone.
“She was a stranger who knew nothing about the person I would become, yet she believed in my future when my own future felt uncertain. Today, her words remind me that sometimes a little hope from one person can keep another person alive inside.
“Today, having survived that chapter of my life and being able to live the future she believed in, her words feel even more powerful. She believed in a future she could not see. I am living that future today.”
Bernardo Caal Xol
Bernardo Caal Xol, a Guatemalan teacher and environmental activist, worked tirelessly to defend communities affected by hydroelectric projects on the Cahabón river, in northern Guatemala. In November 2018, he was sentenced to more than seven years in prison on bogus charges aimed at preventing his human rights work. During Write for Rights 2021 more than half a million actions were taken for Bernardo and in March 2022 he was released.
“The student tells me that in Canada, they have many rivers and lakes. I love knowing that they take care of and protect them there. Being in prison is painful; it’s torture. But the student tells me that I’m a strong and intelligent man and that I deserve all the rivers in the world. I no longer feel the pain of prison because she tells me I’m strong and gives me an award: ‘I deserve the rivers of the world.’
“She inspires me – she wants to be a lawyer in the future ‘because she feels the injustices after learning about my case.’ She is outraged by the Guatemalan government’s criminalization of me; she writes a very profound letter.”
Panusaya “Rung” Sithijirawattanakul
Rung – which means “rainbow” in Thai – became politically active while studying sociology and anthropology at university in the capital, Bangkok. She bravely took part in protests for social and political change throughout 2020. By August, she had become a protest leader. Accused of provoking unrest, she was arrested in March 2021 and imprisoned for 60 days. The authorities denied her bail six times. In defiance, she went on a 38-day hunger strike and was released on 30 April 2021. Rung faces dozens of charges and, if found guilty, life imprisonment. She now lives in exile, outside of Thailand.
Rung featured in Write for Rights 2021, with people around the world calling for her freedom and sending her cards and letters of solidarity.
“Every letter that was written and sent to me while I was imprisoned meant so much to me. Every handwritten message, every drawing, every colour painted across those poster-sized sheets of paper gave me a sense of hope. They reminded me that I was not alone in the movement I was part of.
“When you are in prison, it is incredibly difficult to imagine hope. Everywhere I looked, there was only gray, white, and a sense of bleakness, inside a small, square cell crowded with strangers. Your letters brought some colour from the outside world into my life and brought a little brightness back into my heart. They reminded me that beyond those prison walls, there were still people who saw me, people who knew what I was going through, and people who stood with me.
“With so many letters arriving, they did more than simply give me strength. They also sent a powerful message to those in power that people around the world were watching what was happening in Thailand. “They were watching what was being done to me and to the students who had taken to the streets to demand change. I believe that this international attention and pressure was one of the factors that eventually led to me being granted bail, a right we should have had from the beginning.
“Today, even though I had to leave Thailand and live in exile, I still think about and feel deeply grateful to everyone who helped me, to everyone who wrote a letter, drew a picture, added colour to a page, and sent those pieces of hope across the prison walls to reach me.
“Perhaps to the person who wrote it, it was just one letter. But to me, receiving it on a day when hope was almost impossible to see, that letter meant more than you could ever imagine. I also just found out that, even today, people are still sending letters to me at Amnesty International Thailand’s office. I honestly cannot put into words how that makes me feel.”

Merz seeks swift end to Iran war amid mounting pressure on Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:50:28 UTC
18:50:28 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called for an end to the war involving Iran as quickly as possible, warning that the conflict is placing a growing economic and security burden on Europe, while using his Asian tour to strengthen trade and defense partnerships and address concerns over European protectionism.
Speaking Friday during the final stop of a weeklong visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea, Merz said the war's consequences for Europe remained severe and that diplomatic efforts to end the fighting were a priority.
The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil and gas supplies, has driven up energy prices and intensified pressure on European economies. Germany, with its energy-intensive industrial sector, has been particularly exposed to the economic fallout.
Merz has repeatedly warned against allowing the conflict to become a prolonged war, arguing that the collapse of the Iranian state or uncontrolled instability across the region would have serious consequences for European security, energy supplies and migration.
While acknowledging concerns over Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programs and its support for regional armed groups, the German leader has stressed the need for a negotiated settlement that prevents further escalation.
Berlin has been working with European and regional partners, including France, Britain and Gulf states, to support diplomatic efforts and establish conditions for a lasting agreement.
Merz has also linked the restoration of normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz directly to easing pressure on global energy markets, describing the reopening of the waterway as essential to stabilizing fuel and gas prices.
Germany has indicated that it could contribute to securing the strategic waterway after a cease-fire, potentially deploying minehunters and other military assets. However, Merz has made clear that any such involvement would require a cease-fire, an international mandate, preferably from the United Nations, and approval from the Bundestag.
The conflict has also tested relations between Europe and the United States, with European leaders increasingly concerned about the economic costs of a prolonged military campaign.
Merz has maintained that his relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump remains functional despite differences over the war's direction and how it should end.
Against this backdrop, Merz has sought to strengthen Germany's economic relationships across Asia, a region increasingly important to European trade and industrial supply chains.
Speaking Friday at the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul, he pledged to raise concerns expressed by Asian trading partners about the European Union's proposed "Made in Europe" initiatives with officials in Brussels.
The initiatives, intended to strengthen European industrial production and competitiveness, have raised concerns among some trading partners that the bloc could turn toward protectionism and restrict access to its markets.
"There is a fear that we might be facing a new wave of European protectionism, that we are closing ourselves off from other nations," Merz said.
"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.
Merz said the European Union should take the lead in defending international trade and the rules-based global economic system at a time when free trade faces growing pressure.
"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements," he said, adding that Germany was prepared to work with like-minded partners in Europe and elsewhere to protect and further develop the international economic order.
He noted that international trade had contributed significantly to the prosperity of many countries and that governments were reluctant to abandon the benefits of an interconnected global economy.
His remarks came amid concerns over U.S. tariffs and China's state-backed industrial expansion, which have prompted European countries to reconsider their economic dependencies and strengthen domestic industries.
During his Asian tour, Merz sought to deepen Germany's economic and defense relationships with countries facing similar challenges in an increasingly uncertain international environment.
In South Korea, he met President Lee Jae-myung on Thursday, with the two leaders agreeing to establish an enhanced security partnership.
Merz also pointed to similarities between German and South Korean industries, saying they offered opportunities for closer cooperation.
South Korea's Industry Ministry said nine memorandums of understanding had been signed by companies and organizations from the two countries. The agreements cover cooperation in electricity, energy and biohealth, alongside support for startups and efforts to facilitate access to each other's markets.
The South Korean visit followed earlier stops in Japan and Singapore, where Merz also sought to strengthen economic and strategic cooperation.
