Viet Nam and Kazakhstan bring friendship closer to everyday life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:50:05 UTC
18:50:05 KST

Viet Nam and Kazakhstan bring friendship closer to everyday life
On 10 October 2026, Vietjet launched Ha Noi-Almaty services, expanding travel options between Viet Nam, Kazakhstan and Europe.
The new October routes offer two return flights a week on each route, helping people meet and businesses find partners. New flights, rising trade and investment in green transport are bringing Viet Nam and Kazakhstan closer. The Strategic Partnership relation is opening new opportunities for businesses and travellers.
Having presented my credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on 19 August 2026, I see these connections as a practical way to turn our countries’ mutual trust into benefits for their people.
A friendship looking forward
Our ties reach back to President Ho Chi Minh’s visit to Kazakhstan in 1959. During his August 2023 visit to Viet Nam, President Tokayev presented General Secretary Nguyen Phu Trong with an album commemorating that journey, a reminder of our shared history.
Diplomatic relations followed on 29 June 1992. General Secretary To Lam’s state visit in May 2025 brought a new milestone: a Strategic Partnership. Both countries value peace, independence, sovereignty, the UN Charter and peaceful dispute settlement. Cooperation in international forums and exchanges on reform and integration reinforce that foundation.
Trade gathers pace
Bilateral goods trade reached about USD 564.8 million in the first nine months of 2026, up 44.7 per cent year on year, according to Viet Nam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade. Vietnamese exports rose 35.8 per cent to USD 463.7 million, while imports from Kazakhstan grew 106.5 per cent to USD 101.1 million.
Electronics lead Viet Nam’s exports, with room for agricultural products, processed foods and consumer goods to grow. Viet Nam offers Kazakhstan access to Southeast Asia; Kazakhstan helps connect Viet Nam with Central Asia.
Wheat shows how these strengths can complement each other. Citing Kazakhstan’s Government, Kazinform reported exports of more than 15,000 tonnes to Viet Nam in 2025, following an eight-year pause. Multimodal transport helps cut costs and delivery times, pointing to wider prospects in food and logistics.
The Viet Nam–Eurasian Economic Union Free Trade Agreement, in force since October 2016, provides a platform for growth. Making full use of it requires support on tariff preferences, rules of origin and quality standards, and closer coordination on sanitary and phytosanitary measures, payments and transport.
Investment takes new forms
Six projects involving Vietnamese companies are under way, with Vingroup, Sovico Group, Crystal Bay Tourism Group and Mareven Food Central among the participants. ROX Group is also interested in exploring investment opportunities in Kazakhstan’s energy, infrastructure and real estate sectors. Kusto Group’s operations in Viet Nam add to this two-way investment relationship.
Following a 2025 agreement, the Vietjet Qazaqstan brand is being developed from Qazaq Air. The airline unveiled its new livery and introduced services in Astana in February 2026, opening opportunities for staff training, management exchanges and improved passenger services.
On 23 June 2026, Green SM launched its green mobility service in Almaty. Such projects show what Vietnamese technology-enabled services can offer. Their lasting value depends on meeting local needs, creating jobs and contributing to communities.
Finance offers another avenue. The two countries regularly exchange delegations to share experience in finance, banking, innovation and entrepreneurship via connection with the Astana International Financial Centre, the central bank, Astana Hub and Samruk-Kazyna Fund.
Closer ties between people
In 2025, Viet Nam had welcomed nearly 200,000 Kazakh visitors. Visa exemptions and more convenient flights support further growth. Nha Trang, Phu Quoc, Da Nang and heritage destinations await Kazakh visitors, while Kazakhstan’s landscapes, culture and hospitality offer much for Vietnamese travellers to discover.
Tourism businesses can encourage travel in both directions through familiarisation visits, suitable products and destination promotion. Scholarships, student exchanges and business internships build skills and lasting friendships.
The Vietnamese community in Kazakhstan and Kazakh friends with ties to Viet Nam help sustain these links. The Embassy will work with them, local authorities and educational institutions to support exchanges and cultural preservation, while helping businesses find information and partners.
As the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations approaches in 2027, my priority is to listen and turn shared ambitions into practical cooperation. The success of our Strategic Partnership will be felt in the opportunities it brings to people’s work, studies and daily lives.
H.E. Mr. Nguyen Thanh Le,
Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam to the Republic of Kazakhstan

Speaking at the summit, Tokayev highlighted the significance of the Alley of the Turkic World, inaugurated at the initiative of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, expressing confidence that it would become a symbol of the countries’ enduring brotherhood.

The geopolitical situation in the world continues to deteriorate. The situation in the Middle East, particularly the confrontation around the Strait of Hormuz, is becoming increasingly tense. All this is having a negative impact on global trade and economic relations, as well as transport and logistics chains, including those connecting neighboring Turkic states, said Tokayev.
He added that Kazakhstan strongly condemned attacks by the Houthi armed movement against Saudi Arabia.
Kazakhstan strongly condemns the unjustified attacks by the Houthi armed movement against brotherly Saudi Arabia. We support calls for an end to such unlawful actions, the President stated.
Turning to economic cooperation, Tokayev said Kazakhstan placed particular importance on strengthening economic ties within the OTS framework.
This year, our country's trade turnover with the member states of the Organization has approached 10 billion US dollars. Compared to last year, this figure has increased by 40 percent, he said.

To maintain this momentum, we need to take a number of steps. First and foremost, we must ensure the effective implementation of the Turkic World Vision 2040 program. In this regard, it is important to accelerate the adoption of the Organization of Turkic States Strategy for 2027-2031, he said.

It is fundamentally important that the five-year strategy being adopted focuses on the implementation of specific projects, Tokayev stressed.
He also called for making fuller use of the Turkic Investment Fund, noting that the institution had considerable potential.
This institution has enormous potential, and all the necessary conditions must be created to ensure its full realization, he said.
In addition, Tokayev highlighted the role of the Turkic Chamber of Commerce and Industry in deepening economic integration. He proposed holding a business forum in Kazakhstan in 2027 to give further impetus to cooperation.
We believe that the activities of the OTS Council of Elders are also highly significant. We need to provide this body with financial and other comprehensive support, said the President.

Italian military chopper spirals into deadly crash in Bosnia (VIDEO)
An Italian military helicopter has crashed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, killing four people and injuring 11, the Italian Defense Ministry has confirmed. Dramatic footage shows the aircraft spinning out of control before plunging to the ground.
The CH-47 Chinook, operated by NATO member Italy, crashed on Thursday near the town of Brcko in northern Bosnia. The aircraft was deployed as part of the European Union Force (EUFOR) in the country.
Videos filmed by witnesses show the twin-rotor helicopter spiraling downward while flying at low altitude before crashing into a field.
The accident occurred shortly after takeoff from Brcko airport, according to Italian Ambassador Sarah Castellani. Weather conditions were reportedly favorable.
HELICOPTER CRASH IN BOSNIA KILLS FOUR ON EU PEACEKEEPING MISSION An Italian military helicopter operating under the EU’s Operation Althea crashed in Bosnia, killing 4 people & injuring 11 others. Italy’s Defence Ministry says the cause of the crash is under investigation.
— Subodh Kumar (@kumarsubodh_) October 30, 2026
Investigators are examining several possible causes, including a collision with high-voltage power lines, ANSA reports.
All 15 people aboard were Italian nationals. Two Italian Army personnel and two members of the Italian Red Cross Military Corps are among the dead. The 11 survivors were hospitalized, with none reportedly facing life-threatening injuries.
The helicopter crashed in an uninhabited area near the village of Gorica, narrowly avoiding nearby homes, according to local officials.
The EU-led military mission traces its origins to NATO’s intervention in Bosnia following the 1992-1995 war between Bosnian Serbs, Bosniaks, and Croats. Around 50,000 NATO troops were deployed in 1996 to enforce the peace agreement, before the EU took over the mission in 2004. EU countries to accelerate release of 42.6 million barrels from oil reserves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:46:08 UTC
18:46:08 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
EU member states will accelerate the release of 42.6 million barrels from their strategic oil reserves over the coming months to help contain rising energy prices, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen announced Friday.
The commitment was reaffirmed during talks among European energy ministers in Luxembourg, Belgian news agency Belga reported.
Jorgensen said about half of the planned release would consist of diesel.
The move is part of a broader G7 initiative announced earlier this month to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, with the International Energy Agency coordinating the operation.
However, the EU's contribution amounts to only about four days of consumption across the bloc, raising questions about its potential impact on prices.
"We will monitor the effects," Jorgensen said.
The commissioner warned that the war in the Middle East could keep gas and diesel prices elevated throughout the winter.
"We do not expect a problem with supply itself, but that is little comfort to people who are struggling to pay their bills," he said.
Jorgensen acknowledged that governments may need to provide relief to vulnerable households and sectors dependent on fossil fuels, but stressed that such measures should remain "temporary" and "targeted."
He emphasized that accelerating the green transition and reducing reliance on oil and gas would offer a more sustainable response to high energy costs.
The commissioner also met representatives of European refineries Wednesday to discuss ways to increase production.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul has announced an agreement allowing state police to investigate sexual assault complaints at Cornell University, following criticism of the institution’s handling of a former student’s allegation that she was gang-raped at a fraternity house.
Under the agreement signed by Cornell University and New York State Police on Thursday, survivors who decide to pursue criminal charges can choose whether state police or Cornell University Police will lead their investigations.
They may also request that Ithaca Police or the Tompkins County Sheriff’s Office handle their cases, according to the university.
"Every student deserves to feel safe on their campus. And when someone reports sexual assault, they deserve to be heard, treated with compassion, and know their allegations will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated by law enforcement trained to support survivors,” Hochul said in her statement.
The arrangement follows renewed scrutiny of Cornell’s response to allegations involving a former student, identified as Jane Doe in a civil lawsuit, who says she was pressured to consume drugs and sexually assaulted by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024.
The woman reported the incident to Cornell police. The local district attorney initially declined to pursue charges but reopened the criminal investigation in September 2026. Lawyers for some of the accused men have denied the allegations. The claims have not yet been established in court.
Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation. Separately, former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates was appointed to lead an independent review of Cornell’s handling of sexual misconduct complaints.
The university said the agreement took effect immediately and would remain in place during the independent review.

‘They killed us’: Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announces its closure after decades of repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:45:46 UTC
18:45:46 KST

‘They killed us’: Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announces its closure after decades of repression
Novaya Gazeta, the best-known independent news outlet still operating inside Russia, has announced that it is closing. The day before, it became known that the editorial staff was being evicted from its office in Potapovsky Lane in central Moscow, where journalists had worked for 29 years. As a result, the Anna Politkovskaya museum, located in her former office, will also close. After the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian authorities blocked the outlet’s websites and stripped the newspaper of its registration, and in September 2026 designated Novaya a foreign agent. According to The Economist, the newspaper’s editorial staff held a meeting on October 26 at which the decision was made to close the outlet. On the morning of October 30, Novaya officially announced that it was ceasing operations. Meduza is publishing a translation of the Novaya Gazeta editorial staff’s statement.
They killed us.
On November 9, we will turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down our servers, and leave. The newspaper no longer exists. Russian authorities and Russian security services forced the editorial staff to stop working.
More than 30 years of living alongside the country and its citizens will end for us out on the street, without means of subsistence, under the constant threat of repression.
Our years were happy: filled with creativity and hope, readers, friends, texts, films. At times, those years were desperately bitter.
Bitter, because it was during the rule of this regime — not during the lawless 1990s — that our colleagues were killed for political reasons, for carrying out their professional and civic duty: Igor Domnikov, Yuri Shchekochikhin, Anna Politkovskaya, Stas Markelov, Anastasia Baburova, and Natalia Estemirova.
At the same time as the eviction notice, our donation system, which allowed us to receive contributions from our readers, was shut off. In other words, we were stripped of funds. Entirely.
This is a coordinated action. The banks’ excuses — that they are simply following internal corporate rules — will convince no one. The state’s repressive apparatus, officers of Russia’s Federal Security Service who have embedded themselves inside every organization, set these rules instead. They consider the country their own property.
After military action began, Russian authorities stripped us, like all other journalists, of the ability to talk about the most important and tragic events of our time. They passed laws that brought censorship back into the country, and that censorship then spread to nearly every sphere of human life.
Authorities blocked all of our online resources. The state seized our printing house, and security service officers and censors entrenched elsewhere refused to let us publish the newspaper. Many of our staff were forced to leave the country.
The state then stripped us of our media registration, taking away our right to earn a living through our own work.
Attackers assaulted editor-in-chief and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dmitry Muratov, who nearly lost his eyesight as a result. No criminal case was opened, even though the perpetrators are known.
Then Russian authorities began designating our journalists as foreign agents, starting with the editor-in-chief.
Then Russian authorities brought administrative cases against the editorial leadership.
In Chechnya, our columnist Elena Milashina was abducted and beaten half to death.
Our executive editor Oleg Roldugin was taken hostage, accused of having worked as a journalist. His trial is coming soon.
Authorities searched Novaya Gazeta’s editorial office for hours and also searched the editor-in-chief’s apartment.
In September of this year, Russian authorities designated the entire editorial staff as foreign agents, placing more than 100 journalists and contributors on the registry.
For nearly five years of the war, we managed to keep working, surrounded on all sides by the security services.
And now, that’s it. We have ended up in a “kill zone.”
This is not just our private story. It is the story of a country and a society being finished off the same way.
The FSB, the Justice Ministry, the prosecutor’s office, and others who have privatized the state and usurped power are doing this. This is not Soviet resentment. Behind that label, a military dictatorship has nearly been built.
They say they are defending the constitutional order. No, this is an anti-constitutional order. The Constitution has been raped, beaten, and thrown into prison for an enormous term with its mouth taped shut, just like thousands of the country’s citizens who simply followed its articles, and tens of thousands of other citizens who were forced to become refugees, leaving their homes and heading into the unknown.
Stop saying that this isn’t Stalin’s 1937, and that the repression has some sort of “digital character.” This is state repression. And people, not numbers, are dying in cells. Period.
Human life has lost its meaning and been devalued.
The word “Constitution” provokes sarcasm and laughter. From everyone. Even from judges. Especially from judges. No one believes that it is the country’s basic law, the one the president swore an oath on. Notice that official propaganda has long since stopped calling the president the guarantor of the Constitution.
Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country, and defending them has been equated with a crime. Elections and elected bodies of government have been de facto eliminated. Public institutions have been eliminated. Freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled. Private life has been turned inside out by dirty hands.
Doesn’t Article 29 of the Constitution — “censorship is prohibited” — sound like mockery today? The courts have been destroyed along with law and justice. Having convictions is now treason.
But treason is when the state betrays its own Constitution. This treason is an ongoing crime, unfolding right now before the eyes of the world.
The killing of Novaya Gazeta is further proof of that.
All these years, we wrote about exactly this, for as long as we could. That is exactly why we were killed.
Thank you to everyone who heard us.
The Editorial Staff

A national fundraising day by Swiss Solidarity has raised more than CHF5 million for people impacted by war and famine in Sudan.

+ Impunity is stalling all peace efforts in Sudan. Can it end?

Russia’s Oldest Independent Newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, Announces Closure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:43:00 UTC
18:43:00 KST

Novaya Gazeta, Russia’s oldest and best-known independent newspaper, announced Friday that it will end its run after more than three decades in operation due to growing state pressure against its journalists.
“Novaya Gazeta has been killed. Novaya Gazeta is ending its existence,” editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in an emotional video statement published on the newspaper’s YouTube channel.
“The Russian authorities and security services have forced our newsroom to shut down,” Sokolov said.
Novaya Gazeta said it still plans to release one final edition before turning off its servers and vacating its office in central Moscow on Nov. 9. The total number of people losing their jobs is unclear.
Founded in 1993 with support from former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, Novaya Gazeta built an uncompromising reputation for investigative reporting. The publication routinely exposed government corruption, police brutality, election fraud and human rights abuses in Chechnya, while also probing Russian military operations overseas.
Six of its reporters have been killed over the years in what rights groups believe were retaliatory assassinations linked to their investigative work, including investigative reporter Anna Politkovskaya.
Novaya Gazeta suspended print publication shortly after President Vladimir Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 due to censorship laws that effectively criminalized critical reporting of the war. Courts later revoked its media license, forcing it to publish online.
Novaya Gazeta has faced growing pressure from law enforcement authorities, including the prosecution of its managing editor Oleg Roldugin, who is awaiting trial on accusations of illegally gathering and using personal information following his arrest in April.
Earlier this month, police raided the apartment of editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov before taking him in for questioning and subsequently releasing him. The raid was part of an investigation into Roldugin.
The announcement of Novaya Gazeta’s closure follows reports that it would be evicted from its Moscow office. News of the eviction came as former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov was on his way to France to attend a memorial event to mark the 20th anniversary of Politkovskaya’s murder.
Muratov won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression.” He stepped down as editor-in-chief three years ago after he was declared a “foreign agent.”
Russia’s Justice Ministry designated Novaya Gazeta a “foreign agent” in September of this year, placing it among an already large list of independent news publications the Kremlin has targeted for their critical coverage of the war in Ukraine, including The Moscow Times.
An employee of the newspaper, speaking on condition of anonymity, told The Moscow Times that all signs had indicated the authorities would continue their pressure campaign on Novaya Gazeta, with harsher designations such as “undesirable” or “extremist” likely looming.
“The only step left on this trajectory is the destruction of the people themselves, including criminal charges and arrests,” the employee said. “They already have one of us hostage — Oleg Roldugin.”
In its farewell statement on Friday, Novaya Gazeta said: “We’ve managed to work in tight isolation under the watch of the security services for almost five years of war. And now, we’ve found ourselves in the ‘kill zone’.”
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help.
Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.
Remind me later.

Cyber Ambassador Helen Popp at Tallinn Mechanism meeting in Italy: we are seeing growing international interest in strengthening Ukraine’s cyber resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:42:19 UTC
18:42:19 KST

According to Helen Popp, the meeting reaffirmed the unwavering commitment of member states and observer countries to supporting Ukraine’s cyber resilience. “Russia’s war of aggression affects every aspect of life in Ukraine, and attacks continue in cyberspace as well. It is therefore extremely important to continue strengthening the cyber resilience of Ukraine’s civilian sector and to support the protection and development of the country’s critical digital infrastructure,” Popp said.
The meeting also formally approved Spain’s accession to the Tallinn Mechanism as its 15th member state. Japan was also officially granted observer status. At the invitation of Italy, the Mechanism’s current chair, eight countries attended a Tallinn Mechanism meeting for the first time and expressed interest in becoming members in the future. “Spain’s accession confirms the Mechanism’s international significance and central role in the multifaceted cooperation to support Ukraine. It also demonstrates the Mechanism’s ability to engage an increasing number of countries that wish to make a concrete contribution to strengthening Ukraine’s cyber resilience,” Popp stressed.
The discussions focused on the need to make the Tallinn Mechanism’s work more consistent, efficient and effective, particularly in implementing projects. The importance of public-private cooperation was also emphasised, and several companies and other project implementers shared their experiences, lessons learnt and expectations for future cooperation. “The private sector’s contribution to the joint efforts of the Mechanism is critically important for rebuilding Ukraine and creating a better future for Ukrainians,” the Special Envoy for Digital and Cyber Diplomacy stressed.
One discussion, for example, looked at the challenges faced by Ukrainian public sector institutions in restoring the operation of information and communications technology infrastructure damaged by cyberattacks, drawing on projects implemented in Ternopil and Odesa. Member states and observer countries were encouraged to support similar projects at regional level.
This year, more than €32 million has been allocated to cyber support for Ukraine through Tallinn Mechanism projects, of which approximately €700,000 has been contributed by Estonia. Estonia plans to provide a larger amount in 2027.
On 1 July, Italy took over the rotating chairmanship of the Tallinn Mechanism, also known as the lead country role, from the United Kingdom. Italy will lead the Cyber Support Working Group until the end of December this year. The meeting announced that Finland and Norway will become the Mechanism’s lead countries in the first quarter of next year.
The Tallinn Mechanism is a framework established by Estonia and its Allies to amplify the cyber support of donor countries for Ukraine’s civilian sector.

Divorce: what needs to be taken into account before applying to court
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:41:05 EET
18:41:05 KST

Divorce: what needs to be taken into account before applying to court
Kyiv • UNN
Divorce does not automatically determine the fate of children, property, or loans. A lawyer explained when court proceedings are necessary and why disputes should be separated.
At first glance, divorce appears to be a simple legal procedure. In practice, however, the termination of family relations is often accompanied by a whole range of disputes that go far beyond the divorce itself: determining the children's place of residence, the procedure for parents' participation in their upbringing, child support, division of marital property, use of housing, fulfillment of credit obligations, and other issues that have accumulated during the time the couple lived together. Family law attorney Alina Parkhuta of the Legal Company "Logic" told UNN about the legal nuances in a comment.
When a client seeks advice on divorce, it is important to clarify not only their desire to end the marriage, but also the actual state of the family and property relations between the parties.
"The most common mistake is to perceive divorce as a single process within which the fate of the children, property, and financial obligations will automatically be resolved. In reality, the termination of a marriage is merely one of the possible elements of a family dispute," the attorney explains.
Alina Parkhuta, family law attorney of the Legal Company "LOGIC"
What determines the procedure for divorce
"The procedure for divorce depends on the specific circumstances. If the spouses have no minor children together and both agree to end the marriage, the law allows the marriage to be dissolved out of court. If the spouses have minor children together or one of the spouses does not consent, the matter is decided by a court," Parkhuta says.
Sometimes one of the spouses believes that their refusal can block the divorce process. As the attorney explains, this is not the case: marital relations are based on free will, and a person cannot be forced to remain married simply because the other spouse does not want a divorce.
Lack of consent to divorce is not grounds for preserving the marriage
When considering a claim, Alina Parkhuta explains, the court establishes the parties' actual relationship, the reasons for the termination of family life, and other circumstances relevant to the case.
"The key question is whether continuing to live together and preserving the marriage would conflict with the substantial interests of one of the spouses or their children. The defendant's refusal to consent to the divorce is not, in itself, grounds for preserving the marriage," the attorney emphasizes.
There are cases when one of the spouses does not appear in court, does not receive court correspondence, lives abroad, or otherwise delays the consideration of the case. However, according to the attorney, the defendant's failure to appear does not, by itself, prevent the divorce: if the defendant was duly notified of the date, time, and place of the hearing, the court may, where the grounds provided by law exist, consider the case in their absence.
Having children changes the situation
"Having children significantly expands the range of issues that need to be assessed before or simultaneously with the divorce, since the divorce itself does not automatically determine whom the child will live with. If there is no dispute between the parents, they can independently agree on whom the child will live with, how the child will communicate with the other parent, and in what form each parent will participate in the child's support and upbringing," Alina Parkhuta notes.
If no agreement can be reached, the dispute over the child's place of residence is considered separately. The law, the attorney emphasizes, does not presume an unconditional preference for either the mother or the father: what matters is each parent's attitude toward their responsibilities, their actual involvement in the child's life, the child's age and health, the child's attachment to each parent, living conditions, and other circumstances that make it possible to determine the option that best serves the child's interests.
The termination of a marriage does not deprive the parent who will live separately from the child of parental rights and does not release that parent from the corresponding duties. Divorce is not grounds for one parent to unjustifiably restrict the child's communication with the other parent. If there is a conflict between the parties, the specific arrangements for communication and participation in the child's upbringing often require separate legal regulation.
How is marital property divided
"The widespread belief that after a marriage is dissolved, all property is automatically divided between the husband and wife is mistaken. Dissolution of the marriage does not terminate the regime of joint marital ownership with respect to property acquired during the marriage. If the parties have not divided the property by agreement, the right of joint ownership continues to exist even after the marriage is dissolved," explains a lawyer at Logic.
Importantly, the same applies to joint debts: dissolution of the marriage does not terminate obligations under loan agreements or change the terms agreed with a bank or other creditor.
"A dispute may arise between the spouses themselves over whose interests the loan was taken out for, how the funds were spent, and whether a particular obligation can be considered connected with the needs of the family, but this dispute does not concern the bank and does not release the formal debtor from performing the agreement," emphasizes Parkhuta.
As the lawyer explains, it is not always advisable to combine in one case a claim for dissolution of the marriage, division of property, determination of the child's place of residence, and other claims. If there is a complex property dispute between the parties requiring a real estate valuation, examination of banking transactions, determination of the sources used to acquire the property, or the consideration of a large amount of evidence, combining the claims may substantially prolong the proceedings.
"In such situations, it is often justified to separate the disputes: resolve the issue of terminating the marriage separately, and resolve the dispute over property, alimony, or children in separate proceedings. There is no universal rule here: the procedural strategy depends on the amount of property, the nature of the conflict, and the available evidentiary basis in the particular case," the lawyer says.
According to her, before applying to court, it is worth doing more than filing a standard claim for dissolution of the marriage; a full analysis of the family and property situation should be conducted. It is at this stage that it is determined which claims should be filed together and which separately, what evidence should be collected in advance, and what risks may arise after the marriage ends.
"This approach makes it possible to resolve key issues in advance and minimize the risk of additional disputes arising in the future," the lawyer emphasized.

The chancellor used the trip to promote closer cooperation among “like-minded” middle powers as a counterweight to the trade and economic policies of the US and China.
“The fact remains that the United States is shifting its foreign policy, its foreign economic policy, and redefining its interests. As they do so, we must do the same,” he said.
The same applied to defence policy, Merz added, as he seeks to deepen security cooperation with regional partners.

Spanish train was travelling at 160 kph when it smashed into second one, report finds
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:40:40 CET
18:40:40 KST

By Mireia Merino and Charlie Devereux
MADRID, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Spain’s transport minister on Friday rejected calls for his resignation over the second train accident on his watch to cause mass casualties this year, as authorities worked to identify the victims from a crash that killed at least 69 people.
Lawmakers from across the political spectrum this week condemned Transport Minister Oscar Puente for attributing Wednesday’s crash to a break in protocol by control centre operators rather than accepting responsibility, with rail workers’ unions calling for his immediate dismissal.
The crash, which happened near the town of Urda in central Spain, followed another accident involving the same rail companies on the same line that killed 46 people in January.
It has reopened a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe, as the country prepares for an election that left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has called for November 29.
“My duty now is not to focus on discussing whether I will remain in office, but on solving the problem, determining exactly what happened and providing clear explanations,” Puente said at a press conference on Friday.
At the scene of the crash, large cranes were lifting the mangled wreckage as the Civil Guard listed 64 people as missing in what is already Spain’s deadliest train accident since 2013. It was unclear if all those missing were accounted for in the death toll.
Authorities have carried out 49 autopsies so far and formally identified five people, three women and two men, Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on state television network TVE.
AUTHORITIES CAN’T RULE OUT MORE FATALITIES
No additional bodies were found when rescue teams overturned a train carriage on Thursday, Castilla-La Mancha regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said on TVE.
Identifying the bodies was proving difficult because many were in pieces, he said. On Thursday, rescue teams had placed partial remains in 31 bags.
“We cannot rule out the possibility of more fatalities,” Garcia-Page said.
The collision occurred after several trains were automatically stopped due to the failure of a signalling system, after which the central control centre in Madrid took over. A train operated by state-owned Renfe was authorised to proceed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, according to Puente.
Audio of communications between the control centre and the train drivers obtained by El Pais showed how a controller authorised the Renfe train to continue on its journey at a normal speed, which Puente said disregarded a protocol to travel at no more than 40 kph in such circumstances.
CONTROLLERS SAY FOCUS SHOULD BE ON FAILED SIGNAL SYSTEM
The debate about who was at fault intensified, with unions saying it was unfair to lay the blame on human error.
Raquel Ayllon, a union leader at state-owned infrastructure operator Adif, said controllers were having to operate under difficult working conditions.
“Human error is being criticized and questioned very quickly, while people are not really focusing on the central issue: the failure of the safety system,” Ayllon said on TVE.
Puente said the number of staff working at the control centre in Madrid had almost doubled since 2012 and that the controller who made the call had been working for two hours when the crash occurred.
“I have never used the term ‘human error’, although that is not to say that there was no human error,” he said.
He said the LZB train control system that failed on Wednesday had an average of 170 failures per year, which was about the same as the rest of Europe.
The system was behind schedule for an upgrade, public documents show.
The European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) has been installed across most of Spanish high-speed rail, according to a factsheet by European rail association UNIFE, which developed the new standard.
Thales España, the Spanish arm of the French equipment maker, won a 2021 contract to install the ERTMS on the Madrid-Seville line, site of the two fatal crashes, by early 2026, but the work fell behind and passed to Hitachi Rail in 2024, according to Thales.
Thales declined to comment on the delay of the rollout.
Puente said the ERTMS system on the Madrid-Seville line was expected to begin working in early 2027, adding that the delay was due to the complexity of installing the system while keeping the line in operation.
($1 = 0.8930 euros)
(Reporting by Charlie Devereux, Mireia Merinao, Corina Pons, Emma Pinedo and David Latona; Editing by Sharon Singleton, Aidan Lewis and Xevi Fontdegloria)

Evacuation convoys from Russian-occupied Oleshky split toward Ukraine, Russia, officials say
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Evacuation convoys carrying residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast have separated, with some heading toward Ukrainian-controlled territory and others toward Russia, Ukrainian and Russian officials said on Oct. 30.
Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said he was continuing to personally coordinate the humanitarian mission and was heading back to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Earlier, Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova said that buses carrying evacuees had reached Armiansk in Russian-occupied Crimea, where they were to split into two convoys.
The Ukrainian delegation had traveled to Oleshky via Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, from where they reportedly flew to Belarus before continuing by bus to Ukrainian-controlled territory, David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary faction, said earlier on Oct. 30.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
Residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks have made safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city have frequently been targeted by drones.
Despite efforts by the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and even Pope Leo XIV, a ceasefire agreement has only come about since the intervention of Melania Trump.
Twenty-five buses with a combined capacity of 750 passengers, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility, had been prepared to evacuate residents from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, Lubinets said.
Lubinets's statement came amid reports that Russia had begun evacuating residents ahead of the agreed date.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to leave safely. At the same time, those who have decided to stay can stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian support," Lubinets said.
Lubinets and Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova held a joint press briefing in Armiansk, Russian-occupied Crimea, ahead of the evacuation from Oleshky.
Lubinets said the Ukrainian and Russian delegations were accompanied by media representatives from three countries. However, photos published by Ukraine's Ombudsman's Office show predominantly Russian media outlets.
Around 11:30 a.m. Kyiv time, the Ukrainian delegation had safely reached Oleshky, and the ceasefire had been in effect for 80 hours and was still holding, Lubinets said.
Lubinets added that he was speaking with local residents to hear about their needs and understand what kind of assistance they required most.
Arakhamia said around noon that humanitarian aid had been delivered to Oleshky and that "technical support" was being provided to those wishing to evacuate.
Lantratova also confirmed on social media that the evacuation from Oleshky had begun, with people gradually boarding buses. She added that some residents wanted to travel to Russia, while others wished to go to Ukrainian-controlled territory, without specifying how many people were in each group.
Following the separation of the convoys, Lubinets proposed making humanitarian missions coordinated by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump a regular initiative, saying the operation in Oleshky demonstrated that such agreements could help civilians.
Earlier, Lubinets told TSN on national television that a convoy was traveling from Oleshky to Crimea. According to him, people who had not previously registered for evacuation were also given the opportunity to leave.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi initially said during a public government Q&A session on Oct. 30 that 527 residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky were planning to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory. He later clarified on Telegram that he had shared the figure "by mistake" and that "no exact numbers" were available at the time.
Koretskyi also said during the Q&A session that preliminary medical examinations of residents preparing to leave were expected to be completed by 2 p.m. local time on Oct. 30. He added that the evacuees would then travel to Belarus before crossing into Ukraine.
Under the original evacuation plan, residents wishing to leave Oleshky were expected to depart by 2 p.m. local time on Oct. 30, with security measures arranged for their evacuation. Humanitarian aid distribution was scheduled to begin after 2:30 p.m., according to the ombudsman.
On Oct. 29, Lubinets announced that demining of designated routes had been completed and that a humanitarian convoy was ready to depart. Kherson regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin reported that one person had been injured by the explosion of a Russian mine that day.
Russian state news agency TASS, citing Lantratova, also reported that buses had been prepared for Oleshky residents, including ambulances and a special bus for people traveling with pets.
Kseniia Arkhipova, an evacuation volunteer from Oleshky who is now based in Ukrainian-controlled territory, said that Russia had violated the terms of the agreement by starting the evacuation early.
Footage broadcast by TASS also appears to show civilians being moved with only Russian forces present and before the agreed-upon date of departure, Oct. 30. TASS also showed interviews with people it claimed were evacuated from Oleshky on Oct. 29.
The Russian-installed head of occupied Kherson Oblast, Volodymyr Saldo, claimed on Oct. 27 that residents will have a choice — either to stay in Russia or to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory "to reunite with their families."
But a source familiar with the events unfolding on the ground, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, said on Oct. 29 that Russia was already taking steps to ensure as few people as possible left for Ukraine.
They said that patients at the city's only functioning hospital were being registered and told they faced filtration if they left, Russian forces had refused to go house-to-house to inform sick and immobile people that the evacuation was happening, and those living in outlying villages had been told they could be shot if they approached the assembly point.
Some residents expressed fears in local Telegram chats that they could be taken to "concentration camps."
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha previously warned that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there."
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 29 accused Ukraine of "creating a humanitarian catastrophe" in Oleshky, despite the fact that Russian forces have been in control of the city since 2022.

European air traffic expected to shrink by 110,000 flights amid Middle East tensions

2026-10-30
09:38:06 UTC
18:38:06 KST

Gokhan Yildiz and Emir Yildirim
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East are expected to slow European air traffic growth, leading to a loss of around 110,000 flights in 2026, according to forecasts from aviation agency Eurocontrol.
The European aviation sector performed below growth expectations despite strong passenger demand in the summer.
The number of flights in the European Civil Aviation Conference (ECAC) region is expected to grow by 1.7% this year to 11.2 million, below the previously projected 2.7% growth, marking a 1-percentage-point downward revision.
Developments in the region that prompted changes in flight routes and sent jet fuel prices soaring affected the growth outlook for European aviation, but Eurocontrol expects growth to regain momentum next year, with a projected 3.2% increase to 11.6 million flights in 2027.
The downward revision to this year's growth forecast fueled expectations that the number of flights next year may also fall short of estimates.
Eurocontrol assumes the situation in the Middle East will stabilize by the end of the first quarter of 2027, but a more pessimistic scenario forecasts tensions persisting until the end of the first quarter of 2028, with high fuel costs and weak economic growth limiting air travel demand.
The recovery in air traffic is expected to become more pronounced next year, but the organization noted that the recovery could be stronger in Türkiye and some Eastern Mediterranean countries.
The number of flights across Europe is expected to rise by an average of 2.1% per year from 2026 to 2032, while the total number of flights in the region is estimated to reach around 12.8 million by 2032, according to Eurocontrol.
While the organization expects the medium-term growth outlook to remain largely the same, the number of flights may fall slightly short of previous expectations due to geopolitical developments.
Eurocontrol's network management report recorded an average of 35,679 flights per day in European airspace last month, up 2.5% month-on-month.
The busiest day was Sept. 4, when 37,548 flights were recorded in European airspace. Total delays due to air traffic flow management reached a little over 2.4 million minutes, according to the report.
Capacity constraints, adverse weather and air traffic management issues affected operational performance despite the rise in air traffic.
Geopolitical developments, airspace restrictions, energy prices and air travel demand will determine trends in the coming period, the organization said.

====================================================================================================

British firms test AUKUS underwater tech off San Diego
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:36:54 GMT
18:36:54 KST

Two British companies funded by UK Defence Innovation have taken underwater communications and autonomy software to Maritime Big Play, the trilateral exercise held off San Diego last week, where innovators from Britain, the United States and Australia put emerging AUKUS technologies into the water together, according to UK Defence Innovation.
SEA Ltd of Frome in Somerset and Decision Analysis Services of Basingstoke both received their funding through the AUKUS Maritime Innovation Challenge, the competition run to find undersea communications and autonomy capabilities across the three nations, and both demonstrated technologies aimed at what happens beneath the surface.
SEA demonstrated its Acoustic Deployment Environment Planning Tool, which uses high-resolution environmental data and acoustic modelling to predict and optimise how underwater communications will perform in a given patch of ocean. The toolset builds on systems that have supported the Royal Navy for more than two decades and was developed further with UKDI support ahead of the exercise.
Marcus Donnelly, environmental data science technical lead at SEA, said: “Underwater communications are critical to modern maritime operations, particularly as navies make greater use of autonomous and uncrewed systems. Building on SEA’s decades of acoustic modelling expertise, our Acoustic Deployment Environment Planning Tool software combines high-resolution environmental data with sophisticated acoustic modelling techniques to help operators predict and optimise communications performance in complex underwater environments, supporting situational awareness, command and control, and more effective operations.
“Demonstrating the capability in an operational environment off San Diego will allow us to further test, refine and evolve the technology alongside other advanced maritime capabilities. The toolset has its roots in proven anti-submarine warfare modelling capabilities, including systems that have supported the Royal Navy for more than 20 years, and we see significant long-term potential as reliable underwater communications become increasingly important to future AUKUS and other maritime operations.”
Decision Analysis Services demonstrated the Autonomous Fleet Task Assignment Framework, software written to let a group of uncrewed underwater vehicles divide work between themselves when the link back to a command node is degraded or gone.
Anthony Dunn, lead consultant at Decision Analysis Services, said: “Our Autonomous Fleet Task Assignment Framework (AF-TAF) enables Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) to collaborate with less reliance on C2 orchestration, improving responsiveness and reliability in communications degraded or denied environments. Using distributed decision-making, AUVs dynamically allocate tasks to one another, adapt to changing conditions, and maintain mission effectiveness. Together with an accompanying simulation, AF-TAF supports defence planners in optimising fleet structures and operational scenarios, supporting a more resilient, agile, and capable maritime force for future UK and allied operations.”
Both problems come from the same physical fact, because radio does not travel through seawater. Indeed, submarines and uncrewed underwater vehicles communicate acoustically, at data rates measured in bits where a radio link would carry megabits, over ranges that change with temperature, salinity, depth and the shape of the seabed. A sonar operator who knows how sound will bend that day knows where a message will get through and where it will not, and a fleet of autonomous vehicles that can carry on working while nobody is talking to them removes the dependency altogether.
Both capabilities point at the same future, in which a handful of crewed platforms direct large numbers of uncrewed ones. The Strategic Defence Review’s hybrid navy rests on that arrangement, and the Defence Committee reported this month that the department has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Autonomous underwater systems are meant to help close it.
AUKUS Pillar Two covers the advanced capabilities strand of the partnership, separate from the nuclear-powered submarine programme, and undersea warfare has been one of its more productive areas because all three navies face the same problem in the same water.
Sir Stephen Lovegrove, the Prime Minister’s Special Representative on AUKUS, attended the exercise. SEA and Decision Analysis Services will now use what they learned off San Diego to refine their systems.

The sell-off hit most broader markets in the region, with Seoul diving more than 3%, while Tokyo and Taipei shed more than 2%.
There were also losses in Shanghai, Singapore, Bangkok, Jakarta and Manila, although Hong Kong, Sydney, Mumbai and Wellington rose.
Paris stocks were flat as data showed that the French economy had contracted in the third quarter, compounding concerns about public finances and growing political tensions.
London rose, while Frankfurt fell.
Friday's retreat was a far cry from the optimism seen earlier in the week, when SK hynix said operating profit had soared 632% and AI giant Anthropic reported a first-half revenue surge of about 1,300% in its IPO filing.
Iran fears lift oil
The results have been unable to soothe investor worries about the eye-watering amounts firms are pumping into AI and when that will see a profit, while surging borrowing costs are fuelling fears over company finances.
Focus is now turning to Tuesday's US midterm elections and the impact they could have on the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency, with some speculating that he could ramp up his war on Iran, which could send oil spiking again.
"There's been a lot of talk that once these are out of the way, the US could go all shock and awe on Iran? I'm not sure how the midterms would affect that if he loses control of both Houses," said Michael Hewson, of MCH Market Insights.
"Does the outcome matter for the markets, probably not, although a crude oil price which moves above $120 a barrel could well be another story. This remains a much bigger risk for markets than anything the US midterms might bring about."
Fears of a ramping up in US-Iran hostilities were stoked by a report in the Wall Street Journal saying Trump's top Middle East commander had briefed him on military options for Tehran.
Both main contracts climbed more than 1%, with Brent heading towards $120 a barrel for the first time since April.
Bitcoin, meanwhile, tumbled around 5% to a one-month low of around $76,400 after crypto platform Binance said it had fallen victim to a major hack that had impacted more than $6 billion in funds.
The world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses".
It said later on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion".
"We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze the affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far," it added.
That would be four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date, which saw $1.5 billion (€1.34bn) taken in February 2025 from the Bybit platform.
On currency markets, the yen strengthened against the dollar after the Bank of Japan held steady on interest rates and said inflation had topped its 2% target.

EU lacks basis for talks with US, Russia on Ukraine — source in Brussels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:35:53 UTC
18:35:53 KST

BRUSSELS, October 30. /TASS/. The European Union lacks a common negotiating position that would enable it to engage in talks with the United States and Russia on Ukraine. According to a diplomatic source in Brussels who spoke to TASS, the European Commission’s objective in discussions among EU member states on possible negotiations with Moscow is not to secure a specific outcome, but rather to retain control over the process and prevent divisions from emerging within the bloc.
"The European Commission’s actions in the internal EU debate on potential negotiations with Russia are not aimed at finding a solution to end the conflict in Ukraine. They are directed solely at maintaining control over any attempts at negotiation, in order to prevent any fractures in EU unity regarding the confrontation with Russia and support for Ukraine," the source said.
The source stressed that meaningful negotiations require "a clearly defined negotiating position, including an understanding of possible compromises and the desired outcome."
No Basis for Negotiations
"Any negotiating position adopted by the European Commission on behalf of EU member states must first be agreed upon by the member states within the Council of the EU. Only then can the Commission be granted a clear mandate to conduct the talks. None of these conditions has been met," the source noted.
According to the source, EU member states have failed to formulate a common position identifying the compromises Europe might be prepared to consider in discussions with Washington and Moscow aimed at resolving the conflict in Ukraine.
Instead, the debate within the bloc has focused on who might represent Europe in potential negotiations - a discussion that ultimately led nowhere.
"Brussels is now left with a 20-point document drafted by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, which merely reiterates demands put forward in 2022, without taking current realities into account," the source told TASS.
The document calls for Ukraine’s membership in the EU and NATO, the preservation of its territorial integrity, and the strengthening of its armed forces. However, it makes no mention of what concessions the European Union might be willing to offer to help bring the conflict to an end.
"In short, the European Commission has no substantive basis for negotiations with Russia. Nevertheless, it insists that even technical contacts with Moscow concerning Ukraine must be coordinated by the head of Ursula von der Leyen’s cabinet. In other words, the objective is not to reach an agreement, but to keep the entire discussion surrounding contacts with Russia under its control," the source explained.
Political Masochists
Earlier, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov described EU leaders as "political masochists" for continuing to support Kiev despite the worsening situation in their own countries.
He stressed that European leaders were trying to convince their populations that they must sacrifice "everything - wages, jobs, the scope of healthcare services and, essentially, social benefits" to enable Ukraine to defeat Russia.
Lavrov also recalled recent remarks by German Chancellor candidate Friedrich Merz, who stated: "The main thing for us is not Germany, not the European Union, not NATO, not the US, and not China - the main thing is to defeat Russia."

You can pry Halloween from my cold, witchy fingers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:35:52 UTC
18:35:52 KST

You can pry Halloween from my cold, witchy fingers
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
You can pry the pumpkins from the cold, dead hands of our regular columnist Molly Quell, who is going to celebrate Halloween despite some Dutch naysayers.
I am throwing a Halloween party. I like Halloween. It has cooler vibes than other second tier holidays (Valentine’s Day, Easter) and less stress than the major ones (Christmas, and for Americans/Canadians, Thanksgiving.)
I have gotten some pushback, however, from some of the Dutchies in my life, who are balking at the “Americanisation” of it all.
“What about Sint Maarten?” a Dutch friend asked me, half joking. The traditional Dutch holiday is celebrated on November 11, named after a Roman soldier who converted to Christianity. Children carry paper lanterns and go house to house, singing, in exchange for sweets.
“You are welcome to celebrate it,” I said. “I don’t.”
“I don’t celebrate Halloween,” she retorted.
“I’ll put you down as a ‘no’ then,” I said.
If my friend does celebrate Sint Maarten, she’s in the minority even in the Netherlands. By some estimates, only 30% of kids are out slinging their lanterns (or in some places, hollowed out turnips) for sweet rewards.
In Utrecht the holiday is celebrated widely, as Sint Maarten is the city’s patron saint. Further afield, however, there’s barely a single flame out on a chilly November evening.
Halloween, on the other hand, is everywhere. Hema has pumpkin candles and Takkie in a witch’s hat. There’s trick-or-treating for kids in community centres, spooky canal tours in Amsterdam, horror movies at every Pathé across the country.
That’s significantly better than a hollowed out turnip.
I admit, the broader point my friend was making is correct. American culture is becoming increasingly dominant and, as many become disillusioned with the United States under the current administration, there will be more and more backlash to things seen as symbols of the country.
There are a lot of American things the Netherlands shouldn’t import. I am on record saying we should ban American influencers from moving here. I am also opposed to importing prudish attitudes towards sex.
Takkie in his little witch’s hat is adorable and I am choosing to defend his (and my) right to celebrate Halloween.
I’ve always been a little surprised that Dutch people don’t embrace Halloween more. They love to dress up in absurd costumes for every other holiday. Have you seen Brabant during Carnival?
Plus, there aren’t really any holidays in autumn. In fact, earlier this year I argued that rather than making Liberation Day (May) a public holiday, as prime minister Rob Jetten suggested, we do Prinsjesdag (September) instead.
Half the country shuts down anyway for the annual announcement of the budget (in 2026, this was even more true, as the train lines were sabotaged) and there’s even a bit of a costume element with the hats.
We need something to celebrate in the fall to take our minds off the impending darkness of winter and Halloween is already right there. It already has built-in rituals, themed food (I will die on this hill defending candy corn) and no obligation to spend time with family.
While the pumpkin spice lattes and the knife-wielding maniacs on film may be an American export, Halloween doesn’t originate in the United States. Historians think it started as a Celtic pagan festival and was taken across the pond by Irish and Scottish immigrants.
And what is a bigger rebuff to the current American administration than celebrating immigration?

French economy unexpectedly contracts 0.1% in Q3, missing forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:32:52 UTC
18:32:52 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The French economy unexpectedly contracted 0.1% in the third quarter of 2026, falling well short of market expectations for 0.3% growth, preliminary official data showed on Friday.
The slight decline followed a flat reading in the second quarter, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies.
A sharp deterioration in foreign trade weighed heavily on the economy, deducting 0.6 percentage points from gross domestic product growth after contributing 0.6 percentage points in the previous quarter.
Exports fell 1.7% during the July-September period, driven down by a 9.1% drop in transport equipment shipments, particularly aeronautics, alongside a 7% slump in agricultural exports.
Imports remained virtually flat, edging up 0.1% after expanding 0.9% in the second quarter.
Total production of goods and services slipped 0.1% during the quarter as manufacturing output fell 1.4%, affected by weak car manufacturing, poor summer harvests and reduced power station availability amid heat waves.
Construction output decreased 0.4%, while market services output rose 0.3%, supported by a 1% expansion in information and communication services.
Final domestic demand excluding inventories contributed 0.1 percentage points to growth, matching its performance in the second quarter.
Household consumption growth accelerated to 0.4% from 0.2% in the previous quarter, bolstered by electric vehicle purchases, rebounding electricity spending and recreational services.
Public administration consumption rose 0.3%, continuing its upward trend after a 0.4% increase in the second quarter.
In contrast, total investment, measured as gross fixed capital formation, fell 0.6% in the third quarter following a 0.5% contraction in the preceding three months.
Investment in manufactured goods dropped 1.9% on declines in transport equipment, while construction investment decreased 0.5%.
Changes in inventories provided a positive contribution of 0.4 percentage points to gross domestic product growth, largely driven by aerospace products after a sharp drawdown in the second quarter.

German import prices surge 10.4% in September on Middle East energy shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:32:32 UTC
18:32:32 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
German import prices surged 10.4% year-on-year in September, marking the steepest annual increase since November 2022 as the war in the Middle East drove up energy costs, official data showed on Friday.
Import prices rose 2.1% from the previous month, accelerating from an 8.3% annual increase in August and 6.8% in July, according to the Federal Statistical Office.
The escalation of the Iran war had the largest impact on energy import prices, which surged 61.8% compared to September 2025 and 14.5% compared to August.
Considerable annual increases were recorded across all energy imports, led by electricity at 96.2%, mineral oil products at 81.3%, crude oil at 59.3%, natural gas at 53.9% and hard coal at 25.1%.
Within mineral oil products, prices doubled for lubricating oils, aviation turbine fuel, diesel and heating oil compared to the previous year.
Excluding energy, import prices rose 5.5% year-on-year in September and 0.5% month-on-month.
Intermediate goods import prices climbed 11.1% on an annual basis, driven by a 26.8% jump in non-ferrous metals, with copper up 37.9%, aluminum up 23.4% and precious metals up 22.1%.
Imported capital goods were 4.5% more expensive than a year earlier, while consumer goods edged up 0.2%.
In contrast, imported agricultural products fell 0.9% year-on-year, led by drops in live pigs by 34.9%, raw cocoa by 21.2% and green coffee by 15.2%.
Export prices rose 5.3% year-on-year in September, recording the largest annual increase since February 2023, while edging up 0.6% from August.
The effects of the Iran war were also clearly visible in export prices, with energy exports jumping 58.3% year-on-year and 9.2% month-on-month.
Export prices for mineral oil products rose 74.1% annually, aviation turbine fuel jumped 114.3% and natural gas rose 31.7%.
Intermediate goods exports, which account for a major share of total shipments alongside capital goods, increased 7.2% year-on-year.
Agricultural export prices rose 6.7% compared to September 2025 and climbed 2.8% from the previous month.

Most Ukrainians optimistic about future, unity - KIIS poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:30:43 EET
18:30:43 KST

Most Ukrainians (61%) believe that in 10 years Ukraine will be a prosperous country within the European Union, while 27% share the pessimistic view that in 10 years Ukraine will be a destroyed country with a significant outflow of population, according to a study conducted on October 8-16 by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).
"Over the past year (since December 2025), the level of optimism fluctuates somewhat, but relatively insignificantly. In particular, we do not see significant changes over the past few weeks and months... The current survey was conducted against the backdrop of intensified terror and the 'diesel deal' and further pressure on Ukraine. That is, despite these factors, the level of optimism remains (at least for now) at the same level," KIIS said.
Most Ukrainians (59%) also believe that Ukrainians are overcoming contradictions and moving toward a cohesive nation. At the same time, a third of the population (34% now) believe that internal contradictions are deepening and Ukrainians are heading for a split.
More of the younger respondents see a movement toward a split: it is 24% among respondents aged 60 and older and rises to 41% among those aged 18-29, the study says. There are no significant differences between age groups in views of the future.
KIIS also compared respondents' views of the future, unity and the war, and found that those who share pessimistic views of Ukraine's future and unity also have more pessimistic views on issues of war and peace. In particular, significantly more of them insist that the Ukrainian authorities should have been more accommodating in negotiations and are ready to approve the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Donetsk region.
"Given all the circumstances, including a war that has lasted almost five years and it is unknown when it will end, intensified Russian terror, pressure from some strategic partners, domestic political upheavals and so on, the current level of optimism is high and shows the resilience of Ukrainians. At the same time, optimism or pessimism about the future and the perception of unity remain important components of information security now. As the survey results show, those who succumb to pessimistic narratives are far more ready to end the war on any terms, in fact capitulation. Clearly our Russian enemy understands this and therefore tries to use any pretext to impose and spread despair in society," KIIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetsky said in comments on the study results.
According to him, supporting and, where possible, strengthening healthy optimism about Ukraine's future and the unity of society is now important for preserving the population's moral and psychological resilience and the Ukrainian nation's higher defense capability.
"Responsibility for this lies on all actors, the authorities, the opposition, civil society with the media, and ordinary citizens," Hrushetsky said.
The survey was conducted by telephone interviews (CATI) on a random sample of mobile phone numbers in all government-controlled regions of Ukraine among 1,031 adult respondents. Under ordinary circumstances, the formal statistical error of such a sample (with a probability of 0.95 and a design effect of 1.3) would not exceed 4% for indicators close to 50% and 1.7% for indicators close to 5%. Under wartime conditions, a certain systematic deviation is added to the formal error.

Swiss housing shortage stops many setting up home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:29:28 UTC
18:29:28 KST

Swiss housing shortage stops many setting up home
Due to a lack of affordable housing, tens of thousands of people in Switzerland have put off setting up home independently.
This is a conservative estimate, as the property consultancy Wüest Partner explained in a study published on Thursday. If the housing market were less tight, as many as 40,000 to 50,000 additional households could be created.
Young adults are particularly affected. They are staying with their parents for longer or sharing a flat with others. In some cases, separated couples are also unable to afford a second home.
More
Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
The housing shortage is also leading to a shift in demand towards more affordable regions. As a result, the canton of Zurich is now losing a net total of around 3,500 residents a year to other cantons, particularly Aargau, Thurgau and Schaffhausen. Before the pandemic, Zurich had been gaining around 1,850 people a year from other cantons.
This trend is particularly evident among young adults. The annual net inflow of 15- to 34-year-olds from other cantons to Zurich has halved to around 2,750 people compared with the pre-pandemic period. At the same time, the proportion of young adults living alone has been falling since 2022, particularly in Zurich, Schwyz and Zug.
+ Zurich: Welcome to the world capital of housing shortages!
More new-builds offer little relief
Despite the upturn in construction activity, there is no sign of the situation easing for the time being. Wüest Partner forecasts a net increase of around 45,000 flats by 2026, rising to around 50,000 by 2027.
This means more flats are being built than the approximately 40,000 new households formed annually in recent years But the additional supply is also likely to enable people who have so far postponed setting up a household to do so, thereby triggering new demand.
Consequently, pressure on rents remains high. In the third quarter of 2026, advertised rents across Switzerland were 1.9% higher than the previous year’s level. This was despite the number of rental flats advertised reaching its highest level since early 2024.
The city of Zurich is an exception, where asking rents fell by 1.7%. According to Wüest Partner, this could indicate that a price threshold has been reached which is now barely affordable for many households.
For 2027, property experts anticipate a further rise in asking rents across Switzerland of 0.9%. Rents for existing tenancies, however, are likely to remain stable.
Prices for owner-occupied property are also continuing to rise. In the third quarter, flats cost 5% more than a year earlier, whilst detached houses rose in price by 3.2%. For 2027, Wüest Partner expects further price rises of 3.5% and 3.1% respectively.

Russia's legal siege over assets continues, costing Euroclear hundreds of millions of euros in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:29:15 UTC
18:29:15 KST

Russia's legal siege over assets continues, costing Euroclear hundreds of millions of euros in 2026
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Russian sanctions and countermeasures against the Belgian company Euroclear, which holds over 200 billion euros ($224 billion) in Moscow's immobilized assets, continue to cost the company hundreds of millions of euros, according to an Oct. 30 earnings report.
The EU voted to immobilize all Russian government assets within the bloc promptly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The bloc agreed in December 2025 that the immobilization would remain in place indefinitely.
Belgium, and Euroclear specifically, holds by far the largest share of the Russian government's overseas assets, 204 billion euros ($228 billion), according to Euroclear's latest report.
Even as Euroclear "delivers record business income," the responsibility for upholding EU sanctions against Russia comes with a high financial cost.
"Russia sanctions and countermeasures resulted in a loss of business income of 27 million euros ($30 million) and in direct costs of 233 million euros ($261 million), of which 162 million euros ($181 million) is attributed to provisions for claims in Russian courts," reads the Euroclear report for 2026.
Euroclear is facing "multiple proceedings in Russian courts," including a case launched by the Russian Central Bank that seeks to challenge the immobilization of its assets.
"Euroclear strongly contests the Central Bank of Russia's claim, which is without merit," the company said.
Those costs can be covered by the interest generated from Euroclear's investment in the assets, and the EU has made clear in multiple sanctions packages that it will support companies being adversely affected for upholding the bloc's sanctions regime.
And so far in 2026, Euroclear notes that the assets have generated 3.6 billion euros ($4 billion).
The bulk of the interest earnings is, however, turned into a so-called windfall contribution, which Euroclear transfers to the European Union for the purpose of supporting Ukraine.
Euroclear has so far made five windfall payments since the first payment in July 2024. The total of that assistance stands at 8 billion euros ($9 billion), of which the most recent payment of 1.4 billion euros ($1.6 billion) was made in August 2026.
The Russian assets held by Euroclear are continually being eyed by Ukraine as a potential quick win to bankroll its defense.
Most recently, Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Vsevolod Chentsov and former Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk repeated the idea of transferring the assets to a European custodian, where they could be used to provide immediate financial support, during an event in Brussels on Oct. 28.
The idea was, however, dead on arrival because moving Russia's assets from where they are currently held already introduces legal and business risks for Euroclear, which plays a significant role in the global financial system.
Now, the European Commission is compiling options to maintain financial support for Ukraine. Senior EU officials told the Kyiv Independent that potential use of the assets would be included, but "at the bottom," as the least desired option.

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Air defense systems shot down 1,043 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over various Russian regions overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
