Ukraine's Defense Forces hit the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Russia's Samara Oblast with FP-1 drones early on 30 October, Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said, adding that one of the units hit hydrotreats diesel fuel. The strike came hours after WSJ reported that Ukraine had paused strikes on Russian refineries under pressure from US President Donald Trump until after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Russia is pounding Ukraine's power grid and cities ahead of winter, with a mounting civilian toll, including 14 people killed on a Dnipro railway platform on 29 October. Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on Russian refineries, one of its most effective operations against Moscow, target the oil money that pays for that war. Trump has pressed Kyiv for weeks to stop them, blaming them for high global fuel prices, and Ukraine went quiet without saying so and without getting what it asked for in return, WSJ reported. The Samara strike is the first on Russian oil since then. Kyiv has not said whether the pause is over.
Fires spread across a refinery that makes jet fuel for Russia's military
Residents of Novokuibyshevsk reported drones, explosions, and a fire before dawn. Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ posted the first photos on Telegram at 05:24 Kyiv time, and Russian Telegram channel Astra geolocated the fire to the refinery, citing its open-source analysis of residents' photos.
By morning, Exilenova+ counted at least 11 separate fires at the refinery. Samara Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said air defense and mobile fire groups were repelling an attack, Astra reported. The region had declared a drone alert and closed its airport.
Fire Point said its FP-1 drones scored numerous hits on the refinery grounds, and that one of the units hit hydrotreats diesel fuel. The footage published so far shows several smoke columns over the plant but does not show which units burned. The Rosneft-owned refinery has a design capacity of 8.8 million tons of oil a year and is one of the main producers of jet fuel, according to its website. Astra says it supplies jet fuel to Russia's military. The plant lies about 910 km from the front line. Ukraine's General Staff has not commented.
Ukrainian drones have hit the plant before. Ukraine's military said its forces hit it in August and caused a fire.
It is the first fire at a Russian refinery since 15 October, when Ryazan's governor reported one at the city's refinery. It is also the first reported strike on Russia's oil industry since 20 October, when Ukrainian drones hit a Druzhba pipeline pumping station in Tambov Oblast. WSJ called that strike the last before the pause.
All three Rosneft Samara refineries now offline or reduced as drones halt Kuibyshevsky operations yesterday
WSJ claims: Ukraine paused refinery strikes until after the US midterms
Ukraine's military paused its strikes on Russian refineries after weeks of pressure from Trump shook Kyiv's confidence in US support, people with knowledge of the operations told WSJ. The unofficial pause began early last week and is expected to last until after the midterms, and possibly deeper into November. Units carrying out long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the refinery campaign was effectively on hold once missions already under way were completed, two military officials said. Hours after the report, the Novokuibyshevsk strike called that account into question.
Ukraine's government has not announced a pause. Zelenskyy told reporters in Kyiv on 27 October that “our guys tried to be a little more careful during these days. But they do not have an order” not to hit refineries, according to WSJ. He said drone units were hitting other kinds of targets in Russia.
Trump's envoy Jared Kushner repeated the demand to stop the strikes at a meeting with Zelenskyy in Oslo on 20 October, two US officials told WSJ. One of them called the conversation “very tough.” Kushner, who joined remotely, said he and envoy Steve Witkoff were spending a lot of time, energy, and jet fuel on mediating with Moscow, and that a 30-day pause on refineries would be a way for Ukraine to show gratitude, the official said.
Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
Zelenskyy had asked for something in return, WSJ reported: a mutual energy ceasefire with Russia, Patriot missiles for Ukraine's grid, or permission to use Starlink inside Russia so drones could destroy Russian missile launchers. None of those ideas got far. Some of Kyiv's European backers also nudged Zelenskyy to pause until after the midterms, a senior European official said.
The pause showed in Russia's oil industry. Russian refinery utilization at the end of October was 25% higher than at the start of the month as drone attacks subsided, Reuters reported, according to The Moscow Times.
Russia claims over 1,000 drones for a second night as Moscow's airports close again
Russia's Defense Ministry said it downed 1,043 Ukrainian drones overnight over 19 regions, including Samara Oblast, the Moscow region, and Tatarstan. The night before, it claimed 1,214.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin stated that 862 drones flew toward the Moscow region between 20:30 on 29 October and 07:30 on 30 October, that most were downed on the far approaches, and that 170 were downed on approach to the capital. Russia's aviation agency restricted flights at all four Moscow airports, Astra reported. A day earlier, more than 460 flights were delayed or canceled at Moscow and St. Petersburg airports, Astra counted.
In Starodub, in Russia's Bryansk Oblast, about 35 km from the Ukrainian border, a building of the Konservsushprod plant, which makes canned food for the Russian army, appeared to be on fire in readers' photos and videos, Astra reported, saying the plant was presumably attacked and that its open-source analyst had not verified the footage. The Atesh partisan movement reported a blast in Aleksandrovka in Rostov Oblast, and air defense fire and an explosion in Orel.

From 1 November 2026, a new EU-mandated processing fee of two euros will apply to private individuals' online purchases imported into the European Union (EU) from non-EU countries. International technology and logistics group Omniva explains what these changes will mean for Latvian residents shopping on foreign online stores and platforms.
"It is important to understand that the two-euro fee will not apply to each parcel as a whole, but to each separate goods category listed in the customs declaration. For example, if you order three pairs of trousers, the fee will be two euros. However, if you purchase trousers, a lawnmower and a soup ladle in a single order, the fee will be six euros because these items belong to three different product categories," explained Jānis Andžāns, Head of Communications at Omniva.
The fee will apply to goods imported from countries outside the EU, including China, the United States and the United Kingdom.
It will apply regardless of the value of the goods, including purchases exceeding 150 euros.

As part of the celebrations marking the 70th anniversary of Italy’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations (1956–2026), Italy has donated a new set of uniforms to the UN Office in Geneva for the guides at the Palais des Nations, the historic, recently restored complex of rationalist architecture that houses the work of UN delegates. Every year—as explained in a statement from the Mission—thousands of visitors from all over the world are welcomed to the Palais to learn about the work of the United Nations, discover its prestigious negotiation rooms, and explore from the inside the value and importance of multilateralism. For many, their first point of contact is with a tour guide at the UN complex in Geneva: hence the significance of the uniforms in projecting the Organization’s identity. The uniforms, made from eco-sustainable fabrics, are specifically inspired by the principles of social responsibility promoted by artist Michelangelo Pistoletto and his concept of the “Third Paradise”—a balance between nature, society, and innovation, the statement explains. For the guides, the uniforms thus serve as a reminder of the United Nations’ commitment to collaboration, inclusion, and sustainability. As noted by Permanent Representative Luigi Maria Vignali, by combining Italian creativity with responsible production, the uniforms reflect the very values that underpin the UN’s mission, as well as Italy’s ongoing support for the Sustainable Development Goals. After all, fashion can serve as a universal language of unity, dialogue, and respect for the planet, the statement emphasizes, while also thanking the various companies involved in the initiative.

One of the Philippines' most active volcanoes fired a dark column of ash thousands of metres into the sky on Friday in a "moderately explosive eruption" that lasted nearly six minutes, the state seismology office said.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage in towns and cities surrounding Mount Mayon, but the country's volcano institute raised the alert level from 2 to 3 on its 0-5 scale and called for evacuations within six kilometres of the crater.
The 3,000-metre ash column gradually drifted southwest onto nearby population centres, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology said in a bulletin.
"Mayon is in a new phase of magmatic eruption, with increased chances of lava flows and hazardous PDCs (pyroclastic density currents)... affecting the upper to middle slopes of the volcano in the immediate days to weeks," it said.
It urged local officials to evacuate areas near the crater "due to the danger of PDCs, lava flows, rockfalls and other volcanic hazards", with planes also advised to avoid flying close to the mountain.
The 2,462-metre Mayon, rising in a near-perfect cone about 330 kilometres southeast of Manila, is one of three Philippine volcanoes that have shown elevated levels of activity this year, though no major eruptions occurred.
In June 2023, more than 12,000 people living on its lower slopes were moved to evacuation centres to protect them from ash and toxic gases spewing from its crater.
Earthquakes and volcanic activity are common in the Philippines due to its position on the Pacific "Ring of Fire", where tectonic plates collide.
The country's most powerful eruption in recent decades was Mount Pinatubo in 1991, which killed more than 800 people and produced an ash cloud that travelled thousands of kilometres.

What happens to the brain when you eat peanuts daily? New study reveals striking results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:53:25 UTC
17:53:25 KST

Does eating peanuts every day help to maintain memory as we get older?
A recent scientific study indicates that eating peanuts daily may help improve the brain's response to insulin in areas linked to memory in older adults.
The study was published in the journal "Food & Function", and was carried out by researchers from the medical centre at Maastricht University in the Netherlands, with the aim of examining the effect of regular peanut consumption on the brain's response to insulin with advancing age.
The experiment involved 31 healthy people aged between 60 and 75 years.
The participants ate 60 grams of roasted peanuts with their skins and without salt every day for 16 weeks, then the researchers compared the results with another period during which they did not eat peanuts.
Improved brain response to insulin
The results showed an improvement in the response of areas in the right hemisphere of the brain to insulin, including parts of the hippocampus, the parahippocampal gyrus, the lingual gyrus and the posterior cingulate gyrus, which are areas involved in memory processes and other cognitive functions.
To measure this response, the researchers gave the participants insulin through the nose, then used magnetic resonance imaging based on arterial blood labelling to measure changes in blood flow to brain regions.
Insulin plays a role in a number of brain processes linked to learning, memory and communication between nerve cells.
The brain's response to this hormone may become less effective with advancing age, a change that is associated with age related cognitive decline.
However, the researchers did not demonstrate that eating peanuts prevents cognitive decline or stops dementia from developing, but they observed changes in the response of specific brain regions to insulin.
These findings build on previous research by the same team on the same dietary intervention, published in the journal Clinical Nutrition in 2025, where the results showed a 3.6% increase in total blood flow to the brain, along with a 5.8% improvement in verbal memory after the 16 week intervention period.
The researchers believe that the nutritional composition of peanuts may explain some of these effects, as they contain unsaturated fats, fibre, vitamins, minerals and biologically active plant compounds, as well as plant protein.
Peanuts are also a source of the amino acid L-arginine, which the body uses to produce nitric oxide, a compound that helps regulate blood vessel functions and may in turn be linked to learning and memory processes.
Is eating peanuts enough to protect memory?
These findings still need further research to determine to what extent the recorded changes in the brain's response to insulin are reflected in memory and mental performance.
The experiment was limited to 31 people, and the indicators observed by the researchers are not enough to state with certainty that peanuts provide protection from Alzheimer's or other dementia disorders.
Conducting studies on larger numbers of participants and following them for longer periods would help to clarify this relationship and determine whether the potential benefits continue over time.

North Korean hackers were behind the $6.3 billion attack on the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, according to the U.S. blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs. UNN reports this with reference to Reuters.
Details
"The attacker withdrew approximately $6.36 billion from Binance wallets across ten blockchains, most of it in approximately 20 minutes," TRM Labs said in a blog post on its website.
"TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea's elite hacking unit, based on reliable intelligence both on and off the network. We make this conclusion with a high degree of confidence," TRM Labs stated.
According to Bloomberg, on Friday, October 30, Binance Holdings reported that funds totaling $6.3 billion had been affected, of which $3 billion in cryptocurrency had been frozen, and the company suspended all withdrawal operations while it cooperated with law enforcement and completed a security system upgrade. Withdrawals are expected to resume by Sunday, co-founder Yi He said in a post on X.
The company will cover all losses and "users' funds are safe," the statement said.
The hack dealt a blow to a developing industry seeking to expand into traditional finance. Before this, the largest publicly known cryptocurrency hack occurred at the Bybit exchange in February 2025, when attackers stole tokens worth nearly $1.5 billion.
Previously known episodes of theft and fraud among crypto giants such as FTX and Mt. Gox paved the way for prolonged bear markets that the industry had sought to heal from as part of the new era of cryptocurrency regulation promised by U.S. President Donald Trump.
The largest token, Bitcoin, fell amid news of the attack on Binance, dropping below $77,000 for the first time in more than a month. Later during the Asian trading day, it partially recovered its losses, trading at around $78,400 at 2:45 p.m. Singapore time.

More
Switzerland leads Europe in technology found in Russia’s weapons
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, advisor to the Ukrainian president on international sanctions, told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that 95% of Russian drones and missiles contain mass-produced industrial parts from Swiss companies.
+ Russia’s killer drones still boast Swiss components
It is thought that many of the components find their way into Russian hands via Chinese intermediaries. Some of the Swiss companies manufacture in China.
Vlasiuk has called on Switzerland to better enforce international sanctions to prevent Swiss components from being used by the Russian military.
The Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) told SRF that Swiss companies are obliged to conduct due diligence on customers. They must contractually prohibit the re-export of goods to Russia when exporting or selling to third countries.
An effective and comprehensive enforcement of sanctions against Russia is a priority for the Swiss government, SECO told SRF.

Pentagon urges Baltic NATO allies to tone down rhetoric about Russia, citing remarks likening Putin to a ‘rat in a corner’
Pentagon officials urged several NATO member countries to tone down their rhetoric about the Russian threat during bilateral meetings, according to Reuters sources.
The requests went to Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, among others, the agency’s sources said. It is unclear whether other countries received similar requests.
Elbridge Colby, head of the Pentagon’s policy directorate, was one of the officials who conveyed the requests. He cited public statements by Europeans describing Russia as “cornered like a rat” as an example of inappropriate rhetoric.
It is unclear which statement he meant, but in late September, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal called Putin a “rat in a corner” and suggested that Russia is resorting to sabotage in Europe because it is increasingly bogged down in the war with Ukraine, Reuters said.
At another recent meeting, the Pentagon urged the Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its public statements, according to a source. It was not specified whether Pentagon officials objected to any particular statement.
Colby also recently told a representative of one of the Baltic countries that there should be no “poking” at Russia, according to another source.
The Baltic countries that border Russia have long worried about the Russian threat, particularly because of drones that regularly cross into their territory. European countries also accuse Russia of a series of sabotage acts. One of the most recent incidents occurred in Germany, where a drone carrying explosives was found at Leipzig Airport near a Ukrainian cargo plane.
Putin, for his part, claims Moscow does not want war with Europe and has no plans to attack NATO countries, but says it is prepared for one.

Voter turnout lower in runoffs in the last four presidential elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

17:49:41 KST

News
Voter turnout lower in runoffs in the last four presidential elections
Friday 30 October 2026 09:58
Friday, 30 October 2026, 09:58
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Voter turnout in the runoff has been lower than in the first round in each of the last four presidential elections, according to figures published on the Central Election Commission's website.
The first round of this year's presidential election, held on October 25, saw a record low turnout, with just 22.98% of eligible voters casting their ballots. A runoff is scheduled for Sunday to elect the country's next president.
The Central Election Commission recalls that in 2001, voter turnout stood at just under 42% in the first round, rising to nearly 55% in the runoff. The trend subsequently reversed, with fewer voters participating in the runoff than in the first round.
In the 2021 presidential election, turnout reached 40.5% in the first round and 34.8% in the runoff, a difference of 5.7 percentage points.
The figures for previous presidential elections show the following turnout rates:
2016: 57.5% in the first round and 51.6% in the runoff, a difference of 5.9 percentage points.
2011: 51.8% in the first round and 48% in the runoff, a difference of 3.8 percentage points.
2006: 42.5% in the first round and 41.2% in the runoff, a difference of 1.3 percentage points.

Aid Deliveries and Evacuations in Oleshky Begin After Demining Operation Wraps Up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:49:37 UTC
17:49:37 KST

Russia and Ukraine said Friday that demining operations around the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were finished and that evacuations and aid deliveries in the area could begin.
Efforts have been underway for several weeks to organize a relief operation for the town's residents, who have faced acute shortages of food and medicine. Russia seized Oleshky shortly after President Vladimir Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Both sides of the conflict have praised U.S. first lady Melania Trump for helping broker the ceasefire, which is limited to the area around Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson.
"Demining operations of routes have been completed for the humanitarian mission in Oleshky," Ukraine and Russia said in virtually identical statements. "The humanitarian convoy is ready for departure."
The convoy will head to a local hospital, and residents wishing to leave will be allowed to do so within a specific time frame. Aid packages will then be delivered, the statements read.
Ukraine's human rights chief, Dmytro Lubinets, referred to Melania Trump when he extended Kyiv's "special thanks" to someone who was "personally devoting her time and attention to the humanitarian mission and assistance to civilians in Oleshky."
Still, any hope of wider relief in the war appears to have been dashed away by a series of attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent days, including a strike on the main train station in the southeastern city of Dnipro that killed at least 15 people on Thursday.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine has reported any violations of the ceasefire in Oleshky since it began on Tuesday.
Melania Trump also confirmed in a post on X that the local pause in hostilities, expected to last until Sunday, appeared to be holding as the humanitarian operation got underway.
"The convoy is prepared to safely evacuate over 750 people who voluntarily choose to leave Oleshky. It includes 25 buses, 50 medical professionals and ambulances," she wrote.
Russia's Defense Ministry said Friday that two Russian servicemen had died while clearing mines on a road leading to Oleshky.
Reuters contributed reporting.

University finds plagiarism in Lithuanian PM’s doctoral thesis, gives 6 months to correct
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:47:00 UTC
17:47:00 KST

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has been given six months to correct plagiarism and other academic writing violations in his doctoral thesis, but a university ethics commission has ruled against immediately revoking his doctorate.
The ethics commission at ISM University of Management and Economics identified five cases of plagiarism and two instances of improper text use that did not constitute plagiarism in Sinkevičius’ 2015 dissertation on alcohol consumption, according to its October 26 decision seen by BNS.
The commission concluded that the violations breached the university’s academic integrity principles and requirements for independent doctoral research.
It recommended that the university’s rector instruct the doctoral studies dean to establish requirements for a publicly available list of corrections and proper source attributions within 60 calendar days. Sinkevičius would then have six months from the approval of those requirements to make the corrections.
The revised dissertation would be reviewed by the doctoral committee and published alongside a correction supplement. If Sinkevičius refuses to address the shortcomings within the deadlines, the commission could recommend initiating proceedings to revoke his doctoral degree.
The commission said immediately pursuing revocation would be a disproportionate penalty. It found no violations in the procedures used to evaluate or defend the dissertation.
Sinkevičius acknowledged the findings and pledged to prepare the corrections.
“I conducted the data analysis and formulated the conclusions myself. Therefore, I have never doubted my work, but I do not dispute the violations identified,” he told BNS on Friday.
ISM rector Dalius Misiūnas said the commission had conducted a thorough and professional investigation in accordance with the principles of impartiality and objectivity. The university accepted its findings and would address the identified shortcomings, he said.
The investigation followed allegations of plagiarism that emerged in July. The commission began examining a complaint in August and later received two additional complaints.
Sinkevičius defended his doctoral dissertation at ISM in 2015.

Defense Ministry Chief Baram pushes munitions independence during visit to Covenant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:46:13 UTC
17:46:13 KST

Defense Ministry director-general Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Baram visited Covenant, one of Israel's fast-growing defense-tech companies on Thursday, as part of a series of visits to various defense companies.
According to the Defense Ministry, Baram’s visit “focused on strengthening Israel's munitions independence, expanding the production base, and preserving the State of Israel's qualitative and technological edge in the years ahead.”
The statement added that the visits are part of implementing the Ministry's strategy to strengthen Israel's defense-tech ecosystem.
"The ministry's policy is to encourage and strengthen both defense-tech companies and new start-ups, as well as the established industries. This balance is essential for fostering healthy competition, driving innovation and out-of-the-box thinking, maintaining our qualitative edge, and developing 'the next surprises,’” Baram was quoted as saying during the visit.
According to him, “We must look ahead to an intense security decade and adapt our plans to both global changes and the evolution of the battlefield. Defense exports are a critical growth engine and an enabling tool, not only for strengthening the economy, but also for building the IDF's force and delivering a critical mass of advanced systems to the warfighters on the front lines."
Recognizing the strategic importance of this ecosystem, the Israeli government launched a state‑backed investment initiative last year to strengthen early‑stage defense‑tech ventures. The Defense Ministry has also invested NIS 1.2 billion in start-ups alone, and small- and medium-size companies have signed contracts worth hundreds of millions each.
Last year, the Defense Ministry declared “munition independence” a strategic priority, pushing companies to boost their domestic munition production capacity. Since the outbreak of the wars that began with the deadly Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, Israel has used enormous quantities of munitions, and replenishing its stockpile has become one of the country’s highest priorities.
Anthem
Covenant, which has operations in the US, Germany, and Israel, emerged from stealth last month. Its flagship system, Anthem, is built to deliver heavy payloads at extended ranges while remaining affordable enough to produce in large quantities.
The company has disclosed relatively little about Anthem’s specific performance characteristics, including its precise range, payload, and unit cost. A report in the blog Missile Matters by expert Fabian Hoffman quoted reports saying that the missile has a range of 1,000-1,500 kilometers and has a payload of over 200 kilograms. The report also said that the missile may cost between $500,000 and $6,000 USD per unit.
According to the company, most of Anthem’s components are commercial‑off‑the‑shelf (COTS) parts, supported by long‑term agreements for critical parts. Covenant says this approach allows the missile to be produced quickly and reliably, even during wartime, by drawing on supply chains across allied nations.
The company aims to produce 1,000 Anthem missiles in 2027 in its German and American sites. The report by Missile Matters said that the sites in Israel and Germany “operate as quasi-independent entities with mostly localized supply chains, held under a unique corporate structure” that places them outside US export controls.
Earlier in the month, Denmark announced that it would be procuring the Anthem.

'A lot to do': US Congresswoman Aisha Wahab speaks with TNA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:45:53 UTC
17:45:53 KST

Breadcrumb
'Trying to do the right thing': US Congresswoman Aisha Wahab speaks with The New Arab
At a recent campaign event, US Congresswoman Aisha Wahab spoke with The New Arab about her race to keep her seat in California’s District 14, why many politicians fear speaking out, and how she has been able to build a broad coalition.
As one of the newest members of Congress, who won in a special election after Eric Swalwell resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct, Wahab is in the unusual position of campaigning immediately after taking office.
Though she comes to the 2026 midterms as an incumbent, she is not taking anything for granted, as she once again runs against Melissa Hernandez, the candidate she competed against during the primary.
According to ElectionsCALI, which publishes live prediction markets for California, Wahab is leading Hernandez 92 to 8 (in prediction market odds).
Wahab is the first Afghan American and one of the few Muslims to become a US Congress member. She is also one of a growing number of progressive Democrats speaking out on some of the party’s core issues, including Medicare for All (universal healthcare), taxing billionaires and getting big money out of politics–what many see as part of a new era of grassroots politics.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
You’ve said that some people are afraid of speaking up. What do you mean?
I think people have a lot of fear about talking about the real issues and holding people accountable. Not only holding people accountable, but also holding allies accountable, holding our own party accountable.
What do you think people have the most fear to talk about?
I think it depends on who you’re talking to, and I think that for me it’s always: why are we here? There’s no point in holding the seat if you’re not going to try to make change–on whatever issue you care about–whatever issue you think your community, your district, your constituents care about.
So, for me, you can take a look at my record in the [California state] senate, all of the bills that I’ve brought forward are from my district–some conversation I had, somebody shared a story, somebody shared a problem. Even just in this past week, we’ve had folks say: thank you for this bill at the federal level–you know, protecting women, protecting children, providing for our communities. There’s a lot of work to do.
Is it difficult to talk about things like Israel and Palestine?
I think that it’s definitely getting easier, being the only Muslim in the state legislature [referring to her recent time in the California State Senate], it was hard there. I think there’s this growing movement of accountability and where do our dollars go, and who’s being harmed and for what purpose. When we're talking about our international affairs across the board, there doesn’t seem to be a purpose that’s clear to the American people, and the harm being done does not contribute to a better quality of life over here. And so, as we hold ourselves accountable, our international policies, our dollars, we ask: Where does it go? Why does it go there?
Do you feel, with the person you're following in this seat, more of a responsibility to hold people accountable?
I've always believed in trying to do the right thing. I have several bills that focus on accountability, about going further to provide justice. Whether we're talking about my bill on survivor’s bill of rights, and sexual assault survivors, whether we're talking about closing the spousal rape loophole, whether we’re talking about the bill I did to ban child marriage. I have done a lot of work to not only educate my colleagues that these problems exist, that we have to do more. Even, for example, the Cornell case. I've always had a concern and problem with: why do these universities have their own policing, when it should be regular city jurisdiction law enforcement?
I believe that when we saw Representative [Eric Swalwell] the way we did, I think that there’s more to the story. And I think that by the resignation, it kind of [meant that] everyone in power felt like it absolved anybody of their engagement with him. The reality is that there's a lot of harm when you’re talking about sexual assault and sexual violence–whether it’s children or whether it’s women or whatever the case may be. It affects them mentally, emotionally, physically, spiritually for their entire lives. People don't really talk about the impact that these types of crimes have on victims. And as a daughter of an individual who was murdered, that one action sits with me for a lifetime; that one action affected the entire family. It wasn't just one person that got harmed. So, I think there's a lot to discuss when we’re talking about prioritising victims first; that's always been my goal.
Rhe ad campaigns that were against us–and I'm so glad the San Francisco Chronicle literally wrote that these were false and misleading and distorting her record–because my record is very clear. We have always prioritised victims first.
Even in our campaign, we have the support of people like Bernie Sanders as well as the chiefs of police, as well as sheriff, as well as the attorney general and so many people.
How did you build such a wide coalition?
It’s being able to talk to people directly, being honest, and listening and having an open door of communication. I may not always agree with anybody a hundred percent of the time. But being able to really understand where they’re coming from and find some middle ground is important for doing the best policy.
We had a bill regarding signal jammers. Law enforcement brought that forward to me–our own district, in fact. We worked on it, but we also realised teachers use it so kids don’t cheat in class, so they don’t text each other. So, how do we ensure that people who are using it in crimes get punished for it, but we don’t harm teachers and innocent people.
So, we made it in a way where we threaded the needle and the bill was written in a way that said: if you commit a crime, utlising this type of technology, it’s illegal. But if you use it for people taking tests, it’s not a big deal. I think threading the needle, building policy, writing it a certain way, working with people, understanding that there are multiple sides to a story, for even a tool, we need to prioritise.
I don’t think I’ve seen a coalition so wide. It really spans the spectrum.
We have everybody from Governor Gavin Newsom, Bernie Sanders. We have Adam Schiff, we have Pramila Jayapal–you name it. It's largely because I generally try to work with all people. I don’t really care for labels. I think that that puts you in a box. We want to make sure that we create policy that helps all people, not a specific type of person. Our policies last lifetimes. There's a lot of good you can do and there’s also a lot of harm. So, you need to be able to have those conversations to understand the full nuance of what you are really trying to do. I’m really honoured to be able to have this big, massive coalition. It shows the work that we have done and the conversations we have had. We’re going to try to work with all people.
Do you feel like you’re paving a path for people?
When I was first elected, there were a lot of firsts attached to the progress that I’ve made. I just want people to be able to know that they can do it. Even my own team, for example. My campaign manager has never run a campaign but mine. My team that does my video work had never done photography before. We're bound to make mistakes, we’re bound to fumble, we’re bound to fall down. But the effort is what’s true. If you can try your best, try your hardest, learn from your mistakes and have a goal and work towards that, that is what our efforts are.
I share this because in politics, you don’t need a specific degree. You don't need a specific background. You don’t need to speak a certain way to get elected. You are a representative of the people in your community. For all of them that have fear and doubts, you just want to make sure you persevere through that and also be able to bring people along. That has been genuinely what I've tried, and I may not agree with anybody a hundred percent of the time. But it’s like: where can we work together? That's the goal for me.
How would you feel if someone said that I got into this race because I saw what you were doing?
You know what's funny? We've had people say that and in fact I've had colleagues that ran for their local office because they saw me running for city council years ago. I always say the world is small and since that community, everyone you meet, when you’re able to make an impact, they make an impact on you. They make an impact on their community. You are able to also see where you can do more and be better. Nobody’s perfect, and so as long as people try, do their best, do the work for the people, that’s what I care about. So, when people are interested in running, they have to have the right reasons for why they’re running. I think there are a lot of people who have a lot of ego. A lot of people start to forget why they’re in office, especially with the fundraising component. We talk about that. You don’t want to sell out 'the American Dream'. For me, I try really hard to prioritise the 'American Dream' for everyone. Campaign contributions are not going to change that. In the state legislature, for example, I’ve pushed policies that were not popular among legislators.
For example?
My lobbying reform bill. Because they're so afraid. Their friends are all lobbyists, and I've had a lot of conversations where people were trying to lecture me on that. And I tell them: I appreciate your opinion, but my priority is the 40 million people who rely on the policies being created in this bill. The moment you say that, it kind of level sets them again. And it reminds them of who we really work for. And so even though it's very difficult to pass legislation like that–it gets watered down under the guise of this or that–the goal is to continue to help reform the institution, the work. That's what I care about.
Moving forward, how do you feel about the race?
We've heard rumblings where our opponent and her team met with people in the district and have stated that AIPAC may put in $4 million. I don't know if that’s true. I don't know if that’s them garnering support, or trying to establish more support. I don't know, so we can't assume that we have this in the bag because we’re elected right now. We work every single day. As you can tell, we had literally hundreds of people show up, stand in the burning sun to be able to be part of this. We just want to help, we want to be supportive, work hard for every vote, and see what happens.
How have you done both–run for office while holding office?
I'm very, very proud that we've done a lot of the groundwork ahead of time. I will say that I take my job very seriously. In fact, I voted on every single bill before I got sworn in–in the legislature for the [state] senate. We waited as long as we could before we resigned, and eventually 24 hours before we got sworn in, we resigned. And we started the work. We've just established and found our new district office. We got the short end of the stick in Congress in a lot of ways. They were supposed to have an office for us. That office already had a new tenant. We had to find our own office. There’s a lot of work to do.

China conducts combat readiness patrols around disputed shoal in South China Sea
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:45:33 CET
17:45:33 KST

BEIJING, Oct 30 (Reuters) - China’s military said on Friday its naval and air forces conducted combat readiness patrols around Scarborough Shoal in has long been a flashpoint in tensions between Beijing and Manila in the South China Sea.
The People’s Liberation Army Southern Theater Command, in a statement, said the patrols were “necessary countermeasure in response to the Philippines’ rights-violation and provocative acts” and it has strengthened such patrols this month.
The Philippine embassy in Beijing and the Philippine military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tensions between China and the Philippines resurfaced at the close of a two-day Association of Southeast Asian Nations defence gathering on Thursday, with Beijing accusing an unnamed Philippine politician of obstructing its participation in the event. Manila said China had been given an opportunity at the meeting to state its position.
China claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea via a nine-dash line on its maps that cuts into parts of the exclusive economic zones of Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei and Indonesia. An international arbitral tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision Beijing rejects.
“Such patrols are aimed at further enhancing control and management over relevant waters and airspace, and serve as an effective countermeasure to cope with all sorts of rights-violation and provocative acts,” the Chinese military said.
Separately, the China Coast Guard also conducted law-enforcement patrols in the waters around the shoal on Friday, calling the activities “necessary countermeasure in response to the Philippines’ rights-violation and provocative acts.”
Neither the Chinese military nor the China Coast Guard gave details on which Philippine actions they were referring to.
(Reporting by Beijing Newsroom; Additional reporting by Nestor Corrales in Manila; Editing by Christian Schmollinger and Sharon Singleton)

IN BRIEF: Russia pounds Ukraine’s defense plants, energy sites in massive overnight strike

17:42:57 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Russian forces delivered a massive overnight strike on Ukrainian military-industrial enterprises and their power facilities and hit port infrastructure in the Odessa Region, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has gathered key information about the targets of the strikes.
Defense Ministry statement
- During the past night, the Russian Armed Forces delivered a massive strike by ground-based precision-guided weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on targets in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, the strikes hit Ukrainian military-industrial enterprises engaged in the production and storage of long-and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles, energy facilities providing power for their operation in Kiev, the Kiev and Dnepropetrovsk Regions, and also port infrastructure sites in the Odessa Region and sea vessels used for the needs of the Ukrainian army.
Targets hit
- As the ministry specified later, in the city of Kiev, the strike hit a missile assembly and components plant (the Kiev Radio Plant JSC, Trimen-Ukraine LLC) manufacturing components for reconnaissance and strike drones, including long-range UAVs.
- In Kiev, Russian forces also hit a workshop for assembling and storing unmanned aerial vehicles (Fanplit PrJSC) involved in the production and storage of Fire Point FP-1 and FP-2 long-and medium-range drones.
- In addition, Russian forces hit the PS-330 Novokievskaya power substation in the settlement of Khotov in the Kiev Region, which supported the operation of Ukrainian defense industry enterprises in Kiev.
- Russian forces also struck the PS-330 Svetloye power substation in the settlement of Svetloye in the Dnepropetrovsk Region, which supported the operation of Ukrainian defense industry enterprises in Dnepropetrovsk.
- In addition, Russian forces hit a dry cargo ship in the Black Sea delivering military equipment and dual-use cargo for the needs of the Ukrainian army to the Odessa port.
Situation in Ukraine
- A complete power outage hit Dnepropetrovsk in southeastern Ukraine, Mayor Boris Filatov (blacklisted as a terrorist and extremist in Russia) said.
- The mayor advised Dnepropetrovsk residents to stay at home, whenever possible, as electric public transport (the subway, trolleybuses and trams) had stopped running in the city and only buses were operating on the routes.
- The mayor also recommended that urban residents stock up on enough water for at least one or two days.
- The blackout in Dnepropetrovsk has occurred for the second time over the past 48 hours.
- The city was hit by a complete power outage yesterday evening.
- It was also reported at that time about interruptions in hot water supply to apartments.

Russia's bastion of free press Novaya Gazeta shuts down under Kremlin pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

Russia's bastion of free press Novaya Gazeta shuts down under Kremlin pressure
Newspaper Novaya Gazeta, one of the last vestiges of independent journalism in Russia, announced Friday that it was closing down, citing pressure from authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor and earlier this year detained one of its journalists.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Russia's flagship independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announced Friday it was closing, saying it had been "killed" by state pressure after years of repression targeting its journalists whose reporting was critical of the Kremlin and its Ukraine war.
The closure of Novaya Gazeta – one of the last outlets to openly criticise Russia's offensive – marks the latest outcome of Moscow's campaign against dissenting voices that gained speed after the Kremlin sent troops into its neighbour in 2022.
Since then, the newspaper, long considered a bastion of independent journalism, has seen its media license revoked, while its journalists and editors have been questioned, detained and had their homes searched.
It was also branded a "foreign agent" – a label reminiscent of Soviet-era repression used to stifle dissent.
The paper's Nobel Prize-winning founder, Dmitry Muratov, said the closure was "part of a giant military campaign being waged by the Russian Federation".
"We are fierce opponents of war in all its forms. And we are a part that needed to be destroyed," Muratov, the paper's former editor-in-chief, said.
Novaya Gazeta's current editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, said the paper was "ending its existence" in a statement published on YouTube on Friday morning.
In the emotional video, Sokolov said that "the Russian authorities – the Russian special services – have forced the editorial team to end its work."
Founded in 1993 after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Novaya Gazeta was one of Russia's most reputable and renowned organisations reporting and documenting human rights abuses.
Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, donated some of his Nobel Peace Prize money to help set up the paper.
Rights groups slammed the move.
"Novaya Gazeta will remain THE symbol of free, pluralistic, independent, and rigorous journalism – a model for the entire profession around the world," Reporters Without Borders chief, Thibaut Bruttin, said on Friday.
Amnesty International said the closure was a "devastating loss for everyone in Russia who turns to independent, investigative journalism to uncover the truth."
'Finished off'
Several Novaya Gazeta reporters have been murdered in killings widely seen as retribution for their work.
They include Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia's military during its campaigns in Chechnya.
She was found dead in her apartment block on President Vladimir Putin's birthday in October 2006.
Muratov, who was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his work, had to formally step down as editor-in-chief two years later after being declared a "foreign agent".
The Norwegian Nobel Prize Committee on Friday called on Russian authorities to "end their repression of independent media".
"The closure is a grave blow to freedom of expression and the public's right to information," committee president Jorgen Watne Frydnes said in an email.
Sokolov in his video statement said that Novaya Gazeta for nearly five years of war "managed to operate while completely surrounded by intelligence services. But now, that's it. We've ended up in a kill zone."
"This isn't just our own private story – it's the story of a country and a society that are being finished off in exactly the same way."
The paper, which used to be published several times a week, cut down production inside the country after the war began, but its online version was still available despite court orders.
In recent months, the Russian authorities searched the home of Sokolov and earlier this year arrested one of its journalists, Oleg Roldugin.
"Human rights and freedoms have been abolished, and their defence has been equated with a crime," Sokolov said in the video statement, adding: "Beliefs have become state treason."
"The murder of Novaya Gazeta is yet another piece of evidence. All these years we wrote precisely about this, for as long as we could. Thank you to everyone who listened to us. And the final issue will come out."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Marju Kõivupuu: Halloween won't displace Estonia's mardi and kadri traditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:41:00 UTC
17:41:00 KST

Marju Kõivupuu: Halloween won't displace Estonia's mardi and kadri traditions
No holiday pushes another out of the calendar automatically — people themselves can make the choice about which rituals live on, folklorist Marju Kõivupuu finds.
In the same way, Halloween, which in its present-day form is an import from North America, will not in and of itself destroy Estonians' twin mardi- and kadrisants festivals, held on November 10 and November 25 respectively.
"I have said time and again that no holiday displaces anything on its own, these are choices made by people. For me as a researcher it is interesting to look at what basis we make these choices on," Kõivupuu found in an interview given to R2 hommik.
The folklorist noted that representatives of various faiths tend to label each others' rituals. "That false notion derives precisely from the fact that this or that faith or religion starts to consider itself 'higher' and via that terming belittles others. Christianity took over the holidays connected with marking the old souls' day and honoring the dead, worked them into something more amenable to itself and took them into use," Kõivupuu offered by way of an example.
The same logic holds for Halloween, she said. "Halloween's roots too are indeed in pre-Christian Celtic customs, from which the Christianized Germanic peoples took over that tradition. We now know it as a commercial, entertaining children's holiday that arrived in Europe from America via a circuitous route," the folklorist went on.
Kõivupuu recalled that the Irish carved lanterns which are now characteristic of Halloween from turnips and swedes, but on the European side of the pond. In America, the Europeans found new types of crops, and swapped out the older root vegetables for the pumpkins we now associate with the holiday, just for convenience's sake.
As a theme running through many cultures, the darkening autumn-winter nights serves to bring ancestors' souls back to earth. "If we compare it with our souls' time, then that cloaking is the result of the fact that, according to old beliefs, there is a certain time of the year when the spirits or souls of dead ancestors — whatever we term them — return to earth but want to take the living with them from here," the expert continued.
Kõivupuu added that customs need to be able to breathe, to be dynamic, to stay alive: "A tradition lives when people develop it further. If we give something up, then it stays behind us, but presumably this Halloween was so important that it was adapted according to circumstances."
Equallly, an intentional support and international attention have their place too. "Very few people also know that the Estonian folklore council is currently working in the direction of getting our mardi and kadri day tradition onto UNESCO's representative list of intangible heritage," said Kõivupuu.
Holidays' campaigns on the store shelves
Clever marketing also adds spice to these red-letter days. As a result, international corporations create convenient ready-made solutions so people can celebrate holidays. In the same way, domestic candy producers try to offer children special kadrisants sweets, with the major difference from Halloween being, as Estonian traditions, their lack of a global reach.
As a wider trend, traditional calendar holidays are pushing ever earlier into the commercial sphere, sometimes not even in the most obvious areas. "I went to a building supplies shop at the start of September; I needed a few screws there, and the first thing you could see, in September was already the Christmas trees and elves. I'm sorry, but we still have very plenty of holidays in between; but we can't wait for the holidays any more, they push in from every side," Kõivupuu shared as an anecdote.
The folklorist noted at the same time that more domestic holidays tend to fall below those red-letter days with a bigger commercial footprint, even when children learn the traditional ways thoroughly and wait for sweets at the door when they go "santing" (specifically "mardisandid" on St. Martin's Day (Mardipäev) and "kadrisandid" on St. Catherine's Day (Kadripäev) and originally more akin to carol singing than trick or treating). "Let's be frank, it still stays very, very much in the shadow of that pumpkin holiday, or Halloween," Kõivupuu conceded.
--

Can the US Defense Industry Keep Pace with China’s Military Machine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:39:00 UTC
17:39:00 KST

As modern warfare continues to evolve in its complexity, the sheer quantity of weapons a country possesses is no longer the only decisive factor in an armed conflict. If, for example, a Taiwan crisis were to escalate into a protracted conflict, the central dilemma would be: Is the United States capable of replenishing its weapons and munitions at a pace adequate to sustain the war effort? Would the strategic gain China would obtain from invading Taiwan outweigh the operational costs of the invasion?
The average military planner is busy counting ships, aircraft and missile stockpiles, as well as calculating defense spending. But these figures illuminate only part of what a geopolitical and military power such as the United States needs in order to be combat-ready. Maintaining a sustained combat posture also depends heavily on the companies that produce munitions, components, spare parts and replacement equipment.
Understanding defense readiness requires looking beyond national military preparedness and keeping track of the production capabilities of industrial manufacturers. According to a CSIS assessment, China’s defense industrial base is built to operate under wartime conditions, while the U.S. base remains largely geared toward peacetime production. Being able to assess readiness at the manufacturer level and close any existing gaps will give the United States the strategic wartime advantage it seeks.
China considers wartime industrial readiness a strategic priority. China’s manufacturing scale could make the difference in a protracted conflict in the Asia-Pacific. A Taiwan contingency could include a blockade, sustained maritime operations, missile strikes and loitering munitions, as well as attacks on supporting infrastructure. In this scenario, the United States and its allied forces would need to sustain their aircraft fleets, replenish missile stockpiles, repair ships and maintain a logistics chain across a vast theater of operations. It is in this context that China’s shipbuilding capacity, and its ability to produce, maintain and repair military equipment at scale and in real time, pose a serious industrial challenge for Washington. In 2024, CSIS estimated China’s shipbuilding capacity at roughly 230 times that of the United States, with China acquiring specific high-end weapons systems at five to six times the U.S. rate.
In response to a potential conflict in the Indo-Pacific, in June 2025 the Department of War requested a 13 percent increase in the 2026 defense budget. This increase therefore signals a U.S. industrial-military outlook aimed at deterring China’s ambitions. The increase prioritizes not only the growth and strengthening of U.S. naval power, but also investment in other areas of defense, such as the production of higher-performance fighter jets; at the same time, an increase in stealth units capable of operating from existing aircraft carriers; in turn, initial investments in the “Golden Dome” for Taiwan, which points to increased air defense capability against enemy missiles and aircraft; and finally, investments focused on upgrading nuclear technology.
It is crucial that U.S. lawmakers understand that defense spending is only one part of the equation. The fact that a company holds a defense contract does not mean it has the capacity to accelerate delivery times. Optimizing production often requires new facilities, specialized tooling, skilled workers and an increase in raw-material suppliers. Financing alone does not guarantee a manufacturer’s ability to meet increased demand. A 2025 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that none of the seven major U.S. shipbuilders it examined was in a position to meet the U.S. Navy’s ship delivery targets at the time. Key issues cited included infrastructure and workforce constraints. The key takeaway here is that national budgets and procurement totals alone cannot reveal the delivery times or capacity constraints of individual defense companies.
New ways of evaluating the companies that drive U.S. military power are emerging. As a practical response to the existing gap in manufacturing measurement, DefenseWatch.org has introduced an index. It currently scores 27 companies on a scale of 0 to 100, offering a more structured way to evaluate and rank U.S.-based defense manufacturers. Prime contractors, as well as other companies, are weighted differently according to the index’s unique methodology. The score is calibrated based on quarterly datasets fed into the algorithm from the Federal Procurement Data System (FPDS), SEC filings and notices from the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS).
Rather than analyzing the U.S. defense industrial base as a monolithic entity, the index provides a company-level framework that makes it easier to compare manufacturers’ wartime readiness. The index is not a definitive prediction of wartime performance, but rather a tool that helps structure comparisons and expose potential vulnerabilities in the defense manufacturing industry.
The ability to surge defense production matters as much as, or more than, existing output. In a Taiwan conflict scenario in which the U.S. fires the first military salvo, weapons could be expended faster than peacetime production schedules can replenish them. In this scenario, it is worth being able to identify which manufacturers have the right facilities, workforce and supply arrangements to increase production at any moment. The key metric to watch is not necessarily a company’s current manufacturing capacity, but how quickly it could respond to an extraordinary surge in demand, as well as the cost reductions in manufacturing new technologies; in other words, the use of loitering munitions reduces the operational costs of achieving military objectives and, at the same time, has transformed the modern battlefield, partially replacing the use of conventional weapons and platforms with higher acquisition costs.
CSIS wargames of the Taiwan Strait illustrate the magnitude of the challenge. Across nearly two dozen iterations, U.S. forces typically expended more than 5,000 long-range missiles in three weeks. Replenishment, however, operates on a very different timeline: CSIS reported that producing a Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM) took nearly two years, while the U.S. budget for fiscal year 2023 proposed buying only 88. The figures measure different things—simulated consumption, production lead time and planned procurement—but together they expose the core problem: the U.S. industrial base is not prepared for a potential conflict with China. The Taiwan Strait wargames highlight that, in such a scenario, the U.S. military would likely expend critical weapons far faster than its industrial base can currently replace them.
Key components for helping assess a manufacturer’s viability during a conflict include “Investment Quality,” “Domestic Contribution” and “Adversary Exposure.” “Investment Quality” refers to the ability to assess how much of the capital flowing into a given company is actually used to resolve production bottlenecks and meet reliable delivery schedules. “Domestic Contribution” refers to the extent to which a manufacturer can rely on locally sourced components and labor to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers. This also includes exposure to international imports of components and raw materials, as well as dependence on foreign labor. In a scenario in which U.S. strategic readiness will depend on its ability to operate a self-sufficient industrial base, this may be a crucial metric to assess. “Adversary Exposure” refers to how exposed a manufacturer’s supply chains are to foreign inputs. These risks include partial or full ownership of a defense production entity by a foreign government, as well as international cyber vulnerabilities.
The Defense Watch index methodology takes all of these criteria into account, allowing decision-makers to categorically assess replenishment capacity by manufacturer or across manufacturers. Being able to evaluate a company on the basis of individual information pillars is crucial. Two manufacturers may look equally strong on paper, but in practice one may turn out to underperform in a wartime scenario because of one or more exposed vulnerabilities. Returning to a potential Taiwan crisis, index rankings of this kind can help improve policymakers’ decisions, thereby strengthening deterrence in the Indo-Pacific.
Image caption: Defensewatch.org defense contractor tracking index
At the government level, manufacturer readiness analysis can shed light on where additional industrial investment or supplier diversification deserves attention. Defense planners could leverage the data to examine whether multiple programs depend on the same manufacturer or limited industrial input. Meanwhile, allies such as Japan and Australia could benefit from a clearer understanding of the industrial dependencies and resilience of their defense supply chains.
Industrial readiness is a key component of military power. The key question to keep in mind is this: “If a Taiwan crisis escalated into sustained combat, would Washington know which manufacturers could keep delivering, and would it pinpoint where the industrial base might struggle?” Beyond that, weapons inventories, as well as defense budgets/contracts, are an important, though insufficient, metric to monitor. Being able to readily assess a manufacturer’s surge capacity, investment quality, domestic contribution and adversary exposure adds another lens for understanding the industrial resilience of defense manufacturing. Deterrence depends not only on the military capabilities available to the United States at the outset of a conflict, but on the industrial capacity to sustain them. Measuring that capacity before a crisis arises is a strategic necessity.
Luis Márquez is a lawyer who graduated from the Universidad de los Andes in Venezuela. He holds a diploma in Strategic Intelligence Management, with a specialisation in Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT), from the National Technological University of Argentina. He is currently studying Urban and Port Security at the same institution, further developing his expertise in intelligence, security analysis, and the protection of critical infrastructure.

Ukrainian military forces struck the Novokuibyshevsk Oil Refinery in Russia with FP-1 drones
Kyiv • UNN
The facility has a designed refining capacity of approximately 8.8 million tonnes of oil per year.
On October 30, the Defense Forces struck the Novokuybyshevsk Refinery in Russia’s Samara region using FP-1 drones. This was reported by UNN , citing the Telegram channel of Fire Point — the drone manufacturer.
According to the company, numerous hits were recorded across the plant’s territory. In particular, one of the affected facilities was a diesel fuel hydrotreatment unit.
The Novokuybyshevsk Refinery has a designed processing capacity of approximately 8.8 million tonnes of oil per year.
According to the Telegram channel Exilenova+, at least 11 fire hotspots were recorded at the Novokuybyshevsk Refinery after the strike by the Ukrainian military.
It should be added
Strikes by the Defense Forces on Russian oil refineries are creating additional problems for Russia’s oil refining industry. Damage to critical equipment is forcing enterprises to spend significant sums on repairs, seek alternative suppliers, and reduce the production of petroleum products. At the same time, Russia’s sanctions make it more difficult to obtain foreign technologies and components needed to restore damaged facilities. As experts interviewed by UNN explained , repeated attacks intensify this effect: even after repairs, enterprises remain vulnerable to new strikes. Reduced refining may also create additional pressure on the domestic fuel market and increase the costs of supplying it between regions.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:38:00 UTC
17:38:00 KST

65 years on, many Turkish 'guest workers' in Germany face poverty
October 30, 2026
Düsseldorf Airport is a historically symbolic location. This is where the first Turkish "guest workers," as they were called at the time in Germany, arrived 65 years ago.
At a ceremony there in in mid-September, North Rhine-Westphalia's premier, Henrik Wüst, commemorated the courage of this first generation of migrants and their contribution to Germany's prosperity.
By the time recruitment ended in 1973, some 870,000 Turkish men and women had migrated to Germany for work. They toiled in the coal mines, did piecework on assembly lines or cleaned factory floors. Most settled in Düsseldorf, Cologne or Duisburg. "They have made our country more diverse, more open and stronger," said Wüst. However, he also stressed: "We will have reached our goal only once name, skin color and religion no longer matter."
Some upward mobility among migrants, but discrimination a big problem
According to integration expert Haci-Halil Uslucan, Germany is still a long way from that.
Even 65 years later, he told DW, people of Turkish descent still suffer a great deal of discrimination in Germany.
But he believes that the German Turkish labor recruitment agreement was, in the main, a success story.
"We've seen success in many areas, such as education. Today, we have a large number of college graduates, and we've seen professional advancement. And successful political careers. Take Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, for example," he said.
Uslucan himself is one such a success story. His father came to Berlin from Turkey and worked in the textile industry. Two years later, his father brought his wife and two sons to join him in Germany.
Haci-Halil Uslucan subsequently earned his Ph.D. in psychology and a professor of contemporary Turkish studies at the University of Duiburg-Essen.
One of his most recent research topics addresses the dark side of the labor recruitment agreement. He is examining loneliness, an issue that affects and troubles many former so-called "guest workers."
But poverty is also increasingly taking its toll on some people of Turkish descent reaching retirement age.
With a rate of between 25-30%, poverty in old age is twice as high among migrants in Germany than among Germans, which is about 12-14%, he says, adding that the disability rate and the rate of early retirement are significantly higher among migrants because the first generation did very heavy physical labor.
They are also twice as likely to become unemployed 10 years before reaching retirement age, says Uslucan.
"In addition, their monthly income is lower, they are more likely to have had employment gaps and worked in low-wage sectors. As a result, their pensions are also low."
Pensions €360 lower among Turkish citizens in Germany
An analysis by Germany's pension insurance fund (DRV) for the Mediendienst Integration, an information service for journalists on migration topics, uncovered some alarming figures: In Germany, pensioners with Turkish citizenship receive, on average, about €890 ($997) in pension benefits per month. That is €360 less than German pensioners, who receive €1,250 per month on average.
Even more troubling is that in June 2026, more than three times as many retirees with Turkish citizenship relied on top-up welfare benefits as Germans (9.3% compared to 2.7%).
One reason for this is that many of the Turkish workers who came to Germany were already in the middle of their working lives and consequently has less years to contribute to their pension fund, social scientist Eric Seils of the Hans Böckler Foundation in Düsseldorf told DW.
"But, of course, the most important reason is that they earned less in wages and had a shorter work history. The guest workers who came to Germany often went straight to factories, mines or construction sites. There, they didn't earn high hourly wages because they were often less educated than the Germans," he added.
With deindustrialization in the early 1970s and the oil crisis, many Turkish workers in Germany also lost their jobs.
"There weren't as many good jobs available at traditional industrial companies. Those who weren't as well-educated were more likely to become unemployed than those with an education — and the same was true for Germans. And when working lives are interrupted, that naturally has an impact on retirement benefits at some point."
Few chances for migrant workers to train
Janina Söhn of the Institute for Sociological Research (SOFI) at Göttingen University has also studied the issue of poverty among older immigrants in Germany.
It's a major problem in Germany that nearly one-third of immigrants are at risk of poverty, she said.
"This group faces even greater hardship than, for example, women in general, who already have a higher risk of poverty. And when you then look specifically at female migrants living alone, the figures are truly dire and alarming. If there were no family support, it would be an even sorrier situation."
Older Turkish migrants in Germany also often have limited opportunities to earn extra euros during retirement.
This is because either because they are poorly qualified or because the hard physical labor they performed when they were younger has left them physically unfit.
According to figures from Germany's Federal Employment Agency, the employment rate of for retired Turkish people living in Germany is only half that of Germans (5.2% compared to 10.8%).
"Basically, they face a whole series of disadvantages or hardships in life. That generation of guest workers was brought to Germany and then had to do the worst jobs here, whereas many Germans were able to progress through education and training," Söhn said.
The Turkish workers in Germany didn't get similar chances.
"The people who did these tough jobs, which are always necessary for any economy, paid for it with their health," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

Mexico: world's tallest Catrina unveiled for Día de Muertos in Mexico City
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:37:59 UTC
17:37:59 KST

The monumental female skeleton, roughly the height of an 11-storey building, surpasses the previous record of 28.15 metres set in Puerto Vallarta in 2023.
Created by around 140 artists and technicians from Taller Xibalbá, the figure wears a purple dress stretching more than 27 metres. Visitors gathered beneath the installation to take photographs as workers put the finishing touches to the display. Facing the Metropolitan Cathedral, the Catrina stands at the centre of an enormous ofrenda, a traditional altar honouring the dead, surrounded by a carpet of some 70,000 marigold plants grown in Xochimilco.
The installation pays tribute to Mexican artist José Guadalupe Posada, whose 1913 illustration of a skeletal woman became the inspiration for La Catrina, now one of the most recognisable symbols of Day of the Dead.
The elaborate display also features coloured sawdust carpets and figures inspired by axolotls and alebrijes, Mexico's fantastical folk-art creatures. Celebrated on 1 and 2 November, Day of the Dead brings families together to remember deceased loved ones through photographs, food, flowers and offerings. Marigolds, known as cempasúchil, are traditionally believed to guide spirits home through their colour and scent.
The record-breaking Catrina and its illuminated altar will remain on display until 2 November.

The U.S. Joint Staff has relieved Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia of his post following allegations of him leaking classified information.
ABC News reports this, citing a statement from a senior Pentagon official.
Sylvia served for 11 months as Director of Strategy, Planning, and Policy for the Joint Staff, position known as J-5.
According to the source, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth took ‘immediate action’ to dismiss the general due to a severe violation of his duties.
The investigation found that the official had allegedly shared classified information with the press about the war in Ukraine, the conflict with Iran and other sensitive matters.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell confirmed that the investigation was conducted by the U.S. Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
The case has been referred to the U.S. Department of Justice for possible criminal prosecution of the dismissed general.
Representatives of the Joint Staff initially thanked Brett Sylvia for his service but later retracted the statement in light of the circumstances surrounding the case.
The dismissal marks the latest in a series of personnel changes and early resignations among high command under the current Pentagon chief.
Generals Joseph McGee and Douglas Sims, who had planned to continue serving in senior military positions, had also previously left their posts on the Joint Staff.
Earlier, Poland’s Military Gendarmerie detained a participant in a reservist training course at the Military Medical Academy in Łódź.
He is suspected of espionage. The detainee holds dual Polish and Ukrainian citizenship.
