Bulgaria's CEC Issues Extra Machine Voting Rules After First-Round Disruptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

The Central Election Commission (CEC) has issued additional instructions to municipalities and district election commissions ahead of the runoff to prevent disruptions during machine voting, CEC spokesperson Stoyanka Balova said on BNT.
The new guidelines follow problems during the first round, when some voting procedures were interrupted and ballots were not saved to the machines' flash memory despite voters receiving partial receipts. The CEC is urging voters to follow the operating instructions carefully, particularly by waiting for the audible signal before removing either the control receipt or the voting card.
Assoc. Prof. Dr. Stoyanka Balova said that removing the receipt too early could prevent the voting procedure from being completed and the ballot from being recorded. She also pointed to premature removal of the voting card, which was reported at several polling stations across the country on election day.
The commission has also issued guidance on how polling stations should proceed in the event of a power outage. Technical problems affected 31 voting machines during the first round, including two devices abroad and 29 in Bulgaria. Voting could continue in 27 polling stations where two machines had been provided.
Balova described the number of malfunctioning devices as very small, explaining that some problems occurred during transportation. One machine had a damaged display, while several others failed to start because their motherboards had burned out.
Under the agreement with the service provider, all affected machines must be repaired during the week before the runoff, the CEC said. The commission also confirmed that no payment would be made for machines that were not used.
The first round also exposed shortcomings in ensuring ballot secrecy during machine voting. Some polling stations lacked privacy screens because the clips needed to attach them had not been delivered. The clips will not be available for the runoff, but the CEC has provided alternative instructions for arranging the voting areas.
Balova said polling stations without the required screens must organize the space so that voters can cast their ballots privately without being placed inside fully enclosed, dark booths. At the same time, voters must remain visible to members of the sectional election commissions, she explained, adding that ballot secrecy must be guaranteed through these alternative arrangements.
The CEC also identified inadequate preparation among some sectional election commissions for handling technical problems with voting machines during the first round. It has therefore issued further guidance to commission members ahead of the runoff.
The commission says it is ready to handle a higher turnout, with Balova stressing that the organizational requirements remain unchanged regardless of how many people vote.
She also highlighted the processing of election documentation after the first round. All polling stations abroad had completed the processing of their materials by 6 a.m., while district election commissions submitted their reports as early as Monday.
The CEC spokesperson put the estimated budget for both rounds of the election at approximately 3 million euros. The amount covers the public information campaign, payments to members of district and polling station election commissions and support staff, as well as training activities for both rounds.

ATHENS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Greece has arrested two Greek men and an Albanian national suspected of stealing copper gas pipes from a building, causing a leak that led to a deadly explosion in central Athens last month, authorities said.

French centrists’ feuding increases odds of Le Pen-Melenchon runoff
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:59:25 CET
16:59:25 KST

By Michel Rose
PARIS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Infighting has broken out among centrist candidates for France’s presidential race, splitting the mainstream vote and making a runoff between far-right Marine Le Pen and hard-left Jean-Luc Melenchon more likely.
Opinion polls before next April’s presidential election show Le Penis nearly certain to qualify for a second-round runoff in May and that Melenchon is consistently nudging ahead of mainstream candidates.
Centre-right Edouard Philippe, President Emmanuel Macron’s former prime minister, has so far been the centre’s torchbearer.
But Philippe’s lacklustre campaign, voter weariness near the end of Macron’s two terms, an explosive social and security context and the challenges he faces from within his own camp have hurt his polling, people in Macron’s camp and political analysts say.
“There’s panic on board because there was no scenario planned for this. They hadn’t anticipated the cataclysm under way,” said Philippe Moreau-Chevrolet, a political communications specialist at Sciences Po.
Philippe has also faced criticism over several awkward interventions — including suggesting in a podcast that ideally a newly elected president should have three months to rest before taking office — and political analysts say he is struggling to connect with voters at a time of rising political tensions.
“The terrible thing is that he isn’t cutting through,” Moreau-Chevrolet told Reuters. “They didn’t understand that you have to campaign. There’s a kind of dilettantism.”
The anxiety has sharpened tensions between Philippe and his main rival, Gabriel Attal, another former prime minister. They are locked in a battle over who should step aside for the centrist ticket.
Philippe fell to 15% support in an IFOP-Fiducial poll for Le Figaro newspaper, a six-point drop since September. That is below the 16.5% for Melenchon, who would have enough to qualify for a runoff against Le Pen.
Attal stood at 13%, behind Melenchon and Raphael Glucksmann, a mainstream centre-left candidate.
Under pressure from lawmakers in his camp to abandon his presidential ambitions and rally to Philippe, Attal irritated many Macron allies this week by reviving the idea of a broad centrist primary, a proposal critics say risks fuelling division at a time when moderates can least afford it.
Still, Attal has leverage. As leader of Macron’s Renaissance party, he controls the purse strings of the party machine.
CENTRIST VOTE FRAGMENTS
“It’s catastrophic,” said Jean-Baptiste Moreau, a former lawmaker from Macron’s camp.
“They are attacking one another in the media and they are both collapsing in the polls. We’re heading straight towards an RN-LFI second round,” he said of Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) and Melenchon’s France Unbowed (LFI). “In the current state of opinion, I don’t see how we avoid it.”
The fragmentation stretches beyond the Philippe-Attal feud.
On the centre-left, Glucksmann has gained ground after winning the Socialist primary. On the right, Bruno Retailleau, a former interior minister, and David Lisnard, the free-market mayor of Cannes, are targeting the same moderate electorate.
Philippe’s supporters say reports of his demise are premature. Laurent Marcangeli, a member of Philippe’s party Horizons, acknowledged recent polling setbacks but said the former prime minister remained the only centrist candidate with a realistic path to the runoff.
“He’s still in the race for the second round and to prevent a Le Pen-Melenchon duel,” said Marcangeli, adding that in some polls Attal scored as low as single digits.
Some Macron allies, however, are openly questioning whether either man should carry on. They say any association with Macron, who is finishing his second term at record-low popularity, will weigh on a centrist candidate.
“The two of them are collapsing,” said Perrine Goulet, a lawmaker from Macron ally MoDem. “Any candidate who has been in a Macron government is going to be struggling.”
With Le Pen and Melenchon consolidating support at opposite ends of the spectrum, she said moderates needed to put aside personal ambitions and rally behind a single contender able to unite supporters of Glucksmann through to Retailleau.
“We’re calling on everyone to put their egos aside and find the best candidate,” Goulet said.
“If we keep Glucksmann on one side, Retailleau on the other, Edouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal, we’ll end up with an LFI-RN second round. The danger is simply too great.”
(Editing by Mark John and Timothy Heritage)

By Ibrahim and Ndiamitso
MINNA, Nigeria, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Families of 37 artisinal miners who died in custody in Nigeria want swift justice and the return of property seized during their arrest, saying no financial compensation will make up for their loss.
A presidential panel on Tuesday found that the detainees, who were suspected of being illegal miners, had died from overcrowding, extreme heat, dehydration and neglect while being held by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger state last month.
Nigeria’s government welcomed the panel’s findings, and Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said the panel’s report had been sent to the attorney-general for immediate judicial action. He did not respond to requests for comment on when victims’ families and survivors would receive compensation.
The deaths, including of teenagers, triggered protests in Nigeria, raising new concerns about conditions in detention facilities and the treatment of suspects awaiting trial.
“What we wanted was for our children to be alive and return to us,” said Zainab Salihu, whose son was among the dead.
She said the deaths in detention had led to the deterioration of the health of her husband, who later died. Reuters was unable to verify the circumstances of her husband’s death.
“No matter how much money they give us, it will never bring our children back,” Salihu said.
Dantala Tanko, whose 25-year-old son Suleiman died in detention, is struggling to come to terms with his loss.
“Now he is gone, and this is deeply painful for me. I know he will never return,” he said after praying at his son’s grave.
Some survivors said they appreciated the investigation’s findings, but wanted accountability.
“Officers who demonstrate such disregard for human life should not remain in positions of authority. They must be held accountable, and appropriate disciplinary action should be taken,” said said 25-year-old Dauda Shehu.
Abdulsalam Yakubu, 23, said government action had been slow. He said he wanted the government to return motocycles, phones, mining equipment and gold which he said had been seized during the victims’ arrest.
“We have suffered enough. We are asking for justice, the promised support, and the return of our property so that we can begin to rebuild our lives,” he told Reuters.

Cyberattack on Refrigerators: Pentagon Investigates Series of Malfunctions at Military Bases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:56:54 UTC
16:56:54 KST

The Pentagon is investigating a series of freezer malfunctions at US military bases in August as a suspected cyberattack.
Reuters reported this, citing four sources familiar with the matter.
US military investigators have already contacted their French counterparts to exchange information about a similar cyberattack targeting commercial refrigeration units in Europe.
The Pentagon confirmed that a unit of the U.S. Cyber Command is working in close coordination with interagency and law enforcement partners.
In August, the malfunctions affected at least six military stores at US bases where service members buy groceries.
In some cases, the refrigerators did not simply shut down but switched to defrost mode on their own, causing the temperature inside to rise and food to spoil.
A similar incident occurred in France, where hackers hijacked temperature controllers at more than 350 establishments and stores.
In some cases in France, the temperature in commercial refrigerators was raised so high that the equipment caught fire, with losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
Cybersecurity experts say these vulnerabilities stem from outdated controllers, which were originally designed for standalone operation, being connected to the internet.
Earlier, the Global Food Safety Initiative (GFSI) called for strengthening the security of refrigeration systems, warning that a hacked cooling system can be just as dangerous as a malfunctioning one.
It was previously reported that the Pentagon suffered a data breach affecting more than three million people connected to the US military.
The exposed information includes Social Security numbers and details of the positions held by military personnel and civilian employees.

Bolsonaro's self-exile, ChatGPT blunder cloud political ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:55:00 UTC
16:55:00 KST

Brazilian Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro has faced widespread ridicule and mounting political isolation after fleeing to the United States and declaring himself Brazil's rightful leader following his defeat in Sunday's presidential election.
The 45-year-old's claims sparked a wave of mockery on Brazilian social media, where pop star Anitta jokingly declared herself free of cellulite, one influencer proclaimed himself the "true president" of Twitter, and another announced he had won the next lottery.
The eldest son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro stunned Brazil's political establishment Wednesday when he published a statement challenging the election outcome and presenting himself as the country's legitimate leader. The declaration, however, quickly became an embarrassment after a series of confusing revisions and failed to win support from influential figures within his own political camp.
Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday after leaving Brazil through Argentina and Ecuador, despite a Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his passports as part of ongoing investigations, including a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing.
Hours after arriving in the United States, he published a statement on social media proclaiming himself Brazil's "true president-elect." About an hour later, he deleted the document and replaced it with a revised version describing himself as the country's "leader."
The abrupt change prompted questions about the original statement, which also featured an outdated version of Brazil's coat of arms, abandoned in the 1960s.
A close Bolsonaro ally, right-wing influencer and podcast host Paulo Figueiredo, later blamed the errors on ChatGPT, saying the chatbot had been used to help prepare the document.
Figueiredo, who acts as an unofficial spokesperson for the Bolsonaro family in the United States and initially circulated the statement to journalists, said the document had passed through several drafts involving multiple contributors.
According to Figueiredo, Flavio's younger brother, former Congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, sought ChatGPT's assistance in finalizing the letter. The chatbot allegedly inserted an earlier version of the text and an outdated national emblem.
"When generating the document, AI ended up including an earlier version of the text, in which Flavio presented himself as the true 'president-elect'," Figueiredo wrote on X, adding that the mistakes were discovered only after the document had been distributed to the press.
He said Flavio eventually chose the word "leader" for legal and moral reasons, describing the changes as minor and claiming those involved found the mistake amusing.
OpenAI and Flavio Bolsonaro's press officers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Despite the revised wording, Figueiredo maintained that the senator considered Sunday's election illegitimate and intended to continue challenging the result.
The declaration drew widespread condemnation in Brazilian media, with several outlets describing its language as an attempt to undermine democratic institutions.
O Globo newspaper likened Flavio Bolsonaro to a "lunatic asylum Napoleon," while Folha de S.Paulo dismissed the statement as "pathetic."
Politicians across the political spectrum called for the election results to be respected, further exposing the senator's isolation.
Among the most significant rebukes came from Sao Paulo Gov. Tarcisio de Freitas, a former minister under Jair Bolsonaro who had been considered a leading contender to represent the right in the next presidential race before the former president backed his son.
"We are democrats. The election result is sovereign. What we have seen is the will of the majority of the population, which must be respected," De Freitas told Estadao newspaper.
With Flavio now outside Brazil and his political standing weakened, attention has quickly shifted to who might emerge as the conservative movement's leading figure.
De Freitas, who enjoys strong support in business circles, acknowledged that a presidential bid in 2030 was a possibility.
Other prominent Bolsonaro allies have also rejected claims that the election was stolen.
Rogerio Marinho, who coordinated Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign, said there was no evidence of electoral fraud. Supreme Court Justice Kassio Nunes Marques, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, also issued a statement defending the security and integrity of Brazil's electoral process.
The election authority and international observers have recognized the result, while leaders around the world have acknowledged Lula's victory.
Despite his defeat, Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to lead the opposition from the United States, seeking to maintain his influence over Brazil's conservative movement while remaining outside the country.
His departure has not, however, translated into an immediate loss of political strength for the right. Conservatives secured substantial representation in Congress, and Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) is expected to hold the largest number of seats when the new legislature begins its term in February.
But political analyst Geraldo Monteiro of the State University of Rio de Janeiro said Flavio's attempt to establish himself as a leader in exile was unlikely to command the loyalty he expected.
Rather than a political misstep, Monteiro described the declaration as a calculated effort to preserve his authority over the conservative camp.
"I do not believe he has the means to lead the opposition from afar, as the newly elected officials have already secured their seats and no longer need him," Monteiro told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
He said the statement had drawn a dividing line within the right between politicians willing to demonstrate unwavering loyalty to the Bolsonaro family and those unwilling to become involved in another attempt to undermine democratic institutions.
Monteiro also drew parallels between Flavio's conduct and that of his father, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula.
The backlash has extended to the leadership of Bolsonaro's own party.
On Thursday, PL leader Valdemar Costa Neto visited Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving his sentence under house arrest. Asked about Flavio's statement afterward, Costa Neto made clear that the party was not endorsing the declaration.
"No one approves" of the letter, he said, adding that the party needed to "move forward."

Ebola is a severe viral disease that can cause life-threatening illness and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people. Although the discharge of the final patients represents an important milestone for the MSF facility in Mongbwalu, it does not mean the outbreak has ended or that new cases cannot emerge. The charity's announcement concerns patients being treated at this particular centre, rather than the wider situation across Ituri province or the country.

‘My life is buried here’: Iranian man whose 12 family members were killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:51:08 UTC
16:51:08 KST

‘My life is buried here’: Iranian man whose 12 family members were killed
Hamed Mirzaei lost his wife, parents and many others in a devastating US-Israeli attack on Tehran.
Hamed Mirzaei lost 12 members of his family in an attack on a residential building in Tehran. Among those killed was his wife, 26-year-old Mohadeseh. The young couple had been planning to start a family.
He describes how the United States-Israeli attack on his home on March 9, 2026, changed his life in this first-person account, shared with Al Jazeera:
“Seven months have passed since the bombing. Even now, on many days, when I come to my senses, I find myself back at my destroyed home, searching for my loved ones.
“My grandfather and my father’s uncle built the house that was hit. They divided its apartments among their children. A year ago, when I got married, my wife and I moved into one of the apartments in the same building. We were just beginning to prepare for a child. We were young, with our whole lives ahead of us. Then the bombing happened.
“March 9 was a Monday. At about 1:00 in the afternoon, I left home to check in at work. At 2:30 pm, my wife messaged me, asking me to buy her some headache medicine on my way back. I called her to ask which medicine she wanted, but her phone was busy. We were expecting guests at home, so I called our guest’s phone. That line was busy, too. I hung up, intending to call my wife again.
“I was five minutes from home when I suddenly heard a whistling sound. The first missile had just struck.
“The ground shook beneath my feet from the force of the explosion. With my phone still in my hand, I called my wife again, but her phone was unreachable. I began calling my family members, my grandfather, my father, my mother. All their phones were unreachable.
“Even so, I thought our home had not been hit. I kept telling myself it was impossible that they had struck our house. I thought perhaps a missile had hit somewhere else in our neighbourhood. In those moments, all I wanted was to get home and see that the house was still standing.
“In those same minutes, five more missiles struck our home.
“When I arrived, I saw that everyone in the neighbourhood had come out of their homes, but I still couldn’t bring myself to step into the street. It never even crossed my mind that those missiles could have hit our house. But they had. Even from a distance, it was clear that all that remained of the house was its skeleton.
“When I reached it, everything was burning. All I could think about was getting to the second floor and finding my wife, but the staircase was gone. Several neighbours from the first floor were trapped beneath the rubble. The Red Crescent helped rescue them.
“I thought that if they kept searching, perhaps they would find my family alive somewhere beneath the debris, too. But they didn’t. No one was found that hour. Nor in the hours that followed. By nightfall, no one else had been found in the building. Twelve members of my family were missing, and I still couldn’t bring myself to leave.
“That night, the next day, the day after that, and every day following the attack, I returned to my home. For 20 days, I searched through the rubble and the remnants of the missiles and explosions for my loved ones. There was nothing left.
“My wife was killed. My sister-in-law, who had been a guest in our home, was killed. My father and mother, my grandfather and grandmother, my aunt’s husband and her daughter, my uncle, my father’s cousin, his wife and their child were all killed. Twelve members of my family died in the attack, and people ask me how I am.
“I miss them. I miss them more with every passing day. At first, I thought that perhaps, with time, our grief would ease and we would find some peace. But we haven’t. As each day passes, I feel worse.
“I was an only child, and I always thought that, although I had no brothers or sisters, I had a large family with whom I would grow old. All my life, the members of our extended family had lived together, side by side. Now all those people, and all the love that flowed through our family, have vanished.
“I am the only one left. There is no one else from my family. I am utterly alone.
“I am living proof for anyone who still believes that war can lead to a good outcome. Anyone who thinks war is good should look at what has happened to me and ask themselves: ‘What, in any of this, is good?’
“The building where I was born, the building where my father was born, the building where I had hoped my child would be born, all of it was destroyed in a fraction of a second. My home and my family were wiped out together. And when I miss them, I truly don’t know where to turn or what to look at.
“Seven months have passed since the day they destroyed our home, and every day, when I wake up, I come here to look at the ruins. I cannot bring myself to leave this place. I feel as though my life is buried here, and I return every day, hoping I might find some piece of it. But there is nothing left.
“When someone asks me what I am thinking or how I feel, I cannot answer. Everything I have ever done in my life was for the happiness of my family. Now I no longer have a family for whom I can do anything.
“Every day, I ask myself: ‘Why do I keep going?’ I have no answer.
“The difference between me and my family, who were killed, is that they were buried beneath the rubble, while I am still walking around. Other than that, I am just as dead as they are. The only difference is that my name is not included among the dead.”

How cleaning affects the energy of the home
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:51:00 EET
16:51:00 KST

How cleaning affects the energy of the home
Kyiv • UNN
Folk traditions associate cleanliness with prosperity, while cleaning is advised to begin from the top. The practical benefit is less dust and clutter.
Cleaning can be not only a household chore but also a way to change the atmosphere at home and your own well-being. In folk beliefs, a clean space is associated with prosperity, good luck, and new opportunities. More details about how to tidy up your home, which traditions are associated with cleaning, and what can help make your home more comfortable will be provided by UNN.
Details
In different cultures, cleaning has not only practical but also symbolic significance. It is associated with cleansing from negativity, renewing one's living space, and attracting prosperity. Such beliefs are particularly common in feng shui traditions and folk omens.
Why clutter is associated with negative energy
According to Eastern beliefs, the energy of Qi plays an important role in a person's life. Dust, cluttered corners, and accumulated unnecessary items are believed to hinder its free flow. That is why feng shui followers recommend regularly clearing the home of clutter and not neglecting hard-to-reach places. Particular attention is paid to broken objects, old clothes that are no longer used, and damaged dishes. In folk beliefs, such things symbolize stagnation and tie people to the past, while getting rid of them is perceived as an opportunity to make room for new changes in life. There is also a wholly practical side to this tradition. In particular, when there are fewer unnecessary things at home, it is easier to find what is needed, maintain cleanliness, and organize household life. And the feeling of an orderly space can contribute to calm and comfort.
Where to start when cleansing the home
It is important not to try to do everything at once. First, you can sort through items that have not been used for a long time, clear surfaces, and pay attention to places where dust accumulates. This approach allows you to gradually organize the space and prevents cleaning from becoming an exhausting task.
How to clean properly so that there is more space in the home
In traditions of cleansing the home, not only the result but also the sequence of actions is important. In particular, followers of energy practices advise starting with upper surfaces and gradually moving to lower ones. First, dust is wiped from ceilings, lighting fixtures, and the tops of cabinets. Then they move on to shelves, tables, and other furniture. After that, carpets are cleaned and the floor is washed. This sequence also has a practical advantage: dust and debris that fall while the upper surfaces are being cleaned can be removed at the end.
To remove dust, a dry cloth is used first, and then, if necessary, the surface is wiped with a damp cloth. According to folk beliefs, the floor—and especially the threshold of the home—is best washed with salt, ordinary or sea salt, in order to cleanse the house energetically. Do not forget about corners and remote areas of rooms. In folk beliefs, these are supposedly the places where negative energy accumulates. From the perspective of ordinary cleaning, these areas also require attention, since dust that is not always immediately visible can collect there.
Why it is important to get rid of unnecessary things
If broken or unnecessary items are found during cleaning, it is worth deciding whether there is any reason to keep them at home. Things that are no longer used take up space and make it more difficult to maintain order. In a symbolic sense, letting go of excess is associated with readiness for a new stage of life. Therefore, sorting through a closet, shelves, or a storage room can become a kind of renewal ritual. It is only important not to throw things away thoughtlessly; items that are still suitable for use can, in particular, be given to those who need them.
Which day of the week is best for cleaning
Folk omens attribute special significance to each day of the week. According to these beliefs, the time when order is restored can symbolically influence prosperity, good luck, and the atmosphere in the home.
In some beliefs, Monday is considered an unfavorable day for cleaning, as it is associated with the risk of financial losses.
Tuesday is called a favorable day for tidying up and symbolically attracting monetary energy.
Wednesday is associated with prosperity in affairs and business.
In folk beliefs, Thursday symbolizes cleansing the space and opening up new opportunities.
Friday is advised not to be overloaded with heavy housework, especially if fatigue has accumulated by the end of the week.
Saturday is traditionally considered a convenient time for a thorough cleaning, when one can devote attention to the entire home.
Sunday is often reserved for rest rather than extensive household chores.
How to Finish Cleaning and Refresh the Atmosphere
After tidying up, it is worth airing out the rooms. Fresh air will help refresh the atmosphere in the home, while open windows are symbolically associated with the movement of energy and the release of stagnation. Another important element is one’s own mood. If cleaning is perceived not as an endless obligation but as an opportunity to take care of yourself and your space, the process can become more enjoyable. You can play your favorite music or, after finishing your tasks, create a cozy atmosphere with pleasant lighting or a favorite fragrance.
Some traditions also recommend wiping surfaces with water containing a small amount of salt, considering this a way of symbolically cleansing them. However, this practice has no proven ability to eliminate negative energy. When caring for surfaces, one should follow the manufacturer’s recommendations, as salt water may damage certain materials.
Ideas about the energy of the home, favorable days for cleaning, and money-related omens remain part of cultural traditions. For some, they are important rituals that help them tune in to positive changes. Others view them as interesting customs without literal meaning. At the same time, regular cleaning has clear practical benefits: it helps get rid of dust, organize belongings, and maintain comfort in the home. Getting rid of unnecessary items can also be an opportunity to reconsider habits and arrange everyday life more conveniently. Therefore, the best approach, of course, is to maintain cleanliness at a pace that is comfortable for you, without turning folk omens into strict prohibitions.

Netanyahu survives the election, but Eisenkot holds key to replacing him - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:50:48 UTC
16:50:48 KST

On Tuesday night, Gadi Eisenkot delivered the speech of a man who could already see the Prime Minister's Office on the horizon. He was not alone. The first exit polls pointed to a clear victory for the opposition bloc and the approaching end of Benjamin Netanyahu's tenure.
In the rooms where politicians awaited the actual results, however, the picture gradually changed. Likud climbed to 27 seats, Yashar settled at 21, and the gap between the blocs narrowed. Eisenkot discovered what Shimon Peres had learned long ago: Exit polls are excellent at generating headlines, but somewhat less effective at transferring power.
Netanyahu, for his part, can breathe a sigh of relief. His party is once again the largest, and he remains prime minister. But the good news ends there. The outgoing coalition bloc holds just 53 seats, eight short of the 61 needed for a majority. The opposition bloc has 48, while Ra'am and the Joint List hold 19 between them. These are the numbers according to the latest reported vote count. Anyone looking for a government in them will need to bring something else to the table: Partners willing to sit together.
Voters weakened the outgoing coalition but did not give the opposition parties a majority that would allow them to form a government without reaching new agreements. Netanyahu can remain in office as long as no alternative government is established. Eisenkot must find a way to form one.
The incumbent prime minister's advantage is already clear: He does not need a new agreement to remain in office. While his rivals try to resolve their differences, Netanyahu can use his political connections, maintain his partners' loyalty, and examine who in the opposing camp might prefer a compromise to another election.
The equation Eisenkot must solve begins with the 48 seats held by Yashar, B'Yachad, the Democrats, and Yisrael Beytenu. Ra'am has eight seats, and the Joint List has 11. With Ra'am alone, the opposition bloc would reach 56 MKs; with both Arab factions, it would reach 67.
The arithmetic of a minority government
These are mathematical combinations, not coalition agreements. Eisenkot does not necessarily need 61 votes in favor of his government for it to be sworn in, but he does need a majority in the confidence vote. If all 48 members of the opposition bloc support the government, 53 members of Netanyahu's bloc oppose it, and all 19 members of the Arab factions abstain, the government will fail to win the Knesset's confidence.
To change that outcome, Eisenkot will have to secure additional support or ensure that some of the 53 opponents do not vote against him. Support from Ra'am, for example, could be sufficient numerically if the remaining Arab faction abstains and all 48 opposition-bloc MKs vote in favor. But that calculation depends on agreements that Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman opposed during the campaign.
Although 67 MKs do not belong to Netanyahu's bloc, they have not agreed to form a government together. They may manage to unite around certain measures in the Knesset without agreeing on the identity of the next prime minister. Netanyahu could remain at the head of the executive branch while his rivals assemble a majority against him in parliamentary votes.
For Eisenkot, the challenge is to turn agreement against Netanyahu into agreement in favor of a particular government. Those are two different political tasks.
Netanyahu ran a familiar election campaign: He placed himself at the center, relegated his partners to supporting roles, and portrayed every vote for a small right-wing party as a risk to his continued rule. Likud benefited from this approach far more than its partners did.
Otzma Yehudit won seven seats, United Torah Judaism seven, Shas six, and Religious Zionism and Zehut six. Together with them, Netanyahu reaches 53 seats, eight short of the majority he needs.
No party in the opposition bloc has pledged to join his government, and any attempt to recruit an outside partner could require concessions that anger his existing allies. Yisrael Beytenu has already made clear that even an offer allowing Liberman to serve first in a rotation arrangement would not change his refusal to join a government with Netanyahu.
Relations within the Right could also shift. During the campaign, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich had to defend their voters against Likud's efforts to draw away support. They may now have to choose between loyalty to Netanyahu and concern that a unity government could be formed without them.
Netanyahu needs them to preserve his bloc, but if he wants to form a government, he may have to seek additional partners who would not necessarily agree to sit alongside them. The more Netanyahu signals that he is exploring a broad government, the greater their incentive to make clear what they will not accept.
They could complicate his efforts precisely when he is trying to expand his room for maneuver. From their perspective, however, threatening to dissolve the partnership too early could leave them outside any new arrangement.
Eisenkot faces resistance from his own allies
For Eisenkot, the story begins with success. He entered the election as the leading candidate to replace Netanyahu, pushed Bennett into second place within the camp, and built a party that won 21 seats.
His personal success did not solve the coalition problem. The opposition parties' 48 seats provide a starting point for negotiations, but there is still a long road to swearing in a government.
The disagreements began months earlier, when Eisenkot raised the possibility of forming a minority government. Liberman publicly opposed the idea, while those close to Bennett also viewed it as an attempt by Eisenkot to draw voters away from within the bloc. All three wanted to replace Netanyahu, but they did not agree on how to establish the government that would succeed him.
Yair Golan was quick to propose a course of action. While his partners remained silent, the Democrats chairman called on them to include Ra'am and the Joint List in the calculation of the 67 MKs outside Netanyahu's bloc and to establish a government in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens.
He also criticized the distinction between Jewish and Arab votes. But his call did not produce agreement among the factions. Bennett and Liberman did not join the initiative, and support from both Arab factions for any particular government is far from guaranteed.
Mansour Abbas has already served as a coalition partner in a government headed by Bennett. The Joint List, by contrast, holds different positions on diplomatic and security issues, and cooperation with it would require Bennett and Liberman to cross a political line they have pledged not to cross.
Agreeing to rely on Ra'am does not necessarily indicate a willingness to rely on the Joint List as well. To swear in a government, the parties will have to reach agreements on the confidence vote and subsequently on the budget, security policy, and government decisions. Even outside support will require clarifying the conditions imposed by the factions asked to provide it.
Claims of "election theft" voiced in Likud circles after the polls closed already point to a possible line of attack against a government dependent on the Arab parties: Challenging its legitimacy.
Bennett and Liberman, who pledged not to rely on those factions, would be particularly vulnerable to such criticism.
Senior Yisrael Beytenu figures have spoken of "the sin of arrogance by Gadi and his people" and the "selfish campaign" he conducted. They argue that talk of a minority government supported by Arab parties drove away voters who had already moved to the opposition bloc, and accuse Eisenkot and Golan of returning approximately seven seats to Netanyahu's camp.
That anger is complicating negotiations before they have even begun. Liberman spent years building his political strength around a hard line toward the Arab parties and, ahead of the election, even sought to disqualify Ra'am.
Now, after his party blamed talk of a minority government backed by Arab parties for the loss of seats, it will be difficult for him to agree to such a move.
His refusal would not necessarily rule out every possibility of forming an alternative government, but it would leave Eisenkot without Yisrael Beytenu's seven seats and force him to find another combination.
Bennett faces a similar problem, although his political history complicates it in a different way. He has already formed a government with Ra'am and paid a political price for doing so.
He now leads a party with 12 seats, significantly smaller than Yashar's. Joining an Eisenkot-led government could give him influence, but it could also cement his position as the junior partner of the man who overtook him.
For Bennett, the decision also concerns his political future. If he joins Eisenkot's government, he will have to demonstrate to his voters why they should continue to see him as an independent alternative. If he stays outside, he risks being remembered as the politician who held the power needed to change the government but chose not to use it.
In August, Eisenkot spoke of presenting a government with 58 or 59 seats, without asking anything of the Arab parties. Now the opposition bloc holds only 48 seats.
If all 19 Arab MKs abstain and all 53 members of Netanyahu's bloc vote against the government, Eisenkot will lack a majority in the confidence vote. Conversely, support from Ra'am and abstention by the Joint List could allow a government to be sworn in with 56 votes in favor and 53 against.
Herzog's decision and the battle for the Knesset
Even before that, Eisenkot must deal with President Isaac Herzog.
The president is expected to receive the official results next week, hold consultations with the factions, and decide whom to task with forming a government. Likud is the largest faction, but the central question will be who can demonstrate a realistic chance of forming a government.
If 61 MKs unite in recommending a candidate, that will carry political significance, but recommendations do not guarantee a majority in the confidence vote.
Herzog will have to assess which MK has a chance of forming a government, in accordance with his authority under Basic Law: The Government.
A faction could recommend Eisenkot to prevent Netanyahu from receiving the mandate while still refusing to support his government. Conversely, a faction could decline to recommend him but later allow his government to be sworn in through support or abstention.
The number of recommendations will therefore be important, but it cannot substitute for establishing the agreements needed to win the confidence vote.
Herzog has already called on party leaders to approach consultations with an open mind and avoid another election.
The president can encourage compromises, hold talks, and try to identify a formula for a unity government, but he cannot impose one on the lawmakers who would have to vote for it.
The timetable also matters. Whoever receives the mandate will have 28 days to negotiate, with the possibility of an extension of up to 14 additional days. If that attempt fails, further procedures stipulated by law will become available.
Throughout this period, the outgoing government will remain in office until another is formed. Netanyahu will not be required to leave the Prime Minister's Office after 28 days, even if his rival receives the mandate.
During the mandate period, Eisenkot could try to change the parliamentary balance of power while Netanyahu still serves as caretaker prime minister.
Success in such an effort could restrict the outgoing government's ability to control the legislature and give Eisenkot a political achievement even before he reaches agreement on the composition of a government.
Netanyahu would continue to run the executive branch, but he might struggle to control the parliamentary agenda.
Eisenkot could show his voters that the majority opposed to the outgoing government can deliver results even without a coalition agreement.
To do so, he would have to bring MKs into the plenum repeatedly and ensure that they vote together. If he succeeds in replacing the Knesset speaker or advancing significant legislation, he could point to a tangible achievement and strengthen his position in coalition negotiations.
Failure in the first votes would expose his weakness precisely in the arena where he appears to enjoy a numerical advantage.
For Netanyahu, this would be a particularly uncomfortable scenario. As long as his rivals argue over forming a government, he benefits from the advantages of incumbency.
If they begin cooperating in the Knesset, he will have to contend with a majority whose effectiveness does not depend on agreement over the distribution of ministerial portfolios.
Netanyahu has a clear interest in deepening the divisions between them, particularly over cooperation with the Arab parties.
There is also a trap for Eisenkot. Bennett and Liberman may agree to act against Netanyahu in the Knesset precisely because such votes do not require them to support a minority government under Eisenkot.
Eisenkot could claim parliamentary achievements and apply pressure on the government, but those successes would not necessarily bring him closer to the Prime Minister's Office.
Netanyahu can remain in office as long as no alternative government is formed, even if he struggles to advance his parliamentary agenda.
Unity, Trump, and the possibility of another election
And what of a unity government?
The arithmetic is tempting. Likud and Yashar together hold 48 seats. With Bennett's B'Yachad, they reach 60 even before adding other partners.
But the numbers do not answer the disagreements awaiting the leaders around the negotiating table.
Who would serve first in a rotation? Would Netanyahu agree to a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7? Would Eisenkot agree to serve under him? What would happen to the military conscription law? Would Ben-Gvir and Smotrich be left out? And what would guarantee that any agreement signed would survive the first crisis?
Eisenkot and Bennett have pledged not to sit in a government with Netanyahu.
Breaking that promise would carry a heavy price, but outright refusal does not guarantee a way out of the deadlock either.
Another election could return all sides to the same position, or even give Netanyahu the eight seats he currently lacks. The leaders will have to consider that risk as well.
The political price of a unity government would not be shared equally by Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Netanyahu could present it as an expansion of his government's support base and a means of reducing his dependence on his existing partners.
Eisenkot would have to explain how joining a government headed by the man he sought to replace could be reconciled with breaking the central promise he made to voters.
The rotation question would be central to any such negotiations: Who would serve first, and what would ensure that the other side receives the position when its turn comes?
Even if Eisenkot manages to secure significant policy commitments from Netanyahu, ensuring that the agreement is honored would remain difficult, particularly if Netanyahu serves as prime minister during the first stage.
Then there is Donald Trump.
The US president supported Netanyahu before the election, and he may try to influence the formation of the next government as well.
Washington carries weight in security relations, the Iran issue, and the possibility of offering an Israeli government a shared agenda with the US administration.
If Trump proposes a significant diplomatic or security initiative to Netanyahu and Eisenkot that requires a broad government, he could change their calculations.
Netanyahu could argue that unity is necessary to seize a diplomatic opportunity, while Eisenkot would have to decide whether the opportunity justifies a partnership with Netanyahu.
American pressure could give both leaders a public explanation for a compromise they had initially resisted.
But for that argument to be convincing, a concrete American initiative would be needed, not merely Trump's desire to see a broad Israeli government.
Yet even Trump, for all his influence, does not hold the 61st seat.
Public support for Netanyahu does not turn Liberman into his coalition partner. A meeting at the White House does not resolve the question of a commission of inquiry, and Herzog's decision on whom to entrust with forming a government remains subject to Israeli law, whatever the White House's preferences.
The coming days will first reveal whether Eisenkot can assemble broad enough recommendations to the president.
It will then become clear whether that same majority can act together in the Knesset and whether either leader is prepared to pay the political price of a minority or unity government.
If no agreement is reached, another election remains a possibility.
Netanyahu will continue to head the caretaker government until an alternative government is formed.
Eisenkot, meanwhile, will have to persuade voters who have already voted for change but have not given his camp an agreed path toward achieving it.
Netanyahu can wait in the Prime Minister's Office. Eisenkot must persuade politicians who struggle to agree even on how to replace him.
This is not the result of an exit poll. It is the political outcome of the election.

Louvre heist emboldened art thiefs, leaving Europe's smaller museums on high alert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:50:21 UTC
16:50:21 KST

Two men wearing head torches climbed through a forced-open window at the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum near Parma on the night of March 22 and calmly lifted artworks by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse from the walls.
Within three minutes, they had passed the works, valued at about €9 million ($10 million), to an accomplice and fled. At the museum's main gate, a fourth man discharged a fire extinguisher when the alarm sounded, distracting the custodian.
"Whatever could go wrong, did," said Stefano Roffi, director of the private foundation that runs the museum.
The raid was one of a string of museum thefts in France, Italy and Spain since last year's heist at the Louvre in Paris, raising concerns that criminals are increasingly targeting smaller institutions with fewer resources to protect valuable collections.
"This is where we see the 'Louvre effect'," said Marc Balcells, a Barcelona-based researcher specializing in crimes against cultural heritage. "If the Louvre was so easy to rob, just imagine a tiny museum in a rural area or a smaller town."
Works by Antonello da Messina vanished from a museum in his Sicilian hometown in August, while two Renoirs were stolen from Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera the following month.
In Spain, thieves stole hundreds of historic gold coins from museums in Badajoz and Albacete and made off with a Bronze Age treasure in Villena, near Alicante.
A 2024 survey by France's Culture Ministry found only one in four cultural institutions had an emergency and risk-prevention plan, while nearly half lacked video surveillance.
Who checks when the alarm goes off?
A French parliamentary report in May said museums lacked the resources and preparation to adequately protect artworks and artifacts.
In Italy, the challenge is amplified by the way the country's cultural heritage is spread across hundreds of towns and institutions, a legacy of centuries of fragmented rule.
"That is also what makes our system distinctive: works remain in the places where they were created,” said Antonella Pinna, president of the Italian committee of the International Council of Museums. "But we need to make life harder for criminals."
The council worked with Italy's Culture Ministry and the Carabinieri on museum security guidelines published in 2015, but Pinna said technology alone was not enough.
"If an alarm goes off, someone has to make sure it is checked," she said.
In a narrow street in the Tuscan town of Sansepolcro, the civic museum displays four works by Renaissance master Piero della Francesca, born just steps away in the 15th century.
The Louvre theft "affected us deeply because cultural heritage is central to Sansepolcro's identity. It is our soul," culture councilor Francesca Mercati told Reuters.
After the Louvre raid, officers from the Carabinieri's cultural heritage protection unit recommended more cameras, longer retention of CCTV footage and tighter controls on bags and bulky clothing.
"We immediately implemented those recommendations," Mercati said.
A vast network to protect
The scale of the challenge is daunting.
Italy has more than 4,400 museums and similar institutions, according to national statistics agency ISTAT. Spain has about 1,500 museums, while France has more than 1,200 institutions carrying the official "Musees de France" designation, alongside hundreds of smaller collections.
Protecting such a broad network is particularly difficult for smaller institutions that depend on local funding.
Florence Imbert, a Paris-based security consultant for cultural institutions, said 85% of small French museums were run by local authorities with limited financial resources.
"The budget is key to winning the war," she said.
France's Culture Ministry announced a 33-point security plan in July, backed by €30 million over three years for local museums.
Recent figures suggest concern is warranted. The Carabinieri art squad recorded 17 thefts from Italian museums and galleries in 2025, up from 14 a year earlier.
Europol said in an August report that museum thefts were becoming more forceful and increasingly focused on precious metals, gemstones and other high-value artifacts.
Paintings can't earn the thief a fast buck
Unlike gold or jewelry, which can be broken up or melted down, a well-known painting is difficult to turn into quick cash.
Celebrated works such as those by Renoir can rarely be sold openly, Pinna said. Instead, stolen art is more likely to be hidden, used as leverage in ransom attempts or offered privately.
Even when works are recovered, museums can face significant costs linked to investigations, recovery efforts and upgraded security.
The recent thefts have also reignited debate about insurance.
Most major state-backed museums in Western Europe rely on government indemnity schemes rather than commercial cover, but some institutions have begun reassessing the risks, said Filippo Guerrini-Maraldi, a private wealth and fine art insurance specialist at broker Howden Specialty.
"And for the first time, really, in my 40-year career, I've seen art theft now becoming more of a major, major risk. It was always the minor risk," he said.
Insurers are also turning to technology. Beazley is exploring how AI can be used to analyze CCTV footage to identify suspicious behavior in museums and galleries, helping security staff spot threats sooner, said fine art underwriter Dishni Mahendran.
Balancing prioritizing security vs access
For museum directors and cultural officials, the challenge is how to tighten security without cutting collections off from local communities or diminishing the visitor experience.
"Ultimately, museums must remain easy to access," Imbert said. "People should be able to enter without having to pass through 50 security checks."
Julien Volper, a conservator at Belgium's Africa Museum, said particularly vulnerable treasures should only be displayed when adequate security measures are in place.
"I'm not saying that's the ultimate solution, but it seems better than displaying replicas," he said. "We're not at Disneyland."
In August, the Carabinieri recovered the three artworks stolen from the Parma museum from a cardboard box hidden in an apartment. Five Moldovan nationals were arrested in connection with the theft.
Investigators said wiretaps indicated the suspects had unsuccessfully tried to find buyers in Eastern Europe and Russia.
The works have since returned to the museum in what Roffi called a "homecoming party."
"The theft triggered an outpouring of solidarity in Italy and abroad," he said. The museum now has round-the-clock guards funded by a local cheese consortium.
"It was seen not simply as a theft from a museum, but as an attack on art as a shared cultural heritage."

Is Estonia about to have a surplus of IT specialists?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:33:00 UTC
16:33:00 KST

Is Estonia about to have a surplus of IT specialists?
For years, Estonia has talked about a shortage of programmers and IT workers, but after a huge wave of layoffs this week, is there about to be a surplus instead?
One of Estonia's success stories, Pipedrive, announced on Thursday that most of the people working at the company would lose their jobs. However, the changes brought about by artificial intelligence in the labor market are only just beginning.
Microsoft recently offered voluntary severance packages to around 60,000 employees to cover the costs of AI and data centers. Amazon has cut around 30,000 office jobs in a year, while social media giant Meta has laid off 10 percent of its employees. The International Monetary Fund warned that AI would affect around 40 percent of jobs.
Telia, located next door to Pipedrive, recently announced the elimination of 100 jobs. Business is changing and AI is doing more and more.
"If I had to be an oracle, I would rather think that we will be able to do the same work with increasingly fewer people," said Telia CEO Andre Visse.
Young people have been hit hardest by the change. In Estonia, employment among under-25s working in IT has fallen by nearly a quarter in three years.
"Obviously, we are seeing these changes here, and it is considerably more difficult for young people to enter the labor market today than it perhaps was three years ago," said Urve Mets, head of research at OSKA.
However, Sergei Anikin, who years ago grew Pipedrive's engineering department from 10 people to more than 400, believes that young people are flexible and adopt new ways of working more quickly.
"If I compare young people who had no baggage with someone who, for example, has a stable job, a family and a mortgage, and then suddenly realizes that their skills are no longer actually needed because there is a machine that can do their work better and hundreds of times faster, then I think those people will find it considerably harder to cope with this situation," Anikin said.
Could Estonia soon find itself in a situation where there is no longer a shortage of programmers, but rather a surplus?
"If around 400-500 people are laid off from the sector at once, then that will certainly have an impact on the structure of the workforce, and unemployed people will appear on the market for some time. But I think that will correct itself quite quickly," Visse said.
One distinctive feature of Estonia is that IT specialists are concentrated narrowly in the IT sector, Visse said. AI could change that.
"There is actually quite considerable room for development in bringing more technologically knowledgeable, IT-savvy workers into other sectors and helping us digitalize the entire economy and automate these processes more quickly," Visse said.
There will also be high demand for technology skills in the future, but simply writing code will no longer be enough, Mets said.
"IT knowledge alone is not enough, meaning that every young person could think a little about whether, for example, they see their future work as being more connected to technology in the medical field or perhaps in the industrial sector," Mets said.
Whereas good ideas previously went unrealized because there were not enough people to implement them, AI has eliminated that bottleneck, Anikin said.
"We joke here that no stupid idea will go unrealized, so what will actually become important is the ability to distinguish stupid ideas from good ones," Anikin said.

Zelenskyy thanks US over deal for 500 Patriot missiles but warns delivery could take years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:46:21 UTC
16:46:21 KST

Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian missile and drone attacks. The rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has praised the US for its "strong decision" to approve the sale of 500 much-coveted Patriot missiles to Ukraine - but he has warned that delivery could take years.
The US State Department announced on Friday that Washington had green-lit a package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion as Kyiv continues to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks.
"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media in response.
"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he continued. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on a batch of missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian attacks, and the rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need. Russia has repeatedly sought to target Ukraine's power grid over wartime winter periods as Moscow has looked to break the country's resolve.
Dwindling stocks of interceptors have already encouraged Russia to ramp up missile attacks in recent months, and there are fears this trend could lead to an especially brutal winter for Ukrainians.
"The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses," Zelenskyy said overnight. "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach."
The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including incoming aircraft and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriots through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.
As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.

France aims for 'responsible' 2027 budget as Fitch downgrades outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:27:11 UTC
15:27:11 KST

The US rating agency doubts France's ability to sustainably restore its public finances after the 2027 presidential election, probably followed by parliamentary elections. The government, for its part, reiterates the "absolute necessity" of having a budget adopted by the end of the year.
Equipping France with a "responsible" budget for 2027 is the goal announced by the French government as bad economic news continues to mount.
Ratings agency Fitch has kept France's sovereign debt rating at A+, but has cut its outlook from "stable" to "negative", citing weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a bigger deficit than at its previous review last August.
This verdict comes after figures published by Insee on Friday morning showed that French gross domestic product fell by 0.1% in the third quarter, after stagnating in the second quarter and shrinking by 0.2% in the first.
To justify its decision (source in French), Fitch notably highlighted that "the persistence of political fragmentation" and "a difficult social climate", with the mass protests shaking the country, "further complicate the implementation of a lasting fiscal consolidation".
France's rating is nevertheless supported by "the size, wealth and diversification of its economy, the strength of its institutions, its membership of the euro area and the resilience of its banking sector".
"The absolute need to adopt a budget"
In a statement sent to the media on Friday evening, Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said he "takes note" of the US agency's decision to lower France's outlook.
"This assessment confirms the absolute need to adopt by the end of the year a responsible budget that aims to restore the public finances by reducing our deficit to 5%", he continued, adding that the government was "determined to stay on a path of fiscal consolidation".
"In an uncertain international environment, it is imperative to give economic players visibility", the finance minister concluded.
Earlier in the day, reacting to the fall in GDP on Franceinfo, Roland Lescure had described the French economy as "at a standstill". He had also warned that the country would be heading "into the wall" if the "recovery" budget were not adopted.
"I am saying it, I repeat it and I will repeat it to the end: we need a budget, we need a budget deficit of 5% or less", he hammered home.
But the chances of the text being adopted by a parliamentary vote look more than uncertain, given the lack of a majority in the National Assembly and the approaching presidential election.
49.3, ordinances: Fitch expects a push-through
The political debates taking shape six months before the vote "have not significantly increased Fitch's confidence in the possibility of a lasting reduction in the deficit that could stabilise the debt", the agency notes.
"We believe that the budget should be adopted, thanks to the constitutional mechanisms available to the government despite the lack of a parliamentary majority", the Fitch analysts say.
In the event of deadlock in Parliament, Roland Lescure has indicated that the government does not rule out resorting to article 49.3 of the Constitution, which allows a bill to be passed without a vote unless a motion of no confidence is adopted. Another option would be to use ordinances, a procedure that has never been used to pass a budget since the creation of the Fifth Republic in 1958.
Speaking to Euronews, Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University, believes that a budget adopted by ordinance could reduce uncertainty in the short term, but would not restore long-term fiscal credibility.
"Markets generally prefer a contested decision to a prolonged absence of decision. But if a budget adopted by ordinance is seen as fragile, liable to be called into question after the presidential election or as revealing a lasting inability of the political system to build majorities, the positive effect on [investor] confidence could be limited", the researcher explains.

Why politicians chasing economic growth is a lie | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
What if someone told you the truth about the economy? For years, UK governments have tried spending more, spending less, cutting red tape, leaving the EU, levelling up, and they have still failed to increase growth per person. So what’s the lesson from the great British fairytale? On the latest episode, the rebel economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal explain to Aditya Chakrabortty why they believe praying for growth is a fool’s dream – and why it won’t improve your life
Aditya’s suggested reading list for Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal:
